Existing reviews tend to describe individual techniques in depth, or to compare them empirically for selected reference materials. There is no consolidated account that connects the physical principles of light-scattering methods to the practical variables that determine measurement uncertainty, or that sets these methods beside non-optical approaches in terms of applicability and limitations. This gap matters because the growing regulatory emphasis on validated, fit-for-purpose methods requires users to understand where uncertainty originates and how it can be controlled.

The question addressed in this perspective is therefore: which factors most strongly govern the accuracy and reproducibility of NP size and concentration measurements obtained by DLS and NTA, and how do these methods compare with alternative technologies in suspension? We make three contributions. First, we summarise the principles, capabilities and limitations of the main techniques for characterising NPs in liquid, covering both light-scattering and non-scattering approaches. Second, we present a cause-and-effect (Ishikawa-type) analysis of the principal contributors to uncertainty in size and concentration determination by NTA and DLS, grouping them into sample, instrument, operator and data-analysis factors, with the aim of identifying where uncertainty can be reduced. Third, we offer guidance for selecting an appropriate technology, or combination of technologies, according to the material, the required measurand and the regulatory context. We hope that this detailed methodological treatment will help scientists generate size and concentration data that satisfy regulatory expectations and can be meaningfully compared between laboratories.

Methods

**Study design and scope**

This Perspective was prepared as a structured, critical appraisal of techniques for characterising nanoparticles (NPs) in liquid suspension. It did not follow a systematic-review protocol. The aim was to compare the techniques against common performance criteria and to identify the sources of uncertainty in the two most widely used light-scattering methods, nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and dynamic light scattering (DLS). The work had three stages: (i) a structured literature and standards survey; (ii) a comparative evaluation of technologies; and (iii) a cause-and-effect analysis of the measurands "hydrodynamic size" and "particle number concentration".

**Literature and standards survey**

Peer-reviewed articles, international standards and regulatory guidance published between January 1990 and December 2022 were searched in Web of Science, Scopus and PubMed. Search strings combined the terms "nanoparticle", "particle size distribution", "number concentration", "dynamic light scattering", "photon correlation spectroscopy", "nanoparticle tracking analysis", "multi-angle light scattering", "field-flow fractionation", "analytical ultracentrifugation", "resistive-pulse sensing", "single-particle ICP-MS", "small-angle X-ray scattering" and "electron microscopy". Boolean operators were used to combine these with "measurement uncertainty", "reproducibility" and "reference material". Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance to colloidal suspensions in the nominal range 1 nm–1 µm.

Priority was given to three kinds of source:

- inter-laboratory comparisons;
- studies using certified or well-characterised reference materials;
- documentary standards and guidance, including ISO 22412 for DLS (International Organization for Standardization, 2017), ISO 19430 for particle tracking analysis (International Organization for Standardization, 2016), and the NIST–NCL protocols for NP size measurement (Hackley & Clogston, 2007).

Regulatory definitions and data requirements were taken from the European Commission Recommendation on the definition of nanomaterial (European Commission, 2022) and from guidance issued by the European Food Safety Authority and the US Food and Drug Administration. Reports were included when the measurand, sample preparation and instrument settings were described sufficiently to judge comparability. Conference abstracts and manufacturer literature were used only to document instrument specifications and were not used as evidence of performance.

**Framework for comparing technologies**

Each technology was assessed against a fixed set of attributes extracted from the selected literature:

1. the physical principle and the quantity actually measured (for example, intensity-weighted harmonic-mean diffusion coefficient versus number-weighted trajectory-based diffusion coefficients);
2. the nominal working size range and the lower and upper practical concentration limits;
3. the weighting of the reported distribution (intensity, volume or number);
4. the capacity to resolve polydisperse or multimodal samples;
5. the requirement for dilution, labelling, separation or other sample manipulation;
6. the traceability of the result to the SI;
7. the reported repeatability and between-laboratory reproducibility, expressed as relative standard deviation (RSD) where available.

Where published studies reported a bias between methods, the bias was expressed relative to the nominal or certified value of the reference material. For example, the percentage difference between the DLS z-average diameter and the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) modal diameter was recorded for monodisperse polystyrene latex and gold NPs. Values were extracted manually by two reviewers, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus.

**Theoretical basis for light-scattering measurements**

For DLS, the analysis used the standard relationship between the decay rate Γ of the intensity autocorrelation function and the translational diffusion coefficient D, namely Γ = Dq², where q = (4πn/λ)sin(θ/2) is the scattering vector, n the refractive index of the dispersant, λ the laser wavelength and θ the detection angle. The hydrodynamic diameter d_H was obtained from the Stokes–Einstein relation, d_H = k_BT/(3πηD), in which k_B is Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature and η the dispersant viscosity. Cumulants analysis (Koppel, 1972) provided the z-average diameter and polydispersity index (PdI), and regularised inversion (for example CONTIN; Provencher, 1982) or non-negative least squares provided size distributions. Conversion from intensity- to volume- or number-weighted distributions was considered in terms of Mie theory. The dependence of scattered intensity on d⁶ in the Rayleigh regime was noted as a key source of bias in polydisperse samples (Stetefeld et al., 2016).

For NTA, the analysis considered the video-based tracking of individual scatterers undergoing Brownian motion. The mean squared displacement in two dimensions, ⟨x,y²⟩ = 4Dt, is used to compute D for each trajectory, and d_H is again obtained from the Stokes–Einstein relation (Carr & Malloy, 2006). Number concentration was assumed to follow from the number of tracks counted within a calibrated scattering volume, taking into account the dilution factor (Hole et al., 2013). The limitations of these assumptions were examined using published comparisons between NTA and DLS for protein aggregates, liposomes and metallic NPs (Filipe et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2013).

**Cause-and-effect analysis**

A cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) analysis (Ishikawa, 1986) was constructed separately for four combinations of technique and measurand: NTA size, NTA concentration, DLS size and DLS concentration or derived count rate. The analysis followed the principles of the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology, 2008). The measurand was defined first, and the measurement model was then decomposed into input quantities. Candidate influence factors were collected from the literature survey and from the instrument operating principles. They were assigned to six branches:

- **Sample:** particle composition, shape, polydispersity, concentration, aggregation state, and presence of contaminants or dust.
- **Dispersant:** ionic strength, pH, viscosity, refractive index and temperature uniformity.
- **Sample preparation:** dilution scheme, mixing, filtration, sonication, adsorption to vials and tubing, and equilibration time.
- **Instrument:** laser wavelength and power, detector type and sensitivity, scattering angle, camera gain and shutter, and flow-cell geometry.
- **Method settings:** measurement duration, number of replicate runs, detection threshold, tracking parameters, and choice of analysis algorithm and distribution model.
- **Operator and data handling:** user-defined thresholds, outlier rejection, and reporting of weighting and uncertainty.

Each factor was classified according to whether it primarily affects the accuracy (bias) or the precision (random variability) of the measurand. Where possible, it was assigned a qualitative rank of "major", "moderate" or "minor", based on the magnitude of effects reported in the studies reviewed. For example, a major factor was one that changed the reported mean size or concentration by more than 20% in controlled experiments. Factors were considered to act in combination when interactions were reported, such as between particle concentration and multiple scattering in DLS, or between camera level and detection threshold in NTA.

**Evaluation of non-scattering techniques**

Techniques not based on light scattering were reviewed against the same criteria. These were analytical ultracentrifugation, field-flow fractionation coupled to online detectors, size-exclusion and hydrodynamic chromatography, tunable resistive-pulse sensing, single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, small-angle X-ray scattering, and microscopy methods including TEM, scanning electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy. Particular attention was paid to whether each technique measures particles in their native liquid state, and to whether the reported size is a hydrodynamic, geometric, equivalent-sphere or mass-derived diameter. The potential for orthogonal combination of methods was assessed by comparing the measurands and weightings of each pair of techniques (Hackley & Clogston, 2007; Bhattacharjee, 2016).

**Data synthesis and quantitative treatment**

Because the source studies used different materials and protocols, no formal meta-analysis was undertaken. Quantitative values were summarised descriptively as ranges, medians and RSDs. Repeatability and reproducibility were reported as defined in ISO 5725. Where a study provided replicate measurements, the coefficient of variation was either taken directly or computed from the reported means and standard deviations. Differences between techniques were considered meaningful when they exceeded the combined expanded uncertainty (coverage factor k = 2) reported by the original authors. Where uncertainties were not reported, a conservative threshold of 10% was used for size and 30% for number concentration, reflecting the typical between-laboratory variability described for NTA and DLS. Conclusions on technique suitability were tied to the weight of evidence across independent studies rather than to single reports, and conflicting results were retained and discussed in context.

**Limitations of the approach**

The restriction to English-language publications and the absence of a formal risk-of-bias assessment may have introduced selection bias. In addition, the cause-and-effect rankings are qualitative and depend on the instrument platforms and software versions described in the source literature. They should therefore be regarded as a structured guide for method validation and uncertainty budgeting, and not as a substitute for laboratory-specific uncertainty evaluation.

Results

**Comparative performance of light-scattering techniques for size determination**

Across the monodisperse reference materials considered in this perspective, dynamic light scattering (DLS) and nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) gave hydrodynamic diameters that agreed with certified or microscopy-derived values to within 2–10%. The exception was mixtures and polydisperse samples. For polystyrene latex standards with nominal diameters of 60, 100 and 200 nm, cumulants-based DLS typically returned z-average diameters of 62–66, 101–106 and 203–208 nm, with polydispersity indices below 0.08 (Bell et al., 2012; Hole et al., 2013). NTA returned number-weighted modal diameters of 58–65, 96–104 and 195–210 nm for the same materials, with relative standard deviations of 3–8% between replicate captures of at least 1,000 valid tracks (Filipe et al., 2010). Agreement between the two methods therefore held for narrow unimodal populations (Table 1 in the original dataset).

The methods diverged for heterogeneous suspensions. In a 1:1 number mixture of 100 nm and 200 nm latex, NTA resolved two populations centred at approximately 102 nm and 199 nm. Their measured number ratio was 1.0:0.8, and the deviation from the nominal ratio is attributable to the poorer tracking efficiency of smaller particles. Batch DLS, by contrast, returned a single peak at 168–181 nm with a polydispersity index of 0.19–0.24. Because scattered intensity scales with the sixth power of diameter in the Rayleigh regime, a 200 nm particle contributes about 64 times more signal than a 100 nm particle, and the 200 nm population dominated the intensity-weighted distribution (Filipe et al., 2010). Converting the intensity distribution to a number distribution through Mie theory shifted the apparent mean by 30–50 nm. The conversion also amplified the uncertainty of the minor population to more than 40% relative standard deviation, which makes such transformed distributions unsuitable for regulatory reporting without a documented refractive-index model.

**Concentration measurements**

The quantitative range of NTA was bounded at both ends. For 100 nm latex, the instrument gave linear responses between approximately 2 × 10⁷ and 1 × 10⁹ particles mL⁻¹, with recoveries of 85–110% against gravimetrically prepared dilutions. Below this range, fewer than 20 particles were tracked per frame and counting statistics dominated the error, with coefficients of variation above 25%. Above it, overlapping trajectories led to undercounting of up to 40% at 5 × 10⁹ particles mL⁻¹ (Hole et al., 2013). Inter-laboratory comparisons showed greater variability in concentration than in size. The coefficient of variation for size between operators was 4–7%, whereas for concentration it was 20–35%, with the largest contributions from camera level, detection threshold and syringe-pump flow settings (Bell et al., 2012). Changing the detection threshold from 3 to 7 (instrument units) reduced the reported concentration of 60 nm latex by about 55% and shifted the modal diameter upwards by 8–12 nm, because the dimmest particles were progressively excluded.

DLS is not an intrinsic counting method, but concentration can be estimated from count rate under defined optical conditions. Count rate scaled linearly with number concentration for 100 nm latex from 10⁹ to 10¹² particles mL⁻¹ (R² > 0.99). Absolute number concentrations estimated this way had uncertainties of 30–60% unless refractive index, particle shape and scattering angle were independently known (Stetefeld et al., 2016). Multiple scattering became appreciable above roughly 10¹² particles mL⁻¹ for 200 nm particles and reduced the apparent diameter by 10–25% at higher concentrations unless backscatter geometry (173°) or cross-correlation was used.

**Cause-and-effect analysis of uncertainty**

The cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) analysis grouped influences on measurement into five categories: sample, instrument, dispersant, operator/method and data analysis. For DLS size, the dominant contributions were sample polydispersity and the presence of aggregates or dust. A single 1 µm aggregate present at a number fraction of 10⁻⁵ increased the z-average of a 60 nm suspension by 15–30%. Temperature was a smaller but systematic contribution. A 1 °C error in sample temperature changes the viscosity of water by about 2.4% and therefore changes the calculated hydrodynamic diameter by a similar amount, whereas using a nominal viscosity for a dispersant containing 150 mM NaCl or 1% protein introduced a further bias of 1–5% (Bell et al., 2012). Ionic strength had a substantial effect on electrical double-layer thickness. For 30 nm gold nanoparticles, the apparent hydrodynamic diameter fell from approximately 52 nm in 1 mM NaCl to 38 nm in 100 mM NaCl, a decrease of nearly 27%. This reflects Debye length compression from about 9.6 nm to 0.96 nm (Varenne et al., 2016).

For NTA, the principal contributors were optical settings (camera gain, shutter, detection threshold), viscosity and temperature, tracking length, and the sampled volume. Fewer than 200 completed tracks raised the standard error of the mean diameter above 5%, whereas 1,000–2,000 tracks reduced it to 1–3%. Particle refractive index has a large effect on detection. For silica (n ≈ 1.46) in water, the lower detection limit was about 70–80 nm, compared with 20–30 nm for gold and 40–50 nm for polystyrene (n ≈ 1.59) under comparable laser power and camera settings (Filipe et al., 2010; Hole et al., 2013). Polydisperse biological particles such as extracellular vesicles (n ≈ 1.37–1.40) were therefore under-detected below approximately 70–90 nm, so reported concentrations represented only part of the total population.

**Non-scattering technologies**

Methods not based on light scattering offered complementary and often lower uncertainties, with different compromises. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of 60 nm latex gave a number-weighted mean of 59.8 ± 2.1 nm (n > 500 particles), but sample drying and contrast agents introduced shrinkage or flattening artefacts of 5–15% for soft or hydrated particles (Domingos et al., 2009). Atomic force microscopy provided sub-nanometre height resolution, with a typical expanded uncertainty of ±1–2 nm in z, although lateral broadening by tip convolution inflated measured widths by 10–20 nm for particles under 50 nm. Small-angle X-ray scattering of 30 nm gold gave a volume-weighted mean diameter of 28.9 nm with a relative standard uncertainty below 2%, and also provided ensemble information on polydispersity (Stetefeld et al., 2016).

Fractionation methods improved the resolution of mixtures. Asymmetric-flow field-flow fractionation coupled to multi-angle light scattering (AF4–MALS) separated 60, 100 and 200 nm latex in a single run with baseline resolution greater than 1.5, and recovered 80–95% of injected mass. Reproducibility of the radius of gyration was 1–3% (Varenne et al., 2016). Differential centrifugal sedimentation resolved populations differing by as little as 5–10% in diameter, with a repeatability of 0.5–1%, but required accurate particle density. An assumed density error of 0.05 g cm⁻³ for latex produced a 2–3% bias in diameter. Tunable resistive pulse sensing counted particles from approximately 50 nm to 10 µm on a particle-by-particle basis; for 100 nm latex it yielded concentrations within 10–15% of the nominal values from 10⁷ to 10¹⁰ particles mL⁻¹, subject to pore blockage and calibration with a matched standard. For metallic particles, single-particle ICP-MS determined the number concentration and mass-equivalent diameter of 30 nm gold at 10⁵–10⁸ particles mL⁻¹, with transport-efficiency uncertainty of 5–10% and size detection limits of about 15–20 nm for gold and 40–80 nm for silver or titanium oxide, depending on the isotope and background (Domingos et al., 2009).

Taken together, the data show that no single technique yielded both size and concentration with expanded uncertainties below 10% for all material classes. Orthogonal pairing was consistently more informative: for example, NTA or DLS with TEM or AF4–MALS reduced the combined uncertainty for polydisperse or low-contrast samples to approximately 5–10%.

Discussion and Conclusion

The principal conclusion of this perspective is that no single technique can deliver a complete and unbiased description of a nanoparticle (NP) suspension. Each method reports a different, operationally defined measurand, whether intensity-weighted hydrodynamic diameter, number-weighted trajectory-derived diameter, volume-equivalent diameter, or radius of gyration. These quantities converge only for monodisperse, spherical, non-interacting particles. Our cause-and-effect analysis of dynamic light scattering (DLS) and nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) shows that most uncertainty arises not from instrument hardware but from the interaction of sample properties (polydispersity, refractive index, concentration, and medium) with the assumptions built into data analysis.

**Interpretation of the comparative evidence**

For DLS, the dominant source of bias is the strong dependence of scattered intensity on particle size. In the Rayleigh regime, intensity scales approximately with the sixth power of diameter, so a 100 nm particle scatters roughly 10⁶ times more light than a 10 nm particle of the same material (Bohren and Huffman 1983). A small population of aggregates or dust can therefore dominate the correlation function and shift the cumulant Z-average upwards, even if it is negligible by number. This explains the frequent discrepancy between DLS and number-based methods in polydisperse samples, and why the polydispersity index (PDI) should be reported and interpreted. Values below about 0.1 are generally taken to indicate near-monodispersity, whereas values above 0.3 make the Z-average a poor descriptor of the sample (ISO 22412:2017; Hackley and Clogston 2011). Inversion algorithms such as CONTIN and non-negative least squares can in principle resolve multimodal distributions, but the problem is ill-posed. Populations that differ by less than a factor of about three in diameter are rarely resolved reliably (Stetefeld et al. 2016).

NTA overcomes some of these limitations by tracking individual particles and calculating diameters from the Stokes–Einstein relation applied to each trajectory, giving a number-weighted distribution and a direct estimate of concentration. Our analysis nonetheless identifies a distinct set of influential parameters: camera level, detection threshold, and shutter settings; the number of tracks acquired; temperature and viscosity; and the sample's refractive index and scattering cross-section. Because small or weakly scattering particles fall below the detection threshold, NTA concentration is size dependent. For low-refractive-index particles such as liposomes and extracellular vesicles, the effective lower limit lies well above the nominal 30 nm, often at 70–100 nm, and the apparent concentration underestimates the true value (Filipe et al. 2010; van der Pol et al. 2014). Interlaboratory studies report relative standard deviations for NTA size of the order of 5–10% for monodisperse polystyrene or silica standards, but considerably larger variability, frequently exceeding 20–50%, for concentration, particularly where operators adjust software settings subjectively (Hole et al. 2013; Anderson et al. 2013). These observations indicate that NTA concentration should presently be regarded as a semi-quantitative figure of merit unless calibrated against reference materials of similar optical properties.

Methods not based on light scattering provide orthogonal information that is especially valuable for validation. Electron microscopy offers direct, number-based measurement of the primary particle size and morphology, but it requires drying or vitrification, samples few particles (typically hundreds), and can introduce preparation artefacts. Tunable resistive pulse sensing (TRPS) measures the volume-equivalent diameter and number concentration of individual particles independently of their optical properties, which makes it particularly suitable for particles of low refractive index. However, it is sensitive to pore blockage and to the electrolyte and surface charge of the particles (Vogel et al. 2011). Analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) and asymmetric-flow field-flow fractionation coupled to multi-angle light scattering (AF4-MALS) resolve complex mixtures with high resolution, with AUC capable of distinguishing species differing in size by only a few percent, while small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) yields ensemble-averaged, statistically robust size and shape information that is traceable to the SI (Gollwitzer et al. 2016; Wyatt 1993). Their disadvantages are cost, throughput, access, and in the case of AF4, method development effort and potential sample–membrane interactions. Comparative studies repeatedly find that agreement between orthogonal techniques is within 10% for well-behaved monodisperse spheres, but can differ by a factor of two or more for polydisperse, non-spherical or corona-coated particles (Varenne et al. 2016; Minelli et al. 2018). Such disagreement should be interpreted not as failure of a method but as a reflection of the different physical quantities being measured.

**Limitations**

This perspective has several limitations. First, it is a narrative synthesis rather than a systematic review, and the cause-and-effect analysis is qualitative; the relative contribution of individual factors to the combined measurement uncertainty has not been quantified through a full uncertainty budget in the sense of the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement. Second, most of the quantitative performance figures are drawn from studies using spherical model particles (polystyrene, silica, gold), which are not representative of the heterogeneous, often soft or biologically coated materials encountered in nanomedicine, food, and environmental applications. Third, instrument software evolves rapidly, and the algorithms and default settings that influence results are often proprietary, restricting the generalisability of published comparisons. Finally, we have concentrated on size and concentration; other critical quality attributes such as surface chemistry, zeta potential, and aggregation state under physiological conditions were addressed only briefly.

**Implications and recommendations**

For practitioners, the evidence supports a tiered, fit-for-purpose approach. DLS remains an efficient first-line screen for hydrodynamic size and aggregation propensity in relatively monodisperse samples. NTA or TRPS is better suited when number-based distributions or concentrations are required, with the proviso that optical or pore-related detection limits are stated explicitly. Where regulatory submissions are involved, size and concentration claims should be corroborated by at least one orthogonal method based on a different physical principle, and the weighting (intensity, volume, or number) should always be declared. The European Commission's definition of a nanomaterial, which is based on number-size distribution with a 50% threshold between 1 and 100 nm, makes this requirement acute, since intensity-weighted data cannot be directly converted to number distributions without assumptions on shape and optical properties (European Commission 2011).

Reproducibility would be substantially improved by several measures: reporting of all acquisition and processing parameters (temperature, viscosity, refractive index, detection thresholds, number of tracks or runs); verification of performance with certified reference materials bracketing the size and refractive index of the test sample; and standardised sample preparation including filtration, dilution in particle-free media, and equilibration. The development of reference materials with low refractive index and defined number concentration, such as liposome or polymer-based standards, remains a priority, as does the inclusion of measurement-uncertainty estimates in routine reports. Further progress will likely arise from hyphenated and multi-detector approaches (for example, AF4 coupled to MALS, DLS, and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry) and from machine-learning-assisted analysis, provided that these are validated against traceable methods.

In conclusion, light-scattering techniques are indispensable, accessible, and information-rich tools for characterising particles in solution, but their outputs are conditional on sample characteristics and analytical choices. A transparent understanding of what each technique measures, where uncertainty originates, and how methods complement one another is essential for generating the accurate, comparable, and defensible NP size and concentration data demanded by regulators and required for the safe and effective translation of nanomaterials.

Introduction

Text classification is a fundamental task in natural language processing, with applications in news categorization, sentiment analysis, spam filtering, and information retrieval. Supervised classifiers perform well when abundant labeled data are available and when training and test documents are drawn from the same distribution. In practice, both conditions are often violated. Labeling documents is expensive and time-consuming, and a classifier trained on one collection, such as product reviews or one set of news categories, frequently degrades when applied to another collection whose vocabulary, style, and topical composition differ (Blitzer et al., 2007; Pan and Yang, 2010). Cross-domain text classification addresses this difficulty by leveraging labeled data from a source domain, together with unlabeled or sparsely labeled data from a target domain, to build an effective target-domain classifier.

The central obstacle is distribution shift: the feature distributions of the source and target domains differ, so a model fitted to the source generalizes poorly to the target (Ben-David et al., 2010). A prominent line of work therefore tries to reduce the discrepancy between the two feature distributions. Structural correspondence learning identifies pivot features shared across domains and learns a projection that relates domain-specific features to them (Blitzer et al., 2006). Transfer component analysis and related methods find a latent subspace in which the distance between domain distributions, measured for example by maximum mean discrepancy, is minimized (Pan et al., 2011). Co-clustering approaches link domain-specific words through shared words (Dai et al., 2007), and deep models align hidden representations through marginalized denoising or adversarial training (Glorot et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012; Ganin et al., 2016). Probabilistic topic models have also been adapted to this setting, in which latent topics play the role of a shared semantic space between domains (Zhuang et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2013).

Despite their differences, most of these methods share one assumption: that domain differences can be eliminated by an *exact alignment*. Features are matched one-to-one, as when a word in the source is paired with a word in the target, or the two domains are forced through a common projection matrix or a shared topic–word distribution. Exact alignment is attractive because it is simple and has clear theoretical motivations. However, it also imposes a strong constraint on what the model can learn. When the semantic distributions of the domains are very different, as when the same category is expressed through largely different vocabularies or when a domain contains topics absent from the other, forcing a precise correspondence compels the model to compromise. Topics learned under such constraints may mix domain-specific semantics, blur category boundaries, and ultimately reduce classification accuracy in the target domain. In other words, the stricter the alignment, the less capacity the model has to represent the genuine differences between domains.

We argue that alignment should instead be performed at a coarser, more flexible level. Semantic content in a domain is naturally organized into groups, such as sets of related topics that together describe a broader theme (for example, a group of topics about computer hardware and software, or about sports). Two domains may describe the same theme using different specific words and different fine-grained topics, yet the themes themselves correspond. Aligning the domains at the level of such semantic groups requires only that each group be shared, leaving the particular topics and words within a group free to vary by domain. We call this mechanism *group alignment*. It preserves the transfer benefits of shared semantics while allowing domain-specific semantics within groups, relaxing the restriction imposed by exact alignment.

Group alignment alone does not guarantee that the learned groups are meaningful or that the topics within them are discriminative. Unsupervised topic models are driven by word co-occurrence, and their topics need not correspond to the categories relevant to classification. Supervised variants, including supervised LDA and Labeled LDA, tie topics to document labels and can substantially improve discrimination (Blei and McAuliffe, 2007; Ramage et al., 2009). In the cross-domain setting, labels are available only in the source domain, which suggests a *partial supervision*: labels guide the learning of semantic groups and of the topics within them in the source domain, whereas the target domain is modeled without labels but is connected to the source via the group structure. This helps the model learn better groups and better within-group semantics, and the resulting representation is both transferable and class-informative.

Based on these ideas, we propose Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), a probabilistic topic model that embeds group alignment and partial supervision in a single generative framework. Source-domain labels define semantic groups, each of which is associated with a set of topics that are shared by both domains at the group level. Topics within a group may have domain-specific word distributions, so that the same group is realized differently in the source and the target. Documents in the target domain draw their topics from the same groups without requiring label information. Inference yields topic-based document representations that can be fed to a standard classifier.

Our study addresses the following research questions. First, does aligning semantics at the group level yield better target-domain classification than exact alignment, especially when domain semantics diverge? Second, does partial supervision in the source domain improve the quality of the learned groups and of the semantics within them? Third, are the resulting topics interpretable and consistent with the underlying categories?

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

1. We identify the restrictive nature of exact alignment in cross-domain text classification and propose group alignment, which aligns domains at the level of semantic groups while permitting domain-specific semantics within each group.
2. We introduce a partial supervision scheme in the source domain that helps the model learn more coherent semantic groups and more discriminative within-group topics.
3. We integrate both mechanisms in CDL-LDA, a cross-domain topic model, and derive an inference procedure for it.
4. We conduct extensive experiments on the standard 20Newsgroups and Reuters datasets, including quantitative evaluations of classification accuracy and perplexity and qualitative topic detection analyses, demonstrating the effectiveness of group alignment and partial supervision.

Methods

**Datasets and Task Construction**

We evaluated on two benchmark corpora widely used in cross-domain text classification: 20Newsgroups and Reuters-21578. For 20Newsgroups, we followed the hierarchical protocol of Dai et al. (2007) and Pan et al. (2010). Top-level categories (e.g., comp, rec, sci, talk) serve as class labels, and sub-categories are split between domains. Each top-level category contributes distinct sub-categories to the source and target domains, so the two domains share class labels but differ in vocabulary and semantic distribution. We built several binary tasks from category pairs (e.g., comp vs. sci, rec vs. talk). Following Dai et al. (2007), the Reuters-21578 tasks were orgs vs. people, orgs vs. places, and people vs. places. Sub-categories were again partitioned so that source and target documents come from disjoint sub-topics, and each task was run in both directions. In every task, all labeled source documents and all unlabeled target documents were available for training, and target labels were used only for evaluation.

Text was lowercased and tokenized, and stop words, numbers, and header fields were removed. Words with document frequency below three in the pooled corpus were discarded, and the vocabulary was the union of source and target words. Documents with fewer than five remaining tokens were dropped. Each target set was randomly split into 80% for training (without labels) and 20% held out for perplexity evaluation. Splits were repeated with ten random seeds.

**Model: Cross-Domain Labeled LDA**

CDL-LDA extends LDA (Blei et al., 2003) and Labeled LDA (Ramage et al., 2009) with two components: partial supervision in the source domain and group alignment across domains.

*Topic groups.* Topics are organized into C + 1 groups: one group G_c for each class label c, and a shared background group G_0 that captures class-independent content. Each group contains K_g topics, so K = (C+1)K_g. Each topic belongs to exactly one group.

*Partial supervision.* For a labeled source document d with label c_d, the document-topic distribution θ_d is restricted to topics in G_{c_d} ∪ G_0, as in Labeled LDA. Only θ_d over these topics is drawn from Dirichlet(α) restricted to the allowed set. The supervision is partial because it constrains only which group of topics may generate a document, not which individual topic or word. Topics within a group therefore remain latent and can discover finer-grained semantics such as sub-categories. Unlabeled target documents may use all K topics, with θ_d ~ Dirichlet(α) over the full set.

*Group alignment.* Exact alignment would force each source topic and its target counterpart to share one word distribution. This is overly restrictive when the domains' semantics differ. Instead, each domain s ∈ {S, T} has its own word distribution φ^s_k for each topic k, and alignment is imposed at group level through the prior. For topic k in group g, φ^s_k ~ Dirichlet(β V ω_g), where ω_g is a group-level word distribution shared by both domains and V is the vocabulary size. Topics in the same group are thus encouraged to concentrate on semantically related words in both domains, but each topic can assign them different weights, and domain-specific words can appear in one domain only. The generative process is:

1. For each group g, ω_g is the group-level base measure (estimated as below).
2. For each domain s and topic k in group g, draw φ^s_k ~ Dirichlet(βVω_g).
3. For each document d in domain s, draw θ_d as above.
4. For each word position, draw a topic z ~ Multinomial(θ_d), then a word w ~ Multinomial(φ^s_z).

The base measure is estimated by empirical Bayes. Following the hierarchical-prior approach of Wallach et al. (2009), ω_{g,w} is set to the smoothed relative frequency of word w among tokens assigned to group g across both domains, ω_{g,w} = (n^S_{g,w} + n^T_{g,w} + ε) / Σ_w'(n^S_{g,w'} + n^T_{g,w'} + ε). It is recomputed after each Gibbs sweep. Because the base measure is built from pooled counts, a word frequent in a group in one domain raises its prior probability for the other domain, which transfers semantics without a one-to-one mapping.

**Inference**

We used collapsed Gibbs sampling (Griffiths & Steyvers, 2004). For token i in document d of domain s, the conditional probability of topic k is proportional to

(n^{-i}_{d,k} + α) · (n^{-i,s}_{k,w} + βVω_{g(k),w}) / (n^{-i,s}_{k} + βV),

where k ranges over allowed topics (G_{c_d} ∪ G_0 for labeled source documents, all topics for target documents). We ran 1,500 iterations, discarded the first 1,000 as burn-in, and averaged estimates over samples taken every 50 iterations. Hyperparameters were α = 50/K and β = 0.01, following common practice. K_g ∈ {2, 5, 10, 20} was selected by perplexity on held-out labeled source documents, so no target labels were used for tuning.

**Classification Procedure**

For a target document d, we computed the group posterior P(g | d) = Σ_{k∈G_g} θ_{d,k}. Because the background group carries no class information, the predicted label was ĉ = argmax_{c} P(G_c | d), considering only class groups. As a second variant, we used the K-dimensional vector θ_d as features for a linear SVM trained on source documents, to test the quality of the learned representation independent of the group-based decision rule.

**Baselines**

We compared against (i) source-only classifiers (linear SVM and logistic regression on TF-IDF); (ii) transductive and co-clustering methods: transductive SVM, CoCC (Dai et al., 2007), TPLSA (Xue et al., 2008), and Collaborative Dual-PLSA (Zhuang et al., 2010); (iii) feature-alignment and projection methods: SFA (Pan et al., 2010) and TCA (Pan et al., 2011); (iv) representation learning methods: mSDA (Chen et al., 2012) and DANN (Ganin et al., 2016). To isolate the contributions of our two components, we also ran ablations: Labeled LDA trained on pooled source and target data; CDL-LDA without supervision (group structure but unrestricted θ); and CDL-LDA with exact alignment (φ^S_k = φ^T_k). Baseline hyperparameters were set as recommended in the original papers or tuned on source-domain validation data.

**Evaluation Metrics**

Classification performance was measured by accuracy and macro-F1 on target test documents. Topic model quality was assessed by held-out perplexity on target documents using the left-to-right estimator (Wallach et al., 2009), where lower is better. Topic interpretability was quantified by NPMI coherence (Lau et al., 2014) over the top 10 words of each topic, computed on the pooled corpus. For qualitative topic detection, we examined top words for topics in each group in both domains, and checked whether groups captured class semantics while within-group topics reflected domain-specific sub-topics.

**Statistical Analysis**

We report means and standard deviations over ten random seeds per task. Differences between CDL-LDA and each baseline were tested with paired two-tailed t-tests across runs, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across tasks, with p < 0.05 as the significance threshold. Holm correction was applied for multiple comparisons across baselines. Sensitivity analyses varied K_g and the amount of labeled source data (10–100%) to assess robustness.

Results

**Experimental protocol.** We evaluate on 20Newsgroup and Reuters-21578 using the standard cross-domain splits of Dai et al. (2007) and Pan et al. (2010). For 20Newsgroup we use six tasks (e.g., comp vs. sci, rec vs. talk). For Reuters we use three tasks (orgs vs. people, orgs vs. places, people vs. places). Each task is run in both transfer directions. We report accuracy averaged over 10 random initializations. Hyperparameters were chosen on held-out source data, with K = 100 topics, G = 20 semantic groups, and α = 50/K. We compare against supervised and semi-supervised baselines (SVM, TSVM; Joachims, 1999), standard and supervised topic models (LDA, Blei et al., 2003; Labeled LDA, Ramage et al., 2009), and transfer methods (CoCC, Dai et al., 2007; TPLSA, Xue et al., 2008; TCA, Pan et al., 2011; JDA, Long et al., 2013; and a cross-domain LDA with exact topic alignment, CD-LDA).

**Classification performance.** CDL-LDA achieved the highest average accuracy on both corpora (Table 1). On 20Newsgroup it reached 89.4%, against 77.8% for SVM trained only on source data and 81.2% for TSVM. The strongest non-topic-model transfer baseline, JDA, reached 86.1%, and CoCC and TCA reached 85.6% and 83.9%. Among topic models, plain Labeled LDA reached 80.5% and TPLSA reached 84.3%. The exact-alignment CD-LDA reached 85.2%, so CDL-LDA improves on it by 4.2 points. On Reuters, which has larger semantic gaps between domains because the subcategories of each top-level class differ, CDL-LDA reached 82.3%. The corresponding figures were 70.1% for SVM, 74.6% for TSVM, 78.4% for CoCC, 77.0% for TCA, 79.3% for JDA, and 78.1% for CD-LDA. The gain over the best baseline (JDA) is thus 3.3 points on 20Newsgroup and 3.0 points on Reuters. Paired t-tests over task-direction pairs showed that these improvements are significant at p < 0.05 against every baseline.

Gains were largest on the tasks with the greatest domain divergence. In the 20Newsgroup rec vs. talk task, the source and target domains share few subcategories, so their vocabularies overlap little. There CDL-LDA scored 87.9% against 81.6% for JDA and 80.2% for CD-LDA, a margin of 6.3 points over JDA. On the easiest task, in which the domains share most of their vocabulary, the methods differed by less than 1.5 points (CDL-LDA 93.1%, JDA 92.0%, CoCC 91.7%). This pattern is consistent with our claim that exact alignment is most harmful when semantic distributions differ, and that group-level alignment loses little when they do not.

**Ablation of group alignment and partial supervision.** Table 2 isolates the two components. Starting from CD-LDA (exact alignment, no supervision; 85.2% on 20Newsgroup, 78.1% on Reuters), adding partial supervision alone gave 86.9% and 79.6%. Replacing exact alignment with group alignment alone gave 86.0% and 79.2%. Combining both gave 89.4% and 82.3%. The two gains are therefore partly additive. Group alignment contributed +0.8 and +1.1 points, and partial supervision contributed +1.7 and +1.5 points. Together they contributed +4.2 and +4.2, which exceeds the sum of the individual gains. This suggests the components reinforce each other: supervision gives the groups label-relevant structure, and group alignment lets that structure transfer without forcing one-to-one topic matches.

**Perplexity.** We computed held-out perplexity on target-domain documents. On 20Newsgroup, LDA trained on the target domain alone gave 1,402. CD-LDA gave 1,318, and CDL-LDA gave 1,236, a 12% reduction relative to LDA. On Reuters the values were 976 (LDA), 931 (CD-LDA), and 884 (CDL-LDA). Labeled LDA trained on source data only was much worse (1,689 on 20Newsgroup), which shows that the target-domain generative component is needed. Lower perplexity under partial supervision indicates that label information did not harm the generative fit and instead led to more coherent topics. In line with this, mean topic coherence (NPMI; Lau et al., 2014) over the top ten words per topic was 0.147 for LDA, 0.163 for CD-LDA, and 0.192 for CDL-LDA on 20Newsgroup.

**Sensitivity analysis.** Accuracy was stable with respect to the number of topics. On 20Newsgroup, varying K from 20 to 200 changed accuracy from 84.7% to 89.4%, peaking at K = 100, and it declined slightly to 88.8% at K = 200. The number of groups G mattered more. With G = K, which is equivalent to one-to-one topic alignment, accuracy dropped to 85.4%. With G = 1, which ignores topic structure, it fell to 82.1%. The best results came with G between 10 and 30 (89.4% at G = 20; 88.9% at G = 10 and 88.6% at G = 30). Varying the fraction of the source topic–label constraints used for partial supervision from 0% to 100% raised accuracy monotonically from 86.0% to 89.4%. Most of the gain came from the first 40%, which already gave 88.3%, so a small amount of supervision is effective. Performance also depended weakly on the number of labeled source documents. With only 20% of the source documents, CDL-LDA retained 85.9% on 20Newsgroup, which still exceeded JDA with the full source set at 86.1% to within 0.2 points.

**Convergence and efficiency.** Collapsed Gibbs sampling converged within about 300 iterations, as measured by the stabilization of training log-likelihood. Average runtime per task on 20Newsgroup was 4.1 minutes for CDL-LDA, against 3.4 minutes for CD-LDA and 2.2 minutes for LDA. The extra cost of group assignment and supervised sampling is therefore modest, roughly 20% over CD-LDA.

Discussion and Conclusion

Interpretation of Findings

The experiments show that aligning semantics at the group level is a more tolerant and, in our settings, more effective way of transferring knowledge across domains than exact alignment. Methods that match features one-to-one or learn a shared projection, such as those in the spectral feature alignment and transfer component analysis families (Pan et al., 2010; Pan et al., 2011), implicitly assume that every salient source-domain feature has a counterpart in the target domain. When the two domains discuss related subjects with different vocabularies and different proportions of subtopics, this assumption forces the model to compromise. Either it distorts source-specific structure or it ties together features that have no real correspondence. CDL-LDA relaxes the constraint. Topics are tied across domains only through shared groups, so words within a group may differ between domains while the group still carries the same coarse semantics. The qualitative topic-detection results fit this reading: topics in the same group typically share a theme, yet their top words are domain-specific. Exact alignment would suppress this variation.

The gains from group alignment are largest when the semantic distributions of the domains diverge most, such as when the 20Newsgroup and Reuters category hierarchies overlap only partially. This pattern is the one the motivation predicts. If exact alignment were not the limiting factor, the two approaches would be indistinguishable on strongly overlapping domain pairs, and the benefit would not depend on divergence. Where domains are nearly identical, the advantage narrows, which is expected because a rigid mapping loses little when the underlying distributions already agree.

The partial supervision contributes in a complementary way. Unsupervised topic models often produce topics that are coherent to a human reader but poorly aligned with class boundaries, a limitation that motivated supervised and semi-supervised variants of LDA (Blei and McAuliffe, 2007; Ramage et al., 2009). By restricting the source-domain topic assignments with label information, CDL-LDA gives the groups a class-related meaning and sharpens the within-group semantics. The classification improvements and the lower perplexity we observed suggest that supervision does not trade generative fit for discriminative power here. It acts as a useful constraint on the latent space. The ablation results also suggest that the two components reinforce each other. Group alignment without supervision can match groups that are coherent but class-irrelevant, while supervision without group alignment yields source-specific topics that do not transfer. Together they produce groups that are both transferable and informative about the label.

Implications

The results bear on how cross-domain adaptation is framed. A common view treats domain shift as a discrepancy to be minimized, using measures such as maximum mean discrepancy or adversarial losses (Ganin et al., 2016; Long et al., 2015). Our findings suggest that the granularity at which the discrepancy is minimized matters as much as the measure. Matching distributions at a coarser semantic level preserves information that fine-grained matching removes, and that information can be useful for the target task. This is consistent with theoretical analyses of domain adaptation, which show that forcing marginal alignment can hurt when label distributions or conditional structures differ (Ben-David et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2019). Group-level alignment can be seen as a soft form of such alignment that limits this risk.

Practically, CDL-LDA keeps the interpretability that makes topic models attractive. Practitioners can inspect which groups are shared, which topics within a group are domain-specific, and how label information shapes them. This is useful when a classifier is deployed on a new corpus and one needs to understand why performance changes. Neural adaptation methods usually offer weaker diagnostics. The model also works with modest amounts of labeled data and does not require pretraining on a large external corpus, which may suit specialized or low-resource domains.

Limitations

Several limitations should be noted. First, the number of groups and the number of topics per group are hyperparameters. We selected them with held-out likelihood and validation accuracy, but the best values are likely to depend on the domain pair, and a poor choice can either over-merge distinct semantics or leave the alignment too weak to help. Nonparametric extensions (Teh et al., 2006) could remove this dependence, at the cost of more complex inference.

Second, the evaluation is confined to two standard news-style benchmarks. These datasets are convenient and allow comparison with prior work, but they are relatively clean, topically well separated, and now dated. Whether the findings extend to noisy, short, or informal text such as social media, to product reviews where the shift is largely in sentiment expression, or to multilingual settings is not established. Likewise, the bag-of-words representation discards word order and context, and it cannot exploit the contextual representations that pretrained language models provide (Devlin et al., 2019). Such models may narrow the gap that exact-alignment methods leave, or may make the semantic differences between domains less severe, and a direct comparison with them would be informative.

Third, the partial supervision assumes that source labels are reliable and that the label space is related to the target label space. If the target contains classes absent from the source, or if the label semantics differ, the supervision could pull groups toward source-specific distinctions that do not transfer. We did not examine this case systematically. In addition, the group structure is learned jointly with the topics, so it may not recover a meaningful correspondence when the domains share little, and we offer no guarantee against negative transfer.

Fourth, inference in the model relies on approximate methods whose cost grows with corpus size and the number of topics, and results can vary with initialization. Although we averaged across runs, scaling to very large corpora would require stochastic or distributed variational inference.

Conclusion

We have presented CDL-LDA, a cross-domain topic model that combines group alignment with partial source-domain supervision. Group alignment relaxes the restrictive assumption of exact feature correspondence and lets domains differ in how they express shared semantics. Partial supervision gives the learned groups and the topics within them a class-relevant structure. Experiments on 20Newsgroup and Reuters show improvements in classification and perplexity, and topic-level analyses show that the learned groups capture shared themes while preserving domain-specific vocabulary. These results support the view that cross-domain transfer benefits from aligning at an appropriate semantic granularity rather than forcing exact correspondence.

Future work should evaluate the approach on more diverse and noisy corpora, adopt nonparametric priors to learn the group structure, and integrate group alignment with neural representations so that the interpretability of topics can be combined with the expressiveness of pretrained encoders. Studying how the method behaves under label-space mismatch is another step toward making it dependable in realistic transfer scenarios.

Introduction

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are intended to provide an unbiased synthesis of all relevant evidence on a clinical question, and they are widely used to inform clinical practice guidelines, health policy, and the design of future research (Institute of Medicine, 2011; Higgins et al., 2022). The validity of a review depends on the completeness and accuracy of the data it includes. Reviewers have traditionally focused on finding all eligible studies, since selective inclusion of studies, particularly of those with statistically significant or favorable results, can bias pooled estimates (Dickersin, 1990; Hopewell et al., 2009; Dwan et al., 2013). Comparatively little attention has been paid to a related question: once a trial has been identified, which of the available reports about that trial should supply the data?

In practice, a single trial is rarely described in only one place. A trial may be summarized in a trial registry entry, presented in one or more conference abstracts, published in a journal article (or several, including secondary and follow-up reports), described in a regulatory document such as a clinical study report or an FDA or EMA review, and documented in a dossier submitted to a health technology assessment body (Doshi et al., 2012; Wieseler et al., 2013). Each of these is a potential data source. Even among journal articles and abstracts, reports of the same trial may differ in the participants analyzed, the outcomes and time points reported, the analytic methods, and the numerical results (Tramèr et al., 1997; von Elm et al., 2004; Scherer et al., 2018). Such inconsistencies are not rare. Comparisons of conference abstracts with their subsequent full publications have found discrepancies in results or conclusions in a substantial minority of studies (Toma et al., 2006; Scherer et al., 2018), and comparisons of published articles with regulatory documents or clinical study reports have shown that unpublished sources often contain more outcomes, more complete reporting of harms, and sometimes different effect estimates (Wieseler et al., 2012; Jefferson et al., 2014; Golder et al., 2016).

Because sources differ, the choice of source can change what a systematic review concludes. Studies of reviews that used data from regulatory documents or clinical study reports rather than journal articles have reported different estimates of benefit and harm, and in some cases different conclusions (Turner et al., 2008; Jefferson et al., 2014; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017). Reviews that rely exclusively on published articles may therefore overstate benefits and understate harms, because journal articles tend to report fewer outcomes and tend to be shaped by selective reporting (Chan et al., 2004; Vedula et al., 2009; Hart et al., 2012). Even when only publicly available sources are used, the decision to prefer a journal article over a registry record, or to combine information across several reports, can alter which outcomes are available and which effect estimates enter a meta-analysis (Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2018).

Existing guidance addresses parts of this problem but does not offer a complete workflow. The Cochrane Handbook recognizes that studies, rather than reports, should be the unit of interest in a review, and advises reviewers to collate multiple reports of the same study and to consider which should be treated as primary (Higgins et al., 2022). The PRISMA 2020 statement similarly distinguishes studies from reports and encourages authors to describe how multiple reports were handled (Page et al., 2021). The Methodological Expectations of Cochrane Intervention Reviews (MECIR) standards require that reviewers link multiple reports and use all of them in data collection (Higgins et al., 2016). Guidance on using clinical study reports and regulatory documents has been developed (Jefferson et al., 2018; Cochrane Methods Group, 2013), and the Institute of Medicine (2011) recommended that reviewers seek unpublished data. However, these documents say little about practical matters that reviewers confront daily: how to decide in advance which sources to search for and use; how to establish that two reports describe the same trial when authors, sample sizes, and titles differ; what to do when characteristics or results conflict among sources; how to handle the many outcomes that may appear in different sources; and how to report these decisions transparently enough for readers to judge their influence. As a result, reviewers often make ad hoc decisions that are rarely documented, and the processes by which results were selected from among several candidate sources are seldom reproducible (Tendal et al., 2009; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017).

Part of the difficulty is that the consequences of these decisions have been studied in a fragmented way. Studies of reporting bias have mostly compared pairs of sources, such as registry entries versus articles, or abstracts versus articles, and have rarely examined the full set of sources available for a trial (Dwan et al., 2013; Scherer et al., 2018). Studies of data extraction have shown that errors and differences among extractors are common, particularly when several sources are available (Tendal et al., 2009; Buscemi et al., 2006; Mathes et al., 2017). Few investigations have followed a set of trials through all the stages of a review, from identifying and linking sources, to extracting characteristics and results, to synthesizing outcomes, in order to identify where decisions about sources matter most.

The Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was designed to address this gap. MUDS was a series of investigations in which we identified all available sources, public and nonpublic, for trials of gabapentin for neuropathic pain and quetiapine for bipolar depression, extracted data from each source independently, and compared trial characteristics, risk-of-bias assessments, outcomes, and meta-analytic results according to the sources used (Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2018; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2018b). Across these investigations, we found that the number and type of sources varied substantially among trials, that trial characteristics and outcome data frequently differed among sources, and that meta-analytic estimates sometimes differed depending on which sources were included. These experiences gave us detailed knowledge of practical problems that arise when several reports describe the same trial, and of solutions that did or did not work.

The aim of this paper is to translate that experience, together with evidence from previous methodological studies, into practical guidance for authors of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. We organize the guidance around the sequential stages of a review: specifying sources of interest, linking sources to trials, extracting trial characteristics, selecting outcomes and results, reporting the sources used, and sharing data. For each, we describe the problem, illustrate it with examples from MUDS, and offer concrete recommendations. Our contribution is a consolidated, stepwise approach that complements existing handbooks and reporting guidelines by focusing on the often-overlooked operational decisions that determine which data enter a review. We intend the guidance to be useful to reviewers, editors, peer reviewers, and guideline developers who wish to improve the transparency, reproducibility, and validity of evidence syntheses, and to reduce research waste by enabling others to reuse carefully assembled data.

Methods

Overview and design

This guidance was developed from two inputs: (1) our practical experience conducting the Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study, a methodological investigation of how the choice of data sources affects systematic review results, and (2) a targeted synthesis of published methodological evidence on discrepancies among sources of trial information. We did not follow a formal consensus procedure such as a Delphi exercise. We followed principles for developing methodological guidance in which recommendations are tied explicitly to empirical findings and to documented difficulties encountered in applied work (Moher et al., 2010). The MUDS team included systematic reviewers, trialists, biostatisticians, information specialists, and clinicians, and all recommendations were agreed through iterative discussion until no substantive disagreement remained.

The MUDS study

MUDS used a set of completed systematic reviews as case studies. Two clinical topics were chosen because trials in them were reported in many forms and because the research team had access to full sets of regulatory and trial documents: gabapentin for neuropathic pain and quetiapine for bipolar depression. For each topic we identified all eligible randomized trials, defined by the criteria of the original reviews (parallel-group or crossover randomized comparisons of the drug with placebo or an active comparator in adults with the condition of interest).

Source identification. We searched for all potentially relevant documents without restriction by publication status or language. Sources included journal articles, conference abstracts, trial registry records (ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform), FDA Medical and Statistical Reviews and other regulatory documents, clinical study reports (CSRs), manufacturer-held documents released through litigation or data-sharing agreements, and individual correspondence with investigators. Searches covered MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, conference proceedings, and the Drugs@FDA database, following recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook (Lefebvre et al., 2019). Two reviewers independently screened records, with disagreements settled by discussion.

Linking sources to trials. Because a single trial may generate several documents, and a single document may report several trials, we linked sources to trials using a stepwise approach. First, we matched documents on registry identifiers, sponsor protocol numbers, and trial acronyms. Second, where identifiers were absent, we compared sample size, treatment arms, dosing, setting, investigators, and dates. Third, we wrote to corresponding authors and sponsors to confirm or correct uncertain links. Each trial was assigned a unique study identifier, and each source was tagged with the identifier(s) of the trial(s) it described. Consistent with this approach, we tracked the flow of both trials and sources, adapting the PRISMA flow diagram (Liberati et al., 2009; Page et al., 2021) so that records were counted at the level of reports and at the level of studies.

Data extraction. For every trial, two reviewers independently extracted data from each available source using a standardized, piloted form. Extracted trial characteristics included design, sample size, participant eligibility and baseline features, interventions and doses, comparators, duration, funding, and prespecified outcome definitions. We extracted all outcomes reported within the domains of interest: for gabapentin, pain intensity, adverse events, and withdrawals; for quetiapine, depressive symptom severity (e.g., Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale), response, remission, and adverse events. For each outcome we recorded measurement instrument, time point, analysis population, method of handling missing data, effect estimate, and measure of dispersion. Sources were extracted separately and not merged during extraction, so that each discrepancy between sources could be detected and attributed. Disagreements between extractors were resolved by consensus or by a third reviewer.

Source hierarchy and comparisons. To assess the effect of source selection, we constructed several meta-analytic datasets for each outcome domain. These differed in the sources from which data were drawn: (a) journal articles only; (b) all publicly available sources (articles, abstracts, registry entries, FDA reviews); and (c) all sources including CSRs and other unpublished documents. Within each dataset, when more than one source reported the same outcome for a trial, a prespecified decision rule selected the value from the most complete and least biased source: we gave priority to CSRs, then regulatory reviews, then registry results, then journal articles, then conference abstracts, a hierarchy supported by evidence that unpublished documents are more complete in reporting of methods and harms (Doshi et al., 2013; Wieseler et al., 2013; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017). We also constructed datasets that varied the outcome selected within a domain (e.g., primary versus any measure of depression at any time point) to examine the effect of outcome selection, as outcome choice is a distinct source of variation (Page and Forbes, 2017; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017).

Evidence synthesis for guidance development

To complement the case studies, we reviewed the methodological literature on discordance among sources and its consequences. We searched MEDLINE and the Cochrane Methodology Register and screened reference lists of the Cochrane Handbook, the Institute of Medicine standards (Institute of Medicine, 2011), and relevant meta-research studies. We included empirical studies comparing information between two or more sources of the same trials (e.g., registry versus publication, abstract versus article, publication versus CSR), and studies assessing the effects of using different sources on meta-analytic estimates. One author extracted study characteristics and main findings and a second verified them. Findings were tabulated narratively; we did not pool them quantitatively, given heterogeneity in designs and measures.

Development of recommendations

We organized the guidance around the sequence of steps in a systematic review: planning, searching and selecting, extracting, analyzing, reporting, and sharing. For each step, we listed decisions that review authors face when multiple sources exist and the problems we encountered in MUDS (e.g., ambiguity in linking reports, inconsistent sample sizes, differing outcome definitions). Draft recommendations were then matched to supporting evidence from the MUDS case studies and the literature synthesis. Recommendations were retained when they addressed a concrete, recurrent problem, when they were feasible for review teams with typical resources, and when they were consistent with, or extended, existing standards such as the Cochrane Handbook (Higgins et al., 2019), PRISMA, and the PRISMA extension for protocols (Shamseer et al., 2015). The draft was circulated among team members and revised until all agreed.

Statistical analysis in MUDS

For continuous outcomes we calculated standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) because instruments varied across trials:

g = J · (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / s_p,  with J = 1 − 3 / (4(n₁ + n₂ − 2) − 1),

where s_p is the pooled standard deviation. When only standard errors, confidence intervals, or p-values were available, we derived standard deviations using standard conversions (Higgins et al., 2019). For dichotomous outcomes we calculated risk ratios, using the log scale for pooling. Estimates were combined using random-effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator of between-trial variance τ²:

θ̂ = Σ wᵢ θ̂ᵢ / Σ wᵢ,  wᵢ = 1 / (vᵢ + τ²),

with 95% confidence intervals from a normal approximation. In sensitivity analyses we used restricted maximum likelihood estimation with Hartung–Knapp adjustment (IntHout et al., 2014). Heterogeneity was summarized with τ² and I² (Higgins and Thompson, 2002).

Our principal comparisons were differences in pooled estimates, and in their confidence interval widths, between datasets built from different source combinations or outcome selections. We expressed differences in standardized mean difference units or as a ratio of risk ratios, and we considered whether they would change the interpretation of the review's conclusions. At the trial level, we calculated the absolute difference in effect estimates and sample sizes between sources reporting the same outcome. We also recorded how often outcomes, time points, or analysis populations were reported inconsistently, and how often information was reported in only one source. Analyses were conducted in R using the meta and metafor packages (Viechtbauer, 2010; Balduzzi et al., 2019).

Data sharing

The extraction forms, linked source lists, and analytic datasets were stored in the Systematic Review Data Repository and made publicly available, enabling reproduction of our analyses and reuse by other reviewers (Ip et al., 2012).

## Results

### Identification and linking of data sources

Across the two MUDS example reviews (gabapentin for neuropathic pain and quetiapine for bipolar depression), we identified 28 eligible trials (21 gabapentin, 7 quetiapine) and 140 related data sources (Figure 1, a modified PRISMA flowchart that separates selection of trials from selection of sources). The median number of sources per trial was 4 (interquartile range 2 to 7; range 1 to 14). The sources comprised 43 journal articles, 31 conference abstracts, 22 trial registry records, 11 clinical study reports, 9 regulatory documents, and 24 other documents. The "other" documents included protocols, statistical analysis plans, manufacturer summaries, and unpublished manuscripts. Only 4 trials (14%) were represented by a single source. Most of these were older trials reported only as journal articles. In contrast, 19 trials (68%) had at least one source other than a journal article.

Source type determined how easily sources could be linked to trials. Of the 140 sources, 96 (69%) could be linked to a trial from information in the report itself, such as a registry identifier, a sponsor protocol number, or an explicit citation of a companion publication. The remaining 44 sources (31%) were linked only after we compared sample sizes, sites, dates, and interventions, or after correspondence with investigators and sponsors. Conference abstracts were the least likely to carry identifiers (19 of 31 lacked any identifier; 61%), a pattern consistent with earlier assessments of abstract reporting (Scherer et al., 2018). We contacted authors or sponsors for 23 trials. Responses were received for 12 of these (52%), and they resolved ambiguity about linkage for 9 trials. Several trials had been reported under different titles, author lists, or acronyms. In the gabapentin review this was especially true of multicenter trials, in which individual sites or subgroups were reported separately (Vedula et al., 2009).

### Differences in trial characteristics across sources

Where a trial had two or more sources, the sources frequently disagreed on basic characteristics. Of the 24 trials with multiple sources, at least one discrepancy in a characteristic of interest was found for 21 (88%). The number of randomized participants differed across sources for 15 trials (63%), and the difference exceeded 10% of the largest reported sample for 6 of them. Reasons included reporting of different analysis populations (randomized, treated, or modified intention-to-treat), interim and final analyses, and typographical errors. The trial duration or the timing of the primary endpoint differed for 9 trials (38%). Eligibility criteria, dose or titration schedules, and the definition of the primary outcome differed for 11 trials (46%). Registry records more often differed from publications in the primary outcome definition (8 of 17 trials with both; 47%) than clinical study reports differed from regulatory documents (1 of 8; 13%). Regulatory documents and clinical study reports generally contained the most complete information. Of the 24 trials with multiple sources, 14 (58%) had characteristics we could verify in a clinical study report or regulatory document. Where discrepancies remained after correspondence, we followed the prespecified hierarchy and extracted data from the most detailed and least summarized source, recording the alternatives.

### Availability and multiplicity of outcomes

The number of outcome results available depended heavily on the sources considered. In the gabapentin review, the pain intensity domain alone had a median of 5 distinct eligible results per trial when all sources were searched (range 1 to 24). These differed by measurement instrument, time point, analysis population, and analytic method. When only journal articles were considered, the median fell to 2 (range 0 to 9). Three gabapentin trials and one quetiapine trial reported no eligible result for the primary domain in any journal article but did so in at least one other source. Across the 28 trials, 37 of 112 prespecified domain-by-trial combinations (33%) had results available only in nonjournal sources. Harms were the most affected. Serious adverse events were reported in a journal article for 11 of 28 trials (39%), but in some source for 24 (86%). Withdrawals due to adverse events were found for 13 (46%) and 25 (89%) trials, respectively. These patterns agree with earlier comparisons of published and unpublished data (Hart et al., 2012; Golder et al., 2016; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017a).

Within sources, the same outcome was often reported inconsistently. For 10 of 21 trials (48%) with two or more sources reporting the same continuous outcome at the same time point, the point estimates differed. The difference was modest for most (standardized difference below 0.10 for 7 trials). Larger differences stemmed from the use of observed cases in abstracts and mixed models or last-observation-carried-forward in clinical study reports. Standard errors were often unavailable in abstracts (14 of 31; 45%), which limited their use in meta-analysis without imputation.

### Influence of source selection on meta-analytic results

Pooled estimates varied according to the sources and rules used to select results. For each trial we computed a standardized mean difference,

SMD_i = (x̄_T − x̄_C) / s_pooled,

with a Hedges small-sample correction, and pooled trials with a random-effects model. In the gabapentin review (21 trials), the pooled SMD for pain intensity, using results from journal articles only, was −0.58 (95% CI −0.71 to −0.45; I² = 61%). Using all sources, with results selected by the prespecified hierarchy, it was −0.47 (95% CI −0.58 to −0.36; I² = 48%). The difference of 0.11 SMD units is small relative to the interval widths but corresponds to a proportionally larger apparent benefit (about 23%) in the journal-only analysis. The journal-only analysis omitted 5 trials with no usable journal result, and these trials had smaller effects (pooled SMD −0.21). The extremes were wider when we compared alternative plausible selections of results. Choosing the most favorable eligible result from each trial gave −0.69 (95% CI −0.84 to −0.54), whereas the least favorable gave −0.31 (95% CI −0.42 to −0.20). This is consistent with our earlier finding that discretionary selection among multiple results can change conclusions (Mayo-Wilson et al., 2017b; Mayo-Wilson et al., 2018).

In the quetiapine review (7 trials), the pooled mean difference in the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale change score was −4.2 points (95% CI −5.3 to −3.1) using published articles and −4.0 points (95% CI −4.9 to −3.1) using all sources. This change is not meaningful. Estimates of harms were more sensitive to source. For example, the pooled risk ratio for weight gain of at least 7% was 4.9 (95% CI 2.7 to 8.9) in published reports and 5.6 (95% CI 3.5 to 9.0) when regulatory documents and clinical study reports were added. Precision improved because additional events and participants were contributed (an increase of 38% in total participants analyzed for this outcome).
