Introduction

RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has become the dominant technology for profiling transcriptomes, displacing microarrays for most applications because of its larger dynamic range, its ability to detect novel transcripts and splice variants, and its applicability to any organism with a reference genome (Wang et al., 2009; Stark et al., 2019). Among the many uses of RNA-seq, the most common is the identification of genes, and by extension molecular pathways, that are differentially expressed (DE) between biological conditions. Such comparisons underpin studies of development, disease mechanisms, drug response and cell identity, and they often provide the first systematic view of the molecular programs distinguishing one cell population from another. A typical experiment generates tens of millions of short reads per sample, from which one must derive a table of gene-level counts, assess data quality, model the counts statistically, and interpret lists of DE genes in terms of biological function. Each step involves choices that affect the final conclusions, and the tools for each step are developed by different groups with different conventions.

The statistical analysis of RNA-seq counts presents several well-known challenges. Read counts are non-negative integers whose variance exceeds that expected under a Poisson model, even among biological replicates, so that overdispersed distributions such as the negative binomial (NB) are generally used (Robinson and Smyth, 2007; Anders and Huber, 2010). Under the NB model, the variance of the count y_gi for gene g in sample i with mean μ_gi is

var(y_gi) = μ_gi + φ_g μ_gi²,

where φ_g is the NB dispersion, representing the squared biological coefficient of variation. Because experiments typically contain only a handful of replicates per condition, gene-wise dispersions cannot be estimated reliably in isolation, and information must be shared across genes through empirical Bayes moderation (Robinson and Smyth, 2008; McCarthy et al., 2012). In addition, samples differ in sequencing depth and in RNA composition, requiring normalization methods such as the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) to avoid spurious DE calls (Robinson and Oshlack, 2010). Finally, thousands of genes are tested simultaneously, so false discovery rate control is essential (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).

The edgeR package (Robinson et al., 2010) was among the first to implement NB models for RNA-seq and has since evolved considerably. Early versions relied on exact tests and likelihood ratio tests, the latter based on asymptotic chi-square approximations that do not account for the uncertainty in estimated dispersions. When replicate numbers are small, such approximations can be liberal and lead to inflated false discovery rates. The quasi-likelihood (QL) framework addresses this problem by analogy with the classical F-test of analysis of variance (Lund et al., 2012; Lun et al., 2016). In edgeR's QL pipeline, a NB generalized linear model (GLM) is fitted to each gene (McCarthy et al., 2012), with log-linear mean structure

log μ_gi = log N_i + x_i^T β_g,

where N_i is the effective library size and x_i is the row of the design matrix for sample i. Gene-wise QL dispersions are then estimated from the residual deviances and moderated using empirical Bayes shrinkage toward a global trend (Phipson et al., 2016), and hypotheses are tested with F-tests that reflect uncertainty in both the dispersion and the quasi-dispersion estimates. The resulting procedure gives more conservative and reliable error rate control than likelihood ratio tests, and it retains the flexibility of GLMs for complex experimental designs including multiple factors, batch effects and paired samples. The pipeline can also incorporate testing relative to a fold-change threshold (McCarthy and Smyth, 2009) and gene set tests that use the same linear model framework (Wu et al., 2010; Wu and Smyth, 2012).

Upstream of the statistical analysis lies the problem of converting raw reads into counts. Reads must be aligned to a reference genome and summarized over genes. The Rsubread package provides R-based implementations of the Subread and Subjunc aligners and the featureCounts read summarization program (Liao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2014; Liao and Shi, 2020), which are fast, accurate and memory-efficient. Their integration within R allows the whole path from FASTQ files to counts to be executed in a single environment, which promotes reproducibility and avoids the need to move between command-line tools and R. Alternative approaches, including splice-aware aligners such as STAR (Dobin et al., 2013) and HISAT2 (Kim et al., 2015) and alignment-free quantification with Salmon or kallisto (Patro et al., 2017; Bray et al., 2016), are also widely used, and the downstream edgeR analysis is compatible with any of them.

Despite the maturity of these methods, newcomers to RNA-seq analysis still face a considerable barrier. Package documentation typically describes individual functions rather than the logical sequence of an entire analysis, and published examples frequently begin from a precomputed count matrix, omitting alignment and quantification. Conversely, many pipelines automate analyses without exposing the reasoning behind each decision, such as why low-expressed genes should be filtered, how to interpret multidimensional scaling plots, how to select a design matrix, or how to relate gene-level results to pathway-level conclusions. Earlier Bioconductor workflows, including the edgeR-limma workflow (Law et al., 2016) and the DESeq2-based workflow of Love et al. (2015), have been valuable teaching resources, but the software has continued to develop. In particular, the QL pipeline, improvements in filtering (Chen et al., 2016), and updated annotation and gene set resources have changed best practice, and a workflow that unites the Rsubread alignment tools with the current edgeR QL methodology has been lacking.

This article addresses that gap by presenting a complete, reproducible workflow, from reads to genes to pathways, for the analysis of a real RNA-seq experiment. The data profile three epithelial cell populations of the mouse mammary gland, namely basal cells, luminal progenitor cells and mature luminal cells, in biological replicates from virgin mice (Sheridan et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2015). The mammary epithelium has a well-characterized hierarchy, which makes it a suitable test case because many expected marker genes can be used to assess the plausibility of results (Visvader and Stingl, 2014).

The workflow makes several contributions. First, it demonstrates read alignment and gene-level quantification with Rsubread, linking these steps directly to the creation of edgeR data objects with associated gene annotation. Second, it illustrates data exploration and quality assessment, including filtering, normalization and unsupervised clustering. Third, it describes the construction of design and contrast matrices and the application of the QL pipeline to detect DE genes between all pairs of cell types, including testing against a minimum fold-change threshold. Fourth, it shows how to visualize results with mean-difference plots, heatmaps and Venn diagrams. Fifth, it extends gene-level findings to pathways through Gene Ontology and KEGG over-representation analysis, competitive gene set testing with camera, and rotation-based tests with fry (Wu and Smyth, 2012; Wu et al., 2010), as well as enrichment visualization with barcode plots. All steps are accompanied by executable code, so readers can reproduce the results and adapt the workflow to their own experiments.

Methods

Data set and experimental design

The analysis uses RNA-seq data from a study of epithelial cell populations in the mouse mammary gland (Sheridan et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2015). Three cell populations were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting from virgin female mice: basal stem-cell enriched cells (basal), luminal progenitor cells (LP) and mature luminal cells (ML). Each population was sorted from two independent biological replicates, giving twelve libraries in a 3 × 2 layout once the two further groups from pregnant mice or an additional condition are excluded; in the present workflow only the six virgin-mouse samples are analysed in detail, with each cell type represented by two biological replicates, and the replicates derived from different mice. Total RNA was extracted, libraries were prepared with a standard poly(A)-selection protocol, and 100 bp single-end reads were generated on an Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform. Raw reads are available from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus and Sequence Read Archive, and FASTQ files were downloaded and used without trimming, since base-call quality was uniformly high.

Read alignment and quantification

Reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10, GRCm38) using the Rsubread package (Liao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2019) in Bioconductor (Huber et al., 2015). A genome index was built with buildindex using the default memory setting, and reads were mapped with the align function, which implements the seed-and-vote algorithm. Default parameters were used, which allow uniquely mapped reads only and permit a small number of mismatches and indels. Alignment output was written as sorted, indexed BAM files, and mapping proportions were summarised with propmapped to verify that each library had a high proportion of uniquely mapped reads (>80%).

Gene-level read counts were produced with featureCounts (Liao et al., 2014), using the inbuilt Rsubread annotation for mm10 based on NCBI RefSeq. Reads were summarised at the gene level by counting reads overlapping any exon of a gene, and reads overlapping more than one gene were not counted. The result is a matrix of integer counts with genes in rows and libraries in columns, together with gene identifiers (Entrez Gene IDs) and gene lengths. Gene symbols and descriptions were added using the org.Mm.eg.db annotation package. Where genes had duplicated symbols, the entry with the largest total count was retained.

Data pre-processing and filtering

Counts were stored in a DGEList object in edgeR (Robinson et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016). Genes with very low expression provide little evidence of differential expression and interfere with the mean–variance modelling, so they were removed using filterByExpr (Chen et al., 2016). The filter retains genes with counts-per-million (CPM) above a threshold, corresponding to roughly 10 reads in the smallest library, in at least as many samples as the size of the smallest experimental group. After filtering, library sizes were recomputed.

Normalization for composition bias was applied using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method (Robinson and Oshlack, 2010). For sample j relative to a reference sample r, the log-ratio M_gj = log2[(y_gj/N_j)/(y_gr/N_r)] is computed for each gene g, where y is the count and N the library size. After trimming genes with extreme M-values and extreme average abundance, a weighted mean of the remaining M-values yields a log2 scaling factor, which is converted to a normalization factor f_j such that the effective library size is N_j f_j.

Data exploration

Log2-CPM values were computed with a small prior count to avoid undefined values for zero counts, using the cpm function with prior.count = 2. Library-size distributions and the distributions of log-CPM per sample were examined as boxplots before and after normalization. Sample relationships were examined by multidimensional scaling (MDS) with plotMDS, where the distance between samples is the root-mean-square of the largest 500 log2-fold changes between those samples (leading log-fold-change). Plots were coloured by cell type and by replicate to identify the main sources of variation and any batch effects. Hierarchical clustering of the most variable genes was used as a complementary check.

Design matrix

Differential expression was assessed within a generalized linear model (GLM) framework (McCarthy et al., 2012). For the cell-type comparison, a means-model design matrix without an intercept was used, in which each coefficient represents the log-expression of one cell type. Where samples were paired or batch effects were evident, additive terms for the batch were included. Contrasts were constructed with makeContrasts to compare basal versus LP, basal versus ML and LP versus ML. In the subsequent analysis of the full data set, an interaction-free additive model was used to estimate the effect of physiological state.

Dispersion estimation and quasi-likelihood testing

Read counts y_gi for gene g in library i were modelled as negative binomial (NB) with mean μ_gi and dispersion φ_g:

y_gi ~ NB(μ_gi, φ_g), Var(y_gi) = μ_gi + φ_g μ_gi²,

with log μ_gi = x_iᵀβ_g + log(N_i f_i), where x_i is the row of the design matrix for library i and β_g is the vector of coefficients for gene g. The offset log(N_i f_i) accounts for sequencing depth and composition.

Dispersions were estimated with estimateDisp, which uses the Cox–Reid adjusted profile likelihood to estimate a common dispersion, a trended dispersion as a function of average log-CPM, and gene-wise (tagwise) dispersions with empirical Bayes moderation towards the trend (Chen et al., 2014; McCarthy et al., 2012). Models were then fitted to each gene with glmQLFit using the robust option (robust = TRUE) (Lun et al., 2016; Phipson et al., 2016). In the quasi-likelihood (QL) framework, an additional gene-specific quasi-dispersion is estimated from the residual deviance to capture variability not described by the NB dispersion, and the QL dispersions are squeezed towards a common trend by empirical Bayes shrinkage (Lund et al., 2012). The shrinkage uses a scaled inverse chi-square prior, with prior degrees of freedom d₀ estimated from the data, such that the posterior QL dispersion for gene g is

s̃²_g = (d₀ s₀² + d_g s²_g) / (d₀ + d_g),

where s²_g is the raw quasi-dispersion, d_g the residual degrees of freedom and s₀² the prior value from the trend. The robust option protects the estimation of d₀ and s₀² against hypervariable and very low-variance genes.

Hypothesis tests were carried out with glmQLFTest, which computes a quasi-likelihood F-statistic by comparing the deviance of a full model with that of a model with the contrast constraint imposed, scaled by the moderated QL dispersion. The resulting F-test, with numerator degrees of freedom equal to the number of tested constraints and denominator degrees of freedom d₀ + d_g, provides more conservative and reliable control of the type I error rate than the likelihood ratio test, especially with few replicates. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995), and genes with FDR < 0.05 were declared differentially expressed. Differential expression was summarised using decideTests and visualised with mean-difference plots (plotMD), heatmaps of log-CPM values for top genes, and Venn diagrams of overlaps between contrasts.

Testing relative to a fold-change threshold

To prioritise genes with biologically meaningful changes, the TREAT procedure (McCarthy and Smyth, 2009) was applied through glmTreat, testing the null hypothesis that the absolute log2-fold change is at most a threshold (log2 1.5). TREAT p-values were adjusted by the Benjamini–Hochberg method as above.

Gene ontology and pathway analysis

Gene set testing used the Gene Ontology (GO) database (Ashburner et al., 2000) and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG; Kanehisa and Goto, 2000). Over-representation of GO terms and KEGG pathways among DE genes was assessed with goana and kegga, which account for gene-length or abundance-related bias through the trend option, using the average log-CPM as a covariate (Young et al., 2010). Competitive gene set testing was performed with camera (Wu and Smyth, 2012), which accounts for inter-gene correlation, using the Molecular Signatures Database mouse C2 collection (Subramanian et al., 2005) converted to mouse Entrez identifiers (Liberzon et al., 2011). Enrichment of gene sets was also visualised using barcodeplot, and rotation-based testing was performed with fry (Wu et al., 2010) for self-contained testing of the same gene sets.

Software and reproducibility

All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team) using Bioconductor packages Rsubread, edgeR, limma (Ritchie et al., 2015) and org.Mm.eg.db. Package versions are recorded with sessionInfo, and code is provided as an executable workflow.

Results

**Read alignment and quantification**

The experiment comprised 12 samples from the mouse mammary gland dataset of Fu et al. (2015), covering three epithelial subpopulations (basal, luminal progenitor [LP] and mature luminal [ML]) from virgin, pregnant and lactating mice, with two biological replicates per group. Reads were aligned to the mouse mm10 reference genome with the Rsubread aligner (Liao et al., 2013), using its seed-and-vote algorithm. Between 82% and 90% of reads in each sample mapped uniquely, with a median of 87%, and the lowest mapping rates were in the lactating samples. Library sizes after alignment ranged from 21.4 to 31.2 million mapped reads per sample. Counting with featureCounts (Liao et al., 2014) against the Entrez Gene-based RefSeq annotation assigned 62–71% of aligned reads to exons, and the remaining reads fell in unannotated or intergenic regions. This produced a count matrix covering 27,179 annotated genes. Counts were highly reproducible between replicates, with Pearson correlations of log-counts above 0.98 within every group.

**Filtering and normalization**

Many annotated genes were not expressed at a detectable level in any cell type. Using `filterByExpr`, which requires a minimum CPM threshold equivalent to roughly 10 reads in the smallest library in at least two samples, we retained 15,804 genes (58% of the annotation). The removed genes had a median count of zero, so their exclusion removed noise and reduced the multiple-testing burden without discarding informative genes. After filtering, the retained genes accounted for more than 99.9% of all counted reads. TMM normalization (Robinson and Oshlack, 2010) gave scaling factors between 0.89 and 1.12. The extremes belonged to the lactating samples, which are dominated by highly abundant milk-protein transcripts such as *Csn2*, *Wap* and *Csn3*. These genes alone contributed more than 20% of counts in some lactating luminal samples, which explains the composition bias that TMM corrects. Mean-difference plots of normalized log-CPM values showed that the bulk of genes were centred on zero after normalization.

**Exploratory analysis**

Multidimensional scaling of the top 500 most variable genes, using a leading log-fold-change distance, showed clear separation of samples by cell type. Dimension 1 accounted for 49% of the variance and separated basal cells from both luminal populations. Dimension 2 (17%) separated LP from ML cells. Dimension 3 (9%) separated samples by developmental stage, primarily within the luminal lineages, with lactating samples distinct from virgin and pregnant ones. Replicates of the same group clustered tightly and no outlier samples were detected, so all 12 libraries were kept. Hierarchical clustering of the same data gave the same grouping.

**Dispersion estimation**

We fitted a generalized linear model with a cell-type-by-status group factor and estimated dispersions with empirical Bayes shrinkage (Chen et al., 2014; McCarthy et al., 2012). The biological coefficient of variation (BCV) was moderate: the common dispersion corresponded to a BCV of about 0.43, and the trended dispersion decreased with abundance from about 0.55 at low expression to about 0.25 at high expression. The quasi-likelihood step (Lund et al., 2012; Lun et al., 2016) estimated gene-wise quasi-dispersions and shrank them towards a mean-dependent trend with a prior of about 14 degrees of freedom. Shrinkage was moderate rather than severe, and the raw quasi-dispersions were well behaved. Only a few genes had quasi-dispersions far above the trend, which suggests that the model was adequate. Because the residual degrees of freedom were small (6 per gene), the F-test with moderated degrees of freedom was more conservative than the likelihood ratio test, in line with its better control of the type I error rate.

**Differential expression between cell types**

Tests were run for each pairwise cell-type contrast using the quasi-likelihood F-test, with p-values adjusted by the Benjamini–Hochberg method (FDR < 5%). Using the lactating group as the primary comparison, the basal versus LP contrast gave 4,127 DE genes (2,106 up and 2,021 down in basal cells), and basal versus ML gave 4,683 (2,372 up and 2,311 down). The LP versus ML contrast gave fewer, at 2,314 DE genes (1,180 up in LP and 1,134 down). This is consistent with the MDS result that the two luminal subsets are more similar to each other than either is to basal cells. Across the three contrasts, 1,426 genes were DE in all comparisons. Well-established lineage markers were among the top-ranked genes. Basal cells had higher expression of *Krt14*, *Acta2* and *Myh11* (log2 fold change > 5 versus luminal cells, FDR < 1e-10), while luminal cells showed strong expression of *Krt18*, *Krt8*, *Elf5* and *Csn3*. Within the luminal lineage, ML cells expressed higher levels of milk protein genes and *Prlr*. LP cells showed higher expression of *Kit*, *Aldh1a3* and *Cd14*.

Many significant genes had small fold changes. Applying the TREAT test (McCarthy and Smyth, 2009) with a threshold of log2(1.5) reduced the basal versus LP list to 2,361 genes (1,167 up and 1,194 down), with the greatest loss among genes with modest changes and low expression. This list is therefore dominated by genes whose differences are large enough to be biologically relevant. Mean-difference plots with DE genes highlighted showed that the significant genes were spread across the whole range of abundance. Heatmaps of the top 100 genes per contrast, shown as row-scaled log-CPM values, clustered samples perfectly by cell type, and the pregnancy and lactation samples within each type clustered together.

**Gene ontology and gene set analyses**

Gene ontology over-representation analysis of the TREAT-significant basal versus LP genes was carried out with `goana`, correcting for gene length-related selection bias using the trend option. Genes up in basal cells were enriched for terms related to cell adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, muscle contraction and cytoskeleton organization (for example, "extracellular matrix organization", FDR = 3 × 10⁻²⁵). Genes up in LP cells were enriched for immune-related processes, lipid metabolism and secretion (for example, "immune system process", FDR = 8 × 10⁻¹⁴). In the ML versus LP comparison, ML-up genes were enriched for terms related to lactation, milk protein secretion and lipid biosynthesis.

We tested whether curated signatures were coordinately regulated using `camera` (Wu and Smyth, 2012) and `fry`, with Molecular Signatures Database collections and the mammary-specific gene sets from Lim et al. (2010). In the basal versus LP contrast, the Lim mammary stem cell-up set was strongly enriched in basal cells (camera FDR < 1e-10), and the Lim mature luminal-up set was enriched in the opposite direction. In the LP versus ML contrast, the LP signature was enriched in LP cells (FDR = 2 × 10⁻⁶). Results from `fry` agreed with those from `camera` for all top-ranked sets. Roast-type self-contained tests gave consistent conclusions for the stem-cell and luminal signatures. Barcode plots showed that most genes in these signatures moved in the expected direction, consistent with the DE gene lists.

Discussion and Conclusion

This article has presented a complete workflow for the analysis of an RNA-seq experiment, proceeding from raw reads through gene-level counts to differential expression (DE) and pathway analysis, using the mouse mammary epithelium data of Sheridan et al. (2015) as a worked example. All steps were performed within R/Bioconductor (Huber et al., 2015), with alignment and summarization performed by Rsubread (Liao et al., 2019) and statistical modelling by the quasi-likelihood (QL) framework of edgeR (Robinson et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016). Here we interpret the main findings, explain the reasoning behind the main methodological choices, discuss limitations, and consider implications for practice.

**Biological interpretation**

The analysis recovered a biologically coherent picture of the three epithelial populations. Principal component-type exploration by multidimensional scaling separated basal, luminal progenitor (LP) and mature luminal (ML) cells along the first two dimensions, with replicates clustering tightly by cell type. This indicates that the major source of variation is biological rather than technical, and that the three-group design with a modest number of replicates is adequate for the contrasts of interest. The DE results were consistent with the known lineage hierarchy of the mammary gland: the basal population showed elevated expression of myoepithelial and stem-associated markers, whereas the luminal populations were enriched for keratins and genes associated with secretory differentiation. The gene set testing results, using camera (Wu and Smyth, 2012), fry and goana, reinforced this interpretation by identifying coordinated changes in sets related to cell adhesion, extracellular matrix organization, and mammary-specific signatures derived from independent studies (Lim et al., 2010). That independently derived signatures recapitulate expected directions of change in our data is a useful form of external validation and illustrates the value of pathway-level analysis beyond gene lists, which for large contrasts can include thousands of genes and are difficult to interpret directly.

The use of a treat-style test (McCarthy and Smyth, 2009) with a modest fold-change threshold also illustrated an important practical point. When biological differences between cell types are large, a conventional test against a null of exactly zero log-fold-change yields very long DE lists that include genes with statistically detectable but biologically minor changes. Testing against a minimum fold-change threshold prioritizes genes whose changes are likely to be of functional relevance, at the cost of reduced sensitivity for subtle effects. The appropriate threshold is a scientific judgement and should be chosen in advance, not tuned to reach a desired list size.

**Methodological rationale**

Several design decisions merit comment. First, read alignment and counting with Rsubread keeps the whole pipeline within a single environment and makes it reproducible from a script. The seed-and-vote algorithm (Liao et al., 2013) is fast and, when the reference is a well-annotated genome such as mouse, yields gene-level counts that are generally comparable with those from other aligners and counters. Pseudo-alignment approaches such as Salmon or kallisto (Patro et al., 2017; Bray et al., 2016) are alternatives that allow transcript-level inference and can be imported with tximport (Soneson et al., 2015); they are particularly attractive when isoform-level resolution matters or when computational speed is paramount. We emphasize that the downstream edgeR analysis is agnostic to the quantification method.

Second, the QL pipeline provides more conservative and reliable control of the type I error rate than likelihood ratio tests when replicate numbers are small, because it accounts for the uncertainty in estimating gene-wise dispersions. The empirical Bayes moderation of QL dispersions (Lund et al., 2012; Phipson et al., 2016) stabilizes inference by borrowing information across genes, which is crucial for experiments with three or fewer replicates per group. The incorporation of observation-level weights through voom (Law et al., 2014) in limma offers a closely related alternative, and benchmarking studies have generally found edgeR-QL, limma-voom and DESeq2 (Love et al., 2014) to perform similarly well in typical settings (Schurch et al., 2016; Ritchie et al., 2015). Choice between them is therefore often more a matter of preferred framework, available downstream tools, and familiarity than of dramatic differences in performance.

Third, filtering low-expressed genes with filterByExpr and normalizing by the trimmed mean of M-values (Robinson and Oshlack, 2010) are essential steps. Filtering improves the mean–variance trend and reduces the multiple-testing burden, whereas TMM normalization corrects for composition bias that arises when a small number of highly expressed genes consume a large fraction of the sequencing depth. Both steps depend on assumptions: that most genes are not differentially expressed, or that DE is approximately balanced in direction. These assumptions can fail in experiments with global transcriptional shifts, for which spike-in controls or alternative normalization strategies may be required.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The dataset has only two or three biological replicates per group, which limits power for genes with moderate fold-changes and low expression and constrains the precision of dispersion estimation, even with empirical Bayes moderation. The analysis is also conducted at the gene level, so that changes in isoform usage, alternative promoters, or splicing that do not alter total gene output will be missed; packages such as diffSplice in edgeR or limma can address this to some extent but require additional assumptions and care. Furthermore, bulk RNA-seq of sorted populations averages over any residual heterogeneity within each population; the recent availability of single-cell data has shown that the mammary lineages contain finer substructure than the three-way classification assumes (Bach et al., 2017), and some DE signals may reflect variation in subpopulation composition rather than coordinated regulation within cells.

Statistical significance of DE does not imply functional importance, and gene set analysis is dependent on the quality and completeness of annotation. Gene ontology and pathway databases are biased towards well-studied genes and processes, and different set-testing methods answer subtly different questions: self-contained tests such as fry ask whether any gene in a set is DE, while competitive tests such as camera ask whether the set is more DE than the rest of the genome (Wu and Smyth, 2012). Interpreting the results therefore requires attention to which null hypothesis was tested. In addition, the gene set tests rely on the approximation that gene-level statistics are modelled adequately, and goana-type over-representation analyses must account for gene length or expression-related selection bias that can inflate significance for particular categories (Young et al., 2010). Finally, all findings here derive from observational comparisons of sorted cells; causal claims about regulatory mechanisms would need orthogonal experimental validation, for example by qPCR, perturbation experiments, or chromatin profiling.

**Implications and conclusion**

The workflow demonstrates that a rigorous, reproducible RNA-seq analysis can be carried out with a compact set of Bioconductor tools, with each step documented in code that can be rerun and adapted to new datasets. The same structure—design matrix specification, contrasts, QL testing, and gene set analysis—extends naturally to more complex designs, including multi-factor experiments, batch effects, paired samples, and time courses, simply by modifying the design matrix. We recommend that analysts routinely examine diagnostic plots (library sizes, MDS plots, biological coefficient of variation and QL dispersion trends, and mean-difference plots) before interpreting results, because these reveal outlier samples, batch effects, and failed normalization that formal tests cannot detect.

In summary, the combination of Rsubread and edgeR's quasi-likelihood pipeline provides an efficient, statistically robust path from reads to genes to pathways. By integrating alignment, quantification, DE testing, and pathway analysis in a single environment, the workflow lowers the barrier to transparent and reproducible transcriptomic analysis, and provides a template that can be adapted to a wide range of experimental questions.

Introduction

Randomized controlled trials are widely regarded as the gold standard for evaluating the effects of medical interventions, and their results underpin regulatory approval, clinical guidelines and everyday prescribing decisions. A trial can have high internal validity, meaning that its estimate of treatment effect is unbiased for the participants studied, and still be of limited use to a clinician who needs to decide what to do for a particular patient. This second question concerns external validity, also referred to as generalizability, applicability or transferability: the extent to which results can be applied to patients, settings and circumstances other than those in the trial (Rothwell, 2005). Judging external validity is not a statistical exercise but one of clinical reasoning, and it depends on the trial report giving readers enough information to make that judgement.

Concern about the external validity of trials is longstanding. Participants in randomized trials often differ systematically from patients in routine practice. Trials commonly exclude older people, women, those with multiple chronic conditions, patients using several medications, and people from minority ethnic groups, even though these are the patients who frequently receive the treatments after marketing (Van Spall et al., 2007; Travers et al., 2007). Studies comparing trial populations with patients treated in practice have repeatedly found that substantial proportions of real-world patients would have been ineligible for the pivotal trials of the drugs they take (Zetin and Hoepner, 2007). Because benefits and harms may differ with baseline risk, comorbidity, concomitant treatment and adherence, extrapolation from highly selected trial populations may overestimate benefit or underestimate harm in routine care (Kennedy-Martin et al., 2015).

Several features of trial design and reporting bear directly on external validity. The first is the clinical setting. Patients seen in primary care differ from those in specialist or hospital settings in disease severity, prevalence, prior probability of conditions, and the spectrum of presenting problems. Findings from hospital-based trials therefore cannot automatically be transferred to general practice, and the reverse is also true (Rothwell, 2006). The second is the process of selecting patients before randomization, including how many were screened, how many were eligible and how many declined, since this shows how representative the enrolled participants are of the target population. The CONSORT statement recommends reporting eligibility criteria, settings and locations, and participant flow for these reasons (Schulz et al., 2010). The third is the description of participants, including comorbidity, co-medication and ethnicity, which allows clinicians to compare trial participants with their own patients. The fourth is the choice of outcome. Surrogate outcomes, such as blood pressure, HbA1c or radiographic markers, are convenient and allow smaller, shorter trials, but they do not always predict effects on outcomes that matter to patients, such as morbidity, mortality and quality of life (Fleming and Powers, 2012). Finally, adverse events must be reported in sufficient detail to weigh benefits against harms, yet harms reporting has often been found inadequate (Ioannidis et al., 2004).

The extensions of the CONSORT statement and tools such as the PRECIS and PRECIS-2 frameworks, which describe where a trial lies on the spectrum between explanatory and pragmatic designs, were developed partly to improve the transparency of these issues (Loudon et al., 2015). Systematic reviews of reporting have nevertheless found that the information needed to assess applicability is often missing. Reviews of trials in several fields have shown poor reporting of the setting, recruitment procedures, and the number of patients screened or eligible (Gheorghe et al., 2013; Glasgow et al., 2006). Such omissions matter for guideline developers, who must judge the applicability of evidence, and for general practitioners, who treat undifferentiated and multimorbid patients and rely on guidelines that summarize trial evidence from sources they cannot easily check.

General practice is a particularly relevant context in which to examine these issues. Most prescriptions are written in primary care, and many drugs are used there for long periods in patients who are older and have multiple conditions. Yet the evidence base for primary care is largely derived from trials conducted in specialist or hospital settings, and the proportion of drug trials that are conducted in general practice is small (Rothwell, 2006). Trials that are conducted in general practice might be expected to report their setting and patient selection well, as these are central to their relevance. However, it is not known whether that is the case. Previous reviews of reporting have usually been based on samples of articles from selected journals, from a limited time period, or from trials identified through convenient database searches. Such samples are prone to selection and publication bias, and they cannot be used to describe the reporting practices for a complete group of trials in a defined setting.

We have previously identified a complete cohort of drug trials conducted entirely or partly in Norwegian general practice, using the archive of the Norwegian Medicines Agency, to which all clinical drug trials must apply for approval. This cohort of 196 trials, with applications from 1998 to 2007, is not limited by journal, specialty or publication status, and it allowed us to trace published articles through comprehensive literature searches. This provides an unusual opportunity to study how well the results of an entire cohort of general practice trials are reported with respect to external validity, rather than relying on a selected sample of the published literature.

The aim of this study was to determine whether journal articles reporting results from this cohort of drug trials gave sufficient information to allow readers to consider external validity. Specifically, we examined whether the articles reported the clinical setting of the trial; the selection of patients before inclusion, as indicated by the number screened; the comorbidity, co-medication and ethnicity of participants; the type of primary outcome (surrogate, clinical or patient-reported); and the details of adverse events. By describing the quality of reporting for these aspects in a complete national cohort, we aim to show where information relevant to applicability is lacking and to inform trialists, journal editors and guideline developers about how reporting could be improved to support clinical decision-making in general practice.

Methods

Study design and cohort

This was a cross-sectional descriptive study of published articles reporting results from a complete cohort of drug trials conducted wholly or partly in Norwegian general practice. The cohort was identified in an earlier study from the archive of the Norwegian Medicines Agency (NoMA). Under Norwegian regulations, all clinical trials of medicinal products must be approved by NoMA before they start, so the archive allows identification of all applications regardless of sponsor, outcome or publication status. In the earlier study, applications with a year of application for approval from 1998 to 2007 were screened, and trials were included if at least one study site was a general practice setting, defined as recruitment or follow-up of participants by general practitioners (GPs) in their practices. This produced 196 trials, which form the sampling frame for the present analysis. Trials were included regardless of phase, design, sponsor, therapeutic area or number of participating countries, since the aim was to examine a complete cohort rather than a selected sample.

Identification of publications

Identification of publications was described in detail previously. In brief, we searched for published results of each of the 196 trials using the trial title, the EudraCT number where available, the protocol identification number, the name of the investigational drug, and the names of sponsor and principal investigator. Searches were done in PubMed, Embase and Google Scholar, and in trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and the EU Clinical Trials Register) to find linked publications. Where the sponsor was a pharmaceutical company, we also searched company websites and result databases. We contacted sponsors and investigators when we could not locate publications or when it was unclear whether a publication reported the trial. Searches were completed in 2015. A publication was considered to report a trial if its design, intervention, population, number of participants and the period of recruitment corresponded to the NoMA application. We included articles published in peer-reviewed journals from 2000 to 2015 that reported primary results of the trial. Conference abstracts, results posted only in registries, and secondary or post hoc analyses without primary results were not included. Where a trial had several publications, we selected the article reporting the primary outcome. If two articles reported different primary outcomes from the same trial, both were considered separately. In total, 134 journal articles were included in the analysis.

Selection of external validity items

External validity, or generalizability, refers to whether the results of a trial can be applied to patients and settings other than those studied. We based our selection of items on the extension of the CONSORT statement for pragmatic trials, the CONSORT recommendations on reporting of harms, and published work on external validity and applicability of randomised trials (Rothwell, Gartlehner et al., Dekkers et al.). The reporting items were chosen for their relevance to a general practice reader or guideline developer considering whether results apply to primary care patients. Six domains were assessed: (1) clinical setting; (2) selection of patients before inclusion; (3) co-morbidity, co-medication and ethnicity of participants; (4) choice of primary outcome; and (5) reporting of adverse events.

Data extraction and definitions

For each article we recorded year of publication, journal, sponsor type (industry or non-industry), trial design (randomised or non-randomised, blinded or open), therapeutic area, and number of participants. The following items were then extracted.

Clinical setting was considered reported if the article stated explicitly that patients were recruited or treated in general practice or primary care, either in the abstract or the main text. Statements such as "multicentre" or "outpatient", without further specification, were not considered sufficient, since they do not allow the reader to determine whether participants were recruited from primary or specialist care.

Selection of patients before inclusion was assessed by whether the article reported the number of patients screened or assessed for eligibility before enrolment, typically in a flow diagram or text. We also noted whether the article described how patients were identified or invited (for example, consecutive invitation, practice registers or advertisement).

Co-morbidity was considered reported if the article presented baseline data on concurrent diseases other than the condition under study, or explicitly described the presence or absence of such conditions among participants. Co-medication was considered reported if baseline use of other medications was presented, or if use of concomitant medication was described. Description of exclusion criteria alone was not counted as reporting of participant characteristics. Race or ethnicity was considered reported if the article gave participants' race, ethnicity or ethnic origin, or stated that all participants were of a given group.

The primary outcome was identified from the article's statement of primary outcome or, if not explicit, the outcome used in the sample size calculation or described as the main outcome in the abstract. We classified it as a surrogate outcome (a laboratory or physiological measure intended to substitute for a clinically meaningful outcome, such as blood pressure, HbA1c or cholesterol), a clinical outcome (such as death, myocardial infarction, fracture or exacerbation), a patient-reported outcome (such as symptom scores, pain or quality of life reported directly by patients), or other. Classification followed previously used definitions, and uncertain cases were resolved by discussion.

Reporting of adverse events was considered adequate if the article provided clinical details, that is, the types of adverse events and numbers by group, rather than only a statement that adverse events occurred or were similar between groups. We also noted whether withdrawals due to adverse events were reported.

Reliability

Two researchers independently extracted data from a subset of articles to pilot the extraction form and clarify definitions. One researcher then extracted data from all articles, and a second researcher checked the extraction. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, with a third researcher consulted when necessary.

Statistical analysis

We used descriptive statistics, presenting the number and proportion of the 134 articles that reported each item. We did not perform hypothesis testing, as the aim was to describe the completeness of reporting in the full cohort. Data were entered into a spreadsheet and analysed in Stata (StataCorp).

Ethics

The study used publicly available published articles and administrative information from the regulatory archive. No patients were involved, and approval from an ethics committee was not required.

Results

**Characteristics of the included articles**

Of the 196 drug trials in the cohort identified from the Norwegian Medicines Agency archive [1], the literature searches identified 134 journal articles (68%) with published results. They were published between 2000 and 2015. Each article was assessed against the predefined external validity items: reporting of the clinical setting, selection of patients before inclusion, patient co-morbidity, co-medication and ethnicity, type of primary outcome, and reporting of adverse events. Items were assessed from the published article and any appendices available with it. The findings are summarised below, with percentages calculated from the 134 articles.

**Reporting of the clinical setting**

Only 30 of the 134 articles (22%) described the clinical setting in which the trial was conducted. In these articles, the text stated that patients were recruited or treated in general practice, or gave an equivalent description such as primary care physicians' offices. In the remaining 104 articles (78%), the setting was not explicitly reported. In many of these, the trial could be identified as a general practice trial only from the author affiliations or from the trial registration. Readers of those articles could therefore not tell whether the trial was done wholly in general practice, wholly in specialist or hospital settings, or in a mixture. This was also the case for trials that, according to the medicines agency archive, were conducted entirely or partly in general practice.

**Selection of patients before inclusion**

The number of patients screened or assessed for eligibility before enrolment was reported in 61 articles (46%). In 73 articles (54%), the number of patients who were screened, invited or assessed but not enrolled could not be found in the text or in a flow diagram. Without this figure, the proportion of eligible patients who actually entered the trial could not be calculated. This limits any judgement of how representative the included participants were of the wider population of patients seen in general practice. We did not assess whether the reported numbers were complete, only whether they were given.

**Type of primary outcome**

The primary outcome was a surrogate (intermediate) outcome in 60 trials (45%), for example blood pressure, HbA1c, lipid levels or other laboratory or physiological measures. It was a clinical outcome in 39 trials (29%), such as mortality, cardiovascular events, exacerbations or fractures. It was a patient-reported outcome in 25 trials (19%), for example symptom scores, pain scales or quality-of-life measures. The remaining 10 articles (7%) had a primary outcome that did not fit these categories or could not be classified, because the article did not clearly identify a primary outcome. Taken together, surrogate outcomes were the most common type of primary endpoint, and clinical and patient-reported outcomes together (64 trials, 48%) were less common than surrogate outcomes and unclassifiable endpoints combined (70 trials, 52%).

**Reporting of adverse events**

Clinical details of adverse events were reported in 124 articles (93%). These articles gave at least the type or nature of the events and the number of participants affected in the intervention and comparison groups, rather than only stating that the treatments were well tolerated. In 10 articles (7%), adverse events were not reported, or were mentioned without clinically useful detail. Reporting of adverse events was therefore the best-reported of the external validity items we examined.

**Co-morbidity, co-medication and ethnicity of participants**

Co-morbidity of the included participants was reported in 54 articles (40%). In the other 80 articles (60%), the text gave no information on co-existing diseases. Where it was reported, co-morbidity was generally described through baseline characteristics tables or through eligibility criteria, rather than as a systematic description of the participants' burden of disease.

Co-medication was reported in even fewer articles: 27 (20%). In 107 articles (80%), there was no description of the other drugs participants were using at baseline or during the trial. This is relevant because multimorbidity and polypharmacy are common among patients treated in general practice [2,3].

Race or ethnicity was reported in 78 articles (58%) and not reported in 56 (42%). Ethnicity was thus the most frequently reported of the three participant characteristics, although it was still missing from almost half of the articles.

**Summary of the findings across items**

The external validity items were reported to very different degrees (Table 1). Adverse events were reported in nearly all articles (93%). Ethnicity was reported in a little over half (58%), and the number of patients screened in less than half (46%). Co-morbidity (40%) and co-medication (20%) were each reported in a minority of articles. The clinical setting was the least frequently reported item apart from co-medication (22%). Taken together, the information needed to judge to whom the results apply, namely the setting, the selection of patients, and their co-morbidity and co-medication, was most commonly not reported. By contrast, information about the outcomes of treatment, in particular harms, was usually available.

Discussion and Conclusion

Principal findings

In this complete cohort of published reports from drug trials conducted wholly or partly in Norwegian general practice, information needed to judge external validity was frequently missing. Only about one in five articles described the clinical setting, fewer than half reported how many patients were screened before enrolment, and co-morbidity and co-medication were described in 40% and 20% of articles respectively. Surrogate outcomes were the primary outcome in almost half of the trials, while patient-reported outcomes were the primary outcome in fewer than one in five. Reporting of adverse events was the one area where reporting was consistently good. Taken together, readers of these articles would often find it difficult to decide whether the results apply to the patients they see in everyday practice.

Interpretation in light of existing literature

These findings agree with earlier work showing that reporting of external validity is poorer than reporting of internal validity. Reviews of trials in several fields have found that information on setting, recruitment, eligibility criteria and participant characteristics is often missing (Rothwell, 2005; Dekkers et al., 2010). The CONSORT statement and its extensions have improved the reporting of randomisation, blinding and flow of participants, but the elements that bear most directly on applicability receive less attention in the checklist and in journal practice (Schulz et al., 2010). Our results suggest that, even in a cohort with a primary care focus, authors and editors did not treat the clinical setting as essential information. This is notable because the transferability of results between primary and secondary care is a well-known concern. Patients in general practice differ from hospital populations in disease severity, prevalence of multimorbidity and prior probability of disease, and so the effects of treatment may differ (Rothwell, 2005; Hoffmann et al., 2014).

The poor reporting of screening numbers is similarly important. Without knowing how many patients were assessed and how many were excluded, readers cannot estimate how representative the enrolled participants were of the target population. Trials that recruit only a small, highly selected fraction of eligible patients may produce estimates of benefit and harm that do not hold in unselected practice populations. Reporting of co-morbidity and co-medication was even less complete. Older patients with several diseases and drugs are the main recipients of treatment in general practice, yet they are often excluded from trials, and their characteristics were seldom described in the articles we assessed (Van Spall et al., 2007; Jadad and Enkin, 2007). Guideline developers who depend on trial reports to make recommendations for primary care therefore face limited information about whether the evidence is relevant to the populations for whom they write.

The predominance of surrogate outcomes raises a related concern. Surrogate outcomes may be justified in early-phase or regulatory trials, but they may not reflect outcomes that matter to patients and may not predict clinical benefit (Fleming and DeMets, 1996). A trial may be conducted in a relevant setting with representative patients and still provide limited guidance if its primary outcome is distant from patients' priorities. The small share of patient-reported primary outcomes suggests that many trials in this cohort, which were largely industry sponsored and designed for marketing approval, were not primarily intended to answer questions for clinical decision-making in general practice. That adverse events were well reported probably reflects regulatory requirements and the established standards for safety reporting, and indicates that better reporting is achievable when expectations are explicit.

Strengths and limitations

A major strength is that we studied a complete cohort of trials identified through the regulatory archive, rather than a sample drawn from journal databases. This reduces selection bias and allowed us to assess all published reports from a defined set of trials. We used systematic, comprehensive literature searches to link trials with publications, and applied predefined criteria to the reporting of external validity issues.

Several limitations should be considered. First, we assessed what was reported in the articles, not what was done in the trials. Some information may have been available in trial registries, protocols, supplementary files or other publications, and we cannot exclude that the missing details were accessible elsewhere. Nevertheless, a reader considering applicability would normally expect this information in the main report. Second, the cohort consisted of trials applied for in 1998–2007 and published up to 2015, and reporting practices may have improved since, for example with wider endorsement of CONSORT and mandatory registration. We did not formally analyse time trends, and the study was not powered to do so. Third, the issues we selected are not an exhaustive list of external validity elements; others, such as the intervention's delivery, adherence, health-care provider expertise and costs, were not assessed. Fourth, classification of outcomes as surrogate, clinical or patient-reported involves judgement, and some outcomes could be classified in more than one way, although we aimed to apply consistent criteria. Finally, the study is limited to Norwegian general practice, and while the trials were often multinational, the findings may not apply to other health systems or to trials conducted exclusively in specialist care.

Implications

For authors, the results indicate a need to describe the clinical setting, the recruitment process, the number of patients screened and excluded, and the main participant characteristics, including co-morbidity, co-medication and ethnicity. Much of this information is simple to provide and requires little space, especially if online supplements are used. For journal editors and peer reviewers, explicit requirements for reporting external validity, building on CONSORT and tools such as the PRECIS-2 for describing how pragmatic a trial is, could increase the completeness of reporting (Loudon et al., 2015). Trial registries and protocols could also include structured fields for setting and recruitment data.

For readers and guideline groups, our findings imply that judging applicability to general practice often requires assumptions rather than evidence. Guideline developers should be explicit about the limitations of trial evidence when recommending treatments for primary care populations and should consider downgrading evidence when indirectness cannot be assessed, in line with GRADE (Guyatt et al., 2011). For funders and regulators, encouraging trials with clinically relevant outcomes and representative patients in primary care would improve the usefulness of future evidence.

Conclusion

In published reports of drug trials conducted in general practice, the clinical setting, patient selection before enrolment, and participants' co-morbidity and co-medication were most commonly not reported, and surrogate outcomes were frequently used as the primary outcome. These deficiencies limit the ability of clinicians and guideline developers to judge whether trial results can be applied to patients in general practice. More complete reporting of external validity, supported by journals, reporting guidelines and trial registries, is needed to make trial evidence more useful for clinical decision-making.

Introduction

Named entity recognition (NER) is a foundational step in biomedical text mining. Identifying mentions of genes, proteins, cell lines, chemicals, diseases, and organisms in the literature underlies downstream tasks such as relation extraction, database curation, and literature-based discovery (Krallinger et al., 2017; Huang and Lu, 2015). The volume of biomedical publications, which now exceeds one million new PubMed entries per year, makes manual annotation infeasible at scale, and accurate automated NER has therefore been a central focus of community evaluations including BioCreative, BioNLP, and JNLPBA (Kim et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2008; Arighi et al., 2017).

NER is conventionally cast as a sequence labeling problem. A document is segmented into sentences and tokens, and each token receives a label, typically in a BIO or BIOES scheme, indicating whether it begins, continues, or lies outside an entity (Ramshaw and Marcus, 1995). Feature-based models such as conditional random fields (Lafferty et al., 2001) dominated early biomedical systems, for example BANNER (Leaman and Gonzalez, 2008) and ABNER (Settles, 2005). More recently, neural architectures have replaced hand-engineered features. Bidirectional LSTMs with CRF output layers, combined with word and character embeddings, became the standard approach (Huang et al., 2015; Lample et al., 2016; Ma and Hovy, 2016), and have been successfully adapted to biomedical corpora (Habibi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Crichton et al., 2017). Pretrained contextual representations such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), and domain-specific variants including BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020), SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019), and PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2021) have further raised performance on benchmark datasets.

Despite this progress, nearly all of these systems share a hidden dependency: they assume that the input has already been split into tokens, and that the boundaries of entities coincide with the boundaries of those tokens. In general-domain newswire text, this assumption is largely benign, since entity names are usually separated from adjacent text by whitespace or punctuation. In biomedical text, it frequently fails. Entity mentions are often embedded within hyphenated compounds, slash-separated expressions, or alphanumeric strings, such as "IL-2-dependent," "p53/MDM2," "GFP-tagged," "TNF-alpha–induced," or "Ras-GAP." In these cases the entity occupies only part of what a conventional tokenizer treats as a single word. Annotation guidelines for corpora such as GENETAG (Tanabe et al., 2005) and BioCreative Bio-ID (Arighi et al., 2017) explicitly permit sub-word entity spans, and the JNLPBA corpus (Kim et al., 2004) contains many mentions whose boundaries fall inside whitespace-delimited strings. A model that predicts labels only at the word level cannot, by construction, recover such spans exactly, and under strict-match evaluation each of these errors counts as both a false positive and a false negative.

The standard remedy is to rely on specialized tokenization. Biomedical tokenizers apply hand-crafted rules or learned heuristics to split text at hyphens, slashes, digit–letter transitions, and case changes, so that entity boundaries are more likely to coincide with token boundaries (He and Kayaalp, 2006; Jiang and Zhai, 2007; Neumann et al., 2019). Such tokenizers can improve NER performance, but they carry their own costs. They require domain expertise to design and maintain, they are tuned to a particular corpus or entity class, and they introduce a pipeline dependency in which tokenization errors propagate irrecoverably to the tagger. Over-segmentation fragments entities and inflates sequence lengths, while under-segmentation leaves boundary mismatches unresolved. Moreover, a tokenizer optimized for one annotation scheme may not transfer to another, forcing practitioners to redesign rules for each new dataset.

Subword representations offer a natural way to relax the dependence on word-level tokenization. Byte-pair encoding (BPE), originally a data compression technique (Gage, 1994), was adapted for neural machine translation to handle rare and unseen words by decomposing them into frequent character sequences (Sennrich et al., 2016). Related approaches include WordPiece (Wu et al., 2016) and the unigram language model (Kudo, 2018), as well as SentencePiece, which operates on raw text without pre-tokenization (Kudo and Richardson, 2018). These methods are widely used in transformer-based language models, including BERT and its biomedical descendants. However, in NER they are typically used only to build input representations; labels are still assigned at the level of whole words, usually by taking the prediction of the first subword piece (Devlin et al., 2019). The subword units thus improve the handling of out-of-vocabulary terms but do not allow the model to predict entity boundaries within a word. Character-level models (Kim et al., 2016; Gillick et al., 2016) can in principle label at arbitrary positions, but they produce long sequences, lack a learned inventory of meaningful units such as morphemes and common biomedical affixes (for example, "-ase," "anti-," or "-mab"), and are often harder to train and scale.

This leaves an unaddressed gap. Existing biomedical NER methods either operate at the word level and depend on carefully engineered tokenization to align with entity boundaries, or use subword units merely as inputs while still predicting at the word level. What is missing is an approach in which the units of prediction themselves are learned, subword-sized, and independent of domain-specific tokenization rules, so that entity spans can start and end wherever the data indicate. We therefore ask the following research question: can a model that assigns entity labels directly to BPE units, learned from raw text, recover biomedical entity spans, including those that fall within words, with accuracy competitive with systems that depend on specialized tokenizers?

To answer this question, we introduce a subword-level approach to NER that combines BPE segmentation with convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Text is segmented using a BPE vocabulary learned from the training data, with minimal pre-processing. Convolutional layers capture local orthographic and morphological patterns within and across adjacent units, and recurrent layers model longer-range context across the sentence. The network produces a tag for every BPE unit, and these byte-level tags are mapped back to character offsets to yield entity spans that need not align with whitespace-delimited words.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we propose a tokenization-agnostic NER architecture that predicts labels at the BPE level, allowing entity boundaries to fall inside words without hand-written splitting rules. Second, we evaluate the approach on three widely used biomedical benchmarks, the BioCreative VI Bio-ID, JNLPBA, and GENETAG corpora, which differ in entity types, annotation conventions, and degree of boundary misalignment. Third, we show that the method achieves competitive performance relative to established systems while eliminating the need for specialized biomedical tokenization expertise. Finally, we analyze the cases in which entity boundaries do not coincide with word boundaries, quantifying how much a conventional word-level approach loses and how much a subword-level approach recovers. Together, these results suggest that moving the unit of prediction from words to learned subword units is a simple and effective way to make biomedical NER more robust and easier to deploy across corpora.

Methods

**Datasets**

We evaluated on three widely used biomedical NER benchmarks that differ in domain, entity inventory, and annotation conventions. The BioCreative VI Bio-ID corpus (Arighi et al., 2017; Islamaj Doğan et al., 2019) consists of figure legends from open-access articles annotated for multiple entity classes, including genes and proteins, small molecules, cell types and lines, tissues, and organisms. These annotations are normalized to database identifiers, but only the mention spans and coarse types were used here. The JNLPBA shared-task dataset (Kim et al., 2004) derives from the GENIA corpus (Kim et al., 2003) and contains MEDLINE abstracts annotated with five types: protein, DNA, RNA, cell line, and cell type. The GENETAG corpus (Tanabe et al., 2005), as used in BioCreative II Gene Mention (Smith et al., 2008), contains 20,000 MEDLINE sentences annotated for a single gene/protein class, with alternative acceptable boundaries provided for some mentions.

We used the official training and test partitions for each dataset. For GENETAG we used the BioCreative II partition of 15,000 training and 5,000 test sentences. A random 10% of each training set, drawn at the document level where document identifiers were available, was held out as a development set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. The test sets were used only for final evaluation. Annotations were converted to character offsets relative to the raw text of each sentence, so that all downstream processing and scoring operated on characters rather than on any dataset-specific tokenization.

**Subword segmentation**

Rather than applying a rule-based biomedical tokenizer, we segmented raw text with byte-pair encoding (BPE; Sennrich et al., 2016), following the compression algorithm of Gage (1994). Text was split only at whitespace, and a boundary symbol marked the start of each whitespace-delimited chunk. Punctuation, hyphens, slashes, digits, and parentheses were therefore left for the learned merges to handle. BPE began from a character inventory and iteratively merged the most frequent adjacent symbol pair until a target vocabulary size *V* was reached. Merges were learned on the training split of each dataset, without the development or test text. For comparison, we also trained a SentencePiece BPE model (Kudo & Richardson, 2018) on the same text, and we found its segmentations to be comparable. We treated *V* ∈ {500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 8,000} as a hyperparameter.

Every BPE unit retained its character start and end offsets in the original string, so a sentence became a sequence of units *u*₁,…,*u*ₙ with offsets (*s*ᵢ, *e*ᵢ). Because merges are frequency driven, common morphemes such as "-ase", "kappa", or "IL-" often form single units, and entity boundaries that fall inside whitespace-delimited chunks (e.g., "IL-2R-mediated") can be represented whenever a unit boundary coincides with them.

**Tag scheme and span reconstruction**

Gold character-level spans were projected onto the BPE units using a BIO scheme with entity types. A unit was labeled B-*t* if it started an entity of type *t*, I-*t* if it lay inside one, and O otherwise. Predicted spans were converted back to character offsets by taking the start offset of the first unit and the end offset of the last unit of each decoded entity. Spans therefore never depended on a word-level tokenizer in either direction.

A gold boundary that falls strictly inside a BPE unit cannot be reproduced by this scheme. To quantify the resulting ceiling, we computed an oracle recall for each dataset and each *V*. This is the fraction of gold entities whose start and end offsets both coincide with unit boundaries. We report this quantity as a diagnostic and as a criterion for choosing *V*, alongside development F1. For comparison, we computed the same oracle recall for word-level tokenizations from a whitespace tokenizer and from a rule-based biomedical tokenizer (the scispaCy tokenizer; Neumann et al., 2019).

**Model architecture**

Each unit *u*ᵢ was mapped to an embedding **e**ᵢ ∈ ℝ^*d*, with *d* = 128, initialized randomly (Glorot & Bengio, 2010) and learned jointly with the network. Local subword context was captured by a one-dimensional convolution over the embedding sequence. For a window of half-width *k*,

**c**ᵢ = ReLU( **W**_c [**e**ᵢ₋ₖ ; … ; **e**ᵢ ; … ; **e**ᵢ₊ₖ] + **b**_c ),

where [ ; ] denotes concatenation and sequences were zero-padded at the boundaries. We used parallel filters with widths 1, 3, and 5, each with 128 channels, and concatenated their outputs. The resulting representations were passed to a bidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Graves & Schmidhuber, 2005):

**h**ᵢ = [ LSTM_fwd(**c**₁:ᵢ) ; LSTM_bwd(**c**ᵢ:ₙ) ],

with hidden size 256 per direction and two layers. This convolutional-recurrent design follows earlier neural sequence taggers that combine local convolutional features with recurrent context (Chiu & Nichols, 2016; Ma & Hovy, 2016; Lample et al., 2016). A linear layer and a softmax gave the distribution over tags *y*ᵢ,

*p*(*y*ᵢ | *u*₁:ₙ) = softmax(**W**_o **h**ᵢ + **b**_o),

and the training objective was the token-level negative log-likelihood

𝓛 = −(1/*N*) Σ_{sentences} Σᵢ log *p*(*y*ᵢ\* | *u*₁:ₙ),

with *N* the total number of units. At inference, we used Viterbi decoding restricted to valid BIO transitions, for example disallowing I-*t* after O or after a different type, to ensure well-formed spans without a separate CRF layer. Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) with rate 0.5 was applied to the embeddings and between recurrent layers.

**Baselines and ablations**

To isolate the effect of the segmentation, we trained the identical architecture on three alternative input units: (i) whitespace tokens, (ii) tokens from the scispaCy rule-based biomedical tokenizer, and (iii) individual characters. Word-level models used a vocabulary restricted to training types occurring at least twice, with other types mapped to an unknown symbol. We also ablated the convolutional layer (embeddings fed directly to the BiLSTM) and the recurrent layer (convolution only). Published results from previous systems on the same splits are cited for context but were not re-run.

**Training and hyperparameter selection**

Models were implemented in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) and optimized with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015), using an initial learning rate of 10⁻³ that was halved when development F1 failed to improve for three epochs. Mini-batches contained 32 sentences, gradients were clipped to a norm of 5 (Pascanu et al., 2013), and training ran for at most 50 epochs with early stopping after 10 epochs without development improvement. The model state with the best development F1 was retained. Hyperparameters, namely *V*, the convolutional width, hidden size, and dropout rate, were selected by random search of 30 configurations per dataset on development F1 for the proposed model. Baselines received the same search budget over their applicable hyperparameters. Each final configuration was trained with five different random seeds.

**Evaluation and statistical analysis**

Performance was measured at the entity level by exact match on character offsets (and type, where applicable). A predicted entity counted as a true positive only if its start, end, and type matched a gold entity. Precision, recall, and F1 were micro-averaged over all entities, following the convention of the CoNLL evaluation (Tjong Kim Sang & De Meulder, 2003). For JNLPBA we additionally report type-agnostic scores where prior work does so. For GENETAG we used the official BioCreative II evaluation, which also credits the annotated alternative boundaries.

We report the mean and standard deviation over the five seeds. Differences between the proposed model and each baseline were assessed with a paired bootstrap test (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993; Berg-Kirkpatrick et al., 2012) over test sentences, using 10,000 resamples and the seed-averaged F1 difference as the statistic. Differences with two-sided *p* < 0.05 were regarded as significant. To characterize errors, we categorized false negatives and false positives as boundary errors (overlap with a gold entity of matching type but different offsets), type errors, or complete misses or spurious spans, and we stratified boundary errors by whether the gold boundary lay inside a whitespace-delimited chunk.

Results

**Overall performance**

We evaluated all models on the official test partitions of the three corpora using exact-match entity-level precision, recall, and F1, computed with the original word-level evaluation scripts after projecting byte-level predictions back to character offsets (JNLPBA and GENETAG) or to the annotated spans (Bio-ID). Values are means over five random initializations, with standard deviations in parentheses. Table 1 summarizes the results.

*Table 1. Entity-level performance of the BPE-based CNN–BiLSTM tagger on the test sets.*

| Dataset | Precision | Recall | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| JNLPBA | 74.8 (0.3) | 79.2 (0.4) | 76.9 (0.2) |
| GENETAG | 93.1 (0.2) | 92.4 (0.2) | 92.7 (0.1) |
| Bio-ID | 72.6 (0.5) | 69.9 (0.6) | 71.2 (0.4) |

On JNLPBA, which covers five GENIA categories (protein, DNA, RNA, cell line, and cell type), the model reached an F1 of 76.9. This is comparable to the word-level BiLSTM-CRF models reported for this corpus (Habibi et al., 2017; Yoon et al., 2019) and within about one point of BioBERT (Lee et al., 2020; F1 77.5 as reported). On GENETAG, using the standard evaluation that accepts the alternative annotations (Tanabe et al., 2005), the model reached an F1 of 92.7. This is on par with previously reported neural systems and about 1.5 points below domain-pretrained transformers. On the BioCreative VI Bio-ID corpus (Arighi et al., 2017; Chou et al., 2017), which annotates mentions of genes, cells, tissues, organisms, and small molecules in figure legends, the model reached an F1 of 71.2. Bio-ID is notable for its heterogeneous entity types and the many mentions embedded in compound expressions, and our result compares favorably with the participant systems in the original challenge, which relied on hand-built tokenization and feature engineering.

**Comparison with word-level baselines**

To isolate the effect of tokenization, we trained a word-level BiLSTM-CRF (Lample et al., 2016) with an identical hidden size and the same pretrained embedding initialization. It used either whitespace and punctuation tokenization or the biomedical tokenizer from scispaCy (Neumann et al., 2019). The results are in Table 2.

*Table 2. F1 for different tokenization strategies under a matched architecture.*

| Tokenization | JNLPBA | GENETAG | Bio-ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whitespace + punctuation split | 73.4 | 89.6 | 63.8 |
| scispaCy biomedical tokenizer | 75.9 | 91.8 | 68.5 |
| BPE (ours) | 76.9 | 92.7 | 71.2 |

The BPE-based model outperformed the generic tokenizer by 3.5, 3.1, and 7.4 F1 points on JNLPBA, GENETAG, and Bio-ID, respectively. It also outperformed the domain-specific scispaCy tokenizer by 1.0, 0.9, and 2.7 points. The gains were largest on Bio-ID, whose text contains the most tokens that cross entity boundaries (for example, fusion constructs such as "GFP-tubulin" and prefixed forms such as "p53-dependent"). A paired bootstrap test over test-set sentences (10,000 resamples) indicated that the improvement over the scispaCy baseline was significant on Bio-ID (p < 0.001) and GENETAG (p = 0.02), and borderline on JNLPBA (p = 0.07).

**Boundary-misaligned entities**

We next quantified the impact of tokenization on entities whose boundaries did not coincide with the boundaries produced by the scispaCy tokenizer. These cases represented 3.1% of gold mentions in JNLPBA, 2.4% in GENETAG, and 8.9% in Bio-ID. By construction, a word-level tagger can never recover such mentions exactly, which places an upper bound on its recall. The BPE model correctly recovered 41.7%, 46.3%, and 52.8% of these mentions on the three corpora, respectively. This accounted for roughly one third to one half of its recall advantage over the word-level baseline. On the remaining, boundary-aligned entities, the two approaches differed by less than 0.6 F1 on every corpus, which suggests that the byte-level formulation does not sacrifice accuracy where word-level segmentation is adequate.

**Ablation of model components**

Table 3 reports ablations on the JNLPBA and Bio-ID development sets.

*Table 3. Development-set F1 under architectural ablations.*

| Configuration | JNLPBA | Bio-ID |
|---|---|---|
| Full model (BPE + CNN + BiLSTM) | 77.8 | 72.4 |
| Without CNN layers | 76.1 | 70.2 |
| Without BiLSTM (CNN only) | 74.9 | 68.7 |
