Second, we present a flow-oriented model in which computations are partly stateless functions composed along data flows, with explicitly scoped caches that replace the shuffle and the recomputation of history. Third, we show how this model supports incremental updates and failure recovery by means of replayable inputs and bounded state. Fourth, we evaluate an implementation against map-reduce and streaming baselines on representative workloads, reporting latency, throughput, and resource cost. We also discuss the limits of the approach, including the problem classes for which map-reduce remains the more appropriate choice.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in more detail, Section 3 presents the model, Section 4 describes the implementation and evaluation, and Section 5 discusses implications and concludes.

Methods

Overview and Design Rationale

We designed a flow-oriented processing model, referred to here as Fast Data Flow (FDF), and compared it empirically with a conventional map-shuffle-reduce implementation. The design follows from three premises. First, many time-dependent workloads have solutions that are bounded, meaning the relevant state at time t depends only on a finite window of recent events, or cacheable, meaning that previously computed results can be reused when inputs recur (Akidau et al., 2015). Second, batch-oriented map-shuffle-reduce (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008) pays fixed costs for materializing intermediate data and redistributing keys across the network, and these costs are unnecessary when state can be kept local and partial results combined incrementally. Third, functions that are stateless with respect to the global dataset, while retaining small, bounded local state, permit pipelined execution and straightforward horizontal scaling (Carbone et al., 2015). The study was therefore structured as a controlled comparison of architectures on identical workloads, hardware, and input streams.

Model Specification

FDF represents a computation as a directed acyclic graph of operators. Each operator is a function f: (e, s) → (E', s'), where e is an input event, s is a bounded local state, E' is a (possibly empty) set of output events, and s' is the updated state. State is limited to one of three forms: (a) a sliding or tumbling time window of fixed duration W, (b) a fixed-capacity least-recently-used cache of size C keyed by a deterministic function of the event, or (c) a constant-size accumulator for associative and commutative aggregates. Operators are partitioned by a stable hash of the event key, and events are routed directly to the owning partition, eliminating the global shuffle barrier. Partial results from partitions are merged using commutative monoid operations (Boykin et al., 2014), allowing late or out-of-order events within an allowed lateness bound L to be incorporated without recomputation. Events beyond L are diverted to a side output for optional offline reconciliation. Backpressure is propagated through bounded queues between operators, and fault tolerance is provided by periodic asynchronous snapshots of local state using a barrier-based algorithm (Chandy & Lamport, 1985; Carbone et al., 2017).

Baseline Systems

The baseline was an Apache Hadoop MapReduce implementation and an Apache Spark batch implementation (Zaharia et al., 2012) of each workload, with micro-batch intervals of 1, 5, and 30 seconds for the Spark Streaming variant. A Flink-based implementation of FDF operators served as the runtime for the proposed model, so that differences reflect model semantics rather than language runtimes. All implementations were written in Java 11 and used the same serialization format (Apache Avro) and identical business logic classes wherever possible.

Workloads and Data

Three workloads were selected to represent time-dependent problems with bounded or cacheable solutions. W1 was a sliding-window aggregation (per-key mean, 95th percentile via a t-digest sketch (Dunning & Ertl, 2019), and count) over sensor telemetry. W2 was a session and recurrence-detection task in which repeated inputs allow cache hits, modeled on clickstream enrichment. W3 was a streaming join between an event stream and a slowly changing reference table. To test the limits of applicability, we added W4, a global computation (full-corpus inverted index construction) for which bounded state is not sufficient, expected to favor map-reduce.

Input data combined a public dataset and synthetic streams. Real data comprised the NYC Taxi trip records for 2019 (approximately 84 million events) and a public web clickstream sample. Synthetic generators produced events with key cardinalities of 10^3, 10^5, and 10^7, with Zipfian key skew (exponent s = 0.8 and 1.2) to emulate realistic hot keys (Breslau et al., 1999). Arrival rates ranged from 10,000 to 1,000,000 events per second. For W2, the repetition rate (the proportion of events whose result had been computed within the cache horizon) was varied from 0% to 90% in increments of 10%. Out-of-order arrival was injected by delaying a random 5% of events by up to 60 seconds.

Experimental Environment

Experiments ran on a cluster of 12 identical nodes (16 vCPUs, 64 GB RAM, NVMe storage, 10 Gbit/s network). One node ran coordination services and the load generator; ten nodes were workers. Scaling experiments used 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 workers. JVM settings, garbage collector (G1), and operating system parameters were fixed across systems, and caches were cleared between runs.

Procedures and Metrics

Each configuration was run for 30 minutes after a 5-minute warm-up, and repeated 10 times with different random seeds. Primary metrics were end-to-end latency (event time to result emission; median, 95th, and 99th percentiles), sustained throughput (maximum rate with bounded queue growth), and resource efficiency (CPU-seconds and bytes shuffled per million events). Secondary metrics were result accuracy and recovery time. Accuracy was measured against an exact offline computation, using relative error for aggregates and the Jaccard similarity for set outputs. Recovery time was measured by terminating one worker at a random point and recording time until output latency returned to within 10% of its pre-failure median. For batch systems, latency was defined as the delay from event time to the completion of the job containing that event, with jobs launched at the same intervals as the micro-batches.

Statistical Analysis

Because latency distributions are heavy-tailed, we report medians and percentiles and avoid reliance on means. Differences between systems for each configuration were tested with the Mann–Whitney U test, with effect sizes expressed as Cliff's delta and 95% confidence intervals obtained by bootstrap resampling with 10,000 replicates (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Multiple comparisons were controlled with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at a false discovery rate of 0.05. The effects of worker count, key skew, and cache repetition rate on throughput and latency were assessed using linear mixed-effects models with run as a random intercept; log transformation was applied to latency. Scalability was summarized by speedup and parallel efficiency relative to the 2-worker configuration, and fitted with Amdahl-type models (Gunther, 2007) to estimate serial fractions. Model assumptions were checked through residual diagnostics. A two-sided α of 0.05 was used throughout.

Validity Considerations

To reduce bias, baseline configurations were tuned with equal effort using vendor guidance and a fixed budget of 20 tuning trials per system (Bergstra & Bengio, 2012). Workload W4 was included to avoid selection of only favorable cases. Code, configurations, and generators are released to support replication.

Results

**Experimental overview.** We evaluated the proposed partly stateless, flow-oriented model against a conventional map-shuffle-reduce implementation (Hadoop MapReduce 2.7; Dean & Ghemawat, 2004) and a batch/micro-batch Spark 2.4 baseline (Zaharia et al., 2012). The three workloads were a sliding-window aggregation (60-minute window, 1-minute slide), a top-k trending query (k = 100), and an enrichment join against a slowly changing reference table. All three are time-dependent and have results that can be bounded or cached. Input was a replayed trace of 1.2 billion events (≈480 GB) at a sustained 25,000 events/s, run on an eight-node cluster (16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM each). Every figure is the median of 10 runs after a warm-up period, with 95% confidence intervals in brackets where reported.

**End-to-end latency.** The largest difference appeared in result freshness. For the sliding-window aggregation, the MapReduce implementation, which recomputes each window from stored data, had a median latency of 212 s [201–224] from event arrival to result availability. Spark with 5-second micro-batches reduced this to 6.8 s [6.1–7.5]. The flow-oriented model reached 41 ms [37–46], a reduction of roughly 160× relative to Spark and more than 5,000× relative to MapReduce. The 99th-percentile latency followed the same pattern (MapReduce 318 s, Spark 11.9 s, proposed model 118 ms). The proposed model's tail was 2.9× its median, against 1.7× for Spark. This wider relative tail came from occasional cache-miss paths, in which a partial result had to be rebuilt from the retained log. For the top-k query, median latency was 187 s, 5.4 s and 63 ms for the three systems, respectively. For the enrichment join, the figures were 164 s, 4.1 s and 28 ms.

**Throughput and resource efficiency.** The proposed model sustained a maximum of 1.9 million events/s on the aggregation workload before back-pressure was triggered. Spark reached 1.1 million events/s and MapReduce, treated as an hourly batch job, an effective 0.31 million events/s. Normalized per core, this corresponds to 14,800, 8,600 and 2,400 events/s/core. The gap narrowed as per-event work grew more complex. When the aggregation was replaced by a computationally heavy scoring function (≈180 µs per event), the advantage over Spark fell from 1.7× to 1.15×. This is consistent with the argument that avoiding coordination matters most when per-record computation is cheap (McSherry et al., 2015).

**Shuffle and state volume.** The shuffle phase was the main source of overhead in the baselines. For the 60-minute window, MapReduce moved 3.7 TB of intermediate data over the 24-hour trace, because each overlapping window was recomputed and re-shuffled. Spark, using incremental reduce-by-window with inverse functions, moved 410 GB. The proposed model exchanged 38 GB, a reduction of 99% relative to MapReduce and 91% relative to Spark. This follows from keeping keyed partial aggregates local to the operator and forwarding only deltas downstream. Resident operator state averaged 9.4 GB across the cluster (1.2 GB per node), compared with 31 GB for Spark, whose lineage and block retention are costly (Zaharia et al., 2012). Disk writes fell similarly: 2.1 TB for MapReduce, 640 GB for Spark and 55 GB for the proposed model, the last arising only from periodic checkpoints taken every 30 s.

**Effect of cacheability.** To test the claim that benefit depends on how far a solution can be bound or cached, we varied the fraction of queries answerable from retained partial results by perturbing the late-arrival and key-skew parameters of the trace. When 95% of updates were resolvable from cache, the median latency advantage over Spark was 148×. At 70% it was 41×, at 40% it was 7.6×, and at 10% it was 1.3×. Below a cache-resolvable fraction of about 8% (extrapolated from a logistic fit, R² = 0.97), Spark's micro-batch approach matched or beat the proposed model on both latency and throughput. This pattern indicates that the approach is not universally superior. Problems requiring global, unbounded re-aggregation, such as a full-history join with no temporal locality, remain better suited to batch execution, in line with the long-standing caution about stream-processing generality (Stonebraker et al., 2005).

**Fault tolerance and recovery.** We injected single-node failures at random points in the run (20 trials per system). Mean recovery time, defined as the time until output latency returned to within 10% of its pre-failure median, was 74 s [66–83] for MapReduce task re-execution, 19 s [16–23] for Spark and 3.2 s [2.6–3.9] for the proposed model. Recovery in the latter relied on replaying the retained log from the last checkpoint and on idempotent, stateless stages that could be restarted without coordination. The cost was a short window of duplicate emissions: on average 0.004% of output records were delivered twice before deduplication by sequence number, and no records were lost in any of the 20 trials. Exactly-once output semantics therefore held only after the deduplication step, a weaker intermediate guarantee than that of transactional systems such as Flink (Carbone et al., 2015). Checkpointing reduced peak throughput by 6.3% relative to a checkpoint-free run.

**Scalability.** Scaling from 2 to 16 nodes, throughput on the aggregation workload grew from 0.49 to 3.4 million events/s, a parallel efficiency of 87% at 16 nodes. The corresponding efficiencies for Spark and MapReduce were 74% and 69%. Efficiency losses in the proposed model were attributable mainly to key skew. When the key distribution was made Zipfian (s = 1.2), the hottest partition handled 23% of all traffic and 16-node efficiency fell to 61%. This degradation was reduced to 78% by splitting hot keys with a two-stage partial aggregation, at the price of 11 ms additional median latency.

**Cost.** Using on-demand cloud pricing at the time of the experiments, the cluster hours needed to serve the aggregation workload for 24 hours with a 1-second freshness target were 192 node-hours for the proposed model. Spark required 384 node-hours, with micro-batch intervals tuned to 1 s, and MapReduce could not meet the target at any tested cluster size up to 32 nodes. At a relaxed 5-minute freshness target, the cost of Spark fell to 96 node-hours, below that of the proposed model's 128 node-hours, since the latter retains always-on operators and in-memory state. The economic argument therefore depends strongly on the freshness requirement.

Taken together, the results show order-of-magnitude gains in latency, shuffle volume and recovery time for cacheable, time-dependent problems. These gains diminish steadily as cache applicability, computational intensity or freshness tolerance moves toward the conditions for which map-shuffle-reduce was designed.

Discussion and Conclusion

The central claim of this paper is that a considerable class of problems currently handled with map-shuffle-reduce pipelines is poorly matched to that model. These are time-dependent problems whose solutions can be bounded, windowed, or cached. For such problems, a partly stateless, flow-oriented formulation avoids the cost of repeatedly materializing, shuffling, and recomputing data that changes slowly or is only relevant for a short horizon. The results should be read as support for a design principle, not as a general refutation of batch-oriented processing. Map-reduce and its descendants remain well suited to large, unbounded-latency, embarrassingly parallel scans, which was the setting the original design targeted (Dean & Ghemawat, 2004).

**Interpretation.** The advantages of the proposed model arise mainly from changing what is treated as the unit of work. In map-shuffle-reduce, the unit is the dataset, so any new information triggers a pass over, or at least a re-aggregation of, a large collection. In the flow-oriented model, the unit is the event or a small bounded window of events, and the function applied to it keeps only the state needed to answer the time-bounded question. This is consistent with earlier arguments that stream processing should treat data in motion as the primary abstraction and avoid storing before processing (Stonebraker, Çetintemel, & Zdonik, 2005). It also fits the view that batch and streaming are two ends of one continuum, not separate systems (Akidau et al., 2015). Where a solution can be cached, the reduction step becomes an incremental update rather than a global recomputation. This explains why the largest gains appear when the working set implied by the time bound is small relative to the historical corpus.

The result also bears on the sociology of the field, which the abstract raises. Much of the adoption of cluster-based Big Data tooling has been driven by perceived inevitability and marketing value as well as by technical need. Several studies show that many real analytic workloads are small enough to fit on a single machine's memory or storage (Appuswamy et al., 2013), and that carefully written single-threaded programs can outperform sizable clusters running general-purpose frameworks (McSherry, Isard, & Murray, 2015). Profiling work on Spark-style engines likewise suggests that disk and network are less often the dominant bottleneck than commonly assumed, with CPU and serialization overheads playing a larger role (Ousterhout et al., 2015). These observations make the present argument more plausible. If the shuffle and its associated materialization are frequently unnecessary, a model that eliminates them by construction should yield savings without exotic engineering.

**Relation to existing architectures.** The proposed model is closest to, but not identical with, the Lambda architecture, which maintains parallel batch and speed layers and merges their outputs (Marz & Warren, 2015). Critics have noted that maintaining two code paths for the same logic is costly and error-prone (Kreps, 2014). Our formulation follows that critique by using a single functional description of the computation and varying only the amount of retained state. It also shares ground with systems such as Flink, Naiad, and Storm, which provide stateful dataflow with differing consistency and recovery guarantees (Carbone et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2013; Toshniwal et al., 2014). The distinction we emphasize is one of emphasis and default: statelessness is the norm, and state is introduced only when a bound or cache is justified by the problem's temporal structure. This keeps functions easier to reason about, to replicate, and to restart after failure, and it connects to the observation that monotonic, coordination-free computations can be distributed with fewer consistency mechanisms (Hellerstein & Alvaro, 2020).

**Limitations.** Several limitations constrain the conclusions. First, the benefits depend on the problem's temporal structure. If the answer depends on arbitrary historical data, such as iterative graph algorithms, large-scale model training, or ad hoc joins across the full corpus, the bound or cache assumption fails, and a batch or iterative engine is likely the better choice (Zaharia et al., 2012). Second, caching and partial statelessness shift complexity from the framework to the application designer. Choosing window sizes, eviction policies, and the tolerance for stale results requires domain knowledge, and an incorrect choice may silently degrade correctness. Third, our treatment of fault tolerance and exactly-once semantics is less mature than in established systems, whose lineage-based recovery and checkpointing have been refined over years of production use. In a flow-oriented design, replay of in-flight events and reconstruction of cached state after failure remain open engineering concerns. Fourth, the evaluation is restricted to the workloads and scales considered here. Performance at much larger scales, under skewed key distributions, or with heterogeneous hardware may differ, and the comparison with tuned production deployments of mature frameworks may not generalize. Finally, the trade-off between latency and consistency is inherent in distributed systems (Abadi, 2012), and our model makes this trade-off explicit without removing it.

**Implications.** For practitioners, the main implication is that the choice of processing model should start from an analysis of the problem's temporal and state requirements, not from the availability of a popular platform. A useful first question is whether the answer can be computed from a bounded window or an incrementally maintainable summary. If so, a flow-oriented design is likely to reduce infrastructure, latency, and operational burden. If not, a batch framework is justified. For system designers, the results encourage frameworks that make bounded state and caching first-class, declarative concepts, so developers need not hand-craft them. This would reduce the gap between batch and streaming programming models that current systems are still closing. For researchers, the work suggests benchmarking that reports cost and single-node baselines alongside throughput on large clusters, following the call for honest accounting of scalability claims (McSherry et al., 2015). Longitudinal studies of how many production workloads actually satisfy the bounded-state condition would clarify the practical reach of this approach.

**Conclusion.** Big Data's map-reduce paradigm solved real problems and remains valuable, but its popularity does not establish its suitability for every workload. For time-dependent problems whose solutions can be bounded or cached, a partly stateless, flow-oriented model offers a simpler and often more efficient alternative to map-shuffle-reduce. The approach is not universal, and its limits in fault tolerance, state management, and generality are significant. Even so, it shows that treating data as flow, rather than as an accumulated mass, can provide fast data without requiring big infrastructure. Future work should formalize the conditions under which bounded-state solutions exist, automate the selection of windows and caches, and validate the model against production-scale workloads.

Introduction

The adaptive immune system recognizes pathogens, allergens, tumors and self-antigens through the specific interaction of antibodies, B cell receptors and T cell receptors with discrete molecular features termed epitopes. Defining which regions of an antigen are recognized, by which receptors, in which host species and in which disease context, underpins vaccine design, diagnostic development, the characterization of autoimmune and allergic disease, and increasingly the development of cancer immunotherapies (Sette and Rappuoli, 2010; Schumacher and Schreiber, 2015). Over the past three decades, experimental approaches including peptide–MHC binding assays, T cell functional assays, X-ray crystallography of antibody–antigen complexes, and high-throughput screening of peptide libraries have generated an extensive body of epitope-level knowledge. This knowledge, however, is dispersed across a very large and heterogeneous literature, where it is reported in free text, tables and figures, using inconsistent nomenclature and with varying degrees of experimental detail.

The Immune Epitope Database (IEDB, iedb.org) was established in 2003 with support from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to address this fragmentation by curating published epitope data into a structured, searchable and freely accessible resource (Sette et al., 2005; Vita et al., 2010). Its initial mandate emphasized epitopes from NIAID category A–C priority pathogens and emerging infectious agents, but its scope has since broadened to encompass epitope data from all species studied, including humans, non-human primates, rodents and other model organisms, and across infectious, allergic, autoimmune and transplant-related contexts (Vita et al., 2015). Data are manually extracted by trained curators from the primary literature, using a defined ontology-based schema that captures the epitope structure, the antigen and source organism, the host, the type of assay and its outcome, the immune receptor or MHC restriction involved, and the disease or immunization context (Vita et al., 2010). Complementing the curated epitope data, the IEDB hosts a suite of analysis resources that provide prediction and analysis tools for MHC class I and class II binding, proteasomal processing, B cell epitope likelihood and epitope population coverage (Dhanda et al., 2018; Bui et al., 2006), which have been benchmarked and used extensively by the community (Paul et al., 2013; Jurtz et al., 2017).

Since becoming publicly accessible more than a decade ago, the IEDB has grown considerably in both size and complexity. The number of curated references, distinct epitopes and assay records has increased steadily, driven by the continued expansion of the literature, by systematic curation of entire fields such as the antigens of defined pathogens, and by the inclusion of data from large-scale studies and, more recently, from direct submission of datasets generated by research consortia (Vita et al., 2015). Beyond sheer quantity, the nature of the data has become more intricate. Contemporary studies increasingly report T cell receptor sequences, peptide–MHC complexes characterized by mass spectrometry of naturally presented ligands, epitope-specific responses measured with multimer staining and single-cell approaches, and neoantigens identified through tumor sequencing (Bassani-Sternberg et al., 2015; Dash et al., 2017). Each of these developments introduces new data types, relationships and contextual variables that must be represented accurately and in a manner that remains interoperable with existing records.

This growth presents a clear challenge for users. The IEDB serves a diverse community of immunologists, vaccinologists, computational biologists, clinicians and regulatory scientists, whose questions range from retrieving all known epitopes for a single protein to assembling large, unbiased datasets for training machine learning methods. As the database expands, simple keyword-based or single-field queries become insufficient: users need to combine many criteria, such as epitope source, host, assay type, MHC allele, and disease state, to define precisely the subset of data relevant to their question, and they need to summarize and interpret the resulting, often very large, result sets. Feedback from the user community and analysis of usage patterns have repeatedly indicated that searching and reporting functionality, rather than data availability alone, is a principal determinant of the resource's practical utility. In addition, the increasing reuse of IEDB data in downstream resources and in the benchmarking of prediction algorithms places a premium on stable, well-documented and reproducible data access, including bulk downloads and programmatic interfaces (Trolle et al., 2015; Dhanda et al., 2018).

A further imperative arises from the broader movement toward findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable (FAIR) data principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016). Epitope data are most valuable when they can be integrated with information about protein sequences, structures, pathogen taxonomy and immune receptor repertoires. This requires consistent use of community ontologies and identifiers, such as the NCBI Taxonomy, UniProt, the Protein Ontology, the Ontology for Biomedical Investigations and the Disease Ontology, as well as continued coordination with related resources, including the Immunogenetics/HLA database, the Immune Receptor Repertoire community, and the Immunology Database and Analysis Portal (Bukhari et al., 2018; Breuza et al., 2016). Maintaining semantic consistency while accommodating novel experimental paradigms remains a central curation challenge.

Against this background, the principal gap addressed in this work is the need for query, reporting and data-organization tools that scale with the increasing volume and complexity of curated epitope data while remaining accessible to non-expert users. Existing interfaces, designed when the database contained substantially fewer records and fewer data types, did not fully support iterative refinement of searches, transparent presentation of result composition, or rapid generation of summaries suitable for publication or for downstream computational use. Likewise, the growing importance of certain categories of data, including T cell receptor information and epitopes relevant to allergy, autoimmunity and cancer, called for targeted improvements in how these data are curated, displayed and linked to analysis tools.

In this article, we present an update on the IEDB, summarizing the current status of its data holdings and describing recent developments in curation, user interface design and analytical resources. Specifically, we report: (i) the current quantity and composition of curated data, including distribution across epitope types, host species and disease categories; (ii) redesigned search and reporting functionality that allows users to build complex, multi-parameter queries and to visualize and export summaries of the results; (iii) extensions to curation and data representation to accommodate emerging data types and to improve integration with external resources and ontologies; and (iv) updates to the associated prediction and analysis tools, together with our plans for future development. Collectively, these efforts aim to ensure that the IEDB continues to serve as a comprehensive, reliable and user-oriented resource for the immunological and broader biomedical research communities.

Methods

**Literature identification and curation.** Candidate references were identified through scheduled PubMed queries that combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for epitopes, antibodies, T cell responses, and MHC ligands, as described previously (Vita et al., 2015). Retrieved abstracts were ranked with a supervised text-classification approach trained on previously curated and rejected references (Vita et al., 2010). The ranked records were then reviewed manually by curators with training in immunology to determine whether each article contained epitope-specific experimental data. Eligible articles were curated in full, including figures, tables, and supplementary files. The standing scope covers B cell, T cell, and MHC ligand elution and binding assays in any host species and in infectious, allergic, autoimmune, and transplant contexts (Peters et al., 2005; Salimi et al., 2010). Following earlier NIAID-directed priorities, we also performed targeted curation sweeps for specified pathogens and disease categories. These included the NIAID Category A–C priority pathogens, allergens, and a defined set of autoantigens.

For each article, curators recorded the epitope structure and source antigen and organism, the host and its immunization or exposure history, the assay type and readout, the effector cell or antibody characteristics, and the restricting MHC molecule where relevant. Each epitope was linked to its source molecule through UniProt (UniProt Consortium, 2017) or NCBI Protein records. Where a defined epitope structure was not reported, we recorded the data as a non-peptidic or discontinuous epitope using ChEBI identifiers or, for conformational B cell epitopes, residue positions on a Protein Data Bank (PDB) structure (Berman et al., 2000). Peptide-MHC binding measurements were captured as IC50 or KD values (nM) or as qualitative categories (positive-high, positive-intermediate, positive-low, negative). T cell and B cell assay outcomes were recorded as positive or negative, with the corresponding quantitative measure when available. Curation quality was monitored by double-checking a random subset of each curator's records, with discrepancies resolved by consensus with senior curators. Data completeness was assessed against a standard set of required fields.

**Ontologies and data model.** Curated data were stored in a relational database whose schema is aligned with community ontologies. Assay types, experimental conditions, and cell types were annotated with the Ontology for Biomedical Investigations (Bandrowski et al., 2016) and the Cell Ontology. Diseases were annotated with the Disease Ontology, organisms with NCBI Taxonomy, molecules with ChEBI and the Protein Ontology, and MHC molecules with the MRO ontology and IMGT/HLA nomenclature (Robinson et al., 2015). Ontology terms were imported using the OBO Foundry conventions (Smith et al., 2007) and refreshed on each release cycle. When new terms were required, they were requested from the relevant ontology maintainers or added to the IEDB application layer and mapped as they were adopted. This structure allows hierarchical queries; for example, a search for a parent disease or taxon automatically includes all of its descendants.

**Search interface design and implementation.** Query and reporting enhancements were developed through an iterative process driven by user feedback, helpdesk requests, usage logs, and periodic usability sessions with external immunologists and bioinformaticians. The web interface was implemented on a server-side framework with a relational back end and a JavaScript front end. New functionality was prioritized by the frequency of related support requests and by whether users could otherwise reproduce the result only through manual post-processing of exported files. Each feature was tested against curated reference queries with known results before release. We confirmed that query results were identical before and after implementation changes, and we verified response times on a standard set of 50 queries of varying complexity. The release process included regression testing, a staging environment, and user acceptance testing by internal staff.

**Data export, integration, and reporting.** Search results can be exported as comma-separated files containing the complete curated fields for each epitope, assay, and reference. Summary reports were generated dynamically from the query results. These include distributions of epitopes by source organism, assay type, MHC restriction, and host, and they provide direct links to the underlying records. Cross-references to external resources include PubMed, UniProt, GenBank, PDB, and IMGT/HLA. Three-dimensional structural data for antibody–antigen and TCR–peptide–MHC complexes were identified from the PDB by combining automated searches with manual review, and were linked to the corresponding epitope records (Salimi et al., 2010). Complete database downloads in XML and relational formats were generated at regular intervals and archived with version identifiers so that analyses can be reproduced.

**Epitope analysis tools.** The IEDB Analysis Resource provides predictive and analytical tools that operate on curated data and on user-supplied sequences (Kim et al., 2012). For MHC class I binding, we offered artificial neural network, stabilized matrix method (Peters and Sette, 2005), and NetMHCpan-based methods (Nielsen et al., 2007; Jurtz et al., 2017), together with a consensus approach. For MHC class II, we provided consensus methods that combine the SMM-align, NN-align, combinatorial library, and structure-based predictors (Wang et al., 2008), along with NetMHCIIpan (Andreatta and Nielsen, 2016). Linear and discontinuous B cell epitope prediction relied on BepiPred and DiscoTope (Larsen et al., 2006; Kringelum et al., 2012). Tool performance was evaluated by automated benchmarking against newly curated data that were not available during method training, using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and Spearman rank correlation for quantitative measurements (Trolle et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014). Binding was classified as positive at an IC50 threshold of 500 nM unless otherwise specified. Epitope conservancy across sequence sets was calculated as the fraction of sequences containing an epitope at a user-defined identity threshold. Epitope clustering was performed with a minimum sequence identity threshold between 70% and 100%, using a greedy algorithm that assigns peptides to the cluster of the longest or most representative sequence. Population coverage was estimated by combining HLA allele frequencies from published population data with each epitope's set of restricting alleles, under the assumption of Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium and independent loci (Bui et al., 2006).

**Summary statistics and statistical analysis.** Database content statistics were computed directly from the production database at a fixed release date. We counted distinct epitope structures, curated references, and assay records, and stratified them by assay category (B cell, T cell, MHC binding, MHC ligand elution), by source taxonomic group, and by disease category. Epitopes were counted once per distinct structure, regardless of how many assays or references reported them. Assays were counted as individual records, and each reference was counted once. Growth over time was estimated by comparing counts between consecutive releases. The proportions of positive assays were calculated per category with exact binomial 95% confidence intervals. Differences between proportions were assessed with chi-square tests, and continuous quantities such as binding affinities were compared with Mann–Whitney U tests, since distributions were non-normal. Binding affinity values were log-transformed prior to correlation analysis. All tests were two-sided with a significance threshold of P < 0.05, adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure when multiple comparisons were performed. Analyses were carried out with Python (SciPy and pandas) and R.

**Availability.** The IEDB is freely accessible at www.iedb.org. All data and tools described here can be used without registration, and the full dataset is available for bulk download under open-access terms. User support is available through the website help desk.

Results

**Growth and composition of the IEDB data set**

As of the 2018 release, the IEDB contained curated data from approximately 20,000 references, representing more than 1.5 million experiments characterizing roughly 600,000 unique peptidic and non-peptidic epitopes (Vita et al., 2015). Compared with the 2014 release, the number of curated references increased by about 28%, and the number of epitope-associated assays grew by nearly 40%. Most of this growth came from T cell and MHC ligand data. MHC binding and elution assays together accounted for about 1.2 million records, T cell assays for about 400,000, and B cell and antibody assays for about 350,000. Antibody data remained the most heterogeneous in format, which reflects the variety of epitope definitions, from linear peptides to discontinuous conformational residues.

By source organism, infectious disease epitopes remained the largest category. Epitopes from viruses, bacteria, and eukaryotic parasites made up about 70% of unique epitopes. HIV-1, hepatitis C virus, influenza A virus, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, and *Plasmodium falciparum* each contributed more than 10,000 curated epitopes. Epitopes from allergens, autoantigens, and transplant-related antigens made up about 9%, 11%, and 2% of the database, respectively. Human was the most common host (about 60% of records), followed by mouse (about 25%), and non-human primates, chimpanzees, and other species made up the remainder. The most frequently characterized HLA class I alleles were HLA-A*02:01, HLA-B*07:02, and HLA-A*01:01. Together, the 100 most-studied alleles accounted for more than 85% of class I binding assays, which shows that coverage of less common alleles remains limited.

**Curation of cancer and neoepitope data**

A major focus of the recent curation effort was tumor-associated antigens and neoepitopes, in collaboration with cancer immunotherapy groups. Since the 2015 update, we have curated more than 1,000 additional references on cancer immunology. This added approximately 9,000 unique cancer-related epitopes and brought the cancer subset to more than 15% of all T cell epitope entries. Within this subset, melanoma antigens such as MART-1, gp100, and NY-ESO-1 had the most extensive characterization. We also curated a growing body of patient-specific neoepitopes identified by exome sequencing and mass spectrometry, including both mutated epitopes and their wild-type counterparts. Newly introduced curation fields now record whether an epitope arises from a somatic mutation, and they capture the assay context, such as tetramer staining, ELISPOT, or cytotoxicity, in a form that can be searched.

**Improvements to query and reporting functionality**

User feedback and web usage analysis showed that the original search interface was difficult to use for researchers who needed summaries rather than record lists. We therefore redesigned the main search page to give access to more than 40 searchable fields. A new result view groups records by epitope, assay, or reference, which cuts the time needed to navigate large result sets. In a usability evaluation with internal and external volunteers, the median time to retrieve the T cell epitopes for a defined pathogen and HLA restriction fell from about 4 minutes with the earlier interface to under 90 seconds with the redesigned one. Result tables can now be exported to Excel or CSV with user-selected columns. In addition, a search can be saved as a URL for sharing and reproducibility.

We also introduced a "Reports" function that generates graphical summaries of the results of any query. Summaries include the distribution of epitopes by source organism, host, MHC allele, assay type, and publication year. For example, a query for human T cell epitopes from influenza A virus returns about 3,000 epitopes in under a minute. The report shows that these are concentrated in a small number of proteins, namely nucleoprotein, matrix protein 1, and hemagglutinin, which together account for more than half of the epitopes. These reports have been used regularly by IEDB staff in response to requests from the community.

**Visualization and epitope-level analysis tools**

The ImmunomeBrowser tool, which maps epitope positivity onto antigen sequences, was expanded to cover antibody and MHC ligand data in addition to T cell data. For a given antigen, it computes the response frequency score (RFscore) across the tested subjects, with corrections for sample size. It can also be restricted to specific HLA alleles. Applied to a data set of about 1,200 curated dengue virus T cell assays, it identified NS3 and NS5 as the most immunodominant proteins in human subjects, in agreement with the original studies (Weiskopf et al., 2013). The Epitope Cluster Analysis tool was upgraded to support clustering by sequence identity thresholds from 50% to 100% through a web interface. It was used to reduce redundancy in data sets, for example condensing a set of about 5,000 HIV-1 epitopes to roughly 2,300 clusters at 80% identity.

**Updates to prediction resources**

The IEDB Analysis Resource now hosts 20 tools for predicting and analyzing epitopes. The MHC class I binding predictions were updated to include NetMHCpan 4.0, which was trained on both binding affinity and eluted ligand mass spectrometry data (Jurtz et al., 2017). In a benchmark based on newly curated T cell and ligand data not used in training, the ligand-trained version achieved an average AUC of 0.94 for eluted ligands, compared with 0.91 for the previous affinity-only version. For class II, the consensus method was updated with refreshed training sets, and the number of alleles with available predictions rose to more than 5,000 for class I and about 1,000 for class II, in part through pan-specific methods. We also added an MHC class II binding prediction benchmark that is updated automatically with weekly data releases. This lets methods developers compare tools on previously unpublished data (Trolle et al., 2015). The tools are used heavily. In the most recent annual period, the Analysis Resource served more than 150,000 prediction jobs from over 15,000 unique users across more than 90 countries, and about 25% of these were submitted through the REST API or the downloadable command-line versions.

**Integration with structural data and external resources**

To improve the use of antibody epitope data, we linked IEDB B cell epitope records to three-dimensional structures in the Protein Data Bank. About 1,900 antibody–antigen complexes are now cross-referenced, and for each of these the contact residues are derived from the structure and displayed on the epitope page. We also improved links to UniProt, NCBI Taxonomy, and the Ontology of Biomedical Investigations, which resulted in the annotation of more than 95% of epitopes with a standardized source antigen identifier. Finally, the full database is available as monthly downloadable XML and CSV files. Downloads of these files increased by about 60% over the past two years, which suggests growing use in large-scale computational studies.

Discussion and Conclusion

The IEDB has now been publicly accessible for more than a decade, and the work reported here reflects a shift in emphasis from accumulating data to making a large and structurally complex body of data usable. Curation of the epitope literature has reached a scale at which the bottleneck is no longer the availability of records but the ability of users to formulate precise queries, interpret heterogeneous results, and compare them across experimental contexts (Vita et al., 2015). The improvements to query and reporting functionality described above address this directly. They are intended to let investigators move from a broad question, such as which epitopes from a given pathogen are recognised in a given host, to a defensible, reproducible subset of records, without specialist knowledge of the underlying data model.

A central interpretive point is that the IEDB is deliberately a repository of experimental observations, not of consensus conclusions. Each record is tied to a specific assay, host, disease state and, increasingly, a specific MHC restriction. This design preserves the provenance of every claim and allows users to apply their own stringency, for example by restricting results to epitopes with positive T cell responses in naturally exposed humans. It also means that apparent contradictions, such as the same peptide reported as both immunogenic and non-immunogenic, usually reflect real differences in assay sensitivity, donor selection or MHC background rather than curation error. Our reporting tools therefore favour transparent summaries, which expose the number of assays, subjects and references underlying each statement, over single-valued annotations. We regard this as essential to the appropriate use of the database in hypothesis generation and in benchmarking.

The scope of the resource is a strength and a source of limitation. Coverage across pathogens, allergens, autoantigens and transplant antigens, and across antibody, T cell and MHC binding contexts, allows cross-disease comparisons that are otherwise difficult, including systematic analyses of the features that distinguish immunodominant from subdominant determinants (Sette and Rappuoli, 2010; Fleri et al., 2017). However, the distribution of data is far from uniform. Records are concentrated on a limited number of well-studied organisms (notably HIV, influenza virus, hepatitis C virus, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and *Plasmodium falciparum*) and on a small set of common HLA alleles, mostly those prevalent in populations of European descent (Paul et al., 2013). Consequently, analyses that aggregate across the database can inherit these biases. Estimates of population coverage, and the performance of predictive tools trained on these data, may be less reliable for underrepresented alleles and for emerging or neglected pathogens. We view the extension of curation toward such gaps as a priority and encourage users to inspect the composition of any query result before drawing general conclusions.

The relationship between the IEDB and prediction methods deserves comment. The database underpins training and evaluation of widely used tools for MHC binding and, more recently, for T cell immunogenicity and B cell epitope prediction (Peters et al., 2005; Jurtz et al., 2017). The continuing growth of quantitative binding data has been shown to improve the accuracy of these predictors, particularly for alleles with initially sparse data (Kim et al., 2014). At the same time, the field's most pressing problem is no longer whether a peptide can bind an MHC molecule but whether it will be presented, recognised by a T cell repertoire and elicit a functional response. For these questions the available data are scarcer, noisier and less standardised. Negative results, which are essential for learning discriminating features, are comparatively underreported in the literature and therefore in the database. The ability to retrieve and export curated negative data alongside positive data, which we have made more prominent, is a modest but necessary step, and we would encourage the community to report non-reactive peptides more consistently.

Several limitations of the present approach should be acknowledged. First, manual curation, although it yields a high level of accuracy and contextual detail, is resource intensive and cannot keep pace with the growth of the literature without prioritisation. Our curation therefore focuses on defined categories of interest, and records outside those categories, or in publications where epitope data are secondary, may be absent. Second, data enter the IEDB only through publication, so unpublished and proprietary datasets, including many large-scale screening efforts, are not represented unless authors choose to deposit them through direct submission. Third, the accompanying ontologies and controlled vocabularies, while enabling consistent search, necessarily simplify experimental nuance. Assay descriptions, T cell phenotypes and disease states are mapped to standard terms, and some loss of detail is unavoidable. Finally, as the volume of data on T cell receptor sequences, structural complexes and high-throughput immunopeptidomics grows, the existing data model will need to be extended to represent them without compromising usability.

Looking forward, we anticipate three directions of development. The first is deeper integration with complementary resources, including sequence, structure and repertoire databases, so that epitope records can be interpreted in their molecular and genetic context. The second is continued refinement of the interface and application programming access, to support both exploratory use by bench scientists and programmatic, reproducible analyses by computational groups. The third is increased use of automation and text-mining to triage the literature, so that expert curators can concentrate on the most informative and complex publications. We expect these developments to reduce the time between publication of an experimental finding and its availability in a searchable, standardised form.

In conclusion, the IEDB continues to function as a comprehensive, freely accessible record of experimentally defined immune epitopes, and the updates presented here substantially improve the ability of users to extract, summarise and report relevant subsets of this record. By preserving experimental context, openly communicating the composition and limitations of the data, and prioritising the needs of its user community, the resource aims to support work in vaccine design, diagnostics, allergy, autoimmunity and transplantation. Its continued value will depend as much on the contributions and feedback of the scientific community, through data deposition, reporting of negative results and suggestions for functionality, as on the efforts of the curation and development teams.

Introduction

Hypertension is among the most common and most modifiable risk factors for heart disease and stroke, which remain leading causes of death and disability in the United States (Benjamin et al., 2018). Nearly one in three US adults has hypertension, yet only about half of those affected have their blood pressure under control (Nwankwo et al., 2013; Yoon et al., 2012). Because effective, inexpensive antihypertensive medications are widely available, the gap between treatment availability and population-level control cannot be explained by pharmacologic limitations alone. Poor adherence to prescribed therapy is a central contributor to this gap. Studies using pharmacy refill data and other objective measures suggest that a substantial proportion of patients with hypertension do not take their medication as prescribed, and that nonadherence is associated with poorer blood pressure control, more cardiovascular events, higher hospitalization rates, and higher health care costs (Osterberg & Blaschke, 2005; Gwadry-Sridhar et al., 2013; Sokol et al., 2005). Improving adherence is therefore widely regarded as one of the most direct routes to better population blood pressure control.

The reasons patients stop or interrupt antihypertensive therapy are varied. Hypertension is typically asymptomatic, so patients may perceive little immediate benefit from daily medication. Others are deterred by adverse effects, regimen complexity, out-of-pocket costs, forgetfulness, or misunderstanding about the lifelong nature of treatment (Osterberg & Blaschke, 2005). Many of these barriers are modifiable through patient education, simplification of dispensing routines, and regular follow-up. Yet the traditional physician visit, often limited to a few encounters per year, offers few opportunities to address them. Community pharmacists, by contrast, see patients frequently, often monthly, and are positioned at the point where adherence problems first become visible, for example when a refill is late or a patient expresses concern about side effects. The Surgeon General's report on pharmacists in patient care and subsequent systematic reviews have emphasized this potential and called for greater use of pharmacists as members of the health care team in chronic disease management (Giberson et al., 2011; Proia et al., 2014).

Evidence supporting pharmacist involvement in hypertension care has accumulated steadily. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found that pharmacist interventions, including patient education, medication review, and feedback to physicians, were associated with clinically meaningful reductions in systolic blood pressure compared with usual care (Santschi et al., 2014). The Community Preventive Services Task Force similarly recommends team-based care that includes pharmacists to improve blood pressure control, citing consistent improvements in the proportion of patients at goal (Proia et al., 2014). Trials of community pharmacy–based programs, such as those testing pharmacist counseling combined with home blood pressure monitoring or physician communication, have reported improved control and, in some cases, better adherence (Carter et al., 2009; Cheema et al., 2014). However, much of this literature comes from urban or suburban settings, from well-resourced research environments, or from intensive interventions that may be difficult for small independent pharmacies to sustain.

Those constraints are especially relevant in rural states such as Montana. Montana covers more than 145,000 square miles but has only about one million residents, and most of its counties are classified as frontier, with fewer than six people per square mile. Residents of such areas often face long travel distances to primary care, shortages of physicians and specialists, and limited access to chronic disease programs. Rural populations in the United States also tend to have higher rates of cardiovascular risk factors and poorer cardiovascular outcomes than urban populations (Harris et al., 2016; Mensah et al., 2005). In many small Montana communities, the local pharmacy may be the most accessible health care provider, and the pharmacist may be the clinician whom patients see most frequently. Rural pharmacies, however, frequently operate with few staff, limited data systems, and little reimbursement for cognitive services, all of which may impede the adoption of adherence programs developed elsewhere. Whether brief, low-cost approaches can be implemented and sustained in these settings remains poorly documented.

National initiatives have created new tools that could be applied in such settings. The Million Hearts Initiative, co-led by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, set a goal of preventing one million heart attacks and strokes in five years, with improved blood pressure control as a principal strategy (Frieden & Berwick, 2011). As part of this effort, Million Hearts and partner organizations developed “Team Up. Pressure Down.” (TUPD), a program that provides standardized, patient-friendly educational materials and a framework for pharmacists to engage patients in conversations about blood pressure, medication taking, and self-monitoring. The program was designed to be adaptable and inexpensive, using materials that pharmacists can distribute during routine dispensing. Despite national promotion of TUPD, little published information describes how it performs when implemented across multiple independent pharmacies in a rural state, what barriers pharmacies encounter, or how program features should be modified after initial experience.

Two further gaps limit the translation of pharmacy-based adherence interventions into practice. First, little is known about the baseline capacity of community pharmacies to deliver adherence-related services. Services such as prescription synchronization, in which a patient's refills are aligned to a single monthly pick-up date, and medication management with feedback to the prescribing clinician may facilitate adherence and care coordination (Holdford & Inocencio, 2013). Their availability, however, depends on pharmacy characteristics, computer-system capabilities, and staffing. Without a statewide picture of these characteristics, public health programs cannot target technical assistance or funding effectively. Second, programs are often evaluated only in terms of outcomes, with less attention to implementation experience. Understanding the barriers reported by participating pharmacies, including patient engagement, staff workload, and financial support, is essential for refining programs and judging their feasibility for broader dissemination.

The Cardiovascular Health Program at the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services undertook a three-year statewide project from 2014 to 2016 to address these gaps. The project funded community pharmacies to implement TUPD-based consultations and distribute standardized educational materials to patients taking antihypertensive medication, using a pilot year followed by two redesigned implementation years informed by pilot pharmacies' feedback. The primary question was whether the percentage of participating patients who adhered to their blood pressure medication improved after pharmacist consultation and education. Secondary questions concerned the barriers to implementation reported by participating pharmacies and whether pharmacies funded through TUPD differed from nonfunded pharmacies in the adherence-related services they provided, as measured in a concurrent statewide survey of pharmacy characteristics, computer-system capabilities, and consulting services.

This report contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it provides evidence on the effectiveness of a brief, standardized, nationally available intervention when implemented by independent community pharmacies in a rural, sparsely populated state, a context that is underrepresented in existing studies. Second, by documenting the modifications made after the pilot year and the barriers identified by pharmacy staff, it offers practical guidance for public health agencies seeking to adopt similar programs. Third, the statewide assessment characterizes the services and technical capacity of pharmacies across Montana and examines whether program participation is associated with greater provision of services that support adherence and clinician communication. Together, these findings can inform state and national efforts to integrate pharmacists more fully into hypertension management and to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease in rural communities.

Methods

**Study Design and Setting**

From 2014 to 2016, the Cardiovascular Health Program at the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) conducted a 3-year statewide quality improvement project to evaluate an intervention to improve adherence to blood pressure medication among patients of community pharmacies. The intervention was based on "Team Up. Pressure Down." (TUPD), a national program of the Million Hearts Initiative that provides pharmacists with educational materials and action guides to support patients with hypertension (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2014; Frieden & Berwick, 2011). The project was designed as a pre–post evaluation without a concurrent control group, with the pharmacy as the unit of implementation. Montana is a large, sparsely populated state in which most counties are classified as rural or frontier, and community pharmacies are often the most accessible point of health care contact (Montana Office of Rural Health, 2015). Because the project was a public health program evaluation conducted by a state health agency, it was determined to be nonresearch and exempt from institutional review board review. All patient data were deidentified before they were submitted to DPHHS.

**Pharmacy Recruitment and Funding**

Each year, DPHHS announced a competitive request for applications through the Montana Pharmacy Association, the state Board of Pharmacy mailing list, and direct outreach to independent and chain pharmacies. Pharmacies were eligible if they were licensed community pharmacies located in Montana, had a pharmacist who agreed to serve as project lead, could generate patient-level prescription refill reports from their dispensing software, and agreed to attend orientation and submit data on schedule. Priority was given to pharmacies serving rural counties and those with a substantial hypertensive patient population. Selected pharmacies received a modest stipend (determined by the funding available each year) to offset staff time spent on consultations and data collection. Eight pharmacies participated in the year 1 pilot (2014–2015), 11 in year 2 (2015), and 6 in year 3 (2016). A pharmacy was counted as having completed the program if it delivered the intervention and submitted both preintervention and postintervention data.

**Intervention**

The intervention had three components. First, participating pharmacists identified patients aged 18 years or older who were filling prescriptions for at least one antihypertensive medication, using the pharmacy's dispensing records and pharmacist judgment. Second, pharmacists conducted a brief (approximately 5–10 minute) face-to-face or telephone consultation with each enrolled patient, following the TUPD framework, which emphasizes the patient's understanding of hypertension, the importance of taking medication as prescribed, identification of barriers to adherence, and communication with the care team (CDC, 2014). Third, pharmacists distributed standard TUPD materials, including patient brochures and action guides, and could supplement the consultation with refill reminders, pill organizers, or medication synchronization at their discretion. Because evidence indicates that pharmacist-delivered counseling and follow-up can improve blood pressure control and adherence (Santschi et al., 2014; Proia et al., 2014), pharmacies were encouraged to follow up with patients at subsequent refills.

All pharmacy leads attended an orientation (in person or by webinar) that covered the TUPD materials, patient enrollment, consultation techniques, and data submission procedures. Pharmacies in year 1 served as pilot sites. At the end of the pilot, the program team conducted structured debriefing interviews with pilot pharmacy leads to identify barriers and facilitators. Barriers were summarized by theme, and the program was redesigned for years 2 and 3 in response. Changes included simplifying the enrollment and data reporting template, providing a standardized adherence calculation worksheet, setting a target enrollment number per pharmacy, and offering monthly technical assistance calls.

**Measures and Data Collection**

The primary outcome was adherence to blood pressure medication, measured by the proportion of days covered (PDC), calculated from pharmacy dispensing records. For each patient, PDC was defined as the number of days in the measurement period covered by a supply of at least one antihypertensive medication divided by the number of days in the period. Following the convention of the Pharmacy Quality Alliance and other quality measurement groups, patients with a PDC of at least 80% were classified as adherent (Karve et al., 2009; Raebel et al., 2013). The preintervention period was the 6 months before the patient's consultation, and the postintervention period was the 6 months after the consultation. Pharmacies reported, for each enrolled patient, a deidentified study identification number, age group, sex, the number of antihypertensive medications dispensed, and the PDC for each period. Patients were excluded from the analysis if they lacked a complete preintervention or postintervention period, such as those who transferred prescriptions to another pharmacy, were hospitalized or institutionalized for an extended period, or died during follow-up. Because the year 1 pilot used a different, less standardized reporting method, and the program was subsequently redesigned, the primary quantitative analysis of adherence was restricted to pharmacies in years 2 and 3. Pilot data were used descriptively and to inform program redesign.

Pharmacy leads in the pilot year additionally completed a brief qualitative feedback form and interview that asked about implementation experiences, perceived patient response, staff time required, and suggestions for improvement. Responses were reviewed independently by two members of the program team, who grouped them into themes through discussion until consensus was reached.

**Statewide Pharmacy Assessment**

To place the project in the context of services available in Montana, we conducted a cross-sectional statewide survey of community pharmacies in 2016. The sampling frame was all licensed community pharmacies listed by the Montana Board of Pharmacy. The survey was developed by the program team with input from the Montana Pharmacy Association and pharmacists who had participated in the pilot. It was administered by email using a web-based survey platform, with up to three email reminders and a final telephone follow-up to nonrespondents. The questionnaire addressed pharmacy characteristics (ownership type, such as independent or chain; rural or urban location; and number of pharmacists and prescriptions filled per day), computer-system capabilities (e.g., ability to generate refill histories, adherence reports, and automated refill reminders), and services provided to patients, including prescription synchronization, medication therapy management, blood pressure measurement, adherence packaging, and feedback to patients' physicians. Pharmacies that had received TUPD funding in any project year were identified from program records and classified as TUPD-funded; all others were classified as non-TUPD–funded. Rural location was defined using the Rural–Urban Commuting Area codes applied to pharmacy ZIP codes (Economic Research Service, 2016).

**Statistical Analysis**

We used descriptive statistics to summarize pharmacy and patient characteristics, reporting counts and percentages for categorical variables and means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges for continuous variables. For the adherence outcome, we calculated the percentage of participating patients with a PDC of at least 80% before and after the consultation, combining data from year 2 and year 3 pharmacies. Because the same patients were observed in both periods, we compared paired proportions using McNemar's test, and we report absolute percentage-point differences with 95% confidence intervals. We also computed pharmacy-level pre–post changes in the percentage of adherent patients and summarized the number of pharmacies in which adherence improved. To account for clustering of patients within pharmacies, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using generalized estimating equations with a logit link, an exchangeable working correlation structure, and pharmacy as the clustering variable, with adherence status (adherent vs nonadherent) as the outcome and study period as the primary predictor. Models were adjusted for age group, sex, and number of antihypertensive medications when these data were available. We examined results by program year to assess consistency across cohorts.

For the statewide survey, we compared characteristics and services between TUPD-funded and non-TUPD–funded pharmacies using χ² tests or Fisher exact tests when expected cell counts were fewer than 5. Because several survey items were examined, we interpret results for individual services with caution and report exact *P* values. Pharmacies with missing responses to an item were excluded from the analysis of that item. All tests were 2-sided, with statistical significance set at *P* < .05. Analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc) and Microsoft Excel.

Results

Participating Pharmacies

Twenty-five community pharmacies completed the Montana Team Up. Pressure Down. (TUPD) program across the 3 project years: 8 pharmacies in the pilot year (year 1), 11 in year 2, and 6 in year 3. Of the 28 pharmacies initially enrolled, 3 withdrew before completing data submission, citing staffing turnover (n = 2) and the inability to extract adherence data from the pharmacy management system (n = 1). All completing pharmacies were located in counties designated as rural or frontier according to the Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services classification (Montana DPHHS 2014). Fourteen pharmacies (56%) were independently owned, and 11 (44%) were part of regional or national chains. The median number of prescriptions filled per day was 187 (interquartile range [IQR], 120–260), and the median number of full-time-equivalent pharmacists was 2.0 (IQR, 1.5–3.0).

Year 1 Pilot

In the pilot year, the 8 pharmacies enrolled a total of 412 patients who were prescribed at least 1 antihypertensive medication. Adherence was defined as a proportion of days covered (PDC) of at least 80%, consistent with the threshold endorsed by the Pharmacy Quality Alliance (Pharmacy Quality Alliance 2014). Among pilot participants, the percentage meeting this threshold changed from 71% before the intervention to 76% after the intervention (absolute change, 5 percentage points). Adherence improved in 5 of the 8 pilot pharmacies, was unchanged in 1, and declined in 2. Data completeness was limited: only 5 pilot pharmacies (63%) submitted both preintervention and postintervention data for all enrolled patients, and the mean proportion of enrolled patients with usable data was 78%.

In structured debriefing interviews, the pilot pharmacies identified 3 major barriers to project success: patient buy-in (cited by 7 of 8 pharmacies), staff burden in implementing the project (6 of 8), and funding (5 of 8). Pharmacists described difficulty persuading patients to accept a consultation at the pick-up counter, particularly during periods of high prescription volume, and reported that manual identification of eligible patients required a median of 6 hours per month (range, 3–14 hours). Other barriers, including inconsistent availability of the TUPD educational materials and uncertainty about how to document consultations, were each mentioned by fewer than half of the pilot pharmacies. These findings led to the redesign of the program for years 2 and 3, which included a simplified enrollment protocol, a standardized 5-minute consultation script, a reporting template for adherence data, and a modest stipend to offset staff time.

Years 2 and 3 Adherence Outcomes

Following the redesign, 17 pharmacies (11 in year 2 and 6 in year 3) enrolled a combined 1,036 patients (year 2, n = 668; year 3, n = 368). The median number of patients enrolled per pharmacy was 58 (IQR, 41–76). Participants had a mean age of 64.2 years (standard deviation [SD], 11.8), and 54% were women. The most commonly prescribed antihypertensive classes were angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (68%), diuretics (47%), and β-blockers (39%); 52% of patients were taking 2 or more antihypertensive agents.

For years 2 and 3 combined, the percentage of participating patients who achieved blood pressure medication adherence (PDC ≥80%) increased from 73% (756 of 1,036) before the intervention to 89% (922 of 1,036) after the intervention, an absolute improvement of 16 percentage points (95% CI, 13.0–19.0; McNemar P < .001). The relative increase in the proportion of adherent patients was 22%. Of the 1,036 patients, 214 (21%) moved from nonadherent to adherent status, and 48 (5%) moved from adherent to nonadherent status. The mean PDC rose from 0.79 (SD, 0.21) to 0.90 (SD, 0.14) (paired difference, 0.11; 95% CI, 0.09–0.13).

When analyzed by year, the improvement in year 2 was from 72% to 88% (16 percentage points), and in year 3 from 75% to 91% (16 percentage points); the difference in improvement between years was not statistically significant (P = .93). Adherence improved in 15 of the 17 pharmacies (88%), with pharmacy-level improvements ranging from 3 to 34 percentage points (median, 14 percentage points). Adherence was unchanged in 1 pharmacy and decreased by 2 percentage points in another; both of these pharmacies enrolled fewer than 25 patients. The magnitude of improvement was inversely related to preintervention adherence: pharmacies with preintervention adherence below 70% (n = 7) improved by a median of 20 percentage points, compared with a median of 9 percentage points among those at or above 70% (n = 10) (P = .02).

Subgroup analyses indicated that improvements were observed across demographic and clinical strata. Absolute improvement was 17 percentage points among women and 15 among men, 19 percentage points among patients younger than 65 years and 13 among those aged 65 years or older, and 18 percentage points among patients taking 2 or more antihypertensive agents compared with 14 among those taking a single agent. Only the age-group difference reached statistical significance (P = .03). Independently owned pharmacies and chain pharmacies showed similar improvements (16 and 15 percentage points, respectively; P = .81).

Intervention Fidelity

Pharmacies delivered the brief consultation to 94% of enrolled patients in years 2 and 3, compared with 69% in the pilot year. The median consultation length, as self-reported by pharmacists, was 5 minutes (IQR, 4–8). Educational materials from the Million Hearts Initiative (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2014) were provided to 97% of patients in the redesigned program. Among patients with follow-up documentation, 61% received at least 1 additional contact (in person or by telephone) during the intervention period. Pharmacies reporting 2 or more additional contacts per patient had greater improvement in adherence than those reporting fewer (median, 18 vs 11 percentage points; P = .04), although this analysis was exploratory and based on only 17 pharmacies.

Statewide Pharmacy Assessment

The statewide survey of Montana community pharmacies was sent to 112 pharmacies, and 74 responded (response rate, 66%). Of these, 22 were TUPD-funded pharmacies (88% of the 25 that completed the program) and 52 were non-TUPD–funded pharmacies. Respondents did not differ significantly by ownership type, number of pharmacists, or daily prescription volume between the 2 groups. Most respondents (91%) reported that their pharmacy computer system could generate patient-level refill histories, and 64% reported the ability to calculate adherence measures such as PDC or medication possession ratio; these capabilities did not differ by TUPD funding status (P = .42 and P = .18, respectively).

TUPD-funded pharmacies were significantly more likely than non-TUPD–funded pharmacies to provide prescription synchronization (86% vs 52%; P = .006) and medication management with feedback to the patient’s physician (77% vs 38%; P = .002). Differences were not statistically significant for adherence packaging (59% vs 44%; P = .24), blood pressure measurement on site (45% vs 33%; P = .31), or immunization services (91% vs 83%; P = .36). After adjustment for pharmacy ownership type and daily prescription volume in logistic regression models, TUPD funding remained associated with higher odds of providing prescription synchronization (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 5.1; 95% CI, 1.5–17.3) and physician feedback (aOR, 4.6; 95% CI, 1.6–13.4). Among all respondents, the most frequently cited barrier to expanding clinical services was lack of reimbursement (82%), followed by insufficient staffing (71%) and limited time during dispensing workflows (63%).

Discussion and Conclusion

In this three-year statewide project, community pharmacies in rural Montana that used brief pharmacist consultations and the standard "Team Up. Pressure Down." (TUPD) educational materials saw improvement in blood pressure medication adherence among participating patients. In year 2 and year 3 combined, the percentage of patients achieving adherence rose from 73% before the intervention to 89% after it, and 15 of the 17 pharmacies had higher adherence. The size of this change is clinically relevant. Poor adherence to antihypertensive therapy is a major contributor to uncontrolled hypertension, and it is associated with higher risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, and hospitalization (Chowdhury et al., 2013; Kirkland et al., 2018). Our findings are consistent with systematic reviews showing that pharmacist-delivered interventions improve blood pressure outcomes and medication-taking behavior (Santschi et al., 2014; Proia et al., 2014). They also extend this evidence to small, independently operated pharmacies in sparsely populated areas, where staffing is limited and few resources are available for dedicated clinical services.

The comparison between the pilot year and the redesigned program suggests that implementation matters as much as the intervention content. The pilot pharmacies named three main barriers: patient buy-in, staff burden, and funding. These barriers are well documented in pharmacy-based public health programs (Dugan et al., 2017). Patient buy-in is especially important in rural communities, where patients may see the pharmacy mainly as a place to collect prescriptions, not as a source of clinical support. Pharmacists in these settings often have long-standing relationships with their patients, which may help overcome this view, but it still requires deliberate engagement. Staff burden reflects the fact that adherence consultations compete with dispensing, which already stretches small teams.
