Models were estimated hierarchically: controls only (Model 1), the addition of overall EO (Model 2), its disaggregation into innovativeness, proactiveness and risk-taking (Model 3), and the addition of technological propensity (Model 4). Incremental explanatory power was evaluated using changes in *R*² and *F*-tests. Predictors were mean-centred to ease interpretation and reduce non-essential collinearity. Multicollinearity was checked through variance inflation factors (all below 2.6, against a threshold of 10; Hair et al., 2019). Heteroskedasticity was tested using the Breusch–Pagan test, which indicated mild violations in some specifications. Heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors were therefore reported (White, 1980; Long & Ervin, 2000). Residual normality was inspected with Q–Q plots and the Shapiro–Wilk test, and influential observations were identified through Cook's distance (no case exceeded 4/*n*). Results were unchanged when the few flagged cases were removed.

Two further analyses were undertaken to test the robustness of the results. First, nonparametric bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples was used to derive bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) 95% confidence intervals for all OLS coefficients, which relaxes distributional assumptions about the error term (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Second, because research output is a non-negative count variable, negative binomial regression was estimated on the untransformed (fractionalised, rounded) counts. This approach was preferred to Poisson regression because the likelihood-ratio test of the dispersion parameter rejected equidispersion (α = 0.71, *p* < 0.001) (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013). Incidence-rate ratios (IRRs) were reported alongside coefficients. Consistency of sign, magnitude and significance across the OLS, bootstrapped and negative binomial estimates was taken as evidence of robustness. All hypotheses were tested at α = 0.05 (two-tailed), and effect sizes were interpreted alongside *p*-values in line with current recommendations (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).

**Ethical considerations**

Ethical clearance was obtained from the university's research ethics committee before data collection. Participation was voluntary and informed consent was captured electronically. Responses were anonymised, and data were stored on encrypted institutional servers.

Results

**Sample characteristics and descriptive statistics**

Of the 292 usable responses, 54.5% were from women, and the mean age was 44.3 years (SD = 9.8). Respondents had held an academic post for an average of 11.6 years (SD = 8.4). Of the sample, 63.4% held a doctorate, and 38.7% were at senior lecturer rank or above. Mean annual research output, measured as accredited publication units per annum over the preceding three years, was 3.84 (SD = 3.52; median = 2.9; range = 0–21.5). The distribution was strongly right-skewed (skewness = 1.97) and overdispersed (variance = 12.39, against a mean of 3.84), which motivated the count-based robustness test reported below (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013).

All multi-item scales showed acceptable internal consistency using the conventional threshold of 0.70 (Nunnally, 1978). Cronbach's (1951) alpha was 0.81 for innovativeness, 0.78 for proactiveness, 0.74 for risk-taking and 0.83 for technological propensity. On the seven-point scales, respondents reported moderately high innovativeness (M = 5.21, SD = 0.94) and proactiveness (M = 5.07, SD = 1.02), but markedly lower risk-taking (M = 3.96, SD = 1.17). This pattern is consistent with the risk-averse institutional context often attributed to academia (Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Technological propensity was low (M = 3.18, SD = 1.41). Only 31.2% of respondents reported being aware of crowdfunding as a research-funding mechanism. Actual use was limited: 12 respondents (4.1%) had used crowdfunding and 22 (7.5%) had used crowdsourced R&D, with 34 (11.6%) having used at least one of the two. Respondents who had used at least one such method reported higher mean research output (M = 5.62, SD = 4.31) than non-users (M = 3.60, SD = 3.35). The difference was statistically significant under a Welch correction for unequal variances (t(38.6) = 2.31, p = .026), with a medium effect size (Cohen's d = 0.55; Cohen, 1988).

**Bivariate relationships**

Research productivity was positively correlated with proactiveness (r = .33, p < .001), risk-taking (r = .26, p < .001), technological propensity (r = .22, p < .001) and, more weakly, innovativeness (r = .12, p = .04). Among control variables, productivity correlated with academic rank (r = .29, p < .001), possession of a doctorate (r = .24, p < .001) and years in academia (r = .18, p = .002). It correlated negatively with teaching load (r = −.17, p = .004). The EO dimensions were moderately intercorrelated, most notably innovativeness and proactiveness (r = .58, p < .001), though not to a degree suggesting problematic collinearity. In the regression models, the highest variance inflation factor was 2.31, well below the conventional cut-off of 10 (Hair et al., 2010) and below the more conservative threshold of 5 (O'Brien, 2007). Because all constructs were self-reported, common-method bias was assessed using Harman's single-factor test. A single factor accounted for 24.6% of total variance, well below the 50% level at which concern is typically raised (Podsakoff et al., 2003).

**Ordinary least squares regression**

Table 3 reports the hierarchical OLS results. Model 1, containing only controls (age, gender, rank, doctorate, years in academia, disciplinary field and teaching load), explained 16.0% of the variance in research productivity (R² = .160; F(8, 283) = 6.74, p < .001). Rank (β = .21, p < .001), doctoral qualification (β = .15, p = .01) and teaching load (β = −.13, p = .02) were significant predictors.

Model 2 added the three EO dimensions and technological propensity, and raised R² to .270 (adjusted R² = .239; F(12, 279) = 8.60, p < .001). The increment was significant (ΔR² = .110; F(4, 279) = 10.51, p < .001). Because the Breusch–Pagan test indicated heteroscedasticity (χ² = 11.8, p = .001), heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors were used throughout.

Proactiveness had the strongest association with productivity (b = 0.92, SE = 0.24, β = .24, p < .001). Each one-point increase on the seven-point scale was associated with approximately 0.92 additional publication units per annum, holding other variables constant. Risk-taking was also positive and significant (b = 0.58, SE = 0.20, β = .17, p = .004), as was technological propensity (b = 0.47, SE = 0.18, β = .14, p = .010). By contrast, innovativeness was not significantly related to research productivity once the other predictors were included (b = 0.21, SE = 0.21, β = .06, p = .32). Its modest bivariate correlation therefore appears to reflect shared variance with proactiveness rather than any independent contribution. The effects of rank (β = .18, p = .001) and teaching load (β = −.11, p = .04) remained significant, while the doctorate effect weakened to marginal significance (β = .10, p = .07). Age, gender and disciplinary field were not significant in either model.

**Robustness checks**

Two further tests were applied to assess whether these findings depended on the distributional assumptions of OLS. First, Model 2 was re-estimated using nonparametric bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). The bias-corrected and accelerated 95% confidence intervals excluded zero for proactiveness [0.46, 1.38], risk-taking [0.18, 0.99] and technological propensity [0.11, 0.84], but not for innovativeness [−0.21, 0.62]. Bootstrapped standard errors differed from the HC3 estimates by less than 9% for every coefficient, indicating that the inferences were not sensitive to non-normal residuals.

Second, because publication output is a nonnegative count with evident overdispersion, a negative binomial regression was estimated on the rounded output measure. The dispersion parameter was significantly greater than zero (α = 0.41; likelihood-ratio χ² = 148.3, p < .001), which supported this specification over a Poisson model. The results were substantively consistent with the OLS estimates. Expressed as incidence rate ratios (IRR), each one-point increase in proactiveness was associated with a 19% increase in expected output (IRR = 1.19, 95% CI [1.08, 1.31], p < .001). The corresponding increases were 11% for risk-taking (IRR = 1.11, [1.03, 1.20], p = .006) and 9% for technological propensity (IRR = 1.09, [1.02, 1.17], p = .014). Innovativeness again had no significant effect (IRR = 1.04, [0.94, 1.15], p = .43). Model fit was modest but acceptable (McFadden pseudo-R² = .08), and the direction and significance of all four focal coefficients matched those of the OLS and bootstrap estimates.

**Summary of findings**

Across the three estimation approaches, higher self-reported proactiveness, risk-taking and technological propensity were consistently associated with higher research productivity, with proactiveness showing the largest and most stable effect. Innovativeness, often regarded as the defining characteristic of entrepreneurial orientation, did not independently predict productivity in any specification. The descriptive evidence also shows that novel technological methods such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D were seldom used in this sample, despite the positive association between technological propensity and output.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study asked whether academics who report higher entrepreneurial orientation (EO), and a greater propensity to adopt novel technological methods such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, are more research productive. The evidence from 292 respondents at a large South African university offers qualified support. The aggregate EO measure was positively and significantly associated with research output in the ordinary least squares (OLS) model (β = 0.21, p < 0.01). This result was stable under bootstrapping with 5,000 replications, where the confidence interval excluded zero, and under negative binomial regression, where each one-unit increase in EO corresponded to an estimated 14 per cent increase in the expected output count (incidence rate ratio = 1.14). The convergence of three estimators suggests that the finding is not an artefact of the skewed, over-dispersed distribution typical of publication counts (Cameron and Trivedi, 2013). Innovativeness, by contrast, was not significantly related to productivity, and the adoption of novel technological methods was low across the sample.

The positive EO–productivity relationship is consistent with the view that entrepreneurial dispositions are not confined to commercial settings but shape how individuals pursue opportunities in knowledge-producing organisations (Shane and Venkataraman, 2000; Etzkowitz, 2003). Meta-analytic evidence in firms shows that EO is positively related to performance (Rauch et al., 2009). The present results suggest an analogous mechanism at the level of the individual academic. Proactiveness and risk-taking, two of the core dimensions of EO (Covin and Slevin, 1989; Lumpkin and Dess, 1996), plausibly help scholars pursue collaborators, funding and publication outlets before these are demanded of them, and persist through the high rejection rates and uncertain returns of peer review. In this reading, research productivity reflects not only ability and resources (Fox, 1983) but also an opportunity-seeking orientation. That orientation may be especially valuable in resource-constrained systems, where academics cannot rely on slack resources and must create opportunities themselves.

The non-significant effect of innovativeness (β = 0.06, p = 0.38) is the most theoretically interesting result, and it warrants careful interpretation. One explanation draws on Kuhn's (1962) argument that most scholarly activity is "normal science" conducted within paradigms whose problems, methods and standards of evidence are largely given. If so, productivity within a field may depend more on the efficient execution of well-defined research programmes than on novelty of approach. Innovativeness may even carry costs in the short run, since unconventional topics or methods can face longer review cycles, narrower sets of receptive journals and greater difficulty in securing funding. Incentive structures may reinforce this. South African subsidy arrangements reward accredited publication units (Department of Higher Education and Training, 2015), which may favour incremental, high-throughput output over exploratory work. A second explanation is conceptual: innovativeness, as measured by self-reported openness to new ideas, may not map neatly onto the kind of novelty that is rewarded in academic evaluation. Alternatively, innovativeness may influence the quality or impact of research rather than its volume. Our outcome measure captured quantity, so we cannot rule out that innovative scholars produce fewer but more influential outputs. This distinction deserves direct testing with citation-based or field-normalised indicators.

The low propensity to use crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D is also noteworthy. Fewer than one in ten respondents (approximately 8 per cent) reported having used any such method, and the technological propensity construct was not a significant predictor of productivity once EO was controlled. The absence of an effect should not be read as evidence that these methods are ineffective. Low adoption produces limited variance, which reduces statistical power and makes any underlying relationship hard to detect. Moreover, the literature on crowdfunding indicates that success depends heavily on project quality, network reach and communication of credibility (Mollick, 2014), capabilities that academics may not routinely cultivate. Citizen science and crowdsourcing have likewise delivered substantial gains in data collection and analysis in some disciplines (Wiggins and Crowston, 2011), but their uptake is uneven and depends on disciplinary norms and institutional support. For universities in developing countries, where public research funding is typically scarce and volatile, the underutilisation of these methods may signal an unexploited complement to conventional grant income. This is a possibility rather than a demonstrated benefit, and it requires evidence on costs, ethical governance and reputational risk.

These findings carry several implications. For theory, they support closer synthesis between entrepreneurship and higher-education scholarship. EO has been developed largely in the firm context, yet the evidence here suggests it travels to the individual academic, complementing work on the entrepreneurial university that has concentrated on organisational and commercialisation outcomes (Clark, 1998; Perkmann et al., 2013). The differential behaviour of EO's components also cautions against treating it as a unitary construct, since its dimensions may relate differently to outcomes in contexts where novelty is institutionally constrained (Lumpkin and Dess, 1996). For practice, universities seeking to raise research output might attend to the development of proactive and risk-tolerant dispositions through mentoring, seed funding and tolerance of failure, rather than relying solely on workload and reward instruments. Training in fundraising, project communication and digital engagement might also build the capability needed for alternative funding mechanisms to become viable. For policy, if incentives implicitly penalise novelty, funders and ministries may wish to review whether current metrics encourage the exploratory research that societally important challenges require.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, so causal inference is not warranted. Academics who are already productive may develop greater confidence and proactiveness, and reverse causality cannot be excluded. Self-reports are also vulnerable to common-method bias and social desirability (Podsakoff et al., 2003), although the use of objective output counts as the dependent variable partly mitigates this concern. Second, the sample was drawn from a single South African institution through purposive sampling, which limits generalisability across institutional types, disciplines and national systems. Non-response may also have favoured those more engaged with research. Third, productivity was operationalised as output volume and does not capture quality, impact or societal relevance, and disciplinary differences in publishing conventions may not be fully absorbed by the controls. Finally, the low variance in technological propensity limits the strength of inferences about novel methods.

Future research should employ longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs, multi-institutional samples and field-normalised indicators of quality. It should also examine whether disciplinary paradigms moderate the effect of innovativeness, and whether the adoption of crowdfunding and crowdsourcing yields measurable gains when it occurs at scale. Qualitative work could clarify why adoption is low, whether because of awareness, skills, norms or perceived legitimacy.

In conclusion, academics with stronger entrepreneurial orientation appear to be more research productive, whereas innovativeness alone does not translate into higher output, perhaps because academic work is shaped by paradigms and incentives that reward incremental contribution. Novel technological methods remain underused in the academic context. In resource-constrained higher-education systems, cultivating entrepreneurial dispositions and exploring alternative funding and research methods may offer pragmatic, if still unproven, avenues for strengthening research productivity.

Introduction

Infliximab, a chimeric IgG1 monoclonal antibody against tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), was one of the first biologic agents to change the treatment of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. Randomised trials established its efficacy in Crohn's disease (CD), ulcerative colitis (UC) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Targan et al., 1997; Maini et al., 1999; Rutgeerts et al., 2005). It is now also used for ankylosing spondylitis (AS), psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and plaque psoriasis. These agents have improved disease control and reduced the need for surgery and hospitalisation. Their cost, however, places a considerable burden on health systems and has limited access in many settings. As patents and exclusivity periods on reference biologics expire, biosimilar versions have been developed to broaden access and generate savings. CT-P13 was the first biosimilar monoclonal antibody approved by the European Medicines Agency, in 2013, and was followed by additional infliximab biosimilars in Europe and the United States.

Biosimilars are not generic drugs. Small-molecule generics are chemically identical to their reference products. Biologics are large, structurally complex proteins produced in living cell systems, and their characteristics depend on the cell line and manufacturing process. Even a reference product shows some batch-to-batch variability, for example in glycosylation, so a biosimilar can be highly similar to its reference but cannot be an exact copy (Kurki et al., 2017). Regulatory approval therefore rests on a stepwise comparability exercise. It combines extensive analytical and functional characterisation with non-clinical and pharmacokinetic studies, and usually at least one adequately powered comparative clinical trial. The aim of this exercise is to show no clinically meaningful differences in quality, safety or efficacy. The pivotal infliximab studies, PLANETAS in AS and PLANETRA in RA, demonstrated pharmacokinetic equivalence and comparable efficacy and safety over the study period (Park et al., 2013; Yoo et al., 2013). These trials mainly addressed initiation of therapy or continued dosing of one product, and they were not designed to answer what happens when a patient moves between products.

Switching has become common in practice. Many patients have been stable on reference infliximab for years, and payers, hospitals and national tender systems increasingly move them to a biosimilar for economic reasons. This kind of non-medical switching raises questions that approval studies of biosimilars in treatment-naïve or newly started patients do not fully address. Infliximab is immunogenic, and anti-drug antibodies can accelerate clearance, reduce clinical response and cause infusion reactions (Baert et al., 2003). Because small structural differences could in principle alter immunogenic epitopes, concern has been raised that exposing a patient alternately to two similar but non-identical molecules might provoke new antibody formation or loss of response. Evidence that antibodies to reference infliximab cross-react with CT-P13 in vitro suggests the products share dominant epitopes (Ben-Horin et al., 2016). Such in vitro data do not show what happens in patients over time, and they do not settle whether multiple transitions carry additional risk. Perception-related effects must also be considered. Open-label switching can cause patients to report subjective worsening or discontinue treatment because of negative expectations, a nocebo effect that makes interpretation of uncontrolled switching data difficult.

Regulatory frameworks treat switching and interchangeability differently. The European Medicines Agency evaluates biosimilarity but has historically left decisions on substitution and switching to individual Member States and clinicians. In the United States, the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act created a separate "interchangeable" designation. It allows pharmacy-level substitution without prescriber intervention under state law, and it requires that a product be expected to produce the same clinical result as the reference in any patient and, if administered more than once, that the risk of alternating or switching not exceed the risk of continuing the reference product. Consistent with this, the US Food and Drug Administration guidance on demonstrating interchangeability recommends that sponsors normally conduct a switching study with multiple alternations between reference and proposed product. It also recommends a sufficiently sensitive population and pharmacokinetic endpoints, with comparison against patients who remain on the reference product (US FDA, 2019). The guidance thus sets a high evidentiary standard, involving repeated switches and a control group, that most of the existing clinical literature on infliximab was not designed to meet.

Professional societies in gastroenterology and rheumatology have acknowledged that evidence on switching is incomplete, and they have generally accepted a single, physician-managed switch from reference infliximab to a biosimilar while advising caution about multiple or non-medically driven switches (Danese et al., 2017). The NOR-SWITCH trial, a randomised, double-blind, non-inferiority study, found that switching from reference infliximab to CT-P13 was not inferior to continued reference treatment in terms of disease worsening across several diagnoses, although it was not powered to show equivalence within individual diseases (Jørgensen et al., 2017). Since then, many randomised trials, extension studies, registry analyses and single-centre cohorts have reported outcomes after switching in CD, UC, RA, AS, PsA and psoriasis. Most are observational, uncontrolled, short in follow-up and heterogeneous in design, switching conditions, outcome definitions and concomitant therapy. Much of the information is also available only in congress abstracts, which makes the literature difficult to assemble and appraise. Clinicians, formulary committees and regulators therefore lack a consolidated view of how far the evidence supports the safety and efficacy of switching, and how closely it matches the conditions in which interchangeability is defined.

This systematic review addresses that gap. Its question is whether switching patients between reference infliximab and its biosimilars, in either direction, is associated with changes in efficacy, safety, immunogenicity or drug exposure in patients with inflammatory disorders. We searched the published literature and relevant congress abstracts for studies that reported switching data across all approved indications of infliximab. We describe the study designs and populations, the number and type of switches and the follow-up, and we compare the findings with the evidence standard described in regulatory guidance.

The review makes three contributions. First, it brings together journal and congress data across gastroenterology, rheumatology and dermatology, which have typically been considered separately. Second, it distinguishes randomised, controlled evidence from uncontrolled observational findings and so shows how much of the reassurance comes from each source. Third, it identifies limitations in the current evidence, particularly the scarcity of data on multiple or alternating switches, and highlights the populations and scenarios in which further research is needed to establish interchangeability.

Methods

Study design and reporting

We conducted a systematic review of published evidence on switching between reference infliximab (Remicade, originator) and its biosimilars (CT-P13 and SB2, including the products marketed under various trade names) in patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. The review was planned and reported in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement.[1] The review question was framed with reference to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) draft guidance on interchangeability. This guidance states that, to support a designation of interchangeability, a sponsor should show that the biosimilar produces the same clinical result as the reference product in any given patient, and that the risk of alternating or switching between the two products is not greater than the risk of continuing the reference product.[2] We therefore extracted data that bore on the safety, efficacy, immunogenicity and pharmacokinetics of switching, and recorded the number and direction of switches in each study.

Eligibility criteria

We considered studies of patients of any age with Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis or plaque psoriasis. These are the principal indications for infliximab, and the review covered the indications for which both the reference product and biosimilars are approved. Eligible studies reported outcomes in patients who were switched from reference infliximab to a biosimilar. Studies that also included switches from a biosimilar back to the reference product, or between biosimilars, were eligible if the outcomes of the switch were reported. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), including open-label extension phases of RCTs with a switching component, as well as non-randomised interventional studies, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, registry analyses, case series and pharmacokinetic studies. Case reports, narrative reviews, editorials, commentaries, in vitro studies and studies of patients who started biosimilar treatment without switching were excluded. We also excluded studies that did not report switching outcomes separately from outcomes in biologic-naive patients, as well as studies of non-infliximab biologics. We did not restrict studies by sample size, follow-up duration or country. Only English-language full-text articles and abstracts were considered.

Information sources and search strategy

Published journal articles were identified by searching MEDLINE (via PubMed). The strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for infliximab and its biosimilar products (for example, "infliximab", "CT-P13", "SB2", "Remsima", "Inflectra", "Flixabi", "biosimilar") with terms for switching and related concepts ("switch*", "switching", "transition*", "interchang*", "substitut*", "non-medical switch*", "conversion"). We did not apply a limit on publication date at the lower bound, although biosimilar infliximab had been available only since the early 2010s. Reference lists of retrieved articles and relevant review articles were hand-searched to identify additional eligible reports.

Because much of the available switching evidence was expected to appear first, or only, in congress presentations, we also searched for abstracts. EMBASE was searched using equivalent terms, restricted to conference abstracts. We manually searched the abstract archives and proceedings of relevant congresses for the most recent years in which biosimilar switching data were available. These included meetings of the European Crohn's and Colitis Organisation, Digestive Disease Week, United European Gastroenterology Week, the American College of Gastroenterology, the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR), the American College of Rheumatology and the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology. Where an abstract was later published in full, we treated the full article as the primary source and used the abstract only to supplement information that was not otherwise reported. Abstracts that duplicated one another, or that reported interim data from a study already included, were merged to avoid double counting of patients.

Study selection

All records were exported to reference management software and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria. The full texts of potentially relevant journal articles, and the full abstracts of congress records, were then assessed. For each excluded full-text record, the primary reason for exclusion was documented. Disagreements about eligibility were resolved by discussion and, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. The numbers of records identified, screened, assessed for eligibility and included were tabulated and summarised in a PRISMA flow diagram.

Data extraction

A standardised extraction form was developed and piloted on a subset of studies. For each included study we extracted the following: first author, year and type of publication (journal article or abstract); study design (RCT, open-label extension, prospective or retrospective observational study, registry); country or countries; disease population; number of patients switched; the nature of the switch (reference to biosimilar, biosimilar to reference, or multiple switches); the presence and type of a control group (such as patients continuing on reference product); duration of follow-up; and whether the switch was mandated by protocol, driven by non-medical policy or made by clinician and patient choice. Efficacy outcomes were extracted as reported, using disease-specific measures. These included clinical remission and response, Harvey–Bradshaw Index, Crohn's Disease Activity Index, partial Mayo score, Disease Activity Score in 28 joints, Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index, Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, C-reactive protein, faecal calprotectin, and rates of drug persistence or discontinuation. Safety outcomes comprised adverse events, serious adverse events, infusion reactions, infections and discontinuations due to adverse events. Immunogenicity outcomes comprised the incidence of anti-drug antibodies and neutralising antibodies, with the assay used. Pharmacokinetic outcomes included trough serum infliximab concentrations before and after switching. Where available we also recorded the definitions of the outcomes and the time points of assessment.

Assessment of study quality

Because the review was expected to include mostly uncontrolled observational data, we described the strength of the evidence in terms of design features rather than excluding studies on quality grounds. RCTs were appraised for risk of bias with attention to the domains of the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, namely randomisation, allocation concealment, blinding, completeness of outcome data and selective reporting.[3] For observational studies, we recorded the presence of a comparator, the prospective or retrospective design, the handling of missing data and the potential for confounding, with reference to the criteria of the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale.[4] For abstracts, the limited information available meant that formal quality assessment was not feasible, and this limitation was noted.

Data synthesis and statistical analysis

Considerable heterogeneity was expected in study designs, populations, definitions of outcomes and follow-up durations, and most studies were anticipated to be single-arm. We therefore did not plan a quantitative meta-analysis. Findings were synthesised narratively and organised by study design (RCTs and extension studies followed by observational studies) and by disease area. Within each group we summarised the numbers of patients, the direction and number of switches, and the main efficacy, safety, immunogenicity and pharmacokinetic findings. When studies reported comparisons between switched patients and patients who continued reference product, we reported the effect estimates, confidence intervals and P values as given by the original authors, together with any prespecified non-inferiority or equivalence margins. We did not recalculate statistics or impute missing data. Finally, we judged the evidence against the FDA's interchangeability standard by considering whether the studies assessed multiple alternating switches, whether they were adequately controlled and whether they were powered to detect differences between the switched and non-switched groups.

Results

**Study selection and characteristics**

The MEDLINE search identified 113 journal articles, and the EMBASE and manual congress searches identified 149 abstracts. After screening for data on switching between reference infliximab (Remicade/Remsima-era originator) and a biosimilar, 70 publications were considered relevant and included. Most were uncontrolled, observational, single-arm cohorts or registry analyses, and the rest were open-label extensions of randomised trials. Six randomised, controlled trials contained switching data. Nearly all of the evidence concerned the biosimilar CT-P13 (marketed as Remsima/Inflectra). Smaller bodies of data covered SB2 and, to a lesser extent, other infliximab biosimilars. Studies enrolled patients with Crohn's disease (CD), ulcerative colitis (UC), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), ankylosing spondylitis (AS), psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and plaque psoriasis, and some enrolled mixed inflammatory cohorts. Follow-up after switching was typically 6–12 months, and few studies followed patients beyond 24 months. Every study evaluated a single switch from reference to biosimilar. No study evaluated multiple alternating switches (reference to biosimilar and back to reference), the design called for under FDA interchangeability guidance.

**Randomised controlled trials**

The largest randomised study was NOR-SWITCH, a double-blind, non-inferiority trial that randomised 482 patients on stable reference infliximab to continue the reference product or switch to CT-P13 (Jørgensen et al., 2017). Participants had CD (n = 155), UC (n = 93), spondyloarthritis, RA, PsA or chronic plaque psoriasis. Disease worsening during 52 weeks occurred in 26.2% of patients continuing the reference product and 29.6% of those switched, an adjusted risk difference of −4.4% (95% CI −12.7 to 3.9). This was within the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 15%. In the CD subgroup, worsening was numerically more frequent after switching (36.5% vs 21.2%), but the trial was not powered for individual diseases, and the subgroup did not demonstrate non-inferiority. Rates of adverse events and anti-drug antibodies were similar between arms.

Two randomised trials in rheumatology (PLANETAS in AS and PLANETRA in RA) had extension phases in which patients initially randomised to the reference product were re-randomised or switched to CT-P13 and compared with those who remained on CT-P13 (Park et al., 2017; Yoo et al., 2017). Clinical responses were maintained in both groups. In the PLANETRA extension, ACR20 response rates at about 2 years were broadly similar in patients who maintained CT-P13 and those who switched, at roughly 70–75%. In the PLANETAS extension, ASAS20 and ASAS40 responses and the proportions with partial remission did not differ meaningfully between maintenance and switch groups. Treatment-emergent adverse events and anti-drug antibody rates were comparable between groups in both extensions. An RA extension of the SB2 trial reported similar findings, with ACR20 responses sustained at week 52 and week 78 (approximately 60–70%) and no increase in immunogenicity among patients who switched from the reference product to SB2 (Smolen et al., 2018). The remaining randomised studies were smaller, including trials in CD and in other inflammatory conditions. They also found no statistically significant differences in efficacy, safety or immunogenicity between switched and non-switched patients, although several were not designed or powered to establish non-inferiority of switching.

**Observational studies in inflammatory bowel disease**

Most real-world switching data came from IBD cohorts. Prospective and retrospective studies from the UK, Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Italy, the Czech Republic, Hungary and elsewhere generally enrolled 50–250 patients each. Larger multicentre studies enrolled more than 500. Most reported that 70–90% of patients remained on CT-P13 and in clinical remission 6–12 months after switching. Discontinuation rates were generally 5–15%. Reasons for discontinuation included loss of response, subjective symptoms or adverse events, and a nocebo effect was suspected in some cases. For example, a UK cohort of 143 IBD patients and a Dutch cohort of 83 CD patients both observed no significant changes in disease activity scores, C-reactive protein, faecal calprotectin or trough infliximab concentrations after switching. Several cohorts found stable or slightly increased trough levels and no meaningful increase in anti-drug antibodies, which were detected in fewer than 10% of patients in most studies. Pediatric IBD series, typically 20–100 patients, also reported sustained remission in most patients and no new safety signals. Some studies reported higher withdrawal rates among switched patients, but these were generally in open-label, uncontrolled designs in which patient and physician awareness of the switch could have influenced outcomes.

**Observational studies in rheumatology and dermatology**

The Danish DANBIO registry followed 802 patients with inflammatory arthritis who switched from reference infliximab to CT-P13 (Glintborg et al., 2017). Disease activity was stable over the following year, and about 83% remained on treatment at 1 year. Discontinuations were mainly due to subjective complaints, and the registry authors noted possible nocebo contributions. Other cohorts in RA, AS and PsA, mostly of 30–300 patients, reported stable DAS28, BASDAI, and CRP values, with retention of 80–90% at 6–12 months and a pattern of withdrawals similar to that seen in IBD. Evidence in plaque psoriasis was limited to a small number of studies, including the psoriasis subgroup in NOR-SWITCH (n = 36), and PASI scores remained largely unchanged after switching.

**Safety and immunogenicity**

Across included studies, adverse event rates after switching were similar to those expected for reference infliximab. Infusion reactions, infections and serious adverse events occurred at low and comparable frequencies in controlled studies. In observational cohorts, adverse events leading to discontinuation were reported in about 2–10% of patients. Anti-drug antibody data were available in a subset of studies and showed no consistent increase after switching. Cross-reactivity of antibodies to reference infliximab and biosimilar products was observed, consistent with their similar structure.

**Gaps in the evidence**

Overall, no study reported a clinically important efficacy or safety signal attributable to a single switch. However, controlled data were limited to six RCTs. Most publications lacked comparator arms, many were abstracts with limited detail, and none addressed multiple switches or switching between two biosimilars.

Discussion and Conclusion

This systematic review identified 70 relevant publications describing switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab across inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatic disease, and psoriasis. Across heterogeneous designs and populations, we found no consistent evidence that a single switch from reference infliximab to a biosimilar, principally CT-P13, produces clinically important losses of efficacy, new safety signals, or increased immunogenicity. This is reassuring for clinicians and payers, who increasingly encourage or mandate non-medical switching. The strength of this conclusion is limited, however, by the design and scope of the available evidence.

The most informative data come from the six randomised controlled trials. The largest, NOR-SWITCH, randomised more than 400 patients on stable reference infliximab to continue treatment or switch to CT-P13, and found that switching was non-inferior for disease worsening across the pooled population (Jørgensen et al., 2017). The trial was not powered to demonstrate non-inferiority within individual diagnoses. The numerically larger difference in Crohn's disease, which did not reach statistical significance, shows how subgroup uncertainty remains despite an overall positive result. Randomised extension studies of PLANETAS and PLANETRA, in ankylosing spondylitis and rheumatoid arthritis, found that patients who switched from reference infliximab to CT-P13 maintained efficacy and showed no increase in immunogenicity compared with those who continued on CT-P13 (Park et al., 2017; Yoo et al., 2017). A randomised study in Crohn's disease likewise found no meaningful differences after switching (Ye et al., 2019). Together, these trials suggest that a one-time transition is unlikely to cause harm. They were nevertheless generally designed around non-inferiority margins that tolerate a degree of difference. They usually enrolled patients with stable disease and followed them for a limited period, typically about a year.

The larger body of observational evidence, including national registries such as DANBIO and institutional cohorts in gastroenterology and rheumatology, broadly supports the trial findings (Glintborg et al., 2017; Smits et al., 2017; Avouac et al., 2018). These studies add value because they reflect routine practice, include older and more comorbid patients, and capture outcomes over longer periods. Their limitations are considerable, though. Most lacked a concurrent control group, so apparent stability after switching cannot be distinguished from the natural course of disease in patients selected for stability. Open-label designs, heterogeneous outcome definitions, and variable handling of dose adjustments and concomitant therapy complicate pooling. Publication and reporting bias may also favour studies with uneventful outcomes, particularly among conference abstracts, which made up a large share of the evidence we screened and often lacked methodological detail.

Several observational cohorts reported higher discontinuation rates after switching, typically within the first year, and often driven by subjective complaints, such as subjective worsening or non-specific adverse events, rather than objective inflammatory markers (Tweehuysen et al., 2018; Glintborg et al., 2019). These findings are consistent with a nocebo effect, in which negative expectations about a cheaper replacement drug shape the patient's experience of treatment (Kristensen et al., 2018). If so, the practical risk of switching may depend as much on how the change is communicated as on the molecule. Open-label designs cannot separate these effects. Blinded trials such as NOR-SWITCH offer the cleanest answer, and they showed little difference in discontinuation due to adverse events. Structured patient education and clear communication from the clinical team are therefore reasonable parts of any switching programme, although they were rarely evaluated formally in the included studies.

The principal gap concerns interchangeability as defined by regulators. The US Food and Drug Administration has indicated that demonstrating interchangeability requires data showing that a biosimilar remains equivalent or non-inferior to the reference product after multiple alternations between them (FDA, 2019). The studies we identified overwhelmingly examined one switch, from reference to biosimilar. Very few examined a switch between two biosimilars, a return to the reference product, or repeated alternation. Such scenarios are increasingly relevant as more infliximab biosimilars enter the market and as tenders and formulary changes trigger successive transitions. Immunological theory suggests that repeated exposure to slightly different glycosylation or manufacturing variants might alter immunogenicity, although the high cross-reactivity of anti-drug antibodies between reference and biosimilar infliximab argues against clinically important epitope differences (Ben-Horin et al., 2016). Without data from multiple-switch designs, this remains a theoretical concern. It is nonetheless one that a robust interchangeability claim cannot dismiss.

Other gaps limit generalisability. Most evidence concerns CT-P13, with much less for SB2 and other infliximab biosimilars. Findings cannot be assumed to transfer across products, although all were approved on the basis of comparability exercises. Evidence in plaque psoriasis, ulcerative colitis, and psoriatic arthritis is thinner than in Crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. Data on special populations, including children, pregnant women, and patients with a history of immunogenicity or loss of response, are sparse. Patients with active disease or recent dose escalation are typically excluded from switching studies, so the effect of switching in less stable patients is poorly understood. Pharmacokinetic and immunogenicity endpoints, including trough levels and anti-drug antibodies, were inconsistently reported, and long-term safety outcomes such as malignancy and serious infection require far larger and longer datasets than those available.

This review has its own limitations. We searched MEDLINE for journal articles and EMBASE and congress proceedings for abstracts, so relevant studies indexed elsewhere may have been missed. The heterogeneity of study designs, populations, and outcomes precluded meta-analysis, and our synthesis is narrative. The quality of abstract-only reports could not be assessed fully. Because we did not formally weight studies by risk of bias, the apparent consistency of findings partly reflects the many uncontrolled studies that share similar biases.

In conclusion, the available evidence indicates that a single switch from reference infliximab to a biosimilar is not associated with significant efficacy or safety risks in patients with stable inflammatory disease, and these findings support the use of biosimilars in clinical practice. The evidence base remains narrow, however: it is dominated by single-switch, mostly uncontrolled observational studies of one biosimilar. Future research should include adequately powered, blinded, randomised studies of multiple switches and cross-biosimilar transitions, stratified by diagnosis and using standardised efficacy, pharmacokinetic, and immunogenicity endpoints. Long-term registry follow-up, ideally with consistent reporting and prospective control groups, would help determine whether the reassuring short-term findings persist and identify any vulnerable subpopulations. Until such data are available, clinicians can switch patients with confidence while monitoring them, paying attention to patient communication, and recognising that evidence for repeated switching remains incomplete.

Introduction

Named entity recognition (NER), the task of identifying and classifying mentions of real-world entities in text, is a core component of many natural language processing pipelines. Its output feeds entity linking, relation and event extraction, question answering, and knowledge base population (Mintz et al., 2009; Ling et al., 2015). Progress on NER has been driven largely by a small number of shared benchmarks, most prominently the CoNLL-2003 shared task data (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003) and OntoNotes (Hovy et al., 2006; Pradhan et al., 2013). Neural sequence labelling architectures, from BiLSTM-CRFs (Lample et al., 2016; Ma and Hovy, 2016) to contextualised pretrained representations (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019), have pushed performance on these benchmarks to a level where remaining gains are small. This success is tied to the way the benchmarks represent the task. Each token belongs to at most one entity mention, and the label inventory is small, typically four to eighteen types.

This flat, coarse-grained view discards much of the semantic content of natural language. Entity mentions routinely contain other entity mentions. In "University of California, Berkeley", the organisation contains a state and a city. In "the Bank of China", a financial institution contains a country. Such nested structure is pervasive in news, biomedical text, and other domains, and the inner mentions often matter for downstream tasks. A relation extractor that sees only the outer organisation cannot recover that the organisation is located in, or named for, a particular country. Nested mentions also expose how names are compositionally constructed, which can help with disambiguation and linking. Flat annotation guidelines force annotators to choose a single span, usually the outermost or the one that best fits a narrow set of types, and the resulting models are blind to everything else.

The research community has recognised this limitation. Early work on nested NER used cascaded or layered tagging (Alex et al., 2007) and discontinuous or parse-based approaches (Finkel and Manning, 2009). More recent methods include mention hypergraphs (Lu and Roth, 2015; Muis and Lu, 2017; Katiyar and Cardie, 2018), layered and stacked neural taggers (Ju et al., 2018), transition-based systems (Wang et al., 2018), and span-enumeration models (Sohrab and Miwa, 2018). However, this body of work has been evaluated on a narrow set of resources. The most widely used are the ACE 2004 and 2005 corpora (Doddington et al., 2004; Walker et al., 2006) and GENIA (Kim et al., 2003). ACE contains a small number of coarse entity types, and nesting in it is shallow and often involves pronouns or generic mentions. GENIA is restricted to the biomedical domain and has a specialised ontology. Neither provides a large, fine-grained, general-domain resource with deep nesting. Models for nested NER are therefore tested on data that does not exercise the full range of phenomena they are meant to handle. Conclusions about which approaches work, and why, risk being specific to the idiosyncrasies of these corpora.

Fine-grained entity typing has developed separately. Work on larger type inventories (Fleischman and Hovy, 2002; Ling and Weld, 2012; Gillick et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2018) shows that richer types support more precise downstream inference. Yet fine-grained resources are mostly built either by distant supervision, which introduces noise, or for typing already-identified mentions rather than detecting them. They typically do not annotate nested structure. BBN's pronoun coreference and entity type corpus (Weischedel and Brunstein, 2005) provides a hierarchical inventory of 64 types over the Wall Street Journal, but it is still largely flat in its treatment of mention boundaries. As a result, no existing dataset combines three properties: broad coverage of entity types, genuinely nested annotation, and a text source that is widely studied and linguistically well understood.

This paper presents NNE, a manually annotated dataset of fine-grained, nested named entity mentions over the full Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB; Marcus et al., 1993). Our annotation comprises 279,795 mentions of 114 entity types, with up to six layers of nesting. We build on the BBN type hierarchy and extend it to capture additional distinctions, and we annotate all mentions that fit the scheme, including those embedded within longer names and within non-name noun phrases. Choosing the PTB as the base text has several advantages. The WSJ is a standard newswire benchmark for parsing, tagging, and semantic annotation, and layers such as PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005) and the CoNLL-2003 NER annotation already exist over portions of it. NNE therefore enables comparison with, and joint modelling alongside, syntactic and semantic structure. A large share of nested entity boundaries aligns with constituent boundaries, which makes it possible to study how syntax can inform nested NER and how entity structure can inform parsing.

The goal of NNE is to remove a bottleneck for nested NER research. We argue that a dataset for this task should satisfy three requirements. First, it must be large enough to train and reliably evaluate high-capacity neural models. Second, it must have a sufficiently rich type inventory that nesting is semantically meaningful rather than an artefact of a few coarse classes. Third, it must be annotated consistently, with guidelines and quality control that give confidence in the gold standard. We therefore describe not only the resulting data but also the annotation scheme, the process by which annotators were trained and guided, and measures of inter-annotator agreement. We also analyse the data to characterise how nesting manifests in newswire, including the distribution of types, the depth and structure of nesting, and the relationship between entity structure and the PTB's syntax.

Our contributions are as follows:

1. We release NNE, to our knowledge the largest manually annotated nested NER dataset for English, with 279,795 mentions across 114 fine-grained types and up to six layers of nesting, covering the entire WSJ portion of the PTB.
2. We describe the annotation scheme and process, including type definitions, handling of ambiguous cases, and agreement statistics, so that the resource can be understood, extended, and replicated.
3. We provide a quantitative analysis of the nesting and type distributions and of how the annotation relates to the underlying syntactic structure.
4. We provide standard training, development, and test splits and evaluation of existing nested NER approaches as baselines, to indicate how much difficulty remains once data scale, type granularity, and nesting depth are increased.

We hope that the public release of NNE will encourage the development of new techniques for nested and fine-grained NER and will support research on how entity structure interacts with syntax, linking, and other downstream applications.

Methods

**Corpus selection and preprocessing**

We annotated the complete Wall Street Journal (WSJ) portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB; Marcus et al., 1993), covering sections 00–24. The PTB is the most heavily annotated English newswire resource, with part-of-speech tags, constituency structure, and (through later projects) semantic role and coreference layers. Annotating it lets nested entity structure be studied alongside existing syntactic and semantic information. We kept the PTB tokenization so that mention boundaries align with the treebank. Annotators saw each sentence in its original document order and could see neighboring sentences, which let them resolve ambiguous types (for example, a company name versus its product). We did not use gold parse trees to restrict candidate spans. Mentions were free to cross constituent boundaries wherever the text required.

**Annotation scheme**

Our type inventory began with the BBN Pronoun Coreference and Entity Type Corpus (Weischedel and Brunstein, 2005), which was already annotated over the same WSJ text. We extended it with ideas from the Extended Named Entity Hierarchy (Sekine et al., 2002), the ACE guidelines (Doddington et al., 2004), and the GENIA ontology (Kim et al., 2003). We then ran several rounds of pilot annotation on held-out documents, adding, merging, or splitting types whenever annotators disagreed systematically or found that frequent phenomena had no suitable label. The final scheme has 114 types organized in a three-level hierarchy. Top-level categories include person, organization, geopolitical entity, location, facility, event, product, work of art, law, language, and several numeric and temporal families (e.g., monetary values, percentages, dates, times, cardinal and ordinal numbers, and measurements). Fine-grained subtypes encode distinctions such as the kind of organization (corporation, government body, educational institution) or the kind of numeric expression. Annotators always chose the most specific applicable type, so the hierarchy can be collapsed to coarser labels when needed.

Guidelines defined a mention as a contiguous token span that refers to an entity of one of the scheme's types. Names, numeric expressions, and temporal expressions were annotated, whereas pronouns and generic common-noun phrases were not. Nesting was permitted to arbitrary depth under one structural constraint. Any two mentions must be either disjoint or strictly nested, so partially overlapping spans are not allowed. Identical spans with different types were permitted only for a small set of documented cases of genuine type ambiguity, such as metonymic uses. Where a mention contained others, annotators labeled every inner mention independently. For instance, a company name contains a person name, and a date range contains two dates. Annotators were instructed to label inner mentions even when the surface form was the same as an outer mention's component, and to treat possessives, appositions, and coordinations according to explicit rules in the guidelines. For coordinated structures with shared modifiers, annotators marked each conjunct as its own mention. They did not use discontinuous spans, which keeps the annotation compatible with standard span-based and tree-structured models.

**Annotation procedure**

The annotation team consisted of trained annotators with linguistics backgrounds, who received a guideline document and supervised practice before working on the main corpus. We built a browser-based interface for efficient span selection and hierarchical type assignment. It supports keyboard shortcuts, type search over the hierarchy, and visual display of nested mentions so that annotators can verify structure at a glance. To reduce effort and improve consistency, the tool pre-populated candidate annotations from the existing BBN labels where these were compatible with our scheme, and annotators then corrected, extended, and re-typed them. BBN annotation is flat and uses a different type set, so it served only as a starting point. Every sentence received full manual review, and annotators were encouraged to flag uncertain cases rather than guess.

Annotation proceeded in batches by PTB section. After each batch, a senior annotator reviewed a sample and all flagged items, and recurring problems were resolved through guideline revisions and group discussion. When a guideline changed, earlier batches were searched for affected patterns, using type and string queries over the existing annotations, and corrected. In a final consistency pass, we ran automatic checks to catch structural errors and implausible labelings. These checks looked for partially overlapping spans, mentions whose boundaries split a token, inner mentions of a type not licensed inside a given outer type, and strings that received different labels in different places without a contextual reason. Flagged items were manually adjudicated.

**Quality assessment**

We measured inter-annotator agreement on a subset of documents that were annotated independently by multiple annotators from scratch, without pre-populated labels. Because the number of mentions per sentence is unbounded and there is no natural notion of negative items, chance-corrected coefficients such as Cohen's kappa are poorly defined for this task. Following Hripcsak and Rothschild (2005), we instead treated one annotator's labels as the reference and computed precision, recall, and F1 for the other, which is equivalent to pairwise F1 agreement. A mention counted as matching only if its start, end, and type were all identical. We report agreement at three granularities: unlabeled span match, match at the top level of the hierarchy, and match at the full fine-grained type. This separates disagreements about where mentions are from disagreements about what they are. We also compared agreement at different nesting depths to see whether inner mentions are harder to annotate than outermost ones, and we examined confusion between types to find systematically ambiguous distinctions.

**Dataset statistics and splits**

We computed descriptive statistics over the final corpus: the number of mentions, the frequency of each type, the distribution of mention lengths in tokens, and the distribution of nesting depth. We defined depth as the length of the longest chain of mentions containing a given token. We also counted how many mentions contain other mentions and how many are contained in others, and we tabulated frequent parent–child type pairs to characterize the semantic relationships that nesting captures. To compare with flat NER resources, we computed the proportion of mentions and sentences that a flat annotation would discard, by keeping only outermost mentions.

For experiments we followed the conventional PTB division: sections 02–21 for training, section 22 for development, and section 23 for testing. The remaining sections are distributed with the corpus and can be assigned as additional data.

**Baseline experiments and evaluation**

To show how the dataset can be used, we trained several published nested NER approaches that represent different modeling strategies. These were a transition-based model (Wang et al., 2018), a hypergraph model (Lu and Roth, 2015; Katiyar and Cardie, 2018), and a layered sequence-labeling model that predicts entities from the innermost to the outermost level (Ju et al., 2018), alongside a flat BiLSTM-CRF tagger (Lample et al., 2016) trained on outermost mentions only. All systems were tuned on the development set and evaluated once on the test set. Evaluation used exact-match span-level precision, recall, and F1, requiring identical boundaries and fine-grained type. We report micro-averaged scores overall and broken down by nesting depth. Because the label set is large and imbalanced, we also examined performance on frequent versus rare types. We report results for single runs where cost prevented repetition, and otherwise as means over multiple random seeds, noting that differences smaller than seed variance should not be considered meaningful.

Results

**Corpus statistics.** The NNE annotation covers all 49,208 sentences of the Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB; Marcus et al., 1993), roughly 1.17 million tokens. It contains 279,795 entity mentions, an average of 5.7 per sentence. Every one of the 114 entity types in the hierarchy is attested in the corpus. The type distribution is heavily skewed, as in other newswire annotation (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003; Sekine et al., 2002). The ten most frequent types account for 51.6% of mentions, led by monetary values, cardinal numbers, organizations (corporations), and dates, while the 30 rarest types together account for under 2%.

Nesting is pervasive. Of all mentions, 118,513 (42.4%) are outermost, meaning they are not contained in any larger mention. The remaining 161,282 (57.6%) are embedded in at least one other mention. Annotations reach six layers of nesting, but depth falls off quickly. Mentions at nesting depths 1 through 6 number 118,513, 107,962, 40,741, 10,918, 1,508, and 153 respectively. About 36% of sentences contain at least one nested structure, and 17.3% contain three or more layers. Nesting is also much denser than in ACE-style resources (Doddington et al., 2004; Walker et al., 2006) or GENIA (Kim et al., 2003), where it is limited to a small set of coarse types or a few biomedical categories. NNE has roughly six times as many mentions as the English CoNLL-2003 data and well over twice as many as ACE2005 (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003; Walker et al., 2006). In NNE, 31.4% of mentions share their exact token span with another mention of a different type, such as a *person* that is also a *title-bearing* mention or a *country* that is also a *geopolitical* reference. Nesting is therefore structural as well as lexical.

Nesting patterns are strongly typed. Numeric and temporal types (CARDINAL, MONEY, DATE, PERCENT) account for 44% of mentions at depth 2 or deeper, typically as modifiers inside larger expressions such as "*$ 3.2 billion* contract" or "*the third quarter of 1989*". Organization and person names account for most of the remaining nested material. Common structures include a location inside an organization name (e.g., *New York* in "New York Stock Exchange") and a person name inside a larger organization or title phrase. The five most common parent–child type pairs cover 27.8% of all nested mentions, so a small number of structures carry much of the nesting signal.

**Annotation quality.** Annotation was carried out by trained annotators over the PTB's existing sentence and tokenization boundaries, with a subset annotated twice for agreement. On the doubly annotated sample, annotators reached a mention-level F1 of 94.1 when both span and type had to match exactly, and 96.7 when type was compared only at the parent level of the hierarchy. The remaining disagreements concentrated in a small number of confusable type groups. Distinguishing *organization: other* from *organization: corporation* accounted for the largest share of disagreements, and *facility* versus *geopolitical* usages of place names were also frequently confused. Span disagreements, most often over inclusion of determiners, appositions, and trailing modifiers, were rarer than type disagreements, at 31% versus 69% of all disagreements. Agreement was lower for nested mentions (92.3 F1) than for outermost mentions (95.6 F1), and it decreased with depth. At depth four and beyond, agreement was 87.2 F1, though these mentions make up under 5% of the corpus.

**Experimental splits.** To support comparison across systems, we follow the standard PTB convention. Sections 02–21 are used for training (about 40,000 sentences), section 22 for development, and section 23 for testing. This yields 2,416 test sentences and about 14,000 test mentions. Sections 00, 01, and 24 are also annotated and released but are not used in the standard split.

**Baseline performance.** We evaluated several representative nested-NER approaches, scoring exact match of both span and fine-grained type over all layers. A flat BiLSTM-CRF tagger (Lample et al., 2016) trained only on outermost mentions achieves 91.0 F1 on that layer. This shows that flat recognition of the top-level structure is relatively easy, and also that it discards 57.6% of the annotation. When the same architecture is applied as a cascade, with one tagger per nesting layer, in the manner of Alex et al. (2007) and Ju et al. (2018), it reaches 75.9 precision, 70.4 recall, and 73.0 F1 over the full set of mentions. A transition-based model that builds mention structures incrementally (Wang et al., 2018) improves on this, with 77.4 precision, 71.8 recall, and 74.5 F1. The hypergraph representation of Katiyar and Cardie (2018), adapted to the 114-type inventory, obtains 76.1 F1 on the development set. All systems are far below flat-NER numbers on CoNLL-2003, which is consistent with the greater difficulty of fine-grained, nested prediction. The gap between the best nested system and the outermost-only tagger (about 16 F1 points) reflects both the harder label space and error accumulation through layers.

Performance varies sharply by depth and frequency. For the cascaded model, F1 is 85.2 at the outermost layer, 70.3 at depth 2, 58.9 at depth 3, and below 40 at depths four and above, where training examples are scarce. Recall is the main weakness at greater depth, since an error at an outer layer is often propagated or leaves inner mentions unrecovered. Performance also correlates with type frequency. Types with more than 1,000 training mentions average 80.7 F1, whereas types with fewer than 100 average 38.4. Numeric and temporal types are recognized most reliably (MONEY 93.5, PERCENT 95.1, DATE 88.7). Fine-grained organization and location subtypes, as well as less frequent categories such as *event* and *product* subtypes, are the most difficult.

An error analysis of the transition-based model's outputs on the development set shows that 41% of errors are type confusions with correct spans, 33% are boundary errors, and 26% are missed or spurious mentions. Among the type confusions, over half occur within a single parent category (for instance, between two organization subtypes), which suggests that the hierarchical structure of the inventory could be exploited by future models. Overall, these results show that NNE is a challenging benchmark for nested NER, with substantial headroom, especially for deep nesting and rare types.

Discussion and Conclusion

We have presented NNE, a fine-grained nested named entity corpus covering the full Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank. With 279,795 mentions drawn from 114 entity types and up to six layers of nesting, it is, to our knowledge, considerably larger and more densely annotated than the nested resources most commonly used to benchmark nested NER, such as ACE2005 (Walker et al., 2006) and GENIA (Kim et al., 2003). Annotating the PTB also places NNE alongside rich existing layers, including constituency structure (Marcus et al., 1993), PropBank predicate-argument structure (Palmer et al., 2005), and coreference and entity annotation from OntoNotes (Hovy et al., 2006). We discuss below what the annotation reveals, how it may be used, and where its limitations lie.

**Interpretation.** The central observation motivating this work is that flat NER schemes discard a substantial amount of semantic information. In NNE, a large proportion of mentions are nested inside other mentions, and nesting is not confined to a small set of exotic constructions. Typical examples are organizations containing geopolitical entities, person names embedded in organization names, and numeric or monetary expressions inside longer quantity phrases. Standard flat datasets such as CoNLL-2003 (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003) and the OntoNotes NER layer retain only the outermost or a single selected span, so downstream systems trained on them cannot recover the inner entities. The finer-grained type inventory compounds this loss: distinctions such as those between different kinds of person, organization, and numeric types, or between names and descriptive nominal mentions, are collapsed in coarse four- or eighteen-type schemes. We view the combination of fine granularity and nesting as complementary: nested structure supplies compositional information about how a mention is built, while the fine-grained label supplies information about what each component denotes.

The release of NNE also makes it possible to ask how current models behave when the simplifying assumption of non-overlapping spans is removed. Recent approaches to nested NER, including layered or stacked sequence labelers (Ju et al., 2018; Fisher and Vlachos, 2019), hypergraph representations (Lu and Roth, 2015; Katiyar and Cardie, 2018), span-based classifiers (Sohrmann et al., 2018; Xia et al., 2019), and parsing-inspired methods (Finkel and Manning, 2009), have been evaluated mainly on corpora with limited type inventories or domain-specific text. NNE offers a larger and more varied testbed in which label sparsity, long-tailed type distributions, and deep nesting interact. We expect that the long tail of the 114-type inventory, in particular, will expose weaknesses that are invisible on coarse-grained benchmarks, and that handling structurally deep mentions will require models that go beyond a fixed number of labeling layers.

**Implications.** Because NNE is anchored to the PTB, researchers can study the relationship between named entity structure and syntactic structure. Many nested mentions align with noun phrase constituents, but not all do, and the mismatches are informative: they indicate where the PTB’s flat NP bracketing conceals internal structure (cf. Vadas and Curran, 2007) and where entity boundaries diverge from syntactic ones. This suggests uses in joint modeling of syntax and entities, as well as in evaluating whether syntactic features help nested recognition. The same alignment with PropBank and coreference annotation enables investigation of whether entity types and nested structure improve semantic role labeling, relation extraction, or entity linking. More broadly, nested and fine-grained entities may support applications such as question answering and information extraction in the financial domain, where compound mentions (e.g., a company name containing a place name, or a monetary amount embedded in a description of a transaction) carry the information users seek.

**Limitations.** Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, NNE covers a single genre and period of text: financial newswire from the late 1980s. Models trained on it may not transfer to contemporary news, social media, or other domains, and the entity inventory reflects the preoccupations of business reporting. Second, although annotation followed a detailed scheme and was conducted by trained annotators, fine-grained nested annotation is inherently difficult; decisions about whether a span constitutes a mention, how deeply to nest, and which of many closely related types to assign are subject to genuine ambiguity. Agreement on such a scheme is necessarily lower than on coarse flat annotation, and the resulting labels contain some noise and inconsistency that may place a ceiling on measurable performance. Third, the type hierarchy was designed with particular goals in mind and necessarily reflects design choices; alternative inventories, such as those used in fine-grained typing work (Ling and Weld, 2012; Choi et al., 2018), would segment the space differently, and mapping between schemes is not always one-to-one. Fourth, the annotation is restricted to English and to mentions; it does not include entity linking, coreference among nested mentions beyond what is inherited from other PTB-based layers, or relations between entities. Finally, the standard train/development/test split we provide follows common PTB conventions, which means that evaluation is sensitive to the well-known tendency of the community to overfit to PTB sections.

**Future work.** Several directions follow naturally. Improved modeling of nested structure, particularly approaches that scale to deep nesting and many types, is the most immediate. Cross-domain and cross-lingual extension of the annotation scheme would test its generality. Integrating NNE with existing PTB layers invites multitask and joint approaches. Finally, a more detailed analysis of annotator disagreement could inform both revisions of the guidelines and models that are robust to annotation uncertainty.

**Conclusion.** NNE provides a large, publicly available, fine-grained nested entity resource for English newswire. By preserving the internal structure of entity mentions that flat schemes discard, it supports research on nested NER, on the interaction between entity and syntactic structure, and on downstream uses of richer entity information. We hope that its release encourages the development of new techniques and prompts further annotation of nested structure in other languages and domains.

Introduction

Online reviews have become a central resource for consumers, merchants, and platform operators, and their automatic analysis has driven a large body of work in sentiment analysis, recommendation, and text generation (Pang and Lee 2008; Liu 2012). Most of this work has concentrated on full-length reviews. Many platforms, however, also let users leave tips: short, informal remarks that capture the most salient experience of a visit or purchase, such as "great cocktails, go early for a seat." Tips are typically a single sentence of ten words or fewer. They are written quickly and are easy to read on mobile devices, so they are often the first piece of user-generated text a prospective customer sees. In a sample of Yelp and Foursquare data, tips were on average roughly one-eighth the length of reviews while still conveying a clear evaluative judgment and a specific aspect of the item (Li et al. 2019). Despite this practical value, tips have received much less attention than reviews, and the problem of generating them automatically remains largely unexplored.

Generating tips is useful for two reasons. First, it lowers the effort of contributing content. A system that proposes a draft tip tailored to a user and an item can encourage participation, which in turn improves the coverage of items with few reviews. Second, a tip generator can supply concise explanations for recommendations, which improve user trust and decision efficiency (Zhang and Chen 2020). Both uses require that the generated text read as if it were written by the particular user about the particular item. A generic sentence such as "good food and service" is fluent and nearly always sentiment-consistent, but it is neither informative nor personal.

Prior work on review-related generation has moved toward personalization. Attribute-to-sequence models condition a recurrent decoder on user, item, and rating identifiers to produce reviews (Dong et al. 2017). Explainable recommendation methods generate justifications from aspects or features (Ni and McAuley 2018; Li et al. 2017). Related studies on review summarization and tip generation have used multi-task learning to share representations between rating prediction and text generation (Li et al. 2017; Wang and Ling 2016). These methods generally treat users and items as learned lookup embeddings trained end-to-end with the generation loss. That design has three limitations. First, a deterministic embedding trained for next-word prediction tends to capture the most frequent patterns and neglects the distinctive language habits that define an individual. Second, the same embedding must encode both the user's sentiment preference and the user's writing style, two properties that are only loosely related. Third, rare words that are specific to a user or an item, such as dish names, local idioms, or a reviewer's habitual phrases, are rarely reproduced, because the softmax over a large vocabulary assigns them low probability.

We argue that these limitations can be addressed by modeling persona explicitly.
