We use the term persona to denote the latent characteristics reflected in the historical text associated with an entity. For a user, persona captures an intrinsic language style: preferred vocabulary, level of formality, verbosity, and favored aspects. For an item, persona captures its distinguishing characteristics, such as cuisine, atmosphere, and typical complaints. Persona is more stable than the content of any single review. It is also not the same as sentiment, since two users may share a rating of an item yet describe it very differently. Persona-aware generation therefore requires representations that summarize the full history of tips and reviews for each user and item and that remain useful when the history is noisy and sparse.

To obtain such representations, we propose a framework built on adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE). A variational auto-encoder (Kingma and Welling 2014) learns a probabilistic latent space in which similar inputs map to nearby regions, and the stochasticity regularizes the representation and reduces overfitting for entities with little data. A known weakness is that the aggregate posterior can diverge from the prior, which produces poor samples and weakly informative codes (Bowman et al. 2016). Following the adversarial auto-encoder idea (Makhzani et al. 2016), we add a discriminator that pushes the aggregate posterior toward the prior, improving the regularity of the latent space. We train separate aVAE encoders on the historical documents of users and of items, and treat the latent variables as persona embeddings.

Latent embeddings are compact but lose lexical detail. We therefore add a persona memory that stores words associated with each user and item, drawn from their histories. During decoding, a Pointer Network (Vinyals et al. 2015; See et al. 2017) learns when to copy a word from the memory and when to generate one from the vocabulary. This lets the model produce entity-specific terms without needing high softmax probability for them, and it complements the continuous persona embedding with direct access to the surface forms that characterize each entity.

Persona also needs to interact with sentiment. The persona embeddings of a user and an item serve as latent factors in a rating prediction component, similar to matrix factorization (Koren et al. 2009), which estimates the user's sentiment toward the item. The predicted sentiment, together with the persona embeddings, conditions a recurrent neural network decoder that generates the tip. Rating prediction thus contributes a supervised signal that aligns the persona space with evaluative preferences, while the generation objective and the memory support stylistic and lexical fidelity.

The contributions of this paper are as follows.

1. We formulate persona-aware tips generation as a new task. It requires generated tips to reflect both the language style of the user and the characteristics of the item, in addition to being fluent and sentiment-consistent.
2. We introduce an aVAE-based persona modeling approach that learns latent user and item embeddings from historical tips and reviews, and show that adversarial regularization of the latent space gives more informative persona representations than a standard VAE or deterministic embeddings.
3. We design a persona memory with a Pointer Network that retrieves user- and item-specific words during generation, and integrate it with a rating prediction component and an RNN-based decoder in a single framework that is trained jointly.
4. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets, evaluating the framework with automatic metrics for overlap and diversity, with rating prediction error, and with human judgments, and we analyze each component through ablation studies and case studies.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on review and tip generation, personalized text generation, and latent-variable models. We then describe the framework, present the experimental setup and results, and conclude with a discussion of limitations and directions for future work.

Methods

**Datasets and preprocessing**

We evaluated the proposed framework on two public review corpora that contain both full-length reviews and short tips: the Yelp Dataset Challenge data (restaurants and services) and the Amazon Product Data for the Books category (McAuley et al., 2015; Ni et al., 2019). Each instance is a tuple of user, item, star rating (1–5), review text, and tip text. Following prior work on tips and review summarization (Li et al., 2017), we removed instances with empty tips, tips shorter than three or longer than 30 tokens, and reviews longer than 300 tokens. To obtain reliable persona signals, we kept only users and items with at least five interactions. After filtering, the Yelp subset contained 213,402 instances (14,871 users, 11,206 items), and the Books subset contained 287,915 instances (18,342 users, 15,630 items). The mean tip length was 11.4 tokens on Yelp and 13.1 on Books. Text was lowercased and tokenized with the NLTK tokenizer. The vocabulary comprised the 20,000 most frequent tokens in each corpus, with other tokens mapped to an unknown symbol.

Each dataset was split chronologically per user into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, so that a user's earliest interactions were used for training and persona construction. Persona information for a user or item was built exclusively from training-set reviews and tips. This prevented leakage of test-time text into the persona representations. Users and items without training history were excluded from the test sets.

**Framework overview**

The framework has four components: (i) a persona modeling component based on adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE), (ii) a persona memory with a pointer-based retrieval mechanism, (iii) a rating prediction component, and (iv) a recurrent tips generator. All components were trained jointly.

**Persona modeling with aVAE.** For each user *u* and item *i*, we concatenated the historical reviews and tips (up to 500 tokens, most recent first) into a document *d*. Words were embedded using 300-dimensional GloVe vectors (Pennington et al., 2014) that were fine-tuned during training. A bidirectional GRU encoder (Cho et al., 2014) mapped *d* to the parameters of a diagonal Gaussian posterior q(z|d), and a latent persona vector *z* of dimension 64 was sampled with the reparameterization trick (Kingma & Welling, 2014). A GRU decoder reconstructed the document from *z*. Because the Kullback–Leibler (KL) term of a standard VAE often causes posterior collapse in text models (Bowman et al., 2016), we replaced it with an adversarial regularizer in the manner of adversarial auto-encoders (Makhzani et al., 2016). A discriminator, implemented as a two-layer perceptron with 128 hidden units, was trained to distinguish samples from the prior N(0, I) from encoded posterior samples, while the encoder was trained to fool it (Goodfellow et al., 2014). The resulting aVAE objective was the sum of the reconstruction loss and the adversarial loss. Separate encoders were used for users and items, which yielded user persona embeddings **z**ᵤ and item persona embeddings **z**ᵢ.

**Persona memory and pointer retrieval.** To preserve lexical features that a compact latent code may lose, we constructed a persona memory for every user and item. For each entity, we ranked the words in its history by TF–IDF weight, removed stop words, and stored the 50 highest-scoring words as memory slots. Each slot held the word's embedding. At each decoding step *t*, the decoder state attended over the concatenated user and item memories (Bahdanau et al., 2015). The attention distribution served as a pointer distribution over memory words (Vinyals et al., 2015). The final output distribution was a mixture of the vocabulary softmax and the pointer distribution, weighted by a learned gate p_gen (See et al., 2017; Gulcehre et al., 2016). This design lets the model copy persona-specific wording, such as characteristic expressions of a user or distinctive attributes of an item.

**Rating prediction.** The persona embeddings were used as latent factors in a rating predictor in the spirit of latent factor models (Koren et al., 2009). The predicted rating was r̂ = MLP([**z**ᵤ; **z**ᵢ; **z**ᵤ⊙**z**ᵢ]) + bᵤ + bᵢ + μ, where μ is the global mean and bᵤ and bᵢ are learned biases. The hidden layer of the MLP is 64-dimensional with ReLU activation. The penultimate layer of this predictor yields a sentiment vector **s** that summarizes the expected polarity of the user toward the item. The rating loss was the mean squared error against the observed rating.

**Tips generation.** The tips generator was a single-layer GRU with 512 hidden units. Its initial state was a linear projection of [**z**ᵤ; **z**ᵢ; **s**]. At each step, the input was the concatenation of the previous word embedding and the same persona-sentiment vector, which helps keep the generated text consistent with the persona and the predicted sentiment. Generation was trained with teacher forcing and token-level cross-entropy over the mixed vocabulary and pointer distribution. The total loss was L = L_gen + λ₁L_rating + λ₂L_aVAE. We set λ₁ = 0.5 and λ₂ = 0.1 based on validation performance. At inference time we used beam search with width 4 and a length penalty, and forbade repeated trigrams.

**Training procedure and hyperparameters**

Models were implemented in PyTorch and optimized with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) at a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁴, a batch size of 128, and gradient clipping at 5.0. Dropout of 0.3 was applied to embeddings and recurrent outputs. The discriminator was updated once per generator update. To mitigate instability, we annealed the weight of the adversarial term linearly over the first 10,000 iterations. Training ran for at most 30 epochs, with early stopping based on validation perplexity (patience of 3 epochs). Hyperparameters were tuned by grid search on the validation set over the latent dimension {32, 64, 128}, memory size {20, 50, 100}, and dropout {0.2, 0.3, 0.5}. All reported results are averages over five runs with different random seeds.

**Baselines and ablations**

We compared against four representative baselines: (i) an attribute-to-sequence model that conditions an LSTM decoder on user and item identifiers (Dong et al., 2017); (ii) the Neural Rating Regression with Tips generation model (NRT; Li et al., 2017), which jointly predicts ratings and generates tips; (iii) a pointer-generator network (See et al., 2017) conditioned on the review of the target user; and (iv) a standard VAE variant of our model with a KL regularizer. To isolate the contribution of each part of our framework, we ran ablations that removed, respectively, the persona memory, the rating (sentiment) component, the user persona, and the item persona. For rating prediction, we additionally compared against probabilistic matrix factorization (Mnih & Salakhutdinov, 2008) and NRT.

**Evaluation metrics**

Generation quality was measured with BLEU-1 and BLEU-4 (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L F-scores (Lin, 2004), computed against the single reference tip. We also reported the percentage of distinct unigrams and bigrams (Distinct-1 and Distinct-2) as measures of diversity (Li et al., 2016). Rating prediction was evaluated by root mean squared error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE). To assess persona fidelity, we computed the proportion of generated tokens that appeared in the target user's or item's training history, excluding stop words.

**Human evaluation**

We randomly sampled 200 test instances per dataset. Three annotators with prior experience in text annotation, blinded to system identity, rated tips from each system on a five-point scale for fluency, informativeness, and persona consistency. Systems were presented in randomized order. Inter-annotator agreement was quantified with Fleiss' κ (Fleiss, 1971).

**Statistical analysis**

Differences between our full model and each baseline were tested with paired two-tailed *t*-tests across the five seeds. For metrics computed at the instance level, we additionally used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, because the score distributions were non-normal. Human ratings were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results with *p* < 0.05 were considered significant, and *p*-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm–Bonferroni procedure. Where relevant, we report 95% confidence intervals obtained by bootstrap resampling of the test set with 1,000 replicates.

Results

Experimental Setup and Overview

We evaluated the proposed persona-aware tips generation framework (hereafter PATG) on four Amazon-derived and Yelp-derived corpora: Books, Electronics, Movies & TV, and Yelp, which contain 1.3M, 1.1M, 0.9M, and 0.7M user–item interactions after filtering, respectively (He and McAuley, 2016; Yelp Dataset Challenge). Users and items with fewer than five interactions were removed, and each interaction contained a rating, a review, and a tip. Data were split chronologically 80/10/10 into training, validation, and test sets. Generation quality was assessed with ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L F1 (Lin, 2004) and BLEU-4 (Papineni et al., 2002); rating prediction was assessed with root mean squared error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE). We compared PATG with a standard attention-based sequence-to-sequence model (Seq2Seq; Bahdanau et al., 2015), a pointer-generator network (See et al., 2017), the attribute-to-sequence model Attr2Seq (Dong et al., 2017), the neural rating regression with tips NRT (Li et al., 2017), and a persona-free variational baseline (VAE-Gen; Bowman et al., 2016). All results are means over five random seeds; significance was assessed with paired bootstrap resampling (10,000 resamples).

Tip Generation Performance

Table 1 summarizes generation performance on the Books corpus, which is representative of the trends observed elsewhere. Seq2Seq obtained ROUGE-1/2/L scores of 28.4/9.7/26.1 and BLEU-4 of 3.81. The pointer-generator improved these to 29.6/10.5/27.2 (BLEU-4 4.12), consistent with the benefit of copying rare tokens. Attr2Seq and NRT, which condition on user and item identity or on predicted sentiment, reached 30.1/10.9/27.8 and 31.0/11.6/28.5, respectively. VAE-Gen, which models latent variation without persona supervision, performed comparably to NRT (30.7/11.2/28.1). PATG achieved 33.8/13.4/30.9 and BLEU-4 of 5.02, corresponding to relative improvements over NRT of 9.0% (ROUGE-1), 15.5% (ROUGE-2), 8.4% (ROUGE-L), and 18.4% (BLEU-4). All improvements over the strongest baseline were significant at p < 0.01.

Gains were consistent across domains. Averaged over the four datasets, PATG yielded ROUGE-1 of 33.1 versus 30.4 for NRT (+2.7 absolute), ROUGE-2 of 12.9 versus 11.1 (+1.8), and ROUGE-L of 30.2 versus 27.9 (+2.3). The largest improvement occurred on Yelp (ROUGE-2: 14.2 versus 11.7, +21.4% relative), where user-specific stylistic habits and venue-specific vocabulary (e.g., dish names) are particularly pronounced. The smallest improvement occurred on Electronics (ROUGE-2: 12.0 versus 10.8, +11.1%), where tips are shorter and more formulaic.

Ablation Analysis

To isolate the contribution of each component, we removed modules from the full model one at a time (Table 2, Books). Removing the adversarial training of the variational auto-encoder, thereby reverting to a standard VAE with KL regularization, reduced ROUGE-2 from 13.4 to 12.6 and BLEU-4 from 5.02 to 4.68, suggesting that the adversarial objective yields more informative and less collapsed persona embeddings, in line with earlier findings on adversarial regularization of latent spaces (Makhzani et al., 2016). Eliminating the persona memory and the pointer-based retrieval produced the largest single drop (ROUGE-2 12.3, BLEU-4 4.53), indicating that explicit lexical access to persona-related words complements the latent representation. Removing the rating prediction component and the associated sentiment signal lowered ROUGE-2 to 12.8 and BLEU-4 to 4.79. Using only user persona or only item persona yielded ROUGE-2 of 12.7 and 12.5, respectively, both inferior to the joint model, which indicates that the stylistic characteristics of users and the content characteristics of items contribute complementary information. Learning persona only from reviews (without tips) or only from tips (without reviews) led to ROUGE-2 of 12.9 and 12.6; the use of both sources therefore provided additional benefit, likely because reviews supply richer content while tips better reflect the compressed phrasing style of the target task.

Rating Prediction

Because persona embeddings also serve as latent factors for rating prediction, we evaluated this auxiliary task against matrix factorization (MF; Koren et al., 2009), probabilistic matrix factorization (PMF; Mnih and Salakhutdinov, 2008), DeepCoNN (Zheng et al., 2017), and NRT. On Books, PATG obtained an RMSE of 0.885 and MAE of 0.668, compared with 0.973/0.745 for MF, 0.958/0.731 for PMF, 0.926/0.705 for DeepCoNN, and 0.912/0.690 for NRT. Averaged over datasets, PATG reduced RMSE by 3.1% relative to NRT (0.896 versus 0.925) and by 8.2% relative to MF. The improvement was more pronounced for users with fewer than ten training interactions (RMSE 0.962 versus 1.018 for NRT, a 5.5% reduction), suggesting that the regularized latent persona space is helpful in sparse regimes.

Human Evaluation

Three trained annotators rated 300 randomly sampled tips per model on a five-point scale for fluency, informativeness, and persona consistency (whether the tip plausibly matched the style of the target user and the properties of the target item). Inter-annotator agreement was moderate to substantial (Fleiss’ κ = 0.64). PATG received mean scores of 4.31 for fluency, 3.94 for informativeness, and 3.82 for persona consistency, compared with 4.22, 3.51, and 3.17 for NRT, and 4.18, 3.38, and 3.02 for the pointer-generator. Differences in fluency were small and not significant (p = 0.08 against NRT), whereas gains in informativeness (+0.43) and persona consistency (+0.65) were significant (p < 0.01). In a pairwise preference test, annotators preferred PATG over NRT in 58.3% of cases, judged the outputs equivalent in 16.7%, and preferred NRT in 25.0%.

Diversity and Lexical Characteristics

We additionally measured generation diversity using distinct-1 and distinct-2 (Li et al., 2016). Seq2Seq produced distinct-1/2 of 0.021/0.098, and NRT 0.027/0.121, reflecting the generic outputs common in likelihood-trained decoders. PATG achieved 0.043/0.187, a 59% and 55% relative increase over NRT. Generated tips averaged 9.8 tokens, close to the reference mean of 10.4, whereas Seq2Seq outputs averaged 8.1 tokens. The proportion of generated tips containing at least one persona-memory word retrieved by the pointer mechanism was 61.4%, and the average pointer gate value was 0.27, showing that retrieval is used selectively rather than dominating generation. Among copied tokens, 72% were rated by annotators as appropriate to the target user or item.

Sensitivity and Robustness

We varied the persona embedding dimension from 16 to 256. ROUGE-2 on Books increased from 12.4 at 16 dimensions to 13.4 at 64 and plateaued thereafter (13.3 at 128; 13.2 at 256), with a slight decline attributable to overfitting. The memory size per entity had a similar effect: performance improved up to 50 slots (ROUGE-2 13.4), whereas 10 slots yielded 12.7 and 100 slots 13.3. The weight of the adversarial loss was best at 0.1; values of 0.01 and 1.0 produced ROUGE-2 of 13.0 and 12.8, respectively. For cold-start conditions, in which test users had no more than two historical tips, PATG retained a ROUGE-2 of 11.9, compared with 10.1 for NRT, a gap (+1.8) similar to the full-test gap, demonstrating that persona modeling remains useful but is less beneficial when history is extremely limited, as persona-consistency ratings for this subset fell to 3.41.

Qualitative Analysis

Case studies further illustrated these trends. For a user who habitually writes terse imperative tips, PATG produced “Must read for fans of mystery,” whereas NRT generated the more generic “Great book.” Visualization of persona embeddings with t-SNE showed that users cluster by stylistic attributes such as tip length, with a silhouette coefficient of 0.31 for PATG versus 0.12 for the non-adversarial variant, supporting the quantitative ablation findings.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of the findings.** This study asked whether tips, the short and often overlooked counterpart of full reviews, can be generated more faithfully when the model is aware of the persona of the writer and the characteristics of the item. The experiments support this. On the three evaluation corpora, the full framework improved ROUGE-1 by 1.4 to 2.9 points and BLEU-4 by 0.6 to 1.1 points over the strongest baseline, a neural rating regression model with abstractive tips (Li et al., 2017). It also outperformed an attribute-to-sequence decoder (Dong et al., 2017) by a wider margin. Rating prediction improved as well, with RMSE falling by roughly 3% to 5% relative to matrix factorization (Koren et al., 2009). The gains were not uniform, which is informative in itself. They were largest for users and items with at least ten historical documents (ROUGE-1 gain of about 3.2 points) and smallest for cold-start entities (about 0.8 points). This pattern is what a persona-based account predicts, since the latent representation can only summarize the evidence available to it. It also suggests that most of the benefit comes from real stylistic and topical regularities in the history, not from added capacity.

The ablations clarify which components matter. Removing the persona memory and pointer mechanism reduced ROUGE-2 by about 1.5 points, a larger drop than removing the adversarial regularizer (about 0.7 points). The pointer network (Vinyals et al., 2015) therefore seems to supply something the latent vectors cannot. Fixed-dimensional embeddings capture global style but are poor at reproducing rare, item-specific tokens such as dish names, product features, or idiosyncratic phrases. Copying from a persona-specific memory is a natural remedy, in line with the benefits of copy mechanisms in summarization (See et al., 2017). The latent embeddings, in turn, appear to govern the choice of register, length, and sentiment polarity. Human judges preferred the full model over the best baseline in about 58% of pairwise comparisons on specificity and about 54% on fluency. The larger margin on specificity matches the intended role of the memory.

The adversarial variational auto-encoder was adopted to avoid a well-known weakness of standard VAEs in text, namely posterior collapse, where a powerful recurrent decoder ignores the latent code (Bowman et al., 2016). Matching the aggregated posterior to the prior with a discriminator, as in adversarial auto-encoders (Makhzani et al., 2016), yielded persona embeddings that the decoder actually used. Replacing them with random draws from the prior degraded ROUGE-1 by about 2 points. Qualitative inspection of nearest neighbors in the latent space showed that users cluster by wording habits, such as terse and emphatic versus descriptive, and that items cluster by category and price tier. These observations are suggestive rather than conclusive, because we did not run a controlled probing study to establish which latent dimensions encode which attributes. The coupling with rating prediction was also useful. Using persona embeddings as latent factors for sentiment gave the decoder an explicit polarity signal, and generated tips agreed with the target rating's polarity in about 6% more cases than those from a model without the sentiment pathway. This agrees with earlier evidence that rating and text are best modeled jointly (Li et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2019).

**Limitations.** Several limitations should temper these conclusions. First, persona is inferred entirely from historical text, so the framework depends on data density. Performance for sparse users and new items is only marginally better than baselines, and the approach offers no principled treatment of cold start. Incorporating side information such as demographics, item metadata, or social links could help, though with privacy implications. Second, the training corpora come from English-language consumer platforms with distinct norms of tip writing. We cannot say whether the findings transfer to other languages, domains, or platforms where tips serve different purposes. Third, n-gram overlap metrics such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004) are weak proxies for the qualities we care about. A tip can be useful, stylistically faithful, and factually grounded while sharing few n-grams with a single reference. Our human evaluation involved a limited number of annotators and samples, and agreement was only moderate (Fleiss' kappa of about 0.41), so the preference percentages should be read as indicative. Fourth, the memory selects persona words by frequency- and salience-based heuristics, and this may overweight common terms while missing subtler stylistic cues. Fifth, the recurrent decoder is now surpassed in general fluency by large pretrained Transformers (Radford et al., 2019; Devlin et al., 2019). We did not test whether persona latent variables and memory retrieval would add value on top of such models. It is plausible that part of our improvement reflects the limited capacity of the baseline decoders. Finally, we did not examine factual faithfulness. A persona-conditioned generator may produce fluent tips that attribute features to an item that it does not have, a failure mode that matters if generated tips are shown to consumers.

**Implications.** Despite these caveats, the results have several implications. For research on text generation, they show that modeling who is writing and what is being written about benefits from both distributed and symbolic representations. Latent variables provide a smooth summary of style and sentiment, while a retrieval memory provides lexical precision. This echoes work on persona-conditioned dialogue (Li et al., 2016), but here persona is learned from behavior rather than supplied as explicit profile text, and it covers both sides of the user–item interaction. For recommender systems, the findings support generating short, personalized explanations or summaries. Tips are concise enough to display on mobile interfaces, and conditioning on user persona may make them more relevant to the reader, though we measured only agreement with the writer's own style. For platform designers, the framework could help users compose tips, offer draft suggestions in their own voice, or provide item summaries that reflect different audience preferences. These applications raise concerns about authenticity and manipulation. Automatically generated text that imitates user style could be misused to fabricate reviews, so deployment should include disclosure and detection safeguards.

Future work should pursue four directions: robust persona inference under sparse data, such as meta-learning or hierarchical priors across similar users; evaluation protocols that assess informativeness, faithfulness, and personalization more directly than n-gram overlap; integration of the persona modules with pretrained language models; and controllable generation, in which users or designers can adjust latent persona dimensions to steer tone, length, or aspect coverage.

**Conclusion.** We introduced a persona-aware framework for tips generation that combines adversarial variational persona embeddings, a persona word memory accessed through a pointer network, and a rating prediction component that supplies sentiment to a recurrent decoder. Across experiments, it improved generation quality and rating accuracy over competitive baselines, with the largest gains when historical data were plentiful and with complementary contributions from the latent embeddings and the memory. These results indicate that tips are a worthwhile target for personalized generation and that learning persona from users' and items' own histories is an effective way to capture their distinctive language. The limitations noted above, particularly cold start, evaluation validity, and faithfulness, define the most pressing steps toward practical use.

Introduction

Reading, interpreting, and communicating primary scientific literature is widely regarded as a core competency for undergraduate science majors. Vision and Change in Undergraduate Biology Education identifies communication and collaboration, along with the ability to interpret data, as central competencies that students should develop before graduation (American Association for the Advancement of Science [AAAS], 2011). Similarly, the Next Generation Science Standards and the Association of American Colleges and Universities' LEAP outcomes treat evidence-based argument and oral and written communication as essential learning goals (AAC&U, 2007; NGSS Lead States, 2013). Employers echo these priorities. Surveys of hiring managers consistently rank oral communication and the ability to explain complex information among the skills they most want and most often find lacking in new graduates (Hart Research Associates, 2015). For students entering research, health professions, or industry, the ability to read a research article and present its logic and findings to others is not an optional extra but a foundation for professional practice.

A substantial body of research supports bringing primary literature into the undergraduate classroom. Analyzing journal articles exposes students to the authentic practices of science, including how questions are framed, how methods are chosen, and how conclusions are justified (Hoskins, Stevens, & Nehm, 2007; Hoskins, Lopatto, & Stevens, 2011). Approaches such as CREATE (Consider, Read, Elucidate hypotheses, Analyze and interpret data, Think of the next Experiment) have been associated with gains in critical thinking, epistemological beliefs, and confidence in understanding research (Hoskins et al., 2007; Gottesman & Hoskins, 2013). Other structured strategies, including article annotation, concept mapping, and the Figure Facts approach, similarly scaffold students' reading and interpretation of data (Round & Campbell, 2013; Clark, Bennett, & Rice, 2019). These approaches primarily emphasize reading and analysis, yet reading is only half of the scientific literacy cycle. Scientists must also be able to transform what they have read into a coherent message for an audience.

Presentation of primary literature offers an especially rich opportunity for learning. Having students communicate science orally has been linked to deeper conceptual understanding, because organizing and explaining material to others requires learners to identify main ideas, make inferences, and recognize gaps in their own knowledge (Chi, 2009; Fisher & Frey, 2013). Calls to integrate communication across the science curriculum argue that speaking is not simply a means of assessing learning but a mode of learning in itself (Dunbar, Brooks, & Kubicka-Miller, 2006; Brownell, Price, & Steinman, 2013). Moreover, the ability to communicate science to different audiences is increasingly recognized as a professional responsibility, one that enables scientists to inform public discourse and policy (Brownell et al., 2013).

Despite this evidence, students receive surprisingly little explicit instruction in how to present scientific information. Many biology courses assign oral presentations of journal articles but treat the skills involved as something students will somehow acquire through repeated practice. Instructors rarely have formal training in communication pedagogy, and the constraints of content-heavy curricula leave little time for teaching presentation skills directly (Coil, Wenderoth, Cunningham, & Dirks, 2010; Brownell et al., 2013). As a result, student presentations commonly display recognizable weaknesses. Students may select too much detail, reproduce figures from the original article without adapting them for a live audience, and overload slides with text, a pattern consistent with cognitive load research showing that redundant or dense visual and verbal information impairs comprehension (Mayer, 2009; Sweller, Ayres, & Kalyuga, 2011). Delivery problems, such as reading from slides, limited eye contact, and speaking anxiety, compound these difficulties (Dwyer & Davidson, 2012). Critically, these difficulties are not merely cosmetic. When students cannot decide what to include or how to sequence an argument, instructors may be unable to determine whether the difficulty lies in communication or in understanding the science itself.

One underused resource for addressing this problem is the campus communication center. Communication centers, also called speaking centers or oral communication labs, are academic support units that provide training and feedback to students, faculty, and staff on oral presentation, group communication, and related skills (Yook & Atkins, 1999; Turner & Sheckels, 2011). Their staff are typically trained in communication pedagogy, audience analysis, and the use of visual aids, and many centers have developed research-informed approaches to coaching speakers (Dannels & Gaffney, 2009). Evidence from the communication-across-the-curriculum literature suggests that discipline-based instructors and communication specialists bring complementary expertise: instructors understand disciplinary content and norms, while communication specialists understand how audiences process messages and how speakers can be coached to improve (Dannels, 2002; Dannels & Martin, 2008). However, collaborations between biology faculty and communication centers are rarely described in the biology education literature, and when they are, they tend to consist of generic, one-size-fits-all workshops or referrals to center services rather than integrated, content-specific instruction. Generic presentation advice may fail to address the particular demands of presenting scientific data, such as deciding which figures to show, explaining experimental design to non-specialists, or conveying uncertainty and the limits of inference. Little guidance exists for biology instructors who wish to build the kind of partnership that would produce authentic, discipline-specific training.

This article addresses that gap by describing the development, implementation, and apparent outcomes of a partnership between a biosciences instructor and a communication center director. Together, we designed a workshop for undergraduates in a laboratory course who were required to present articles from the primary literature. The workshop targeted three skills: selecting content, designing slides, and delivering the presentation orally. It used authentic, course-specific materials and models drawn from student work rather than abstract examples. Our guiding question was whether and how a collaboratively designed, content-based workshop could improve the quality of student presentations of primary literature, including the extent to which presentations reflected understanding of the underlying science.

We make three contributions. First, we provide a replicable description of a workshop that integrates disciplinary and communication expertise, offering a concrete model for instructors who lack formal communication training. Second, we report observations of student performance before and after the workshop was introduced, suggesting that explicit instruction in presentation skills can support, rather than compete with, conceptual learning. Third, we reflect on the processes that made the partnership productive, with the aim of encouraging other biology educators to seek out campus communication resources and build similar collaborations to teach scientific communication more effectively.

Methods

**Course context and participants**

The study took place in a sophomore- and junior-level Molecular Cell Biology Laboratory at a mid-sized public university in the United States. The course is required for biology majors and enrolls about 50 students per year in sections of 24 or fewer. In addition to a semester-long investigative project, students complete a primary-literature module in which each student gives an individual 10-minute slide presentation (plus 3 minutes of questions) on a research article related to their project. Articles were drawn from a curated list of 20 papers and assigned randomly, so that each student presented an article they had not previously encountered. The assignment, article list, grading weight (10% of the course grade), and timeline were identical across the two cohorts compared here.

We used a quasi-experimental, two-cohort design. The comparison cohort (Fall 2017; n = 46) completed the presentation module with the instructor's customary guidance, which consisted of a written assignment description, a rubric, and a brief in-class overview of presentation expectations. The intervention cohort (Fall 2018; n = 49) completed the same module after participating in the workshop described below. Random assignment was not feasible because the course is offered once per year. To assess baseline comparability, we collected class standing and cumulative GPA from institutional records and compared these between cohorts. The study was classified as exempt by the institutional review board (protocol #-----), and students consented to the use of their recorded presentations and records for research. Presentations from non-consenting students (two in 2017, one in 2018) were excluded from analysis.

**Partnership and workshop design**

The workshop was co-designed over approximately three months by the course instructor (a biosciences faculty member) and the director of the campus communication center, who has a background in speech communication and communication-across-the-curriculum pedagogy (Dannels 2001). Planning meetings followed a backward-design approach (Wiggins and McTighe 2005). We first articulated the performance we wanted to see, then identified common weaknesses in earlier presentations (for example, slides reproducing entire figures, listing methods without linking them to questions, and reading from notes), and then built activities to address each. The instructor contributed disciplinary expertise on what constitutes the central question, evidence, and conclusion of a primary article, consistent with data-centered approaches to reading the literature (Round and Campbell 2013; Hoskins et al. 2007). The center director contributed expertise in audience analysis, visual design, and delivery, drawing on principles of multimedia learning (Mayer 2009) and scientific presentation practice (Alley 2013).

The resulting workshop was a single 75-minute session held in the fourth week of the term, four weeks before presentations. It was co-facilitated by both partners and had three modules. In *content selection*, students identified the research question, hypothesis, key figures, and take-home message of a short sample article, and practiced "figure triage": deciding which two or three figures and which methods details a specific audience of peers needed to follow the argument. In *slide design*, students critiqued and redesigned slides using assertion–evidence principles (one claim per slide, a descriptive sentence headline, minimal text, simplified and annotated figures). In *oral delivery*, students rehearsed 90-second segments in triads, using a structured observation sheet to give feedback on eye contact, pacing, vocal variety, and the use of the slide to guide the audience through a figure.

All examples and activities used authentic content-based materials. Student models were de-identified, consented presentations from earlier course offerings, selected to represent weaker, adequate, and strong performance on each dimension and annotated with the rubric language. After the workshop, students could book optional 30-minute rehearsal consultations at the communication center, and the number who did so was recorded.

**Outcome measures**

Presentations were video recorded, and slide files were archived. Performance was assessed with an analytic rubric adapted from the instructor's existing rubric and the communication center's presentation criteria, following guidance on rubric development by Stevens and Levi (2013). The rubric contained 12 items grouped into four dimensions: (1) *scientific understanding* (accuracy of explanation of the question, methods rationale, and interpretation of data; ability to answer questions), (2) *content selection and organization* (focus on a clear narrative, appropriate depth), (3) *slide design* (text economy, figure clarity, visual consistency), and (4) *oral delivery* (eye contact, vocal delivery, independence from notes, pacing within the time limit). Each item was scored on a four-level scale (1 = beginning, 2 = developing, 3 = proficient, 4 = exemplary), and dimension scores were the mean of the constituent items. We interpreted "apparent understanding" as what a presenter demonstrated in explanation and responses, not as a direct measure of learning.

Two raters (the course instructor and a trained graduate teaching assistant who did not teach the course in either year) scored all presentations. Presentations from the two cohorts were randomized, stripped of semester identifiers where possible, and scored in a single session after a 2-hour calibration using five practice presentations that were not part of the data set. Because the instructor could not be fully blind to workshop content, rater drift was monitored by having each rater rescore 10 randomly selected presentations two weeks later. Dimension scores used in analysis were the mean of the two raters.

**Reliability**

Inter-rater agreement on individual items was quantified with quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa (Cohen 1968),

κ_w = 1 − (Σ w_ij o_ij) / (Σ w_ij e_ij), with w_ij = (i − j)² / (k − 1)²,

where o_ij and e_ij are the observed and chance-expected proportions of ratings in cells *i* and *j*, and *k* = 4 is the number of categories. Agreement on dimension scores was assessed using a two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement, average-measures intraclass correlation coefficient, ICC(2,k) (Shrout and Fleiss 1979). We considered κ_w and ICC values above 0.70 acceptable, and interpreted values following Landis and Koch (1977).

**Statistical analysis**

Because rubric scores are ordinal and distributions were bounded and skewed, we used nonparametric tests. Cohort differences in each of the four dimension scores, and in the total score, were tested with two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests. The effect size was reported as

r = Z / √N,

where Z is the standardized test statistic and N is the total number of presentations, with r of about 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 interpreted as small, medium, and large (Cohen 1988). We also report Cliff's delta, δ = [P(X₂ > X₁) − P(X₂ < X₁)], with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals based on 5,000 resamples. Because four dimensions were tested, we controlled the familywise error rate with the Holm–Bonferroni procedure (Holm 1979) and report adjusted *p* values; the total score was treated as a secondary descriptive comparison.

To examine whether cohort differences could be explained by student characteristics, we fit a proportional-odds ordinal regression for each dimension, with the rounded mean score as the outcome and cohort, cumulative GPA, and class standing as predictors:

logit P(Y ≤ j) = α_j − (β₁·Cohort + β₂·GPA + β₃·Standing), j = 1, 2, 3.

The proportional-odds assumption was examined with a Brant test. We report odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for the cohort term. Baseline GPA and standing were compared using a Mann–Whitney U test and a chi-square test, respectively. Finally, we compared the proportion of presentations that fell within the 10-minute time limit between cohorts using Fisher's exact test, and descriptively summarized use of optional consultations. All analyses were performed in R (version 4.2) with the *irr*, *effsize*, and *MASS* packages, and α = 0.05 was used throughout.

# Results

## Study populations and scoring reliability

Presentation data came from two consecutive offerings of the upper-level laboratory course. In the baseline offering (before the workshop), 46 students gave 15-minute presentations of a primary research article. In the offering that included the workshop, 51 students gave the same assignment. The two cohorts had similar demographics, majors, and prior grade point averages (mean GPA 3.21 vs. 3.26; Welch's *t*-test, *p* = 0.62). Instructors, article pool, and assignment instructions were unchanged between offerings.

Recorded presentations were scored by two raters blind to cohort. The raters were the course instructor and a trained graduate teaching assistant, and they used a four-dimension rubric. The dimensions were content selection, slide design, oral delivery, and conceptual understanding, each scored 0–4, for a maximum total of 16. Interrater agreement was good. The intraclass correlation for total score was ICC(2,k) = 0.84 (95% CI 0.77–0.89), and weighted Cohen's κ for individual dimensions ranged from 0.71 (oral delivery) to 0.82 (slide design), which corresponds to "substantial" to "almost perfect" agreement (Landis & Koch, 1977; Hallgren, 2012). Final scores are the mean of the two raters.

## Overall rubric performance

Total presentation scores rose substantially after the workshop was introduced. The mean total score was 9.6 (SD = 2.4) in the baseline cohort and 12.6 (SD = 1.9) in the workshop cohort (Mann–Whitney *U* = 391, *p* < 0.001). Effect size was calculated as Cohen's *d* using the pooled standard deviation:

$$d = \frac{\bar{X}_{\text{post}} - \bar{X}_{\text{pre}}}{s_{p}}, \qquad s_{p} = \sqrt{\frac{(n_{1}-1)s_{1}^{2} + (n_{2}-1)s_{2}^{2}}{n_{1}+n_{2}-2}}$$

With *s*<sub>p</sub> = 2.15, the overall effect was *d* = 1.40, a large effect by conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988). The proportion of presentations scoring at least 12 of 16 (75%) increased from 15% (7/46) to 69% (35/51). The proportion scoring 8 or lower fell from 33% (15/46) to 4% (2/51).

## Performance by rubric dimension

Gains were not uniform across dimensions (Table 1). Because four comparisons were made, *p*-values were adjusted with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). All four comparisons remained significant after adjustment.

**Table 1.** Mean (SD) rubric scores by dimension (0–4 scale).

| Dimension | Baseline (*n* = 46) | Workshop (*n* = 51) | Cohen's *d* | Adjusted *p* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Content selection | 2.0 (0.7) | 3.1 (0.6) | 1.69 | < 0.001 |
| Slide design | 2.4 (0.7) | 3.3 (0.6) | 1.38 | < 0.001 |
| Oral delivery | 2.8 (0.6) | 3.1 (0.6) | 0.50 | 0.02 |
| Conceptual understanding | 2.4 (0.8) | 3.1 (0.7) | 0.93 | < 0.001 |
| **Total (0–16)** | **9.6 (2.4)** | **12.6 (1.9)** | **1.40** | **< 0.001** |

The largest improvements were in content selection and slide design, the two skills most directly targeted by the workshop's authentic, content-based exercises. Oral delivery showed the smallest gain, a moderate effect (*d* = 0.50). Baseline delivery scores were already the highest of the four dimensions, which suggests a ceiling effect. Conceptual understanding, as inferred from raters' judgments of whether students accurately explained the rationale, methods, and interpretation of the featured experiments, also improved substantially (*d* = 0.93). The rubric measures apparent understanding from the presentation rather than independent mastery, so this result is interpreted cautiously.

## Objective features of slides and delivery

Several quantifiable features of the presentations changed in ways consistent with the rubric results (Table 2). Slide decks in the baseline cohort contained a mean of 9.8 figures or tables (SD = 3.4) drawn from the source article, compared with 5.6 (SD = 1.7) in the workshop cohort (*p* < 0.001). Students therefore selected fewer data displays and presumably explained them in more depth. Mean text density fell from 62 words per slide (SD = 21) to 28 (SD = 11; *p* < 0.001). The percentage of figures with an explicit takeaway title (a full-sentence claim rather than a topic label) rose from 11% to 74%. Of the 46 baseline presentations, 28 (61%) exceeded the 15-minute limit, compared with 9 of 51 (18%) in the workshop cohort, χ²(1, *N* = 97) = 19.2, *p* < 0.001, φ = 0.44.

|---|---|---|---|
| Figures/tables per presentation, mean (SD) | 9.8 (3.4) | 5.6 (1.7) | < 0.001 |
| Words per slide, mean (SD) | 62 (21) | 28 (11) | < 0.001 |
| Figures with sentence-style takeaway title (%) | 11 | 74 | < 0.001 |
| Presentations exceeding time limit (%) | 61 | 18 | < 0.001 |

## Relative improvement

To express gains relative to the maximum possible improvement, we calculated a normalized difference between cohort means (cf. Hake, 1998):

$$g = \frac{\bar{X}_{\text{post}} - \bar{X}_{\text{pre}}}{X_{\max} - \bar{X}_{\text{pre}}}$$

For total score, *g* = (12.6 − 9.6)/(16 − 9.6) = 0.47. Dimension-level values were 0.55 for content selection, 0.56 for slide design, 0.25 for oral delivery, and 0.44 for conceptual understanding. Because these values compare different cohorts rather than the same students over time, they describe between-cohort differences, not individual learning gains.

## Student perceptions of the workshop

Of the 51 students in the workshop cohort, 49 (96%) completed an anonymous end-of-term survey. On a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree), students agreed that the workshop helped them decide which figures to include (mean = 4.5, SD = 0.7; 90% agreed or strongly agreed). Agreement was similar for designing clearer slides (mean = 4.4, SD = 0.8; 86%) and for explaining data to a non-expert audience (mean = 4.1, SD = 0.9; 78%). Fewer students reported increased confidence in delivery (mean = 3.7, SD = 1.0; 63%), which parallels the smaller observed gain in oral delivery scores. Overall, 94% (46/49) said they would recommend retaining the workshop in future offerings.

Open-ended comments (*n* = 41 students providing responses) were coded inductively by two researchers using thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Three themes accounted for most comments. The first was the value of working with article-specific models (22 comments, 54%). Students described seeing "before and after" versions of slides built from a familiar paper as the most useful activity. The second was a shift in perspective from reporting everything to building an argument (17 comments, 41%). The third was the usefulness of practicing with feedback from the communication center director and peers (14 comments, 34%). Four students (10%) wished for additional time for delivery practice.

## Instructor observations

The course instructor also noted qualitative changes in question-and-answer sessions. In the baseline cohort, instructors recorded that audience questions most often asked presenters to clarify what a figure showed. In the workshop cohort, questions more often concerned experimental design and alternative interpretations. We did not formally code these observations, so they are reported only as supporting context. Instructor grading time for the presentation component did not change noticeably, and the workshop required a single 75-minute session plus one 30-minute follow-up consultation per student group.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study describes a partnership between a biosciences instructor and a campus communication center director that produced a workshop on presenting primary literature in an undergraduate laboratory course. After the workshop was introduced, student presentations were noticeably stronger in content selection, slide design, and delivery, and students appeared to explain the underlying science more accurately. These observations are consistent with calls to integrate primary literature and science communication into undergraduate biology (American Association for the Advancement of Science, 2011; Hoskins et al., 2007; Kozeracki et al., 2006). They also suggest that the barrier to doing so may lie less in instructor willingness than in the availability of expertise and structured support.

Interpreting the improvement

Several mechanisms plausibly contributed to the gains, and the design of the workshop does not allow them to be fully separated. First, the workshop gave students explicit criteria for what makes a scientific presentation effective. Without such criteria, novices tend to reproduce the structure of the paper, giving each section equal weight and including figures they do not fully understand (Hoskins et al., 2007; Round & Campbell, 2013). Teaching content selection forced students to decide which question, result, and interpretation the audience most needed. Making that decision requires deeper processing of the article than summarizing it does. The apparent improvement in conceptual understanding may therefore be a byproduct of the communication training rather than a separate effect. This interpretation fits with work showing that explaining and teaching material to others promotes learning (Fiorella & Mayer, 2013) and that writing and speaking in a discipline serve as tools for thinking as well as for reporting (Reynolds et al., 2012).

Second, the use of authentic, content-based materials and student models probably mattered. Worked examples and exemplars help novices form accurate mental representations of quality, and they reduce the cognitive load of figuring out expectations while also mastering difficult content (Sadler, 1989; Sweller et al., 1998). Because the examples came from the same disciplinary context as the assignment, students could see how general principles, such as limiting text, aligning visuals with a single message, and pacing explanations of data, applied to figures they would soon be presenting. Generic presentation training often fails to transfer for this reason (Barnett & Ceci, 2002).

Third, the communication center director contributed expertise in design and delivery that most biology instructors have not been trained to teach. Principles from cognitive psychology and multimedia learning, including the benefits of reducing extraneous text and coordinating narration with visuals (Mayer, 2009), are well established in communication scholarship but seldom appear in disciplinary training. The instructor, in turn, ensured that the advice respected the conventions of scientific argumentation, such as attention to controls, sample sizes, and the limits of inference. Neither partner alone could have produced the same workshop, which supports the argument that effective science communication instruction is best delivered through collaboration across expertise (Dannels, 2001; Mercer-Mapstone & Kuchel, 2017).

Limitations

Several limitations temper these conclusions. The comparison relied on cohorts before and after the workshop, so differences in student preparation, instructor experience, grading emphasis, or the particular articles assigned could have contributed to the observed improvement. Presentations were evaluated by course staff who knew about the intervention, which creates the potential for expectancy bias. Our assessment of conceptual understanding was inferred from how accurately students explained methods and results during their presentations and in follow-up questions, rather than from an independent concept inventory or a pre/post test of primary-literature comprehension. Thus we use the phrase "apparent understanding" deliberately. Presenting well can mask misunderstanding, and, conversely, a halting presentation can hide real comprehension (Dunlosky et al., 2013). Future work should pair presentation rubrics with validated measures such as the Critical Thinking Assessment Test or instruments of scientific reasoning, and should use blind or multiple raters with reported inter-rater reliability.

The study was also conducted in a single course at one institution, with a modest number of students. The extent to which the findings generalize to larger enrollments, other subdisciplines, or institutions lacking a well-resourced communication center is uncertain. We also did not follow students into later courses, so we cannot say whether the skills persisted or transferred to other settings, such as research group meetings, conference posters, or professional writing. Finally, we did not systematically collect student perceptions of the workshop, such as changes in communication apprehension or self-efficacy, which are important outcomes in their own right and often predict persistence in the sciences (Chemers et al., 2011).

Implications for practice

Despite these limitations, the experience offers practical lessons for biology educators. First, instructors should look beyond their departments for expertise. Many campuses have communication centers, writing centers, or teaching and learning units whose staff are eager to work with disciplinary faculty but are rarely approached by STEM instructors. The partnership here began with a modest request and grew into a shared design effort. Such collaborations require time for each partner to learn the other's vocabulary and goals, so early conversations about learning outcomes and assessment criteria are essential.

Second, the workshop was built around the assignment itself rather than around abstract advice. Aligning instruction with a graded task that students care about, and using materials drawn from the course, increases relevance and likelihood of uptake. Third, the use of student models, with permission and appropriately anonymized, allowed students to critique realistic examples and calibrate their own work. Fourth, the workshop is a relatively low-cost intervention, a single session supplemented by a rubric, that can be adapted to other courses. Instructors with limited class time can use it in place of, rather than in addition to, content delivery, because the preparation of the presentations itself requires students to engage with the primary literature.

Finally, institutional recognition matters. Sustaining partnerships like this one depends on communication centers having adequate staffing and on departments valuing communication instruction as part of the curriculum rather than as an optional extra. Embedding communication outcomes in program-level learning goals would encourage the repeated, scaffolded practice that research suggests is necessary for durable skill development (Ambrose et al., 2010; Dannels, 2001).

Conclusion

Teaching students to present primary literature is a worthwhile goal that biology faculty are seldom equipped to pursue alone. By combining disciplinary knowledge with communication expertise, this collaboration produced a workshop that was associated with clearer, better-organized presentations and more convincing evidence of conceptual understanding. Although more rigorous evaluation is needed, the approach is feasible, adaptable, and grounded in established principles of learning and communication. We encourage biology educators to seek out campus communication professionals as partners, to share and test their designs across contexts, and to assess both communication and conceptual outcomes so that the field can build a stronger evidence base for teaching science communication.

# 1. Introduction

The Web of Data has grown into a large, decentralised collection of knowledge graphs published under the Resource Description Framework (RDF). Datasets such as DBpedia, Wikidata, GeoNames, and a growing number of domain-specific life-science, government, and cultural-heritage sources expose billions of statements through SPARQL endpoints, dumps, and dereferenceable IRIs (Bizer et al., 2009; Schmachtenberg et al., 2014). The Linked Data principles promised that publishing structured data with shared identifiers and explicit links would let applications traverse and combine sources as easily as documents are navigated on the Web (Heath & Bizer, 2011). In practice, however, combining data from independent RDF publishers remains difficult, and much of the value of the Web of Data stays unrealised.

A first obstacle is semantic heterogeneity. Datasets are created by different communities for different purposes, under different technical constraints. There is no "one model fits all": each context imposes its own requirements, and modellers make different decisions about granularity, class and property design, the reuse of existing vocabularies, and the representation of the same real-world entity as an IRI, a literal, or a structured node. As a result, the same notion, such as a country, a gene, a person, or a postal code, is represented in incompatible ways across datasets (Euzenat & Shvaiko, 2013). Ontology alignment, schema mapping, and entity-resolution techniques address parts of this problem, but they are costly to apply across many sources and often assume that the datasets to be reconciled are already known and understood.

A second obstacle remains even if semantic heterogeneity is assumed to be solved or mitigated. Querying and accessing data spread across distributed RDF datasets is not straightforward, because it is hard to determine how the datasets can be related to one another. Federated query processing engines such as FedX (Schwarte et al., 2011) and SPLENDID (Görlitz & Staab, 2011) can execute a query across several endpoints, but the query author must still know which datasets contain relevant data and which resources or values in one dataset correspond to those in another. Explicit `owl:sameAs` links are one means of connecting datasets, but they cover only a small fraction of possible connections, are unevenly distributed, and are frequently misused or semantically inconsistent (Halpin et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2010). Many useful relations are never materialised as triples. Two datasets may, for example, both contain a literal such as an ISO country code, a DOI, a taxonomic name, or a geographic coordinate, so that a join over this value would be meaningful, yet nothing in either dataset or its metadata says so. Consumers therefore have to inspect schemas, sample data, and read documentation manually. This process is complex, fastidious, and difficult to reproduce or automate.

Dataset-level metadata is the natural place to record such knowledge. The Vocabulary of Interlinked Datasets (VoID) (Alexander et al., 2009) is the W3C-recognised vocabulary for describing RDF datasets and their relationships. It provides terms for dataset statistics, vocabularies used, access methods, partitions by class and property, and linksets, which are collections of RDF links between two datasets. Related efforts, including DCAT (Albertoni et al., 2024), the Data Cube and PROV vocabularies, SPARQL Service Description, and the Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) and ShEx for structural description, cover complementary aspects such as catalogues, provenance, endpoint capabilities, and constraints. Nevertheless, the VoID linkset concept has a significant limitation. A `void:Linkset` describes triples that actually exist, whose subject is in one dataset and whose object is in another. It cannot describe a relationship that holds only implicitly, because two resources, whether IRIs or literals, share a value or satisfy some commonality, and no triple connects them. Nor does VoID provide guidance on how to model such connections consistently, so that tools and humans can discover and exploit them.

This gap motivates the research question that guides our work: *How can the implicit, non-materialised relationships between independent RDF datasets be described in a standard, machine-readable, and reusable way, so that they improve interoperability and make cross-dataset querying easier?* We break this into three sub-questions. (i) What vocabulary extensions are needed to express connections between literals and IRIs drawn from different datasets? (ii) Which data model patterns allow these connections to be described uniformly across heterogeneous datasets? (iii) What benefits does this description give to data consumers and to query-federation scenarios?

To answer these questions, we present VoIDext, an extension of VoID. Our central idea is the *virtual link*: a connection between resources, namely literals and IRIs, from different RDF datasets that have some commonality, such as an identical value, a shared identifier scheme, or a mappable representation. It is "virtual" because it is not asserted as an RDF triple in either dataset but is described at the metadata level, so the datasets stay untouched and independent. A collection of such links between two datasets is described as a *Virtual Link Set*, which is analogous to a VoID linkset but covers connections that are not materialised.

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

1. **A vocabulary extension.** We introduce VoIDext, which adds the Virtual Link Set concept and associated properties to VoID. These let publishers declare which elements of two datasets can be related, and on what basis.
2. **Data model patterns.** We define a set of patterns for describing virtual links in different situations, including literal-to-literal, IRI-to-literal, and IRI-to-IRI connections, so that descriptions are consistent and can be generated and interpreted automatically.
3. **An analysis of benefits.** We discuss how virtual links improve interoperability between heterogeneous, independent datasets. They support dataset discovery, make query formulation easier, and reduce the effort of understanding how datasets relate. They also do not require modifying or republishing the source data.
4. **Application to real datasets.** We exemplify and apply the approach to several widely used RDF datasets, showing that the vocabulary and patterns can express useful cross-dataset relationships in practice.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on dataset description, linking, and federated querying. Section 3 presents the VoIDext vocabulary and patterns. Section 4 applies them to real datasets, and Section 5 discusses benefits and limitations before concluding.

Methods

Overview and Design Rationale

We followed a design-science approach in which the artifact is a lightweight extension of the Vocabulary of Interlinked Datasets (VoID) (Alexander et al., 2011). The work had four stages: (1) requirements elicitation from published linked data practices and from the limits of existing dataset-description vocabularies; (2) vocabulary design, including formal definitions of the Virtual Link Set concept and associated data model patterns; (3) instantiation on a set of widely used RDF datasets; and (4) evaluation through competency questions and federated query experiments. We reused existing vocabularies wherever possible, following established vocabulary-engineering guidance (Poveda-Villalón et al., 2014; Suárez-Figueroa et al., 2012), and restricted new terms to what VoID, DCAT (Albertoni et al., 2024), and SPARQL Service Description (Williams, 2013) could not express.

Requirements Elicitation

Requirements were gathered by analyzing the VoID specification, in particular void:Linkset, which assumes that links are explicit RDF triples (e.g., owl:sameAs or rdfs:seeAlso) between resources in two datasets. We then reviewed cases where datasets are related without such triples: two datasets that share a literal value (an ISO country code, a gene symbol, a postal code, a label), or that share an IRI pattern without materialized links. These were identified through the literature on link discovery and data integration (Ngomo & Auer, 2011; Nentwig et al., 2017) and through inspection of the dataset catalogue of the Linked Open Data cloud (McCrae et al., 2018). From this analysis we derived competency questions (Grüninger & Fox, 1995) of the form "Which datasets can be joined with dataset A, through which properties or classes, and on which kind of values?" and "What is the nature of the commonality between two resources, and how can it be queried?" These questions guided vocabulary scope and later evaluation.

Definition of Virtual Links

We define a virtual link as a non-materialized connection between a resource (IRI or literal) in dataset D₁ and a resource in dataset D₂ that share a commonality, expressed by a comparison function. Formally, given a source set S₁ of terms selected from D₁ by a path or class expression, a target set S₂ from D₂, and a relation r (e.g., strict equality, case-insensitive string equality, or equality after a transformation such as IRI-to-local-name extraction), a virtual link exists for every pair (a, b) ∈ S₁ × S₂ for which r(a, b) holds. Virtual links are not asserted as triples in either dataset. Instead, they are described at the metadata level, and can be realized at query time through SPARQL FILTER expressions or joins over shared values. This distinguishes them from materialized links, which are typically produced by link discovery tools such as Silk (Volz et al., 2009) or LIMES (Ngomo & Auer, 2011).

Vocabulary Design Procedure

The design followed a simplified NeOn/Ontology 101 workflow (Noy & McGuinness, 2001; Suárez-Figueroa et al., 2012): specification, conceptualization, formalization in OWL 2 and RDFS, and implementation in Turtle. The new class void-ext:VirtualLinkSet is defined as a subclass of void:Linkset so that existing VoID consumers can still interpret it. Additional properties describe the subject and object dataset (reusing void:subjectsTarget and void:objectsTarget), the classes or properties from which the linked values are drawn, the commonality type, and optional transformation expressions. Each term was given labels, definitions, and domain/range axioms kept deliberately weak to avoid unintended inferences. The ontology was checked for consistency with the HermiT reasoner and for pitfalls with OOPS! (Poveda-Villalón et al., 2014). It was published with dereferenceable IRIs and content negotiation, following the linked data principles (Heath & Bizer, 2011).

Data Model Patterns

To guide dataset publishers, we defined reusable data model patterns, in the sense of ontology design patterns (Gangemi & Presutti, 2009). Each pattern is documented with intent, competency questions, structure, and an example. The patterns cover: (a) literal-to-literal virtual links, (b) IRI-to-IRI links through a shared identifier scheme, (c) literal-to-IRI links where a literal encodes an identifier of a resource in the other dataset, and (d) links mediated through a third dataset or a shared vocabulary. Patterns were derived inductively from the cases found during requirements elicitation until no new structural variants appeared.

Datasets

We applied the approach to several RDF datasets widely used on the Web: DBpedia (Lehmann et al., 2015), Wikidata (Vrandečić & Krötzsch, 2014), GeoNames, and, in the life sciences, UniProt (The UniProt Consortium, 2023) and Bio2RDF resources (Callahan et al., 2013). These were chosen because they cover different knowledge domains, use different modelling styles, are available through public SPARQL endpoints, and are known to be only partially interlinked. For each dataset we recorded the endpoint, the named graphs, the relevant classes and properties, and the existing VoID description where available. Exploratory SPARQL queries (class and property enumeration with counts, and sampling of literal values) were used to characterize the candidate values for virtual links. Queries were executed with result limits and timeouts so as to respect endpoint usage policies, and query dates were recorded because the datasets change over time.

Procedure for Creating Virtual Link Set Descriptions

For each dataset pair, we (1) identified candidate properties with value types likely to be shared (codes, names, identifiers); (2) estimated overlap by counting distinct values in each dataset and computing the size of their intersection through SPARQL queries; (3) selected the appropriate pattern and comparison relation; (4) authored the VirtualLinkSet description in Turtle; and (5) validated it with SHACL shapes (Knublauch & Kontokostas, 2017) that check required properties and dataset references.

Evaluation and Analysis

Evaluation had three components. First, the competency questions were translated into SPARQL queries over the generated metadata, and we checked whether each could be answered. Second, for each virtual link set we executed a federated SPARQL query (using the SERVICE keyword; Buil-Aranda et al., 2013) that joins the two datasets using only the information in the description, and recorded the number of joined results. Third, we compared the reachable joins with those available through VoID alone, as the number of dataset pairs connectable without manual inspection.

The analysis is descriptive. We report counts of distinct values, intersection sizes, and an overlap ratio, defined as |S₁ ∩ S₂| / min(|S₁|, |S₂|), together with query success and execution time. Because endpoint load and caching affect timing, each query was run three times and the median was reported. No inferential statistics were applied, since the evaluation aims to demonstrate feasibility and expressiveness rather than to test population-level hypotheses.

Results

**Experimental setup and datasets.** We applied VoIDext to seven publicly available RDF datasets that are widely used and differ in domain and modelling style: DBpedia (2022-09 release), Wikidata (truthy dump, 2023-03), GeoNames, LinkedGeoData, DrugBank, UniProt (reviewed Swiss-Prot subset) and the Bio2RDF release of PubMed. Together they contain about 9.4 billion triples. Following the original VoID specification (Alexander et al., 2011), we first generated the standard dataset descriptions, then extended them with virtual link sets (`voidext:VirtualLinkSet`) and the accompanying data model patterns. Each dataset pair has up to 21 possible combinations, and we examined all of them. Candidate virtual links were defined over IRIs and literals (e.g., labels, ISO country codes, InChIKeys, UniProt accessions, geographic names). We measured the overlap of each candidate with Jaccard and containment coefficients over distinct values, computed on SPARQL endpoints or local dumps.

**Virtual links discovered.** From the 21 dataset pairs we identified 64 candidate virtual links. After manual validation by two annotators (Cohen's κ = 0.81), 52 (81.3%) were retained as semantically valid, i.e. the connected resources denoted the same entity or a directly corresponding one. The remaining 12 were rejected as coincidental string matches, such as homonymous place names or short gene symbols shared across organisms. Of the 52 valid links, 31 (59.6%) connected literal values to literal values, 14 (26.9%) connected literals to IRIs, and 7 (13.5%) connected IRIs to IRIs through a shared key that was not expressed as an explicit `owl:sameAs` statement. Only 9 of the 21 dataset pairs (42.9%) were already connected by explicit RDF links in the datasets themselves, in line with earlier observations that the Linked Data cloud is sparsely interlinked (Schmachtenberg et al., 2014; Hogan et al., 2012). Virtual links raised the number of connected pairs to 19 of 21 (90.5%).

**Quality of the overlap.** Containment varied widely by link type. For the ISO 3166 country-code link between GeoNames and DBpedia, the Jaccard coefficient was 0.87 (249 shared codes). For the DrugBank–UniProt link through UniProt accessions, containment of DrugBank targets in UniProt was 0.94 (4,102 of 4,364 distinct accessions). By contrast, the label-based link between DBpedia and LinkedGeoData reached only 0.31 Jaccard overall, though it rose to 0.58 after language-tag normalisation and case folding. Across all valid links the median Jaccard coefficient was 0.42 (IQR 0.19–0.73). Recording these coefficients in the `void:` statistics of each virtual link set (shared distinct values, source and target coverage) allowed us to rank links automatically. Ranking by containment placed 40 of the 52 valid links (76.9%) above all 12 rejected candidates in the top-quartile band, so the descriptor offers a usable first filter for deciding which links merit manual inspection.

**Effect on query formulation.** To evaluate whether the descriptions help data consumers, we defined 30 cross-dataset information needs, such as "drugs targeting proteins annotated with a given GO term, together with the countries where the associated research was published". Each need was expressed as a federated SPARQL 1.1 query in two conditions. In the baseline condition, six participants (graduate students and Semantic Web practitioners) had access only to the standard VoID descriptions and the public endpoints. In the VoIDext condition, they also had the virtual link sets and patterns. Participants produced a correct query (one returning the gold-standard answer set) for 128 of 180 tasks (71.1%) in the baseline condition and 163 of 180 (90.6%) with VoIDext (McNemar χ² = 21.4, p < 0.001). The median time to a correct query fell from 14.5 to 6.2 minutes (a 57% reduction; Wilcoxon signed-rank, p < 0.001). Failures in the baseline condition were mostly caused by missing join keys (58%) and by incorrect assumptions about literal formats (27%). With VoIDext, only 9 of the 17 failures involved a join path, and the rest were SPARQL syntax errors unrelated to the datasets' interoperability.

**Effect on federated execution.** We also tested whether virtual link sets can support source selection in federated engines. For the 30 queries, we compared a FedX-style engine (Schwarte et al., 2011) using ASK-based source selection with the same engine configured to prune sources using VoIDext statistics. Pruning reduced the mean number of remote requests per query from 214 to 97 (−54.7%) and the median end-to-end latency from 18.3 s to 9.8 s (−46.4%). Result sets were identical for 28 of the 30 queries. For the remaining two, both involving the low-containment label link (Jaccard 0.31), pruning discarded a source that held a small number of relevant bindings, reducing recall to 0.91 and 0.84. This points to a trade-off: when containment is below roughly 0.4, statistics-based pruning should be combined with probing queries. Queries that depended only on links with containment ≥ 0.7 (19 queries) showed no recall loss.

**Cost of description.** The additional metadata is small. The 52 virtual link sets and 17 instantiated patterns amounted to 3,846 triples, compared with 1,912 triples for the standard VoID descriptions of the seven datasets, an overhead of about 2×, which is negligible next to the 9.4 billion triples described. Computing the overlap statistics took 6.8 hours in total on a single server with 64 GB of RAM, dominated by the Wikidata and DBpedia comparisons (4.1 hours). Pairs involving only the smaller datasets took under 10 minutes. Once stored, the descriptions can be reused without recomputation until the underlying datasets are updated.

**Pattern coverage.** The data model patterns captured the structure of all 52 valid links.
