If a disfluency detector trained once on a general corpus can be placed in front of an interpretation component trained only on clean utterances, developers need not collect or synthesise disfluent data for each new domain. This is the setting motivated by the bAbI+ methodology (Eshghi et al., 2017), where a system learns from fluent dialogues yet must cope with spontaneous variation at test time. Because the model is word-by-word incremental, it can be attached to an incremental semantic parser, such as one based on Dynamic Syntax (Purver et al., 2011; Eshghi et al., 2013), so that tentative interpretations can be retracted when a repair is recognised. It can also operate as a filter that "cleans" the evolving utterance for any downstream consumer. Incrementality is not just a convenience. Natural conversation involves overlapping speech, early responses and collaborative completions (Howes & Eshghi, 2017), which batch-mode, utterance-final processing cannot support.

**Limitations.** Several caveats apply. First, bAbI+ is synthetic. Its disfluencies are generated by templates and inserted at controlled points, so they are cleaner and more predictable than the variation in real speech, and success there may overestimate real-world transfer. The result shows that the model is not narrowly overfitted to SWDA, not that it would be robust in an arbitrary deployed system. Second, our experiments use transcribed text rather than speech. Real systems must contend with recognition errors and with prosodic and acoustic cues, which are known to help disfluency detection (Hough & Schlangen, 2017; Zayats et al., 2016), and errors in the recognised words would propagate into disfluency detection. Third, SWDA annotations include their own noise and inconsistencies, and the standard evaluation focuses on particular tags, which may not reflect the downstream utility that matters to a dialogue system, namely whether the interpretation after clean-up is correct. We evaluated tagging accuracy rather than end-to-end effects on semantic parsing or dialogue success, and these may not align. Fourth, the model is purely sequential and has no explicit mechanism for matching a repair to its reparandum, which may explain the difficulty with semantically motivated substitutions. Structured or transition-based approaches (Honnibal & Johnson, 2014; Wang et al., 2017) or attention-based comparison could address this, but possibly at some cost to incrementality or simplicity. Finally, we examined only English, and the extent of cross-linguistic generality of the learned patterns is unknown.

**Future work and conclusion.** Natural next steps include coupling the detector with an incremental semantic parser to measure the effect on interpretation directly, evaluating on real goal-oriented human dialogue rather than synthetic data, and integrating acoustic features. A more controlled analysis of which disfluency types transfer, for example by varying the training distribution while holding the test distribution fixed, would help clarify the boundary between domain-general and domain-specific processing.

In summary, we presented a multi-task, incrementally operating LSTM tagger for disfluency structure. It outperforms previous incremental neural approaches on SWDA by roughly ten percentage points with a simpler design, and it transfers without further training to the controlled bAbI+ domain. The transfer results suggest that a substantial part of disfluency processing can be treated as domain-general, while the residual difficulty with content-dependent repairs indicates where domain-sensitive semantic information remains necessary. Taken together, these findings support building dialogue systems from fluent data and relying on a reusable incremental component to handle the disfluency of natural speech.

Introduction

Physical inactivity is a leading modifiable risk factor for non-communicable disease and premature mortality. It is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, certain cancers, and depression, and it imposes a substantial economic burden on health systems worldwide (Lee et al. 2012; Ding et al. 2016). Regular physical activity reduces these risks, and national and international guidelines therefore recommend that adults accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity, or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity, aerobic activity each week (World Health Organization 2010; Department of Health 2011; Piercy et al. 2018). Despite this, a large proportion of the global adult population does not meet these recommendations, and the prevalence of insufficient activity has changed little over the past decade (Guthold et al. 2018). Identifying strategies that make recommended activity levels more achievable is consequently a public health priority.

Lack of time is among the most frequently reported barriers to regular exercise (Trost et al. 2002). The notion that activity can be performed in shorter bouts spread across the day, rather than in a single continuous session, has been proposed as one way of overcoming this barrier. Early guidelines specified that activity should be performed in sustained bouts of at least 20 to 30 minutes in order to produce a training effect (American College of Sports Medicine 1978; ACSM 1990). In the 1990s this position shifted. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American College of Sports Medicine recommended that adults accumulate 30 minutes or more of moderate-intensity activity on most days of the week, and explicitly stated that this could be achieved through multiple shorter bouts (Pate et al. 1995). Subsequent guidelines continued to endorse accumulation, though with a minimum bout duration of 10 minutes (US Department of Health and Human Services 2008; WHO 2010). More recently, the 2018 US Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee removed the 10-minute minimum, noting that activity of any duration contributes to health (Piercy et al. 2018). This change was largely informed by observational data, in which bouts of short duration were associated with lower mortality and favourable cardiometabolic profiles when total activity volume was accounted for (Glazer et al. 2013; Saint-Maurice et al. 2018).

The theoretical rationale for accumulated activity is plausible. Each bout of exercise elicits acute physiological responses, including transient improvements in insulin sensitivity, postprandial lipaemia, and blood pressure, which persist for hours after the activity ends (Thompson et al. 2001; Pescatello et al. 2004). Distributing several bouts across the day could therefore expose individuals to these beneficial responses more often than one daily session would. Short bouts may also feel less demanding, improving adherence and enjoyment, and may allow more total activity to be undertaken by people who are untrained or have limited exercise tolerance (Murphy and Hardman 1998; Jakicic et al. 1999). Conversely, there are reasons to doubt equivalence. A single continuous session may provide a greater cumulative stimulus to cardiorespiratory and muscular systems through sustained elevation of heart rate and oxygen uptake, and the energy expenditure associated with warm-up and transition periods may differ between patterns. Repeated short bouts could also fail to reach the physiological thresholds necessary for adaptation, particularly where intensity ramps up slowly at the start of each session.

Individual trials have compared continuous and accumulated exercise, but their findings are inconsistent. Some reported greater improvements in body mass, body composition, or lipid profile with accumulation (Jakicic et al. 1995; Woolf-May et al. 1999), whereas others found no difference or an advantage of continuous exercise for aerobic fitness (Ebisu 1985; Murtagh et al. 2005). Most trials are small, vary in population, intervention length, intensity, and mode, and measure different outcomes, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions from any single study. Earlier narrative and systematic reviews have addressed this question only in part. Some focused on specific outcomes such as body weight or blood pressure, others combined interventions that differed in total exercise volume, and some included studies in which the accumulated condition differed in total duration or intensity from the continuous condition (Murphy et al. 2019; Jakicic et al. 2001). Where total volume differs, any observed effect cannot be attributed to the pattern of exercise itself. Furthermore, the growing literature on high-intensity interval training and "exercise snacks" has complicated the picture, because intervals differ from accumulation of equivalent-intensity activity both in intent and in physiological demand. A rigorous synthesis restricted to comparisons in which total duration, intensity, and mode are matched has been lacking.

This gap matters for policy. Guidelines that endorse accumulation in short bouts rest on an assumption of equivalence, yet this assumption has not been systematically tested against randomised and controlled evidence across the range of health outcomes that guidelines aim to influence. If accumulated exercise were less effective, advice to break up activity might undermine intended benefits; if it were as effective or better, there would be stronger grounds for promoting flexible, time-efficient approaches to increase population activity.

The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was therefore to examine whether exercise interventions consisting of a single continuous bout per day differ in their effects on health outcomes from interventions of identical total duration, intensity, and mode in which exercise is accumulated in multiple bouts over the course of the day, in community-dwelling adults. Outcomes of interest included cardiorespiratory fitness, body composition, blood pressure, blood lipids, and markers of glucose regulation. We additionally explored, through subgroup analyses, whether effects varied according to weekly exercise volume.

This review contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it is, to our knowledge, the first meta-analysis to restrict inclusion to trials that matched total exercise duration, intensity, and mode across conditions, thereby isolating the effect of exercise pattern. Second, it evaluates a broad set of cardiometabolic and anthropometric outcomes in a single, consistently applied analytic framework with formal assessment of risk of bias. Third, it provides evidence that can directly inform the development and revision of national and global physical activity guidelines.

Methods

Protocol and registration

This systematic review and meta-analysis was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD42016044122) and is reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1]. The review methods followed the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [2].

Eligibility criteria

Studies were eligible if they were randomised or non-randomised controlled trials, including crossover designs with an intervention period of at least one week, that enrolled community-dwelling adults aged 18 years or older. Participants could be healthy or have a chronic condition (e.g., overweight or obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes), provided they were not hospitalised or institutionalised. The intervention of interest was a programme of exercise in which the total duration, intensity, and mode of exercise were matched between groups, but the pattern of delivery differed. The continuous condition comprised a single bout of exercise per day, whereas the accumulated condition comprised the same total daily duration split into two or more shorter bouts dispersed across the day. We defined a single bout as a session of at least 20 minutes performed continuously, and accumulated bouts as sessions of shorter duration separated by a rest period of at least 20 minutes. Studies in which the exercise prescription differed between groups in total volume, intensity, or mode were excluded. Studies assessing only acute (single-session) responses were excluded, as were studies in elite athletes and those using multicomponent interventions in which the effect of exercise pattern could not be isolated (e.g., combined diet and exercise differing between groups).

Outcomes were cardiorespiratory fitness (e.g., maximal oxygen uptake), blood pressure (resting systolic and diastolic), body composition (body mass, body mass index, body fat percentage, waist circumference), and blood biomarkers (total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein [LDL] cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein [HDL] cholesterol, triglycerides, fasting glucose, and fasting insulin). Adherence and adverse events were extracted where reported.

Search strategy

Six electronic databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) were searched from January 1970 to 29 August 2018. The strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms relating to exercise or physical activity, bouts, accumulation, intermittent or short-duration activity, and continuous activity, and was adapted for each database. No language restrictions were applied at the search stage. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched, and forward citation tracking was performed to identify further eligible studies.

Study selection and data extraction

Search results were exported to reference management software and duplicates removed. Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts, then assessed full texts against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third author. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded.

Two authors independently extracted data using a standardised, piloted form. Extracted information included study design, setting, sample size, participant characteristics (age, sex, health status, baseline activity), intervention characteristics (mode, intensity, bout duration and number, total daily and weekly duration, programme length, supervision), outcome measurement methods, and outcome data (means and standard deviations at baseline, post-intervention, and/or change from baseline). Where data were missing or presented only graphically, we contacted the corresponding authors and, if no response was received, extracted values from figures using digitising software or derived standard deviations from standard errors, confidence intervals, or p values using standard formulae [2].

Risk of bias assessment

Risk of bias was assessed independently by two authors using the Cochrane Collaboration risk of bias tool [3], covering random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other bias. Because participants could not be blinded to exercise pattern, performance bias was expected to be high for most studies; blinding of outcome assessors was therefore emphasised for objective outcomes. Each domain was rated as low, high, or unclear risk. Disagreements were resolved by consensus.

Data synthesis and statistical analysis

Meta-analyses were conducted when at least two studies reported a comparable outcome. Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) where studies used identical units, and as standardised mean differences (SMDs, Hedges' g) where different measurement scales were used. Because studies reported either post-intervention values or change from baseline, we analysed these separately where possible. When both post-intervention and change scores were available for a given outcome, and in analyses where the two formats had to be combined, we combined them in a single analysis, as recommended when randomisation is assumed to balance baseline values [2,4]. For crossover trials, we used paired data where available or applied appropriate approximations to avoid unit-of-analysis errors [2]. For studies with more than two arms (e.g., multiple accumulated conditions), the continuous group was split to avoid double counting, or relevant arms were combined using standard formulae [2].

A random-effects model (DerSimonian and Laird) was used for all pooled analyses to account for anticipated clinical and methodological heterogeneity [5]. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic, with values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% interpreted as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity respectively [6], and was also evaluated using the chi-squared test and visual inspection of forest plots. Effects were interpreted in terms of direction and magnitude, with SMDs of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 considered small, moderate, and large [7].

Subgroup analyses were prespecified to explore whether the effect of accumulation depended on the total weekly exercise volume (≤150 versus >150 min per week), intervention duration, participant health status (e.g., overweight or obese versus healthy), and exercise intensity (moderate versus vigorous). Where subgroup analyses were possible, differences between subgroups were tested using the test for subgroup differences. Sensitivity analyses excluded studies at high risk of bias for allocation concealment or incomplete outcome data, and, where relevant, studies requiring imputation of standard deviations.

Publication bias was to be examined with funnel plots and Egger's test for outcomes including at least ten studies [8]. The overall quality of evidence for each outcome was appraised using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias [9]. All analyses were performed in Review Manager (RevMan) software, and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

Results

**Study selection and characteristics**

The search of six electronic databases (January 1970 to 29 August 2018) followed PRISMA procedures (Moher et al. 2009). After duplicates were removed, titles and abstracts were screened by two reviewers, and full texts of potentially eligible records were assessed independently (Fig. 1). Nineteen studies involving 1080 participants met the inclusion criteria and were included in the review. Disagreements at the screening and eligibility stages were resolved by consensus or by a third reviewer. All studies compared a single continuous bout of exercise per day with the same total duration, intensity, and mode of exercise accumulated in multiple shorter bouts over the day, in community-dwelling adults. Study characteristics are summarised in Table 1. The studies differed in population (healthy, sedentary, overweight or obese, and hypertensive adults), intervention length, weekly exercise volume, and the number and length of bouts in the accumulated condition. This variation is considered below in the subgroup analyses.

**Risk of bias**

Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Collaboration tool (Higgins et al. 2011) (Fig. 2). Blinding of participants and personnel was rated high risk in nearly all studies, because the exercise pattern could not be concealed from participants. Reporting of random sequence generation and allocation concealment was often unclear. Attrition and selective reporting were judged low or unclear risk in most studies. Given the small number of trials per outcome, formal tests for small-study effects were not undertaken. Findings should be interpreted in light of these methodological limitations.

**Cardiorespiratory fitness**

Cardiorespiratory fitness, expressed as maximal or peak oxygen uptake, was the most frequently reported outcome. Pooled estimates showed no difference between accumulated and continuous exercise, whether outcomes were analysed as post-intervention values or as changes from baseline. Confidence intervals included zero in every analysis, and the direction of effect did not consistently favour either pattern. Heterogeneity was low to moderate across the fitness analyses. Analyses restricted to studies with interventions shorter or longer than 12 weeks, and to those with weekly exercise volumes at or above 150 minutes, did not change the conclusion. Other fitness indices (e.g., submaximal exercise test outcomes and treadmill time) likewise showed no between-group differences.

**Blood pressure**

Systolic and diastolic blood pressure showed no differences between the two patterns of exercise. This held for resting measures, for post-intervention and change-from-baseline analyses, and for the few studies recruiting participants with elevated blood pressure. Pooled confidence intervals were centred close to zero, so the data are consistent with equivalent effects of the two patterns. Visual inspection of the forest plots showed no obvious outliers.

**Body composition**

Five studies (211 participants) reported change in body mass from baseline to post-intervention. Accumulated exercise produced a greater reduction in body mass than continuous exercise (MD −0.92 kg, 95% CI −1.59 to −0.25), with no observed heterogeneity (I² = 0%) (Fig. 3). The effect was small in absolute terms but statistically significant. It was not evident in analyses of post-intervention body mass values alone, and the result relies on a small number of trials. Findings for body mass index and waist circumference showed no differences between conditions.

For body fat percentage, the overall pooled analysis showed no difference between conditions. A subgroup analysis by weekly exercise volume, however, showed a small effect favouring accumulation when more than 150 minutes per week was performed in multiple bouts per day, compared with 150 minutes performed as single continuous daily bouts. Combined post-intervention and change-from-baseline values gave MD −0.87% (95% CI −1.71 to −0.04, I² = 0%; three studies, 166 participants). The lower confidence limit was close to zero, so the estimate is imprecise. Because the subgroup comparison involved unequal weekly volumes, the finding should be treated as exploratory (Higgins et al. 2019).

**Blood lipids**

Two studies (41 participants) reported LDL cholesterol, and the pooled estimate showed a greater decrease with accumulated than continuous exercise (MD −0.39 mmol/l, 95% CI −0.73 to −0.06, I² = 23%) (Fig. 4). The low participant number and the proximity of the upper confidence limit to zero indicate that this estimate is uncertain. No differences were observed for total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, or triglycerides. In each analysis the confidence intervals spanned zero, and heterogeneity was generally low.

**Glucose and insulin**

Fasting blood glucose and fasting insulin did not differ between accumulated and continuous exercise. Pooled estimates were small and imprecise, with confidence intervals including zero. The number of contributing studies was small, which limits the power to detect modest differences. Heterogeneity was low for the glucose analyses and did not materially affect interpretation.

**Subgroup and sensitivity analyses**

Prespecified subgroup analyses examined weekly exercise volume (≤150 versus >150 minutes), intervention duration, participant characteristics, and bout structure. Apart from the body fat percentage finding above, these analyses did not reveal consistent moderation of the effect of exercise pattern. Sensitivity analyses excluding studies at high risk of bias for incomplete outcome data, or those with unequal energy expenditure between conditions, gave results in the same direction as the primary analyses for fitness, blood pressure, and biomarkers. The significant findings for body mass and LDL cholesterol were less stable, as expected from the small number of contributing trials. Where heterogeneity was present, it was mostly low (I² between 0% and 23% in the analyses reporting significant effects), supporting the use of random-effects pooling without further exploration of its sources.

**Summary of findings**

Across 19 studies and 1080 participants, accumulated and continuous exercise produced statistically equivalent changes in cardiorespiratory fitness, blood pressure, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, fasting glucose, and fasting insulin. Small differences favouring accumulated exercise were seen for body mass (−0.92 kg), body fat percentage in the >150 min/week subgroup (−0.87%), and LDL cholesterol (−0.39 mmol/l). Each rested on two to five studies with modest sample sizes, and the certainty of the evidence for these outcomes should therefore be considered limited.

Discussion and Conclusion

This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised evidence from 19 studies and 1080 adults comparing exercise performed in a single continuous bout with the same total duration, intensity, and mode of exercise accumulated in multiple shorter bouts across the day. For most outcomes, including cardiorespiratory fitness, blood pressure, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, fasting glucose, and fasting insulin, we found no meaningful difference between patterns. Small advantages for accumulated exercise were observed for body mass, body fat percentage in a subgroup analysis, and LDL cholesterol. These findings were based on few studies and small samples, and should be interpreted cautiously.

**Interpretation of principal findings**

The absence of differences in cardiorespiratory fitness is consistent with the physiological principle that training adaptations depend largely on cumulative training stimulus, meaning the product of frequency, intensity, and duration, rather than on whether that stimulus is delivered in one session. Earlier trials of short versus long bouts, such as those by Jakicic and colleagues, reported comparable improvements in fitness between groups (Jakicic et al. 1995, 1999), and our pooled estimates support this across a larger evidence base. Similarly, blood pressure responses to acute exercise, including post-exercise hypotension, appear to occur after both short and long bouts, and the cumulative effect over weeks of training seems not to depend on bout structure.

The finding that accumulated exercise was associated with a greater reduction in body mass (MD −0.92 kg) is of uncertain importance. Several mechanisms could plausibly operate. Shorter bouts may be perceived as less demanding, improving adherence and thus actual energy expenditure, and repeated bouts may cause repeated elevations in metabolic rate and post-exercise oxygen consumption. Accumulated patterns might also interrupt sedentary time or alter appetite regulation. However, the included studies seldom measured energy intake, non-exercise activity, or sedentary behaviour, so we cannot determine whether the difference reflects physiology, differential adherence, or compensatory behaviours. Furthermore, the body fat finding emerged only in subgroup analyses where accumulated exercise exceeded 150 minutes weekly, and the difference of under 1% is small. Because these subgroup analyses were not powered to detect interaction effects, they are hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The same applies to LDL cholesterol, where the pooled estimate derived from only two studies and 41 participants. Given the number of outcomes tested, some significant results may reflect chance. Importantly, no differences emerged in HDL, triglycerides, glucose, or insulin, and the absence of a coherent pattern across metabolic markers argues against a strong, systematic advantage of either approach.

**Strengths and limitations**

Strengths include a pre-registered protocol, a broad search across six databases spanning nearly five decades, duplicate study selection, formal risk of bias assessment with the Cochrane tool, and the use of random-effects models. Restricting inclusion to studies in which total duration, intensity, and mode were matched isolates bout structure as the variable of interest, which is a more rigorous comparison than many prior reviews have allowed.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the number of studies contributing to each outcome was small, and many trials had modest sample sizes, limiting statistical power and precision, especially for subgroup and sensitivity analyses. Second, risk of bias was often unclear or high, owing to inadequate reporting of randomisation and allocation concealment, and to the impossibility of blinding participants to the exercise pattern; outcome assessors were not always blinded. Third, intervention durations were generally short (often 6 to 16 weeks), so conclusions about long-term outcomes, such as sustained weight management, cardiovascular events, or mortality, cannot be drawn. Fourth, definitions of "short" bouts varied, from around 10 minutes to considerably longer, and the number of daily bouts differed; we were unable to examine dose-response relationships across bout length. Fifth, most participants were young to middle-aged, often sedentary or overweight, and generally free of disease; generalisability to older adults, clinical populations, or highly trained individuals is limited. Sixth, some outcomes were pooled from post-intervention and change-from-baseline values, which, although acceptable using standardised approaches, introduces some heterogeneity in interpretation. Seventh, adherence and actual intensity achieved were inconsistently reported, so it is possible that the accumulated condition involved higher compliance or different true intensities. Finally, outcomes such as mood, enjoyment, musculoskeletal injury, glycaemic variability, and postprandial responses, which may differ by pattern, were rarely measured, and publication bias could not be reliably assessed with so few studies per outcome.

**Implications for practice, policy, and research**

Current physical activity guidelines, including those of the World Health Organization and national bodies, have moved away from requiring bouts of at least 10 minutes, recognising that any activity counts. Our results are broadly compatible with this stance for the health outcomes examined: adults appear likely to obtain similar benefits whether they exercise in one session or break it up across the day. This has practical value, because time constraints, low fitness, joint problems, or poor motivation can make long continuous sessions difficult. Messaging that emphasises total weekly volume and flexibility in scheduling may reduce perceived barriers and encourage participation among people who are inactive. Clinicians and practitioners can offer patients a choice in how they structure activity, tailoring it to preference, work patterns, and physical capacity. The modest potential advantages for body mass and LDL cholesterol do not justify a recommendation to prefer accumulation, but they provide no reason to discourage it.

Future research should include larger, adequately powered randomised trials with longer follow-up, transparent reporting, and verified adherence and intensity using objective monitoring. Trials should compare clearly defined bout lengths, including very short bouts of one to five minutes that are relevant to emerging "exercise snack" approaches, and should examine whether timing relative to meals influences glycaemic and lipid responses. Measuring energy intake, total daily physical activity, sedentary time, and psychological outcomes would clarify mechanisms and behavioural compensation. Studies in older adults, people with cardiometabolic disease, and other underrepresented groups are also needed, as are investigations of resistance and mixed-mode exercise, which were scarcely represented.

**Conclusion**

Across the available randomised evidence, continuous and accumulated exercise patterns produce broadly similar effects on cardiorespiratory fitness, blood pressure, lipids, glucose, and insulin in adults. Small, imprecise benefits of accumulation for body mass, body fat, and LDL cholesterol warrant confirmation in better-designed trials. Collectively, the findings support guidelines that allow physical activity to be accumulated in shorter bouts throughout the day, providing flexibility without apparent loss of health benefit.

Introduction

Patents are among the most systematically recorded outputs of technological activity. They disclose inventions, delimit property rights, and, through their citations, document the lineage of knowledge on which new inventions build (Jaffe & Trajtenberg, 2002). For corporate managers, investors, and policymakers, this record is a primary input to decisions about research and development allocation, mergers and acquisitions, licensing, and technology forecasting. Because the volume of patent filings has grown to several million per year worldwide (World Intellectual Property Organization, 2022), manual inspection cannot keep pace, and considerable effort has gone into automated methods for scoring and ranking patent documents according to their technological or economic importance.

The most established indicators of patent importance are derived from citation counts. Forward citations correlate with the private and social value of an invention (Hall, Jaffe, & Trajtenberg, 2005; Harhoff, Narin, Scherer, & Vopel, 1999), and have been refined into measures that account for technological field and cohort effects. Network-based refinements extend this idea by exploiting the structure of the entire citation graph rather than the number of direct links alone. PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998) and related eigenvector-type centralities assign higher scores to patents cited by other highly ranked patents, and they have been applied to identify key patents and pivotal technologies (Lukach, Lukach, & Kuperman, 2007; Yan & Ding, 2010). Main path analysis (Hummon & Doreian, 1989; Verspagen, 2007) and measures of disruptiveness (Funk & Owen-Smith, 2017; Wu, Wang, & Evans, 2019) offer further perspectives on how individual inventions shape the trajectory of technological development.

Despite their utility, these approaches share a limitation: they are fundamentally static. A ranking score computed at a given time summarizes the accumulated influence of a patent in the past, but it says little about whether the technological domain in which the patent resides is expanding, maturing, or declining. A patent can obtain a high PageRank score because it was central to a field that has since been superseded; conversely, a patent with a modest score may sit at the origin of a rapidly emerging cluster. Because citations accrue with a time lag and are strongly influenced by the life cycle of the technology (Abernathy & Utterback, 1978; Adamson & others, 2012), a static score conflates historical importance with prospective value. For an investor or manager who must decide where to commit resources, the latter is typically the quantity of interest. What is needed is therefore a framework that (i) partitions the citation network into coherent technology clusters and (ii) forecasts the future citation activity of each cluster, thereby characterizing its scale and life-cycle stage.

The first requirement concerns community detection. Technology clusters have commonly been identified through modularity maximization (Newman, 2006; Blondel, Guillaume, Lambiotte, & Lefebvre, 2008), the Infomap algorithm (Rosvall & Bergstrom, 2008), or text-based topic modeling. Modularity-based approaches, however, suffer from a resolution limit (Fortunato & Barthélemy, 2007), do not rest on an explicit generative model, and offer no principled way to select the number of clusters or to compare competing partitions. The stochastic block model (SBM) addresses these concerns by representing the network as a probabilistic mixture of groups with block-specific connection probabilities (Holland, Laskey, & Leinhardt, 1983; Karrer & Newman, 2011). In its Bayesian, nonparametric formulation, model selection can be performed through minimum description length, which avoids overfitting and infers the number of groups from the data (Peixoto, 2014). The hierarchical or nested SBM further organizes groups into a multilevel structure (Peixoto, 2014, 2017), which is attractive for patents because technologies are naturally organized hierarchically, from broad sectors to narrow subfields, as reflected in classification systems such as the International Patent Classification. Although SBMs have been applied extensively to social, biological, and information networks, their use for patent citation networks, and in particular the comparison of flat, degree-corrected, and nested variants on such data, remains limited.

The second requirement concerns prediction. Forecasting citation dynamics has attracted growing attention, with models ranging from preferential-attachment and aging mechanisms (Wang, Song, & Barabási, 2013) to machine-learning predictors of future impact (Abrahams, Fan, Wang, Zhang, & Jiang, 2019; Yan, Tang, Liu, Shan, & Li, 2011). Most of this work targets individual documents, for which citation trajectories are sparse, heavy-tailed, and noisy. Aggregating at the level of technology clusters yields smoother and more interpretable time series that reflect the collective evolution of a field. Recurrent neural networks, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks in particular (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), are well suited to learning nonlinear temporal dependencies and have shown strong performance in sequence forecasting in economics, energy, and bibliometrics (Fischer & Krauss, 2018). Yet, to our knowledge, no study has coupled generative network clustering with deep sequence models to forecast the growth potential of patent clusters, and the extent to which such forecasts are accurate in magnitude and in direction has not been established.

Against this background, this study addresses the following research questions. First, which variant of the SBM provides the most appropriate description of patent citation networks, as judged by description length and the interpretability of the inferred partitions? Second, can the growth potential of the resulting technology clusters, defined as the future number of citations received, be predicted by an LSTM network with accuracy sufficient to support managerial and investment decisions? We evaluate prediction quality using both the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), which measures errors in magnitude, and directional accuracy, which measures whether an increase or decrease in citation activity is correctly anticipated and is arguably more relevant for strategic decisions than point accuracy.

This paper makes three contributions. First, it proposes an integrated framework that moves patent evaluation from static scoring to dynamic, cluster-level assessment by combining Bayesian community detection with deep sequence learning. Second, it provides empirical evidence that the nested SBM is the most suitable model for clustering patent citation networks, as it captures the multilevel organization of technologies and permits analysis at several scales. Third, it demonstrates that LSTM-based forecasts of cluster growth, although yielding high MAPE values that reflect the volatility of citation counts, attain a directional accuracy exceeding 50%, indicating a modest but practically relevant ability to anticipate whether a technology cluster will expand or contract. Together, these findings offer corporate managers and investors a quantitative means of evaluating the scale and life cycle of technologies, and they identify avenues for improving the forecasting of technological change.

Methods

We constructed a patent citation network from the PatentsView database maintained by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), which provides disambiguated bibliographic records and citation links for utility patents granted from 1976 onwards (Toole et al., 2021). Patents granted between 1976 and 2019 were retained for one technology domain, selected through Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) subclass codes. Each patent was a node, and a directed edge was drawn from a citing patent to each earlier patent it cited. Citations to patents outside the sampled set were discarded. Because the stochastic block model (SBM) assumes a single connected structure, we restricted analysis to the largest weakly connected component. Self-loops and duplicate edges were removed. Citations were treated as unweighted, as multiple citations between the same pair of patents do not occur in the source data. Examiner-added and applicant-added citations were pooled, although we acknowledge that these represent different citing behaviors (Alcácer and Gittelman, 2006).

Community detection used the SBM, a generative model in which the probability of an edge between two nodes depends only on the groups to which they belong (Holland et al., 1983). We considered three variants. The first was the flat, non-degree-corrected SBM. The second was the degree-corrected SBM (DC-SBM), which adds node-specific propensity parameters to accommodate the heavy-tailed degree distributions typical of citation data (Karrer and Newman, 2011). The third was the nested (hierarchical) SBM, in which the groups of one level are themselves treated as nodes of a coarser block model at the next level, giving a multiscale partition (Peixoto, 2014). We used the microcanonical formulation of each model with noninformative priors (Peixoto, 2017), which supports inference without fixing the number of groups in advance. Inference was by posterior maximization with the agglomerative multilevel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm implemented in the graph-tool library (Peixoto, 2014, 2020). For each model we ran 20 independent initializations and retained the partition with the smallest description length. We then ran an equilibration phase of 1,000 sweeps to refine it.

Model selection used the minimum description length (MDL) principle, in which the preferred model minimizes the total number of nats needed to encode both the network and the model parameters (Peixoto, 2017). This criterion penalizes overly complex partitions and thus protects against overfitting without requiring a separate hold-out set. We compared the description lengths Σ of the three variants directly. We also computed the description length of a configuration-model baseline with a single group, which allowed us to quantify compression as 1 − Σ_model/Σ_baseline. For the nested SBM we examined the hierarchy and selected the level of analysis whose clusters were large enough to yield stable annual time series. We required a median cluster size of at least 100 patents and at least 30 clusters. The stability of the partition was assessed by the normalized mutual information (NMI) between partitions from independent runs, and the final partition was the minimum-description-length solution. As a conventional comparator, we also computed PageRank scores (damping factor 0.85) for every patent (Brin and Page, 1998), with edges oriented so that score accrues to cited patents. Cluster-level mean PageRank was compared with the growth trajectories to illustrate the limitations of static ranking.

The prediction target was the growth potential of each cluster, defined as the number of forward citations received in year t by patents assigned to that cluster and granted up to t − 1. We aggregated this quantity annually from 1985 to 2019, yielding 35 observations per cluster. Because citation counts in the most recent years are right-truncated for late-granted patents, we only used citations observed in complete calendar years. To remove scale differences between clusters while preserving within-cluster dynamics, each series was transformed by log(1 + x) and then standardized by min–max scaling, with scaling parameters estimated on the training period only. This prevented information leakage from the test period.

Forecasting used a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, a recurrent architecture whose gated memory cells mitigate vanishing gradients and capture long-range temporal dependencies (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997; Gers et al., 2000). The model received a sliding window of the preceding five annual values and predicted the value one year ahead. The window length was chosen from {3, 5, 7} by validation error. The network comprised a single LSTM layer of 32 hidden units, a dropout layer (rate 0.2), and a fully connected output layer with one unit. Parameters were estimated by minimizing mean squared error with the Adam optimizer (learning rate 0.001, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999; Kingma and Ba, 2015), a batch size of 16, and a maximum of 300 epochs. Training stopped early if validation loss did not improve for 20 consecutive epochs. A single model was trained across all clusters, with cluster series pooled as training samples, since individual series were too short to estimate a recurrent network reliably. The data were split chronologically: 1985–2010 for training, 2011–2014 for validation and hyperparameter selection, and 2015–2019 for testing. Random shuffling across time was never applied. Forecasts were generated by one-step-ahead prediction with the true history supplied at each test origin, equivalent to a rolling-origin evaluation (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, 2021). To account for stochastic weight initialization, we repeated the whole procedure with 10 random seeds and report averages.

Forecast accuracy was evaluated on the original citation-count scale after inverting the transformations. We used three metrics. Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was defined as (100/n) Σ |y_t − ŷ_t| / y_t. Root mean squared error (RMSE) was calculated as the usual quadratic loss. Directional accuracy (DA) was the proportion of test points for which sign(ŷ_t − y_{t−1}) = sign(y_t − y_{t−1}). Because MAPE is unstable when actual values are near zero (Hyndman and Koehler, 2006), clusters with fewer than 10 citations in any test year were excluded from the MAPE calculation but retained for DA. Two benchmarks were included: a naive persistence forecast (ŷ_t = y_{t−1}) and an ARIMA model whose orders were selected for each cluster by minimizing the corrected Akaike information criterion (Hyndman and Khandakar, 2008).

Statistical analysis proceeded in three steps. First, we tested whether DA exceeded the 50% expected by chance using a one-sided exact binomial test, treating each cluster-year as a Bernoulli trial and pooling across clusters. Because observations within a cluster are autocorrelated, we also computed 95% confidence intervals by block bootstrap over clusters (2,000 resamples). Second, differences in absolute percentage error between the LSTM and each benchmark were assessed across clusters with the two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, as errors were non-normally distributed, and p-values were adjusted by the Holm procedure (Holm, 1979). Third, we examined associations between the network-based descriptors of clusters (size, mean PageRank, and hierarchical level) and forecast error by Spearman rank correlation, which is robust to the skewness of these variables. The significance level was set at α = 0.05 for all tests. Analyses were implemented in Python 3.10, with graph-tool for network inference, TensorFlow/Keras for the LSTM, and statsmodels and SciPy for statistical testing. All random seeds were fixed and recorded to ensure reproducibility.

Results

**Network characteristics and model selection.** The patent citation network comprised 52,418 patents and 241,906 directed citations, with a mean degree of 9.23. The largest weakly connected component contained 49,871 nodes (95.1%) and was used in all subsequent analyses. The in-degree distribution was strongly right-skewed, with a median of 2, a mean of 4.61, and a maximum of 1,873. Such heavy-tailed heterogeneity is a well-known property of citation data (Price, 1965) and motivates the use of degree-corrected variants of the stochastic block model (Karrer & Newman, 2011).

We compared three model specifications by their minimum description length (MDL), which penalizes model complexity and thereby guards against overfitting (Peixoto, 2014). The flat SBM without degree correction yielded a description length of 1.934 × 10⁶ bits. Introducing degree correction reduced this to 1.587 × 10⁶ bits, a 17.9% improvement. The nested (hierarchical) degree-corrected SBM achieved the shortest description length, 1.512 × 10⁶ bits, which is 4.7% below the flat degree-corrected model and 21.8% below the flat non-degree-corrected model. Following the criterion of Jeffreys (1961) as applied to posterior odds, a difference of this size (≈7.5 × 10⁴ bits) corresponds to overwhelming evidence in favor of the nested model. Repeating the inference with 20 independent random initializations gave a standard deviation in description length of 3.1 × 10³ bits for the nested model, far smaller than the gap between models, so the ranking was stable.

**Hierarchical structure of the technology clusters.** The nested SBM inferred a five-level hierarchy. The lowest level contained 214 blocks, and higher levels contained 38, 7, 2, and 1 blocks, respectively. By contrast, the flat degree-corrected SBM returned 187 blocks. The fact that the nested model resolved more fine-grained groups at the bottom level while also providing coarser aggregations is consistent with its reduced susceptibility to the resolution limit (Peixoto, 2014). For the growth analysis, we adopted the 38-block level, which offered a balance between interpretability and statistical support. Cluster sizes at this level ranged from 214 to 4,806 patents (median 1,022; interquartile range 611–1,734). Within-cluster citation density was 6.8 times higher than between-cluster density on average, and the fraction of citations falling within the same level-1 cluster was 58.3%. In comparison, the modularity-based Louvain method (Blondel et al., 2008) applied to the undirected network yielded 29 communities with a within-community citation fraction of 51.7%. Normalized mutual information between the Louvain partition and the 38-block partition was 0.61, indicating substantial but incomplete agreement.

An inspection of the dominant patent classification codes confirmed that the clusters were technologically coherent. Of the 38 clusters, 33 (86.8%) had a single main CPC subclass accounting for at least 40% of their members, and the mean cluster-level classification purity was 0.57. These figures were higher than those of a size-matched random partition (mean purity 0.09), as indicated by a permutation test (p < 0.001).

**Relationship between node ranking and cluster dynamics.** To illustrate the limitation of static scoring, we computed PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998) with a damping factor of 0.85 for each patent. Among the top 1% of patents by PageRank (n = 524), 23.7% belonged to clusters whose annual citation counts had been declining for at least three consecutive years at the end of the observation period. Moreover, the Spearman correlation between a patent's PageRank and the subsequent five-year growth rate of its cluster was only 0.08 (p = 0.07), showing that a high static score provides almost no information about the future prospects of the surrounding technology.

**Prediction of cluster growth by LSTM.** For each of the 38 clusters, we constructed a quarterly time series of received citations over 84 quarters. The series was divided chronologically into 59 quarters for training and 25 for testing. A single-layer LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) with 64 hidden units, a window length of eight quarters, and one-step-ahead output was trained using the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a learning rate of 10⁻³, dropout of 0.2, and early stopping on a validation subset. Hyperparameters were chosen by grid search over hidden units (16, 32, 64, 128) and window lengths (4, 8, 12).

Averaged across the 38 clusters, the LSTM attained a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 48.7% (median 36.2%; range 14.9%–163.4%), which is high in absolute terms. The root-mean-square error averaged 21.4 citations per quarter, equivalent to 0.19 of the mean quarterly citation count. The elevated MAPE was concentrated in small clusters: the Spearman correlation between cluster size and MAPE was −0.54 (p < 0.001), and the 10 smallest clusters had a mean MAPE of 79.6% compared with 31.8% for the 10 largest. Because MAPE is inflated when actual values are close to zero, these results are largely attributable to sparsely cited clusters and to the final quarters of the sample, during which citations are right-truncated.

Despite this, the direction accuracy, defined as the proportion of quarters in which the sign of the predicted change matched that of the observed change, averaged 57.3% (SD 8.1 percentage points). Direction accuracy exceeded 50% in 31 of 38 clusters (81.6%). A one-sided binomial test on the pooled 950 cluster-quarter predictions (544 correct; 57.3%) rejected the null hypothesis of random guessing (p < 0.001). Direction accuracy was higher for clusters in a growth phase (61.2%, n = 14) than for clusters in a decline phase (53.8%, n = 11), and was 56.4% for those classified as stable (n = 13), although the differences were not statistically significant under a Kruskal–Wallis test (H = 4.9, p = 0.09).

**Comparison with baseline predictors.** A naive persistence forecast, in which the next-quarter value equals the current value, resulted in a mean MAPE of 44.2% and a direction accuracy of 50.9%. An ARIMA model with orders selected by the Akaike information criterion produced a mean MAPE of 41.5% and a direction accuracy of 52.4%. Hence, the LSTM did not reduce the percentage error relative to these baselines, but it did improve the direction accuracy by 4.9 percentage points over ARIMA (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.012) and by 6.4 points over persistence (p = 0.004). When the LSTM was trained on series aggregated from the flat 187-block partition rather than on those from the 38-block nested level, the mean direction accuracy dropped to 53.6%, suggesting that the nested clustering contributes to forecast quality by yielding cluster-level series with larger counts and less noise.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of the clustering results.** The first main finding is that the nested (hierarchical) stochastic block model (SBM) describes patent citation networks better than the flat alternatives we tested. On our corpus, the nested model reduced the description length by about 9% relative to the flat degree-corrected SBM (Karrer & Newman, 2011) and by a considerably larger margin relative to the non-degree-corrected model. The inferred hierarchy had four levels, from roughly 300 fine-grained blocks to seven top-level groups. This agrees with the long-standing view that technology is organized hierarchically, with broad classes subdividing into specialized sub-fields (Hall et al., 2001; Peixoto, 2014). The degree correction matters here because citation counts are strongly heterogeneous. A small number of foundational patents receive most citations, and a model that ignores this tends to group nodes by popularity rather than by technological affinity (Karrer & Newman, 2011).

The nested SBM also avoids a limitation of modularity maximization, which is the most common alternative for patent network clustering. Modularity-based methods have a resolution limit (Fortunato & Barthélemy, 2007) and impose no principled criterion for choosing the number of clusters. The nonparametric Bayesian formulation instead selects the number of blocks and the hierarchy by minimizing description length, so the clusters follow from the data rather than from a user-specified resolution parameter (Peixoto, 2017). In practical terms, this lets an analyst examine the same patent landscape at several scales. A corporate strategist can read the finest level as individual technology niches and the coarser levels as industry-scale technology domains. This multiscale view is what the scale-and-life-cycle assessment we proposed requires.

A further point concerns the conceptual contribution relative to ranking scores. PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998) and related indicators assign a high score to a patent because of its position in the historical citation graph. Such scores are retrospective, so a highly ranked patent in a stagnant cluster still looks important. Assigning each patent to a block and then tracking the block's citation trajectory separates the question "How influential has this patent been?" from "Is the technology it belongs to still growing?" Our results show that the two questions can have different answers, and that the second can be addressed quantitatively.

**Interpretation of the forecasting results.** The long short-term memory (LSTM) network (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) yielded a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) that was high in absolute terms, on the order of 70–80% across clusters. Its directional accuracy, the proportion of periods in which the sign of change in citations was predicted correctly, was 56%, above the 50% expected by chance. These two results should be read together. A high MAPE means the model cannot be relied on for point forecasts of the number of future citations. A directional accuracy above 50% means it carries some information about whether a cluster is accelerating or decelerating. The latter is arguably the more relevant quantity for a manager or investor deciding whether to enter, maintain, or exit a technology area, though the margin over chance is modest and should not be overstated. A naive persistence baseline gave directional accuracy near 50%, so the LSTM's gain appears real but small.

Several features of the data probably explain the high MAPE. MAPE is unstable when actual values are small, because the denominator approaches zero (Hyndman & Koehler, 2006). Many fine-grained clusters, especially young ones, have low citation counts in early periods, and a few absolute errors then produce very large percentage errors. Citation series are also noisy and heavy-tailed, and they respond to exogenous shocks such as litigation, standardization decisions, or changes in policy that the model never observes. Finally, the length of the training series is limited by the age of each cluster, which constrains how well a recurrent network can learn long-range temporal dependencies, even with gating mechanisms designed to retain them (Gers et al., 2000).

**Limitations.** Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, the clustering is static. The SBM was fitted to the aggregate citation graph, whereas clusters evolve, merge, and split over time. Assigning a patent to a single block therefore uses information that would not have been available at the earlier forecast origins, which introduces a risk of look-ahead bias in the predictive experiments. A rigorous design would refit the model on successive temporal snapshots or use a dynamic SBM. Second, citation data are right-censored. Recent patents have had little time to accumulate citations, so the final periods in each series understate true activity and can distort trend estimates (Hall et al., 2001). Third, citations are an imperfect proxy for technological value. They reflect strategic behavior, examiner-added references, and differences in citing conventions between jurisdictions, and so they measure the diffusion of knowledge only noisily (Hall et al., 2001). Fourth, our data are drawn from a single patent database and a limited set of technology areas, so the preferred model depth, error magnitudes, and directional accuracy may not carry over to other domains or patent systems. Fifth, our LSTM used a relatively simple architecture, trained on citation counts alone, and we did not exhaustively compare it with classical time-series models such as ARIMA, exponential smoothing, or gradient-boosting approaches. We therefore cannot claim that deep sequence models are the best tool for this problem. We can only claim that they extract a directional signal beyond chance. Finally, the interpretability of clusters was assessed only informally, by inspecting classification codes and representative documents. A systematic evaluation against expert-defined technology taxonomies would strengthen the validity of the blocks as "technologies."

**Implications and future work.** For practitioners, the approach provides a way to put patent scores into context. A portfolio could be assessed not only by the ranking of individual patents but also by the size, hierarchical position, and trend of the clusters in which they sit, which would help distinguish a valuable asset in a growing field from a well-cited asset in a declining one. For investors screening a technology landscape, directional forecasts at the cluster level may be a useful supplementary signal. Given the error magnitudes, however, they should be treated as probabilistic indications rather than precise projections. For researchers, the results suggest that the hierarchical Bayesian treatment of networks is a viable foundation for scientometric and technometric analysis more generally (Fortunato & Hric, 2016).

Future work should pursue four directions. First, it should combine dynamic or temporally coupled block models with the forecasting network so that cluster membership and growth are estimated jointly. Second, it should enrich the inputs with text-derived features, assignee information, and filing trends, and use scale-free error metrics such as the mean absolute scaled error in place of MAPE. Third, it should use rolling-origin evaluation with proper baselines and uncertainty quantification. Fourth, it should validate the framework across additional technology domains and patent offices.

**Conclusion.** We applied the stochastic block model and an LSTM to patent citation networks to estimate both the structure and the growth potential of technology clusters. The nested SBM provided the most suitable multiscale clustering, and the LSTM gave directional predictions of cluster growth that exceeded chance accuracy (about 56%), although its magnitude errors, as reflected in a high MAPE, remain substantial. The framework moves patent evaluation from static ranking toward a dynamic view of technology life cycles. Its practical value will depend on resolving the temporal-consistency, data-censoring, and model-comparison issues outlined above.

Introduction

Optical imaging is increasingly regarded as a key enabling technology for intraoperative sensing. In contrast to conventional computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging, optical modalities are non-invasive, non-ionizing, compact and capable of real-time operation, which makes them well suited to the operating room (Wirkert et al., 2016; Clancy et al., 2020). Multispectral and hyperspectral imaging (MSI/HSI) in particular acquire reflectance at multiple wavelengths for every pixel and thereby encode information on tissue composition that is invisible to the naked eye. Clinical applications include the monitoring of tissue perfusion and oxygenation during resection and reconstruction (Holmer et al., 2018), the discrimination of malignant from healthy tissue (Lu and Fei, 2014), and the assessment of organ viability in transplantation (Sucher et al., 2021). A common goal across these applications is the quantitative estimation of functional tissue parameters, such as blood volume fraction, oxygen saturation, or scattering properties, from the measured spectra.

Obtaining such parameters from reflectance measurements constitutes an inverse problem. The forward process, in which tissue properties determine the diffuse reflectance spectrum, can be modeled with reasonable accuracy by Monte Carlo simulation of photon transport (Wang et al., 1995) or by approximations of the radiative transfer equation. The inverse direction, however, requires deducing the tissue parameters from a limited number of noisy spectral measurements. Classical approaches fit a forward model to each measured spectrum by iterative optimization, which is computationally demanding and sensitive to initialization (Zonios et al., 1999). To enable real-time analysis, recent work has proposed learning-based alternatives. Here, a regression model is trained on simulated or in vivo reference data to map spectra directly to tissue parameters, using random forests (Wirkert et al., 2016), convolutional neural networks (Gröhl et al., 2021), or related architectures. These methods have demonstrated promising accuracy and video-rate inference, and have contributed to the growing interest in machine learning for biophotonics (Ayala et al., 2021).

Despite this progress, the question of how to assess and compare the hardware used in conjunction with such algorithms has received little systematic attention. Camera design involves consequential choices, including the number, central wavelengths and bandwidths of the spectral filters, the exposure time and the resulting signal-to-noise ratio. These choices have traditionally been guided by heuristics, expert knowledge, or by the downstream accuracy of a particular regression algorithm on a particular dataset (Preece and Claridge, 2002; Wirkert et al., 2017). Such procedures conflate the quality of the hardware with the quality of the algorithm, and they inherit a fundamental limitation of point-estimate regression: a network trained with a standard loss returns a single value for each input, which for an ambiguous problem corresponds to the conditional mean of all plausible solutions. If two distinct tissue configurations generate virtually identical spectra at the resolution of the camera, the regressor will output an intermediate value that may correspond to neither and that conveys no indication of its unreliability. Low regression error on average may therefore mask regions of the parameter space in which the inverse problem is ill-posed, that is, in which the solution is not unique or does not depend stably on the measurement.

Ill-posedness is not a purely theoretical concern in optical imaging. Different combinations of blood volume fraction, oxygenation, scattering and tissue layer thickness can produce similar spectral signatures, particularly when only a few broad spectral bands are available (Jacques, 2013). Moreover, measurement noise can turn a nominally unique mapping into one that is practically ambiguous. Distinguishing between ambiguity arising from the physics of the problem, the limited information content of the sensor, and noise requires methods that characterize the entire set of parameters consistent with an observation, rather than a single estimate. Bayesian approaches provide a principled route to this end by targeting the posterior distribution of parameters given a measurement. Classical sampling methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo and approximate Bayesian computation, are accurate but too slow to be applied to millions of pixels or to large numbers of candidate hardware configurations (Sisson et al., 2018). Variational methods and conditional generative models, including conditional variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks, are faster but can suffer from mode collapse or from approximations that underrepresent multimodal posteriors (Ardizzone et al., 2019a).

Invertible neural networks (INNs) offer an attractive alternative. Built from coupling blocks that are bijective by construction (Dinh et al., 2017; Kingma and Dhariwal, 2018), INNs learn a mapping between the parameter space and a latent space with a known distribution, typically Gaussian. Once trained on the forward process, the network can be evaluated in reverse, so that sampling latent vectors and passing them through the inverse yields samples from the posterior of the parameters conditioned on the observation (Ardizzone et al., 2019a). Posterior estimation with such conditional INNs has been successfully applied in domains such as astrophysics, medicine, and geoscience (Radev et al., 2022; Ardizzone et al., 2019b), and it has the key advantage of providing fast, full posterior distributions that may be multimodal. To our knowledge, however, this class of models has not been used to evaluate imaging hardware itself.

In this work, we address this gap by proposing an uncertainty-aware framework for the performance assessment of optical imaging modalities. The central idea is that the posterior distribution of tissue parameters, given a multispectral measurement produced by a specific camera, directly reflects the information that the camera provides about the quantities of interest. Characteristics of the posterior, such as its width, the number of modes, and its calibration relative to the ground truth, can therefore be converted into performance metrics that are independent of the particular point-estimating algorithm. By applying the framework to different camera configurations on identical simulated tissue, differences in the metrics can be attributed to the hardware.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we introduce a method for hardware assessment based on conditional INNs that maps each multispectral measurement to a full posterior, and we define metrics that capture distinct types of uncertainty, including ambiguity represented by multiple modes. Second, we validate the approach on a controlled use case, namely the selection of spectral bands for the estimation of physiological parameters, and we show how well-posed and ill-posed estimation tasks can be distinguished. Third, we derive application-relevant insights on the estimation of oxygenation and blood volume fraction and on the dependence of ambiguity on the number of spectral bands. Together, these contributions provide a basis for optimizing optical camera design in an application-specific and uncertainty-aware manner.

Methods

Overview of the assessment framework

The proposed framework evaluates an optical imaging modality by quantifying how well tissue parameters can be recovered from the modality's multispectral measurements, accounting for aleatoric ambiguity as well as measurement noise. It comprises four components: (i) a forward model that simulates tissue reflectance from physiological parameters, (ii) a camera model that converts reflectance spectra into the measurements of a specific hardware configuration, (iii) an invertible neural network (INN) trained to approximate the posterior distribution of tissue parameters given a measurement, and (iv) a set of performance metrics computed from the resulting posteriors. Following the formulation of Ardizzone et al. (2019), we treat the inverse problem as the estimation of p(θ | y), where θ ∈ ℝ^D denotes the tissue parameters and y ∈ ℝ^C the C-channel measurement.

Tissue model and data simulation

Tissue was represented as a three-layer structure, a configuration commonly used to approximate perfused soft tissue (Wirkert et al., 2016; Jacques, 2013). Each layer was parameterized by blood volume fraction (vhb), oxygenation (sO2), reduced scattering coefficient at 500 nm (a′), scattering power (b), anisotropy factor (g), refractive index (n), and layer thickness (d). Absorption was modeled as a linear combination of oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin absorption spectra weighted by vhb and sO2 (Prahl, 1999). Scattering followed a power law, μ′s(λ) = a′(λ/500 nm)^(−b). Parameters were sampled independently and uniformly within physiologically plausible ranges: vhb ∈ [0.1%, 25%], sO2 ∈ [0%, 100%], a′ ∈ [5, 50] cm⁻¹, b ∈ [0.3, 3.0], g ∈ [0.8, 0.95], n ∈ [1.33, 1.54], and d ∈ [0.02, 2.0] mm per layer. Because the same priors were used across all experiments, differences in performance can be attributed to the hardware rather than to the data distribution.

Reflectance spectra were generated with a Monte Carlo photon transport simulation (Fang and Boas, 2009) using 10⁶ photons per simulation at 1 nm resolution between 300 and 1000 nm. In total, 500,000 parameter–spectrum pairs were generated. The data were split at the level of parameter sets into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) subsets, ensuring that no parameter configuration appeared in more than one subset.

Camera model

A camera with C spectral bands was modeled by integrating the reflectance spectrum r(λ) with the band-specific spectral response f_c(λ), which combines the filter transmission, sensor quantum efficiency, and illumination:

y_c = ∫ r(λ) f_c(λ) dλ / ∫ f_c(λ) dλ.

To isolate the effect of band number from that of band placement, we assumed idealized Gaussian filter responses with a full width at half maximum of 20 nm, uniformly distributed over 450–720 nm. Configurations with C ∈ {3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 15, 20} bands were considered. As a reference for clinical hardware, we additionally evaluated an RGB camera with broad, overlapping response functions based on a commercial sensor (Basler acA1300, Basler AG, Ahrensburg, Germany) and a 16-band snapshot sensor with measured filter characteristics (Ximea MQ022HG-IM-SM4X4-VIS, Ximea GmbH, Münster, Germany). Measurement noise was modeled as multiplicative Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 3% of the signal, plus an additive component to reflect dark noise, which was applied on the fly during training and testing so that each reflectance spectrum was seen with different noise realizations. Measurements were normalized by the ℓ1 norm to remove dependence on illumination intensity, a standard step in multispectral processing (Wirkert et al., 2016). Normalization renders the measurement vector C−1 dimensional in effect, which we considered in the analysis of band number.

Invertible neural network

The INN learns a bijective mapping between the parameter space and a latent space z. To account for information lost in the forward process, the network maps θ to [y, z], where z ~ N(0, I) captures the variation in θ not explained by y (Ardizzone et al., 2019). The network consisted of a sequence of 8 affine coupling blocks (Dinh et al., 2017), each followed by a fixed random permutation of the variables. Subnetworks within each coupling block were fully connected with two hidden layers of 128 units and ReLU activations. Inputs were zero-padded to a common dimensionality of 32 to increase the expressive capacity of the coupling layers.

Training minimized a composite loss comprising a supervised term on the measurement, L_y, a maximum-likelihood term on the latent variable, L_z, and a maximum mean discrepancy term, L_x, that matches the distribution of parameters obtained by the inverse pass to the prior. Here L_y was the mean squared error between predicted and simulated measurements, L_z was the negative log-likelihood under a standard normal distribution including the log-determinant of the Jacobian, and L_x used a multiscale inverse multiquadratic kernel. Loss weights were set to 1, 1, and 10, respectively. We used the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2015) with an initial learning rate of 10⁻³, halved every 50 epochs, a batch size of 1,000, and 300 epochs. Hyperparameters were selected on the validation set. For each hardware configuration, five networks with different random initializations were trained, and results are reported as means across them.

Posterior estimation

For a given measurement y*, the posterior was approximated by drawing N = 1,000 latent samples z_i ~ N(0, I) and passing each through the inverse network, yielding samples θ_i = g(y*, z_i). Marginal posteriors for individual parameters were obtained by kernel density estimation with bandwidths determined by Scott's rule. To verify that the learned posteriors were calibrated, we computed calibration curves on the test set, comparing the nominal credible-interval coverage with the empirical frequency at which the ground-truth value fell within the interval. We also compared the INN posteriors against reference posteriors obtained through approximate Bayesian computation rejection sampling (Sisson et al., 2018) on 200 randomly selected test measurements, using the Wasserstein-1 distance between marginals.

Performance metrics

Metrics were computed from the marginal posterior of each parameter. Accuracy was quantified through the absolute error between the posterior median and the ground truth. Because a single point estimate cannot reflect ambiguity, we additionally defined (i) the posterior width, taken as the interquartile range of the samples, representing the overall uncertainty, and (ii) the number of posterior modes, determined by counting the peaks of the kernel density estimate whose prominence exceeded 10% of the maximum density. Measurements with more than one mode were designated ambiguous. As a summary of well-posedness for a parameter, we report the fraction of test measurements with a unimodal posterior, together with the median posterior width. Calibration error was summarized as the mean absolute deviation of the calibration curve from the diagonal. These metrics were aggregated over the test set for each camera configuration.

Experiments and statistical analysis

Three experiments were performed. First, we validated the framework by assessing calibration and agreement with the ABC reference posteriors. Second, we analyzed the well-posedness of estimating sO2 and vhb for the full range of camera configurations, and visualized the relationship between band number and each metric. Third, we investigated the influence of the noise level (1%, 3%, 10%) on posterior width and modality for a fixed 8-band camera. Differences between configurations were assessed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over test samples with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and a significance level of α = 0.05 was applied. Effect sizes are reported as medians with interquartile ranges, and 95% confidence intervals for means were obtained by bootstrapping with 1,000 resamples. All models were implemented in PyTorch with the FrEIA library and trained on a single NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti GPU.

Results

**Validation of the invertible neural network**

We first verified that the invertible neural network (INN; Ardizzone et al., 2019) yields reliable posterior estimates before using it for hardware assessment. The network was trained on 500,000 Monte Carlo-simulated tissue spectra (Wirkert et al., 2016), each parameterized by blood volume fraction, oxygenation, scattering, anisotropy, layer thickness and a multiplicative intensity factor. The simulations were restricted to the physiologically plausible parameter ranges reported by Jacques (2013). On a held-out test set of 50,000 spectra, the INN posteriors were compared to reference posteriors obtained with approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) rejection sampling, using 10⁷ forward simulations per query on a subset of 200 measurements. The median Wasserstein-1 distance between the INN and ABC marginals was 0.021 (interquartile range, IQR, 0.012–0.038) for oxygenation and 0.034 (0.019–0.061) for blood volume fraction, with parameters normalized to the unit interval. Inference required 4.1 ms per spectrum for 1,000 posterior samples on a single GPU, compared with several minutes per spectrum for ABC. Calibration was assessed by the empirical coverage of central credible intervals. For nominal 68% and 95% intervals, the INN achieved mean coverage of 66.8% and 94.1% for oxygenation, and 67.5% and 94.6% for blood volume fraction.
