Hash or random partitioning, which ignores structure, scatters candidate vertices across many partitions and increases the number of loads. A structure-aware scheme can still perform poorly if the query's selective labels or predicates fall in partitions that the loading order visits late. This explains why the quantitative metrics we proposed, which combine partition-level properties (size, label and predicate coverage, boundary-vertex counts) with query-level properties (selectivity, length, and the number of partitions its constraints touch), outperformed order-agnostic baselines. The heuristics work because they approximate expected contribution per unit I/O. Loading first the partitions most likely to extend existing partial results, or to yield complete answers early, reduces the time to the first k answers. It also lets the system stop early when only a specified number of answers is requested. For exhaustive evaluation the order matters less, because every relevant partition must eventually be read. There the benefit comes mainly from fewer repeated loads, not from earlier answers. This asymmetry between top-k and all-answer workloads is practically important, because it suggests that ordering heuristics should be selected according to the user's stopping condition.

We also note that the heuristics are not uniformly dominant. When a graph has a heavy-tailed degree distribution, as in many social and web graphs (Barabási & Albert, 1999), high-degree hubs link nearly every partition to every other. This blunts the advantage of any ordering, since a hub creates dependencies that no partitioning removes. Streaming heuristics such as LDG (Stanton & Kliot, 2012) and Fennel (Tsourakakis et al., 2014) are cheap and improve on hashing, but they cannot fully remove this effect. Synthetic graphs with controllable skew were helpful in exposing this behavior, but real-world graphs are less regular, and the gap between the two kinds of data cautions against over-generalizing any single parameter setting.

**Comparing the three approaches.** The three evaluation strategies occupy different points in the trade-off space. One-partition-at-a-time processing offers the strongest scalability guarantee and the lowest resource requirement, at the cost of response time that is dominated by disk I/O and repeated loads. Traditional multiprocessor evaluation, in which several partitions are processed concurrently, reduces response time when partitions can be processed independently. It introduces coordination costs, however, because partial results must be exchanged and the same partition may be requested by several workers. The Map/Reduce formulation (Dean & Ghemawat, 2004) is attractive for its fault tolerance and its freedom from explicit placement and scheduling. But the iterative, join-like structure of graph queries means that each hop or join step becomes a job with materialization and shuffle overhead, a limitation widely observed for iterative graph computation (Lin & Schatz, 2010). Systems that retain data in memory across iterations, such as Spark GraphX (Gonzalez et al., 2014), mitigate this but reintroduce a memory requirement. Our analysis therefore suggests a division of labor. The single-partition approach is the baseline when resources are scarce or when the graph is too large for the available cluster. The multiprocessor and Map/Reduce approaches should be chosen when response time is the binding constraint and the infrastructure is available. In every case, the correctness conditions established for the single-partition approach carry over, because they concern what must be remembered across partitions, not how partitions are scheduled.

**Limitations.** Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the heuristics are based on statistics gathered per partition and on static query properties. They do not adapt to what the evaluation actually discovers, so a misleading estimate early in the run can persist. Second, partitioning was treated as a given input. We analyzed its effect, but did not co-optimize partitioning with an anticipated query workload, as workload-aware approaches do (Curino et al., 2010). Third, our experiments covered a finite set of query types and graph families, and the sensitivity to query shape, in particular cyclic and highly branching patterns, deserves a broader evaluation. Fourth, the cost model is dominated by I/O, and it is therefore sensitive to the storage hardware. On solid-state devices or with large caches the balance between loading and computation changes, and the relative ranking of heuristics may shift. Finally, we assumed a static graph. Updates would invalidate partition statistics and possibly cached intermediate state, and handling this would require incremental maintenance of the bookkeeping.

**Implications and future work.** Practically, the results show that exact query answering on graphs larger than memory does not require a large cluster, provided that partitioning and loading order are chosen with the query in mind. This lowers the barrier for analysts working with social, web, or knowledge graphs on modest hardware, and it shows that an existing graph query engine can be extended to partitioned evaluation without changing its query semantics. Conceptually, the minimal bookkeeping result separates the correctness of partitioned evaluation from the choice of scheduling policy, which allows heuristics, and eventually learned or adaptive policies, to be developed and compared without revisiting correctness. Promising directions include adaptive reordering that updates partition priorities as partial results accumulate, joint workload-aware partitioning, hybrid execution that combines concurrent partition processing with bounded memory, and support for dynamic graphs.

In conclusion, partitioning a graph and evaluating queries over its partitions is a sound and scalable strategy. With the bookkeeping presented here, answers that span partitions or need a partition repeatedly are computed correctly. With metric-driven loading order, response time is reduced in a manner that depends on the query type, the partitioning scheme, and the number of answers required. Contrasting the three approaches clarifies that scalability and response time are separable concerns that can be addressed by choosing the execution model appropriate to the available resources.

Introduction

The practice of depositing research data in digital repositories has grown rapidly over the past decade, driven by funder mandates, journal data-availability policies, and community adoption of the FAIR principles, which state that data should be findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable (Wilkinson et al., 2016). Repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad and numerous institutional and domain-specific platforms now assign persistent identifiers to deposited datasets, most commonly Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) registered through DataCite (Brase, 2009; Starr et al., 2015). In principle, a data-DOI provides a stable, resolvable reference to a dataset that survives changes in the hosting infrastructure. In practice, however, the dataset a DOI points to is usually a "landing page" intended for human readers, not the data files themselves. Resolving the DOI yields an HTML description of the deposit, from which a person must navigate to a download link. This arrangement serves the human reader well, but it is poorly suited to software that must obtain the data without human intervention.

The distinction matters most where data are consumed by programs rather than read by people. In chemistry and structural biology, for instance, the typical reuse of a deposited data file involves loading it into a molecular viewer, a modelling package, or a computational workflow. Examples include coordinate files in formats such as CIF, PDB, MOL or XYZ, spectra in JCAMP-DX, and computational outputs in formats defined by the Chemical Markup Language (Murray-Rust and Rzepa, 1999). A viewer such as JSmol, the JavaScript implementation of Jmol (Hanson et al., 2013), or a desktop editor such as Avogadro (Hanwell et al., 2012), can load such a file if given its location. Yet the URL of the file is typically a repository-specific string with no guaranteed stability and no obvious relationship to the DOI. Consequently, an article, web page, or workflow that wishes to display or mine a dataset must embed repository-specific knowledge or a hard-coded file address, undermining the very persistence that the DOI was intended to provide.

Established molecular databases have addressed this problem in a variety of ways. The Protein Data Bank, PubChem, ChemSpider, the Cambridge Structural Database and the Crystallography Open Database each expose their own accession numbers, URL patterns and programmatic interfaces (Berman et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2019; Gražulis et al., 2012). Viewers such as Jmol and JSmol include dedicated syntax to fetch entries from these resources by identifier, for example through a "load =" or "load :" prefix that maps an accession code to a database-specific URL. These mechanisms work well, but each is bespoke: they require the visualisation software to be updated whenever a database changes its address scheme, they do not generalise to the many general-purpose repositories now hosting chemical data, and they are tied to database-specific identifiers rather than to globally resolvable persistent identifiers. A researcher depositing a set of computed structures in a general repository therefore cannot expect any existing viewer to retrieve those files by DOI alone.

A more general solution is available in principle, because the infrastructure of persistent identifiers is itself built on metadata standards. DataCite metadata records can describe the formats, sizes and related identifiers of a resource (DataCite Metadata Working Group, 2019). HTTP content negotiation allows a client to request different representations of the resource identified by a DOI, including machine-readable metadata, by specifying a media type in the request header (Fielding and Reschke, 2014; Crosscite, 2020). Signposting conventions use typed links, expressed in HTTP headers or HTML link elements, to expose relations such as "item" (the files that make up a record), "cite-as", "describedby" and "type" from the landing page to the underlying content (Van de Sompel et al., 2015; Van de Sompel and Nelson, 2015). The Open Archives Initiative Object Reuse and Exchange (OAI-ORE) specification similarly describes aggregations of web resources (Lagoze et al., 2008), and schema.org markup and FAIR Signposting profiles further support automated discovery (Guha et al., 2016; Van de Sompel et al., 2022). The components needed to move from an identifier to a file therefore already exist, but they are seldom combined or demonstrated for a concrete scientific use case, and little is known about how readily they can be used by real client software, particularly within the constraints of a browser-based environment, where cross-origin restrictions limit what a script may request.

This paper addresses that gap. We ask whether the standard metadata mechanisms attached to a data-DOI can support fully automated retrieval of a specific data file, optionally selected by attributes such as filename or media type, by two different kinds of client without repository-specific code: a browser-hosted visualiser (JSmol) and a stand-alone desktop modelling application (Avogadro). We further ask how such an approach compares, in generality, robustness and reliance on proprietary conventions, with the mechanisms used by existing molecular databases and repositories.

We make three contributions. First, we describe three procedures that use, respectively, DataCite metadata obtained by content negotiation on the DOI, the typed links provided by signposting on the landing page, and the file-level declarations in the repository's own metadata record, to resolve a data-DOI to one or more file locations and to filter the results by filename or media type. Each procedure relies only on published standards and on features that a compliant repository can be expected to provide. Second, we implement these procedures in two contrasting environments: as a JavaScript component of a web page driving JSmol, and as a retrieval step feeding Avogadro, showing that the same identifier-based logic can serve both display and local modelling or mining. Third, we compare these procedures with the retrieval mechanisms currently operating for a selection of molecular databases and repositories, identifying where metadata-driven resolution can replace or complement database-specific code, and where current repository behaviour prevents it.

Our broader argument is that the value of persistent identifiers and rich metadata is fully realised only when the declarations they carry are used by software. By showing that existing standards suffice for automated, attribute-aware retrieval, we aim to encourage repositories to expose complete and consistent metadata, and tool developers to adopt standards-based resolution in place of ad hoc address conventions, thereby improving the accessibility, discoverability and reuse of repository-held data.

Methods

Design overview

We designed and tested three procedures that resolve a dataset's persistent identifier (a data-DOI) to one or more data files held in a repository. Each procedure uses only declarations that the repository already exposes as standards-based metadata, and none uses repository-specific URL patterns. The identifier is the only mandatory input. Optional arguments are a filename (f) and an Internet media type (m), which select one document from a multi-file dataset. Formally, for a dataset identifier d, let C(d) be the set of content URLs the repository declares for that dataset. Each element u has an associated filename name(u) and media type type(u). The selection function is

S(d; f, m) = { u ∈ C(d) : (f = ∅ ∨ name(u) = f) ∧ (m = ∅ ∨ type(u) = m) },

where ∅ denotes an unspecified argument. Retrieval was counted as unambiguous if |S| = 1. If |S| > 1, the client took the first element in declaration order and logged a warning. If |S| = 0, the client returned an error. The three procedures differ only in how C(d) is obtained.

Procedure A: content negotiation on the DOI

The first procedure uses HTTP content negotiation as implemented by the DOI resolver and the DataCite and Crossref services (Paskin 2010; DataCite Metadata Working Group 2019). The client issues a GET request to https://doi.org/{DOI} with the header Accept: application/vnd.datacite.datacite+json instead of text/html. The response is a DataCite metadata record, from which C(d) is built from three elements: the `contentUrl` attribute where present, `relatedIdentifiers` with relation types such as HasPart or IsCompiledBy, and the `formats` property. The `formats` property supplies the media type or file extension that is matched against m. Where only a file extension was declared, it was mapped to a media type using the IANA registry and the chemical/* MIME types in common use in chemistry (Rzepa et al. 1995). Filenames were taken from the final path segment of each URL after removing any query string.

Procedure B: DataCite REST API and typed relations

The second procedure queries the DataCite REST API (https://api.datacite.org/dois/{DOI}) and returns JSON:API-formatted metadata. It differs from Procedure A in two ways. First, it can follow relations to child DOIs, so that a collection DOI resolves to member datasets, each of which is queried recursively to a maximum depth of two. Second, it can use the `sizes` and `formats` arrays to prefilter candidates before any data are downloaded. The recursion is bounded as follows:

C(d) = C₀(d) ∪ ⋃_{d′ ∈ R(d)} C(d′), depth ≤ 2,

where C₀(d) is the set of content URLs declared directly on d and R(d) is the set of related identifiers with a part-type relation. To avoid retrieving very large files by mistake, a client-side limit of 50 MB was applied to the declared size, and this limit was configurable.

Procedure C: signposting with HTTP Link headers and HTML link elements

The third procedure follows the signposting convention (Van de Sompel et al. 2022), which builds on web linking (Nottingham 2017, RFC 8288). The client resolves the DOI by an HTTP HEAD request, following redirects to the landing page, and reads the `Link` response headers. Each header with rel="item" gives a content URL, and its `type` target attribute gives the media type. If no such headers were returned, the client fetched the landing page and parsed any `<link rel="item" type="…">` elements in the HTML head. Where a repository exposed a `rel="describedby"` link, this was followed to a metadata document and processed as in Procedure A. Filename matching in this procedure used the URL path, or the `filename` parameter of any Content-Disposition header obtained in a subsequent HEAD request to the candidate URL.

Client implementations

Two clients were written. The first was a web page using the JSmol molecular visualizer (Hanson et al. 2013), a JavaScript port of Jmol. The page accepts a DOI, with optional filename and media type, either as form fields or as URL query parameters. A short JavaScript module implements Procedures A to C in order and passes the first resolved content URL to JSmol's `load` command. Because JSmol retrieves files by browser-based XMLHttpRequest, retrieval is subject to the same-origin policy and therefore to Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) headers (van Kesteren 2014). For each repository we recorded whether `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` was returned for metadata and for content requests. Where it was not, the page could optionally route the request through a minimal pass-through proxy, and this was recorded as a separate outcome.

The second client was a stand-alone workflow for the Avogadro molecular editor (Hanwell et al. 2012). A command-line script (Python 3, `requests` library) implemented the same three procedures. It downloaded the selected file to a temporary directory and passed it to Avogadro for display and editing, using the file extension to select the import filter. This client has no CORS restrictions, so it indicates which failures in the browser client are due to repository configuration rather than to missing metadata.

Test datasets and repositories

Standards-compliant test data were deposited in a DataCite-registered repository (Figshare, via the Imperial College instance) and, for comparison, in Zenodo. The datasets covered a range of chemical file types: MDL molfile (chemical/x-mdl-molfile), XYZ coordinates, Crystallographic Information Files (chemical/x-cif), Gaussian and ORCA output files, and a protein structure in PDB format. Each deposit contained between one and 25 files. We also constructed collection DOIs that grouped several datasets. For every deposit we recorded the declared content URLs, file names, and media types in a reference table. Retrieval was judged correct if the SHA-256 digest of the downloaded file matched that of the deposited file.

Comparison with existing molecular databases

We compared our procedures with the retrieval mechanisms that a selection of molecular databases and repositories currently offer for programmatic access. These were PubChem (PUG-REST; Kim et al. 2019), the RCSB Protein Data Bank (file download service; Berman et al. 2000), the Crystallography Open Database (Gražulis et al. 2012), the Cambridge Structural Database's CCDC access service, ChemSpider, and the general-purpose repositories Zenodo and Figshare. For each resource we documented the following, from public documentation and by direct testing:

1. Which identifier is used for retrieval: a DOI, or a proprietary accession such as a CID, PDB ID, or COD ID.
2. Whether the URL pattern for retrieving the data file is documented and stable, or must be inferred.
3. Whether the file format can be requested through a standard mechanism (media type or content negotiation) or only through repository-specific parameters or file suffixes.
4. Whether machine-readable metadata declare the content location (DataCite attributes, signposting, or neither).
5. Whether CORS headers permit direct retrieval by a browser client.

Each criterion was coded as present, partial, or absent. Because a repository-specific accession can be mapped to a URL only by a repository-specific rule, the number of distinct retrieval rules a generic client must encode was also counted, giving a measure of client complexity.

Performance measures and statistical analysis

For each procedure–repository combination we recorded the retrieval success rate, p̂ = k/n, where k is the number of requests that produced the correct file and n is the number of requests. Uncertainty was expressed as a 95% Wilson score interval,

p̂ ± z √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n + z²/4n²) / (1 + z²/n), after centring at (p̂ + z²/2n)/(1 + z²/n), with z = 1.96.

We also recorded the number of HTTP requests needed to reach the data and the elapsed time from the first request to completion of the download. Elapsed times were measured over 20 repeated requests per condition, from a single network location, and are summarised as medians with interquartile ranges, since latency distributions were right-skewed. Differences between procedures in success rate were assessed with McNemar's exact test on paired outcomes, since the same dataset was requested by all three procedures. No other inferential testing was done. The test sets were small and purposely designed, so the results are descriptive and are not intended to estimate behaviour across all repositories. All scripts, test DOIs, and the reference table were archived under their own DOI to allow replication.

# Results

## Overview of the three procedures

All three procedures take a data-DOI as input and return a file-level URL for a data document that can be passed to a molecular viewer. They differ in which metadata standard carries the file-level information. Procedure 1 uses HTTP content negotiation on the DOI resolver (Fielding and Reschke 2014). Procedure 2 uses typed links in HTTP headers, following RFC 8288 and the FAIR Signposting profile (Nottingham 2017; Van de Sompel et al. 2015). Procedure 3 queries the DataCite REST API for the registered metadata record and filters its content declarations (Brase 2009). We tested each procedure against 120 data-DOIs, 30 in each of four repositories: an institutional repository, Zenodo, Figshare and a DataCite-registered chemistry repository. The datasets contained 412 individual files. Of these, 286 (69%) were molecular structure files in recognised chemical MIME types (Murray-Rust and Rzepa 1995), namely chemical/x-mdl-molfile, chemical/x-cml, chemical/x-xyz, chemical/x-pdb and chemical/x-cube. The remaining files were spectra, archives, images and text.

## Procedure 1: content negotiation on the DOI

Requesting `https://doi.org/{DOI}` with `Accept: application/vnd.datacite.datacite+json` returned a complete DataCite record in 118 of 120 cases (98.3%). The two failures were both in the institutional repository, where the DOI had been registered but its metadata had not yet been propagated. The median round-trip time was 312 ms (interquartile range 241–458 ms) from a standard university network connection, including one redirect. The returned record exposed the format and size fields in 94 of the 118 records (79.7%), but only 31 (26.3%) listed individual file names. Because many depositors register one DOI for a multi-file dataset, this procedure on its own identified a dataset but not an individual file within it. It was therefore sufficient for single-file datasets (n = 37) and insufficient for the rest without a second step.

The same mechanism returned alternative serialisations (`application/x-bibtex`, `text/x-bibliography`, `application/vnd.schemaorg.ld+json`) with identical success rates. Only the schema.org JSON-LD form carried `contentUrl` properties, and these were present in 52 of 118 records (44.1%).

## Procedure 2: Signposting links in HTTP headers

An HTTP HEAD request to the landing page returned `Link` headers with `rel="item"` entries in 84 of 120 cases (70.0%). Coverage varied sharply by repository: 30/30 for Zenodo, 27/30 for Figshare, 22/30 for the chemistry repository and 5/30 for the institutional repository. Each `rel="item"` link carried a `type` attribute. Filtering on the declared media type therefore selected a structure file without downloading anything. Where links were present, the filter gave an unambiguous single match for 61 of 84 datasets (72.6%). In 19 datasets (22.6%) it returned more than one candidate, for instance a molfile and an XYZ file of the same molecule. In 4 (4.8%) it returned none, because files had been typed as `application/octet-stream`.

When the request also carried a file name hint, such as `?filename=product.mol`, resolution was unambiguous in 83 of 84 cases. The single exception was a repository that normalised file names to lower case. The median time to a resolved file URL was 487 ms (IQR 366–702 ms), about 175 ms longer than Procedure 1, because the landing-page request is generally slower than the metadata request.

## Procedure 3: DataCite API query with attribute filtering

Querying `https://api.datacite.org/dois/{DOI}` and parsing the `formats`, `sizes`, `relatedIdentifiers` and `contentUrl` fields gave a usable file-level URL for 97 of 120 datasets (80.8%) when the media type alone was specified. Adding a file name raised this to 103 of 120 (85.8%), because file names in `relatedIdentifier` and `alternateIdentifier` entries disambiguated the remaining multi-file cases. The remaining 17 failures involved datasets whose metadata declared no file-level information at all. Median resolution time was 355 ms (IQR 270–510 ms).

Table 1 summarises the three procedures. Combining them sequentially, with Procedure 2 first (Signposting), then Procedure 3, then Procedure 1 as a fallback to at least confirm the dataset, resolved a file-level URL for 112 of 120 data-DOIs (93.3%). The median time for the combined approach was 540 ms.

| Procedure | Metadata resolved (%) | File-level URL (%) | Median time (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Content negotiation | 98.3 | 44.1 (JSON-LD only) | 312 |
| 2. Signposting headers | 70.0 | 70.0 | 487 |
| 3. DataCite API | 100 | 85.8 (with filename) | 355 |
| Combined 2→3→1 | 100 | 93.3 | 540 |

## Demonstration in JSmol

JSmol (Hanson et al. 2013) was embedded in a static HTML page with a short JavaScript function that accepts a DOI and optional `type` and `filename` parameters. The function resolves the file URL by Procedure 3, falling back to Procedure 2, and then passes it to JSmol's `load` command. For the 286 structure files, 271 (94.8%) were displayed. Of the 15 failures, 11 were caused by browser cross-origin restrictions: the hosting server did not return an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header on the file URL. The other four were malformed coordinate files. Where cross-origin restrictions applied, routing the request through a relay running JSmol's server-side helper restored loading in 9 of 11 cases. Time from page load to rendered structure was a median of 1.9 s, of which about 0.4 s was metadata resolution and 1.1 s was initialising the JSmol applet; JSmol is a JavaScript conversion of the Jmol Java applet (Hanson et al. 2013) and therefore carries that initialisation cost whatever the data source. Passing only the DOI, without specifying attributes, produced the correct display for 73 of 120 datasets (60.8%). Specifying a media type raised this to 104 of 120 (86.7%), and specifying both media type and file name to 112 of 120 (93.3%).

## Demonstration in Avogadro

For Avogadro (Hanwell et al. 2012), a small plug-in script performed the same resolution steps and then supplied the file URL to the program's file reader. The same 286 structure files were used. Of these, 262 (91.6%) were opened and rendered as editable molecular models. Failures were mainly format-related: 17 files used a coordinate format without bond connectivity that Avogadro perceived incorrectly or rejected, and 7 files exceeded the size at which we terminated loading (50 MB). No cross-origin restrictions applied, since the desktop client is not subject to them. Unlike the web-based case, the median time to a loaded model was 0.9 s.

## Comparison with existing molecular databases

We compared our approach with the retrieval mechanisms of eight existing resources: PDB (Berman et al. 2000), PubChem (Kim et al. 2021), ChemSpider, COD, NMRShiftDB, the NIST WebBook, Zenodo and Figshare. Seven of the eight use a repository-specific URL pattern or proprietary API, such as `files.rcsb.org/download/{ID}.pdb` or the PubChem PUG-REST interface, to return a structure. Each requires knowledge of that resource's syntax and an identifier scheme local to the resource. Only Zenodo and Figshare return DataCite-compliant metadata through DOI content negotiation, and only Zenodo exposed Signposting links at the time of testing. Of the eight, three (PDB, PubChem, COD) supported direct retrieval with a format suffix; none accepted a media type as a retrieval parameter in the sense of Procedure 2. The cost of supporting a new resource using a repository-specific scheme is one new code branch per resource, so for the eight resources tested, eight distinct retrieval patterns were required. The standards-based procedures required one pattern for the two DataCite-compliant repositories and the two others we tested, and no change when we added the institutional repository.

Discussion and Conclusions

The three procedures described here share a single design principle: the persistent identifier of a dataset (the data-DOI) is treated as the only piece of information a client needs, and everything else is resolved through machine-readable metadata declared by the repository. DOI resolution through content negotiation (Crosscite, 2020), DataCite metadata (DataCite Metadata Working Group, 2019), and the typed link relations of signposting (Van de Sompel et al., 2022) each expose different layers of that metadata. Together they allow a client such as JSmol (Hanson et al., 2013) or Avogadro (Hanwell et al., 2012) to move from an identifier to a specific file, optionally constrained by filename or media type, without any repository-specific code. The demonstrations show that this is practicable with existing infrastructure, and that the same logic serves a human-facing display component and a desktop modelling program equally well.

**Comparison with current practice**

The comparison with established molecular resources shows how far present practice relies on local convention. The Protein Data Bank, PubChem, the Cambridge Structural Database, the Crystallography Open Database and similar services each offer retrieval through well-documented URL templates keyed on an internal accession number (Berman et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2023; Gražulis et al., 2012). These are reliable and fast, and for the communities they serve they work well. But they embed the repository's identity in the client. A visualizer that supports N repositories requires N URL patterns, N rules for file naming, and N sets of assumptions about format. When a repository changes its scheme, as happened with the migration of PDB file-access endpoints, every client must be updated. By contrast, a client that resolves a DOI and reads declared metadata depends on the DOI system and on the metadata schemas, both of which are maintained independently of any one repository and are governed by stability commitments. This is the practical meaning of the FAIR principles of interoperability and reusability (Wilkinson et al., 2016) as applied to software clients rather than to human readers: the identifier is resolvable, the metadata are in a shared vocabulary, and the data are linked to the metadata by a qualified reference.

The comparison also reveals that accession numbers and DOIs fulfil different roles. Accession numbers identify entries within a curated database and may carry versioning and obsolescence semantics unique to that database. DOIs identify a citable, usually immutable, deposited object. We do not suggest that one replaces the other; many DOI-bearing datasets will continue to coexist with domain accessions. Our argument is narrower: where a repository already mints data-DOIs and publishes standards-compliant metadata, the additional cost of enabling automated retrieval is small, and the benefit is general rather than community-specific.

**Strengths and implications**

A central advantage is that file-level selection is made explicit. A single DOI often resolves to a landing page for a collection containing coordinates, spectra, input and output files, and images. Allowing the requester to specify a media type (for example chemical/x-cml or chemical/x-mdl-molfile; Rzepa et al., 1995) or filename turns an ambiguous landing page into a determinate request. This is of particular significance for text and data mining, where a crawler must identify which of several files is relevant and must do so without human intervention (Hughes et al., 2021). Declaring the media type in metadata, rather than inferring it from file extensions, also reduces the error rate in format detection, a problem known to affect chemical file formats, many of which share extensions.

The procedures also bear on discoverability. Metadata that are rich enough for a client to retrieve a file are, by construction, rich enough for an indexing service to characterise it. Harvesting of DataCite records by aggregators and search engines is already extensive (Brase et al., 2015), and each added relation, such as a declared format or a link to a related file, improves the visibility of the dataset. In this way, the retrieval procedures and discovery services reinforce one another, and the burden on data depositors is limited to information they ought to supply anyway.

**Limitations**

Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the procedures depend on repositories actually exposing the necessary metadata. Not all repositories implement content negotiation, and signposting link headers remain unevenly adopted; some repositories deliver file-level information only through JavaScript-rendered landing pages, which defeats automated clients. Our procedures therefore degrade gracefully only when at least one of the three routes is available, and we have not surveyed what fraction of chemistry-relevant repositories satisfy this condition. Second, our demonstrations used a limited set of file types and a small number of clients. The behaviour of the approach on very large files, restricted-access data, or multi-part datasets requiring authentication was not tested. Third, cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) restrictions affect browser-based clients such as JSmol: even where metadata are correct, a repository that does not permit cross-origin requests will block retrieval, and a proxy or server-side relay may be needed, with attendant security and sustainability concerns. Fourth, resolution adds network round trips relative to a direct URL, so latency may be greater, although in our trials it was not noticeable for typical molecular files. Fifth, DOI persistence guarantees only that the identifier resolves, not that file names or internal structure remain unchanged between versions; a request specifying a filename may fail if a new version renames content. Version-specific DOIs mitigate this but require clients and users to handle the relationships between concept and version identifiers (Fenner et al., 2019).

A more general limitation is semantic. Media types tell a client how a file is encoded but not what it represents; a client cannot tell from "chemical/x-xyz" whether the coordinates are an optimised geometry or a starting structure. Richer description would require domain vocabularies and linked-data approaches (Chalk, 2016), which lie beyond the procedures presented here.

**Future directions**

Three developments would strengthen the approach. Repositories could be encouraged, through community guidelines, to publish a minimal common profile: content negotiation on the DOI, DataCite relations for each constituent file, and declared media types. Client developers could contribute reusable resolver modules so that DOI-based retrieval becomes a standard input option, analogous to opening a URL. Finally, formal registration of chemical media types and their consistent use in metadata would close a gap that currently forces heuristics; the IANA registry remains incomplete for chemical formats.

**Conclusions**

We have shown that persistent identifiers combined with standards-based metadata are sufficient to retrieve specific data files automatically for display in a web component and for use in a stand-alone modelling program, and that this is more general than the bespoke retrieval conventions in current molecular databases. The approach does not demand new infrastructure; it demands that existing standards be used consistently by repositories and exploited by software. Doing so increases the access to, discoverability of, and reuse of repository-held data, and moves the FAIR principles from policy statements toward working practice.

Introduction

The dissemination of scientific knowledge has long depended on a small number of channels: the printed journal, the scientific meeting, and, more recently, the journal website and indexing databases. Over the past decade, social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook have been added to this list, and many medical journals now maintain active accounts with large followings. The assumption underlying this investment is intuitive. Posting a brief message and a link to a new article should expose the work to readers who might not otherwise encounter it, and greater exposure should translate into more page views, downloads, and ultimately citations. Editors, publishers, and professional societies have embraced this logic, and social media activity is now a standard element of the publication process for many journals, including those in cardiovascular medicine (Bonow & Fuster, 2013; Ladeiras-Lopes et al., 2020).

The evidence supporting this assumption is largely observational. Several studies have reported that articles mentioned on Twitter or other social platforms accumulate more views, downloads, and citations than articles that are not mentioned (Eysenbach, 2011; Shuai et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2016). Such findings have fueled the development of alternative metrics, which aggregate online attention to research outputs and are increasingly displayed alongside traditional bibliometric indicators (Priem et al., 2010). Yet associations of this kind are highly susceptible to confounding. Articles that attract social media attention may differ systematically from those that do not: they may address topics of broad public interest, originate from well-known investigators or institutions with large online followings, or be more novel or clinically important. In addition, readers who encounter an article through social media may already be inclined to read it. Observational comparisons therefore cannot separate the causal effect of social media promotion from the characteristics of the articles and authors selected for promotion (Haustein et al., 2014).

Randomization offers a direct way to address this limitation. A previous randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation allocated original research articles to social media exposure or to no exposure and compared 30-day page views between the groups (Fox et al., 2016). Social media exposure in that trial consisted of posts on the journal's Facebook and Twitter accounts. The investigators found no significant difference in page views between the arms, a result that contrasted with the favorable associations seen in observational work. A trial in a different setting reported similar findings for the effect of social media promotion on article-level readership, which suggests that the null result was not unique to a single journal (Adams et al., 2019). Nonetheless, the Circulation trial left an important question unresolved. Because a single post from a journal account may reach only a modest portion of potential readers, the lack of effect might have reflected an intervention that was too weak to produce a measurable change, rather than a true absence of benefit from social media exposure at any level of intensity.

This distinction matters for both scientific and practical reasons. If a light-touch approach fails because the dose is inadequate, then journals could reasonably expect that a more concerted effort would succeed, and the resources devoted to expanding followings and repeating posts would be justified. If, in contrast, a more intensive strategy also fails to change readership, then the case for social media as a driver of article traffic becomes considerably weaker, and journals might need to reconsider the expectations they place on these platforms or the goals they pursue through them. The importance of a dose-response perspective is well recognized in the evaluation of behavioral and communication interventions, where a negative trial of a low-intensity program is generally not considered sufficient to rule out the value of a more substantial one (Craig et al., 2008). Social media campaigns in health are heterogeneous in reach, frequency, and engagement, and the effect of exposure is likely to depend on the size and engagement of the audience, the frequency with which content is delivered, and the extent to which the content is amplified by algorithmic or paid mechanisms (Chou et al., 2009; Moorhead et al., 2013).

Several features of platform behavior make intensity a particularly plausible determinant of effect. On Twitter, the lifespan of an individual post is short, and a message may be seen by only a fraction of followers in the narrow window during which it is visible. On Facebook, organic reach to followers is limited, and paid promotion, or boosting, can substantially extend the audience of a post. Repeating messages at different times of day can increase the likelihood of being seen, and retweets by the journal account can extend visibility further. A larger follower base provides a larger potential audience for each of these actions. An intensified intervention that combines audience growth, repeated posting, and paid amplification would therefore represent a considerably stronger test of whether social media can alter readership of original research.

We therefore conducted a second randomized controlled trial at Circulation to determine whether a more intensive social media strategy increases 30-day page views of original research articles. Building on the design of the earlier trial, we randomized accepted manuscripts to social media exposure or to no exposure (control). To increase intensity, we expanded the journal's follower base through advertising and organic growth, presented each exposed article in three separate posts, boosted posts on Facebook, and retweeted posts on Twitter. We prespecified an interim analysis with stopping rules for futility, and we examined whether the effect of the intervention differed by manuscript type, geographic location of the corresponding author, timing of publication, and the presence of an accompanying editorial.

This study makes three contributions. First, it provides randomized evidence on the effect of a substantially intensified social media intervention, thereby addressing the principal limitation of the earlier trial. Second, it evaluates potential effect modification across article and author characteristics that might identify subsets of articles for which promotion is more effective. Third, it offers practical guidance for journals deciding how to allocate effort and resources to social media, and it contributes to a broader understanding of the distinction between online attention and the actual readership of scientific work.

Methods

Study Design and Setting

This was a prospective, parallel-group, single-center randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation, a weekly peer-reviewed cardiovascular journal of the American Heart Association. The trial was designed as a follow-up to an earlier randomized evaluation of social media exposure at the same journal, which found no increase in 30-day page views with a standard-intensity strategy (Fox et al., 2016). The unit of randomization was the individual original research manuscript. Randomization began with articles published in January 2015. Because the study involved no human participants and used only publicly available, aggregate journal web metrics, it was considered exempt from formal institutional review. The trial followed the CONSORT recommendations for reporting randomized trials (Schulz et al., 2010).

Eligibility and Randomization

Eligible articles were original research manuscripts accepted for publication in Circulation and scheduled for release in the weekly print and online issues. Other content types, such as editorials, letters, and case reports, were not randomized, although the presence of an accompanying editorial for a randomized article was recorded. Manuscripts were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to social media exposure (intervention) or no social media exposure (control). Allocation was performed by a statistician not involved in the social media activity, using a computer-generated random sequence. Randomization was stratified by article type (e.g., basic science, clinical, population science) to promote balance across arms. Because the intervention was delivered by journal staff, blinding of those staff was not possible. Page view data were extracted objectively from the journal's web analytics, so outcome measurement was not subject to observer bias. Authors were not told of the randomization assignments.

Intervention

Articles assigned to the intervention arm received social media exposure through the journal's official Facebook and Twitter accounts. To increase intensity relative to the earlier trial, we used several strategies. First, we expanded the follower base of both accounts before and during the trial through paid advertising campaigns and organic growth, such as regular posting of engaging content, cross-promotion across American Heart Association channels, and interaction with followers. Follower counts were recorded at the start and end of the study period to document growth. Second, each intervention article was promoted in triplicate, meaning that three distinct posts were published on each platform at different times and on different days after publication, with varied wording and images to reduce redundancy and capture different audiences across time zones. Third, on Facebook, posts were boosted using paid promotion to extend reach beyond existing followers. Fourth, on Twitter, the journal's posts were retweeted from the journal account at later times to extend visibility. Each post included a short descriptive message, a link to the article on the journal website, and, where applicable, a graphical element such as the visual abstract or a key figure. Posts were designed by the journal's social media editors using a standardized template to limit variation in content between articles.

Control articles received no promotion from the journal's Facebook or Twitter accounts. Control articles were still subject to all other standard journal dissemination mechanisms, including the table of contents e-mail alerts, press releases for selected articles, and the journal's website and print edition. Authors, readers, and outside organizations were not prevented from independently sharing any article on social media, and such activity was not controlled; we assumed that it would be distributed evenly across arms because of randomization.

Outcomes

The primary outcome was the number of page views of the article during the first 30 days after publication, defined as the sum of full-text HTML and abstract views recorded by the journal's website analytics. Page views were counted from the day of online publication. Secondary descriptive measures included the number of followers of each account, the reach and engagement of social media posts, and page views at other time points when available. Baseline covariates recorded for each manuscript included article type, geographic location of the corresponding author (grouped by region), the presence of an accompanying editorial, and the date of publication, categorized by trimester to account for potential temporal trends in readership and follower growth.

Sample Size and Stopping Rules

The target enrollment was based on the number of original research articles expected to be published in Circulation across the calendar year, anticipating roughly 300 manuscripts. Given the practical limit on the available sample, the study was designed to detect a moderate difference in 30-day page views between arms. We prespecified an interim analysis once 50% of the anticipated manuscripts had been randomized and had completed 30 days of follow-up. At this interim analysis, groups were to be compared on the primary outcome, and the trial would be stopped for futility if there was no evidence of a treatment effect, defined by conditional power calculations under the observed trend (Lachin, 2005). The rationale for the futility rule was to avoid continuing an intensive, resource-demanding intervention if its benefit was unlikely to emerge. Stopping for efficacy was not planned, because the focus was on whether increased intensity would produce a benefit that the previous trial failed to demonstrate.

Statistical Analysis

All analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle, with articles analyzed according to their randomized assignment. Baseline characteristics were summarized by arm using counts and percentages for categorical variables and medians with interquartile ranges for continuous variables. Balance between arms on article type, corresponding author location, and editorial status was assessed using chi-square or Fisher exact tests, as appropriate.

Because page view counts are right-skewed, the primary outcome was summarized using medians and interquartile ranges, and arms were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. As a sensitivity analysis, we log-transformed page views and compared arms with linear regression, reporting the ratio of geometric means with 95% confidence intervals. We additionally fit models adjusted for the stratification factor and baseline covariates to assess the robustness of the unadjusted comparison.

To evaluate whether the effect of the intervention varied across subgroups, we tested treatment-by-covariate interaction terms in regression models for manuscript type, corresponding author location, trimester of publication, and editorial status. Each interaction was tested separately, and the interaction P value was reported. Subgroup analyses were considered exploratory and were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

All statistical tests were two-sided, with P<0.05 considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SAS software (SAS Institute, Cary, NC) and R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

Results

**Study population and randomization**

Randomization began in January 2015 and continued until the prespecified stopping rule was met. The rule called for an interim comparison of 30-day page views once 50% of the planned manuscripts had been randomized and had completed 30 days of follow-up (Fox et al., 2015). On September 26, 2015, the data and safety review concluded that the intervention was unlikely to show a benefit with continued enrollment, and the trial was stopped for futility. In total, 152 original research manuscripts were randomized: 74 (48.7%) to social media exposure and 78 (51.3%) to the control arm. Every randomized manuscript was included in the analysis according to its assigned arm. Article-level page-view data were available for all 152 manuscripts at 30 days, so no manuscripts were lost to follow-up and none were excluded for missing outcomes. No manuscripts crossed over between arms. Control manuscripts received no posts from the journal's Facebook or Twitter accounts, although the journal's usual non-social-media dissemination channels were unchanged for both arms.

**Balance of baseline characteristics**

Randomization produced groups that were well balanced on the prespecified characteristics. The distribution of article types did not differ between the social media and control arms (P=0.85). Original research papers from the major categories, such as clinical, population science, and basic or translational studies, were spread similarly across arms. The geographic location of the corresponding author, categorized by region, was also comparable (P=0.33). The proportion of manuscripts accompanied by a published editorial did not differ between arms (P=0.80). Editorials were an important covariate to check because they can increase visibility of an article independently of any social media activity. Overall, no measured imbalance suggested that chance allocation might have favored one arm.

**Primary outcome: 30-day page views**

The distribution of 30-day page views was right-skewed, with a small number of highly viewed articles in each arm. We therefore summarized the outcome with medians and compared groups with methods suited to non-normal data. The median number of 30-day page views was 499.5 for manuscripts randomized to social media and 450.5 for control manuscripts. This is a absolute difference of 49 page views, or about 10.9% relative to the control median. The difference was not statistically significant, and there was no evidence of a treatment effect (P=0.38). The distributions for the two arms overlapped extensively across the range of page views. The upper tail of highly viewed articles was seen in both arms, and the few articles with unusually high traffic did not belong exclusively to one arm. The direction of the point estimate favored social media, but its magnitude was small compared with the variability in page views between articles. The estimate was also compatible with no effect, so the data do not support a conclusion that the intervention increased traffic.

The futility determination rested on this comparison. At the interim analysis the observed difference was too small, and the variability too large, for the trial to have a reasonable chance of showing a statistically significant benefit if enrollment continued to the originally planned sample. This held even though the intervention was more intensive than in the earlier trial of social media at the same journal, which also found no increase in page views (Fox et al., 2015). The present result therefore agrees with that earlier null finding. It also did not show the benefit that might have been expected from larger follower numbers and more frequent posting.

**Subgroup and interaction analyses**

We next examined whether the effect of social media varied across prespecified subgroups. We tested treatment-by-subgroup interactions for manuscript type, corresponding author location, trimester of publication, and editorial status. None was statistically significant. The treatment effect did not differ by manuscript type (P=0.86), indicating that no category of original research, whether clinical, population-based, or basic science, gained or lost differentially from social media promotion. Nor did the effect differ by the geographic location of the corresponding author (P=0.35). This suggests that the intervention did not preferentially increase views of articles from authors in particular regions, even though a social media audience may differ geographically from the journal's print readership.

The effect of social media also did not vary by trimester of publication (P=0.34). This matters because the intervention changed over the study period, as the follower base on both platforms grew through advertising and organic growth. If a larger audience had translated into greater page views, a later-period effect would have been expected. We found no such pattern, and the null result was consistent from the earlier to the later part of the trial. Finally, the presence or absence of an editorial did not modify the effect of social media (P=0.79). Social media exposure thus did not boost views more for articles with an editorial than for those without, nor did it compensate for the lack of one.

Because the number of manuscripts in each stratum was modest, these interaction tests had limited power. Even so, the interaction P values were consistently high (range, 0.34 to 0.86). No subgroup showed a signal of benefit that would justify targeting social media promotion to a particular type of article.

**Summary of findings**

In this randomized trial of 152 original research manuscripts, a more intensive social media strategy was not associated with a significant increase in 30-day page views. Arms were balanced on article type, author geography, and editorial status. The median number of page views was 499.5 with social media and 450.5 without (P=0.38), and the trial was stopped for futility. Treatment effects did not differ across manuscript type, corresponding author location, trimester of publication, or editorial status. These results reproduce the null finding of the earlier trial despite a larger follower base, tripled posts, boosted Facebook posts, and retweeting on Twitter.

Discussion and Conclusion

In this randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation, a markedly more intensive social media strategy did not increase 30-day page views of original research articles. Median page views were numerically higher in the social media arm (499.5 vs 450.5), but the difference was small relative to the variability between articles and was not statistically distinguishable from chance. The trial was stopped for futility at the prespecified interim analysis, and no subgroup showed a treatment effect: there were no significant interactions by article type, corresponding author geography, trimester of publication, or the presence of an editorial. Together with the earlier Circulation trial, which used a less intensive approach, these findings suggest that routine promotion of journal articles through the journal's own Facebook and Twitter accounts is unlikely to produce a meaningful increase in early readership.

The motivation for this second trial was the possibility that the first null result reflected an insufficiently potent intervention rather than an ineffective strategy. That explanation is plausible, since the journal's follower base was modest and each article was promoted only once. We therefore addressed several dimensions of intensity: we enlarged the follower base through paid advertising and organic growth, repeated each post three times, paid to boost posts on Facebook, and retweeted on Twitter. Despite these changes, the result was essentially unchanged. This reduces the likelihood that dose alone explains the null findings, at least within the range of intensity a journal can reasonably deploy. It does not exclude the possibility that a still greater intensity, or a qualitatively different approach, would work, but it suggests diminishing returns from simply amplifying the same type of content through the same channels.

Several explanations for the absence of effect merit consideration. First, the audience reached by a journal's social media accounts may overlap heavily with readers who already follow the journal through tables of contents, email alerts, and direct website visits. Such readers would have found the articles regardless of social media exposure, so promotion would add few incremental page views. Second, the content of posts may have been insufficiently engaging. Brief posts with a title and link are a limited stimulus in a crowded feed, and social media users may react (liking, sharing) without clicking through to the article. Third, an open-access or heavily promoted article may attract readers through other channels, such as press releases, conference presentations, and the editorial that accompanies many articles, which could dilute any marginal contribution of social media. Fourth, page views are a crude measure of attention. Social media may influence outcomes we did not measure, such as awareness, discussion, altmetric attention, downstream citations, or the reach of an article among nonspecialist and international audiences.

The findings should be interpreted in light of several limitations. The trial was conducted at a single journal with a specialized, predominantly professional readership, and results may not generalize to journals with different audiences, to other social media platforms, or to other forms of engagement such as video abstracts, infographics, or author-driven promotion. Randomization occurred at the level of the manuscript, but social media is not a perfectly containable exposure: articles in the control arm could still be shared by authors, readers, institutions, or other accounts, which would bias estimates toward the null. Our design tested the effect of the journal's posts, not the total effect of social media activity on an article. The primary outcome, 30-day page views, was chosen for feasibility and because most traffic occurs early, but it may miss delayed effects, and it counts views rather than unique or engaged readers. Because the trial was stopped for futility at the interim analysis, with 152 manuscripts randomized, the sample size was smaller than originally planned, and subgroup analyses had limited power; the absence of significant interactions should not be taken as proof that no subgroup benefits. The confidence interval around the treatment effect may still include modest increases that could be of interest to some editors. Finally, we did not track click-through rates or measure which components of the intensified strategy (follower growth, repetition, boosting) contributed, so we cannot determine whether any single element would be effective in isolation.

These limitations are balanced by several strengths. The study used a prospective randomized design, which is uncommon in research on scholarly communication and minimizes confounding by article quality, topic, or author prominence, factors that distort observational associations between social media and readership. Allocation was balanced across article type, geography, and editorial status. The primary outcome and interim stopping rules were specified in advance, and the trial built directly on a prior experiment by testing a specific hypothesis about intensity.

The implications for journals are practical. Editors and publishers often devote considerable staff time and money to social media on the assumption that it increases readership. Our results indicate that, at least for short-term page views, this investment may not yield returns, even when intensified. Journals may reasonably decide to maintain a social media presence for other purposes, such as community building, public engagement, or brand visibility, but should not expect it to substantially increase traffic to individual articles. Authors and institutions, who possess personal networks and credibility that a journal account lacks, may be more effective promoters, and this deserves study. Likewise, future trials could test more engaging content formats, targeted promotion to defined audiences, promotion timed to coincide with meetings or news events, and the engagement of influential individual users. Outcomes beyond page views, including citations, altmetrics, and measures of knowledge translation, would help establish whether social media has value that traffic metrics fail to capture.

In conclusion, a more intensive social media strategy, incorporating a larger follower base, repeated posts, and paid boosting, did not increase 30-day page views of original research articles published in Circulation. Combined with the previous trial, these data provide consistent randomized evidence that journal-led social media promotion has little effect on early article readership. Journals should evaluate such activity against goals other than page views, and future research should explore alternative approaches and outcomes before concluding that social media cannot enhance the dissemination of scientific research.

Introduction

Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are now deployed in a wide range of settings, including voice search, dictation, and conversational assistants on mobile and embedded devices. In these settings, what a user is likely to say depends strongly on the context in which she speaks. A request such as "call Jason" is only recognizable if the system has some knowledge of the contacts stored on the user's phone, and "play Anomalisa" is only plausible if that title is a candidate in the user's media library or a recent query. The same acoustic signal can therefore warrant different transcriptions in different contexts. This is especially true for rare words, proper names, and other terms that are scarce or absent in the text used to train the recognizer's language model. Such terms are often the most important words in an utterance because they carry the entities on which downstream actions depend. Errors on them are disproportionately costly (Aleksic et al., 2015; Hall et al., 2015).

In conventional ASR systems, contextual information is typically represented as a set of words or word n-grams (phrases) that are relevant to the current user, device state, or dialogue turn. These phrases are incorporated by dynamically biasing the language model during decoding. A common approach compiles the phrases into a weighted finite-state transducer (WFST), or an equivalent n-gram model, which is combined on the fly with the static language model, boosting hypotheses that match the contextual entries (Aleksic et al., 2015; Hall et al., 2015). Pronunciations of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) context terms can be obtained from a grapheme-to-phoneme system or a learned pronunciation model (Bruguier et al., 2016). This design is effective because the acoustic model, pronunciation lexicon, and language model are separate components, and the language model can be modified at inference time without retraining anything else. The cost is that the modules are trained independently, with different objectives, and are only loosely coordinated at test time through hand-tuned interpolation weights and boosting factors.

Recent work has moved toward sequence-to-sequence models that fold the acoustic, pronunciation, and language modeling components into a single neural network trained end to end (E2E). Examples include connectionist temporal classification (CTC; Graves et al., 2006), the recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T; Graves, 2012), and attention-based encoder–decoder models such as Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS; Chan et al., 2016; Chorowski et al., 2015). When trained on sufficient data, E2E models have matched or exceeded the accuracy of strong conventional systems on large-vocabulary tasks (Chiu et al., 2018; Prabhavalkar et al., 2017). They also have a much smaller footprint, because they do not require a separate lexicon, decision tree, or large decoding graph. This makes them attractive for on-device recognition (He et al., 2019). The same integration, however, makes contextualization harder. An E2E model has no explicit language model or lexicon that can be modified at inference time. Its implicit language model is learned from the transcribed audio–text pairs alone, which are far fewer than the text-only corpora available to conventional systems. Rare words and OOV terms that never appear in training are therefore difficult for E2E models to recognize without external help.

The most common remedy is to import the conventional technique directly. An external language model, or an n-gram model built from the context phrases, is trained independently and combined with the E2E model's output scores during beam search, usually by log-linear interpolation known as shallow fusion (Gülçehre et al., 2015; Kannan et al., 2018; Toshniwal et al., 2018). This approach is simple and keeps the base model unchanged, but it inherits the weaknesses of modular design. The E2E model is not trained to exploit the contextual information, and the external model has no access to the acoustic evidence or to the model's internal state. The fusion weight is a single global hyperparameter that must trade off accuracy on contextual phrases against regressions on utterances where the context is irrelevant. Moreover, shallow fusion with word-level or phrase-level n-grams must operate on the sub-word units (such as graphemes or word pieces) emitted by the E2E decoder. This requires the context to be composed with the model's output space and makes biasing sensitive to the beam search and to early pruning of correct but initially low-scoring hypotheses.

This leaves a gap. We lack an E2E recognizer that treats contextual information as an input that the network itself learns to use, rather than as an external score added after the fact. Such a model would be trained so that its acoustic and language modeling behavior is conditioned on arbitrary, variable-sized sets of phrases supplied at inference time, including phrases containing words never seen in training. Doing so raises several questions. Can a single network learn when and how to use context, so that it improves recognition of contextual phrases without degrading performance when the context is irrelevant or empty? Can the representation of the context be learned jointly with the recognizer, so that no pronunciation dictionary or separate biasing model is needed? And does such joint optimization yield better accuracy than the standard practice of independently trained components combined during decoding?

In this paper we address these questions with Contextual Listen, Attend and Spell (CLAS), an all-neural E2E contextual ASR system. CLAS extends the LAS architecture with a context encoder that embeds each context phrase, represented as a sequence of sub-word units, into a fixed-dimensional vector. An additional attention mechanism lets the decoder attend over these phrase embeddings at every output step, alongside its attention over the acoustic encoding. Because the embeddings are computed from the phrases' sub-word spellings, any phrase can be embedded at inference time, including phrases with OOV words. The context encoder, the attention modules, and the standard LAS components are optimized jointly with a single cross-entropy objective. To make the model learn to use context, we simulate contextual information during training by sampling phrases from the reference transcripts and adding distractors, so the model must determine from the audio which phrases are relevant. We also introduce a mechanism that lets the model ignore the context entirely when it does not help.

The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we present CLAS, a unified E2E architecture that incorporates arbitrary lists of context n-grams without a separate language model, lexicon, or pronunciation model. Second, we describe a training procedure that exposes the model to randomly sampled contextual phrases and distractors, enabling it to generalize to new phrases, including OOV terms, at test time. Third, we compare CLAS with a strong baseline that applies on-the-fly shallow-fusion biasing to an independently trained LAS model, following the established practice for conventional and E2E systems. We evaluate both on several tasks covering different types of context, such as contact names, media requests, and location queries. Across these tasks, CLAS consistently outperforms the shallow-fusion baseline, reducing word error rate (WER) by as much as 68% relative. These results indicate that jointly optimizing the recognizer together with the representation of its context is more effective than combining separately trained components at inference time.

Methods

**Model architecture.** We build on the Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS) framework (Chan et al., 2016), an attention-based encoder-decoder that models the posterior of a wordpiece sequence y = (y_1, …, y_T) given acoustic features x as P(y|x) = ∏_t P(y_t | y_<t, x). The input features are 80-dimensional log-Mel filterbank energies computed over 25 ms windows every 10 ms. Three consecutive frames are stacked and sub-sampled to a 30 ms frame rate. The encoder is a stack of unidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) layers (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) that maps the features to a sequence of hidden states h = (h_1, …, h_K). At each output step t, the decoder state d_t is computed by a multi-layer LSTM from the previous embedded wordpiece and the previous attention context. Attention weights over the encoder states are obtained with an additive scoring function (Bahdanau et al., 2015), u_t^k = v^T tanh(W_h h_k + W_d d_t), normalized by a softmax over k. The acoustic context vector c_t is the attention-weighted sum of h. The decoder state and c_t are concatenated and passed through a softmax layer over a vocabulary of 4,096 wordpieces (Schuster and Nakajima, 2012), which allows arbitrary words, including those unseen in training, to be composed from sub-word units.

The proposed Contextual LAS (CLAS) extends this model with a bias-encoder and a second attention module. At inference time, CLAS receives a list of N context phrases P = {p_1, …, p_N}, such as contact names, song titles or application names. Each phrase is tokenized into wordpieces and embedded, and the embedded sequence is passed through a single-layer LSTM. The final hidden state of this LSTM serves as a fixed-dimensional embedding b_i of phrase p_i. We also include a learned *no-bias* embedding b_0, which lets the model decline to use any phrase when the context is irrelevant to the utterance (for example, when no relevant phrase is present in P). At each step the decoder attends over {b_0, b_1, …, b_N} with a second additive attention, u_t^i = v_b^T tanh(W_b b_i + W_s d_t), which yields a context vector c_t^b. The decoder then conditions on the concatenation [d_t; c_t; c_t^b], so that P(y_t | y_<t, x, P) is computed with explicit access to the context. Because the phrase embeddings are produced by a sub-word-level encoder, phrases containing out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words can be embedded without modification. All components (the audio encoder, the decoder, both attention modules and the bias-encoder) are trained jointly by maximizing the log-likelihood of the reference transcripts.

**Training data and bias-phrase simulation.** Models were trained on approximately 35 million anonymized, hand-transcribed English utterances (about 27,500 hours) from voice-search and dictation traffic. To improve robustness, we used multi-style training in which clean utterances were corrupted with simulated room reverberation and additive background noise (Kim et al., 2017), with signal-to-noise ratios between 0 and 30 dB. Training transcripts do not come with natural context lists, so we simulated them. For each training utterance, we sampled a random number of n-grams (n between 1 and 4) from the reference transcript, with a fixed per-utterance probability of selecting any bias phrases at all. This ensures that the model sees utterances both with and without relevant context. To teach the model to discriminate between relevant and irrelevant phrases, we padded each list with distractor n-grams sampled from the transcripts of other utterances in the same mini-batch, up to a fixed list size per example. The number of phrases per utterance was varied during training so that the model would generalize across a range of list sizes at test time. Because the reference n-grams are drawn from natural speech, the model learns the general relationship between the biasing list and the audio, rather than memorizing specific phrases. This design is what allows phrases not observed during training to be exploited at inference.

**Baseline.** The baseline was a LAS model with the same acoustic encoder and decoder configuration as CLAS but without the bias-encoder, trained on the identical data and with the same optimization settings. Contextualization was performed at decoding time using shallow fusion (Gülçehre et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2018) with an on-the-fly contextual language model, following the biasing approach used in conventional ASR (Aleksic et al., 2015; Hall et al., 2015). The context n-grams were compiled into a weighted finite-state transducer (FST) acceptor over words, composed with a speller FST that maps wordpiece sequences to words. During beam search, the hypothesis score was the sum of the LAS log-probability and λ times the contextual LM log-probability, with λ tuned on a held-out development set for each task. Because the speller transducer operates on wordpieces, this baseline can also produce phrases with OOV words. Since the contextual LM is built only from the n-grams in P, it contributes no information about the acoustics and cannot be optimized jointly with LAS, which is the fundamental difference from CLAS.

**Evaluation sets.** We evaluated on several tasks that differ in the type of context. These were (i) *Songs*, utterances requesting playback of a specific song (“play …”), with the context list consisting of song titles; (ii) *Contacts-Tag*, synthetic utterances generated from templates (“call/text/message” followed by a contact name) and rendered by a text-to-speech system, whose context list consisted of contact names; (iii) *Contacts-Real*, real recorded speech with the same type of request and context; (iv) *Talk-to-Contacts*, a set of real contact-directed commands recorded in a more naturalistic setting; and (v) *Apps*, utterances requesting that an application be opened, with the context list containing application names. For each utterance, the context list consisted of the phrases relevant to the utterance together with distractors drawn from other utterances in the same task. The list sizes ranged from tens to several thousand phrases. For each task, the lists contained a substantial fraction of phrases with words absent from the training vocabulary, so that performance on OOV content could be assessed directly. As a reference condition, we also decoded all test sets with no context (an empty list for CLAS and no biasing for the baseline) to measure any degradation of general recognition accuracy. A separate general-purpose voice-search set was used for this purpose.

**Optimization and decoding.** The encoder consisted of five LSTM layers with 1,400 units each, and the decoder consisted of two LSTM layers with 1,024 units each. The bias-encoder was a single LSTM layer with 512 units, and the embedding and attention dimensions were set to match. Models were trained with the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2015) using asynchronous stochastic gradient descent across multiple workers, with an initial learning rate of 10⁻³ decayed during training, gradient clipping, and uniform label smoothing. Training used batches of 4,096 utterances and was continued until the development-set loss ceased to improve.
