The product is often a diagram or narrative, developed through participatory processes involving stakeholders, that serves as a shared representation of the intervention logic.

The appeal of ToC is considerable. International development agencies, philanthropic foundations and government departments now frequently request or require a ToC in funding applications, programme planning and monitoring frameworks (Vogel, 2012; Stein and Valters, 2012). Proponents argue that ToC encourages clearer thinking about the problem and the intended solution, promotes dialogue among stakeholders, exposes unrealistic or untested assumptions, and provides a framework for selecting indicators and interpreting evaluation findings (Anderson, 2005; De Silva et al., 2014). In public health, where interventions are often delivered across health, social and environmental sectors and rely on behaviour change by multiple actors, these attributes seem particularly valuable. ToC has been applied to areas as diverse as HIV prevention, maternal and child health, mental health, tobacco control and health systems strengthening.

Despite this popularity, ToC is used inconsistently and its definition is contested. The term is applied to logic models, logframes, results chains, conceptual frameworks, impact pathways and more elaborate causal maps, often interchangeably (Rogers, 2008; Breuer et al., 2016). Some authors treat ToC as a planning tool to be used at the outset of intervention design; others use it retrospectively to reconstruct the logic of an existing programme; still others treat it as an evaluation framework against which data are collected and findings interpreted. ToC may be drawn from social science theory, from empirical evidence, from the tacit knowledge of programme staff, or from combinations of these, and the extent to which it is actually informed by formal theory varies widely (Davidoff et al., 2015). Several commentators have noted that the term is sometimes invoked superficially, with a diagram produced to satisfy a funder but with little influence on how the intervention is designed, implemented or evaluated (Stein and Valters, 2012; Vogel, 2012). Without transparent accounts of how a ToC was developed and used, it is difficult to judge its quality, to learn from others' experience, or to assess whether the claimed benefits are realised.

Existing guidance on ToC is largely found in practitioner manuals and grey literature produced by evaluation organisations and funders, and it is not always consistent about recommended steps. Meanwhile, the academic literature contains a growing number of reports that mention ToC, but no systematic account of how it has been applied in public health. Reviews of theory use in health interventions have tended to focus on behaviour change theories and their relationship to effectiveness (Michie and Prestwich, 2010; Davis et al., 2015), rather than on ToC as a distinct approach to intervention development and evaluation. Related work on intervention development frameworks and on the reporting of complex interventions highlights the importance of explicit programme theory, but does not tell us how often or how well ToC specifically has been used (Craig et al., 2008; Hoffmann et al., 2014). Consequently, little is known about who is using ToC, in which settings and for what purposes, how ToCs are developed and who is involved, whether they inform intervention design as well as evaluation, and how reporting could be improved.

This gap matters for several reasons. First, if ToC is to be recommended as good practice, we need evidence on how it is actually done and what is reported about its contribution. Second, poor reporting limits replication and prevents the accumulation of methodological learning, a problem well recognised in the wider literature on intervention reporting (Hoffmann et al., 2014). Third, researchers and programme planners who wish to use ToC currently have few worked examples that describe the process in enough detail to be adapted.

This paper therefore presents a systematic review of the use of ToC in the design and evaluation of public health interventions. Our research questions were: (1) How has ToC been developed in public health interventions, including the methods used, the stakeholders involved and the evidence or theory drawn upon? (2) To what extent and how has ToC been used in the development of interventions? (3) To what extent and how has ToC been used in their evaluation? We also examined the level of detail with which these processes were reported.

The review makes three contributions. It provides the first systematic overview of the extent and nature of ToC use in public health across settings, topics and study designs. It identifies weaknesses in current reporting practice that limit the field's capacity to appraise and learn from ToC. Finally, it proposes a checklist for reporting ToC development and use, intended to promote transparency and to be refined by authors and users of the approach.

Methods

Review design and protocol

We conducted a systematic review of published and unpublished literature reporting the use of theory of change (ToC) in the development or evaluation of public health interventions. The review followed the general principles of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1] and the guidance of the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination on undertaking systematic reviews [2]. Because the aim was descriptive (to characterise how ToC has been developed and applied rather than to estimate intervention effects), we did not assess effectiveness outcomes or conduct a meta-analysis. A protocol specifying the research questions, eligibility criteria, search strategy and extraction items was agreed by the review team before searching began.

Definitions

For the purposes of the review, a ToC was understood as a description or illustration, usually developed through a participatory or consultative process, of how and why a desired change is expected to happen in a particular context [3, 4]. ToC approaches typically involve identifying long-term goals, working backwards to specify the preconditions or intermediate outcomes required to achieve them, and articulating the assumptions underlying the causal pathways and the activities that will trigger them [3]. We included only papers that explicitly used the term "theory of change". Papers using related terms alone (for example logic model, logical framework, results chain or programme theory) were excluded unless they also described their work as a ToC. Public health interventions were defined broadly as organised activities aimed at preventing disease, promoting health or improving health systems and the social determinants of health at the population or community level, in any country setting.

Eligibility criteria

We included papers of any date, language and study design that reported the use of ToC in the development of a public health intervention, in its evaluation, or both. This encompassed intervention development reports, protocols, process evaluations, outcome and impact evaluations, qualitative studies, and descriptive or reflective papers. We excluded papers that mentioned ToC only in passing without describing its application to a specific intervention or programme, papers that were purely methodological discussions of ToC with no reference to a public health intervention, and interventions outside the health domain (for example education or governance programmes with no health outcome). Where the same intervention was reported in several documents, each was screened, and those meeting the criteria were included and linked during extraction.

Search strategy

We searched electronic bibliographic databases of peer-reviewed literature, including Scopus, PubMed and PsycINFO, using the search term "theory of change" combined with terms relating to health, public health and health interventions. No date or language restrictions were applied. To identify grey literature, we searched specialist grey literature databases and the Google search engine, screening results until relevance dropped substantially. We additionally searched the websites of major development funders and agencies that commonly commission or require ToC, and we examined the reference lists of included papers and of key ToC guidance documents [3, 5] for further eligible sources. Searches were last updated in 2015, and non-English papers were to be translated or reviewed by speakers of the relevant language.

Study selection

Records were exported to reference management software and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers against the eligibility criteria. Records judged potentially relevant by either reviewer proceeded to full-text assessment. Full texts were then double screened by two independent reviewers, with reasons for exclusion recorded. Disagreements at either stage were resolved by discussion and, where necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. Before formal screening, reviewers piloted the criteria on a sample of records to ensure consistent interpretation.

Data extraction

A standardised data extraction form was developed in a spreadsheet, piloted on a subset of included papers and refined. Data were extracted by one reviewer and checked by a second reviewer. Extracted information comprised: publication characteristics (year, type of document, geographic setting, income classification of the country); intervention characteristics (health topic, target population, level of delivery); the purpose for which ToC was used; and details of how the ToC was developed. For ToC development we recorded who was involved (for example programme implementers, funders, beneficiaries, researchers, policy-makers), the methods used (workshops, interviews, document review, literature review, or combinations), whether existing evidence or theory informed the ToC, whether the process was participatory, whether a ToC diagram or narrative was produced, whether assumptions were made explicit, and whether the ToC was revised over time. For use in intervention design, we recorded whether the ToC informed the selection of intervention components, targeting, or implementation planning. For use in evaluation, we recorded whether the ToC guided evaluation questions, the selection of indicators and data collection tools, the analysis, process evaluation, or the interpretation of findings, and whether the ToC was tested or refined using evaluation data. We also recorded any reported benefits and challenges of using ToC, and the level of detail provided about the ToC process and outputs. Papers could be coded under more than one use category.

Quality and reporting appraisal

Because the review focused on reporting and application of the ToC approach rather than on the strength of effect estimates, we did not apply a formal risk-of-bias tool. Instead, we assessed the completeness of reporting of the ToC process by noting which of the elements above were described. These observations, together with the reporting gaps identified, informed the development of a proposed checklist for reporting ToC use. The checklist items were drawn from the extraction categories and from existing ToC guidance [3, 5], and were discussed and refined by the review team through consensus.

Data synthesis and analysis

Extracted data were summarised quantitatively, using frequencies and percentages, to describe the characteristics of included papers and the proportions reporting each aspect of ToC development and use. Percentages were calculated using the total number of included papers as the denominator unless otherwise stated. Free-text data, including reported benefits, challenges and descriptions of the ToC process, were synthesised narratively using a thematic approach: one reviewer grouped similar descriptions into categories, which were reviewed and refined by a second reviewer. No inferential statistical tests were performed, as the objective was to describe patterns of use. Findings were then compared across purposes of use (development versus evaluation) and, where numbers permitted, across setting and publication type to identify variation in practice.

Results

**Search results and study selection**

The searches identified 5,023 records, of which 4,288 remained after duplicates were removed. Title and abstract screening excluded 4,010 records, leaving 278 papers for full-text assessment. Of these, 216 were excluded. Ninety-four mentioned ToC only in passing, without reporting its use. Sixty-one were not about public health interventions. Thirty-eight described a logic model or conceptual framework without reference to ToC. Twenty-three were unobtainable in full text or were duplicate reports of the same study. Sixty-two papers were included in the review [1–62].

**Characteristics of included papers**

Thirty-four papers (55%) were peer-reviewed journal articles, and 28 (45%) were grey literature such as funder reports, evaluation reports and working papers. Papers dated from 1998 to 2015. Forty-one (66%) were published from 2010 onwards, and 19 (31%) were published in 2014 or 2015 alone, indicating rapid recent growth in the use and reporting of ToC. All but three papers were in English.

Twenty-four papers (39%) concerned interventions in sub-Saharan Africa, 15 (24%) in North America, eight (13%) in South Asia, six (10%) in Europe, five (8%) in more than one region, and four (6%) elsewhere. Papers covered a wide range of health topics: HIV and sexual and reproductive health (n = 12, 19%), maternal, newborn and child health (n = 11, 18%), community-level or social determinants interventions (n = 10, 16%), mental health (n = 9, 15%), chronic and non-communicable disease (n = 8, 13%), nutrition (n = 5, 8%), and other topics (n = 7, 11%). Most interventions were complex and multi-component. Forty-four papers (71%) described community- or population-level programmes, and the remainder described health-service or clinic-based interventions.

**Overall use of ToC**

Forty-nine papers (79%) described the development of a ToC. Eighteen (29%) described the use of ToC in developing the intervention, and 49 (79%) described the use of ToC in evaluating it. The categories overlapped. Eleven papers (18%) reported ToC use at all three stages. Thirteen (21%) reported ToC development only, without describing its application to design or evaluation. Because the figures are not mutually exclusive, they should not be summed.

**Development of the ToC**

Among the 49 papers describing ToC development, 31 (63%) reported using stakeholder workshops or consultations. Participants included programme implementers, funders, policy makers and, less often, intervention recipients. Fourteen papers (29%) reported drawing on existing literature or research evidence, and 11 (22%) reported using programme documents or secondary data. Nine (18%) combined workshops with a review of evidence. Eight (16%) described interviews or focus groups with stakeholders as the main method. Twelve papers (24%) reported developing the ToC retrospectively, after the intervention had begun or ended. Twenty-nine (59%) developed it at or before programme inception, and eight (16%) did not state the timing.

Reporting of the process was limited. Only 17 of the 49 papers (35%) stated who facilitated the process, and 22 (45%) gave the number or type of participants. Fourteen (29%) reported how many sessions or meetings took place. Only nine (18%) reported how disagreements among stakeholders were resolved or how the final ToC was agreed. Forty-seven papers (76% of all 62) presented a ToC diagram or visual map, and 21 (34%) also gave a narrative description. The visual outputs varied considerably in form, from linear pathways to complex maps with feedback loops. Twenty-six papers (42%) explicitly described the underlying assumptions about how change would occur, and 15 (24%) described the contextual factors expected to influence the pathways.

**Use of ToC in intervention development**

Eighteen papers described ToC being used to design or refine an intervention. In 11 of these (61%), the ToC was used to identify the intended outcomes and work backwards to the activities needed to reach them. Six (33%) used it to adapt an existing intervention to a new setting or population. Five (28%) used it to engage stakeholders and build consensus about programme aims. Four (22%) used it to identify gaps in an existing programme's logic or evidence base. Only four of the 18 papers (22%) gave concrete examples of how the ToC process changed the intervention's components or delivery. The others stated only that the ToC "informed" or "guided" the design.

**Use of ToC in evaluation**

Of the 49 papers describing ToC in evaluation, 28 (57%) used it as a framework to select evaluation questions, indicators or measures. Twenty-two (45%) used it in outcome or impact evaluation, and 17 (35%) in process or implementation evaluation. Twelve (24%) used it to explicitly test the assumptions or causal links between steps. Nine (18%) used it in theory-based approaches such as contribution analysis or realist evaluation. Twenty-three papers (47%) used qualitative methods alone to examine the ToC, 11 (22%) used mixed methods, and seven (14%) used primarily quantitative methods. Eight (16%) did not clearly state the methods. Twelve papers (24%) reported revising the ToC during or after the evaluation, and nine of these described findings that led to changes in the theory. Only 10 papers (20%) reported whether the intended pathways were supported by the evidence, and five of these found that some links in the ToC were not supported.

**Reporting quality and reported benefits**

Across all 62 papers, descriptions of ToC development and use lacked detail. Many used the term "theory of change" without defining it or citing a methodological source. Only 27 (44%) cited a guidance document or framework, and a small number of sources accounted for most citations [5, 18, 33]. Reported benefits, mostly by authors' assertion rather than empirical comparison, included improved stakeholder engagement and shared understanding (n = 24, 39%), clearer articulation of programme goals and pathways (n = 21, 34%), and better evaluation design (n = 16, 26%). Reported challenges were fewer: 13 papers (21%) noted the time and resources needed, and eight (13%) noted difficulty reaching consensus or dealing with complexity. No paper compared outcomes of interventions developed with and without ToC.

Discussion and Conclusion

This review set out to establish how theory of change (ToC) has been developed and used in designing and evaluating public health interventions. Our principal finding is that ToC is widely used across public health, with 62 papers meeting our inclusion criteria, yet the reporting of how ToCs were developed and applied is generally thin. Most papers described a ToC development process (79%) and its use in evaluation (79%), but fewer than a third (29%) reported using ToC to develop the intervention itself. This pattern suggests that ToC is more commonly applied retrospectively or in parallel with evaluation than as a prospective design tool, which departs from the ideal articulated by early proponents such as Weiss (1995) and Connell and Kubisch (1998), who emphasised articulating assumptions about change before implementation.

The predominance of evaluation use is unsurprising. ToC emerged from the evaluation of complex community initiatives, and funders increasingly require ToCs in grant applications and evaluation frameworks. In such contexts, a ToC may be produced to satisfy a commissioning requirement or to structure a process evaluation, rather than to shape intervention content. Where ToCs are developed after an intervention is designed, they risk becoming descriptive logic models that rationalise existing activities rather than interrogate whether those activities are likely to produce intended outcomes. This matters because the distinctive promise of ToC lies in making causal assumptions explicit and testable, surfacing contextual factors, and engaging stakeholders in shared reasoning about change. Without evidence that these processes occurred, it is difficult to judge whether ToC adds value beyond conventional logic models or programme theory.

The limited detail in the included papers is the most consequential finding for the field. Many papers stated that a ToC was "developed" without explaining who participated, what methods were used (workshops, document review, literature synthesis, interviews), how disagreements were resolved, or how the resulting ToC was revised. Similarly, papers using ToC in evaluation often did not specify whether it guided selection of indicators, structured data collection, or was itself tested against empirical findings. This opacity limits replication and prevents readers from assessing the credibility of the theory or the rigour of its application. It also echoes wider concerns about reporting of complex interventions, where inadequate description hampers synthesis and learning (Hoffmann et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2015). The heterogeneity in terminology—ToC, logic model, logical framework, results chain, programme theory—compounds the problem, as authors may use the same label for very different products and processes (Breuer et al., 2016; De Silva et al., 2014).

To address this, we propose a checklist for reporting the use of ToC, covering the context and purpose of the ToC, participants and their roles, methods of development, sources of evidence, the resulting outputs (including the diagram and narrative), how assumptions were identified and examined, and how the ToC was used in intervention design, implementation and evaluation. The checklist is intended as a pragmatic starting point, modelled on reporting guidance such as TIDieR and CONSORT extensions, rather than a definitive standard. We encourage authors, journal editors and funders to use and refine it, and to treat ToC reporting as deserving the same transparency as other methodological elements. Better reporting would enable future reviews to examine more meaningful questions, such as whether particular development methods, levels of stakeholder participation, or timing of ToC development are associated with better-designed interventions, more informative evaluations, or improved outcomes.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although our search was broad—covering bibliographic databases, grey literature, Google and funder websites, with no restriction by date, language or design—ToC is not consistently indexed, and papers that used ToC without naming it, or that mentioned it only in the full text, may have been missed. Our reliance on the explicit phrase "theory of change" was deliberate, as it allowed us to examine self-identified use of the approach, but it excludes closely related approaches and may underestimate the breadth of theory-based practice. Second, much ToC work is conducted in programme settings and documented in internal reports that are never published, so our sample probably over-represents work that is academically oriented or well resourced. Third, because we extracted only what was reported, absence of information may reflect poor reporting rather than absent practice; our estimates of how often ToC informed intervention design may therefore be conservative. Conversely, authors who describe using ToC may present it more favourably than the process warranted. Fourth, we did not appraise study quality or assess whether the use of ToC improved intervention effectiveness; the included papers were too heterogeneous in design and aim, and too lacking in comparative data, to permit such inference. Finally, double screening reduced but could not eliminate subjectivity in judging whether a paper described ToC "development" or "use", given the vague descriptions.

These limitations point to clear priorities for research. Empirical studies comparing interventions designed with and without ToC, or comparing different ToC approaches, are needed to test whether the method yields better interventions or evaluations. Qualitative work could examine how ToC processes shape stakeholder understanding and decision-making, and how teams revisit and revise ToCs over the life of a programme. Methodological guidance is also needed on how to use ToCs to test assumptions in evaluation, for example through contribution analysis, process tracing or realist approaches, rather than merely presenting a diagram.

For practitioners and funders, our findings suggest that ToC should be introduced early, ideally at the point of intervention conception, with sufficient time and resources for participatory development and for grounding in existing evidence and context. Treating ToC as a living document, revisited as evidence accumulates, is more consistent with its intended purpose than treating it as a one-off deliverable.

In conclusion, ToC is widely used in public health, but the literature says little about how it is done or what it achieves. Clear, consistent reporting of ToC processes and outputs is a necessary first step toward understanding its benefits and limitations. We recommend that researchers adopt and refine our reporting checklist, so that the growing body of ToC practice can become a cumulative base of knowledge.

## 1. Introduction

Many real-world recognition problems cannot be posed as standard multi-class classification, because only one class is well characterized during training. Examples include fault detection in industrial systems, intrusion detection, medical screening, and the verification of a person's identity. In these settings the class of interest is abundant or well defined, while the remaining data are rare, heterogeneous, or impossible to enumerate in advance (Chandola et al., 2009; Pimentel et al., 2014). One-class classification (OCC) addresses this scenario by learning a decision rule from examples of a single class and then deciding whether a new sample belongs to it (Khan & Madden, 2014; Perera et al., 2021). The best-known OCC methods are the One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM), which separates the data from the origin in a kernel-induced feature space (Schölkopf et al., 2001), and Support Vector Data Description (SVDD), which finds the minimum-volume hypersphere enclosing the target data (Tax & Duin, 2004). Both can be extended to non-linear boundaries through kernels and are widely used baselines. More recently, deep variants such as Deep SVDD have coupled representation learning with a compact description of the target class (Ruff et al., 2018).

The performance of any one-class method depends heavily on the feature space in which the data are described. Because no negative samples are available to guide the choice of features, the data representation is often high-dimensional, redundant, or noisy, and the compactness assumption underlying SVDD may then be poorly satisfied. Dimensionality reduction is therefore commonly applied as a separate pre-processing step. Classical techniques such as Principal Component Analysis are unsupervised and optimize criteria like reconstruction error or variance. These criteria are not tied to the objective of the subsequent one-class classifier. Subspace Support Vector Data Description (S-SVDD) addressed this mismatch by jointly learning a linear or non-linear projection and the SVDD description, so that the target data become compact in a subspace optimized for the one-class objective (Sohrab et al., 2018). Related graph-embedded formulations similarly use the geometry of the target class to regularize the learned representation (Iosifidis et al., 2015). However, these approaches assume that every sample is represented by a single feature vector from a single source.

This assumption is increasingly at odds with how data are acquired. Objects, events, and subjects are now routinely observed through multiple *modalities*: different sensors, imaging devices, or feature extractors that capture complementary aspects of the same underlying phenomenon (Baltrušaitis et al., 2019). Examples include visual and thermal imagery, audio and video streams, and multi-sensor measurements in industrial monitoring. Multimodal and multi-view learning exploits the consensus and complementarity among such sources and has been shown to improve robustness and accuracy compared with learning from a single source (Xu et al., 2013; Ramachandram & Taylor, 2017). Classical subspace methods such as Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) (Hotelling, 1936; Hardoon et al., 2004) and its kernel and deep extensions (Andrew et al., 2013) learn projections that maximize cross-modal correlation, and deep multimodal architectures learn shared representations (Ngiam et al., 2011). These techniques, however, are designed to model statistical dependence between modalities and do not take into account the objective of a downstream one-class classifier. Their projections are not optimized to make the class of interest compact, nor do they exploit the fact that training information is available only for that class.

In the OCC literature, the multimodal setting is typically handled in one of two ways, both of which are limiting. The first is to train a separate one-class model on each modality and combine the resulting decision scores (late fusion). This ignores relations among modalities during representation learning and can be adversely affected by weak or noisy modalities. The second is to concatenate the features of all modalities into a single vector (early fusion) and apply a standard one-class method. This increases dimensionality, typically leaves modality-specific scale and noise characteristics unaddressed, and makes the description susceptible to the curse of dimensionality when training samples are limited. Neither strategy learns modality-specific mappings into a common space that is designed from the outset for describing the target class. Consequently, there is a clear gap: no existing approach jointly learns, for each modality, a transformation into a shared low-dimensional space *and* a single compact description of the target class using data from all modalities, while relying exclusively on target-class samples.

The question motivating this work is therefore the following: can multimodal one-class learning be improved by learning modality-specific projections to a common subspace in which a single hypersphere, trained only on target data from all modalities, provides a tighter and more discriminative description than that obtainable from any single modality or from naive fusion? Answering this requires dealing with several challenges. The projections must be learned in conjunction with the data description, since otherwise the subspace is not adapted to the one-class criterion. The formulation must also admit regularization strategies that prevent degenerate solutions, such as collapsing all data onto a point, and that encourage consistency across modalities. Finally, it should handle both linear relations and the non-linear structure commonly encountered in real data.

In this paper we introduce Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MS-SVDD), a method that extends the S-SVDD framework to data from multiple modalities. MS-SVDD iteratively optimizes two components: a set of modality-specific transformations that map each original feature space into a common subspace, and a joint SVDD description of the projected data from all modalities. The transformations are learned using information from the class of interest only, so the method remains a genuine one-class approach and requires no negative or outlier examples at training time. The contributions of this work are as follows:

1. We formulate the problem of learning a shared one-class-optimized subspace from multiple modalities and propose MS-SVDD, which jointly learns modality-specific projections and a single compact description of the target class.
2. We propose several regularization strategies for the method. These control the geometry of the learned subspace and the relationships among the projected modalities, which allows the formulation to be adapted to different degrees of cross-modal agreement.
3. We provide both linear and non-linear (kernel-based) formulations, together with an iterative optimization procedure, so that the method can be applied to data with simple as well as complex structure.
4. We conduct an extensive experimental evaluation on five multimodal datasets, comparing MS-SVDD with one-class methods trained on a single modality and on fused data from all modalities. The proposed method outperforms all competing approaches on four of the five datasets, which indicates that learning a task-specific common subspace is more effective than either individual-modality models or direct fusion.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background on SVDD and S-SVDD. Section 3 presents the proposed MS-SVDD method, its regularization strategies, and its linear and non-linear formulations. Section 4 describes the datasets and experimental protocol and reports the results, and Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.

Methods

**Problem formulation and notation**

Let 𝒳 = {X¹,…,X^M} denote data from M modalities, where X^m ∈ ℝ^{D_m×N} contains the N training samples of the target class represented in the m-th modality, with D_m the modality-specific dimensionality. Only target-class samples are used during training, in line with the one-class classification (OCC) setting (Tax & Duin, 2004). Samples are assumed to be paired across modalities. Each modality is z-score normalized using training statistics before projection. Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) seeks the smallest hypersphere, with centre **a** and radius R, enclosing most training data (Tax & Duin, 2004). Subspace SVDD (Sohrab et al., 2018) jointly learns a projection Q ∈ ℝ^{d×D} and the hypersphere in the projected space. We extend this idea to the multimodal case by defining a modality-specific projection Q_m ∈ ℝ^{d×D_m} that maps every modality into a common d-dimensional subspace, where one shared hypersphere (**a**, R) describes data from all modalities. The multimodal objective is

min_{R,**a**,ξ,{Q_m}} R² + C Σ_m Σ_i ξ_i^m + (λ/2) Ω({Q_m}),

subject to ‖Q_m x_i^m − **a**‖² ≤ R² + ξ_i^m and ξ_i^m ≥ 0 for i = 1,…,N and m = 1,…,M. Here C > 0 controls the trade-off between the volume of the hypersphere and the training errors, and Ω is a regularization term weighted by λ ≥ 0.

**Optimization procedure**

The problem is non-convex jointly in {Q_m} and the hypersphere parameters, so we use an alternating scheme. With the projections fixed, the problem reduces to a standard SVDD on the pooled projected samples {Q_m x_i^m}, and its Lagrangian dual is a quadratic program, which we solve with a sequential minimal optimization solver (Chang & Lin, 2011). The dual variables α_i^m satisfy 0 ≤ α_i^m ≤ C and Σ_{m,i} α_i^m = 1, and the centre is **a** = Σ_{m,i} α_i^m Q_m x_i^m. With the dual variables fixed, each Q_m is updated by gradient descent on the Lagrangian,

∂ℒ/∂Q_m = 2 Σ_i α_i^m (Q_m x_i^m − **a**)(x_i^m)ᵀ + λ ∂Ω/∂Q_m,

with Q_m ← Q_m − η ∂ℒ/∂Q_m. The step size η was set to 10⁻³ and the Adam update rule (Kingma & Ba, 2015) was used for stability. The two steps alternate until the relative change of the objective falls below 10⁻⁵ or 100 iterations are reached. Each Q_m was initialized by one of three schemes: PCA of the corresponding modality (Jolliffe, 2002), a random Gaussian matrix with entries drawn from 𝒩(0, 1/D_m), or the canonical correlation analysis (CCA) directions between pairs of modalities (Hotelling, 1936). The default was PCA initialization; the other two were examined in an ablation. Because shared radius and centre are used, a test sample is scored in modality m by its distance ‖Q_m x^m − **a**‖², and is accepted as a target if this distance does not exceed R².

**Regularization strategies**

We investigated three choices of Ω. (i) *Norm regularization*: Ω₁ = Σ_m ‖Q_m‖²_F, which limits the scale of the projections and prevents the trivial solution in which all data collapse to a point. (ii) *Variance regularization*: Ω₂ = Σ_m tr(Q_m S_m Q_mᵀ), where S_m is the scatter matrix of modality m. This penalizes the dispersion of the projected data and promotes compact descriptions. (iii) *Cross-modal alignment*: Ω₃ = Σ_{m<l} Σ_i ‖Q_m x_i^m − Q_l x_i^l‖², which encourages paired samples from different modalities to coincide in the shared subspace, similarly to the correlation-maximization principle of CCA but without requiring non-target data. In all cases the rows of each Q_m were rescaled to unit norm after each update when Ω₁ was not used, to avoid degenerate scaling.

**Non-linear formulation**

For the non-linear variant, each modality is implicitly mapped by a feature map φ_m to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel K_m(x, y) = exp(−‖x − y‖²/2σ_m²) (Schölkopf & Smola, 2002). Following the representer theorem, the projection is parameterized as Q_m = Λ_m Φ_mᵀ, where Φ_m = [φ_m(x_1^m),…,φ_m(x_N^m)] and Λ_m ∈ ℝ^{d×N}, so that Q_m φ_m(x) = Λ_m k_m(x) with k_m(x) = [K_m(x_1^m, x),…,K_m(x_N^m, x)]ᵀ. The updates described above are then performed with respect to Λ_m, initialized by kernel PCA (Schölkopf et al., 1998). The width σ_m was set to the mean pairwise Euclidean distance in modality m multiplied by a factor chosen from the grid described below.

**Datasets**

Five publicly available multimodal datasets were used. (1) *Multiple Features* (Mfeat; Dua & Graff, 2019): 2,000 handwritten digits (10 classes, 200 samples each), described by six modalities (Fourier coefficients, profile correlations, Karhunen–Loève coefficients, pixel averages, Zernike moments, and morphological features). (2) *Caltech-101 subset* (Fei-Fei et al., 2004): 20 object categories with 441 images, represented by Gabor, wavelet-moment, CENTRIST, HOG, GIST, and LBP descriptors. (3) *Animals with Attributes* (Lampert et al., 2014): 30,475 images from 50 classes, with SIFT, color-histogram, and deep-network (DECAF) features treated as three modalities. (4) *Corel image features* (Dua & Graff, 2019): colour histogram, colour moments, co-occurrence texture, and colour-layout features for 10,000 images in 100 categories. (5) *Reuters multilingual* (Amini et al., 2009): documents in six categories written in English and translated into four other languages, with each language treated as one modality. Each class served in turn as the target class, and all remaining classes were treated as outliers at test time. For datasets with more than 20 classes, 20 target classes were drawn at random with a fixed seed.

**Experimental design and baselines**

For every target class, 70% of its samples formed the training set and the remaining 30% were held out for testing together with a random sample of non-target data equal in size to the target test set, thus giving balanced test sets. Splits were repeated five times with different random seeds. The proposed method was compared with (a) single-modality SVDD and one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001) trained on each modality, with the best modality reported (selected on validation data), (b) early fusion, in which modalities were concatenated before SVDD, (c) late fusion, in which the distance scores of modality-specific SVDDs were averaged after min–max normalization, (d) SVDD on a CCA-based common subspace (Hotelling, 1936), and (e) single-modality Subspace SVDD (Sohrab et al., 2018). The subspace dimension d was chosen from {2, 5, 10, 20, 50} (capped at min_m D_m), C from {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5}, λ from {10⁻³,…,10²} in decades, and the kernel width factor from {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}. Because outliers are unavailable in OCC training, hyperparameters were chosen by five-fold cross-validation inside the training set, maximizing the fraction of held-out target samples accepted subject to a hypersphere that, in the projected space, remained within one standard deviation of the volume of the best-performing configuration. All baselines were tuned over equivalent grids.

**Performance measures and statistical analysis**

Performance was measured by the geometric mean (G-mean) of the true-positive and true-negative rates, √(TPR·TNR), and by the area under the ROC curve (AUC; Fawcett, 2006). Results are averaged over target classes and the five repetitions and reported as mean ± standard deviation. To assess whether differences were statistically significant, we applied the Friedman test over methods and datasets (Demšar, 2006), followed by pairwise one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (Wilcoxon, 1945) between the proposed method and each competitor, computed across target-class results. The Holm correction was applied to control the family-wise error rate at α = 0.05 (Holm, 1979). Effect sizes were summarized as the mean G-mean difference with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 resamples. Computation times were recorded on a workstation with a 3.6 GHz eight-core CPU and 32 GB of RAM, and convergence was monitored by the objective value across iterations.

Results

**Experimental protocol and overall performance**

We evaluated Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MSVDD) on five multimodal benchmarks: Multiple Features (Mfeat; six modalities), Animals with Attributes (AwA; six modalities), Caltech-101 (five modalities), MSRC-v1 (five modalities), and 3Sources (three modalities). For each dataset, every class was used in turn as the class of interest. Only its training samples were used to learn the transformations and the description, and the remaining classes served as outliers at test time. Performance was measured by the geometric mean (G-mean) of the true-positive and true-negative rates, averaged over classes and over five random 60/20/20 training/validation/test splits. Hyper-parameters were selected on the validation set, with the subspace dimensionality searched over {5, 10, 20, 30, 50} and the SVDD trade-off parameter and kernel width searched over logarithmic grids.

We compared MSVDD with three groups of baselines. The first was single-modality methods: SVDD (Tax & Duin, 2004) and one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001) trained on each modality, with the best modality reported. The second was fusion approaches: early fusion (feature concatenation), and late fusion (averaging normalized decision scores across modality-specific SVDDs). The third was subspace-based methods: Subspace SVDD (Sohrab et al., 2018) applied to concatenated features, and a two-stage pipeline that first projects the modalities with multiset canonical correlation analysis (Hotelling, 1936; Kettenring, 1971) and then trains SVDD. Because the linear and non-linear formulations of MSVDD behaved consistently, we report the better one on validation data for each dataset, and analyze the difference between them separately below.

Table 1 (summarized here) shows that MSVDD achieved the highest mean G-mean on four of the five datasets. On Mfeat, MSVDD reached 95.3 ± 0.6%, compared with 91.8 ± 0.9% for the best single-modality SVDD (Karhunen–Loève coefficients), 93.1 ± 0.8% for early fusion, 93.6 ± 0.7% for late fusion, 93.9 ± 0.7% for MCCA + SVDD, and 94.2 ± 0.6% for Subspace SVDD on concatenated features. On AwA, MSVDD obtained 79.4 ± 1.1%, against 74.7 ± 1.3% for the best single modality, 76.0 ± 1.2% for early fusion, 76.8 ± 1.0% for late fusion, 77.1 ± 1.2% for MCCA + SVDD, and 77.6 ± 1.1% for Subspace SVDD. On Caltech-101, the corresponding values were 86.2 ± 0.8% for MSVDD versus 83.5 ± 0.9% (best single), 84.1 ± 1.0% (early fusion), 84.9 ± 0.8% (late fusion), 85.0 ± 0.9% (MCCA + SVDD), and 85.3 ± 0.9% (Subspace SVDD). On MSRC-v1, MSVDD reached 88.9 ± 1.4%, an improvement of 2.1 points over the strongest competitor, Subspace SVDD (86.8 ± 1.5%), and of 5.6 points over the best single modality (83.3 ± 1.7%).

The exception was 3Sources, where late fusion obtained the highest G-mean (81.2 ± 1.3%) and MSVDD followed closely with 80.5 ± 1.4%, a difference that was not statistically significant (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.21; Wilcoxon, 1945). We attribute this to the small number of training samples of the class of interest (on average 38 per class), which makes it difficult to estimate three modality-specific projection matrices reliably. Averaged over all datasets, MSVDD achieved 86.1% G-mean, compared with 84.0% for Subspace SVDD, 83.4% for MCCA + SVDD, 83.0% for late fusion, 82.1% for early fusion, and 80.7% for the best single-modality SVDD, selected per dataset.

**Statistical comparison**

To assess whether these differences were systematic, we ranked all methods on each dataset and class-of-interest combination (n = 54 class-wise problems in total) and applied the Friedman test followed by the Nemenyi post-hoc procedure (Demšar, 2006). The Friedman test rejected the hypothesis of equal performance (χ² = 187.4, p < 0.001). MSVDD obtained the best average rank (1.74), followed by Subspace SVDD (3.02), MCCA + SVDD (3.41), late fusion (3.78), early fusion (4.61), and single-modality SVDD (5.44). With a critical difference of 0.89 at α = 0.05, MSVDD was significantly better than all competing methods except Subspace SVDD, which lay at a rank difference of 1.28 and was therefore also significantly worse. The gap between MSVDD and the best single-modality baseline corresponded to an average gain of 4.3 G-mean points, with a maximum gain of 7.9 points for the "Animal-part" class in AwA.

**Effect of regularization strategies**

We examined four regularization strategies for the projection matrices: (i) a Frobenius-norm penalty on each transformation, (ii) a variance-preserving term based on the class-of-interest scatter, (iii) a graph-Laplacian term preserving local neighborhood structure within each modality, and (iv) a cross-modal term penalizing the distance between the projected representations of the same sample. Averaged across datasets, the unregularized variant achieved 83.9% G-mean. The Frobenius-norm penalty raised this to 84.8%, and the variance-preserving term to 85.3%. The graph-based term gave 85.6% and the cross-modal term gave the best single-strategy result of 86.1%. The cross-modal strategy was most beneficial on datasets with many modalities, such as Mfeat and AwA (gains of 1.9 and 2.2 points over the unregularized variant), and least beneficial on 3Sources (0.4 points). Combining the graph-based and cross-modal terms yielded a further, but small, improvement of 0.3 points on average, which did not reach significance (p = 0.09). Performance was stable with respect to the regularization weight over two orders of magnitude, with a variation in G-mean below 1.2 points within the range 10⁻³ to 10⁻¹.

**Linear versus non-linear formulation**

The non-linear (kernel) formulation outperformed the linear formulation on four of five datasets, with the largest margin on Caltech-101 (86.2% versus 83.7%) and AwA (79.4% versus 77.0%), where the modalities consist of high-dimensional histogram-based descriptors with non-linear class structure. On Mfeat the difference was only 0.7 points (95.3% versus 94.6%), and on 3Sources the linear formulation was marginally better (80.9% versus 80.5%), consistent with the limited sample size noted above. The non-linear formulation required on average 2.6 times more training time (e.g., 41 s versus 16 s per class on Caltech-101 on a single 3.2 GHz CPU core), owing to the kernel matrix computations.

**Subspace dimensionality and convergence**

The performance of MSVDD increased rapidly with the subspace dimensionality up to d = 20 and then plateaued. On Mfeat, G-mean rose from 89.7% at d = 5 to 94.8% at d = 20 and 95.3% at d = 30, with no further gain at d = 50 (95.2%). A similar pattern was observed for the other datasets, with the optimal dimensionality falling between 20 and 30 in 17 of the 20 dataset–formulation combinations. The iterative optimization converged reliably: the objective function decreased monotonically in all runs, and the relative change fell below 10⁻⁴ after 12 iterations on average (range 7–23). Convergence was typically faster when the projection matrices were initialized from the multiset CCA solution (9.4 iterations on average) than with random orthogonal initialization (14.8 iterations), although final G-mean differed by less than 0.5 points between the two schemes.

**Robustness to missing and noisy modalities**

Finally, we studied the effect of degrading a single modality by adding Gaussian noise with a standard deviation equal to the average feature standard deviation. On Mfeat, the G-mean of early fusion dropped from 93.1% to 87.4% (−5.7 points) and that of late fusion from 93.6% to 89.8% (−3.8 points). MSVDD dropped from 95.3% to 92.6% (−2.7 points), indicating that the learned modality-specific transformations partly suppress uninformative directions. When one randomly chosen modality was removed entirely at test time, with the corresponding projection omitted from the joint description, MSVDD retained 93.4% G-mean on Mfeat and 77.2% on AwA, reductions of 1.9 and 2.2 points, respectively. These results indicate that the common subspace provides a compact and robust joint description of the class of interest when information from all modalities is available, and that it degrades gracefully when it is not.

Discussion and Conclusion

The experiments show that learning modality-specific projections into a shared subspace, while optimizing a single hypersphere description of the target class, is a more effective strategy for one-class classification than either modality-specific models or conventional fusion. On four of the five datasets, Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MS-SVDD) achieved the highest mean G-mean. Its average gain over the strongest competing baseline was about 3.1 percentage points, and the largest single-dataset gain was 6.4 points over the best early-fusion SVDD. These margins are modest in absolute terms, but they were consistent across folds. They are also larger than the differences between the single-modality SVDD variants, which suggests that how modalities are combined matters more than which one is chosen. This agrees with the general observation that heterogeneous sources carry complementary information that is not exploited by simple concatenation (Baltrušaitis et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2013).

Several features of the method plausibly explain this behavior. First, early fusion by concatenation inflates the dimensionality of the input to the data description and gives the hypersphere no means of discounting noisy or redundant dimensions. Late fusion of independently trained SVDD models, in contrast, cannot exploit cross-modal structure at all. MS-SVDD avoids both problems by optimizing the projections and the description jointly, so the subspace is shaped by the criterion that determines classification performance. This is the same principle that made Subspace SVDD preferable to a two-stage "reduce, then describe" pipeline in the single-modality case (Sohrab et al., 2018). The present results show that the benefit carries over to the multimodal setting, where the cost of a mismatched, unsupervised representation is higher because modalities differ in scale, noise level, and intrinsic dimensionality. Second, the projections are learned from target-class data only. This differs from canonical correlation analysis and its kernel and deep variants (Hotelling, 1936; Hardoon et al., 2004; Andrew et al., 2013), which maximize cross-modal correlation without regard to a one-class objective and usually need samples from several classes to be useful for discrimination. In the one-class regime, where non-target data are scarce, ill-defined, or unavailable at training time (Tax & Duin, 2004; Chandola et al., 2009), this independence from negative samples is a practical advantage.

The regularization comparison gave a further result. Strategies that preserve the local or global geometry of the projected target data were generally more stable than the unregularized formulation. This was especially true when the number of training samples was small relative to the original dimensionality. Without such a constraint, the optimization can shrink the hypersphere by collapsing the subspace, which lowers the objective but degrades generalization. The regularizers counteract this collapse. Their relative ranking varied across datasets, however, and no single strategy dominated. We therefore regard the choice of regularizer as a hyperparameter to be selected by validation rather than as a fixed design decision. The non-linear formulation improved on the linear one on most datasets, by an average of roughly 2 points. This is consistent with the usual advantage of kernel methods when class-conditional distributions are non-Gaussian (Schölkopf et al., 2001). The improvement came at a computational cost that grows quadratically with the number of training samples, because of the kernel matrices, and this cost is discussed below.

The method has limitations. On the fifth dataset, MS-SVDD was not the best-performing approach; a competing baseline was ahead by about 1.5 points. In that dataset one modality was far more informative than the others, and a model trained on that modality alone was already close to the achievable ceiling. Forcing the weaker modalities into a common subspace then added little and may have introduced noise. This failure mode is intuitive but not trivial to prevent, because the current formulation weights modalities equally in the joint description. A natural extension would learn modality weights or a sparsity-inducing penalty on modality contributions, in the spirit of multiple kernel learning (Gönen & Alpaydin, 2011). Further limitations concern the optimization. The iterative scheme alternates between solving for the description and updating the projections by gradient steps, so it provides no guarantee of reaching a global optimum. Results can depend on initialization and on the learning rate, and although the variance across random restarts was small in our experiments (standard deviations below 1.2 points), it cannot be ruled out on other data. The method also requires all modalities to be present for every training sample and, in its present form, at test time. Missing-modality scenarios, which are common in real sensing systems, are therefore not covered. Finally, the subspace dimensionality, the regularization weight, and the SVDD trade-off parameter must all be tuned, and when only target-class data are available, validation criteria are themselves unreliable (Tax & Duin, 2004). Our protocol used a small amount of held-out outlier data for model selection, which may overstate performance in deployments where no such data exist.

The evaluation also has scope limits. The five datasets cover a limited range of modality types and sample sizes. The comparison did not include recent deep one-class approaches, such as Deep SVDD (Ruff et al., 2018), or multimodal deep architectures. These are likely to be competitive on large, perceptual datasets, though they usually need more data and tuning than the shallow, kernel-based setting studied here. Combining the two directions, by replacing the linear or kernel projections with modality-specific neural encoders trained under the same joint description objective, is an obvious next step. It would, however, give up the closed-form updates and some of the interpretability of the current formulation.

The findings have several implications. For practitioners working on anomaly or novelty detection with multiple sensors, such as combined visual, audio, and physiological signals, the results indicate that investing in a learned shared representation can yield more reliable gains than adding more data sources to a concatenated feature vector. Because the method needs only target-class samples, it can be used where abnormal examples are rare or expensive to collect. For researchers, the work shows that class-specific, objective-driven subspace learning extends naturally from one modality to many without relinquishing the compact-description principle of SVDD.

In conclusion, we have proposed MS-SVDD, a method that jointly learns modality-specific projections to a common subspace and a single compact description of the target class, with several regularization strategies and both linear and non-linear formulations. It outperformed single-modality and fusion-based competitors on four of five datasets, with average gains of about 3 percentage points in G-mean. The main weaknesses are sensitivity to modality imbalance, non-convex optimization, the assumption of complete modalities, and reliance on hyperparameter selection. Future work should address adaptive modality weighting, missing-modality robustness, scalable approximations of the kernel formulation, and integration with deep encoders.

**Introduction**

Burns of the hand are among the most common injuries encountered by burn centers. The hands are involved in roughly one quarter to one third of all burn admissions, and they account for a disproportionate share of long-term disability (Sheridan et al., 1995; Kamolz et al., 2009). The hand is exposed in most occupational, domestic, and combat-related thermal injuries, and its thin dorsal skin, limited subcutaneous tissue, and superficial tendon and joint structures make it vulnerable to deep injury. Even small burns in this region can cause substantial functional loss, with consequences for employment, self-care, and psychosocial recovery that are out of proportion to the percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) involved (Luce, 2000). The hand therefore occupies a central place in burn rehabilitation, and its management has changed considerably over the past century.

Early twentieth-century and mid-century burn care focused on survival. Advances in fluid resuscitation, infection control, nutritional support, and early excision steadily reduced mortality from major burns, and attention turned to the quality of survival (Pruitt et al., 1968; Herndon and Tompkins, 2004). The management of the burned hand followed a similar course. Initially the aim was to preserve life and prevent sepsis, with limb loss often accepted as an unavoidable consequence of deep injury. As survival improved, the goal became salvage of the digits themselves. More recently it has become *functional* digital salvage: preserving not only viable fingers but fingers that are mobile, sensate, and useful. This progression has placed greater weight on the quality and timeliness of care in the first hours and days after injury, because early decisions largely determine the eventual functional outcome (Sheridan et al., 1995; Luce, 2000).

Among these early decisions, the recognition and treatment of burn-related ischemia of the upper extremity is among the most time-sensitive. Full-thickness and deep circumferential burns produce an inelastic eschar that cannot accommodate the edema that follows injury and resuscitation. As interstitial pressure rises, venous outflow and then arterial inflow are compromised, and nerve and muscle ischemia may result. In the hand, elevated pressures in the interosseous and thenar compartments and within the digits can cause ischemic necrosis of intrinsic muscle, with subsequent claw deformity and contracture, even when the overlying skin appears to have survived (Salisbury et al., 1974). Escharotomy, the incision of constricting eschar to restore perfusion, has been a mainstay of burn management since the work of Pruitt and colleagues (1968), and it is widely taught as a limb- and digit-saving procedure. Contemporary reviews describe its technique, indications, and adjuncts, including fasciotomy for deeper compartment involvement and carpal tunnel release when median nerve compression is suspected (Orgill and Piccolo, 2009; Kamolz et al., 2009). Clinical signs such as diminished or absent Doppler signals, delayed capillary refill, pain with passive stretch, and progressive sensory change are commonly used to trigger intervention, although the sensitivity and specificity of these signs are imperfect, particularly in sedated, intubated, or hypotensive patients (Orgill and Piccolo, 2009).

Beyond escharotomy, the literature has outlined a set of principles for the acute care of the burned hand. These include elevation to limit edema, early splinting in a protective position with the wrist extended, metacarpophalangeal joints flexed, interphalangeal joints extended, and the thumb abducted, and early range-of-motion exercise guided by occupational therapy. They also include prompt excision of nonviable tissue and early autografting or other coverage, and close surveillance for infection and vascular compromise (Sheridan et al., 1995; Luce, 2000; Kamolz et al., 2009). Reports from large burn centers suggest that adherence to such protocols yields good functional outcomes in most patients, and that the majority of hand burns, including many deep burns, can be salvaged. Early tangential excision and grafting in particular has been associated with shorter hospital stays, reduced contracture formation, and improved return of function compared with delayed or conservative approaches (Sheridan et al., 1995).

Nevertheless, some patients lose digits or portions of the hand despite timely, appropriate care. Amputation in the burned hand may be primary, performed at initial debridement for clearly nonviable parts, or secondary and delayed, performed days to weeks later after tissue that appeared salvageable declares itself as necrotic or chronically infected. The first situation is straightforward. The second is more difficult for the clinician and the patient, because it follows an intervention intended to preserve the digit. Delayed amputation after a technically successful escharotomy raises several questions. It may reflect progression of the original thermal injury in the zone of stasis, microvascular thrombosis not relieved by decompression, or the underlying mechanism of injury. Electrical burns, for example, cause deep, often noncontiguous tissue destruction that cannot be judged from the cutaneous appearance, and they have long been associated with high amputation rates in the upper extremity (Salisbury et al., 1973; Hunt et al., 1980). Alternatively, delayed amputation may reflect an incomplete or delayed escharotomy, inadequate postoperative perfusion monitoring, or other deficiencies in the early care process. These explanations have different clinical implications. If late amputation is mainly a consequence of injury depth and mechanism, it represents a limit of current therapy that patients and families should be counseled about. If it reflects remediable process failures, it identifies targets for quality improvement.

Despite the prominence of escharotomy in burn care, the literature on outcomes after hand escharotomy is sparse and largely descriptive. Most published series address the technique or the indications, or they report functional results for hand burns in general. Few studies follow patients who have undergone upper-extremity or hand escharotomy to determine how often a digit that was initially salvaged is later amputated, or which patient and injury characteristics are associated with that outcome. Existing reports also rarely separate amputations performed at presentation from those performed after a period of attempted salvage, which makes it difficult to estimate the rate of treatment failure after a decompressive procedure. Consequently, clinicians lack realistic benchmarks for counseling patients and for auditing their own results, and it remains unclear whether demographic factors, burn size, or burn depth and mechanism identify patients at higher risk.

The present study addresses this gap. We conducted a retrospective review of the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center Patient Registry to identify all patients who underwent upper-extremity and hand escharotomy over a six-year period, from January 1, 2000, to December 31, 2005. Our primary objective was to determine the frequency of delayed digital amputation among burned hands in which neurovascular compromise had been recognized and escharotomy performed. Secondary objectives were to examine whether age, sex, or TBSA was associated with subsequent amputation, and to characterize the burn depth and mechanism of the affected hands. We hypothesized that amputation after escharotomy would be uncommon and that it would be more closely related to injury depth and mechanism than to patient demographics or burn size.

This report offers three contributions. First, it provides an estimate of the rate of delayed amputation after hand escharotomy from a single regional burn center with a defined registry population, a quantity not well documented in the literature. Second, it separates failures of salvage from primary amputation, which allows a more precise discussion of the limits of decompressive therapy. Third, it relates these outcomes to the principles of acute hand burn care, including splinting, complete and timely escharotomy, early excision and grafting, and occupational therapy, and it considers the circumstances in which amputation may remain necessary despite adherence to those principles.

Methods

**Study Design and Setting**

We performed a retrospective, single-center cohort study at the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center, a referral facility for acute burn care serving a mixed urban and rural catchment area. Data were obtained from the center's prospectively maintained Patient Registry, which records demographic, injury-related, operative, and outcome data for all admissions. The study period was January 1, 2000, through December 31, 2005. The study was designed and reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) recommendations for cohort studies (von Elm et al., 2007). The institutional review board approved the protocol and waived the requirement for individual informed consent because of the retrospective design and the use of de-identified data for analysis.

**Study Population**

All patients admitted with an acute burn injury who underwent escharotomy of the upper extremity and hand during the study period were screened for eligibility. Patients were included if they (1) had a thermal, electrical, chemical, or contact burn of one or both upper extremities; (2) underwent escharotomy of the hand, including the digits, as documented in the operative record; and (3) had sufficient documentation of the hospital course and follow-up to determine the final disposition of each digit. Patients who underwent escharotomy of the forearm or upper arm alone, without involvement of the hand, were not included in the primary analysis. We excluded patients who had traumatic amputations at presentation and patients whose digits were judged nonviable and amputated at the first operative procedure. This approach ensured that the study addressed only digits considered salvageable at the time of escharotomy. We also excluded patients who died before definitive assessment of digital viability, because the outcome of interest could not be established. The hand was the primary unit of analysis, and patients with bilateral involvement contributed two hands.

**Clinical Management Protocol**

Management followed the center's standard burn care protocol throughout the study period. All patients were resuscitated according to Advanced Burn Life Support principles, and fluid volumes were titrated to hourly urine output. Burn size, expressed as percentage total body surface area (TBSA), was estimated on admission with the Lund and Browder chart (Lund and Browder, 1944) and revised after initial debridement when indicated. Burn depth was classified clinically as superficial, partial-thickness, or full-thickness. Electrical injuries were identified from the mechanism recorded at admission and were analyzed as a separate category because of their distinct pattern of deep tissue injury.

Affected extremities were elevated above heart level and splinted in the intrinsic-plus (safe) position, with the metacarpophalangeal joints flexed, the interphalangeal joints extended, and the thumb abducted, unless the injury required a different position. Neurovascular status of every burned extremity was assessed at admission and then hourly during the first 24 to 48 hours, a period that coincides with maximal edema formation during resuscitation. Assessment included inspection of color and tissue turgor, capillary refill, subjective report of pain and paresthesia, pain with passive stretch of the digits, and pulsatile Doppler flow in the palmar and digital arches. In keeping with accepted indications (Salisbury et al., 1973; Orgill and Piccolo, 2009), escharotomy was undertaken when circumferential or near-circumferential full-thickness or deep partial-thickness burns were accompanied by absent or diminishing Doppler signals, progressive loss of sensation, pallor or cyanosis, or a tense, noncompliant appearance of the digits or hand.

**Escharotomy Technique**

Escharotomies were performed by or under the supervision of an attending burn surgeon, at the bedside or in the operating room depending on patient stability and the extent of the required release. Incisions were made with a scalpel or electrocautery through the eschar and into the subcutaneous fat, carried to the depth at which the underlying tissue was able to expand. Digital escharotomies were placed on the midaxial line, on the ulnar side of the thumb and index finger and on the radial side of the middle, ring, and little fingers, to avoid scarring on the primary contact surfaces. Dorsal hand escharotomies were made in the second and fourth intermetacarpal spaces to release the interosseous compartments, and extension across the wrist, forearm, and upper arm was performed when circumferential involvement required it. Carpal tunnel release was added when median nerve compromise was suspected. Complete release was defined as extension of the incisions across the entire length of constricting eschar, with documented restoration of Doppler signals or improvement in perfusion after the procedure. The date and time of escharotomy relative to injury, and the extent of release, were abstracted from the operative notes. Because intrinsic muscle ischemia can occur despite adequate skin release (Salisbury et al., 1974), the operative notes were also reviewed for any additional fasciotomy.

After escharotomy, wounds were dressed with topical antimicrobial agents, and early tangential or fascial excision with autografting was performed when the patient's physiologic condition permitted. Occupational therapy consultation was obtained for custom splinting and for the initiation of active and passive range-of-motion exercises. Digits with progressive demarcation or necrosis were observed until the line of demarcation was clear and were then amputated electively at the level of viable tissue.

**Data Collection and Variables**

A single reviewer abstracted data from the registry and the inpatient and outpatient medical records using a standardized collection form; a second reviewer independently verified a random sample of the records to assess abstraction accuracy. Collected variables included age, sex, mechanism of burn (flame, scald, contact, electrical, chemical), percentage TBSA, depth of the hand burn, the presence of inhalation injury, laterality, the time from injury to escharotomy, the extent of escharotomy, timing of excision and grafting, and the length of hospital stay. For every hand, we recorded whether neurovascular compromise was documented before escharotomy, whether perfusion was restored, and whether any digit later required amputation.

**Outcome Definitions**

The primary outcome was delayed amputation of one or more digits in a hand that had undergone escharotomy of a digit judged salvageable. Delayed amputation was defined as a digital amputation, at any level, performed after the initial escharotomy and attributable to subsequent necrosis, as documented in the operative and pathology records. The amputation rate was calculated as the number of hands requiring delayed amputation divided by the total number of hands that underwent escharotomy. Secondary outcomes included the number and level of digits amputated and the association of amputation with burn depth, burn mechanism, TBSA, age, and sex.

**Statistical Analysis**

Continuous variables are presented as means with standard deviations or as medians with ranges, depending on the distribution as assessed by the Shapiro-Wilk test. Categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages. Patients and hands that did and did not require delayed amputation were compared. Continuous variables were compared with the Student t test or the Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate, and categorical variables with the Fisher exact test, given the small number of events expected. Associations of TBSA and age with amputation were additionally examined with point-biserial correlation coefficients. Because hands from the same patient are not statistically independent, we repeated the principal comparisons at the patient level, classifying a patient as having had an amputation if either hand was affected. We did not develop a multivariable regression model, because the number of outcome events was too small to support one without overfitting. The analysis is therefore descriptive and hypothesis-generating. All tests were two-tailed, and a P value less than .05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed with SPSS statistical software (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). Missing data were not imputed, and the denominator for each variable is reported wherever it differs from the total cohort.

Results

**Patient and Burn Characteristics**

The registry search identified 34 patients who underwent upper extremity or hand escharotomy between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2005, and all met the inclusion criteria. Together they had 57 burned hands: 23 patients (68%) had bilateral hand involvement and 11 (32%) had unilateral involvement. There were 24 men (71%) and 10 women (29%). Mean age was 41.2 years (SD 16.8; range 19–78), and 4 patients were older than 65 years. Mean total body surface area (TBSA) burned was 28.4% (SD 17.9; median 24%; range 4%–75%). Eleven patients (32%) had a TBSA burned greater than 40%, and 9 (26%) had an inhalation injury. Flame burns were the most common mechanism (18 patients, 53%), followed by electrical injury (6, 18%), scald (5, 15%), contact burn (3, 9%), and chemical burn (2, 6%). The 6 patients with electrical injury accounted for 8 of the 57 hands (14%). The remaining 49 hands (86%) had thermal or chemical injuries.

Burn depth was assessed from the operative and clinical documentation for each hand. Twenty-one hands (37%) had full-thickness injury involving at least part of the dorsal hand or digits, and 36 hands (63%) had deep partial-thickness injury. Circumferential or near-circumferential digital involvement was documented in 31 hands (54%). These proportions are consistent with earlier series in which escharotomy was reserved for deep, circumferential injuries with clinical or Doppler evidence of impaired perfusion (Salisbury et al., 1973; Sheridan et al., 1995).

**Indications and Timing of Escharotomy**

All 57 hands underwent escharotomy because of clinical neurovascular compromise. Documented findings were loss or diminution of Doppler signals in the digital arteries (47 hands, 82%), pallor or delayed capillary refill (38 hands, 67%), and tense swelling with progressive paresthesias in the 19 patients (56%) who were awake and able to cooperate with examination. Forearm or carpal tunnel decompression was performed in 41 hands (72%) in addition to hand and digital incisions. Dorsal interosseous compartment release was performed in 29 hands (51%), and digital escharotomies were performed in 52 hands (91%), with a mean of 3.6 digits per hand (range 1–5).

Median time from injury to escharotomy was 4.0 hours (interquartile range, 2.5–8.0; range 1–18 hours). Forty-nine hands (86%) were decompressed within 8 hours of injury. Thirty-one patients (91%) were treated at, or transferred directly to, the burn center before escharotomy, and 3 patients (9%) had the procedure at a referring facility. Restoration of Doppler signals or capillary refill was recorded immediately after release in 54 of 57 hands (95%). The 3 hands without immediate reperfusion all belonged to patients with electrical injury, and each subsequently required amputation.

**Acute Management**

Early splinting in the intrinsic-plus (safe) position was documented for 52 hands (91%), generally within 24 hours of admission, and occupational therapy consultation occurred a median of 1 day after admission (range 0–4). Tangential or fascial excision and autografting of the hand was performed at a median of 5 days after injury (range 2–14) in 49 hands (86%). Forty-one hands (72%) were excised within the first 7 days. The remaining 8 hands (14%) healed or were managed nonoperatively, or were excised after the study period of acute care had concluded. Split-thickness skin grafts were used in 43 hands, and 6 hands required pedicled or free flap coverage for exposed tendon or joint. Sheet grafts were used for the dorsal hand in 31 of the 43 grafted hands (72%). This strategy is consistent with recommendations that favor early excision and sheet grafting of the hand to limit joint stiffness and scarring (Sheridan et al., 1995; Kamolz et al., 2004). Median hospital stay was 31 days (range 6–112 days), and 3 patients (9%) died during the index admission from causes unrelated to the hand injury, all with TBSA greater than 60%.

**Delayed Amputation**

Despite prompt recognition of neurovascular compromise and technically adequate escharotomy, 6 of the 57 hands (10.5%; 95% confidence interval, 4.0%–21.5%) required delayed amputation of one or more digits. These hands belonged to 5 patients (15% of the cohort), one of whom required bilateral amputations. A total of 11 digits were amputated, with a median of 2 digits per affected hand (range 1–3). Seven amputations were at or distal to the proximal interphalangeal joint, 3 were at the proximal phalanx level, and 1 was a ray resection of the small finger. Amputation was performed a median of 19 days after injury (range 8–42 days). In every case the digit had initially appeared salvageable, with return of perfusion after escharotomy, and progressed over days to dry gangrene or deep infection with exposed, nonviable bone or joint. Fifty-one hands (89.5%) maintained all digits through the end of follow-up, which had a median duration of 14 months (range 3–48 months). The 6 hands with delayed amputation had a median of 2 additional operations (range 1–4) beyond the amputation procedure, compared with 1 additional operation (range 0–3) in hands that did not require amputation.

**Factors Associated with Amputation**

Table 2 summarizes the comparison of patients with and without amputation. Mean TBSA burned was 31.2% (SD 20.1) in patients who required amputation and 28.0% (SD 17.8) in those who did not (p = 0.71).
