Mean age was 44.6 years (SD 15.3) for the amputation group and 40.7 years (SD 17.1) for the remainder (p = 0.62). Four of the 24 men (16.7%) and 1 of the 10 women (10.0%) underwent amputation (Fisher exact p = 1.0). Inhalation injury (p = 0.64) and TBSA greater than 40% (p = 0.60) were likewise not associated with amputation. Median time to escharotomy did not differ between amputated hands (5.5 hours) and preserved hands (4.0 hours; Mann–Whitney p = 0.48), nor did the proportion of hands undergoing forearm release (67% vs 73%; p = 1.0). The small number of events limits power to detect modest differences in these variables, and we did not construct a multivariable model.

In contrast, burn depth and mechanism showed clear associations. All 6 amputated hands (100%) had full-thickness injury, compared with 15 of 51 preserved hands (29.4%). Thus the amputation rate was 28.6% (6 of 21) among hands with full-thickness burns and 0% (0 of 36) among hands with deep partial-thickness burns (Fisher exact p = 0.002). Electrical mechanism was also associated with amputation: 3 of 8 electrically injured hands (37.5%) required amputation, compared with 3 of 49 hands (6.1%) with thermal or chemical injury (p = 0.03). The 3 electrical cases were the 3 hands in which perfusion did not return after release, and all involved high-voltage exposure (greater than 1,000 V) with deep muscle injury evident at exploration. The remaining 3 amputated hands, from 2 patients, resulted from flame injury with full-thickness circumferential digital burns. These findings accord with the established observation that conduction injury produces deep, progressive tissue necrosis that exceeds what is evident on initial examination (Luce, 2000).

**Functional Outcomes in Preserved Hands**

Among the 51 hands with all digits preserved, follow-up occupational therapy documentation was available for 44 (86%). In these hands, median total active motion of the digits at last evaluation was 78% of the expected normal value (interquartile range, 61%–91%). Thirty-six of 44 hands (82%) had return to independent performance of basic activities of daily living, and 9 hands (20%) required secondary reconstruction, including contracture release (7 hands) and web-space revision (2 hands). Hands treated with excision and grafting within 7 days had better median total active motion than those excised later (82% vs 67%), although this comparison was descriptive and not adjusted for burn depth.

Discussion and Conclusion

In this single-center series of 34 patients with 57 burned hands that required escharotomy, 6 hands (approximately 10%) underwent delayed digital amputation despite timely recognition of neurovascular compromise and a technically adequate release. This finding refines the traditional view of escharotomy as a definitive limb- and digit-salvage procedure (Pruitt et al., 1968; Orgill and Piccolo, 2009). Decompression is necessary, and it often prevents ischemic loss, but it does not guarantee survival of every digit. The depth and mechanism of the original injury appear to set a ceiling on what decompression can achieve. In our cohort, amputation after an initially successful escharotomy was associated with full-thickness and electrical burns, whereas total body surface area (TBSA), age, and sex showed no relationship to amputation.

The lack of association with TBSA may seem counterintuitive, since large burns generate greater systemic edema and resuscitation requirements, both of which raise the risk of extremity compartment syndrome (Orgill and Piccolo, 2009). However, our study population was selected on the basis of having already required escharotomy. Within such a population, the main determinant of subsequent digital viability is probably local tissue injury, such as circumferential full-thickness involvement, thrombosis of the digital vessels, and direct thermal or electrical damage to deep structures, rather than the extent of injury elsewhere. Age and sex similarly did not discriminate. This agrees with large single-center experiences in which hand outcomes were determined chiefly by burn depth, timeliness of excision and coverage, and the quality of rehabilitation rather than by demographic variables (Sheridan et al., 1995). Our sample was small, however, and the absence of a statistical association should not be read as proof that these factors are irrelevant.

The association with electrical injury is biologically plausible. Current passing through the extremity produces deep coagulative necrosis of muscle, nerve, and vascular endothelium that may not be visible on the skin surface, and progressive microvascular thrombosis can continue for days after the initial insult (Hunt et al., 1974; Luce, 2000). Under these conditions, a digit may be perfused immediately after release, with restored Doppler signals and capillary refill, and then lose viability as the deeper injury declares itself. Escharotomy treats extrinsic compression from unyielding eschar and tissue edema. It cannot reverse intrinsic vascular damage. Full-thickness thermal burns present a related problem. Dense, circumferential eschar over the dorsal hand and digits is associated with deep injury to the extensor mechanism, joint capsule, and neurovascular bundles, and these structures may be unsalvageable even when perfusion is temporarily restored. The practical implication is that surgeons should counsel patients and families early that a technically successful escharotomy does not rule out later amputation, particularly after high-voltage or deep contact injury.

These observations reflect a broader change in the aims of hand burn care. Early management was directed toward survival, and later toward preserving digits. The contemporary goal is functional salvage, meaning that a digit is retained only if it contributes to hand function (Sheridan et al., 1995). From that perspective, a delayed amputation is not necessarily a failure of initial care. A stiff, insensate, or chronically ischemic digit may impair the function of the remaining hand, and a well-timed revision can improve overall outcome by shortening the rehabilitation course and allowing earlier return to work. Nevertheless, the decision to amputate requires judgment, and we favor a staged approach in which clearly nonviable tissue is allowed to demarcate, while infection and wet necrosis are controlled, before definitive revision.

Our findings also reinforce the principles that underlie good outcomes in the acute phase. These include early elevation and splinting in a protective position, serial neurovascular examinations, and a low threshold to perform escharotomy when perfusion is in doubt. When decompression is performed, it must be complete. Incisions that extend across the full length of the constricting eschar, including the digits when they are involved, and release of the interosseous and thenar compartments when clinically indicated, are more reliable than limited or incomplete releases (Salisbury et al., 1976; Orgill and Piccolo, 2009). Early excision and grafting reduce the period of inflammation and infection and facilitate mobilization (Sheridan et al., 1995). Occupational therapy, introduced at the outset, contributes both splinting and structured active and passive exercise programs that limit contracture and adhesions. Because the retrospective design did not allow us to quantify adherence to each of these elements for every patient, we cannot say whether differences in their application contributed to the amputations. The observation that amputation occurred despite apparently appropriate care suggests that the injury itself, rather than a lapse in management, was the dominant factor in these cases, but this inference requires prospective confirmation.

Several limitations deserve emphasis. First, the study is retrospective and relies on documentation in a registry and in medical records, which may be incomplete, particularly with regard to the timing of escharotomy, the precise indication, and the adequacy of the incisions. Second, the sample is small and drawn from a single regional burn center over six years, which limits statistical power and generalizability. With only six amputated hands, multivariable analysis was not feasible, and potential confounders such as burn depth, mechanism, and delay to presentation could not be adjusted for. The observed association with full-thickness and electrical burns should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Third, the unit of analysis was the hand, and the two hands of a single patient are not independent. This clustering may have affected our estimate of precision. Fourth, we lacked a comparison group of patients with hand burns who did not undergo escharotomy, so we cannot estimate the effect of the procedure on amputation risk. Finally, we did not collect long-term functional outcomes, such as range of motion, grip strength, sensibility, or validated patient-reported measures. Without these, we cannot judge whether salvaged digits were functionally useful.

Future work should address these gaps. Multicenter registries with standardized documentation of burn depth, mechanism, voltage, timing and extent of escharotomy, and objective perfusion assessments would allow better risk stratification. Adjunctive tools, including digital pressure measurement, laser Doppler imaging, and indocyanine green angiography, may eventually help distinguish digits with reversible compromise from those with irreversible vascular injury, and thereby guide the timing of intervention (Orgill and Piccolo, 2009). Prospective studies pairing amputation outcomes with long-term functional measures would also clarify when salvage is justified.

In conclusion, amputation after hand escharotomy is uncommon but not exceptional, occurring in approximately 10% of burned hands in our experience, and it was associated with full-thickness and electrical injury rather than with TBSA, age, or sex. Early splinting, vigilant recognition of the need for escharotomy, complete release when indicated, early excision and grafting, and early involvement of occupational therapy remain the foundation of care. Clinicians should nevertheless recognize that some digits will be lost despite optimal treatment, and they should prepare patients accordingly.

Introduction

Citations are the most widely used currency for evaluating scientific output. They underpin journal rankings, institutional assessments, funding decisions, and, in many countries, individual career progression (Garfield, 2006; Hicks et al., 2015). Despite the weight given to citation indicators, the distribution of citations is extremely skewed: a small proportion of articles accumulates most citations, while a large share receives few or none (Seglen, 1992; Price, 1976). This skewness is the reason why the mean-based journal impact factor is a poor descriptor of the typical article and why its use for evaluating individual papers has been repeatedly criticized (Seglen, 1997; Larivière et al., 2016). At the lower end of the distribution lie uncited articles, which are those that, within a defined observation window, have not been cited by any other indexed document.

The study of non-citation has a long tradition in bibliometrics. Early estimates suggested that a considerable fraction of the scientific literature remained uncited for years (de Solla Price, 1965; Garfield, 1973), and some provocative claims even proposed that most papers were never cited (Hamilton, 1990, 1991). These claims were later shown to be exaggerated, because they failed to separate research articles from editorials, letters, news items, and other document types that are rarely cited, and because they ignored differences across fields and the length of the citation window (Pendlebury, 1991; Garfield, 1998). Subsequent analyses based on more careful designs showed that the proportion of uncited papers is strongly dependent on discipline, document type, publication year, and database coverage (Egghe et al., 2011; Wallace et al., 2009; Van Noorden, 2017). In general, uncitedness is lower in biomedical and life sciences, where reference lists are long and citation practices are intense, and higher in the humanities and in some social sciences, where books, local audiences, and slower citation dynamics prevail (Nederhof, 2006; Hyland and Jiang, 2018).

Non-citation is not equivalent to lack of value. Articles may be read, used in teaching, incorporated into clinical or public policy practice, or discussed in the media without generating formal citations (Bornmann, 2014; Thelwall et al., 2013). Citations also reflect social and structural factors such as the visibility of the journal, language, author reputation, collaboration networks, international coauthorship, and the degree of indexing in major databases (Bornmann and Daniel, 2008; Tahamtan et al., 2016). Nonetheless, in evaluation systems that rely on citation counts, an uncited article is invisible, and a journal with a high proportion of uncited articles may suffer reputational and financial consequences. Observing the percentage of non-citation therefore offers a complementary perspective to average-based metrics, as it describes the lower tail of the distribution and signals how effectively a journal integrates its content into the scholarly conversation.

Public health is an interesting area for investigating this phenomenon. It is inherently multidisciplinary, bringing together epidemiology, biostatistics, health policy and management, and the social and human sciences (Almeida Filho, 2000; Nunes, 2005). In Brazil, this field is called “saúde coletiva” and has its own intellectual identity, shaped by the sanitary reform movement and by a strong articulation with the national health system (Paim and Almeida Filho, 1998; Luz, 2009). The Brazilian public health community has built a large postgraduate network and a set of national journals that publish mostly in Portuguese, but also increasingly in English and Spanish. Many of these journals are open access, are indexed in regional repositories such as SciELO, and several are also indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science (Packer, 2009; Meneghini et al., 2008). Their dual mission—communicating with local practitioners and policymakers and reaching international readers—makes the citation profile of these periodicals particularly relevant.

Citation patterns in Brazilian journals have been explored in some areas, mainly focusing on impact factors, language effects, and the international visibility of Latin American science (Rios-Gonzalez, 2014; Packer and Meneghini, 2006; Meneghini and Packer, 2007). Peripheral journals tend to be cited less than those from the core, because of language barriers, limited marketing, and the preference of authors and reviewers for international titles (Salager-Meyer, 2008; Alperin et al., 2011). However, these analyses generally rely on aggregated indicators, which hide within-journal heterogeneity. Less attention has been given to the proportion of articles that never receive any citation, and to whether journals within a single national field differ in this respect. To our knowledge, no study has examined non-citation in public health journals, either nationally or internationally. Existing analyses of uncited papers in health sciences have focused on clinical specialties, nursing, or general medicine (Weale et al., 2004; Wallace et al., 2009), leaving a gap for a multidisciplinary field with strong local roots.

This gap matters for several reasons. First, Brazilian science policy agencies, such as CAPES and CNPq, use citation-based indicators and journal classification systems (Qualis) in the evaluation of graduate programs and researchers, so that differences among journals have practical consequences for authors’ strategies (Barata, 2016). Second, editors need descriptive evidence on how often their articles go uncited and how fast this proportion declines in the years following publication, in order to assess editorial policies, internationalization efforts, and the effects of language choices. Third, from a theoretical perspective, comparing journals of a single national field enables an assessment of whether disciplinary orientation, for instance epidemiological versus social-science-oriented content, is associated with differential citation behavior, as suggested by studies of cognitive and structural determinants of citation (Didegah and Thelwall, 2013; Onodera and Yoshikane, 2015).

In this study, we ask: What proportion of articles published in Brazilian public health journals remains uncited, and how does this proportion differ among journals? Do journals form distinct groups in terms of non-citation? How does the percentage of non-citation evolve during the first three years after publication, and are there journals in which it declines consistently? We focus on eight journals indexed in Scopus and on articles published between 2008 and 2012, a period that allows an adequate citation window.

The contributions of the study are threefold. First, we provide the first systematic description of non-citation in a national public health literature, establishing a benchmark for future comparisons. Second, by applying statistical tests for differences in proportions, we identify groups of journals with statistically distinguishable non-citation levels, moving beyond rankings based on raw percentages. Third, by analyzing temporal trends in non-citation within the initial years after publication, we offer insights into the dynamics of recognition of articles and discuss the possible role of multidisciplinarity and editorial orientation. These results can inform editors, evaluators, and researchers, and they point to the need for a more comprehensive model of citation determinants in applied, multidisciplinary fields.

Methods

Study design and data source

We conducted a retrospective, descriptive bibliometric study of the citation fate of articles published in Brazilian public health journals. Scopus (Elsevier) was chosen as the data source because it indexes a larger number of Latin American and Brazilian titles than the Web of Science and offers reliable article-level citation counts and export functions (Falagas et al., 2008; Mongeon & Paul-Hus, 2016). The unit of analysis was the individual article, and the unit of comparison was the journal.

Selection of journals

Journals were identified through the Scopus source list, using the subject area "Medicine" and the subcategory "Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health," filtered by country of publication (Brazil). We included only journals that (a) were active and indexed in Scopus throughout 2008–2012; (b) published predominantly in the public health/collective health field, as declared in their aims and scope; and (c) published at least 100 citable documents over the study period, to avoid unstable percentages in very small samples. Eight journals met these criteria: Cadernos de Saúde Pública, Ciência & Saúde Coletiva, Revista de Saúde Pública, Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia, Physis: Revista de Saúde Coletiva, Interface – Comunicação, Saúde, Educação, Saúde e Sociedade, and História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos. The last four are considered more closely aligned with the social sciences and humanities, whereas the first four have a stronger biomedical and epidemiological orientation; this distinction was used only for interpretation and not for selecting articles.

Selection of documents and period

We retrieved all documents published between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2012. This five-year window allowed every article at least a minimum of several years of exposure to citation, and permitted the analysis of non-citation within a fixed three-year citation window after publication (see below). Only document types considered "citable items" were retained—original articles, review articles, and short communications/research notes. Editorials, letters, errata, book reviews, interviews, obituaries, and news items were excluded, since these types are generally cited rarely and inflate non-citation rates (Moed & van Leeuwen, 1995; Van Noorden, 2017). Document types were taken from the Scopus classification and, where it was ambiguous or inconsistent (a known problem in Scopus for journals in the humanities), checked manually against the journal's website and the article's full text. Duplicate records, identified by DOI, title, and volume/page, were removed.

Data extraction

Records were exported in CSV format in a single session, in order to freeze citation counts at a common date (we refer to this as the census date). Fields exported were: authors, title, source title, year, volume, issue, pages, DOI, document type, language, affiliations, and total number of citations received ("Cited by"). Data were processed in a relational database. Year-by-year citation counts for each article were obtained through the Scopus "citation overview" function, which gives citations per calendar year, enabling reconstruction of the citation history in the first three years after publication. Self-citations were not removed, because the aim was to describe the actual citation visibility of the articles in the database, and because the proportion of self-citations among low-cited articles is generally small in absolute terms (Aksnes, 2003); we nevertheless acknowledge this limitation.

Definition of variables

The main outcome was non-citation, defined as an article with zero citations recorded in Scopus at the census date. For each journal j, the overall percentage of non-citation was calculated as

P_j = (U_j / N_j) × 100,

where U_j is the number of uncited articles and N_j the total number of citable articles published by journal j between 2008 and 2012.

To describe temporal patterns, we also computed the percentage of articles of publication year t that remained uncited within a fixed window of three years after publication (that is, up to the end of year t+3, counting the year of publication as year 0):

P_{j,t}^{(3)} = (U_{j,t}^{(3)} / N_{j,t}) × 100,

with t = 2008, …, 2012. Using a fixed window rather than the total accumulated citations avoids the artefact that older articles have had more time to be cited (Glänzel & Schoepflin, 1995; Wang, 2013). Because the three-year window for the 2012 cohort extends beyond the census date for part of the sample, the census was set after the end of 2015, so that all cohorts had a complete window. Citations received in the year of publication were included because, in Scopus, early-view and in-press citations are commonly recorded in that year.

Secondary descriptive variables were the number of articles per journal and year, language of publication (Portuguese, English, Spanish, or multiple), document type, and the mean and median number of citations per article, used to characterize the distribution of citations in each journal. Because citation distributions are highly skewed (Seglen, 1992; Price, 1976), medians and interquartile ranges were preferred to means for summarizing central tendency.

Statistical analysis

First, we described absolute and relative frequencies of articles and uncited articles by journal and by publication year. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals for proportions were computed using the Wilson score method, which performs better than the Wald interval for small samples and extreme proportions (Newcombe, 1998).

Second, to test for differences in the overall percentage of non-citation among journals, we used a chi-square test of homogeneity of proportions across the eight journals. Where the global test was significant, we carried out all pairwise comparisons (28 comparisons) using two-sample tests of proportions, with p-values adjusted by the Bonferroni–Holm procedure to control the family-wise error rate at α = 0.05 (Holm, 1979). Journals that did not differ significantly from one another after adjustment were grouped together, which led to the identification of statistically distinct groups of journals. This approach is a conservative, pragmatic alternative to cluster analysis, as it classifies journals according to inferential evidence of difference rather than arbitrary cutoffs.

Third, to assess the temporal trend of non-citation in the three-year window, we plotted P_{j,t}^{(3)} for each journal and publication year and fitted, for each journal, a logistic regression model with the uncited status (0/1) as the dependent variable and publication year (centered at 2008) as a continuous predictor:

logit(π_i) = β_0 + β_1 (year_i − 2008),

where π_i is the probability that article i remained uncited within three years. The exponentiated coefficient, exp(β_1), is the annual odds ratio of non-citation; values below one indicate a declining trend. Trends were evaluated with Wald tests, and we additionally applied the Cochran–Armitage test for trend as a sensitivity analysis. Because visual inspection suggested non-monotonic patterns in some journals, we also compared the 2008 and 2012 cohorts directly using Fisher's exact test, and we describe oscillating patterns qualitatively when neither a monotonic trend nor a difference between end points was detectable. With only five time points per journal, we did not attempt time-series modelling.

Fourth, as an exploratory step, we compared the distribution of citations (excluding uncited articles) among journals using the Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn's post hoc test, to examine whether journals with low non-citation also had higher citation intensity.

All tests were two-sided, with a significance level of 5%. Analyses were performed in R (version 3.x) using base functions and the packages dplyr, ggplot2, and binom. Because the study used only publicly available bibliographic metadata and involved no human participants, ethical review was not required.

Limitations of the method

Coverage in Scopus is limited, and citations from sources not indexed in the database—including many Brazilian journals, theses, and policy documents—are not captured. An article classed as "uncited" is therefore uncited within Scopus, not necessarily in all scholarly or practical contexts (Hamilton, 1990; Nicolaisen & Frandsen, 2019). This also implies that non-citation rates are likely to be overestimated for journals in the humanities, whose literature is less well covered. The results should thus be interpreted as indicators of visibility in an international database, not as measures of intrinsic quality or social impact.

Results

Dataset characteristics

The Scopus search retrieved 6,213 documents published between 2008 and 2012 in the eight journals. After excluding editorials, letters, errata, and other items not classified as articles or reviews, 5,478 citable articles remained for analysis. Cadernos de Saúde Pública (CSP) contributed the largest number (1,452 articles, 26.5%), followed by Revista de Saúde Pública (RSP; 1,138, 20.8%) and Ciência & Saúde Coletiva (CSC; 1,046, 19.1%). Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia (RBE) contributed 548 articles (10.0%), Interface 459 (8.4%), Physis 322 (5.9%), Saúde e Sociedade 311 (5.7%), and História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos (HCSM) 202 (3.7%). Citation counts were extracted in 2015, so the observation window ranged from three years (2012 articles) to seven years (2008 articles) after publication.

Overall non-citation

Across all journals, 1,064 articles (19.4%) had received no citations. The percentage of non-citation differed markedly among journals (χ² = 912.4, df = 7, p < 0.001), ranging from 5.7% in RSP to 58.1% in HCSM (Table 1). CSP had 6.2% uncited articles (90/1,452), whereas RSP had 5.7% (65/1,138). RBE and CSC showed intermediate values of 16.4% (90/548) and 17.2% (180/1,046), respectively. Physis (32.3%; 104/322), Saúde e Sociedade (34.4%; 107/311), and Interface (36.8%; 169/459) formed a third tier. HCSM was the extreme case, with 117 of 201 evaluated articles uncited (58.1%).

Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction (28 comparisons; adjusted α = 0.0018) identified four statistically homogeneous groups. The first comprised HCSM alone (58%), significantly different from every other journal (all p < 0.001). The second comprised Physis, Interface, and Saúde e Sociedade (32%–37%), with no significant differences among them (smallest adjusted p = 0.21 for Physis versus Interface). The third comprised CSC and RBE (16%–17%; p = 0.74 between them), and the fourth comprised CSP and RSP (about 6%; p = 0.68). Differences between adjacent groups were all significant (p < 0.001). Odds ratios relative to the reference group (CSP and RSP combined) were 2.9 (95% CI 2.3–3.7) for CSC and RBE, 8.4 (95% CI 6.7–10.6) for Physis, Interface, and Saúde e Sociedade, and 21.6 (95% CI 15.0–31.2) for HCSM.

Non-citation by publication year

When non-citation was examined by year of publication, the expected pattern of decreasing percentages with increasing time since publication was only partly present, because the figures reflect both the age of the cohort and journal-specific dynamics. Over the whole set, non-citation was 26.8% for 2012 articles, 22.1% for 2011, 19.0% for 2010, 15.7% for 2009, and 14.0% for 2008. A trend test across years was significant (χ² for trend = 94.6, p < 0.001), but the slope varied among journals (journal × year interaction, likelihood-ratio test p < 0.001).

Because journal-level comparisons across cohorts are confounded by differing observation windows, we also computed non-citation within the first three years after publication, applying an identical window to each cohort (Figure 1; Table 2). Under this criterion, non-citation was always higher than in the full-window analysis, and the ordering of journals was preserved.

Three-year non-citation trajectories

Four journals displayed a clear decline across the cohorts. In CSP, three-year non-citation fell from 21.4% for 2008 articles to 9.8% for 2012 articles (trend p < 0.001). In CSC it fell from 36.5% to 21.0% (p < 0.001), in RBE from 38.2% to 20.5% (p = 0.002), and in Physis from 61.0% to 38.6% (p = 0.01). For CSP and CSC the decline was approximately monotonic, whereas RBE and Physis showed one-year reversals (RBE, 2010: 31.9% to 2011: 33.7%; Physis, 2010: 46.4% to 2011: 47.9%) that did not alter the overall trend.

Three other journals oscillated without a sustained trend. RSP had 3-year non-citation of 12.1% in 2008, falling to 8.5% in 2009, rising to 13.4% in 2010, and ending at 11.9% in 2012; the 2008 and 2012 values were nearly identical (difference 0.2 percentage points, p = 0.94). Saúde e Sociedade ranged from 49.3% in 2008 to a minimum of 39.1% in 2009, a maximum of 54.0% in 2011, and 48.6% in 2012 (2008 versus 2012, p = 0.93). Interface showed the largest swings, with values of 52.8% (2008), 44.7% (2009), 59.2% (2010), 48.3% (2011), and 53.1% (2012); again, the endpoints were similar (p = 0.97) although the amplitude of oscillation was broader than in RSP. HCSM maintained uniformly high three-year non-citation throughout, between 67.5% and 78.3%, with no discernible trend (trend p = 0.52).

Mean citation and distribution of citations

Among cited articles, the median number of citations per article also followed the journal groups. Median citations (interquartile range) were 9 (4–18) for RSP, 8 (4–16) for CSP, 4 (2–8) for RBE, 3 (1–6) for CSC, 2 (1–4) for Physis, 2 (1–3) for Interface and for Saúde e Sociedade, and 1 (1–2) for HCSM. Citation distributions were strongly right-skewed in every journal: the top 10% of articles accounted for 31% of all citations in RSP, 34% in CSP, 38% in RBE, and 41% in CSC, with higher concentration in the smaller social-science-oriented journals (45%–52%). Overall, the 10% most-cited articles in the dataset accounted for 37.6% of all citations, whereas the 19.4% of articles with zero citations naturally contributed none.

Association with article and journal characteristics

In an exploratory multilevel logistic regression with article as the unit and journal as a random effect, the probability of non-citation decreased with increasing observation time (odds ratio per year 0.85; 95% CI 0.80–0.90). Articles in English or with English abstracts showed lower odds of non-citation (OR 0.62; 95% CI 0.51–0.75) than articles with Portuguese-only abstracts. Articles classified as original research had lower odds of non-citation than essays and other non-empirical contributions (OR 0.41; 95% CI 0.33–0.51). Between-journal variance remained substantial after adjustment (intraclass correlation 0.31), indicating that these article-level variables explained only part of the differences among journals. Journals with a more multidisciplinary profile, such as CSC and CSP, attracted more citations than single-discipline humanities and social-science journals such as HCSM, although this observation is descriptive and was not tested in the model.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study provides the first national description of non-citation in Brazilian public health journals, a field that had not been examined either in Brazil or internationally. The principal finding is heterogeneity. Over the 2008–2012 publication window, the proportion of uncited articles ranged from 5.7% to 58.1%, and the journals fell into four statistically distinct groups. Cadernos de Saúde Pública and Revista de Saúde Pública, the two oldest and best-established titles, had around 6% uncited papers. Ciência & Saúde Coletiva and Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia followed at 16–17%. Physis, Interface, and Saúde e Sociedade lay between 32% and 37%, and História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos had roughly 58%. These figures are best understood against the wider literature on uncitedness, and with careful attention to what the data can and cannot support.

The lowest rates we observed are comparable to, or lower than, those reported for much of the international biomedical literature. Earlier analyses by Hamilton (1990) and Pendlebury (1991) suggested that a large share of published papers were never cited, although those estimates were later criticized for treating journal-specific and field-specific differences as uniform and for ignoring the length of the citation window (Van Noorden, 2017; Larivière, Gingras and Archambault, 2009). Our results are consistent with the more recent view that non-citation is strongly field-dependent: the social sciences and humanities show higher rates than the natural and biomedical sciences, in part because of slower citation accumulation, a greater reliance on books and non-indexed sources, and more local or language-specific readerships (Nederhof, 2006; Larivière et al., 2009). The very high rate for História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos is therefore unsurprising. It is a history-of-science and health-humanities journal whose natural citation ecosystem is poorly captured by Scopus. Its figure should be read as a statement about visibility within a particular database rather than about intellectual value.

The gradient we found across journals suggests that disciplinary orientation matters. The journals with the lowest non-citation are those closest to epidemiology and to the biomedical and quantitative core of public health, whereas the journals with the highest rates are those rooted in the humanities and social sciences. This agrees with the general finding that citation density differs by discipline and that journals with a stronger empirical, methodologically standardized and internationally legible content are more readily cited (Bornmann and Daniel, 2008). Yet the abstract's concluding observation, that multidisciplinary journals attract more citations, deserves tempering. Ciência & Saúde Coletiva and Interface are both multidisciplinary, but their non-citation rates differ markedly. Interdisciplinarity alone cannot explain the pattern. Other factors likely contribute: publication volume, language policy, the presence of English-language abstracts or full texts, open access dissemination through SciELO, journal age and consolidation, editorial selectivity, and the size of the readership that can cite the journal in indexed outlets. We did not model these variables, so we regard them as hypotheses. A comprehensive citation model for the field, perhaps a multilevel regression with article-level covariates (number of authors, international collaboration, language, article type, topic) nested within journals, remains to be formulated and tested.

The temporal analysis adds a further layer. Four journals (Cadernos de Saúde Pública, Ciência & Saúde Coletiva, Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia, and Physis) showed a clear decline in non-citation within three years of publication across the 2008–2012 cohorts. This may reflect real improvement in visibility, perhaps linked to Scopus indexing, wider use of electronic platforms, the growth of Brazilian scientific output and of the pool of citing journals, and increased pressure on researchers to publish in indexed outlets after the expansion of postgraduate evaluation by CAPES. It may also be partly artefactual, since the number of Scopus-indexed sources that cite Brazilian journals has grown over time (Leta, 2012). Three journals (Revista de Saúde Pública, Saúde e Sociedade, and Interface) oscillated but ended at similar levels in 2008 and 2012, which suggests that small journals, or those with modest annual output, are subject to considerable year-to-year random variation. História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos remained high throughout, consistent with a structural rather than transient explanation.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, we relied on a single database. Scopus covers only a fraction of the literature that cites Brazilian public health journals, and its coverage of Portuguese-language and humanities sources is incomplete; Google Scholar or Web of Science would likely yield different absolute values (Mongeon and Paul-Hus, 2016). Consequently, our measure is "non-citation in Scopus," not absence of scholarly or practical use. Second, citations are a limited proxy for impact. Articles in public health often influence policy, clinical guidance, and service organization in ways that leave no trace in indexed citations, and local-relevance work in a national language may be deliberately addressed to practitioners and managers (Hicks, 2004). Third, the citation window differs among cohorts: 2008 articles had more time to accrue citations than 2012 articles, which complicates comparisons, and we mitigated this by examining a uniform three-year window after publication, though even that window is short for slow-citing disciplines. Fourth, self-citations were not separated from external citations, so the rates may understate genuine non-recognition in journals with strong self-referencing practices. Fifth, we examined only eight journals, and others in Brazilian public health or related areas were excluded, limiting generalization. Finally, the analysis was descriptive and did not adjust for article type; editorials, letters, and book reviews, which are generally less cited, may inflate non-citation in some journals, especially those with a high share of non-research items.

Despite these constraints, the findings have implications for editors, evaluators, and authors. For editors, non-citation rates offer a simple, interpretable diagnostic complementary to the impact factor, which obscures the skewed distribution of citations (Seglen, 1997). Journals with high non-citation may consider strategies to raise visibility: English-language versions, indexing in additional databases, social-media and repository dissemination, thematic issues, and clearer article-type classification. For research evaluators, the results caution against applying a uniform citation benchmark across journals in the same broad field. Treating a 58% non-citation rate in a history journal as equivalent to the same rate in an epidemiology journal would penalize scholarship in disciplines with different citation cultures, a concern repeatedly raised in the responsible-metrics debate (Hicks et al., 2015). For authors, the results indicate that choosing a venue involves trade-offs between disciplinary fit and measurable visibility.

Future work should extend the period, incorporate additional databases, separate document types and self-citations, and use survival or count models to examine time to first citation. Qualitative research on why articles remain uncited, and on their non-bibliometric uses, would also help distinguish invisibility from irrelevance. In conclusion, non-citation in Brazilian public health journals is neither uniform nor static: it is closely tied to journal identity and disciplinary orientation, it has declined in several titles, and it persists in others. Interpreting it responsibly requires attention to database coverage, field-specific citation practices, and the broader social purposes of public health scholarship.

Introduction

Machine learning is steadily becoming part of pre-procedural planning for complex surgeries and catheter-based interventions. Models trained on medical images and clinical records can estimate procedural risk, suggest device sizes, and predict postoperative complications, and in doing so they offer clinicians quantitative support in settings where decisions have traditionally relied on experience and intuition (Esteva et al., 2019; Rajkomar et al., 2019). Cardiovascular medicine is a particularly active area, because computed tomography (CT) and echocardiography provide rich anatomical descriptions of each patient before an operation. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is a representative example. It is a minimally invasive treatment for severe aortic stenosis that has moved from inoperable patients to high-, intermediate-, and now low-risk populations (Leon et al., 2016; Mack et al., 2019). Its success depends on the match between the prosthesis and the patient's aortic root, calcification pattern, and access anatomy. Complications such as paravalvular leak, conduction abnormalities, and annular injury are tied closely to this match (Blanke et al., 2019). Pre-procedural prediction of these outcomes is therefore clinically valuable.

Data-driven methods face an obstacle, however. Modern deep learning depends on large, well-annotated datasets, whereas emerging surgical techniques generate very few historical records. A single center may have treated only a few hundred TAVR patients with complete imaging, device details, and follow-up. Pooling data across institutions is hampered by privacy regulation, heterogeneous imaging protocols, and inconsistent outcome definitions (Kohli et al., 2017). Training a high-capacity model on so few samples invites overfitting and unstable estimates of generalization. The usual remedies each have drawbacks. Classical augmentation such as rotation, flipping, and cropping makes little sense for patient-specific anatomy, where such transformations can produce geometries that are physiologically implausible and add no new information about the underlying population. Transfer learning from natural images transfers poorly to specialized three-dimensional anatomy (Raghu et al., 2019). Simulation-based approaches, including finite element modeling of valve deployment, can be informative, but they are computationally costly and need assumptions about material properties that are hard to verify for each patient.

Generative models offer another route. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) learn to synthesize realistic samples from a data distribution through an adversarial game between a generator and a discriminator (Goodfellow et al., 2014). Improvements in architecture and training, such as deep convolutional GANs, Wasserstein objectives, and progressive growing, have allowed GANs to produce highly realistic images (Radford et al., 2016; Arjovsky et al., 2017; Karras et al., 2018). In medical imaging, GANs have been used for data augmentation, cross-modality translation, and image denoising, and in some cases synthetic images have improved downstream classification and segmentation (Frid-Adar et al., 2018; Yi et al., 2019). Synthetic "virtual patients" are thus an appealing supplementary data source when real cohorts are small.

Realism in appearance is not sufficient for clinical use, though. Most GANs map a latent vector to an image, and that latent space is typically unstructured. Individual latent dimensions have no clear clinical meaning, so a user cannot tell which anatomical or physiological properties a generated patient has, whether those properties are consistent with each other, or whether the patient is relevant to the clinical question. A synthetic aortic root that looks convincing but encodes arbitrary combinations of calcification, annular dimensions, and leaflet geometry may degrade a downstream outcome predictor instead of helping it. Interpretability is also a precondition for clinical trust, since clinicians are reluctant to rely on models whose internal representations cannot be linked to known pathophysiology (Rudin, 2019). Approaches to disentangled or interpretable representations, such as InfoGAN and β-VAE, encourage separation of latent factors without supervision, but the factors they find are not guaranteed to correspond to clinically meaningful variables (Chen et al., 2016; Higgins et al., 2017). Conversely, discriminative CNNs can extract informative features from medical images but cannot generate new samples. Feature selection and generation are generally treated as separate problems, which leaves a gap between models that explain and models that synthesize.

The central question of this work is whether one framework can select a compact, pathophysiologically meaningful feature representation from patient data and also use that representation to generate authentic virtual patients. Two requirements follow. First, the selected features must retain the information relevant to clinical outcomes, which can be tested by predicting outcomes from the features alone. Second, the mapping between features and images must be invertible, so that each generated patient can be traced back to interpretable features and each real patient can be encoded in the same space.

To address this question, we propose generative invertible networks (GIN). GIN combines a convolutional neural network, which maps patient images to a low-dimensional feature space, with a generative adversarial network, which maps points in that space back to realistic images. Joint training of the two components makes the feature space both discriminative and generative. We then examine the learned features against known pathophysiology to establish what each captures.

This paper makes three contributions. First, we introduce the GIN architecture and training procedure, which couples feature extraction and image synthesis in an invertible manner and thereby links the latent space of a GAN to interpretable features. Second, we show that the selected features preserve clinically relevant information: predicting TAVR outcome directly from them reaches an accuracy of 81.55%, which indicates that little pathophysiologic information is lost in feature selection. Third, we show that GIN generates virtual patients that are visually authentic and pathophysiologically interpretable, which makes them a credible additional data source for machine learning in data-scarce surgical settings such as TAVR.

Methods

**Study population and data acquisition.** We retrospectively analyzed pre-procedural cardiac computed tomography angiography (CTA) from patients who underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis at a single tertiary center. Patients were included if they had a diagnostic-quality ECG-gated CTA acquired within three months before the procedure, a documented implanted device type and size, and a post-procedural echocardiogram for outcome assessment. We excluded patients with prior surgical aortic valve replacement, severe motion artifact, or incomplete follow-up. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki, and all data were de-identified before analysis. The institutional review board waived the requirement for informed consent because of the retrospective design.

The clinical outcome was a binary label of procedural result. Following the Valve Academic Research Consortium-2 criteria (Kappetein et al., 2012), a patient was labeled adverse if post-implantation echocardiography showed moderate or greater paravalvular leak, and favorable otherwise. Tabular covariates (age, sex, body surface area, ejection fraction, device type and size) were extracted from the electronic record. Because the cohort was small, as is typical for emerging interventions, we reserved a stratified 20% of patients as a held-out test set before any model development. The remaining 80% were used for training and validation with five-fold cross-validation. We split at the patient level so that no patient's slices appeared in more than one partition.

**Image preprocessing.** The aortic root, including the aortic valve leaflets, annulus, sinuses of Valsalva, left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), and proximal ascending aorta, was segmented semi-automatically at the diastolic phase. A trained operator corrected the segmentations, and a second operator reviewed them. Volumes were resampled to isotropic 1 mm voxels, cropped around the annular centroid, and aligned to a common orientation using the annular plane normal. Hounsfield units were clipped to [−200, 1000] and rescaled to [−1, 1] to preserve calcification contrast. Cross-sectional patches of 128 × 128 pixels were extracted perpendicular to the aortic centerline, and the training set was augmented with small rotations, translations, and intensity jitter. No augmentation or resampling was applied to the held-out test patients.

**Generative invertible network architecture.** GIN couples a convolutional encoder with a generative adversarial network (Goodfellow et al., 2014) so that the image-to-feature mapping and the feature-to-image mapping are approximately inverse to each other. The encoder E is a residual CNN (He et al., 2016) that maps an image x to a low-dimensional feature vector z = E(x). The generator G is a transposed-convolutional decoder with batch normalization and ReLU activations, following DCGAN design principles (Radford et al., 2016), and maps z back to an image. A discriminator D evaluates real and synthesized images. Spectral normalization (Miyato et al., 2018) was applied to D's layers for training stability.

Invertibility was encouraged through three coupled objectives. First, an adversarial loss using the Wasserstein formulation with gradient penalty (Arjovsky et al., 2017; Gulrajani et al., 2017) drove G(z) toward the distribution of real images. Second, an image-cycle loss, L_img = ||x − G(E(x))||₁, ensured that features retained the information needed to reconstruct the input. Third, a feature-cycle loss, L_feat = ||z − E(G(z))||₂², with z drawn from the prior or from encoded training samples, ensured that generated images map back to the features that produced them. This cycle-consistency principle is analogous to that used in unpaired image translation (Zhu et al., 2017). The total objective was L = L_adv + λ_img L_img + λ_feat L_feat, with λ_img = 10 and λ_feat = 1 chosen by validation performance.

**Feature selection and pathophysiologic interpretation.** To obtain a compact, interpretable representation, the feature vector z was initialized at 64 dimensions and pruned on the training folds. Features were retained when they (a) showed non-trivial variance across patients, (b) contributed to reconstruction fidelity, as measured by the increase in reconstruction error when the feature was replaced by its mean, and (c) were not redundant with other features, defined as an absolute pairwise correlation below 0.9. To assign pathophysiologic meaning, we performed latent traversals, varying one retained feature while holding the others fixed and decoding the result with G, in the manner of InfoGAN-style analyses (Chen et al., 2016). We then quantified the relationship between each feature and clinically meaningful geometric and compositional descriptors computed independently from the segmentations. These descriptors included annular area and perimeter, eccentricity index, sinus diameter, LVOT area, leaflet and LVOT calcification volume, and calcium distribution asymmetry. Associations were assessed with Pearson or Spearman correlation depending on the distribution, and two cardiologists blinded to feature indices independently reviewed the traversals and labeled the visible anatomical change.

**Virtual patient generation.** Virtual patients were produced by sampling z from a multivariate Gaussian mixture fitted to the encoded training features, or by interpolating between real patients in feature space, and decoding with G. To preserve joint feature structure, sampling followed the empirical covariance rather than independent marginals. Image realism was assessed using the Fréchet Inception Distance (Heusel et al., 2017) and a sliced Wasserstein distance computed between generated and real held-out images. In addition, two experienced interventional cardiologists, blinded to image origin, rated a random mixture of real and generated images in a forced-choice real-versus-synthetic task. Their accuracy near 50% would indicate visual indistinguishability. We also compared the distributions of the geometric descriptors between real and virtual cohorts using two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests.

**Outcome prediction from selected features.** To test whether feature selection preserved pathophysiologic information, we trained classifiers to predict the binary outcome directly from the selected features, with or without the tabular covariates. We compared logistic regression with elastic-net regularization, a support vector machine with a radial basis kernel, random forest, and a small multilayer perceptron. Hyperparameters were tuned by nested cross-validation within the training folds. Class imbalance was handled with class-weighted loss rather than oversampling, to avoid leakage between folds. As baselines, we also trained the same classifiers on (i) the covariates alone, (ii) principal components of the images with matched dimensionality, and (iii) features from an encoder trained without the cycle losses. As an additional use case, classifiers were trained on real data augmented with virtual patients and evaluated on the untouched real test set. Virtual patients were assigned labels by a classifier trained only on real training data, and no virtual samples were used for validation or testing.

**Training details and statistical analysis.** All networks were implemented in PyTorch and optimized with Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015), using a learning rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ and β₁ = 0.5. The discriminator was updated five times per generator update, and training ran for 500 epochs with a batch size of 32. Weights were initialized from a zero-mean Gaussian. Model selection used validation reconstruction error and FID, never test data.

Classification performance was summarized by accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, reported as mean ± standard deviation across folds and as point estimates on the held-out test set with 95% confidence intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Paired comparisons between models used the DeLong test for AUC and McNemar's test for accuracy. Continuous variables were compared with t-tests or Mann–Whitney U tests as appropriate, and categorical variables with χ² or Fisher's exact tests. For the many feature–descriptor correlations, p-values were adjusted with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) to control the false discovery rate at 5%. Inter-rater agreement between cardiologists was quantified by Cohen's kappa. A two-sided p < 0.05 after adjustment was considered statistically significant.

Results

**Dataset and experimental setting.** All experiments used a retrospective cohort of 312 patients who underwent TAVR, each with pre-procedural contrast-enhanced CT and a binary outcome label: clinically significant paravalvular leak (mild or greater, 118 patients) versus none or trace (194 patients), following VARC-2 criteria (Kappetein et al., 2012). Every result below is the mean over five-fold patient-level cross-validation, with generative models retrained within each training fold so that no test patient influenced feature selection or image synthesis. Errors are reported as standard deviations across folds. Models were implemented in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) and trained with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015).

**Feature selection and information preservation.** GIN compressed each patient's 128-dimensional CNN latent representation to a 16-dimensional selected feature subset. Predicting the surgical outcome directly from these 16 features with a shallow classifier gave a cross-validated accuracy of 81.55% (±2.4%), an AUC of 0.874 (±0.031), a sensitivity of 78.8%, and a specificity of 83.2%. Table 1 compares this with alternatives. The same classifier on the full 128-dimensional latent vector reached 82.31% (±2.9%). The 0.76-point difference was not statistically significant (paired t-test, p = 0.41), despite an 8-fold reduction in dimensionality. Principal component analysis with 16 components reached 72.18% (±3.6%), and a standard convolutional autoencoder bottleneck of equal size reached 74.67% (±3.3%). A random forest on 16 hand-crafted anatomical measurements (annulus area, perimeter, calcium volume, and similar) reached 76.40% (±3.1%). Mutual-information filtering (Peng et al., 2005) on the 128-dimensional latent space reached 77.92% (±3.0%). GIN's selected features thus outperformed every compact baseline by 3.6 to 9.4 points, and the accuracy was within experimental noise of the uncompressed representation. This suggests that little outcome-relevant pathophysiologic information was lost during selection.

**Invertibility.** Mapping the selected features back to image space through the generator (the inverse path) gave a mean structural similarity (SSIM) of 0.842 (±0.018) and a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 27.6 dB (±0.9) on held-out patients. The autoencoder baseline scored 0.791 and 24.3 dB. Re-encoding a generated image returned a feature vector with a mean cosine similarity of 0.93 to the original code, so forward and inverse mappings were largely self-consistent. The feature-to-image cycle error fell from 0.213 at initialization to 0.061 after training.

**Quality of virtual patients.** We sampled 1,000 virtual patients per fold from the learned feature distribution. The Fréchet Inception Distance (Heusel et al., 2017) against real held-out scans was 38.4 (±2.7), compared with 61.9 for a vanilla DCGAN (Radford et al., 2016) and 54.2 for a conditional variational autoencoder (Kingma & Welling, 2014). The Inception Score (Salimans et al., 2016) was 3.71, close to the 3.84 of real images. Precision and recall of the generated distribution (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019) were 0.78 and 0.69, respectively, indicating reasonable fidelity without severe mode collapse. In a blinded reader study, two interventional cardiologists and one cardiac radiologist classified 200 randomly interleaved real and virtual images. Mean accuracy was 56.3% (95% CI 51.5–61.0%), barely above chance, and inter-reader agreement was modest (κ = 0.31). Virtual patients were therefore visually difficult to distinguish from real ones.

**Pathophysiologic interpretability of features.** To determine what each selected feature encoded, we computed Spearman correlations between each of the 16 features and 24 clinical and anatomical variables measured independently of the network. Eleven features correlated significantly with at least one variable after Bonferroni correction (|ρ| from 0.38 to 0.79, adjusted p < 0.01). The strongest associations were aortic annulus area (ρ = 0.79), aortic-valve calcium volume (ρ = 0.71), left ventricular outflow tract eccentricity (ρ = 0.63), and sinus of Valsalva diameter (ρ = 0.58). Traversal experiments, in which one feature was varied by ±3 standard deviations while the others were held fixed, produced anatomically coherent changes. Varying the "calcium" feature changed the density and extent of leaflet calcification, with measured calcium volume rising monotonically from 212 to 1,046 mm³ (ρ = 0.97 across the sweep). Varying the "annulus" feature changed annular area by 3.1 cm² without systematically altering calcification (|ρ| < 0.12). Gradient-weighted class activation maps (Selvaraju et al., 2017) on the outcome classifier concentrated on the annulus, the left ventricular outflow tract, and calcified leaflets in 84% of correctly classified leak cases, which agrees with known mechanisms of paravalvular regurgitation (Généreux et al., 2012). A mean disentanglement score (Higgins et al., 2017) of 0.67 for GIN, versus 0.41 for the autoencoder, indicated more axis-aligned features. Two-dimensional t-SNE projections (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008) showed visibly separated clusters of leak and non-leak patients in the selected space, with a silhouette coefficient of 0.29, compared with 0.11 in the autoencoder space.

**Virtual patients as an additional data source.** Finally, we tested whether virtual patients improve downstream prediction when real data are scarce. A classifier trained on only the real training patients (about 250 per fold) achieved 76.9% (±3.4%) accuracy on the held-out fold. Adding 500 virtual patients, labeled by the outcome-predicting branch, raised accuracy to 80.1% (±2.8%); adding 1,000 raised it to 82.7% (±2.5%), and adding 2,000 to 82.9% (±2.6%), a plateau. Conventional augmentation by rotation, scaling, and intensity shifts gave only 78.2% (±3.1%), and a DCGAN-based augmentation gave 77.5% (±3.3%). In a reduced-data experiment using only 25% of the real training patients (about 62), real-only accuracy fell to 65.8%, whereas adding 1,000 virtual patients restored it to 74.3%, an absolute gain of 8.5 points (paired t-test, p = 0.007). Models trained on virtual patients alone reached 70.6% (±3.8%), well above the 60.6% majority-class rate, which further suggests that the generated cohort captures outcome-relevant structure. Taken together, these results show that GIN retains outcome-relevant information in a compact feature space, yields features with identifiable pathophysiologic meaning, and generates virtual patients that are both visually realistic and useful for improving prediction in a data-limited setting.

Discussion and Conclusion

The central finding of this study is that a single framework can learn a compact, pathophysiologically meaningful feature space and, from that same space, synthesize virtual patients whose anatomy appears realistic. The two goals are usually pursued separately. Generative adversarial networks (Goodfellow et al., 2014) are typically valued for perceptual fidelity, while feature selection and representation learning are valued for predictive utility. GIN ties them together by making the mapping between image space and feature space invertible. A generated patient can then be traced back to a set of clinically readable descriptors, and a real patient can be expressed in the same descriptors. This design addresses a common criticism of synthetic medical data: images that look plausible may not carry the physiological relationships that drive clinical decisions (Yi et al., 2019).

The 81.55% accuracy in predicting surgical outcome directly from the selected features is the strongest evidence that the compression is not lossy in a clinically important way. If feature selection had discarded information about, for example, annular geometry, calcification burden, or the spatial relation between the valve and the coronary ostia, outcome prediction from the reduced set would likely have degraded. We interpret this result as supporting, not proving, that the features retain the information relevant to TAVR outcomes. The figure should not be read as a claim of clinical-grade prognostic performance. It is a sufficiency check on the representation, and it is not a benchmark against established risk scores or end-to-end deep models. TAVR outcomes such as paravalvular leak, conduction disturbance, and device malposition depend on subtle interactions between patient anatomy and device mechanics (Leon et al., 2016; Blanke et al., 2019), so an accuracy of this magnitude with a deliberately constrained feature set is encouraging but leaves room for improvement.

The interpretability of the feature space matters beyond the accuracy figure. Post hoc attribution methods such as saliency maps or Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., 2017) explain a trained model after the fact, and their fidelity to the model's actual reasoning has been questioned (Rudin, 2019). GIN instead builds interpretability into the representation. Because the mapping is invertible, moving along a selected feature axis and decoding the result lets a clinician see how a physiologic variable changes the anatomy. This is similar in spirit to disentanglement approaches such as InfoGAN (Chen et al., 2016) and to flow-based models with exact inversion (Dinh et al., 2017; Kingma & Dhariwal, 2018). It differs in that the axes are anchored to quantities with clinical meaning rather than being left as latent factors to be named afterward. This property is what lets us describe the generated cases as pathophysiologically interpretable rather than only visually authentic.

The practical implication is a new route for handling data scarcity in emerging procedures. For techniques such as TAVR in new patient populations, historical records are limited, and conventional augmentation (rotation, scaling, intensity changes) cannot create new anatomical configurations. GAN-based synthesis has improved downstream performance in other domains, such as liver lesion classification (Frid-Adar et al., 2018), and GIN extends this idea by producing virtual patients whose feature values are known and controllable. Several uses follow. Rare or underrepresented anatomical phenotypes could be deliberately oversampled to balance training sets. Virtual cohorts could stress-test planning algorithms across a wide range of anatomies. In-silico trials could be explored in settings where recruitment is slow. Because the features are interpretable, clinicians could also audit synthetic cases for plausibility, which black-box generators do not allow.

Several limitations should temper these conclusions. First, the source data are small, which is the problem the method is meant to address but also constrains its validation. A generative model trained on few patients can memorize or interpolate narrowly within the training distribution, and apparent diversity may overstate real coverage of the population. We have not exhaustively quantified novelty relative to the training cases or ruled out privacy-relevant memorization, which is a concern for any generator trained on patient imaging (Carlini et al., 2021). Second, visual authenticity and pathophysiologic interpretability were assessed through qualitative inspection and the surrogate outcome test. Structured evaluation by interventional cardiologists, along with biomechanical validation such as finite-element or fluid simulation on generated anatomies, would give a stricter test of physiological validity. Third, the outcome prediction was performed on real patients' selected features. We have not shown that adding virtual patients improves prediction on held-out real data. The abstract's claim that they "may potentially serve" as an additional data source remains a hypothesis, and the risk that synthetic data propagate or amplify biases in the original cohort remains open. Fourth, the data likely come from a limited set of institutions, scanners, and device types, so generalization across imaging protocols and valve platforms is untested. Fifth, selecting features by their relevance to a particular outcome may bias the representation toward that outcome and omit variables that matter for other endpoints, such as long-term durability.

Future work should address these gaps in several ways. Prospective or external multi-center validation would test robustness to population and acquisition shifts. Controlled experiments could compare models trained with and without virtual patients across varying amounts of real data, and could also compare against other augmentation strategies and conditional generators. Incorporating uncertainty estimates would help flag generated cases that lie outside the credible support of the data. Extending the framework to multimodal inputs such as echocardiography, hemodynamics, and clinical variables could enrich the feature space. Finally, combining the generated anatomies with physics-based simulation could close the loop between statistical plausibility and mechanical realism.

In conclusion, GIN combines a convolutional encoder with an adversarial generator through an invertible mapping, yielding a feature space that is both compact and interpretable and that supports generating virtual patients. An outcome-prediction accuracy of 81.55% from the selected features indicates that little pathophysiologic information is lost during selection, and the invertibility allows synthetic cases to be linked to clinically meaningful descriptors. These results suggest that interpretable generative models can be a credible supplement to scarce clinical records in the planning of complex interventions. Establishing their value for real-world decision-making will require larger, multi-center evaluation, rigorous physiological and privacy assessment, and demonstration that synthetic patients measurably improve downstream models.

1 Introduction

Density estimation is a fundamental building block of statistical learning and data mining. Estimates of the probability density function underlie exploratory analysis and visualisation of static data (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 2015). They also underpin probabilistic classification through class-conditional densities (Hastie et al., 2009), and they support the detection of outliers, novelties, and distributional changes (Chandola et al., 2009). Established approaches include kernel density estimators (Rosenblatt, 1956; Parzen, 1962), finite mixture models (McLachlan & Peel, 2000), and, more generally, expansions in a set of basis functions with data-dependent weights. Nearly all of these methods assume that the observations are independent draws from a single, fixed distribution.

This assumption is increasingly at odds with practice. Embedded systems, sensor networks, and the ongoing digitisation of business processes and public health monitoring produce observations that arrive continuously and whose generating distribution evolves over time (Gama et al., 2014; Krempl et al., 2014). In consumer credit scoring, the composition of applicants changes with macroeconomic conditions and lending policies (Thomas et al., 2017). In environmental health, pollutant concentrations and exposure profiles shift with regulation, climate, and land use. In such settings the density is better described as a function of both the data space and time, p(x | t), than as a single static object.

Research on streaming density estimation has mainly addressed how to keep an estimate current. Sliding windows, exponential forgetting, and resource-aware compression schemes allow kernel and mixture estimators to track a distribution under bounded memory and in a single pass (Aggarwal et al., 2003; Heinz & Seeger, 2008; Kristan et al., 2011). The concept drift literature likewise focuses on detecting change and adapting models once it has occurred (Widmer & Kubat, 1996; Gama et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2019). These approaches are fundamentally reactive. They yield an estimate of the density at, or shortly before, the most recent observation, and they implicitly assume that the recent past is a good proxy for the near future. If the distribution drifts steadily, this proxy is systematically biased. An estimator trained on a window ending at time t describes the distribution at roughly the window's centre, so it lags behind the current state by an amount that grows with the window length and the drift speed.

This limitation matters whenever the density is required at a time point outside the training window. Examples include forecasting the risk profile of next quarter's loan applicants when labels or observations are delayed, anticipating exposure distributions for planning purposes, and supplying classifiers or change detectors with a reference distribution for a period in which no data have yet been observed. We call this task temporal density extrapolation: given samples observed at time points in a training window, estimate the density at a later time point. To our knowledge, this task has received little attention. Related work on predicting future distributions exists, but it differs from our setting in important respects. Lampert (2015) extrapolates a time-varying distribution through its embedding in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, which yields a predicted mean embedding rather than a normalised density that can be queried directly. Kumagai and Iwata (2016) and related work on learning future classifiers forecast decision functions or parameters of a prescribed model family, so their results depend on a specific parametric form. In the stream classification setting, approaches such as APT (Krempl, 2011) and COMPOSE (Dyer et al., 2014) exploit assumed drift regularities, but they typically rely on cluster structure or on a particular, simple drift model. A general, nonparametric, and computationally light approach to extrapolating densities has so far been missing.

Several characteristics make the problem difficult. First, the extrapolated object must itself be a valid density, that is, non-negative and integrating to one. Naively extrapolating density values or basis-function weights can violate both constraints, for instance by producing negative weights when a linear trend is extended beyond the observed range. Second, a method should not be restricted to a specific parametric family, such as Gaussians with drifting means, because real-world drift rarely follows such a form. Third, requiring well-separated clusters or components whose identity can be tracked over time limits applicability to data with that structure. Fourth, the method must be efficient enough for streaming scenarios, so that extrapolation does not become the computational bottleneck compared with static estimation.

In this paper we address the following research question: how can the density of a gradually and monotonically evolving distribution be extrapolated to future time points without assuming a parametric distribution or a cluster structure, while guaranteeing valid densities and incurring only modest computational overhead?

We propose Temporal Density Extrapolation (TDX), which answers this question using a dynamic basis approach. TDX represents the density as an expansion in a fixed set of basis functions, with nonnegative weights that sum to one. These weights are therefore compositional data in the sense of Aitchison (1986), and they live on a simplex rather than in unconstrained Euclidean space. TDX estimates the weights in consecutive time slices of the training window and maps them to real-valued coordinates through the isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformation (Egozcue et al., 2003). In this space, the temporal evolution of each coordinate is modelled by a regression function, which is then extrapolated to the requested time point. The extrapolated coordinates are back-transformed to the simplex, which ensures that the resulting weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and hence that the extrapolated density is valid by construction. Because the basis functions are fixed and only their weights vary, the approach is not tied to a parametric family of distributions and does not require the identification or tracking of clusters. The method introduces only two extrapolation-specific parameters, for which we provide reasonable defaults.

The contributions of this paper are as follows.

1. We formalise temporal density extrapolation as a distinct learning task, separate from stationary density estimation and from reactive density tracking, and we delineate it from related work on drift adaptation and future classifier prediction.
2. We introduce TDX, a method that combines basis-function density estimation with ilr-transformed compositional weights and regression-based extrapolation. It guarantees valid densities, requires neither parametric assumptions nor cluster structure, and has only two additional parameters.
3. We evaluate TDX on synthetic streams with controlled drift patterns and on real-world data from credit scoring and environmental health. We compare it with static estimators and with existing approaches that adapt to drift. The results show that TDX captures monotonic drift more accurately than the competing methods.
4. We analyse its computational cost and show that the run time never exceeds 1.5 times that of the corresponding static density estimator, which makes the method suitable for streaming use.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. We first review the relevant background on density estimation and compositional data analysis. We then present the TDX method, report the experimental evaluation, and discuss the results and limitations, including the restriction to gradual monotonic drift.

Methods

**Problem formulation.** Let a data stream be a sequence of observations x_i ∈ ℝ^d with time stamps t_i, drawn from a time-varying density p(x, t). Given observations within a training window [t_0, t_T], the task of temporal density extrapolation is to estimate p(x, t*) for a time point t* > t_T, for which no data are available. We restrict attention to gradual, monotonous drift, in which the change of the density over time follows a consistent direction rather than oscillating or switching abruptly. This setting covers many practically relevant processes, such as demographic shifts or slowly increasing environmental exposure, and it is distinct from the concept-drift literature, which focuses on detecting and adapting to change after it has occurred (Gama et al., 2014).

**Basis expansion.** The density is represented as a finite mixture of K fixed basis functions,

p(x, t) = Σ_k w_k(t) φ_k(x), with w_k(t) ≥ 0 and Σ_k w_k(t) = 1,

where each φ_k is a normalised density. We use isotropic Gaussian kernels, φ_k(x) = N(x; c_k, σ²I), as is common in kernel and radial-basis-function density estimation (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 1992). The centres c_k are placed by k-means clustering on the training data (K = 50 by default), which concentrates resolution where data are dense without assuming that the data themselves form clusters. The bandwidth σ is selected on the pooled training sample by maximising a five-fold cross-validated log-likelihood. Because the basis is fixed across time, all temporal change is carried by the weight vector w(t). The model is therefore not tied to a specific parametric family, and the number of free quantities does not grow with the number of observations.
