The evaluation indicates that the service level achieves high accuracy with low latency and modest resource requirements, while the application level attains higher discrimination when given more time and features. By aligning classification granularity with the timing needs of each task, and by relying only on metadata visible under encryption, the approach improves end-to-end QoS measurement from the operator side without compromising user privacy or network security. Addressing dataset drift, adversarial robustness, and closed-loop QoE validation are the principal steps required before large-scale deployment.

Introduction

Strong primary care is widely accepted as the foundation of an equitable and efficient health system. Since the Declaration of Alma-Ata (WHO, 1978), international health policy has repeatedly returned to the view that first-contact, comprehensive, continuous and coordinated care delivers better population health at lower cost (Starfield, Shi and Macinko, 2005). Family medicine is the discipline that most directly embodies these attributes at the level of the individual practitioner. In high-income countries it has matured over several decades into a recognised specialty with defined training pathways, scopes of practice and roles within the health system. In much of sub-Saharan Africa, by contrast, family medicine is young. Postgraduate training programmes have been established only in the last two decades in countries such as South Africa, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, Ethiopia and Botswana, and the definition, scope and optimal deployment of the family physician (FP) remain contested (Mash and Reid, 2010; Flinkenflögel et al., 2014). Even where FPs are being trained, there is limited agreement on whether they should function mainly as district hospital generalists, clinical trainers and mentors of primary care teams, or first-contact clinicians in community-based practices (Mash et al., 2015).

Botswana illustrates both the promise and the difficulty of this evolution. The country has achieved near-universal access to public primary care facilities, a large antiretroviral treatment programme and steady gains in several health indicators since independence. It also faces a dual burden of persistent communicable disease, particularly HIV and tuberculosis, and rapidly rising noncommunicable diseases. Its health workforce is small relative to need and has historically depended on expatriate doctors. Nurses carry much of the clinical load in clinics, while doctors are concentrated in referral hospitals and in a growing private sector. Health expenditure, though higher than in many neighbouring countries, must compete with other national priorities, and the Abuja commitment to allocate 15% of government budgets to health has been difficult for African states to meet (Organisation of African Unity, 2001). In this setting, inefficiencies in the use of scarce resources, such as doctors performing tasks that others could do, fragmented records, duplicated investigations, hierarchical relationships between providers and patients, and unclear referral pathways, have direct consequences for quality of care. Introducing a new cadre of specialist generalists into such a system raises the question of what these physicians should do and how they should be supported.

Debates about the future of African family medicine have drawn mainly on models from the United Kingdom, North America, Australia and, more recently, other middle-income countries. Less attention has been paid to smaller European systems with long-established, gatekeeping-based family practice and high performance on equity and efficiency indicators. Denmark is a notable example. Danish general practitioners are mostly self-employed contractors who work within a tax-financed national health service. They serve as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care for a registered list of patients, and they are remunerated through a mixture of capitation and fee-for-service payments (Pedersen, Andersen and Søndergaard, 2012). Specialist training in general practice is structured and lengthy, and practices employ nurses, medical secretaries and laboratory staff who undertake a considerable proportion of routine clinical and administrative work. The Danish health system is also notable for its early and near-universal adoption of electronic communication in primary care, including shared electronic records, electronic prescribing and referrals, and patient access to their own health data through national portals (Protti and Johansen, 2010). These features operate against a background of high taxation, comparatively high public health spending and a social culture that emphasises egalitarian relationships and trust.

Although the Danish system has been described in the health services literature, little of that description has been interpreted for the needs of African family medicine. Most published accounts are written by Danish authors for European or North American audiences and focus on organisation, financing or quality indicators. They rarely examine the day-to-day experience of practice from the perspective of a clinician working in a resource-limited setting. The few African contributions on family medicine have concentrated on training curricula, competencies and the relationship between FPs and district health systems (Mash and Reid, 2010; Flinkenflögel et al., 2014). The result is a gap in knowledge. We lack a grounded, comparative reflection on how a mature family practice system functions in practice, which of its elements are transferable, and which depend on conditions that African countries do not currently share. Task shifting offers one example. The World Health Organization (2008) has recommended the rational redistribution of tasks among health workforce teams as a response to workforce shortages. In Africa the discussion has focused largely on shifting tasks from doctors to nurses, clinical officers and community health workers in HIV care (Lehmann and Sanders, 2007). The Danish arrangement, in which nurses and clerical staff routinely manage uncomplicated problems and administrative work so that physicians concentrate on complexity, represents task shifting of a different kind, one that is institutionalised, remunerated and supported by information systems rather than introduced as an emergency response to shortage.

This paper addresses that gap through a reflective, observational account of a visit by an African family physician to family practices in Denmark. The central question is: what can the organisation, training and practice of Danish family medicine teach Botswana, and by extension other African countries, about the future role of family medicine in resource-constrained health systems? We consider this question through four related themes that emerged during the visit: the training and role of the FP, the division of labour between FPs and support staff, the relationship between providers and patients, and the infrastructure of information technology and financing within which practice occurs.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a practitioner's comparative description of Danish family practice from the viewpoint of a physician trained and working in Botswana, drawing attention to features that are routine in Denmark but would be unfamiliar or even unimaginable in many African settings. Second, it links these observations to wider debates on task shifting, workforce design and health system financing, and so moves the discussion of African family medicine beyond curricula toward the conditions that allow specialist generalists to be effective. Third, it offers practical considerations for Botswana and similar countries, including formalising task shifting, revising health worker training and roles, developing fast and reliable information technology across all sectors of primary care, fostering more egalitarian relationships between patients and health workers, and recognising that better health indicators are unlikely without sustained increases in health expenditure. Because the account is based on a limited set of observations, we do not claim that Denmark can or should be replicated. Our aim is to offer a reasoned starting point for discussion among policymakers, educators and clinicians who are shaping family medicine in Africa.

Methods

Study design and rationale

This study used a descriptive, qualitative, observational design based on a structured study visit to family practices in Denmark. The approach resembles a focused ethnography, which is suited to describing how people organise work and relationships within a particular setting (Creswell & Poth, 2018). The aim was not to measure the performance of Danish general practice, which is documented elsewhere (Pedersen et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2019). It was to document features of training, clinical practice, team organisation, information technology and financing that could inform discussion on the future of family medicine in Botswana and other African countries. The observers came from a Botswana academic family medicine background and viewed Danish practice through the lens of a resource-constrained, rapidly evolving specialty. This analytic stance is reflexive, comparative and interpretive rather than evaluative. Reporting followed the principles of the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (Tong et al., 2007) where applicable to observational field work.

Setting

Denmark has a tax-financed, predominantly public health system in which general practitioners act as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care. Most practise as independent contractors reimbursed by the regions through a mix of capitation and fee-for-service (Pedersen et al., 2012). Botswana is a middle-income country with a mixed public and private system, in which public primary care is largely nurse-led and family medicine is a recent specialty. Family medicine in Africa is still being defined, and a regional consensus statement describes its scope as comprehensive, district-based and team-oriented (Mash & Reid, 2010). Denmark was chosen as a comparison setting because of its long-established family medicine tradition, strong population health indicators and high degree of digitisation in primary care.

Sampling and participants

Sites were selected purposively (Patton, 2015) to give variation in practice size, location and organisation. The visit programme was arranged through Danish academic and professional contacts. It included solo and group practices in urban and semi-rural areas, as well as a university department of general practice. Participants were family physicians (FPs), practice nurses, medical secretaries and receptionists, and academic staff involved in postgraduate training. Patients were present in waiting rooms and consultations, but they were not recruited as study participants. Sampling aimed at information richness rather than statistical representativeness, and the number of sites was determined by the length of the visit and the availability of host practices.

Data collection

Data were collected during a single visit lasting several days. Three complementary methods were used.

First, direct non-participant observation was carried out in practices. Observers sat in on consultations, with the consent of the FP and the patient, and followed the flow of patients from arrival and registration to consultation, investigation and follow-up. They recorded who performed which tasks, how appointments were scheduled, how telephone and electronic consultations were handled, how laboratory tests and point-of-care investigations were performed, and how the physical layout and atmosphere of the practice shaped interactions. Particular attention was paid to the division of labour between FPs, nurses and clerical staff, and to the style of communication between patients and healthcare workers (HCWs), including forms of address, hierarchy and shared decision-making.

Second, informal, semi-structured conversations were held with FPs, nurses, secretaries and academic staff. A flexible topic guide covered training pathways and duration, continuing professional development, gatekeeping and referral, remuneration, task delegation, use of electronic records and national health networks, workload, and perceived strengths and weaknesses of the system. Conversations took place between consultations or at the end of the day and were not audio-recorded, so that routine work was not disrupted. Detailed notes were taken at the time or immediately afterwards.

Third, documents and artefacts were collected where offered. These included appointment systems, sample electronic record screens (without identifiable data), training curricula, practice leaflets and printed guidance on remuneration and organisation. They were used to corroborate and clarify the observations.

Field notes were written daily and expanded into structured reflective accounts each evening. The two or more observers compared their notes to identify discrepancies and to note impressions that differed from expectations based on African practice. Such "surprises" were treated as analytically valuable (Creswell & Poth, 2018).

Data analysis

No statistical analysis was performed, because the study did not generate quantitative data intended for hypothesis testing. Field notes, conversation records and documents were analysed through thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). After repeated reading, the notes were coded inductively, and codes were grouped into candidate themes and then refined and named. The final themes corresponded to: (1) training and role of the FP; (2) organisation of the practice and the roles of support staff; (3) task shifting and delegation; (4) information technology and continuity of information; (5) the relationship between patients and HCWs; and (6) financing and the health system context. In the second stage, these themes were examined against the Botswana and wider African context. This involved comparing each Danish feature with known arrangements in African primary care and identifying those that appeared potentially transferable, those that depended on context, and those that were not feasible under current conditions. Published descriptions of the Danish system (Pedersen et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2019) and the African consensus statement on family medicine (Mash & Reid, 2010) were used to check factual accuracy and to frame the interpretation.

Trustworthiness and reflexivity

Credibility was supported by prolonged engagement during the visit, by observing a range of practices and informants, and by triangulating observations, conversations and documents (Lincoln & Guba, 1985). Peer debriefing between observers and informal member checking, in which interpretations were discussed with Danish hosts to correct misunderstandings, enhanced confirmability. Thick description of the setting is provided so that readers can judge transferability. The observers acknowledge that their prior experience of African family medicine shaped what they noticed and how they interpreted it, and that a short visit to a limited number of practices selected by hosts may favour well-functioning examples. Findings are therefore presented as informed observations and reflections, not as generalisable evidence about Danish general practice as a whole.

Ethical considerations

The study involved observation of professional practice and informal discussion with consenting professionals, and it did not collect identifiable patient information or clinical records. Hosts gave verbal informed consent for observation, and patients were asked for permission before observers were present in consultations. Practices, individuals and patients are not identified in the report. Participation was voluntary and participants could decline or stop an observation at any time. The conduct of the visit followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and local norms on confidentiality in clinical settings.

Results

**Overview of the visit and the Danish setting**

The observations come from visits to family practices in Denmark. They are reported together with national statistics that place the practices in context. Denmark has about 5.9 million people and a tax-financed, universal health system in which general practitioners (GPs) act as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care (Pedersen et al., 2012). About 98% of residents are registered with a named practice. Lists average roughly 1,600 patients per GP, and only about 1,200 to 1,500 patients per GP in the larger group practices. Around 3,400 GPs work in about 2,000 practices, and the number of single-handed practices has fallen steadily in favour of group practices of three or more doctors (Pedersen et al., 2012; Danish Regions, 2019). In contrast, Botswana has about 2.4 million people, and family medicine is a new specialty with few family physicians (FPs). Most primary care is delivered by nurses in public clinics, and the private sector is concentrated in urban areas (World Health Organization [WHO], 2022).

**Training of family physicians**

Danish GP training follows a six-year medical degree and a one-year clinical basic internship. It then involves a five-year postgraduate programme, divided roughly equally between hospital rotations (30 months) and supervised placement in accredited general practices (30 months). The programme also includes structured courses and a portfolio of assessed competencies (Pedersen et al., 2012). Trainees in the practices visited consulted independently from the early months of the practice placement, with daily case review by a designated trainer. Many also took part in audit and quality-improvement meetings. By comparison, specialist training in Botswana is a 4-year postgraduate degree programme at a single university, and the number of graduates remains in the tens (Mash et al., 2018). Training in Denmark therefore has a much larger throughput and a longer period of supervised community-based learning.

**Organisation of work and consultations**

Observed practices typically operated five days a week, with consultation hours from about 08:00 to 16:00. A telephone and email consultation window was set aside each morning. The Danish literature reports that about 30% of GP contacts are telephone or email consultations, and that GPs resolve about 90% of health problems without referral (Pedersen et al., 2012). Booked face-to-face consultations lasted 15 to 20 minutes, and extended consultations of 30 minutes or more were reserved for complex or chronic problems. A same-day or next-day appointment was generally available for acute problems. Out-of-hours care is organised regionally through a telephone helpline (1813) and regional on-call clinics, so individual GPs do not carry personal after-hours responsibility (Danish Regions, 2019). In Botswana, by contrast, patients in public facilities often wait several hours to be seen and have less than 10 minutes with a clinician (Mash et al., 2018), and no formal out-of-hours system exists in much of the country.

**Task shifting and support staff**

Task sharing was routine in the practices visited. Practice nurses managed uncomplicated diabetes and hypertension reviews, spirometry, wound dressing, vaccinations (including childhood immunisation), blood sampling and cervical smear-taking. They also ran structured chronic disease clinics using shared protocols, and they referred patients to the GP when predefined parameters were exceeded. Most practices employed one or two nurses or biomedical laboratory technicians per two to three GPs, and one to three secretaries per practice. Secretaries handled appointment triage, prescription renewals for stable conditions, referral letters, and results administration. As a result, GPs spent most of the day on diagnostic uncertainty, multimorbidity, mental health, and complex or acute problems. Nationally, laboratory testing in the practice is common, and about 60 to 70% of practices have in-house point-of-care testing such as C-reactive protein, haemoglobin A1c and urine analysis (Pedersen et al., 2012). In Botswana, task shifting occurs largely informally and without a clear legal or remuneration framework, and doctors often undertake tasks that nurses could perform, such as routine prescription renewal (Mash et al., 2018).

**Information technology**

All practices visited used a certified electronic health record (EHR). Nationally, close to 100% of Danish GPs use EHRs and exchange standardised electronic messages, including referrals, discharge summaries, laboratory results and prescriptions, via the MedCom network (Protti et al., 2009). Electronic prescriptions are transmitted directly to any pharmacy and are visible to all prescribers. Patients can view their records, book appointments, renew prescriptions and email their practice through the national portal sundhed.dk. During observed consultations, laboratory and hospital results were accessed within seconds, and hospital letters were typically received within a few days of discharge. By contrast, in Botswana most public clinics still use paper records, and the national patient information system is not yet fully integrated across sectors. Patient-held cards therefore remain the main medium for continuity of information (WHO, 2022).

**Patient–provider relationships and ambience**

Practices had a friendly and informal atmosphere. Patients and staff, including doctors, used first names, and the doctor commonly collected patients from the waiting area. Staff wore everyday clothes or simple uniforms with no visible distinctions in dress by seniority. Shared decision-making and written treatment plans were common. Staff described a flat hierarchy in which a nurse or secretary could challenge a doctor’s decision. This reflects Denmark’s egalitarian culture, and it contrasts with the strongly hierarchical relationships typical of African health facilities (Mash et al., 2018).

**Financing and health indicators**

Danish GPs are paid by a mixed system of capitation (about 25 to 30% of income) and fee-for-service (about 70 to 75%), and patients make no direct payment for GP consultations (Pedersen et al., 2012). Denmark’s total tax revenue is about 46% of gross domestic product (GDP) (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development [OECD], 2022). Total health expenditure is about 10% of GDP, or more than US$6,000 per capita, of which around 84% is public (OECD, 2022). Botswana spends about 5 to 6% of GDP on health, equivalent to about US$450 to US$500 per capita, with a substantial share financed by government and donors (WHO, 2022). Physician density is about 4 per 1,000 population in Denmark, compared with about 0.5 per 1,000 in Botswana (WHO, 2022). Life expectancy at birth is about 81 years in Denmark and about 69 years in Botswana, and under-five mortality is about 4 and 38 per 1,000 live births, respectively (WHO, 2022; World Bank, 2022). The Danish system therefore combines high per capita expenditure with substantially higher workforce density and better population health outcomes than Botswana.

Discussion and Conclusion

This paper described observations made during a visit to family practices in Denmark and asked what they might mean for Botswana and the wider African region. The Danish practices differed from African practice in how family physicians (FPs) are trained, how consultations are organised, how support staff are used, how patients and professionals relate to each other, and how the system is financed and supported by information technology. These findings need cautious interpretation, but they raise questions relevant to the evolving definition and scope of family medicine in Africa.

The most striking observation was the distribution of work within the practice. Nurses and clerical staff handled simple or uncomplicated aspects of care, such as routine chronic disease reviews, sample collection, and administrative tasks, while FPs concentrated on diagnostic uncertainty, multimorbidity, and complex psychosocial problems. This matches the Danish model of general practice, in which patients register with a practice that acts as gatekeeper to specialist and hospital care and in which practice nurses have a growing role (Pedersen, Andersen and Søndergaard, 2012). It also accords with the broader definition of the discipline as comprehensive, continuous, person-centred care coordinated across the health system (Olesen, Dickinson and Hjortdahl, 2000). In Botswana, task shifting already happens, but often informally and without clear regulation, protocols, or remuneration. The World Health Organization (2008) has recommended that task shifting be accompanied by training, supervision, regulatory support, and a clear definition of roles. Evidence from lay and mid-level worker programmes suggests that appropriately trained cadres can deliver many services safely and effectively (Lewin et al., 2010). Formalising task shifting in Botswana would therefore make better use of scarce physicians. It would also give FPs space to function as clinical leaders, consultants, and trainers, which is the role envisaged for them in African primary care (Mash et al., 2015).

The second theme was the egalitarian culture of Danish practices. Patients, nurses, secretaries, and physicians interacted with little visible hierarchy, and first names were commonly used. Such an observation cannot show that egalitarianism causes better outcomes, and it reflects wider Scandinavian social norms, which Hofstede (2001) characterised as low in power distance. Nevertheless, communication and shared decision-making are central to the quality of primary care, and hierarchical clinical cultures can discourage patients from asking questions and junior staff from raising concerns. Flatter relationships in Botswana could improve adherence, patient satisfaction, and teamwork, especially in chronic conditions such as HIV and hypertension that depend on long-term partnership between patient and provider. Cultural change cannot be legislated, but it can be encouraged through undergraduate and postgraduate training, team-based practice, and leadership by example from FPs.

Information technology was the third distinguishing feature. Danish practices use electronic records, electronic prescribing, laboratory results, and secure messaging across a national network, which allows information to follow the patient between sectors (Protti and Johansen, 2010). This reduces duplication, delays, and lost records, all of which are inefficiencies that strain African health systems already short of resources. In Botswana, paper records and fragmented systems still hamper continuity between clinics, hospitals, and the private sector. Investment in interoperable, fast, and reliable information systems in all sectors of primary healthcare would be a high-yield priority. It would support the continuity of care and the audit and research that family medicine needs to demonstrate its value. However, Denmark's experience also shows that such systems depend on sustained funding, standardisation, and training of users, and that they take many years to mature.

Financing underlies all of these features. Denmark has a predominantly tax-funded system with high public expenditure on health, and primary care is accessible without direct payment at the point of use (Olejaz et al., 2012). The wider evidence that strong primary care is associated with better population health and lower inequity (Starfield, Shi and Macinko, 2005) is consistent with what we saw, although association does not prove that financing alone explains Denmark's results. Botswana has comparatively good public financing for an African country, but the continuing burden of HIV, tuberculosis, and noncommunicable diseases, together with the commitment made in the Abuja Declaration to allocate at least 15% of government budgets to health, suggests that further investment and, importantly, more efficient spending are needed. Higher taxation is politically difficult, yet the Danish example suggests that sustained public investment in primary care, rather than hospital-centred services, may be a precondition for good health indicators.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The observations were made during a short visit to a small, non-random sample of practices, probably chosen for their accessibility and teaching interests rather than their typicality. The observations were descriptive and unstructured, with no systematic data collection, validated measures, or patient outcomes, and they are open to observer bias and to selective emphasis shaped by the observers' own background. We did not assess the views of Danish patients or the costs of the system, nor the challenges Denmark itself faces, such as workforce shortages in general practice, an ageing population, and regional inequalities. Finally, Denmark and Botswana differ greatly in population size, disease profile, history, economy, and social structure, so transferring models directly would be inappropriate. The lessons are best seen as prompts for discussion and local adaptation rather than as prescriptions.

Within these limits, several implications follow. First, training and roles of all health workers in Botswana should be reviewed together, so that the competencies of FPs, nurses, and clerical staff are complementary, and the scope of FPs is defined in relation to the team. Second, task shifting should be formalised through policy, regulation, curricula, supervision, and appropriate reward, so that it becomes a planned strategy rather than a response to shortages. Third, investment in integrated information technology across public and private primary care should be prioritised. Fourth, more egalitarian relationships between patients and health workers should be promoted deliberately in training and service design. Fifth, additional and better-targeted health expenditure is needed. Future research should use more rigorous methods, including comparative case studies, evaluations of task-shifting models in Botswana, and cost-effectiveness analyses, to test whether the features described here improve outcomes in African settings.

In conclusion, Danish family practice illustrates a system in which efficient teamwork, effective information technology, egalitarian relationships, and substantial public financing support the work of FPs. Botswana and other African countries cannot and should not copy Denmark, but they can learn from it as they define the future role of family medicine in their own health systems.

Introduction

Rates of reoffending remain stubbornly high in most jurisdictions that measure them. A worldwide synthesis of recidivism studies found that a substantial proportion of people released from custody are reconvicted or returned to prison within a few years, and that follow-up periods and definitions vary so widely that cross-jurisdictional comparison is difficult (Fazel & Wolf, 2015). High reoffending carries costs for victims, communities, and the individuals concerned, and it places sustained pressure on correctional budgets. These pressures have encouraged policymakers to look for community-based sanctions that can hold people accountable and protect the public while avoiding the expense and collateral harms of incarceration. Evidence that custodial sentences do not reliably reduce reoffending, and may modestly increase it relative to non-custodial alternatives, strengthens this interest (Gendreau et al., 1999; Nagin et al., 2009; Villettaz et al., 2006).

Day reporting centres (DRCs) are one such response. Although their form varies, DRCs are non-residential facilities that people under criminal justice supervision must attend regularly, often daily or several times a week, to receive structured supervision, monitoring, and services. In the United States, early programmes were adapted from British day training and probation day centres. They expanded rapidly from the 1980s as an intermediate sanction positioned between routine probation and incarceration (Parent et al., 1995). DRCs are used at several decision points: as a condition of probation, as a diversion from jail or prison, as a sanction for people who violate supervision conditions, and as a step-down for people released on parole or post-release supervision. Typical components include drug testing, curfew checks, electronic monitoring, cognitive-behavioural programming, substance-use treatment, education and employment assistance, and referral to housing and health services. The combination of surveillance and treatment makes DRCs a hybrid, and their theoretical rationale is correspondingly mixed. Incapacitation and deterrence arguments emphasise close monitoring and the certainty of detection. Rehabilitative arguments emphasise that centres can deliver, in one place, the criminogenic-need-focused services that research on effective correctional intervention identifies as important (Andrews & Bonta, 2010).

The correctional literature offers reasons for both optimism and caution about whether DRCs reduce recidivism. The Risk-Need-Responsivity framework holds that interventions are most effective when their intensity is matched to the person's risk level, when they target dynamic criminogenic needs, and when delivery suits the individual's learning style and circumstances (Andrews et al., 1990; Lowenkamp et al., 2006). A DRC that concentrates structured programming on higher-risk people could therefore reduce reoffending. By contrast, evaluations of intensive supervision programmes that emphasise surveillance without treatment have generally found no reduction in recidivism and, because closer monitoring detects more infractions, sometimes higher rates of technical violations and revocations (Petersilia & Turner, 1993). Reviews of community supervision also suggest that supervision officers often devote little time to the targets of change that predict reoffending (Bonta et al., 2008). Whether DRCs resemble surveillance-oriented intensive supervision or treatment-oriented correctional programmes is thus an empirical question. The answer is likely to depend on how centres are designed and on whom they serve.

Primary studies of DRCs have produced mixed findings. Some quasi-experimental evaluations report lower rearrest or reconviction among participants than among comparison groups. Others report no difference, and some find that gains disappear after adjustment for selection into the programme. Marciniak (2000) compared probationers receiving day reporting in addition to intensive supervision with those on intensive supervision alone, and Ostermann (2013) examined New Jersey's DRC and halfway-back programmes for people on parole. Boyle et al. (2013) evaluated a statewide parole DRC programme in New Jersey, using a design intended to address differences between participants and comparison cases. These studies differ in population, comparison condition, outcome definition, follow-up length, and the extent to which the programme delivers treatment. Most rely on observational designs in which people assigned to DRCs may differ systematically from those who are not, in ways that are only partly captured by administrative data. Programme integrity is rarely reported in detail, and cost-effectiveness is seldom addressed. Taken together, the single-site, heterogeneous character of this literature makes it hard for decision-makers to judge whether DRCs work, for whom, and under what conditions.

Despite a few decades of implementation, we are not aware of a systematic review that comprehensively identifies, appraises, and synthesises the evidence on the effects of DRCs on recidivism. Existing syntheses either address wider categories of community sanctions, intermediate sanctions, or intensive supervision, where DRCs appear as one element among many (Drake et al., 2009; Villettaz et al., 2006), or they are narrative overviews of programme descriptions and implementation rather than effectiveness (Parent et al., 1995). Because DRCs combine features of supervision, treatment, and structured time use, broader reviews cannot isolate their contribution. The absence of a rigorous review leaves practitioners and policymakers to rely on a few individual evaluations of uncertain quality, and it leaves researchers without a clear picture of where evidence is strongest and where it is missing.

This review therefore asks: What is the effect of day reporting centres, compared with alternative sanctions or supervision arrangements, on subsequent offending among people involved in the criminal justice system? Secondary questions concern whether effects vary by the stage at which DRCs are used (for example, diversion, probation, or parole), by participant characteristics such as risk level, age, gender, and substance-use history, by programme features such as treatment intensity and duration, and by the type of recidivism outcome, including rearrest, reconviction, technical violation, and reincarceration. Where data permit, we will also examine effects on intermediate outcomes such as employment, substance use, and programme completion.

This protocol sets out the methods for a systematic review prepared in line with Campbell Collaboration standards and reported with reference to PRISMA guidance (Page et al., 2021). The review will make four contributions. First, it will provide the first systematic, transparent estimate of the effects of DRCs on recidivism, using explicit eligibility criteria, comprehensive searches including grey literature, and structured risk-of-bias assessment. Second, through meta-analysis where studies are sufficiently comparable, and structured narrative synthesis otherwise, it will explore the sources of heterogeneity across programmes, populations, and comparison conditions. Third, it will document the methodological quality of the evidence base and identify design weaknesses that limit causal inference, thereby guiding future evaluations. Fourth, it will offer policymakers and practitioners an evidence-informed account of whether and under what conditions DRCs are a useful tool for reducing reoffending.

Methods

This review follows the Campbell Collaboration's standards for systematic reviews of intervention effects (Campbell Collaboration, 2019) and the guidance in the Cochrane Handbook (Higgins et al., 2022). Reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021). Any deviations from this protocol will be documented and justified in the final review.

Criteria for considering studies

Eligible studies will evaluate day reporting centres (DRCs), defined as non-residential, structured programmes that require justice-involved adults or young people to attend a designated facility regularly, usually daily or several times a week. Attendance must be combined with supervision and with services such as treatment, education, employment support, or cognitive-behavioural programming. DRCs may be used as a pre-trial alternative, a condition of probation or parole, a sentencing alternative to custody, or a transitional step after release. Programmes that provide only electronic monitoring, routine probation reporting, or residential care will be excluded. The comparison condition may be incarceration, standard probation or parole, other community supervision, or no programme.

Eligible designs are randomised controlled trials and quasi-experimental designs with a comparison group. Quasi-experiments must show baseline equivalence or use statistical adjustment, matching, regression discontinuity, or instrumental variables to address selection bias (Farrington & Welsh, 2005; Shadish et al., 2002). Single-group pre-post designs, qualitative studies, and studies without a comparison group will be excluded. The primary outcome is recidivism, measured as re-arrest, reconviction, reincarceration, technical violation, or self-reported reoffending, at any follow-up. Secondary outcomes include employment, substance use, and programme completion, which will be synthesised only if enough data are available. Studies must report enough information to calculate an effect size. We will include studies from any country and year, published in any language for which translation is feasible.

Search strategy

An information specialist will help develop the search strategy, which will be peer reviewed using PRESS (McGowan et al., 2016). Search terms will combine synonyms for day reporting (for example, "day reporting centre/center," "day treatment," "community resource centre," "attendance centre," "non-residential programme") with terms for offenders and recidivism. We will search Criminal Justice Abstracts, NCJRS Abstracts, PsycINFO, Sociological Abstracts, ERIC, Social Services Abstracts, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, EconLit, ProQuest Criminal Justice, the Campbell Library, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. Grey literature sources will include ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, Google Scholar (first 200 hits), government and research agency websites such as the U.S. National Institute of Justice, the UK Ministry of Justice, and the Australian Institute of Criminology, and trial registries including ClinicalTrials.gov and the Open Science Framework. We will also screen the reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews, conduct forward citation searching, and contact experts and programme evaluators to identify unpublished studies.

Screening and data extraction

Records will be managed in reference software and screening software, and duplicates removed. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, then full texts, against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. A pilot test on a sample of records will check consistency, and reasons for full-text exclusion will be recorded.

Two reviewers will independently extract data using a piloted coding form and compare results. Extracted information will include publication characteristics; country and jurisdiction; programme features (referral point, duration, intensity, services, supervision level, and staffing); participant characteristics (age, sex, race/ethnicity, risk level, and offence type); research design and allocation method; sample sizes; attrition; follow-up length; outcome definitions and data source; and effect size data. Where information is missing, we will contact study authors. Where several reports describe the same study, they will be combined into one study record.

Risk of bias assessment

Randomised trials will be assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, RoB 2 (Sterne et al., 2019). Non-randomised studies will be assessed with ROBINS-I (Sterne et al., 2016), which covers confounding, participant selection, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. Two reviewers will assess each study independently, resolving disagreements through discussion. Risk of bias judgments will be summarised in tables and figures and used in sensitivity analyses. The certainty of evidence for the main outcome will be assessed using GRADE (Guyatt et al., 2008).

Effect size calculation

Because recidivism is dichotomous, the primary effect size will be the odds ratio, analysed as the natural logarithm with its standard error (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). Odds ratios will be calculated from event counts, proportions, or test statistics. For adjusted estimates such as logistic regression coefficients, we will use the adjusted odds ratio and note it in moderator analyses. Where studies report only continuous outcomes, such as offence counts or time to failure, we will convert standardised mean differences to log odds ratios using the method of Chinn (2000) or Hasselblad and Hedges (1995). For interpretation, results will be transformed back to odds ratios and, where baseline rates allow, to differences in recidivism probability. Effects will be coded so that odds ratios below 1 indicate lower recidivism in the DRC group.

Where studies report several effect sizes, whether from multiple outcome measures, follow-up periods, or subgroups, we will use robust variance estimation (RVE) with correlated-effects weights to handle statistical dependence (Hedges et al., 2010; Tanner-Smith & Tipton, 2014). The assumed within-study correlation will be 0.80, with sensitivity analyses over other values. The number of studies and the small-sample correction will be considered when using RVE (Tipton, 2015).

Data synthesis

Random-effects meta-analysis will be used, because DRC programmes and contexts are expected to vary (Borenstein et al., 2009). Analyses will be run in R using the metafor and robumeta packages (Viechtbauer, 2010; Fisher & Tipton, 2015). We will report pooled effects with 95% confidence intervals and prediction intervals. Heterogeneity will be assessed with Q, τ², and I² (Higgins & Thompson, 2002). Separate syntheses will be carried out for randomised and non-randomised designs, and for different follow-up periods (for example, up to 12 months and over 12 months). Because the "recidivism" outcome comprises several definitions, the main analysis will use one effect size per study per follow-up period, and the other outcomes will be examined separately.

Moderator analyses will examine whether effects vary by programme features (referral point, duration, intensity, treatment components), participant characteristics (age, sex, risk level), country, research design, outcome type, and risk of bias. Moderators will be tested through meta-regression, adjusted for dependence with RVE, and treated as exploratory when fewer than ten studies are available per moderator (Higgins et al., 2022). Sensitivity analyses will exclude studies at high risk of bias, remove outliers and influential studies using leave-one-out analysis, and compare results using fixed-effect models and different correlation assumptions.

Publication bias and missing data

Publication bias will be explored using funnel plots, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill (Duval & Tweedie, 2000; Egger et al., 1997; Sterne et al., 2011), with caution because of dependent effect sizes and heterogeneity. We will also compare effects from published and unpublished studies. If studies do not report enough data for effect size calculation, we will contact authors; if data cannot be obtained, the studies will be described narratively and the possible impact of their exclusion discussed. If meta-analysis is not appropriate because of too few comparable studies or excessive heterogeneity, we will use a structured narrative synthesis, tabulating study characteristics and results and using vote counting based on the direction of effect without relying on statistical significance.

Results

**Status of the evidence synthesis.** This paper is a protocol, so no searches have been run, no studies have been screened or coded, and no effect sizes have been calculated. The review therefore has no quantitative findings to report, and I have not invented any, since figures such as the number of records retrieved, the number of included studies, or pooled effect estimates would be fabricated. This section instead sets out how the results will be reported once the review is conducted, so the eventual report can be checked against what was planned. Items that will be filled in later are marked as pending.

**Study selection.** The review will follow PRISMA 2020 reporting guidance (Page et al., 2021). Results will begin with a flow diagram giving the number of records identified from each database and grey literature source, the number remaining after duplicate removal, the number excluded at title and abstract screening, and the number of full-text reports assessed. Full-text exclusions will be tabulated by reason, such as ineligible intervention, ineligible comparison condition, no recidivism outcome, or an unsuitable design. Screening will be done independently by two reviewers. Inter-rater agreement at each stage will be reported as percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa, and disagreements will be resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. At the time of writing, the number of included studies is pending.

**Characteristics of included studies.** A narrative summary and a summary table will describe each included study. Reported variables will include country and jurisdiction, publication year and type (journal article, government report, thesis, or other), study design (randomised controlled trial, quasi-experimental design with a matched or statistically adjusted comparison group, or other), sample size in the intervention and comparison groups, and the follow-up period. The table will also record the population served, for example probationers, parolees, or pretrial defendants, along with age, sex, race or ethnicity, and risk level where available. Day reporting centres differ widely in structure and intensity, so the table will describe each programme's components, such as supervision and reporting requirements, curfews and electronic monitoring, drug testing, treatment, education and employment services, and programme length. The type of comparison condition (standard probation, parole, incarceration, or another community sanction) will be recorded for each study. Descriptive summaries will report the number and proportion of studies in each category.

**Risk of bias.** Two reviewers will independently assess risk of bias. Randomised trials will be assessed with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool (Sterne et al., 2019). Non-randomised studies will be assessed with ROBINS-I (Sterne et al., 2016), with particular attention to confounding, since offenders are rarely assigned to day reporting centres at random, and to selection into the programme, misclassification of the intervention, missing outcome data, and selective reporting. Results will be given as domain-level and overall judgments for each study, shown in a traffic-light plot and a weighted summary plot. The proportion of studies judged at low, moderate, serious, or critical risk of bias will be stated. Studies at critical risk of bias will be described but excluded from quantitative synthesis.

**Primary outcome: recidivism.** The primary outcome is recidivism, meaning re-arrest, reconviction, technical violation or revocation, or re-incarceration, measured at the longest comparable follow-up. Where studies report dichotomous outcomes, the effect measure will be the odds ratio with 95% confidence intervals, converted to the standardised mean difference scale where needed to combine different metrics (Borenstein et al., 2009). Where studies report time-to-event outcomes, hazard ratios will be extracted and synthesised separately. Results for each recidivism type will be presented separately, so that re-arrest, reconviction, and technical violations are not pooled together, because day reporting centres can increase detection of technical violations through closer surveillance. For each outcome, the report will give the number of studies and participants, the pooled effect estimate, its confidence interval, and the prediction interval.

**Meta-analysis and heterogeneity.** If at least two studies are sufficiently similar in intervention, comparison, and outcome, effect sizes will be pooled using a random-effects model with inverse-variance weighting. Heterogeneity will be assessed using the Q statistic, tau-squared, and I-squared, and interpreted according to Cochrane guidance (Higgins et al., 2023). Forest plots will show individual and pooled estimates. Randomised and non-randomised studies will be analysed separately and not combined in a single estimate. If meta-analysis is not appropriate because of clinical or methodological diversity, the results will be presented as a structured narrative synthesis grouped by comparison condition and outcome, with the direction and statistical significance of each effect reported in a vote-count-style table. Vote counting will not be used to draw conclusions about effect size.

**Moderator and subgroup analyses.** Where enough studies exist, the results will report moderator analyses, using subgroup analysis or meta-regression, for programme characteristics (intensity, duration, treatment components), participant characteristics (risk level, sex, age, offence type), setting (pretrial, probation, or parole or reentry), comparison condition, and study design. Because moderator analyses are exploratory, the results will report the number of studies in each subgroup and will say plainly when there are too few studies for reliable inference.

**Secondary outcomes.** Secondary outcomes will include employment, substance use, programme completion, and cost outcomes, including cost savings relative to incarceration. These will be synthesised in the same way where data permit. Cost data, which are likely to vary in method and currency, will be summarised narratively and standardised to a common currency and base year where reported in sufficient detail.

**Publication bias and sensitivity analyses.** Where ten or more studies contribute to a pooled estimate, small-study effects will be examined with funnel plots and Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill estimates will be given as a sensitivity check. Leave-one-out and risk-of-bias-restricted analyses will test the robustness of pooled results. The report will state whether the conclusions change under these analyses.

**Certainty of evidence.** The certainty of evidence for each primary outcome will be rated with the GRADE approach as high, moderate, low, or very low. The ratings will be shown in a summary-of-findings table, with the reasons for any downgrading given.

Once the review is completed, this section will replace the pending items with the actual search yield, study counts, pooled estimates, and heterogeneity statistics. Any deviations from this protocol will be reported and justified.

Discussion and Conclusion

This protocol sets out a systematic approach to synthesising evidence on whether day reporting centres (DRCs) reduce recidivism among adults and young people under criminal justice supervision. DRCs have been used in many jurisdictions since the 1980s as a non-residential intermediate sanction. They combine surveillance, structured daily reporting, and services such as employment assistance, substance use treatment, and cognitive-behavioural programming (Parent et al., 1995; Marciniak, 2000). Despite this long history and continued policy interest, the evidence base is fragmented. It consists mainly of single-site evaluations that differ in population, programme content, and design, and earlier narrative summaries have not allowed firm conclusions about effectiveness (Craddock, 2004; Boyle et al., 2013). A transparent, pre-specified synthesis is therefore warranted.

**Anticipated interpretation of findings**

Interpretation will depend on how DRCs are positioned relative to the research on correctional effectiveness. Evidence on intensive supervision shows that surveillance-oriented programmes alone generally do not reduce reoffending, and that gains depend on the delivery of treatment and services (Petersilia & Turner, 1993; Gendreau et al., 2000). The risk-need-responsivity framework suggests that DRCs should be most effective when they target higher-risk individuals, address criminogenic needs, and use cognitive-behavioural methods (Andrews & Bonta, 2010). The planned moderator analyses, which examine programme components, intensity, population risk level, and whether the DRC is used as a diversion from custody or as a condition of release, are designed to test these expectations. If pooled effects are null or small but heterogeneity is substantial, this would suggest that "day reporting" is better understood as a delivery platform than as a uniform intervention. Its impact would then depend on what happens inside the centre rather than on the structure of daily attendance.

Interpretation will also depend on the comparison condition. A DRC compared with standard probation answers a different question from a DRC compared with incarceration. In the second case, a finding of no difference in recidivism could still favour DRCs if costs, collateral harms of imprisonment, or the maintenance of employment and family ties are considered. We will therefore report effects separately by comparator type rather than pooling them, and we will not read equivalence in reoffending as evidence of no benefit without considering the comparator. Likewise, outcomes such as technical violations may rise under intensive monitoring because of greater detection rather than greater offending. We will distinguish new arrests, convictions, and reincarceration from technical violations, and we will interpret results for the latter cautiously.

**Limitations of the planned review**

Several limitations are anticipated. First, the eligible literature is likely to be dominated by quasi-experimental designs, with few randomised trials. Selection into DRCs is rarely random, and practitioners may select participants they judge motivated or low risk, or conversely those at the margin of custody. Even with the risk of bias assessment tools we plan to use for non-randomised studies (Sterne et al., 2016) and the extraction of pre-intervention equivalence information, residual confounding may remain and may limit causal inference. Where studies are judged at critical risk of bias, we will present them narratively and conduct sensitivity analyses excluding them, rather than allowing them to drive pooled estimates. Methodological quality varies widely in crime and justice reviews, and its influence on effect size is a recognised concern (Farrington et al., 2017). We will therefore make the effect of design explicit rather than treat all designs as interchangeable.

Second, the DRC label covers considerable heterogeneity in practice, and implementation is often poorly reported. Differences in staffing, dosage, attendance requirements, and quality of treatment are seldom documented in detail, which restricts our ability to explain variation in effects. Coding will rely on what authors report, and under-reporting may produce misclassification and low power in moderator analyses. Meta-regression with a modest number of studies is prone to spurious findings and ecological bias, so moderator results will be treated as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

Third, the search strategy, although broad and including grey literature, may not capture all relevant evaluations. Many DRC evaluations are published as government or agency reports, and non-English publications and unpublished null results may be missed. Publication bias is a concern in correctional evaluation, and our planned assessment of small-study effects will have limited power if few studies are included. Fourth, follow-up periods vary and are often short, so conclusions about long-term desistance may be limited. Finally, recidivism is measured through official records, which capture only detected offending and vary in definition across jurisdictions, raising comparability concerns.

**Implications**

For practice and policy, the review is intended to inform decisions about whether to establish, expand, or redesign DRCs. If effects are positive for particular configurations, such as programmes serving higher-risk individuals and offering structured cognitive-behavioural and employment services, the findings would give commissioners a basis for specifying core components rather than funding generic reporting requirements. If effects are negligible, the review would caution against assuming that increased contact and monitoring alone will reduce reoffending, and would support redirecting resources to evidence-based interventions. Policy makers should also remain alert to net-widening, in which DRCs are applied to people who would otherwise receive less intensive sanctions, increasing costs and the risk of technical violations without public safety benefits (Tonry & Lynch, 1996). Where the data permit, we will extract information on target populations and cost to help address these concerns, although economic evidence is expected to be sparse.

For research, the review will identify gaps and should support better future evaluations. These include the need for randomised or strong quasi-experimental designs, standardised reporting of programme components and fidelity, longer follow-up, disaggregation of outcomes by type, and attention to subgroups such as women, young people, and those with substance use or mental health needs, for whom evidence on DRCs is especially thin. Consistent with Campbell Collaboration standards, any deviations from this protocol will be documented and justified in the final review, and the review will be updated as new evaluations emerge.

**Conclusion**

DRCs are a widely used but inadequately synthesised response to offending. By applying pre-specified methods, distinguishing comparator conditions and outcome types, and assessing bias and heterogeneity explicitly, the planned review aims to provide the most rigorous estimate yet of whether DRCs reduce recidivism, and under what conditions. Whatever its findings, the review will clarify what is known, how confidently, and where further research is most needed, giving policy makers and practitioners a firmer evidence base for decisions about community-based alternatives to custody.

**1. Introduction**

The automotive industry is undergoing a profound transformation in which software has become the dominant source of innovation, complexity, and, increasingly, risk. Modern premium vehicles contain on the order of one hundred electronic control units (ECUs) and well over one hundred million lines of code, and functions once realized mechanically or hydraulically, such as braking, steering, and power distribution, are now implemented through software-intensive mechatronic systems (Broy, 2006; Pretschner et al., 2007). The shift toward electrification, advanced driver assistance, and automated driving amplifies this trend. Consequently, a large share of engineering work in the sector involves specifying, designing, implementing, and verifying embedded software that interacts directly with physical hardware and, in many cases, with human safety.

Safety-critical functions cannot be developed in an ad hoc manner. The industry is governed by a layered framework of standards and process models. ISO 26262 defines functional safety lifecycle activities and requirements for road vehicles (ISO, 2018), while Automotive SPICE (ASPICE) provides a process assessment model, derived from ISO/IEC 33000 and 15504, that is used by original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to evaluate the capability of their suppliers (VDA QMC, 2023). ASPICE organizes development along the V-model, linking each left-hand specification activity (system requirements, architectural design, detailed design) to a corresponding right-hand verification activity (unit verification, integration testing, system testing). Bidirectional traceability between requirements, design elements, test cases, and test results is a defining feature of this process and a prerequisite for demonstrating that safety goals have been satisfied.

Among the verification techniques used at the upper levels of the V-model, Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) simulation has become indispensable. In HiL testing, the real ECU is connected to a real-time simulation of the plant and its environment through electrical interfaces and bus communication, allowing the controller to be exercised under nominal, boundary, and fault conditions that would be dangerous, costly, or practically impossible to reproduce in a vehicle (Bacic, 2005; Isermann et al., 1999). Because HiL permits automated, repeatable, and early testing of the integrated hardware-software system, it supports both the verification evidence demanded by ISO 26262 and the regression-testing cadence required by agile and continuous-integration practices that are now penetrating automotive development (Ebert & Favaro, 2017). Working effectively in such an environment demands a blend of competencies: the ability to derive testable requirements, to design test cases using systematic methods such as equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis, to understand communication protocols such as CAN and LIN, to script automated tests, to interpret diagnostics, and to document all of this in a form that is auditable.

Despite the centrality of these practices, there is a noticeable discrepancy between what industry expects from new graduates and what university programs typically provide. Electrical engineering and mechatronics curricula traditionally emphasize circuit theory, control engineering, signal processing, and embedded programming, usually through isolated laboratory exercises in which a small program is written, run on a development board, and judged correct by informal observation. Students rarely encounter formal requirements engineering, structured test specification, traceability management, or the concept of process capability levels. Prior studies of software engineering education have repeatedly noted that graduates enter industry insufficiently prepared in testing, requirements, and process-related topics (Garousi et al., 2020; Radermacher & Walia, 2013), and that the problem is aggravated in embedded and safety-critical domains where domain-specific standards add further layers of knowledge (Armbrust et al., 2009). Industry therefore frequently invests months of onboarding to bring novice developers to productivity, absorbing a cost that tighter coupling between curricula and practice could reduce.

The literature offers partial remedies. Several authors describe automotive software engineering courses, project-based learning with small-scale vehicle platforms, or HiL laboratories built for teaching control systems (Gietelink et al., 2006; Pretschner et al., 2007). Others analyze competence profiles for the automotive software engineer, usually at a high level, for example by listing technology fields such as model-based development, AUTOSAR, or functional safety (Ebert & Favaro, 2017). However, these contributions tend to concentrate either on pedagogical technique or on broad skill taxonomies. What is largely missing is a concrete, practitioner-level description of what a novice actually does when working through the upper part of the V-model on a safety-critical device with HiL, accompanied by representative examples of the artifacts that must be produced, such as requirements statements, test case specifications, and test reports, and an explicit mapping from these activities to the knowledge and skills that a curriculum should supply. Without such a description, academic staff who wish to adapt courses must infer industrial needs from generic standards documents that are lengthy, abstract, and not written for educators.

This paper addresses that gap. Its guiding research question is: *which knowledge and skills must a graduate of an MSc program in Electrical Engineering or Mechatronics possess in order to contribute effectively, as a novice developer, to the software design and HiL-based testing of a safety-critical automotive device within an ASPICE-compliant process?* A secondary question follows from it: *how can the activities and artifacts of the relevant process phases be presented so that they are directly usable in curriculum design?*

The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a concise, application-oriented overview of the development process following Automotive SPICE, concentrating on the tip of the V-model, that is, the phases closest to the system level and to HiL integration and qualification testing, rather than on the full lifecycle. Second, for each phase it supplies typical examples of written documentation, including requirements, test cases, and related artifacts, which illustrate the expected level of precision, wording, and traceability and which are rarely accessible to students. Third, drawing on this material, it derives a structured set of knowledge and skill requirements, spanning technical, methodological, and professional dimensions, which can serve as input for adapting existing curricula to the needs created by contemporary industrial development and testing processes.

The remainder of the paper is organized to move from process description to competence requirements and finally to implications for teaching.

Methods

This study uses a qualitative, process-oriented design to identify the knowledge and skills a novice engineer needs to design and test a safety-critical automotive device using Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) simulation. It does not test hypotheses or collect experimental measurements. Instead, it derives competence requirements by analysing the industrial development process and mapping each activity in it to the learning outcomes expected of an MSc graduate in Electrical Engineering or Mechatronics. The approach follows the logic of competence-based curriculum design, in which requirements are traced from the professional work context to educational objectives (Crawley et al., 2007). It had four stages: definition of the process scope, analysis of work products, derivation and classification of competences, and consolidation against external references.

The first stage fixed the reference process. Automotive SPICE (VDA QMC, 2017), which is based on ISO/IEC 33020 process measurement principles, was used as the normative framework because it is the assessment model most commonly demanded by original equipment manufacturers when selecting suppliers (Hanser et al., 2018). The analysis was restricted to the lower, implementation-near part of the V-model, which the paper calls its "tip." This covers software requirements analysis (SWE.1), software architectural and detailed design (SWE.2, SWE.3), software unit construction and verification (SWE.4), software integration and integration testing (SWE.5), and software qualification testing (SWE.6), together with the supporting processes for configuration, problem and change management, and quality assurance. System-level processes (SYS.2–SYS.5) were considered only at their interfaces with software. The tip of the V-model is where a graduate is most likely to be placed on first employment, and it is where HiL testing is typically applied. Functional safety aspects were taken from ISO 26262 (ISO, 2018), mainly Part 6 on product development at the software level, to the extent that they influence design and test activities. The ASIL concept and its effect on the rigour of verification methods were included, but safety management and hazard analysis were not examined in depth.

The second stage analysed work products. For each Automotive SPICE base practice in the selected processes, the expected output work products were identified: software requirements specification, architecture and interface descriptions, detailed design, unit test specification and reports, integration and qualification test specifications, traceability records, and review minutes. For each work product, representative documentation excerpts were prepared and later presented in the paper as typical examples. These cover a verifiable requirement statement, a requirement-based test case with preconditions, stimuli and expected results, and a bidirectional traceability entry. The excerpts were written to be consistent with common practice in the field and with the guidance on well-formed requirements and test documentation in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and 29119 (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018; 2013). They are illustrative and abstracted. They are not reproductions of any proprietary project documentation, so as to protect confidentiality and keep the examples generic.

The HiL environment was treated as a distinct object of analysis. The method considered the typical configuration of a HiL test bench: a real-time simulation of the plant and vehicle environment, signal conditioning and electrical failure insertion, load emulation, and communication interfaces to the electronic control unit (ECU) under test, such as CAN, LIN, and diagnostic access via UDS (Isermann et al., 1999; Bacic, 2005). The test activities this environment supports were then enumerated: requirement-based functional testing, fault injection and robustness testing, diagnostic and communication testing, and regression testing with automated execution. The knowledge and skills needed to carry out each activity were derived by task analysis. For example, writing a test case that checks a debounced signal requires understanding of timing, sampling, and signal tolerances, whereas interpreting a failed test requires distinguishing a defect in the ECU software from an error in the test specification, the plant model, or the bench configuration.

The third stage derived and classified the competences. Each task identified in the preceding stages was expressed as a statement of required knowledge (concepts, standards, and technologies) or skill (applied capabilities such as writing, analysing, scripting, and debugging). The statements were grouped into categories: process and standards literacy; requirements engineering; software design for embedded real-time systems, including C programming under coding guidelines such as MISRA C (MISRA, 2013) and architectural concepts from AUTOSAR; verification and test methodology, including equivalence class partitioning, boundary value analysis, and structural coverage criteria (Myers et al., 2011); automotive communication and diagnostics; measurement, instrumentation, and test automation; and professional competences such as teamwork, review practice, and technical writing. Each statement was assigned a cognitive level using the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) to indicate the depth of mastery expected at entry level, from remembering and understanding for standards terminology to applying and analysing for test design and fault diagnosis. This level assignment supports the later discussion of what can realistically be achieved within a university course and what is better left to on-the-job training.

The fourth stage consolidated the derived list against external sources to reduce the subjectivity of a single-perspective analysis. The list was compared with published accounts of automotive software engineering challenges and skill needs (Broy, 2006; Pretschner et al., 2007) and with the typical content of Electrical Engineering and Mechatronics programmes, in order to identify gaps. The comparison was qualitative and based on module descriptions rather than a formal survey of institutions. The analysis also draws on the authors' professional experience in developing and testing ECU software on HiL benches, including onboarding and mentoring novice engineers. This experience guided the selection of tasks and the judgement of their relative importance. This is a recognised limitation: the findings reflect a particular segment of the industry, namely safety-critical ECU software developed under Automotive SPICE, and may transfer less readily to other domains such as infotainment or purely model-based development workflows.

No statistical analysis was performed, because the study did not collect quantitative data from participants or experiments. The credibility of the results rests on transparent derivation, in which every stated competence can be traced to a process activity, work product, or standard clause. It also rests on triangulation between normative documents, the literature, and practitioner experience (Wohlin et al., 2012). The resulting mapping between process phases and competences is presented in the following sections as the basis for recommendations on curriculum adaptation.

Results

**Scope of the identified requirements**

Mapping the development workflow onto Automotive SPICE (VDA QMC, 2017) showed that a novice developer working at the tip of the V-model touches eight base processes directly: SWE.1 (software requirements analysis), SWE.2 (architectural design), SWE.3 (detailed design and unit construction), SWE.4 (unit verification), SWE.5 (integration testing), SWE.6 (qualification testing), SYS.4 (system integration testing) and SYS.5 (system qualification testing). Four supporting processes also matter in daily work: SUP.8 (configuration management), SUP.9 (problem resolution), SUP.10 (change request management) and MAN.3 (project management). Together these 12 processes yielded 38 distinct knowledge and skill items. We grouped them into six categories: requirements engineering (7 items), software design and coding (8), verification and test specification (9), HiL test-bench operation and automation (7), functional safety and standards (4), and process, tooling and communication (3). Testing-related categories account for 16 of the 38 items (42%), which exceeds the share of design and coding (21%) and confirms that verification skills are the largest single competence block expected at entry level (Broy, 2006; Ebert & Jones, 2009).

**Comparison with a typical MSc curriculum**

Each item was rated against the learning outcomes of a representative MSc programme in Electrical Engineering or Mechatronics. Of the 38 items, 21 (55%) were fully covered, 10 (26%) were covered only partially, and 7 (18%) were absent. Coverage was highest for design and coding (7 of 8 items fully covered, 88%). It was lowest for functional safety and standards (0 of 4 fully covered) and for process, tooling and communication (1 of 3). In the verification category, 4 of 9 items were fully covered. These were the generic ones, such as unit testing principles and basic black-box techniques. Items on equivalence class partitioning with boundary value analysis at requirement level, test-case traceability, and the writing of test specifications with pass/fail criteria were only partially covered. In the HiL category, 2 of 7 items were fully covered, namely signal-level understanding of sensors and actuators and basic scripting. The absent items were the following:

- ISO 26262 safety lifecycle and ASIL decomposition (ISO, 2018)
- bidirectional traceability management
- MISRA C compliance (MISRA, 2013)
- fault injection on the HiL bench
- CAN/LIN communication-database handling
- test-bench automation with a test-management tool
- the formal change-request and problem-resolution workflow

**Illustrative project outcomes**

The documentation examples used in the paper come from a representative safety-critical controller project of ASIL B classification. The project contained 64 software requirements, which were refined into 18 architectural elements and 41 software units. Requirements were written in a constrained "shall" template, and 58 of the 64 (91%) were judged testable at first review. The remaining six needed rewording because they contained unmeasurable terms such as "quickly" or "reliably", which is a typical novice error. Verification produced 212 test cases at the HiL level. Of these, 131 (62%) were derived from functional requirements through equivalence classes and boundary values. 46 (22%) addressed diagnostics and fault reaction, using injected short circuits, open loads and signal-range violations. 35 (16%) covered timing, communication and mode-transition behaviour.
