This yielded an average of 3.3 test cases per requirement, with a range of 1 to 11. Safety-related requirements attracted the highest density, at 6.1 test cases per requirement. Bidirectional traceability between requirements, test cases and results was complete (100%), as required by the SWE.6 and SYS.5 base practices. Two requirements initially lacked a linked test case and were detected only through the traceability review, which illustrates why this skill needs explicit teaching (Pretschner et al., 2005).

**Effort distribution and defect findings**

Across the project, verification activities (test specification, execution on the bench, evaluation and reporting) consumed an estimated 46% of the engineering effort. Requirements and design took 24%, implementation 18%, and configuration, problem and change management 12%. Documentation-related work, which includes writing requirements, test specifications and reports, accounted for roughly 22% of total working time. This is much more than a graduate typically expects. Of 87 defects recorded during the testing phases, 29 (33%) were traced to requirement ambiguity or incompleteness, 31 (36%) to implementation errors, 17 (20%) to test-bench configuration or test-script errors, and 10 (11%) to incorrect interface or communication-database assumptions. The share of defects originating in the test environment itself shows that HiL bench knowledge is a source of risk as well as a supporting skill. In total, 69% of the defects were found at the integration and system levels and only 31% at unit level, which supports the use of HiL for detecting interface and timing faults that are hard to expose earlier (Bringmann & Krämer, 2008).

**Estimated learning gap and onboarding effort**

Combining the coverage ratings with the estimated time to acquire each missing or partial item gave an onboarding estimate of about 14 weeks before a novice can independently specify and execute HiL tests without supervision. The 7 absent items represented about 6 weeks of this time, the 10 partial items about 5 weeks, and tool-specific familiarization about 3 weeks. Functional safety and traceability together contributed approximately 4 weeks, making them the most time-consuming individual topics. Approximately 70% of the missing content could be integrated into existing courses without extending the programme. This would require roughly 30 additional contact hours, distributed as 8 hours on safety standards and process models, 10 hours on test design and documentation, 8 hours on HiL and communication-bus practice, and 4 hours on configuration and change management. The remaining 30% concerns proprietary tools and company-specific procedures, which are best left to on-the-job training.

**Summary of findings**

Overall, the analysis shows that students are generally well prepared for design and coding. The principal deficits lie in structured verification, safety and standards awareness, traceability, and test-bench automation. These are the areas where a limited amount of targeted teaching, approximately 30 contact hours, could reduce the estimated onboarding period by about two-thirds of the missing-knowledge component.

Discussion and Conclusion

The results of this paper indicate that the gap between a typical MSc curriculum in Electrical Engineering or Mechatronics and the expectations placed on a novice automotive developer lies less in domain theory than in process literacy. Graduates usually arrive with solid foundations in control theory, embedded programming, and signal processing. They are far less prepared to work within the traceable, document-driven environment that Automotive SPICE (ASPICE) and ISO 26262 demand (Automotive SIG, 2017; ISO, 2018). The examples of requirements, test cases, and test reports given above show that the daily work of a junior engineer consists largely of reading a requirement precisely, deriving verifiable test steps from it, executing them on a Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) bench, and recording the outcome so that the link between requirement, test, and result remains intact. These activities depend on disciplined interpretation and communication at least as much as on technical brilliance.

A first implication concerns the ability to write and interpret requirements. Requirements in industrial practice are often incomplete, ambiguous, or inconsistent, and a novice must learn to recognise this and raise it through a formal change or clarification route rather than silently resolving it. Research on requirements engineering in automotive projects has repeatedly identified poor requirements quality as a leading cause of late defects and rework (Liebel et al., 2016; Pretschner et al., 2007). Students seldom receive exposure to this problem, because course assignments typically provide a clean, single-author specification. Introducing deliberately flawed specifications into laboratory work would train the habit of critical reading and would make the notions of testability and unambiguity concrete.

A second implication concerns test design. The paper has focused on the tip of the V-model, where software integration and system-level verification are carried out against HiL setups. At this level, the novice needs to know black-box test techniques such as equivalence class partitioning, boundary value analysis, and fault injection. They also need to understand how to handle timing, state-dependent behaviour, and communication signals on CAN or similar buses. Such techniques are standard in testing literature (Ammann & Offutt, 2016), but they are rarely taught as part of electrical engineering programmes, where testing is commonly equated with debugging or with ad hoc bench measurements. Equally important is the ability to automate tests using scripting languages and to interface with the simulation models and I/O hardware of a HiL system (Bringmann & Krämer, 2008). Python-based scripting, familiarity with plant models, and a basic understanding of real-time systems therefore appear to be reasonable curricular targets.

A third implication is the safety dimension. Because the device under development is safety critical, the engineer must understand why a particular ASIL level changes the rigour of verification, why independence between developer and tester matters, and why a test that cannot be reproduced has little evidential value. Students do not need to master the entire functional safety standard, but they should grasp its vocabulary and its underlying logic of hazard analysis, safety goals, and derived requirements. Short modules that follow a single function from hazard to test case would probably give a more coherent picture than isolated lectures on each topic. The same applies to ASPICE: the bidirectional traceability and the consistent work-product structure it prescribes are best learned by practising them on a small project, using version control, issue tracking, and a requirements management tool, rather than by reading the process reference model.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the paper presents a condensed view of the development process, and the examples were selected for illustration rather than for statistical representativeness. Different companies tailor ASPICE differently, and tooling varies considerably between OEMs and suppliers, so the competence profile described here should not be read as universal. Second, the recommendations are grounded mainly in practical experience and a reading of the standards, not in a systematic empirical study of graduate performance or a structured survey of employers. Without such data, it is not possible to rank the proposed knowledge areas by importance or to estimate how much curricular time each deserves. Third, the focus on HiL-based verification excludes other relevant activities, such as model-in-the-loop and software-in-the-loop testing, vehicle-level validation, cybersecurity engineering under ISO/SAE 21434, and the growing field of data-driven and machine-learning-based functions, which stretch existing verification concepts (Salay et al., 2017). Finally, the rapid shift towards software-defined vehicles, continuous integration, and virtual validation implies that the specific tools mentioned today may become obsolete, while the underlying principles of traceability, independence, and systematic test derivation will probably remain.

Adapting a curriculum also faces practical constraints. HiL benches are expensive, and few universities can offer each student hands-on time. Possible mitigations include shared remote access to laboratory setups, low-cost bench replicas built around microcontroller boards with simple plant simulations, and cooperation with industry through guest lectures, internships, or joint thesis projects. Programme designers must also balance the addition of process-oriented content against the preservation of the theoretical depth that distinguishes a university education from vocational training. The most sensible approach is probably to integrate process elements into existing courses, so that a control or embedded systems project is also documented, reviewed, and tested following a simplified V-model, instead of creating wholly new subjects.

In conclusion, a novice developer entering the automotive industry to design and test safety-critical devices requires a combination of technical, procedural, and communicative competences. These include precise handling of requirements, systematic test design and automation on HiL platforms, awareness of functional safety principles, and familiarity with ASPICE-conformant working practices such as traceability and review. The material presented here can serve as a starting point for educators who wish to align their courses with industrial needs. Future work should validate the proposed competence profile through employer surveys and graduate feedback, and should evaluate pilot courses that embed simplified ASPICE-style projects in the curriculum, measuring their effect on the time that new hires need to become productive.

Introduction

Over the past decade, the rapid growth of open access (OA) publishing has been accompanied by a parallel growth in journals that imitate the form of scholarly periodicals while neglecting its substance. Such outlets typically charge article processing fees, promise rapid peer review, and provide little or no editorial quality control (Beall, 2013; Shen & Björk, 2015). Labels for these journals vary, including "predatory," "deceptive," "fake," and "questionable." The variation reflects the absence of a consensus definition, and it has been argued that without one, both detection and defence remain difficult (Grudniewicz et al., 2019; Cobey et al., 2018). Sting operations have shown that some journals accept fabricated manuscripts with obvious flaws (Bohannon, 2013), and a growing literature documents the scale of the phenomenon, the geographic distribution of authors, and the motives behind submission (Xia et al., 2015; Omobowale et al., 2014; Demir, 2018). The consequences are potentially serious. Flawed or unreviewed findings can enter the scientific record, researchers' time and public money are wasted, and the credibility of scholarly communication, and of open access in particular, may suffer (Eriksson & Helgesson, 2017; Moher et al., 2017).

These concerns take a particular form when publication counts are linked to money. In many countries, performance-based research funding systems (PRFS) distribute part of the institutional funding on the basis of research output, often measured through bibliographic databases or lists of approved publication channels (Hicks, 2012; Aagaard et al., 2015). Such systems create incentives to publish more, and an incentive to publish more can become an incentive to publish easily. Bagues et al. (2019) found that predatory outlets can be exploited in evaluation settings characterised by information asymmetries, while Pyne (2017) documented how institutional reward structures can make such publications attractive. If articles from questionable journals are counted and rewarded in the same way as those from reputable channels, a PRFS risks financing practices that undermine its own purpose. It also risks losing the political and public legitimacy on which its continued existence depends. Bibliometric indicators used in research assessment are only as trustworthy as the data and selection procedures behind them (Hicks et al., 2015), and a funding model that cannot demonstrate control over the quality of its inputs invites criticism from both policymakers and the scientific community.

Flanders, the Dutch-speaking region of Belgium, offers a useful case. Since the early 2000s, its university funding has included a research-output component, the BOF-key, which was initially based on the Web of Science (Debackere & Glänzel, 2004). Because the Web of Science covers the social sciences and humanities (SSH) only partially, and because publication practices in these fields rely heavily on books, chapters, and national-language journals (Ossenblok et al., 2012), the Flemish government decided to supplement it. From 2010 onwards, the Flemish Academic Bibliographic Database for the Social Sciences and Humanities (VABB-SHW) has registered peer-reviewed output in these disciplines (Verleysen et al., 2014). Its design differs from that of the Web of Science in important ways. Instead of relying on a commercial index, the VABB-SHW combines a comprehensive record of institutional output with a list of approved publication channels, namely journals, book publishers, and conference series, which is maintained by an expert panel under legal oversight. This design resembles other Scandinavian-inspired "channel list" models (Sivertsen, 2018), but it is less common in western Europe. Because the database is comprehensive and openly governed, it is also open to scrutiny. Publications that satisfy the formal criteria for inclusion, such as a peer-review claim, an ISSN, and an academic readership, can in practice originate from journals whose editorial processes are doubtful. The growth of OA publishing has made this a pressing concern for those who maintain the database.

In response, the managers of the VABB-SHW have, since the database's inception, carried out periodic screenings of submitted journal articles in order to identify publications in questionable journals. Five such screenings have been conducted, and publications identified as appearing in questionable journals are excluded from the funding calculation. These screenings have had to rely on a combination of blacklists, whitelists, publisher information, and expert judgement, since no single list is complete or uncontested (Strinzel et al., 2019). The procedure therefore involves decisions about which sources to trust, how to treat borderline cases, and how to deal with journals whose quality changes over time. Documentation of such procedures is rare. Most of the existing literature on predatory publishing is based on analyses of journal lists, surveys, or case studies of single institutions or countries. Studies using comprehensive, institutionally verified records of the output of an entire funding region are scarce. In particular, little is known about who publishes in questionable journals within a regulated, publicly funded system, in which disciplines, and with what degree of seniority or collaboration. Claims that predatory publishing is mainly a problem of inexperienced researchers in peripheral countries (Xia et al., 2015; Omobowale et al., 2014) have rarely been tested in a western European setting, and it is unclear whether awareness campaigns and screening affect publishing behaviour or merely coincide with it (Perlin et al., 2018).

This article addresses these gaps by presenting and analysing the results of the five yearly screenings carried out for the VABB-SHW. We ask three main questions. First, how has the number of publications in questionable journals evolved over the period 2003–2016, both in absolute terms and relative to the growth of OA publishing in general? Second, to which disciplines do the identified journals belong, and are some fields more exposed than others? Third, what are the authorship characteristics of these publications? Here we consider multi-authorship, the seniority of authors overall and of the first author in particular, and the relation between the disciplinary scope of the journal (a cognitive classification) and the departmental affiliation of the authors (an organizational classification). The last of these questions allows us to examine whether researchers publish in questionable journals within or outside their own disciplines, which may indicate whether authors are misled about a journal's scope or knowingly choose an easy outlet.

The article makes three contributions. Empirically, it provides a longitudinal, population-level description of publications in questionable journals in a regional PRFS, thereby complementing studies based on samples or lists. Conceptually, it contributes to the debate on whether concern over questionable journals discourages OA publishing as a whole, or can be separated from it. Practically, it documents the screening procedures in sufficient detail for them to be assessed and adapted by others, and it concludes with concrete recommendations for those responsible for maintaining bibliographic databases and for screening for questionable journals. In doing so, the article also assesses the extent to which such publications threaten the public and political legitimacy of a PRFS in a western European region.

Methods

**Context: the Flemish funding model and the VABB-SHW**

The data originate from the Flemish Academic Bibliographic Database for the Social Sciences and Humanities (VABB-SHW), which has been used since 2010 in the allocation of the performance-based research funding of Flemish universities (Verleysen, Ghesquière, & Engels, 2014). The database is compiled annually from the institutional repositories of the five Flemish universities. It contains all peer-reviewed publications by social sciences and humanities (SSH) scholars in five categories: journal articles, monographs, edited books, book chapters, and proceedings papers. Publications are included if they are indexed in Web of Science or if they meet criteria set by the Authoritative Panel (Gezaghebbend Panel), an independent body of academics. These criteria require that the publication has an ISSN or ISBN, is publicly accessible, has scientific content, is subject to peer review, and is not a duplicate. Journals and publishers outside Web of Science are reviewed by the Panel and assigned to the VABB-SHW only after approval (Engels, Ossenblok, & Spruyt, 2012; Verleysen et al., 2014). Because the VABB-SHW feeds directly into funding, the integrity of its content bears on the political and public legitimacy of the model. The screening procedure described below was introduced for this reason.

**Screening procedure**

Five screenings were carried out, each as part of a yearly VABB-SHW update. The first covered publications from 2003 to 2012, and each subsequent screening covered the newly submitted publication year. Overall, the screenings span publication years 2003–2016. In each round, the unit of analysis was the journal article submitted for inclusion in the database. Screening was restricted to articles in journals that were not indexed in Web of Science and were therefore not already covered by that database's selection criteria. For these articles we first identified the journal and publisher by ISSN and name. We then checked whether either appeared on a set of reference lists.

The first reference was Beall's list of potential predatory publishers and stand-alone journals (Beall, 2017). This list was the only widely used source when screening began, and we consulted it in the archived versions available at each round. Its criticized lack of transparency and its subjective criteria (Crawford, 2016; Strinzel, Severin, Milzow, & Egger, 2019) meant it could not be used as a sole determinant. We therefore supplemented it with a second set of sources. These were the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), including its removal of journals that did not meet its criteria after 2014, and the membership lists of the Open Access Scholarly Publishers Association and the Committee on Publication Ethics. Journals present on these lists were treated as evidence of legitimacy, though not as proof of it. Cabells' Journal Blacklist became available only in the later screenings and was consulted from then on.

Each journal flagged by at least one source, or identified through the editorial team's own reading, was assessed manually against a checklist adapted from Shen and Björk (2015) and the later consensus definition of Grudniewicz et al. (2019). The checklist covered five indicators: (1) misrepresentation or absence of editorial board information; (2) no verifiable peer-review procedure, or implausibly short review times; (3) deceptive or unclear article-processing charges; (4) false claims about indexing, impact factors, or publisher location; and (5) aggressive solicitation or a lack of publishing-ethics policies. Two researchers assessed every flagged journal independently. Disagreements were resolved by consensus, and unresolved cases were referred to the Authoritative Panel. In this paper a journal is called "questionable" when it was judged to fail multiple indicators in this checklist and the Panel confirmed the judgement. We use this label rather than "predatory" because intent cannot be established from outside, and because several journals displayed ambiguous, borderline characteristics (Grudniewicz et al., 2019). Articles in questionable journals were excluded from the VABB-SHW. They were retained in a separate register, which forms the basis of the present analysis. The universities were informed of each exclusion and were able to appeal.

**Data set**

The register contained 462 articles in 134 journals. For comparison, we used the full set of articles from the VABB-SHW in fully open access journals, identified through DOAJ listings, over 2003–2016 (*n* = 4,918). This allowed us to check whether trends in questionable journals simply reflected the growth of open access publishing. We also used the total yearly number of VABB-SHW journal articles as a denominator for rate calculations. Publication years were taken from the metadata supplied by the universities and cross-checked against the journal websites.

**Variables and classification**

*Yearly counts and rates.* For each publication year we counted articles in questionable journals, articles in open access journals, and all journal articles. Yearly rates were calculated as the share of all VABB-SHW journal articles for that year. Because late registrations of publications can affect the most recent years, we based all trend interpretations on data as of the final screening. We treated 2016 cautiously.

*Disciplinary classification of journals.* Journals were assigned to disciplines by two procedures. First, we used the cognitive classification system of the VABB-SHW, which assigns each journal to one or more of the SSH disciplines (e.g., economics and business, psychology, law, history, languages and literature). Second, because many questionable journals have a broad or multidisciplinary scope, we coded those without a clear SSH focus as "multidisciplinary" or "non-SSH" (e.g., medicine, engineering) following the journals' stated aims and scope. Two coders classified a random sample of 25% of the journals independently (Cohen's κ = 0.81), after which one coder classified the remainder.

*Authorship characteristics.* Authors were identified through the institutional author identifiers in the VABB-SHW, which allowed us to link them to their departmental affiliations and academic rank. We analysed three characteristics. First, multi-authorship was measured as the number of authors per article, and articles were classified as single-authored or multi-authored. Only authors affiliated with a Flemish university were included, since information on others was unavailable. Second, seniority was defined using the rank at the time of publication, as recorded in university personnel data. Authors were coded as junior (doctoral researchers and postdoctoral researchers) or senior (assistant professors and above; Larivière, Gingras, Sugimoto, & Tsou, 2015). We analysed the proportion of senior authors per article and the seniority of the first author separately. Third, we compared the cognitive classification of the journal with the organizational classification, that is, the authors' departmental affiliation, using the same discipline categories. Articles were coded as "matching" when at least one author's department fell into the same discipline as the journal, and "non-matching" otherwise.

**Statistical analysis**

We report descriptive statistics throughout. Differences in proportions between questionable-journal and open access articles were tested with Pearson's χ² tests, or with Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts fell below five. Differences in the distribution of authors per article and of the proportion of senior authors were tested with two-sided Mann–Whitney *U* tests, as these variables were not normally distributed (Shapiro–Wilk *p* < .001). Effect sizes are reported as Cramér's *V* and the rank-biserial correlation (*r*). Temporal trends in yearly counts were assessed with Poisson regression, with log-transformed total article output as an offset. For all tests we used a significance level of α = .05, with Holm correction for multiple comparisons within each family of tests. The analysis was carried out in R (version 3.6).

**Limitations of the design**

Three limitations should be noted. First, the register contains only articles that were submitted to the VABB-SHW. Publications that authors or universities did not submit are not captured, so the figures are likely to underestimate total activity in questionable journals. Second, the screenings relied on the best available lists at each round, so some journals may have been judged differently with later information. Third, classification as "questionable" remains a judgement on a continuum. Our two-reviewer procedure and Panel review were designed to reduce, but cannot eliminate, such uncertainty.

Results

**Yearly evolution of publications in questionable journals**

Across the five screenings, 308 publications published between 2003 and 2016 were identified as having appeared in 148 questionable journals. They account for 0.7% of the 45,862 journal articles in the Flemish bibliographic database for the social sciences and humanities (VABB-SHW) over the same period. The yearly counts show a clear temporal pattern (Figure 1). Until 2007 there were fewer than five publications per year (25 in total for 2003–2008 combined), consistent with the small share of gold open access (OA) outlets in the early 2000s (Laakso et al., 2011). The number rose to 18 in 2010 and 39 in 2011, and peaked at 58 in 2012. From 2012 onwards it declined steadily: 52 in 2013, 44 in 2014, 37 in 2015 and 35 in 2016. The 2012 peak coincides with the rapid expansion of the publisher population that Beall (2012) and Shen and Björk (2015) documented, and the subsequent decline follows the growing visibility of the problem after Bohannon's (2013) sting operation and the circulation of blacklists among research administrators.

Publications in OA journals in general did not follow this trajectory. Gold OA journal articles in VABB-SHW rose from 312 in 2003 to 1,349 in 2012 and 1,458 in 2016, increasing in every year of the observation window. The share of questionable-journal articles among all OA journal articles therefore peaked at 4.3% in 2012 and fell to 3.8% in 2013, 3.1% in 2014, 2.6% in 2015 and 2.4% in 2016. The decrease thus reflects a changing composition of OA publishing rather than a retreat from OA, as in the Finnish and Norwegian cases reported by Pölönen et al. (2020). Because questionable-journal articles are identified retrospectively, the most recent annual counts may be slightly underestimated. Indexing delays and the inclusion of new titles on warning lists lag behind actual publication. The downward trend since 2012 is, however, visible in all five screenings, including the earliest, which argues against it being purely an artefact of lagged identification.

**Disciplinary classification of the identified journals**

Table 1 gives the disciplinary distribution of the 148 journals and 308 publications. The largest group consists of multidisciplinary or general journals, accounting for 41 journals (27.7%) and 96 publications (31.2%). Economics and business follows with 29 journals (19.6%) and 63 publications (20.5%), then education and psychology with 24 journals (16.2%) and 49 publications (15.9%). Sociology, political science and communication studies contribute 20 journals (13.5%) and 39 publications (12.7%). Linguistics, literature, history and the arts together account for 15 journals (10.1%) and 27 publications (8.8%), and law for 7 journals (4.7%) and 13 publications (4.2%). The remaining 12 journals (8.1%; 21 publications, 6.8%) could not be assigned to a single discipline in the classification used.

Relative to the overall size of each domain in VABB-SHW, economics and business and education and psychology are over-represented. They contribute 36.4% of the questionable-journal publications but only 24.1% of all journal articles in the database. In contrast, the humanities and law are under-represented. These fields have strong national-language publishing traditions and a more limited supply of English-language OA titles from the publishers concerned. The pattern fits earlier observations that questionable outlets mainly attract authors in fields with large volumes of applied or policy-oriented output and a strong English-language orientation (Shen & Björk, 2015; Demir, 2018). The number of publications per journal is low: 112 journals (75.7%) appear only once in the data, 26 (17.6%) twice, and 10 (6.8%) three times or more. The most frequent journal contributes 11 publications.

**Authorship characteristics**

*Multi-authorship.* Single-authored articles account for 119 of the 308 publications (38.6%). A further 96 (31.2%) have two authors and 93 (30.2%) have three or more, with a maximum of eight. The mean number of authors per publication is 2.1, which is lower than for OA journal articles overall (2.4) and for all journal articles in the database (2.2). The proportion of single-authored publications is significantly higher for questionable journals than for OA journals in general (38.6% versus 33.4%; χ² = 4.1, df = 1, p = 0.04), but the effect size is small (Cramér's V = 0.03). The relatively high share of sole authorship suggests that publishing in a questionable journal is often an individual decision, which is relevant for deciding who can be approached for awareness-raising.

*Seniority.* The 308 publications involve 647 author instances, from 412 unique authors affiliated with Flemish institutions. Authors were classified as senior if they held a tenured or tenure-track academic position at the time of publication, and as early career if they were doctoral students, postdoctoral researchers or other temporary research staff. Of the author instances, 267 (41.3%) were senior and 380 (58.7%) were early career. The mean proportion of senior authors per publication is 0.43, compared with 0.37 for OA journal articles in general (Mann–Whitney U, p = 0.01). The first author is a senior researcher in 107 of the 308 publications (34.7%), against 31.0% for OA journal articles in general; this difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.22). Early-career first authors predominate, at 65.3% of the publications, but the substantial senior involvement shows that questionable journals are not simply a problem of inexperienced researchers. This is in line with findings by Frandsen (2017) and Eykens et al. (2019) that experienced researchers also publish in such outlets. Seniority is moreover unevenly distributed across years. The proportion of publications with a senior first author is 29.3% in 2010–2012 (n = 115) and 38.9% in 2013–2016 (n = 149), which suggests that the decline since 2012 is driven mainly by fewer early-career authors.

*Cognitive and organizational classification.* To assess how well the disciplinary scope of the journal (cognitive classification) matches the first author's departmental affiliation (organizational classification), we compared the two for the 212 publications in journals with a single disciplinary scope; the 96 multidisciplinary publications were analysed separately. For 148 of the 212 publications (69.8%) the first author's department matched the discipline of the journal. For the remaining 64 (30.2%) it did not. In these cases the first author was frequently affiliated with engineering, applied sciences or biomedical departments but had published in a business, education or social science journal. Mismatches are more frequent among early-career first authors (34.6%) than among senior first authors (21.1%; p = 0.03). Among the 96 multidisciplinary publications, 58 first authors (60.4%) belonged to social science departments, 22 (22.9%) to humanities departments and 16 (16.7%) to other domains. Taken together, these results indicate that most identified publications are discipline-internal, so that questionable journals appear to function as substitutes for regular disciplinary outlets rather than as outlets for out-of-field work. A sizeable minority nonetheless suggests a degree of opportunism or a lack of familiarity with the target field's publication norms.

Discussion and Conclusion

The five screenings conducted within the Flemish performance-based research funding system show that publications in questionable journals form a small and, since 2012, declining share of the output registered in the VABB-SHW. This is not a trivial finding. Studies of "predatory" publishing have often stressed the rapid growth of the phenomenon (Shen & Björk, 2015) and the ease with which journals with little or no peer review can be mistaken for legitimate outlets (Bohannon, 2013). Our data point in a different direction for a regulated, nationally curated database. In the period studied, the yearly number of identified publications peaked at roughly 0.5% of all journal articles submitted and then fell, while the number of articles in bona fide open access journals rose every year. Awareness of questionable publishing therefore appears to have reduced the use of suspect outlets without discouraging open access publishing as such. This distinction matters politically, because warnings about questionable journals are sometimes used, implicitly or explicitly, to cast doubt on open access in general (Beall, 2012). Our results suggest that researchers can and do tell the two apart, or at least are guided by institutional signals that do.

Several mechanisms may explain the decline after 2012. The most likely is the combined effect of increased media attention, the circulation of Beall's lists, and the screening itself. Because researchers know that articles in journals judged questionable are excluded from the funding allocation key, the screening acts as a deterrent as well as a filter. We cannot disentangle these influences with the present design, and the decline may partly reflect substitution, with authors moving to journals that are less visible to screeners yet only marginally better in quality. The finding that authors did not systematically cluster in one discipline, although humanities and some social science fields were overrepresented relative to their share of total output, is consistent with earlier work indicating that publication pressure and the absence of clearly established journal hierarchies make some fields more exposed (Hicks, 2012; Hammarfelt & de Rijcke, 2015).

The authorship analysis challenges the stereotype that questionable journals attract only inexperienced or peripheral researchers (Xia et al., 2015; Omobowale et al., 2014). Both early-career and senior researchers published in them. The average proportion of senior authors on articles in questionable journals was somewhat higher than on articles in open access journals, and first authors were drawn from all career stages. Such a pattern is difficult to reconcile with an account based purely on naïveté. It suggests that some authors knowingly use these outlets for speed or low rejection risk, while others, particularly those working outside the core of their discipline, lack the cues needed to evaluate an unfamiliar title. The mismatch we observed between the cognitive classification of the journal and the departmental affiliation of the authors supports the second interpretation: a considerable share of publications appeared in journals whose scope lay outside the authors' home discipline. Evaluative heuristics that work within a specialty, such as familiarity with editorial boards or reputations, are less reliable when authors publish across disciplinary borders. Multi-authorship, in turn, may dilute individual responsibility, since a co-author who did not select the journal has little opportunity to check it (Cobey et al., 2018). Awareness campaigns should therefore address senior researchers and co-authors, not only doctoral students.

For the legitimacy of the funding system, the relevant question is whether the volume identified threatens public and political confidence. At the observed rates, the financial distortion is negligible, since the allocation depends on relative shares of weighted output across universities and very small numbers cannot shift it appreciably. The reputational risk is different in kind. A single case in which public money rewarded publication in a journal without genuine peer review can be publicized far beyond its statistical weight. A system that screens regularly and transparently, and can show that identified items were removed, is better placed to defend its integrity than one that does not. Our results thus support the view that a modest, continuing investment in screening is proportionate. At the same time, they caution against relying on screening alone. A purely exclusionary approach shifts attention to what is being counted rather than to the quality of what is being published (Hicks et al., 2015), and the incentives that make low-barrier outlets attractive remain intact.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, our analysis is restricted to publications submitted for inclusion in the VABB-SHW and therefore says nothing about articles that authors chose not to register or that were never submitted. Second, the identification of questionable journals is inherently contested. Beall's lists were discontinued and criticized for opaque criteria and for bias against journals from the Global South, and later blacklists and whitelists overlap only partially (Strinzel et al., 2019). Our procedure combined several sources with expert assessment of individual journals, but misclassification in both directions is possible, and the dichotomy between questionable and legitimate journals oversimplifies a continuum of practices (Grudniewicz et al., 2019). Third, the screenings were carried out at different times and with slightly refined procedures, which complicates strict comparison of yearly rates, especially for the most recent publication years, where later retrospective screening could still raise counts. Fourth, the seniority variable is a proxy based on institutional position and cannot capture actual experience or the degree of each author's involvement in choosing the journal. Finally, the study concerns one western European region with a particular combination of a comprehensive database, a peer-review-based authoritative panel, and a strong incentive structure, so generalization to other systems should be cautious.

The study nevertheless allows a set of practical recommendations. Those responsible for bibliographic databases should combine several lists and criteria rather than depend on a single source, and should document and publish the decision rules applied. Screening should be systematic and recurring, because journals change their practices and new titles emerge. Flags raised during data entry, such as unfamiliar publishers or large mismatches between journal scope and author affiliation, could support earlier detection. The disciplinary scope of the journal can be compared with the authors' departmental affiliations as a low-cost warning indicator, although it should trigger review rather than automatic exclusion. Universities should combine this with information directed at all career stages, including senior researchers, and with accessible guidance for choosing journals, such as the "Think. Check. Submit." checklist. Finally, a procedure for authors to contest classifications is necessary to ensure fairness, especially for researchers publishing in regional or emerging outlets.

In conclusion, publications in questionable journals constitute a limited but persistent phenomenon in Flemish social sciences and humanities output. They have declined since 2012, while open access publishing has continued to grow, and they involve researchers of all seniority levels. Although these patterns do not indicate a systemic threat to the funding model, they underline the need for transparent screening, continuing education, and critical reflection on the incentives that sustain the market for questionable publishing. Future research should follow authors longitudinally, examine the motives behind journal choice through surveys or interviews, and assess whether screening in a funding context changes publication behavior or merely redirects it.

Introduction

The therapeutic alliance, broadly understood as the collaborative and affective bond between a clinician and a patient, together with their agreement on the goals and tasks of care, is one of the most robust and consistently documented contributors to outcome in mental health treatment (Bordin, 1979; Horvath et al., 2011). Meta-analytic evidence from psychotherapy research shows a modest but reliable association between alliance quality and symptom change, which holds across treatment modalities, patient diagnoses and measurement approaches (Flückiger et al., 2018). Evidence from inpatient and community mental health settings points in the same direction: stronger alliances are associated with greater treatment adherence, higher satisfaction, fewer involuntary admissions, reduced symptom severity and better functioning (Priebe & McCabe, 2006; Howgego et al., 2003; Dunster-Page et al., 2017). In services where psychological therapy is not the primary mode of care, these relationships may be among the most important mechanisms through which people experience help.

Nurses are the largest professional group in mental health services and typically have the most sustained and intensive contact with service users, particularly in inpatient, crisis and community case management contexts. It is therefore unsurprising that the nurse–patient relationship has long been positioned as the foundation of psychiatric and mental health nursing practice. Peplau's (1952) interpersonal relations theory framed the relationship as the vehicle through which therapeutic change occurs, and subsequent policy and professional frameworks have continued to emphasise therapeutic engagement as a core nursing function (Department of Health, 2006; Cutcliffe & Barker, 2004). Qualitative studies consistently show that service users value nurses who are available, respectful, empathic and genuinely interested in them as people, and that these qualities are often more salient to their experience of care than specific interventions (Shattell et al., 2007; Cleary et al., 2012). Conversely, perceptions of nurses as controlling, dismissive or absent are associated with experiences of coercion, alienation and disengagement from services (Bee et al., 2015).

Despite this centrality, building and sustaining an effective alliance in mental health nursing is far from straightforward. Nurses work in environments characterised by high acuity, restrictive practices, staff shortages, administrative burden and the competing demands of risk management and recovery-oriented care (Bowers, 2014; Hamilton & Manias, 2006). The dual role of nurses as both caregivers and agents of control, including in the use of legal powers, observation, seclusion and restraint, creates inherent tension for the development of trust (Moreno-Poyato et al., 2016). Service users may enter care with histories of trauma, stigma or negative experiences of services, and symptoms such as paranoia, withdrawal or cognitive disorganisation can make engagement difficult for both parties. Studies of nurses' time use suggest that direct, meaningful interaction with patients comprises a small proportion of the working day (Sharac et al., 2010), and staff burnout, moral distress and negative attitudes towards particular patient groups, for example those with personality disorder, may further erode relational quality (Bowers et al., 2006; Koekkoek et al., 2006). The alliance is thus not simply a matter of individual nurse skill but is shaped by organisational, interpersonal and contextual factors.

Given its importance and its fragility, one would expect a substantial body of work testing ways to strengthen nurse–patient relationships. A number of broader literatures are relevant. In psychotherapy research, alliance-focused training, feedback-informed treatment and interventions to repair ruptures have been evaluated, with some encouraging results (Safran et al., 2011; Lambert & Shimokawa, 2011). In mental health services more generally, interventions such as shared decision making, structured models of inpatient care (for example, Safewards; Bowers et al., 2015), recovery-focused training and clinical supervision have been proposed to improve the quality of staff–patient interactions. However, these approaches have usually been developed for psychotherapists or multidisciplinary teams, and it is not clear how far their findings transfer to the particular role, setting and constraints of nursing. Existing reviews have tended either to examine alliance correlates and outcomes (Howgego et al., 2003; Hartley et al., 2020), to synthesise qualitative accounts of what constitutes a good relationship (Hartley et al., 2020; Moreno-Poyato et al., 2016), or to focus on interventions in psychotherapy rather than nursing practice (Flückiger et al., 2018). We are not aware of a systematic review that has specifically collated and appraised interventions intended to improve the therapeutic alliance between mental health nurses and the people they care for, while also requiring that studies include an explicit measure of alliance.

This gap matters for several reasons. First, without an overview of what has been tested, nurses, educators and service managers lack an evidence base on which to design training, supervision or ward-level initiatives, and risk investing in approaches whose effects on relationships have never been demonstrated. Second, the heterogeneity of theoretical models, intervention components, settings and outcome measures in this area makes it difficult to identify promising mechanisms or to see where replication is needed. Third, careful appraisal of methodological quality is needed to establish whether the existing evidence can bear the weight placed on it by policy and practice. Finally, the relational aspects of nursing are increasingly threatened by system pressures, and a clear account of the state of the evidence can help argue for research investment in this area.

The present review therefore aimed to identify, collate and critique studies reporting on interventions designed to improve the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance in mental health care settings. Specifically, we sought to answer the following questions: (1) What interventions have been evaluated with the aim of improving the therapeutic alliance between nurses and mental health service users? (2) What theoretical and procedural approaches underpin these interventions? (3) What is the evidence that these interventions change alliance, as measured by validated or explicit alliance measures? (4) What is the methodological quality of the available evidence?

This paper makes three contributions. It provides the first systematic synthesis of intervention research focused on nurse–patient alliance in mental health care, applying rigorous search, extraction, reliability and quality assessment procedures. It characterises the range of intervention approaches and their theoretical foundations, offering a map of the field for practitioners and researchers. And it identifies the limitations of current evidence and sets out specific recommendations for designing more robust studies, with the aim of stimulating a renewed research agenda on supporting staff to build relationships that benefit both service users and nurses themselves.

Methods

Design and reporting

We conducted a systematic review following a protocol agreed by the author team before screening began. Reporting adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Page et al., 2021). Because we anticipated substantial heterogeneity in interventions, settings and outcome measures, we planned a narrative synthesis structured according to guidance from the Economic and Social Research Council (Popay et al., 2006), rather than meta-analysis.

Eligibility criteria

Eligibility was defined using a PICOS framework. Participants were nursing staff (registered nurses, nursing assistants, healthcare assistants and equivalent grades) and the adult or adolescent patients receiving mental health care from them, in inpatient, community or forensic settings. Studies were eligible if the intervention was explicitly directed at improving the nurse–patient therapeutic relationship, whether delivered to nurses, to patients, or to both. Eligible interventions included training programmes, supervision or reflective practice models, structured communication approaches, and organisational or ward-level changes. Studies were required to include at least one validated or purpose-designed quantitative or qualitative measure of therapeutic alliance, working alliance or closely related constructs such as therapeutic relationship, rapport or engagement, completed by nurses, patients or observers. Comparators could be usual care, waiting list, alternative interventions or pre-intervention baselines. We included randomised and non-randomised controlled trials, controlled and uncontrolled before-and-after studies, and mixed-methods evaluations with an intervention component. We excluded studies in which the alliance was reported only as a predictor or correlate of outcome without an intervention, studies of therapeutic alliance with non-nursing professionals only, and studies in general health settings. Only original journal articles published in English were included; conference abstracts, dissertations, editorials and protocols were excluded. No restriction was placed on publication date.

Search strategy

We searched Excerpta Medica database (Embase), PsycINFO, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE) and Cumulative Index of Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) from inception to the search date. Search terms were developed with an information specialist and combined four concepts using Boolean operators: (i) nursing staff (e.g. nurs*, "mental health nurs*", "psychiatric nurs*", "healthcare assistant*"); (ii) mental health care (e.g. psychiatr*, "mental health", "mental illness", inpatient*, forensic); (iii) therapeutic alliance (e.g. "therapeutic alliance", "therapeutic relationship*", "working alliance", "nurse-patient relation*", rapport, engagement); and (iv) intervention (e.g. intervention*, training, program*, trial, evaluation, "supervision"). Controlled vocabulary (MeSH, Emtree, CINAHL headings, APA thesaurus terms) was combined with free-text terms in title and abstract fields, and strategies were adapted for each database. The reference lists of all full-text papers meeting inclusion criteria were hand-searched, and a forward citation search of included papers was conducted using Google Scholar to identify further eligible work.

Study selection

Records were exported to reference management software and duplicates removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, followed by independent full-text assessment of potentially relevant papers. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted where consensus was not reached. Inter-rater reliability at each screening stage was evaluated using Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960):

κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e)

where p_o is the observed proportion of agreement and p_e is the proportion of agreement expected by chance, calculated from the marginal totals of each rater's include/exclude decisions. Values were interpreted using the conventions of Landis and Koch (1977), with 0.61–0.80 indicating substantial and >0.80 almost perfect agreement. Reasons for exclusion at full-text stage were recorded.

Data extraction

Data were extracted using a pre-determined form piloted on two studies and refined before use. Extracted information comprised: bibliographic details; country and setting; study design; sample size and participant characteristics (nurses and patients); intervention description, theoretical underpinning, dose, mode of delivery and provider; comparator; alliance measure(s), respondent and time points; other outcomes; main findings, including effect estimates, p values and confidence intervals where reported; attrition; and author-stated limitations. One reviewer extracted data from all papers, and a second independently extracted data from all included studies. Agreement was assessed as percentage agreement across extraction fields and, for categorical fields, by Cohen's kappa. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus with reference to the original papers. Where necessary, corresponding authors were contacted to clarify missing information.

Quality appraisal

Methodological quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies developed by the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP; Thomas et al., 2004), which is suitable for diverse intervention designs and has demonstrated content and construct validity (Armijo-Olivo et al., 2012). The tool rates six domains: selection bias, study design, confounders, blinding, data collection methods, and withdrawals and dropouts. Each domain is rated strong, moderate or weak, and a global rating is assigned: strong (no weak ratings), moderate (one weak rating) or weak (two or more weak ratings). Two reviewers independently appraised each study, and agreement on domain ratings and global ratings was quantified using weighted kappa, which assigns partial credit to near agreement on an ordinal scale:

κ_w = 1 − (Σ w_ij o_ij) / (Σ w_ij e_ij)

where o_ij and e_ij are the observed and expected frequencies in cell (i, j) and w_ij are linear disagreement weights. Disagreements were resolved by discussion. Quality ratings were not used as grounds for exclusion, but were used to inform interpretation of the findings, in line with recommendations that appraisal should contextualise rather than determine inclusion in reviews of heterogeneous evidence (Higgins et al., 2022). Where qualitative or mixed-methods components were present, these were described narratively and not given a separate quality score.

Data synthesis

Given the anticipated heterogeneity of interventions, populations and alliance measures, we did not pool results statistically. Instead, the synthesis proceeded in three stages: (i) tabulating study characteristics and findings to enable preliminary description; (ii) grouping studies by intervention type and theoretical basis, and exploring patterns in the direction and size of effects within and across groups; and (iii) considering how methodological quality, respondent perspective (nurse, patient, observer) and measurement approach might explain differences in findings. For each study, we recorded whether the intervention produced a statistically significant improvement in alliance at the conventional threshold of p < 0.05 and, where sufficient data were reported, calculated standardised effect sizes to aid comparison. For between-group continuous outcomes, we used Cohen's d:

d = (M₁ − M₂) / SD_pooled, where SD_pooled = √[((n₁ − 1)SD₁² + (n₂ − 1)SD₂²) / (n₁ + n₂ − 2)]

and for pre–post designs the standardised mean change, using the baseline standard deviation. Effect sizes were interpreted as small (0.2), moderate (0.5) or large (0.8) (Cohen, 1988), and, where possible, 95% confidence intervals were derived from reported statistics. Because effects calculated from uncontrolled designs are vulnerable to regression to the mean and secular trends, we interpreted them cautiously and distinguished them from those derived from controlled comparisons. Qualitative findings were synthesised descriptively, with attention to concordance or discordance with the quantitative results. We did not formally assess publication bias, because the small number of studies and the diversity of outcomes precluded funnel plot or similar methods (Sterne et al., 2011); however, we reflected on its likely influence in interpreting the findings. Results were not formally graded for certainty of evidence, but strengths and limitations of the evidence base were considered narratively.

Results

**Study selection**

The database searches returned 8,214 records (Embase n = 2,397; PsycINFO n = 2,146; MEDLINE n = 2,018; CINAHL n = 1,653). After removing 2,871 duplicates, 5,343 titles and abstracts were screened. Of these, 5,121 were excluded as clearly irrelevant, usually because they were not about nurse–patient relationships, did not evaluate an intervention, or used no alliance measure. The remaining 222 full-text articles were assessed against the eligibility criteria. A total of 214 were excluded, most commonly because they did not include a validated or explicit alliance measure (n = 97), evaluated an intervention delivered by non-nursing staff or an unspecified mixed workforce (n = 58), or were not original empirical reports (n = 41). The remaining 18 exclusions were for non-English language, non-mental-health settings, or duplicate publication. Hand-searching of reference lists and forward citation searching identified one further eligible paper, and eight papers were included in the final synthesis. Inter-rater agreement was good at title and abstract screening (κ = 0.79, 95% CI 0.74–0.84) and excellent at full-text screening (κ = 0.88, 95% CI 0.81–0.95). Agreement on data extraction was 93% across extracted fields, and all disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Study characteristics**

The eight papers were published between 2011 and 2019 and were conducted in the United Kingdom (n = 3), Australia (n = 2), Sweden (n = 1), the Netherlands (n = 1) and the United States (n = 1). Three studies were randomised controlled trials, one of which was a cluster trial (Bowen et al., 2014; Carter and Nguyen, 2016; Eriksson et al., 2011). Two were non-randomised controlled studies (Hughes et al., 2018; Lindqvist et al., 2013) and three were uncontrolled pre–post designs (Okafor et al., 2017; Reyes et al., 2019; Walsh and Patel, 2015). Four studies took place in acute inpatient wards, one in a forensic or secure setting, two in community mental health teams, and one across mixed inpatient and community services.

Across studies, 389 nurses and 1,046 service users contributed data (median per study: 38 nurses, range 12–112; 118 service users, range 41–286). Nurse samples were predominantly female (range 58–76% where reported). Service user samples were diagnostically heterogeneous. Most had psychotic or mood disorders, and two studies recruited people with a primary diagnosis of schizophrenia-spectrum disorder. Follow-up ranged from immediate post-intervention to 12 months (median 3 months), and only two studies followed participants beyond six months.

**Interventions and alliance measures**

The interventions fell into three broad categories. Four were staff training programmes teaching specific communication or therapeutic skills. These comprised motivational interviewing (Bowen et al., 2014), a cognitive-behavioural communication skills package (Reyes et al., 2019), Peplau-informed interpersonal training (Lindqvist et al., 2013), and a de-escalation and relational security curriculum (Eriksson et al., 2011). Two evaluated reflective or supervisory processes: group reflective practice (Hughes et al., 2018) and clinical supervision (Okafor et al., 2017). The final two were structural or organisational interventions, namely protected one-to-one engagement sessions (Carter and Nguyen, 2016) and a recovery-oriented care planning approach (Walsh and Patel, 2015). Intervention intensity varied considerably, from a single six-hour workshop to monthly supervision over 12 months. Only three studies reported fidelity assessment, and only one used independent ratings of recorded sessions.

Alliance was measured with five instruments: the Working Alliance Inventory (WAI or WAI-SR; n = 3), the Scale to Assess the Therapeutic Relationship (STAR; n = 2), the Helping Alliance Questionnaire (n = 1), the California Psychotherapy Alliance Scale (n = 1), and a bespoke therapeutic relationship scale (n = 1). Five studies relied on service user ratings, one on nurse ratings only, and two collected both. No study used observer-rated alliance as its primary outcome.

**Intervention effects**

Four of the eight studies (50%) reported a statistically significant improvement in alliance on their primary measure. Where possible, standardised mean differences were computed as

d = (M₁ − M₂) / SD_pooled,

using the between-group difference for controlled studies and the pre–post change for uncontrolled studies. Pre–post effect sizes should be treated cautiously because they are not protected against regression to the mean or testing effects.

Among the randomised trials, Bowen et al. (2014) found that service users of nurses trained in motivational interviewing (n = 62) reported higher WAI-SR scores at three months than those receiving usual care (n = 62; d = 0.41, 95% CI 0.05–0.77, p = .02). Eriksson et al. (2011) reported a moderate effect on patient-rated alliance in a secure unit (d = 0.62, 95% CI 0.08–1.16, p = .03), although the sample was small (n = 58) and the effect was not sustained at 12-month follow-up. The cluster trial of protected engagement sessions (Carter and Nguyen, 2016; 12 wards, n = 286) found no significant difference in patient-rated STAR scores (adjusted mean difference 2.1 points, 95% CI −1.3 to 5.5, p = .22). The intracluster correlation coefficient was 0.07, and the trial appeared underpowered for the design effect.

Of the non-randomised controlled studies, Lindqvist et al. (2013) reported significantly greater improvement in the intervention group on nurse- and patient-rated alliance (d = 0.48, p = .01), though baseline differences between groups were present and were adjusted for only partly. Hughes et al. (2018), which evaluated reflective practice groups across six wards (n = 142 service users), found no significant between-group difference (d = 0.12, 95% CI −0.21 to 0.45, p = .48).

Of the uncontrolled studies, only Reyes et al. (2019) reported significant improvement following communication skills training (pre–post d = 0.55, p < .01, n = 41 service users). The clinical supervision study (Okafor et al., 2017; d = 0.19, p = .27) and the recovery-oriented care planning study (Walsh and Patel, 2015; d = 0.10, p = .61) reported non-significant changes. Neither reported a power calculation.

Considering intervention type, three of four training programmes yielded significant effects, compared with none of the two reflective or supervisory interventions and none of the two structural interventions. Effects varied by rater: in the two studies collecting both nurse and patient ratings, nurse-rated alliance improved more than patient-rated alliance (mean difference in standardised effect 0.27). Because of the clinical, methodological and measurement heterogeneity, meta-analysis was judged inappropriate and a narrative synthesis was undertaken. No study reported adverse effects of the interventions.

**Methodological quality**

Quality was appraised using a standardised tool for quantitative studies, with two reviewers rating independently (initial agreement 87%; weighted κ = 0.81). Overall, none of the eight studies was rated strong, three were rated moderate (Bowen et al., 2014; Eriksson et al., 2011; Carter and Nguyen, 2016), and five were rated weak. Selection bias was a particular concern, with only two studies providing evidence that participants were representative of the target population. Two of the three RCTs clearly described adequate randomisation and allocation concealment, and none of the studies blinded outcome assessors or participants to allocation, which is perhaps unsurprising but notable given the largely subjective, self-reported outcome measures. Attrition was substantial: among the six studies reporting follow-up rates, retention ranged from 52% to 91% (median 74%), with differential dropout in two studies. Only three studies reported sample size justification. Confounding was appropriately controlled in just two of the five non-randomised or uncontrolled studies. Notably, the four studies with significant findings were not systematically higher in quality than those with null findings; two of the four significant studies were rated weak.

Discussion

This review set out to identify and critique interventions designed to improve the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance in mental health settings. Only eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Four reported statistically significant improvements in alliance, and most were limited by small samples, weak designs, or inadequate reporting. Given that the therapeutic relationship is widely regarded as the foundation of mental health nursing (Peplau, 1952; Cutcliffe et al., 2018) and a reliable predictor of outcome across psychological therapies (Flückiger et al., 2018), the scarcity of rigorous intervention research is striking. Our findings suggest that the profession's rhetorical commitment to the alliance has not been matched by a systematic effort to test how it can be strengthened.

Several explanations for this gap merit consideration. First, the alliance has often been treated as a by-product of good practice or personal disposition rather than a skill that can be taught and measured. Nursing education tends to emphasise therapeutic use of self, and the assumption that relational capacity is intrinsic may discourage the development of structured interventions. Second, the conceptual diversity of the alliance complicates evaluation. The studies we identified drew on different theoretical traditions, including psychodynamic, recovery-oriented, motivational, and skills-based models, and used measures developed for different purposes. Some instruments were adapted from psychotherapy research (e.g., the Working Alliance Inventory; Horvath & Greenberg, 1989), whereas others were designed for nursing contexts. Few had been validated for use with inpatients, people experiencing acute psychosis, or involuntarily detained patients. The "alliance" captured by these tools may therefore differ substantially, limiting comparison across studies and making meta-analysis inappropriate. Third, inpatient and community mental health environments present practical barriers to trials: high staff turnover, fluctuating patient populations, crisis-driven workloads, and the challenge of obtaining consent from people who are acutely unwell. These factors help explain the prevalence of small, uncontrolled, or quasi-experimental studies, yet they do not excuse the lack of methodological innovation, such as stepped-wedge or cluster designs, that could accommodate such complexity.

The heterogeneity of the interventions is itself informative. Some targeted staff skills through training, others altered the structure of care (for example, scheduled one-to-one time or consistent allocation of key workers), and others attempted to change how patients engaged with staff. Interventions that combined skills training with supervision or reflective practice appeared somewhat more promising than brief standalone training, consistent with wider evidence that single-session education rarely produces durable behaviour change (Beidas & Kendall, 2010). This accords with implementation research indicating that organisational support, leadership, and opportunities for practice are needed to sustain relational change (Damschroder et al., 2009). However, with so few studies, we cannot draw firm inferences about which components are active. Moreover, most studies assessed alliance shortly after the intervention, so we know little about whether gains persist or translate into improved clinical outcomes, reduced coercion, or better staff wellbeing.

A further concern is that alliance was frequently measured from a single perspective, usually the nurse's. Nurse and patient ratings of alliance often diverge, with clinicians typically rating the relationship more favourably (Tryon et al., 2018). Interventions evaluated solely through staff report may therefore overstate benefit, particularly when staff are aware of the study aims and have participated in the training being evaluated. Patient-rated measures are essential, and the field would benefit from the inclusion of qualitative data to capture what service users experience as meaningful relational care. The limited involvement of service users in designing and evaluating these interventions was notable and is at odds with principles of coproduction now central to mental health policy.

The quality appraisal indicated risk of bias in most studies, including lack of randomisation, absence of blinding, inadequate control of confounders, and incomplete reporting of attrition and intervention fidelity. Several papers did not provide sufficient detail for replication, and few described how intervention delivery was monitored. Without fidelity assessment, null findings cannot be distinguished from poorly implemented interventions, and positive findings cannot be attributed with confidence to the intended mechanism. Reporting guidelines such as TIDieR (Hoffmann et al., 2014) and the CONSORT extension for nonpharmacological trials would improve transparency and cumulative learning.

Limitations of the review should be acknowledged. We restricted inclusion to English-language journal articles, which may have excluded relevant work published elsewhere or in grey literature such as dissertations and service evaluations. Our requirement that studies include a measure of alliance excluded interventions that targeted relational practice but assessed only related constructs, such as empathy, therapeutic optimism, or attitudes towards patients. This decision strengthened conceptual coherence but may have narrowed the evidence base. Terminology for the nurse–patient relationship is inconsistent (therapeutic relationship, working alliance, engagement, rapport), and despite a broad search strategy and forward citation tracking, some relevant studies may have been missed. The small number and heterogeneity of included studies precluded quantitative synthesis, so our conclusions rest on narrative synthesis and are necessarily tentative. Finally, although data extraction and quality assessment involved independent evaluation with reliability checks, quality tools inevitably involve subjective judgement.

Several implications follow. For research, there is a need for conceptually grounded, theory-informed interventions developed in collaboration with nurses and service users, with explicit hypotheses regarding mechanisms of change. Future studies should use validated, patient-rated alliance measures appropriate for the setting, complemented by staff ratings and outcomes such as service engagement, perceived coercion, incidents of aggression, and nurse burnout. Adequately powered cluster-randomised trials, with process evaluations and follow-up beyond immediate post-intervention, would substantially improve the evidence base. Consensus on core outcome measures would facilitate synthesis. Researchers should also consider how interventions can be embedded within routine practice, using clinical supervision and organisational change to support skills over time, rather than relying on isolated training events.

For practice and education, our findings do not indicate that existing efforts to improve relationships are ineffective; rather, they show that their effectiveness has rarely been tested. Services should therefore be cautious in claiming that particular programmes enhance alliance and should build evaluation into their implementation. In the meantime, organisations can create conditions known to facilitate relational care, such as manageable workloads, protected time for meaningful interaction, continuity of nursing staff, and reflective supervision, while recognising that these too require empirical evaluation.

In conclusion, the evidence for interventions to support nurses in developing and sustaining therapeutic relationships with people using mental health services is sparse and methodologically weak, despite the central importance of the alliance to care quality and outcomes. Some approaches show promise, but confidence in their effectiveness is low. A renewed, rigorous, and collaborative research agenda is needed to determine what works, for whom, and in which contexts, so that nursing staff are supported by evidence in the relational work that lies at the heart of their role.

Introduction

High-heeled shoes, commonly defined as footwear in which the heel is substantially elevated above the forefoot, occupy a distinctive place in contemporary fashion and gender presentation. Surveys in Western countries indicate that a large proportion of women wear them at least occasionally, and a substantial minority wear them regularly for work or social occasions (Frey, 2000; Menz and Morris, 2005). Beyond their practical function, high heels are widely understood as a marker of femininity and sexual allure, and they form part of the visual vocabulary through which female gender identity is performed and perceived (Morris et al., 2013). This symbolic weight helps explain why high heels have persisted across centuries and cultures despite repeated criticism of their discomfort and potential for harm.

The musculoskeletal consequences of high heel wear have been studied for several decades. Raising the heel shifts body weight anteriorly, increases forefoot loading, and alters the kinematics of the ankle, knee, hip and lumbar spine during standing and walking (Cowley et al., 2009; Speksnijder et al., 2005). Such changes have been proposed as mechanisms for forefoot pain, deformity of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (hallux valgus), acute ankle and foot injuries, and more proximal pain. Increased knee joint loading in women walking in heels has led to the hypothesis that habitual wear may predispose to osteoarthritis, particularly in the patellofemoral and medial tibiofemoral compartments (Kerrigan et al., 1998). The evidence addressing these hypotheses comes from two largely separate research traditions. Epidemiological studies, mainly cross-sectional or case–control in design, relate self-reported or observed footwear exposure to clinical outcomes in populations. Biomechanical studies, usually laboratory-based experiments with small samples, quantify joint kinematics, kinetics, muscle activity and plantar pressure under controlled conditions. The first approach captures outcomes that matter to patients but is vulnerable to confounding, recall bias and uncertainty about causal direction. The second offers mechanistic insight and precise measurement but relies on surrogate outcomes whose relationship to long-term disease is uncertain. Consequently, each tradition alone provides an incomplete picture of the health burden attributable to high heels.

Several narrative and systematic reviews have synthesised parts of this literature. Some have concentrated on the effects of heel height on gait and posture (Cowley et al., 2009), others on foot problems and footwear in specific populations (Menz and Morris, 2005), and still others on particular joints or outcomes. These reviews differ in scope, inclusion criteria and methodological rigour, and their conclusions are not always consistent, partly because they address different outcomes and use different standards of evidence. To our knowledge, no review has examined the epidemiological and biomechanical evidence side by side, nor has any attempted to relate biomechanical changes to the outcomes observed in epidemiological studies. This is a clear limitation, because the two bodies of evidence are complementary: where epidemiological data are sparse or inconclusive, as might be expected for long-latency outcomes such as osteoarthritis, biomechanical findings may indicate plausible risk, whereas epidemiological findings can show whether predicted harms materialise in real-world wearers.

A further limitation of the existing literature concerns the scope of harm. Almost all research has focused on injury or disease in the wearer, which we term first-party harm. High heels, particularly those with narrow, rigid heel tips, can also injure other people, for example when a wearer treads on or strikes a bystander, or when the shoe is used as a weapon. Such second-party injuries have been reported in the form of isolated case reports and descriptive series, but they have not been systematically collated, and their frequency and severity are unknown. Without such evidence, assessments of the public health significance of high heels remain incomplete.

Perhaps the most striking omission is the lack of attention to why women choose to wear high heels. Discussions of footwear-related harm often implicitly treat the behaviour as irrational or as the product of social pressure alone. Yet there is experimental evidence that heels change how women are perceived and how men behave towards them. Controlled studies suggest that women wearing high heels are rated as more attractive, that heel height can influence judgements of femininity, and that men may be more likely to approach or assist women who wear them (Guéguen, 2013, 2015; Morris et al., 2013). If such psychosexual benefits are real, they constitute a substantive reason for wearing heels and must be weighed against the health costs in any balanced appraisal. They also help to explain why educational messages about foot health have had limited impact on behaviour. To date, however, these studies have not been brought together in a review, and their relationship to the health literature has not been explored.
