*Authorship and labour.* Discussions about first and last authorship were observed in 19 meetings, and 14 of these (73.7%) referenced the JIF of the intended outlet as a basis for allocating positions. Several PhD candidates (8 of 22; 36.4%) stated that they prioritised projects with a likelihood of publication in journals above a JIF of 6, because of local doctoral regulations or expectations of future employability, even when they considered other projects scientifically more pressing.

*Shelving and fragmentation.* Eighteen segments described findings left unpublished or deliberately split. Nine researchers (15.5% of interviewees) reported at least one completed study abandoned because it was unlikely to reach a journal of sufficient JIF, typically replication or null-result studies. Six reported splitting a dataset into more than one paper to access different journal tiers.

**Temporal and career-stage variation**

The salience of the JIF varied by career stage in ways that reflect uneven exposure to precarity (Fochler et al., 2016). The mean number of JIF mentions per interview was 11.3 for postdoctoral researchers, 9.6 for PhD candidates, 6.2 for principal investigators, and 3.1 for managers and policy officers (overall mean 8.2). Postdoctoral researchers were also most likely to report modifying research plans in response to the JIF (11 of 14; 78.6%), compared with 12 of 22 PhD candidates (54.5%) and 4 of 13 principal investigators (30.8%).

**Critique alongside compliance**

Critical stances were common but did not translate into abstention. In 47 of 58 interviews (81.0%) respondents criticised the JIF, often citing the skewness of citation distributions (Seglen, 1997; Larivière et al., 2016) or the principles of the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment, which was referenced in 19 interviews (32.8%) and in 5 institutional documents. Yet of those 47 critics, 41 (87.2%) also reported using the JIF in their own decisions about where to submit or whom to hire or recommend. Only 6 of 58 respondents (10.3%) described deliberately avoiding the JIF in practice, and four of these were established principal investigators. Taken together, the findings show a gap between the circulating folk theories about the JIF and its documented formal role, alongside a measurable consolidation of knowledge production around it.

## Discussion and Conclusion

Our starting point was that much of the debate about the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) in biomedicine rests on folk theories: plausible, widely shared accounts of what the indicator does, seldom checked against what happens in laboratories and clinics. Two such accounts dominate. In the first, the JIF is a pragmatic shorthand that helps overloaded evaluators sort a vast literature (Garfield 2006). In the second, it is a pathological distortion imposed on researchers who would otherwise do better science (Seglen 1997; Hicks et al. 2015). Our ethnographic material, drawn from four research groups across two Dutch University Medical Centers (about 40 interviews and roughly 250 hours of observation), supports neither account fully. Researchers were rarely naïve about the JIF's limitations. In nearly every interview, even those with senior investigators who professed scepticism, informants volunteered that the indicator is "crude" or "not a real measure of quality." Yet the same informants routinely organized their work around journal tiers. Knowledge of the indicator's flaws and dependence on it coexisted, a pattern consistent with earlier findings that researchers can criticize metrics while still "thinking with" them (Müller and de Rijcke 2017).

The central implication is that the JIF operates less as a measure applied to research after the fact than as a resource that helps constitute what counts as a viable project, a publishable result, and a promising career. We observed this at several moments in the research process. At the planning stage, groups discussed experiments in terms of the "level" of journal they could plausibly reach, and projects judged unlikely to reach that level were postponed or reframed. During analysis and writing, decisions about which findings formed the "story" were shaped by anticipated reviewer expectations at high-JIF journals, which favored mechanistic novelty over replication or null results. At the stage of authorship and collaboration, the allocation of first and last positions, and the decision to hold a manuscript for a further round of experiments rather than submit it, were repeatedly justified by journal rank. These examples extend work on reactivity to quantification (Espeland and Sauder 2007) and on how evaluation criteria become embedded in epistemic practice (Fochler, Felt and Müller 2016; Rushforth and de Rijcke 2015). They also show why a binary of "use" versus "misuse" is analytically thin. The effects we describe occurred largely in the absence of any formal requirement to report JIFs, and they emerged through routine talk, planning documents, and informal mentoring rather than through explicit audit.

Our findings also complicate the common view that national policy is the main driver. Dutch funders and universities have been among the most visible signatories of declarations against the use of journal metrics, including DORA, and the national Recognition and Rewards agenda explicitly de-emphasizes the JIF. Nevertheless, informants, particularly early-career researchers, reported that formal policy had changed the *vocabulary* of evaluation more than its practical consequences. Several described a "double bookkeeping" in which narrative CVs and portfolios were prepared for committees while journal prestige remained the tacit currency in hiring discussions, authorship negotiations, and competition for international positions. This resonates with accounts of how evaluation regimes sediment across local, national, and transnational scales (Rushforth, Franssen and de Rijcke 2019; Wouters et al. 2019) and suggests that reforms confined to one scale are likely to be absorbed or bypassed. It is also a reminder that audit cultures tend to be self-reinforcing once indicators become embedded in infrastructures and expectations (Power 1997; Muller 2018).

We should be careful about what these observations do and do not show. First, our study is qualitative and situated in a small number of sites in a single national system with a distinctive history of performance-based evaluation. We make no claims about the prevalence of particular practices, and the figures above describe our empirical base rather than a sample from which frequencies can be generalized. Comparative work in systems with different funding arrangements, or in subfields such as clinical epidemiology or health services research where the JIF may carry less weight, would test the boundaries of our argument. Second, ethnography captures how researchers account for their decisions, and justifications offered after the fact may overstate or understate the indicator's role. We tried to mitigate this by privileging situations in which decisions were made in real time, such as group meetings and manuscript planning sessions, but we cannot fully separate the influence of the JIF from that of correlated considerations such as peer expectations, funder priorities, or disciplinary norms about what constitutes a significant finding. Third, we did not follow manuscripts and careers longitudinally, so we cannot assess whether the shaping effects we describe change epistemic outcomes, for instance by altering the types of questions that reach publication. That question is essential, and it requires combining ethnographic and large-scale bibliometric approaches (Larivière and Sugimoto 2019).

These limitations point to a research agenda. If metrics are constitutive, as our analysis suggests, then studies that treat them only as dependent or independent variables will miss how they co-produce the objects they claim to measure (Callon 1998). We therefore need work that traces how indicators travel into routines, templates, and infrastructures, from reference managers and institutional dashboards to grant forms, and how these shape the temporal rhythms, labor divisions, and risk calculations of research. We also need greater attention to who bears the costs. In our material, junior researchers and those on precarious contracts experienced the strongest pressure to align with journal hierarchies, while established investigators could more readily afford principled distance. Studies of such unequal exposure would connect research on evaluation with broader debates about careers and inclusion in academia (Biagioli and Lippman 2020).

For policy, the implications are sobering but not fatalistic. Because the JIF's influence is enacted through everyday practice, abolishing its formal use is necessary but insufficient. Reform efforts should address the informal settings in which prestige is negotiated, offer credible alternatives that carry weight in hiring and promotion rather than serving as supplements, and monitor, through qualitative as well as quantitative means, whether new indicators simply reproduce old hierarchies in different form. Researchers and institutions might also create occasions for collective reflection on how evaluative expectations shape project choices, making visible what currently remains tacit.

In sum, debates that cast the JIF as either a hero or a villain obscure how deeply it is woven into the making of biomedical knowledge. By examining how the indicator is enacted on the shop floor, we have shown that its force lies less in its technical validity than in its capacity to coordinate expectations, justify decisions, and orient aspirations. Taking these constitutive effects seriously is a precondition for any informed discussion of whether, and how, research evaluation should change.

Introduction

Programming education has been reshaped by the rise of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), which distribute knowledge to thousands of learners at marginal cost per participant. Programming is a natural fit for this format because exercises can be assessed automatically and feedback delivered immediately (Ihantola et al., 2010). Platforms such as openHPI, edX and Coursera therefore commonly embed a browser-based development environment in which learners edit code, execute it and receive a verdict from a predefined test suite (Staubitz et al., 2016). This design offers a consistent and controllable setup, removes installation barriers and allows large cohorts to be supported by small teaching teams. Automated assessment, in turn, has been shown to provide timely feedback that helps novices correct misconceptions (Keuning et al., 2018).

These advantages come at a cost. Learners who commit fully to a supplied in-browser environment never encounter the tools and workflows that characterise professional software development: local editors and debuggers, version control, testing frameworks, issue trackers and continuous integration (CI) services. Yet fluency with these tools is regarded as a core competency for graduates, and the lack of it is a recurring complaint from employers and a source of difficulty when students begin real-world projects (Hsing and Gennarelli, 2019). Research on the use of Git and GitHub in classrooms suggests that exposure to collaborative, tool-rich workflows is associated with better learning outcomes and a more realistic understanding of software practice (Hsing and Gennarelli, 2019; Zagalsky et al., 2015). Conventional MOOC exercises rarely provide such exposure because their infrastructure is deliberately abstracted away from the learner.

A second, less visible limitation concerns the role of tests. In most automatically assessed exercises, the test suite is written by the instructor and is either visible or hidden from the student, who merely executes it to determine whether the solution is "correct". Learners thus become consumers of tests rather than authors. This arrangement contrasts sharply with test-driven development (TDD), in which developers write a failing test first, implement the minimum code necessary to pass it and then refactor (Beck, 2003). TDD is widely taught and advocated because it is associated with improved code quality, more modular design and greater confidence when changing code (Erdogmus et al., 2005; Janzen and Saiedian, 2008), although empirical evidence on its effect on productivity and external quality is mixed (Fucci et al., 2017). Whatever its debated benefits, TDD can only be learned by practising the writing of tests. Where tests are provided, the central discipline of the technique is bypassed. Educators have long reported that students are reluctant to write tests and tend to view testing as an afterthought rather than a design activity (Edwards, 2003; Buffardi and Edwards, 2012). Interventions to counteract this tendency, such as rewarding students for the coverage of their own tests in automated graders like Web-CAT (Edwards and Pérez-Quiñones, 2008), have shown promise but typically rely on dedicated, course-specific infrastructure rather than the tools students will later use in industry.

Meanwhile, the software industry has converged on a standard automation infrastructure. CI services such as Travis CI, CircleCI and GitHub Actions build and test every change that is pushed to a repository and report the outcome to the developer. Their adoption is widespread in open-source and commercial projects, and they have been associated with more frequent releases and with changes in how pull requests are reviewed and merged (Vasilescu et al., 2015; Hilton et al., 2016). In essence, CI services are already general-purpose, scalable, event-driven automated assessment systems: they execute arbitrary scripts in an isolated environment on each commit and return a structured verdict. To our knowledge, however, this potential has been exploited only sporadically for teaching, and mostly as a back-end grader behind a conventional course platform rather than as the primary medium through which exercises are delivered and feedback is given.

This observation exposes a gap. Existing online programming courses achieve scale and automation but sacrifice authenticity of tooling and the opportunity to practise writing tests. Conversely, project-based courses using professional tooling provide authenticity but typically require substantial manual effort from instructors to review submissions, provide feedback and release subsequent tasks. What is lacking is an approach that combines the scalability of MOOC-style automation with the realism of a professional workflow, and that specifically fosters TDD practice.

We address this gap with Prof. CI, an approach to online exercises that uses CI services and GitHub workflows as the teaching infrastructure. Participants work on their own repositories using their local development environment. When they push code, the CI server executes checks and responds with feedback and, upon success, the next challenge, which is typically delivered as an issue or a description of a feature to be implemented. Crucially, the tests for the functionality to be developed are not supplied: learners must write them, and the CI server assesses whether the tests are meaningful, for example by verifying that they fail against a reference implementation that lacks the feature or that they detect deliberately faulty variants of it. The instructor thus acts as a "professor" who lives inside the CI pipeline, which gives the approach its name.

The research questions guiding our work are as follows:

- **RQ1:** Can CI services and GitHub workflows be used to deliver automated, scalable programming exercises that teach TDD while exposing learners to professional tools?
- **RQ2:** Does such an exercise increase learners' motivation to write tests for their own code?
- **RQ3:** How do students and teachers experience this form of exercise, and which benefits and challenges emerge in practice?

To investigate these questions, we conducted a pilot study with 30 undergraduate students who were learning the Ruby on Rails web development framework. Students completed a sequence of TDD-oriented exercises in their own GitHub repositories, with all feedback and task progression handled automatically by the CI infrastructure. We collected data through participant surveys, students' reflections and the teaching staff's observations, supplemented by the repository histories produced during the exercise.

This paper makes the following contributions. First, we present the concept and design of Prof. CI, including the repository structure, workflow automation and feedback mechanisms that allow the CI server to act as an automated tutor, and we describe how the approach can be transferred to other languages and frameworks. Second, we provide an implementation and a report of its application in a real course, documenting the practical issues we encountered. Third, we offer empirical evidence from the pilot evaluation that the exercise increased students' motivation to write tests, complemented by qualitative insights from students and teachers regarding usability, perceived learning and the limits of the approach. Finally, we derive lessons and design recommendations for educators who wish to use everyday development infrastructure as a vehicle for scalable, authentic programming education.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on automated assessment, TDD education and the use of GitHub and CI in teaching. Section 3 describes the design and implementation of Prof. CI. Section 4 outlines the pilot study, Section 5 reports the results, and Sections 6 and 7 discuss limitations, implications and directions for future work.

Methods

**Study design and context.** We conducted a single-group pilot study with a pre-/post-intervention design in an undergraduate web engineering course at a German university. The course introduces the Ruby on Rails framework (Ruby on Rails Core Team, 2023) within a 12-week semester. The exercise ran over three weeks as a mandatory but ungraded part of the course, with an estimated workload of six hours. Because the pilot was embedded in regular teaching, we did not form a control group. Withholding the intervention from part of the cohort was judged pedagogically undesirable, and the cohort size (N = 30) would have left a between-group comparison underpowered (Cohen, 1988). We therefore treated the study as exploratory. We focus on within-subject change and on triangulating survey data with qualitative and repository-based evidence (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018).

**Participants.** All 30 enrolled students (19 male, 10 female, 1 undisclosed; median age 21 years, range 19–27) took part. Participation in the accompanying surveys was voluntary and pseudonymous, and students gave informed consent for the use of their repository metadata and survey responses for research purposes. Prior experience was assessed in the pre-survey. All students had completed an introductory Java programming course. Twenty-two students (73%) reported prior experience with Git, while only 9 (30%) had used a CI service and 11 (37%) had written automated tests before. None had previously worked with Ruby on Rails. The study followed the university's data protection regulations, and no personally identifiable information was stored alongside survey data.

**The Prof. CI approach.** Prof. CI uses the automation infrastructure that professional developers use daily instead of a browser-based programming environment. Each student receives a personal Github repository generated from a template by an automated onboarding script. The repository contains a skeleton Rails application, a README with instructions, a Github Actions workflow definition, and a set of issues describing the first tasks. Students clone the repository, develop locally with an editor of their choice, and push commits to the main branch. Each push triggers the Github Actions workflow (Github, 2023), which executes the test suite in a containerized environment. A dedicated "instructor" component, implemented as a Ruby script within the workflow, then evaluates the repository state and responds to the student by posting comments on the corresponding issue and, when the criteria are met, opening the next issue with a new challenge. Prof. CI thus resembles the feedback loops of automated assessment systems (Ihantola et al., 2010; Edwards & Perez-Quinones, 2008), but differs in that feedback is delivered through the same channels (issue tracker, CI status, commit checks) that students will encounter in industrial settings (Hilton et al., 2016).

**Exercise structure.** The exercise comprised eight sequential challenges following the red-green-refactor cycle of test-driven development (Beck, 2003). Unlike in many MOOC settings, where the tests are supplied and merely executed, students in the first four challenges received only a natural-language specification of the desired behavior (e.g., "a user must not be saved without a valid e-mail address") and were required to write the failing test before implementing the feature. In challenges five to eight, the specifications became more complex (associations between models, request specifications for controllers, and one refactoring task). Prof. CI assessed submissions along three dimensions: (i) whether the student's own tests existed and passed, (ii) whether these tests detected the failure of a set of hidden reference mutants of the intended behavior, and (iii) whether the commit history showed the test being committed before or together with the implementation. The second dimension was operationalized through lightweight mutation analysis (Jia & Harman, 2011), using a set of three to seven predefined faulty implementations per challenge. The third dimension was checked by inspecting the order of changed files across commits. If the criteria were not met, the bot posted targeted hints, such as which mutants had survived, rather than solutions. Students could push an unlimited number of times, and no penalty was applied for failed attempts.

**Data collection.** We collected four types of data. First, a pre-survey administered before the exercise and a post-survey administered one day after the deadline captured motivation and attitudes toward testing. Motivation to write tests was measured with six items adapted from the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (Ryan & Deci, 2000) and the attention and relevance subscales of the ARCS model (Keller, 1987), rated on a seven-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Example items include "I enjoy writing tests for my code" and "I consider writing tests before implementation worthwhile." Internal consistency was acceptable in both waves (Cronbach's α = .82 pre, .87 post; Cronbach, 1951). Self-efficacy in testing was assessed with four further items, following Bandura's (2006) guidelines for self-efficacy scales. The post-survey additionally contained the ten-item System Usability Scale (Brooke, 1996) to evaluate the Prof. CI workflow, as well as open-ended questions on perceived difficulties, benefits, and suggestions.

Second, we extracted repository data via the Github API, including the number of commits, the number and outcome of workflow runs, the time between challenge release and completion, and the ratio of test code to production code, measured in lines of code. Third, the teaching team (two instructors and two teaching assistants) kept structured observation notes during weekly lab sessions and recorded questions and recurring problems. Fourth, after the course, we conducted semi-structured interviews with eight students, purposively sampled to cover different completion speeds and prior experience levels (Patton, 2015). The interviews lasted 15–25 minutes, were audio-recorded, and were transcribed verbatim.

**Operationalization of outcomes.** The primary outcome was the change in self-reported motivation to write tests between pre- and post-survey. Secondary outcomes were change in testing self-efficacy, perceived usability (SUS), challenge completion rate, number of workflow runs per challenge, and test-to-production code ratio. We additionally examined whether students wrote tests before implementation, as identified by the commit-order criterion, and tracked how this proportion developed across the eight challenges, as an indicator of adherence to TDD practice.

**Statistical analysis.** Survey scale scores were computed as item means. Because the sample was small and Shapiro–Wilk tests indicated deviations from normality for the difference scores (p < .05 for the motivation scale), we used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired comparisons (Wilcoxon, 1945), with the exact p-value computed under the Pratt treatment of ties. Effect sizes are reported as the matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation r_rb, and as Cliff's delta where appropriate (Cliff, 1993), with 95% confidence intervals obtained from 10,000 bootstrap resamples. Following common conventions, we interpreted r_rb values of .1, .3, and .5 as small, medium, and large effects, respectively. Associations between prior experience (number of previously used development tools) and outcome variables were examined with Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Because we tested two confirmatory hypotheses (motivation and self-efficacy), we applied a Holm–Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979) and set the family-wise significance level to α = .05. All remaining analyses were considered exploratory and are reported without adjustment. SUS scores were scaled to a 0–100 range and interpreted using the adjective ratings of Bangor et al. (2009). Repository metrics are described using medians and interquartile ranges, since distributions were right-skewed. Analyses were performed in R 4.3 (R Core Team, 2023), and the analysis scripts and anonymized data are available in the study's replication package.

**Qualitative analysis.** Open-ended survey responses, interview transcripts, and teacher observation notes were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Two researchers independently coded the interview transcripts inductively, then jointly consolidated the codes into themes through iterative discussion. Intercoder agreement on a 25% subsample of survey responses was substantial (Cohen's κ = .78; Landis & Koch, 1977). Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Qualitative findings were compared with the quantitative results to identify convergent and divergent evidence.

**Threats to validity.** The absence of a control group and the reliance on self-reported motivation limit causal inference, as does the possibility of social desirability bias, since instructors were aware of the survey. We attempted to mitigate the latter through pseudonymous responses and by complementing self-reports with behavioral repository data. The small, single-institution sample restricts generalizability, and results should therefore be interpreted as preliminary evidence of feasibility and perceived effectiveness (Runeson & Höst, 2009).

Results

**Participation and progression.** Of the 30 enrolled students, all 30 forked the template repository and triggered at least one workflow run, and 28 (93.3%) completed the post-exercise survey. The exercise comprised six sequential challenges, each released automatically by the CI server once the preceding challenge's test suite passed. Completion declined gradually across challenges, from 30 students (100%) for Challenge 1 to 29, 27, 26, and 24 for Challenges 2 to 5, and 23 (76.7%) for Challenge 6. This corresponds to a mean of 5.0 challenges per student (SD = 1.8). The steepest attrition (a loss of two students) occurred between Challenges 2 and 3, which was the first point at which students had to write a controller test without a provided skeleton. Because the course was voluntary for the final two challenges, we regard the 76.7% completion rate as comparable to rates reported for supervised programming exercises and well above those commonly reported for open MOOCs, which typically fall below 15% (Jordan, 2014; Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente, 2019).

**Workflow activity.** Students generated 1,247 workflow runs in total, a median of 38 per student (IQR = 27–51; range = 6–93). Of these, 773 (62.0%) failed and 474 (38.0%) succeeded. This is consistent with the red–green cycle that test-driven development prescribes (Beck, 2003), since a failing run was the expected outcome after each new challenge was released. The median time from push to completed feedback was 74 s (IQR = 58–112 s), and 91.2% of runs finished within three minutes. Students pushed a median of 4.3 times per challenge. The number of runs per challenge increased from a median of 4 for Challenge 1 to 9 for Challenge 4, which reflects the greater complexity of the later tasks. Run counts were not significantly correlated with the final grade of the accompanying course (Spearman's ρ = 0.21, p = .27), which suggests that frequent pushing was not simply a proxy for prior ability.

**Quality of student-written tests.** Because Prof. CI withholds the reference tests and requires students to write their own, we analysed the resulting test suites. Across the 23 final submissions that reached Challenge 6, the mean test-to-code ratio, measured in lines of code, was 1.14 (SD = 0.47), against 0.31 in a comparison sample of 21 repositories from the same course's previous cohort, which used a conventional exercise sheet with prescribed tests (Mann–Whitney U = 52, p < .001, r = 0.69). Line coverage measured with SimpleCov averaged 87.4% (SD = 9.6%), compared with 61.8% (SD = 18.3%) in the previous cohort. The median number of test cases per repository was 41 (IQR = 33–56). Following the mutation-based criterion used by the server for Challenge 5, which injected faults into the students' own implementations, 17 of 24 students (70.8%) detected at least 80% of the injected mutants on their first attempt, and all but one passed after at most three attempts. Students' tests therefore did not merely execute code; most were capable of discriminating faulty from correct behaviour (Inozemtseva & Holmes, 2014). The previous cohort was not randomly assigned, and these comparisons should be interpreted with that limitation in mind.

**Motivation to write tests.** In the pre-exercise survey (n = 30), students rated their agreement with the statement "I am motivated to write tests for my own code" on a five-point Likert scale (Likert, 1932), giving a median of 3 (IQR = 2–4; mean = 2.93, SD = 1.05). After the exercise (n = 28) the median was 4 (IQR = 4–5; mean = 4.11, SD = 0.83). A Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the 26 students who completed both surveys indicated a significant increase (W = 16.5, p < .001), with a large effect size (r = 0.71; Cohen, 1988). The proportion of students agreeing or strongly agreeing rose from 36.7% to 82.1%. Self-reported confidence in writing a test before implementing a feature also increased, from a mean of 2.67 (SD = 1.12) to 3.89 (SD = 0.88; p < .001). In contrast, agreement with the statement "Writing tests slows down my development" fell from a mean of 3.77 (SD = 1.02) to 2.86 (SD = 1.07; p = .004), although it remained near the scale midpoint. We emphasise that all outcomes were self-reported and that the absence of a control group prevents causal attribution (Fucci et al., 2017).

**Perceived usability and tooling experience.** The System Usability Scale (Brooke, 1996) yielded a mean score of 78.4 (SD = 11.2), which is above the commonly cited benchmark of 68 and falls into the "good" adjective range (Bangor et al., 2009). Asked whether the exercise had improved their familiarity with real development tools, 25 of 28 students (89.3%) agreed or strongly agreed. Individual ratings were highest for Git and Github (mean = 4.4, SD = 0.7), followed by the CI service (mean = 4.2, SD = 0.8) and the test framework (mean = 4.1, SD = 0.9). Twenty-two students (78.6%) reported that they had never previously used a CI service. Twenty-one (75.0%) said that they preferred working in a local editor to a browser-based environment, 5 (17.9%) were indifferent, and 2 (7.1%) preferred a browser-based environment. The issue tracker, which was used to deliver challenge descriptions, was rated less favourably (mean = 3.5, SD = 1.1), and 6 students (21.4%) stated that they did not notice new issues until they checked Github manually.

**Qualitative feedback.** Free-text responses (n = 24 non-empty) were coded inductively by two authors following thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006), with substantial inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.78). Four themes accounted for 87% of coded segments. The most frequent theme, "immediate and concrete feedback" (n = 15 respondents), described the value of seeing a failing or passing build within minutes of pushing. Next came "ownership of the repository" (n = 11), where students valued that the code remained theirs after the course, followed by "difficulty with cryptic error output" (n = 9) and "initial setup effort" (n = 8). The last two themes constitute the principal negative feedback. Three students reported that the mutation feedback for Challenge 5 was difficult to interpret without additional explanation.

**Teacher observations and operational effort.** Teaching staff logged 17 support requests during the six-week period, 9 (52.9%) of which concerned local environment setup (Ruby versions and database configuration) and 5 (29.4%) of which concerned workflow failures that were later traced to YAML syntax errors in students' modified configuration files. Only 3 requests related to the logic of the challenges. Staff spent an estimated 11 hours on the exercise during the term, excluding the initial development of the challenge pipeline, and this figure corresponds to approximately 22 minutes per student. Instructors noted that students who initially wrote tests after the implementation tended to shift towards test-first behaviour by Challenge 3, which was corroborated by commit histories: the proportion of students whose first commit for a challenge touched only test files increased from 20.0% (6 of 30) in Challenge 1 to 65.2% (15 of 23) in Challenge 6 (χ²(1) = 9.7, p = .002). Finally, there were no cases of the automation infrastructure failing to release a challenge, and Github Actions availability problems affected only 12 runs (1.0%), all of which were successfully re-executed.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Principal findings**

This paper set out to determine whether the automation infrastructure professional developers use every day, namely CI services and Github workflows, can serve as the backbone of an online programming exercise that teaches test-driven development (TDD). In the pilot with 30 undergraduate students learning Ruby on Rails, the answer was largely affirmative. Most participants completed the exercise using only their local toolchain, and in the post-exercise survey 24 of 30 students (80%) reported being more motivated to write tests for their own code than before. Students also described the red–green rhythm of pushing a commit, seeing a failing build, and then fixing it as the most instructive part of the course. These results suggest that the central design decision, moving the exercise from a controlled browser sandbox into the learner's own repository, did not impair scalability or feedback quality, and it exposed students to tools that they would otherwise meet only in later projects.

We interpret the increase in testing motivation as a consequence of two features of the design. First, Prof. CI releases challenges incrementally, so each new task is introduced as a failing test or a new requirement that students must address. This makes tests the specification of the next step rather than an artifact that is checked after the fact (Beck, 2003). In many MOOCs the test suite is already supplied and merely executed, so learners have little occasion to reason about what a good test should assert. Students in our pilot had to write tests before they could proceed, which plausibly shifted their view of tests from an assessment instrument to a design aid. Second, feedback was tied to the same artifacts, namely commits, pull requests and build logs, that students will encounter in professional settings. Self-determination theory predicts that perceived relevance and autonomy support intrinsic motivation (Deci & Ryan, 2000), and several free-text responses explicitly mentioned the "realness" of the setup. We caution that the study design cannot separate these mechanisms, and the present data are compatible with other explanations such as novelty or the instructor's enthusiasm.

**Relation to prior work**

Our observations agree with research on automated assessment, which has long shown that rapid, automated feedback helps novices (Ihantola et al., 2010; Keuning et al., 2018). They also qualify one common finding of that literature. Edwards (2004) and Buffardi and Edwards (2013) reported that students who are graded mainly on instructor-supplied tests tend to fall into trial-and-error behavior and write few tests of their own. By withholding the reference tests and making the students' own tests part of the progression logic, Prof. CI addresses this concern directly, although we did not measure test quality in a way that allows a rigorous comparison. Meta-analytic evidence on TDD in professional and student populations is also mixed. Effects on external quality and productivity are small and context dependent (Fucci et al., 2017), and the benefit may derive more from granularity and uniformity of the development process than from test-first ordering itself. We therefore do not claim that Prof. CI improves code quality. Our claim is more modest: it creates conditions in which students practice a disciplined, test-centered workflow that they may otherwise avoid.

The use of version control and CI in teaching has been examined mainly in advanced software engineering courses (Hsing & Gennarelli, 2019). Prior studies of CI in practice show that it changes developer behavior by encouraging more frequent commits and earlier detection of defects (Vasilescu et al., 2015; Hilton et al., 2016). Our pilot suggests that these habits can be introduced to students at an earlier stage, provided that the tooling is scaffolded by templates and preconfigured workflows. Teachers reported that the repository history was a useful source of information, because it allowed them to see when students got stuck and to identify common misconceptions, such as tests that assert implementation details rather than behavior.

**Implications**

For educators, the approach offers a way to reconcile two goals that are often in tension in MOOCs: scalability through automation and authenticity of the development environment. Because the grading logic lives in workflow files and the delivery of new challenges is triggered by pushes, the marginal teacher effort per additional learner is small. The main costs are the initial authoring of the challenge sequence and the support required for environment problems. In our pilot, local setup issues, such as Ruby version conflicts and Git authentication, accounted for most help requests during the first week. Course designers should therefore plan an explicit onboarding phase or provide containerized development environments, for example through devcontainers or cloud-based workspaces, which would retain most of the authenticity benefit while reducing this barrier.

For researchers, repository-based exercises generate fine-grained process data (commit frequency, time between failing and passing builds, test-to-code ratios) that are difficult to collect in browser-based environments and are not limited to final submissions. Such data could support analyses of how novices actually practice TDD, including whether they write tests first, which was not verifiable in our pilot beyond commit order.

**Limitations**

Several limitations constrain the interpretation of our results. The sample was small (N = 30), drawn from a single course at one institution, and self-selected to the extent that students chose to complete the survey. Without a control group working in a conventional browser-based environment, we cannot attribute the observed motivation gains to the Prof. CI design rather than to maturation, course content, or a general enthusiasm for the topic. Motivation was assessed through self-report, which is subject to social desirability bias, particularly because instructors were involved in administering the survey. We did not evaluate whether increased motivation translated into better tests, as measured by, for example, mutation scores or coverage in later assignments, nor whether the effect persisted after the course ended. Moreover, the approach relies on commercial infrastructure. Dependence on Github's pricing, usage limits and terms of service, as well as questions about student data privacy, may restrict adoption in some institutions and jurisdictions. Finally, the exercise targeted a specific framework with a strong testing culture; Rails conventions make testing comparatively easy to set up, and the transferability to ecosystems with weaker test tooling remains to be shown.

**Future work**

Future studies should use controlled or quasi-experimental designs with larger cohorts, combine self-reports with behavioral repository data, and assess test quality objectively. It would also be valuable to investigate adaptive challenge sequences that respond to the quality of a student's tests, as well as feedback that goes beyond pass/fail, such as automated hints derived from mutation analysis. Extending Prof. CI to other languages and testing frameworks would clarify how general the approach is.

**Conclusion**

Prof. CI demonstrates that CI services and Github workflows can be repurposed as a scalable, automated teaching platform for TDD. In a pilot with 30 undergraduates, the approach was feasible, was well received, and increased students' self-reported motivation to write tests, while giving them practical experience with local editors, issue tracking, version control and CI. Although the evidence is preliminary and the effect on code and test quality remains untested, the results indicate that authentic development infrastructure need not be sacrificed for the sake of scalability in online programming education.

Introduction

Malaria remains one of the most important parasitic diseases worldwide. The World Health Organization estimated roughly 219 million cases and 435,000 deaths in 2017, with about 93% of cases and 94% of deaths occurring in the WHO African Region (World Health Organization, 2018). Despite the substantial gains of the early 2000s, when scaled-up vector control, artemisinin-based combination therapy and improved diagnostics reduced the global burden by around 40% (Bhatt et al., 2015), progress has stalled in several high-burden countries. Malaria is also strongly heterogeneous. Transmission intensity varies over small distances and across seasons and years, shaped by climate, land use, vector ecology, human movement, socioeconomic conditions and the coverage of interventions (Gething et al., 2011; Kabaria et al., 2017). This heterogeneity means that national averages obscure the foci and periods of risk that matter most for control and elimination. The concern is sharper in low and middle-income countries (LMICs), where resources are limited and targeting is essential.

Spatio-temporal modelling has become a central tool for characterising this heterogeneity. By describing how disease risk varies jointly over space and time, such models support mapping of burden, early warning and forecasting of epidemics, identification of hotspots and high-risk periods, and evaluation of interventions (Hay et al., 2009; Pigott et al., 2015). The field has expanded rapidly for several reasons. Georeferenced data are now far more abundant, including national household surveys with GPS coordinates such as the Demographic and Health Surveys and Malaria Indicator Surveys, health facility records from routine information systems such as DHIS2, and the parasite rate databases compiled by the Malaria Atlas Project (Guerra et al., 2007; Gething et al., 2011). Satellite remote sensing now provides rainfall, temperature, vegetation indices and other environmental measures at high temporal and spatial resolution (Hay et al., 2006). At the same time, computational advances have made hierarchical Bayesian geostatistical inference practical on large datasets. Markov chain Monte Carlo, and more recently the integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) with the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) approach, now allow flexible models to be fitted routinely (Rue et al., 2009; Lindgren et al., 2011).

The methods in use are diverse. At the area level, studies typically model counts of cases y_it in district i and time t using Poisson or negative binomial likelihoods, for example

y_it ~ Poisson(E_it θ_it), log θ_it = α + x_itᵀβ + u_i + v_i + γ_t + δ_it,

where E_it is the expected count or population at risk, x_it are covariates, u_i and v_i are spatially structured and unstructured random effects (often with a conditional autoregressive prior; Besag et al., 1991), γ_t is a temporal term (such as a random walk or seasonal harmonic), and δ_it is a space-time interaction (Knorr-Held, 2000). For point-referenced survey data, a geostatistical binomial model is common, with logit(p(s,t)) = x(s,t)ᵀβ + w(s,t), where w is a Gaussian process with Matérn covariance that may be separable or non-separable in space and time (Diggle et al., 1998; Gething et al., 2012). Alongside these, authors have used spatial scan statistics for cluster detection (Kulldorff, 1997), generalised additive models, spatio-temporal autoregressive and distributed-lag models for climate-driven forecasting, machine-learning approaches such as random forests and boosted regression trees, and mechanistic or hybrid models combining transmission dynamics with spatial structure (Smith et al., 2012; Reiner et al., 2015). Each approach rests on different assumptions about stationarity, dependence structure, interaction between space and time, and the relation between covariates and risk. The choice of approach also interacts with the scale of analysis, ranging from microspatial studies at household or village level to continental mapping, and with the quality, completeness and denominators of the underlying data.

The covariates that enter these models are equally varied. Environmental and climatic variables, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, vegetation indices, elevation and hydrology, are used most often because of their biological relevance to vector and parasite development (Craig et al., 1999; Mordecai et al., 2013). Many studies also include socioeconomic indicators, housing quality, urbanisation, population density, access to health care, intervention coverage (insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, treatment) and human mobility, though these tend to be less consistently available and measured, and their inclusion is less standardised. Decisions about lagged effects, spatial resolution matching, collinearity, variable selection and how to handle covariates that are themselves modelled or interpolated are made inconsistently, and often without clear justification. Likewise, the practices used to validate models vary from simple in-sample fit statistics (deviance information criterion, R²) to out-of-sample cross-validation, spatial block validation and prospective forecast evaluation using proper scoring rules (Roberts et al., 2017; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). Where validation does not account for residual spatial and temporal autocorrelation, predictive performance is easily overstated.

Existing reviews have addressed parts of this landscape but not its entirety. Earlier syntheses have focused on the use of geographic information systems and remote sensing in malaria epidemiology (Hay et al., 2006; Eisele et al., 2012), on early warning systems and climate-based forecasting (Thomson et al., 2006; Zinszer et al., 2012), on mapping of parasite prevalence (Hay et al., 2009), or on specific techniques. Few have systematically compared the full set of spatio-temporal approaches, the covariates used and the validation strategies adopted across settings. Consequently, researchers and national malaria control programmes who wish to build a model for a specific purpose, whether burden estimation, forecasting or intervention targeting, have little consolidated guidance on which methods have been applied under which data conditions, which covariates have proven informative, and how models have been assessed. This gap matters particularly in LMICs, where data are sparse, noisy and often reported at aggregated administrative scales, and where methodological choices can directly shape resource allocation. Because the literature is heterogeneous in aims, designs and outcomes, a scoping review is more appropriate than a conventional systematic review with meta-analysis. A scoping approach allows the extent, range and nature of evidence to be mapped, key concepts and gaps to be identified, and a foundation for best-practice recommendations to be laid (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010; Tricco et al., 2018).

The overarching question of this review is: what spatio-temporal modelling approaches have been used to assess the burden of malaria in LMICs within the limits of malaria transmission, and what covariates and validation techniques have accompanied them? Specific objectives are to (i) describe the aims and settings of spatio-temporal malaria modelling studies, including the spatial and temporal scales and the data sources used; (ii) catalogue and classify the statistical and mathematical modelling frameworks applied; (iii) summarise the covariates included and how they were processed; (iv) document the model validation and performance assessment procedures; and (v) identify methodological gaps and derive recommendations to guide future modelling decisions.

This review makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured, comprehensive synthesis of spatio-temporal malaria modelling over five decades (1968–2018), including grey literature that is often missed by conventional searches. Second, it links modelling choices to data characteristics, spatial scale and purpose, enabling a more transparent approach to method selection. Third, it highlights under-used methods, weaknesses in validation and reporting, and priority areas for research, supporting more rigorous and reproducible modelling in settings where it is most needed. The review follows the PRISMA-P reporting guidance (Moher et al., 2015) and is registered in PROSPERO (CRD42017076427).

Methods and Analysis

Study design and reporting framework

This scoping review follows the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), as refined by Levac et al. (2010) and the Joanna Briggs Institute (Peters et al., 2015). The protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement (Moher et al., 2015; Shamseer et al., 2015), and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42017076427) before screening began. The final review will be reported using PRISMA guidance, including a flow diagram of study selection. A scoping design was chosen because the aim is to map the range of spatio-temporal approaches, covariates and validation practices, not to pool effect estimates. The review proceeds through five stages: (1) identifying the research question; (2) identifying relevant studies; (3) selecting studies; (4) charting the data; and (5) collating, summarising and reporting the results.

Research question and eligibility criteria

The review question is: what spatio-temporal modelling approaches, covariates and validation techniques have been used to assess the burden of malaria in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) within the limits of malaria transmission? Eligibility was structured using the Population–Concept–Context framework. The population comprises human malaria cases, infection prevalence, incidence or mortality, at any spatial scale from household to continental. The concept is the application of a statistical, mathematical or geostatistical model that explicitly incorporates both spatial and temporal dimensions, for example Bayesian hierarchical models, spatio-temporal geostatistical models, space–time scan statistics, generalised additive or autoregressive models with spatial structure, and mechanistic models with spatial components. The context is any LMIC, as defined by the World Bank income classification, lying within the spatial limits of malaria transmission (Gething et al., 2011; Guerra et al., 2008). Studies were included if published between January 1968 and April 2018, in any language for which translation was feasible, and as primary research, methodological papers, theses or technical reports. Studies were excluded if they were purely spatial or purely temporal with no joint modelling, if they were conducted in high-income or non-endemic settings, if they considered only vector distribution or entomological outcomes without human burden, or if they were commentaries, editorials or narrative reviews without original modelling. Reference lists of excluded reviews were hand-searched for eligible primary studies.

Search strategy

A comprehensive search will be conducted of PubMed, Web of Science, JSTOR, Cochrane CENTRAL via Wiley, Academic Search Complete, MasterFILE Premier, CINAHL and MEDLINE via EBSCOhost, and Google Scholar. The search strategy was developed with an information specialist and combines controlled vocabulary (e.g. MeSH) with free-text terms in three concept blocks joined by the Boolean operator AND: (i) malaria ("malaria" OR "Plasmodium" OR "falciparum" OR "vivax"); (ii) spatio-temporal methods ("spatio-temporal" OR "spatiotemporal" OR "space-time" OR "geostatistic*" OR "Bayesian hierarchical" OR "disease mapping" OR "geographic information system*" OR "remote sensing" OR "kriging" OR "CAR model" OR "INLA"); and (iii) burden or outcome terms ("prevalence" OR "incidence" OR "burden" OR "transmission" OR "mortality" OR "risk"). Terms within each block are joined by OR. A country-level filter listing LMICs, adapted from the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care group filter (Cochrane EPOC, 2017), will be used to improve specificity. The search will be piloted in PubMed, peer-reviewed using the PRESS checklist (McGowan et al., 2016), and adapted to the syntax of each database. Because Google Scholar returns very large numbers of records ranked by relevance, the first 200 hits for each search string will be screened (Haddaway et al., 2015).

Grey literature will be sought through OpenGrey, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, the World Health Organization Global Malaria Programme repository, the Malaria Atlas Project, the MEASURE DHS and Malaria Indicator Survey publications, conference proceedings of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene and the Multilateral Initiative on Malaria, and institutional repositories of African universities. Experts in malaria spatial epidemiology will be contacted to identify unpublished work.

Study selection

All records will be exported to EndNote, where duplicates will be removed, and then imported into Rayyan (Ouzzani et al., 2016) for screening. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, then abstracts, then full texts against the eligibility criteria. Before formal screening, a calibration exercise on a random sample of 50 records will be undertaken to refine the criteria and ensure consistent interpretation. Inter-rater agreement at each stage will be quantified using Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960):

κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e),

where p_o is the observed proportion of agreement and p_e is the agreement expected by chance. A kappa of at least 0.61 will be considered substantial agreement (Landis and Koch, 1977). Disagreements will be resolved by discussion, and where consensus cannot be reached, by a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage will be recorded and reported in the PRISMA flow diagram.

Data charting

A standardised data charting form will be piloted on ten studies and iteratively refined by the review team. Two reviewers will independently chart data, with a third verifying a 10% random sample. Extracted variables will include: bibliographic details; country and region; spatial scale and unit of analysis (point-referenced, village, district, national, continental); study period and temporal resolution; data source (routine surveillance, household surveys, health facility records, cohort or sentinel data); malaria outcome (parasite prevalence, clinical incidence, mortality, parasite species); study aim (mapping, forecasting, early warning, risk factor identification, intervention evaluation, cluster detection); modelling framework (frequentist or Bayesian; geostatistical, areal/lattice, or mechanistic); specification of spatial and temporal random effects (e.g. Gaussian process, conditional autoregressive, random walk, autoregressive AR(1), harmonic seasonal terms); inference and computational tools (MCMC, INLA, SPDE, software); treatment of spatial and temporal autocorrelation, zero inflation, overdispersion and non-stationarity; covariates (climatic, environmental, demographic, socioeconomic, intervention coverage, health system and access, and their spatial and temporal resolution and lags); and model validation and performance assessment techniques (e.g. cross-validation, hold-out data, mean absolute error, root mean square error, correlation, area under the curve, deviance information criterion, posterior predictive checks). To illustrate the model classes anticipated, a typical Bayesian space–time formulation for count data is

Y_it ~ Poisson(E_it θ_it), log θ_it = α + x_itᵀβ + u_i + v_i + γ_t + δ_it,

where u_i is a spatially structured effect, v_i an unstructured effect, γ_t a temporal effect and δ_it a space–time interaction (Knorr-Held, 2000). Geostatistical alternatives replace u_i with a latent Gaussian field S(s,t) with Matérn covariance (Diggle and Giorgi, 2019). Authors will be contacted where key information is missing.

Quality appraisal

Consistent with scoping review guidance, formal risk-of-bias assessment is not required and will not be used to exclude studies (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005). However, to inform best-practice recommendations, the reporting transparency of each study will be descriptively appraised, including whether data sources, model specification, priors, convergence diagnostics and validation procedures were stated, and whether uncertainty was quantified and mapped.

Synthesis and analysis

Charted data will be summarised descriptively, using frequencies and proportions, to show the distribution of studies by year, geographic region, spatial scale, outcome and model class. A qualitative thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) will be used to group and evaluate studies around four themes: aims, spatio-temporal methodology, covariates employed and model validation techniques. Coding will be conducted inductively in NVivo by two reviewers, with themes developed through iterative discussion. Studies will further be cross-tabulated by method and aim, and by covariate class and spatial scale, to identify methodological trends, gaps and areas of consensus. Findings will be synthesised into recommendations for model choice, covariate selection and validation, which will be explicitly linked to the characteristics of the data and the intended use of the model.

Patient and public involvement and ethics

Patients and the public were not involved in the design of this review. Because the review uses only published and publicly available data, ethical approval is not required. Results will be disseminated through a peer-reviewed publication and presentations at malaria and spatial epidemiology conferences.

# Results

## Study selection

The search covered January 1968 to April 2018 and identified 6,214 records: 5,873 from the electronic databases and 341 from grey literature sources (unpublished reports, conference proceedings and dissertations). After removing 1,982 duplicates, 4,232 records were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 3,801 were excluded, leaving 431 articles for full-text review. A further 244 were excluded at this stage: 109 had no explicit spatio-temporal component, 52 were set outside malaria-endemic low- and middle-income settings or outside the transmission limits (Guerra et al., 2008), 48 had no malaria burden outcome, and 35 gave insufficient methodological detail (mostly conference abstracts). In total, 187 studies met the inclusion criteria and entered the thematic synthesis. Inter-reviewer agreement was substantial to almost perfect at both stages (Cohen's κ = 0.82 for title and abstract screening; κ = 0.87 for full-text review). Disagreements were resolved by consensus without a third reviewer.

## Characteristics of included studies

The earliest eligible study was published in 1999, in the period when geostatistical methods were first applied to malaria survey data (Kleinschmidt et al., 2000; Diggle et al., 2002). Publication volume rose steeply thereafter. Twelve studies (6.4%) appeared before 2005, 41 (21.9%) between 2005 and 2010, and 134 (71.7%) between 2011 and April 2018.

Most studies were from sub-Saharan Africa (128; 68.4%), followed by Asia (38; 20.3%) and the Americas (15; 8.0%). Six studies (3.2%) were multi-regional or global. Kenya (n = 21), Tanzania (n = 17), Uganda (n = 14), Mali (n = 11) and Mozambique (n = 10) were the most frequently studied African countries. Within Asia, Thailand, India and Indonesia predominated, and in the Americas, Brazil, Colombia and Peru.

By spatial scale, 71 studies (38.0%) worked at the subnational or district level and 62 (33.2%) at the national level. Thirty-one (16.6%) worked at the village or household level, and 23 (12.3%) were continental or multi-country analyses such as the Malaria Atlas Project (Hay et al., 2009; Gething et al., 2011; Bhatt et al., 2015). Outcomes were mainly clinical incidence or case counts (82; 43.9%) and parasite prevalence (74; 39.6%). Fewer studies modelled entomological indices such as vector density or entomological inoculation rate (12; 6.4%), malaria mortality (9; 4.8%), or other outcomes such as anaemia or treatment-seeking (10; 5.3%).

Data came from three main sources. Routine health management information systems or passive surveillance supplied 78 studies (41.7%). National household surveys such as the Malaria Indicator Surveys, Demographic and Health Surveys and MICS supplied 69 (36.9%). Active surveillance, cohort or purpose-designed cross-sectional surveys supplied 24 (12.8%). The remaining 16 (8.6%) used other sources or combined data.

## Study aims

The principal aim of 98 studies (52.4%) was disease mapping or risk estimation, including prediction at unsampled locations. Another 46 (24.6%) examined environmental, climatic or socioeconomic determinants of malaria, 24 (12.8%) developed forecasting or early-warning systems (for example, Thomson et al., 2006), and 19 (10.2%) evaluated interventions such as insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying or mass drug administration.

## Spatio-temporal modelling approaches

Table-level synthesis showed considerable methodological heterogeneity (see Figure 2). Bayesian hierarchical models were the most common (63 studies; 33.7%). Most of these were geostatistical models with a Gaussian random field of the form

*y*(*s*,*t*) | *p*(*s*,*t*) ~ Binomial(*n*(*s*,*t*), *p*(*s*,*t*)),

logit *p*(*s*,*t*) = **x**(*s*,*t*)ᵀ**β** + *S*(*s*) + *u*(*t*) + *ε*(*s*,*t*),

where *S*(*s*) is a spatially structured Gaussian process, typically with a Matérn covariance, *u*(*t*) is a temporal effect, and *ε* is an unstructured error term (Diggle et al., 2002; Gosoniu et al., 2006). Of these 63 studies, 41 used Markov chain Monte Carlo estimation and 22 used integrated nested Laplace approximation with the stochastic partial differential equation approach (Rue et al., 2009; Lindgren et al., 2011). The latter appeared only after 2012. The share of Bayesian approaches rose from 18.2% of studies published before 2011 to 41.0% of those published from 2011 onwards.

Frequentist regression approaches, including generalised linear and additive models with spatial autocorrelation terms, simultaneous or conditional autoregressive structures, or generalised estimating equations, were used in 39 studies (20.9%). Spatial scan statistics and other cluster detection methods featured in 25 studies (13.4%), usually to identify hotspots (Kulldorff, 1997; Bejon et al., 2010). Time-series methods, such as seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average models and wavelet analyses, were used in 21 studies (11.2%), almost all in forecasting. Machine-learning or ensemble approaches, such as boosted regression trees and random forests, were applied in 14 (7.5%), and mechanistic or mathematical transmission models coupled to spatial data in 11 (5.9%). The remaining 14 (7.5%) used other or hybrid techniques.

Temporal structure was treated in several ways. Fifty-eight studies (31.0%) analysed discrete time slices or aggregated periods separately, 47 (25.1%) included first-order autoregressive or random-walk temporal effects, and 31 (16.6%) used harmonic or other seasonal terms. A full space–time interaction term was fitted in 29 studies (15.5%). Only 12 studies (6.4%) allowed non-stationary spatial covariance, and 32 studies (17.1%) were purely spatial in their estimation despite using multi-year data.

## Covariates

Environmental and climatic covariates were used far more often than socioeconomic or health-system covariates (Figure 3). Rainfall was used in 141 studies (75.4%), temperature in 128 (68.4%), and vegetation indices (NDVI or EVI) in 112 (59.9%). Elevation (83; 44.4%), humidity (54; 28.9%), distance to water bodies (52; 27.8%) and land cover (47; 25.1%) were also common, as were climate-driver indices such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (9; 4.8%). Most remotely sensed data came from MODIS, TRMM or WorldClim products.

Among socioeconomic and demographic variables, intervention coverage (net ownership or use, indoor residual spraying) appeared in 74 studies (39.6%), household wealth indices in 69 (36.9%), population density in 58 (31.0%), urban–rural classification in 41 (21.9%), and distance to health facilities in 27 (14.4%). Of the 141 studies using rainfall, 68 (48.2%) included lagged effects, typically of one to three months. Temperature lags were less commonly examined (41 of 128; 32.0%). Covariate selection was usually based on stepwise or univariable screening (96 studies; 51.3%), with fewer using Bayesian variable selection or penalised regression (17; 9.1%).

## Model validation and reporting

Only 97 studies (51.9%) reported any form of validation, and 90 (48.1%) reported none beyond model fit. Information criteria (AIC, BIC or DIC) were used for model comparison in 108 studies (57.8%). Among those validating predictive performance, cross-validation was used in 52, hold-out datasets in 31, and external independent data in 14. Predictive accuracy was summarised by mean absolute or root mean squared error (49 studies), correlation between observed and predicted values (38), area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (17) and coverage of prediction or credible intervals (12). Residual spatial autocorrelation was checked in 45 studies (24.1%). Uncertainty in predictions was mapped or reported in 71 studies (38.0%), most often among Bayesian analyses (58 of 63; 92.1%). Fewer than one in five studies (34; 18.2%) made data or code available.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation and anticipated contribution**

Spatio-temporal modelling has become central to how malaria burden is quantified, forecast and targeted in low and middle-income countries (LMICs). Several developments drive this: wider availability of georeferenced survey and surveillance data, global malaria mapping initiatives (Hay et al., 2009; Bhatt et al., 2015), and computational advances that make hierarchical Bayesian inference tractable for large datasets (Rue et al., 2009; Lindgren et al., 2011). Yet the methodological literature has grown without a consolidated account of which approaches are used, under what data conditions, with which covariates, and how their predictive performance is judged. This scoping review addresses that gap. It is not a meta-analysis of effect sizes. Its purpose is to chart the breadth of practice and to identify where practice is consistent, where it is idiosyncratic, and where it is deficient.

Three themes are expected to structure the interpretation of the findings. The first concerns model class. Malaria models in LMICs span a continuum from regression with residual spatial correlation, through geostatistical models with Gaussian random fields (Diggle et al., 1998; Gething et al., 2011), to areal conditional autoregressive formulations (Besag et al., 1991) and mechanistic or hybrid models. A generic formulation covers many of these:

g(μ_it) = β₀ + **x**ᵀ_it **β** + S(s_i) + T(t) + ψ(s_i, t) + ε_it,

where μ_it is expected prevalence or incidence at location i and time t, **x**_it is a vector of covariates, S is a spatially structured effect, T is a temporal trend or seasonal term, ψ is a space–time interaction, and ε is unstructured error. The review will interpret how studies parameterise each component. In particular, it will examine whether the interaction term is specified at all, since omitting it implicitly assumes that spatial patterns are temporally stable, an assumption that sits uneasily with malaria's seasonality, epidemic potential and response to intervention scale-up (Noor et al., 2014).

The second theme concerns covariates. Climatic and environmental predictors such as temperature, rainfall, humidity and vegetation indices are expected to dominate, reflecting their biological basis in vector and parasite development (Craig et al., 1999; Mordecai et al., 2013) and their free availability from remote sensing. The interpretive question is whether this dominance reflects scientific rationale or data convenience. Socioeconomic factors, housing, urbanisation, human movement and intervention coverage (insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, case management) are comparatively harder to obtain at fine resolution, yet they often determine local transmission intensity and its change over time (Bhatt et al., 2015; Tatem et al., 2017). If the included studies underuse these variables, the policy relevance of resulting maps for programme evaluation will be limited. Covariate lag structures, scale mismatches between predictor and outcome, and collinearity handling are further features that influence inferential credibility, and the review will document how often they are addressed.

The third theme concerns validation. Predictive claims depend on out-of-sample assessment, and spatially autocorrelated data make random hold-out or naive cross-validation optimistic (Roberts et al., 2017). The review will therefore catalogue whether studies use spatial or temporal blocking, independent datasets, or only in-sample fit criteria such as DIC or AIC, and whether predictive uncertainty is reported and calibrated. Where validation is absent or weak, maps used for resource allocation may convey spurious precision.

**Implications for practice and policy**

The synthesis is intended to support modelling decisions in settings with limited data and analytic capacity. Practical guidance is expected to cover matching model complexity to data type (cross-sectional prevalence surveys, routine health facility counts, entomological data), the circumstances in which geostatistical versus areal approaches are preferable, and the minimum reporting needed for reproducibility. Routine surveillance data, increasingly digitised through platforms such as DHIS2, are subject to reporting incompleteness, variable care-seeking and changing diagnostic practices (Alegana et al., 2013), and models that ignore these issues may misattribute artefacts to epidemiology. A clear map of how researchers handle such problems will help national malaria programmes and collaborating modellers prioritise methodological safeguards. As countries move toward subnational stratification and elimination, models that deliver fine-scale, uncertainty-aware estimates of transmission and its temporal change are essential to target limited interventions (Cairns et al., 2012). Identifying gaps, for example few applications to low-transmission or pre-elimination settings, to vivax malaria, or to forecasting with operational lead times, will also help set a research agenda.

**Strengths and limitations**

The review has several strengths. The protocol was prospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD42017076427) and follows PRISMA-P reporting standards (Moher et al., 2015), with a scoping framework (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010) suited to a heterogeneous methodological literature. The search spans multiple biomedical and multidisciplinary databases and grey literature, which is important because much spatial modelling appears in geography, statistics and environmental science outlets that biomedical indices cover poorly. Independent duplicate screening reduces selection bias, and thematic extraction around aims, methods, covariates and validation yields a structured, comparable description.

Limitations should be acknowledged. First, restricting the search to January 1968–April 2018 means that more recent advances, including machine learning, deep learning and the integration of mobile phone and satellite-derived human mobility data, will be under-represented; the findings should be read as a snapshot of practice up to that date. Second, limiting inclusion to LMICs within malaria transmission limits, and to English-language sources if applied, may omit relevant work and introduce language and publication bias. Third, scoping reviews do not formally appraise study quality or risk of bias; descriptive frequency of a method says nothing about its adequacy, and popularity of an approach may reflect software availability or disciplinary habit rather than performance. Fourth, reporting heterogeneity is likely to constrain extraction, because model specifications, priors, validation procedures and covariate processing are often incompletely described, and qualitative thematic grouping involves subjective judgements, mitigated but not eliminated by dual review. Fifth, because outcomes (prevalence, incidence, mortality, vector density) and scales differ, direct comparison of predictive accuracy across studies will not be possible, and recommendations will necessarily be conditional and based on convergent practice rather than head-to-head evidence. Finally, a focus on published work may over-represent settings with high research capacity and good data, such as East Africa, and under-represent others, so the generalisability of any recommendations across regions should be judged cautiously.

**Conclusion**

Spatio-temporal modelling offers powerful means of characterising malaria burden and informing control and elimination in LMICs, but its value depends on appropriate model structure, relevant and well-processed covariates, honest accounting for data limitations, and rigorous validation. By systematically mapping the approaches, covariates and validation strategies used to date, this scoping review will provide a basis for more consistent, transparent and policy-relevant modelling. It will also highlight methodological gaps, including temporal dynamics, uncertainty quantification, low-transmission settings and out-of-sample evaluation, that future studies and funders should prioritise. Dissemination through peer-reviewed publication and conferences in malaria and spatial epidemiology will help translate these findings to modellers and programme planners.

1. Introduction

Continuous deployment (CD) is a software engineering practice in which code changes are automatically built, tested, and released to end users through an automated deployment pipeline (Humble and Farley, 2010). Organizations adopt CD to shorten release cycles, obtain faster customer feedback, and reduce the manual effort of releasing software. Industry surveys associate frequent, automated deployment with better organizational performance and faster recovery from failures (Forsgren et al., 2018). A central enabler of CD is infrastructure as code (IaC), the practice of provisioning and configuring computing infrastructure through machine-readable scripts rather than manual procedures (Humble and Farley, 2010; Rahman et al., 2019a). Tools such as Puppet, Chef, and Ansible let practitioners specify the desired state of servers, services, and dependencies in source code. That code can then be version-controlled, reviewed, tested, and executed repeatedly and consistently across environments.

Treating infrastructure as software also exposes it to the defects that affect any other software artifact. A defect in an IaC script can propagate to every machine on which the script is executed, and so can compromise the reliability of the whole deployment pipeline. Misconfigured infrastructure has been implicated in widely reported service disruptions, including a 2017 outage of Amazon's Simple Storage Service that followed an erroneous operational command and affected a large number of dependent websites and services (Amazon Web Services, 2017). Prior empirical work shows that such defects are not rare. Jiang and Adams (2015) observed that infrastructure code in open source projects co-evolves with, and is often as change-prone as, production code. Rahman and Williams (2018) found that defect-related commits constitute a substantial share of the commits to IaC scripts in several open source repositories. Defective IaC scripts can cause frequent deployment failures and consume considerable developer effort, which undermines the benefits that motivate CD in the first place.

Researchers and practitioners have begun to study the quality of IaC along several lines. A systematic mapping study found that research on IaC remains sparse relative to its adoption in industry, and that few studies have examined the relationship between source code characteristics and script quality (Rahman et al., 2019a). Sharma et al. (2016) catalogued configuration smells in Puppet code and showed that they can be detected with static analysis, and Schwarz et al. (2018) extended this line of work to Chef. Hanappi et al. (2016) and Hummer et al. (2013) proposed approaches for testing the idempotence and convergence of configuration scripts. These studies are valuable, but they mostly rely on smells and rules defined a priori by researchers or tool builders. They do not establish which properties of IaC source code are actually associated with defects observed in practice. Without empirical evidence of this kind, practitioners lack data-driven guidance on where to focus code review and testing, and researchers lack a principled basis for building automated defect prediction models for IaC.
