Its criteria are ethical and practical, including judgment, perceptiveness, and responsibility. Scientific measurement may inform it but cannot exhaust it.

*Patient preferences* can be defined as expressions of values and personal ends. Their authority derives from respect for persons and informed consent. They are legitimate whether or not they improve outcomes.

On this account, research tells clinicians what is likely to work on average, expertise determines what is fitting in this case, and patient values determine what counts as a good outcome. The three components then answer different questions (empirical, practical, and normative), and none reduces to another. This differentiation is what a tripartite model requires and what the current EBPP definition does not deliver.

Discussion and Conclusion

This paper has argued that evidence-based practice in psychology (EBPP) is tripartite in name but not in structure. The American Psychological Association's definition (APA Presidential Task Force on Evidence-Based Practice, 2006) names three components: the best available research, clinical expertise, and patient characteristics, culture, and preferences. In the literature that operationalises the definition, however, the second and third components are routinely redescribed in scientific terms. Expertise becomes the application of empirically supported principles, assessment skills that can be validated, or competencies that can be trained and measured. Patient preferences become moderators of treatment outcome, variables to be entered into trials and meta-analyses (Norcross et al., 2006; Spring, 2007). When all three components are defined by science, they are no longer independent sources of authority. EBPP then reduces to one component with two sub-parts.

The conflation has several plausible sources. One is the inheritance from evidence-based medicine. Sackett and colleagues (1996) presented clinical expertise and patient values as essential companions to external evidence. Yet the movement's methodological apparatus, including evidence hierarchies, systematic reviews, and appraisal tools, addressed only the evidential component. The remaining two were left as slogans without epistemologies of their own (Tonelli, 2006; Greenhalgh et al., 2014). A second source is professional. Psychology's claim to legitimacy rests on being a science-based profession, so any component that cannot be expressed in scientific terms risks appearing arbitrary or unaccountable. A third is the regulatory and economic setting. Payers, guideline developers, and training bodies need auditable standards, and only what can be measured can be audited. Together these pressures favour definitions of expertise and preference that are operational, quantifiable, and, ultimately, scientific.

Defining the other two components extra-scientifically does not make them unscientific or anti-scientific. It means that their standards of adequacy are not exhausted by those of empirical research. Clinical expertise includes what Aristotle called phronesis, practical wisdom in particular cases, as well as the tacit, perceptual, and relational knowledge described by Polanyi (1966) and Schön (1983). It also includes the interpretive judgement through which clinicians decide whether general findings bear on this person in this situation (Montgomery, 2006). Cartwright and Hardie (2012) show that evidence of efficacy in a study population does not by itself license the claim that an intervention will work for a given individual. Bridging that gap requires local causal knowledge and judgement that no trial supplies. Patient preferences, in turn, are not merely predictors of dropout or outcome. They express what a person values, what risks they will tolerate, and what kind of life they are trying to build. This is a normative matter, and the accounts of shared decision-making (Charles et al., 1997; Elwyn et al., 2012) and values-based practice (Fulford, 2004) both treat it as such. Studying preferences as moderators is useful, but it cannot replace the patient's authority to decide among options that research cannot rank.

This reading has an interpretive payoff. Several long-standing disputes in the field, such as those over manualisation, the weight given to common factors, and the status of "empirically supported treatments," may be partly disputes over which component of EBPP is dominant (Messer, 2004; Wampold & Imel, 2015; Westen et al., 2004). If the three components are not commensurable on one scale, then appeals to "the evidence" cannot settle such disputes. A clinician who departs from a guideline because of a patient's considered refusal is not necessarily less evidence-based. She may be exercising a legitimate component of the model that science cannot overrule.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the argument is conceptual and relies on the APA's definition and a selective reading of the literature. I have not systematically surveyed how training programmes, guidelines, or practitioners actually operationalise the three components, and the degree of scientocentrism in practice may differ from that in the definitional literature. Empirical work, such as content analyses of guideline documents or qualitative studies of clinical decision-making, could test the claim. Second, "extra-scientific" is a contested term. Some philosophers of science hold that values and judgement are already embedded in scientific practice (Upshur et al., 2001), which would blur the boundary on which my argument relies. My claim is therefore modest: the authority of expertise and preference does not derive from, and cannot be exhausted by, the methods of empirical research. Third, I have not offered a full positive epistemology of clinical expertise or patient values. I have only indicated where such accounts might be found, in practical philosophy, phenomenology, and bioethics. Fourth, there is a risk of misuse. Critics of evidence-based approaches have sometimes invoked "expertise" or "preference" to justify practices unsupported by any evidence (Lilienfeld et al., 2013). Recognising independent components does not license ignoring research. It requires that the components be balanced, and that departures from the evidence be reasoned and transparent.

The implications are practical as well as theoretical. For training, programmes should teach clinical judgement and the elicitation of values as disciplined competencies with their own literatures, not as add-ons to empirical content. Reflective practice, case-based reasoning, ethics, and the study of narrative could be given the standing now reserved for methodology and statistics. For guideline development, panels should state explicitly where recommendations rest on research and where they rest on value judgements, and should present options so that patient choice is a real decision point rather than a residual category (Upshur, 2002). For research, outcome studies should treat preferences as more than covariates, for example by examining how deliberation about values shapes the course of therapy. For professional regulation, accountability could be extended beyond treatment fidelity to the quality of reasoning and the documentation of shared decisions.

In conclusion, EBPP in its current form is better described as a science-centred model with two scientised satellites than as a tripartite one. This is not an argument against research evidence, which remains indispensable to ethical practice. It is an argument that a model claiming to integrate three sources of authority must let each be defined on its own terms. Restoring that independence would make EBPP more faithful to its stated ideal and more candid about the judgements and values that inevitably enter psychological care. It would also give clinicians and patients a clearer account of why, in a given case, they may rightly weigh the evidence against what they know and what matters.

Introduction

The credibility of biomedical research rests on the integrity of the data from which its conclusions are drawn. Clinical trials and large observational studies now generate heterogeneous data at unprecedented scale, including imaging, genomics, wearable-sensor streams, and electronic health record extracts. These data pass through many hands and systems between acquisition and publication. Each transfer, transformation, and analysis step is an opportunity for error, undocumented modification, or, in rare cases, deliberate misconduct. Concerns about reproducibility have intensified in recent years: large-scale replication efforts have shown that a substantial fraction of published findings cannot be reproduced (Open Science Collaboration, 2015), and surveys of researchers indicate that most have failed to reproduce another scientist's experiments (Baker, 2016). Although many factors contribute, incomplete provenance and uncertainty about whether analyzed data match the data originally collected are persistent and addressable contributors.

Regulators and funders have responded with explicit expectations for data governance. Good Clinical Practice guidance (ICH E6) and the FDA's 21 CFR Part 11 require that electronic records be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, and accurate, the principles summarized by the acronym ALCOA, and that audit trails record changes to data. The FAIR principles similarly emphasize that data should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, with rich provenance (Wilkinson et al., 2016). In practice, however, audit trails are typically implemented within individual software systems under the control of a single administrator or institution. A database administrator with sufficient privileges can alter both a record and its log, and external parties such as journal reviewers, regulators, or collaborating sites have little means of independently verifying that a dataset is unchanged since collection. Trust is therefore placed in institutions and procedures rather than in verifiable evidence. This weakness is magnified in multi-site studies, where data are aggregated from independent organizations with differing infrastructure and incentives.

Blockchain technology offers a plausible mechanism for strengthening this evidentiary chain. A blockchain is an append-only, replicated ledger in which records are grouped into blocks, each cryptographically linked to its predecessor through a hash, so that retroactive modification of any entry invalidates all subsequent blocks unless a majority of participants collude (Nakamoto, 2008). Because cryptographic hash functions such as SHA-256 are deterministic, collision-resistant, and sensitive to any change in input, a short digest recorded on a ledger can serve as a compact, tamper-evident fingerprint of an arbitrarily large file. Verification then reduces to recomputing the digest of a data asset and comparing it with the immutable record: for a file *d* and stored value *h*, the asset is considered authentic if H(*d*) = *h*. Smart-contract platforms such as Ethereum extend this model by enabling programmable logic and widely replicated, publicly auditable state (Wood, 2014).

Healthcare and biomedical research have been identified as promising application domains. Reviews describe uses including electronic health record sharing, consent management, supply chain tracking, and clinical trial management (Azaria et al., 2016; Kuo et al., 2017; Mettler, 2016). Several proposals address clinical trial integrity specifically. Benchoufi and colleagues demonstrated a blockchain-based approach to timestamping informed consent (Benchoufi et al., 2017), and Nugent and colleagues showed that smart contracts could help prevent outcome switching and selective reporting by committing protocols to a ledger prior to data collection (Nugent et al., 2016). Other work has explored blockchain-based audit logging and data-sharing frameworks for medical records and trial data (Zhang et al., 2018; Omar et al., 2019). Collectively these studies suggest that blockchain can supply independent verification, but most are conceptual designs, small proofs of concept, or focused on a single trial stage such as consent or registration.

Several gaps limit the translation of these ideas to large research environments. First, much of the literature concentrates on protocol registration or consent rather than on the data themselves as they move through acquisition and analysis pipelines. Data integrity in practice depends on continuous capture of hashes as files are generated, ingested, and transformed, ideally without burdening investigators. Second, there is a tension between public and private ledgers. Public networks such as Ethereum provide strong decentralization and allow anyone to validate a claim without trusting the originating institution, but transaction fees, limited throughput, and public exposure of metadata make them impractical for logging every event in a high-volume research data flow. Private, permissioned chains offer low cost, high throughput, and access control compatible with privacy regulations such as HIPAA and the GDPR, but their trust guarantees are weaker, since a small consortium or single organization could in principle rewrite the ledger. Third, existing proposals seldom document integration with operational data science infrastructure, including data ingestion tools, containerized analysis environments, and administrative interfaces that research staff can use. Finally, provenance for downstream analysis, in which derived datasets and results are linked to their source data and the transformations applied, is rarely captured alongside the original acquisition record, although it is essential for reproducing and auditing reported findings (Moreau et al., 2008).

These gaps motivate the question addressed in this work: can a blockchain-based architecture be integrated into the data acquisition and analysis pipeline of a large biomedical research center to provide scalable, low-cost, and publicly verifiable assurance of data integrity and provenance? We hypothesized that a hybrid design, combining a private permissioned blockchain for high-volume logging with periodic anchoring of its state to a public blockchain, could retain the throughput, cost, and confidentiality advantages of private ledgers while inheriting the tamper resistance and independent verifiability of a public network. Anchoring approaches of this kind have been used for timestamping and notarization in other settings, but their application to research data governance within an operational data science platform has not been well described.

In this paper we present TrialChain, a platform designed to meet this need. The contributions of this work are as follows. (1) We describe a hybrid architecture in which a private MultiChain blockchain records cryptographic hashes of research data assets and the events that modify them, and the state of this chain is periodically synchronized to the public Ethereum network to enable external validation. (2) We detail integration with an existing institutional data science platform, using Apache NiFi to hash and log data automatically during acquisition so that integrity records are generated as a by-product of routine data flow rather than as a separate manual task. (3) We implement a microservice architecture deployed with Docker and an administrative web application written in Python for managing the platform, together with an API that allows data assets and analysis results to be validated rapidly on demand. (4) We extend logging beyond original data to downstream modifications and analysis steps, thereby documenting provenance across the research lifecycle. Together, these elements provide a practical data governance solution for auditing the acquisition and analysis of biomedical research data and for giving collaborators, reviewers, and regulators cryptographic evidence of data authenticity.

Methods

System Overview and Design Requirements

TrialChain was developed at a large biomedical research center to provide tamper-evident provenance for data acquired in clinical and translational studies. Requirements were gathered through consultation with data managers, biostatisticians, and compliance staff, and were organized around the ALCOA+ principles of data integrity (attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, and complete) (Woodley et al., 2018). The platform had to (i) record a cryptographic fingerprint of each data asset at the time of acquisition, (ii) record derived assets and the transformations that produced them, (iii) permit independent verification by parties without access to the internal network, (iv) avoid storing protected health information (PHI) on any ledger, and (v) operate at transaction volumes consistent with high-throughput imaging, genomic, and electronic data capture workflows at low marginal cost.

A hybrid architecture was selected. A permissioned private blockchain handles high-frequency logging, while periodic anchoring to the public Ethereum network provides externally verifiable timestamps and immutability (Nakamoto, 2008; Wood, 2014). This design follows earlier proposals for anchoring private ledgers to public chains to inherit their security properties (Gipp et al., 2015).

Private Blockchain Infrastructure

The private ledger was implemented with MultiChain (Greenspan, 2015), chosen for its permission management, native data streams, and absence of per-transaction fees. Three validating nodes were deployed on separate virtual machines in different failure domains within the institutional data center. Consensus used MultiChain's round-robin mining with a target block time of 15 seconds and a mining diversity parameter set to two-thirds of validators, so that a single compromised node could not unilaterally append consecutive blocks. Connect, send, receive, create, and admin permissions were assigned by role; ingestion services held write permissions only to specific streams, while auditors held read-only permissions.

Three streams were created: assets, which stores records of original data; transformations, which stores records of derived data and analysis steps; and anchors, which stores receipts of public-chain synchronizations. Each stream entry was a JSON document containing no PHI. Fields included a study identifier (pseudonymized), asset type, SHA-256 digest, file size, acquisition timestamp, the identity of the submitting service account, a schema version, and, for derived assets, the digests of all parent assets, a digest of the executed code or workflow definition, and a parameter hash.

Microservice Architecture and Administrative Application

All components were containerized with Docker and orchestrated with Docker Compose in development and with a container orchestration cluster in production. Services comprised the MultiChain nodes, a ledger gateway exposing a REST API, a hashing and registration service, an anchoring service, a PostgreSQL database for operational metadata and indexing, and an administrative web application. The administrative application was written in Python using the Flask framework and provided functions for user and role management, stream configuration, study registration, review of ledger entries, and initiation of verification reports. Authentication used institutional single sign-on via OpenID Connect, and all administrative actions were themselves logged to the ledger. The REST API was documented with the OpenAPI specification and secured with token-based authorization and TLS.

Integration with the Data Science Platform

TrialChain was integrated with an existing institutional data science platform that ingests data from electronic data capture systems, imaging archives, laboratory instruments, and sequencing cores. Data movement is orchestrated by Apache NiFi, and we added custom NiFi processors that intercept each flowfile at acquisition. For each file, the processor computed a SHA-256 digest (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2015) in streaming mode, assembled the metadata record, and submitted it to the ledger gateway. For structured data such as tabular exports, records were canonicalized before hashing (sorted keys, normalized whitespace and encoding, and fixed numeric formatting) so that semantically identical content produced identical digests. For multi-file assets such as imaging studies, a Merkle tree was constructed over the constituent file digests and only the root was registered (Merkle, 1988). Given leaf digests h_1,…,h_n, parent nodes were computed as

h_parent = H(h_left ‖ h_right),

where H is SHA-256 and ‖ denotes concatenation; when a level contained an odd number of nodes the last digest was duplicated. This allowed inclusion of any individual file to be proven with a logarithmic-size path.

Downstream analyses executed on the platform, including preprocessing pipelines and statistical scripts run in containerized notebooks and workflow engines, called the same API to register outputs. Each derived-asset record referenced its parents, forming a directed acyclic provenance graph that is consistent with the W3C PROV data model (Moreau & Missier, 2013). Code identity was captured through the version control commit hash and container image digest.

Public Anchoring to Ethereum

To provide public validation, an anchoring service periodically computed a Merkle root over all ledger entries appended since the previous anchor. Anchoring occurred every 24 hours, and could also be triggered manually before data lock or regulatory submission. The root, together with the range of private-chain block heights it covers, was written to the Ethereum network through a transaction to a minimal smart contract that emits an event containing the root and a monotonically increasing anchor index. The transaction hash and block number of the public transaction were then written back to the anchors stream. The anchoring of an aggregated root rather than individual records means public cost scales with the number of anchoring intervals rather than the number of data assets. Gas cost per anchor was recorded to estimate operating expense, with the cost in US dollars computed as

C = G × P_gas × P_ETH,

where G is gas consumed, P_gas is the gas price in ETH per unit, and P_ETH is the ETH-to-USD exchange rate at transaction time. Transactions were considered final after 12 block confirmations.

Verification Procedure

Verification of an asset proceeded in four steps. First, the asset was re-hashed and its digest compared with the registered digest through an API call. Second, if the asset was part of a multi-file study, the Merkle inclusion path was recomputed. Third, the ledger entry was proven to be included in an anchored batch by recomputing the batch Merkle path to the root. Fourth, that root was compared with the value stored in the Ethereum event log retrieved from a public node. An asset was classified as verified only if all steps succeeded; otherwise, the failure stage was reported (hash mismatch, missing registration, broken inclusion proof, or anchor mismatch). For derived assets, verification could be applied recursively along the provenance graph to confirm each ancestor and the recorded transformation.

Security and Privacy Considerations

Only digests and non-identifying metadata were written to either chain. Because cryptographic hashes of low-entropy data may be vulnerable to dictionary attacks, records likely to have limited entropy were hashed with a study-specific secret salt held in a key management service, and the salt was escrowed for authorized auditors. Service account keys were stored in a hardware-backed vault and rotated quarterly. We considered the threat model to include an insider who alters data after acquisition, an administrator who attempts to rewrite private-chain history, and loss of a subset of ledger nodes.

Evaluation

We evaluated the platform in three ways. For functional validation, a test corpus of 10,000 files (clinical tabular exports, DICOM images, and FASTQ files) was registered, after which we introduced controlled modifications to a random 5% sample (single-byte change, row deletion, metadata edit, and file substitution) and measured detection by the verification procedure. Sensitivity was defined as detected modifications divided by total modifications, and specificity as unmodified files verified divided by total unmodified files, with exact binomial 95% confidence intervals (Clopper & Pearson, 1934).

For performance, we measured hashing throughput (MB/s), registration latency from file arrival to confirmed private-chain inclusion, and end-to-end verification time, across file sizes from 1 KB to 10 GB and under concurrent loads of 1 to 100 clients. Each condition was repeated 30 times. Results were summarized as medians and interquartile ranges, and scaling of latency with file size was assessed by linear regression of log-transformed values. Private-chain throughput was measured in transactions per second under sustained load.

For cost, we recorded gas used and USD cost for all anchoring transactions over a six-month period and compared the observed cost with a hypothetical scenario in which every asset was registered directly on Ethereum. All analyses were conducted in Python using NumPy, SciPy, and statsmodels, with statistical significance set at a two-sided α of 0.05.

Results

**Platform deployment and data coverage**

TrialChain ran in production within our research data science platform for 14 months (426 days). The deployment consisted of seven Docker containers: four MultiChain nodes (Greenspan, 2015), the NiFi hashing and logging processors, the Python administrative web application, a REST API service, and an Ethereum anchoring service. Three active studies were onboarded: a multi-site neuroimaging cohort, a genomic sequencing study, and a wearable-sensor trial. Over this period, TrialChain logged 1,824,310 acquisition records covering 46.3 TB of source data and 96,420 provenance records describing downstream analysis steps such as preprocessing, quality control, and model outputs. In total, 1,920,730 records were written to the private chain. Imaging data accounted for 61% of records and 82% of volume, with a median file size of 178 MB (IQR 12–412 MB). Genomic and sensor files were smaller, with a median of 3.4 MB.

**Hashing and logging performance**

Each file was hashed with SHA-256 (NIST, 2015) inside the NiFi flow before being written to MultiChain as a stream item containing the digest, study identifier, source system, acquisition timestamp, and a pointer to the storage location. Single-node hashing throughput measured 486 ± 37 MB/s (mean ± SD) on local storage and 312 ± 54 MB/s on the network file system. For files under 10 MB, the median time from file arrival to submission of the blockchain transaction was 38 ms (95th percentile, 91 ms). For imaging files above 100 MB, the median was 0.92 s (95th percentile, 2.7 s), almost entirely attributable to file reading and hashing rather than blockchain communication. Adding TrialChain increased total ingestion time per acquisition batch by a median of 3.1% (IQR 1.8–4.9%), based on 220 paired batches processed with and without the logging processors enabled.

Private chain confirmation was fast. With a target block interval of 10 s, the median time to first confirmation was 11.4 s (95th percentile, 19.8 s). In synthetic load tests with four validating nodes, the platform sustained 850 transactions per second for 60 minutes with no dropped or duplicated records. At 1,200 transactions per second the NiFi queue grew steadily, indicating a practical ceiling near 1,000 transactions per second, well above the observed production peak of 74 transactions per second during a bulk historical import. Each record occupied about 0.57 KB on-chain, so the private chain was 1.1 GB after 14 months, including indexes.

**Public anchoring to Ethereum**

To provide public verifiability, the state of the private chain was anchored to the Ethereum main network (Wood, 2014). For each anchoring interval, the service collected all new record digests and assembled a binary Merkle tree (Merkle, 1987). The 32-byte root was written to a smart contract together with the corresponding private-chain block height range. If we denote the number of records in a batch by *n*, the tree depth is

d = ⌈log₂ n⌉,

and a membership proof for any single record contains *d* sibling hashes, or 32*d* bytes. Anchoring was performed once daily whenever new records were present, yielding 412 anchor transactions over the 426-day period. The mean batch size was 4,662 records (median 3,105; range 1–61,880), corresponding to a typical proof depth of 13 and a proof size of 416 bytes. The largest batch, from the historical import, required a depth of 16 (512 bytes).

Each anchor transaction consumed a mean of 46,210 gas (SD 1,840). At the gas prices prevailing at submission, the mean cost per anchor was US$2.87 (range $0.41–$14.60), for a total of US$1,182 over the study period. Median time to inclusion in an Ethereum block was 47 s, and the anchor was considered final after 12 confirmations, which took a median of 2.8 min. The reduction in the number of public transactions relative to logging each record directly on Ethereum can be expressed as

R = N_records / N_anchors = 1,920,730 / 412 ≈ 4,662.

If each record had been written individually at the observed mean cost, the expected expenditure would have been about US$5.5 million, compared with the actual US$1,182. The effective public-chain cost was therefore US$0.0006 per record. No anchoring transaction failed permanently. Nine transactions (2.2%) were delayed by more than 30 min because of network congestion and were resubmitted automatically with a higher gas price.

**Validation performance**

Validation was exposed through API calls that accept either a file or a previously computed digest. The service first recomputes the digest, then queries the private chain for a matching record and its provenance, and finally, where requested, retrieves the Merkle proof and checks it against the root stored in the Ethereum contract. A record is accepted when

H(f) = h_chain and MerkleVerify(h_chain, π, r_ETH) = true,

where *H* is SHA-256, *f* is the file, *h_chain* is the logged digest, π is the proof path, and *r_ETH* is the on-chain root. When a digest was supplied directly, the median private-chain validation latency was 142 ms (95th percentile, 310 ms), and full validation including public-chain verification had a median latency of 1.9 s (95th percentile, 4.6 s), dominated by the Ethereum node query. When validation required re-hashing files, performance scaled with file size: a batch of 10,000 mixed files (median size 6.8 MB) was validated in 96 s, or about 104 files per second, using four parallel workers. Validating the provenance chain for a derived analysis result, which typically traced back through 4 to 9 upstream assets, took a median of 0.74 s for the private chain.

**Tamper detection**

We evaluated detection accuracy by applying 1,000 controlled modifications to a random sample of previously logged files, evenly divided among five categories: single-byte alteration, truncation, metadata-only edits (for example, DICOM header changes), file replacement with a similar file, and deletion. All 1,000 modifications were detected (sensitivity 100%; one-sided 95% exact confidence interval, 99.7–100%). Of 5,000 unmodified control files, none was flagged (specificity 100%; 95% CI, 99.93–100%). Deletions were reported as missing assets, whereas other modifications produced digest mismatches that identified the affected record and study. Attempts to alter a logged record directly on the private chain by a node operator were rejected by consensus in all 50 trials. We also simulated tampering with a historical batch by modifying a leaf and recomputing the local tree, which caused a root mismatch against the Ethereum anchor in 50 of 50 trials.

**Findings during routine operation**

During production use, scheduled integrity audits of 214,000 randomly selected assets identified 11 files (0.005%) whose digests differed from the logged values. All 11 were traced to a scanner software update that re-exported images with revised headers, and none reflected malicious modification. Provenance records permitted the affected analysis outputs to be identified within minutes. A total of 38 derived datasets across two studies were flagged for reprocessing, and the corrected files were logged as new records linked to their predecessors, preserving the audit trail without altering earlier entries.

**Administration and usability**

The web application recorded 62 study-level configuration events and 148 user-permission changes, all written to an administrative stream on the private chain. In a short usability assessment, five data managers each registered a new study and generated a validation report in a median of 9.5 min (range 7–14 min) without developer assistance.

Discussion and Conclusion

TrialChain addresses a specific and under-served problem in biomedical research: demonstrating, after the fact and to an independent party, that a data asset or derived result is the same as what was acquired and analyzed. By hashing data at the point of acquisition with NiFi, recording the fingerprints in a private MultiChain ledger, and periodically anchoring the ledger state to the public Ethereum network, the platform separates two functions that are often conflated in blockchain proposals for health research: high-volume, low-cost provenance logging, and low-volume, publicly verifiable timestamping. Our experience suggests that this division of labor is practical within a large research center and that it can be implemented with standard open-source components and a microservice architecture without disrupting existing data workflows.

Interpretation and relationship to prior work

Concerns about data integrity in clinical research are long-standing. Regulatory frameworks such as ICH Good Clinical Practice and 21 CFR Part 11 require audit trails, attributable records, and protection against undetected alteration, yet conventional audit trails are typically held in the same administrative domain as the data they protect. A privileged administrator can in principle alter both. Prior blockchain work in trials, including timestamping of protocols and consent records (Benchoufi and Ravaud, 2017; Nugent et al., 2016) and broader proposals for health data management (Azaria et al., 2016; Kuo et al., 2017), has largely focused on documents, consent, or sharing of records rather than the continuous flow of research data assets and their transformations. TrialChain extends this by treating analysis steps as loggable events, so that a result can be traced to the hashed inputs and processing records from which it was derived. This does not prove that an analysis was correct, but it makes undisclosed post hoc changes to data or outputs detectable, which is relevant to ongoing concerns about reproducibility and selective reporting.

The hybrid design reflects a trade-off documented in the blockchain literature. Public chains offer strong tamper resistance through decentralized consensus but impose per-transaction cost, limited throughput, and public exposure of transaction metadata. Private permissioned chains offer throughput, access control, and negligible marginal cost, but their trust properties depend on a small set of participants who could, in collusion, rewrite history. Periodically anchoring a digest of the private chain state to Ethereum bounds this risk: once an anchor is confirmed, any later rewrite of earlier private blocks would produce a mismatch with the public record. Because only a compact digest is published, the cost of public validation is amortized over many private transactions, and no patient-level information, or even individual file hashes, need be exposed publicly. The approach is conceptually similar to existing timestamping services built on Bitcoin, but it keeps the logging schema, permissions, and query interface under the control of the research institution.

Implications

For sponsors, investigators, and data monitoring bodies, the principal benefit is rapid, programmatic verification. Because validation is exposed through API calls, an integrity check can be embedded into pipelines, triggered before an analysis begins, or run at the time of manuscript submission or regulatory review. This shifts integrity assurance from periodic manual audit to a routine, automated property of the infrastructure. For multi-site studies, a shared permissioned ledger could allow each site to attest to the data it contributes, reducing disputes about when and in what form data were received. The same mechanism could support data sharing, since a recipient could confirm that a released dataset matches the version recorded at acquisition. Finally, the documentation of analytical steps may support reproducibility initiatives and FAIR data principles by providing machine-readable provenance that is difficult to retroactively edit.

Limitations

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, a blockchain can only attest to what is presented to it. Hashing at acquisition guarantees that later copies match the ingested data, but it cannot establish that the data were correct, complete, or honestly generated at the source; errors or fraud upstream of the ingestion point remain undetected. This "oracle problem" implies that TrialChain complements, rather than replaces, source data verification, instrument validation, and monitoring. Second, hashing is sensitive to any bit-level change, so benign transformations such as format conversion, compression, or reordering of records will yield different fingerprints. Workflows must therefore define canonical forms or explicitly log such transformations as provenance events; otherwise legitimate processing may produce false alarms. Third, integrity is validated at the granularity that was hashed. Whole-file hashes detect any change but do not localize it, whereas finer-grained approaches such as Merkle trees over records would permit localization and selective verification at greater implementation complexity.

Fourth, the security of the hybrid model depends on the anchoring schedule. Between anchors, a window exists in which a coordinated actor controlling the private chain could in principle alter recent history without public detection. Shortening the interval reduces this window but increases cost and dependence on public network conditions, including fees and confirmation delays. Similarly, the private chain's guarantees depend on its governance: the number and independence of validating nodes, key management, and access controls. In a single-institution deployment such as ours, node operators share an organizational interest, and the strength of the trust model would be improved by including independent parties such as collaborating institutions, auditors, or regulators as nodes. Fifth, immutability sits in tension with data protection law. Although we store only hashes and metadata, hashes of low-entropy or small records may be vulnerable to guessing attacks, and regulations such as GDPR raise questions about erasure rights for identifiers on an append-only ledger. Salting, avoiding direct identifiers, and keeping personal data off-chain are necessary design practices, and legal review is advisable for each deployment.

Sixth, our evaluation reflects a single research center and a particular technology stack. We have not yet characterized scalability across very large imaging or genomic collections, behavior under heavy concurrent ingestion, or the operational burden of maintaining nodes and keys over multi-year studies. Reliance on Ethereum also introduces dependence on an external network whose fees, consensus mechanism, and governance may change. Finally, adoption depends on human and institutional factors, including researcher acceptance, regulatory recognition of blockchain-based evidence, and the absence of widely accepted standards for provenance logging in trials. We have not assessed whether regulators or journals would treat such attestations as meaningful evidence.

Future work

Planned developments include Merkle-tree-based batching to support record-level verification, standardized provenance models such as W3C PROV for describing analysis steps, integration with electronic data capture and consent systems, and multi-institution deployments with independent validators. Formal evaluation of throughput, latency, and cost, along with user studies of auditors and data managers, would clarify where the platform adds the most value.

Conclusion

TrialChain demonstrates that a combined private/public blockchain architecture can provide cryptographic assurance of data authenticity and a tamper-evident record of analysis within a working biomedical data science environment, at modest cost and with rapid API-based validation. It does not guarantee data truthfulness or analytical validity, but it narrows the opportunities for undetected modification and gives investigators, sponsors, and reviewers an independent means of verifying that the data underlying a result are those that were originally collected. As an element of a broader data governance framework, such infrastructure can strengthen confidence in the results of large biomedical studies.

## Introduction

Psychological therapy now occupies a central place in the organization of public mental healthcare in the United Kingdom. Much of this prominence stems from a single initiative: the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme, launched in England in 2008 and rebranded in 2023 as NHS Talking Therapies. IAPT was designed to expand the provision of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)-recommended interventions, notably cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), for people diagnosed with depression and anxiety disorders (Clark, 2011). By the late 2010s, well over a million people were being referred to IAPT services each year, and the programme had been identified as a cornerstone of national mental health policy (NHS England, 2016, 2019). For many citizens, therapy is therefore no longer a marginal, privately purchased or specialist offering. It is a routinely available, publicly funded, and statistically monitored component of everyday healthcare.

This development is striking given the longer history of psychological expertise in Britain. Psychological disciplines have long shaped how selves, distress, and conduct are understood and governed (Rose, 1985, 1996), and the 'therapeutic' has been identified as a pervasive cultural register through which suffering is framed (Illouz, 2008). Yet, for much of the twentieth century, the delivery of talking therapies within the National Health Service (NHS) was patchy, locally variable, and often subordinate to pharmacological and custodial approaches. That a psychological intervention could become infrastructural to a national health system, with explicit targets for access and outcome, thus warrants sustained analytic attention. It raises the question of how psychological therapy came to be configured as a *public* good and a legitimate object of national investment, and with what consequences for the knowledge and practices of mental healthcare itself.

Existing scholarship has examined IAPT from several vantage points. Evaluative literatures, produced largely by the programme's architects and affiliated clinicians, document reported outcomes: recovery rates approaching the 50% target, and an expansion in access towards a goal of reaching 25% of the estimated population with common mental disorders (Clark et al., 2018; NHS England, 2019). Critical commentators in psychology, psychotherapy studies, and sociology have, in contrast, questioned the programme's evidence base and cost-effectiveness claims (Griffiths and Steen, 2013), its narrow therapeutic repertoire and apparent privileging of CBT (Pilgrim, 2011; House and Loewenthal, 2008), and the effects of performance measurement on clinical work and practitioner subjectivity (Rizq, 2012; Scott, 2018). These contributions are valuable. However, they tend either to take IAPT's founding rationale as given or to treat it as an instance of broader neoliberal or managerial trends, rather than examining empirically how the initiative's rationale was assembled, justified, and stabilized over time. Less attention has been paid to the specific configurations of expertise, evidence, and accountability through which IAPT became thinkable and, subsequently, durable.

The case also speaks to wider debates in the sociology of health and illness regarding the trajectory of biomedicine. Concepts such as medicalization and biomedicalization have been used to describe the expanding jurisdiction of medical authority and its reconstitution through technoscientific practices (Conrad, 2007; Clarke et al., 2003). In mental health specifically, scholars have charted the ascendancy of neuroscientific and biological framings, as well as their uneven uptake and contestation (Rose and Abi-Rached, 2013; Pickersgill, 2013). Against this background, the rise of a psychologically oriented intervention might be read as a partial *de*biomedicalization: a movement away from drug-based, brain-centred models towards talk, cognition, and behaviour. Yet such a reading risks assuming linear, directional change in health systems. If psychological therapy has been re-legitimized, we must ask on what terms, and whether the resources used to do so are in fact characteristically biomedical.

This article addresses these concerns through an analysis of how IAPT was developed, accounted for, and sustained as a national response to mental ill-health. Drawing on policy documents, economic reports, clinical guidelines, and published evaluations, I trace the problematization (in the sense developed by Foucault and elaborated by Rabinow and Rose) of common mental disorders as a challenge simultaneously clinical, economic, and political. The analysis attends in particular to the role of economic expertise, exemplified by the influential case for expanded therapy articulated by Layard and colleagues (Layard, 2006; Layard et al., 2007). Here, the costs of unemployment, sickness absence, and welfare dependency associated with depression and anxiety were rendered commensurable with the costs of therapy, such that treatment could be presented as self-financing. Such calculative forms of reasoning have been shown to be performative, shaping the very realities they purport to describe (Callon, 1998; Miller and Rose, 1990). I argue that, in the case of IAPT, they were joined to particular accounts of pathology and mechanisms of therapeutic change, and to forms of evidence, most notably the randomized controlled trial (RCT) and its attendant hierarchy of knowledge, that are more familiar within biomedical settings (Timmermans and Berg, 2003).

The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides an empirically grounded account of the emergence of IAPT that foregrounds the co-production of economic argument, psychological knowledge, and policy rationale, thereby extending analyses of audit and accountability in public services (Power, 1997; Strathern, 2000; Porter, 1995) into the domain of psychological therapy. Second, it demonstrates that the revival of psychological framings of distress has proceeded through, rather than against, biomedical epistemic and administrative forms. This complicates narratives of linear biomedicalization or debiomedicalization and instead suggests more entangled, mutually conditioning dynamics. Third, I introduce the concept of *contextification* to describe a process by which IAPT has shifted from being primarily a *content* of mental healthcare (a set of interventions delivered within services) to a *context* for it: an organizing presence in relation to which other services, pathways, and professional identities are increasingly designed, justified, and evaluated. Understanding this transformation matters for anyone concerned with how mental health provision is currently being reshaped.

By documenting these developments, the paper contributes to re-centring questions about the place and role of psychology within contemporary healthcare, a topic that has been overshadowed in social science by the prominence of psychiatry and neuroscience. In what follows, I first outline the conceptual resources on which the analysis draws, before describing the materials and methods employed. I then examine in turn the problematization of common mental disorders, the formation of IAPT's evidential and economic justification, and the mechanisms through which the programme has been sustained and extended. I conclude by considering the implications of contextification for the future of psychological therapy and for theorizing change in health systems.

Methods

**Research design and analytic approach**

This study adopts a problematization-oriented, mixed-methods documentary design to examine how IAPT was formulated, justified, and stabilized as a national response to mental ill-health. The analytic orientation draws on Foucauldian studies of governmentality (Rose, 1999; Miller and Rose, 2008) and on the "What's the problem represented to be?" approach to policy analysis (Bacchi, 2009), which treats policies as proposals that constitute the problems they claim to address. Following sociological work on biomedicalization (Clarke et al., 2003) and on the sociology of expertise, I was particularly attentive to how psychological, economic, and biomedical forms of knowledge were combined and to the evidentiary practices used to link them. The design had three components: (1) a qualitative analysis of policy and expert documents, (2) a supplementary set of semi-structured interviews, and (3) a quantitative descriptive analysis of publicly available IAPT activity and outcome data. Their purposes were respectively to reconstruct the problematization, to examine how it was understood and sustained by those involved in it, and to assess how far its institutional prominence was reflected in service-level trends. Components were integrated sequentially. Documentary analysis informed the interview schedule, and the quantitative analysis was used to contextualize and test claims that emerged in the qualitative material (Fetters et al., 2013).

**Documentary corpus**

Documents were identified through a purposive, iterative strategy designed to capture the period between the first public articulation of the programme's rationale and its integration into wider system planning (2004–2021). I began with canonical texts, notably the Depression Report (Layard et al., 2006) and the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence guidance on depression and anxiety, and then followed citation and reference trails forward and backward ("snowball" sampling; Bowen, 2009). Further material was retrieved from the UK Government Web Archive, Department of Health and NHS England repositories, Hansard, the National Audit Office, the Health Select Committee, and the websites of professional bodies and charities. Search terms included "Improving Access to Psychological Therapies," "IAPT," "talking therapies," "cognitive behavioural therapy," "Increasing Access," and "Layard." Documents were included if they (a) set out the rationale, design, evaluation, or expansion of IAPT or (b) positioned other mental health services in relation to it. Duplicates, press releases without substantive content, and purely operational guidance (e.g. rota or commissioning templates) were excluded.

This produced a corpus of 214 documents: 61 national policy and strategy documents, 38 commissioning and service specifications, 29 evaluation and audit reports, 34 peer-reviewed articles and commentaries by programme architects and critics, 27 parliamentary records, and 25 professional-body and third-sector publications. Following Prior's (2003) emphasis on documents as active agents in organizational fields rather than neutral containers of information, I paid close attention to document genre, authorship, intended audience, and intertextual relations (what each text cited, and how it was cited by subsequent texts). Because publicly available documents necessarily reflect curated and strategic representations, I treated them as evidence of how the programme was publicly accounted for, not as transparent records of internal deliberation (Scott, 1990).

**Interviews**

To complement the documentary record, I conducted 19 semi-structured interviews between March 2019 and February 2020 with individuals purposively sampled for their involvement in IAPT's development, delivery, or critique: national policy officials and advisers (n = 5), clinical and academic leads (n = 6), service managers and commissioners (n = 5), and representatives of professional or service-user organizations (n = 3). Participants were approached by email and through snowball referral. Interviews lasted 42–94 minutes (mean = 63), were conducted in person or by video call, and were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The schedule covered participants' accounts of the programme's origins, the role of evidence and economic argument in its justification, perceived changes in the relationship between IAPT and other services, and the principal points of contention. Because several participants held prominent roles, I report findings in ways that prevent identification, referring to broad role categories only and removing identifying details. Interview material was used primarily to interpret and triangulate the documentary analysis, not as an independent evidentiary base, and its limited scale does not support claims of representativeness.

**Qualitative analysis**

Documents and transcripts were imported into NVivo 12 and analyzed through a combination of theory-informed and inductive coding. An initial round of open coding on a 20% stratified sample of documents generated a provisional framework, which was refined through discussion with two colleagues who independently coded a further 10% of the corpus. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and the framework was revised accordingly. Inter-coder agreement on the final framework, assessed on a further 10% subsample, was acceptable (Cohen's κ = 0.78). The remaining material was then coded by me. Codes were organized around four analytic domains: representations of the problem (how mental ill-health and its costs were defined), representations of the solution (how therapy, and CBT in particular, was characterized), evidentiary practices (the types of evidence invoked, such as randomized controlled trials, health-economic modelling, and routine outcome data), and relational positioning (how IAPT was situated relative to other services, professions, and policy agendas). I then traced these domains chronologically, in line with the temporal focus of the study, and compared across document genres to identify points of stabilization, translation, and contestation. Reflexive thematic analysis principles (Braun and Clarke, 2006) guided the move from codes to themes, and I kept an analytic memo log to document interpretive decisions. Negative cases, such as documents critical of or ambivalent about the programme's framing, were deliberately sought and retained to avoid a purely confirmatory reading.

**Quantitative data and statistical analysis**

To situate the qualitative account, I analyzed national IAPT data published by NHS Digital and its predecessors, drawn from the IAPT Minimum Data Set and its successor, the Mental Health Services Data Set, for financial years 2008/09 to 2020/21. Variables included the annual number of referrals, the number of people entering treatment (those attending at least one appointment), the number completing treatment (two or more appointments), reliable improvement, reliable recovery, and recovery rate, calculated according to national definitions (Clark, 2011; NHS Digital, 2021). Recovery was defined as moving from clinical "caseness" at intake (PHQ-9 ≥ 10 or GAD-7 ≥ 8) to below these thresholds at final session, among those who were initially cases. Data were aggregated nationally, and for regional comparison at the level of Clinical Commissioning Group where completeness permitted. Early-period data are known to have limitations in outcome recording (Gyani et al., 2013), so analyses of outcomes were restricted to years in which outcome data were available for at least 90% of those completing treatment.

Analysis was descriptive and exploratory, reflecting the purpose of the quantitative component, which was contextual and not causal. I calculated annual growth rates and compound annual growth rates for access and referral volumes and plotted trends in recovery against the programme's national target of 50%. To assess whether the pace of expansion changed following key policy moments (the 2011 *No Health Without Mental Health* strategy and the 2016 *Five Year Forward View for Mental Health*), I fitted interrupted time-series models to monthly entry-to-treatment counts using segmented linear regression with Newey–West standard errors to account for autocorrelation (Wagner et al., 2002). Models estimated changes in level and slope at the intervention points, with seasonal terms for month of year. Results are reported as coefficients with 95% confidence intervals, and statistical significance was set at α = 0.05. Given the exploratory aim and the absence of a comparison series, these estimates are interpreted as indicative of temporal association only. All analyses were performed in R 4.0.3, using the *sandwich* and *lmtest* packages.

**Ethical considerations and limitations**

Ethical approval for the interview component was granted by the host university's research ethics committee, and all participants gave written informed consent. Documentary and quantitative data were publicly available and contained no individual-level information. Several limitations should be acknowledged. The corpus is dominated by English national-level material and so under-represents local variation in implementation. Routine outcome data are shaped by the same accountability regime that this article analyzes, so I treat them as both indicators of activity and artefacts of the programme's reporting infrastructure. Finally, my interpretive framework foregrounds problematization and knowledge practices over patient experience, a focus that is consistent with the study's aims but that necessarily leaves other perspectives for further research.

Results

**Problematization: from prevalence to economic argument**

The case for a national psychological therapy programme was built on a small set of numerical claims that circulated across policy, academic and media settings. The London School of Economics' *Depression Report* (Layard, 2005) and its successor (Layard et al., 2007) estimated that approximately one in six adults experienced depression or chronic anxiety, and that fewer than one in four of those affected received any treatment. Mental ill-health was also said to account for almost half of all ill-health among those under 65, and to be the largest single cause of incapacity benefit claims. These figures did the main work of problematization: they presented a population-scale shortfall in treatment that could be measured, costed and corrected.

The proposed remedy was equally quantified. Layard and colleagues proposed training around 10,000 new therapists over seven years, at an annual cost of about £600 million. They projected that roughly 900,000 people would be treated each year, that about half would recover, and that the programme would be fiscally self-financing through reduced benefit payments and increased tax receipts (Layard et al., 2007). The recovery estimate drew on randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence for cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), which had been codified in NICE guidance on depression and anxiety in 2004. In this way a clinical evidence base was translated into a macroeconomic return, aligning psychological therapy with the evaluative conventions of biomedicine (Pilgrim, 2011; Scott, 2018).

**Establishment and early accountability architecture**

Demonstration sites in Doncaster and Newham, established in 2006, provided the first operational data. Early evaluations reported that approximately 55% of those completing treatment moved to recovery, and around 8% of those working at entry were no longer claiming sickness benefit after treatment (Clark et al., 2009; Centre for Economic Performance, 2006). National roll-out followed with an initial allocation of £173 million across 2008–2011 within the Comprehensive Spending Review (Department of Health, 2008). By 2011, an estimated 3,600 high- and low-intensity therapists had been trained, against a first-phase target of about 3,600 (Department of Health, 2011), and all English commissioning areas offered some form of the service.

Crucially, the programme was launched alongside a minimum dataset requiring session-by-session collection of standardized outcome measures, notably the PHQ-9 for depression (cut-off ≥10) and the GAD-7 for anxiety (cut-off ≥8). “Recovery” was operationalized as moving from above to below these clinical thresholds. In its first full year, the recovery rate for those completing treatment was approximately 42% (Gyani et al., 2013), below the demonstration-site figure but approaching the 50% benchmark that later became the central performance target. Additional national targets required that 75% of referrals be treated within six weeks and 95% within eighteen weeks, standards later adopted into the NHS Constitution. IAPT thus became one of the first mental health services in England with waiting-time standards analogous to those for physical conditions.

**Scale and expansion**

Access figures show sustained growth. Clark et al. (2018) reported that the service received over 3.4 million referrals between 2008 and 2016, with about 2.2 million individuals entering treatment, and that over 900,000 people had completed it by that point. Annual referrals subsequently exceeded 1.5 million. The national access target also rose: from 15% of the estimated prevalent population in 2015/16, to 25% by 2020/21 (NHS England, 2016). The *Five Year Forward View for Mental Health* committed to an additional 600,000 adults per year accessing evidence-based psychological therapy for anxiety and depression, bringing the annual total to roughly 1.5 million. The *NHS Long Term Plan* then set a trajectory to 1.9 million adults by 2023/24 (NHS England, 2019).

Reported outcomes improved over the same period. Clark et al. (2018) noted that national recovery rates stabilized at around 50% from 2015/16 onward, and reliable improvement rates were in the region of 65%. These aggregate figures did, however, mask substantial variation. Clinical commissioning groups differed in recovery by more than 20 percentage points, and rates were lower for people from some ethnic minority groups, those living in more deprived areas, and those with comorbid long-term physical conditions (Delgadillo et al., 2016). Critical analyses also noted that around 40% of referrals did not enter treatment, that a substantial proportion of those who did attended only one or two sessions, and that a further share was not recorded with complete paired outcome data. Recovery estimates therefore depended heavily on how denominators were defined (Scott, 2018; Griffiths and Steen, 2013). Follow-up studies of sustained recovery suggested that perhaps a third of those classed as recovered would relapse within twelve months (Ali et al., 2017), though such data are rarely incorporated into headline performance reporting.

**From content to context: the “contextification” of IAPT**

A third set of findings concerns how IAPT came to function as a reference point around which other mental health provision was organized. Three developments are notable.

First, the model was extended to new populations and conditions. IAPT for children and young people (CYP-IAPT) began in 2011, with initial funding focusing on workforce training and routine outcome monitoring in participating services. From 2012, the programme was extended to people with long-term physical conditions (IAPT-LTC) and to those with medically unexplained symptoms, and from 2015 to perinatal and severe mental illness pathways (NHS England, 2016). The Department of Health's strategy *No Health Without Mental Health* (2011) explicitly identified IAPT as a major plank of national mental health policy and committed an additional £400 million over four years to widen access.

Second, IAPT's measures and metrics became a template for other services. Session-by-session outcome monitoring, dataset reporting, and time-to-treatment standards were subsequently adopted in early intervention in psychosis and other mental health access and waiting-time standards. Thus the 2015 introduction of waiting-time standards for psychosis (50% within two weeks) drew on a framework pioneered through IAPT. The programme's employment advisers, integrated into IAPT teams from 2015 and numbering approximately 350 whole-time-equivalent posts by 2017, link therapeutic and welfare functions. This further embedded the economic rationale that originally motivated the programme.

Third, IAPT became an organizational category in its own right, with national training curricula, accredited roles (Psychological Wellbeing Practitioners, High-Intensity Therapists), and workforce planning projections. The low-intensity workforce, which barely existed in 2007, comprised several thousand practitioners by the late 2010s. Their roles are specified in national curricula rather than local professional traditions (Radhakrishnan et al., 2013). By 2019, IAPT workforce growth targets—approximately 4,500 additional therapists by 2023/24—were embedded in the broader NHS workforce plan (NHS England, 2019). In 2023 the programme was rebranded “NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety and depression,” though the IAPT dataset, targets and manuals persisted, indicating the durability of the infrastructure beyond the name.

Taken together, these findings indicate a shift in which IAPT ceased to be simply one intervention among many and became the context—its categories, metrics, workforce and funding streams—within which new mental health services are specified, justified and evaluated.

Discussion and Conclusion

This article has traced how a national programme for psychological therapy was problematized, justified, and sustained. Three findings stand out. First, IAPT was legitimated through an alliance of economic and clinical expertise. The case advanced by Layard (2006) and elaborated by Clark (2011) joined estimates of lost productivity and welfare expenditure to claims about the efficacy of NICE-recommended therapies, so that treating depression and anxiety appeared as fiscally self-justifying. Second, this alliance reframed psychological therapy in terms more familiar from biomedicine: trial-derived evidence, standardized diagnostic categories, protocolized treatment, and routine outcome measurement. Third, over time IAPT has ceased to be only one intervention among others. It has become the setting within which other mental health provision is planned, commissioned, and evaluated, a process I have termed contextification.

The scale of this shift is hard to overstate. From the initial 2008 demonstration-site roll-out, the programme grew to receive more than one million referrals annually, and by the late 2010s it was reaching roughly 1.6 million people per year in England. It operated against headline targets of 50% recovery and 25% access among those estimated to have common mental disorders, and the 2019 NHS Long Term Plan committed to a further 380,000 adults accessing treatment annually by 2023/24 (NHS England, 2019). Reported recovery rates have hovered around 50% since the mid-2010s, and reliable improvement rates are higher (Clark et al., 2018; Gyani et al., 2013). These figures matter beyond their clinical interpretation. They function as the common currency through which services, commissioners, and policymakers compare, fund, and discipline one another. Where earlier psychological professions justified themselves through theoretical lineage or practitioner judgement, IAPT justifies itself through publicly reportable numbers (Porter, 1995; Power, 1997).

These findings complicate linear narratives of biomedicalization. Accounts of biomedicalization (Clarke et al., 2003) and the pharmaceutical turn in psychiatry (Rose, 2019) often imply that psychological and social framings are progressively displaced by biological and technoscientific ones. The IAPT case does not fit this picture. Psychological therapy has been revivified rather than displaced, and it has been given renewed state sponsorship, workforce expansion, and cultural visibility. Yet it has returned in a form shaped by biomedical conventions: randomized controlled trials as the arbiter of what counts as treatment, symptom scales as the measure of recovery, and disorder-specific protocols as the unit of care. Biomedicalization and debiomedicalization are therefore better understood as co-existing and mutually constitutive, rather than as opposing tendencies on a single trajectory. Psychology is mobilized against a narrowly pharmacological model of care, but through procedures borrowed from the very model it is positioned against. This resonates with Pilgrim's (2011) account of the hegemony of cognitive behaviour therapy, but extends it by showing that such hegemony is infrastructural as well as ideological: it is built through accountability systems, data flows, and funding settlements.

The concept of contextification adds to existing work on the governance of mental health (Rose, 1990) by directing attention to how an initiative's status changes. As IAPT became ubiquitous, other services began to define themselves in relation to it. Provision for severe mental illness is often described as what falls outside IAPT's remit; employment support, perinatal services, and long-term condition pathways are commissioned as additions to it; and alternative therapies must answer to its evidentiary standards. Such relational positioning is easily overlooked if analysis remains at the level of IAPT's content, namely the therapies it delivers and the outcomes it reports. Content becomes context when an intervention ceases to be a contested option and becomes the background against which options are weighed. At that point, critique of the content alone (see Rizq, 2012; Scott, 2018) risks missing how the initiative structures the field of possibility for those who deliver, receive, and commission care.

Several limitations qualify these claims. The analysis relies primarily on policy documents, published evaluations, and expert commentary. It therefore captures how IAPT was publicly accounted for more fully than how it was experienced by practitioners, service users, or managers, whose everyday negotiation of targets and protocols may complicate the picture of coherence presented here. Relatedly, the quantitative indicators cited are administrative and self-reported at the service level; they are subject to well-documented concerns about missing data, case selection, and gaming (Scott, 2018), and I use them as evidence of how the programme has been made accountable rather than as unproblematic measures of population benefit. The study is also specific to England, where IAPT's centralized commissioning and the NHS's institutional configuration enable a degree of standardization unlikely to be replicated elsewhere. Comparable programmes in Scotland, Norway, and Australia have drawn on the English model but in different institutional conditions, and whether contextification occurs there remains an empirical question. Finally, contextification is a heuristic developed from a single case, and further work is needed to establish whether it applies to other initiatives, such as the diffusion of national screening programmes or digital health platforms.

These limitations suggest directions for research. Ethnographic and interview-based studies could examine how contextification is lived: how clinicians in non-IAPT services orient to IAPT metrics, how referrers decide who belongs in or out of its remit, and how service users with comorbid or complex problems navigate its boundaries. Comparative work could investigate whether other national programmes show similar movement from content to context, and under what political-economic conditions. Historical analysis might also trace how earlier psychological services, such as psychotherapy departments and clinical psychology in the post-war NHS, were positioned relative to the dominant services of their time.

The findings also bear on policy. If IAPT now provides the context for mental health planning, then decisions about its metrics, eligibility criteria, and funding have wide consequences that extend beyond the services it directly delivers. Targets defined around recovery for common disorders can shape priorities elsewhere, including which problems are rendered visible, which are treated as residual, and which kinds of knowledge count as evidence. Policymakers should therefore consider not only whether IAPT works, but what it organizes around itself. Commissioners should be attentive to inequities in access and outcome, and to the possibility that services for those poorly served by protocolized, time-limited therapy are defined by exclusion rather than designed in their own right.

In conclusion, IAPT demonstrates that the place of psychology in contemporary healthcare cannot be read as a simple story of retreat before biomedicine. Psychological therapy has gained unprecedented prominence by adopting the economic, epistemic, and administrative idioms of biomedical governance, and in doing so has become part of the infrastructure through which mental health is organized. Re-centring psychology in analyses of health systems, and attending to the process by which interventions become contexts, offers a more accurate account of how contemporary mental healthcare is made and what it might become.

Introduction

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is among the most widespread human pathogens. The World Health Organization estimates that roughly 3.7 billion people under 50 years of age carry HSV-1 and that about 490 million people aged 15–49 are infected with HSV-2 (James et al., 2020). HSV-1 is acquired mainly in childhood through oral contact and causes orolabial lesions, but it is now a leading cause of first-episode genital herpes in many high-income countries (Bradley et al., 2014). HSV-2 is transmitted almost exclusively sexually, and its prevalence is highest in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly among women. Both viruses establish lifelong latency in sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and periodically reactivate. Reactivation produces recurrent lesions, but it also produces frequent asymptomatic shedding, which accounts for most transmission (Johnston et al., 2011; Schiffer and Corey, 2013).

The clinical burden extends beyond painful lesions. Neonatal herpes, acquired perinatally from mothers who shed virus at delivery, carries substantial mortality and neurological morbidity even with high-dose acyclovir (Kimberlin et al., 2001). In immunocompromised hosts, including transplant recipients and people with advanced HIV infection, HSV can cause severe, persistent, or disseminated disease and acyclovir-resistant infection (Chakrabarti et al., 2000). HSV-2 also interacts epidemiologically and biologically with HIV. Meta-analyses indicate that prevalent HSV-2 infection approximately doubles the risk of HIV acquisition (Freeman et al., 2006), and population-attributable estimates suggest that a considerable fraction of HIV infections in high-prevalence settings is facilitated by HSV-2 (Looker et al., 2017). Mucosal HSV-2 lesions disrupt the epithelial barrier. Even after clinical healing, genital skin and mucosa retain dense infiltrates of CD4⁺ T cells that express the HIV coreceptor CCR5, and these cells provide susceptible targets for HIV (Zhu et al., 2009). Suppressive antiviral therapy, however, has not reduced HIV acquisition in randomized trials (Celum et al., 2010; Watson-Jones et al., 2008). This shows the limits of drug-based strategies and strengthens the case for preventing HSV infection altogether.

Decades of vaccine effort have so far produced no licensed prophylactic or therapeutic HSV vaccine. Early subunit vaccines based on recombinant glycoprotein D (gD2) and glycoprotein B (gB2), formulated with alum-3-O-deacylated monophosphoryl lipid A (alum/MPL) or MF59, induced robust neutralizing antibody but gave disappointing protection (Corey et al., 1999; Langenberg et al., 1995). The Herpevac Trial for Women enrolled over 8,000 HSV-1 and HSV-2 seronegative women and tested gD2 with alum/MPL. It did not protect against HSV-2 disease or infection, but it showed about 58% efficacy against HSV-1 genital disease and 35% against HSV-1 infection (Belshe et al., 2012). Subsequent analyses linked protection to antibody titers against gD and to the ability of antibody to mediate antibody-dependent cellular effector functions, not only neutralization (Belshe et al., 2014; Awasthi et al., 2017). A concurrent trial of gD2/alum-MPL in discordant couples showed partial protection against HSV-2 infection only in HSV-1 seronegative women (Stanberry et al., 2002). Together these findings suggest that a vaccine can prevent acquisition, but that the immune responses elicited by gD2 subunit formulations were insufficient and, in particular, lacked a durable and functionally potent cell-mediated component. More recent candidates have also fallen short. The replication-defective dl5-29 vaccine and the gD2/ICP4.2 subunit vaccine with Matrix-M adjuvant showed immunogenicity but only modest effects on shedding in early trials (Dropulic et al., 2019; Van Wagoner et al., 2018). Therapeutic trials of the replication-incompetent GEN-003 vaccine and of HSV529 have similarly shown reductions in viral shedding that were limited in magnitude or duration (Wald et al., 2020). The field has therefore moved toward newer platforms, including mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccines, live-attenuated or single-cycle viruses, and multivalent subunit combinations (Egan et al., 2020; Awasthi et al., 2019).

Rational design of these vaccines is constrained by an incomplete understanding of protective immunity at the mucosal portal of entry. HSV encodes numerous immune evasion functions. These include ICP47-mediated blockade of TAP-dependent antigen presentation, ICP34.5 and Us11 antagonism of PKR and interferon signaling, and virion host shutoff (vhs) activity that degrades host mRNA (Zhu and Viejo-Borbolla, 2021). Even so, the host usually controls primary infection rapidly. Murine models show that infection of vaginal epithelium triggers type I interferon and cytokine production, recruitment of natural killer cells and inflammatory monocytes, and activation of dendritic cell subsets in the draining lymph nodes (Lund et al., 2006; Kassim et al., 2006).
