Duplicate DOIs, incorrect DOIs, and DOIs unregistered in the receiving database all occurred in our data, and the duplicates in particular create a dilemma that cannot be resolved without compromising either publication counts or citation counts. As UID-based citation linking becomes standard, the presence of a valid UID may become decisive for whether a publication or a database enters a bibliometric analysis. Future research should replicate the evaluation across disciplines, systems, and time points, develop benchmark data sets for match validation, and quantify the effect of different duplicate-handling strategies on indicators at several organizational levels.

Introduction

The 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak was the largest and most complex filovirus epidemic recorded. It caused more than 28,000 reported cases and more than 11,000 deaths, mostly in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone (WHO Ebola Response Team, 2016). Earlier outbreaks in Central Africa had typically been confined to remote rural areas and were contained within weeks or months by classical measures: rapid case detection, isolation, contact tracing, safe burials, and community engagement (Chowell & Nishiura, 2014). In 2014, however, the virus spread into densely populated urban settings and across porous borders, in health systems already weakened by decades of conflict and underinvestment. Health workers were infected at disproportionately high rates, and the supply of trained staff, laboratories, vehicles, and basic communication infrastructure was overwhelmed (Kieny et al., 2014; Gostin & Friedman, 2015). Under these conditions, the speed and quality of information flow, from the village to the district, the national command center, and international partners, became a decisive factor in the response.

Paper-based reporting was the default in most affected areas. Case investigation forms, contact lists, laboratory request forms, and daily follow-up sheets were completed by hand, transported physically, and entered later into spreadsheets or databases. This introduced delays of days to weeks, transcription errors, duplicate records, and difficulty reconciling data from different sources (Fäh et al., 2015; Tom-Aba et al., 2015). Incomplete contact lists and poor linkage between laboratory results and clinical records were widely reported as obstacles to timely control. The consequence was that decision makers often worked with outdated or inconsistent epidemiological pictures, which hampered resource allocation and the identification of transmission chains (Frieden et al., 2014).

Mobile health (mHealth), defined by the World Health Organization as medical and public health practice supported by mobile devices such as phones, tablets, and other wireless equipment (WHO, 2011), was widely proposed as a way to address these gaps. Mobile phone penetration in sub-Saharan Africa had grown rapidly during the preceding decade, often outpacing access to electricity, roads, and fixed-line networks (GSMA, 2014). mHealth tools had already been used for disease surveillance, community health worker support, and data collection in low-resource settings, with growing evidence of improved data timeliness and completeness (Braa et al., 2012; Aranda-Jan et al., 2014). Previous outbreaks, including cholera in Haiti and Zimbabwe, H1N1 influenza, and Marburg and Ebola in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, had also seen mobile or electronic systems deployed for outbreak response, although generally at small scale and with limited evaluation (Freifeld et al., 2010; Black et al., 2013). The 2014-2015 outbreak thus offered both an urgent need and an unprecedented opportunity to apply these technologies at scale.

During the epidemic, a large and heterogeneous set of mHealth initiatives emerged. Governments, ministries of health, international agencies, nongovernmental organizations, academic groups, technology companies, and volunteer developers built or adapted tools for many purposes. These included electronic case reporting, contact tracing and follow-up, laboratory result transmission, mapping of cases, mobile-based symptom checkers, health worker training, public messaging and rumor tracking, and monitoring of returning travelers (Sacks et al., 2015; Tom-Aba et al., 2015; Oluwafemi et al., 2015). Some were adaptations of platforms already used in other contexts, such as DHIS2, Open Data Kit, CommCare, and Magpi, whereas others were developed specifically for the outbreak. Many reports describe rapid deployment, often within weeks, and several suggest that mobile data collection improved the timeliness of contact follow-up and shortened the delay between data capture and analysis (Tom-Aba et al., 2015; Fäh et al., 2015). Digital tools have therefore been credited as a major contribution to improved control of EVD in the later phases of the epidemic (Kamadjeu et al., 2015).

Despite this enthusiasm, the evidence base on what was actually developed and used remains fragmented. Information about tools is scattered across peer-reviewed articles, conference abstracts, technical reports, press releases, and project websites, and the terminology used to describe functions varies widely. Existing overviews have generally been narrative or have focused on single projects, a single country, or a single functionality such as contact tracing (Sacks et al., 2015; Danquah et al., 2019). Moreover, rapid, parallel development by many actors raised concerns about duplication of effort, lack of interoperability, limited alignment with national information systems, unclear data governance, and low sustainability beyond the emergency period (Heeks, 2006; Kamadjeu et al., 2015). Without a structured overview, it is difficult for public health agencies and developers to know which tools exist, what core functions they cover, and which combinations of features appear most useful for outbreak response. This hampers the building on earlier experience and risks repeating fragmented development in future outbreaks, including recent resurgences of EVD and other epidemic-prone diseases.

Outbreak control relies on a chain of linked activities that are not independent. Surveillance detects and reports suspected cases; case management ensures isolation, care, and clinical documentation; contact tracing identifies and follows people at risk of developing disease; and laboratory data management confirms or excludes infection and feeds results back to clinicians and epidemiologists. A tool that addresses only one step may speed up that step but leave bottlenecks elsewhere, and data silos can prevent the integrated view needed for decision making. Systems covering several of these functions within a single platform may reduce duplicate data entry and facilitate real-time linkage of cases, contacts, and test results (Tom-Aba et al., 2015). Whether such integrated tools were common during the 2014-2015 outbreak, however, has not been systematically assessed.

We therefore conducted a systematic review of mHealth tools developed or used in the context of the 2014-2015 West Africa EVD outbreak. Our research question was: what mobile tools were reported for EVD management in 2014 and 2015, and which core functionalities (surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management) did they support? Our objectives were to identify and describe the available tools, to characterize their functionalities and the extent to which they were integrated, and to highlight the most promising approaches to guide future mHealth development for infectious disease control.

This review makes three contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first systematic inventory of mHealth tools from this outbreak, using a reproducible search of multiple databases and independent dual review, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). Second, it offers a functionality-based classification that allows tools to be compared on the activities central to outbreak response rather than on their technical architecture alone. Third, it identifies tools that combine several core functions and may therefore be priority candidates for further development, evaluation, and preparedness planning.

Methods

Study design and reporting framework

We conducted a systematic review of mobile health (mHealth) tools developed or deployed in response to the 2014–2015 West Africa Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009; Liberati et al., 2009). Because the objective was to describe and compare tool functionalities rather than estimate intervention effects, no meta-analysis was planned, and the review was not registered in a prospective protocol registry. We defined mHealth in accordance with the World Health Organization as medical and public health practice supported by mobile devices such as mobile phones, smartphones, tablets, and patient-monitoring devices (WHO, 2011). A "tool" was defined as a distinct software application, platform, or system with a named identity or a clearly described, reproducible set of functions, irrespective of whether it was developed de novo or adapted from an existing platform.

Search strategy and information sources

We searched Google Scholar, MEDLINE (via PubMed), CAB Abstracts (Global Health), POPLINE, and Web of Science for reports published between January 1, 2014 and December 31, 2015. No language restrictions were applied. The following search string was used and adapted to the syntax of each database: ("outbreak" OR "epidemic") AND ("mobile phone" OR "smartphone" OR "smart phone" OR "tablet" OR "mHealth") AND ("Ebola" OR "EVD" OR "VHF" OR "Ebola virus disease" OR "viral hemorrhagic fever") AND ("2014" OR "2015"). Searches were run on titles, abstracts, and keywords where the database allowed; for Google Scholar, which does not support field-restricted searching to the same degree, the full-text option was used and the first 200 records, sorted by relevance, were screened, a pragmatic cut-off commonly applied for this engine (Haddaway et al., 2015). Because mHealth implementations are often documented outside indexed journals, we additionally screened the reference lists of included records and of relevant narrative reviews, and examined grey literature such as reports from the WHO, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Médecins Sans Frontières, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, and technology developers' websites when these were cited in or linked from retrieved records. Records in languages other than English or French were translated using machine translation and verified by a fluent colleague when available.

Eligibility criteria

Records were eligible if they (1) described one or more specific mHealth tools; (2) explicitly stated that the tool was developed, adapted, or used in the context of the 2014–2015 West Africa EVD outbreak (including pilot, preparedness, or neighboring-country settings linked to this outbreak); and (3) provided sufficient information to characterize at least one functionality. We included original research articles, implementation reports, conference abstracts, technical reports, and descriptive commentaries that contained primary information on a tool. We excluded records that (1) referred to mHealth only in general terms without identifying a specific tool; (2) addressed other outbreaks or diseases without reference to the 2014–2015 EVD epidemic; (3) were purely opinion pieces, editorials, or news items with no original description of a tool; (4) concerned non-mobile information technology solutions only (e.g., desktop-only software, call-center-only services without a mobile application component); or (5) were duplicates. Where a tool was described in several records, these were grouped under a single tool entry, and the most informative record was used as the primary source, with additional records used to complete missing data.

Study selection

All retrieved records were exported to a reference manager and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then retrieved and independently assessed by the same two reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved by discussion and, when consensus could not be reached, by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the title-and-abstract stage was quantified using Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960):

κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e),

where p_o is the observed proportion of agreement and p_e is the proportion of agreement expected by chance. Values above 0.60 were interpreted as substantial agreement (Landis & Koch, 1977). The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram, indicating the number of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons), and included.

Data extraction

A standardized data extraction form was developed in Microsoft Excel, piloted on a random sample of five included records, and refined to resolve ambiguities. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and discrepancies were reconciled through consensus. For each tool we recorded: name, developer or implementing organization, type of developer (government, nongovernmental organization, academic institution, private sector, or international agency), country or countries of deployment, publication type and year, development stage (concept or prototype, pilot, or field deployment), platform and hardware (e.g., Android, iOS, basic feature phone with SMS/USSD, tablet), connectivity requirements (online, offline-capable with synchronization), open-source status, and target users (e.g., health workers, laboratory staff, contact tracers, community members, the general public).

The principal data of interest were the functionalities of each tool. Based on the epidemiological workflow of EVD response (WHO, 2014) and previous typologies of mHealth functions (Labrique et al., 2013), we predefined four core functionalities:

1. Surveillance: collection, transmission, or analysis of data on suspected, probable, or confirmed cases and deaths, including event-based reporting, alert generation, and mapping.
2. Case management: support for clinical care of patients, including registration, triage, symptom assessment, monitoring of clinical progress, treatment documentation, and patient tracking within treatment facilities.
3. Contact tracing: identification, listing, and daily follow-up of contacts of confirmed cases over the 21-day incubation period, including symptom monitoring and referral.
4. Laboratory data management: ordering of tests, sample tracking, and transmission or reporting of laboratory results.

Additional functionalities were recorded inductively and grouped as health education and risk communication, training and decision support for health workers, logistics and supply management, and other. A functionality was coded as present only when it was explicitly described in the source; where information was absent or unclear, it was coded as "not reported" rather than "absent." This approach was chosen because incomplete reporting is common in implementation documents and would otherwise bias estimates downward.

Quality and risk of bias considerations

Because included records were predominantly descriptive reports and not comparative studies, formal risk-of-bias instruments for effectiveness studies were not applicable. Instead, we assessed the completeness of reporting for each tool by counting the number of extracted descriptive items (out of the items listed above) for which information was available, and we recorded whether any form of evaluation (e.g., usability testing, accuracy assessment, or outcome measurement) was reported. This allowed us to describe the strength of the evidence base without excluding tools on the basis of quality.

Data synthesis and statistical analysis

Findings were synthesized narratively and quantitatively through descriptive statistics. Categorical variables were summarized as absolute frequencies and percentages. Because the extent of reporting varied among tools, the denominator for each functionality was the number of tools for which information on that functionality was reported, rather than the total number of tools; proportions were therefore calculated as

p_f = n_f / N_f,

where n_f is the number of tools with functionality f and N_f is the number of tools with available information on f. Where informative, 95% confidence intervals for proportions were computed using the Wilson score method (Wilson, 1927). We cross-tabulated functionalities to identify tools combining all four core functions and examined the overlap among functionalities using a matrix of co-occurrence. Exploratory comparisons of functionality profiles by developer type, platform, and development stage were performed using Fisher's exact test, given the small expected cell counts, with a two-sided significance level of 0.05; because these analyses were exploratory, no adjustment for multiple testing was made and results were interpreted cautiously. Analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2016) and Microsoft Excel.

Results

**Study selection and characteristics of included publications**

The search strategy identified 1220 records across Google Scholar, MEDLINE, CAB Abstracts (Global Health), POPLINE, and Web of Science. After removal of duplicates and screening of titles, abstracts, and full texts against the eligibility criteria, 1143 records were excluded. Most of these discussed Ebola virus disease (EVD) or mobile technology in general terms without describing a specific mHealth tool, or were opinion pieces, commentaries, or news items. This left 77 original publications (6.31% of all records), which reported on 58 distinct mHealth tools developed or deployed in the context of the 2014-2015 West Africa EVD outbreak. Agreement between the two independent reviewers at the full-text stage was high (Cohen κ=0.86), and disagreements were resolved by consensus without recourse to a third reviewer.

Of the 77 publications, 23 (30%) appeared in 2014 and 54 (70%) in 2015, reflecting a lag between tool deployment and reporting. Thirty-eight (49%) were peer-reviewed journal articles, 21 (27%) were conference abstracts or proceedings, and 18 (23%) were technical or institutional reports. One publication was in French; all others were in English. Several tools were described in more than one publication; for example, CommCare, the Open Data Kit (ODK)-based tools, and the Surveillance and Outbreak Response Management and Analysis System (SORMAS) were each covered in at least three reports. A further 11 tools were described in only a single conference abstract, which limited the detail available for data extraction.

**Overview of identified tools**

The 58 tools varied widely in origin and purpose. Developers included international and nongovernmental organizations, ministries of health, academic groups, and private technology companies. A substantial share were built on existing open-source or commercial platforms such as ODK, CommCare, Magpi, KoBoToolbox, Epi Info, and DHIS2, and were adapted for EVD rather than designed de novo. Reported deployment settings were concentrated in the three most affected countries (Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone). Some tools were used only in neighboring countries or were prototypes that were never deployed in the field. Where operating system information was available, Android was the dominant platform. Smartphones or tablets were used for data entry, whereas basic feature phones were used mainly by tools relying on short message service (SMS) or interactive voice response.

Information on whether a tool had been used in the field, as opposed to only developed or piloted, was available for most tools. A minority had undergone any formal evaluation of usability, data quality, or effect on outbreak outcomes. The majority of reports were descriptive and did not provide quantitative performance indicators.

**Functionalities offered by the tools**

Functionalities were extracted across four predefined core domains: surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management. The denominator differed for each domain because the publications did not report equally on each. The proportions below are therefore based on the number of tools for which information on the respective functionality could be determined.

*Surveillance.* Surveillance was the most frequently supported functionality. Of the 55 tools with sufficient information, 34 (62%) offered surveillance functions, such as case reporting, alert notification, syndromic or event-based data collection, and the geographic visualization of cases. Many of these were form-based data-collection applications for health facility or community-level reporting, and several included mapping dashboards that updated as data were synchronized to a central server.

*Case management.* Of the 45 tools for which information was available, 10 (22%) supported case management. Typical features included electronic patient records for isolation and treatment units, tracking of patients' clinical status and symptoms over time, bed and resource management, and recording of discharge or outcome. Most of these tools were designed for use in Ebola treatment centers or holding facilities rather than at community level.

*Contact tracing.* Among 38 tools with relevant information, 7 (18%) provided contact tracing functionality. These tools enabled the listing of contacts of confirmed or probable cases, scheduling and recording of daily follow-up visits, and flagging of contacts who developed symptoms or were lost to follow-up. Some also supported automated assignment of contacts to field teams and tracking of follow-up completeness.

*Laboratory data management.* Laboratory functionality was the least common. Only 3 of 51 tools (6%) supported laboratory data management, including the registration of samples, the transmission of test results to clinicians or surveillance officers, and the linkage of laboratory results to case records. Reports describing mobile solutions for reducing delays in the return of laboratory results were notably scarce, despite the recognized importance of timely diagnostics during the outbreak.

**Tools combining multiple functionalities**

Most tools addressed a single functionality, typically surveillance or data collection, and relatively few integrated multiple components of the outbreak response. Only 3 tools (5% of the 58 identified tools) supported all four core functionalities: Community Care, Sense Ebola Followup, and SORMAS. Community Care and Sense Ebola Followup were based on mobile data collection, offline operation, and synchronization with central databases. SORMAS was designed as an integrated, open-source system linking surveillance, case and contact management, and laboratory workflows. A small number of additional tools covered two or three of the four functionalities, most commonly the combination of surveillance with contact tracing or of surveillance with case management. Tools that combined contact tracing with laboratory data management, or case management with laboratory data management, but without surveillance, were not identified.

**Additional functionalities and technical features**

Beyond the four core domains, some tools offered supplementary features. These included health education and information dissemination to the public or health workers (for example via SMS or interactive messaging), training and decision support for frontline workers, communication and coordination among health workers, symptom self-assessment, and crowdsourced or social media-based event detection. Such features were generally standalone applications and were not integrated with case or contact data. Offline data collection with later synchronization was reported for most of the tools designed for field use, reflecting the unreliable connectivity in affected areas. Reports on data security, patient privacy, and data ownership were limited, and few publications described how personally identifiable information, such as the location and health status of contacts, was protected.

**Summary of findings**

In summary, of 1220 records screened, 77 publications described 58 mHealth tools for EVD management. Surveillance functionality was far more common (62%) than case management (22%), contact tracing (18%), or laboratory data management (6%). Only 3 tools (Community Care, Sense Ebola Followup, and SORMAS) incorporated all four functionalities. Evidence on formal evaluation, effectiveness, and sustainability was sparse across all tools.

Discussion

Principal findings

This systematic review identified 58 mHealth tools reported in connection with the 2014–2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak, drawn from 77 original publications among 1220 records screened. The tools were concentrated heavily in surveillance (62% of those for which this could be assessed), with markedly fewer supporting case management, contact tracing, or laboratory data management. Only three tools (Community Care, Sense Ebola Followup, and the Surveillance and Outbreak Response Management and Analysis System, SORMAS) covered all four functionalities. These findings suggest that mHealth development during the outbreak was largely reactive, fragmented, and driven by local or institutional needs rather than coordinated against a shared functional specification for outbreak response.

The predominance of surveillance functionality is unsurprising. Electronic data capture on mobile devices was already well established in low-resource settings before 2014, and tools such as the Open Data Kit and DHIS2 could be rapidly adapted for syndromic reporting and case notification (Brunette et al., 2013; Braa et al., 2012). Surveillance forms are comparatively simple, require limited clinical logic, and fit the reporting structures of ministries of health and international agencies. By contrast, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory integration demand longitudinal patient or contact records, interoperability with other systems, and stronger data governance. These are harder to build and deploy under emergency conditions. The low share of tools addressing laboratory data is particularly notable, as delays in returning test results were repeatedly identified as a bottleneck in the response (WHO Ebola Response Team, 2014; Kucharski et al., 2015).

Interpretation and implications

The finding that few tools integrated all four functions has practical importance. Ebola control depends on a chain of linked activities: detecting suspected cases, isolating and treating them, confirming diagnoses, and identifying and following contacts. Where each step is supported by a separate application, data must be re-entered, reconciled, or transferred manually, introducing delay and error. Fragmentation of this kind was a recognized problem in earlier outbreak responses and in the 2014–2015 epidemic, when parallel paper and electronic systems coexisted (Tom-Aba et al., 2015; Sacks et al., 2015). Integrated platforms offer the possibility of a single record linking a contact to a case, a laboratory result, and a clinical outcome, thereby enabling near-real-time epidemiological analysis. The three tools identified here are therefore reasonable candidates for further development, although inclusion of all four functions is a necessary rather than sufficient indicator of quality.

Importantly, our classification is based on the functionalities described, not on demonstrated effectiveness. Few of the included reports presented evaluation data on completeness, timeliness, usability, or impact on transmission. Consequently, we cannot conclude that the tools with the broadest functionality performed best in the field. Several narrower tools may have performed well within their intended niche, and the value of an application depends heavily on context: network coverage, device availability, user training, language, and the capacity of the health system to act on the data. Experience from SORMAS and similar systems suggests that adoption depends on co-design with end users and on alignment with existing workflows and national policy (Fähnrich et al., 2015). Likewise, evaluations of mHealth in other settings have repeatedly shown that technically sound tools fail to scale without sustained institutional support and funding (Labrique et al., 2013; Tomlinson et al., 2013).

Relation to previous work

Earlier reviews of mHealth have documented the field’s rapid growth alongside a thin evidence base, particularly for infectious disease outbreaks (Free et al., 2013; Aranda-Jan et al., 2014). Reports from the Ebola response itself have tended to be descriptive or experiential, emphasizing speed of deployment, the use of mobile phones for call-center and hotline operations, and the potential of mobile network data for mobility analysis (Wesolowski et al., 2014; Sacks et al., 2015). Our review adds a structured inventory organized by core outbreak-response functions, which may help developers and funders identify gaps. The marked underrepresentation of contact tracing and laboratory management tools indicates where investment might yield the largest gains, and the example of the three comprehensive tools provides a starting template for functional requirements in future outbreaks of Ebola and other pathogens requiring contact tracing, such as Lassa fever, Middle East respiratory syndrome, and, subsequently, COVID-19.

Limitations

Several limitations should be considered. First, the search was restricted to publications between January 2014 and December 2015, and many tools were documented only in grey literature, conference presentations, organizational reports, or app-store descriptions that were not captured by bibliographic databases. The number of tools actually deployed was likely larger than the 58 identified, and publication bias may favor tools developed by academic groups or large organizations. Second, the search strategy required terms for both “outbreak/epidemic” and specific device terms, and used relatively narrow vocabulary; relevant reports using terms such as “digital health,” “eHealth,” “SMS,” or “electronic data collection” may have been missed. Third, functionality was extracted from published descriptions, which vary in detail. Absence of a described feature does not prove its absence in the software, and the denominators differed across functionalities because information was not available for every tool, which complicates direct comparison of proportions. Fourth, we did not assess methodological quality or effectiveness, because the heterogeneity and descriptive nature of the sources precluded the use of standard risk-of-bias instruments; consequently, the review characterizes concepts and designs rather than outcomes. Finally, some tools were prototypes or concepts that were never deployed in affected areas, and our review did not systematically distinguish between pilot, deployed, and scaled tools, which limits inferences about real-world use.

Recommendations and future research

Several recommendations follow. Developers should adopt open standards and interoperable architectures so that surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory modules can be exchanged between systems and with national health information platforms such as DHIS2. Preparedness plans should designate preapproved, tested tools before outbreaks occur, rather than relying on ad hoc development under emergency conditions. Governance issues, including data protection, consent, and the ethics of linking personal contact information to surveillance records, require explicit attention (Mohr et al., 2015). Furthermore, transparent reporting frameworks for mHealth evaluation, such as the mHealth Evidence Reporting and Assessment (mERA) checklist, should be applied to deployments so that effectiveness, cost, and usability data accumulate (Agarwal et al., 2016). Prospective evaluations comparing integrated and stand-alone tools on indicators such as time from symptom onset to isolation, proportion of contacts followed, and laboratory turnaround time would provide the evidence needed to move beyond functionality-based appraisal.

Conclusions

Of 58 mHealth tools reported in the context of the 2014–2015 Ebola outbreak, most addressed surveillance, whereas few supported case management, contact tracing, or laboratory data management, and only Community Care, Sense Ebola Followup, and SORMAS offered all four functions. These three tools appear the most promising foundations for future development, provided they are rigorously evaluated, interoperable, and embedded in national systems. Future mHealth efforts for infectious disease control should prioritize integrated, evaluated, and sustainably supported platforms prepared in advance of the next outbreak.

Introduction

Open access (OA) has moved from a marginal ideal to a central organizing principle of scholarly communication. The Budapest Open Access Initiative of 2002, the Bethesda Statement and the Berlin Declaration of 2003 articulated the premise that peer-reviewed research, much of it publicly funded, should be freely available for reading, reuse and text mining (Suber, 2012). Over two decades, this premise has been translated into funder mandates, institutional policies and new publishing models. The growth is measurable. Piwowar et al. (2018) estimated that at least 28% of the scholarly literature was OA in 2015, with a markedly higher share among recently published articles. The Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) now lists more than 20,000 peer-reviewed journals, and PubMed Central (PMC) archives millions of full-text biomedical articles. Plan S, launched by cOAlition S in 2018, marked a qualitative shift. It requires that publications from funded research be available immediately under open licenses, with fewer exceptions for hybrid or delayed-access routes (Schiltz, 2018). Many journals and publishers are now adapting to a policy environment that links funding eligibility to publishing practices.

This transition raises the requirements for journals. Subscription-era indicators, such as print circulation, library holdings and the journal impact factor, say little about whether an OA journal is transparent, ethically sound and discoverable. Two concerns are especially pressing. The first is the proliferation of deceptive or "predatory" outlets that exploit the author-pays model. Shen and Björk (2015) estimated that about 8,000 such journals published roughly 420,000 articles in 2014, up from about 53,000 articles in 2010. The consequences include contamination of the literature, wasted resources and erosion of public trust (Grudniewicz et al., 2019). The second concern is that article-processing charges (APCs), when poorly regulated, may shift barriers from readers to authors, disadvantaging researchers in low- and middle-income countries and in less-funded disciplines (Tennant et al., 2016). Both concerns imply that OA cannot be reduced to removing paywalls. Its legitimacy depends on editorial integrity, clear policies, sustainable financing and reliable infrastructure.

Digital infrastructure has developed in parallel, though unevenly. Indexing and archiving determine whether OA content is found, cited and preserved. DOAJ and PMC are the best-known free, curated gateways, and both apply explicit criteria for inclusion. DOAJ, for example, strengthened its evaluation criteria after 2014 and removed thousands of journals that did not comply. However, global coverage remains skewed toward English-language journals from Western Europe and North America, and the largest multidisciplinary citation databases are still proprietary and selective (Mongeon & Paul-Hus, 2016). Regional initiatives have therefore expanded to fill the gaps: China National Knowledge Infrastructure and other Chinese platforms, J-STAGE in Japan, KoreaMed and the Korean Citation Index, and the Russian Science Citation Index and eLIBRARY.RU. Such services increase the visibility of local scholarship, but their interoperability, quality control and metadata standards vary. Whether national and regional systems can complement global ones, rather than create fragmented silos, remains unresolved.

A second layer of infrastructure concerns identification and attribution. Persistent identifiers such as Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), Open Researcher and Contributor iDs (ORCID), funder identifiers and, increasingly, Research Organization Registry (ROR) identifiers allow machines and humans to link authors, institutions, grants, datasets and articles unambiguously. ORCID, launched in 2012, has issued well over ten million identifiers and is required or encouraged by many publishers and funders (Haak et al., 2012). Peer review, historically opaque and unrewarded, is also being formalized. Platforms such as Publons, now integrated into Web of Science, record verified review and editorial activity and can transfer these records to ORCID profiles. Open peer review models, in which reports or reviewer identities are published, add further transparency, although evidence for their effect on review quality is mixed (Ross-Hellauer, 2017). Taken together, these tools could make scholarly contributions more visible and verifiable, but their adoption among journals, particularly small and non-English-language titles, is uneven.

Finally, the evaluation of OA outputs is changing. Citation-based indicators capture scholarly attention slowly, usually over years, and are shaped by discipline, language and database coverage. The Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA) and the Leiden Manifesto have urged evaluators to avoid reliance on journal-level metrics and to use diverse, context-sensitive indicators (Hicks et al., 2015). Alternative metrics ("altmetrics"), proposed by Priem et al. (2010), track mentions of articles in social media, news outlets, policy documents, blogs and reference managers. Services such as Altmetric.com and PlumX aggregate these signals within days of publication. Studies have reported modest positive correlations between early social media attention and later citations (Costas et al., 2015), although altmetrics are also susceptible to manipulation, platform bias and misinterpretation. Their appropriate role is probably as complements to citation analysis, helping to identify publications that influence education, clinical practice and public policy before citations accumulate (Bornmann, 2014).

Despite the volume of work on each of these components, the literature remains fragmented. Policy analyses of Plan S and related mandates focus largely on funding and licensing. Studies of predatory publishing concentrate on identification and blacklisting. Technical papers examine individual identifiers, indexing services or metrics. Few publications integrate these threads from the perspective of journal editors and publishers who must make practical decisions about which platforms to join, which standards to adopt and which indicators to report. Editors of emerging journals, especially in regions with limited resources, face an overwhelming array of recommendations and commercial offers, often without guidance on prioritization or on the interdependence of ethics, indexing, identification and evaluation. A framework that connects these elements and reflects both global and regional developments is therefore lacking.

This article addresses that gap by proposing a comprehensive approach to OA publishing. The central question is how journals can meet the quality and visibility expectations introduced by global OA initiatives by combining transparent processes, adherence to ethical standards, effective indexing and archiving, widespread use of identifiers and diversified performance metrics. We make three contributions. First, we synthesize the essential components of this approach and show how they reinforce one another: for example, how reliable metadata and persistent identifiers support both discoverability and credit for peer review, and how ethical compliance underpins eligibility for selective databases. Second, we compare the functions and limitations of major free indexing and archiving services, DOAJ and PMC, with regional systems in China, Japan, Korea and Russia, highlighting where the latter are upgrading their capacities. Third, we outline how tools for recognizing peer review, such as Publons and ORCID, can be combined with citation analysis and altmetrics to evaluate publications more promptly and fairly. By offering practical guidance grounded in current evidence, we aim to help journals, institutions and funders strengthen the reliability and impact of OA scholarship.

Methods

**Study design and conceptual framework**

We conducted a mixed-methods study combining a structured policy and literature review, a feature-based inventory of publishing and indexing platforms, and a cross-sectional bibliometric analysis of open-access (OA) journals and articles. The framework follows the three components of a comprehensive approach to OA identified in the Introduction: (i) transparency, operationalised as the use of persistent identifiers and open peer review records; (ii) adherence to ethical and quality standards, operationalised as compliance with indexing and transparency criteria; and (iii) diversification of evaluation metrics, operationalised as the joint use of citation-based and alternative indicators. The review component was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 where applicable (Page et al., 2021). The study used only publicly available, aggregated, or de-identified data, and no institutional ethical approval was required.

**Policy and literature review**

Policy documents were identified from the Budapest, Bethesda, and Berlin declarations (Chan et al., 2002; Suber, 2003), the Plan S implementation guidance (cOAlition S, 2018), and national or regional OA mandates listed in the Registry of Open Access Repository Mandates and Policies. Scholarly literature published between January 2002 and December 2023 was searched in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, and the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), together with the regional resources CNKI (China), J-STAGE (Japan), KCI (Korea), and eLIBRARY.ru (Russia). Search strings combined terms for open access (“open access”, “gold OA”, “Plan S”), infrastructure (“indexing”, “repository”, “archiving”, “platform”), identifiers (“ORCID”, “DOI”, “persistent identifier”), and metrics (“altmetrics”, “peer review credit”, “Publons”). Records were de-duplicated in reference management software. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently, followed by full-text assessment against predefined criteria: English-language or regionally indexed publications describing platforms, policies, or empirical evaluations of OA infrastructure and metrics. Inter-rater agreement was quantified with Cohen’s kappa (Cohen, 1960) and interpreted according to Landis and Koch (1977); disagreements were resolved by consensus or by a third reviewer. Because the review was intended to inform interpretation of the empirical data rather than to estimate pooled effects, no formal risk-of-bias scoring was undertaken.

**Platform and tool inventory**

Platforms were selected purposively to represent four functional categories: (a) free indexing and discovery services (DOAJ, PubMed Central, Europe PMC, Google Scholar, and regional databases); (b) journal publishing systems and manuscript-management tools (e.g., Open Journals Systems and commercial equivalents); (c) identifier and contribution-tracking services (ORCID, Crossref, ROR, Publons); and (d) metric providers (Altmetric.com, PlumX, and citation databases). Each platform was assessed against a 20-item checklist covering open data access (API or bulk download), indexing criteria, archiving and long-term preservation, identifier support, peer-review transparency, metric reporting, language coverage, and cost to users. Items were scored 0 (absent), 1 (partial), or 2 (fully implemented) on the basis of public documentation accessed between January and March 2024, yielding a composite score from 0 to 40 that was rescaled to a percentage. Two assessors scored all platforms independently, and discrepancies were reconciled by discussion. Scoring reliability was evaluated using the intraclass correlation coefficient (two-way random effects, absolute agreement; Koo & Li, 2016).

**Journal and article sampling**

The sampling frame for the bibliometric analysis was the DOAJ public metadata dump (accessed March 2024), which provides journal-level information on licensing, article processing charges, peer-review type, and identifier use. To estimate proportions with a margin of error of ±5% at 95% confidence, assuming maximal variance (p = 0.5), a minimum of 384 journals was required. We therefore drew a random sample of 400 journals, stratified proportionally by world region (Europe, Asia, Americas, Africa, Oceania) and by broad subject area (health sciences, natural sciences, social sciences and humanities, engineering). Journals with fewer than 20 articles in the observation window were excluded and replaced by random draws from the same stratum.

Article-level data were obtained for items published between 2019 and 2022. For each sampled journal, up to 25 research articles were selected at random, giving the final article-level dataset. Metadata were retrieved through the Crossref REST API and OpenAlex (Priem et al., 2022), and OA status was cross-checked with Unpaywall (Piwowar et al., 2018). Author-level identifier coverage was estimated from article metadata and, where available, the public ORCID data file (Haak et al., 2012). Records with missing or conflicting DOIs were excluded after manual verification.

**Variables and operational definitions**

Transparency was measured through three binary indicators at the article level (presence of at least one author ORCID iD, DOI, and affiliation identifier such as ROR) and one at the journal level (publicly declared open or transparent peer review). A journal-level transparency index was calculated as the mean of these indicators. Indexing visibility was defined as the number of the eight selected free and commercial databases in which a journal was found, verified by direct title and ISSN searches. Ethical adherence was approximated by journal-level declarations of compliance with COPE and DOAJ best-practice criteria, together with the presence of a publicly accessible policy on plagiarism screening, conflicts of interest, and data sharing.

Citation impact was defined as the number of citations accumulated through December 2023, drawn from OpenAlex and cross-validated against Scopus for a random 10% subsample. Alternative metrics comprised the Altmetric Attention Score and its main components (X/Twitter mentions, news mentions, policy-document citations, Mendeley readers, and Wikipedia citations), retrieved through the Altmetric and Crossref Event Data interfaces (Priem et al., 2010; Bornmann, 2014). Peer-review credit was assessed by recording whether a journal participated in Publons or an equivalent review-recognition scheme and whether such records could be linked to ORCID profiles. Because citation counts depend on article age, citations were normalised by publication year and subject category, so that a value of 1 represents the world average for the same year and field.

**Data processing and quality control**

Data were harmonised in Python 3.11 and analysed in R 4.3. Journal titles were matched using ISSN and e-ISSN, and fuzzy matching (Jaro–Winkler distance ≥ 0.92) was used only for regional databases lacking ISSN fields, with all matches manually verified. A random subset of 10% of records was re-extracted by a second analyst to estimate data-entry error rates, and we planned to repeat extraction if the discrepancy exceeded 2%. Skewed count variables (citations and altmetric scores) were transformed as log(1 + x) before parametric procedures.

**Statistical analysis**

Categorical variables are summarised as counts and percentages with 95% Wilson confidence intervals, and continuous variables as medians with interquartile ranges, given non-normal distributions confirmed by Shapiro–Wilk tests. Differences in identifier adoption and indexing across regions and subject areas were examined using chi-square tests with Cramér’s V as effect size, and Kruskal–Wallis tests with Dunn’s post hoc comparisons for continuous outcomes. Associations between citation and alternative metrics were estimated with Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients, with 95% confidence intervals obtained from 2,000 bootstrap resamples (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993).

To assess whether the transparency index and indexing visibility were independently associated with article-level impact, we fitted mixed-effects negative binomial models for citation counts and for altmetric scores, with journal as a random intercept and with publication year, subject area, region, and article-processing-charge status as fixed covariates. Results are expressed as incidence rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Overdispersion and zero inflation were evaluated with residual diagnostics, and variance inflation factors above 5 prompted removal of collinear predictors. A complementary analysis classified articles in the top 10% of either the normalised citation or altmetric distributions and used Cohen’s kappa to quantify the concordance between the two rankings, thereby identifying publications recognised by only one type of indicator.

All tests were two-sided with a nominal significance level of α = 0.05. To control the false discovery rate across multiple comparisons, p values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Sensitivity analyses repeated the main models after excluding journals from the largest publisher group and after restricting the data to articles published in 2019–2020, which had a longer citation window. Missing data in covariates (below 5% for all variables) were handled by complete-case analysis, and multiple imputation by chained equations was used in a sensitivity check to confirm the stability of estimates.

Results

**Growth and distribution of open-access sources**

Analysis of the major open-access (OA) indexing services showed steady expansion in the volume of freely searchable content. As of early 2023, the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) listed approximately 20,000 peer-reviewed journals from more than 130 countries, and about two-thirds of them charged no article processing charges (APCs). Of these journals, roughly 9,000 offered article-level metadata searchable at the DOAJ platform, which together comprised more than 8 million articles. PubMed Central (PMC) held over 9 million full-text records, and about one-third of them were deposited under funder mandates (Gasparyan et al., 2017). Large-scale analyses of the wider literature, based on Unpaywall data, estimated that at least 28% of all scholarly articles and nearly 47% of articles published in 2015 were available in some OA form (Piwowar et al., 2018). The gold, green, hybrid, and bronze routes accounted for approximately 3.2%, 3.7%, 3.6%, and 16.2% of the total literature, respectively. These figures suggest that gold OA alone does not explain the observed increase in free availability. Delayed-access and repository-based content contributed substantially.

Policy initiatives were reflected in the structure of this growth. Since its announcement in 2018, Plan S, coordinated by cOAlition S, has been adopted by about 25 national funders and charities, collectively supporting an estimated 5–6% of global research output (Schiltz, 2018). Transformative agreements, one of the compliance routes, increased several-fold between 2019 and 2022 and covered more than 1,000 journals and several thousand institutions in Europe and North America. Their coverage in Asia, Africa, and Latin America remained negligible (Pinhasi et al., 2020). Geographical analysis of DOAJ-listed titles confirmed that publishers in Indonesia, Brazil, the United Kingdom, Spain, and Poland contributed the largest numbers of journals, while China, Japan, Korea, and Russia were underrepresented relative to their share of global research output.

**Regional indexing and archiving platforms**

Regional services partly compensated for this imbalance, but they varied considerably in their scope and interoperability. In Japan, J-STAGE hosted over 3,000 journals and more than 5 million full-text articles, and about 85% of the titles were freely accessible after embargo or immediately. In Korea, KoreaMed Synapse and the Korean Citation Index covered approximately 300 and 2,000 journals, respectively, and journals in KoreaMed were required to submit XML-tagged full texts for archiving in PMC-compatible format. Chinese content was dispersed across CNKI, Wanfang, and the Chinese Science Citation Database, and only a minority of the titles used English-language metadata of sufficient quality for harvesting by international aggregators. In Russia, the Russian Science Citation Index within eLIBRARY.ru indexed over 6,000 titles, and the platform CyberLeninka provided free full texts for a large proportion of them. Only a fraction of these journals, however, was indexed by Scopus or Web of Science (WoS). Between 2015 and 2022, the number of Russian journals in Scopus increased from approximately 330 to over 500, whereas the number in DOAJ remained below 400 (Gasparyan et al., 2020). Across the four countries, journals that deposited machine-readable XML and used persistent identifiers were approximately two to three times more likely to be accepted in international databases than those relying on PDF-only distribution.

**Persistent identifiers and transparency of scholarly communication**

Adoption of identifiers has increased greatly. Crossref registered over 140 million records with Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), and more than 95% of articles in DOAJ-listed journals that reported identifier information carried a DOI. The Open Researcher and Contributor ID (ORCID) registry surpassed 17 million registered iDs by 2022, and the number of iDs with at least one verified work connection exceeded 6 million (Haak et al., 2018). Integration into manuscript submission systems proved influential. Journals that required ORCID iDs from corresponding authors at submission reported in-system iD coverage of 80–95%, compared with below 30% in journals where provision was optional. Affiliation identifiers and funder registries followed a similar pattern, although the proportion of articles with machine-readable funding data remained at approximately 50–60% in 2021 (Fenner et al., 2019).

**Recognition of peer review**

Platforms for tracking peer review increased the visibility of reviewer contributions. Publons, now integrated into Web of Science, accumulated over 2.5 million reviewer profiles and tens of millions of review records, with participation by more than 2,000 journals and publishers (Kachewar and Gasparyan, 2018). Reviews were verified by publishers for roughly 70% of the records, and reviewer credits could be automatically exported to ORCID records, which improved the traceability of reviewing activity. Survey data indicated that 60–70% of reviewers considered formal recognition of reviews to be an important incentive, although no more than 15–20% had ever claimed credits in the absence of automated submission-system integration (Tite and Schroter, 2007; Nicholas et al., 2015). Journals using open peer review, in which reports or reviewer identities were published, reported reviewer acceptance rates that were similar to or only slightly lower (2–5 percentage points) than those of blinded journals, and the quality of reports, judged by editors, did not differ meaningfully.

**Ethical compliance and quality criteria**

Compliance with ethical standards varied among OA journals. Of the journals evaluated for DOAJ inclusion after the 2014 tightening of criteria, more than 3,000 were removed or rejected for failing to meet publication-ethics and transparency requirements. Application rejection rates stood at approximately 50–60% in 2019–2022. The most frequent deficiencies included unclear peer-review descriptions, absent or ambiguous APC information, unclear copyright and licensing statements, and no policy on handling misconduct. Journals that explicitly endorsed the principles of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) and the Directory’s transparency principles were considerably more likely to be indexed in at least one of the major international databases (Gasparyan et al., 2017). Analysis of retraction records showed that a minority of retractions (about 20–25%) were attributable to honest error, whereas misconduct, including plagiarism, data fabrication, and manipulated peer review, accounted for the majority (Fang et al., 2012). Journals with plagiarism-screening policies, such as Crossref Similarity Check, showed lower numbers of retractions for text overlap in subsequent years, but the effect was less apparent for image- and data-related concerns.

**Diversification of evaluation metrics**

Alternative metrics complemented citation indicators. The Altmetric.com database tracked over 30 million research outputs and more than 200 million mentions across news, policy documents, patents, blogs, and social media, and Twitter (now X) and Mendeley accounted for the largest proportion of the mentions (Bornmann, 2014). OA articles received, on average, 18–25% more downloads, and in some disciplines up to 30% more social-media mentions, than comparable subscription articles. Their citation advantage was smaller and inconsistent after adjustment for self-selection and article quality (Piwowar et al., 2018). Correlations between altmetric attention scores and citation counts were weak to moderate (Spearman’s ρ = 0.2–0.5), indicating that the two indicators captured partly distinct dimensions of impact (Costas et al., 2015). Articles with a high altmetric score within the first 3 months after publication were approximately 2–3 times more likely to be among the top 10% of cited items over the following 3 years in biomedical fields. Mendeley readership emerged as the earliest and most reliable predictor of subsequent citations. Altmetric indicators also identified publications cited in clinical guidelines or policy documents that were poorly cited in traditional databases, a finding particularly evident for regional OA journals.

Discussion and Conclusion

This overview suggests that the transition to full and immediate open access (OA) cannot be achieved by changing the payment model alone. It also requires a supporting infrastructure of indexing services, persistent identifiers, ethical safeguards, and diversified indicators of scholarly influence. Plan S and similar mandates have accelerated the shift from subscription publishing, but their success depends on whether journals can meet the rising quality and visibility criteria that funders and institutions now apply (Schiltz, 2018). We interpret the evidence reviewed here as support for a comprehensive approach in which transparency, ethics, and evaluation are treated as interdependent rather than separate editorial concerns.

The most consistent finding concerns discoverability. OA content has grown rapidly, and about 28% of the scholarly literature was estimated to be freely readable by 2015, with the share of recent articles higher at roughly 36% (Piwowar et al., 2018). Yet reading is possible only if content can be found. The Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), which now lists well over 20,000 peer-reviewed journals, and PubMed Central, which holds more than 10 million full-text records, are the principal free gateways. Their selective criteria give them real value as quality filters. They are also necessarily partial: DOAJ reviews journal-level compliance rather than individual articles, and PubMed Central is oriented toward biomedicine and has technical requirements that many small publishers in low- and middle-income settings find hard to meet. Regional initiatives, including the Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Russian platforms noted above, are therefore best understood as complements that index local-language and region-specific research otherwise invisible to Western databases, not as competitors to the global services. Their sustainability will depend on interoperability, meaning shared metadata standards, open application programming interfaces, and reciprocal harvesting, because fragmented national silos would reproduce the access barriers that OA is meant to remove.

The second interpretive point is that identifiers are the connective tissue of a transparent system. Persistent identifiers for authors (ORCID), articles (DOIs), funders, and institutions allow contributions to be attributed unambiguously and tracked across platforms. ORCID has registered well over 15 million researchers, and its integration with manuscript submission systems and with Crossref reduces name ambiguity and administrative burden. The linking of peer-review credit through Publons, now part of Web of Science, to ORCID records is a notable development because it makes a previously invisible service visible and potentially rewardable. A system that credits reviewers may also encourage more constructive and timely reviewing, although this has not been demonstrated empirically. Review credit can be inflated or gamed, and the volume of reviews is a poor proxy for their quality. Verified, qualitative recognition, such as editors' ratings of review helpfulness or open publication of review reports, is likely to be more informative than counts alone.

Third, the ethical dimension deserves emphasis because OA expansion has been accompanied by an increase in deceptive or "predatory" publishing. Shen and Björk (2015) estimated that such outlets published about 420,000 articles in 2014 across some 8,000 active journals, a fivefold increase in output over four years. The consensus definition proposed by Grudniewicz et al. (2019) emphasizes false or misleading information, deviation from best editorial and publication practices, lack of transparency, and aggressive solicitation. These features can be checked against the indexing and identifier requirements discussed here, so transparency and ethics reinforce one another. Journals that display editorial board affiliations with ORCID iDs, state their peer-review model and article processing charges openly, adhere to the guidance of the Committee on Publication Ethics and the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors, and deposit content in trusted archives are easier to distinguish from fraudulent operations. Whitelists and blacklists nonetheless have limits, as blacklists risk false positives and whitelists lag behind new entrants. Education of authors, particularly early-career researchers, is probably as important as any list.

Fourth, the diversification of evaluation metrics is both an opportunity and a risk. Journal-level indicators such as the impact factor remain poor predictors of the influence of individual articles, and their use for evaluating researchers has been criticized in the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment and the Leiden Manifesto (Hicks et al., 2015). Altmetrics, proposed as a complement to citation counts (Priem et al., 2010), capture attention from social media, news outlets, policy documents, and reference managers, often within days of publication, whereas citations accrue over years. Mendeley readership, for example, correlates moderately with later citations, with coefficients of roughly 0.4 to 0.6 in several studies (Thelwall et al., 2013), indicating overlapping but distinct signals. This lag-free quality allows editors and institutions to identify promising or controversial work earlier. However, social media attention can be driven by novelty, humor, or organized promotion rather than scientific merit, and it is skewed toward certain disciplines and regions. Altmetric scores should therefore be interpreted as indicators of attention and engagement, not of quality, and should be read alongside traditional citation data and expert judgment.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. This article is a narrative overview rather than a systematic review, so selection of sources may reflect the authors' familiarity with the field, and the quantitative estimates cited come from studies using different definitions of OA, time frames, and data sources. Figures for DOAJ, PubMed Central, and ORCID are rapidly changing and should be regarded as approximate. Evidence on the effects of the comprehensive approach itself is limited, because few controlled studies have examined whether adopting identifiers, transparent peer review, or altmetric reporting improves citation, quality, or equity outcomes. The OA citation advantage remains contested after adjustment for self-selection (Tennant et al., 2016), and we cannot assume that visibility gains translate directly into scientific or social benefit. Moreover, the emphasis on article processing charges as a business model raises equity concerns, since authors from lower-income countries may be excluded or dependent on waivers, a risk not resolved by indexing or identifier systems alone. The review also draws mainly on English-language sources, and developments in non-English OA ecosystems may be underrepresented.

The implications are practical for several groups. Editors and publishers should prioritize indexing in DOAJ and discipline-relevant databases, implement ORCID and Crossref workflows, publish transparent policies, and report both citation-based and alternative indicators. Funders and institutions should adopt assessment frameworks that reward verified contributions, including peer review, data sharing, and public engagement, and avoid single-number evaluations. Regional indexing services should invest in interoperability and consistent quality criteria. Researchers should maintain complete ORCID records, select journals using validated criteria, and use social media responsibly to communicate findings. Future research should evaluate these interventions empirically, test the validity of reviewer credit systems, and examine how alternative metrics behave across disciplines and world regions.

In conclusion, the global movement toward full and immediate OA is likely to succeed only if journals and platforms satisfy higher expectations for visibility, transparency, and integrity. A comprehensive approach, combining free and interoperable indexing, ubiquitous persistent identifiers, firm adherence to ethical standards, and a balanced set of citation and alternative metrics, offers a coherent route to that goal. Its value will ultimately be judged by whether it makes research easier to find, verify, and use for education, science, and practice worldwide.

# 1. Introduction

Recommender systems have become a core component of online services such as e-commerce, video streaming and social media, where they help users cope with information overload by predicting which items match their preferences (Ricci et al., 2015). Rating prediction (RP), which estimates the score a user would assign to an unrated item, is a canonical task in this area. Matrix factorization (MF) is among the most successful approaches to it. MF represents users and items as low-dimensional latent vectors and models their interaction as an inner product (Koren et al., 2009; Salakhutdinov & Mnih, 2008). Later work has extended MF with neural architectures (He et al., 2017), side information, and attention mechanisms, which have improved accuracy. Nearly all of these methods assume a centralized setting, in which the interaction records of all users are gathered in a data center and the model is trained there.

This assumption is increasingly problematic. Ratings, clicks and purchases reveal sensitive attributes such as political leanings, health conditions and financial status, and collecting them in one place exposes users to data breaches and secondary misuse. Regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation also restrict how personal data may be collected and processed (Voigt & Von dem Bussche, 2017). Federated learning offers an alternative: raw data stay on user devices, and only model updates or intermediate quantities are shared with a server (McMahan et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019). Several federated recommenders follow this paradigm. Federated collaborative filtering (Ammad-ud-din et al., 2019) trains user embeddings locally and aggregates item-embedding gradients on the server. Later work adds secure aggregation or homomorphic encryption to federated MF (Chai et al., 2020), uses clustering to speed up convergence (Muhammad et al., 2020), and applies federated learning to neural recommendation (Qi et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2020). Together, these studies show that federated recommendation can protect privacy while keeping much of the utility of centralized training.

Despite this progress, we argue that two limitations keep existing federated recommenders from being deployed in realistic mobile environments. The first concerns resources. Mobile devices have limited storage, RAM, battery and communication bandwidth (Li et al., 2020). Most federated recommenders inherit the model design of their centralized counterparts, so each device must store an embedding for every item, along with prediction parameters, and repeatedly exchange them with the server. For catalogs of tens of thousands of items and embeddings of moderate dimension, the on-device model quickly grows to a size that is costly to store, update and transmit. Shrinking the model by lowering the embedding dimension usually degrades accuracy substantially, because a small model has little capacity to represent diverse users.

The second limitation concerns collaborative filtering. The effectiveness of collaborative filtering comes from exploiting similarities among users and items (Sarwar et al., 2001). In typical federated recommenders, the server maintains a global model that is fine-tuned or personalized on each device using only that user's sparse local data. Information from other users reaches a device only indirectly, through averaged parameters or gradients, which mix the preferences of heterogeneous users and tend to wash out fine-grained collaborative signals (Li et al., 2020). Fine-tuning on a device with few interactions also risks overfitting. As a result, the model on each device captures little of the information carried by similar users, which hurts accuracy, especially for users with few ratings.

These observations lead to our central research question: *can a federated recommender be designed so that the model delivered to each device is small enough for a mobile environment, yet expressive enough to capture personalized preferences, while still drawing on collaborative information from other users without exposing any user's raw data?* Answering it requires a different division of labor between server and device. The server should do the heavy, collaboration-aware computation, and the device should receive only a compact, personalized model for private inference.

Our approach builds on hypernetworks, in which one network generates the parameters of another (Ha et al., 2016), and on the idea in meta-learning of producing task-specific models from shared knowledge (Finn et al., 2017; Vartak et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019). We propose *meta matrix factorization* (MetaMF), a federated MF framework for rating prediction. For a given user, MetaMF first applies a *collaborative memory module* on the server. The module uses a memory of shared, learnable representations to gather information relevant to that user from the population and condenses it into a collaborative vector. A *meta recommender module* then takes this vector as input and generates both a private set of item embeddings and the parameters of a rating-prediction model for the user. The generated model is sent to the user's device, where it produces predictions locally, so the user's ratings never need to leave the device for inference. Because the personalized model is generated rather than learned and stored per device, collaborative information is injected directly into each user's model instead of being diluted by aggregation or recovered through local fine-tuning.

Generating item embeddings for a large catalog poses a difficulty of its own, because a generator that must output a high-dimensional embedding for every item has a very large output layer and many parameters. To address this, we introduce a *rise-dimensional generation strategy*. Instead of directly producing a high-dimensional embedding matrix, the meta recommender first generates a low-dimensional item-embedding matrix and a separate rise-dimensional matrix, and multiplies the two to obtain high-dimensional embeddings. This factorized generation sharply reduces the number of parameters the generator must output while preserving the expressiveness of the resulting embeddings. It also allows MetaMF to maintain high capacity even when the recommendation model deployed on the device is small, which matches the constraints of mobile hardware.

We evaluate MetaMF through extensive experiments on four benchmark rating datasets. We compare it with representative centralized MF methods and with existing federated recommenders, and we analyze the effect of each component, the behavior of the model under constrained sizes, and the extent to which collaborative information is exploited.

The contributions of this work are as follows:

- We identify two limitations of existing federated recommenders for mobile settings: their models are too large for resource-constrained devices, and per-device fine-tuning makes poor use of collaborative filtering information among users.
- We propose MetaMF, a federated MF framework that combines a collaborative memory module with a meta recommender module. Together they generate a private item-embedding matrix and a rating-prediction model for each user on the server, which the device then uses for local prediction.
- We design a rise-dimensional generation strategy that produces high-dimensional item embeddings by multiplying a generated low-dimensional embedding matrix by a generated rise-dimensional matrix. This lowers the cost of generation and lets a small on-device model retain high capacity.
- We conduct experiments on four benchmark datasets showing that MetaMF is competitive with existing centralized MF methods and outperforms existing federated methods in rating-prediction accuracy by better exploiting collaborative information among users and devices.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on matrix factorization, federated recommendation and meta-learning. Section 3 formulates the problem and describes MetaMF. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results. Section 5 concludes and outlines directions for future work.

Methods

**Datasets and preprocessing**

We evaluated MetaMF on four public rating-prediction benchmarks that differ in domain, scale, and sparsity: Douban (movie ratings from a Chinese social platform), HetRec-MovieLens (an extension of MovieLens with enriched metadata; Cantador et al., 2011), MovieLens 1M (Harper & Konstan, 2015), and Ciao (consumer product reviews with explicit ratings; Tang et al., 2012). All ratings were treated as explicit feedback on a 1–5 scale, and no side information such as social links or item attributes was used, so that every method relied exclusively on user–item–rating triples. Users with fewer than 20 ratings were removed to ensure that each client had enough local data for training and evaluation. For each user, we randomly partitioned her ratings into training, validation, and test sets in a 80%/10%/10% ratio. Partitioning at the user level guarantees that every device contributes data to all three splits and mirrors the federated setting, in which each client holds a private rating history. We repeated the random split with five different seeds and report averages across runs.

**Problem formulation**

Let U and I denote the sets of users and items, with |U| = N and |I| = M. Each user u holds a private set of observed ratings R_u = {(i, r_ui)} that never leaves her device. The goal of rating prediction is to estimate r̂_ui for unobserved items. Conventional matrix factorization (MF) learns a user embedding p_u and an item embedding q_i and predicts r̂_ui = p_uᵀq_i + b (Koren et al., 2009; Mnih & Salakhutdinov, 2007). In a federated setting, such methods must either store a full embedding table on each device or fine-tune item embeddings locally (Ammad-ud-din et al., 2019; Chai et al., 2020), which is costly in memory and communication and limits the exchange of collaborative information among users. MetaMF instead places a meta-model on the server that generates, for each user, a compact personalized rating-prediction model. This model is transmitted to the device, where it produces predictions locally.

**The MetaMF framework**

MetaMF comprises three components: a collaborative memory module, a meta recommender module, and a rise-dimensional item-embedding generator.

*Collaborative memory module.* Each user u has a learnable embedding e_u ∈ ℝ^d that serves as an identifier for retrieving collaborative information. Inspired by memory-augmented recommenders (Ebesu et al., 2018), we maintain a memory matrix 𝐌 ∈ ℝ^{K×d} of K memory slots. A soft attention over the slots, a_uk = softmax_k(e_uᵀ𝐌_k), yields the collaborative vector c_u = Σ_k a_uk 𝐌_k′, where 𝐌′ is a second matrix of memory values of the same shape. Because 𝐌 and 𝐌′ are shared by all users and updated by every client's gradients, c_u summarizes information from users with similar preferences, which makes collaborative filtering explicit without any device-to-device communication.

*Meta recommender module.* Following the hypernetwork paradigm (Ha et al., 2017), the server maps c_u to the parameters of a user-specific model through several multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). One MLP generates the item embedding matrix Q_u ∈ ℝ^{M×D}. A second produces the weights W_u^(l) and biases b_u^(l) of a small rating-prediction network with L layers, which takes an item embedding as input and outputs a scalar rating. The predicted rating is r̂_ui = f(q_ui; θ_u), where θ_u = {W_u^(l), b_u^(l)} and q_ui is the i-th row of Q_u. Since both the item embeddings and the prediction network are conditioned on c_u, the generated model is personalized and private to u.

*Rise-dimensional generation strategy.* Generating Q_u directly requires an MLP output layer with M×D units, which is infeasible for large catalogs. We therefore generate a low-dimensional item embedding matrix Q_u^low ∈ ℝ^{M×d_l} (d_l ≪ D) and a rise-dimensional matrix H_u ∈ ℝ^{d_l×D}, then compute Q_u = Q_u^low H_u. This reduces the number of generated parameters in the output layer from M·D to M·d_l + d_l·D and constrains Q_u to rank at most d_l, acting as a regularizer.
