In our main experiments, d = 64, K = 100, d_l = 8, D = 64, and the prediction network has L = 2 layers with 8 hidden units. These values yielded the lowest validation error in a grid search over d ∈ {32, 64, 128}, K ∈ {50, 100, 200}, d_l ∈ {4, 8, 16}, and hidden width ∈ {8, 16, 32}.

**Federated training procedure**

Training follows a client–server protocol in the spirit of federated averaging (McMahan et al., 2017). In each communication round, the server samples a batch of B clients. For each sampled user u, the server computes c_u, generates (Q_u, θ_u), and sends them to the device. The device calculates the squared-error loss on its local training ratings, L_u = (1/|R_u|) Σ (r_ui − r̂_ui)², and returns the gradients with respect to the generated parameters. Raw ratings, and the items a user has rated, are never uploaded. The server back-propagates these gradients through the generator and memory module and updates all shared parameters (the user embeddings, 𝐌, 𝐌′, and the MLP weights). Optimization used Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a learning rate of 1e-3, weight decay of 1e-4, batch size B = 64, and up to 100 epochs. Early stopping was applied when validation root mean squared error (RMSE) did not improve for 10 consecutive epochs. At inference, the server generates the model for each user once, and the device then computes predictions offline.

**Baselines**

We compared MetaMF with centralized and federated methods. Centralized baselines were probabilistic matrix factorization (PMF; Mnih & Salakhutdinov, 2007), the classical biased MF of Koren et al. (2009), neural collaborative filtering (NCF; He et al., 2017), and AutoRec (Sedhain et al., 2015). Federated baselines were FedMF (Chai et al., 2020), federated collaborative filtering (FCF; Ammad-ud-din et al., 2019), and a federated version of NCF trained with federated averaging. All baselines were tuned on the validation set with the same search protocol; embedding sizes were selected from {8, 16, 32, 64, 128}, and regularization coefficients from {1e-5, …, 1e-2}. For federated baselines, local fine-tuning of item embeddings was performed for five local epochs per round, consistent with the original implementations.

**Evaluation metrics and resource analysis**

Predictive accuracy was measured by RMSE and mean absolute error (MAE) on the held-out test ratings, computed over all test interactions. Lower values indicate better performance. To assess suitability for mobile environments, we additionally report the number of parameters transmitted to and stored on each device, the model size in kilobytes (32-bit floats), and the per-user inference time on a single CPU thread. We also conducted ablation studies by (i) removing the collaborative memory module and replacing c_u with e_u, (ii) removing the rise-dimensional strategy by generating Q_u directly, and (iii) varying the number of memory slots K and the low dimension d_l to quantify sensitivity.

**Statistical analysis**

All results are reported as mean ± standard deviation over five independent runs, each using a different data split and random initialization. Differences between MetaMF and the strongest competing method on each dataset were evaluated with a two-sided paired t-test on per-run RMSE and MAE, with significance declared at p < 0.05. Because multiple baselines and datasets were compared, we applied Holm–Bonferroni correction to control the family-wise error rate. To examine whether gains were concentrated among particular user groups, we also stratified users into terciles by number of training ratings and computed RMSE within each stratum. All experiments were implemented in PyTorch and run on a single NVIDIA GPU; code and splits will be released to support reproducibility.

Results

**Experimental protocol.** We evaluated MetaMF on four benchmark datasets: Douban, Hetrec-MovieLens, MovieLens 1M (Harper & Konstan, 2015), and Ciao (Tang et al., 2012). Each dataset was split 80%/10%/10% into training, validation, and test sets. We report mean squared error (MSE) on the test set, where lower is better, averaged over five runs with different random seeds. We compared MetaMF with two groups of baselines. The centralized group comprises probabilistic MF (Mnih & Salakhutdinov, 2007), non-negative MF (Lee & Seung, 2001), classical MF (Koren et al., 2009), and neural collaborative filtering (NeuMF; He et al., 2017). The federated group comprises FedMF (Chai et al., 2020) and FedRec (Lin et al., 2020), both of which fine-tune a local model on each device. Unless stated otherwise, all differences discussed below were significant under a paired *t*-test (*p* < 0.01).

**Comparison with centralized methods.** MetaMF achieved competitive accuracy against centralized MF-based models on all four datasets, although it never accesses raw user–item interactions on a shared device. On Douban, MetaMF obtained an MSE of 0.6221, against 0.6320 for MF, 0.6355 for NMF, 0.6508 for PMF, and 0.6179 for NeuMF. On Hetrec-MovieLens, MetaMF reached 0.7268, improving on MF (0.7425) and NeuMF (0.7312). On MovieLens 1M, MetaMF obtained 0.7722, compared with 0.7803 for MF and 0.7716 for NeuMF, so the gap to the strongest centralized model was below 0.1%. On Ciao, the sparsest dataset, MetaMF obtained 1.0391 and outperformed every centralized baseline, including NeuMF (1.0524, a 1.3% reduction) and MF (1.0687, a 2.8% reduction). Averaged over the four datasets, MetaMF reduced MSE by 1.9% relative to MF and was within 0.4% of NeuMF. This suggests that generating user-specific models from a collaborative vector captures much of the nonlinear interaction structure that NeuMF models explicitly.

**Comparison with federated methods.** The advantage of MetaMF was largest against the federated baselines. On Douban, FedMF and FedRec reached MSEs of 0.6903 and 0.6765, whereas MetaMF reached 0.6221, a 8.0% relative reduction against the stronger baseline. The corresponding reductions against FedRec were 8.0% on Hetrec-MovieLens (0.7268 vs. 0.7897), 5.6% on MovieLens 1M (0.7722 vs. 0.8176), and 8.4% on Ciao (1.0391 vs. 1.1346). Across datasets, MetaMF lowered MSE by 7.5% on average compared with FedRec and by 9.6% compared with FedMF. These gains are consistent with our central hypothesis. Methods that fine-tune a model on each device rely on a user's own sparse ratings and cannot transfer information between users. In MetaMF, the collaborative memory module aggregates information from similar users on the server, so each generated model reflects collaborative filtering signals. The gains were also larger on the two sparser datasets (Douban, Ciao), where a single user's data is least informative.

**Performance across user activity levels.** To test whether the gains stem from better collaborative filtering, we stratified test users by training-set rating count. For users with fewer than 20 ratings, MetaMF reduced MSE by 10.3% relative to FedRec on MovieLens 1M, and by 11.7% on Ciao. For users with more than 100 ratings, the reductions fell to 4.9% and 5.8%, respectively. Federated fine-tuning thus degrades most when local evidence is scarce, whereas MetaMF substitutes information from comparable users. The gap to centralized MF showed the same pattern. For low-activity users, MetaMF was 2.4% better than MF on MovieLens 1M, while for high-activity users it was 0.9% worse, which indicates that the collaborative vector is most valuable where the user's own history is weakest.

**Model size and communication cost.** A principal motivation of this work is the resource limit of mobile devices. On MovieLens 1M (3,706 items), FedMF and FedRec each store a 128-dimensional embedding for every item on the device, amounting to roughly 474K item parameters (about 1.9 MB in 32-bit precision). The RP model generated by MetaMF for each user used low-dimensional private item embeddings of size 8 that were expanded on-device through a shared rise-dimensional matrix. This reduced the transmitted per-user model to about 41K parameters (0.16 MB), an 91% reduction in downlink payload per round. Even so, MetaMF improved on FedRec by 5.6% in MSE. When we constrained the centralized MF and FedRec models to the same parameter budget, their MSE rose to 0.7961 and 0.8374, respectively, so MetaMF's advantage widened to 8.0% against the size-matched FedRec. MetaMF therefore showed a high capacity even with a small RP model.

**Ablation of the rise-dimensional generation strategy.** We compared the full model with a variant that directly generates the high-dimensional item embedding matrix. The direct variant required a meta recommender module with 4.87M parameters on MovieLens 1M, while the rise-dimensional version needed only 0.62M, an 87% reduction. Accuracy did not suffer: the direct variant reached an MSE of 0.7788 and the rise-dimensional version 0.7722. We observed the same ordering on Douban (0.6290 vs. 0.6221) and Ciao (1.0452 vs. 1.0391). Factorizing generation into a low-dimensional item matrix and a rise-dimensional matrix thus acts as a low-rank regularizer, as well as lowering the parameter count of the generator, in line with the parameter-efficiency rationale of hypernetworks (Ha et al., 2017).

**Ablation of the collaborative memory module.** Replacing the collaborative memory with a randomly initialized, user-specific vector learned independently of other users raised MSE from 0.6221 to 0.6489 on Douban (+4.3%), from 0.7268 to 0.7535 on Hetrec-MovieLens (+3.7%), from 0.7722 to 0.7904 on MovieLens 1M (+2.4%), and from 1.0391 to 1.0873 on Ciao (+4.6%). Removing the meta recommender's user-specific generation of the RP model, so that all users share one set of parameters, produced larger losses of 5.1% to 7.8%. Both components therefore contribute, and the generation of private models matters more than the memory read alone.

**Hyperparameter sensitivity.** The dimension of the collaborative vector influenced accuracy modestly. On MovieLens 1M, MSE decreased from 0.7869 at dimension 16 to 0.7722 at dimension 64 and then plateaued (0.7719 at 128). The number of memory slots showed a similar saturation: 100 slots gave 0.7801, 200 slots 0.7722, and 400 slots 0.7725. We adopted dimension 64 and 200 slots as defaults. MetaMF also converged within about 40 training epochs on all datasets, comparable to centralized MF.

Discussion and Conclusion

Interpretation of the main findings

This study set out to determine whether a federated rating predictor can meet the resource constraints of mobile devices while still exploiting collaborative filtering signals across users. Our results support both aims. Across four benchmark datasets, MetaMF achieved rating-prediction error comparable to centralized matrix factorization baselines such as PMF (Mnih & Salakhutdinov, 2008) and neural variants such as NeuMF (He et al., 2017), and it improved over existing federated approaches, including FedRec (Lin et al., 2020) and FedMF (Chai et al., 2020). Several lines of evidence suggest that these gains come from the architectural choices of MetaMF rather than from increased capacity on the device.

First, the advantage over federated baselines is consistent with the view that on-device fine-tuning is a weak mechanism for sharing collaborative information. In methods that personalize a global model locally, each device updates parameters using only its own sparse ratings, and cross-user structure enters only indirectly through aggregated gradients. In MetaMF, the collaborative memory module builds a user-specific collaborative vector by attending over a shared memory, so similarity between users is encoded explicitly at inference time. The meta recommender module then converts this vector into private item embeddings and prediction parameters. In this sense, personalization is moved from local optimization to server-side generation, which allows a user with few interactions to borrow statistical strength from users with similar profiles. This interpretation is consistent with our finding that the improvement was largest for users with sparse histories, a pattern often observed when collaborative signals compensate for limited individual data (Koren et al., 2009).

Second, the ablation results indicate that the components contribute complementary effects. Removing the collaborative memory yielded the largest degradation, suggesting that the collaborative vector, rather than the generator alone, carries most of the useful cross-user information. Removing the rise-dimensional strategy had a smaller effect on accuracy but a substantial effect on the size of the generator, indicating that its primary role is to make generation tractable. By producing a low-dimensional item embedding matrix and expanding it through a rise-dimensional matrix, the model reduces the number of generator parameters roughly in proportion to the ratio between the intermediate and final embedding dimensions. This reflects a general low-rank principle: high-dimensional embeddings often lie close to a lower-dimensional subspace, so factorized generation loses little information while saving considerable computation (Hu et al., 2022; Ha et al., 2017).

Third, MetaMF retained strong performance even when the delivered recommendation model was small. This points to a useful asymmetry. The server may hold a large, expressive generator, whereas the device receives only a compact, user-specific model. Hypernetwork-style generation (Ha et al., 2017) therefore shifts capacity from the device to the server without requiring raw interaction data to leave the device for inference. The effective capacity of the system is thus not the size of the delivered model but the size of the family of models the generator can produce.

Implications

For practice, the results suggest that federated recommendation need not be limited to small shared models with local fine-tuning. A design in which the device stores a few kilobytes to megabytes of generated parameters, performs inexpensive forward passes, and avoids local training can substantially reduce memory, energy, and communication demands, which are the bottlenecks typically cited for mobile deployment (Kairouz et al., 2021). Because only a collaborative vector and generated parameters are exchanged, the communication pattern is also simpler than repeated multi-round gradient exchange. For research, the findings suggest that meta-learning and hypernetwork techniques provide a promising alternative to the dominant paradigm of federated averaging with personalization (McMahan et al., 2017; Fallah et al., 2020), particularly when heterogeneity among clients is large and the quality of recommendations depends on relationships between clients.

Limitations

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The most important concerns privacy. Although MetaMF keeps the final predictions on the device, the server-side generation step requires the server to form a representation of each user. Whether this collaborative vector or the generated embeddings could leak information about a user's ratings, for instance through membership or attribute inference attacks (Shokri et al., 2017), was not formally analyzed. We did not integrate differential privacy (Dwork & Roth, 2014), secure aggregation, or other cryptographic protections, and doing so would likely reduce accuracy by an amount that we have not measured. Our privacy claims should therefore be read as relative to centralized training rather than as formal guarantees.

Second, our experiments were conducted in a simulated federated environment. Resource consumption was estimated from model size and computational cost rather than measured on physical devices, and we did not model client dropout, asynchronous participation, or unreliable networks. Real-world behavior may differ, especially when user populations change over time.

Third, the approach has scalability and cold-start constraints. The generator and collaborative memory reside on the server, so their cost grows with the number of items and users, and the item-embedding generation step may become expensive for catalogs far larger than those in our benchmarks. New users with no ratings receive a collaborative vector that depends on limited information, and new items require extending the generator. We also evaluated only explicit rating prediction with error metrics. Performance on implicit feedback and ranking metrics, which dominate industrial settings (Cremonesi et al., 2010), remains untested. Finally, the datasets are of moderate size and may not capture the sparsity and popularity skew of production systems, and hyperparameters such as memory size and embedding dimensions were tuned on these datasets, which may limit generalization.

Future directions and conclusion

Future work should address the above limitations by combining MetaMF with formal privacy mechanisms and quantifying the accuracy–privacy trade-off, by testing on real devices under realistic network conditions, and by extending the framework to implicit feedback, top-N ranking, and the use of side information. Techniques such as quantization and pruning of the generated models could further reduce on-device cost.

In conclusion, we proposed MetaMF, a federated matrix factorization framework in which a collaborative memory and a meta recommender generate private item embeddings and prediction models for each user, with a rise-dimensional strategy making the generation efficient. Experiments on four benchmarks showed competitive accuracy relative to centralized methods and superior accuracy relative to existing federated methods, along with a small on-device footprint. These results indicate that generating personalized models from collaborative information is an effective and resource-conscious alternative to local fine-tuning for federated rating prediction.

Introduction

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), principally cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancers and chronic respiratory disease, are the leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for roughly two-thirds of global mortality (World Health Organization, 2011). Their economic burden is substantial. Bloom and colleagues (2011) projected cumulative global output losses of approximately US$30 trillion between 2011 and 2030. The costs also include health-care expenditure, lost productivity and reduced quality of life for individuals and families. A considerable proportion of this burden is attributable to modifiable risk factors, and poor diet is among the most important (Lim et al., 2012). Dietary patterns characterised by high intakes of energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods, sugar-sweetened beverages, saturated fat and sodium, together with low intakes of fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, are consistently associated with obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and increased all-cause mortality (Lim et al., 2012; World Health Organization, 2003). Modelling studies suggest that population-level dietary change could deliver sizeable health gains at relatively low cost (Cecchini et al., 2010). The combined economic and social costs of NCDs therefore provide a compelling rationale for strategies that target dietary behaviour.

Overall dietary patterns are built from many individual, repeated decisions about what to eat. These discrete food choices, such as selecting fruit rather than a confectionery snack, ordering a sugar-sweetened beverage, or trimming visible fat from meat, are the proximal behaviours that interventions must ultimately change. Discrete food choices are also more amenable to precise definition and measurement than global dietary patterns, and they are the level at which many policy instruments, such as menu labelling, price signals and school food standards, operate. Effective intervention requires an understanding of the psychological processes that underpin these decisions. Interventions that are explicitly grounded in theory are widely recommended because theory specifies the mechanisms through which behaviour is expected to change and allows these mechanisms to be tested (Craig et al., 2008; Michie & Prestwich, 2010). Theoretical models thus provide the conceptual order that allows programme designers and policy makers to identify the elements that drive behaviour and to select appropriate intervention techniques.

Among social cognition models, the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB; Ajzen, 1991) is one of the most frequently applied in health research. The TPB, an extension of the Theory of Reasoned Action (Fishbein & Ajzen, 1975), proposes that the proximal determinant of behaviour is intention, which reflects the motivation to perform the behaviour. Intention is in turn determined by three constructs: attitude (the overall evaluation of performing the behaviour), subjective norm (perceived social pressure to perform or not perform the behaviour) and perceived behavioural control (PBC; perceived ease or difficulty of performing the behaviour). Because many behaviours are not fully under volitional control, PBC is additionally proposed to exert a direct effect on behaviour to the extent that it reflects actual control (Ajzen, 1991). The model's parsimony, its clear operational definitions and its generalisability across behaviours have made it attractive to researchers and practitioners alike.

Meta-analytic evidence supports the predictive utility of the TPB across health domains. Armitage and Conner (2001), in a review of 185 independent studies, found that the TPB accounted for 39% of the variance in intention and 27% of the variance in behaviour. Subsequent syntheses have reported similar findings for physical activity (Hagger et al., 2002), and for a range of health behaviours using prospective designs (McEachan et al., 2011). Reviews of the intention–behaviour relationship indicate that intentions explain approximately 28% of the variance in behaviour (Sheeran, 2002), although experimental evidence suggests that even medium-to-large changes in intention produce only small-to-medium changes in behaviour (Webb & Sheeran, 2006). The TPB has also been subject to substantial criticism. Critics have questioned whether it omits important determinants such as habit, affect and automatic processes, whether its constructs are sufficiently distinct, and whether it has generated interventions that effectively change behaviour (Sniehotta et al., 2014). These concerns are especially pertinent for food choice, which is often habitual, cue-driven and shaped by hedonic and environmental factors that lie outside conscious deliberation.

The TPB has nevertheless been widely used to study eating behaviour, and the primary literature now spans a diverse array of food choices. These include increasing consumption of fruit and vegetables, choosing low-fat or whole-grain foods, limiting sweets, snacks and fast food, and avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages. Existing reviews of the TPB and diet have been valuable but limited in important respects. Some have examined dietary behaviour as a single undifferentiated category, or combined food choice with other health behaviours such as physical activity and substance use (Armitage & Conner, 2001; McEachan et al., 2011). Others have focused on a single food group, most commonly fruit and vegetable intake (Guillaumie et al., 2010), or have encompassed a broad set of social cognitive determinants without focusing on TPB relationships. Aggregating across heterogeneous food behaviours may mask meaningful differences in the strength of TPB associations. Conceptually, there are good reasons to expect such differences. Choosing to consume a health-promoting food (an approach behaviour) may be governed by different processes than refraining from a health-compromising but palatable food (an avoidance behaviour), the latter requiring self-regulation against strong hedonic temptations and ready availability. Perceived control may matter more for behaviours that involve resisting temptation than for those that are simply performed. Likewise, the relative influence of attitudes, social norms and control may vary with the characteristics of those making the choice, including age and gender, because developmental stage and social roles shape both autonomy over food and sensitivity to social influence (Conner & Norman, 2005). Yet these potential moderators have rarely been tested systematically within a single synthesis restricted to discrete food choices.

A second limitation concerns the evidential basis of earlier reviews. Rapid growth in the number of TPB food choice studies in recent years means that earlier syntheses omit a considerable body of evidence, and few have systematically sought unpublished work, which may reduce the risk of publication bias. Without a current, comprehensive and behaviourally specific synthesis, researchers lack the quantitative information needed to judge when the TPB is an appropriate framework for understanding dietary decisions, and to prioritise the constructs that interventions should target.

The primary aim of the present systematic review and meta-analysis was therefore to quantify the associations between TPB variables and discrete food choice behaviours. Specifically, we estimated pooled effect sizes for the relationships of attitude, subjective norm and PBC with intention; of intention and PBC with behaviour; and, where data permitted, the inter-correlations among predictors. A secondary aim was to examine the extent and sources of heterogeneity in these associations. Using meta-regression, we tested whether effect sizes were moderated by the type of food choice behaviour (health-promoting versus health-compromising foods, and approach versus avoidance behaviours) and by participant characteristics (age and gender).

This review makes three contributions. First, it provides up-to-date, precise estimates of TPB relationships specific to food choice, drawing on both published and unpublished studies. Second, by testing behavioural and demographic moderators, it moves beyond the question of whether the TPB predicts food choice to consider when and for whom it does so, thereby informing the selection of theory in relation to the nature of the target behaviour. Third, it identifies the constructs most strongly associated with intention and behaviour, offering an empirical basis for prioritising intervention targets while recognising the limits of the model in explaining dietary behaviour.

Methods

**Search strategy and eligibility criteria**

The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). Electronic searches were run in PsycINFO, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses from database inception to the search date. Search strings combined terms for the theory (e.g., "theory of planned behavio*", "theory of reasoned action", "perceived behavio* control", "subjective norm*", "attitude*", "intention*") with terms for food choice (e.g., "food choice", "diet*", "fruit", "vegetable*", "snack*", "fat", "sugar", "soft drink*", "fast food", "eating"). Terms were adapted to the indexing vocabulary of each database. The reference lists of included studies and of earlier reviews of the TPB and health behaviour (Armitage & Conner, 2001; McEachan et al., 2011) were hand-searched. Authors were contacted when the data needed for effect size calculation were not reported.

Studies were eligible if they (a) were published in English as a peer-reviewed journal article or as an unpublished doctoral or master's dissertation; (b) used the TPB (Ajzen, 1991) as the primary theoretical framework; (c) measured at least one TPB construct (attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control [PBC], or intention) and a measure of a discrete food choice behaviour; and (d) reported a bivariate association between constructs, or sufficient information to compute one. Discrete food choice behaviours were defined as the selection, purchase, or consumption of a specific food or food group (e.g., fruit, fast food), as opposed to composite dietary patterns, weight management, or general "healthy eating" indices. Studies were excluded if they focused on clinical populations requiring prescribed diets, on eating disorders, or on breastfeeding or infant feeding practices, or if they reported only multivariate or structural equation modelling results without zero-order correlations. Where several publications reported on the same sample, the report with the most complete data was retained.

**Study selection and data extraction**

Titles and abstracts were screened by one reviewer, and a second reviewer independently screened a random 20% subset; disagreements were resolved by discussion. Full texts of potentially relevant records were assessed independently by two reviewers against the eligibility criteria. Data were extracted using a standardised form, piloted on five studies, covering bibliographic details, country, sample size, mean age, percentage female, study design, time lag between measures, TPB constructs assessed, type of behavioural measure (self-report versus objective), and the correlations among constructs. Extraction was performed by one reviewer and verified by a second; discrepancies were resolved by consensus.

**Coding of moderator variables**

Three moderators were specified a priori. First, *type of food choice behaviour* was coded as (a) consumption of health-promoting foods (e.g., fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, low-fat options), (b) consumption of health-compromising foods (e.g., fast food, sugar-sweetened beverages, high-fat snacks), or (c) avoidance or limitation of health-compromising foods. This classification distinguished approach behaviours from avoidance behaviours, which are thought to differ in their volitional demands (Conner & Armitage, 2002). Second, *participant age* was coded as the sample mean age, and categorically as children/adolescents (<18 years), young adults (18–25 years), and adults (>25 years) where the continuous value was not reported. Third, *gender composition* was coded as the percentage of female participants in the sample. Samples with no gender information were excluded from the gender analyses. Coding was completed independently by two reviewers (κ = 0.91 for behaviour type), with disagreements resolved by discussion.

**Methodological quality**

Study quality was appraised using an adapted checklist drawing on criteria used in earlier TPB meta-analyses (Cooke & French, 2008; McEachan et al., 2011). Items addressed the use of a prospective design, the use of validated or elicitation-based TPB measures, the correspondence between attitudinal and behavioural measures with respect to target, action, context, and time (Ajzen & Fishbein, 1977), the reporting of reliability coefficients, the reporting of attrition, and the use of an objective behavioural measure. Each item was scored 0 or 1, and total scores were examined descriptively and used in sensitivity analyses.

**Effect size computation**

The effect size of interest was the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (*r*) for each bivariate association in the TPB: attitude–intention, subjective norm–intention, PBC–intention, intention–behaviour, and PBC–behaviour. Where studies reported more than one correlation for the same relationship (e.g., multiple foods or multiple items), correlations were averaged within the study after Fisher's *z* transformation to avoid inflating the weight of any single sample (Borenstein et al., 2009). Where studies reported effect sizes for independent subgroups (e.g., males and females), each subgroup was treated as a separate sample for moderator analyses and combined for overall analyses. Correlations were transformed to Fisher's *z*, with variance *v* = 1/(*n* − 3), for all analyses and back-transformed to *r* for presentation. Where only standardised regression coefficients or *t*, *F*, or χ² statistics were available, these were converted to *r* using standard formulae (Peterson & Brown, 2005; Lipsey & Wilson, 2001).

**Meta-analytic procedure**

Pooled mean effect sizes (*r*+) and 95% confidence intervals were calculated using inverse-variance weighted random-effects models with the DerSimonian and Laird (1986) estimator of between-study variance (τ²). A random-effects approach was selected because the included studies differed in populations, behaviours, and measurement, so that a single common effect could not be assumed (Hedges & Vevea, 1998). Pooled effects were interpreted using Cohen's (1992) conventions, whereby *r* = 0.10, 0.30, and 0.50 represent small, medium, and large effects, respectively. Statistical significance was set at α = .05, two-tailed.

Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's *Q* statistic and the *I*² index, which expresses the proportion of total variability attributable to between-study differences rather than sampling error; values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% were taken to indicate low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins et al., 2003). Ninety-five percent prediction intervals were also computed to indicate the range of true effects expected in future studies.

**Moderator analyses**

Sources of heterogeneity were investigated using random-effects meta-regression, with the Knapp–Hartung adjustment applied to standard errors to reduce the risk of false-positive results when the number of studies is modest (Knapp & Hartung, 2003). Categorical moderators (type of food choice behaviour; age group) were entered as dummy-coded variables, with consumption of health-promoting foods as the reference category for behaviour type. Continuous moderators (mean age; percentage female) were entered as centred predictors. Each moderator was tested separately for each TPB relationship, provided at least four independent samples were available per category. Because age and gender composition may covary with the type of food behaviour studied, the robustness of significant effects was examined in multivariable models including all moderators simultaneously where sample size permitted. The proportion of between-study variance explained by each moderator was expressed as an adjusted *R*². For the behavioural relationships, we additionally examined whether the follow-up interval (in days) and the use of self-reported versus objective measures altered the results.

**Sensitivity analyses and publication bias**

Robustness was examined by repeating analyses using a leave-one-out procedure, by excluding unpublished dissertations, and by excluding studies with the lowest quality scores. Outliers were identified as studies whose standardised residuals exceeded ±2.58, and analyses were repeated with and without them. Publication bias was evaluated by visual inspection of funnel plots, Egger's regression test (Egger et al., 1997), and Duval and Tweedie's (2000) trim-and-fill procedure, which estimates the number of missing studies and the adjusted pooled effect. Rosenthal's fail-safe *N* was also calculated to estimate the number of null studies required to reduce a pooled effect to non-significance. All analyses were conducted in Stata (StataCorp, College Station, TX) using the *metan*, *metareg*, and *metabias* commands.

Results

**Study selection and characteristics**

The search of electronic databases and reference lists yielded 3,214 records after duplicates were removed. Of these, 2,987 were excluded on the basis of title and abstract. The full texts of 227 articles were assessed for eligibility, and 181 were excluded, most commonly because the behaviour was not a discrete food choice (n = 74), because the TPB constructs were not measured according to published guidelines (n = 49), or because the necessary effect sizes could not be obtained from the authors (n = 38). The final sample comprised 42 journal articles and four unpublished dissertations, which reported 51 independent datasets and a total of 14,826 participants (median n = 213, range 52–2,160). Studies were conducted in Europe (45%), North America (28%), Australasia (17%) and Asia (10%). The mean age of participants ranged from 12.8 to 61.3 years, and the median proportion of female participants was 66% (range 0–100%). Most studies used prospective designs with follow-up intervals of 1 to 4 weeks (78%), and behaviour was nearly always self-reported (94%). The target behaviours were categorised as choosing health promoting foods (e.g. fruit, vegetables, wholegrain products; k = 26), choosing health compromising foods (e.g. fast food, snacks, sugar-sweetened beverages; k = 12) and avoiding health compromising foods (e.g. limiting dietary fat or sugar; k = 13). Meeting Cohen's (1992) conventions, effect sizes of r = 0.10, 0.30 and 0.50 were interpreted as small, medium and large, respectively.

**Associations between TPB variables and intention**

Pooled associations with intention are summarised in Table 2. Attitude showed the strongest association with intention (k = 48, N = 13,904, r+ = 0.54, 95% CI 0.50–0.58), which was large in magnitude. Perceived behavioural control (PBC) was moderately to strongly associated with intention (k = 47, N = 13,611, r+ = 0.42, 95% CI 0.37–0.47), as was subjective norm (SN; k = 44, N = 12,988, r+ = 0.37, 95% CI 0.32–0.42). The confidence intervals for attitude did not overlap with those for SN, indicating that attitude was a significantly stronger correlate of intention than SN. Heterogeneity was substantial for all three associations (attitude: Q = 521.3, p < 0.001, I² = 91%; PBC: Q = 601.7, p < 0.001, I² = 92%; SN: Q = 478.2, p < 0.001, I² = 91%), which justified the use of random-effects models and the exploration of moderators.

**Associations between TPB variables and behaviour**

Intention was moderately associated with subsequent behaviour (k = 45, N = 12,570, r+ = 0.45, 95% CI 0.40–0.49; Q = 389.6, p < 0.001, I² = 89%). PBC was less strongly related to behaviour (k = 38, N = 10,912, r+ = 0.27, 95% CI 0.22–0.32; Q = 302.4, p < 0.001, I² = 88%). Associations between attitude and behaviour (k = 31, r+ = 0.31) and between SN and behaviour (k = 27, r+ = 0.19) were also observed, although these are not core paths in the model and are not considered further. Taken together, the results indicate that the TPB variables had medium to large associations with intention and small to medium associations with behaviour.

**Publication bias**

Visual inspection of funnel plots revealed slight asymmetry for the attitude–intention association, and Egger's regression test was significant for this relationship (p = 0.03). Duclan and Tweedie's trim-and-fill procedure imputed four studies, resulting in an adjusted estimate of r+ = 0.51 (95% CI 0.46–0.55), which remained large. No evidence of small-study effects was found for the other associations (Egger's p values 0.11–0.64). Fail-safe N calculations indicated that between 1,840 (SN–intention) and 6,215 (attitude–intention) null studies would be needed to reduce the pooled estimates to non-significance, suggesting that the findings are robust.

**Moderator analyses: type of food choice behaviour**

Results of the meta-regression analyses of behaviour type are shown in Table 3. The attitude–intention (Q_between = 2.9, p = 0.24) and SN–intention (Q_between = 3.4, p = 0.18) associations did not differ significantly across behaviour types. The PBC–intention association varied marginally (Q_between = 5.8, p = 0.055), being stronger for avoiding health compromising foods (r+ = 0.49) than for choosing health promoting foods (r+ = 0.40).

By contrast, behaviour type significantly moderated both paths to behaviour. For the intention–behaviour association, the pooled effect was significantly larger for choosing health promoting foods (k = 24, r+ = 0.49, 95% CI 0.44–0.54) than for avoiding health compromising foods (k = 11, r+ = 0.34, 95% CI 0.26–0.42; B = −0.15, SE = 0.05, p = 0.004). The association for choosing health compromising foods (k = 10, r+ = 0.43, 95% CI 0.34–0.51) did not differ significantly from that for health promoting foods (B = −0.06, SE = 0.06, p = 0.31).

The PBC–behaviour association was likewise moderated by behaviour type (Q_between = 14.6, p = 0.001). The strongest association was found for choosing health compromising foods (k = 9, r+ = 0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.44), which was significantly larger than that for choosing health promoting foods (k = 20, r+ = 0.27, 95% CI 0.21–0.33; B = 0.09, SE = 0.04, p = 0.03). The association was weakest for avoiding health compromising foods (k = 9, r+ = 0.14, 95% CI 0.05–0.23), which was significantly lower than that for choosing health promoting foods (B = −0.13, SE = 0.05, p = 0.008). Thus, PBC was most strongly related to behaviour when the behaviour involved choosing health compromising foods, and least strongly when it involved avoiding them. Residual heterogeneity remained high after the inclusion of behaviour type (I² = 82–87%), indicating that further unexplained variability remained.

**Moderator analyses: participant characteristics**

Mean participant age significantly moderated the intention–behaviour association (B = 0.004 per year, SE = 0.002, p = 0.02), with stronger associations in older samples. When age was categorised, the pooled intention–behaviour correlation was r+ = 0.34 (95% CI 0.24–0.43, k = 8) for samples of adolescents (mean age < 18 years), r+ = 0.43 (95% CI 0.37–0.49, k = 26) for young adults (18–35 years) and r+ = 0.54 (95% CI 0.46–0.61, k = 11) for samples with a mean age above 35 years (Q_between = 9.7, p = 0.008). Age did not significantly moderate the PBC–behaviour association (B = 0.002, SE = 0.002, p = 0.31) or any of the associations with intention (all p > 0.10).

The proportion of female participants was unrelated to the attitude–intention (B = 0.001, p = 0.42), SN–intention (B = 0.001, p = 0.37) and PBC–intention associations (B = 0.000, p = 0.89). Similarly, gender composition did not moderate the intention–behaviour (B = 0.001, SE = 0.001, p = 0.20) or PBC–behaviour associations (B = −0.001, SE = 0.001, p = 0.46). Sensitivity analyses that excluded the four unpublished dissertations, or studies using single-item behavioural measures, produced pooled estimates that differed from the primary estimates by no more than 0.03 and did not change the pattern of significant moderators.

Discussion

This review synthesised evidence from 46 sources to quantify the associations among Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) constructs and discrete food choice behaviours. Across studies, TPB variables showed medium to large associations with intention and behaviour. Attitude was the strongest correlate of intention (r+ = 0.54), followed by perceived behavioural control (PBC; r+ = 0.42) and subjective norm (SN; r+ = 0.37). Intention was moderately associated with behaviour (r+ = 0.45), and PBC was more weakly associated with behaviour (r+ = 0.27). These magnitudes are broadly consistent with earlier syntheses of the TPB across health behaviours (Armitage & Conner, 2001; McEachan et al., 2011) and with dietary reviews that examined broader or more heterogeneous outcomes (Mc Dermott et al., 2015). The present findings add specificity by restricting the outcome to discrete food choices and by examining whether the nature of the choice and the characteristics of the sample alter the strength of the relationships.

The dominance of attitude over SN and PBC suggests that food choices are driven chiefly by evaluative beliefs about the consequences of eating particular foods, including taste, health, and convenience. Food decisions are frequent, low-effort, and typically made autonomously, so personal appraisals may carry more weight than perceived social expectations. The comparatively modest contribution of SN is a recurrent finding in the TPB literature (Armitage & Conner, 2001), and it may partly reflect the limited sensitivity of conventional injunctive norm measures. Descriptive norms or identification with referent groups may better capture social influence in eating contexts (Rivis & Sheeran, 2003), and future primary studies should measure these constructs more routinely. The intention–behaviour association (r+ = 0.45) corresponds to a substantial but incomplete translation of motivation into action. This is consistent with the well-documented intention–behaviour gap (Sheeran, 2002) and with the habitual, cue-driven nature of much eating behaviour, in which automatic processes and environmental affordances can override deliberate intentions (Wood & Neal, 2007). The relatively weak direct PBC–behaviour association (r+ = 0.27) may likewise reflect difficulties in measuring control beliefs, since PBC captures both self-efficacy and perceived external constraints, which may influence food choices in different ways.

The moderator analyses constitute the main novel contribution of this review. The nature of the food choice behaviour significantly influenced the strength of the associations. PBC–behaviour associations were higher for choosing health-compromising foods than health-promoting foods. One interpretation is that consumption of energy-dense, palatable foods is more strongly shaped by perceived barriers, such as temptation, availability, and self-regulatory capacity, so individual differences in perceived control translate more directly into differences in behaviour. By contrast, health-promoting choices may be constrained by more distal factors, including cost, access, and skills, that are only partly captured by PBC. In addition, both intention–behaviour and PBC–behaviour associations were stronger for approach behaviours (choosing health-promoting foods) than for avoidance behaviours (avoiding health-compromising foods). Avoidance requires sustained inhibition of habitual or hedonically rewarding responses, and may therefore be more vulnerable to lapses, dependence on momentary cues, and failures of self-control (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006). Such behaviours may be better predicted by models that incorporate self-regulatory and implementation processes alongside motivation. Taken together, these results indicate that the TPB does not operate uniformly across the dietary domain and that the theory’s explanatory value depends on the behavioural target.

Participant characteristics also moderated associations. Intention–behaviour associations were higher in older than in younger participants. Older adults may possess more stable preferences and more consolidated routines, as well as greater autonomy over food purchasing and preparation, which would permit intentions to be enacted more reliably. Younger participants, particularly adolescents, often have less control over food availability, are more influenced by immediate social and environmental contexts, and may have less crystallised intentions, weakening the translation of intention into behaviour (Ajzen, 2011). These findings underscore the importance of tailoring both theoretical expectations and intervention strategies to the developmental stage of the target group.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the included studies were predominantly cross-sectional or short-term prospective designs with self-reported behaviour. Self-report is vulnerable to recall error and social desirability bias, and the common-method variance it generates may inflate correlations between TPB constructs and behaviour (Armitage & Conner, 2001). The effect sizes reported here therefore reflect associations rather than causal effects, and should not be assumed to indicate that changing TPB variables will produce equivalent changes in behaviour; experimental evidence indicates that medium-to-large changes in intention yield only small-to-medium changes in behaviour (Webb & Sheeran, 2006). Second, heterogeneity across studies was considerable for most associations. Although moderator analyses explained part of this variability, substantial residual heterogeneity remained, probably attributable to differences in measurement, follow-up interval, population, and cultural context. Third, the number of studies in some moderator categories was small, limiting statistical power and precluding examination of interactions among moderators. Moderators were also tested one at a time, so confounding among, for example, behaviour type and age cannot be excluded. Fourth, the review was restricted to correlational data and to studies reporting sufficient statistics, which may introduce selective reporting; although unpublished dissertations were included to reduce publication bias, small-study effects cannot be ruled out. Fifth, the focus on discrete food choices, while enhancing conceptual clarity, limits generalisation to overall dietary patterns, which comprise many interrelated decisions. Finally, most studies were conducted in high-income Western settings, and the applicability of the findings to other cultural and economic contexts remains uncertain. Few studies assessed the sufficiency of the TPB by including additional predictors such as habit, past behaviour, or moral norm, so we could not evaluate the incremental variance explained by such constructs.

These findings have implications for research and practice. For intervention designers, the strength of attitude as a correlate of intention suggests that messages targeting beliefs about outcomes of food choices are a logical focus, particularly when the goal is to build motivation. However, the moderate intention–behaviour association and the weaker association for avoidance behaviours imply that motivational strategies alone will be insufficient. Interventions should combine belief-based components with techniques that support enactment, such as action and coping planning, self-monitoring, and modification of the food environment. For choices involving health-compromising foods, strategies that bolster perceived control and reduce exposure to cues may be particularly valuable. Policy makers should recognise that individual-level cognitive determinants account for only part of the variance in food choice and that structural measures addressing availability, price, and marketing are required to complement educational approaches, especially for younger populations with limited autonomy.

For researchers, the variability in TPB associations across behaviours strongly suggests that the nature of the target behaviour should be carefully considered before selecting a theoretical framework. Future studies should employ objective or multi-method behavioural measures, longer follow-up periods, and designs that permit causal inference, such as randomised experiments that manipulate TPB constructs. Extending the model with habit strength, self-regulatory constructs, and affective components may improve prediction, especially for avoidance behaviours.

Conclusion

The TPB explains a meaningful proportion of variability in intention and discrete food choices, with attitude the most influential correlate of intention. However, the model’s performance varies according to the type of food choice and participant age, indicating that it is not equally suited to all dietary behaviours. Theory selection and intervention design should therefore be matched to the specific behaviour and population of interest.

Introduction

Regular physical activity (PA) in adolescence is associated with better cardiometabolic health, mental wellbeing, cognitive functioning and academic outcomes, and it tends to track into adulthood (Janssen & LeBlanc, 2010; Poitras et al., 2016). Despite this, the majority of young people worldwide do not meet the recommendation of an average of 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous PA per day, and global surveillance data show that adolescent girls are consistently less active than boys (Guthold et al., 2020). In England, activity levels decline markedly across the secondary school years, and the gender gap widens during this period (Sport England, 2023). Girls' disengagement from PA during early adolescence therefore remains a persistent public health concern, and interventions that address it need to be both effective and acceptable to the girls they target.

Enjoyment is one of the most consistent correlates of youth PA. Self-determination theory proposes that activities experienced as intrinsically satisfying, and that fulfil needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness, are more likely to be sustained (Ryan & Deci, 2000). Empirical work supports this, showing that PA enjoyment is positively associated with participation and predicts later engagement among young people (Dishman et al., 2005; Fairclough et al., 2016). For adolescent girls, however, enjoyment can be undermined by competitive and performance-oriented school PE and sport environments, concerns about body image and peer judgement, and a lack of choice in the activities offered (Biddle et al., 2005; Slater & Tiggemann, 2010). Qualitative studies indicate that girls value opportunities to be active in supportive, non-judgemental settings and in the company of friends (Coakley & White, 1992; Casey et al., 2009).

The social context is therefore central. Peers shape adolescents' PA through modelling, encouragement, companionship and normative influence, and friends' activity levels are associated with one's own (Fitzgerald et al., 2012; Sawka et al., 2013). The presence of peers also increases the likelihood that PA is experienced as enjoyable (Salvy et al., 2009; Smith, 1999). Adolescence is a developmental stage in which the importance of peer relationships rises while parental and teacher influence becomes relatively less salient (Brown & Larson, 2009). It follows that peer networks represent a promising, yet potentially under-used, channel through which to promote PA among girls.

Peer-led approaches harness this potential by having trained peers, rather than teachers or researchers, deliver or support intervention content. Theoretically, they draw on social learning theory and diffusion of innovations, which suggest that behaviours spread through credible, similar and trusted social contacts (Bandura, 1986; Rogers, 2003). Peer-led models in health promotion, including smoking prevention, sexual health education and mental health, have shown promising outcomes (Campbell et al., 2008; Stok et al., 2016). In the PA domain, peer-led initiatives have often been used to motivate other young people, and reviews suggest they can be an effective and low-cost way to engage pupils, with benefits for the peer leaders themselves in the form of leadership skills, confidence and a sense of responsibility (Ginis et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2017). Notable examples include the Peer-Led Activity for Girls (PLAN-A) and the Peer Education approach used in the Active Teen Leaders Avoiding Screen-time (ATLAS) programme (Lubans et al., 2016; Sebire et al., 2018). Even so, systematic reviews conclude that the evidence for peer-led PA interventions is limited and heterogeneous, with small numbers of studies, variable quality, and little attention to how peer delivery operates in practice (Owen et al., 2017; Yip et al., 2016). Peer-led strategies remain relatively underused and, consequently, understudied in school-based PA interventions, particularly those designed specifically for adolescent girls.

A further limitation of the existing literature is that peer-led interventions are often designed with limited input from, and evaluation by, those involved in delivery. Complex interventions benefit from careful early-phase evaluation of feasibility and acceptability before progression to larger trials (Bowen et al., 2009; Skivington et al., 2021). Such work asks whether an intervention can be delivered as intended, how it is received by participants and implementers, and what refinements are needed. Without it, effectiveness trials risk testing approaches that are poorly implemented or unappealing to the target group, wasting resources and potentially reinforcing the view that nothing works for girls. Qualitative methods are particularly suited to this stage because they illuminate the processes, relationships and contextual factors that determine whether peer-led delivery is viable (Moore et al., 2015). Notably, few studies have examined peer-led PA interventions that incorporate multiple tiers of support, such as university student mentors training school-based peer leaders who then reach the wider year group, and there is little understanding of how communication between peer leaders and their peers influences engagement.

To address these gaps, the Girls Peer Activity (G-PACT) intervention was developed as a novel peer-led mentoring programme for Year 9 girls (aged 13–14 years) in secondary schools in North-West England. G-PACT used a three-tier model. At Tier 1, undergraduate students acted as Mentors who delivered educational and leadership training. At Tier 2, Year 9 girls nominated by teachers acted as Leaders who received this training. At Tier 3, the wider Year 9 cohort served as Peers whom Leaders were encouraged to support and motivate to engage in more PA. The model was designed to use peer networks as the vehicle for dissemination, while providing Leaders with near-peer guidance from Mentors who were closer in age and experience than teachers or researchers.

The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the G-PACT peer-led mentoring intervention from the perspectives of all stakeholders. Specifically, we sought to explore how Leaders, Peers, Mentors and teachers experienced the intervention, which aspects of the design and delivery worked well, and which required refinement. The research questions were: (1) Is the G-PACT intervention feasible to deliver within secondary school settings? (2) Is the intervention acceptable to Leaders, Peers, Mentors and teachers? and (3) How can the processes linking the tiers, particularly Leader–Peer communication, be improved?

This study makes three contributions. First, it provides one of the few evaluations of a multi-tier peer-led mentoring model targeting adolescent girls' PA, extending the limited peer-led literature. Second, by triangulating focus group and interview data across four stakeholder groups, it offers a rounded account of implementation processes rather than outcomes alone. Third, it generates practical, evidence-informed recommendations for refining the intervention, particularly the communication processes between Leaders and Peers, to inform future definitive evaluation.

Methods

Study Design and Theoretical Framing

This study used a qualitative, multi-perspective design to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the Girls Peer Activity (G-PACT) intervention. Feasibility and acceptability were examined as part of early-stage development, in line with the UK Medical Research Council framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions (Skivington et al., 2021) and recommendations for feasibility studies (Bowen et al., 2009; Eldridge et al., 2016). Focus groups and semi-structured interviews were chosen because they allow participants to discuss shared experiences and to generate detailed accounts of how an intervention was received (Braun & Clarke, 2013). The study adopted a pragmatic orientation, prioritizing practical knowledge to refine the intervention before any larger evaluation (Kelly & Cordeiro, 2020). Ethical approval was granted by the university research ethics committee, and the study followed the British Educational Research Association (2018) guidelines. Reporting followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (Tong et al., 2007).

Setting and Participants

Three mixed-sex state secondary schools in West Lancashire, North-West England, took part. Schools were approached through existing university partnerships and were purposively selected to vary in size and catchment area. All 249 Year 9 girls (13–14 years) in the three schools were invited to participate. The study used a three-tier model. Tier 1 comprised Mentors, undergraduate students from sport and exercise-related degree programs who were recruited by advertisement and selected after interview. Tier 2 comprised Leaders, Year 9 girls nominated by teachers on the basis of perceived communication skills, social influence, and willingness to take part. Tier 3 comprised Peers, the remaining Year 9 girls in each school. Teachers who liaised with the project in each school were also invited to take part.

Focus groups and interviews were conducted with 40 Leaders (eight focus groups), 185 Peers (28 focus groups), six Mentors (two focus groups), and four teachers (three interviews; one interview involved two teachers). Peer and Leader groups were organized by school and, where possible, by existing class or friendship groupings, in order to promote ease of discussion (Kitzinger, 1995). Groups contained approximately five to seven participants. Parents or guardians gave written informed consent for all girls, and the girls themselves gave written assent. Mentors and teachers provided written informed consent. Participants were told that participation was voluntary, that they could withdraw at any time, and that their responses would remain confidential and would not be shared with teachers.

The G-PACT Intervention

G-PACT was developed using peer-led approaches (Campbell et al., 2008; Stok et al., 2016) and self-determination theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000), with a focus on enjoyment, autonomy, and relatedness in physical activity (PA). Mentors delivered a series of educational and leadership training sessions to Leaders in each school during school time. Sessions addressed the benefits of PA, enjoyment and motivation, communication and leadership skills, and strategies for planning and promoting activities. Leaders were then encouraged to share this information with their Peers and to promote and organize PA opportunities within the school day, for example during break times and lunch times, and in extracurricular sessions. Mentors visited the schools regularly to support Leaders, provide feedback, and help overcome problems. Teachers provided logistical support, including room bookings and equipment. The Peers received the intervention indirectly, through contact with Leaders in informal and organized settings.

Data Collection

Data were collected at the end of the intervention period, in school, in a private room. Separate topic guides were developed for each participant group, informed by the feasibility and acceptability literature (Sekhon et al., 2017) and reviewed by the research team. Questions for Leaders explored their experiences of training, their role, communication with Peers, barriers and facilitators to delivery, and perceived impact. Questions for Peers examined awareness of G-PACT, interactions with Leaders, perceptions of the activities, and suggestions for improvement. Mentors were asked about the training content and delivery, support for Leaders, and the practicalities of working in schools. Teachers were asked about organizational demands, integration into school routines, and perceived value and sustainability. Guides were piloted informally and refined for clarity and age-appropriateness. Prompts and probes elicited elaboration, and the girls were encouraged to share differing views.

Sessions were facilitated by members of the research team experienced in qualitative research with young people, who were not responsible for delivering the training. Focus groups with girls lasted approximately 20–40 minutes, which fit within lesson periods, and Mentor groups and teacher interviews lasted approximately 30–60 minutes. All sessions were audio-recorded with permission and transcribed verbatim. Transcripts were anonymized, with pseudonyms or participant codes replacing names and identifying details. Field notes were made after each session to record contextual observations and initial impressions.

Data Analysis

Data from all groups were pooled and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006, 2019). Pooling allowed the triangulation of perspectives across the tiers of the intervention and across stakeholders, providing a fuller account of feasibility and acceptability (Carter et al., 2014). The analysis followed six phases. First, two researchers read and re-read the transcripts to become familiar with the data. Second, they generated initial codes inductively across the dataset, using NVivo software to organize the data. Third, codes were collated into candidate themes. Fourth, themes were reviewed against the coded extracts and the full dataset, and some were merged, split, or discarded. Fifth, themes were defined and named. Sixth, illustrative quotations were chosen for reporting. Although coding was inductive, the interpretation of themes was guided by the feasibility and acceptability domains of the theoretical framework of acceptability (Sekhon et al., 2017), including perceived effectiveness, burden, and affective attitude, as well as by practical considerations of recruitment, delivery, and communication.

Consistent with a reflexive approach, themes were treated as constructed through the researchers' engagement with the data rather than as emerging independently, so inter-coder agreement statistics were not calculated (Braun & Clarke, 2019). Instead, rigor was supported through several strategies (Lincoln & Guba, 1985; Smith & McGannon, 2018). Two researchers coded independently and acted as critical friends to each other, discussing alternative interpretations until consensus on the thematic structure was reached. Reflexive notes were kept to document analytic decisions and consider how the researchers' backgrounds and assumptions might shape interpretation. Triangulation across participant groups and schools was used to identify convergent and divergent accounts, and deviant cases were actively sought. Data were treated as sufficiently rich when later groups yielded no new aspects relevant to the research questions, though this was interpreted in terms of information power rather than saturation (Malterud et al., 2016). Themes were discussed with the wider research team before the final thematic structure was agreed.

Because the study was qualitative and aimed to assess feasibility and acceptability, no inferential statistics were used. Participation numbers and the number and duration of groups were summarized descriptively to indicate the reach and scope of the data collection.

Results

**Participation and data collection**

Of the 249 Year 9 girls (13–14 years) invited from the three participating schools, 225 (90.4%) contributed data to the evaluation as either Leaders or Peers. Across the three schools, 38 focus groups and three interviews were completed, giving 41 data collection events with 235 participants in total. The Leader focus groups (n = 8) involved 40 girls, a mean of 5.0 per group, or about 2.7 groups per school. The Peer focus groups (n = 28) involved 185 girls, a mean of 6.6 per group. This was 74.3% of the 249 invited girls, or 82.2% of the 225 contributing girls. Two focus groups were held with Mentors (n = 6; mean = 3.0 per group), and three interviews were held with four teachers, one of which was a paired interview. All three schools delivered the three-tier model through to the end of the intervention period, and data were obtained from all tiers in every school. These recruitment, retention, and data-completeness figures meet the commonly used criteria for feasibility (Bowen et al., 2009; Eldridge et al., 2016).

Thematic analysis of the pooled transcripts (Braun & Clarke, 2006, 2019) produced three overarching themes. The first was acceptability of the training and role for Leaders and Mentors. The second was feasibility and fit within the school context. The third was the Leader–Peer relationship and communication. These themes are organised below using the acceptability and feasibility constructs of Sekhon et al. (2017) and Bowen et al. (2009). Illustrative quotations are labelled by participant tier and school.

**Theme 1: Acceptability of the training and the Leader role**

Leaders in all eight focus groups described the training sessions delivered by the Mentors as enjoyable, relevant, and different from normal lessons. Leaders valued the interactive format and the opportunity to practise leadership skills such as motivating others, organising activities, and communicating clearly. As one Leader explained, "It wasn't like being taught at school, it was more like being with older friends who actually listened" (Leader, School 2). Mentors were seen as credible and approachable role models because they were close in age and not part of the school's formal hierarchy. Leaders reported greater confidence, a sense of responsibility, and pride in being chosen. Several Leaders also described becoming more active themselves because they felt they had to "set an example" (Leader, School 1).

The six Mentors described the role as worthwhile and as developing their own skills in facilitation, planning, and working with adolescents. They also reported challenges, mainly in adapting content when Leaders had different levels of confidence and in coordinating timetables with school commitments. Mentors suggested that more structured resources and a short pre-intervention orientation would help future cohorts. Teachers regarded the Leader selection process as acceptable and workable. However, they noted that identifying girls who were influential but not already highly active could broaden the reach of the intervention. In their view, the programme's emphasis on enjoyment rather than performance was an important strength.

**Theme 2: Feasibility and fit within the school context**

All three schools implemented the three-tier model, and teachers described the demands on staff as manageable because the Mentors delivered the training and the Leaders drove the peer-facing activity. Teachers highlighted several practical barriers. These included competing academic priorities, limited availability of space during lunch and after school, and variation in weather and facilities. The timing of training sessions was the most frequently noted logistical issue, with Leaders sometimes missing lessons or break times to attend. Leaders from all three schools said that the amount of training felt appropriate, though some wanted additional time to plan activities with Mentors before delivering them to their Peers.

Mentors and teachers agreed that the model could be sustained with modest resources, provided that a named staff member acted as a liaison and that Mentor travel and scheduling were organised in advance. Teachers viewed the Mentor-led delivery as a way to introduce a PA programme without adding to their workloads, but they felt that more explicit teacher involvement might help maintain momentum after the Mentors' input ended. Taken together, these findings suggest the intervention can be delivered as planned within secondary school settings, with minor changes to scheduling and communication.

**Theme 3: The Leader–Peer relationship and communication**

The Peer focus groups (28 groups, 185 girls) showed that awareness and understanding of G-PACT were more variable among Peers than among Leaders. Peers in most groups knew that some girls in their year had been selected as Leaders, but many were unclear about the aims of the project or what Leaders were supposed to do. A typical comment was, "We knew they did something with the mentors, but they never really told us what it was for" (Peer, School 3). Where Leaders communicated clearly, for instance by inviting friends to try an activity, suggesting a lunchtime session, or sharing ideas in the form tutor group, Peers described feeling encouraged and more willing to join in. Peers said they were more receptive when the messages were informal, came from friends, and emphasised fun and choice rather than fitness or competition.

Peers also identified barriers to engagement that related to the Leader role. Some perceived Leaders as part of a particular friendship group, which made them feel excluded or reluctant to participate. Others said they felt self-conscious about being seen to be active or being judged by boys in mixed-sex settings. Several Peers reported not knowing when or where activities would take place, which reflected the limited communication channels available to Leaders. Leaders themselves confirmed these difficulties, reporting that they were uncertain how to approach Peers outside their immediate friendship networks and that they sometimes found it hard to maintain Peers' interest. Both Leaders and Peers suggested using social media groups, tutor-time announcements, and posters, as well as giving Leaders more training in communication and inclusion.

**Summary**

Across the 41 data collection events and 235 participants, the findings indicate that G-PACT was feasible and acceptable to Leaders, Mentors, and teachers, with high participation across all tiers and all schools. The main area for refinement was the Leader–Peer interface, where clearer communication, broader inclusion, and better information about activities were needed to extend the reach of the intervention to the wider Year 9 cohort.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of G-PACT, a three-tier peer-led mentoring intervention in which undergraduate Mentors trained Year 9 girls (Leaders) to promote physical activity (PA) among their wider cohort (Peers). The findings suggest that the model was feasible and acceptable for Leaders and Mentors, and that the Mentor-Leader tier was the strongest part of the design. The Leader-Peer tier needs refinement, particularly in how information and encouragement were communicated. These findings fit a broader pattern in school-based PA research. Interventions for adolescent girls often show small or inconsistent effects (Owen et al., 2017), and the way a programme is delivered, not only what it contains, may shape its reception.

The positive reception among Leaders and Mentors is consistent with self-determination theory, which proposes that autonomy, competence, and relatedness support sustained motivation (Deci & Ryan, 2000). Leaders were trusted with a meaningful role, trained by near-peer Mentors, and given opportunities to apply new skills. These conditions plausibly support all three needs. Near-peer Mentors may also have occupied a useful middle position, since they were older and credible but less hierarchical than teachers. This echoes social cognitive theory, which holds that role models perceived as similar and attainable strengthen observational learning and self-efficacy (Bandura, 1986). That Mentors also valued the experience suggests the tiered structure may carry reciprocal benefits, such as employability skills, and these could support recruitment and retention if the model is scaled. These interpretations are tentative, because the present data describe perceptions of the experience and do not test mechanisms.

The more equivocal finding concerned the relationship between Leaders and Peers. Peers were often unclear about what Leaders were doing, why, and how to take part. This suggests that a training programme for Leaders is not enough to ensure that messages reach and resonate with the intended audience. Peer-led interventions depend on the quality of interpersonal transmission, and Leaders are adolescents who must negotiate their own status and friendships while taking on a role that may set them apart. Large-scale peer-led approaches have worked when peer supporters were chosen through social-network methods that identified influential students rather than by staff nomination alone (Campbell et al., 2008). In G-PACT, teachers selected the Leaders, which was pragmatic and probably improved reliability and safeguarding. However, teacher-nominated students may not always be those with the most influence over peers' PA choices, and this may partly explain the weaker reach. Future iterations could test hybrid selection that combines teacher knowledge with peer nomination or network data.

Communication difficulties may also reflect a lack of structure and shared language. Intervention components that are well specified, with clear behavioural targets, defined delivery opportunities, and explicit prompts, are more likely to be implemented as intended (Michie et al., 2011). Leaders may need concrete communication scripts, scheduled and visible activity sessions, and guidance on adapting their approach to different friendship groups, including less active or less confident girls. Peers' preferences for how they receive information, including social media and informal messaging, also deserve attention, although these channels bring safeguarding and school-policy considerations. Because Peers wanted enjoyable, low-pressure, non-competitive activities, in line with research on girls' PA preferences (Yungblut et al., 2012), involving them in co-designing activity offers could improve fit and ownership.

The three-tier structure also has implications for school staff. Teachers' views were important for judging feasibility, since time, space, and competing priorities frequently limit what schools can deliver. Whole-school buy-in and designated staff liaison are commonly cited facilitators of PA intervention implementation. The model's reliance on university-based Mentors reduces teacher workload but raises questions about sustainability beyond a research partnership. Options include training sixth-form students as Mentors, or embedding the programme within existing leadership awards.

These findings should be interpreted in light of several limitations. First, the study involved three mixed-sex schools in one region of North-West England, which limits transferability to other settings, including single-sex schools, rural areas, and more ethnically diverse or differently resourced communities. Second, Leaders were selected by teachers, so their experiences may be more favourable than those of students who were less confident or engaged. Third, focus groups are susceptible to social desirability and group dynamics, particularly among adolescents, and quieter participants may have contributed less. Pooling the data from different participant groups allowed triangulation, but it may have blurred distinct perspectives. Fourth, the evaluation focused on feasibility and acceptability, so it cannot indicate whether G-PACT changes PA, enjoyment, or psychosocial outcomes. Perceived acceptability does not guarantee behavioural effects (Sekhon et al., 2017). Finally, the intervention's duration limits conclusions about the maintenance of Leader activity and Peer engagement over time. Following established guidance, findings from feasibility work should be treated as informing refinement rather than as evidence of effectiveness (Eldridge et al., 2016; Bowen et al., 2009).

Despite these limitations, the study has several strengths. It gathered data from all tiers of the model, including Peers, whose views are rarely examined in peer-led research. It also used a theoretically informed, structured approach to adolescent girls' PA, a group with persistently low participation. The qualitative approach gave rich insight into how the intervention was experienced and where it needs to change.

Several recommendations follow. Future development should strengthen the Leader-Peer interface by providing communication training, clear role descriptions, visible and regular activity opportunities, and feedback loops through which Peers can shape the programme.
