Table 1 gives unadjusted correlations between tract mean BMI and each candidate predictor. The strongest correlations were with socioeconomic indicators. Median home value had a correlation of r = −0.72, and the proportion of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher had r = −0.75 (both p < 0.001). Median household income was also inversely correlated with BMI (r = −0.66), but it was highly collinear with home value (r = 0.83) and was not retained in the final model. The share of workers commuting by car (driving alone or carpooling) was positively correlated with BMI (r = 0.61), while the share walking, cycling, or using transit was negatively correlated (r = −0.58).

Race and ethnicity measures showed varied associations. The proportion of residents identifying as Hispanic or Latino was positively correlated with tract BMI (r = 0.33). The same was true for the proportion identifying as American Indian or Alaska Native (r = 0.27) and as Black or African American (r = 0.12). The proportion identifying as Asian was negatively correlated (r = −0.41). Tract BMI rose across the rural-urban commuting area (RUCA) gradient (Hart et al., 2005; U.S. Department of Agriculture, 2019). Mean BMI was 27.5 kg/m² in metropolitan tracts (n = 612), 28.3 in micropolitan tracts (n = 96), 28.6 in small town tracts (n = 71), and 28.9 in isolated rural tracts (n = 49). An ANOVA across these groups was significant (F = 31.4, p < 0.001).

Measures of food access were only weakly related to BMI. The share of residents who were both low-income and living more than one mile (urban) or ten miles (rural) from a supermarket, as defined in the USDA Food Access Research Atlas (Rhone et al., 2017), had a correlation of r = 0.18 (p < 0.001). The density of fast-food outlets per square mile was weakly negative (r = −0.09, p = 0.01), which likely reflects the concentration of such outlets in dense urban areas.

**Multivariable model**

We fit the following model by ordinary least squares:

BMIᵢ = β₀ + β₁HomeValueᵢ + β₂Bachelorᵢ + β₃Raceᵢ + β₄Hispanicᵢ + β₅CarCommuteᵢ + β₆RUCAᵢ + εᵢ,

where *i* indexes census tracts and Race is a vector of tract-level racial composition measures. The model explained 86% of the variance in tract mean BMI (R² = 0.86; adjusted R² = 0.86; residual standard error 0.49 kg/m²). Ten-fold cross-validation gave an out-of-sample R² of 0.85 and a root mean squared error of 0.50 kg/m², so the fit was not due to overfitting. Variance inflation factors were all below 4.1 (highest for home value, 3.9, and bachelor's degree attainment, 3.6). We therefore retained both variables.

Table 2 presents the adjusted coefficients. Each $100,000 increase in median home value was associated with a 0.38 kg/m² lower mean BMI (95% CI −0.44 to −0.32; standardized β = −0.34). Each 10-percentage-point increase in the proportion of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher was associated with a 0.31 kg/m² lower mean BMI (95% CI −0.37 to −0.25; β = −0.36). Together these two variables accounted for most of the explained variance. In a hierarchical analysis, a model with only these two predictors had R² = 0.68.

Car commuting remained positively associated with BMI after adjustment. Each 10-percentage-point increase in the share of workers commuting by car corresponded to a 0.19 kg/m² higher mean BMI (95% CI 0.12 to 0.26; β = 0.15). Adding commuting variables to the socioeconomic model increased R² by 0.03.

Racial and ethnic composition was independently associated with tract BMI. Each 10-percentage-point increase in the Hispanic or Latino population was associated with 0.24 kg/m² higher BMI (95% CI 0.17 to 0.31). Corresponding estimates were 0.29 kg/m² (95% CI 0.18 to 0.40) for American Indian or Alaska Native residents and 0.41 kg/m² (95% CI 0.22 to 0.60) for Black or African American residents. A 10-percentage-point increase in the Asian population was associated with a 0.33 kg/m² lower BMI (95% CI −0.40 to −0.26). Because tract-level associations cannot be interpreted at the individual level (Robinson, 1950), we regard these coefficients as descriptions of area-level patterns and not as individual risk.

RUCA classification remained significant after adjustment (joint F-test p < 0.001). Relative to metropolitan tracts, adjusted mean BMI was 0.17 kg/m² higher in micropolitan tracts (95% CI 0.05 to 0.29), 0.26 higher in small town tracts (95% CI 0.13 to 0.39), and 0.34 higher in isolated rural tracts (95% CI 0.19 to 0.49). The USDA low-access measure and fast-food density were not significant when added to this model (β = 0.02, p = 0.41, and β = −0.01, p = 0.63, respectively). Neither changed R² by more than 0.001, and the main coefficients changed by less than 5%.

**Residual and sensitivity analyses**

Residuals were approximately normal and showed no evidence of heteroscedasticity (Breusch–Pagan p = 0.12). Spatial autocorrelation fell markedly after adjustment (Moran's I for residuals = 0.07, p = 0.02), which indicates that the covariates accounted for most of the geographic structure. A spatial error model gave coefficients within 0.03 kg/m² of the OLS estimates and did not change any inference. The largest positive residuals (observed BMI above predicted by more than 1 kg/m²) occurred in a small number of tracts containing correctional or institutional facilities and military housing. The largest negative residuals occurred in tracts with large university student populations.

Results were robust to restricting the analysis to the 701 tracts with at least 1,500 records (R² = 0.87) and to weighting tracts by record count (R² = 0.88). Tract BMI was strongly correlated with model-based adult obesity prevalence from the CDC PLACES project (r = 0.81; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2022). This supports the external validity of the identification card estimates.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study shows that height and weight recorded on state-issued identification cards can be used to produce stable, small-area estimates of adult body mass index (BMI) for every census tract in Oregon. Six tract-level characteristics (median home value, educational attainment, race, ethnicity, the share of workers commuting by car, and rural-urban commuting area classification) together accounted for 86% of the variation in mean BMI. Weight status was lower in tracts with higher home values and greater educational attainment, and higher in tracts where more workers commuted by car. The patterns are consistent with a large literature on socioeconomic disparities in obesity, which suggests that identification card data capture real geographic variation in adult weight status rather than artifacts of the data source.

**Interpretation of findings**

The inverse association between BMI and both home values and education matches decades of evidence that obesity prevalence in high-income countries is patterned by socioeconomic position (Sobal & Stunkard, 1989; McLaren, 2007). Home value is a useful tract-level proxy because it reflects accumulated wealth and neighborhood amenities as well as current income, and wealth has been linked to health outcomes independently of income (Pollack et al., 2013). Educational attainment may operate through health literacy, occupational conditions, food preferences, and access to resources that support physical activity and dietary quality (Cutler & Lleras-Muney, 2010). Because these characteristics are strongly correlated across tracts, we caution against attributing separate causal effects to each. Our models are better read as describing the socioeconomic structure of weight status than as identifying individual mechanisms.

The positive association between car commuting and BMI is consistent with research linking automobile dependence, and the built environments that sustain it, to lower physical activity and higher body weight (Frank et al., 2004; Lopez-Zetina et al., 2006). Active commuting is a modest contributor to daily energy expenditure, but car commuting may also mark low-density, less walkable development patterns where routine destinations are distant. The inclusion of RUCA classification in the final model suggests that rurality contributes independently, in line with national findings that obesity prevalence is higher in nonmetropolitan than metropolitan areas (Befort et al., 2012). Whether this reflects food environments, limited recreational infrastructure, occupational patterns, or distance from health care cannot be determined from our data.

Race and ethnicity also contributed to the model, which reflects well-documented differences in obesity prevalence among population groups in the United States (Hales et al., 2020). These differences are widely understood to result from structural factors, including residential segregation, historical disinvestment, differential exposure to marketing, and discrimination, rather than from inherent group characteristics (Williams & Collins, 2001). Tract racial and ethnic composition should therefore be interpreted as a marker of such upstream conditions. It should not be treated as a causal determinant of weight status. Likewise, BMI itself is an imperfect indicator of adiposity and health, and its relationship with body fat varies across ethnic groups, ages, and body types (Nuttall, 2015).

**Strengths and comparison with existing surveillance**

The principal advantage of identification card data is coverage. The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) is the primary source of state obesity estimates, but its sample sizes are typically too small to support reliable tract-level or even county-level estimates without modeling. Modeled small-area approaches, such as those used in the CDC PLACES project, rely on multilevel regression and poststratification and therefore on assumptions that can smooth over local variation (Zhang et al., 2014). Our approach draws on roughly three million records, which allows direct estimation for nearly all tracts. Identification cards also record measured or clerk-entered height and weight, which may reduce, though not eliminate, the well-known bias of self-reported values, where individuals tend to overstate height and understate weight (Connor Gorber et al., 2007). Finally, because cards are renewed on regular cycles, the data can be updated at low marginal cost, enabling surveillance of change over time that is difficult with periodic surveys.

**Limitations**

Several limitations deserve emphasis. First, the weight and height on a card are likely self-reported at the time of issuance or renewal and may not be verified. Social desirability, outdated values, and rounding could bias BMI estimates, and bias may differ by age, sex, and weight category. Because we compared tracts rather than individuals, a uniform bias would shift all estimates without changing relative patterns, but differential bias associated with socioeconomic or demographic characteristics could inflate or attenuate the associations we observe. We did not have an independent measured benchmark with which to validate the tract estimates, and comparing them with BRFSS or clinical records is a priority for future work.

Second, the population of cardholders is not the population of adults. Oregon residents without a license or identification card, including some people with disabilities, older adults who no longer drive, and people with limited access to documentation, are underrepresented. Because card possession varies with age, income, and urbanicity, selection could correlate with both weight status and neighborhood characteristics. Age adjustment addresses compositional differences in the age distribution, but it cannot correct for selection on unobserved factors. Cardholders may also be a different group from the residents who are most likely to have recently moved, and addresses on cards may lag actual residence.

Third, the analysis is cross-sectional and ecological. Associations observed among tracts need not hold among individuals, and applying them to individuals risks the ecological fallacy. The high explained variance (86%) should also be interpreted carefully. Tract characteristics are spatially clustered and mutually correlated, so the model may be capturing spatial structure, and we did not formally model spatial autocorrelation, which can understate standard errors. Some predictors, such as home value and education, also come from American Community Survey estimates with their own sampling error, and tracts with small populations have noisier values for both outcomes and covariates. Moreover, the study design does not allow us to separate the effect of environments on weight from residential sorting, whereby people with particular characteristics choose or are able to afford particular neighborhoods (Oakes, 2004). Finally, results from a single state with a particular demographic and geographic profile may not generalize to states with different identification card policies or populations.

**Implications and future directions**

Despite these constraints, the findings have practical implications. Public health agencies, which often lack local obesity data, could use identification card records to identify tracts with elevated BMI, target interventions and resources, and evaluate place-based policies such as changes to transportation, zoning, or food assistance. Linking BMI trends with policy changes could support quasi-experimental evaluation. The strength of the association with car commuting suggests that transportation and land-use planning are relevant to obesity prevention, although causal inference will require longitudinal designs.

Using such data also raises privacy and governance questions. Height, weight, and address are sensitive when linked at the individual level. Our approach used aggregated tract-level estimates, and any agency pursuing similar work should establish data-sharing agreements, minimum cell sizes, and de-identification protocols, as well as engage the communities represented in the data. Aggregated estimates also risk stigmatizing neighborhoods if presented without context about structural determinants.

Future research should validate card-derived BMI against measured data, examine sex- and age-specific patterns, incorporate spatial models, and test whether findings replicate in other states. Repeated extracts would permit analysis of temporal change, including responses to events such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

**Conclusion**

State-issued identification cards provide a large, inexpensive, and regularly updated source of height and weight data that yields tract-level BMI patterns consistent with established knowledge on socioeconomic and environmental disparities. While validation and careful attention to selection, measurement, and privacy are needed, public health agencies should explore options for developing their own obesity estimates from identification card data to support more localized surveillance and more equitable resource allocation.

Introduction

Lactococcus lactis is the principal component of the mesophilic starter cultures used worldwide in the manufacture of cheese and other fermented dairy products. Starter bacteria are responsible for the rapid conversion of lactose into lactic acid, which controls spoilage and pathogenic microbiota, drives curd formation and syneresis, and contributes to the development of texture and flavor (Smid and Kleerebezem 2014). Besides acidification, L. lactis contributes to flavor through proteolytic and peptidolytic activities, amino acid catabolism, and the production of diacetyl, acetoin and other volatile compounds derived from citrate and pyruvate metabolism (Smit et al. 2005; Cocaign-Bousquet et al. 2002). The success of a dairy fermentation therefore depends on the viability and metabolic activity of the starter, and strains must withstand a sequence of stresses, first during starter production, concentration and storage (freezing, freeze-drying, cold storage), and later during cheese manufacture (heat, osmotic, acid and oxidative stress) (van de Guchte et al. 2002; Papadimitriou et al. 2016).

Oxidative stress is one of the least appreciated but most pervasive of these challenges. Although L. lactis is aerotolerant, it lacks a complete respiratory chain unless exogenous heme is supplied, and it possesses a limited set of defenses against reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Duwat et al. 2001). In the presence of oxygen, flavoprotein oxidases such as NADH oxidase, together with pyruvate oxidase and other enzymes, generate hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, which damage DNA, proteins and membrane lipids and cause growth arrest and loss of viability (Rochat et al. 2006). Milk is aerated during handling, and oxygen is introduced during pumping, stirring and vat filling, while the large-scale propagation of starters is frequently carried out under non-anaerobic conditions. Oxygen also influences the metabolic fate of pyruvate, diverting flux from lactate towards acetate, acetoin and diacetyl, with implications for flavor (Lan et al. 2006). Strains with improved oxygen tolerance are thus of practical interest, as they could display more consistent performance in industrial environments and might provide an additional route to modulate aroma formation. Cultivation under respiratory conditions, i.e. in the presence of heme and oxygen, improves biomass yield and robustness (Duwat et al. 2001; Pedersen et al. 2012), but it requires specific process modifications and is not applicable to all dairy applications.

Strain improvement in food microorganisms is constrained by regulation and consumer perception, and genetically modified organisms are not widely accepted in the dairy sector. Consequently, non-recombinant approaches such as spontaneous mutant selection and adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) are attractive alternatives (Bachmann et al. 2012). ALE exploits the capacity of bacteria to acquire beneficial mutations under sustained selective pressure, and it has been used to improve industrially relevant traits in lactic acid bacteria, including acid and thermal tolerance, osmotolerance, growth in specific substrates, and bacteriophage resistance (Derkx et al. 2014; Zhu et al. 2020). A particularly interesting feature of this approach is that selection under one stress frequently results in cross-protection against other stresses, as a result of the overlap in cellular responses and of global regulatory changes (Mols and Abee 2011). Selecting for a trait that depends on a global physiological response, such as the integrity and remodeling of the cell envelope, could therefore be a way to obtain strains with generally more robust phenotypes.

The cell envelope is the first barrier against environmental insults, and its stress response is well characterized in L. lactis. Envelope-targeting agents trigger the CesSR and other two-component systems, which induce a regulon that includes genes involved in cell wall biosynthesis, modification of the envelope and protein quality control (Martínez et al. 2007; Roces et al. 2012). Lcn972 is a non-lantibiotic bacteriocin produced by L. lactis IPLA972 that inhibits cell wall biosynthesis in sensitive lactococci by binding to lipid II, the cell wall precursor, at the septum, thereby impairing septum formation and cell division (Martínez et al. 1996; Martínez et al. 2008; Roces et al. 2009). Its narrow spectrum, restricted to L. lactis, and its mode of action make it a suitable agent to impose controlled cell envelope stress on lactococcal starters. Previous work has shown that the response to Lcn972 involves the CesSR system, the overexpression of the stress-inducible protein encoded by the *lcn972* resistance-associated locus, and the activation of genes of unknown function, and that spontaneous resistant mutants carry mutations affecting sugar metabolism, in particular the phosphotransferase system component *ptnD*, as well as other envelope-related genes (Roces et al. 2012; Kramer et al. 2008; Tymoszewska et al. 2017). Notably, resistance to Lcn972 in mutants of the laboratory strain L. lactis IPLA947 or its derivatives has been linked to altered growth, cell wall properties and metabolic regulation, which in turn may influence how cells handle other stresses (Roces et al. 2012). Whether resistance to cell wall-active bacteriocins can be harnessed to improve technological robustness of an industrial starter has not been explored.

The strain L. lactis IPLA947 is a well-characterized, phage-resistant dairy starter used in the manufacture of artisanal and industrial cheeses, with good acidifying properties and a genome that has been sequenced and annotated (Rodríguez-Alonso et al. 2009; Flórez et al. 2016). Given its industrial relevance, it is an appropriate model on which to test whether cell envelope stress-driven adaptive evolution may generate variants with enhanced technological traits. Importantly, any improvement in stress tolerance must not come at the expense of the core functions of the starter, namely rapid acidification, a stable lactose-to-lactate conversion and an adequate contribution to flavor. Trade-offs between stress resistance and growth, which are well described for mutants affected in global regulators or in carbon catabolite control (Ferenci 2016), can render stress-tolerant variants useless for dairy applications.

In this work, we applied adaptive evolution under cell envelope stress by consecutive exposure of L. lactis IPLA947 to increasing doses of Lcn972, and we screened the resulting derivatives for cross-protection against oxidative stress. We hypothesized that resistance to this envelope-active bacteriocin would select for variants with modified envelope physiology and/or metabolic regulation that would confer a more robust phenotype in the presence of oxygen. We characterized the selected mutant, L. lactis R5, regarding its survival after hydrogen peroxide challenge, its growth in aerobic and respiratory conditions, and its tolerance to the stresses encountered during starter production and storage, namely cold storage and freeze-drying. We then evaluated its performance as a dairy starter in aerated milk cultures, its acidification kinetics, its lactose consumption and organic acid production, and the profile of volatile compounds in experimental cheese curds. Our results show that Lcn972 resistance can be used to obtain a stable, oxygen-tolerant derivative that retains the technological properties of the parental strain and displays an enhanced capacity to produce acetoin, supporting the use of cell envelope stress as a driver of intra-strain diversification in industrial lactococci.

Materials and Methods

Bacterial strains, media and growth conditions

Lactococcus lactis subsp. lactis IPLA947, a dairy starter strain from the IPLA-CSIC collection, was the parental strain. Cultures were routinely grown at 30 °C without shaking in M17 broth (Oxoid) supplemented with 0.5% glucose (GM17) or in reconstituted skim milk (RSM, 10% w/v; Scharlau) for milk experiments. Stocks were stored at −80 °C in 20% glycerol. Lcn972 was produced and partially purified from L. lactis IPLA972 supernatants by cation-exchange chromatography, as described previously (Martínez et al. 1996), and its activity was quantified by the agar well diffusion assay against L. lactis subsp. cremoris MG1363 and expressed in arbitrary units (AU) per ml. Where indicated, hemin (5 µg/ml) was added to GM17 to promote respiratory metabolism (Duwat et al. 2001).

Adaptive evolution under Lcn972 stress

Adaptive evolution was carried out by consecutive exposure to Lcn972. An overnight culture of IPLA947 was diluted 1:100 in GM17 containing a sub-inhibitory concentration of Lcn972 (initially 0.5× the minimum inhibitory concentration, MIC), incubated for 24 h, and transferred daily into fresh medium with the bacteriocin concentration raised stepwise whenever growth was visible (OD600 > 0.5). MIC was determined by broth microdilution in 96-well plates, defined as the lowest concentration preventing visible growth after 24 h. After about 30 transfers (approximately 200 generations), the final population was plated on GM17 agar, and isolated colonies were tested for Lcn972 MIC. Clones with the highest MIC were selected and passaged ten times (about 70 generations) in GM17 without bacteriocin to test phenotypic stability; MIC was re-determined after this passage. One stable clone, designated R5, was selected for further characterization. Strain identity relative to the parent was confirmed by RAPD-PCR fingerprinting with primer OPA-3 (Ward and Roberts 1994) and by confirmation of the absence of bacteriophage-induced changes through plaque assays.

Hydrogen peroxide challenge

Exponential-phase cultures (OD600 ≈ 0.5) of IPLA947 and R5 were harvested, washed twice in 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 7.0), and resuspended to approximately 10^8 CFU/ml. Hydrogen peroxide (Sigma) was added to final concentrations of 5–20 mM and cells were incubated at 30 °C for 30 min. Residual H2O2 was neutralized with catalase (100 U/ml), and viable counts were determined by plating serial dilutions on GM17 agar. Survival was expressed as

S (%) = (N_t / N_0) × 100,

where N_t and N_0 are CFU/ml after and before treatment, respectively. Log reductions, log10(N_0/N_t), were also calculated.

Growth under aerobic and anaerobic conditions

Growth was monitored in GM17 in 250 ml flasks containing 50 ml of medium incubated at 30 °C with orbital shaking at 200 rpm (aerobic) or static in sealed tubes filled to the top (limited oxygen). OD600 was recorded every hour and specific growth rates (µ, h⁻¹) were obtained from the slope of ln(OD600) versus time during the exponential phase:

µ = (ln OD₂ − ln OD₁)/(t₂ − t₁).

Dissolved oxygen was measured with a fiber-optic oxygen sensor (PreSens) in selected experiments. To assess respiratory metabolism, the same experiments were performed in GM17 with and without hemin, and growth, final OD600, and biomass were compared.

Milk acidification

RSM was inoculated with 1% (v/v) of overnight cultures washed in sterile saline, or at ~10^6 CFU/ml, and incubated at 30 °C. For aerated cultures, 100 ml of milk in 500 ml flasks was shaken at 200 rpm, whereas static incubation in filled bottles served as the low-oxygen control. pH was recorded continuously with a data logger (CINAC system; Spinnler and Corrieu 1989) or measured at defined intervals. The maximum acidification rate (Vmax, pH units/min), time to reach pH 5.3 (t5.3), and final pH after 24 h were calculated from the pH curves.

Survival during cold storage and freeze-drying

For cold storage, cells from stationary-phase cultures were harvested, resuspended in RSM or in 0.9% NaCl, and stored at 4 °C for 28 days; viable counts were determined weekly. Freeze-drying was performed on cells harvested in late exponential phase, washed, and resuspended in 10% (w/v) skim milk supplemented with 5% sucrose. Aliquots (1 ml) were frozen at −80 °C for 2 h and lyophilized for 24 h (Telstar Lyoquest). Survival was calculated as the ratio of CFU/ml after versus before freeze-drying, after rehydration in the original volume of sterile water, and viability was also monitored after 1 and 3 months of storage at 4 °C.

Cheese manufacture

Experimental miniature cheeses were manufactured in duplicate on two independent days from pasteurized whole cow’s milk (72 °C, 15 s). Milk (2 l per vat) was warmed to 32 °C, inoculated with 1% active starter (approximately 10^7 CFU/ml), and 0.02% CaCl2 and 0.02% (v/v) commercial chymosin (Maxiren) were added. After coagulation (≈ 40 min), curd was cut, gently stirred, scalded at 36 °C, drained, moulded and pressed, and brined in 12% NaCl for 2 h. Cheeses were ripened at 12 °C for 30 days. Counts of lactococci were obtained on GM17 at 0, 1, 15 and 30 days. pH was recorded in milk, curd and cheese with a penetration electrode.

Analysis of sugars and organic acids

Lactose, galactose, lactic acid, acetic acid, citric acid, and other organic acids were quantified by HPLC from milk fermentations and cheeses. Samples were diluted in 0.01 N H2SO4, centrifuged, and filtered through 0.22 µm membranes. Separation was achieved on an Aminex HPX-87H column (Bio-Rad) at 65 °C with 3 mM H2SO4 as mobile phase at 0.6 ml/min, using refractive index and UV (210 nm) detection. Concentrations were calculated using external calibration curves.

Volatile compound analysis

Volatile compounds in 30-day curds were analysed by headspace solid-phase microextraction coupled to gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (HS-SPME-GC-MS). Grated cheese (3 g) with 2-methyl-3-heptanone as internal standard was equilibrated at 40 °C for 10 min, and volatiles were extracted for 30 min using a DVB/CAR/PDMS fibre (Supelco). Compounds were desorbed at 250 °C and separated on a DB-WAX capillary column with a temperature gradient from 40 to 220 °C. Mass spectra were acquired in electron impact mode (70 eV), and compounds were identified by comparison with NIST library spectra, retention indices, and authentic standards when available. Relative abundance was expressed as peak area ratios to the internal standard.

Statistical analysis

All experiments were performed with at least three independent biological replicates, unless otherwise stated. Data are expressed as means ± standard deviation. Differences between R5 and IPLA947 were analysed with two-tailed Student’s t tests, or with one-way or two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons (e.g. time-course and concentration-dependent data). Normality and homogeneity of variance were verified with Shapiro–Wilk and Levene’s tests; non-parametric Mann–Whitney tests were used otherwise. For volatile compounds, peak area ratios were log-transformed before analysis, and a principal component analysis was performed to visualize differences between cheese groups, with false discovery rate correction (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995) applied to multiple comparisons. Differences were considered significant at P < 0.05. Analyses were performed in R (version 4.1) and GraphPad Prism 8.

Results

Isolation of a stable Lcn972-resistant mutant with enhanced oxidative stress survival

Consecutive exposure of L. lactis IPLA947 to increasing concentrations of Lcn972 in M17 broth supplemented with glucose (GM17) yielded several resistant derivatives. After five rounds of exposure, the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) for the population rose from 40 to more than 640 arbitrary units (AU) ml⁻¹. One clone, designated R5, was selected after it retained the resistant phenotype (MIC ≥ 640 AU ml⁻¹) following approximately 100 generations of growth without bacteriocin, which indicated a stable genetic change rather than a transient physiological adaptation. Resistance was comparable to that reported for spontaneous Lcn972-resistant mutants of L. lactis IPLA947 and other strains (Roces et al., 2012; Kramer et al., 2008). Under standard anaerobic conditions in GM17, R5 and the parental strain displayed similar maximum specific growth rates (0.62 ± 0.03 and 0.60 ± 0.02 h⁻¹, respectively; P > 0.05), so the acquisition of resistance carried no obvious fitness penalty.

Because cell envelope stress responses frequently overlap with other stress responses in lactococci (Pinto et al., 2011), we compared the survival of both strains after challenge with hydrogen peroxide. Cells in exponential phase were exposed to 5 mM H₂O₂ for 30 min and survival was calculated as N/N₀. The wild type showed a reduction of about 3.1 log units, whereas R5 decreased by only 1.4 log units, giving a difference in survival of roughly 1.7 log units (P < 0.01). Thus R5 exhibited about 50-fold greater survival under oxidative challenge. Survival after exposure to other stresses, including heat (52 °C), acid (pH 4.0) and 0.3 M NaCl, did not differ significantly between the strains (differences < 0.4 log units), suggesting that the improvement was relatively specific to oxidative stress.

Growth and acidification under aerobic conditions

The impact of this phenotype on growth was evaluated in aerated cultures (shaking at 200 rpm) in GM17. Under these conditions the wild type slowed markedly, with a specific growth rate of 0.35 ± 0.02 h⁻¹, whereas R5 grew at 0.48 ± 0.03 h⁻¹, a 37% increase (P < 0.01). R5 also reached a higher final optical density at 600 nm (1.9 ± 0.1 versus 1.5 ± 0.1). In static cultures the differences were negligible. The relative growth advantage of R5 in the presence of oxygen was therefore consistent with its greater tolerance to peroxide, a major product of NADH and pyruvate oxidase-type reactions in lactic acid bacteria (Condon, 1987; Marty-Teysset et al., 2000).

In reconstituted skim milk (10% w/v) cultures incubated at 30 °C with agitation to aerate the medium, the wild type reduced the pH to 5.2 ± 0.1 after 24 h, whereas R5 reached 4.7 ± 0.1 (P < 0.05). Final viable counts were about 0.5 log CFU ml⁻¹ higher for R5 (9.2 versus 8.7 log CFU ml⁻¹). In non-aerated milk, however, the acidification curves were superimposable, with both strains reaching pH 4.6 within 8 h and showing equal maximum acidification rates (approximately 0.012 pH units min⁻¹ at the steepest part of the curve). Thus the benefit of the mutation was confined to oxygenated conditions.

Respiration, cold storage and freeze-drying

L. lactis can switch to respiratory metabolism when supplemented with heme and oxygen, resulting in higher biomass and improved survival (Duwat et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2012). We therefore tested whether the improved oxygen behavior of R5 extended to respiration-permissive conditions. In cultures supplemented with 1 µg ml⁻¹ hemin and aerated, both strains displayed the expected increase in biomass relative to cultures without heme (final OD₆₀₀ of 3.0–3.3 for both), and the specific growth rates did not differ statistically (0.55 ± 0.03 h⁻¹ for the wild type and 0.57 ± 0.02 h⁻¹ for R5). Likewise, survival after 7 days of storage in the stationary phase at 4 °C was equivalent in respiratory and fermentative cultures, with a loss of 0.3–0.6 log units in each. The benefit of R5 was thus masked by heme, which presumably confers oxygen detoxification through the respiratory chain and catalase activity.

Storage under cold conditions was also examined for cells suspended in milk. After 21 days at 4 °C, viable counts decreased by 0.5 ± 0.2 log units for the wild type and 0.4 ± 0.2 for R5 (P > 0.05). Survival after freeze-drying in 10% skim milk with 5% sucrose was 38 ± 6% for the wild type and 41 ± 7% for R5, and after 3 months at 4 °C the remaining viability was again indistinguishable (approximately 0.8 log reduction in both cases). Therefore, the oxidative stress advantage did not translate into improved technological robustness during cold storage or lyophilization.

Fermentation profile and acidification in cheese-like conditions

To determine whether the mutation altered the metabolic performance of the starter, lactose consumption and organic acid production were quantified by HPLC in milk fermentations at 30 °C. After 24 h, lactose decreased from 47.5 ± 0.8 g l⁻¹ to 2.1 ± 0.4 g l⁻¹ with the wild type and to 2.3 ± 0.5 g l⁻¹ with R5. Lactic acid concentrations were 41.2 ± 1.5 and 40.6 ± 1.2 g l⁻¹, respectively, and traces of acetic and formic acid (below 0.5 g l⁻¹) were similar in both strains. Citrate levels were not significantly affected. No differences were therefore noted in homolactic fermentation, as expected from the identical acidification kinetics.

Cheese manufacture and volatile compounds

Experimental miniature cheeses were manufactured in triplicate using either strain as the sole starter. Curd pH at the end of manufacture (5.3 ± 0.1) and moisture content (approximately 56%) were equivalent. Cell counts in the curd were 9.0 ± 0.2 log CFU g⁻¹ for both strains, indicating that R5 grew and was retained in the matrix to the same extent as the parental strain.

Volatile compounds were extracted by headspace solid-phase microextraction and analyzed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. Across the 30 compounds identified (acids, alcohols, ketones, aldehydes and esters), most showed similar abundance in the two sets of cheeses. The notable exception was 3-hydroxy-2-butanone (acetoin), which increased approximately 2.5-fold in curds made with R5 (P < 0.01). Diacetyl and 2,3-butanediol showed upward trends (about 1.5-fold) that did not reach significance. Acetoin is a key flavor compound associated with buttery notes in fresh cheeses and results from α-acetolactate decarboxylation and diacetyl reduction (Smid and Kleerebezem, 2014). The elevated acetoin points to a redirected pyruvate flux in R5, possibly connected to NADH reoxidation under oxidative conditions, although branched-chain aldehydes and other amino acid–derived volatiles were unchanged.

Collectively, these results show that selection for Lcn972 resistance produced a stable derivative with increased survival to H₂O₂ and better aerobic growth and acidification, while preserving the performance of the parental strain in standard dairy processes and enhancing acetoin production in curd.

Discussion

Adaptive laboratory evolution is increasingly used to generate robust industrial strains without recourse to recombinant DNA, which remains a practical barrier in food applications. Here we used sublethal, increasing exposure to the cell wall-active bacteriocin Lcn972 as a selective pressure and obtained a stable derivative of L. lactis IPLA947, strain R5, whose most notable acquired trait was enhanced tolerance to oxidative challenge. The result is of interest because Lcn972 resistance was not selected for on the basis of oxygen physiology; the link between the two phenotypes suggests that cell envelope perturbation and oxidative stress share common adaptive routes in lactococci, in line with earlier reports that envelope-targeting agents induce broad stress responses in L. lactis (Martínez et al., 2007; Roces et al., 2012). Because Lcn972 binds lipid II and interferes with septum formation and cell wall synthesis (Martínez et al., 2008), mutations that rebalance peptidoglycan metabolism, membrane composition or the redox state of the cell could plausibly confer cross-protection. Cell envelope stress also engages two-component systems such as CesSR and the regulators that coordinate envelope and oxidative responses (Martínez et al., 2007), and cross-protection between antimicrobial peptides and other stressors has been described in other Gram-positive bacteria (Cotter and Hill, 2003). We therefore interpret the R5 phenotype as a pleiotropic consequence of a regulatory or structural change in the envelope, although the specific mutation(s) remain to be identified. Whole-genome resequencing and transcriptomic comparison with the parental strain will be necessary to test this hypothesis and to rule out the contribution of unrelated mutations accumulated during serial passage.

The improved behavior of R5 in aerobic conditions was evident in faster growth in broth and in lower final pH in aerated milk, which suggests that the trait is relevant in a food matrix and not only in laboratory media. Oxygen is a recognized stressor for lactococci: although they are aerotolerant, reactive oxygen species generated by NADH oxidase, pyruvate oxidase-like activities and flavoprotein autoxidation damage DNA, proteins and lipids, and lactococci lack catalase and have a limited arsenal of detoxifying enzymes (Duwat et al., 2001; Rochat et al., 2006). Increased tolerance to H2O2 would be expected to prolong viability and metabolic activity during processes involving vigorous agitation, such as starter propagation and the early stages of vat filling. However, enhanced oxygen tolerance did not extend to respiratory conditions. In the presence of heme, L. lactis switches to respiration, with increased biomass and improved long-term survival (Duwat et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2012), and one might have expected R5 to benefit differently. The absence of additional gains suggests that the protective mechanism acquired by R5 is independent of the respiratory pathway, or that heme already alleviates oxidative damage sufficiently so that any advantage of R5 is masked. This distinction is useful from an applied perspective, as it indicates that R5 improves performance under standard fermentative conditions, which are the ones used by most dairies, without requiring supplementation with heme.

Equally informative are the traits that did not change. Oxidative stress tolerance is often assumed to correlate with resistance to other technological stresses, since cold storage and freeze-drying damage cells in part through oxidation of membrane lipids and proteins (Rault et al., 2007; Santivarangkna et al., 2008). Nevertheless, R5 did not show higher survival after cold storage or freeze-drying. Cryotolerance and desiccation tolerance are multifactorial and depend strongly on membrane fluidity, cytoplasmic solute accumulation and the growth phase at harvest, so oxidative protection alone may not suffice. The result also shows that the evolved phenotype is relatively specific and was not accompanied by a generalized stress-resistant state. Although a broader gain in robustness would have been attractive, specificity can be considered an advantage, because pleiotropic stress resistance is sometimes linked to slower growth or reduced acidification, trade-offs that are unacceptable in a starter (Bachmann et al., 2012).

From a technological standpoint, the central finding is that R5 retained the milk acidification rate, lactose consumption and organic acid profile of the wild type. Mutants selected under strong pressure often display fitness costs or altered carbon flux, and resistance to bacteriocins that target the cell wall can impair growth or autolysis. The absence of such costs in R5 supports its suitability as a dairy starter and indicates that selection with Lcn972 can yield mutants whose functionality in milk is preserved. The significant increase in acetoin in curds made with R5 is the most notable metabolic difference. Acetoin and diacetyl derive from α-acetolactate, whose formation and conversion depend on pyruvate partitioning and on the NADH/NAD+ ratio (Hugenholtz, 1993; Smid and Kleerebezem, 2014). Under oxygen exposure, NADH oxidase activity modifies the redox balance and generally promotes diversion of pyruvate towards C4 compounds. An altered redox state or enhanced oxidative capacity in R5 would therefore be consistent with higher acetoin, although we did not measure intracellular cofactors or enzyme activities. Acetoin contributes a buttery note and is a precursor of diacetyl, so its increase could modify the sensory profile of cheese, probably in a favorable way in fresh and lactic-type varieties. Whether the change is perceptible, desirable and stable throughout ripening can only be established by sensory analysis and by studies with ripened cheeses, which were beyond the scope of this work.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study is based on a single evolved isolate from one parental strain, so we cannot say how reproducible the phenotype is across independent evolutionary lineages or across other L. lactis strains. Second, the genetic basis of the phenotype is unknown, which limits mechanistic interpretation and the assessment of the stability of the trait under industrial propagation, although the mutant was stable over repeated subculture. Third, cheese-making trials were performed at laboratory scale, and the interaction of R5 with bacteriophages, with adjunct cultures and with the variable oxygen levels of industrial vats were not evaluated. Finally, resistance to Lcn972 may alter susceptibility to other cell wall-active agents or to phage adsorption, and these properties should be examined before commercial use.

Despite these caveats, the work has practical implications. It demonstrates that adaptive evolution under envelope stress is a simple, non-GMO route to diversify industrial lactococci and to uncover phenotypes, such as oxidative stress tolerance, that are not obviously connected to the selective agent. Such strains could be valuable for starter production and for processes in which aeration is unavoidable, and could extend the repertoire of strains available for rotation schemes. In conclusion, L. lactis R5 combines improved oxidative stress tolerance with unaltered acidification and organic acid production and with increased acetoin formation in curd, supporting its potential as a dairy starter. Future work should define the underlying mutations, test the strain in ripened cheeses at pilot scale, and explore whether sequential or combined selective pressures can generate strains that also improve resistance to cold and drying.

Introduction

Concern about the growing distance between people and the natural world has become a central theme in environmental scholarship, education, and public health. Louv's (2005) popular account of "nature-deficit disorder" gave wide currency to the idea that urbanized, screen-saturated societies are producing generations estranged from the outdoors, and a large empirical literature has since documented the psychological, physical, and civic benefits of contact with nature. Exposure to green space is associated with reduced stress, improved attention, and better mental health (Kaplan 1995; Ulrich et al. 1991; Bratman et al. 2019), while childhood experiences outdoors are linked to environmental concern and pro-environmental behavior in adulthood (Wells and Lekies 2006; Chawla 2020). Scholars have developed numerous constructs to capture these relationships, including connectedness to nature (Mayer and Frantz 2004), nature relatedness (Nisbet, Zelenski, and Murphy 2009), and biophilia (Wilson 1984; Kellert and Wilson 1993). Collectively, this work has sought to explain how and why people come to feel part of, or apart from, the natural world.

Most of this research, however, relies on structured scales that ask respondents to agree or disagree with researcher-defined statements. Such instruments are valuable for measuring the strength of a connection, but they reveal little about the content of people's thoughts when they contemplate nature. A respondent who scores low on connectedness may be bored by nature, afraid of it, indifferent to it, or simply unaccustomed to it; one who scores high may be thinking of tranquil forests, of recreation, or of ecological interdependence. Because the meanings attached to nature are socially constructed and historically contingent (Cronon 1995; Williams 1980), the associations that come to mind are likely to vary with the social positions and experiences of those who hold them. Few scholars have therefore asked the simple, prior question of what people tend to ponder when they think of nature, and fewer still have examined how those thoughts differ across social groups.

This gap matters because the "positive" framing that dominates the literature may obscure a more ambivalent reality. Nature has long evoked fear as well as reverence. Tuan (1979) documented the landscapes of fear that shape human settlement and imagination, and Ulrich (1993) and Öhman and Mineka (2001) argued that humans are predisposed to learn fear of certain natural stimuli such as snakes, heights, and darkness. Wilderness, in the American imagination, has been simultaneously sublime and menacing, a site of both spiritual renewal and mortal danger (Nash 2001; Cronon 1995). Environmental psychologists have likewise noted that fear of crime, getting lost, or encountering dangerous animals can deter outdoor recreation (Jorgensen and Anthopoulou 2007; Bixler and Floyd 1997). Bixler and Floyd (1997), for example, found that disgust, fear, and discomfort with wildland settings were associated with a preference for indoor activities among adolescents. These fears are not merely individual quirks but may be patterned by social experience.

Research on race and the outdoors suggests that this patterning is substantial. Historical exclusion, segregation, and racial violence in rural and wild places have shaped the relationships many Black, Indigenous, Latino, and Asian American communities have with parks and wilderness (Finney 2014; Taylor 2016; Mock 2018). Studies of outdoor recreation have traced differential participation to a combination of marginality, discrimination, cultural preferences, and unequal access (Floyd 1999; Washburne 1978; Flores, Falco, and Morales 2018). Lynching and the legacy of plantation landscapes, for example, complicate any assumption that rural nature is a universally safe or restorative space (Finney 2014; Kimmerer 2013 offers a contrasting Indigenous perspective emphasizing reciprocity rather than fear). At the same time, scholars caution against essentializing. Minority communities have deep traditions of farming, fishing, gardening, and environmental stewardship (Taylor 2016; Mohai, Pellow, and Roberts 2009), and survey evidence frequently shows that racial and ethnic minorities express equal or greater environmental concern than whites (Pearson, Schuldt, and Romero-Canyas 2016). Characterizing minorities as uniformly fearful or disconnected would thus be both empirically and ethically problematic.

Race, moreover, is only one of several dimensions along which thoughts about nature may vary. Gender has been associated with differences in fear of crime and of natural hazards in outdoor settings (Pain 2001; Valentine 1989), and with differing environmental attitudes more generally (Zelezny, Chua, and Aldrich 2000). Social class and parental education shape access to leisure time, travel, camps, and parks (Stodolska and Shinew 2010), and first-generation college students may bring distinctive experiences and constraints to higher education (Stephens et al. 2012). Age and life stage influence both exposure and attitude. Academic interest or major is another plausible influence: students in environmental or natural science fields receive sustained exposure to ecological concepts, fieldwork, and hazard knowledge that could alter what they associate with nature (Hungerford and Volk 1990). Yet these factors are seldom analyzed together, and when they are not, apparent racial differences may reflect confounding with class, gender, or educational background. An intersectional and multivariate approach is needed to separate these influences (Crenshaw 1991; Finney 2014).

College and university students constitute a useful population for such an inquiry. They are at a formative stage in which environmental identities and career orientations are consolidating, and they are the future leaders, professionals, and voters whose decisions will shape environmental policy. Campuses are also increasingly diverse in race, class, and generational status, allowing comparisons across groups that share a common institutional context. Moreover, educators who aim to foster environmental literacy and outdoor engagement need to understand the associations students bring with them, including fear, danger, and loathing, if programs are to be welcoming and effective (Chawla 2020; Rickinson et al. 2004).

This study therefore addresses two research questions. First, how do college and university students think about nature, and in particular, how often do they bring to mind concepts of fear, danger, disconnection, and loathing, such as predators, natural hazards, human-made hazards, getting lost, and loathsome or hateful places? Second, which social and academic factors, including race and ethnicity, gender, age, social class, parental education, first-generation status, and academic interest, are most significant in shaping those thoughts? Using open-ended responses from 287 American students, coded into thematic categories and analyzed through descriptive and multivariate techniques, the paper offers three contributions. It shifts attention from the strength of human–nature connection to the content of students' thoughts about nature. It highlights the negative and ambivalent associations that tend to be overshadowed in the literature. And it demonstrates that although race matters, it operates alongside academic interest, gender, age, and family educational background, cautioning against simplistic narratives of minority disconnection from nature.

Methods

**Research Design and Data Collection**

The study used a cross-sectional survey design with a mixed approach to analysis. Open-ended responses were systematically coded into categories (Krippendorff, 2019), and the resulting binary indicators were then analyzed with descriptive and multivariate statistics (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). This approach suited the research question. Closed-ended instruments such as the Connectedness to Nature Scale (Mayer & Frantz, 2004) or the New Ecological Paradigm (Dunlap et al., 2000) measure attitudes toward researcher-defined constructs. Our aim was to learn what students spontaneously think about when they contemplate nature, so respondents had to be free to name their own ideas.

Data were collected from undergraduate students at two public universities in the United States during one academic term. Instructors in a range of general education and discipline-specific courses distributed an anonymous online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform, following tailored-design principles for web surveys (Dillman et al., 2014). Courses were chosen deliberately to reach students with different academic interests, including environmental science, biology, sociology, business, education, and the humanities. Participation was voluntary, and some instructors offered a small amount of extra credit, with an alternative assignment of equal effort available. The institutional review board at the lead author's university approved the protocol and classified it as exempt. Informed consent was obtained electronically before respondents could begin the survey.

A total of 301 students opened the survey. Fourteen were excluded because they did not complete the open-ended prompt or the demographic items, leaving an analytic sample of 287 (95.3% of those who started). Because the sample is non-probability and drawn from a limited number of courses, the findings are not generalizable to all American students. We treat the analysis as exploratory and focus on the direction, magnitude, and consistency of associations rather than population estimates.

**Instrument and Measures**

The questionnaire contained an open-ended prompt followed by demographic and background items. The prompt read: "When you think of nature, what thoughts, ideas, images, or feelings come to mind? Please list or describe as many as you wish." It was deliberately neutral. It did not mention fear, danger, or any other valence, so that such themes would emerge only if respondents introduced them (Kellert, 1996). Responses ranged from single words to multi-sentence paragraphs.

*Dependent variables.* Responses were coded for eight concepts that prior scholarship links to negative or ambivalent relationships with nature: (1) disconnection from or lack of contact with nature; (2) predators or dangerous animals; (3) getting lost; (4) loathsome or hateful places (e.g., statements that nature is disgusting, dirty, boring, or hated); (5) fear; (6) danger; (7) natural hazards (e.g., storms, wildfires, floods, venomous insects); and (8) human-made hazards (e.g., pollution, toxic exposure, development, climate disruption). These categories build on research on fear and avoidance of natural settings (Bixler & Floyd, 1997; Ulrich, 1993), on racialized experiences of outdoor spaces (Finney, 2014; Flores et al., 2018; Mott, 2018), and on the notion of "nature-deficit" (Louv, 2005). Each concept was coded 1 if the respondent mentioned it at least once and 0 otherwise. We analyzed presence rather than frequency of mention because the responses were brief and counts would have conflated verbosity with salience.

*Independent variables.* Race/ethnicity was collapsed into a binary variable (white = 1; racial/ethnic minority = 0) because cell sizes for individual groups were too small for stable estimation. Gender was coded as woman = 1 and man = 0. Seven respondents who identified as non-binary or declined to answer were retained in descriptive tables but excluded from multivariate models for lack of power. We discuss this limitation below. Age was measured in years. Class standing (first-year through senior) was entered as an ordinal variable treated as continuous after sensitivity tests with dummy coding produced substantively identical results. Parental education was the highest level attained by either parent (ordinal, 1 = less than high school to 6 = graduate degree). First-generation status was coded 1 if neither parent had completed a four-year degree. Because parental education and first-generation status are conceptually and empirically related, they were never entered in the same model. Academic interest was operationalized as whether a student's major or intended major was in a natural resource, environmental, or life science field (1) or another field (0). Using major as a proxy for interest follows prior work on how disciplinary socialization shapes environmental orientations (Hand & Van Liere, 1984).

**Coding Procedure and Reliability**

Coding followed a hybrid deductive–inductive strategy (Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006). A preliminary codebook was derived from the literature, and two coders then independently read a random 20% subsample (n = 57) and proposed additional categories and clarified decision rules. Definitions and exemplar quotations were revised in two rounds. Both coders then independently coded the full dataset, blind to respondent demographics. Intercoder agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa:

κ = (p₀ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ),

where p₀ is observed agreement and pₑ is agreement expected by chance. Kappa values for the eight categories ranged from 0.78 to 0.91, which Landis and Koch (1977) classify as substantial to almost perfect. Disagreements were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached, and the consensus codes were used in all analyses.

**Statistical Analysis**

Analysis proceeded in three stages. First, we calculated frequencies and percentages for each concept for the full sample and by race/ethnicity, gender, and academic interest. Bivariate associations between the binary outcomes and categorical predictors were tested with Pearson's chi-square test, or Fisher's exact test when any expected cell count was below five. Effect sizes were reported as phi or Cramér's V. For continuous and ordinal predictors we used point-biserial correlations and Mann–Whitney U tests. Because we examined eight outcomes, we report exact p-values and treat results near conventional thresholds cautiously instead of relying on a single cutoff (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).

Second, we estimated a binary logistic regression model for each dependent variable. For respondent *i* and outcome *k*, the model was

ln[ Pᵢₖ / (1 − Pᵢₖ) ] = β₀ₖ + β₁ₖ White + β₂ₖ Woman + β₃ₖ Age + β₄ₖ Class + β₅ₖ ParEd + β₆ₖ NatSci,

where Pᵢₖ is the probability that respondent *i* mentioned concept *k*. A parallel set of models replaced ParEd with a first-generation indicator (FirstGen). Coefficients are reported as odds ratios, OR = exp(β), with 95% confidence intervals. An OR below 1 for White indicates that white students had lower odds than minority students of mentioning the concept, net of controls. Because odds ratios can overstate differences when outcomes are common (Norton et al., 2018), we also computed average marginal effects, which express the change in predicted probability, holding other covariates at observed values.

Third, we evaluated model adequacy and robustness. Multicollinearity was assessed with variance inflation factors, with values above 5 treated as problematic. Overall fit was assessed using likelihood-ratio chi-square tests against the null model, the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (Hosmer et al., 2013), and McFadden's pseudo-R²:

R²_McF = 1 − ln L_M / ln L₀,

where L_M and L₀ are the likelihoods of the fitted and intercept-only models. Discrimination was summarized with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. For outcomes with few positive cases, such as getting lost and predators, we followed the events-per-variable guideline of Peduzzi et al. (1996) and judged whether estimates were stable. Where separation or sparse data were a concern, we re-estimated models with Firth's (1993) penalized likelihood and report both sets of results when they differ. Cases with missing data on any predictor were few (fewer than 2%) and were handled by listwise deletion. Analyses were conducted in Stata 17 and R 4.3, with two-tailed tests and α = .05.

Finally, because our analytic aim includes showing that racial/ethnic minority students are not uniformly fearful of or disconnected from nature, we examined the proportion of minority respondents who mentioned each concept alongside the group differences, and we read the uncoded text for illustrative quotations. This keeps the focus on within-group variability and guards against the ecological fallacy of treating a binary group contrast as a characterization of every group member (Finney, 2014).

**Results**

**Sample Characteristics and Coding Outcomes**

The analytic sample comprised 287 students. Of these, 155 (54.0%) identified as white and 132 (46.0%) as racial/ethnic minorities (49 Black, 40 Hispanic/Latino, 28 Asian/Asian American, and 15 multiracial or other). Women made up 61.3% of respondents. Mean age was 21.4 years (SD = 4.2). Roughly one-third (34.8%) were first-generation college students, and 29.3% were enrolled in programs with an explicit nature-related focus (environmental science, biology, geology, forestry, or related fields). Responses to the open-ended prompt were coded into binary indicators for each theme (1 = mentioned, 0 = not mentioned), following conventional procedures for content analysis (Krippendorff, 2019). Intercoder agreement on the themes analyzed here was high (Cohen's κ = .82 to .91).

Across the sample, the most frequently mentioned themes in this cluster were natural hazards (21.9%), danger (18.8%), and fear (14.3%). Less common were human-made hazards (12.5%), disconnection (11.5%), predators (9.8%), loathsome or hateful places (8.7%), and getting lost (7.3%). Most respondents, then, did not associate nature with these ideas, consistent with research showing that positive, restorative associations dominate public thinking about nature (Kellert, 1996; Louv, 2005).

**Bivariate Differences by Race/Ethnicity**

Table 1 (not reproduced here) shows that white students were significantly less likely than minority students to mention six of the eight themes (Pearson χ² tests, df = 1). Fear was mentioned by 9.0% of white students and 20.5% of minority students, χ² = 7.60, p = .006, φ = .16. For danger the figures were 13.5% and 25.0%, χ² = 6.12, p = .013, φ = .15. Disconnection showed 6.5% and 17.4%, χ² = 8.43, p = .004, φ = .17. Predators showed 5.2% and 15.2%, χ² = 8.08, p = .004, φ = .17. Getting lost showed 3.9% and 11.4%, χ² = 5.90, p = .015, φ = .14. Loathsome or hateful places showed 4.5% and 13.6%, χ² = 7.46, p = .006, φ = .16. By conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988) these effects are small to modest.

No significant racial differences emerged for natural hazards (20.6% of white vs. 23.5% of minority students, χ² = 0.32, p = .57) or human-made hazards (11.0% vs. 14.4%, χ² = 0.78, p = .38). Both groups appear similarly likely to think of floods, storms, wildfires, pollution, and similar threats.

These differences should not be read as evidence of widespread fear or alienation among minority students. Even for the most frequently mentioned theme, fear, 79.5% of minority respondents did not mention it. Among minority subgroups, fear was mentioned by 22.4% of Black students (11 of 49), 22.5% of Hispanic students (9 of 40), 14.3% of Asian students (4 of 28), and 20.0% of the multiracial/other group (3 of 15). Fisher's exact tests found no significant heterogeneity among these groups (p = .81), although the small cell sizes limit statistical power. Disconnection followed a similar pattern, with the highest proportion among Black students (22.4%) and the lowest among Asian students (10.7%). Most minority students did not describe nature in these terms, a finding in line with scholarship challenging deficit portrayals of minority communities' relationships with the outdoors (Finney, 2014; Mott, 2019).

**Multivariate Models**

To assess whether racial differences persisted after accounting for other characteristics, each binary theme was modeled with logistic regression (Hosmer et al., 2013):

$$\ln\left(\frac{P(Y_i=1)}{1-P(Y_i=1)}\right)=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{Minority}_i+\beta_2\text{Female}_i+\beta_3\text{Age}_i+\beta_4\text{ParentEd}_i+\beta_5\text{FirstGen}_i+\beta_6\text{NatureMajor}_i$$

Parental education was measured as the highest level attained by either parent (1 = less than high school to 6 = graduate degree). Coefficients are reported as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals. Variance inflation factors were below 2.1 for all predictors, indicating no serious multicollinearity, and Hosmer–Lemeshow tests indicated adequate fit for all models (all p > .20). Nagelkerke R² ranged from .08 (human-made hazards) to .21 (loathsome or hateful places).

*Race/ethnicity.* Net of the controls, minority status significantly increased the odds of mentioning six themes. The adjusted ORs were 2.31 for fear (95% CI = 1.10–4.84, p = .027), 2.05 for danger (1.04–4.03, p = .038), 2.78 for disconnection (1.20–6.44, p = .017), 3.01 for predators (1.21–7.49, p = .018), 2.66 for getting lost (1.03–6.85, p = .043), and 3.22 for loathsome or hateful places (1.26–8.21, p = .014). Race was not significant in the natural hazards model (OR = 1.14, p = .68) or the human-made hazards model (OR = 1.31, p = .50).

*Academic interest.* Nature-related academic interest was the most consistent non-racial predictor, significant in five of the eight models. Students in nature-related fields were more likely to mention natural hazards (OR = 2.14, 1.13–4.05, p = .019) and human-made hazards (OR = 2.67, 1.18–6.04, p = .018). They were less likely to mention disconnection (OR = 0.31, 0.10–0.94, p = .038), predators (OR = 0.38, 0.14–0.99, p = .048), and loathsome or hateful places (OR = 0.22, 0.06–0.80, p = .021). Thus, academic exposure appears to shift attention toward environmental processes and threats and away from alienation and aversion, a pattern consistent with work on how environmental education shapes nature connectedness (Zylstra et al., 2014).

*Gender.* Women were more likely than men to mention danger (OR = 2.28, 1.16–4.49, p = .017) and predators (OR = 2.52, 1.01–6.30, p = .048). The fear model showed a similar direction, but the effect was not significant (OR = 1.74, p = .13). Gender was unrelated to the remaining themes. This agrees with research on gendered perceptions of risk in outdoor spaces (Pain, 2001).

*Age.* Each additional year of age reduced the odds of mentioning fear by 8% (OR = 0.92, 0.85–0.99, p = .031) and getting lost by 10% (OR = 0.90, 0.82–0.99, p = .035). Age was not significant in the other models.

*Parental education and first-generation status.* Higher parental education was associated with lower odds of mentioning disconnection (OR = 0.72 per unit, 0.55–0.94, p = .016) and of mentioning human-made hazards (OR = 0.78, 0.62–0.98, p = .033). First-generation students were more likely than continuing-generation students to mention loathsome or hateful places (OR = 2.94, 1.15–7.51, p = .024) and danger (OR = 2.01, 1.01–4.00, p = .047). Neither variable was significant in the remaining models.

**Summary of Findings**

Overall, race/ethnicity remained a significant predictor of fear, danger, disconnection, predators, getting lost, and loathsome or hateful places after controlling for gender, age, family background, and academic interest. However, the absolute proportions of students reporting these thoughts were modest, and academic interest, gender, age, parental education, and first-generation status each significantly shaped at least one outcome. Racial differences were therefore real but not exhaustive of the variation in how students thought about nature.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study set out to determine what college students think about when they contemplate nature and which demographic and academic characteristics shape those thoughts, with particular attention to fear, danger, disconnection, and loathing. Three broad conclusions emerge. First, white students were less likely than racial and ethnic minority students to report thoughts of disconnection, predators, getting lost, loathsome or hateful places, fear, and danger. Second, this pattern was neither uniform nor deterministic, and race was not the only significant predictor. Third, academic interest, gender, age, parental education, and first-generation status also had significant effects in multivariate models, and in several cases these effects were as informative as race.

The racial and ethnic differences are consistent with a long line of scholarship showing that the meanings attached to natural spaces are historically and socially situated. Work on the racialized history of American wilderness and outdoor recreation suggests that minority groups have encountered exclusion, violence, and unequal access in rural and wild settings (Finney, 2014; Taylor, 2016). Such histories plausibly generate associations between nature and danger that white students, whose families have not experienced those constraints, are less likely to hold. Our finding that minority students were more likely to mention predators and getting lost may reflect not only direct experience but also inherited narratives, such as those of lynching, slavery, or border crossings, that infuse landscapes with threat (Lanier, 2016; Mock, 2020). Likewise, thoughts of disconnection may reflect structural limits on access to parks and green space, which are distributed unequally by race and income (Rigolon, 2016), rather than any cultural indifference to the natural world. Interpreting these results as evidence of minority "fear" of nature would therefore misplace the explanation in individuals rather than in the social conditions that structure their encounters with it.

That caution is reinforced by the second finding: it would be inaccurate to describe minority students as universally fearful of or disconnected from nature. Many minority respondents offered thoughts of beauty, calm, family, and recreation, and many white respondents reported fear and danger. This heterogeneity echoes critiques of the "minority nature deficit" narrative, which argues that simple comparisons of participation rates conceal diverse and sometimes deep relationships with land, including agricultural, spiritual, and subsistence traditions (Johnson & Bowker, 2004; Finney, 2014). Our results suggest that difference in the probability of a particular thought should not be conflated with an absence of connection. Differences of degree, not kind, characterize the data.

The multivariate results further complicate any race-only account. Academic interest, particularly majoring in or being drawn to environmental and natural science fields, significantly predicted thoughts about natural hazards, disconnection, predators, human-made hazards, and loathsome or hateful places. Students whose studies orient them toward the environment may possess more detailed ecological vocabulary and be more aware of hazards, whether geological, biological, or anthropogenic. This is consistent with research indicating that environmental education and disciplinary socialization alter the conceptual frames through which people interpret nature (Kellert, 2012; Louv, 2005). Alternatively, selection effects may operate: students already attentive to risk, degradation, or contamination may self-select into these fields. Cross-sectional data cannot separate these mechanisms. Gender effects fit prior evidence that women report greater fear of crime and victimization in isolated outdoor settings (Pain, 2001; Hughes & Morrison, 2018), and the age, parental education, and first-generation effects point toward the role of class-linked exposure, cultural capital, and family experience in shaping associations with nature. First-generation students, for example, may have had fewer opportunities for recreational travel or park visitation, which could heighten both unfamiliarity and apprehension (Kuo, Barnes, & Jordan, 2019).

Taken together, these findings support an intersectional rather than single-axis interpretation (Crenshaw, 1991). Race, gender, class background, and field of study jointly influence what nature means to students, and the substantive significance of race often diminished or changed when other variables were controlled. For theory, this suggests that frameworks such as biophilia (Wilson, 1984) and the nature deficit perspective, which emphasize innate or universal affinities, must be supplemented by sociological accounts attending to power, history, and inequality. Fear, danger, and loathing are not aberrations from a natural human bond with nature; they are meaningful responses to particular social and ecological conditions, and in some cases reasonable ones.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The sample of 287 students is modest and was drawn from a limited number of institutions, so generalization to all American college students is unwarranted. Smaller racial and ethnic groups had to be aggregated into a minority category to maintain statistical power, which masks meaningful differences among, for example, Black, Latino, Asian American, and Indigenous students, whose histories with land differ substantially. The open-ended prompt, coded into thematic categories, captures what came to mind but not the intensity, valence, or context of those thoughts; a student who mentions "predators" may be expressing fear, respect, or scientific interest. Coding decisions inevitably involve interpretation, although we sought consistency through documented procedures. Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, causal claims about academic interest or parental education are not justified, and unmeasured variables such as rural versus urban upbringing, prior outdoor experience, disability, religion, or experiences of discrimination may account for part of the observed variation. Finally, a student sample is younger and more educated than the general public, and thus represents a particular, albeit important, stage in the formation of environmental attitudes.

These limitations suggest directions for future research. Larger and more diverse samples would permit disaggregation of racial and ethnic groups and the testing of interaction effects among race, gender, and class. Mixed-methods designs, combining surveys with interviews or photo elicitation, could clarify why particular thoughts arise and how they are felt. Longitudinal studies could examine whether coursework, field experiences, or outdoor programming actually change students' associations, helping to distinguish socialization from selection.

The findings also carry practical implications. Campus sustainability offices, outdoor recreation programs, and environmental curricula often assume that students approach nature with a shared set of positive expectations. Our results indicate that some students approach it with legitimate concerns about safety, belonging, and access. Programs may therefore be more effective if they address these concerns directly through inclusive leadership, transparent safety practices, affordable equipment and transportation, and curricula that acknowledge the histories of exclusion and environmental injustice (Taylor, 2016; Rigolon, 2016). Presenting nature solely as a refuge may alienate students for whom it has also been a site of risk, whereas acknowledging hazards, both natural and human-made, may build trust and relevance. Because first-generation and lower-income students were distinct in some outcomes, outreach should also attend to class-based barriers.

In sum, college students think about nature in varied ways, and fear, danger, disconnection, and loathing are more common among racial and ethnic minority students, yet are shaped by gender, academic interest, and family background as well. Understanding these thoughts as products of social context rather than individual deficiency offers a more accurate and more constructive foundation for environmental scholarship, education, and engagement.

Introduction

Antibiotic resistance is among the most pressing threats to global health, and the use of antibiotics in food-producing animals is widely regarded as one contributor to its emergence and spread (World Health Organization, 2017; O'Neill, 2016). Livestock production accounts for a substantial share of global antibiotic consumption. Recent estimates suggest that more antimicrobials are administered to animals than to humans in many countries, and that global veterinary consumption will continue to rise with growing demand for animal protein (Van Boeckel et al., 2015; Van Boeckel et al., 2017). Resistant bacteria and resistance determinants selected in animals can reach humans through the food chain, direct occupational contact, and environmental pathways such as manure application and contaminated water (Marshall and Levy, 2011; Wegener, 2003). Although the quantitative contribution of agricultural use to the overall burden of resistant human infections remains debated, the biological plausibility of this contribution has motivated regulatory action across many jurisdictions.

Policy responses have varied considerably in scope and design. Sweden prohibited the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in 1986, and Denmark phased out growth promoters in the 1990s and subsequently introduced additional controls on prescribing and veterinary profit from drug sales (Aarestrup et al., 2010; Wierup, 2001). The European Union banned avoparcin in 1997 and then extended its prohibition to all antibiotic growth promoters in 2006 (European Commission, 2005). More recently, the European Union has restricted routine prophylactic use and reserved certain antimicrobials for human medicine (Regulation (EU) 2019/6). In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration withdrew approval for fluoroquinolone use in poultry in 2005 and, through Guidance for Industry #209 and #213, phased out the use of medically important antibiotics for growth promotion and required veterinary oversight of remaining uses by 2017 (Food and Drug Administration, 2012; 2013). Other countries have restricted individual antibiotics, such as colistin in China in 2017 and in several Southeast Asian nations thereafter (Walsh and Wu, 2016; Wang et al., 2020). Voluntary industry initiatives, including "no antibiotics ever" labeling, represent a market-driven form of restriction that is more stringent than most regulation, in that it excludes therapeutic use. These policies therefore differ in important ways: some target a single drug, some a drug class, some particular indications such as growth promotion or disease prophylaxis, and some all uses of antibiotics.
