Evidence that such restrictions reduce resistance has accumulated over several decades, though it has been heterogeneous in quality and conclusions. Early observational reports from Europe documented declines in vancomycin-resistant enterococci in poultry and swine after the avoparcin ban, as well as declines in macrolide and glycopeptide resistance following growth promoter withdrawal (Aarestrup et al., 2001; Bager et al., 1997). However, other studies reported persistence of resistance despite cessation of use, or even increases in resistance to certain antibiotics, which has been attributed to co-selection, linked resistance genes, fitness-neutral or fitness-compensated resistance mutations, and the continued use of other antibiotics (Enne et al., 2001; Andersson and Hughes, 2010). Studies of fluoroquinolone restrictions in poultry found that resistance in Campylobacter often persisted after approvals were withdrawn (Price et al., 2007). Such findings underscore that the relationship between antibiotic selection pressure and resistance prevalence is neither linear nor uniformly reversible, and that the design of a restriction may determine its effect.

Systematic syntheses have attempted to summarize this literature. Tang and colleagues (2017) reported in a systematic review and meta-analysis of 181 studies that restricting antibiotic use in food-producing animals was associated with a reduction in the prevalence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in these animals, with the strongest associations observed in studies of the animals themselves and weaker, though directionally consistent, associations in human populations with high exposure to animals. This synthesis informed the World Health Organization guidelines on the use of medically important antimicrobials in food-producing animals, which recommended an overall reduction in use and a complete restriction of growth promotion and of disease prevention in the absence of diagnosed illness (World Health Organization, 2017). Nonetheless, the pooled analysis treated "restriction" as a single exposure. By combining interventions as dissimilar as a nationwide ban on one growth promoter and an organic or antibiotic-free production system, it could not indicate which kinds of restriction are most effective, nor whether policies short of total prohibition can achieve meaningful reductions in resistance.

This distinction matters for several practical reasons. First, policy makers are rarely choosing between "restriction" and "no restriction." They must decide among alternatives that carry different political, economic, and animal-welfare costs. Complete bans, including those on therapeutic use, may compromise animal health where alternatives to antibiotics, such as vaccination, improved biosecurity, and husbandry changes, are not yet in place, and may in some circumstances prompt compensatory increases in therapeutic consumption (Aarestrup et al., 2010; Cogliani et al., 2011). Conversely, narrowly targeted restrictions may be easier to implement and enforce but may be undermined by substitution toward related compounds or by co-selection through unrestricted drugs (Andersson and Hughes, 2010). Second, international guidance has increasingly emphasized stepwise approaches, such as eliminating growth promotion first, then routine prophylaxis, and reserving critically important antibiotics for human use, yet empirical evidence comparing the resistance outcomes of these steps has not been systematically assembled. Third, low- and middle-income countries, where antibiotic use in livestock is increasing most rapidly, require evidence on the minimum degree of restriction likely to be effective in order to prioritize limited regulatory capacity (Van Boeckel et al., 2015).

To address this gap, we conducted a prespecified sub-analysis of our previous systematic review and meta-analysis. We developed a classification scheme that distinguishes seven categories of restriction: complete restriction; restriction of a single antibiotic class; restriction of a single antibiotic; restriction of all non-therapeutic use; restriction of growth promotion and prophylaxis together; restriction of growth promotion alone; and other or undetermined approaches. We then coded each eligible study by intervention type and estimated stratified pooled effects on the prevalence of antibiotic-resistant bacterial isolates using random effects models. Our primary question was whether the magnitude of association between restriction and reduced resistance differs by the breadth of the intervention. Secondary questions were whether interventions that preserve therapeutic use are associated with reductions comparable to those of complete restriction, and whether narrowly targeted restrictions on one antibiotic or class are associated with reductions in resistance.

This analysis makes three contributions. It provides, to our knowledge, the first quantitative comparison across the principal types of antibiotic restriction applied in food-producing animals. It identifies where the evidence base is concentrated and where it is absent, notably for combined restriction of growth promotion and prophylaxis. Finally, it offers evidence on the effectiveness of intermediate policy options that can inform the design of national and international strategies for restricting antibiotics in animal agriculture.

Methods

**Study design and data source**

This study is a pre-specified stratified sub-analysis of a previously published systematic review and meta-analysis, which examined whether restricting antibiotic use in food-producing animals is associated with changes in antibiotic resistance in animals and humans (Tang et al., 2017). The parent review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). Its search strategy, eligibility criteria, and data extraction procedures are described in full elsewhere and are summarised here. Briefly, we searched multiple electronic bibliographic databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, together with the Web of Science and the grey literature, for studies published up to the search date. We also screened reference lists of relevant articles. Eligible studies were primary investigations that compared the prevalence or occurrence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria between a group exposed to an intervention restricting antibiotic use in food-producing animals and a comparison group. Comparison groups could be unrestricted contemporaneous controls or the same population before the restriction. Studies in any language were considered, and eligible designs included randomised and non-randomised trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, and before-and-after studies. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts, and disagreements were resolved by consensus or by a third reviewer. The parent review identified 181 eligible studies.

**Study selection for the present analysis**

All studies from the parent review that provided data amenable to quantitative synthesis were considered for inclusion. Studies were eligible if they reported, for both the intervention and comparison groups, the number of bacterial isolates tested and the number resistant to at least one antibiotic, or if these quantities could be derived from the published data. Studies reporting only narrative findings, or whose data could not be reconciled into a numerator and denominator of isolates, were excluded from the quantitative analysis. This yielded 127 studies for the stratified analysis.

**Classification of restriction approaches**

Because the parent review pooled heterogeneous interventions, we developed an a priori classification scheme to characterise the scope of each antibiotic restriction. The scheme was based on the policy landscape for antibiotic use in agriculture, in which regulatory approaches differ according to the antibiotics affected and the indications for which use remains permitted (World Health Organization, 2017). Seven mutually exclusive categories were defined:

1. Complete restriction: prohibition of all antibiotic use, including therapeutic use, as in organic or antibiotic-free production systems.
2. Single antibiotic-class restriction: restriction of one antibiotic class, such as fluoroquinolones or glycopeptides, regardless of indication.
3. Single antibiotic restriction: restriction of one specific agent, such as avoparcin.
4. All non-therapeutic use restriction: prohibition of growth promotion and routine disease prevention, with therapeutic use retained.
5. Growth promoter and prophylaxis restriction: prohibition of both growth promotion and prophylactic use only.
6. Growth promoter restriction: prohibition of growth promotion only.
7. Other or undetermined: interventions that did not fit the above categories or whose scope could not be determined from the report.

Two reviewers independently coded each study using the full text of the report and any regulatory documents it cited. Where the description of the intervention was ambiguous, we classified the study conservatively according to the information explicitly stated and assigned it to the "other or undetermined" category if necessary. Inter-rater agreement was quantified with Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960), and discrepancies were resolved through discussion with a third investigator. Studies reporting more than one distinct intervention, for example separate comparisons for different antibiotics or populations, contributed one independent comparison per intervention type to the corresponding stratum.

**Data extraction**

From each study we extracted the following variables: first author, year of publication, country, study design, animal species (cattle, swine, poultry, or other), bacterial species or genus tested, antibiotic or antibiotic class for which resistance was measured, sampling source (for example faecal, carcass, or retail meat), and the numbers of resistant and total isolates in the intervention and comparison groups. When studies reported resistance to multiple antibiotics or in multiple bacterial species, we extracted each combination as a separate estimate. We then accounted for within-study dependence in the analysis, as described below. Data extraction was performed in duplicate, and discrepancies were reconciled by consensus.

**Outcome measure**

The primary outcome was the difference in the prevalence of antibiotic-resistant bacterial isolates between intervention and comparison groups, expressed as an absolute risk difference. Negative values indicate lower resistance in the restriction group, and we report the magnitude of the reduction in percentage points. For each comparison, the risk difference was calculated as the proportion of resistant isolates in the intervention group minus that in the comparison group, with variance estimated using the standard binomial approximation. To ensure the stability of variance estimates when proportions approached 0 or 1, we also repeated the analyses after applying the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation to the proportions (Freeman and Tukey, 1950).

**Statistical analysis**

Pooled estimates were obtained for each intervention category using random-effects meta-analysis according to the DerSimonian and Laird method (DerSimonian and Laird, 1986), selected a priori owing to the anticipated clinical and methodological diversity among studies. To account for the inclusion of multiple correlated estimates from the same study, we first combined estimates within each study before pooling, so that each study contributed a single summary effect to its stratum. We also performed sensitivity analyses using robust variance estimation (Hedges et al., 2010) to confirm that this approach did not materially affect the results. Results are presented as pooled risk differences with 95% confidence intervals, together with forest plots for each stratum.

Between-study heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q test and quantified with the I² statistic, which describes the proportion of total variability attributable to heterogeneity rather than chance (Higgins et al., 2003). We interpreted I² values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. To formally compare effects across the intervention categories, we conducted subgroup analyses and tested for between-subgroup differences using a random-effects meta-regression with intervention type as a categorical moderator, using complete restriction as the reference category. Strata with fewer than three studies were analysed and reported but interpreted cautiously, since estimates of between-study variance are imprecise with so few observations (Borenstein et al., 2010). The "other or undetermined" category was reported for completeness but was not used to draw inferences about the effectiveness of any specific approach.

To explore whether the findings were robust, we conducted several pre-specified secondary analyses. First, we restricted the analysis to studies in which the resistance outcome concerned bacteria of public health importance, such as *Escherichia coli*, *Enterococcus* species, *Salmonella* species, and *Campylobacter* species. Second, we repeated the stratified analyses by animal species and by study design (comparing controlled studies with before-and-after studies). Third, we performed leave-one-out analyses within each stratum to determine whether any single study exerted undue influence on the pooled estimate.

Publication bias was evaluated visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger's regression test (Egger et al., 1997) for strata containing at least ten studies, which is the minimum recommended for these methods to have adequate power (Sterne et al., 2011). Where asymmetry was detected, we applied the trim-and-fill method (Duval and Tweedie, 2000) to assess the potential effect of missing studies on the pooled estimates.

All hypothesis tests were two-sided, and statistical significance was defined as P<0.05 without adjustment for multiple comparisons, given the exploratory nature of the stratified analyses. Analyses were performed using Stata (StataCorp, College Station, TX) and cross-checked in R using the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010).

Results

**Study selection and characteristics**

Of the 181 studies in the original systematic review (Tang et al., 2017), 127 (70.2%) reported data on the proportion of resistant bacterial isolates in a form suitable for quantitative synthesis and were included in this sub-analysis. The remaining 54 studies were excluded because they reported only qualitative findings, gave no denominators, or presented resistance as continuous minimum inhibitory concentration data without dichotomised outcomes. Included studies were published between 1975 and 2016, and 83 (65.4%) were published after 2000. Most were conducted in Europe (n=71, 55.9%), followed by North America (n=29, 22.8%), Asia (n=17, 13.4%) and other regions (n=10, 7.9%). Poultry (n=61), swine (n=42) and cattle (n=33) were the most commonly studied species; some studies examined more than one species. The most frequently examined organisms were *Escherichia coli* (n=58), *Enterococcus* species (n=39), *Campylobacter* species (n=24) and *Salmonella* species (n=21). In total, the 127 studies contributed 1,142 distinct resistance estimates (antibiotic–organism–species combinations) with a median sample of 214 isolates per estimate (interquartile range, 86–512).

**Distribution of intervention types**

The distribution of studies across the seven categories was uneven (Table 1). Complete restriction was the most commonly studied intervention (n=51, 40.2%), followed by restriction of all non-therapeutic use (n=33, 26.0%) and restriction of growth promoters alone (n=19, 15.0%). Seven studies (5.5%) examined restriction of a single antibiotic and three (2.4%) examined restriction of a single antibiotic class. No study evaluated restriction of growth promotion and prophylaxis together. The remaining 14 studies (11.0%) were coded as other or undetermined, usually because the policy or farm-level intervention could not be matched to a defined category from the information supplied. Studies of complete restriction were predominantly organic or antibiotic-free farm comparisons (n=38), whereas studies of growth promoter restriction were almost entirely evaluations of national or regional bans, primarily in Denmark and other European Union countries (n=16), as in the avoparcin and broader growth promoter bans (Bager et al., 1997; Aarestrup et al., 2001). Studies of single antibiotic and single class restrictions mainly evaluated the withdrawal of fluoroquinolones or avoparcin from poultry production.

**Pooled effect of restriction by intervention type**

Across all 127 studies, restriction of antibiotic use was associated with a pooled absolute reduction in the prevalence of antibiotic resistance of 14% (95% confidence interval [CI] 11–17; I²=94%), consistent with our earlier report (Tang et al., 2017). When stratified by intervention type using random effects models (DerSimonian and Laird, 1986), the magnitude of association differed across categories (Figure 1).

Complete restriction was associated with a 15% absolute reduction in the prevalence of resistance (95% CI 11–19; 51 studies; I²=92%). Restriction of all non-therapeutic use was associated with a 9% reduction (95% CI 5–13; 33 studies; I²=90%). Restriction of growth promoters alone produced the largest point estimate, a 30% reduction (95% CI 18–42; 19 studies; I²=96%), although the confidence interval was wide. Studies in the other/undetermined category yielded a 17% reduction (95% CI 9–25; 14 studies; I²=89%).

In contrast, neither of the narrowly targeted interventions was significantly associated with reduced resistance. Single antibiotic-class restriction was associated with an 11% reduction with a confidence interval spanning the null (95% CI −4 to 26; 3 studies; I²=81%), and single antibiotic restriction was associated with a 6% reduction (95% CI −3 to 15; 7 studies; I²=78%). Because these two strata contained few studies, their estimates were imprecise and the absence of statistical significance should not be interpreted as evidence of no effect. Nevertheless, point estimates for both were lower than that for complete restriction, and the lower confidence limits indicated that modest increases in resistance could not be excluded.

A test for subgroup differences indicated statistically significant variation in effect size across intervention types (Q=14.8, df=5, p=0.011). Exploratory pairwise comparisons suggested that the difference between growth promoter restriction and non-therapeutic restriction was the largest (difference 21 percentage points; 95% CI 7–35), whereas complete restriction and non-therapeutic restriction did not differ significantly (difference 6 percentage points; 95% CI −1 to 13). Complete restriction and growth promoter restriction also did not differ significantly (difference −15 percentage points; 95% CI −28 to 1). Thus, interventions that permitted therapeutic use were not meaningfully less effective than those prohibiting all use.

**Heterogeneity**

Heterogeneity was substantial within every stratum (I² 78%–96%), and stratification by intervention type explained only a small proportion of the total between-study variance (R²=11%). Heterogeneity was lowest among the single antibiotic and single class studies, which also contained the fewest studies. In univariable meta-regression, the pooled reduction was larger for Gram-positive than for Gram-negative organisms (difference 8 percentage points; 95% CI 2–14; p=0.008), a pattern driven largely by enterococcal studies of growth promoter bans. Effect sizes did not differ significantly by animal species (p=0.37) or study region (p=0.21). In a multivariable model including intervention type, organism Gram stain, and study design (before–after versus concurrent comparison), the direction of the effect for each intervention type was unchanged, and the contrast between broad and narrowly targeted interventions remained of similar magnitude (adjusted difference 9 percentage points; 95% CI 1–17).

**Sensitivity analyses and publication bias**

Results were robust to several sensitivity analyses. Excluding studies at high risk of bias (n=22) yielded pooled reductions of 14% (95% CI 10–18) for complete restriction, 8% (95% CI 3–13) for non-therapeutic restriction, and 27% (95% CI 14–40) for growth promoter restriction; estimates for single antibiotic and single class restrictions remained non-significant. When only one resistance estimate per study was retained (the antibiotic with the greatest sample size), the pooled estimates differed by no more than 3 percentage points from the primary analysis for any category. Leave-one-out analyses showed that no single study changed the statistical significance of any stratum-specific estimate, although removal of the largest Danish growth promoter evaluation reduced that stratum's estimate to 24% (95% CI 13–35). Restricting the analysis to studies of antibiotics classified as critically important by the World Health Organization produced slightly larger reductions for complete restriction (17%; 95% CI 12–22) and similar findings for other categories.

Visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger's test suggested possible small-study effects for complete restriction (p=0.03) and non-therapeutic restriction (p=0.04), with smaller studies reporting larger reductions. Trim-and-fill adjustment lowered the corresponding pooled estimates to 12% (95% CI 8–16) and 7% (95% CI 3–11), respectively, without altering the overall conclusion. There was no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry for growth promoter restriction (p=0.41), and the strata of single antibiotic and single class restrictions were too small to assess reliably.

Discussion and Conclusion

In this stratified analysis of 127 studies, restrictions on antibiotic use in food-producing animals were associated with lower levels of antibiotic resistance across most intervention types. Complete restrictions were associated with a 15% reduction in resistance, and less prohibitive approaches, including those that permitted therapeutic use, were associated with reductions of 9% to 30%. Interventions targeting a single antibiotic class or a single antibiotic were not significantly associated with reduced resistance, although these estimates rested on only three and seven studies, respectively. Two practical conclusions follow. Broad restrictions appear more effective than narrow ones, and the evidence does not show that eliminating all use, including therapeutic use, is necessary to achieve meaningful reductions in resistance.

The weaker effect of narrow restrictions is biologically plausible. Antibiotic resistance determinants are frequently carried on mobile genetic elements that link genes conferring resistance to several unrelated drug classes, so selection pressure exerted by one agent can maintain resistance to others (Schwarz et al., 2001; Andersson and Hughes, 2010). Restricting one drug or class while others remain in use may therefore leave co-selection intact. The Danish experience with growth promoters is consistent with this. Glycopeptide resistance in enterococci fell after avoparcin was withdrawn, but macrolide and other resistance declined more slowly, and the pattern varied by species and by the persistence of linked determinants (Aarestrup et al., 2001; Wegener, 2003). The ceftiofur experience in Quebec also suggests that narrow interventions can have measurable effects on specific resistance phenotypes (Dutil et al., 2010), but such gains may be offset when producers substitute other drugs, a form of therapeutic displacement that single-agent restrictions do not prevent. Because our single-agent and single-class estimates were imprecise, we do not interpret them as evidence of no effect. They show only that the available data cannot distinguish a modest benefit from none, and they argue against relying on narrowly targeted bans as a stand-alone strategy.

The finding that restrictions permitting therapeutic use were similarly effective as complete restrictions is perhaps the most policy-relevant result. Complete restrictions were typically implemented in production systems, such as organic or antibiotic-free programs, that differ systematically from conventional systems in husbandry, stocking density, biosecurity, and herd health management. These co-interventions may explain the effect of such programs as much as the restriction itself, and may account for why a more prohibitive approach did not yield a proportionally larger reduction. Conversely, bans on growth promotion and routine non-therapeutic use typically eliminate the continuous, low-dose exposures that are thought to be especially favorable to selection and dissemination of resistance (Cogliani et al., 2011; Van Boeckel et al., 2015). Retaining the ability to treat sick animals protects animal welfare and allows policies to be more acceptable to producers and veterinarians, and our findings suggest this need not substantially compromise the resistance benefits. This is consistent with the direction of recent policy, including the European Union prohibition of antibiotic growth promoters in 2006, the United States Food and Drug Administration's Guidance for Industry #209 and #213, and the World Health Organization guidelines recommending complete restriction of growth promotion and of disease prevention in the absence of diagnosed illness (WHO, 2017). Our results provide empirical support for the practical effectiveness of these intermediate approaches.

No study examined restrictions on growth promoters and prophylaxis jointly, an important gap because this combination mirrors the scope of several recent regulatory frameworks. Prophylactic and metaphylactic uses are often indistinguishable in practice from treatment, and in jurisdictions that ban growth promotion alone, reclassification of former growth-promoting use as prevention has been described (Cogliani et al., 2011). Evaluations that distinguish these indications, ideally with quantitative use data at herd level, would help clarify whether the apparent effectiveness of growth promoter bans persists when prophylactic use is allowed to expand.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. First, this is a secondary analysis of a previously published systematic review, and stratification reduced the number of studies per category, in some cases to very few. Subgroup estimates were consequently imprecise, and between-category comparisons have limited statistical power and are susceptible to confounding by study-level characteristics. Intervention types were not randomly allocated across studies, and they differ in host species, bacterial species, resistance phenotypes, geographic setting, and time since implementation. We could not adjust meaningfully for these factors, and the apparent differences between categories should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than as definitive comparative effectiveness estimates. Second, the classification scheme was developed post hoc, and the intervention described in a study may not fully reflect the restriction actually experienced by animals. Compliance, concurrent use of non-restricted agents, and the extent of the pre-intervention exposure were rarely quantified. Third, most included studies were observational, often comparing farms with and without restrictions or sampling before and after a policy change, and are vulnerable to selection bias, secular trends, and ecological confounding. The substantial heterogeneity typical of this literature was present here and was only partly explained by intervention type. Fourth, the outcome of interest was the proportion of resistant isolates, which depends on sampling strategy, laboratory methods, and breakpoints, and which does not capture absolute abundance of resistance genes or downstream human health outcomes. Reductions in resistance among animal isolates do not necessarily translate to equivalent reductions in human infections, and the reverse is also possible, given the multiple pathways, including food, environment, and occupational contact, by which resistance moves between reservoirs (Van Boeckel et al., 2019). Fifth, as in any meta-analysis, publication bias may have favored the reporting of significant reductions, and the evidence base is concentrated in high-income countries, particularly in Europe and North America, where baseline surveillance and regulatory infrastructure are strongest. The generalizability of our findings to low- and middle-income settings, where animal antibiotic consumption is projected to increase most rapidly, remains uncertain.

Despite these limitations, the consistency of direction across most intervention types strengthens confidence that restricting antibiotic use in animals reduces resistance, even if the magnitude varies. Future research should prioritize prospective evaluations with standardized, quantitative reporting of antibiotic consumption and of resistance outcomes, including genomic and metagenomic measures. Such studies should compare specific policy designs directly and should examine whether reductions in animal reservoirs lead to measurable benefits for human health. Studies in low- and middle-income countries and in aquaculture and other underrepresented production sectors are particularly needed.

In conclusion, broad interventions that restrict antibiotic use across multiple agents appear more effective in reducing antibiotic resistance than restrictions that target a single drug or class. Interventions that allow therapeutic use performed similarly to complete restrictions, suggesting that outright bans are not required to achieve substantial reductions. These findings support policies that eliminate growth promotion and routine non-therapeutic use while preserving veterinary treatment, and they caution against dependence on narrowly targeted restrictions alone. Policymakers should pair such restrictions with robust surveillance of both antibiotic use and resistance so that effects can be monitored and policies refined as evidence accumulates.

Introduction

Speech is produced by a coordinated sequence of movements of the articulators, including the lips, jaw, tongue, velum, and larynx. These movements continuously reshape the vocal tract, the airway extending from the glottis to the lips. By modulating airflow and creating different resonant cavities, the time-varying vocal tract shape determines the acoustic properties of the speech signal (Fant, 1970; Stevens, 1998). Vocal tract configurations therefore carry rich information about the underlying speech production mechanism, and understanding the mapping between vocal tract geometry and acoustics remains a central problem in speech science, with implications for phonetics, speech technology, clinical assessment, and the study of language variation (Narayanan et al., 2014; Lingala et al., 2016).

Progress on this problem has depended on instrumentation for observing articulation. Electromagnetic articulography, ultrasound, X-ray microbeam, and video of the face each provide partial views, capturing flesh-point trajectories, the tongue surface, or the external lips (Whalen et al., 2005; Stone, 2005). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is attractive because it is non-invasive, involves no ionizing radiation, and provides a view of the entire vocal tract, including regions such as the pharynx and velum that are hard to reach by other modalities. Advances in fast acquisition and reconstruction have made real-time MRI (rtMRI) of speech practical, with frame rates sufficient to capture dynamic articulation in the midsagittal plane during natural, continuous speech (Narayanan et al., 2004; Bresch et al., 2008; Lingala et al., 2016). Large rtMRI corpora, such as the USC-TIMIT database and related multi-speaker collections, now allow quantitative study of articulation across many speakers (Narayanan et al., 2014).

Most computational work on rtMRI speech data has relied on hand-designed or semi-automatic representations of the vocal tract. These include air–tissue boundary segmentation, cross-distance functions along the vocal tract midline, and region-of-interest time series that capture constriction formation at the lips, tongue tip, tongue body, and velum (Kim et al., 2014; Bresch & Narayanan, 2009; Proctor et al., 2010). Such representations are interpretable and have supported insights into coarticulation, compensatory articulation, and the composition of articulatory gestures (Browman & Goldstein, 1992). However, they require segmentation or parameterization pipelines that may be sensitive to image quality and speaker anatomy, and they may discard information that is not captured by the chosen parameters. A complementary strategy is to learn representations directly from the image sequences, letting the data determine which spatial and temporal features are informative about the speech sounds being produced.

Deep learning provides tools for this strategy. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn hierarchical visual features and have achieved strong results in image recognition (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015; He et al., 2016). For video, the challenge is to also model temporal dynamics. Approaches include 3D convolutions (Ji et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2015), two-stream networks combining appearance and motion (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014), and architectures that couple per-frame CNN features with recurrent networks such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) are a prominent example of the last family: a CNN extracts deep visual features from each frame, and a recurrent layer integrates them over time, making the model deep in both space and time (Donahue et al., 2015). Such models have been successful in action recognition, video description, and other sequence-learning tasks, and have also been applied to visual speech recognition from lip images (Assael et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2017). Applying them to rtMRI of the full vocal tract is a natural extension, but one that has received comparatively little systematic attention.

There is a gap in the existing literature. Studies of automatic recognition from articulatory data have mostly used point-tracking measurements or lip-region video, or have used articulatory features as auxiliary inputs to acoustic recognizers (King et al., 2007; Hueber et al., 2010). Work that learns directly from the full midsagittal rtMRI video to identify speech content is limited, and it is not well understood how standard video-classification architectures behave on this kind of data. Vocal tract videos differ from the natural-scene videos for which these architectures were designed. The images are grayscale, the spatial layout is highly constrained and consistent across frames, and the discriminative information lies in subtle, spatially localized constrictions and their timing rather than in large-scale object motion or scene context. Moreover, the sequences of interest, such as vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) utterances, are short and the relevant dynamics are brief and coarticulated, so assumptions about the value of long temporal context or of pretrained appearance features may not carry over. It is therefore unclear whether design choices that benefit generic video and sequence classification, including network depth, recurrent configuration, and sequence length, transfer to speech.

This paper takes a step towards automatic mapping of vocal tract shape geometry to speech acoustics by addressing a closely related question: can speech content be identified directly from the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract in rtMRI, using video action recognition techniques? We focus on identifying VCV sequences, which isolate consonant articulation in a controlled vowel context and are a standard probe of coarticulation and articulatory dynamics. We ask how LRCN-style models perform on this task, how their performance depends on parameter settings such as the CNN and recurrent components, and whether the behavior observed differs from that known for generic video or sequence classification.

The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we formulate speech identification from rtMRI as a video classification problem and apply LRCN models that combine deep CNN feature extraction with recurrent sequence modeling to 2D rtMRI of VCV utterances from 17 speakers. Second, we conduct a comparative evaluation of this class of models under various parameter settings and for several classification tasks, providing an empirical characterization of what matters for this data. Third, we report that model behavior in speech classification differs markedly from that in generic sequence or video classification tasks, which suggests that architectures and training practices developed for natural video should be adapted for articulatory imaging. Together, these findings inform the design of data-driven models linking vocal tract dynamics and speech, and they provide a baseline for future work on acoustic mapping from articulation.

Methods

**Data**

We used a database of two-dimensional real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rtMRI) of the midsagittal vocal tract acquired from 17 native speakers of American English during the production of vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences. Image acquisition followed the established protocol for rtMRI of speech production (Narayanan et al., 2004; Narayanan et al., 2014). Participants lay supine in a scanner. A fast spiral gradient-echo sequence with a flexible receiver coil placed around the head and neck was used to image a single midsagittal slice that covered the lips, tongue, velum, larynx, and pharyngeal wall. The reconstructed image sequences had a temporal resolution of approximately 20–25 frames per second and a spatial resolution of a few millimeters per pixel. Reconstructed frames were stored as grayscale video. Audio was recorded simultaneously through a noise-cancelling optical microphone and denoised (Bresch et al., 2006), so the acoustic signal could be used to segment utterances. Audio was used only for segmentation and was not an input to any classifier.

Each speaker produced a set of VCV tokens with a symmetric vowel context, in which the same vowel precedes and follows the consonant. The inventory crossed a set of English consonants spanning stops, nasals, fricatives, and approximants with the corner vowels /a/, /i/, and /u/. Each token was repeated several times in a carrier-free, isolated manner. Individual tokens were cut from the continuous recording using the acoustic signal. Each clip began shortly before the onset of the first vowel and ended shortly after the offset of the second vowel, and we manually checked the boundaries. Tokens with visible motion artifacts, incomplete articulations, or acquisition failures were discarded. Each remaining clip was labeled with its VCV identity, and by derivation with its consonant and with its vowel context.

**Preprocessing**

Frames were cropped to a fixed region of interest around the vocal tract, resized to 224 × 224 pixels by bilinear interpolation, and replicated across three channels so that ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks could be used directly (Deng et al., 2009). Intensities were normalized per speaker, by subtracting that speaker's mean and dividing by that speaker's standard deviation. This reduces inter-speaker differences in coil sensitivity and overall brightness. Because the number of frames varied across tokens with speaking rate, every clip was converted to a fixed length of T frames. Clips longer than T were uniformly subsampled, and shorter clips were padded by repeating the last frame. We treated T as a design parameter (see below). No horizontal flipping was applied, since the sagittal view has a fixed anatomical orientation. Training-time augmentation consisted of small random translations and rotations (±5°), small brightness and contrast jitter, and mild temporal jitter of the sampled frame indices, applied identically to all frames of a clip.

**Model architecture**

The main model was a Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Network (LRCN; Donahue et al., 2015). A convolutional network processes each frame independently and yields a fixed-length feature vector. The sequence of feature vectors is passed to a recurrent network, whose outputs are mapped to class probabilities. We used VGG-16 (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015) as the main visual feature extractor and took the activations of its penultimate fully connected layer. ResNet-style backbones (He et al., 2016) and a small CNN trained from scratch were used as alternatives. The temporal component was a long short-term memory (LSTM) network (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), which we compared with a gated recurrent unit variant (Cho et al., 2014). The final hidden state, or alternatively the mean of the outputs across time steps, was fed to a softmax layer. Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) was applied before the recurrent and output layers.

To place the LRCN results in context, we trained three reference models on the same splits: (i) a frame-wise CNN whose per-frame predictions were averaged over the clip, which ignores temporal order; (ii) a late-fusion CNN that concatenates features over time (Karpathy et al., 2014); and (iii) a 3D convolutional network that learns joint spatiotemporal filters (Tran et al., 2015). Comparing these tests whether explicit sequence modeling helps beyond what is captured by static vocal tract shape.

**Experimental design**

We defined three classification tasks. In the *VCV identification* task, the model predicted the full VCV label, so the consonant and the vowel context had to be inferred together. In the *consonant classification* task, clips from all vowel contexts were pooled and labeled only by the consonant, which required invariance to the surrounding vowel. In the *vowel classification* task, clips were labeled by vowel context regardless of consonant.

For each task we varied several parameters, one at a time around a default configuration. The parameters were: (a) clip length T, from short clips of about 10 frames to longer clips of about 30 frames; (b) the number of LSTM units (64, 128, 256) and layers (1 or 2); (c) the CNN backbone; (d) initialization, either ImageNet-pretrained weights with the convolutional layers frozen, pretrained weights fine-tuned end to end, or random initialization; and (e) unidirectional versus bidirectional recurrence. We also ran a comparison with the label set restricted to consonants grouped by manner of articulation, to examine whether errors concentrate within articulatory classes.

**Training and evaluation protocol**

To estimate generalization to unseen speakers, we used speaker-independent evaluation. The 17 speakers were partitioned into folds for cross-validation, so that all tokens from a speaker were in the test set of exactly one fold. In each fold, a subset of the remaining speakers (about 10%) was held out as a validation set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection, and no test speaker data influenced model selection. For comparison we also ran a speaker-dependent condition in which tokens from every speaker were split across training and test sets by repetition, to quantify the gap caused by inter-speaker variability in vocal tract anatomy.

Networks were trained by minimizing categorical cross-entropy with the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015). The initial learning rate was 1e-4 for pretrained layers and 1e-3 for newly initialized layers. It was reduced when validation loss plateaued. We used mini-batches of 16 clips, weight decay for regularization, and early stopping with a patience of 10 epochs. Class frequencies were balanced by construction, but we monitored per-class performance. Models were implemented in a standard deep learning framework and trained on a single GPU. Each configuration was run with several random seeds.

**Statistical analysis**

The primary metric was classification accuracy on the held-out speakers, and we also report macro-averaged F1 to guard against class-specific effects. Results are given as mean ± standard deviation across cross-validation folds and seeds. Confusion matrices aggregated over folds were examined to characterize systematic confusions, for example among consonants sharing a place of articulation. Differences between model configurations were assessed on matched folds with paired t-tests, or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests when normality was doubtful, and p-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons with the Holm–Bonferroni procedure. When two classifiers were compared on the same test clips, McNemar's test was used. Chance level for each task was computed from the number of classes and reported with the results. Differences were considered significant at an adjusted α of 0.05.

Results

**Experimental outcomes and overall performance.** All results are leave-speakers-out accuracies, averaged over a 5-fold cross-validation in which the 17 speakers of the rtMRI corpus (Narayanan et al., 2014; Lingala et al., 2017) were partitioned so that no test speaker appeared in training. Each fold was repeated with three random initializations, and we report mean ± standard deviation. We considered three tasks: (i) consonant identification from the VCV clip (C-task, 8 classes), (ii) vowel-context identification (V-task, 3 classes), and (iii) joint identification of the full VCV token (VCV-task, 24 classes). Chance levels are 12.5%, 33.3%, and 4.2%, respectively.

The baseline LRCN (Donahue et al., 2015) used a VGG-16 encoder pretrained on ImageNet (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015), a single-layer LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) with 256 hidden units, and 20 frames per clip sampled uniformly. It reached 71.4 ± 2.8% on the C-task, 88.9 ± 1.9% on the V-task, and 63.7 ± 3.1% on the VCV-task. The vowel context was therefore recognized much more reliably than the intervening consonant, consistent with the larger and more sustained tongue and jaw displacements of vowels in midsagittal images. Most joint-task errors came from consonant confusions; only 7.9% of VCV errors involved an incorrect vowel with a correct consonant.

**Effect of the visual feature extractor.** Table-level comparisons across encoders showed a pattern that differs from generic action recognition. With the LSTM fixed, the pretrained VGG-16 reached 71.4% on the C-task, ResNet-50 (He et al., 2016) reached 70.2 ± 3.0%, and a small four-layer CNN (about 0.4M parameters) trained from scratch reached 72.6 ± 2.6%. Differences among these three were within one standard deviation and not significant (paired t-test across folds, p > 0.2). The VCV-task showed the same ordering: 63.7% (VGG-16), 62.5% (ResNet-50), and 64.9% (small CNN). Deeper hierarchical features therefore did not help, even though they typically yield large gains on UCF-101 and similar benchmarks (Donahue et al., 2015). Fine-tuning the pretrained backbones raised C-task accuracy by only 1.1 points for VGG-16 (72.5%), whereas freezing them lowered it to 66.8 ± 3.3%. This suggests that ImageNet features transfer only partially to grayscale, single-view articulatory images.

**Effect of recurrent configuration.** Increasing LSTM hidden size from 64 to 128, 256, and 512 units produced C-task accuracies of 67.9%, 70.1%, 71.4%, and 71.0%, so performance saturated at about 256 units. Stacking two LSTM layers gave 71.8 ± 2.9%, a negligible change, and a third layer reduced accuracy to 69.5% with higher variance. Bidirectional LSTMs gave a modest gain (73.2 ± 2.5%), which is plausible because VCV identity depends on both the closing and releasing gestures around the consonant. Replacing the LSTM with a GRU gave 71.0%, statistically indistinguishable from the LSTM. Notably, a frame-level baseline that averaged CNN features over time with no recurrence reached 64.3 ± 3.4% on the C-task. The recurrent layer thus contributed about 7 points, and 9 points when bidirectional, which confirms that temporal ordering carries information beyond static posture. This benefit is smaller than the typical gap between frame-averaging and recurrent models in generic video classification.

**Effect of temporal sampling.** We varied the number of frames per clip (8, 12, 20, 30, and all frames, with a median of 46 at the native frame rate of roughly 83 frames per second after downsampling). C-task accuracies were 66.1%, 69.0%, 71.4%, 71.9%, and 70.3%, respectively. Gains therefore plateaued at about 20–30 frames. Using all frames lowered accuracy and increased training time by 2.1×. Clips subsampled non-uniformly, with higher density around the consonantal constriction located by the minimum of the articulator-opening trajectory, achieved 74.1 ± 2.6% with 20 frames. Thus, where frames are placed mattered more than how many were used, in contrast with generic action recognition, where longer clips usually improve accuracy.

**Effect of spatial input and speaker variability.** Cropping the image to a region around the vocal tract (from 84×84 full frames to a 64×64 crop) improved C-task accuracy from 71.4% to 74.8 ± 2.4%, suggesting that background and shoulder pixels are distracting. Intensity normalization per speaker added another 1.6 points (76.4%). Per-speaker accuracy on the C-task ranged from 58.2% to 85.7% (interquartile range 69.3–80.1%), and the weakest speakers were those with the lowest signal-to-noise ratios or atypical head positioning. Adding data augmentation (random shifts of ±4 pixels, rotations of ±5°, and brightness jitter) raised the mean to 78.0 ± 2.2%, but temporal augmentation by speed perturbation (0.8–1.2×) reduced accuracy to 75.9%, again suggesting that articulatory timing itself is discriminative.

**Per-class behavior and confusions.** In the best configuration (bidirectional LSTM, cropped and normalized input, augmentation, targeted sampling), accuracies were 80.3 ± 2.1% on the C-task, 91.6 ± 1.5% on the V-task, and 70.8 ± 2.9% on the VCV-task. Per-consonant F1 scores were highest for the bilabial /p/ (0.91) and the velar /k/ (0.86), which have visually salient closures, and lowest for the alveolar pair /t/–/d/ (0.62 and 0.58). Confusion matrices showed that 64% of consonant errors involved a voicing counterpart with the same place and manner (e.g., /p/–/b/, /t/–/d/, /s/–/z/), which is expected because voicing is largely controlled at the glottis and is poorly captured in midsagittal images. When voicing pairs were merged into a single class, C-task accuracy rose from 80.3% to 90.2 ± 1.7%. Place-of-articulation errors accounted for only 21% of the remaining confusions.

**Comparison with generic video benchmarks.** Together, these results indicate a marked contrast with generic sequence classification. Pretrained depth, longer clips, and larger recurrent stacks, which usually yield gains, provided little or none here. Compact encoders, tight spatial cropping, and a short, well-targeted temporal window proved more beneficial.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study examined whether action-recognition architectures, in particular Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN; Donahue et al., 2015), can identify vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences from the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract in 2D real-time MRI (rtMRI). The main finding is that these models can extract linguistically meaningful information from articulatory video, but their behavior differs from what is usually reported for generic video classification. The differences concern which architectural components help, how much temporal context matters, and which kinds of classes are confused.

In benchmarks such as UCF-101, much of the performance of CNN-RNN hybrids comes from appearance cues. Scene context, objects, and body pose are highly discriminative, and the recurrent layer adds a comparatively modest gain by aggregating frame-level evidence (Karpathy et al., 2014; Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014; Donahue et al., 2015). Vocal tract rtMRI offers none of these cues. Every frame shows the same anatomy in the same view, and the class information lies in small, continuous deformations of the tongue, lips, velum, and larynx, and in the timing of constrictions relative to one another. A deep visual extractor must therefore be sensitive to subtle contour displacements, not to object-level semantics. This is probably why features transferred from natural-image pretraining, which are strong for generic action recognition, were less advantageous here. Feature transferability declines as the source and target domains diverge (Yosinski et al., 2014), and grayscale mid-sagittal tissue boundaries are far from ImageNet statistics. We therefore interpret the performance gap between speech and generic video tasks as largely a domain-mismatch effect, along with the fact that the discriminative signal is spatially localized and low in contrast.

The temporal dimension also behaves differently. In generic video classification, a few sampled frames are often enough to identify an action. In speech, the identity of a VCV token depends on when a constriction is formed and released and on how the surrounding vowels shape the movement. This is the coarticulatory structure described by Öhman (1966) and formalized as overlapping gestures in articulatory phonology (Browman & Goldstein, 1992). Because consonantal gestures are superimposed on a continuously moving vowel-to-vowel trajectory, the same consonant produces different image sequences in different vowel contexts, while different consonants can share similar vowel transitions. A model that relies on frame-level appearance will thus confuse tokens whose articulatory differences are brief and local, such as place contrasts among consonants formed with similar tongue-body configurations. Recurrent modeling is useful in principle (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), but its benefit depends on the quality of the per-frame representation, and on the frame rate and clip length being adequate to capture short constriction events. Our comparisons across parameter settings, such as sequence length and recurrent configuration, are consistent with this picture. Sensitivity to temporal sampling was greater than is typical in generic action recognition, where adjacent frames are highly redundant.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, the database contains 17 speakers, which is large by rtMRI standards (Narayanan et al., 2014; Lingala et al., 2016) but small by deep learning standards. Inter-speaker differences in vocal tract anatomy, head position, and speaking style add variability that a small cohort cannot fully cover. Performance under speaker-independent evaluation is the more relevant measure of generalization, and it should be interpreted cautiously, since individual speakers may still be partly memorized by high-capacity networks. Second, the data are 2D mid-sagittal images acquired at limited frame rates. This view omits lateral channel shaping, such as the grooving involved in sibilants and lateral approximants, and some of the spatial detail in the oral cavity and pharynx. Temporal blurring at the frame rates used may also obscure rapid events like stop releases and taps. Third, VCV tokens are controlled, read stimuli. They isolate consonantal gestures cleanly but are far from continuous, spontaneous speech, in which reduction, prosodic modulation, and long-range coarticulation make the mapping from shape to phonetic identity less direct. Fourth, we evaluated classification of discrete, pre-segmented tokens, which sidesteps the problems of segmentation and alignment that any practical system would face. Finally, we did not systematically compare against architectures that learn spatiotemporal features jointly, such as 3D convolutions (Tran et al., 2015) or inflated two-stream networks (Carreira & Zisserman, 2017), nor against explicit articulatory representations such as segmented contours or region-of-interest time series (Bresch & Narayanan, 2009). These alternatives could change the relative conclusions.

Despite these caveats, the findings have several implications. For speech science, the ability of a general-purpose video model to separate VCV classes supports the view that vocal tract shape dynamics contain rich, learnable information about linguistic content. Analyzing which classes are confused and which image regions drive decisions could give data-driven evidence on which articulators and time points are most informative for particular contrasts, complementing the hypothesis-driven analyses typical of articulatory phonetics (Toutios & Narayanan, 2016). For speech technology, the results are a modest step toward mapping vocal tract geometry to acoustics. They resemble work on visual speech recognition from lip video (Assael et al., 2016) and on articulatory-to-acoustic mapping from ultrasound and other modalities (Csapó et al., 2020), but they use a view of the full vocal tract that includes the internal articulators. Such mappings could support silent-speech interfaces, assessment of disordered speech production, and articulatory-informed acoustic modeling. Methodologically, the contrast with generic video classification suggests that architectures and pretraining strategies should be designed for articulatory data instead of being imported unchanged. Promising directions include self-supervised or domain-specific pretraining on large rtMRI corpora, higher temporal resolution, attention or temporal-convolution models that focus on brief constriction events, and multimodal training that uses the synchronized acoustic signal as supervision.

In conclusion, LRCN-style models can identify VCV sequences from rtMRI of vocal tract shaping, but their behavior departs markedly from that seen in generic sequence and video classification. Appearance-based pretrained features contribute less, temporal sampling matters more, and errors reflect articulatory and coarticulatory similarity. Future work should test speaker-independent generalization on larger cohorts, extend to continuous speech and richer imaging views, and compare against spatiotemporal and articulatorily informed architectures. The aim is models that classify speech from vocal tract dynamics and also help explain how articulation produces speech sounds.

Introduction

Information hiding is the practice of concealing the existence of a piece of information, or its association with a particular carrier, so that only intended parties can detect or recover it. Its best-known branches are steganography, which hides a secret message inside innocuous-looking data, and digital watermarking, which embeds information in a host object for purposes such as copyright protection and tracing (Cox et al., 2007; Fridrich, 2009). Since Simmons' (1984) formulation of the prisoners' problem, steganography has been modelled as covert communication between two parties through a channel monitored by a warden. Security is then defined by the warden's inability to distinguish cover objects from stego objects (Cachin, 1998). Under this model, research has concentrated on embedding secret data into a cover object, such as an image, audio clip, video, or text, while keeping statistical and perceptual distortion small. Practical progress ranges from early least-significant-bit and transform-domain methods (Provos and Honeyman, 2003; Westfeld, 2001) to content-adaptive schemes based on distortion minimisation and syndrome-trellis codes (Filler et al., 2011), with steganalysis advancing in parallel through rich feature models and machine learning (Fridrich and Kodovský, 2012).

Beyond multimedia files, the information hiding community has extended the notion of carrier to communication systems. Network steganography and covert channels hide data in protocol fields, packet timing, or traffic patterns (Zielińska et al., 2014; Mazurczyk et al., 2016; Wendzel et al., 2015). More recently, online social networks (OSNs) have been used as covert media. Researchers have shown that user-generated content on public platforms can carry censorship-resistant messages (Burnett et al., 2010), that social-network structure and activity can support covert botnet command and control (Nagaraja et al., 2011; Pantic and Husain, 2015), and that images and text posted on social media can be turned into stego carriers. These developments reflect a general trend: as digital life moves to large, open, high-volume platforms, such platforms offer both new opportunities for concealment and new difficulties for detection.

Despite this diversity, almost all existing approaches share one structural assumption: a *cover* exists. The cover may be selected from a database, modified in place, synthesised from the message, or, in so-called coverless approaches, chosen or retrieved because its natural features already map to message bits (Zhou et al., 2015). Generative methods using neural networks (Hayes and Danezis, 2017) also produce a concrete cover-like object that carries the payload. In every case the hidden information is attached to a bounded object or message stream that the warden can, in principle, isolate and test. This assumption shapes both attack and defence. Steganalysis is typically framed as a binary classification problem on individual objects, or as pooled analysis over a batch of objects from one source (Ker, 2006). Even when real-world conditions are acknowledged, such as unknown cover sources, mismatched training data, and the sheer volume of traffic, the detection target remains a set of identifiable objects (Ker et al., 2013).

This assumption leaves a gap. Contemporary digital environments consist of vast numbers of human and automated agents continuously performing actions: posting, replying, liking, following, retweeting, tagging, and joining groups. The fact that certain actions occurred, with certain attributes (who, when, what type, in what order, toward which targets), is itself observable by anyone with access to the platform. Such activity patterns can encode information without requiring any single content object to be modified or even to be unusual. To our knowledge, the literature has not treated this observable activity space as the carrier in a general, systematic framework. Existing OSN-based schemes typically either embed data in the content of posts or in the traffic and behaviour of a specific malware-like structure, and they do not generalise to a design in which an arbitrary set of entities and activities in an arbitrary digital world encodes the message. Consequently, we lack both a unifying model and an understanding of the security implications when the cover effectively becomes the entire observable digital world.

This paper addresses the following research question: *can information be hidden not in a chosen or generated cover object, but in the very fact that particular digital activities, with particular attributes, were carried out in particular ways by selected human and computer entities in a receiver-observable digital world, and what does this imply for applications and for detection?* Answering it requires specifying how a message can be mapped onto activity patterns, how a receiver can observe and decode them, how the sender and receiver share the necessary secret (for example, the selected entities, activity types, and mapping rules), and how such a scheme behaves with respect to security notions that were developed for object-based covers.

We make the following contributions. First, we propose a general framework for information hiding in digital activities. In it, the sender and receiver agree on a digital world (for example, one or several OSNs), a set of entities within it (such as accounts), and a family of activities and attributes through which the message is expressed. The traditional notion of cover nearly disappears: the whole selected digital world, together with the activity it contains, plays the role of the cover. Second, we discuss application areas in both security and non-security settings. For steganography, the framework offers a channel that does not require producing a suspicious stego object. For non-security uses, such as gaming (for instance, treasure-hunt or puzzle designs where clues are carried by activity patterns), it offers a new interaction medium. Third, we analyse the implications for steganalysis. Because there is no isolated object to inspect, we argue that detection would require monitoring and analysing the whole digital world constantly and in real time, a task likely to be more complex, less effective, and less efficient than existing object-based steganalysis, and one calling for fundamentally new techniques. Fourth, we present a proof-of-concept system, implemented as a mobile app built on Twitter activities, showing that the framework can be realised in a real platform. We also outline ongoing work on a hybrid system that spans several online social networks.

The rest of this paper is organised as follows: we first formalise the framework and its components, then describe the Twitter-based implementation, and finally discuss security considerations, applications, and directions for future work.

Methods

**Framework formalization.** We model the selected digital world as a tuple W = (E, A, T, O), where E = {e_1, …, e_n} is a set of human or computer entities (here, online social network accounts), A is a set of activity types (posting, reposting, liking, following, replying), T is a discrete sequence of time slots, and O is the observation function that determines which activities a receiver can see. An activity is a tuple a = (e, α, v, t), where e is the acting entity, α is the activity type, v is a vector of attributes (e.g., target account, hashtag, text length, or media presence), and t is the slot in which it occurred. The sender and receiver share a secret key K and a public specification of W. The hidden message is carried by the fact that a particular ordered set of activities occurred, not by the content of any cover object. This follows the prisoners' problem setting (Simmons, 1984) and the usual requirement that security rest on the key rather than on secrecy of the scheme (Kerckhoffs, 1883; Cachin, 1998). Because every activity in W is a potential carrier, no cover is chosen or modified.

**Message preparation.** The plaintext is compressed and encrypted with AES-256 in counter mode, using a subkey derived from K by HMAC-SHA256 (Bellare et al., 1996). A short header with message length and sequence number is prepended. The result is protected with a Reed–Solomon code (Reed & Solomon, 1960) over GF(2^8), which tolerates the missing or spurious activities expected on a public platform, where unrelated users act concurrently, posts may be deleted, and rate limits may delay actions. The coded stream is split into symbols of b bits.

**Codebook and embedding.** A key-seeded pseudorandom generator, built from HMAC-SHA256 in counter mode, produces for each slot t a codebook C_t. This is an injective map from the 2^b symbol values to distinct activity tuples drawn from the permitted set. Because the codebook changes with t, repeated symbols do not yield repeated activity patterns. To embed symbol s_t, the sender performs the activity C_t(s_t). Decoding is the inverse lookup. The activity choice also determines how many bits each slot carries: if an slot offers m distinguishable tuples, its nominal capacity is log₂ m bits. Embedding capacity therefore grows with the number of controlled accounts, the activity types used, and the attribute resolution. Additional key-derived rules decide which accounts act and when, so that the volume and timing of activity per account stay close to that account's historical behavior. This is meant to reduce statistical deviation from benign activity, in line with the aim of avoiding distributional differences between cover and stego behavior (Cachin, 1998; Hopper et al., 2002).

**Synchronization and reception.** The receiver knows K, the start time, and the slot length. It polls the public timelines and relationship lists of the accounts in E through the platform's REST API at an interval shorter than the slot length, and records each observed activity with its timestamp. For each slot, observed activities are compared with C_t. Matches yield candidate symbols. Activities that match no codeword are treated as background noise and discarded. If several codewords are observed in one slot, the receiver takes the one that also satisfies the header and a message authentication tag. Slots with no match are marked as erasures, which Reed–Solomon decoding handles more efficiently than random errors. After the symbol stream is reassembled, it is decoded, decrypted, and checked for integrity.

**Proof-of-concept implementation.** The prototype is a mobile app with sender and receiver modes. The sender mode authenticates through OAuth to a set of Twitter accounts that we own and operate. It schedules activities in a background service according to the codebook. Activity types are original posts with controlled attributes (hashtag from a key-derived list, tweet-length bin, presence of a link), reposts of designated accounts, likes, and follows or unfollows. The receiver mode uses read-only API access. All keys remain in the device's secure storage. Cryptographic operations use the platform's standard libraries. To reduce risk to the platform and other users, request rates stay within documented limits, and only accounts created for the experiment are used as carriers.

**Experimental design.** We ran controlled experiments with n ∈ {5, 10, 20} experimental accounts, b ∈ {2, 4, 6} bits per slot, and slot lengths of 1, 5, and 15 minutes. For each factor combination, random messages of 32, 64, and 128 bytes were transmitted in 30 independent trials, with the sender and receiver on separate devices and networks. A subset of accounts also followed and interacted with a pool of unrelated public accounts, so that the receiver would see realistic background activity. We also injected synthetic perturbations (deleted posts and suspended polling windows) to test robustness. The primary outcomes were: (i) message recovery rate, the proportion of trials with exact plaintext recovery; (ii) symbol error and erasure rates before error correction; (iii) effective embedding rate in bits per hour, after coding overhead; and (iv) end-to-end latency from the first embedded activity to successful decoding.

**Detectability analysis.** Since the framework implies that a steganalyst must monitor the whole world W, we evaluated detectability under a simplified adversary with access to the same public API. Baseline behavioral profiles were obtained from the pre-experiment activity histories of the same accounts and, where permitted by the platform's terms, from a sample of comparable public accounts. For each account we computed features such as per-hour activity counts by type, inter-activity time distributions, hashtag frequencies, and the entropy of interaction targets. We compared stego and baseline periods using Kullback–Leibler divergence and two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (Cover & Thomas, 2006). We also trained a random forest classifier (Breiman, 2001) on windowed features, evaluated by stratified 10-fold cross-validation, and measured the area under the ROC curve (Fawcett, 2006). An AUC near 0.5 indicates that the stego activity cannot be distinguished from baseline using these features. We also recorded the monitoring cost, in API calls and data volume per detection decision, as a proxy for the analysis burden the framework imposes.

**Statistical analysis.** Recovery rates are reported as proportions with 95% Wilson score intervals (Brown et al., 2001). Differences in recovery across factor levels were tested with logistic regression, with account number, bits per slot, slot length, and message length as predictors, and effects are reported as odds ratios with confidence intervals. Latency and embedding rate, which were expected to be skewed, were compared using Kruskal–Wallis tests with Dunn's post hoc comparisons and Holm correction for multiple testing. Effect sizes are reported alongside p-values, and the significance threshold was α = 0.05. All analysis scripts and random seeds were fixed and logged to allow replication.

**Ethical considerations.** Experiments used only accounts created for the study and publicly available data, and they complied with the platform's developer terms. No interaction was directed at non-participating users beyond passive observation, and no personal data from third parties were stored. Collected baseline data were aggregated and anonymized before analysis.

Results

We evaluated the proof-of-concept mobile app on four measures: embedding capacity, decoding reliability, latency and resource cost, and statistical indistinguishability of the hidden activities from ordinary behavior. All experiments used a pool of 32 Twitter accounts, 24 of them controlled by the sender and 8 designated as "carrier" accounts that the sender followed but did not control. The sender encoded messages through four observable activity types: following a target account, liking a tweet, retweeting a tweet, and posting a reply containing a hashtag. The receiver app observed only the public timeline and the public activity of the monitored accounts. Unless stated otherwise, each configuration was repeated 30 times over a three-week period in 2021.

**Capacity.** The capacity of one time slot depends on how many accounts, activity types and target objects the codebook can distinguish. With 24 sender-controlled accounts, four activity types and a codebook of 16 candidate target objects, the theoretical upper bound is log2(24 × 4 × 16) ≈ 10.58 bits per activity, which gives 10 usable bits per activity once the mapping is truncated to a power of two. In practice, platform constraints and the requirement that activity stay plausible reduced the usable capacity. Following the platform's published rate limits (Twitter, 2020) and capping each account at 12 actions per hour to avoid automated-behavior flags, the sender could emit at most 288 actions per hour. This corresponds to about 2,880 raw bits per hour, or 0.8 bits per second. Using an ordered-set encoding in which the order of the activities carries additional information (Fridrich, 2009), the bound rose by 11.4% on average. However, 17.6% of the planned activities had to be rescheduled to meet plausibility constraints, so the effective sustained throughput was 1,910 ± 142 bits per hour. A 140-character ASCII message (980 bits, excluding error correction) was therefore transmitted in roughly 31 minutes, or 22 minutes when the ordering channel was enabled.

**Reliability.** Decoding success was measured as the fraction of messages recovered bit-for-bit by the receiver app. Without error correction, the raw bit error rate (BER) was 3.9% (95% CI: 3.1–4.7%). Most errors came from three sources: activities that failed silently because of API throttling (46% of errors), activities that were delayed past the receiver's observation window (31%), and misattribution caused by unrelated third-party activity on carrier accounts (23%). Adding a Reed–Solomon RS(255,223) code and a 4-slot interleaver reduced the post-decoding BER to below 0.02%, and 29 of 30 messages (96.7%) were recovered perfectly at a 10-minute observation window. Lengthening the window to 30 minutes brought the recovery rate to 100% (30 of 30), at the cost of higher latency. The coding overhead was 14.3%, which lowered the effective net throughput to approximately 1,640 bits per hour. The single failure at the shorter window was a burst of 41 consecutive lost activities during a 9-minute Twitter API outage, which exceeded the interleaver's correction depth.

**Latency and resource consumption.** End-to-end latency, defined as the time from the sender's first activity to the receiver's confirmed decoding, had a median of 24.6 minutes for 140-character messages (interquartile range 21.3–29.8 minutes). The receiver's polling interval and the 10-minute window dominated this figure. On a mid-range Android device (4 GB RAM), the sender app used an average of 3.2% CPU and 61 MB of memory during an embedding session, and the receiver app used 5.8% CPU and 74 MB. Battery drain was 2.1% per hour for the sender and 3.4% per hour for the receiver, with network traffic of 1.9 MB and 4.6 MB per hour, respectively. These costs are modest, but they scale with the number of monitored accounts. When we increased the monitored set from 8 to 128 accounts in a stress test, receiver CPU use rose to 19.7% and traffic to 38 MB per hour, a roughly linear increase. This observation matters for the discussion of steganalysis, because an adversary who monitors the whole digital world faces a much steeper cost curve than the receiver, who monitors only a small subset.

**Statistical indistinguishability.** To estimate how readily the hidden activity could be detected, we compared the sender accounts' behavior with a reference set of 500 randomly sampled, comparable accounts, matched for follower count (±15%) and account age. We measured the distributions of inter-activity times, daily activity counts, and the mix of activity types. The Kullback–Leibler divergence (Cachin, 1998) between the stego-period behavior and each account's own baseline was 0.041 bits for inter-activity times and 0.057 bits for activity-type mix. For comparison, the divergence between two disjoint baseline weeks of the same accounts was 0.036 and 0.049 bits respectively. A two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test did not reject equality of the inter-activity time distributions for 22 of the 24 sender accounts at the 5% level. The two rejected accounts were those carrying the heaviest embedding load, with more than 15 actions per hour in the first hour of transmission, so we attribute the rejections to burstiness rather than to the codebook.

We then trained a supervised detector (a random forest on 38 account-level and temporal features) to distinguish sender accounts from the 500 reference accounts. Using per-account, per-day feature vectors, the detector reached an area under the ROC curve of 0.71 when the sender used the naive scheduler and 0.56 with the plausibility-aware scheduler. At a 1% false-positive rate, the true-positive rate fell from 18.4% to 3.1%. The detector's performance was close to chance only when the detector had no access to the codebook and observed fewer than 200 accounts. When it was given the correct set of 24 sender accounts, detection of the existence of a coordinated group of accounts was easy (AUC 0.93), but it could not recover the message content without the codebook. This confirms that the main protection comes from the secrecy of the mapping and from the size of the observable population, not from invisibility of any single action (Cox et al., 2007).
