Finally, a preliminary test with a hybrid configuration, in which 8 of the 24 sender accounts were replaced with accounts on a second social network, increased capacity by 9.7% and reduced the receiver-side recovery rate to 93.3% (28 of 30), mainly because of unsynchronized clocks and differing API delays.

Discussion and Conclusion

The central claim of this paper is that information can be hidden in the fact that particular digital activities, with particular attributes, occurred in particular ways in a receiver-observable digital world, rather than in a designated cover object. The proof-of-concept Twitter application shows that this is technically feasible. A sender and a receiver who share a key and a mapping can convey a message through selected account activities such as following, liking, retweeting and posting, and the receiver can recover it by observing the public activity space. The sections above treat this as an engineering result. Here we consider what it means for information hiding theory, where it falls short, and what follows for security and non-security uses.

Classical steganography is organised around the prisoners' problem (Simmons, 1984) and its formalisations, in which a cover is chosen or generated, modified, and compared with an unmodified distribution (Cachin, 1998; Hopper et al., 2002). Security is then the statistical indistinguishability of cover and stego objects, and practical research has focused on minimising embedding distortion within a cover model (Fridrich, 2009; Pevný et al., 2010). Our framework weakens the premise of this model. When the "cover" is the whole selected digital world, there is no single object whose distribution can be tested, and the embedding action is not a perturbation of existing content but the selection and timing of ordinary activities. Distortion-minimisation therefore gives way to a different design question: how closely do the activities chosen as carriers resemble the background behaviour of the entities involved? This is closer to the modelling of covert timing and storage channels (Lampson, 1973; Wendzel et al., 2015) than to media steganography. It differs in that the channel is built from semantically meaningful, socially embedded events rather than from protocol artefacts, and in that the sender may distribute the signal across several accounts and platforms.

A consequence for steganalysis is that the detector's task changes from classifying a suspect object to deciding whether any subset of a very large, heterogeneous and fast-changing activity stream carries a signal. Without a bounded suspect object, the usual feature-extraction and classifier pipeline (Westfeld and Pfitzmann, 2000) does not apply directly. Detection needs continuous collection, per-entity behavioural baselines, and some means of identifying which entities and activities to correlate. These requirements raise the monitoring cost, and we expect detection to be more complicated, less effective and less efficient than for conventional schemes. We do not claim this advantage is guaranteed. A warden who suspects a particular platform, account cluster or time window can reduce the search space considerably. Platform operators also hold information, such as account creation metadata, client identifiers and network-level traces, that outside observers lack. Our security argument is therefore economic and probabilistic, not information-theoretic. It rests on the expectation that the warden's cost grows with the size of the digital world, whereas the sender and receiver need to observe only the part they have agreed on.

Several limitations qualify these results. First, capacity and reliability have not been characterised systematically. Each activity carries few bits, and the activity-to-bit mapping must tolerate deleted posts, suspended accounts, rate limits and API changes. The square-root-law literature (Ker et al., 2008) suggests that secure payload will grow sublinearly with the number of carrier activities under reasonable detector assumptions, and similar behaviour is likely here, though we have not shown it. Second, the framework depends on the receiver being able to observe the relevant activities, so it inherits the availability, privacy settings and terms of service of the chosen platforms. A platform that changes its API or visibility rules can disable a channel without notice. Third, our implementation relied on one social network, so the evidence for cross-platform hybrids remains prospective, and the hybrid system under development must still show that coordinating across platforms improves robustness and deniability without adding correlatable patterns. Fourth, we have not evaluated the scheme against an adaptive adversary. Realistic evaluation needs models of ordinary user behaviour, which are hard to build and which drift over time. Bots and automated accounts are common on social networks, but platforms increasingly try to detect coordinated inauthentic behaviour, which could make synthetic carrier accounts the weakest point. Fifth, the sender's activities must look natural at the account level, yet the content, timing and social graph of an account are themselves rich features. Embedding schemes that ignore the dependence between a user's activities leave statistical traces, as earlier work on practical steganography repeatedly found (Provos and Honeyman, 2003).

These limitations suggest an agenda of three parts. The first is formalisation: a model that defines the observable digital world, the entity set, the activity space and the warden's observation and computation budget, so that security can be stated relative to explicit resource bounds. The second is an empirical study of carrier selection. This would learn behavioural models from real platform data and test whether activities chosen under them are distinguishable from background behaviour, in the way image steganography matured through adversarial benchmarking (Fridrich, 2009). The third is the development of steganalysis suited to this setting, probably based on streaming anomaly detection, graph analysis and cross-platform correlation.

The framework also has implications beyond covert communication. The same mechanism can support non-security uses, because a message hidden in a set of activities can serve as a puzzle, a game mechanic or an authentication token that participants discover by observing a shared environment. Examples include alternate-reality games, geocaching-style scavenger hunts, and lightweight signalling between cooperating applications. Dual use is unavoidable. A channel that is hard to monitor can protect journalists and dissidents under censorship, but it can equally coordinate malicious actors, and defenders of platforms may need to consider activity-level channels alongside content-level ones. We believe it is better to describe the framework openly so that both communities can study it than to leave it unexamined.

In conclusion, we have proposed a general information hiding framework in which the digital world observed by the receiver becomes the cover and the hidden message is encoded in what particular entities do and how they do it. A Twitter-based mobile app demonstrates the concept, and a multi-network hybrid is in progress. The framework redefines the cover concept, changes the problem faced by steganalysts, and extends information hiding to new applications. Its practical security, capacity and robustness remain open questions that require formal modelling, large-scale behavioural evaluation and adversarial testing.

# 1. Introduction

Empirical software engineering relies on observable artifacts such as source code, version histories, and defect reports to derive claims about how software is built and maintained. Such claims are rarely confined to the data from which they were drawn. A technique that performs well on a set of open-source projects is commonly presented as a general solution, and a result observed in one period is implicitly assumed to hold in the next. This assumption is seldom tested, even though software projects change continuously through new features, shifting teams, refactoring, and evolving development practices. The question this article asks is whether a researcher's conclusions will still hold a year from now for the same software projects.

There are reasons to doubt that they will. Menzies and Shepperd (2012) argued that many findings in software analytics are unstable, and that "conclusion instability" is a central obstacle to building a cumulative body of knowledge. Subsequent work has shown that conclusions often vary across data sets, learners, and experimental configurations (Menzies et al. 2013; Shepperd et al. 2014; Tantithamthavorn et al. 2016). Findings that appear robust on one collection of projects may weaken or reverse on another. Most of this work examines variation across space, that is, across projects, data sets, or methods. Far less attention has been paid to variation across time, even though software evolves and any practical use of a prediction model is necessarily temporal.

Defect prediction is a particularly informative setting in which to study this problem. It has been an active research area for more than two decades, with the goal of identifying files, modules, or changes likely to contain defects so that limited quality-assurance effort can be directed effectively (Zimmermann et al. 2009; Hall et al. 2012). A large body of work proposes new learners, features, and transfer strategies, and reports improvements over prior approaches. Cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), in which a model trained on one or more source projects predicts defects in a different target project, has received particular attention because it addresses the common situation where a project lacks sufficient historical data to train its own model (Turhan et al. 2009; Zimmermann et al. 2009; Nam et al. 2013). Comparative studies have identified approaches that appear to outperform others (Herbold et al. 2018; Hosseini et al. 2019), and such rankings are routinely taken as guidance for both researchers and practitioners.

However, the way defect prediction models are usually evaluated can obscure temporal instability. Standard protocols, including k-fold cross-validation and random train/test splits, ignore the chronological order of the data. They allow models to be trained on instances from the future of the instances being predicted, a form of information leakage that no practitioner could replicate in deployment (Tan et al. 2015; Jimenez et al. 2019). In addition, defect labels are often derived with delay, since a defect may be discovered long after the code that introduced it. Evaluations that disregard this lag can overstate performance. Even when time is respected, evaluations typically report a single aggregate figure computed over a whole history. A single number hides how performance fluctuates between releases or periods, so a method that looks superior on average may be superior only in some intervals. Aggregation therefore masks exactly the temporal behavior on which a practitioner's decision to adopt a model depends.

This gap matters for several reasons. First, a defect predictor is deployed on future releases, so the relevant evidence is its performance on data that postdate its training. Second, if the ranking of techniques changes from one release to the next, a study that selects the "best" approach from one evaluation window cannot support a claim that this approach will remain best. Third, the metrics used to quantify performance may themselves behave differently over time. Defect-prone ratios shift between releases, and metrics such as F-Score are sensitive to class imbalance, whereas the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) is more robust to it (Yao and Shepperd 2020; Chicco and Jurman 2020). Reporting only one metric may thus provide an incomplete view of stability.

In this article, we empirically investigate the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models. We adopt a time-aware evaluation approach in which models are trained only on data available in the past and are evaluated only on data from the future. Instead of one aggregate result, we examine performance as a function of the evaluation period, and we compare how conclusions drawn in one period compare with those drawn in subsequent periods. We measure performance with three complementary indicators: F-Score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and MCC. We then ask whether the relative performance of CPDP approaches, and the conclusions one would draw about them, remain consistent as the evaluation window moves forward in time.

Our study is guided by the following research questions:

**RQ1: How does the performance of cross-project defect prediction models vary across time periods?** We quantify the variability of F-Score, AUC, and MCC when the same models are evaluated on successive periods of the same projects.

**RQ2: Are conclusions about the relative performance of defect prediction approaches stable over time?** We examine whether the ranking of approaches, and the statistical significance of differences between them, persist across evaluation periods or change from one period to the next.

**RQ3: How sensitive is conclusion stability to the choice of performance metric?** We compare the three metrics to determine whether instability is an artifact of a particular measure or a more general phenomenon.

This work makes the following contributions. First, we present, to our knowledge, one of the first systematic investigations of time-based conclusion stability in cross-project defect prediction, shifting the focus from stability across data sets to stability across time for the same projects. Second, we provide a time-aware evaluation procedure in which training uses only past data and testing uses only future data, avoiding the leakage inherent in conventional cross-validation and allowing performance to be tracked period by period. Third, we show empirically that the performance of defect predictors, in terms of F-Score, AUC, and MCC, varies depending on the period evaluated, and that conclusions drawn in one period are frequently not reproduced in another. Fourth, we show that the next release of a product, particularly one that differs substantially from its predecessor, can drastically alter prediction performance. Finally, we offer practical guidance: in the absence of evidence of conclusion stability, researchers should restrict claims about defect prediction performance to the contexts in which they were evaluated, and should report results over multiple time periods rather than as a single aggregate. We also make our evaluation scripts and data available to support replication and extension.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on defect prediction, cross-project transfer, and conclusion stability. Section 3 describes the data, the prediction approaches, and our time-aware evaluation design. Section 4 presents results for each research question. Section 5 discusses implications and threats to validity, and Section 6 concludes.

## Methods

### Research Questions

We examine the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) through three research questions. **RQ1:** How much does the performance of CPDP models, measured by F-Score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), vary across successive evaluation periods? **RQ2:** Do comparative conclusions, such as "learner A outperforms learner B", remain consistent across periods? **RQ3:** Is the magnitude of change between consecutive releases associated with the change in predictive performance?

### Data

We studied 10 open-source Java projects from the Apache Software Foundation (e.g., Ant, Camel, Cassandra, Lucene, POI, and Synapse) that satisfy four criteria: (i) at least five tagged releases, (ii) a public issue tracker with bug reports linked to commits, (iii) at least 100 classes per release, and (iv) a release history of at least three years. This yielded 74 releases (4–12 per project) published between 2008 and 2020, containing 61,204 class-level instances in total. Release dates were taken from version-control tags and verified against project archives.

For each class in each release we computed 20 static product metrics, including the Chidamber–Kemerer suite, size and complexity measures, and coupling and cohesion indicators (Chidamber & Kemerer, 1994; Jureczko & Madeyski, 2010). Metrics were extracted using the same tool version across all releases to prevent measurement drift.

Defect labels were derived with the SZZ algorithm (Śliwerski et al., 2005). Bug-fixing commits were identified through issue identifiers in commit messages, restricted to issues typed as "Bug", and mapped to the bug-introducing changes of the files they modify. A class was labeled defective if it was modified by a bug-fixing commit within 180 days after the release date and the corresponding change was traceable to code present in that release. SZZ is known to introduce noise (da Costa et al., 2017), so we excluded fixes for issues reopened more than once and fixes touching more than 20 files, since these are likely to be tangled changes. The proportion of defective classes ranged from 6% to 41% per release (median 17%).

### Time-Aware Evaluation Design

Standard k-fold cross-validation and random train/test splits permit training on data that postdate the test data, which inflates estimates and obscures temporal effects (Tan et al., 2015; Jimenez et al., 2019). We therefore adopted a strictly chronological protocol. Every release *r* of every project *p* served once as a test set. The training set consisted only of instances from releases of *other* projects (the cross-project condition; Zimmermann et al., 2009) satisfying two conditions. First, the release date plus the 180-day labeling window precedes the release date of *r*. Second, the defect labels used for training were recomputed using only bug-fix information available at that cut-off. This removes both look-ahead in the instances and look-ahead in the labels, a subtle form of leakage that occurs when labels are collected after the prediction date (Herbold et al., 2018). Releases of project *p* itself never entered training, so the setup is a pure CPDP scenario.

To define evaluation periods, we grouped test releases into non-overlapping calendar half-years, yielding 22 periods between 2009 and 2020, of which 17 contained at least three test releases. We restricted the analysis to those 17 periods so that per-period summaries were not dominated by a single release. Performance within a period was summarized by the median across its test releases. As a reference condition, we also ran a time-agnostic CPDP evaluation in which, for each test release, the training set comprised all releases of other projects regardless of date. This allowed us to quantify how much the ignoring of temporal ordering changes conclusions.

### Learners and Preprocessing

We selected four learners that are widely used in the defect-prediction literature (Hall et al., 2012; Ghotra et al., 2015): logistic regression (LR), naïve Bayes (NB), random forest (RF; Breiman, 2001) with 100 trees, and a gradient-boosted decision tree ensemble (GBT). Beyond these, we included a CPDP-specific approach, the nearest-neighbor relevancy filter of Turhan et al. (2009), applied before fitting LR (NN-LR). All metrics were log-transformed (log(x+1)). Because metric distributions differ strongly between projects, features were z-standardized using training-set statistics only (Zimmermann et al., 2009; Herbold et al., 2018). Class imbalance was handled by class-weighting in the loss function rather than resampling, which keeps the test distribution untouched and avoids synthetic instances. Hyperparameters were kept at library defaults to isolate temporal effects from tuning variability. Stochastic learners (RF, GBT) were repeated 30 times per test release with different random seeds, and the median over runs was used. All models used a fixed probability threshold of 0.5 for the threshold-dependent metrics.

### Performance Measures

We report three complementary measures. The F-Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall for the defective class. AUC measures threshold-independent ranking performance (Lessmann et al., 2008). MCC is a balanced correlation between observed and predicted classes that remains informative under class imbalance (Matthews, 1975; Chicco & Jurman, 2020; Yao & Shepperd, 2021):

MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)).

MCC was set to 0 when any marginal sum was zero. Using three measures with different sensitivities to base rate and threshold allows us to check whether instability is an artifact of a single metric.

### Operationalizing Conclusion Stability

We define a *conclusion* as a statement about performance that a researcher might report from a single evaluation, either an absolute statement (e.g., "learner A achieves an AUC above 0.70") or a comparative statement (e.g., "A outperforms B"). A conclusion is *stable* if it holds in the evaluation periods beyond the one in which it was drawn. We assessed this using four indicators.

1. **Dispersion (RQ1).** For each learner and measure, we computed the range, interquartile range, and coefficient of variation (CV) of the period-level medians. We also counted the proportion of periods in which a performance threshold satisfied in the first period (AUC ≥ 0.70, MCC ≥ 0.30, F-Score ≥ 0.40; cf. Hall et al., 2012) was violated.
2. **Comparative consistency (RQ2).** For every learner pair and period, we determined the winner using the paired, per-release performance values. The significance of differences was tested with the two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Wilcoxon, 1945), with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons at a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). Effect sizes were quantified using Cliff's δ, interpreted as negligible (|δ| < 0.147), small (< 0.33), medium (< 0.474), or large (otherwise) (Romano et al., 2006). A pairwise conclusion was labeled *stable* if the same learner won with a non-negligible effect in at least 80% of periods. We additionally computed the learner ranking in each period and measured agreement across periods using Kendall's coefficient of concordance *W* (Kendall & Smith, 1939) and the Spearman rank correlation between rankings of consecutive periods.
3. **Sign reversal rate.** The fraction of learner pairs whose winner changed sign between consecutive periods, with at least one period showing a significant difference.
4. **Time-aware versus time-agnostic gap (RQ1–RQ2).** The paired difference in each performance measure between the two evaluation protocols, tested with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and the number of pairwise conclusions that differ between the protocols.

### Release Change Analysis (RQ3)

To characterize how much a product changes between releases, we compared the metric distributions of each test release with those of its immediate predecessor in the same project. For each of the 20 metrics, we computed the two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic and the Jensen–Shannon divergence between binned distributions, and averaged these across metrics to obtain a release dissimilarity score. We also recorded churn-based descriptors (the proportion of added, deleted, and modified classes). We then calculated the Spearman correlation (ρ) between dissimilarity and the absolute change in AUC, F-Score, and MCC relative to the previous release of the same project. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples) were reported. We additionally contrasted performance change for the upper versus lower quartile of dissimilarity using Mann–Whitney *U* tests with Cliff's δ.

### Threats Mitigation and Reproducibility

To limit dependence on a single labeling choice, we repeated the analysis with 90- and 365-day labeling windows. We also repeated it with quarterly periods, which changes period boundaries. Conclusions were considered robust only if they appeared under all variants. All analyses were implemented in Python (scikit-learn) and R, with fixed random seeds, and all scripts and derived data sets are provided in a replication package.

Results

**RQ1: How stable is cross-project defect prediction performance across time periods?**

We first evaluated each of the five learners (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and a CART decision tree) under a time-aware cross-project protocol. For every target project and each evaluation window, models were trained exclusively on defect data from other projects that had been observed before the window began, and tested on the target project's modules created or changed during the window. In total, this procedure produced 1,214 train–test pairs across 41 projects and 24 consecutive windows of six months each.

Performance varied considerably across windows. Averaged over all learners and projects, the median F-Score was 0.41 (IQR 0.27–0.55), the median AUC was 0.67 (IQR 0.58–0.76), and the median MCC was 0.19 (IQR 0.06–0.33). These values are lower than those typically reported under time-agnostic cross-validation, where we obtained a median F-Score of 0.53, AUC of 0.74, and MCC of 0.31 on the same data. The difference was statistically significant for all three measures (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001) with moderate-to-large effect sizes (Cliff's δ = 0.38, 0.41, and 0.44 for F-Score, AUC, and MCC, respectively), consistent with earlier warnings that ignoring temporal order inflates estimates (Tan et al., 2015; Jimenez et al., 2019).

Within-project variability over time was also substantial. For a given project and learner, the median range (maximum minus minimum) of AUC across windows was 0.29, and that of MCC was 0.41. In 63% of projects, the best-performing window had an MCC at least three times that of the worst-performing window, and in 18% of projects, MCC changed sign, i.e., the model performed better than chance in some windows and worse in others. The coefficient of variation of F-Score across windows averaged 0.46 (SD = 0.19), far higher than the 0.12 observed across ten repetitions of random cross-validation. Hence, the variation was not attributable to stochastic training effects alone.

We also quantified consecutive-window change. Between adjacent windows, the absolute change in AUC had a median of 0.07 but a heavy tail: the 90th percentile was 0.21, and 7.4% of transitions exceeded 0.30. Large changes frequently coincided with major releases. For transitions spanning a major release, the median absolute change in MCC was 0.16, compared with 0.07 for transitions within a release series (Mann–Whitney U, p < 0.001, δ = 0.35). This suggests that a substantive revision of a product can alter predictive performance abruptly, in line with observations of concept drift in software data (Menzies et al., 2012; Turhan, 2012).

**RQ2: Do conclusions about the relative ranking of learners remain stable over time?**

Most defect prediction studies draw conclusions of the form "learner A outperforms learner B." We therefore examined how often such rankings persisted from one window to the next. For each window, we ranked the five learners by mean AUC across target projects and tested for differences using a Scott–Knott ESD procedure (Tantithamthavorn et al., 2017).

The top-ranked learner changed in 58% of consecutive window pairs. Random Forest was ranked first most often (39% of windows), followed by Logistic Regression (24%), Naive Bayes (17%), SVM (12%), and CART (8%). However, Random Forest was ranked in the statistically best group in only 71% of windows, and in 11 of the 24 windows, at least one simpler learner was statistically indistinguishable from it. Kendall's τ between rankings of adjacent windows had a median of 0.40 (IQR 0.00–0.60), and in 21% of cases the correlation was zero or negative, indicating that the order of learners in one period offered little information about the next.

To mimic a typical single-snapshot study, we randomly drew 1,000 individual windows and drew a "conclusion" about which learner was best. We then checked whether this conclusion was reproduced in a different window sampled from the following year. Only 46% of such conclusions replicated, and the probability of replication declined as the temporal gap grew: 52% for a gap of one window, 44% for two to three windows, and 38% for four or more. The corresponding Spearman correlation between the gap and replication outcome was ρ = −0.31 (p < 0.001). Under F-Score the replication rate was 43%, and under MCC it was 41%, suggesting that the choice of metric does not remedy instability.

**RQ3: Does conclusion stability depend on the evaluation metric and on dataset characteristics?**

Stability differed across metrics. When we computed the Kendall's coefficient of concordance (W) of learner rankings across all 24 windows, we obtained W = 0.34 for F-Score, W = 0.47 for AUC, and W = 0.29 for MCC (all p < 0.01, but all well below the conventional 0.7 threshold for strong agreement). AUC was therefore the most stable measure, albeit with limited absolute stability. Moreover, the three metrics disagreed about the best learner in 37% of windows, so conclusions drawn from one metric did not reliably carry over to another.

We then investigated what explained instability. We characterised each train–test pair by the defect rate of the test window, the shift in the distribution of product metrics between training and test data (measured by the mean Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic over 20 features), and the relative amount of code churn in the window. A mixed-effects regression with project as a random intercept explained 36% of the variance in MCC (marginal R² = 0.36; conditional R² = 0.52). Distribution shift was the strongest predictor (standardised β = −0.31, p < 0.001): a one standard deviation increase in the KS statistic was associated with a 0.09 decrease in MCC. Test-window defect rate had a positive association (β = 0.18, p < 0.001), reflecting the greater ease of discriminating when positive instances are less rare, and churn was negatively associated (β = −0.12, p = 0.004). Windows containing a major release had a mean KS statistic of 0.34, compared with 0.21 for others (p < 0.001), which corresponds with the drops in performance observed in RQ1.

The class imbalance of the test data also changed over time. The median defect rate was 17%, but it ranged from 3% to 46% across windows within the same project, with a median within-project range of 14 percentage points. Because F-Score and MCC are sensitive to base rates (Zhang & Zhang, 2007), part of the variation in these metrics originates from changes in the data rather than in the learner. Indeed, AUC was less correlated with defect rate (Spearman ρ = 0.14) than F-Score (ρ = 0.52) or MCC (ρ = 0.33).

**Sensitivity analyses**

We assessed robustness of these findings along three dimensions. First, we repeated the analysis with three-month and twelve-month windows. The median range of AUC across windows was 0.34 and 0.21, respectively, so shorter windows exhibited more volatility, but the qualitative findings were unchanged: the top learner changed in 64% and 46% of consecutive pairs, respectively. Second, we applied standard transfer approaches, namely Burak filtering (Turhan et al., 2009) and a transformation-based method (Nam et al., 2013), before training. These techniques improved median AUC by 0.03–0.05 but did not reduce the variability: the coefficient of variation of F-Score remained 0.43–0.47, and the top learner changed in 55–60% of consecutive pairs. Third, restricting the analysis to the 14 projects with at least 20 windows of data and more than 100 defective modules per window yielded similar results (median AUC 0.69, top-learner change rate 54%), indicating that the instability is not simply an artefact of small samples.

Overall, the results show that performance estimates and, more importantly, comparative conclusions about defect predictors are strongly dependent on the time period in which they are evaluated.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of the findings.** Our results show that the conclusions drawn from cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) experiments depend on when the evaluation is performed. When models were trained only on past releases and tested on future ones, performance fluctuated considerably between consecutive evaluation periods. The median F-score across projects ranged from 0.31 to 0.62, AUC from 0.58 to 0.81, and MCC from 0.05 to 0.44. The spread in MCC is the most telling, since MCC is a more conservative indicator of classifier quality on imbalanced data than F-score or AUC (Yao & Shepperd, 2020; Chicco & Jurman, 2020). In several periods, a model that appeared adequate under F-score had an MCC close to zero, meaning its predictions were barely better than chance. In 38% of the consecutive period pairs we examined, the relative ranking of the best and second-best approaches reversed. A researcher who evaluated at one point in time could therefore have reported a different "best" technique than one who evaluated a few months later on the same projects.

This instability is consistent with earlier warnings that conclusions in software analytics rarely transfer across contexts (Menzies et al., 2012; Zimmermann et al., 2009; Herbold et al., 2018). It also extends them. Prior work mostly examined instability across data sets, whereas we show that it persists across time within a fixed set of projects. Temporal instability is arguably the more troubling of the two. A researcher can state in a paper that a conclusion holds only for the projects studied, but the projects themselves change underneath the claim. Ekanayake et al. (2012) observed that prediction quality fluctuates as project activity changes, and our findings suggest the same fluctuation affects cross-project models, which add distributional mismatch between source and target on top of temporal change.

We offer several explanations for this behavior, though our design cannot isolate each one. First, software evolves non-uniformly. Major refactorings, new features, and changes in team composition shift the relationship between code metrics and defect-proneness, a form of concept drift well known in the data-stream literature (Gama et al., 2014). The largest performance drops in our data followed releases with unusually large churn, in line with the intuition that a release differing substantially from its predecessor invalidates patterns learned from earlier ones. Second, defect labels are themselves time-dependent. Defects discovered after a release are only partially observable at the time of evaluation, and bug-fix linkage is known to be noisy and biased (Bird et al., 2009; Herzig et al., 2013; Tantithamthavorn et al., 2015). Evaluations that ignore this delay can mix information from the future into training, which inflates performance (Jimenez et al., 2019). Third, the proportion of defective instances varies by period, which affects threshold-dependent measures such as F-score more than rank-based ones such as AUC. This is why the three measures did not always move together.

**Implications.** For researchers, the main implication is that claims about defect prediction performance should be scoped to the period and context in which they were evaluated. Statements such as "approach A outperforms approach B" are, on our evidence, incomplete unless qualified by the time window, the releases involved, and the evaluation measure. We recommend three practices. First, adopt time-aware evaluation in which training data strictly precede test data. Randomized cross-validation, still common in the field, can leak temporal information and produce optimistic, non-reproducible estimates (Tantithamthavorn et al., 2017). Second, report performance as a distribution over multiple time windows rather than a single point estimate, so that readers can judge stability as well as central tendency. Third, report MCC alongside F-score and AUC, because the divergence among the three exposes cases where apparent success is an artifact of class imbalance or threshold choice.

For practitioners, the findings caution against deploying a cross-project model on the strength of past benchmark results. A model that performed well on last year's releases may fail on the next one, particularly after major changes. Teams should monitor predictive performance continuously, retrain when it degrades, and treat the outputs of a CPDP model as one input to quality assurance rather than as a reliable oracle. This is consistent with work on online and just-in-time prediction, which emphasizes adapting to recent data (Kamei et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2015). More broadly, our results support calls for greater caution in generalizing from empirical software engineering studies (Shepperd et al., 2014; Menzies & Shepperd, 2012) and for conclusion stability to be treated as a first-class evaluation criterion alongside accuracy.

**Limitations.** Several threats to validity should be considered. Regarding construct validity, we relied on defect labels derived from issue trackers and version control histories, which contain mislabeling and missing links. Because such noise may itself change over time, some of the observed instability could reflect labeling quality rather than model behavior. We mitigated this by using a fixed labeling procedure across all periods but could not eliminate it. Regarding internal validity, we examined a limited set of learners and metric sets with default or lightly tuned hyperparameters. More aggressive tuning, ensemble methods, or transfer learning approaches such as bellwether selection (Krishna et al., 2016) might be more stable. We also defined evaluation windows by calendar periods and releases, and different segmentation choices could alter the magnitude of the fluctuations, although the qualitative pattern was preserved across the alternative window lengths we tried. Regarding external validity, our sample consists of open-source projects with sufficiently long histories, and commercial or short-lived projects may behave differently. Finally, regarding conclusion validity, we describe instability descriptively and with non-parametric tests, and we did not model its causes formally. Our explanations in terms of drift, label delay, and class prevalence remain hypotheses for future testing.

**Future work.** Three directions seem especially promising. The first is to quantify which release characteristics, such as churn, developer turnover, or architectural change, predict a drop in performance, so that practitioners can anticipate when a model needs retraining. The second is to develop drift-detection mechanisms tailored to defect prediction. The third is to test whether stability-oriented training strategies, such as weighting recent data or selecting source projects dynamically, yield more consistent performance over time.

**Conclusion.** We have shown that the conclusions of cross-project defect prediction studies are not stable over time. Under a time-aware evaluation, F-score, AUC, and MCC all varied substantially across periods, and the apparent superiority of particular approaches frequently reversed. Because the next release of a product may differ markedly from its predecessor, broad claims about defect prediction performance risk being contradicted by future data. Researchers should therefore restrict their claims to the contexts in which they were evaluated, report results across multiple time windows with robust measures such as MCC, and treat conclusion stability as an explicit property to be assessed rather than assumed.

Introduction

Microsurgical free tissue transfer has become a cornerstone of reconstructive surgery. It is used to restore form and function after tumor resection, trauma, burns, and chronic wounds, and in the head and neck, breast, and extremities. With experienced teams and refined techniques, reported success rates now exceed 95% in many high-volume centers (Khouri et al., 1998; Pohlenz et al., 2012). Even so, vascular compromise at the anastomosis remains the leading cause of flap loss. Arterial inflow obstruction or venous outflow obstruction, usually due to thrombosis, kinking, compression, or vasospasm, occurs in roughly 5% to 25% of cases, depending on the series and the type of flap (Chen et al., 2007; Kroll et al., 1996). Most of these events occur within the first 48 to 72 hours after surgery (Kroll et al., 1996).

The prognosis of a compromised flap depends strongly on how quickly the problem is recognized. Muscle and other metabolically active tissues tolerate warm ischemia poorly, and the no-reflow phenomenon limits reperfusion after prolonged ischemia (Wang et al., 2015). Salvage rates are high when re-exploration takes place within a few hours of vascular compromise. They fall sharply when the diagnosis is delayed, reaching about 30% or lower for flaps explored late (Yii et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2007). Reliable early detection is therefore as important to flap survival as the original operation.

Many monitoring methods have been proposed. Clinical observation of skin color, capillary refill, temperature, turgor, and bleeding on pinprick is still the most widely used approach and the standard against which other techniques are compared (Smit et al., 2010). It costs little and needs no equipment. However, it is subjective and depends on the experience of the examiner. Intermittent assessment can miss events that develop between rounds, and nighttime examination under poor lighting is unreliable. Clinical signs also tend to appear late, when ischemia is already established. Buried flaps and those without a skin paddle, such as free jejunum or muscle flaps used in pharyngeal and intraoral reconstruction, cannot be assessed by skin appearance at all.

Several adjunctive technologies have been developed to address these limitations. Handheld Doppler ultrasonography detects flow in the pedicle or in perforators, but it is operator dependent and intermittent, and it can give false reassurance when the signal comes from adjacent vessels (Smit et al., 2010). Implantable Doppler probes allow continuous monitoring of anastomotic flow but need a second invasive procedure to place and remove, may dislodge, and have been reported to produce false-positive results (Rozen et al., 2008). Laser Doppler flowmetry and photoplethysmography give continuous measures of microcirculatory perfusion. They are sensitive to motion, probe position, and ambient light, and they provide relative rather than absolute values (Hölzle et al., 2006). Tissue oxygen tension, pH, and temperature probes, microdialysis, and fluorescence angiography with indocyanine green offer physiological information. Their drawbacks include invasiveness, cost, the need for specialized personnel, and the lack of true continuous bedside measurement (Udesen et al., 2000; Smit et al., 2010). No single technique has become a universal standard, and the search for a monitor that is noninvasive, continuous, objective, and simple to use is still active.

Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) is an optical technique that may meet these requirements. Biological tissue is relatively transparent to light in the near-infrared range of about 700 to 900 nm. In this range oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin have distinct absorption spectra, so measuring light attenuation at several wavelengths allows the relative concentrations of each chromophore to be estimated. From these, a regional tissue oxygen saturation can be calculated (Jöbsis, 1977). Because the signal comes mainly from small vessels (arterioles, capillaries, and venules), NIRS reflects the balance between oxygen delivery and consumption in the microvascular bed. It does not require pulsatile flow. NIRS has been used for years to monitor cerebral oxygenation during cardiac and carotid surgery and in neonatal intensive care, and in muscle physiology and the evaluation of peripheral vascular disease (Murkin and Arango, 2009). Its use in reconstructive surgery has been explored more recently. Early clinical studies in breast reconstruction and in head and neck and extremity flaps suggested that falling tissue oxygen saturation accompanies both arterial and venous compromise and may precede visible clinical changes (Keller, 2009; Repez et al., 2008; Steele et al., 2011). Different devices, probe designs, and algorithms have been used, however, and published experience is still heterogeneous. Many reports concentrate on breast flaps or on small series. Descriptions of the temporal relationship between the fall in regional oxygen saturation and the onset of visible color change are limited. This relationship determines whether the technique has practical value for earlier intervention and salvage. Information on how NIRS performs across the varied flap types and recipient sites seen in routine practice is also limited, particularly for the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy (INVOS) system, which uses a disposable adhesive sensor with a continuous bedside display.

The gap this study addresses can be stated briefly. Flap surveillance still relies largely on subjective clinical examination, and the available adjuncts are invasive, intermittent, or technically demanding. NIRS is promising, but evidence is needed on whether continuous, noninvasive measurement of regional oxygen saturation can reliably detect arterial and venous insufficiency in a mixed series of free flaps, and whether it does so before clinical signs appear.

We therefore asked whether postoperative monitoring of regional oxygen saturation with the INVOS system can detect vascular compromise in free flaps early enough to allow successful salvage. We prospectively monitored 57 patients undergoing free tissue transfer. We recorded regional oxygen saturation continuously after surgery and compared the trends with clinical findings and with the outcomes of re-exploration.

This study makes three contributions. First, it describes the use of the INVOS system as a continuous, noninvasive flap monitor in a consecutive clinical series. Second, it documents the temporal behavior of regional oxygen saturation in cases of arterial and venous insufficiency, particularly its decline before pallor or congestion became visible. Third, it reports that all patients in whom insufficiency was detected were salvaged by re-exploration, which supports NIRS as a practical addition to postoperative flap monitoring.

Methods

Study Design and Patients

We conducted a prospective, single-center observational study of consecutive patients who underwent microsurgical free tissue transfer in our department of plastic and reconstructive surgery. A total of 57 patients were enrolled. Eligible patients were adults who had free flap reconstruction with a cutaneous or musculocutaneous component large enough to accommodate the optical sensor. Reconstructive indications included head and neck cancer defects, breast reconstruction, and traumatic or oncologic defects of the extremities. We excluded patients with flaps that had no skin paddle (e.g., buried flaps), patients with severe skin pigmentation disorders or extensive scarring at the planned sensor site, and patients who could not be monitored for at least 72 hours. The institutional review board approved the protocol. All patients gave written informed consent, and the study followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Recorded demographic and clinical variables were age, sex, comorbidities (diabetes mellitus, hypertension, smoking history), flap type, recipient site, ischemia time, and anastomotic details.

Surgical Procedure and Standard Postoperative Care

Experienced microsurgeons performed all operations under general anesthesia. Anastomoses were done under an operating microscope with 9-0 or 10-0 monofilament nylon. Arterial anastomoses were end-to-end or end-to-side according to recipient vessel conditions. Venous anastomoses were done by hand-sewn technique or with a coupling device. Venous outflow was reconstructed with one or two veins depending on flap type. Intraoperative vessel patency was confirmed by the milking test and by inspecting flap bleeding after reperfusion. We did not use routine postoperative anticoagulation beyond a standard protocol of low-dose aspirin and adequate hydration, with unfractionated heparin given only at the surgeon's discretion in high-risk cases. After surgery, patients were nursed in a warm room (about 25–28 °C) with the flap kept free of external pressure and with controlled head and limb positioning. Standard clinical monitoring was performed in parallel with the investigational device. It consisted of hourly assessment of flap color, temperature, turgor, capillary refill, and bleeding on pinprick for the first 24 hours, then every 2–4 hours until postoperative day 3, and every 8 hours thereafter. These clinical criteria have long been the reference standard for detecting vascular compromise (Disa et al., 2001; Smit et al., 2010). The nursing staff and clinicians who made clinical decisions applied the same criteria as for any patient. The clinical team also knew the oximetry readings, so decisions about re-exploration were made on the combined clinical and device data.

Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Monitoring

Regional tissue oxygen saturation (rSO2) was measured with the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy (INVOS) oximeter (Somanetics, Troy, MI). The device uses the principle of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), which exploits the relative transparency of biological tissue to light at 700–1000 nm and the differing absorption spectra of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin (Jöbsis, 1977). The oximeter uses two wavelengths (approximately 730 and 810 nm) generated by a light-emitting diode in a disposable adhesive sensor. Two silicon photodiode detectors placed at different distances from the emitter (shallow and deep) record the returning light. Subtracting the shallow signal from the deep signal reduces the contribution of superficial tissue, so that the reported value reflects mainly a mixed arteriolar, capillary, and venular compartment in the underlying tissue (Irwin et al., 1995; Stranc et al., 1998). The result is displayed continuously as a percentage (rSO2), and the device updates it every few seconds. Because the measurement is not pulsatile, it can be used in flaps with low or absent pulse pressure.

Sensors were applied in the operating room immediately after completion of the anastomoses and reperfusion, once the flap was stable and bleeding had been controlled. The sensor was placed on the skin paddle, away from the pedicle and from the flap edges and suture lines, and avoiding visible superficial veins. Placement was chosen to minimize interference from ambient light. The sensor was covered with an opaque dressing and fixed with minimal pressure so that it would not compress the flap. A second sensor was placed on normal skin at a comparable site near the flap as an internal reference for systemic changes in oxygenation. The position of the probe was marked so that it could be replaced at the same site if it detached. Baseline rSO2 was defined as the mean value over the first 30 minutes of stable recording after reperfusion. The readings were then recorded continuously through the first 72 hours and afterwards at the time of each clinical assessment until postoperative day 7 or until the patient was discharged. We also recorded systemic variables that might influence tissue oxygenation, including arterial oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry, hemoglobin concentration, blood pressure, body temperature, and use of vasopressors.

Definition of Vascular Compromise and Management

Because there are no validated absolute thresholds for rSO2 in free flaps, we defined alert criteria in advance, informed by earlier reports of NIRS in flaps (Repez et al., 2008; Steele, 2011). A vascular event was suspected if flap rSO2 fell by 20% or more relative to its own baseline value and the decrease persisted for at least 10 minutes without a corresponding fall in the reference-site value or in arterial saturation. The investigators also recorded whether the pattern suggested arterial insufficiency (a rapid, steep decline to low values) or venous insufficiency (a more gradual decline). A decrease triggered immediate clinical examination of the flap, verification of positioning and dressing, and exclusion of technical artifacts. If clinical examination also suggested compromise, or if rSO2 continued to decline despite correction of reversible causes, the patient was taken back to the operating room for re-exploration. The final diagnosis of arterial or venous insufficiency was made at re-exploration, based on the finding of a thrombosed or kinked vessel at the anastomosis or in the pedicle. We recorded the time of the first rSO2 alarm, the time at which clinical signs (pallor or congestion, change in capillary refill) were first noted, and the time of return to the operating room. Salvage was defined as survival of the flap without partial or total necrosis at hospital discharge and at the first outpatient follow-up.

Outcome Measures and Statistical Analysis

The primary outcome was the ability of rSO2 monitoring to detect arterial or venous insufficiency, and in particular whether a decrease in rSO2 preceded visible changes in flap color. Secondary outcomes were the interval between the rSO2 alarm and clinical recognition, the flap salvage rate after re-exploration, and device-related problems such as signal loss, probe displacement, or skin reaction. Continuous variables are summarized as mean ± standard deviation or median and range, as appropriate, and categorical variables as counts and percentages. Baseline rSO2 values and the lowest values recorded during vascular events were compared with those in uneventful flaps using the Mann–Whitney U test. Within-patient changes from baseline to the time of the event were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Differences among flap types were assessed with the Kruskal–Wallis test. We estimated the sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values of the predefined rSO2 criterion against the final operative diagnosis, with exact 95% confidence intervals. Reproducibility was checked by comparing the values obtained after sensor replacement at the marked site with the preceding values, using the intraclass correlation coefficient. A two-sided p value less than 0.05 was considered significant. All analyses were carried out with SPSS software (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY).

Results

**Patient and flap characteristics**

Fifty-seven patients (34 women and 23 men) underwent microsurgical free tissue transfer and were monitored with the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy (INVOS) system. Mean age was 52.4 ± 13.8 years (range 19–78). Reconstructions were performed for breast (n = 19), head and neck (n = 15), lower extremity (n = 17), and upper extremity or trunk (n = 6) defects. The flaps were anterolateral thigh (n = 21), deep inferior epigastric perforator (n = 12), radial forearm (n = 8), latissimus dorsi (n = 6), fibular osteocutaneous (n = 5), and other flaps (n = 5). Mean ischemia time was 74 ± 19 minutes. Venous anastomoses were end-to-end, with one vein in 41 flaps and two veins in 16. The sensor was applied to the skin paddle in the operating room immediately after reperfusion. Monitoring continued for a mean of 96 ± 12 hours, giving a total of about 5,470 monitored flap-hours. The sensor stayed in place in 55 of 57 patients (96.5%) for the full planned period. In the other 2 patients the probe adhesive was removed early because of local skin irritation, and monitoring continued with clinical examination alone.

**Baseline and normal-course oxygen saturation values**

The initial regional oxygen saturation (rSO2) measured 30 minutes after reperfusion averaged 69.3 ± 6.1% (range 54–83%) across all 57 flaps. In the 53 flaps with an uncomplicated course, mean rSO2 was 70.1 ± 5.8% at baseline. It remained stable over the monitoring period, measuring 70.8 ± 5.5% at 24 hours, 71.4 ± 5.2% at 48 hours, and 72.0 ± 5.6% at 72 hours. Fluctuation within individual uncomplicated flaps was small, with a mean coefficient of variation of 4.3%. Baseline values differed modestly by flap type. Muscle and musculocutaneous flaps averaged 66.2 ± 5.4%, and fasciocutaneous and perforator flaps averaged 71.5 ± 5.7% (p = 0.02). Within each flap, however, relative changes from baseline were consistent. Age, sex, and recipient site were not significantly associated with baseline rSO2 (all p > 0.05). Our uncomplicated-flap values are consistent with those previously reported for cutaneous free flaps (Repez et al., 2008; Keller, 2009).

**Vascular compromise and detection**

Four of the 57 flaps (7.0%) developed vascular compromise: one arterial insufficiency (1.8%) and three venous insufficiencies (5.3%). All four were detected by a fall in rSO2 that preceded any visible change in flap color, capillary refill, or temperature.

The arterial event occurred in a radial forearm flap used for hand reconstruction. rSO2 fell from a baseline of 72% to 51% over 20 minutes on postoperative day 1 (a 29% relative decrease) and then reached 34% within 1 hour. The flap became visibly pale about 3.5 hours after the first decline. Re-exploration revealed thrombosis at the arterial anastomosis. After thrombectomy and revision, rSO2 returned to 68% within 40 minutes, and the flap survived completely.

The three venous events involved one anterolateral thigh flap, one deep inferior epigastric perforator flap, and one fibular osteocutaneous flap. They occurred at 6, 14, and 31 hours after surgery. rSO2 fell gradually rather than abruptly, from baselines of 70%, 66%, and 68% to 43%, 41%, and 47%, respectively. The mean fall was 38.6% of baseline, compared with a maximum fluctuation of 9.8% in uncomplicated flaps. The decline began a mean of 4.7 hours (range 3–7 hours) before congestion was apparent on clinical examination. Venous thrombosis at the anastomosis was found in two flaps, and kinking of the pedicle by a hematoma was found in one. After revision, rSO2 returned to within 10% of baseline in a mean of 55 minutes (range 35–80), and all three flaps survived.

Across the four complications, the mean lead time between the first significant rSO2 decline and the first clinical sign was 4.4 ± 1.6 hours. Detection was therefore earlier than clinical observation in 4 of 4 cases (100%). The overall flap salvage rate after re-exploration was 4 of 4, and overall flap survival was 100% (57/57), with no partial or total flap loss.

**Diagnostic thresholds**

In an exploratory analysis, we compared the rSO2 values of the four compromised flaps with those of the 53 uncomplicated flaps. A relative decrease of at least 20% from baseline sustained for more than 10 minutes identified all four vascular events (sensitivity 100%). An absolute rSO2 below 50% was also reached in all four. In the uncomplicated group, a 20% relative decrease occurred transiently in 3 flaps (5.7%). Each episode was attributed to probe displacement or external compression, and it resolved on repositioning within 15 minutes with no intervention. This corresponded to a specificity of 94.3% and a positive predictive value of 57.1% (4 of 7 alerts). The negative predictive value was 100%. Because the number of events was small, these estimates have wide confidence intervals (sensitivity 95% CI 39.8–100%) and should be interpreted cautiously.

Venous insufficiency was characterized by a slower, progressive decline (mean slope −2.9% per hour), whereas arterial insufficiency produced a rapid decline (−17% per hour). This difference was descriptive only, given the single arterial case. The rSO2 values in both complication types were lower than the values at which clinicians would intervene on the basis of appearance alone (Steele, 2011).

**Concordance with clinical assessment and safety**

Clinical assessment by experienced nurses and surgeons, performed hourly during the first 24 hours and every 2 hours thereafter, agreed with the rSO2 trend in 53 of 57 flaps (93.0%). Disagreement occurred only in the four complicated cases, where rSO2 changed first. No re-exploration was performed solely because of an rSO2 alert in the absence of other findings, and no unnecessary re-explorations occurred. No adverse events attributable to the device were observed apart from the two instances of mild skin irritation (3.5%) noted above. Data acquisition was uninterrupted by ambient light in 55 patients, and the readings were reproducible on repeat sensor placement, with a mean difference of 2.1 ± 1.4 percentage points in 12 patients who had the sensor repositioned.

Discussion and Conclusion

The principal finding of this study is that continuous regional oxygen saturation (rSO2) measured by in-vivo optical spectroscopy detected vascular compromise in all four flaps that developed it (one arterial and three venous), and that the fall in rSO2 preceded the visible change to a pale or congested color. All four flaps were salvaged by re-exploration. These findings suggest that near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) can supplement conventional bedside assessment and, in some circumstances, give an earlier warning of thrombosis at the anastomosis.

Flap salvage depends on how quickly a failing anastomosis is recognized. Salvage rates fall sharply as the interval between thrombosis and re-exploration lengthens, because the no-reflow phenomenon and irreversible ischemic injury develop progressively (Smit et al., 2010). Clinical observation of color, capillary refill, turgor, and temperature remains the most widely used monitoring method, and in experienced hands it is effective (Disa et al., 2001). However, it is subjective, depends on the observer, and is intermittent. Changes may be subtle in dark-skinned patients, under poor lighting, or during the night when staffing is reduced. Implantable and handheld Doppler devices, laser Doppler flowmetry, and tissue pH or temperature probes have each been proposed to address these limitations, but each has drawbacks, including false-positive and false-negative signals, operator dependence, probe displacement, the need for invasive placement, and the inability to give a quantitative, continuous reading of tissue status (Hirigoyen et al., 1995; Kind et al., 1998; Smit et al., 2010). Our results suggest that NIRS addresses several of these concerns. The probe is applied to the skin, it requires no interpretation of an audible signal, and it gives a numerical trend that can be reviewed by any member of the care team.

The physiologic basis for this performance is straightforward. Near-infrared light penetrates several millimeters to centimeters of tissue and is differentially absorbed by oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin. Because about 75% of the blood in a tissue bed is venous, the measured signal mainly reflects the oxygenation of the venous and capillary compartments (Irwin et al., 1995; Stranc et al., 1998). This explains why the technique is sensitive to both failure modes. Arterial occlusion removes oxygen delivery while tissue extraction continues, which lowers saturation. Venous occlusion produces stagnant, progressively deoxygenated blood, which also lowers saturation. Because tissue oxygenation falls before the skin changes color, a fall in rSO2 would be expected to precede any visible change, as we observed. Other investigators using similar technology have reported comparable early detection and high salvage rates, and some have reported lower flap loss after introducing tissue oximetry, particularly in breast reconstruction (Keller, 2009; Lin et al., 2011; Steele, 2011; Repez et al., 2008). A systematic review of NIRS-monitored free flaps likewise found high sensitivity and specificity and a high rate of salvage when intervention was prompted by a change in saturation (Newton et al., 2020). Our experience agrees with these reports and adds to the evidence that the technique can be used in routine practice.

Several limitations must be considered. First, this was a single-series, uncontrolled study with no concurrent comparison group monitored by clinical examination alone or by another device. We therefore cannot say that NIRS performed better than conventional monitoring, or that the four salvages would not have occurred without it. The statement that rSO2 fell "before" visible change relies on retrospective comparison of the trend with the recorded clinical findings, and a prospective design with blinded, time-stamped clinical assessments would give a more rigorous estimate of the lead time. Second, only four vascular events occurred among 57 patients. This number is too small to define reliable sensitivity, specificity, or predictive values, to establish an absolute or relative threshold for intervention, or to compare arterial and venous compromise. Our data also cannot show whether NIRS would miss events or produce false alarms in larger or more varied populations. Third, our cohort was heterogeneous in flap type, recipient site, and skin thickness. Absolute rSO2 values depend on probe-to-tissue geometry, flap thickness, subcutaneous fat, skin pigmentation, and hematoma or edema (Steele, 2011). Interpretation should therefore rely on the individual patient's baseline and trend rather than on a single universal cutoff. Fourth, the technique has recognized pitfalls. Ambient light, probe movement, and poor contact can produce artifact, and an isolated reading should be confirmed against the clinical examination. NIRS also monitors only the tissue under the probe, so partial flap necrosis, or compromise in an area remote from the probe, may be missed. Buried flaps with no skin paddle cannot be monitored directly by surface probes. Finally, we did not perform a formal cost analysis. The price of the device and disposable probes must be weighed against reductions in the cost of failed reconstruction, reoperation, and prolonged hospitalization, as well as against nursing time spent on hourly checks.

Despite these limitations, the findings have practical implications. A continuous quantitative trend allows less experienced staff to recognize deterioration and escalate care without relying on subtle visual cues. It may also reduce the frequency of disturbing the patient for manual examination and may support a more objective, standardized postoperative protocol. Because the device is noninvasive, it avoids the risks associated with implanted probes, such as bleeding, infection, and pedicle injury at removal. We recommend that NIRS be used as an adjunct to clinical examination, not a replacement for it, with any significant drop from baseline triggering immediate bedside assessment and a low threshold for re-exploration.

Future work should include prospective, multicenter studies with larger numbers of flap failures, direct comparison against other monitoring methods, and predefined alarm criteria, such as an absolute decrement or a rate of decline in rSO2 over a given interval. These studies should also stratify results by flap type and patient characteristics and include a formal cost-effectiveness analysis.

In conclusion, in this series of 57 free tissue transfers, monitoring with in-vivo optical spectroscopy detected both arterial and venous insufficiency early, before visible changes in flap color, and allowed successful salvage of all four compromised flaps. The method is noninvasive, continuous, and reproducible, and it is easy to apply at the bedside. Although larger controlled studies are needed to define thresholds and confirm its diagnostic accuracy, NIRS is a promising and practical method for the postoperative monitoring of microsurgical free tissue transfers.

Introduction

Nanotechnology, broadly defined as the manipulation of matter at the nanoscale (approximately 1–100 nm) to exploit novel physicochemical properties, has been heralded as an enabling technology with applications across medicine, energy, electronics and, increasingly, the agri-food sector (Roco 2003; Chaudhry et al. 2008). In food production, potential applications include nano-encapsulation of nutrients and flavours, nano-sized additives and carriers designed to improve bioavailability, texture or shelf life, nanosensors for detecting pathogens and spoilage, nano-formulated agrochemicals, and packaging materials with enhanced barrier, antimicrobial or monitoring properties (Duncan 2011; Rashidi and Khosravi-Darani 2011). Proponents argue that such applications may enhance food safety, reduce waste, improve nutrition and lower the environmental burden of agriculture. Market analysts have projected substantial growth in the sector, although the actual number of commercially available nano-enabled food products remains uncertain, in part because of inconsistent definitions, limited labelling requirements and commercial reluctance to publicise the use of nanomaterials (Chaudhry et al. 2008; Gruère 2012).

The history of food technologies suggests that technical feasibility and economic promise do not guarantee commercial success. Genetically modified (GM) foods, food irradiation and, to a lesser extent, cloning have all encountered public resistance that constrained their adoption, particularly in Europe (Frewer et al. 2011; Siegrist 2008). Consumer responses to such technologies are shaped not only by perceived risks and benefits but also by trust in institutions, perceived naturalness, moral and ethical concerns, and the extent to which individuals feel able to exercise control over their exposure (Frewer et al. 2004; Siegrist 2008). Because food is ingested, intimately linked to health and identity, and embedded in cultural practices, technologies applied to it are often judged more stringently than those applied to non-food products. Early experience with controversial technologies has therefore led policymakers and industry to emphasise the need for early engagement with public perceptions, so that innovation trajectories can be aligned with societal expectations rather than corrected after opposition has crystallised (Macnaghten et al. 2005; Stilgoe et al. 2013).

Nanotechnology presents particular challenges in this regard. Public awareness of nanotechnology has consistently been low, with many survey respondents reporting that they have heard little or nothing about it (Satterfield et al. 2009; Gaskell et al. 2005). Attitudes are therefore often formed on the basis of limited knowledge, heuristics, affect and trust in the actors involved, and may be highly sensitive to how information is framed (Scheufele and Lewenstein 2005; Cobb and Macoubrie 2004). At the same time, scientific uncertainty about the toxicology, environmental fate and long-term health effects of engineered nanomaterials remains considerable, and regulators have struggled to establish definitions, risk assessment methods and labelling provisions appropriate to nano-enabled foods (Chaudhry et al. 2008; Grieger et al. 2012). This combination of public unfamiliarity, scientific uncertainty and evolving regulation creates conditions in which consumer acceptance may be fragile and open to rapid change, for example following media coverage or a perceived safety incident.

A growing empirical literature has examined public and stakeholder responses to nanotechnology in food. Studies have employed surveys, focus groups, deliberative workshops, choice experiments and experimental auctions to assess awareness, perceived risks and benefits, trust, willingness to buy and willingness to pay (WTP) for nano-enabled products (e.g. Siegrist et al. 2007, 2008; Roosen et al. 2009; Bieberstein et al. 2013). Several findings recur: applications in food packaging tend to be viewed more favourably than nanomaterials incorporated directly into food, and perceived benefits to consumers and society appear to carry more weight than generalised technological promise (Siegrist et al. 2007, 2008). Yet the evidence is dispersed across disciplines, including risk perception psychology, food science, agricultural and consumer economics, science communication and science and technology studies. These fields differ in their theoretical frameworks, methodologies, sampled populations and outcome measures, which makes it difficult to draw coherent conclusions. Findings on the role of knowledge, gender, age, trust, and cultural context are mixed, and WTP estimates are derived under diverse elicitation conditions, in different countries and for different product types, limiting comparability. Expert perspectives, which shape research priorities, regulation and communication, have been examined less frequently than lay views and are rarely considered alongside them.

Existing reviews have tended to address nanotechnology perception in general rather than food applications specifically, or to concentrate on risk and regulatory aspects rather than consumer acceptance (Frewer et al. 2014; Grieger et al. 2012). Narrative reviews are valuable but are vulnerable to selective inclusion of studies and unclear appraisal criteria. A systematic review, with explicit search strategies, inclusion criteria and transparent procedures for appraisal and synthesis, offers a more reproducible means of integrating heterogeneous evidence and identifying consistent determinants of acceptance as well as gaps in knowledge. To our knowledge, no previous systematic review has aggregated empirical research from across disciplines on both attitudes toward, and willingness to pay for, applications of nanotechnology in the agri-food chain, while also including expert perspectives.

The present study addresses this gap. Its central research question is: what socio-psychological, cultural, affective and informational factors determine consumer (and expert) acceptance of, and willingness to pay for, nanotechnology applied to agri-food production? Subsidiary questions concern how acceptance differs between application types (for example packaging versus food-integrated nanomaterials), how perceived risks, benefits and trust shape attitudes, and how methodological approaches influence the evidence generated.

This paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured, reproducible synthesis of peer-reviewed empirical research on acceptance of agri-food nanotechnology, using a formal protocol and independent appraisal by two researchers supported by qualitative analysis software. Second, through thematic analysis it identifies key themes that organise the determinants of acceptance and may inform future theory building and measurement. Third, it draws out implications for developers, regulators and communicators, in particular concerning the importance of demonstrable benefits, transparent governance and the cultivation of trust, thereby supporting the development of nano-enabled food products that are consistent with societal expectations.

Methods

Review design and protocol

A systematic review methodology was adopted to identify, appraise and synthesise empirical evidence on consumer and expert acceptance of nanotechnology applied to agri-food production. The approach followed established guidance for systematic reviews in the social and health sciences (Centre for Reviews and Dissemination 2009; Higgins and Green 2011) and the reporting conventions of the PRISMA statement (Moher et al. 2009). Because the evidence base was expected to combine quantitative surveys, experimental valuation studies and qualitative work (focus groups, interviews, deliberative exercises), a narrative, thematic synthesis was planned in advance rather than a statistical meta-analysis (Thomas and Harden 2008; Popay et al. 2006). A written protocol specified the review question, search strategy, eligibility criteria, screening procedure, data extraction and synthesis approach before the searches were run.

Review question and scope

The review question was: what is known about consumer and expert attitudes towards, acceptance of, and willingness to pay (WTP) for nanotechnology applied to food production, including food, food packaging, and agricultural inputs? Agri-food nanotechnology was defined broadly to include nano-enabled ingredients, additives and supplements (nanoencapsulation, nano-sized delivery systems), food contact materials and packaging (antimicrobial, barrier and sensing materials), and agricultural applications (nano-pesticides, fertilisers and veterinary products). Studies on non-food nanotechnology applications were considered only when they included comparative data on food applications.

Search strategy

Electronic databases were searched from the earliest available date to the search date. The databases covered the social sciences, food science, agriculture, economics and general science: Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect, PubMed, ProQuest, EconLit and Google Scholar. Search strings combined terms for the technology, the domain and the outcome using Boolean operators, for example: (nano* OR nanotechnolog* OR nanomaterial* OR nanoparticle*) AND (food* OR agri* OR packag* OR “food production”) AND (consumer* OR public OR attitude* OR perception* OR accept* OR “willingness to pay” OR WTP OR risk OR benefit OR trust). Terms were adapted to the syntax of each database and piloted to confirm that a set of known relevant papers was retrieved. Searches were supplemented by hand-searching the reference lists of included papers and of earlier narrative reviews of public perceptions of nanotechnology, and by forward citation tracking of key studies. Results were exported to reference management software and duplicates were removed.

Eligibility criteria

Papers were included if they: (i) reported primary empirical data (quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods); (ii) were published in peer-reviewed journals in English; (iii) used a sample of adults aged 18 years or over; (iv) focused on consumer or expert acceptance of agri-food nanotechnology; and (v) examined attitudes towards, or willingness to pay for, one or more applications of agri-food nanotechnology. Experts (for example scientists, regulators, industry representatives and other stakeholders) were included where their views on acceptance, risk or governance were reported, as these perspectives inform and contrast with lay views (Siegrist et al. 2007). Exclusions were: conference abstracts, editorials, commentaries and opinion pieces; purely theoretical or modelling papers lacking primary data; technical papers on nanomaterial properties, toxicity or detection; studies of minors; studies not concerned with food, packaging or agriculture; and secondary analyses or reviews that did not report new empirical findings. No restrictions were placed on country of study or study design.

Study selection

Selection proceeded in three stages. First, titles were screened against the eligibility criteria. Second, abstracts of potentially relevant records were reviewed. Third, full texts of remaining papers were obtained and assessed. Two researchers independently performed screening at the abstract and full-text stages.
