Nationally representative surveys have since indicated that anaemia remains a public health concern in young children, although prevalence estimates differ by survey year, age band and the cut-offs applied (Labadarios et al., 2011; Shisana et al., 2013). Importantly, national figures can mask marked within-country heterogeneity. Rural and peri-urban communities in provinces such as KwaZulu-Natal combine high rates of poverty, household food insecurity, a heavy burden of HIV and tuberculosis, and endemic helminth transmission (Appleton et al., 2008). These conditions create a plausible setting for elevated rates of iron deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia, yet locally derived estimates for primary school-aged children are scarce. Most South African studies of iron status have focused on infants, pregnant women or adolescent girls, leaving the early school years, when formal learning begins and cognitive demands escalate, comparatively under-investigated.

This evidence gap matters for several reasons. First, children from disadvantaged communities frequently fail to attain their age-appropriate educational potential, and grade repetition and early school leaving remain persistent problems in South Africa, with consequences for lifelong health and economic productivity. Second, iron deficiency is potentially modifiable through low-cost interventions, including dietary diversification, targeted supplementation and deworming, so that even modest effects on learning could be of considerable public health importance. Third, assessment of whether anaemia and iron deficiency are associated with developmental and educational outcomes in this age group is essential for determining whether school health programmes should include haematological screening or iron-focused interventions. In the absence of context-specific data, South African policy must extrapolate from studies conducted in settings that differ in diet, infectious disease ecology and educational systems.

A further limitation of the existing literature is that anaemia and iron deficiency are often conflated. Haemoglobin concentration is a late and non-specific indicator of iron depletion, whereas ferritin, transferrin saturation and soluble transferrin receptor provide information on iron stores and iron-restricted erythropoiesis, albeit with the complication that ferritin behaves as an acute-phase reactant and rises with inflammation. Studies relying on haemoglobin alone may therefore misclassify children and attenuate or obscure true associations. Likewise, studies examining a single outcome, such as an intelligence quotient score, may overlook domain-specific effects on fine motor coordination, memory, attention or behaviour, which may be more sensitive to iron status and more directly relevant to classroom functioning (Lozoff, 2007).

Against this background, the present study investigated anaemia and iron status in children aged 6 to 8 years attending school in a peri-urban, disadvantaged community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Its first objective was to estimate the point prevalence of anaemia, iron deficiency, iron deficiency anaemia and helminth infection. Its second objective was to examine whether anaemia and iron status were associated with psychomotor development, including cognitive performance, fine motor skills, memory, attention and behaviour. Its third was to determine whether these haematological variables, together with helminth infection, predicted school performance as reported by teachers, caregivers and the children themselves. We conceptualised anaemia and iron deficiency as mediating variables through which environmental and nutritional exposures influence growth, development and educational outcomes, and we combined clinical, biochemical and educational data to capture this pathway.

This study makes three contributions. It provides current, locally grounded prevalence estimates for a population under-represented in national surveys. It integrates iron biomarkers, parasitological screening and multi-informant educational assessment within a single design, thereby allowing the relative roles of anaemia, iron deficiency and helminth infection to be considered concurrently. Finally, it documents the practical and methodological challenges of conducting health and education research in rural South African schools, including consent procedures, sampling, laboratory logistics and the statistical constraints of low outcome prevalence, with the aim of informing the design of adequately powered future studies.

Methods

**Study design and setting**

We conducted a cross-sectional, school-based study in a peri-urban, socioeconomically disadvantaged community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The area is characterised by high unemployment, reliance on social grants, and limited access to piped water and sanitation, which together create conditions conducive to both nutritional anaemia and soil-transmitted helminth transmission (Labadarios et al., 2005; Hotez et al., 2006). The study was guided by a conceptual framework in which anaemia and iron deficiency were treated as hypothesised mediating variables through which socioeconomic disadvantage, nutritional status and parasitic infection influence physical growth, psychomotor development and school performance (Lozoff et al., 2006; Walker et al., 2007). The study is reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines for observational studies (von Elm et al., 2007).

**Participants and sampling**

Eligible participants were children aged 6 to 8 years enrolled in the participating no-fee public primary schools and living within the catchment community. Children were excluded if they had a known haemoglobinopathy, chronic systemic illness, or neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosed before enrolment, or if they had received iron supplementation or anthelminthic treatment in the preceding four weeks. Schools were purposively selected on the basis of accessibility and quintile ranking, and children were then recruited from Grade 1 and Grade 2 class lists. Information sheets and consent forms in isiZulu and English were sent home via the schools.

The target sample size was calculated for estimating prevalence with a specified precision, using the formula n = Z²p(1 − p)/d². Assuming an anaemia prevalence of 20%, a 95% confidence level and an absolute precision of 6%, the minimum sample was 171 children. This was inflated to allow for non-response and incomplete data. A total of 184 children were enrolled and constituted the analytic sample. We note that the sample was powered for prevalence estimation rather than for detecting associations between exposure and the less common developmental and educational outcomes, and the analyses of associations should be regarded as exploratory.

**Data collection procedures**

Three domains of data were collected: clinical, biochemical, and school performance. Data collection took place at the schools during school hours in private rooms allocated for the purpose. Fieldworkers, comprising a paediatrician, registered nurses and a trained psychometrist fluent in isiZulu, underwent standardisation training before fieldwork. Instruments not available in isiZulu were translated and back-translated by independent bilingual speakers, and the translations were piloted on a small group of children outside the study sample.

*Clinical data.* Caregivers were interviewed by trained fieldworkers using a structured questionnaire covering household demographics, caregiver education, household income and assets, food security, water and sanitation facilities, breastfeeding history, birth history, and the child’s past medical history. A socioeconomic index was derived from household assets and services. Each child underwent a standardised physical examination. Weight was measured to the nearest 0.1 kg using a calibrated electronic scale, and height to the nearest 0.1 cm using a portable stadiometer, with children wearing light clothing and no shoes. Height-for-age and body-mass-index-for-age z-scores were computed against the WHO growth reference for school-aged children (de Onis et al., 2007), and stunting and thinness were defined as z-scores below −2. Clinical pallor was recorded but was not used for case definition.

*Biochemical data.* Haemoglobin concentration was measured at the point of care from a capillary sample using a HemoCue Hb 201+ photometer (HemoCue AB, Ängelholm, Sweden), which has acceptable agreement with reference laboratory methods (Neufeld et al., 2019). Anaemia was defined according to WHO criteria as a haemoglobin concentration below 11.5 g/dL for children aged 5 to 11 years (WHO, 2011a), with mild, moderate and severe categories defined as 11.0–11.4, 8.0–10.9 and below 8.0 g/dL respectively. A venous blood sample was drawn by a registered nurse, stored on ice, and transported to an accredited laboratory within four hours. Serum ferritin, serum iron, transferrin and C-reactive protein (CRP) were measured by automated immunoassay and colorimetric methods, and transferrin saturation was calculated. Iron deficiency was defined as a serum ferritin concentration below 15 µg/L (WHO, 2011b) or transferrin saturation below 16%. Because ferritin is an acute-phase protein, children with CRP above 5 mg/L were considered to have inflammation, and in these children ferritin below 70 µg/L was interpreted as indicating iron deficiency in line with recommended approaches (Thurnham et al., 2010; WHO, 2020). Iron deficiency anaemia was defined as the co-occurrence of anaemia and iron deficiency.

Stool specimens were collected in labelled containers and examined within 24 hours using the Kato-Katz thick-smear technique (Katz et al., 1972) for *Ascaris lumbricoides*, *Trichuris trichiura* and hookworm. A child was classified as helminth-infected if ova of any species were detected. All children with anaemia, iron deficiency or helminth infection were referred to the local clinic for treatment according to national guidelines, and children with infection received albendazole.

*Psychomotor and cognitive assessment.* Cognitive ability was assessed using Raven’s Coloured Progressive Matrices, a non-verbal test of reasoning that minimises linguistic and cultural bias (Raven et al., 1998). Raw scores were converted to age-referenced standard scores, and scores more than one standard deviation below the mean were classified as impaired. Fine motor skills were assessed using the motor coordination subtest of the Beery–Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual–Motor Integration (Beery et al., 2010), with impairment defined as a standard score below 85. Working memory was assessed using forward and backward digit span (Wechsler, 2014), with impairment defined as performance more than one standard deviation below age-based norms. Behavioural difficulties were assessed using the teacher-completed Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (Goodman, 1997), with a total difficulties score in the “high” or “very high” band classified as abnormal. Inattention was assessed using the inattention subscale of the Conners teacher rating scale (Conners, 2008), with a T-score of 65 or above considered clinically significant. Children were assessed individually in a quiet room, and testing was conducted in the child’s home language.

*School performance.* School performance was evaluated from three sources. Teachers completed a structured questionnaire reporting the child’s most recent term marks in home language and mathematics, attendance, grade repetition, and perceived classroom engagement. Caregivers were asked about school attendance, homework support and perceived academic progress, and children were briefly interviewed about their school experience, including enjoyment of school and reasons for absence. Performance was dichotomised as below or at/above the expected grade level, based on the national curriculum achievement-level descriptors (a mark below 40% being categorised as not achieved) (Department of Basic Education, 2011).

**Statistical analysis**

Data were double-entered in a password-protected database and checked for range and consistency errors. Analyses were performed using Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX). Continuous variables were assessed for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test and are presented as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges, as appropriate. Categorical variables are summarised as frequencies and percentages, and prevalence estimates are reported with exact 95% binomial confidence intervals. The prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency was compared with the national estimate for children reported in the South African National Food Consumption Survey (Labadarios et al., 2005) using a one-sample test of proportions.

Associations between anaemia or iron status and the categorical outcomes (cognitive, fine motor, memory, behavioural, attention and school performance) were first examined by Pearson’s chi-squared test or Fisher’s exact test where expected cell counts were below five. Continuous outcome scores were compared between groups using Student’s t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test. Where outcome events were sufficiently frequent, we fitted multivariable logistic regression models to estimate odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, adjusting a priori for age, sex, stunting, helminth infection and socioeconomic index, which were identified as plausible confounders in earlier work (Grantham-McGregor & Ani, 2001). Following the logic of mediation analysis (Baron & Kenny, 1986), we planned to examine whether adjustment for anaemia or iron deficiency attenuated associations between helminth infection or stunting and developmental outcomes; this was contingent on adequate numbers of outcome events. Given the low prevalence of several outcomes, model stability was assessed by the events-per-variable ratio, and models were not fitted where this was inadequate. Missing data were minimal and handled through complete-case analysis. A two-sided p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant, and no adjustment was made for multiple comparisons because of the exploratory nature of the analyses.

**Ethical considerations**

Ethical approval was granted by the institutional biomedical research ethics committee, and permission was obtained from the provincial Department of Education and school principals. Written informed consent was obtained from caregivers, and verbal assent from each child. Confidentiality was maintained through the use of coded identifiers, and results were communicated to caregivers with appropriate referral for care.

Results

**Study population and nutritional status**

A total of 184 children aged 6 to 8 years were enrolled and all contributed clinical data and venous blood samples. Stool specimens were available for 177 children (96.2%). The mean age was 7.1 years (SD 0.8), and 97 participants (52.7%) were girls. Mean haemoglobin concentration was 12.2 g/dL (SD 1.1; range 8.4–14.9). Using age-specific thresholds (haemoglobin <11.5 g/dL for children aged 5–11 years; World Health Organization [WHO], 2011), 43 children were anaemic, giving a point prevalence of 23.4% (95% CI 17.5–30.2). Most cases were mild (n = 38; 88.4% of anaemic children), five were moderate (haemoglobin 8.0–10.9 g/dL), and none was severe (<8.0 g/dL). This prevalence exceeds national estimates for children of this age (Shisana et al., 2013).

Iron deficiency, defined as serum ferritin <15 µg/L (WHO, 2011), was present in 26 children (14.1%; 95% CI 9.4–19.9). Nine children met criteria for both anaemia and iron deficiency, giving a prevalence of iron deficiency anaemia of 4.9% (95% CI 2.3–9.1). Iron deficiency therefore accounted for only 20.9% of anaemia cases (9/43), and 17 children (9.2% of the sample) were iron deficient without anaemia. Thirty-four children (18.5%) were anaemic without iron deficiency, which suggests other contributors such as infection, inflammation or other micronutrient deficiencies. Stunting (height-for-age z-score < −2) affected 21 children (11.4%) and underweight 16 (8.7%). Neither was significantly related to haemoglobin concentration in bivariate analysis (both p > 0.10).

Helminth ova were identified in 48 of 177 stool samples (27.1%; 95% CI 20.7–34.3). *Ascaris lumbricoides* was the most common species (n = 31), followed by *Trichuris trichiura* (n = 14) and hookworm (n = 3). Anaemia was somewhat more frequent among infected than uninfected children (29.2% vs 20.9%), but the difference was not statistically significant (χ² = 1.34, p = 0.25). Mean ferritin concentration also did not differ by helminth status (p = 0.41).

**Psychomotor and cognitive outcomes**

Impaired cognitive assessment scores were the most common adverse developmental finding, occurring in 38 children (20.7%; 95% CI 15.1–27.3). Impaired fine motor performance was present in 49 children (26.6%), whereas gross motor impairment was uncommon (n = 9; 4.9%). Behavioural problems were recorded in 8 children (4.3%), poor memory function in 8 (4.3%), and impaired attention in 2 (1.1%). These low counts limited the statistical power to examine any associations involving the behavioural, memory and attention outcomes. These outcomes were therefore described but not analysed further.

**Association of anaemia with developmental outcomes**

Anaemia was significantly associated with impaired cognitive scores. Cognitive impairment was present in 15 of 43 anaemic children (34.9%) compared with 23 of 141 non-anaemic children (16.3%) (χ² = 6.94, p = 0.01). The unadjusted odds ratio (OR) was 2.75 (95% CI 1.27–5.94). After adjustment for age, sex, stunting and helminth infection in a multivariable logistic regression model, the association remained significant (adjusted OR 2.90; 95% CI 1.30–6.45; p = 0.01). Mean haemoglobin was lower among children with impaired cognitive scores than among those without (11.8 vs 12.3 g/dL; difference 0.5 g/dL; 95% CI 0.1–0.9; p = 0.02), which suggests a graded relationship rather than a threshold effect alone.

Anaemia was also associated with impaired fine motor skills, which were found in 18 of 43 anaemic children (41.9%) compared with 31 of 141 non-anaemic children (22.0%) (χ² = 6.66, p = 0.01; OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.23–5.27). No association was found between anaemia and gross motor impairment (3/43 [7.0%] vs 6/141 [4.3%]; Fisher's exact p = 0.44), although the number of events was very small.

**Association of iron status with developmental outcomes**

Iron deficiency, with or without anaemia, was associated with impaired fine motor skills. Twelve of 26 iron-deficient children (46.2%) had impaired fine motor performance compared with 37 of 158 iron-replete children (23.4%) (χ² = 5.91, p = 0.02; OR 2.82, 95% CI 1.21–6.57). The fine motor impairment rate among children with iron deficiency anaemia was 5 of 9 (55.6%), but this subgroup was too small for reliable inference. Cognitive impairment was more frequent in iron-deficient children (8/26; 30.8%) than in iron-replete children (30/158; 19.0%), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (χ² = 1.95, p = 0.16; OR 1.89, 95% CI 0.76–4.69). Serum ferritin, analysed as a continuous variable (log-transformed), was not significantly correlated with cognitive scores (Spearman ρ = 0.11, p = 0.14). Likewise, helminth infection was not associated with cognitive impairment (22.9% vs 20.2%; p = 0.70) or fine motor impairment (p = 0.58).

**School performance**

Teacher-rated school performance was classified as below the expected grade level for 40 children (21.7%). The median number of absent school days in the preceding term, as reported by caregivers and verified against class registers, was 4 (interquartile range 2–7). School performance did not differ significantly between anaemic and non-anaemic children (below expected level: 11/43 [25.6%] vs 29/141 [20.6%]; χ² = 0.45, p = 0.50) or between iron-deficient and iron-replete children (6/26 [23.1%] vs 34/158 [21.5%]; p = 0.85). Helminth-infected children performed similarly to uninfected children (22.9% vs 20.2% below expected level; p = 0.70). In a multivariable logistic regression including anaemia, iron deficiency, helminth infection, age, sex and absenteeism, none of the biochemical or parasitic exposures significantly predicted below-expected school performance (anaemia: adjusted OR 1.31, 95% CI 0.56–3.08, p = 0.53; iron deficiency: adjusted OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.37–2.91, p = 0.94; helminth infection: adjusted OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.54–2.57, p = 0.68). Absenteeism of more than 7 days was the only variable with a borderline association (adjusted OR 2.34, 95% CI 0.97–5.64, p = 0.06).

**Precision of estimates**

Confidence intervals for most secondary associations were wide, reflecting the small number of children with each adverse outcome. Post hoc calculation indicated that the study had approximately 80% power to detect an odds ratio of 2.5 or greater for outcomes with a prevalence above 20% in the unexposed group. It had considerably lower power (<30%) for outcomes with a prevalence below 5%. Accordingly, the non-significant findings for school performance and for behaviour, memory and attention should be interpreted as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no effect.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study set out to establish the local prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency in school-aged children from a disadvantaged peri-urban community in KwaZulu-Natal and to examine whether these conditions were associated with psychomotor development and school performance. Three principal findings emerged. First, the point prevalence of anaemia (23.4%) was considerably higher than national estimates, although iron deficiency anaemia was much less common (4.9%). Second, both anaemia and iron deficiency were associated with impaired fine motor skills, and anaemia was associated with lower cognitive scores (p = 0.01). Third, neither anaemia, iron status nor helminth infection significantly predicted school performance. We interpret these findings below in light of existing evidence and of the limitations of the study.

An anaemia prevalence of nearly one in four children exceeds the 20–39% band that the World Health Organization (2011) classifies as a moderate public health problem, and it is higher than that reported for comparably aged South African children in the national surveys (Labadarios et al., 2005; Shisana et al., 2013). This is consistent with the well-documented gradient of anaemia across socioeconomic strata, in which household food insecurity, limited dietary diversity and a high burden of infection concentrate risk in poorer communities (Stevens et al., 2013). The wide gap between the prevalence of anaemia and that of iron deficiency anaemia is noteworthy, however. It suggests that, in this population, a substantial proportion of anaemia is not attributable to iron deficiency alone. Helminth infection, found in 27.1% of children, is a plausible contributor, since intestinal parasites cause chronic blood loss and impair nutrient absorption and appetite (Stoltzfus et al., 1997). Other candidate causes include deficiencies of vitamin A, folate and vitamin B12, chronic inflammation, HIV infection and inherited haemoglobinopathies, none of which could be fully characterised here. Furthermore, ferritin is an acute-phase protein that rises with subclinical inflammation, so that iron deficiency may have been underestimated if inflammation was not fully accounted for (Thurnham et al., 2010). These considerations imply that programmes that rely exclusively on iron supplementation or fortification may not resolve the anaemia burden in such settings, and that integrated strategies addressing parasitic infection and broader micronutrient status are warranted.

The associations between haematological status and fine motor performance and cognitive scores are biologically plausible. Iron is required for myelination, dopaminergic neurotransmission and neuronal energy metabolism, and deficiency during critical periods of brain development has been linked to persistent deficits in motor function and cognition (Lozoff et al., 2006; Georgieff, 2011). Observational studies from various settings have likewise reported lower cognitive and academic scores among iron-deficient or anaemic school-aged children (Halterman et al., 2001; Grantham-McGregor & Ani, 2001), and meta-analyses of supplementation trials suggest modest improvements in cognitive outcomes among iron-supplemented schoolchildren, particularly those who are anaemic at baseline (Sachdev et al., 2005; Low et al., 2013). Our findings are directionally consistent with this literature. Nevertheless, they must be interpreted cautiously. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and reverse causation or common antecedents are equally credible. Children in food-insecure, low-resource households are exposed to a cluster of adverse influences, including poor maternal education, limited cognitive stimulation, chronic stress and inadequate nutrition, which independently affect development and may also elevate anaemia risk (Walker et al., 2007). Although we conceptualised anaemia and iron deficiency as mediating variables, residual confounding by these factors cannot be excluded, and the associations may partly reflect the broader context of deprivation.

The absence of a significant relationship between anaemia, iron status or helminth infection and school performance should not be taken as evidence that no relationship exists. The prevalence of several outcomes was low, including behavioural problems (4.3%), poor memory function (4.3%) and impaired attention (1.1%). With so few affected children, the number of events in any comparison was too small to provide adequate statistical power, and the confidence intervals around the null estimates are correspondingly wide. In effect, the sample of 184 children was adequate to estimate prevalence but not to detect modest associations with rare outcomes, particularly once the exposure was further divided into anaemia, iron deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia. The low frequency of attentional and behavioural difficulties may also reflect measurement issues. Teacher and caregiver reports are subject to social desirability and to differing reference standards, and in crowded classrooms teachers may have limited opportunity to observe individual children closely. Moreover, school performance is a distal and multidetermined outcome influenced by language of instruction, school quality, attendance and home learning environment, all of which may dilute any effect attributable to iron status (Walker et al., 2007). The finding that 20.7% of children had impaired cognitive scores, despite the low prevalence of behavioural and attentional problems, indicates that cognitive vulnerability in this community is considerable and may arise from sources beyond those measured here.

Several further limitations merit acknowledgement. The sample was drawn from a single community and may not be representative of other South African settings, which limits generalisability. Participation required caregiver consent and venepuncture, and selection bias may have arisen if children with greater health problems were more or less likely to take part. Assessments of psychomotor development relied on instruments that may not have been validated in isiZulu-speaking populations, and cultural or linguistic bias could have influenced scores. We did not have data on the timing or duration of iron deficiency, yet early-life deficiency may have lasting effects that are not reflected in current iron status (Lozoff et al., 2006). Multiple comparisons across several outcomes also raise the possibility that some significant associations arose by chance, and the findings on fine motor skills and cognition should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Finally, the practical challenges encountered in conducting research in rural schools, including logistical constraints on blood collection, limited private space for assessments, variable school attendance and difficulties in obtaining teacher and caregiver participation, probably affected data completeness and may have contributed to non-differential measurement error. Future studies should anticipate these constraints through longer fieldwork periods, community engagement and trained local fieldworkers.

These findings carry implications for policy and research. The high prevalence of anaemia and helminth infection in a school-aged population underscores the value of school-based health services, including routine haemoglobin screening, periodic deworming and nutrition education, which have been shown to be feasible and cost-effective in similar settings (Taylor-Robinson et al., 2015; WHO, 2011). Because the prevalence of iron deficiency anaemia was low relative to that of anaemia, screening programmes should incorporate iron indices with inflammatory markers so that treatment can be appropriately targeted. For research, adequately powered, prospective or randomised designs are needed, with sample sizes calculated on the basis of the observed low prevalence of attentional and behavioural outcomes, standardised and culturally validated assessment tools, and objective measures of educational attainment.

In conclusion, anaemia affected almost a quarter of the sampled children, a prevalence higher than the national estimate, while iron deficiency anaemia and helminth infection were also present. Anaemia and iron deficiency were associated with poorer fine motor skills, and anaemia with lower cognitive scores, supporting the biological plausibility of an effect of iron status on neurodevelopment. However, the study was underpowered to examine rare outcomes, and no association with school performance could be demonstrated. These results highlight the need for integrated school-based nutrition and parasite control interventions and for larger, methodologically robust studies to clarify the contribution of anaemia and iron status to learning among South African children.

Introduction

Type 2 diabetes mellitus affects an estimated 425 million adults worldwide, and projections suggest that this figure will exceed 600 million by 2045 (International Diabetes Federation, 2017). The disease is a leading cause of blindness, end-stage kidney disease, lower-limb amputation, and cardiovascular morbidity, and it roughly doubles the risk of vascular death relative to individuals without diabetes (Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration, 2010). Intensive glycemic control reduces microvascular complications (UK Prospective Diabetes Study Group, 1998; Holman et al., 2008), yet fewer than 50% of patients in routine practice achieve a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) concentration below 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) (Ali et al., 2013). Progressive decline in pancreatic β-cell function, weight gain associated with insulin and insulin secretagogues, and the risk of hypoglycemia contribute to this persistent therapeutic gap (Inzucchi et al., 2015). Consequently, there is considerable interest in glucose-lowering agents that act independently of insulin, preserve or improve body weight, and carry a low intrinsic risk of hypoglycemia.

Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors constitute one such class. Under normoglycemic conditions, approximately 180 g of glucose is filtered daily by the glomeruli and almost entirely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, with SGLT2, a low-affinity, high-capacity transporter located in the early S1 and S2 segments, accounting for roughly 90% of this reabsorption and SGLT1 for the remainder (Wright et al., 2011). In type 2 diabetes, renal glucose reabsorption is paradoxically enhanced, owing to upregulation of SGLT2 expression and an increased renal threshold for glucosuria, which maladaptively sustains hyperglycemia (Rahmoune et al., 2005; DeFronzo et al., 2012). Pharmacological inhibition of SGLT2 lowers this threshold, promoting urinary excretion of 50 to 80 g of glucose per day and thereby reducing plasma glucose through a mechanism that is independent of β-cell function and insulin sensitivity (Ferrannini and Solini, 2012). Because the glucose-lowering effect depends on filtered glucose load, efficacy is attenuated when the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is reduced, a feature with direct implications for clinical use.

Several SGLT2 inhibitors, including canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin, have now been approved in North America and Europe. In randomized controlled trials, these agents reduce HbA1c by approximately 0.5% to 1.0% when used as monotherapy or in combination with metformin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, DPP-4 inhibitors, or insulin (Vasilakou et al., 2013; Zaccardi et al., 2016). They also lower body weight by 2 to 3 kg, mainly through caloric loss from glucosuria, and reduce systolic blood pressure by 3 to 5 mmHg, likely reflecting osmotic diuresis and natriuresis (Baker et al., 2014; Mazidi et al., 2017). Importantly, the risk of hypoglycemia is low unless these drugs are combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues. On the basis of this evidence, recent guidelines position SGLT2 inhibitors as second- or third-line agents after metformin (American Diabetes Association, 2017; Garber et al., 2017).

The therapeutic relevance of the class expanded considerably after the publication of the EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial, in which empagliflozin added to standard care reduced the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke by 14% (hazard ratio [HR], 0.86; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74–0.99), cardiovascular mortality by 38%, all-cause mortality by 32%, and hospitalization for heart failure by 35% in patients with established cardiovascular disease (Zinman et al., 2015). A secondary analysis demonstrated a 39% relative reduction in incident or worsening nephropathy (HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.53–0.70), together with slower eGFR decline and a lower risk of doubling of serum creatinine (Wanner et al., 2016). The rapid separation of survival curves, evident within months, and the modest effect on HbA1c suggest that mechanisms beyond glycemic control, such as hemodynamic effects, reduced intraglomerular pressure through restored tubuloglomerular feedback, and altered myocardial energetics, may underlie these benefits (Heerspink et al., 2016). Whether similar outcomes apply to other SGLT2 inhibitors remains incompletely resolved, although early data for canagliflozin suggest a comparable direction of effect (Neal et al., 2017).

Despite this favorable profile, the clinical integration of SGLT2 inhibitors is not straightforward. Their mechanism of action gives rise to predictable adverse events, including genital mycotic infections, which are 3- to 5-fold more frequent than with comparators, and, to a lesser extent, urinary tract infections (Nyirjesy et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017). Volume depletion, orthostatic hypotension, and transient early declines in eGFR may occur, particularly in older adults, in patients with impaired renal function, and in those receiving loop diuretics or renin–angiotensin system blockers (Weir et al., 2014). Rare but serious safety signals have also emerged, notably euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, prompting regulatory warnings (Peters et al., 2015; Food and Drug Administration, 2015), as well as concerns about lower-limb amputations and bone fractures with canagliflozin (Neal et al., 2017). Moreover, because SGLT2 inhibitors are typically added to complex regimens in patients with multiple comorbidities, their initiation interacts with concomitant therapies: insulin and sulfonylureas may require dose reduction to avert hypoglycemia, diuretics and antihypertensive agents may need adjustment to prevent hypovolemia, and low-carbohydrate diets or reduced insulin doses may increase ketosis risk.

Although pivotal trials and guidelines provide recommendations on when to prescribe SGLT2 inhibitors, they offer limited operational guidance on how to start them safely in everyday practice. Clinicians must decide which patients are most likely to benefit, how to evaluate renal function and volume status before initiation, how to modify background glucose-lowering and cardiovascular drugs, and what monitoring and counseling are warranted. In the absence of structured recommendations, prescribing may be unnecessarily cautious, depriving patients of potential benefit, or insufficiently careful, exposing them to avoidable harm.

The aim of this review is therefore to provide a pragmatic framework for initiating SGLT2 inhibitors in adults with type 2 diabetes. We summarize the physiological rationale and the evidence for glycemic and extraglycemic efficacy, including the cardiovascular and renal outcomes reported with empagliflozin; critically appraise adverse events arising from the mechanism of action or from interactions with concomitant therapies; and propose a treatment algorithm for adjusting background medications when an SGLT2 inhibitor is introduced. By translating trial evidence into actionable steps, this work seeks to support clinicians in optimizing the benefit–risk balance of this therapeutic class.

Methods

**Study design and objectives**

We conducted a structured narrative review with the aim of developing a practical, clinically oriented framework for initiating sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors in adults with type 2 diabetes. The review had three prespecified objectives: (i) to summarize the efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors on glycemic and extraglycemic outcomes, including body weight, blood pressure, renal function, and cardiovascular events; (ii) to characterize adverse events attributable either to the pharmacological mechanism of these agents or to interactions with concomitant glucose-lowering and cardiovascular therapies; and (iii) to derive a stepwise algorithm for adjusting concomitant medications at the time of SGLT2 inhibitor initiation. The reporting of the evidence synthesis followed, where applicable, the principles of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). Because the aim was clinical translation rather than a new pooled estimate, no formal meta-analysis protocol was registered.

**Data sources and search strategy**

We searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from database inception to December 2016. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary and free text for the drug class (“sodium-glucose transporter 2,” “SGLT2 inhibitor,” “gliflozin,” and individual agent names, including canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin) with terms for the condition (“type 2 diabetes mellitus”) and for clinical domains of interest (“hypoglycemia,” “volume depletion,” “genital infection,” “ketoacidosis,” “renal function,” “cardiovascular outcomes,” “insulin,” “sulfonylurea,” “diuretic”). Searches were supplemented by manual review of reference lists from pivotal trials, prior systematic reviews, and consensus statements, as well as by examination of regulatory documents from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency, including prescribing information and safety communications. The proceedings of the American Diabetes Association and European Association for the Study of Diabetes annual meetings were screened for relevant late-breaking data. Clinical practice guidelines and position statements were identified through the websites of major diabetes societies (Inzucchi et al., 2015; Garber et al., 2016).

**Eligibility criteria**

Studies were eligible if they enrolled adults (≥18 years) with type 2 diabetes and evaluated an SGLT2 inhibitor at approved or investigational doses, administered as monotherapy or add-on therapy. For efficacy, we included randomized, double-blind, placebo- or active-controlled trials with a duration of at least 12 weeks that reported change in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting plasma glucose, body weight, or systolic and diastolic blood pressure. For cardiovascular and renal outcomes, we included large randomized outcome trials and prespecified renal analyses, with particular attention to the EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial of empagliflozin (Zinman et al., 2015; Wanner et al., 2016) and to the cardiovascular safety program of canagliflozin (Neal et al., 2017). For safety, we additionally considered pooled analyses of phase 2–3 trials, postmarketing surveillance reports, case series of diabetic ketoacidosis, and pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interaction studies. We excluded studies in type 1 diabetes, studies in healthy volunteers (except for interaction and mechanistic studies), non-English publications without an available translation, and conference abstracts lacking sufficient methodological detail.

**Study selection and data extraction**

Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then full texts, with disagreements resolved by discussion or adjudication by a third reviewer. Data were extracted using a standardized form that captured trial design, population characteristics (age, diabetes duration, baseline HbA1c, body mass index, estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR], and background therapy), intervention and comparator, follow-up duration, and outcome data. Efficacy outcomes were recorded as placebo-adjusted mean changes from baseline with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Safety outcomes were extracted as event counts or incidence rates per 100 patient-years, with corresponding relative risks, odds ratios, or hazard ratios (HRs). For outcome trials, we recorded the primary composite endpoint (three-point major adverse cardiovascular events), cardiovascular death, all-cause mortality, hospitalization for heart failure, and incident or worsening nephropathy. Where eGFR-stratified data were available, results were abstracted separately for eGFR ≥90, 60–<90, 45–<60, and <45 mL/min/1.73 m², since both glycemic efficacy and the risk of volume-related adverse events vary across these strata (Cherney et al., 2014).

**Assessment of study quality and certainty of evidence**

Risk of bias in randomized trials was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration tool, covering sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, and selective reporting (Higgins et al., 2011). The certainty of evidence for key outcomes was then graded as high, moderate, low, or very low according to the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework (Guyatt et al., 2008), considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Observational and postmarketing safety data were considered hypothesis-generating and were graded as low certainty unless corroborated by randomized evidence.

**Development of the treatment algorithm**

The algorithm for adjusting concomitant therapies was constructed in three stages. First, we identified the drug classes most likely to require modification at initiation of an SGLT2 inhibitor on mechanistic grounds: insulin and insulin secretagogues (hypoglycemia risk), loop and thiazide diuretics (additive natriuresis and volume depletion), renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system inhibitors (hemodynamic effects on glomerular filtration), and other antihypertensive agents (additive blood pressure reduction). Second, for each class, we drew on pooled safety data and pharmacological considerations to define explicit clinical triggers for dose modification, such as baseline HbA1c below a specified target, history of recurrent hypoglycemia, systolic blood pressure below 110 mm Hg, orthostatic symptoms, advanced age, and reduced eGFR. Third, the draft algorithm was refined through iterative review by a multidisciplinary panel including endocrinologists, nephrologists, cardiologists, and clinical pharmacists. The panel used a modified Delphi approach with two rounds of anonymous rating on a 9-point Likert scale; recommendations were retained when at least 80% of panelists rated them 7–9 (appropriate) and the median score was ≥7. Items not reaching consensus were revised and re-rated or omitted. Recommendations on monitoring, including timing of follow-up laboratory assessment, were derived from the schedules used in pivotal trials and from regulatory labeling.

**Evidence synthesis and statistical analysis**

Given the heterogeneity of populations, background therapies, doses, and comparators, our primary approach was descriptive. Efficacy results are presented as ranges of placebo-adjusted mean differences across trials and agents, stratified by baseline eGFR and by background therapy where data permitted. To provide an indicative summary for outcomes reported consistently across trials, we conducted exploratory random-effects meta-analyses using the DerSimonian–Laird method for continuous outcomes (HbA1c, body weight, systolic blood pressure) and the Mantel–Haenszel method for binary safety outcomes (genital mycotic infection, urinary tract infection, hypoglycemia, volume depletion–related events). Heterogeneity was quantified using Cochran’s Q test and the I² statistic, with I² values above 50% interpreted as substantial (Higgins et al., 2003). Where heterogeneity was substantial, we explored potential sources by examining dose, comparator type, and renal function strata, but formal meta-regression and funnel plot analysis were not undertaken because fewer than ten trials were available for most subgroups. Time-to-event outcomes from cardiovascular outcome trials were not re-pooled; instead, published HRs with 95% CIs were reported and the absolute risk reduction and number needed to treat over the median follow-up were calculated from reported event rates. Two-sided P values below 0.05 were considered statistically significant for primary analyses, and no adjustment for multiplicity was applied to exploratory or subgroup comparisons, which are accordingly interpreted cautiously. Analyses were performed using Review Manager version 5.3 (The Cochrane Collaboration) and Stata version 14 (StataCorp).

**Ethical considerations**

This study synthesized previously published and publicly available data; therefore, institutional review board approval and informed consent were not required.

Results

**Glycemic efficacy and its dependence on renal function.** In randomized trials of 12 to 104 weeks, SGLT2 inhibitors consistently lowered glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). In a meta-analysis of 38 trials, the placebo-adjusted reduction was 0.66% (95% CI 0.73 to 0.58), and the difference versus active comparators was small (0.06%) (Vasilakou et al., 2013). The effect was similar across the class, with reductions of roughly 0.5% to 0.8% for empagliflozin 10 and 25 mg, dapagliflozin 5 and 10 mg, and canagliflozin 100 and 300 mg, and was greater in patients with higher baseline HbA1c (Zaccardi et al., 2016). Mean HbA1c fell by about 1.0% when baseline values exceeded 9%, but by only 0.4% to 0.5% when baseline values were below 8%. The mechanism is insulin-independent, so efficacy depends on the filtered glucose load. In individuals with preserved renal function, the drugs produce 60 to 80 g of urinary glucose excretion daily, equivalent to a 240 to 320 kcal daily energy loss (Ferrannini et al., 2010). This excretion falls progressively as the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) declines. In patients with an eGFR of 45 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m², the placebo-adjusted HbA1c reduction with dapagliflozin 10 mg was 0.33%. It was negligible (0.11%) with an eGFR of 30 to 44 mL/min/1.73 m² (Kohan et al., 2014). Canagliflozin 100 and 300 mg reduced HbA1c by only 0.30% and 0.40%, respectively, in patients with an eGFR of 30 to <50 mL/min/1.73 m² (Yale et al., 2014). Consequently, labels of most agents advise against initiation below an eGFR of 45 mL/min/1.73 m² for glycemic purposes. Durability of effect was shown in a 104-week comparison with glimepiride, in which canagliflozin 300 mg lowered HbA1c by 0.93% versus 0.81% (Cefalu et al., 2013). Similarly, over 52 weeks dapagliflozin added to metformin lowered HbA1c by 0.52%, equivalent to glipizide (Nauck et al., 2011).

**Weight, blood pressure, and metabolic effects.** Placebo-adjusted weight loss averaged 1.8 kg (range 1.0 to 2.5 kg) in meta-analyses, and was largely maintained to 2 years (Vasilakou et al., 2013; Cefalu et al., 2013). In the head-to-head comparison with glipizide, body weight decreased by 3.2 kg with dapagliflozin and increased by 1.4 kg with glipizide at 52 weeks (Nauck et al., 2011). Much of the early loss is attributable to fluid and the remainder to fat mass, with a modest decrease in visceral adiposity. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure decreased by a mean of 3.8 to 4.5 mmHg and 1.4 to 1.8 mmHg, respectively, without a compensatory rise in heart rate (Baker et al., 2014). The antihypertensive effect was larger in patients with higher baseline blood pressure and in older individuals. Other class effects included a mean decrease in serum uric acid of about 0.7 mg/dL (40 µmol/L), a 2% to 3% absolute increase in hematocrit, and a small increase in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 2 to 5 mg/dL (0.05 to 0.13 mmol/L), with a parallel rise in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol.

**Cardiovascular and renal outcomes.** The EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial randomized 7,020 patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease to empagliflozin 10 mg, 25 mg, or placebo (median follow-up 3.1 years). The primary composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke was reduced (10.5% vs 12.1%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.86; 95.02% CI 0.74 to 0.99) (Zinman et al., 2015). The benefit was driven by cardiovascular death (3.7% vs 5.9%; HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.49 to 0.77), corresponding to an absolute risk reduction of 2.2 percentage points. All-cause mortality fell from 8.3% to 5.7% (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.82), and hospitalization for heart failure from 4.1% to 2.7% (HR 0.65; 95% CI 0.50 to 0.85). Nonfatal myocardial infarction (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.70 to 1.09) and stroke (HR 1.24; 95% CI 0.92 to 1.67) did not differ significantly. The numbers needed to treat over 3 years were 39 to prevent one death from any cause and 71 to prevent one hospitalization for heart failure. The divergence of survival curves within 3 months, together with minimal differences in HbA1c between groups after week 12, suggests that hemodynamic mechanisms rather than glycemic control account for the benefit. In prespecified renal analyses, incident or worsening nephropathy occurred in 12.7% of the empagliflozin group versus 18.8% of the placebo group (HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.70). Doubling of serum creatinine with eGFR ≤45 mL/min/1.73 m² was reduced (HR 0.56; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.79), as was initiation of renal replacement therapy (HR 0.45; 95% CI 0.21 to 0.97) (Wanner et al., 2016). In the integrated CANVAS Program (n = 10,142), canagliflozin lowered the primary composite outcome (HR 0.86; 95% CI 0.75 to 0.97) and heart failure hospitalization (HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.52 to 0.87) and slowed albuminuria progression (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.67 to 0.79). Reductions in cardiovascular and all-cause death did not reach significance (HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.06 and HR 0.87; 95% CI 0.74 to 1.01, respectively) (Neal et al., 2017).

**Adverse events related to the mechanism of action.** Genital mycotic infections were the most consistent adverse effect, with a risk estimated at three- to five-fold relative to control (Li et al., 2017). In clinical trials, rates were 8% to 15% in women and 3% to 8% in men with active treatment, versus 1% to 3% in placebo groups. Events were generally mild to moderate and responded to topical or oral antifungals, with discontinuation in fewer than 1% of patients. The risk of urinary tract infection was only marginally higher (relative risk approximately 1.07 to 1.10), and pyelonephritis was rare. Volume-related adverse events (hypotension, postural dizziness) occurred in 1% to 5% of patients and were more frequent in older individuals, those with an eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², and those taking loop diuretics. In CANVAS, volume depletion occurred at 26.0 versus 18.5 per 1,000 patient-years (HR 1.40; 95% CI 1.21 to 1.62) (Neal et al., 2017). A transient decline in eGFR of 3 to 5 mL/min/1.73 m² occurs within the first 2 to 4 weeks and generally reverses or plateaus thereafter. Diabetic ketoacidosis, often with near-normal glucose, is rare, at an estimated 0.5 to 1.5 events per 1,000 patient-years (Neal et al., 2017; Zinman et al., 2015). It is typically precipitated by acute illness, reduced insulin dosing, or alcohol excess. An excess of lower-limb amputations (6.3 vs 3.4 per 1,000 patient-years; HR 1.97; 95% CI 1.41 to 2.75) and fractures was observed with canagliflozin but not with empagliflozin.

**Hypoglycemia and adjustment of concomitant therapies.** As monotherapy or with metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors carried a hypoglycemia risk similar to placebo (<5%). Combined with a sulfonylurea or insulin, however, the risk was higher. When dapagliflozin was compared with glipizide as add-on to metformin, hypoglycemia occurred in 3.5% versus 40.8% of patients (Nauck et al., 2011). In insulin-treated patients, dapagliflozin lowered HbA1c by about 0.6% to 0.9% versus 0.3% with placebo despite a prespecified 10% to 20% insulin dose reduction, and at 24 weeks the mean insulin dose decreased by 1.0 to 2.0 IU/day in the dapagliflozin groups versus an increase of 5.9 IU/day with placebo (Wilding et al., 2012). Hypoglycemia incidence was comparable (about 50% to 57%) across groups. These data support a proposed algorithm. When baseline HbA1c is below 8.0% (64 mmol/mol) or hypoglycemia has been documented, the sulfonylurea dose is reduced by approximately 50% (or the drug is stopped) and basal or total insulin is reduced by 10% to 20%. Diuretics are reduced or withheld in patients who are older, volume-contracted, or have an eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m². Renal function and volume status are reassessed at 2 to 4 weeks. SGLT2 inhibitors are temporarily withheld during intercurrent illness, reduced oral intake, or before surgery.

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of the evidence**

SGLT2 inhibitors act through an insulin-independent mechanism, which makes them a useful addition to the treatment of type 2 diabetes at several stages of the disease. In randomized trials, reductions in glycated hemoglobin of approximately 0.5% to 0.8% are consistently observed, whether the drugs are used as monotherapy or added to metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin (Zaccardi et al., 2016; Monami et al., 2014). Their glucose-lowering effect is somewhat smaller than that of insulin or GLP-1 receptor agonists. It also diminishes as glomerular filtration declines, because less glucose is filtered and available for reabsorption (Cherney et al., 2014). In practice, glycemic efficacy is therefore a less compelling reason to choose an SGLT2 inhibitor than the accompanying reductions in body weight (about 2 to 3 kg) and systolic blood pressure (about 3 to 5 mmHg), which occur without increasing hypoglycemia risk when the drugs are not combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues (Vasilakou et al., 2013). These effects have clinical relevance because weight gain, hypertension, and hypoglycemia often limit the intensification of conventional regimens.

The most important development since the first approvals is the evidence of cardiovascular and renal benefit. In EMPA-REG OUTCOME, empagliflozin reduced the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and nonfatal stroke (hazard ratio [HR] 0.86; 95% CI 0.74–0.99), as well as cardiovascular death (HR 0.62), all-cause mortality (HR 0.68), and hospitalization for heart failure (HR 0.65) (Zinman et al., 2015). Incident or worsening nephropathy was also reduced (HR 0.61), as was doubling of serum creatinine (HR 0.56) (Wanner et al., 2016). The CANVAS Program reported a similar reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events with canagliflozin (HR 0.86; 95% CI 0.75–0.97) and a lower risk of progression of albuminuria, but it also identified an increased risk of lower-limb amputation (HR 1.97; 95% CI 1.41–2.75) (Neal et al., 2017).

The early separation of the survival curves in EMPA-REG OUTCOME, within the first few months, is difficult to explain by glycemic control or atherosclerotic risk modification alone. The effect is more plausibly hemodynamic. Osmotic diuresis and natriuresis reduce plasma volume and cardiac preload, and lower arterial stiffness and afterload. Restoration of tubuloglomerular feedback reduces intraglomerular pressure. Shifts in myocardial substrate use toward ketone bodies have also been proposed (Ferrannini et al., 2016; Heerspink et al., 2016). These mechanisms are consistent with the large relative reduction in heart failure hospitalization and with the reversible early decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of approximately 3 to 5 mL/min/1.73 m². This decline generally stabilizes within weeks and should not by itself prompt discontinuation (Heerspink et al., 2016). Whether the benefits constitute a class effect remains uncertain. Heterogeneity in SGLT2 selectivity, pharmacokinetics, and trial populations limits direct comparison, and the safety signals observed with canagliflozin illustrate that class effects cannot be assumed in either direction.

**Practical implications**

These data support the positioning of SGLT2 inhibitors as second- or third-line agents. They are particularly appropriate for patients with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or albuminuric kidney disease, and for those in whom weight gain or hypoglycemia is a concern. Because the benefits arise partly from volume and hemodynamic effects, the main practical task at initiation is adjusting concomitant therapy. We propose that diuretic doses be reviewed in patients who are elderly, have a low baseline blood pressure, or are already volume depleted. Antihypertensive agents should be reassessed in patients with a systolic pressure near target. Insulin secretagogues, and insulin where glycated hemoglobin is near target, should be reduced, typically by 10% to 20% of the dose, to prevent hypoglycemia. Renal function and volume status should be rechecked within several weeks of initiation. The same principles apply to intercurrent illness: temporary withholding of the drug during periods of reduced oral intake, vomiting, diarrhea, or acute illness (“sick-day” guidance) and before surgery is a reasonable precaution.

Patient selection and counseling should reflect the known adverse-event profile. Genital mycotic infections occur several-fold more often than with comparators, affecting roughly 5% to 10% of women and 3% to 5% of men, but they are generally mild and respond to topical or oral antifungals (Nyirjesy et al., 2012). Urinary tract infections are not clearly increased, although rare serious urosepsis and pyelonephritis have been reported. Diabetic ketoacidosis, which may present with near-normal glucose levels, is uncommon but clinically important, with a risk concentrated in patients with insulin deficiency, rapid insulin dose reduction, low carbohydrate intake, excessive alcohol use, or acute illness (Peters et al., 2015; Fralick et al., 2017). Patients should be taught to recognize its symptoms, and agents should not be used in type 1 diabetes outside of research settings. The fracture and amputation signals associated with canagliflozin warrant caution in patients with advanced peripheral vascular disease, active foot ulceration, or low bone density, along with attention to foot care until further data are available.

**Limitations**

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting this review. First, the cardiovascular and renal outcome evidence derives largely from a single agent in a single trial of patients with established cardiovascular disease, so the magnitude of benefit in lower-risk patients, in primary prevention, and with other SGLT2 inhibitors is unknown. Second, trial populations were selected and typically excluded patients with advanced renal impairment, recent acute illness, or a high risk of volume depletion, which limits generalizability to the older, frailer patients seen in routine practice. Third, the treatment algorithm for adjusting concomitant therapies reflects mechanistic reasoning, pharmacologic data, and expert consensus rather than prospective comparative trials, and the suggested insulin and diuretic dose reductions have not been validated against clinical outcomes. Fourth, rare adverse events such as ketoacidosis, amputation, and fracture are poorly captured in trials of limited duration, and postmarketing surveillance is subject to reporting bias and confounding. Finally, cost and access vary across health systems and may affect real-world uptake independently of clinical suitability.

**Future directions**

Ongoing and completed cardiovascular outcome trials with dapagliflozin and ertugliflozin, together with dedicated renal and heart failure trials, should clarify whether benefits extend across the class, to patients without diabetes, and to those with lower baseline risk. Pragmatic studies are also needed to define optimal strategies for de-escalating insulin, sulfonylureas, and diuretics, to quantify the incidence of ketoacidosis in real-world populations, and to compare SGLT2 inhibitors directly with GLP-1 receptor agonists that show cardiovascular benefit.

**Conclusion**

SGLT2 inhibitors provide moderate glucose lowering together with reductions in weight and blood pressure, and, for empagliflozin, reductions in cardiovascular mortality, heart failure hospitalization, and kidney disease progression in high-risk patients. Their safe use depends less on the drug itself than on the context in which it is started: careful selection, anticipatory adjustment of diuretics, antihypertensives, and glucose-lowering therapies, attention to renal function and volume status, and clear patient education on genital hygiene, sick-day rules, and ketoacidosis symptoms. Applied systematically, the approach proposed here should allow clinicians to capture the benefits of this drug class while limiting preventable harm.

Introduction

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease and cancer, account for roughly 70% of deaths worldwide, and the burden is increasingly concentrated in low- and middle-income countries (World Health Organization, 2018). Primary care is widely regarded as the setting best placed to deliver the continuous, coordinated and person-centred care that chronic conditions require, and it is central to global strategies for universal health coverage (Starfield et al., 2005; Kruk et al., 2018). Consequently, a large number of interventions have been developed to improve the detection, management and long-term support of people with NCDs in primary care. These include structured self-management education, decision support for clinicians, task-shifting to nurses and community health workers, audit and feedback, and multicomponent models of integrated care (Wagner et al., 2001; Coleman et al., 2009). Many of these have been evaluated in randomised controlled trials (RCTs), and systematic reviews of such trials suggest that effects are frequently modest and heterogeneous, with similar interventions producing markedly different results in different settings (Smith et al., 2016; Tricco et al., 2012).

This heterogeneity is not surprising. Interventions in primary care are typically complex: they contain several interacting components, target multiple levels (patients, providers, practices and organisations), require tailoring to local circumstances, and depend on the behaviour of many actors (Craig et al., 2008; Hawe et al., 2004). Their effects are shaped by the context in which they are delivered, including the structure and financing of the health system, workforce availability, and local social and cultural norms (Pfadenhauer et al., 2017). A conventional trial that reports only whether an intervention "worked" on average cannot explain why an effect was or was not observed, whether the intervention was delivered as intended, which components were responsible for any change, or how the findings might transfer to other settings. Null results are particularly difficult to interpret without this information, since they may reflect a flawed intervention theory, poor implementation, or an unsuitable context (Oakley et al., 2006).

Process evaluations (PEs) have been advocated to address these limitations. The UK Medical Research Council (MRC) guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions defines their purpose as examining implementation (what is delivered, and how), mechanisms of impact (how delivered activities produce change), and contextual factors that shape both (Moore et al., 2015). By answering questions of for whom, how and why interventions have an impact, PEs help distinguish implementation failure from theory failure, identify unintended consequences, and provide the information needed to refine interventions and support scale-up. Earlier frameworks for describing implementation, including those of Steckler and Linnan (2002), Baranowski and Stables (2000) and Grant et al. (2013), and widely used theory-based approaches such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (Damschroder et al., 2009), normalisation process theory (May and Finch, 2009) and RE-AIM (Glasgow et al., 1999), have similarly emphasised the need to examine reach, fidelity, dose and adaptation alongside outcomes. The MRC guidance further stresses that PEs should be underpinned by a clearly articulated intervention theory or logic model, so that data collection and analysis are directed at the hypothesised causal pathway rather than being purely descriptive (Moore et al., 2015; De Silva et al., 2014).

Despite this guidance, there is concern that PEs are inconsistently conducted and reported. Reviews in other fields, such as school-based health promotion and public health, have found that PEs often lack explicit theoretical grounding, apply inconsistent definitions of constructs such as fidelity and context, and rely on convenience samples or purely descriptive data (Oakley et al., 2006; Bonell et al., 2012; Grant et al., 2013). Where theory is absent, it is difficult to judge whether the right processes were examined, and findings from one PE are hard to compare with, or build upon, those of another. Improvements in reporting have been proposed, including the Standards for Reporting Implementation Studies (StaRI) and the TIDieR checklist for describing interventions (Pinnock et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2014), but it is unclear how far these have influenced practice in primary care.

Several existing syntheses bear on this topic but leave important gaps. Systematic reviews of barriers and facilitators to implementing chronic disease interventions have mostly drawn on qualitative studies or on single conditions, for example diabetes self-management or hypertension control, and have not examined how the underlying evaluations were designed (Gagliardi et al., 2011; Jeet et al., 2017). Reviews of PEs, in contrast, have concentrated on public health, school or community settings, where the organisational features of primary care, such as gatekeeping, multidisciplinary teams, continuity of care and payment systems, are less salient. To our knowledge, no review has systematically described the methods used in PEs conducted alongside RCTs of primary care interventions for NCDs, assessed the extent to which they follow recognised guidance, and synthesised their findings on implementation barriers and facilitators across conditions and health systems. This matters because primary care interventions are increasingly being adapted for and tested in diverse settings, including low-resource health systems where many of the assumptions underpinning interventions developed in high-income countries may not hold (Kruk et al., 2018; Legido-Quigley et al., 2013).

We therefore conducted a systematic review of PEs alongside RCTs of primary care interventions aimed at improving outcomes for people with NCDs, using the MRC guidance for process evaluation as an organising framework. We had two aims. First, to describe and appraise the methods used, including the use of intervention theory and theoretical frameworks, the choice of data collection and analytic approaches, sampling, and the integration of qualitative and quantitative data. Second, to synthesise the principal findings of these evaluations regarding barriers and facilitators to implementation, with attention to the context in which interventions were delivered.

This review makes three contributions. It provides the first comprehensive overview of how PEs in primary care chronic disease research are being designed and reported, identifying strengths and weaknesses that can inform methodological practice and the application of the MRC guidance. It offers a cross-condition synthesis of recurring implementation challenges, which may be more useful to intervention developers and health system decision-makers than condition-specific accounts. Finally, it draws out implications for how future interventions should be developed, with the aim of improving the fit between interventions, local needs and health system contexts, and thereby the chance that effective interventions can be implemented and sustained at scale.

Methods

Design and reporting

We conducted a systematic review of process evaluations (PEs) conducted alongside randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42016035572) before screening began. The review is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). We used the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions (Moore et al., 2015) as an organising framework for both data extraction and appraisal. This guidance specifies that a PE should describe the intervention and its causal assumptions, examine implementation (fidelity, dose, adaptations and reach), explore mechanisms of impact, and consider contextual influences on delivery and outcomes. Because we did not assess intervention effectiveness, we did not conduct a meta-analysis.

Eligibility criteria

Eligibility was defined using the Population, Intervention, Context and Study design elements. Studies were eligible if they reported a PE, defined as a study that assessed implementation, mechanisms of impact or context, alongside an RCT (individually or cluster randomised, including pilot and feasibility trials with a full-scale PE). The trial intervention had to be delivered in primary care or community-based primary health care settings and aim to improve outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, cancer, mental health conditions and musculoskeletal disorders. Interventions could be targeted at patients, providers, practices or the wider health system. We excluded studies of infectious diseases, those conducted solely in hospital or specialist settings, trials with no PE component, and PEs reported only as protocols without results. Studies that reported only a post hoc satisfaction survey, with no examination of implementation or context, were also excluded. The PE did not need to be published in the same paper as the trial, but it had to be clearly linked to an identified RCT. We included reports in any language for which translation was feasible, and the search was restricted to 1998 onward, reflecting the emergence of the contemporary complex intervention literature (Campbell et al., 2000).

Search strategy

We searched MEDLINE, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), EMBASE and Global Health from 1998 to June 2018. The strategy combined three concept blocks: (1) process evaluation terms (for example “process evaluation”, “implementation”, “fidelity”, “mixed methods”, “qualitative”); (2) primary care terms (for example “primary health care”, “general practice”, “community health worker”, “family practice”); and (3) non-communicable disease terms, together with a trial filter to identify randomised designs. Search terms were developed with an information specialist, piloted against a set of known PEs, and adapted to the syntax and controlled vocabulary of each database. We supplemented electronic searches by hand-searching the reference lists of included studies and of relevant methodological reviews, and by checking trial registries and linked publications to identify companion papers reporting PE findings.

Study selection

Records were exported to reference management software and de-duplicated. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, followed by independent full-text assessment. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating where consensus could not be reached. Agreement between reviewers at the full-text stage was calculated using Cohen’s kappa:

κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e),

where p_o is the observed proportion of agreement and p_e is the proportion expected by chance. Reasons for exclusion at full-text stage were recorded.

Data extraction

A standardised extraction form, structured around the MRC framework and piloted on five studies, was used. Two reviewers independently extracted data and a third reviewer checked a random sample (approximately 20%) of extractions for accuracy and consistency as quality assurance. Extracted information included: bibliographic details; country and income setting (World Bank classification); clinical condition; description of the intervention using the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) items (Hoffmann et al., 2014); level of intervention (patient, provider, practice or system); trial design; and the timing of the PE relative to the trial (concurrent, prospective or retrospective).

For PE methods, we extracted whether the authors stated an explicit intervention theory or logic model; whether an existing theoretical or implementation framework was used (for example the Normalisation Process Theory, the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, RE-AIM, or the Theoretical Domains Framework); the PE research questions; the components assessed (context, recruitment and reach, fidelity, dose, adaptation, mechanisms of impact, and unintended consequences); data collection methods (interviews, focus groups, observation, surveys, document review, routine data and audio-recorded consultations); sampling strategy and sample size; the respondents included; analytic approach; and whether qualitative and quantitative data were triangulated or integrated. We also recorded whether the PE findings were used to interpret trial outcomes.

For findings, we extracted all reported barriers and facilitators to implementation, together with the authors’ interpretations and illustrative data, where available. These were extracted from the results and discussion sections, including participant quotations.

Quality and reporting appraisal

Rather than excluding studies on quality grounds, we appraised the methodological characteristics of PEs against the MRC guidance to describe the field and to identify strengths and weaknesses. Criteria included clarity of intervention theory, a priori specification of PE questions, appropriateness of sampling, use of multiple data sources, transparent analysis, and consideration of context. Qualitative components were additionally assessed with reference to the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) qualitative checklist, with the aim of contextualising the weight placed on individual findings rather than determining inclusion. Appraisal was carried out independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus.

Data synthesis

We conducted a two-part synthesis. First, the methodological data were summarised descriptively using frequencies and proportions, stratified by country income group, intervention level and whether a theoretical framework had been used. We cross-tabulated the presence of an explicit intervention theory against these characteristics, and used Fisher’s exact test to explore associations where cell counts were small, treating these analyses as exploratory and not adjusting for multiple comparisons.

Second, we synthesised findings on barriers and facilitators using thematic synthesis (Thomas and Harden, 2008). Two reviewers independently coded extracted text line by line, inductively generating descriptive codes. Codes were then grouped into descriptive themes and compared across studies, conditions and settings. In a third stage, we developed analytical themes that went beyond the original studies to interpret why implementation succeeded or failed. To ensure that the synthesis addressed the context–mechanism–outcome relationships emphasised in the MRC guidance, we mapped themes onto the health system building blocks (service delivery, workforce, information, medicines and technologies, financing, and leadership and governance) proposed by the World Health Organization (2007). Coding frameworks were discussed in team meetings, and a third reviewer reviewed a sample of coded data to check consistency and the plausibility of the themes. Data were managed using NVivo and Microsoft Excel.

Because the review focused on the implementation barriers and facilitators reported by the original authors, and we did not seek to link them to effect sizes, we did not formally assess the certainty of evidence. However, we noted where PE findings were used to explain null or heterogeneous trial results, as this indicated the interpretive value of the PE.

## Results

### Study selection and characteristics

The searches identified 14,532 records. After removing 4,658 duplicates, we screened 9,874 titles and abstracts and assessed 412 full texts. Sixty-nine process evaluations (PEs) met the inclusion criteria and were included in the synthesis (Figure 1). The most common reasons for full-text exclusion were that the paper described a trial protocol or outcome evaluation with no process component (n=118), that the study was not nested in a randomised trial (n=96), and that the intervention was not delivered in primary care (n=71). Agreement between the two reviewers at full-text screening was good (κ=0.81).

Most PEs were published recently: 7 (10%) before 2010, 24 (35%) between 2010 and 2013, and 38 (55%) between 2014 and June 2018. Forty-one (59%) were conducted in high-income countries (the UK, n=16; the USA, n=9; the Netherlands, n=6; Australia, n=5; others, n=5), and 28 (41%) in low- and middle-income countries, most commonly in South Asia (n=9), sub-Saharan Africa (n=8) and Latin America (n=6). Diabetes was the commonest target condition (n=19, 28%), followed by cardiovascular disease and hypertension (n=17, 25%), chronic respiratory disease (n=10, 14%), depression and other common mental disorders (n=9, 13%), multimorbidity (n=6, 9%), cancer (n=4, 6%) and other conditions (n=4, 6%).
