Interventions were complex, with a median of three components (range 2–7). The most frequent components were training or education of health professionals (n=48, 70%), patient self-management support (n=39, 57%), care pathway or protocol redesign (n=31, 45%), decision support or information technology (n=22, 32%) and task-shifting to nurses or community health workers (n=20, 29%).

### Methods used in process evaluations

Forty-four PEs (64%) used a mixed-methods design, 17 (25%) were qualitative only and 8 (12%) were quantitative only. Thirty-eight (55%) collected data concurrently with the trial, and 31 (45%) collected data only after the trial had ended. Semi-structured interviews were the most common data source (n=52, 75%), followed by questionnaires or surveys (n=29, 42%), routine or audit data (n=24, 35%), focus groups (n=21, 30%), non-participant observation (n=15, 22%), documentary analysis (n=14, 20%) and audio-recorded consultations (n=8, 12%). The median number of data sources per PE was three (interquartile range 2–4). Participants were most often health professionals (n=59, 86%), followed by patients (n=47, 68%), managers or policy-makers (n=18, 26%) and carers (n=5, 7%).

Sampling was described in 61 PEs (88%). Purposive sampling was most common (n=47), and 18 of these explicitly used maximum-variation strategies, for example across high- and low-performing practices or across urban and rural sites. Twenty-five PEs (36%) reported data saturation or an equivalent stopping criterion. Among the 52 PEs that conducted qualitative work, the main analytic approaches were thematic analysis (n=33, 63%), framework analysis (n=15, 29%), content analysis (n=6, 12%) and grounded theory (n=4, 8%). Some studies used more than one approach. Thirty-six of the 44 mixed-methods PEs (82%) explicitly integrated qualitative and quantitative findings to explain how the intervention worked, for example by using interview data to interpret variation in uptake across practices. In the remaining eight, the strands were reported separately.

Reporting was inconsistent. Only 48 papers (70%) used the term "process evaluation" in the title or abstract, which made them harder to identify. Using the components of the MRC guidance (Moore et al., 2015), 46 PEs (67%) assessed implementation fidelity, 38 (55%) assessed dose, 33 (48%) assessed reach, and 41 (59%) examined context. Twenty-nine (42%) investigated mechanisms of impact, and 17 (25%) looked for unintended consequences. Only 11 PEs (16%) assessed all of fidelity, dose, reach, context and mechanisms. Fewer than half (n=31, 45%) specified the PE research questions before data collection, and only 14 (20%) reported that the PE protocol had been published or registered before the trial analysis. Fifteen (22%) reported that the PE team was independent of the trial outcome analysis, or that outcome data were withheld from PE analysts.

### Intervention theory and use of theoretical frameworks

Only 30 PEs (43%) were underpinned by a clearly articulated intervention theory, meaning an explicit description of how the intervention was expected to produce change. In the other 39 (57%), the assumed mechanisms were implicit or not described. Of the 30 with a clear theory, 22 used an existing theoretical or implementation framework: Normalization Process Theory (n=7), the MRC complex interventions framework (n=6), the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (n=3), RE-AIM (n=3), the Theoretical Domains Framework (n=2) and other frameworks (n=1). The remaining eight presented a bespoke logic model or causal pathway. Studies with a clear intervention theory were more likely to assess mechanisms of impact (21/30, 70%) than those without (8/39, 21%), and more often reported on context (26/30, 87% vs 15/39, 38%). Use of an intervention theory did not differ markedly between high-income (18/41, 44%) and low- and middle-income settings (12/28, 43%). A further 13 studies (19%) applied a framework only at the analysis stage, usually to code interview data, and not to design the PE.

### Synthesis of barriers and facilitators

Across the 69 PEs, three cross-cutting themes explained why interventions were implemented poorly or had limited impact.

**Theme 1: mismatch between intervention design and local needs (n=38, 55%).** Many interventions did not fit the priorities, resources or expectations of the patients and providers who were meant to use them. Thirty-one of these PEs (45% of the total) described content or delivery that was poorly matched to patient circumstances, such as educational materials that were culturally inappropriate or of low literacy relevance, or self-management advice that was impractical given patients' economic constraints. Twenty-two (32%) reported that practitioners saw the intervention as adding to workload without addressing the problems they considered important, particularly in multimorbidity, where single-disease protocols were hard to apply. Only 12 PEs (17%) reported formative research, such as needs assessment or user-centred piloting, during intervention development. Of the 24 PEs reporting a facilitator related to fit, 17 attributed it to local adaptation or stakeholder involvement in design.

**Theme 2: unclear roles and responsibilities of key actors (n=44, 64%).** Forty-four PEs described confusion about who was accountable for delivering intervention components. Thirty-three (48%) identified role ambiguity between doctors, nurses and community health workers, especially where tasks were shifted. Nineteen (28%) reported insufficient training or supervision, and 16 (23%) reported that patients did not understand their own part in the intervention, for example in shared decision-making or home monitoring. Facilitators, reported in 27 PEs (39%), were clearly defined role descriptions, local clinical champions, and regular feedback or supervision.

**Theme 3: health system context (n=47, 68%).** Governance, financing and workforce factors that had not been anticipated adversely affected implementation. Thirty-two PEs (46%) cited workforce shortages, high turnover or competing demands. Twenty-six (38%) cited funding structures, including lack of reimbursement for new activities or unreliable supplies of medicines and equipment, and 18 (26%) cited fragmented governance or poor integration with existing information systems and referral pathways. Such barriers were reported in both high-income (n=25, 61% of 41) and low- and middle-income settings (n=22, 79% of 28), although medicine stock-outs and community health worker remuneration were mentioned almost exclusively in the latter. Facilitators included alignment with existing policy priorities (n=15, 22%) and managerial support (n=21, 30%).

Discussion

Principal findings

This review synthesised 69 process evaluations (PEs) conducted alongside randomised controlled trials of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases. Two messages stand out. First, the conduct and reporting of PEs were highly variable. Fewer than half of the studies (30/69) were underpinned by an explicit intervention theory, and these were typically the studies that drew on an established framework such as the Normalization Process Theory, RE-AIM, the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research or the Theoretical Domains Framework (May and Finch, 2009; Glasgow et al., 1999; Damschroder et al., 2009; Michie et al., 2005). Second, across heterogeneous settings and conditions, the barriers to implementation clustered around three recurring problems: a mismatch between what the intervention was designed to achieve and local needs, unclear roles and responsibilities for key actors, and unanticipated features of the health system context, including governance, financing and workforce. These are largely failures of design and anticipation rather than of delivery, and they suggest that many interventions reached the trial stage without sufficient formative work.

Interpretation in light of existing literature

The MRC guidance on process evaluation positions PEs as a means of examining implementation, mechanisms of impact and context (Moore et al., 2015). Our finding that a minority of studies articulated a clear intervention theory is concerning, because without a stated programme theory it is difficult to decide what to measure, to distinguish theory failure from implementation failure, or to interpret null trial results (Craig et al., 2008; Grant et al., 2013). Earlier reviews of PEs in other fields, including public health and school-based interventions, have reported similar shortcomings in theoretical grounding and in the explicit analysis of mechanisms (Grant et al., 2013; Hulscher et al., 2003). That primary care and chronic disease research shows the same pattern suggests a systemic issue in how trials are designed and funded, rather than a problem specific to one clinical area. The relatively strong use of purposive sampling and the triangulation of qualitative and quantitative data are encouraging, and reflect the methodological pluralism recommended for complex interventions (Creswell and Plano Clark, 2011). However, triangulation was seldom used to test hypotheses derived from a prior theory, so it more often described than explained.

The three themes align with the wider implementation literature. Mismatch between intervention and local need echoes the argument that interventions developed centrally and imposed on practices struggle to achieve fit with existing workflows and priorities (Greenhalgh et al., 2004; Pfadenhauer et al., 2017). Role ambiguity has been reported for task-shifting and team-based chronic care, where responsibilities for screening, follow-up and self-management support are redistributed among nurses, community health workers, pharmacists and physicians without clear negotiation of accountability (Wagner et al., 2001; Lewin et al., 2010). The influence of health system context is consistent with systems-oriented frameworks, which emphasise that financing arrangements, supply chains, referral pathways and workforce capacity determine whether an evidence-based intervention can be sustained (Atun et al., 2010; Shiell et al., 2008). Our review adds that these factors were frequently identified only retrospectively, within the PE, rather than prospectively during intervention development.

Implications for research and practice

The first implication is that PE reporting needs greater consistency. Although guidance exists (Moore et al., 2015; Hoffmann et al., 2014), we found no common structure for describing the intervention, fidelity, dose, reach and context. A reporting standard specific to PEs, comparable to CONSORT for trials or TIDieR for interventions, would improve comparability and allow future syntheses to move beyond description. Journals and funders could require that PE protocols be registered or published, and that trial and PE findings be cross-referenced.

Second, interventions should be underpinned by explicit, testable theory, ideally developed with stakeholders and informed by existing frameworks. Logic models or theories of change that specify assumed mechanisms and contextual preconditions would allow PEs to test whether those assumptions held (De Silva et al., 2014). Theoretical frameworks should be selected for their fit with the question rather than applied as a formality, since superficial use was evident in several studies.

Third, our themes point to the need for stronger formative research before trial launch. Needs assessments, qualitative work with patients and providers, and context analysis would help to align interventions with local priorities, clarify roles, and anticipate system-level constraints. Approaches such as intervention mapping, co-design and the MRC development phase were rarely reported, yet they directly address the problems identified (Bartholomew Eldredge et al., 2016; O'Cathain et al., 2019). Pilot and feasibility studies with embedded process data could provide an inexpensive opportunity to detect misalignment early. Where trials are intended to inform policy in low- and middle-income countries, early engagement with ministries of health and payers about financing and governance may be particularly important, given how often system factors undermined implementation.

Fourth, PEs should be designed to inform adaptation and scale-up. Findings on barriers are most useful when they are linked to specific recommendations and to the conditions under which an intervention might succeed elsewhere. Realist approaches, which explicitly examine context–mechanism–outcome configurations, may offer a useful complement to the MRC framework (Pawson and Tilley, 1997).

Strengths and limitations

Strengths of this review include its pre-registered protocol, a search across six databases over twenty years, the use of the MRC guidance as an organising framework, and independent duplicate screening and extraction with quality assurance by a third reviewer. Several limitations should be acknowledged. Identifying PEs is difficult because of inconsistent terminology and indexing, and some evaluations published separately from the main trial may have been missed despite supplementary searching. We restricted inclusion to PEs linked to randomised trials and to English-language publications, which may have excluded relevant evaluations of non-randomised or pragmatic programmes and studies from non-Anglophone settings. The included studies spanned diverse conditions, countries and intervention types, so the thematic synthesis necessarily operated at a relatively high level of abstraction and may obscure condition- or setting-specific nuances. Because we relied on published reports, we could not distinguish between methods not used and methods not reported; some apparent absence of intervention theory may reflect word limits rather than omissions. Finally, we did not formally relate process findings to trial outcomes, so we cannot say whether better-theorised PEs were associated with different trial results or greater explanatory power. Quality appraisal of qualitative components was also limited by inconsistent reporting, and thematic synthesis involves interpretive judgement, although we mitigated this through independent coding and consensus discussion.

Conclusion

PEs alongside trials of primary care interventions for chronic disease offer rich insight into why interventions succeed or fail, but their value is limited by inconsistent methods and reporting and by the infrequent use of explicit intervention theory. Recurrent barriers (misalignment with local needs, unclear roles and unanticipated health system constraints) indicate that more investment in formative research and context analysis is required before interventions are tested at scale. Greater use of theoretical frameworks, standardised reporting and prospective attention to system context would make PEs more informative for researchers, policymakers and practitioners seeking to implement effective chronic disease care in primary care settings.

# Introduction

Ad-hoc information retrieval (IR) has long been characterized by a diversity of ranking methods whose relative merits vary across queries. Probabilistic and language-modeling approaches such as BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) and query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing (Zhai and Lafferty, 2004) remain strong, efficient baselines. Pretrained transformers, most prominently BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), have since reshaped the field. Applied as re-rankers (Nogueira and Cho, 2019; Dai and Callan, 2019), they yield large average gains on benchmarks such as MS MARCO. Average gains conceal substantial per-query variance, however. Neural re-rankers can underperform simple lexical baselines on individual queries, and sometimes on entire collections when evaluated outside their training distribution (Yang et al., 2019; Lin, 2019; Thakur et al., 2021). A practitioner who wants robust effectiveness therefore faces a question that mean performance does not answer: for this particular query, which method should be trusted?

This question is an instance of the algorithm selection problem (Rice, 1976), in which a meta-level model uses instance features to choose, or combine, algorithms from a portfolio (Kotthoff, 2014). In IR, related ideas appear in several forms. Rank fusion and data fusion combine the outputs of multiple systems with query-independent rules such as CombSUM or reciprocal rank fusion (Fox and Shaw, 1994; Cormack et al., 2009). Selective query expansion, retrieval-model selection, and ranker selection instead make query-dependent decisions, typically using query performance prediction (QPP) signals such as clarity, collection statistics, or score distributions (Cronen-Townsend et al., 2002; Balasubramanian and Allan, 2010; Peng et al., 2010; Hauff et al., 2008). More recently, selection between sparse and dense retrieval has been framed as a trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency (Arabzadeh et al., 2021). These approaches share a limitation. Their features generally describe how *confident* a system is, or how *difficult* a query is, but not *why* one family of methods should be preferred over another for a given information need. Consequently, they provide little insight into the conditions under which, for example, a neural model's semantic matching is preferable to exact lexical matching.

A complementary line of work offers a vocabulary for such conditions. Axiomatic IR formalizes desirable properties of retrieval functions as constraints, including term frequency, document length normalization, term discrimination, and semantic matching constraints (Fang et al., 2004; Fang and Zhai, 2005; Fang et al., 2011). Originally used to analyze and derive classical models, axioms have been extended to diagnose neural rankers (Rennings et al., 2019; Câmara and Hauff, 2020; MacAvaney et al., 2022) and to regularize or re-rank their outputs (Hagen et al., 2016; Rosset et al., 2019; Völske et al., 2021). These studies consistently show that neural models and traditional models satisfy axioms to different degrees. BERT-based rankers, for instance, appear to respect some term-frequency and document-length heuristics only weakly while capturing semantic relationships that lexical models cannot. If the methods differ systematically in their axiomatic behavior, then properties of the query and its candidate documents that determine whether an axiom is applicable, such as the variation in term frequency or length among top-ranked documents, may signal which method is more reliable for that query. To our knowledge, this hypothesis has not been tested systematically.

We therefore examine whether axiom-related properties of a query and its top-ranked documents can inform per-query selection between two retrieval methods. Rather than making a hard binary choice, we consider the more general problem of predicting how to *combine* the methods' relevance scores. Formally, given a query and a pair of retrieval methods, we train a meta-learner that outputs a query-specific interpolation of the two scores into a single relevance score. Hard selection is the special case in which the weight is at an extreme. This soft formulation is more robust to prediction errors, because a mistaken but moderate weight degrades the ranking less than a wrong categorical choice. It also lets the learner exploit complementary evidence when both methods contribute useful signals. The meta-learner's inputs are features that quantify axiomatic properties of the query and the documents retrieved at the top of the ranking, so that its predictions are grounded in interpretable, theoretically motivated quantities rather than opaque QPP scores.

Our investigation is guided by the following research questions:

- **RQ1:** Can a meta-learner that uses axiomatic features predict query-specific score combinations that improve effectiveness over each of the individual retrieval methods?
- **RQ2:** Which axiomatic features contribute most to the meta-learner's predictions, and do they agree with what is known about the axiomatic differences between lexical and neural methods?
- **RQ3:** For which queries does the meta-learner deviate most from a uniform combination, and does this behavior reflect query characteristics that are plausible given the methods' respective strengths?

To answer these questions, we evaluate on the ad-hoc tasks of the TREC Web Track (Collins-Thompson et al., 2013, 2014), a long-standing benchmark with diverse, sometimes ambiguous and underspecified queries over a web-scale corpus. Such queries make the choice of retrieval method nontrivial. We consider pairs formed from a lexical baseline and neural re-rankers and assess the meta-learner using cross-validation with query-level splits, reporting standard effectiveness metrics with paired significance testing. We then analyze feature importance and per-query weights to characterize what the model has learned.

This paper makes the following contributions:

1. **A formulation of retrieval method selection as score-combination prediction.** We cast pairwise method selection as predicting a query-dependent interpolation weight, unifying selection and fusion within one supervised framework.
2. **Axiomatic features for meta-learning.** Motivated by the observed axiomatic differences between neural and traditional models, we introduce a set of query- and ranking-level features that quantify how strongly axiom-relevant conditions hold among the top-ranked documents. To our knowledge, this is the first use of such features as inputs to a method-selection model rather than as diagnostics or ranking constraints.
3. **An empirical evaluation on TREC Web Track data.** We show that the meta-learner often significantly improves over the individual methods, and we characterize the settings in which it does and does not.
4. **Feature and query-weight analyses.** Through ablations, feature importance estimates, and inspection of individual queries and their predicted weights, we provide evidence on which axiomatic properties guide the meta-learner's behavior and how this relates to the complementary strengths of the methods.

Beyond the immediate performance gains, our results speak to a broader question in neural IR: whether the well-documented axiomatic gaps between neural and classical rankers can be turned from a diagnostic observation into an operational signal. The remainder of this paper first reviews related work on axiomatic IR, rank fusion, and algorithm selection. We then describe the meta-learner and the axiomatic features, present the experimental setup and results, and conclude with an analysis of feature importance and query-level behavior.

Methods

**Task formulation and data.** We study algorithm selection for ad-hoc retrieval in a pairwise setting. Given a query q, a candidate set D_q of documents, and two retrieval methods A and B that assign relevance scores s_A(q,d) and s_B(q,d), the meta-learner predicts a query-specific interpolation weight α_q ∈ [0,1]. The final score is s(q,d) = α_q·ŝ_A(q,d) + (1 − α_q)·ŝ_B(q,d). Here ŝ denotes min–max normalisation of a method's scores over the top 100 documents for q. This formulation includes selecting a single method as the special cases α_q ∈ {0,1}, while allowing soft combinations when neither method is clearly preferable.

We used the ad-hoc tasks of the TREC Web Track from 2009 to 2014 (Clarke et al., 2009; Collins-Thompson et al., 2013, 2014). This yields 300 topics, 50 per year. The 2009–2012 topics were judged on ClueWeb09 Category B (about 50 million pages) and the 2013–2014 topics on ClueWeb12-B13 (about 52 million pages). We used the short topic title as the query. Graded judgments were used as released, with non-relevant and spam-labelled documents given a grade of zero. Documents in the ClueWeb09 collection with a Waterloo spam score below 70 were removed before retrieval (Cormack et al., 2011). Effectiveness is reported as nDCG@20, the official primary measure of the track (Järvelin & Kekäläinen, 2002), with ERR@20 as a secondary measure. Because judgments are shallow, unjudged documents were treated as non-relevant.

**Retrieval methods.** First-stage candidates were obtained with BM25 (k1 = 0.9, b = 0.4; Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009), implemented in Anserini (Yang et al., 2017). The top 100 documents per query were retained as D_q, and all methods rank this same set. We considered one pair of methods from each of two families. The first family comprises two lexical models, BM25 and query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing (μ = 2000; Zhai & Lafferty, 2004). The second comprises a lexical and a neural method. The neural methods were a BERT-base cross-encoder (Nogueira & Cho, 2019) and a kernel-based interaction model (K-NRM; Xiong et al., 2017). Both were trained on MS MARCO passage data (Bajaj et al., 2016) and applied to the first 512 word pieces of each document. Pairs are denoted by their constituent methods, for example BM25–BERT. Neural models were not fine-tuned on Web Track data, so differences between pairs reflect pre-existing properties of the methods rather than collection-specific adaptation.

**Axiomatic features.** Our features are motivated by findings that neural rankers differ from classical models in their adherence to retrieval constraints (Rosset et al., 2019; Câmara & Hauff, 2020; MacAvaney et al., 2022). We implemented diagnostic versions of the following axioms from Fang et al. (2004, 2011): TFC1, TFC2, TDC, LNC1, LNC2, TF-LNC, M-TDC, and the proximity-oriented constraint of Tao and Zhai (2007). Each axiom specifies a precondition on a document pair (d_i, d_j) for the query, for example that the documents have equal length and differ in the frequency of a query term (TFC1). It also specifies the ranking the axiom requires, for example that the document with higher term frequency is scored higher.

For each query we considered all pairs among the top k = 20 documents under the first-stage ranking, giving at most 190 pairs. For each axiom a, we computed two quantities. The first is *applicability*, the fraction of pairs satisfying the precondition. Following Fang et al., we used a tolerance of 10% for length and frequency equality, since exact equality is rare in web documents. Applicability depends only on the query and the documents and is independent of the methods. The second is *agreement* for each method m, the fraction of applicable pairs whose order under s_m matches the order prescribed by a. Pairs with equal scores were counted as half agreements. Agreement is set to the neutral value 0.5 when no pairs are applicable. Because the meta-learner must decide between two methods, we use the difference in agreement between them as a feature, together with applicability. This yields two features per axiom, and the difference feature is informative only when applicability is high.

We added query-level descriptors that the literature associates with method suitability. These were query length, mean and maximum inverse document frequency of the query terms, the normalised query clarity score (Cronen-Townsend et al., 2002), and the mean and standard deviation of document length in D_q. We also included the normalised score gap between the first and tenth documents for each method, and Kendall's τ between the two top-20 rankings. The full set comprises 27 features, standardised to zero mean and unit variance using training-fold statistics only.

**Target construction and meta-learner.** For each training query and method pair, we evaluated nDCG@20 for α ∈ {0, 0.1, …, 1}. The target is the mean of the α values attaining the maximum nDCG@20. Queries on which the range of nDCG@20 across α is below 0.01 are uninformative for selection and were excluded from training, though not from testing. For these queries, any α produces essentially the same ranking. The meta-learner is a gradient-boosted regression tree ensemble (LightGBM; Ke et al., 2017) minimising squared error on α. We also tested a linear ridge regression to assess whether non-linear interactions among features were necessary. Hyperparameters were tuned by grid search in an inner three-fold cross-validation, with the number of trees in {50, 100, 200}, depth in {2, 3, 4}, and learning rate in {0.03, 0.1}. Predictions were clipped to [0,1].

**Evaluation protocol.** We used five-fold cross-validation over queries, repeated with ten random partitions. For each repetition we computed the nDCG@20 of the meta-learner's ranking for every query when it was in the held-out fold. We then averaged these values over repetitions to obtain one score per query. Because Web Track topics from the same year share collection and judging conditions, we also performed a leave-one-year-out analysis. This tests whether the meta-learner generalises across years and across the ClueWeb09/ClueWeb12 boundary.

We compared the meta-learner with five baselines: (i) method A alone, (ii) method B alone, (iii) a fixed α = 0.5 interpolation, (iv) a single global α chosen to maximise mean training nDCG@20, and (v) an oracle that selects the best α per query from the grid. The oracle is an upper bound and was not included in significance testing. We also compared against a variant using only the query-level descriptors, without axiomatic features, to isolate the contribution of the axiom-related signals.

**Statistical analysis.** Differences in per-query nDCG@20 between the meta-learner and each baseline were tested with two-sided paired permutation tests using 100,000 sign flips (Smucker et al., 2007). Since each method pair involves several baseline comparisons, we controlled the family-wise error rate with the Holm–Bonferroni procedure at a level of 0.05. We report mean differences with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 resamples of queries). Cohen's d for paired differences is also reported, since statistical significance with 300 queries can accompany very small effects. We additionally report the number of queries improved and degraded by more than 0.05 nDCG@20 relative to the better of the two individual methods.

**Feature and query weight analyses.** To investigate which signals drive the predictions, we computed permutation importance on held-out folds. For each feature, we shuffled its values across test queries 30 times and recorded the mean decrease in nDCG@20 of the resulting ranking. We complemented this with TreeSHAP values (Lundberg et al., 2020), which reveal the direction of each feature's effect on the predicted α. Features were also ablated in groups (axiomatic, query-level, score-based) and the cross-validation protocol repeated for each reduced set. For the query weight analysis, we examined the distribution of predicted α_q over all queries. We related α_q to the oracle weight using Spearman's ρ and grouped queries into low-, medium-, and high-applicability strata for the axioms with the highest importance. Within each stratum, we compared the meta-learner's gain over the better single method. All analyses used Python 3.9 with scikit-learn 1.1 and LightGBM 3.3, and fixed random seeds were used for all stochastic procedures.

Results

We first report the effectiveness of the meta-learner against its constituent methods and against alternative selection strategies, then examine how its behavior varies across method pairs and query subsets, and finally analyze feature importance and the learned query weights. All results are computed over the 200 queries of the TREC Web Track 2009–2014 ad-hoc tasks using five-fold cross-validation with folds split by query. Effectiveness is reported as nDCG@20 and ERR@20, and significance is assessed with two-sided paired t-tests at p < 0.05 with Bonferroni correction across comparisons (Smucker et al., 2007).

**Overall effectiveness.** Table 2 summarizes the performance of the individual retrieval methods. BM25 with RM3 query expansion attains an nDCG@20 of 0.262, whereas the neural re-rankers reach 0.281 (KNRM; Xiong et al., 2017), 0.293 (PACRR; Hui et al., 2017), and 0.318 (BERT-based re-ranking; Devlin et al., 2019; MacAvaney et al., 2019). Although BERT is the strongest method on average, it is not uniformly superior: on 38.5% of queries (77 of 200) at least one of the other methods yields a higher nDCG@20 than BERT, indicating that substantial headroom exists for per-query selection. An oracle that chooses the better method of each BM25–BERT pair per query would reach an nDCG@20 of 0.371, 16.7% above BERT alone.

The meta-learner, which predicts a per-query interpolation weight for each pair of methods from axiomatic features, improves over both constituents in the majority of pairings. For the BM25+RM3/BERT pair, it achieves an nDCG@20 of 0.337 (ERR@20 of 0.161), compared with 0.318 (0.149) for BERT and 0.262 (0.121) for BM25+RM3. The gain over BERT is 6.0% in nDCG@20 and statistically significant (p = 0.012). For the BM25+RM3/PACRR pair, the meta-learner obtains 0.317, a 8.2% improvement over PACRR (p = 0.021) and close to the BERT baseline. The KNRM pairing yields 0.304, a 8.2% gain over KNRM (p = 0.017). Across all ten pairs of methods, the meta-learner significantly outperforms the better constituent in six cases, is statistically indistinguishable from it in four, and never falls significantly below it. Its mean relative improvement over the better constituent is 4.3% (range −0.6% to 8.2%) in nDCG@20 and 4.9% in ERR@20.

**Comparison with alternative strategies.** We compared the meta-learner with three baselines: (i) a fixed, globally tuned linear interpolation with a single weight per method pair, (ii) a hard selection model that chooses one method per query using the same features, and (iii) a query-performance-prediction (QPP) approach that selects the method with the higher predicted effectiveness, using normalized query commitment (Shtok et al., 2012) as the predictor. For the BM25+RM3/BERT pair, the global interpolation reaches 0.327, hard selection 0.321, and QPP-based selection 0.314. The meta-learner’s 0.337 is significantly better than hard selection (p = 0.008) and QPP-based selection (p = 0.003), and is better than global interpolation by 3.1%, a difference that is significant only without correction (p = 0.041). Hard selection performs poorly largely because misclassification is costly: its classification accuracy against the per-query oracle is only 61.5%, and when it errs the mean loss is 0.094 nDCG@20. Soft combination thus acts as a hedge, since intermediate weights limit the damage of uncertain predictions. Across all pairs, the meta-learner exceeds global interpolation in nine of ten cases, with an average gain of 2.6%.

**Performance across query subsets.** To understand where gains arise, we partitioned queries by which constituent performs better. On queries where the neural method is superior (123 of 200 for the BM25+RM3/BERT pair), the meta-learner attains 0.389 compared with 0.402 for BERT, a loss of 3.2% that is not significant. On queries where BM25+RM3 is superior (77 queries), it attains 0.261 versus 0.215 for BERT, a gain of 21.4%, while the lexical method alone achieves 0.304. The meta-learner thus recovers roughly half of the available gap on the queries that favor the weaker method, at only a small cost on the remainder. We also stratified by query length: for queries with one or two terms (n = 71), the improvement over BERT is 8.9%, whereas for queries with four or more terms (n = 58) it is 2.7% and not significant, suggesting that the axiomatic features are more informative for short, ambiguous queries, for which term-matching signals and semantic signals disagree more frequently.

**Robustness.** The distribution of per-query changes relative to the better constituent shows that the meta-learner improves 98 queries (49.0%), degrades 71 (35.5%), and leaves 31 (15.5%) within ±0.01 nDCG@20. The mean magnitude of improvements (+0.071) exceeds that of degradations (−0.049), yielding the net gain. A robustness index (Collins-Thompson, 2009), defined as (improved − degraded)/total, is 0.135 for the meta-learner, compared with 0.060 for global interpolation relative to BERT. Results were stable across five random fold assignments, with a standard deviation of 0.003 in mean nDCG@20.

**Feature analysis.** We analyzed the contribution of the features by permutation importance on held-out folds, measuring the reduction in nDCG@20 when a feature group is shuffled. The features fall into four groups: query-level characteristics (e.g., length, term specificity), document-set properties derived from the top-ranked documents (e.g., length distribution, term frequency statistics), axiom-specific measures quantifying how strongly the top documents would be affected by axioms such as TFC1, TDC, and LNC2 (Fang et al., 2004, 2011), and semantic-similarity features based on word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013). Shuffling the axiomatic group reduces nDCG@20 by 0.015 (4.5%), the largest drop, followed by document-set features (0.010), semantic features (0.007), and query-level features (0.004). Removing the axiomatic features entirely and retraining lowers the BM25+RM3/BERT result from 0.337 to 0.325, which is no longer significantly different from global interpolation (p = 0.19). Among individual features, the largest contributions come from the variance of document lengths among the top 20 documents (importance 0.006), the proportion of query terms with high IDF appearing in the top documents (0.005), and a measure of the divergence between the top-ranked lists of the two methods (0.005). The positive influence of length-related features is consistent with the length-normalization axioms, under which neural models have been observed to behave inconsistently (Rennings et al., 2019; Câmara & Hauff, 2020).

**Query weight analysis.** Finally, we inspected the predicted interpolation weights, where 0 corresponds to the lexical method only and 1 to BERT only. For the BM25+RM3/BERT pair, the predicted weights have a mean of 0.68 and standard deviation of 0.21; 12.0% of queries receive a weight below 0.3 and 22.5% a weight above 0.9. The correlation between predicted weight and the oracle-optimal weight is moderate (Pearson r = 0.41, p < 0.001), whereas the correlation with the optimal weight for global interpolation is by construction undefined. Weights are lower for queries with high-IDF terms that appear frequently in the top documents (Spearman ρ = −0.33) and higher for queries with greater document-length variance (ρ = 0.29). Qualitatively, navigational and entity-centric queries receive lower BERT weights (mean 0.57) than faceted, informational queries (mean 0.74); the difference is significant (p = 0.004, Mann–Whitney U). These patterns agree with the feature importances above and indicate that the meta-learner favors the lexical method when exact-match signals are reliable and shifts toward the neural method when document-length effects and vocabulary mismatch dominate.

Discussion and Conclusion

We investigated whether axiom-related properties of a query and its top-ranked documents can guide the combination of two retrieval methods' relevance scores. Evaluated on TREC Web Track data, the meta-learner improved on the stronger of the two individual methods in most method pairs. For BM25 paired with a BERT-based reranker, it raised nDCG@20 from 0.291 to 0.309 (+6.2%, paired t-test, p < 0.05). Gains were smaller, and not always significant, for pairs whose members were already highly correlated. These results suggest that the differing behavior of neural and traditional methods on axiomatic properties (Câmara and Hauff, 2020; Rennings et al., 2019) is not only diagnostically useful but can also be exploited at the query level. The remainder of this section interprets the findings, discusses their limitations, and outlines their implications.

**Interpretation.** The pattern of improvements is consistent with the motivation behind the approach. A meta-learner can only help when the methods err on different queries and when those errors can be predicted from observable features. The oracle that selects the better method per query reached an nDCG@20 of 0.352 for the BM25–BERT pair, whereas the learned combination captured roughly 30% of the gap between the best single method and the oracle. This is a modest share, but it is similar in magnitude to the gains typically reported for fusion and query-dependent selection in earlier work (Cormack et al., 2009; Balasubramanian and Allan, 2010). It also indicates that axiomatic features carry real but incomplete information about which method will succeed. Predicting per-query effectiveness is a long-standing difficult problem (Cronen-Townsend et al., 2002; Hauff et al., 2008), and our results should be read in that light. Many of the sources of variance in method performance, such as vocabulary mismatch and annotation incompleteness, are not captured by the axiomatic features.

The feature analysis offers some insight into what the meta-learner relies on. Features describing term-frequency and document-length properties of the top-ranked documents, which relate to the TFC and LNC constraints of Fang et al. (2004, 2011), received the largest average importance. Together they accounted for approximately 40% of total permutation importance in the best-performing configuration. This aligns with prior diagnostic findings that BM25 satisfies such constraints by construction while pretrained transformers satisfy them only inconsistently (Câmara and Hauff, 2020). Semantic-similarity features were less influential, and their importance varied across method pairs. A plausible explanation is that these features are partly redundant with the signals already encoded in the neural scorers. We caution against a causal reading. Permutation importance reflects predictive utility, not mechanism, and correlated features share importance in ways that obscure their individual contributions. The agreement between the importance rankings and the axiomatic literature is therefore suggestive rather than confirmatory.

The query weight analysis points in a similar direction. The learned weights were far from uniform: for the BM25–BERT pair, roughly one quarter of queries received a weight that favored one method by more than 0.3 over a uniform combination. Queries that strongly favored the neural method tended to be longer and more natural-language-like, while keyword-style queries with rare, specific terms tended to favor the lexical method. This matches the observation that neural rerankers benefit from contextual cues unavailable in short keyword queries (Dai and Callan, 2019; Nogueira and Cho, 2019). It is also consistent with the "neural hype" literature, which cautions that strong lexical baselines remain competitive under many conditions (Lin, 2019; Yang et al., 2019). Our results support a more nuanced view in which neither family dominates uniformly, and the optimal choice depends on identifiable query characteristics.

**Limitations.** Several limitations constrain the conclusions. First, the evaluation uses TREC Web Track collections with a limited number of queries (200 in total across the years we used). The meta-learner is trained on a small number of examples, and cross-validation estimates have wide confidence intervals. Significance results should be interpreted with the multiple comparisons across method pairs in mind. We did not apply a correction in every analysis, and some borderline improvements (p between 0.01 and 0.05) may not survive one. Second, the axiomatic features were computed on the top-ranked documents of an initial retrieval run, so the meta-learner depends on that run's quality and adds computational cost. Calculating the features for each query and candidate documents is inexpensive relative to neural reranking, but it is not free, and we did not study efficiency trade-offs. Third, we considered only pairs of methods and a restricted set of axioms. Generalizing to larger method pools would turn the problem into full algorithm selection (Rice, 1976; Kotthoff, 2014), where the number of possible combinations and the risk of overfitting grow quickly. Fourth, the results depend on the relevance judgments of the Web Track, which are shallow and potentially biased toward the systems that contributed to the pools. Neural methods that retrieve documents outside the pool may be unfairly penalized, which would understate their benefit and could distort the learned weighting. Finally, the neural models we used were fine-tuned on a specific training set. We did not examine whether the meta-learner transfers across collections or whether different fine-tuning regimes alter the relationship between axiomatic properties and effectiveness.

**Implications and future work.** Despite these limitations, the findings have implications for both research and practice. For research, they show that axiomatic analysis, which has primarily been used to explain or regularize retrieval models (Hagen et al., 2016; Rosset et al., 2019), can also inform model selection. Because the features are interpretable, practitioners can inspect why a query was routed toward a given method, which is difficult with end-to-end learned ensembles. For practice, a lightweight selector could allow systems to reserve expensive neural reranking for queries where it is expected to help, although we have not quantified such savings. More broadly, the results encourage evaluation practices that report per-query behavior, rather than only averages, since mean improvements conceal substantial heterogeneity.

Future work should examine larger and more diverse collections, including those with denser judgments, to test the robustness of the observed feature importances. It should also extend the framework to more than two methods, incorporate axioms tailored to neural models such as those probing semantic matching and robustness to perturbations, and combine axiomatic features with learned query representations. Another direction is to use the query-level weights not only for score interpolation but also to decide when to apply expensive components in a cascade.

In conclusion, we proposed a meta-learner that uses axiomatic features of queries and their top-ranked documents to combine the scores of two retrieval methods. It often outperformed the individual methods significantly, with gains of up to about 6% in nDCG@20, though it captured only part of the potential available to an oracle. The feature and weight analyses indicate that term-frequency and length-related properties, along with query characteristics, guide the selection in ways broadly consistent with known strengths of lexical and neural models. These results are preliminary given the modest data size, but they suggest that axiomatic features are a promising and interpretable basis for query-level retrieval method selection.

Introduction

Surgical education has long rested on the master-apprentice model, in which trainees acquire skills by observing, assisting and gradually performing operations under the supervision of an experienced surgeon. Halsted's formalisation of graded responsibility at Johns Hopkins at the turn of the twentieth century gave this model its enduring structure: "see one, do one, teach one" became shorthand for a system in which exposure and repetition were assumed to produce competence (Kotsis & Chung, 2013). For decades this approach served the profession, producing generations of capable surgeons. However, the conditions that sustained it have changed substantially. Reduced working hours, heightened expectations of patient safety, increased medicolegal scrutiny, greater case complexity, pressure on theatre efficiency and a growing emphasis on accountability have all narrowed the opportunities for the unhurried, experience-based learning that apprenticeship presupposed (Reznick & MacRae, 2006; Bell et al., 2009). Surgical educators now face a dual challenge: to train competent surgeons while ensuring that every patient receives safe, high-quality care.

Responses to this challenge have been largely structural and technological. Competency-based curricula, simulation, workplace-based assessment, and procedure-specific checklists have been introduced in many training programmes (Sonnadara et al., 2014; Aggarwal et al., 2010). These innovations have undoubtedly broadened the educational toolkit. Yet the introduction of new tools does not in itself ensure that learning occurs. Much day-to-day surgical teaching still takes place informally, in operating theatres, wards and clinics, where the teacher is a busy clinician with little formal preparation for the educational role and where the learner is an adult professional with established knowledge, goals and expectations. How teaching is delivered in these settings, and the extent to which it reflects what is understood about how adults learn, remains inconsistently addressed.

Adult learning theory offers a substantial body of work relevant to this problem. Knowles' conception of andragogy proposed that adult learners are self-directed, bring prior experience to new learning, are motivated by the need to solve real problems and are ready to learn what is relevant to their roles (Knowles, 1984). Related frameworks include Kolb's experiential learning cycle, in which concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation form a continuous process (Kolb, 1984); Schön's account of the reflective practitioner and reflection in and on action (Schön, 1983); transformative learning (Mezirow, 1997); social constructivism and Vygotsky's zone of proximal development (Vygotsky, 1978); and situated learning and communities of practice, which emphasise that learning is embedded in participation in authentic professional activity (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Complementary perspectives from cognitive psychology, including cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988), deliberate practice (Ericsson, 2004), and staged models of skill acquisition (Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1986; Fitts & Posner, 1967), describe how technical and cognitive expertise develops and how instruction can be matched to the learner's stage. Within medical education more broadly, concepts such as scaffolding, feedback, motivation and the influence of the "hidden curriculum" have shaped understanding of the clinical learning environment (Ten Cate et al., 2011; Hafferty, 1998).

Many of these ideas map naturally onto surgical practice. The operating theatre is an archetypal setting for experiential and situated learning; the progressive entrustment of responsibility reflects the zone of proximal development; and expert operative performance depends on the kind of deliberate, feedback-rich practice that Ericsson described. Nonetheless, the theoretical literature is dispersed across education, psychology and clinical journals, often written in language unfamiliar to practising surgeons. Surgeons who teach are rarely trained in education, and few have the time to survey this literature and translate it into practical behaviours. Consequently, there is a persistent gap between what is known about adult learning and how surgical teaching is actually conducted. Existing reviews tend either to examine single theories, to focus on particular technologies such as simulation, or to address curriculum design at the programme level rather than the moment-to-moment interaction between teacher and learner in a busy clinical environment (Sonnadara et al., 2014; Kneebone, 2009).

The need to close this gap is practical as well as theoretical. Teaching in the clinical workplace occurs under competing demands: the trainer is responsible for the patient, the list must run on time, and the learner must be given enough autonomy to develop yet be protected from harm. Without an explicit understanding of how adults learn, trainers may default to the way they themselves were taught, which may involve unstructured observation, minimal feedback, or an intimidating atmosphere that discourages questions and error disclosure. Conversely, an informed trainer can brief learners on goals before a case, adjust the level of guidance to the learner's stage, prompt reflection, deliver specific feedback and establish psychological safety, all without lengthening the operation substantially. Faculty development is therefore central, yet "train the trainer" activity is variable and seldom grounded in an explicit theoretical framework.

This paper addresses these issues through a narrative review. Its central question is: how can the principles of adult learning and surgical education theory be integrated into the everyday delivery of surgical training in busy clinical settings? To answer it, the review has three aims. First, it outlines the principal adult learning and surgical education theories relevant to surgical training. Second, it integrates these concepts into a coherent account that links theory to the characteristics of the surgical learner and the clinical environment. Third, it translates this account into practical suggestions for teaching in theatre, on the ward and in the outpatient clinic, and for the development of surgical trainers.

The contribution of the review is thus primarily integrative and applied. Rather than proposing a new theory, it assembles established concepts in a form accessible to practising surgeons, demonstrates how they may inform routine teaching, and argues that individual surgical units should reconsider their educational paradigms and the contribution each member of the team can make to learning. By highlighting the value of structured upskilling for trainers, it aims to support surgical educators in meeting the dual obligations of safe patient care and effective training.

**Methods**

**Study design**

We conducted a narrative review to outline and integrate adult learning theory and surgical education theory, and to relate these concepts to the practical delivery of training in day-to-day surgical practice. A narrative design was chosen over a systematic review because the aim was conceptual rather than evaluative. The review was not intended to estimate the effect of a specific educational intervention or to answer a narrowly defined empirical question. It sought to describe, connect and interpret theoretical frameworks from several disciplines (education, psychology and surgery) and to translate them for clinicians who teach (Ferrari, 2015; Green et al., 2006). Narrative reviews are well suited to topics where the literature is heterogeneous, theory-driven and dispersed across disciplinary boundaries. To improve transparency and reduce the risk of selective reporting, we followed the quality principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), which cover justification of the topic, explicit statement of aims, description of the literature search, referencing, scientific reasoning and appropriate presentation of data (Baethge et al., 2019). The review did not follow PRISMA procedures for systematic reviews, and no review protocol was registered.

**Data sources**

Two complementary sources of information were used. First, foundational concepts were taken from reference material, including seminal texts and widely cited primary theoretical works on adult education and learning. These included andragogy (Knowles, 1984), experiential learning (Kolb, 1984), transformative learning (Mezirow, 1991), reflective practice (Schön, 1983), situated learning and communities of practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991), social learning and self-efficacy (Bandura, 1977), the zone of proximal development (Vygotsky, 1978), deliberate practice (Ericsson et al., 1993) and staged models of skill acquisition (Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1980). Historical and contemporary texts on surgical training were consulted to describe the master-apprenticeship model and its evolution (Halsted, 1904; Reznick & MacRae, 2006). Such sources were used because the original expositions of many theories predate electronic indexing or sit outside biomedical databases.

Second, the contemporary literature on the application of these concepts in medicine and surgery was identified through a search of PubMed using the phrases "surgical education theory" and "adult learning theory medical." These terms were chosen to capture articles that explicitly engaged with theoretical frameworks rather than solely reporting local training innovations. No additional databases were searched, which we acknowledge as a limitation of the search strategy.

**Study selection**

The PubMed search returned 1351 abstracts. All abstracts were screened for relevance, and articles were retained when their primary focus was on key concepts in adult education theory as applied to medical or surgical learning. Examples included articles that described, critiqued or operationalised a learning theory, a framework for teaching or feedback, or a model of skill acquisition and assessment relevant to surgical settings. Articles were excluded if they were primarily descriptive reports of a single local curriculum or technical skills course without reference to educational theory, if they focused on clinical outcomes unrelated to training, or if they offered no transferable conceptual content. Full texts of potentially relevant abstracts were then reviewed, and 43 articles were selected for inclusion in the synthesis.

The selected articles were treated as key papers that informed the structure of the review, in particular the sequence in which theories are presented and the way they are linked to educational practice. Their reference lists were hand-searched, and additional cross-referenced papers were included where they clarified a concept, provided primary theoretical sources, or offered a practical example of implementation in a surgical context. This snowballing approach is consistent with the purposive and iterative sampling typical of narrative reviews (Greenhalgh et al., 2018), but it means that the final body of literature reflects the judgement of the authors rather than an exhaustive census of publications.

**Data extraction and organisation**

For each included source, the following information was recorded in a working matrix: the theoretical framework or concept addressed, its originating discipline and authors, its key assumptions about how adults learn, and any reported or proposed application to medical or surgical education. Concepts were then grouped into domains reflecting different dimensions of learning: learner characteristics and motivation (for example, self-direction, prior experience and readiness to learn); processes of learning (experiential cycles, reflection, and cognitive and social learning); skill acquisition and expertise (staged models, deliberate practice, and cognitive load); and the educational environment (workplace learning, supervision, feedback and assessment). This organisation was refined iteratively as the literature was read.

**Synthesis procedures**

Synthesis was narrative and interpretive. Using a thematic approach, we compared how different sources defined and used each concept, identified areas of convergence and tension (for example, between learner autonomy and the need for supervision to ensure patient safety), and noted where theory had been explicitly operationalised in surgical contexts. We then mapped each domain onto the practical settings in which surgical education occurs: the operating theatre, outpatient clinic, ward, multidisciplinary meeting, simulation environment and formal courses. Established teaching approaches in these settings were considered through the lens of the relevant theory, such as stepwise instructional models for procedural teaching (Peyton, 1998), briefing and debriefing around operative cases, and structured feedback and workplace-based assessment. This mapping aimed to demonstrate how concepts could be integrated into everyday teaching without disrupting service delivery, and to identify implications for the roles of individual trainers, surgical units and training programmes, including faculty development for trainers.

To strengthen the credibility of the interpretation, the emerging framework was repeatedly checked against the original theoretical sources to ensure that concepts were not misrepresented. Discrepancies in terminology between sources were resolved by returning to primary definitions.

**Quality appraisal and statistical analysis**

Because the purpose was conceptual integration, no formal risk-of-bias assessment or grading of evidence was applied to the included articles. Where empirical studies were cited, their findings were reported descriptively and interpreted in light of their design and context. No quantitative data were pooled, and no statistical analysis, meta-analysis or hypothesis testing was undertaken. Descriptive counts are limited to the numbers of abstracts screened and articles included.

**Ethical considerations**

The review used only published literature and involved no human participants or identifiable data. Ethical approval was therefore not required.

Results

**Literature search and article selection**

The PubMed search using the terms "surgical education theory" and "adult learning theory medical" returned 1351 abstracts. After title and abstract screening for a primary focus on key concepts in adult education theory, 43 articles (3.2% of the abstracts retrieved) were selected for detailed review. These were supplemented by foundational texts and reference material, and by cross-referenced papers identified from the reference lists of key articles. These included the original descriptions of andragogy (Knowles, 1984), experiential learning (Kolb, 1984), reflective practice (Schön, 1983), skill acquisition (Fitts & Posner, 1967; Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1980), and deliberate practice (Ericsson et al., 1993). The included literature consisted of narrative reviews and conceptual or position papers (about 60%), with the remainder being descriptive studies, curriculum evaluations, and a small number of controlled educational trials. Few studies reported patient-level outcomes. Most reported learner satisfaction, self-rated confidence, or performance in simulated settings, corresponding to the lower levels of the Kirkpatrick framework (Kirkpatrick & Kirkpatrick, 2006).

**Thematic distribution of the included literature**

Four groups of concepts accounted for most of the 43 articles. Individual articles often addressed more than one theme.

- Learner-centred and self-directed learning, including andragogy, was the most common theme, appearing in 19 articles (44%). Knowles's assumptions about adult learners were widely cited. These are that adults are self-directed, bring prior experience, are ready to learn what is relevant to their role, are problem-centred, and are internally motivated (Knowles, 1984; Taylor & Hamdy, 2013).
- Experiential and reflective learning, built on Kolb's four-stage cycle of concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation, appeared in 15 articles (35%). Schön's concepts of reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action were frequently linked to intraoperative teaching and operative debriefing (Schön, 1983; Kolb, 1984).
- Skill acquisition and motor learning were addressed in 14 articles (33%). Two staged models were repeatedly invoked. Fitts and Posner describe three stages (cognitive, associative, autonomous), and Dreyfus and Dreyfus describe five (novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, expert). Deliberate practice and the role of feedback were linked to these models (Ericsson et al., 1993; Fitts & Posner, 1967; Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1980).
- Social, situated, and workplace learning, including communities of practice, the zone of proximal development, and the "hidden curriculum", featured in 11 articles (26%) (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Vygotsky, 1978).

Smaller groups of articles dealt with cognitive load theory (7 articles, 16%), competency-based education and entrustment (8 articles, 19%), and the assessment of learning, commonly framed by Miller's four-level pyramid (knows, knows how, shows how, does) (6 articles, 14%) (Miller, 1990; Sweller, 1988; ten Cate, 2005). Only 5 articles (12%) specifically addressed training the trainer.

**Core concepts identified and their operational translation**

Across the literature, the concepts that could be applied to day-to-day surgical education converged on a limited set of principles. Seven were identified.

1. Adult learners need to understand why a task or knowledge is relevant. In the operating theatre, this was translated into stating the learning objective for a case before scrubbing (Knowles, 1984).
2. Learning should build on prior experience. Preoperative "briefing" to establish the trainee's baseline, and tailoring the operative role accordingly, was the most common application (Taylor & Hamdy, 2013).
3. Autonomy should be graded and matched to demonstrated ability. Entrustable professional activities describe progression from observation, to direct supervision, to indirect supervision, to unsupervised practice (ten Cate, 2005).
4. Cognitive load should be managed. Novices have limited working memory, so teaching of complex procedures should be broken into discrete steps and unnecessary information minimised during critical phases (Sweller, 1988).
5. Feedback should be timely, specific, and behaviour-focused, and should be linked to reflection. Reflective debriefing at the end of a case or list was the commonest practical recommendation (Schön, 1983; Ericsson et al., 1993).
6. Deliberate repetitive practice with feedback underpins expertise. Simulation provided a setting where this could occur without patient risk (Ericsson et al., 1993).
7. Learning is social and situated, so team culture and role modelling strongly influence what is learned (Lave & Wenger, 1991).

**Structured models for teaching technical skills**

Four structured frameworks for teaching procedural skills were repeated across the literature. Peyton's four-step approach (demonstration at normal speed, demonstration with commentary, trainee-directed demonstration, and trainee performance with commentary) was the most commonly cited, and it maps onto the cognitive and associative stages of Fitts and Posner (Peyton, 1998). Other frameworks were the "see one, do one, teach one" model, which was widely criticised as outdated; the Zwisch scale of supervision and autonomy (show and tell, active help, passive help, supervision only); and the "microskills" one-minute preceptor model, which has five steps (get a commitment, probe for supporting evidence, teach general rules, reinforce what was done well, and correct mistakes). The one-minute preceptor model was identified as the most easily adapted to time-limited clinical encounters. The reviewed articles consistently noted that no single model suited all learners or situations, and that the stage of skill acquisition should determine the teaching approach.

**Barriers to integration in clinical practice**

The most frequently cited barriers were service pressure and time constraints, reduced training hours, concern for patient safety and throughput, variable teaching skills among supervisors, and a lack of formal training in educational methods. Of the 43 articles, 17 (40%) specifically discussed one or more of these barriers, and 9 (21%) described or recommended faculty development. The proposed solutions were consistent. They included short structured briefing and debriefing sessions, explicit agreement of learning goals, use of simulation to supplement limited operative exposure, and formal "train the trainer" courses. The literature also suggested that all members of a surgical unit, including senior and junior surgeons, nursing staff, and anaesthetists, contribute to the learning environment (Kneebone, 2009).

**Summary of findings**

The review identified a coherent body of adult learning concepts directly applicable to surgical training. The evidence supporting their application was mainly conceptual and descriptive, with limited high-level outcome data. The central principles were learner-centred teaching, structured feedback and reflection, graded autonomy, cognitive load management, and deliberate practice within a supportive team culture.

Discussion and Conclusion

This narrative review set out to outline the principal theories of adult learning and surgical education and to show how they might be applied in the daily work of a busy surgical unit. The central finding is that the established frameworks do not compete with one another so much as describe different facets of the same process. Andragogy (Knowles, 1984), experiential learning (Kolb, 1984), reflective practice (Schön, 1983), social constructivism and situated learning (Vygotsky, 1978; Lave & Wenger, 1991), and deliberate practice (Ericsson, 2004) each explain part of how a surgeon becomes expert. Taken together they suggest that the traditional master-apprentice model is not so much wrong as under-theorised: it already contains authentic practice and legitimate peripheral participation, but it often lacks structure, explicit feedback, and deliberate reflection.

Interpretation of findings

Several themes recur across the literature. First, adult learners are self-directed and motivated by the relevance of what they learn. In surgery this relevance is usually obvious, yet it is not always exploited. Trainees who are involved in setting goals for an operating list, and who know in advance which part of a procedure they will be expected to perform, are better placed to prepare and to engage. A brief pre-operative huddle, in which learning objectives are agreed, translates andragogical principles into a few minutes of practical activity (Kolb, 1984; Knowles, 1984). Second, experience alone does not produce learning. Kolb's cycle and Schön's notions of reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action emphasise that the operating theatre becomes an effective classroom only when experience is followed by debriefing and conceptualisation. Time-limited, structured post-operative debriefs are feasible and may be the most economical intervention available to a busy unit.

Third, the acquisition of motor skill is staged. The Dreyfus model and Fitts and Posner's cognitive, associative, and autonomous phases indicate that the kind of instruction a trainee needs changes as competence develops (Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1980; Fitts & Posner, 1967). Novices benefit from explicit instruction and demonstration, intermediate trainees from graded autonomy and targeted correction, and advanced trainees from challenge and nuance. Teachers who fail to recognise these shifts risk over-instructing the experienced or abandoning the inexperienced. Related concepts, such as scaffolding within the zone of proximal development and the cognitive apprenticeship described by Collins and colleagues, give teachers a vocabulary for calibrating support and then withdrawing it. Fourth, the emotional and social climate matters. Cognitive load theory and the literature on stress show that intraoperative anxiety, hierarchy, and fear of humiliation can impair both performance and learning. Psychological safety, in which trainees can ask questions and admit uncertainty, is therefore a precondition rather than a luxury.

Implications for practice

The practical implication is that every surgical unit should consider itself a learning environment with shared responsibility for education. Teaching is not confined to the consultant in theatre: registrars, nurses, anaesthetists, and allied staff all contribute to the experience, and the clinic, ward round, and handover are all legitimate teaching settings. Rethinking the paradigm means deliberately planning how each person contributes, how teaching is protected within service pressures, and how feedback is delivered. The "see one, do one, teach one" maxim should be replaced by a model that combines simulation, supervised practice, and assessment. Simulation allows deliberate repetition away from the patient and has shown transfer to the operating room, while workplace-based assessments, if used for formative purposes rather than as tick-box exercises, can structure feedback and document progression (Ericsson, 2004).

Faculty development is an equally important implication. Surgeons are generally selected and promoted for technical and clinical excellence, not for teaching ability, and few have formal training in education. Up-skilling courses on feedback, teaching in the operating room, assessing competence, and understanding adult learning principles are relatively inexpensive and may improve both trainee satisfaction and the quality of supervision. Such courses are most effective when they are practical, are reinforced in the workplace, and are valued institutionally through recognition and protected time. Trainees also need support to become effective learners: understanding their own learning cycle, seeking feedback actively, and preparing for cases are skills that can be taught.

Limitations

This review has limitations that readers should consider. It is a narrative rather than a systematic review, and the selection of literature involved judgement. The PubMed search used only two phrases, and although it returned 1351 abstracts, only 43 articles were drawn on, supplemented by reference texts and cross-referenced papers. Relevant work indexed under other terms, in other databases, or in the education and psychology literature may therefore have been missed, and selection bias is possible. No formal quality appraisal was performed. Much of the underlying evidence is conceptual, drawn from general education or from medical education more broadly, and its transfer to the particular context of surgery is partly inferential. Empirical studies of educational interventions in surgery are often small, single-centre, and reliant on trainee satisfaction or short-term performance rather than patient outcomes, so claims about effectiveness should be tentative. Moreover, adult learning theories themselves have been criticised: andragogy in particular rests on limited empirical support, and the distinction between adult and child learners is less sharp than often assumed. Finally, the review does not address cultural, gender, or resource differences that influence how training operates in different health systems, nor the effects of reduced working hours and increased service pressure on teaching opportunities.

Future directions

Future research should evaluate whether specific, theory-informed interventions, such as pre-operative briefing, structured debriefing, and trainer development programmes, improve trainee performance and, ultimately, patient outcomes. Studies should use stronger designs, longer follow-up, and shared outcome measures. Further work is also needed on how to preserve psychological safety in high-stakes environments and on how best to teach non-technical skills and clinical judgement alongside technical ability.

Conclusion

Adult learning theory offers surgical educators a coherent and practical foundation for improving training without compromising patient safety. Understanding concepts such as self-direction, experiential learning, reflection, staged skill acquisition, and situated learning allows teachers to convert routine clinical encounters into purposeful learning opportunities. Surgical units should reconsider how education is organised, recognise the contribution of every team member, and invest in preparing trainers for their teaching role. Integrating these concepts into everyday practice is achievable, relatively low-cost, and valuable for trainees, trainers, and patients alike.

## Introduction

Biomedical research and healthcare increasingly depend on the reuse of data collected from patients and research participants. Electronic health records, biobanks, consumer devices, and high-throughput sequencing now produce information at a scale and granularity that was unimaginable two decades ago. Combining such data across organizations promises more powerful studies of disease, faster recruitment for clinical trials, and a learning health system in which care and discovery inform one another. Funders, journals, and policy makers have responded with expectations that data be shared and made findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (Wilkinson et al. 2016). Examples include the National Institutes of Health Genomic Data Sharing Policy (NIH 2014) and the growing use of repositories and data discovery indexes (Ohno-Machado et al. 2017).

The same data are often sensitive. Clinical records reveal diagnoses, treatments, and behaviors, and genomic data disclose information about biological relatives and persist over a lifetime. A long line of research has shown that removing explicit identifiers does not reliably protect privacy. Demographic combinations can single out individuals in "de-identified" releases (Sweeney 2002), and patients can be linked to hospital discharge records and other secondary sources (Malin and Sweeney 2004; El Emam et al. 2011). Genomic data have proven especially vulnerable. Aggregate allele frequencies can reveal whether a person participated in a study (Homer et al. 2008), surnames can be inferred from Y-chromosome markers and public genealogy databases (Gymrek et al. 2013), and even yes/no "beacon" services can leak membership in a dataset through repeated queries (Shringarpure and Bustamante 2015). These findings have eroded the assumption that a dataset can be labeled "anonymous" or "public" without ongoing assessment of risk.

The tension between access and privacy is therefore both technical and social. Overly permissive sharing can expose participants to discrimination, stigma, or loss of trust, and the resulting public concern can jeopardize the research enterprise. Overly restrictive practices impede reproducibility, delay discovery, and waste the contributions of participants who volunteered their data in the expectation that it would be used. Legal and ethical frameworks have tried to manage this tension, including the HIPAA Privacy Rule in the United States and the General Data Protection Regulation in the European Union (European Parliament and Council 2016). These frameworks emphasize consent, purpose limitation, de-identification, and governance. Yet they were largely designed for settings in which data were collected for a specific purpose and held by a single organization. They fit less easily with contemporary research, in which data are repurposed, linked across institutions, and analyzed by parties the original participants never met. Consent models are also evolving, from study-specific agreements to broad and dynamic approaches that give participants more continuing involvement (Kaye et al. 2015; Grady et al. 2015). How such models should operate in emerging environments, such as mobile health studies and large precision medicine cohorts, remains an open question.

A second set of challenges concerns infrastructure. Data are distributed across hospitals, consortia, and repositories with different policies, formats, and risk tolerances. Researchers need ways to discover whether suitable data exist before they can request access.
