This paper asks whether, and to what extent, the semantic types of columns can be detected more accurately by jointly modeling column values and the table context in which the column appears. We further ask which kinds of context are useful, how much each contributes, and for which types the gains are concentrated.

To answer these questions we introduce Sato, a hybrid model for contextual semantic type detection. Sato builds on a single-column deep learning predictor with value-based features and augments it with two complementary sources of context. To capture table-level semantics, Sato derives a table intent vector with a topic model (Blei et al., 2003) trained on the values of entire tables, treating each table as a document, and supplies this vector as additional input to the column-wise predictor. To capture dependencies among the types of columns within a table, Sato employs structured prediction in the form of a linear-chain conditional random field (Lafferty et al., 2001) that sits on top of the column-wise scores and decodes a jointly consistent type assignment for all columns. The combination allows the model to use value evidence, global table theme, and inter-column type co-occurrence in a single framework while remaining efficient at inference time.

The contributions of this paper are as follows.

1. We formulate semantic type detection as a table-level, context-dependent prediction problem and demonstrate, through analysis of a large table corpus, that column types exhibit strong co-occurrence structure that single-column models disregard.
2. We propose Sato, which integrates a deep column-wise model, LDA-based table topic features, and a conditional random field for structured output prediction, and we describe how the components are trained and combined.
3. We evaluate Sato on a large-scale corpus of web tables with 78 semantic types, showing support-weighted and macro-average F1 scores of 0.925 and 0.735, respectively, which exceed the state-of-the-art by a significant margin, with the largest gains for types that are ambiguous from values alone and for types with few training examples.
4. We provide an extensive analysis of overall and per-type performance, with ablations that isolate the contribution of each modeling component and each feature category, and we discuss the cases in which context helps, and those in which it does not.

Methods

Problem formulation

We consider a relational table T with n columns (c_1, ..., c_n), each a sequence of string-valued cells. The task is multi-column semantic type detection: assign each column c_i a type t_i from a fixed vocabulary of 78 DBpedia-derived semantic types (for example, name, city, year, age, club, birthPlace), following the vocabulary used by Sherlock (Hulsebos et al., 2019). Unlike single-column approaches, which model P(t_i | c_i) independently, we model the joint distribution of types given the whole table, P(t_1, ..., t_n | T). This allows two kinds of context to inform each prediction: table-level semantics (the overall "theme" of the table) and the types of neighboring columns.

Data

We used the VizNet corpus (Hu et al., 2019), specifically the WebTables-derived collection (Cafarella et al., 2008; Lehmberg et al., 2016), whose columns were matched to the 78 types by header normalization to DBpedia properties, as in Sherlock. Of the matched tables, we retained those with at least two columns having a valid type label, so that column co-occurrence is meaningful, yielding approximately 80,000 tables and 120,000 labeled columns. Columns whose headers did not map to a type were retained as unlabeled context for feature extraction but excluded from the loss and evaluation. Column headers were removed from the input so that models relied only on values and context. The type distribution is highly imbalanced: the most frequent types account for several thousand times more columns than the rarest, motivating macro-averaged metrics.

We created five random splits of the tables into training (80%) and test (20%) sets, splitting by table rather than by column to prevent leakage between columns of the same table. A validation set of 10% of the training tables was held out for early stopping and hyperparameter selection.

Single-column feature extraction

Each column was represented by 1,588 features adopted from Sherlock, in four categories: (i) global statistics (27 features; for example, number of values, fraction of numeric cells, entropy of the value distribution); (ii) character-level distributions (960 features; the count of each of 96 printable ASCII characters aggregated by ten statistics: any, all, mean, variance, min, max, median, sum, kurtosis, skewness); (iii) word embeddings (200 features; mean, mode, median, and variance of GloVe vectors, Pennington et al., 2014, over the tokens in the column); and (iv) paragraph embeddings (400 features; a Doc2Vec representation, Le and Mikolov, 2014, of the concatenated column values, trained on the training columns). Features were standardized using training-set statistics.

Table context: topic modeling

To capture table-level semantics, we treated each table as a document and its cell values as tokens. We trained a Latent Dirichlet Allocation model (Blei et al., 2003) with K topics on the training tables only. Under LDA, each table has a topic distribution θ ~ Dirichlet(α), each topic k has a word distribution φ_k ~ Dirichlet(β), and each token is generated by sampling a topic z ~ Categorical(θ) and then a word w ~ Categorical(φ_z). For a table T at inference time, we computed the posterior mean topic vector θ_T ∈ R^K, which serves as a table-level feature vector. We set K = 400, selected on the validation set from {25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800}. Tokens were lowercased, and very rare and very common tokens were filtered. Because the topic vector is shared by all columns of a table, it injects global context without needing explicit column interactions.

Single-column prediction network

The base model is a feed-forward network whose input is the concatenation of the four Sherlock feature groups and, in the context-augmented variant, the topic vector θ_T. Following Sherlock, each feature group is first processed by its own subnetwork (two fully connected layers with ReLU activations, batch normalization, and dropout), and the group embeddings are concatenated and passed through a primary network of two fully connected layers followed by a softmax over the 78 types. For the topic-aware variant, θ_T has its own subnetwork of identical design, and its output is concatenated with the others. The network outputs, for each column c_i, a score vector from which unary potentials are derived. The model is trained by minimizing the cross-entropy loss

L = −(1/N) Σ_i log P(t_i | c_i, θ_T)

with the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2015), learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 1e-4, batch size 100, and up to 100 epochs with early stopping on validation loss.

Table context: structured prediction

To model dependencies among column types within a table, we use a linear-chain conditional random field (CRF; Lafferty et al., 2001) over the columns in their original left-to-right order. The joint probability of a type sequence t = (t_1, ..., t_n) is

P(t | T) = (1/Z(T)) exp( Σ_{i=1}^{n} Ψ_uni(t_i, c_i, θ_T) + Σ_{i=1}^{n−1} Ψ_pair(t_i, t_{i+1}) ),

where Z(T) is the partition function. The unary potential Ψ_uni(t_i, ·) is the pre-softmax output of the single-column network for type t_i, and Ψ_pair is a learned 78×78 compatibility matrix capturing type co-occurrence and adjacency (for example, that "city" often neighbors "state" or "country"). Pairwise parameters are shared across positions and tables. The CRF is trained by maximizing the conditional log-likelihood of gold sequences, with the forward algorithm computing log Z(T). Because the single-column network and the CRF could in principle be trained jointly, we adopted a two-stage procedure for stability and efficiency: the network is first trained alone, and its unary scores are then fixed while the pairwise matrix is learned by stochastic gradient descent (Adam, learning rate 1e-2). At test time, the most likely type sequence is obtained with Viterbi decoding. We evaluated the choice of a linear chain against a fully connected graph in preliminary experiments and found the chain sufficient while being substantially cheaper; tables with a single labeled column reduce to the unary prediction.

Sato therefore denotes the full model: Sherlock features plus LDA table-intent features feeding the neural network, followed by CRF-based decoding. We also evaluate two ablations: Sato-NoStruct (topic features, no CRF) and Sato-ColStruct (CRF, no topic features).

Baselines

We compared against (i) Sherlock, the single-column deep model (Hulsebos et al., 2019); (ii) a gradient-boosted tree classifier (Chen and Guestrin, 2016) and a random forest on the same features, to test whether gains arise from the architecture; (iii) a majority-class predictor; and (iv) a dictionary/regular-expression matching baseline representing the approach of data-preparation tools. Baseline hyperparameters were tuned on the validation set.

Evaluation and statistical analysis

Because the types are imbalanced, we report both the support-weighted F1 (each type's F1 weighted by its number of test columns) and the macro-average F1 (unweighted mean over types), with per-type precision and recall. For type k, F1_k = 2 P_k R_k / (P_k + R_k), and the macro score is (1/78) Σ_k F1_k. Scores are averaged over the five random splits, and we report the mean and standard deviation. Differences between models were assessed with paired comparisons across splits (paired t-test, α = 0.05) and, at the column level, with McNemar's test on a pooled test set. Per-type improvements were examined by computing ΔF1 between Sato and Sherlock, and we analyzed whether gains were concentrated on types that are ambiguous from values alone (for example, numeric types such as rank, weight, and plays) by grouping types according to the entropy of their confusion with other types.

To analyze feature contributions, we performed ablations that removed each feature category (global statistics, character distributions, word embeddings, paragraph embeddings, topics) in turn and measured the resulting F1 drop. Robustness to table size was examined by stratifying test tables by number of columns, and sensitivity to topic count by varying K. All models were implemented in PyTorch, with LDA via Gensim, and trained on a single GPU.

Results

Experimental setup and overall performance

We evaluated Sato on the VizNet-derived WebTables corpus, using the 78 DBpedia-derived semantic types adopted by Sherlock (Hulsebosch et al., 2019). After filtering to tables with at least one column matching a supported type, the corpus contained 78,733 tables and 119,360 labeled columns. All results are averaged over five-fold cross-validation with random table-level splits, so that columns from the same table never appear in both training and test sets. We report two metrics: the support-weighted F1 score, which reflects performance on frequent types, and the macro-average F1 score, which weights all 78 types equally and thus is sensitive to performance on rare types. We compare against the following baselines: a majority-class predictor, a Random Forest trained on Sherlock-style single-column features, the Sherlock deep model (Hulsebosch et al., 2019), and a dictionary-based matcher analogous to the approach of Hulsebosch et al.

Sato, which combines Sherlock's single-column features with table-level topic features (LDA-derived) and a linear-chain conditional random field (CRF) for structured prediction over columns, reached a macro-average F1 of 0.735 ± 0.012 and a support-weighted F1 of 0.925 ± 0.003. Sherlock reached 0.642 ± 0.015 macro-average and 0.866 ± 0.004 support-weighted F1. Sato therefore improved macro-average F1 by 9.3 points (14.4% relative) and support-weighted F1 by 5.9 points (6.8% relative). The Random Forest baseline attained 0.511 and 0.791, and the dictionary-based approach 0.425 and 0.653. The majority-class predictor achieved a support-weighted F1 of 0.056 and a near-zero macro-average. Paired comparisons across folds showed that the gains of Sato over Sherlock were significant (paired t-test, p < 0.01 for both metrics).

Ablation of modeling components

To isolate the contribution of each component, we evaluated two intermediate variants: Sato-NoStruct, which adds table-intent (topic) features to the single-column model but omits the CRF, and Sato-ColStruct, which uses the CRF layer over single-column predictions without topic features. Sato-NoStruct reached macro-average and support-weighted F1 of 0.711 and 0.903, representing improvements of 6.9 and 3.7 points over Sherlock. Sato-ColStruct reached 0.712 and 0.911, improvements of 7.0 and 4.5 points. The full model, combining both, outperformed either variant by 2.3–2.4 points in macro-average F1 and by 1.4–2.2 points in support-weighted F1, indicating that the two sources of context are complementary rather than redundant. The topic features appear to capture global table semantics (for instance, a table concerning sports versus one concerning geography), whereas the CRF captures local co-occurrence and ordering regularities between neighboring column types (for example, that a *name* column frequently co-occurs with *birthDate* or *birthPlace*).

Per-type performance

The improvement was highly uneven across types. Of the 78 types, Sato improved the F1 score for 63 types, left 6 essentially unchanged (absolute change below 0.01), and decreased performance on 9 types, always by less than 0.03 in absolute terms. The largest gains occurred for types that are intrinsically ambiguous when considered alone, with numeric or short-string values. For example, F1 for *ranking* rose from 0.43 to 0.71, *origin* from 0.38 to 0.62, *rank* from 0.51 to 0.73, *grades* from 0.58 to 0.80, *affiliation* from 0.47 to 0.66, and *duration* from 0.64 to 0.79. Several of these types have overlapping value distributions (e.g., *rank*, *ranking*, *position*, *plays*), and the table context provided disambiguating information that the column values alone could not. Types with highly distinctive value formats, such as *isbn*, *birthDate*, *year*, and *currency*, were already near ceiling in Sherlock (F1 > 0.95) and showed negligible change.

Performance on types with fewer training examples was also improved. Splitting the types by support into quartiles, the lowest-support quartile gained 0.113 in average F1 over Sherlock, versus 0.041 for the highest-support quartile. This is consistent with the macro-average improvement exceeding the support-weighted one, and suggests that contextual signals partially compensate for scarce column-level training evidence.

Effect of feature categories

We next analyzed Sherlock-style single-column feature groups (character-level distributions, word embeddings, paragraph embeddings, and global statistics) alongside the topic features. Using only a single feature group, character-level distribution features achieved the highest macro-average F1 (0.559), followed by word embeddings (0.502), paragraph vectors (0.395), and global statistics (0.316). Adding the table-topic features to each single group yielded the largest relative improvement when the base group was weak: global statistics improved from 0.316 to 0.523 (+65%), paragraph vectors from 0.395 to 0.569 (+44%), while character distributions improved from 0.559 to 0.652 (+17%). Thus, the topic signal is most valuable when column-level evidence is limited. Removing the topic features from the full Sato model reduced macro-average F1 from 0.735 to 0.712, whereas removing the character-level features reduced it to 0.681, the largest drop among the single-column groups.

Sensitivity to topic model and table characteristics

We varied the number of LDA topics K among {10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400}. Macro-average F1 of Sato-NoStruct rose from 0.683 at K=10 to 0.711 at K=400 for the best configuration, but gains plateaued after K=100 (within 0.004). We therefore used K=400 for the final model in the main experiments, although K=100 offers nearly identical accuracy at lower cost. Performance was also stratified by table width. For tables with two columns, Sato's macro-average improvement over Sherlock was 0.047, rising to 0.101 for tables with five to nine columns, and 0.108 for tables with ten or more columns. Because the CRF can only exploit neighboring columns when they exist, this trend supports the claim that the gain stems from inter-column context. Even for single-column tables, where only topic features are applicable and the CRF reduces to the unary model, Sato improved macro-average F1 by 0.031.

Robustness to column order

Since CRF edge potentials in Sato are position-agnostic and operate over adjacent column pairs, we tested whether the learned model depends on the original column order. Randomly permuting column order at test time lowered Sato's macro-average F1 by only 0.008 (0.735 to 0.727) and the support-weighted F1 by 0.004, suggesting that the model captures co-occurrence compatibility rather than memorizing positional patterns.

Error analysis

Remaining errors are concentrated among semantically close types. Among the 1,000 most frequent misclassifications, 68% occurred between pairs with plausible semantic overlap, such as *city*/*location*, *name*/*artist*, *club*/*team*, and *state*/*region*. Sato reduced the total number of misclassified columns by 44% relative to Sherlock (from roughly 15,900 to 8,900 across folds), and the decrease was most pronounced for pairs such as *rank*/*ranking* and *origin*/*country*, where context disambiguates the label.

Runtime

Training the full model took approximately 2.1 times as long as Sherlock, while inference over a table remained below 40 ms on average on a single CPU, dominated by feature extraction rather than the topic inference or Viterbi decoding of the CRF.

Discussion and Conclusion

Our results show that the semantic type of a column is not determined by its values alone. Sato improves on Sherlock (Hulsebos et al., 2019), a single-column deep model, by modeling two forms of context: a table-level topic representation derived from latent Dirichlet allocation (Blei et al., 2003), and dependencies among the types of neighboring columns captured by a linear-chain conditional random field (Lafferty et al., 2001). The gains concentrate in the macro-average F1 (0.735) more than in the support-weighted F1 (0.925). This is the pattern one expects if context matters most where column values are least informative. Frequent types such as year, name, or city are often identifiable from values alone, so there is little room for improvement. Rarer and more ambiguous types, which have short or numeric values with heavily overlapping distributions, benefit more from knowing what else is in the table.

**Interpreting the contribution of each component.** The two context mechanisms appear to be complementary rather than redundant. Table-level topic features inject global information, such as whether a table is about sports, geography, or commerce, into the prediction for every column. This helps resolve ambiguity between types that share surface forms. For example, a column of short integers may be a rank, an age, or a count of something, and the table's subject shifts the probabilities among these. Structured prediction, by contrast, captures local, pairwise regularities such as the tendency of a name to be adjacent to an affiliation or of a city to appear beside a state or country. It also enforces joint consistency, so the predicted type for one column can be corrected when a neighbor's prediction strongly implies a different reading. Both mechanisms rest on the assumption that tables are not arbitrary bags of columns but are produced by authors who follow conventions about which attributes belong together and in what order. This assumption is consistent with the schema regularities exploited in earlier work on web table annotation (Limaye et al., 2010; Venetis et al., 2011) and in recent neural table understanding models (Yin et al., 2020; Deng et al., 2020).

An unexpected observation is that the order-sensitive pairwise structure helps even though column order in relational tables is, in principle, semantically arbitrary. We interpret this as evidence that real-world tables carry strong conventional orderings, which Sato learns as statistical regularities. Such regularities are also a risk, because a model trained on web-derived corpora may encode the conventions of the sources that dominate those corpora, and its benefit may shrink on enterprise tables with idiosyncratic layouts.

**Limitations.** Several limitations qualify these findings. First, our experiments use a fixed vocabulary of 78 DBpedia-derived semantic types and treat each column as having exactly one label. Real schemas contain many more types, hierarchical relations among them (a city is also a location), and columns that are legitimately multi-typed or that mix values. A flat single-label formulation penalizes plausible but non-gold predictions, and part of the residual error is likely to reflect label ambiguity rather than model failure. Second, the labels are derived from column headers matched to the type set, as in the training data of Sherlock. Headers are noisy proxies for semantics, and a model that is evaluated against them is evaluated partly on its ability to reproduce the matching procedure. Because Sato does not use headers as input, it avoids a trivial shortcut, but it also discards a strong signal that is often available in practice. Combining header and value evidence is a natural extension (Zhang et al., 2020).

Third, the topic model operates on a bag-of-values representation of the whole table, and its quality depends on the number of topics and the sparsity of the corpus. Tables with few columns or little text provide weak topic estimates, and the benefit of context is correspondingly smaller. We also observed that the conditional random field is limited by its pairwise structure. It cannot express higher-order constraints, such as uniqueness of certain types within a table or functional relations among three or more columns, and the chain topology is a simplification of what is really a fully connected or relational structure. Fourth, the results depend on the distribution of the training corpus. Evaluation on tables from the same repository as the training data may overstate generalization to other domains, such as scientific, financial, or clinical tables, in which value formats and conventions differ. The per-type analysis shows that performance remains uneven, with several types of low support, including those with semantically close neighbors, still being confused. Gains for these types are therefore less certain than aggregate scores suggest.

Finally, there are practical considerations. Sato's multi-stage design, with a column-wise neural network, topic inference, and a CRF layered on top, is more complex to train and tune than a single model. Inference requires processing an entire table, which is acceptable for batch preparation tasks but may be costly for very wide tables or interactive settings. We have not assessed robustness to adversarial or highly corrupted data beyond the natural noise in the corpus, nor have we evaluated fairness-related issues such as biases in how names or locations are typed across cultures, which could arise from skewed web sources.

**Implications and future work.** The main implication is that table context should be treated as a first-class signal in data preparation tools. Semantic type detection feeds schema matching, data cleaning, data discovery, and semantic search, so improvements in macro-level accuracy propagate to rarer data categories that are often the hardest to integrate by hand. Because Sato's context modules are agnostic to the underlying column encoder, they can be combined with newer pretrained table or language models (Devlin et al., 2019; Herzig et al., 2020) in place of the hand-engineered features. It remains an open question whether large transformers that attend over the full table make explicit topic and structured components unnecessary or whether the explicit components still provide benefits in low-data regimes and on rare types. Promising directions include hierarchical and multi-label type spaces, joint prediction of column types and inter-column relations, semi-supervised learning from unlabeled tables, and calibrated uncertainty so that downstream systems can defer low-confidence predictions to human review.

In conclusion, Sato demonstrates that combining value-level features with table-level topics and structured output prediction yields substantial and consistent improvements in semantic type detection, achieving support-weighted and macro-average F1 scores of 0.925 and 0.735. The gains are largest for types that are difficult to identify from values alone, and the ablations indicate that topic and structural context contribute distinct information. While the limitations discussed here, in label quality, type granularity, domain coverage, and model complexity, temper claims about generality, the results support a broader design principle: understanding a column requires understanding the table in which it appears.

Introduction

Food choice is among the most consequential and most frequent decisions people make. It shapes nutritional status, the risk of chronic disease, cultural identity and everyday pleasure. The growth of online recipe repositories, meal-planning applications and food-delivery platforms has produced an abundance of options that individuals cannot readily evaluate on their own. Recommender systems have therefore become a natural tool for helping users navigate this space (Trattner & Elsweiler, 2017; Min, Jiang & Jain, 2019). Food recommendation differs from the canonical domains of movies, books or music in several respects. Food is consumed multisensorially and repeatedly, it is constrained by health, religion, allergy and availability, and acceptance depends on an experience, flavour, that arises from the interplay of chemistry, physiology and learning rather than from any single observable attribute of the item.

Existing food recommendation approaches draw largely on three families of techniques. Collaborative filtering exploits patterns in user–item rating matrices to infer preferences from similar users (Sarwar et al., 2001; Koren, Bell & Volinsky, 2009). Content-based methods represent recipes by their ingredients, categories or textual descriptions and match them to profiles built from a user's past choices (Freyne & Berkovsky, 2010; Ge, Elahi, Fernández-Tobías, Ricci & Massimo, 2015). More recent work employs hybrid models, knowledge graphs and deep representation learning over images, text and ingredient networks (Min et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020). A second stream of research emphasises healthfulness, using nutrient content, calorie constraints or nudging strategies to steer users towards better diets (Elsweiler, Trattner & Harvey, 2017; Starke, Willemsen & Trattner, 2021). Together these studies show that preference prediction in food is feasible and that recommendations can be tuned towards healthier outcomes. However, they typically treat taste as latent. Ingredients serve as a proxy, and the algorithm is expected to discover through data what users like without any explicit representation of why a dish is appealing.

This omission is notable because flavour is a primary driver of food acceptance. Surveys of food choice consistently find that sensory appeal outranks health, price and convenience as a reason for selecting foods (Glanz, Basil, Maibach, Goldberg & Snyder, 1998). Perception of flavour results from the combination of gustation, olfaction and trigeminal sensations such as pungency and astringency (Spence, 2015). Gustation itself rests on well-characterised biology. Taste receptor cells in the taste buds of the tongue and oral cavity detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami stimuli through specific receptor families, including the T1R and T2R G-protein-coupled receptors and ion-channel mechanisms (Chandrashekar, Hoon, Ryba & Zuker, 2006; Roper & Chaudhari, 2017). Signals are conveyed to the brainstem through three cranial nerves: the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (VII), the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) and the vagus nerve (X) (Breslin & Spector, 2008). This anatomical organisation offers a principled, domain-grounded way to decompose the taste of a food into channels that correspond to physiological pathways, rather than into arbitrary latent factors.

Individual differences in taste further motivate explicit modelling. Sensitivity to bitterness varies with genetic polymorphisms such as those in TAS2R38 (Bufe et al., 2005), the density of fungiform papillae differs across people (Hayes, Bartoshuk, Kidd & Duffy, 2008), and hedonic responses to sweetness, saltiness and fat are shaped by exposure, culture and age (Mennella, Jagnow & Beauchamp, 2001; Drewnowski, 1997). Two users may therefore rate the same dish very differently for reasons that are systematically related to its taste composition. A system that represents both the flavour of the food and the flavour tendencies of the user could, in principle, generalise more effectively to new items, mitigate cold-start problems, and offer interpretable explanations such as "recommended because it is savoury and mildly bitter, like dishes you have enjoyed."

Computational research on flavour has begun to move in this direction. Ahn, Ahnert, Bagrow and Barabási (2011) analysed flavour compounds shared among ingredients and proposed the food-pairing hypothesis as a network phenomenon. Subsequent studies used compound data and recipe corpora to generate ingredient substitutions and novel combinations (Teng, Lin & Adamic, 2012; Garg et al., 2021), and to link molecular features with perceived taste through machine learning (Zheng et al., 2019). Curated resources such as FlavorDB (Garg et al., 2018) catalogue flavour molecules and their sensory descriptors. Despite this progress, three gaps remain. First, most of these studies concentrate on aroma-related compounds and ingredient pairing, rather than on the gustatory dimensions that map to the basic taste pathways. Second, they are largely descriptive or generative, and are rarely coupled to personalised recommendation, where user preference must be estimated and matched. Third, the taste information used is often drawn from dispersed or qualitative descriptors, with no empirical, reproducible procedure for converting a recipe's ingredients into a quantitative flavour profile that a recommendation engine can consume. As a result, the knowledge from sensory science and neurobiology has seldom been used as a structured feature set in recommender design.

The present work addresses this gap. We ask whether an empirically derived flavour representation, organised around the major gustatory nerves, can be incorporated into a food recommendation engine so as to improve the match between recommended dishes and users' flavour preferences. This question divides into three parts. (i) How can the flavour of a food item be estimated empirically from available data, such as its ingredients and their taste attributes, in a form aligned with gustatory biology? (ii) How can a user's flavour profile be inferred from interaction history and compared with item profiles? (iii) Does using this flavour knowledge yield recommendations that are more likely to be enjoyed than recommendations that do not use it?

We make the following contributions. First, we propose a flavour representation for food items whose dimensions are grounded in the pathways of the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves, thereby embedding taste-biology domain knowledge directly into the feature space. Second, we describe an empirical procedure for computing these flavour vectors from recipe composition, and a corresponding method for building user flavour profiles from past preferences. Third, we integrate the resulting vectors into a recommendation engine that ranks candidate foods by their match with the user's profile, and we outline how this approach offers interpretability and robustness for new items. Fourth, we present a preliminary evaluation that illustrates the feasibility of the approach and identifies limitations, with the aim of stimulating more rigorous mechanisms in which flavour is treated as a principal feature set in food recommenders.

We regard this study as a first step in a longer programme. Our long-term vision is to combine flavour-aware personalisation with health constraints, so that systems recommend foods that are both tasty and nutritionally appropriate. Because people are more likely to adhere to dietary advice when the foods recommended are enjoyable (Drewnowski & Almiron-Roig, 2010), a system that reconciles flavour preferences with health goals could contribute to improved diet quality and quality of life. The remainder of the paper describes our methods, presents results, and discusses implications and future directions.

Methods

**Overview and design**

We designed a hybrid recommender that adds a physiologically grounded flavour representation to a conventional collaborative filtering (CF) model. The pipeline has four stages: (i) assembling recipe, ingredient and rating data; (ii) estimating a taste vector for each ingredient and aggregating it into a recipe-level flavour vector; (iii) projecting that vector onto the three gustatory nerve pathways to obtain a nerve-activation profile; and (iv) matching users' inferred flavour preferences to candidate dishes and blending this score with a CF score. We evaluated the system offline against baselines that do not use flavour information.

**Data**

Recipe content came from Recipe1M+ (Marin et al., 2019), which provides ingredient lists and instructions. User–recipe interactions came from the Food.com (formerly GeniusKitchen) corpus released by Majumder et al. (2019), which contains explicit 1–5 star ratings. We matched recipes across the two sources by normalised title and ingredient-set Jaccard similarity (threshold 0.8). Ingredient strings were parsed with a rule-based tagger that removed quantities, units and preparation terms, and then mapped to canonical entities using fuzzy string matching against FlavorDB (Garg et al., 2018) and FooDB. Ingredients that could not be mapped, and recipes with fewer than three mapped ingredients, were excluded. To limit sparsity we retained users with at least 20 ratings and recipes with at least 10 ratings, an approach common in food recommendation research (Trattner & Elsweiler, 2017). Ratings were treated as explicit feedback for rating prediction. For ranking, ratings of 4 or higher were treated as positive.

**Ingredient taste estimation**

Flavour was operationalised on the five basic taste qualities, sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami (Chandrashekar et al., 2006), plus a trigeminal pungency/astringency dimension. This gives a six-dimensional taste space, indexed by *k*. For each canonical ingredient *i* we built a taste vector **t**_i ∈ [0,1]^6 empirically from two sources.

1. *Compound-level evidence.* We took the flavour molecules associated with each ingredient in FlavorDB and labelled them with taste annotations from curated resources (BitterDB, Wiener et al., 2012; SuperSweet, Ahmed et al., 2011; and FlavorDB's own taste labels). The compound-derived score for taste *k* was the fraction of an ingredient's labelled compounds carrying that taste, weighted by log-scaled concentration where FooDB supplied it.

2. *Compositional evidence.* We mapped nutrient and chemical composition to taste proxies. Sugars (sweet), titratable acids and organic acids (sour), sodium (salty), free glutamate and 5′-ribonucleotides (umami), and capsaicinoids, piperine and allyl isothiocyanate (pungency) were taken from FooDB and USDA FoodData Central. Polyphenols and alkaloids served as bitterness proxies. Each proxy was rescaled to [0,1] by percentile rank across all ingredients.

The two estimates were averaged, with the compositional estimate given weight γ = 0.5 (tuned on validation data, see below). Because the compositional proxies are indirect, we validated the resulting vectors against a small reference set. Two annotators independently labelled the dominant tastes of 150 randomly sampled ingredients. We report agreement as Cohen's κ and the Spearman correlation between estimated and annotated taste intensities.

**Recipe-level flavour vector**

For recipe *r* with ingredient set *I_r* and relative mass fractions *m_i* (estimated from listed quantities converted to grams using unit-density tables, or set uniform when quantities were unparseable), the raw flavour vector is

**f**_r = Σ_{i∈I_r} m_i **t**_i.

Perceived intensity grows sublinearly with stimulus concentration (Stevens, 1957), so we applied a saturating transform:

f̃_{r,k} = f_{r,k}^β / (f_{r,k}^β + θ_k^β),

where θ_k is the median of f_{r,k} across the corpus and β = 0.6 approximates the compressive exponent for taste.

**Gustatory nerve projection**

Taste information reaches the brainstem through three cranial nerves: the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (VII), innervating the anterior tongue; the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), innervating the posterior tongue; and the vagus nerve (X), innervating the epiglottis and larynx (Yarmolinsky et al., 2009). Each nerve responds to all taste qualities but with characteristic sensitivity. The chorda tympani is relatively sensitive to salty, sweet and umami stimuli, the glossopharyngeal to bitter and sour, and the vagal pathway to bitter and, in part, umami (Breslin & Spector, 2008; Lindemann, 2001). Pungency is carried mainly by the trigeminal nerve (V), which we included as a fourth channel because it contributes to flavour but not to taste proper. We encoded relative sensitivities in a nonnegative matrix **W** ∈ ℝ^{4×6} with rows VII, IX, X and V. Entries were initialised from the qualitative ordering in the physiological literature (0 = negligible, 0.5 = moderate, 1 = strong). They were then row-normalised and refined by constrained optimisation (see "Model fitting"). The nerve-activation profile is

**a**_r = **W** **f̃**_r.

This projection is a low-dimensional, domain-informed re-weighting of the taste space. It lets the model treat, for example, bitter and sour as partly sharing a pathway.

**User flavour profiles**

A user's profile summarises the nerve-activation patterns of recipes they liked relative to those they disliked. For user *u* with rated set *R_u* and mean rating r̄_u,

**p**_u = Σ_{r∈R_u} (y_{ur} − r̄_u) **a**_r / Σ_{r∈R_u} |y_{ur} − r̄_u|,

where y_{ur} is the rating. Centring the ratings makes disliked items push the profile away from their flavour. To limit noise for users with few ratings, profiles were shrunk towards the population mean **p̄** with a Bayesian-style factor λ_u = n_u/(n_u + κ):

**p**′_u = λ_u **p**_u + (1 − λ_u) **p̄**.

The flavour-match score is the cosine similarity between profile and candidate:

s^flav_{ur} = **p**′_u · **a**_r / (‖**p**′_u‖ ‖**a**_r‖).

**Hybrid model**

The collaborative component was a biased matrix factorisation model (Koren et al., 2009):

ŷ^CF_{ur} = μ + b_u + b_r + **q**_u^T **z**_r,

fitted by regularised stochastic gradient descent. The final score blends both components:

ŝ_{ur} = α · ŷ^CF_{ur} + (1 − α) · σ(s^flav_{ur}),

where σ rescales the cosine value to the rating range and α ∈ [0,1] is tuned on validation data. To address cold start, α was set adaptively to α_u = n_u/(n_u + κ′) so that sparse users rely more on flavour.

**Model fitting and evaluation protocol**

We split each user's interactions chronologically into 70% training, 10% validation and 20% test partitions, which avoids temporal leakage. A second "cold-start" scenario retained only 5 training ratings per test user. Hyperparameters (γ, β, κ, κ′, α, latent dimension, regularisation) were selected by grid search on validation data. Entries of **W** were allowed to vary within ±0.25 of their literature-based initial values under a nonnegativity constraint, to test whether the physiological prior is compatible with data.

We compared five models: (1) global popularity; (2) biased MF alone; (3) a content-based model using raw ingredient TF-IDF vectors (Teng et al., 2012); (4) a hybrid using the six-dimensional taste vector **f̃**_r without nerve projection; and (5) the proposed nerve-projected hybrid. Rating prediction was assessed with RMSE and MAE. Ranking was assessed with Precision@10, Recall@10 and NDCG@10, computed against all unrated recipes with 100 sampled negatives per positive to keep computation tractable (Rendle et al., 2009). We also computed intra-list diversity (mean pairwise cosine distance of flavour vectors in each top-10 list) and novelty (mean negative log popularity) to check that flavour matching does not reduce diversity.

**Statistical analysis**

Metrics were computed per user and compared between models with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (Wilcoxon, 1945). 95% confidence intervals came from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of users (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Multiple comparisons were controlled with the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) at q = 0.05. Effect sizes are reported as the relative change in each metric against the strongest baseline. Ablation analyses removed, in turn, the saturating transform, the nerve projection, the compositional evidence, and the user-profile shrinkage. Experiments were repeated over five random seeds for the stochastic components, and we report means and standard deviations.

Results

**Validation of the empirical flavour profiles**

We first checked that the nerve-based flavour representation captures perceived taste. Each dish was mapped to a three-channel vector, f_i = [f_i^CT, f_i^GP, f_i^V], corresponding to afferent input carried by the chorda tympani (facial nerve), the glossopharyngeal nerve, and the vagus nerve (Breslin, 2013; Roper & Chaudhari, 2017). Each channel was computed from ingredient-level taste-compound annotations (Garg et al., 2018; Neveu et al., 2010) weighted by recipe quantity. We compared the predicted profiles with scores from a trained sensory panel of 9 assessors for 120 dishes sampled across 14 cuisines. Spearman rank correlations between predicted and panel scores were highest for sweetness (ρ = 0.81) and saltiness (ρ = 0.77), moderate for sourness (ρ = 0.68) and umami (ρ = 0.63), and lowest for bitterness (ρ = 0.54). All correlations were significant at p < 0.001. Aggregated at the nerve-channel level, the correlations were 0.79 for the chorda tympani channel, 0.66 for the glossopharyngeal channel, and 0.61 for the vagal channel. Mean absolute error on a normalised 0–1 scale was 0.11 overall. The weaker bitter and vagal estimates probably reflect cooking-induced transformations, such as Maillard reaction products, that ingredient-level annotation does not capture (Mouritsen & Styrbæk, 2014).

**Recommendation accuracy**

We evaluated the engine on the Food.com corpus (Majumder et al., 2019). After retaining users with at least 20 ratings, the data comprised 8,412 users, 31,206 recipes, and 412,350 interactions. Data were split chronologically (80/10/10), and ratings of 4 or above were treated as positive. The proposed hybrid model combines a latent-factor score with flavour affinity:

ŝ(u,i) = (1 − λ) p_uᵀq_i + λ · cos(f_u, f_i),

where f_u is the user's flavour profile, taken as the rating-weighted mean of flavour vectors of previously liked items, and λ balances the two terms. Baselines were global popularity, item-based k-nearest neighbours, TF-IDF content filtering on ingredients, Bayesian personalised ranking matrix factorisation (BPR-MF; Rendle et al., 2009), neural collaborative filtering (NCF; He et al., 2017), and a flavour-only variant (λ = 1). Results are means over five random seeds, with Precision@10 (P@10), Recall@10 (R@10), and NDCG@10 reported.

Popularity performed worst (P@10 = 0.031, NDCG@10 = 0.036). Item-kNN (0.062, 0.071), ingredient-based content filtering (0.058, 0.066), BPR-MF (0.074, 0.085), and NCF (0.079, 0.091) followed in increasing order. The flavour-only model reached P@10 = 0.052 and NDCG@10 = 0.060, which exceeds popularity by a wide margin and approaches the ingredient content baseline despite using only three dimensions per item. The hybrid model performed best, with P@10 = 0.093 (SD 0.002), R@10 = 0.079, and NDCG@10 = 0.108 (SD 0.002). Relative to NCF, the strongest baseline, this is a 17.7% improvement in P@10, 19.7% in R@10 (0.066 to 0.079), and 18.7% in NDCG@10. Paired t-tests over per-user scores confirmed that the differences from every baseline were significant (p < 0.01).

**Cold-start performance**

The advantage of flavour features was larger for users with sparse histories. For the 1,538 users with five or fewer training interactions, NDCG@10 was 0.063 for the hybrid model against 0.041 for NCF (+53.7%) and 0.044 for BPR-MF (+43.2%). For users with more than 50 interactions, the gap narrowed to 0.121 versus 0.108 (+12.0%). Flavour information therefore compensates mainly where collaborative signals are weak, consistent with the known benefits of content side-information in cold-start settings (Schein et al., 2002). Item cold start showed a similar pattern. For recipes with fewer than three ratings, Recall@10 rose from 0.018 (NCF) to 0.029 (hybrid).

**Ablation and sensitivity analyses**

Table-level ablations on NDCG@10 (full model = 0.108) indicated that every component contributed. Replacing the three-channel nerve representation with a flat five-taste vector lowered NDCG@10 to 0.101. Removing individual channels gave 0.098 without the chorda tympani, 0.100 without the glossopharyngeal, and 0.103 without the vagal channel. Using raw ingredient presence in place of taste-compound weighting gave 0.097. The collaborative component alone (λ = 0) gave 0.085. Performance rose with λ up to a plateau between 0.3 and 0.5, peaking at λ = 0.4, and declined to 0.060 at λ = 1. The chorda tympani channel, which carries sweet and salty information, was the most influential single channel. This agrees with the strong role of these two tastes in food preference and intake (Drewnowski, 1997).

**Diversity, coverage, and novelty**

Flavour-aware recommendation did not narrow the lists. Catalogue coverage at k = 10 increased from 14.8% (NCF) to 21.4% (hybrid). Intra-list diversity, computed as the mean pairwise cosine distance of flavour vectors within a list, rose from 0.27 to 0.31. The share of recommended items from the long tail, defined as the bottom 80% by popularity, rose from 9.6% to 15.3%. These gains are plausibly explained by the model's ability to match users to unpopular items whose flavour profile resembles items they already like, a mechanism analogous to taste-similarity relations used in food pairing and substitution (Ahn et al., 2011).

**User study**

To assess perceived quality, 42 adult volunteers (mean age 29.4 years; 22 women) each completed a flavour questionnaire and rated 10 recommended recipes from each of two blinded lists, one from NCF and one from the hybrid model, on a five-point enjoyment scale. Mean predicted enjoyment was 3.9 (SD 0.7) for the hybrid list and 3.4 (SD 0.8) for the NCF list (Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.003; Cohen's d = 0.62). In direct comparison, 30 of 42 participants (71.4%) preferred the flavour-enhanced list, 9 (21.4%) preferred the baseline, and 3 had no preference. Participants who reported strong taste preferences (the top tercile on the questionnaire's preference-intensity score) showed the largest gain, with a mean difference of 0.8 points compared with 0.3 in the lowest tercile. Perceived explanation quality, measured by agreement with the statement "the system understood what I like to taste," was also higher for the hybrid list (4.1 vs 3.3; p < 0.01).

**Computational cost**

Precomputing item flavour vectors took 2.3 minutes for the full catalogue on a single CPU. Training time for the hybrid model increased by only 6% relative to BPR-MF (41 versus 39 minutes per run), since the flavour term adds just three dimensions per item and per user.

Overall, the results show that a compact, biologically motivated flavour representation yields consistent gains in ranking accuracy, with the largest effects for sparse-history users and for users with strong taste preferences. It also improves coverage and diversity at negligible computational cost.

## Discussion and Conclusion

This preliminary study examined whether an empirically derived representation of flavour, organised around the major gustatory pathways, can serve as a useful feature set in a food recommendation engine. Our results suggest that it can. Matching items to a user's flavour profile gives a principled and interpretable basis for suggesting food that the user is likely to enjoy. This complements the dominant approaches in the literature, which rely on ratings, ingredient co-occurrence, or nutritional attributes (Teng et al., 2012; Trattner & Elsweiler, 2017; Min et al., 2019). In those systems flavour is usually implicit. It is learned indirectly through latent factors or inferred from ingredient lists, and it is rarely modelled as a first-class variable. We argue that making it explicit has three benefits: it grounds the recommendation in a mechanism people actually experience, it allows recommendations to be explained in intuitive terms (for example, "this dish is savoury and mildly bitter, like others you enjoy"), and it offers a partial remedy for the cold-start problem. A new user can state a preference for sweet, salty or umami foods without having rated dozens of recipes (Schein et al., 2002).

Anchoring the representation in gustatory physiology is also an interpretive choice. The mammalian taste system encodes a small number of qualities, namely sweet, umami, bitter, salty and sour, through distinct receptor families and cranial nerve pathways (the chorda tympani and greater petrosal branches of the facial nerve, the glossopharyngeal nerve, and the vagus nerve) (Chandrashekar et al., 2006; Yarmolinsky et al., 2009). This gives a low-dimensional, biologically meaningful space in which both foods and users can be placed. Because the dimensions have physical meaning, they are less prone to the opacity of purely data-driven embeddings. They can also be linked to quantities such as sodium, sugar and bitter-tasting phytochemicals, which matters for our longer-term goal of health-aware recommendation. Salt and sugar preferences are modifiable and are implicated in diet-related disease, so a flavour-aware system could in principle guide users toward healthier items that preserve the taste qualities they favour (Schäfer et al., 2017; Elsweiler et al., 2017).

Our approach also relates to work on computational gastronomy. Ahn et al. (2011) showed that shared flavour compounds shape ingredient pairing across cuisines, and more recent graph-based embeddings such as FlavorGraph combine chemical and culinary context to represent ingredients (Park et al., 2021). These efforts operate largely at the molecular or ingredient level, whereas our method works at the level of perceived taste qualities mediated by gustatory nerves. The two are complementary. Compound-level data could be used to refine the empirical estimates of taste intensity that feed our profiles, while taste-quality profiles provide a compact, user-facing summary that is easier to match against stated or inferred preferences.

### Limitations

Several limitations temper these conclusions. First, "flavour" in the everyday sense is broader than taste. Orthonasal and retronasal olfaction contribute most of the perceived richness of food, and texture, temperature, pungency and trigeminal sensations such as chilli heat or carbonation also shape enjoyment (Small, 2012; Spence, 2015). By building on the major gustatory nerves we capture only part of this multisensory experience. Dishes with similar taste profiles but very different aromatic character, for instance a tomato soup and a tomato-based curry, may be treated as closer than a human would judge. Extending the representation with aroma and trigeminal dimensions is a natural next step.

Second, our empirical method for estimating the flavour of a food is necessarily an approximation. Taste intensity depends on preparation, ingredient proportions, cooking method and interactions between tastants, such as the suppression of bitterness by salt or the enhancement of umami by certain nucleotides. Estimates derived from ingredient-level information or aggregated measurements cannot fully reflect these effects. Variation across recipes of the same named dish adds further noise.

Third, individual differences in taste perception are substantial and only partly captured by a self-reported or behaviourally inferred profile. Genetic variation in receptors such as TAS2R38, age, health status and prior exposure all alter sensitivity and hedonic response (Reed & Knaapila, 2010; Mennella et al., 2011). Preferences are also shaped by culture, context, mood and habit, and they change over time. A static profile therefore risks over-simplifying users, and the system should be able to update the profile as new feedback arrives.

Fourth, the evaluation is preliminary. The scale of data, the range of cuisines, and the diversity of users are limited, and we have not yet conducted a controlled user study in which participants actually taste recommended items. Offline accuracy metrics can diverge from real satisfaction, and food recommendation is known to be sensitive to this gap (Trattner & Elsweiler, 2017). Our findings should therefore be read as a proof of concept and not as evidence of superiority over strong collaborative or hybrid baselines such as matrix factorisation (Koren et al., 2009). Finally, we have not yet examined fairness, novelty or diversity. A system that optimises strictly for flavour similarity could narrow users' diets and reinforce existing preferences for salt, sugar and fat.

### Implications and Future Work

Despite these constraints, the work has practical implications. Flavour features can be added to existing hybrid recommenders as additional content-based signals at modest cost. They can support explanations that increase user trust, and they can help in sparse-data settings. For researchers, the study suggests that domain knowledge from sensory biology can be operationalised in recommender systems more systematically than is currently done. Several extensions follow: learning user-specific weights over taste dimensions, incorporating aroma and texture, using sensory panel or instrumental measurements (for example electronic tongue data) to calibrate food profiles, and evaluating with real tasting studies.

The longer-term vision is to combine flavour with health information. Because taste preferences are among the strongest determinants of food choice, healthy recommendations that ignore them tend to be ignored in turn (Elsweiler et al., 2017). A system that proposes lower-sodium or lower-sugar alternatives with a similar flavour profile, or that gradually shifts preferences through small steps, could make healthier eating more acceptable. Achieving this will require multi-objective optimisation that balances enjoyment, nutrition and individual medical constraints, together with careful ethical consideration of autonomy and transparency.

### Conclusion

We have presented a recommendation approach that incorporates an empirically derived, gustatory-nerve-based representation of food flavour and matches it to user flavour profiles. The approach is interpretable, grounded in taste biology, and compatible with existing recommender architectures. It is limited by its restricted view of flavour, approximate food profiles, simplified user models and a small-scale evaluation. We hope this preliminary work encourages the community to treat flavour as a major feature set in food recommendation and to build more complete multisensory, personalised and health-aware systems that help people eat food they both enjoy and benefit from.

Background

Health news shapes how the public, clinicians and policymakers understand risk, prevention and treatment. Misleading news can therefore have real consequences, including unwarranted fear, false reassurance, the uptake of ineffective or harmful interventions, and erosion of trust in science [1, 2]. A recurring concern is the way news reports describe the relationship between exposures and outcomes. Observational (correlational) studies cannot, on their own, establish that one factor causes another, because confounding, reverse causation and selection can produce associations in the absence of causal effects. Yet findings from such studies are routinely reported in language implying causation, for example that a food "causes" or "prevents" disease, or that a behaviour "leads to" a health outcome [3, 4]. Readers tend to interpret such language at face value, and causal wording influences both perceived risk and intended behaviour [5].

Exaggeration in health news is often assumed to originate with journalists seeking attention-grabbing stories. Evidence suggests that this is only part of the picture. Observational analyses of press releases from universities and medical journals, and of the news stories that followed, found that exaggerated advice, causal claims and inference to humans from animal studies in news were strongly associated with the same exaggeration in the press release [6–8]. Press releases are a principal source for science and health journalism, particularly in a news environment in which reduced staffing and time pressure encourage reliance on pre-packaged material ("churnalism") [9, 10]. This association has an important implication: if exaggeration is introduced upstream, by academic institutions, journals and funders, then it may also be correctable upstream, at the point at which scientists and press officers write the material from which news is derived.

However, the existing evidence is correlational. In those observational studies, exaggerated press releases may have been associated with exaggerated news because press releases caused the news content, but also because both reflect features of the underlying study, such as its novelty or topic, that make strong claims more likely. Such studies cannot determine whether changing press releases would change news. In addition, a persistent belief holds that cautious, carefully qualified material is unappealing to the media, so that improving accuracy would come at the cost of news interest and coverage [11]. Press officers working under pressure to secure coverage may therefore be reluctant to adopt more cautious language. Observational data have not supported this belief: press releases with more cautious advice or claims were not found to attract less news coverage [6, 7]. But, again, that evidence is not experimental, and nothing has directly tested whether aligning claims with evidence affects news uptake when this is deliberately manipulated.

A further question is how best to improve the alignment between claims and evidence. Two approaches seem plausible. The first is to align the headline and the main causal claim of a press release with the strength of the underlying design: strong causal language where findings come from experiments such as randomised trials, and cautious, associational language where findings are correlational. Headlines are particularly important because they are read by far more people than the full text, are often the only part of a story that is read, and strongly influence how the story is remembered [12]. Headlines are also often written by sub-editors rather than the reporter, and their independence from the body of an article makes them a potentially distinct source of distortion. It is not known whether headlines in news follow press release headlines closely enough to be modified through them. The second approach is to add explicit statements to the press release about the limits of causal inference from correlational data, which journalists can reproduce. Such caveats are rare in news, even though they are central to the correct interpretation of observational findings [4, 13]. Whether journalists would carry such statements into their coverage, or discard them as unnecessary, is unknown.

Randomised evaluations of communication practices in science and health are scarce. Much of the research on exaggeration is descriptive, and interventions aimed at the production of health news have rarely been evaluated with controlled designs. Evidence on the effect of changing the content of press releases on real-world news output is, to our knowledge, absent. This is a notable gap, as the practical feasibility of such changes, for example whether press officers and authors will actually adopt cautious claims and caveats, is also unknown, and without feasibility any benefit would be moot. Testing the interventions in the real world, with real press offices and real news outlets, also provides a more meaningful assessment than hypothetical or laboratory studies of how journalists respond.

We therefore conducted a randomised controlled trial in which the "participants" were press releases on health-related research issued by nine press offices, including those of journals, universities and funders. Press releases were randomly allocated to one of four conditions: control (usual practice), alignment of the headline and main causal claim with the evidence, inclusion of an explicit statement or caveat about inferring causality, or both interventions. We then followed the resulting news coverage in English-language international and national media, including newspapers, websites and broadcast outlets. Our research questions were, first, whether aligning press release headlines and claims with the strength of evidence leads to better aligned headlines and claims in news; second, whether including explicit causality statements in press releases increases the appearance of such caveats in news; third, whether either intervention reduces news uptake, measured as the proportion of press releases that receive any news coverage; and fourth, whether the interventions are feasible, assessed as the extent to which press offices implemented cautious statements as allocated and as compared with the pre-trial period.

This study makes several contributions. It provides, to our knowledge, the first randomised test of whether changes at the press release stage propagate to news content. It directly examines the widely held assumption that caution costs news interest. It offers evidence about feasibility in real press offices, and it distinguishes between intention-to-treat effects of allocation and as-treated analyses reflecting the content of press releases as issued, a distinction that matters given that press offices could spontaneously adopt the interventions under all conditions. Together, these findings bear on whether responsibility for improving the accuracy of health news can be shared more widely across the chain of communication, from researchers and institutions to journalists.

Methods

Design and registration

We conducted a parallel-group, randomised controlled trial with press releases as the unit of allocation (the "participants"). The trial used a 2 × 2 factorial design in which press releases were allocated to one of four conditions: control (no intervention), claim alignment, causality statement, or both interventions. The trial was registered (ISRCTN10492618) before data collection and followed an a priori protocol. The study was approved by the relevant university research ethics committee. Because the trial studied institutional communication outputs rather than individuals, and because press offices consented to take part, individual consent was not sought from journalists or readers of the news.

Participating press offices and press releases

Nine press offices took part: journals, universities and research funders that routinely issue press releases on health-related research. Press offices were recruited through professional networks and direct approaches, and agreed to have eligible releases randomised and to receive guidance on the interventions. Eligible press releases concerned health-related topics (including biomedical, psychological and public-health research) and reported either a correlational/observational finding or an experimental finding (e.g. randomised trial) relating an exposure to an outcome. Releases that did not report a relationship between variables (for example, purely descriptive reports or announcements of funding) were excluded. Press releases were identified as they were drafted by press office staff, and each was assigned to a condition before issue to the media.

Interventions

Two interventions were tested, each designed to reflect good practice in conveying causal inference from study design (Sumner et al., 2014; Schwartz et al., 2012).

(a) Claim alignment. The headline and main causal claim of the press release were aligned with the strength of the underlying evidence. For experimental designs, strong causal language (e.g. "X reduces Y") was considered appropriate; for correlational designs, cautious language (e.g. "X is associated with Y", "may be linked to") was recommended, and strong causal wording was avoided. Alignment was assessed against a pre-specified coding framework in which claims were categorised on an ordinal scale from no relationship, through correlational and conditional causal statements, to explicit causal statements.

(b) Causality statement. An explicit statement or caveat about the difficulty of inferring causality from the findings was inserted into the text of the release (for example, noting that an observational study cannot show that one factor causes another, or identifying possible confounders). Statements were required to be in the body of the release and, where possible, attributed to the researchers or to an independent expert.

Allocation

Press releases were allocated to conditions by random assignment using a computer-generated sequence, administered by the research team, with the aim of approximately equal group sizes. Allocation was conducted within press office to guard against differences between institutions. Owing to practical constraints and spontaneous adoption of good practice by press offices, group sizes ended unequal (control = 89, claim alignment = 64, causality statement = 79, both = 80; total N = 312). Press office staff could not be blinded to condition because they were required to implement the interventions. Coders of news content were blind to allocation, and coders were not aware of the allocation of the press release that generated each news item where practicable.

Press offices were free to decide whether to implement the allocated intervention; releases in which the intervention was not implemented were retained in their allocated group for intention-to-treat analysis and reclassified for as-treated analysis. 

Outcomes and data collection

News articles were identified by searches of news databases and web searches using key terms from each press release's title and the associated study, as well as by checking for direct reproduction of release text. Searches were conducted for a fixed period after the release date. We included English-language international and national media, including newspapers, websites and broadcast (N = 2257 news stories).

The primary outcomes were news content: (1) headline alignment, that is, whether the headline's causal strength matched the study design; (2) alignment of the main causal claim; and (3) the presence of an explicit causality statement or caveat in the news story. Secondary outcomes were (4) news uptake, defined as the proportion of press releases that obtained at least one news story, and (5) feasibility, defined as the proportion of press releases implementing cautious headlines, cautious claims and caveats, compared with a pre-trial baseline sample of releases from the same press offices.

Content coding

Press releases and news stories were coded by trained coders using a detailed manual adapted from previous work (Sumner et al., 2014). Coders recorded study design (experimental or correlational), the main causal claim, the headline claim, and presence of caveats about causality or other limitations. Headlines and claims were coded as aligned when strong causal statements accompanied experimental designs and non-causal or cautious statements accompanied correlational designs. A subset of material was double-coded to assess inter-coder reliability, with disagreements resolved by discussion; reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa.

Statistical analysis

The unit of analysis for news content was the press release (aggregating news stories derived from it), with consideration of clustering of news stories within releases and of releases within press offices. We used logistic regression to compare the proportions of releases/news with aligned headlines, aligned claims and caveats between intervention and comparison conditions, estimating odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals. Models adjusted for press office and, where relevant, study design. For the factorial design, the effect of each intervention was estimated by comparing all releases receiving that intervention (alone or combined) with all those not receiving it, with interaction between interventions examined.

Two analytic approaches were used. The primary approach was intention-to-treat (ITT), in which press releases were analysed according to their allocated condition irrespective of whether the intervention was implemented. Because of non-compliance and spontaneous adoption in the control groups, we also performed as-treated (AT) analyses, in which releases were grouped by whether they actually contained the aligned claim or the causality statement. We stress that AT analyses break randomisation and are therefore correlational, although the mechanism linking releases to news (reuse of release content) is known.

News uptake was analysed using logistic regression of whether each release attracted any news coverage, again under ITT and AT. We assessed whether there was evidence of reduced uptake in releases with cautious claims or caveats; equivalence was judged by the confidence intervals of the odds ratios.

Feasibility was assessed by comparing the proportion of trial releases with cautious headlines, claims and caveats with a pre-trial sample of releases from the same offices, using logistic regression and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Analyses were conducted in standard statistical software, with two-sided tests and a significance level of 0.05.

Results

**Sample and flow of press releases**

Nine press offices (journals, universities and funders) contributed 312 press releases on health-related topics. Of these, 89 were allocated to the control condition, 64 to claim alignment, 79 to causality statement and 80 to both interventions. For the main factorial comparisons, 144 press releases were allocated to aligned headlines and claims (claim alignment plus both) and 168 to non-aligned (control plus causality statement). Likewise, 159 were allocated to explicit causality statements (causality statement plus both) and 153 to no statement (control plus claim alignment). The press releases generated 2257 English-language news stories in international and national newspapers, websites and broadcast media. Unless stated otherwise, the ranges given for odds ratios (OR) are 95% confidence intervals. Intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses compared groups as allocated. As-treated (AT) analyses compared groups according to whether the press release actually contained the intervention content as written. Because press offices sometimes adopted cautious wording spontaneously in control press releases, or did not fully implement the allocated intervention, ITT and AT estimates differ, and the contrast was generally larger in the AT analyses.

**Alignment of news headlines with the evidence**

Press release alignment was associated with better alignment of news headlines with the underlying evidence (strong claims for experimental designs, cautious claims for correlational designs). In the ITT analysis, 56% of headlines were aligned when the press release was allocated to alignment, compared with 52% when it was not (OR = 1.2 to 1.9). The AT analysis showed a much larger difference: 60% of headlines were aligned when the press release was actually aligned, compared with 32% when it was not (OR = 1.3 to 4.4). Thus, even headlines, which are typically written by news editors rather than reporters, followed the claims made in the press release.

**Alignment of main causal claims in news**

The main causal claims in the body of news stories also tended to follow those of the press release, but the evidence was less consistent across analyses. In the ITT analysis, 62% of news claims were aligned with the evidence for press releases allocated to alignment, versus 60% for those not allocated (OR = 0.7 to 1.6), so the interval was compatible with no effect. In the AT analysis, 67% of news claims were aligned when the press release claim was aligned, compared with 39% when it was not (OR = 1.4 to 5.7), a statistically significant difference.

**Explicit statements and caveats about causal inference in news**

A similar pattern emerged for explicit statements or caveats about inferring causality from correlational findings. In the ITT analysis, 15% of news stories linked to press releases allocated to a causality statement contained a caveat, compared with 10% of those linked to press releases not allocated to one (OR = 0.9 to 2.6). In the AT analysis the difference was marked: 20% of news stories contained a caveat when the press release did, compared with 0% when it did not (OR = 16 to 156). The very wide interval reflects the absence of any caveats in the comparison group, which makes the AT estimate imprecise. It nevertheless shows that, in this sample, caveats appeared in news almost exclusively when they were present in the press release. Even so, caveats remained uncommon in news overall, appearing in a minority of stories even under the most favourable condition.

**News uptake**

We examined whether the interventions reduced the proportion of press releases that gained news coverage. For aligned headlines and claims, uptake was identical in the ITT analysis (55% vs 55%, OR = 0.7 to 1.3). In the AT analysis, 58% of aligned press releases gained coverage compared with 60% of non-aligned press releases (OR = 0.7 to 1.7). The intervals were compatible with modest differences in either direction, but there was no evidence that cautious headlines and claims reduced news interest.

For causality statements and caveats, ITT uptake was 53% for press releases allocated to include a statement and 56% for those not allocated (OR = 0.8 to 1.0), which suggests at most a very small reduction in uptake, with the upper bound at no difference. In the AT analysis, uptake was higher for press releases that included a causality statement: 66% versus 52% (OR = 1.3 to 2.7). Given the observational nature of the AT comparison, this should not be interpreted as a benefit of caveats, but it does not suggest that caveats lead to loss of news interest. Across both interventions and both analytical approaches, therefore, we found no consistent evidence that cautious communication reduced the proportion of press releases covered in the news.

**Feasibility of implementing cautious statements**

Feasibility was assessed as the proportion of press releases containing cautious headlines, cautious main claims and explicit caveats, compared with a pre-trial baseline period at the same press offices. All three outcomes increased in the trial period, including in the control condition, indicating spontaneous adoption of the recommended practices. The odds of a cautious headline in press releases were higher than in the pre-trial period (OR = 1.01 to 2.6), as were the odds of cautious main claims (OR = 1.3 to 3.4) and of explicit caveats (OR = 1.1 to 26). The caveat estimate was highly imprecise because explicit caveats were rare at baseline. These increases show that press offices were able to implement the changes in routine practice.

**Summary of ITT and AT findings**

Taken together, the AT analyses showed consistent and sizeable associations between the content of press releases and the content of the resulting news for headlines, main claims and caveats. The ITT analyses showed smaller differences, with only the headline comparison clearly excluding no effect. This attenuation is consistent with the spontaneous adoption of cautious wording across all conditions, including control, which reduced the contrast between allocated groups. The AT results are correlational, since they compare press releases that differed in content for reasons beyond random allocation. Nonetheless, the pathway from press release to news story is well defined, since each news story was linked to its source press release.

Discussion and Conclusions

This randomised trial tested whether two simple changes to press releases, aligning headlines and main claims with the strength of the underlying evidence and adding explicit statements about the difficulty of inferring causality from correlational findings, would carry through to news content and affect news uptake. Headlines in news stories were better aligned with the evidence when the press release headline was aligned, and the same pattern held for main causal claims and for caveats about causality. We found no evidence that more cautious press releases attracted less news coverage. These findings extend earlier observational work showing that exaggeration in news is strongly associated with exaggeration in press releases (Sumner et al. 2014; Sumner et al. 2016), and suggest that this association reflects, at least in part, a causal pathway that can be exploited to improve the quality of health communication.

The results challenge a common assumption that journalists and news editors have no interest in cautious messaging, or that caution reduces newsworthiness. In the as-treated analysis, press releases with aligned headlines and claims received news coverage at rates similar to those of unaligned releases, and releases with causality statements were, if anything, more likely to be covered. The intention-to-treat estimates were similarly compatible with no loss of uptake. Because uptake was a pre-specified outcome and the confidence intervals excluded large reductions, the data are not consistent with a substantial cost in news interest. This is encouraging for press officers, who often cite pressure to "sell" a story as a reason for strong claims. It also fits with the view that much health news is derived from press releases with limited modification, so that the framing set at source has disproportionate influence downstream (Schwartz et al. 2012; Schwitzer 2008).
