After filtering, Gowalla contained 18,737 users, 32,510 POIs, and 1,278,274 check-ins (density 0.21%). Foursquare contained 24,941 users, 28,593 POIs, and 1,196,248 check-ins (0.17%). Yelp contained 30,887 users, 18,995 POIs, and 860,888 check-ins (0.15%). Because the task is based on implicit feedback, each user *u* was represented as a binary vector **x**_u ∈ {0,1}^M, where M is the number of POIs and x_uj = 1 indicates at least one check-in at POI *j*. Repeated visits were collapsed into a single positive observation. For each user, we randomly assigned 70% of check-ins to training, 10% to validation for hyperparameter selection and early stopping, and 20% to testing. The split was repeated with five different random seeds.

**Problem formulation.** Let U and P denote the user and POI sets, and let g_j ∈ ℝ² be the coordinates of POI *j*. The task is to estimate, for each user *u*, a reachability score ŷ_uj for every unvisited POI *j* and to return the top-*k* ranked POIs. Candidate sets for ranking comprised all POIs absent from a user's training and validation records.

**Model architecture.** SAE-NAD is an autoencoder that maps **x**_u to a latent representation (encoder) and reconstructs a dense score vector over all POIs (decoder). The encoder is a self-attentive encoder (SAE). Each POI *j* has an input embedding **e**_j ∈ ℝ^d. Let E_u ∈ ℝ^{n_u×d} stack the embeddings of the n_u POIs visited by user *u*. Rather than average these embeddings or weight them equally, we adopt the multi-dimensional structured self-attention of Lin et al. (2017) to capture several aspects of preference:

A_u = softmax(W₂ tanh(W₁ E_uᵀ)),

where W₁ ∈ ℝ^{t×d} and W₂ ∈ ℝ^{r×t} are learnable parameters, t is the attention hidden size, r is the number of attention aspects (attention "hops"), and the softmax is taken over the user's visited POIs, so that each row of A_u ∈ ℝ^{r×n_u} sums to one. The attended representation is S_u = A_u E_u ∈ ℝ^{r×d}. This is flattened and passed through a fully connected layer with a nonlinear activation to produce the user latent vector **z**_u ∈ ℝ^{h}: **z**_u = σ(W_z vec(S_u) + **b**_z). Each aspect can thus emphasize a different subset of the user's check-ins, for example work-related versus leisure venues, as in Vaswani et al. (2017).

The decoder is a neighbor-aware decoder (NAD). A standard autoencoder decoder would compute ŷ_uj = σ(**w**_jᵀ**z**_u + b_j) and ignore geography. To incorporate geographical context, we add a neighbor term that raises the reachability of POIs that are both similar to, and near, the user's visited POIs. For each POI pair (l, j), we define the neighbor influence

K_lj = ⟨**q**_l, **q**_j⟩ · exp(−‖g_l − g_j‖² / (2ρ²)),

where **q**_j ∈ ℝ^d are decoder-side POI embeddings, ⟨·,·⟩ is the inner product, and the second factor is a radial basis function (RBF) kernel with bandwidth ρ (Schölkopf & Smola, 2002). The final score is

ŷ_uj = σ(**w**_jᵀ**z**_u + b_j + ∑_{l ∈ P_u} K_lj / |P_u|),

with P_u the set of POIs visited by *u*. The inner product models latent similarity, while the RBF kernel decays smoothly with distance. In practice, the kernel is truncated to each visited POI's 100 nearest neighbors, so the neighbor term costs O(|P_u|·100) per user rather than O(|P_u|·M). Distances were computed with the haversine formula.

**Training procedure.** Because only positive feedback is observed, we treated unobserved entries as weak negatives and optimized a weighted binary cross-entropy:

ℒ = −∑_u ∑_j [x_uj log ŷ_uj + α(1−x_uj) log(1−ŷ_uj)] + λ‖Θ‖²,

in which α < 1 downweights unobserved entries (Hu et al., 2008) and Θ denotes all parameters. To avoid computing the loss over all M entries, we sampled five unobserved POIs per positive per epoch. Dropout with rate 0.5 was applied to the latent layer to reduce overfitting (Srivastava et al., 2014), as in denoising and collaborative autoencoders (Wu et al., 2016). Parameters were initialized with the Xavier scheme and optimized with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with learning rate 0.001, mini-batches of 256 users, and a maximum of 200 epochs. Training stopped if validation Recall@10 failed to improve for 10 consecutive epochs. We searched the embedding dimension d ∈ {32, 50, 64, 128}, number of attention aspects r ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 8}, attention size t ∈ {20, 50, 100}, RBF bandwidth ρ ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 5} km, negative weight α ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}, and regularization λ ∈ {10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁴}. Selection used the validation set, one factor at a time around a default configuration. Unless otherwise stated, the reported results use d = 50, r = 3, t = 50, and ρ = 1 km.

**Baselines.** We compared SAE-NAD against representative methods from three families. (i) Classical implicit-feedback and geographical models: WRMF (Hu et al., 2008), Bayesian personalized ranking matrix factorization (BPRMF; Rendle et al., 2009), RankGeoFM (Li et al., 2015), and IRenMF (Liu et al., 2014). (ii) Neural collaborative models: neural collaborative filtering (NeuMF; He et al., 2017), CDAE (Wu et al., 2016), and Mult-VAE (Liang et al., 2018). (iii) Neural POI recommenders: PACE (Yang et al., 2017) and ASMF (Ma et al., 2018). Baseline hyperparameters were tuned on the same validation sets using the ranges recommended in the original publications. To isolate component contributions, we also trained ablated variants: SAE-NAD without attention (mean pooling in place of A_u, "AE-NAD"), without the neighbor term ("SAE-only"), and with the neighbor term but with the RBF kernel removed ("SAE-NAD w/o RBF").

**Evaluation metrics.** Performance was assessed with Precision@k, Recall@k, and Mean Average Precision (MAP@k) at k ∈ {2, 5, 10}, standard top-*k* metrics for POI recommendation (Liu et al., 2017). For user *u*, Precision@k = |R_u^k ∩ T_u|/k and Recall@k = |R_u^k ∩ T_u|/|T_u|, where R_u^k is the ranked top-*k* list and T_u is the set of held-out test POIs. MAP@k averages, over users, the average precision computed at the rank positions of correctly retrieved POIs within the top *k*. Users with no test POIs were excluded, and all metrics were averaged across users.

**Statistical analysis.** Each model was trained and evaluated under five random splits and initializations, and we report means with standard deviations. Differences between SAE-NAD and the strongest baseline on each dataset and metric were tested with a two-sided paired *t*-test across the five runs, with significance at *p* < 0.05. Because multiple metrics were tested, we applied Holm–Bonferroni correction to control the family-wise error rate (Holm, 1979). Relative improvement was computed as (M_ours − M_best baseline)/M_best baseline. Sensitivity to d, r, and ρ was assessed by varying one parameter at a time while holding others at their defaults, and we also stratified users by training check-in count (quartiles) to examine robustness to data sparsity. All experiments were implemented in TensorFlow and run on a single NVIDIA GPU.

Results

Overall performance comparison

Table 2 reports Precision@k (P@k), Recall@k (R@k) and MAP@k for k ∈ {5, 10, 20} on Gowalla, Foursquare and Yelp. All values are averaged over five random splits (80% training, 5% validation, 15% test). We compare SAE-NAD with seven baselines: WRMF (Hu et al., 2008), a weighted matrix factorization model for implicit feedback; GeoMF (Lian et al., 2014) and IRenMF (Liu et al., 2014), which incorporate geographical influence into matrix factorization; RankGeoFM (Li et al., 2015), a ranking-based geographical factorization model; PACE (Yang et al., 2017), a deep embedding model that jointly learns user and POI representations with context prediction; CDAE (Wu et al., 2016), a denoising autoencoder for collaborative filtering; and Mult-VAE (Liang et al., 2018), a variational autoencoder with a multinomial likelihood.

SAE-NAD achieved the best performance on every dataset and metric. On Gowalla, it obtained P@10 = 0.1562, R@10 = 0.1317 and MAP@10 = 0.0845. The strongest baseline, Mult-VAE, obtained 0.1388, 0.1156 and 0.0702, so the relative gains are 12.5%, 13.9% and 20.4%. On Foursquare, the P@10, R@10 and MAP@10 of SAE-NAD were 0.1263, 0.1581 and 0.0953. The best baseline there, PACE, achieved 0.1117, 0.1392 and 0.0794, so the improvements are 13.1%, 13.6% and 20.0%. On the sparsest dataset, Yelp, SAE-NAD obtained P@10 = 0.0618, R@10 = 0.0702 and MAP@10 = 0.0341, against 0.0547, 0.0613 and 0.0278 for the strongest baseline (Mult-VAE), corresponding to gains of 13.0%, 14.5% and 22.7%. The differences were statistically significant in every case (paired t-test, p < 0.01 over the five splits). Improvements were largest at k = 5 and decreased slightly as k grew. For instance, the P@5 gain over the best baseline on Gowalla was 14.8%, against 11.2% for P@20. This pattern suggests that the model ranks the most relevant POIs more accurately at the top of the list, which matters most in practical recommendation.

Several secondary trends can be seen among the baselines. First, the nonlinear models (PACE, CDAE and Mult-VAE) consistently outperformed the linear factorization methods WRMF and GeoMF. Averaged over the three datasets, Mult-VAE improved MAP@10 by 24.6% over WRMF. This supports the premise that user–POI interactions are poorly captured by inner products in a latent space. Second, geographically aware factorization models outperformed their geography-agnostic counterpart. IRenMF and RankGeoFM gained 6.8% and 9.3% in R@10 over WRMF on Gowalla, which confirms the value of spatial context. Third, the autoencoder baselines CDAE and Mult-VAE did not exploit coordinates at all, yet they surpassed the geography-aware matrix factorization methods on Gowalla and Yelp. SAE-NAD combines the nonlinear modeling capacity of the autoencoder family with explicit geographical information, and it outperformed both groups.

Ablation study

To quantify the contribution of each component, we evaluated four variants: (i) AE, in which both the self-attentive encoder and the neighbor-aware decoder are removed, leaving a plain autoencoder; (ii) SAE, which keeps only the self-attentive encoder; (iii) NAD, which keeps only the neighbor-aware decoder; and (iv) the full SAE-NAD. Figure 3 shows MAP@10 and R@10 for these variants. On Gowalla, the plain AE reached MAP@10 = 0.0671. Adding the self-attentive encoder raised this to 0.0749 (+11.6%), and adding the neighbor-aware decoder raised it to 0.0772 (+15.1%). The full model reached 0.0845, which is 25.9% above the plain AE. The two components thus contribute complementary rather than redundant information, because the gain of the combined model is nearly additive. Similar patterns were observed on Foursquare (AE 0.0731, SAE 0.0812, NAD 0.0846, SAE-NAD 0.0953) and on Yelp (AE 0.0248, SAE 0.0280, NAD 0.0297, SAE-NAD 0.0341). The neighbor-aware decoder was the more important component on all three datasets. The gap was largest on Foursquare, where check-ins are strongly clustered in urban areas and proximity is therefore highly informative.

We also compared the multi-dimensional attention mechanism with a standard single-vector additive attention (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and with uniform weighting of checked-in POIs. Replacing multi-dimensional attention with single-vector attention reduced R@10 by 3.9% on Gowalla and 4.4% on Foursquare. Uniform weighting reduced it by 7.8% and 8.6%, respectively. Using the RBF kernel alone in the decoder, without the POI-embedding inner product, decreased MAP@10 by 5.7% on Gowalla, and using the inner product alone, without the RBF kernel, decreased it by 6.9%. Hence both the semantic similarity between POIs and their geographical proximity are needed for the decoder to be effective.

Hyperparameter sensitivity

We examined the sensitivity of SAE-NAD to the latent dimension d, the number of attention dimensions r, and the RBF kernel bandwidth. Performance increased with d from 20 to 100 and then saturated. On Gowalla, R@10 rose from 0.1189 at d = 20 to 0.1301 at d = 50 and 0.1317 at d = 100, with no meaningful improvement at d = 200 (0.1314). We therefore fixed d = 100 for the main experiments. For the number of attention dimensions, performance improved steadily from r = 1 (R@10 = 0.1262) to r = 5 (0.1317). Beyond r = 10 it declined slightly (0.1298 at r = 20), probably because of overfitting with highly sparse check-in histories. The RBF bandwidth had a clear optimum. Very small values made the geographical influence too local to propagate to useful neighbors, and very large values made the kernel nearly uniform, so that distant POIs were treated like close ones. The best MAP@10 was reached at intermediate values, and results varied by less than 3% within the neighborhood of the optimum, which indicates reasonable robustness. Finally, the dropout rate had a moderate effect, with 0.3–0.5 giving the best results on all datasets.

Performance across user activity levels

Because check-in data are heavily long-tailed, we split test users into three groups according to the number of training check-ins: inactive (fewer than 10), moderate (10–30) and active (more than 30). On Gowalla, the inactive group made up 41.2% of users. For this group, SAE-NAD obtained R@10 = 0.0963, against 0.0794 for Mult-VAE (+21.3%) and 0.0781 for PACE (+23.3%). The advantage narrowed for active users, where SAE-NAD improved on Mult-VAE by 8.9% (0.1804 versus 0.1657). Geographical neighbors compensate for limited interaction history, and the attention mechanism can emphasize the few informative check-ins that sparse users have. For active users, the baselines already have sufficient data to estimate preferences, which leaves less room for improvement. A similar trend appeared on Yelp, where the improvement for inactive users was 19.7%, against 9.4% for active ones.

Efficiency

We finally compared training cost on a single NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti GPU. SAE-NAD converged in approximately 40 epochs on Gowalla, with an average of 11.3 seconds per epoch, so total training took about 7.5 minutes. This is comparable to CDAE (about 6.8 minutes) and much faster than PACE (about 31 minutes), which requires joint training of user and POI embeddings with context prediction. The RBF kernel is computed once from the POI coordinates and can be reused throughout training, so the neighbor-aware decoder adds only 9% to the per-epoch time of the plain autoencoder. These results indicate that the accuracy gains of SAE-NAD do not come with prohibitive computational costs.

Discussion and Conclusion

The experiments reported above show that combining a self-attentive encoder with a neighbor-aware decoder yields consistent improvements over strong baselines on three LBSN datasets. SAE-NAD improved Precision@k, Recall@k, and MAP@k at every cutoff we examined. Relative to the strongest competing method, the gains were most pronounced on the sparsest dataset, where Recall@10 increased by roughly 8–12%. In this section we interpret these results, relate them to prior work, and discuss limitations and implications.

**Interpretation of the main findings.** Three observations stand out. First, autoencoder-based collaborative filtering clearly benefits from non-linear modeling of user–POI interactions. Linear and bilinear factorization approaches, including weighted matrix factorization (Hu et al., 2008) and its geographically augmented variants (Lian et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015), were consistently outperformed by neural approaches such as those of Wu et al. (2016) and Liang et al. (2018). This pattern is consistent with the view that check-in behavior is governed by interacting factors, such as category preference, spatial convenience, and social or temporal routines, which a single inner product of latent vectors cannot easily express. The performance gap between our model and these baselines supports this interpretation.

Second, the ablation results indicate that the two components contribute complementary gains. Replacing the multi-dimensional attention with mean pooling over checked-in POI embeddings reduced performance substantially. This suggests that treating all visited POIs as equally informative discards useful signal. A user's history typically mixes habitual visits, such as a workplace cafeteria, with more preference-revealing ones, such as an infrequently visited specialty venue. Attention weights learned in multiple subspaces allow the encoder to emphasize different subsets of the history for different latent aspects, in the spirit of structured self-attention (Lin et al., 2017) and Transformer-style architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017). The case studies we examined showed that different attention dimensions concentrated on semantically coherent groups of POIs, such as dining venues versus transit-adjacent locations. These are qualitative observations from a limited set of users, however, and should not be read as proof that each dimension encodes a distinct interpretable factor. Prior analyses have cautioned that attention weights are not always faithful explanations of model behavior (Jain & Wallace, 2019).

Third, removing the neighbor-aware decoder, or replacing the RBF kernel with a uniform or purely distance-thresholded alternative, degraded accuracy. The decoder raises the predicted reachability of POIs that are both geographically close to and embedding-similar to a user's visited POIs. This reflects the first law of geography as it operates in human mobility: users tend to visit places near those they already know (Ye et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2012). A key difference from earlier approaches is that geography is not imposed as a hard prior or a separate additive score. It enters multiplicatively with learned POI similarity, so a nearby but dissimilar POI receives less boost than a nearby and similar one. This design likely explains why our model outperformed methods that model geographical influence through independent distributions, such as the multi-center Gaussian formulation of Cheng et al. (2012) or the kernel density estimation used by Zhang and Chow (2013). Sensitivity analyses further showed that performance varied smoothly with the kernel bandwidth and the number of attention dimensions, which suggests that the gains do not depend on narrow hyperparameter tuning.

**Limitations.** Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, our model treats check-in histories as unordered sets. Sequential and temporal dynamics, including time-of-day effects, recency, and transition patterns between consecutive visits, are not modeled. Recurrent and attention-based sequential recommenders (Feng et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019) capture such dynamics and may be preferable for next-POI prediction, whereas our formulation targets general, long-term preference modeling. Second, the neighbor-aware decoder relies on pairwise POI distances and a single global kernel bandwidth. Urban density varies greatly: a 500-meter radius is a reasonable neighborhood in a dense downtown but not in a suburban area. A location-adaptive bandwidth might therefore be more appropriate. Third, the computational cost of the decoder grows with the number of POIs, because each user's reachability is computed against all candidate locations and their neighbors. Although this was manageable on our datasets, scaling to city- or country-level catalogs with millions of POIs would require sparsification, approximate nearest-neighbor search, or negative sampling. Fourth, the model uses only check-in data and POI coordinates. Textual reviews, categories, social ties, and images, all of which have been shown to help in related work, are not exploited, and the cold-start problem for new users and new POIs remains unaddressed.

There are also limitations of evaluation. Our datasets come from a small number of platforms and regions, and the sparsity levels and spatial distributions may not represent other settings. We followed the common practice of removing users and POIs with very few check-ins and of randomly splitting each user's history into training and test portions. Such protocols can overstate performance relative to a chronological split, and they ignore exposure bias: unobserved POIs are not necessarily disliked, and check-ins reflect what users were able and inclined to visit, not only what they prefer. Finally, the reported improvements are averages over users; we did not systematically examine whether gains are uniform across user groups, for instance travelers versus locals, or across popular versus long-tail POIs. Recommenders trained on implicit feedback are known to favor popular items (Abdollahpouri et al., 2019), and it remains to be verified whether our model mitigates or amplifies this tendency.

**Implications and future work.** From a methodological standpoint, the results suggest that contextual information such as geography is best integrated where it interacts with the learned representation, here the decoder, rather than as an external post hoc re-ranking. This principle may extend to other contextual signals, such as temporal proximity or category hierarchies, by defining analogous kernels over those spaces. From a practical standpoint, the improvement on sparse data is encouraging for deployments in which most users have few recorded visits. Nevertheless, because location histories are highly sensitive, practitioners must consider privacy. Approaches such as federated training or differential privacy could be combined with autoencoder-based recommenders, although their effect on accuracy would need to be measured.

In conclusion, we proposed SAE-NAD, an autoencoder that encodes user histories with multi-dimensional self-attention and decodes them with a neighbor-aware, RBF-weighted mechanism that incorporates geographical context. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrated consistent gains over state-of-the-art baselines, and ablation and sensitivity analyses confirmed the contribution of each component. Future work will incorporate sequential and temporal information, adaptive spatial kernels, auxiliary content, and cold-start handling, and will examine fairness, popularity bias, and privacy in large-scale deployments.

Introduction

Insufficient physical activity is among the leading modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, several cancers, and premature mortality. Globally, physical inactivity is estimated to account for 6% to 10% of the burden of major noncommunicable diseases and for roughly 9% of premature deaths (Lee et al., 2012). Despite the well-documented benefits of regular activity, only about one in four U.S. adults meets national guidelines for both aerobic and muscle-strengthening activity (Blackwell & Clarke, 2018; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018). The burden of inactivity is not distributed evenly. Adults in rural areas report less leisure-time physical activity and have a higher prevalence of obesity than their urban counterparts, with national estimates of obesity of approximately 40% in rural settings versus 33% in urban settings (Befort et al., 2012). Rural residents also face structural barriers to activity, including dispersed destinations, limited recreational infrastructure, fewer programs, and constrained public health resources (Frost et al., 2010; Bauman et al., 2012).

A substantial evidence base now exists on how to promote physical activity at the population level. The Community Guide for Preventive Services, developed by the Community Preventive Services Task Force, recommends a portfolio of strategies spanning three broad domains: informational approaches (e.g., community-wide campaigns), behavioral and social approaches (e.g., social support in community settings and individually adapted health behavior change), and environmental and policy approaches (e.g., creation of or enhanced access to places for physical activity combined with informational outreach) (Kahn et al., 2002; Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2016). Socioecological models further hold that sustained behavior change is most likely when individual-level support is combined with change in the social, physical, and policy contexts in which people live (Sallis et al., 2006; Sallis et al., 2012). Community-wide multicomponent interventions grounded in these principles are therefore a promising means of shifting population activity levels.

Evidence for such interventions, however, derives disproportionately from large urban and suburban settings, from clinical or school samples, or from rural communities with relatively stable and demographically homogeneous populations. Systematic reviews of rural physical activity interventions have consistently noted the small number of well-evaluated studies, short follow-up periods, and limited attention to implementation processes and contextual fit (Umstattd Meyer et al., 2016; Based on these gaps, rural communities remain underrepresented in the dissemination literature). Moreover, "rural" is not a monolithic category. Micropolitan communities, defined by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget as having an urban core of 10,000 to 49,999 residents, occupy an intermediate position: they are larger and more service-rich than remote rural towns, yet they typically lack the public transit, parks and recreation departments, and philanthropic and academic infrastructure of metropolitan areas. How evidence-based recommendations should be adapted for mid-size rural communities is not well understood.

This gap is compounded in micropolitan communities that have become new immigrant destinations. Beginning in the 1990s, immigration from Latin America and elsewhere shifted away from traditional gateway states and cities toward the rural Midwest and South, often driven by labor demand in meatpacking, food processing, and agriculture (Massey, 2008; Lichter, 2012). Many Midwestern towns have consequently experienced rapid demographic change within a single generation, with linguistically and culturally diverse newcomers settling alongside long-term residents. Immigrant and Latino adults in the United States often report lower rates of leisure-time physical activity than non-Latino White adults, and activity patterns tend to decline with acculturation and time in the United States (Crespo et al., 1996; Marquez & Bryan, 2011). Newcomers in new destinations may also confront language barriers, long and physically demanding work shifts, limited transportation, unfamiliarity with local resources, and strained institutional capacity to serve them (Lichter, 2012). Interventions developed elsewhere cannot be assumed to translate without modification into such settings, and the literature offers few examples of community-wide physical activity interventions designed for communities that are simultaneously rural and rapidly diversifying.

Lay health advisor models, also described as promotores de salud or community health workers, offer one plausible approach to bridging these gaps. Lay health advisors are trusted community members who receive training to provide social support, information, and navigation to peers, and they have been shown to improve health behaviors and outcomes in underserved and minority populations (Balcázar et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2014). Evidence from Latino and rural communities indicates that peer-led walking groups and other group-based activities can increase physical activity while building social capital and local capacity for sustaining programs (Ayala et al., 2011; Cleland et al., 2012). Because lay leaders are embedded in community networks, they can also serve as conduits for informational campaigns and as advocates for environmental and policy improvements. Yet few studies have integrated a lay health advisor approach with the full range of Community Guide recommendations in a single community-wide effort, and fewer still have done so in a micropolitan new destination.

Closing this gap also requires attention to how evidence-based interventions are adapted and evaluated. Adaptation frameworks emphasize the systematic modification of intervention content, delivery, and context to improve fit while preserving core functions (Escoffery et al., 2018), and community-based participatory research principles stress shared decision-making between researchers and community partners throughout this process (Israel et al., 1998). Evaluation frameworks such as RE-AIM encourage assessment not only of effectiveness but also of reach, adoption, implementation, and maintenance, which are dimensions of particular relevance to resource-constrained settings (Glasgow et al., 1999). Community-wide interventions are difficult to evaluate with a single design, and combining population-level surveillance with longitudinal cohort data, observational measures of the environment, and qualitative and process data can yield a more complete account of what changes, for whom, and why.

In this paper, we describe the design and early implementation of Active Ottumwa, a community-wide intervention to increase physical activity in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents in the rural southeastern part of the state. Ottumwa has experienced substantial demographic change linked to employment in meatpacking and related industries, and now has a sizable and growing Latino population. Active Ottumwa is part of a community-academic partnership in which local organizations and residents helped to shape the intervention. The initiative adapts strategies recommended by the Community Guide across behavioral and social, campaign and informational, and environmental and policy domains, using trained lay health advisors, referred to here as physical activity leaders, as the central delivery mechanism for group-based activities such as walking groups, tai chi, and yoga.

The overarching research question is whether a multicomponent, lay health advisor–based intervention grounded in Community Guide recommendations can increase physical activity among residents of a micropolitan new destination community. Secondary questions concern the reach of the intervention across population subgroups, the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted strategies, and the contextual factors that facilitate or constrain implementation.

This report makes three contributions. First, it extends the evidence base on physical activity promotion to a setting that is underrepresented in the literature: a mid-size rural community undergoing immigration-driven demographic change. Second, it documents a transparent process for adapting and integrating evidence-based, multilevel strategies through a community-academic partnership, including the training and deployment of 45 physical activity leaders and the execution of a five-channel communication campaign. Third, it presents a multi-method evaluation design, combining a cross-sectional community survey, a longitudinal cohort, observational data, key informant interviews, and project records, that may serve as a model for evaluating community-wide interventions in similar settings. By describing implementation in detail, we aim to inform practitioners and researchers seeking to translate evidence-based recommendations into the diverse rural communities where they are most needed.

Methods

**Study Setting and Design**

Active Ottumwa is a community-wide, multi-component intervention developed within a community-academic partnership in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents in the southeastern part of the state. Ottumwa is a new immigrant destination. Meatpacking and related industries have drawn growing Latino and Pacific Islander populations, and the city is more ethnically and linguistically diverse than most rural Iowa communities. The partnership includes university researchers, local public health and healthcare organizations, city and parks officials, schools, faith-based organizations, and residents. Consistent with community-based participatory research principles (Israel et al., 1998), partners helped prioritize physical activity as a health concern, review intervention materials for cultural and linguistic appropriateness, and interpret early findings. We used a single-community, pre-post design with multiple data sources. A convergent mixed-methods framework guided evaluation, so quantitative and qualitative data were collected in parallel and integrated at interpretation (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). The study protocol was approved by the University of Iowa Institutional Review Board, and all participants gave informed consent in English or Spanish.

**Intervention Development and Components**

We selected intervention strategies from the Community Guide for Preventive Services recommendations for physical activity (Task Force on Community Preventive Services, 2002; Kahn et al., 2002) and adapted them through partner review of local assets, barriers, and resources. Three categories of approaches were implemented.

*Behavioral and social approaches.* The central strategy used a lay health advisor model. Lay health advisors, termed physical activity leaders, were recruited through partner organizations, workplaces, churches, and neighborhood networks, with deliberate outreach to residents who were bilingual or who were trusted in immigrant communities. Eligible leaders were aged 18 years or older, lived or worked in Ottumwa, and were willing to lead or support at least one activity for 12 months. Leaders completed a structured training of about 8 hours covering physical activity guidelines (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018), group facilitation, safety and injury prevention, motivational communication, and program logistics. Content was informed by social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1986), emphasizing self-efficacy, modeling, and social support. Leaders then established community-based walking groups, tai chi classes, and yoga classes in locations and at times chosen by participants. Leaders could also receive refresher sessions and ongoing technical support from study staff.

*Campaign and informational approaches.* We developed a community-wide communication campaign delivered over five channels: local print media, radio, social media, community events with printed materials, and signage or flyers placed at partner sites. Messages were tested with community members, and key materials were produced in English and Spanish. The campaign promoted the benefits of physical activity, publicized local opportunities including leader-led groups, and encouraged use of existing parks and trails.

*Environmental and policy approaches.* Working with city and parks partners, we identified and promoted low-cost changes that support activity, such as wayfinding and trail signage, publicized walking routes, and improved access to existing facilities. We also documented policy discussions and actions relevant to active living, including shared-use arrangements and municipal planning efforts.

**Evaluation Framework**

Evaluation followed the RE-AIM framework (Glasgow et al., 1999), assessing reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance. Evaluation methods comprised a cross-sectional community survey, a longitudinal cohort, systematic observation, key informant interviews, and project records.

**Cross-Sectional Community Survey**

To assess population-level change, we planned repeated cross-sectional surveys of adult Ottumwa residents at baseline and at the end of the intervention period. Households were sampled from an address-based frame, and one adult per household was selected using the next-birthday method. Residents could complete the survey online, by mail, or by interviewer-assisted telephone or in-person administration, in English or Spanish. The instrument assessed leisure-time and transportation-related physical activity with the International Physical Activity Questionnaire short form (Craig et al., 2003), along with perceived neighborhood environment, social support for activity, self-efficacy, awareness of Active Ottumwa messages and programs, and sociodemographic characteristics. Awareness items measured exposure to each campaign channel and participation in leader-led activities. Survey weights adjusted for unequal selection probability and for nonresponse and were calibrated to American Community Survey estimates for age, sex, and ethnicity.

**Longitudinal Cohort**

We recruited a cohort of adult residents through community events, partner organizations, leader networks, and direct outreach, including both people who participated in leader-led programs and those who did not. Participants completed baseline and 12-month assessments, with additional follow-up planned. Data collection included self-reported physical activity (Craig et al., 2003), sociodemographic and health characteristics, and psychosocial measures. A subsample wore hip-mounted accelerometers for 7 days, with valid wear defined as at least 10 hours per day on at least 4 days (Troiano et al., 2008). Height, weight, and blood pressure were measured by trained staff using standard protocols. Retention strategies included flexible scheduling, bilingual staff, reminder contacts through multiple modes, and modest participation incentives. Retention was calculated as the proportion of baseline participants completing the 12-month assessment, and we compared baseline characteristics of completers and non-completers to evaluate differential attrition.

**Observational Data**

We used the System for Observing Play and Recreation in Communities (SOPARC; McKenzie et al., 2006) to estimate the number, activity level, and demographic characteristics of people using selected parks, trails, and other public spaces. Trained observers conducted scans at fixed target areas several times daily on multiple days across seasons, with a subset of scans double-coded to assess interrater reliability using Cohen’s kappa. Observations were scheduled before and after implementation of campaign and environmental components to assess changes in use.

**Key Informant Interviews**

Semi-structured interviews were conducted with purposively sampled stakeholders, including physical activity leaders, city officials, healthcare and school representatives, and leaders from immigrant communities. The interview guide was informed by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (Damschroder et al., 2009) and addressed perceived barriers and facilitators, community readiness, intervention acceptability, and prospects for sustainability. Interviews lasted 30 to 60 minutes, were conducted in English or Spanish, and were audio recorded and professionally transcribed. Spanish-language transcripts were translated and checked by a bilingual team member. Recruitment continued until thematic saturation was reached (Guest et al., 2006).

**Project Records**

Project records documented implementation processes and reach. These included the number of leaders recruited, trained, and retained; their demographic characteristics; the number, type, location, and frequency of activity sessions; attendance counts; leader activity logs; campaign outputs and dissemination dates; and partner meeting notes. Fidelity was assessed by comparing implemented activities with the planned protocol, and documented adaptations were classified by type and rationale.

**Statistical and Qualitative Analysis**

Analyses will follow the RE-AIM domains. Descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, medians, and proportions, will summarize leader characteristics, session attendance, campaign exposure, and participant characteristics. Reach will be estimated as the proportion of survey respondents and cohort members reporting participation in Active Ottumwa activities, and representativeness will be examined by comparing participants with the Ottumwa population using chi-square tests and standardized differences.

For cross-sectional survey data, changes between baseline and follow-up in meeting aerobic physical activity guidelines (at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-to-vigorous activity) will be evaluated with weighted logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, education, and income. Continuous outcomes such as weekly minutes of activity will be modeled using linear or generalized linear models with appropriate transformation for skewness. For the cohort, we will use linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants to estimate change from baseline to 12 months (Fitzmaurice et al., 2011), and generalized estimating equations (Liang & Zeger, 1986) for binary outcomes. Models will include time, exposure to the intervention (participation in leader-led activities and campaign awareness, modeled as dose), and their interaction, with adjustment for covariates. Missing data will be addressed with multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption, and sensitivity analyses will examine complete-case results and inverse-probability weighting for attrition. Accelerometer data will be summarized as daily minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity using established cut points. Observational SOPARC data will be analyzed as counts of users per scan with Poisson or negative binomial regression comparing pre- and post-implementation periods, adjusting for season, day type, and area. Two-sided P values below .05 will indicate statistical significance, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals will be emphasized. Analyses will be conducted in Stata or R.

Interview transcripts will be analyzed using directed content analysis (Hsieh & Shannon, 2005), with an initial codebook based on CFIR constructs and iterative addition of inductive codes. Two coders will independently code a subset of transcripts, resolve discrepancies by consensus, and calculate intercoder agreement before coding the remainder in qualitative analysis software. Community partners will review summarized findings as a member-checking step. Quantitative and qualitative results will be integrated through joint displays to explain variation in reach, implementation, and effectiveness.

Results

**Intervention implementation**

Implementation of Active Ottumwa followed the three categories of strategies recommended by the Community Guide for Preventive Services: behavioral and social, campaign and informational, and environmental and policy approaches (Kahn et al., 2002; Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2017). Results are reported using RE-AIM dimensions where applicable (Glasgow et al., 1999). At the time of writing, the project was in its second year of intervention delivery.

**Physical activity leaders and behavioral and social strategies.** Forty-five lay health advisors, termed physical activity leaders (PALs), were recruited and trained across two training cohorts (n = 26 and n = 19). Recruitment drew on churches, worksite wellness programs, the community college, ethnic community organizations, and the local school district. The mean age of PALs was 44.3 years (SD 12.1; range 21–71), and 38 (84.4%) were women. Twenty-one PALs (46.7%) identified as Hispanic or Latino, 3 (6.7%) as Pacific Islander, and 21 (46.7%) as non-Hispanic White, which broadly reflects the demographic composition of the target community. Twenty-eight PALs (62.2%) reported a language other than English as their primary language at home, and 17 (37.8%) delivered sessions in Spanish or bilingually. All 45 completed the 8-hour core training, and 41 (91.1%) remained active at 12 months after training.

Active PALs established 34 recurring physical activity groups: 22 walking groups, 7 tai chi classes, and 5 yoga classes. Over the first 18 months of implementation, 1,846 sessions were documented in PAL logs, with a median of 48 sessions per group (interquartile range [IQR] 26–71). Mean attendance was 9.4 participants per session (SD 4.2), and 612 unique individuals attended at least one session, equivalent to approximately 2.4% of the city’s adult population. Of these participants, 71.6% were women, 38.4% identified as Hispanic or Latino, and 52.1% were aged 50 years or older. Among participants attending at least four sessions (n = 347), the median number of sessions attended was 14 (IQR 7–29). Walking groups accounted for 64.9% of all sessions, tai chi for 20.8%, and yoga for 14.3%. Tai chi sessions attracted the highest proportion of adults aged 60 years or older (58.2%), whereas yoga sessions had the highest proportion of participants younger than 40 years (44.0%).

**Communication and informational campaign.** The campaign used five channels: local radio (English and Spanish), a local newspaper, social media, printed materials distributed through community venues, and signage and banners along walking routes. Across the campaign period, 1,240 radio spots were broadcast (608 in Spanish), 36 newspaper features or columns were published, and 214 social media posts generated 48,310 impressions and 3,972 engagements. A total of 18,500 printed materials were distributed through 52 community sites, and 31 route signs were installed. In the cross-sectional community survey conducted after the first campaign wave, 41.7% of respondents (n = 412 of 988) reported awareness of the Active Ottumwa name or logo. Awareness was highest for printed materials (27.3%) and radio (22.6%), and lower for social media (12.9%) and newspaper (11.4%). Awareness was lower among respondents with less than a high school education (28.5%) than among those with at least some college education (47.2%; χ² = 19.4, p < 0.001), but did not differ significantly between Hispanic (39.1%) and non-Hispanic (42.6%) respondents (p = 0.41).

**Environmental and policy approaches.** Working with the city parks department, the public works office, and the school district, the project team and community partners completed audits of 14 walking routes and 6 parks using the Community Pedestrian Audit Tool. Audits identified a mean of 5.2 environmental barriers per route, most commonly missing or damaged sidewalks (38%) and inadequate lighting (24%). Based on these findings, partners installed lighting and wayfinding markers on 4 routes, and the city council adopted a resolution to prioritize sidewalk repairs near 3 elementary schools. Two worksites and one school district adopted written policies allowing walking breaks or community use of facilities outside school hours.

**Cohort recruitment and retention**

The longitudinal cohort comprised 402 adults recruited through door-to-door outreach, community events, and PAL networks. Mean age at baseline was 47.6 years (SD 15.3), and 64.7% were women. Participants self-identified as Hispanic or Latino (33.1%), Pacific Islander (7.5%), non-Hispanic White (51.2%), and other race or ethnicity (8.2%). Nearly one-third (31.8%) reported less than a high school education, and 44.3% reported annual household income below $35,000. Mean body mass index was 30.1 kg/m² (SD 6.7), and 38.6% of participants met the criteria for obesity. At 12 months, 331 participants (82.3%) completed follow-up assessment. Attrition was slightly higher among men (23.1%) than women (14.6%; p = 0.02) and among participants younger than 35 years (24.8%) than among those aged 35 years or older (15.9%; p = 0.03), but did not differ by ethnicity or education.

**Baseline physical activity and preliminary findings**

At baseline, 46.5% of cohort participants met the federal aerobic guideline of at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity per week (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018), based on self-report using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire short form (Craig et al., 2003). Median self-reported weekly moderate-to-vigorous activity was 120 minutes (IQR 20–300). Among the 214 participants who wore accelerometers for at least four valid days, mean daily wear time was 13.1 hours (SD 1.4), and mean moderate-to-vigorous activity was 19.8 minutes per day (SD 15.6); 18.2% met the guideline on the basis of accelerometer-measured activity, which was substantially lower than the self-reported proportion, consistent with known overreporting in questionnaire-based measures (Prince et al., 2008). Hispanic participants reported more occupational activity but fewer minutes of leisure-time activity (median 30 vs. 60 minutes per week; p = 0.008) than non-Hispanic participants.

At 12 months, the proportion meeting the guideline by self-report increased from 46.5% to 54.4% among the 331 participants with complete data (absolute change +7.9 percentage points; McNemar p = 0.01). Median weekly minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity increased from 120 to 150 (Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.004). In a mixed-effects model adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, education, and season, the estimated mean change was +24.6 minutes per week (95% CI 8.3 to 40.9). Among accelerometer-wearing participants with valid data at both time points (n = 158), mean moderate-to-vigorous activity increased by 2.7 minutes per day (95% CI 0.4 to 5.0; p = 0.02). Participants who reported attending at least one PAL-led session (n = 119) showed larger gains in self-reported weekly activity (+46.2 minutes; 95% CI 21.5 to 70.9) than those who did not (+14.8 minutes; 95% CI −3.9 to 33.5), although this comparison was not randomized and should be interpreted cautiously given potential self-selection. These findings are preliminary and are not intended to estimate the causal effect of the intervention, which will be assessed with comparison community data and the second cross-sectional survey wave.

**Qualitative and observational data**

Key informant interviews (n = 22) conducted at 12 months indicated that PALs were viewed as trusted and culturally credible messengers. Eighteen informants (81.8%) identified PAL-led groups as the most visible component of the initiative. Commonly cited barriers included winter weather, limited childcare, and variable work schedules, particularly for shift workers in meatpacking and manufacturing. Direct observation of walking routes (n = 1,120 observation periods across 10 routes) recorded a mean of 11.8 people per hour per route, an increase of 26% relative to the pre-intervention mean of 9.4 (p = 0.03), though differences varied by route and season.

Discussion and Conclusion

This paper describes the design and early implementation of Active Ottumwa, a community-wide, multicomponent intervention to promote physical activity in a micropolitan new destination community. Effectiveness findings are not yet available, so our interpretation is confined to feasibility and implementation. Within that scope, the results suggest that evidence-based recommendations from the Community Guide for Preventive Services can be adapted to a mid-size rural setting with a rapidly diversifying population. In the second year of implementation, 45 lay health advisors (physical activity leaders) have been trained to deliver behavioral and social strategies such as walking groups, tai chi, and yoga. A communication campaign has been completed across five channels, and the longitudinal cohort has been recruited and has completed baseline and 12-month assessments. Together, these milestones indicate that a community-academic partnership can mobilize a multilevel intervention in a setting that is underrepresented in the physical activity literature.

Three features of the intervention warrant interpretation. First, the study draws on the three strategy domains recommended by the Community Guide: behavioral and social approaches, campaign and informational approaches, and environmental and policy approaches (Kahn et al., 2002; Heath et al., 2012). Most evidence supporting these strategies comes from urban or large-metropolitan settings, or from single-component interventions delivered in clinical or school contexts. Rural communities differ in infrastructure, population density, transportation, and the availability of recreational facilities, all of which shape the opportunity structure for activity (Befort et al., 2012; Sallis et al., 2006). By applying the recommendations as a coordinated package, Active Ottumwa reflects an ecological perspective, in which individual behavior is influenced by interpersonal, organizational, community, and policy factors acting together (Sallis et al., 2006). Whether the package yields effects greater than its components is an empirical question that our mixed-methods evaluation can address only partially.

Second, the lay health advisor model is the main mechanism through which adaptation occurred. Lay health advisors and community health workers have been used to extend the reach of health promotion into groups that often have limited contact with formal services, and they have shown promise for improving physical activity and other health behaviors (Balcazar et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2014). In new destination communities, where recent immigrants may face language barriers, unfamiliarity with local resources, and long or irregular work hours, trusted peers may be better placed than outside professionals to build social support and tailor activities to local preferences (Massey, 2008; Lichter, 2012). Recruiting and training 45 leaders in the first phase of implementation suggests that there is community interest in these roles. Offering a range of activities, including low-cost, low-equipment options such as walking, tai chi, and yoga, may also have lowered barriers to participation. Our process data do not yet establish how many residents these leaders have reached or how consistently classes were attended, and these data are needed before conclusions can be drawn about reach and dose.

Third, the intervention was developed and carried out as a community-academic partnership. Principles of community-based participatory research emphasize shared decision-making, co-learning, and attention to local context, and these have been linked to greater relevance, acceptability, and sustainability of interventions (Israel et al., 1998; Wallerstein & Duran, 2006). Cultural adaptation frameworks similarly argue that preserving the core elements of an evidence-based intervention while adapting delivery, language, and content can improve engagement without sacrificing fidelity (Castro et al., 2004; Barrera & Castro, 2006). Our experience suggests that adaptation was more feasible when community partners helped decide which components to retain, modify, or add. The tension between fidelity and fit remains, however, and we have not yet quantified the extent to which adaptations altered the intensity or delivery of the underlying strategies.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The most important is that the present report describes implementation and does not test outcomes. Claims about changes in physical activity, health, or the built environment must await analysis of the full dataset. Second, the evaluation design lacks a randomized or concurrent comparison community. Cross-sectional surveys and a single-site cohort can detect change over time, but secular trends, concurrent local initiatives, and other unmeasured influences may confound observed changes, and causal inference will be limited. Third, the longitudinal cohort is subject to attrition and selection. Participants who agree to be followed may be more motivated or better connected than those who decline, and loss to follow-up may be greater among more mobile or more recently arrived residents, which would threaten both internal and external validity. Fourth, many physical activity measures rely on self-report, which is prone to recall and social desirability bias and may perform differently across language and cultural groups (Prince et al., 2008). We have supplemented surveys with observational data, key informant interviews, and project records, but triangulation cannot fully remove measurement error. Finally, because Ottumwa is a single community with a specific demographic, economic, and political history, the findings may not generalize to all new destination or rural communities, even though the adaptation process may be transferable.

Despite these limitations, the study has strengths that merit emphasis. It addresses a population and setting that are underrepresented in the intervention literature, namely mid-size rural communities that have become immigrant destinations. It uses a multilevel, multicomponent strategy aligned with consensus recommendations. And it employs a multi-method evaluation that can address questions of implementation and context alongside outcomes. The RE-AIM framework, which emphasizes reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance, offers a useful structure for synthesizing these data and for judging public health impact beyond statistical significance (Glasgow et al., 1999). The project records and interviews should be particularly informative on adoption by community organizations and on the factors that influence maintenance once external funding ends. Sustainability is a persistent concern for community-based programs, and the long-term value of the leader network will depend on whether local institutions assume responsibility for training, coordination, and space (Shediac-Rizkallah & Bone, 1998).

The early implementation experience carries several implications for practice and research. For practitioners and local health departments in comparable communities, the results suggest that investing in a cadre of trained peer leaders, offering varied and inexpensive activity options, and coordinating communication through multiple channels are feasible first steps. They also suggest that environmental and policy change, though slower and less visible than program delivery, should be pursued in parallel, because programs alone are unlikely to produce population-level change if the surrounding environment remains unsupportive (Heath et al., 2012). For researchers, our experience highlights the value of documenting adaptation decisions and implementation processes in sufficient detail that others can replicate or modify them. Future work in new destination communities should also examine how language, work schedules, documentation status, and perceived safety shape participation, as these factors are rarely captured in standard physical activity measures.

In conclusion, Active Ottumwa demonstrates that evidence-based recommendations can be translated into a coordinated, community-led effort in a micropolitan new destination community. The first two years have produced a trained network of 45 physical activity leaders, a completed multichannel communication campaign, and a cohort with baseline and 12-month data. Whether these achievements translate into meaningful and sustained increases in physical activity will be determined by the forthcoming outcome analyses. Regardless of the results, the lessons from implementation should help guide efforts to reduce physical inactivity in the many rural communities experiencing demographic change.

# Introduction

Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the leading infectious causes of death worldwide. The World Health Organization estimated that 10.4 million people developed TB and 1.8 million died of the disease in 2015, with the greatest burden in South-East Asia, the Western Pacific and sub-Saharan Africa (World Health Organization 2016). Treatment of drug-susceptible TB uses a standardised six-month regimen: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for four months. When taken correctly, this regimen cures more than 85% of patients (World Health Organization 2016). Its effectiveness is limited, however, by adverse drug reactions, which can lead to interruption or modification of therapy, poor adherence, treatment failure, relapse and the emergence of drug resistance (Yee et al. 2003; Tostmann et al. 2008).

The best-characterised toxicity of first-line anti-tubercular agents is drug-induced liver injury (DILI). Isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide are all potentially hepatotoxic, and reported incidence varies from about 2% to 28% depending on the case definition, the regimen, the population and the intensity of monitoring (Tostmann et al. 2008; Saukkonen et al. 2006). Anti-tubercular DILI can range from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to acute liver failure requiring transplantation, and it carries a recognised case fatality (Saukkonen et al. 2006). Other clinically important reactions include cutaneous hypersensitivity, peripheral neuropathy (chiefly isoniazid-related), gastrointestinal intolerance, hyperuricaemia and arthralgia (pyrazinamide), haematological abnormalities, and optic neuritis (ethambutol). Clinical risk factors for toxicity, including older age, female sex, malnutrition, chronic alcohol use, viral hepatitis and HIV co-infection, explain only part of the observed variability (Yee et al. 2003; Tostmann et al. 2008). Some patients develop severe reactions despite having no identifiable risk factors, while others tolerate the full regimen without difficulty. This pattern has prompted interest in host genetic determinants of susceptibility.

Pharmacogenetic research has concentrated on genes encoding enzymes that metabolise anti-tubercular drugs. N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) acetylates isoniazid to acetylisoniazid, and individuals are classified as rapid, intermediate or slow acetylators by combinations of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) such as *NAT2*5*, *6* and *7*. Slow acetylators clear isoniazid more slowly, which may increase the formation of hepatotoxic metabolites through alternative pathways involving cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1) (Huang et al. 2002). Glutathione S-transferase M1 (GSTM1), a phase II detoxification enzyme, is frequently deleted (null genotype), and this may compromise the clearance of reactive intermediates. Variants in *CYP2E1*, *GSTM1*, *GSTT1*, *GSTP1*, and more recently in genes involved in drug transport (e.g. *SLCO1B1*), immune response (e.g. HLA alleles) and oxidative stress, have also been investigated. Since the early report that slow acetylator status was associated with isoniazid-related hepatitis (Huang et al. 2002), dozens of candidate-gene studies have been published, mostly in East Asian, South Asian, Brazilian and European populations.

Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses have attempted to synthesise this literature, and their conclusions are mixed. Meta-analyses of *NAT2* slow acetylator status have generally reported a statistically significant association with anti-tubercular hepatotoxicity, with pooled odds ratios (ORs) of roughly 3 to 5 (Sun et al. 2008; Wang et al. 2012; Cai et al. 2012). For *CYP2E1* and *GSTM1*, results have been less consistent. Some analyses found an increased risk for the *CYP2E1* c1/c1 genotype or the *GSTM1* null genotype, whereas others found no association, or associations confined to particular ethnic groups (Sun et al. 2008; Cai et al. 2012). Discrepancies of this kind may reflect differences in search strategies, inclusion criteria, genetic models, the handling of heterogeneity, and publication dates. They may also result from the small sample sizes of many primary studies and from differences in how hepatotoxicity was defined, for example transaminase thresholds of two, three or five times the upper limit of normal with or without symptoms.

Existing reviews also share methodological and scope limitations that restrict their usefulness. First, many applied restrictive eligibility criteria, such as limiting inclusion to case–control studies, to a single ethnic group, to publications in English or Chinese, or to a single gene or SNP. This risks omitting relevant evidence and introducing selection bias. Second, many did not formally assess the methodological quality or risk of bias of included studies, although genetic association studies are prone to well-described problems. These include population stratification, inappropriate selection of controls, non-blinded genotyping, deviation from Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, inconsistent outcome definitions and selective reporting (Little et al. 2009). Where quality was assessed, it was seldom used to explore heterogeneity or to test the robustness of pooled estimates. Third, nearly all published syntheses addressed hepatotoxicity alone. Other toxicity outcomes, including peripheral neuropathy, cutaneous reactions, haematological toxicity and visual disturbance, have not been systematically summarised, even though primary studies exist for several of them. Fourth, the number of genetic variants examined has been small, concentrated on *NAT2*, *CYP2E1* and *GSTM1*, while a growing number of primary studies have examined other candidate genes, and genome-wide approaches have begun to appear. Finally, the most recent searches in existing meta-analyses are now several years old, and the primary literature has since expanded considerably.

A comprehensive and up-to-date synthesis is therefore needed. For clinicians and TB programmes, the practical question is whether genotype-guided dosing or monitoring could reduce harm. Pharmacogenetic testing is already used for other drugs, such as abacavir and thiopurines, and *NAT2*-guided isoniazid dosing has been proposed as a way of reducing toxicity without compromising efficacy. Whether such strategies are justified depends on the strength, consistency and specificity of the underlying associations, and on whether these differ by ancestry, since allele frequencies, such as the high prevalence of slow acetylators in some populations, vary widely. A rigorous review that covers all genetic variants, all anti-tubercular drugs and all toxicity outcomes can identify which associations are well supported, which are inconclusive, and where further primary research is most needed.

The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to evaluate comprehensively the evidence for associations between any genetic variant and toxicity associated with anti-tubercular drugs in patients with TB. Our primary research question is: among patients with TB who are receiving or commencing anti-tubercular treatment, are specific genetic variants associated with an increased or decreased risk of drug-related toxicity outcomes? We will include cohort studies, case–control studies and randomised controlled trials, and will not restrict inclusion by drug, variant, outcome or language where translation is feasible. Where data are sufficiently similar, we will pool estimates of effect for each genotype and outcome using meta-analyses stratified by ethnicity, and we will assess study quality, heterogeneity and potential publication bias.

This protocol makes three contributions. First, it pre-specifies a transparent and reproducible methodology, registered in PROSPERO (CRD42017068448) and reported in line with PRISMA-P guidance (Moher et al. 2015), to limit selective reporting and post hoc analytic decisions. Second, it broadens the scope of previous work beyond hepatotoxicity and a handful of candidate genes, and so may provide the first systematic summaries for many gene–outcome pairs. Third, by incorporating quality assessment and ethnicity-stratified analyses, it aims to clarify whether apparent inconsistencies in earlier meta-analyses reflect true population differences, methodological weaknesses or chance, and thereby to inform future pharmacogenetic research and the development of personalised TB treatment.

Methods

**Protocol and reporting**

This protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement (Moher et al. 2015) and registered prospectively with PROSPERO (CRD42017068448). The completed review will follow the PRISMA reporting guideline (Liberati et al. 2009) and the recommendations of the Human Genome Epidemiology Network (HuGENet) for systematic reviews of genetic association studies (Little et al. 2009). Any deviation from this protocol will be documented, dated, and justified in the final report and in the PROSPERO record.

**Eligibility criteria**

We will include randomised controlled trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and case–control studies (including nested designs) that recruited patients with tuberculosis, either established on anti-tuberculosis treatment or commencing it, and that genotyped participants to investigate the effect of one or more genetic variants on any anti-tuberculosis drug-related toxicity outcome. Patients of any age, ethnicity, HIV status, or disease site (pulmonary or extrapulmonary), and with drug-sensitive or drug-resistant disease, will be eligible. Any first- or second-line anti-tuberculosis drug, in any regimen, dose, or duration, will be considered.

The exposure of interest is any germline genetic variant, whether a single-nucleotide polymorphism, insertion–deletion, copy-number variant (such as *GSTM1* and *GSTT1* null genotypes), or inferred haplotype or metaboliser phenotype. Comparison will be between genotype categories, using the reference genotype defined in each study. The primary outcome is any drug-related toxicity event, categorised a priori as hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, cutaneous reactions, haematological toxicity, gastrointestinal intolerance, visual or auditory toxicity, renal toxicity, and other events. Studies will be included regardless of how toxicity was defined, but definitions (e.g. alanine aminotransferase thresholds relative to the upper limit of normal, symptom requirements, causality assessment) will be extracted for use in subgroup analyses. We will exclude studies in which toxicity was not attributed to anti-tuberculosis therapy, studies of latent infection prophylaxis only, genome-wide expression or somatic studies, case reports, reviews, and conference abstracts without sufficient data. No language restrictions will be applied; non-English papers will be translated where necessary.

**Information sources and search strategy**

We will search MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS, and Web of Science from inception to the date of the search, which will be rerun before analysis to capture recent publications. The strategy will combine three concept blocks using Boolean operators: (i) tuberculosis and individual anti-tuberculosis drug names (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin, and second-line agents); (ii) genetic terms, including polymorphism, genotype, allele, variant, pharmacogenetics, and gene names such as *NAT2*, *CYP2E1*, and *GSTM1*; and (iii) toxicity terms, including adverse drug reaction, hepatotoxicity, liver injury, neuropathy, and rash. Controlled vocabulary and free-text terms will be adapted to each database, and the MEDLINE strategy will be peer-reviewed by a second author and an information specialist using the PRESS checklist (McGowan et al. 2016). We will additionally hand search the reference lists of included studies and previous systematic reviews, and contact experts in the field to identify unpublished or ongoing studies.

**Study selection**

Search results will be imported into reference management software and de-duplicated. One author will screen all titles and abstracts to identify potentially relevant studies and will then obtain full texts and assess eligibility against the criteria above. At both stages, a second author will independently screen or assess a random 10% sample of records. Agreement will be quantified using Cohen's kappa; if agreement is substantially below acceptable levels (κ < 0.60), the screening criteria will be clarified and the second reviewer's sample will be extended. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion or, if necessary, by a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage will be recorded, and the selection process will be summarised in a PRISMA flow diagram. Where multiple reports describe overlapping participants, we will include the report with the largest sample or most complete data and cross-reference the others.

**Data extraction**

Two authors will independently extract data using a standardised form piloted on a subset of studies and refined before full use. Extracted items will include: bibliographic details; study design, setting, and recruitment period; participant characteristics (sample size, age, sex, ethnicity, HIV status, baseline liver function, alcohol use, comorbid hepatitis); treatment regimen, dosing, and duration; genes and variants investigated, with reference SNP identifiers, genotyping method, and quality control procedures; toxicity outcome definitions, severity grading, and time to onset; and the number of participants with and without the outcome in each genotype category. Where available, we will also extract adjusted effect estimates with their confidence intervals and the covariates adjusted for. Where data are missing or unclear, we will contact corresponding authors. Discrepancies between extractors will be resolved by consensus.

**Quality assessment**

Two authors will independently assess study quality. For cohort and case–control studies we will use the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (Wells et al. 2000), supplemented with items specific to genetic association studies derived from the STREGA statement (Little et al. 2009) and published quality criteria (Thakkar et al. 2008). These additional items include whether genotyping was performed blind to outcome status, whether genotyping quality control and error rates were reported, whether Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) was assessed in controls or non-affected participants, whether population stratification was addressed, and whether outcome ascertainment was consistent across genotypes. Randomised trials will be assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (Higgins et al. 2011). Quality scores will not be used to exclude studies but will inform sensitivity analyses, and the overall strength of evidence for each genotype–outcome association will be graded with the Venice criteria (Ioannidis et al. 2008), which consider the amount of evidence, replication, and protection from bias.

**Data synthesis and statistical analysis**

We will first describe the included studies narratively and in tables, grouped by gene, variant, and outcome. Where at least two sufficiently homogeneous studies report the same variant and outcome, we will perform meta-analysis. Because allele frequencies and linkage disequilibrium structure differ across populations, analyses will be stratified by ethnicity (e.g. East Asian, South Asian, African, European, admixed or other), using the ethnic groups defined by study authors and, where ambiguous, by the study location.

For each variant we will estimate odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for toxicity comparing genotype groups, under the genetic model most appropriate to the variant, namely allelic, dominant, recessive, and codominant (heterozygote and homozygote versus reference) models. For *NAT2*, we will additionally analyse inferred acetylator status (slow, intermediate, rapid), with classification criteria recorded for each study. Relative risks or hazard ratios from cohort studies and trials will be pooled separately when reported, and adjusted and unadjusted estimates will be analysed separately. Studies with zero cells will have a continuity correction of 0.5 applied.

Pooled estimates will be obtained using the DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model (DerSimonian and Laird 1986), given the expected clinical and methodological diversity; fixed-effect estimates will be presented for comparison. Heterogeneity will be assessed by Cochran's Q test (p < 0.10 considered significant) and quantified with the I² statistic, with values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% interpreted as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity (Higgins et al. 2003). Where heterogeneity is notable, we will explore it through subgroup analyses and random-effects meta-regression, with prespecified covariates: drug regimen, toxicity definition, age group (children versus adults), HIV status, study design, and study quality. Where fewer than ten studies are available, meta-regression will not be undertaken.

Sensitivity analyses will examine the effect of excluding studies with low quality scores, studies deviating from HWE in controls (p < 0.05), and studies contributing outlying estimates, and will compare results using a Knapp–Hartung adjustment for small numbers of studies. Publication bias will be assessed by visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger's regression test (Egger et al. 1997) for analyses including ten or more studies. Given the number of genotype–outcome comparisons anticipated, we will interpret results with caution and report the possibility of false-positive findings.

All analyses will be performed in Stata or R (using the *meta* and *metafor* packages), with two-sided p values and a significance threshold of 0.05. If meta-analysis is inappropriate owing to insufficient or highly heterogeneous data, results will be synthesised narratively.

Results

**Status of the evidence and scope of this section**

This article is a protocol. The searches, screening, data extraction, and quality assessment described in the Methods have not yet produced pooled estimates, so there are no empirical findings to report. We have not invented effect sizes, study counts, or heterogeneity statistics. This section instead reports the quantitative parameters fixed in advance for the review (registered as PROSPERO CRD42017068448) and sets out the format in which results will be presented. The thresholds below are the proposed analysis plan. They will be fixed at registration and any later deviation will be reported.

**Search and selection parameters**

Four bibliographic databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS, and Web of Science) will be searched. Reference lists of eligible studies and of relevant prior reviews will be hand searched, and experts in the field will be contacted to identify unpublished or in-press studies. One reviewer will screen all titles and abstracts. A second reviewer will independently screen a random 10% sample. The same approach will be used for full-text eligibility assessment, again with a 10% independent sample. Agreement between reviewers will be quantified with Cohen's kappa (Cohen 1960). We propose that kappa values below 0.60 (conventionally "moderate" or worse agreement) will trigger discussion of the eligibility criteria and a further 10% sample (Landis and Koch 1977). Disagreements will be resolved by consensus or by arbitration by a third author.

The flow of records will be reported according to PRISMA (Moher et al. 2009; Shamseer et al. 2015). The final report will give the number of records identified per database, the number remaining after de-duplication, the number excluded at the title and abstract stage, the number of full texts assessed, and the number excluded with reasons. The final tally of included studies will be stratified by design (cohort, case–control, or randomised controlled trial), by the population's ethnic ancestry, and by the candidate gene or variant investigated.

**Characteristics of included studies**

Two authors will independently extract data using a pre-piloted form. The form will record the following items:

- Study design and setting.
- Sample size for each genotype group.
- Participants' age, sex, and self-reported or genetically inferred ethnicity.
- HIV status and other comorbidities.
- Treatment regimen, including drugs, doses, and duration.
- Genotyping method.
- Outcome definition and ascertainment.
- Follow-up duration.
