Third, by documenting heterogeneity in diagnostic methods, breakpoints and reporting, it identifies concrete priorities for standardisation and data sharing, which are prerequisites for effective, coordinated and sustainable laboratory-based AMR surveillance in Cameroon and comparable settings.

Methods

Study design and reporting standards

We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of published and unpublished studies reporting antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacteria isolated from humans, animals and the environment in Cameroon. The review was designed and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Page et al., 2021). A One Health framework was applied throughout, in line with the tripartite definition of the interconnected health of people, animals and ecosystems (World Health Organization [WHO], Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO] and World Organisation for Animal Health [OIE], 2019). Studies were therefore classified a priori into three compartments: human (clinical and community samples), animal (livestock, poultry, aquaculture and companion animals, including animal-derived foods) and environment (water, soil, hospital surfaces and effluents). The protocol was prepared before the searches began and followed the structure recommended for reviews of prevalence data (Munn et al., 2015).

Search strategy

PubMed, Google Scholar and African Journals Online (AJOL) were searched for articles published in English or French. The search combined Medical Subject Headings and free-text terms in three concept blocks using Boolean operators: (i) resistance ("antimicrobial resistance", "antibiotic resistance", "drug resistance, microbial", "multidrug resistance", "susceptibility", "ESBL"); (ii) setting ("Cameroon", "Cameroun", and the names of the ten administrative regions); and (iii) host or source ("human", "patient", "animal", "livestock", "poultry", "environment", "water", "hospital"). French equivalents were used for searches targeting French-language records. Because Google Scholar returns results ranked by relevance and in very large numbers, only the first 200 records of each search string were screened (Haddaway et al., 2015). Reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews were hand-searched to identify additional records. Grey literature, including theses, dissertations, conference abstracts and institutional reports, was identified through web searches and by directly contacting corresponding authors and national laboratories, who were asked to share unpublished or free-text data. The last search was run in the final week of the search period, and all records were exported to a reference manager for removal of duplicates.

Eligibility criteria

Studies were eligible if they (i) were conducted in Cameroon; (ii) reported original phenotypic or genotypic data on antimicrobial susceptibility of bacterial isolates recovered from humans, animals or the environment; (iii) specified the bacterial species and the antibiotics tested; (iv) reported the number of isolates tested and the number resistant (or percentages from which these could be derived); and (v) used a recognised susceptibility testing method, namely disk diffusion, broth microdilution, agar dilution, gradient diffusion, or automated systems, interpreted according to the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) or the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) breakpoints, or equivalent guidance such as the Comité de l'Antibiogramme de la Société Française de Microbiologie (CA-SFM). Studies were excluded if they were reviews, editorials, case reports with fewer than ten isolates, in vitro evaluations of plant extracts or novel compounds, studies on mycobacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites, studies in which data from Cameroon could not be disaggregated from those of other countries, or studies in which the denominator of tested isolates was not identifiable. When the same dataset was published more than once, the most complete report was retained.

Study selection

Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria, and potentially relevant articles were retrieved in full text. Two reviewers independently assessed the full texts, and disagreements were resolved by discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram showing the numbers of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons) and included.

Data extraction

A standardised extraction form was piloted on five articles and then applied to all included studies. The following variables were extracted: first author, year of publication, year(s) of sampling, region of Cameroon, setting (hospital, community, farm, market, water body), One Health compartment, sample type, population characteristics, sample size, bacterial species, number of isolates tested, antibiotics tested with the number of resistant isolates, susceptibility testing method and interpretive standard, and the reported resistance mechanisms (for example extended-spectrum β-lactamase [ESBL] or methicillin resistance). Antibiotics were grouped by class following the WHO Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification and the WHO AWaRe categories (WHO, 2021). Intermediate results were classified as non-susceptible and pooled with resistant isolates only where the original authors did not report the categories separately. Data were extracted independently by two reviewers and cross-checked, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Authors were contacted to clarify missing or ambiguous information.

Definition of outcomes

The primary outcome was the proportion of isolates resistant to a given antibiotic for each pathogen–antibiotic pair. The secondary outcome was the prevalence of multidrug resistance (MDR), defined as acquired non-susceptibility to at least one agent in three or more antimicrobial classes (Magiorakos et al., 2012). Where studies did not report MDR directly but provided isolate-level resistance profiles, MDR was derived using this definition. Studies in which MDR was defined differently by the authors were retained only if the definition was compatible with the above criterion. Intrinsic resistance was excluded from the numerator and denominator where it could be identified.

Quality assessment

Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed independently by two reviewers using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (Munn et al., 2015), which evaluates sampling frame, sampling method, sample size adequacy, description of subjects and setting, coverage of the data analysis, validity of the methods for identifying the condition, standardisation of measurement, statistical analysis and response rate. Each item was scored as met or not met, and studies were classified as low (≥7 items met), moderate (4–6) or high (≤3) risk of bias. Quality scores were used to explore heterogeneity in sensitivity analyses rather than as grounds for exclusion.

Statistical analysis

Analyses were stratified by One Health compartment, bacterial species and antibiotic. Pooled prevalence was estimated only where at least three studies contributed data to a pathogen–antibiotic pair. Proportions were transformed using the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation to stabilise variances and to avoid exclusion of studies with proportions near 0% or 100% (Freeman and Tukey, 1950; Barendregt et al., 2013). Pooled estimates were obtained with DerSimonian–Laird random-effects models and back-transformed for presentation, with 95% confidence intervals (CI) (DerSimonian and Laird, 1986). Random-effects models were selected a priori because of anticipated differences in study populations, laboratory methods and sampling periods. Heterogeneity was quantified with Cochran's Q test and the I² statistic, with I² values of 25%, 50% and 75% considered to represent low, moderate and high heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins et al., 2003), and with the between-study variance τ². Because high heterogeneity is expected in prevalence meta-analyses, 95% prediction intervals were also computed for the main pooled estimates.

Potential sources of heterogeneity were explored through subgroup analyses by administrative region, setting (hospital versus community), sampling period (before 2010, 2010–2015, after 2015), susceptibility testing method and risk-of-bias category, and by univariable random-effects meta-regression on the same covariates where at least ten studies were available. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were used to assess the influence of individual studies on pooled estimates. Publication bias was evaluated by visual inspection of funnel plots and by Egger's regression test for small-study effects where ten or more studies were available (Egger et al., 1997), with a P value below 0.05 considered significant.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarise study characteristics, regional distribution, the number of bacterial species and antibiotics tested, and resistance across antibiotic classes. All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.2) using the packages meta and metafor (Balduzzi et al., 2019; Viechtbauer, 2010), and maps and figures were produced with ggplot2. All tests were two-sided, and statistical significance was set at P < 0.05 unless otherwise stated.

Ethical considerations

This review used only published and aggregated unpublished data, and no individual patient information was collected; formal ethical approval was therefore not required. Data shared by authors were used with their consent.

Results

**Study selection and characteristics**

The database searches and contact with authors yielded 428 records. After removal of 117 duplicates, 311 titles and abstracts were screened and 214 were excluded as irrelevant. The full texts of 97 articles were assessed for eligibility (Page et al., 2021). Of these, 31 were excluded because they lacked antibiotic susceptibility data disaggregated by pathogen (n = 14), had no clear sampling denominator (n = 9), reported fewer than 10 isolates (n = 5) or were duplicate reports of the same dataset (n = 3). Sixty-six studies, published between 2005 and 2022, were retained for qualitative synthesis, and 61 contributed to at least one pooled estimate (Supplementary Table S1).

Geographically, the studies came mainly from four regions: Centre (24; 36.4%), South-West (16; 24.2%), West (13; 19.7%) and Littoral (9; 13.6%). The remaining four (6.1%) came from the North-West, Adamawa, North and Far North regions combined, and no study was identified from the East or South regions. Forty-five studies (68.2%) addressed AMR in humans, 9 (13.6%) in animals and 12 (18.2%) in the environment. The human studies were mostly hospital-based, cross-sectional laboratory analyses of clinical specimens (urine, blood, stool, wound and genital swabs). Most animal studies sampled poultry, cattle or pigs at farms or abattoirs. Environmental studies sampled hospital effluents, surface and well water, and market or hospital surfaces. Disk diffusion was the predominant susceptibility method (53 studies; 80.3%), and only 21 studies (31.8%) stated adherence to a named interpretive standard (CLSI or EUCAST). Based on the adapted Joanna Briggs Institute prevalence checklist, 38 studies (57.6%) were rated as moderate quality, 17 (25.8%) as high and 11 (16.7%) as low.

**Bacterial species and antibiotics tested**

Across all sectors, 19 bacterial species were tested against 48 antibiotics spanning all major classes: penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, macrolides, sulfonamides/trimethoprim, glycopeptides and phenicols. In human studies, *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae* and *Staphylococcus* spp. were the most frequently reported organisms, appearing in 23, 19 and 18 studies, respectively. *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (n = 12), *Salmonella* spp. (n = 10) and *Enterococcus* spp. (n = 6) followed. Resistance was documented for every antibiotic class tested.

**Resistance in human isolates**

The pooled prevalence of resistance in *E. coli* was highest for the oldest, most widely used agents: amoxicillin or ampicillin, 87.3% (95% CI 81.4–91.5; 21 studies); tetracycline, 76.9% (68.2–83.8; 11 studies); and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, 78.4% (70.9–84.4; 17 studies). Resistance was lower for third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, 38.6% [29.7–48.4]; ceftazidime, 41.2% [31.5–51.5]) and for ciprofloxacin (29.8% [21.6–39.6]) and gentamicin (24.3% [17.1–33.3]). Pooled carbapenem resistance was low (imipenem, 3.4% [1.6–7.1]), although isolated reports of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales were noted [S14, S31, S47]. Using a threshold of resistance to three or more antibiotic classes, the pooled MDR prevalence in *E. coli* was 47.1% (95% CI 37.3–57.2; 23 studies).

For *K. pneumoniae*, the pooled MDR prevalence was 51.0% (95% CI 42.0–59.9; 19 studies). Resistance to ceftriaxone was 52.7% (41.8–63.4), to ceftazidime 49.6% (38.2–61.1), to ciprofloxacin 34.5% (24.9–45.5) and to gentamicin 40.2% (30.1–51.3). The intrinsic resistance of *K. pneumoniae* to ampicillin was reflected in a pooled estimate of 94.1% (88.2–97.1). Imipenem resistance was 5.8% (2.9–11.3).

For *Staphylococcus* spp. (predominantly *S. aureus*, 14 of 18 studies), the pooled MDR prevalence was 45.2% (95% CI 38.0–54.7; 18 studies). The pooled prevalence of methicillin resistance among *S. aureus* was 31.6% (24.1–40.2; 12 studies), with resistance to penicillin of 91.2% (85.0–94.9), to tetracycline of 52.4% (42.6–62.0), to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole of 58.7% (47.9–68.8) and to erythromycin of 41.3% (32.2–51.0). Resistance to gentamicin and ciprofloxacin was 22.5% (15.2–32.0) and 20.1% (13.5–28.9), respectively. No vancomycin resistance was reported in *S. aureus*, although 3 of 6 studies on *Enterococcus* spp. reported vancomycin-resistant isolates, with a pooled prevalence of 7.9% (3.1–18.4).

Among the less frequently studied species, *P. aeruginosa* showed pooled resistance of 36.4% (26.0–48.2) to ceftazidime, 31.0% (21.3–42.7) to ciprofloxacin and 14.2% (8.1–23.7) to imipenem. Non-typhoidal and typhoidal *Salmonella* from humans showed pooled ampicillin resistance of 62.8% (51.2–73.0) and ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility of 18.7% (10.9–30.0).

**Resistance in animal isolates**

The nine animal studies reported on *Salmonella* spp. (n = 6), *E. coli* (n = 5), *Staphylococcus* spp. (n = 3) and *Campylobacter* spp. (n = 1) isolated mostly from poultry (6 studies), followed by cattle (2) and pigs (1). The pooled MDR prevalence in animal-derived *Salmonella* spp. was 46.2% (95% CI 39.2–53.5; 6 studies). Resistance in these isolates was highest for tetracycline (68.3% [57.4–77.5]), ampicillin (51.9% [40.6–63.0]) and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (47.7% [36.0–59.7]). Resistance to ciprofloxacin (14.6% [8.2–24.5]) and to ceftriaxone (9.8% [5.0–18.2]) was lower. Poultry-derived *E. coli* showed very high resistance to tetracycline (83.5% [74.1–89.9]) and to ampicillin (71.2% [58.8–81.2]), and a pooled MDR prevalence of 58.4% (45.0–70.7; 5 studies). Colistin resistance was investigated in only two studies, both reporting resistant isolates in poultry (pooled prevalence, 9.3% [3.4–23.2]).

**Resistance in environmental isolates**

Twelve studies addressed environmental samples. *Staphylococcus* spp. were reported in 8 studies and exhibited a pooled MDR prevalence of 67.1% (95% CI 55.2–77.2). This was the highest MDR estimate of any pathogen–source combination in this review. Environmental *E. coli* (n = 6 studies) and *Pseudomonas* spp. (n = 4) displayed pooled MDR prevalences of 52.3% (38.4–65.9) and 43.7% (29.6–58.8), respectively. Hospital effluents and hospital surfaces yielded higher MDR prevalences than community water sources (60.5% vs 38.9% for pooled Gram-negative isolates; between-subgroup *p* = 0.03). Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) production was assessed in 7 environmental and 14 human studies, with pooled ESBL prevalences among Enterobacterales of 21.4% (12.8–33.5) and 34.7% (26.0–44.5), respectively.

**Heterogeneity, subgroup analyses and publication bias**

Between-study heterogeneity was substantial for nearly all pooled estimates (I² range 71.4–97.2%; Higgins et al., 2003), consistent with the use of random-effects models (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). For *E. coli* MDR, I² was 92.6% (τ² = 0.41). Subgroup analyses explained part of this variation. MDR prevalence in *E. coli* was higher in studies published after 2015 than before (54.8% vs 38.1%; *p* = 0.04), and in hospitalized than in community-based participants (56.3% vs 33.9%; *p* = 0.01). Differences between regions were not statistically significant (*p* = 0.18), but this comparison was limited by the small number of studies outside the four main regions. Sensitivity analysis excluding low-quality studies changed the pooled MDR estimates by less than 3 percentage points for each of the principal pathogens. Visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger's regression test suggested small-study effects for *E. coli* (*p* = 0.03) but not for *K. pneumoniae* (*p* = 0.21) or *Staphylococcus* spp. (*p* = 0.34).

Discussion

This systematic review and meta-analysis provides one of the first syntheses of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) across human, animal and environmental compartments in Cameroon. From 66 eligible studies, we found that 19 bacterial species were tested against 48 antibiotics, and that resistance was present in every antibiotic class examined. The pooled multidrug resistance (MDR) estimates were high and similar across compartments: 47.1% for *Escherichia coli*, 51.0% for *Klebsiella pneumoniae* and 45.2% for *Staphylococcus* spp. in human studies, 46.2% for *Salmonella* spp. in animal studies, and 67.1% for *Staphylococcus* spp. in environmental studies. Taken together, these figures suggest that first-line empirical therapy is likely to fail in a substantial proportion of bacterial infections in the country. They are consistent with the high burden attributed to bacterial AMR in sub-Saharan Africa, where attributable and associated mortality was estimated to be the highest worldwide (Murray et al., 2022).

The dominance of *E. coli*, *K. pneumoniae* and *Staphylococcus* spp. in the human literature mirrors the priority pathogens identified by the World Health Organization and the pathogens most frequently reported in African surveillance syntheses (Tadesse et al., 2017; WHO, 2021). The MDR prevalence of roughly 45–51% in these organisms is comparable to estimates from other low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and compatible with a setting in which antibiotics are widely available without prescription, diagnostic stewardship is limited, and empirical treatment is the norm (Founou et al., 2017; Okeke et al., 2005). The comparatively high MDR in *K. pneumoniae* is particularly worrying because this species is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and hospital-acquired infection, and is commonly associated with extended-spectrum β-lactamase production, which narrows the therapeutic options to carbapenems that are scarce and costly in Cameroon (Founou et al., 2017). The environmental estimate for *Staphylococcus* spp. (67.1%) was the highest we observed. This suggests that hospital effluents, surface waters, markets and farm environments may act as reservoirs and conduits for resistant organisms and resistance determinants, as described elsewhere in Africa. However, the estimate rests on only eight studies and should be interpreted cautiously.

The similarity of MDR estimates in humans and animals supports a One Health reading of resistance in Cameroon, although our data cannot demonstrate transmission directions. Antibiotic use in livestock, particularly in intensive poultry and pig production, is substantial in LMICs and is projected to rise with increasing demand for animal protein (Van Boeckel et al., 2015, 2019). Tetracyclines, penicillins, sulphonamides and quinolones are commonly used for prophylaxis and growth promotion, often without veterinary oversight. This selective pressure is plausibly reflected in the 46.2% MDR we found in *Salmonella* spp. from animals. Because *Salmonella* is foodborne, resistant strains could reach humans through the food chain, direct contact or contaminated water. Nevertheless, only nine animal studies and twelve environmental studies were identified, compared with 45 human studies. This imbalance shows that the One Health framing is not yet matched by the research effort, and that the human clinical perspective still dominates AMR research in the country. Few studies used comparable sampling frames or molecular typing that would allow resistant clones or plasmids to be tracked across compartments, so integrated analyses remain largely out of reach.

The geographic distribution of the evidence is also uneven. More than a third of the studies (36.4%) came from the Centre Region and a further 24.2% from the South-West, with the West and Littoral contributing 19.7% and 13.6%, respectively. Only four studies (6.1%) came from all other regions combined. This clustering around major urban centres and university-affiliated hospitals reflects the location of laboratories and research funding rather than epidemiological need. The pooled estimates are therefore likely to represent tertiary-care and peri-urban populations, whereas the northern and eastern regions, with distinct livestock systems, population movement across borders and limited health access, are essentially unobserved. National policy based on these data risks over-generalising from a few settings.

Heterogeneity was a further challenge. Studies differed in specimen type, population, laboratory methods, breakpoints (CLSI versus EUCAST, or none stated), the number and selection of antibiotics tested, and the definition of MDR. Although we used random-effects models to accommodate between-study variation, the pooled prevalences should be seen as descriptive summaries of the available literature and not as precise population-level estimates. Many studies were hospital-based convenience samples of patients already suspected of having infection, probably inflating resistance relative to community carriage, and a considerable share of isolates came from patients who had received prior antibiotics. Small sample sizes also contributed to wide confidence intervals for several pathogen–antibiotic pairs. The inconsistent application of MDR definitions, such as those proposed by Magiorakos et al. (2012), limits comparability between studies and with other countries. These problems are typical of AMR evidence in LMICs and underscore the fragmentation of surveillance reported across the continent (Iskandar et al., 2021).

This review has limitations. We searched PubMed, Google Scholar and African Journals Online and included English and French publications, supplemented by grey literature obtained from authors. Even so, reports in institutional repositories, theses and unpublished laboratory records may have been missed, and publication bias favouring high-resistance findings cannot be excluded. Extraction depended on the information reported, and the quality of laboratory methods could not be uniformly verified. Pooling across years obscures temporal trends, and we could not consistently stratify by age, ward, or community versus hospital origin. Finally, most studies reported phenotypic resistance only, so we cannot comment on the genetic mechanisms and mobile elements that drive dissemination.

These findings have several implications. First, the high levels of resistance to commonly used antibiotics call for the revision of national standard treatment guidelines using local susceptibility data, and for the promotion of culture-guided therapy where laboratory capacity allows. Second, the heterogeneity in methods supports the adoption of harmonised protocols aligned with WHO GLASS and the national action plan: standardised breakpoints, a minimum core panel of antibiotics, common MDR definitions, and quality assurance through external proficiency testing. Third, surveillance should be extended beyond referral hospitals to peripheral facilities, livestock production systems, markets, slaughterhouses and water sources, with shared data platforms linking the ministries responsible for health, livestock and the environment. Fourth, integrating whole-genome sequencing, even in a small number of reference laboratories, would allow the clonal and plasmid-mediated spread of resistance between compartments to be investigated directly. Fifth, interventions targeting antibiotic use, such as enforcing prescription-only sales, strengthening veterinary oversight, and improving infection prevention, sanitation and hygiene, should be implemented alongside surveillance and evaluated for their effect on resistance.

In conclusion, resistance to commonly prescribed antibiotics is high in Cameroon, with MDR frequently approaching or exceeding 50% among key pathogens in human, animal and environmental settings. However, the evidence base is fragmentary, geographically concentrated and methodologically heterogeneous. Closing these gaps through standardised diagnostics and reporting, broader geographic and sectoral coverage, sustained data sharing and coordinated action among all stakeholders is essential for defining the national AMR burden and for guiding effective, evidence-based control strategies.

Introduction

Armed conflict, persecution, and political instability have displaced unprecedented numbers of people worldwide, and children and adolescents account for roughly half of the global refugee population (UNHCR, 2018). Resettlement countries such as Australia, Canada, the United States, and many European states receive children who have often experienced war-related violence, loss of family members, protracted displacement, and disrupted education before arrival. These cumulative exposures place refugee children at elevated risk of post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, and behavioural difficulties (Fazel, Reed, Panter-Brick, & Stein, 2012; Bronstein & Montgomery, 2011). Yet mental health outcomes are not determined by pre-migration trauma alone. A substantial body of work indicates that post-migration stressors, including insecure legal status, poverty, discrimination, social isolation, and difficulties in the new educational environment, make an independent and sometimes greater contribution to psychological distress than the premigration events themselves (Miller & Rasco, 2004; Li, Liddell, & Nickerson, 2016). Because post-migration conditions are modifiable, they represent a priority target for intervention.

Schools are among the most important of these post-migration contexts. For resettled children, school is frequently the first sustained point of contact with the host society, and it occupies a large proportion of their waking hours. Beyond its educational function, school provides opportunities to form peer friendships, to learn the host language, to encounter adult role models, to re-establish routine and a sense of normality, and to gain access to health and welfare services (Fazel et al., 2012; Rutter, 2006). Ecological models of development suggest that these proximal settings and the relationships within them shape children’s adaptation, and that schools mediate between the child, the family, and the wider community (Bronfenbrenner, 1979; Ager & Strang, 2008). Schools may therefore serve as protective environments that buffer the effects of earlier adversity, or, where they are marked by bullying, racism, or exclusion, as further sources of stress (Mace, Mulheron, Jones, & Weaver, 2014; Kia-Keating & Ellis, 2007).

The concept of school climate offers a useful organising framework for understanding these effects. School climate refers to the quality and character of school life, reflecting shared norms, values, and interpersonal relationships, teaching and learning practices, and organisational structures (Cohen, McCabe, Michelli, & Pickeral, 2009; Thapa, Cohen, Guffey, & Higgins-D’Alessandro, 2013). In the general student population, positive school climate is associated with better academic achievement, reduced behavioural problems, and improved emotional wellbeing (Thapa et al., 2013; Wang & Degol, 2016). Related constructs, such as school connectedness and belonging, have been consistently linked to lower rates of depression and substance use among adolescents (Bond et al., 2007; Allen, Vella-Brodrick, & Waters, 2016). It is plausible that these dimensions matter at least as much for refugee students, who must also navigate language barriers, interrupted prior schooling, cultural unfamiliarity, and the expectations of teachers and peers who may know little about their circumstances.

Existing research suggests that a range of school-level factors may influence refugee children’s emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes. These include supportive teacher–student relationships (Kia-Keating & Ellis, 2007), peer acceptance and the absence of bullying and discrimination (Fazel, Garcia, & Stein, 2016), culturally responsive and inclusive policies and curricula (Block, Cross, Riggs, & Gibbs, 2014), language support, parental engagement, and teacher training in trauma and refugee experiences (Baak, 2019; Matthews, 2008). Alongside these, specialised school-based programmes, such as cognitive-behavioural and creative interventions, have been evaluated, though these typically target individual symptoms rather than the broader school environment (Tyrer & Fazel, 2014; Fazel & Betancourt, 2018). Acculturation, understood as the psychological and sociocultural changes that occur through sustained contact between cultural groups (Berry, 1997), is closely tied to these processes, since schools are principal sites in which language acquisition, identity negotiation, and the formation of cross-cultural friendships take place.

Despite this recognised importance, the evidence base is difficult to use in practice. First, it is methodologically heterogeneous. Studies include large quantitative surveys, small qualitative investigations, ethnographies, programme evaluations, and mixed-methods designs, conducted in diverse national contexts with children of varied ages, origins, and migration histories. Second, the studies investigate numerous and disparate school factors, using inconsistent terminology and measures, so that “school climate”, “school connectedness”, “belonging”, and “inclusion” are often used interchangeably or are not defined at all. Third, much relevant evidence is effectively hidden. Many qualitative and mixed-methods studies of refugee education address broader questions, such as the experiences of resettlement or the perspectives of teachers and parents, and report findings about the school environment as secondary themes that are not captured in titles, abstracts, or keywords. Such material is easily missed by conventional database searches. Fourth, relevant work is dispersed across disciplines, including psychiatry, psychology, education, public health, sociology, and migration studies, and a considerable proportion appears in grey literature, such as government and non-government organisation reports and theses.

Previous reviews have addressed adjacent questions but have not resolved these limitations. Systematic reviews of the mental health of refugee children have largely concentrated on prevalence and on risk factors at the individual and family levels (Bronstein & Montgomery, 2011; Reed, Fazel, Jones, Panter-Brick, & Stein, 2012). Reviews of school-based interventions have focused on the effectiveness of structured programmes delivered to children, generally measuring symptom reduction (Tyrer & Fazel, 2014; Nocon et al., 2017). Reviews of refugee education have tended to be narrative and thematic, and often have not used systematic search strategies or formal quality appraisal (Block et al., 2014; Mace et al., 2014). To our knowledge, no review has systematically synthesised quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods evidence on the relationship between whole-school environmental factors and both emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes for refugee students. As a result, educators and policymakers lack a consolidated, quality-appraised account of which features of school life support refugee students’ mental health and integration, and how these features operate.

The present protocol describes a systematic review designed to address this gap. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P; Moher et al., 2015) and methods appropriate to mixed studies reviews (Pluye & Hong, 2014), the review will ask: what school factors are associated with the emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes of students from refugee backgrounds? It adopts an extensive search strategy, including grey literature and citation tracking, to capture evidence embedded in broader studies. By synthesising heterogeneous evidence within a convergent narrative framework, the review aims to identify evidence-based school factors that promote good mental health and positive resettlement trajectories, and to provide a basis for practical recommendations for schools, policymakers, and future research. Publishing the protocol in advance, and registering it prospectively, enhances transparency and reduces the risk of selective reporting.

Methods

Protocol design and registration

This protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidance (Moher et al. 2015), and the completed review will be reported following the PRISMA statement (Moher et al. 2009). Because the literature on school environments and refugee wellbeing includes quantitative, qualitative and mixed-methods designs, the review is conceived as a mixed studies review (Pluye and Hong 2014). The protocol was registered prospectively with PROSPERO (CRD42017077570). Any amendments to the methods will be documented in the registration and reported in the final manuscript.

Review question and conceptual framing

The review asks: which school environmental factors (school climate) are associated with the emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes of students from refugee backgrounds? School climate is defined broadly as the quality and character of school life, encompassing interpersonal relationships, teaching and learning practices, safety, institutional environment, and organisational and community links (Cohen et al. 2009; Thapa et al. 2013). This definition is operationalised using the domains of the Bronfenbrenner ecological framework applied to refugee resettlement (Bronfenbrenner 1979; Ager and Strang 2008), which permits school-level factors to be distinguished from individual, family and wider community factors. Outcomes are grouped into (a) emotional wellbeing and mental health, including symptoms of depression, anxiety and posttraumatic stress, strengths and difficulties, self-esteem, and subjective wellbeing, and (b) resettlement outcomes, including acculturation, sense of belonging, social connectedness, school engagement, and academic achievement.

Eligibility criteria

Eligibility was specified using a Population–Exposure–Outcome–Study design structure.

Population: Children and adolescents aged 5 to 18 years who are from refugee backgrounds, including refugees, asylum seekers, and those with refugee-like experiences, and who are attending primary or secondary school in a resettlement country. Studies with mixed samples will be included where data for refugee students can be extracted separately or where refugee students constitute the majority (≥50%) of the sample. Studies of children in refugee camps or in countries of first asylum will be excluded, as the review focuses on resettlement contexts. Studies reporting only the views of parents, teachers or other stakeholders will be included where the outcomes pertain to refugee students.

Exposure: Any measured or described school-level factor, such as teacher–student relationships, peer relationships and bullying, school policies, anti-racism and inclusion practices, language support and welcoming programs, curriculum, extracurricular activities, family–school engagement, staff training, and the physical or organisational environment. Individual-level clinical or therapeutic interventions delivered in schools (for example, trauma-focused therapy) will be excluded unless the study reports on school environmental features rather than treatment efficacy.

Outcomes: At least one emotional wellbeing or resettlement outcome as defined above.

Study design: Peer-reviewed empirical studies using quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods designs will be included. Grey literature, including theses, government and non-government organisation reports, will also be eligible. Editorials, commentaries, opinion pieces, and reviews will be excluded, although reference lists of relevant reviews will be hand-searched. Articles must be available in English. Searches will be limited to 1990 onward, reflecting the period in which contemporary resettlement programs and school climate research developed.

Information sources and search strategy

Six electronic databases will be searched: MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and ERIC. The search strategy was developed with a health sciences librarian and combines controlled vocabulary (for example, MeSH and thesaurus terms) with free-text terms in three concept blocks: (1) refugee population (refugee*, asylum seek*, displaced, humanitarian entrant*, forced migra*); (2) school setting and climate (school*, student*, adolescent*, child*, climate, connectedness, belonging, teacher*, peer*, bullying, inclusion, ethos, environment); and (3) outcomes (mental health, wellbeing, psychological, emotional, depress*, anxiety, posttraumatic, acculturat*, adjustment, adaptation, integration, resettle*, engagement). Blocks will be combined with Boolean operators and adapted to the syntax of each database. The MEDLINE strategy will be piloted against a set of known relevant articles to test sensitivity before finalisation, and the full strategy will be peer reviewed using the PRESS checklist (McGowan et al. 2016).

To reduce publication bias and capture qualitative findings that are often reported within broader studies, the database searches will be supplemented by: searches of grey literature sources including ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, OpenGrey, and Google Scholar (first 200 results); searches of websites of relevant international organisations (such as UNHCR, UNICEF, the International Organization for Migration, and national refugee education and health agencies); sequential, site-specific internet searches; consultation with subject area experts to identify additional published and unpublished work; and backward and forward citation searching of all included articles.

Study selection

All records will be exported to EndNote and, after removal of duplicates, uploaded to Covidence for screening. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, followed by independent full-text assessment of potentially relevant articles. Before formal screening, reviewers will pilot the criteria on a random sample of 50 records to calibrate decisions. Disagreements will be resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted if consensus cannot be reached. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage will be recorded, and the selection process will be presented in a PRISMA flow diagram. Interrater agreement will be calculated using Cohen’s kappa (Cohen 1960):

κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e),

where p_o is the observed proportion of agreement and p_e is the proportion expected by chance.

Data extraction

A standardised extraction form will be piloted on three studies and refined. Two reviewers will independently extract data, with a third checking a sample for accuracy. Extracted items include: bibliographic details; country of study and resettlement context; study aim and design; sampling and setting; participant characteristics (age, gender, country of origin, time since arrival, visa status); school type; the school factors examined and how they were measured or described; outcome measures and instruments; main quantitative results (effect sizes, confidence intervals, p values) and qualitative themes with illustrative quotations; and authors’ conclusions. For qualitative and mixed methods studies, findings reported in results and discussion sections, including participant data and author interpretations, will be extracted. Where information is missing, study authors will be contacted by email up to two times.

Quality appraisal

Methodological quality will be assessed independently by two reviewers using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) 2018 version (Hong et al. 2018), which provides criteria for qualitative studies, randomised trials, non-randomised studies, quantitative descriptive studies and mixed-methods studies, allowing a consistent approach across heterogeneous designs. Each study will be rated against the relevant criteria as yes, no or can’t tell. In line with MMAT guidance, a single summary score will not be used to exclude studies; instead, the profile of ratings will be reported and considered in the interpretation of findings. Grey literature will be appraised using the same tool where it reports empirical research. Disagreements will be resolved by consensus or with a third reviewer.

Data synthesis

Given anticipated heterogeneity in designs, school factors, measures and outcomes, meta-analysis is not planned. A convergent qualitative synthesis design will be used (Hong et al. 2017), in which quantitative and qualitative data are transformed and integrated in a single synthesis. Quantitative results will be “qualitised”, that is, converted into narrative descriptions of the direction and strength of association between school factors and outcomes, and assembled with qualitative findings. Following the thematic synthesis approach of Thomas and Harden (2008), two reviewers will code findings line by line, develop descriptive themes inductively, and then generate analytical themes organised around school climate domains and outcome categories. The synthesis will be conducted in NVivo. Narrative synthesis procedures from the Economic and Social Research Council guidance (Popay et al. 2006) will guide tabulation of study characteristics, exploration of relationships within and between studies, and assessment of the robustness of the synthesis. Where adequate data exist, subgroup patterns will be explored by age group (primary versus secondary), resettlement country, and time since arrival.

Assessment of confidence in the evidence

Confidence in the qualitative findings will be assessed using GRADE-CERQual (Lewin et al. 2018), and consideration will be given to the consistency of quantitative findings across studies, the risk of bias indicated by MMAT, and the directness of evidence. Reporting biases will be considered through the breadth of grey literature searching and comparison of published and unpublished findings.

Ethical considerations

As the review uses published and publicly available data, ethical approval is not required.

Results

**Status of the review and the absence of study findings**

This article is a protocol, so no search has been run, no records have been screened, and no data have been extracted or synthesised. The review is registered prospectively (PROSPERO CRD42017077570). This section therefore does not report effect estimates, counts of included studies, or quality ratings, and none are invented here. It sets out the results the review will report, the quantities that will be calculated, the thresholds that will govern their interpretation, and how they will be presented, so that the final report can be checked against a pre-specified plan. This follows PRISMA-P guidance that protocols specify outputs and decision rules in advance (Shamseer et al., 2015; Moher et al., 2009).

**Planned reporting of study identification and selection**

The first results will be the flow of records through the review, shown in a PRISMA flow diagram (Moher et al., 2009). The diagram will give the number of records identified from each of the six databases (MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science and ERIC). It will give separate counts for grey literature sources, targeted website and site-specific internet searches, expert consultation, and backward and forward citation searching of included articles. It will then report records remaining after deduplication, records excluded at title and abstract screening, full-text articles assessed, full-text articles excluded with a reason for each exclusion, and the final number of studies included in the synthesis. Exclusion reasons will be tabulated using a hierarchy applied in a fixed order (for example, population not refugee-background; no school-level exposure; no emotional wellbeing or resettlement outcome; non-empirical report). This ensures each excluded article is counted once.

The contribution of each source to the final set of included studies will be reported as a yield, defined as

Yield_s = n_included,s / N_identified,s,

where *n*_included,s is the number of included studies first identified through source *s*, and *N*_identified,s is the total number of records that source returned. We will also report the number of included studies found only through supplementary methods (grey literature, citation chasing, expert consultation). A large share of such studies would support the premise of this review that relevant evidence is "hidden" in broader qualitative and mixed-methods work and is not indexed by school-climate or refugee-mental-health terms.

**Planned reporting of inter-rater reliability**

Two reviewers will screen independently at both stages. Agreement will be quantified with Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960):

κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e),

where *p*_o is the observed proportion of agreement and *p*_e is the proportion expected by chance, calculated from each reviewer's marginal include/exclude frequencies. Kappa will be reported separately for title and abstract screening, full-text screening, data extraction on categorical fields, and quality appraisal. Values will be interpreted using the conventional bands of Landis and Koch (1977): 0.61–0.80 substantial and 0.81–1.00 almost perfect agreement. If kappa at any stage falls below 0.61 in a calibration sample (the first 10% of records), reviewers will discuss and clarify criteria, then re-screen the sample before continuing. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion and, if necessary, a third reviewer. The number and proportion of conflicts resolved at each stage will be reported.

**Planned description of included studies**

Included studies will be summarised in a characteristics table. Fields will include author and year, country of resettlement, country or region of origin of participants, participant age and school level, sample size, design (qualitative, quantitative non-randomised, quantitative descriptive, randomised, or mixed methods), setting (mainstream school, language or intensive English centre, or other), the school factor examined, and the outcome domain. Descriptive counts will be reported for each field, with the number and percentage of studies in each category. Studies will be grouped by design according to the MMAT categories (Hong et al., 2018). We expect a heterogeneous evidence base, and design-wise counts will allow readers to judge how much the synthesis relies on each type of evidence.

School factors will be categorised using an a priori framework derived from school climate literature, with domains such as relationships and belonging, teacher practices and support, peer relations and bullying or discrimination, school policies and programmes, language support, and home–school and community links (Thapa et al., 2013). Categories not anticipated in advance will be added inductively and flagged as emergent. The number of studies contributing to each domain will be reported. Outcomes will be grouped into emotional wellbeing (for example, depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, self-esteem, life satisfaction, strengths and difficulties) and resettlement or acculturation outcomes (for example, academic engagement and achievement, language acquisition, school belonging, social integration, and attendance).

**Planned reporting of methodological quality**

Methodological quality will be appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (Hong et al., 2018). For each study, the five design-specific criteria will be rated "yes", "no" or "can't tell". Following MMAT guidance, we will not compute a single summed score. Instead, we will present a criterion-level table for every included study and report, by design category, the number and percentage of studies meeting each criterion. For mixed-methods studies, the additional criteria on integration and on the divergence between qualitative and quantitative components will be reported (Pluye & Hong, 2014). Quality will not be used to exclude studies. It will be used to examine confidence in each thematic finding through a sensitivity analysis in which findings are re-examined after excluding studies that meet fewer than half of the applicable criteria.

**Planned reporting of the synthesis**

Synthesis will follow a convergent qualitative approach in which quantitative and qualitative findings are transformed into a common narrative form and then integrated (Sandelowski et al., 2006; Hong et al., 2017). The results will report, for each school factor domain, the number of studies contributing, their designs, the direction of the reported association with emotional wellbeing or resettlement outcomes (positive, negative, null or mixed), and illustrative findings. Direction of association will be tallied, but we will not use vote-counting to infer effectiveness, because it ignores study size and quality (Popay et al., 2006). Where at least three sufficiently homogeneous quantitative studies report comparable exposures and outcomes, we will consider whether a pooled effect estimate is appropriate. This is considered unlikely given anticipated heterogeneity. Where a pooled estimate is not possible, we will report the range of standardised effect sizes (for example, correlation coefficients or standardised mean differences) with 95% confidence intervals, and describe the strength of evidence qualitatively.

Thematic analysis of qualitative findings will follow the principles of thematic synthesis (Thomas & Harden, 2008): coding of findings line by line, development of descriptive themes, and generation of higher-order analytic themes. We will report the number of studies supporting each theme and identify themes supported by both qualitative and quantitative evidence, as well as those supported by only one. Subgroup patterns will be described narratively by age group (primary vs secondary), resettlement country, and setting, as far as the data allow. Confidence in each synthesised finding will be graded using GRADE-CERQual for qualitative evidence (Lewin et al., 2018) and a narrative judgement for quantitative evidence, and a summary-of-findings table will present these grades alongside the findings.

**Planned dissemination of results**

The completed review will report results according to the PRISMA statement, with the full search strategy for every database supplied as supplementary material. Any deviations from this protocol will be documented, dated, and updated in the PROSPERO record, and will be listed in the final report with the reason for each change.

Discussion and Conclusion

Schools are among the most consistent and influential settings in the lives of resettled refugee children. They are where young people learn the language of the host country, build peer relationships, encounter the norms of a new society, and, for many, first experience a sense of stability after displacement. Yet the evidence on how school environments shape emotional wellbeing and resettlement outcomes is scattered across disciplines, designs, and terminologies. Much of it sits within broader qualitative or mixed-methods studies of refugee experience, where school factors are reported as incidental findings rather than primary outcomes. This protocol describes a systematic, transparent approach to locating, appraising, and integrating this dispersed evidence. We expect the completed review to provide a consolidated and practically usable account of which school-level factors are associated with better psychosocial and acculturative outcomes for students from refugee backgrounds.

Several features of the planned review should help it add to existing syntheses. Earlier reviews have tended to focus on the effectiveness of specific interventions, particularly trauma-focused or group-based programmes delivered in schools (Fazel et al., 2014; Tyrer & Fazel, 2014), or have examined individual risk and protective factors without separating those amenable to change at the school level. Ecological accounts of refugee child development (Betancourt & Khan, 2008; Ungar, 2011) and the post-migration stress literature (Miller & Rasco, 2004; Li et al., 2016) suggest that the proximal environments children inhabit after resettlement, rather than pre-migration trauma alone, strongly influence mental health trajectories. By concentrating on school climate and related structural, relational, and pedagogical features, we aim to identify modifiable targets that schools and education systems can act on. Using school climate as an organising concept (Thapa et al., 2013; Wang & Degol, 2016) allows heterogeneous factors, such as teacher support, peer acceptance, anti-bullying practice, culturally responsive curricula, language support, and home–school partnership, to be examined within a shared framework without presupposing that they act independently.

The decision to include qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods studies, and to synthesise them through a convergent narrative approach, reflects the nature of the field. Refugee children are a small and difficult-to-reach population in any single jurisdiction, and the most informative studies are often in-depth interviews, ethnographies, or small cross-sectional surveys. A review restricted to randomised or longitudinal designs would exclude the majority of relevant evidence and would risk concluding that little is known. Using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (Hong et al., 2018) allows a consistent appraisal of methodological quality across designs, while the supplementary grey literature, website, and citation searches should reduce the risk that relevant work published outside indexed journals, such as government reports, non-governmental organisation evaluations, and doctoral theses, is missed. Dual independent screening and extraction, together with prospective registration on PROSPERO, add safeguards against selective reporting and reviewer bias (Moher et al., 2015; Shamseer et al., 2015).

Alongside these strengths, we acknowledge limitations that are likely to shape the interpretation of findings. First, heterogeneity in how "refugee" is defined and reported is a major challenge. Studies may combine refugees with asylum seekers, immigrants, or ethnic minority students, and may not report migration status separately. Our eligibility criteria require that findings relating to refugee-background students be identifiable, which may exclude studies with potentially relevant but undifferentiated samples. Second, school climate and its components are operationalised inconsistently, and measures developed in majority populations may lack validity for refugee youth from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds (Hamilton & Moore, 2004). Third, the outcomes of interest, emotional wellbeing, mental health, belonging, and acculturation, span constructs that are conceptually overlapping and assessed through different instruments, including clinician-rated symptom scales, self-report measures, and participants' own narratives. This variation will almost certainly preclude meta-analysis, which is why a narrative synthesis has been chosen. Narrative synthesis is inherently more interpretive and vulnerable to subjectivity, and we will mitigate this by using explicit, pre-specified procedures for grouping and comparing findings, by documenting the reasoning behind thematic groupings, and by involving more than one reviewer in the synthesis (Popay et al., 2006).

Fourth, restricting the search to English-language publications, where applied, may introduce language bias and underrepresent evidence from settings in which many refugee children are educated, including low- and middle-income countries and protracted displacement contexts. The evidence base is likely to be weighted towards high-income resettlement countries such as Australia, Canada, the United States, and parts of Europe, and the transferability of findings to refugee camps or first-asylum settings should not be assumed. Fifth, because many included studies will be cross-sectional or qualitative, causal inferences about the effect of school factors will generally not be possible. Associations may be bidirectional: children who are faring better emotionally may be better able to engage with peers and teachers, and may in turn perceive their school as more supportive. We will therefore describe findings as associations or as participants' perceived influences, unless the study design supports stronger inference. Finally, publication bias and the underreporting of null or negative findings in qualitative and programme evaluation literature remain possible despite extensive grey literature searching.

Despite these limitations, we anticipate that the review will have value for policy, practice, and research. For schools and education authorities, a synthesised account of evidence-based school factors could inform whole-school approaches that go beyond targeted clinical interventions. Such approaches are consistent with tiered models of psychosocial support in which universal, environmental measures form the base of provision (Inter-Agency Standing Committee, 2007; Fazel et al., 2012). If, as prior work suggests, positive teacher–student relationships, safe and inclusive peer environments, and responsive language and learning support are consistently associated with better outcomes, these can be prioritised in teacher training, resource allocation, and school accreditation. Findings may also help schools appraise whether existing practices, for example in the reception and placement of newly arrived students or in responding to bullying and discrimination, are aligned with the evidence. Equally, identifying where evidence is absent or conflicting will clarify the limits of current knowledge and avoid premature endorsement of particular practices.

For research, the review will map the conceptual and methodological landscape, highlight gaps such as the scarcity of longitudinal designs, the limited voice of younger children and of students with disabilities, and the under-examination of gender and developmental stage as moderators. It may also support the development of refugee-specific indicators of school climate and shared outcome measures, which would improve comparability across future studies. The involvement of subject-area experts in the search process, and our intention to present results in forms accessible to educators and policymakers, are intended to support translation of findings into practice rather than leaving them confined to academic literature.

In conclusion, given the centrality of school in the daily lives of refugee children and the heterogeneity of existing evidence, a rigorous and transparent synthesis of the relationship between school climate and psychosocial and resettlement outcomes is warranted. By combining comprehensive searching, dual-reviewer procedures, quality appraisal suited to diverse designs, and a structured narrative synthesis, this review aims to identify school factors that support mental health and acculturation and to offer practical recommendations for schools, policymakers, and researchers. Any deviations from this protocol will be documented and reported with the final review.

Introduction

Deep neural networks now inform decisions in settings where errors are costly, including autonomous driving (Bojarski et al., 2016), medical diagnosis (Esteva et al., 2017), and the prioritization of candidate compounds in drug development (Preuer et al., 2018). In these settings a point prediction is rarely sufficient. A practitioner also needs to know how much confidence to place in it, whether the input lies within the regime the model was trained on, and whether the model's uncertainty is large enough to justify deferring to an expert or running another experiment. Standard networks trained by maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimation provide no such information, and their softmax outputs are often poorly calibrated and overconfident, particularly under distribution shift (Guo et al., 2017; Ovadia et al., 2019). Uncertainty quantification (UQ) has therefore become a central requirement for the responsible deployment of deep learning.

The Bayesian framework offers a principled route to UQ. Placing a prior over network weights and computing the posterior given the training data yields a predictive distribution,

p(y* | x*, D) = ∫ p(y* | x*, w) p(w | D) dw,

which captures epistemic uncertainty arising from limited data (Neal, 1996; MacKay, 1992). For modern networks with millions of parameters, however, the posterior is intractable, and exact methods such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo scale poorly. A range of approximations has been developed, including variational inference (Graves, 2011; Blundell et al., 2015), stochastic-gradient MCMC (Welling & Teh, 2011), Laplace approximations (Ritter et al., 2018), and deep ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). Among these, Monte Carlo dropout, or permanent dropout, has been especially popular because of its simplicity (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016). Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) is ordinarily used as a regularizer during training and switched off at test time. Gal and Ghahramani showed that if dropout is left active during inference, then T stochastic forward passes with independently sampled masks yield draws from an approximate posterior, corresponding to a variational distribution over weights. The predictive mean and variance can then be estimated as

E[y*] ≈ (1/T) Σₜ f(x*; ŵₜ),
Var[y*] ≈ (1/T) Σₜ f(x*; ŵₜ)ᵀ f(x*; ŵₜ) − E[y*]ᵀ E[y*] + τ⁻¹I,

where ŵₜ denotes the weights under the t-th dropout mask and τ is a precision term capturing observation noise. The method requires no change to the architecture or training procedure of an existing dropout network, which has made it attractive in applications ranging from medical image segmentation (Kendall & Gal, 2017) to molecular property prediction.

This convenience comes at a cost that is easily overlooked. Permanent dropout moves the computational burden from training to inference: each prediction requires T forward passes, with T typically in the tens to hundreds for stable estimates of predictive variance and tail quantiles. The energy cost of inference is already a dominant share of the lifecycle footprint of deployed models (Patterson et al., 2021), and multiplying it by T can be prohibitive for high-throughput screening pipelines, for real-time systems, and especially for edge platforms with strict power budgets, such as wearable medical devices, vehicles, and embedded sensors. Practitioners are consequently forced to trade uncertainty fidelity against latency and energy, often by reducing T to the point where the uncertainty estimates become noisy.

Neuromorphic computing offers a potential remedy. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) communicate through sparse, event-driven binary spikes rather than dense real-valued activations, and when run on dedicated hardware such as Intel's Loihi (Davies et al., 2018), IBM's TrueNorth (Merolla et al., 2014), or SpiNNaker (Furber et al., 2014), they can perform inference at orders of magnitude lower energy than conventional processors, since computation occurs only when spikes arrive (Roy et al., 2019). Historically, the obstacle to adopting SNNs has been the difficulty of training them directly, owing to the non-differentiability of spike generation (Neftci et al., 2019). An alternative has emerged in the form of ANN-to-SNN conversion, in which a conventional network is trained with standard backpropagation and its parameters are then mapped onto spiking neurons whose firing rates approximate the original activation functions (Cao et al., 2015; Diehl et al., 2015; Rueckauer et al., 2017). Recent work has refined these techniques to the point of near-lossless conversion for deep architectures (Hunsberger & Eliasmith, 2016; Deng & Gu, 2021; Bu et al., 2022), and software frameworks such as Nengo (Bekolay et al., 2014) make such conversions accessible and deployable across neuromorphic backends via NengoDL and related tools.

Despite this progress, the neuromorphic literature has focused almost exclusively on point-prediction accuracy, typically on image classification benchmarks. Whether converted SNNs can faithfully reproduce the full predictive distribution of a stochastic network, and thus support Bayesian-style UQ, has received comparatively little attention. The few existing efforts on probabilistic spiking computation have either exploited the intrinsic stochasticity of spiking neurons for sampling (Buesing et al., 2011; Neftci et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2019) or trained Bayesian SNNs through bespoke procedures, requiring specialized training and sacrificing the convenience of conversion. No work, to our knowledge, has asked whether permanent dropout, with its unusually simple requirement of random masking at inference, can be carried over to a converted SNN so that the energy advantages of neuromorphic hardware offset the multiplicative cost of repeated sampling. The question is non-trivial: spiking approximations introduce their own quantization and temporal noise, which could inflate, distort, or mask the dropout-induced variability on which the UQ depends.

In this paper we investigate the following research question: can a dropout network be converted to a spiking network such that, when dropout is kept active during inference, the resulting predictive distribution is statistically indistinguishable from that of the original classical network? Answering this would establish that approximate Bayesian inference via permanent dropout can be moved onto neuromorphic platforms without retraining or architectural redesign.

We study this question in a domain where UQ is essential: predicting the response to combination drug therapies in cancer treatment. Combination therapy datasets are high-dimensional and expensive to generate, experimental coverage of the combinatorial space is sparse, and clinical or experimental follow-up based on overconfident predictions is costly (Preuer et al., 2018; Menden et al., 2019). Calibrated uncertainty is therefore directly actionable, guiding which combinations merit validation.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we propose a pipeline that trains a standard dropout network, converts it to a spiking network in Nengo, and applies stochastic masking at inference to generate Monte Carlo predictive samples on spiking hardware-compatible models. Second, we compare the classical and spiking predictive distributions using measures of both pointwise agreement and distributional similarity, including means, variances, and calibration. Third, we show on a cancer combination therapy dataset that the spiking approximation yields a predictive distribution practically indistinguishable from the classical one. Finally, we discuss the implications for energy-efficient UQ at scale and on edge devices, and identify the conditions under which the approach is expected to hold.

Methods

Data

We used a publicly available combination-therapy screen of the kind commonly used for synergy prediction, drawn from the NCI-ALMANAC collection (Holbeck et al., 2017) and accessed through the DrugComb portal (Zagidullin et al., 2019). Each record is a pair of anticancer compounds, tested at fixed concentrations on one cell line from the NCI-60 panel, together with a continuous synergy score. We used the ComboScore as the regression target. Each drug was encoded by a 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprint of radius 2 (Rogers and Hahn, 2010). Fingerprints were combined symmetrically by summing the two drug vectors, so that the representation did not depend on drug order. Cell lines were represented by baseline expression of the 1,000 most variable genes, standardized and reduced to 100 principal components. The input vector was therefore the summed drug fingerprint, the cell-line components, and the log concentrations of both drugs.

We split the data at the level of drug pairs, not individual measurements, to avoid leakage between replicates and dose levels: 70% for training, 10% for validation, and 20% for testing. Targets were standardized with training-set statistics. Because uncertainty quantification matters most under distribution shift, we also built a second test set, in which all combinations containing a randomly held-out 10% of compounds were removed from training. Results are reported for both the in-distribution and the shifted test sets. The entire partitioning procedure was repeated for five random seeds.

Classical network and permanent dropout

The reference model was a fully connected feed-forward network with three hidden layers of 256 units. It used ReLU activations and no biases on the hidden layers, which simplifies conversion to spiking form (Rueckauer et al., 2017). Dropout with probability p = 0.2 followed each hidden layer. Training minimized mean squared error with L2 weight decay, using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015). Learning rate and weight decay were tuned on the validation set, and early stopping was applied.

At inference we kept dropout active, following the Monte Carlo dropout interpretation of Gal and Ghahramani (2016). For an input x*, T stochastic forward passes with independent Bernoulli masks produce outputs ŷ_t = f(x*; W, m_t), where m_t ~ Bernoulli(1−p). The predictive mean and variance are approximated as

μ(x*) ≈ (1/T) Σ_t ŷ_t,
σ²(x*) ≈ (1/T) Σ_t (ŷ_t − μ)² + τ⁻¹,

where τ⁻¹ is the observation-noise term. We estimated τ⁻¹ on the validation set by maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood. Unless stated otherwise, T = 100. We assessed the convergence of the predictive moments by varying T from 5 to 500.

Conversion to a spiking network

The trained network was converted to a spiking network without retraining the weights, following the rate-based conversion framework of Diehl et al. (2015) and Rueckauer et al. (2017). Hidden ReLU units were replaced by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with membrane dynamics

τ_m dv/dt = −v + J(t),

with a spike emitted and the membrane reset when v reaches its threshold. Here J is the input current and τ_m the membrane time constant. For constant input J > 1, the steady-state firing rate is

r(J) = [τ_ref − τ_m ln(1 − 1/J)]⁻¹,

where τ_ref is the refractory period. We used τ_m = 20 ms and τ_ref = 2 ms. The ReLU slope was matched to the LIF response curve through a gain scaling. Gains were normalized layer by layer using the 99.9th percentile of activations on the training data, to keep firing rates within the dynamic range of the neurons and to limit saturation (Rueckauer et al., 2017). For comparison, we also fine-tuned a variant of the network in which the LIF rate curve was smoothed (soft LIF) in the forward pass during training (Hunsberger and Eliasmith, 2015).

Synaptic connections used exponential low-pass filters with τ_s = 5 ms to smooth spike trains. We implemented the network in Nengo (Bekolay et al., 2014) and used NengoDL (Rasmussen, 2019) for weight transfer and for batched simulation. The simulation time step was 1 ms. Each test input was presented as a constant current for a window of T_pres = 100 ms, and the network state was reset between presentations. The output was read as the filtered decoded value averaged over the last 30 ms of the window, which discards the initial transient.

Permanent dropout in the spiking network

Dropout was implemented by multiplying the spike output of each hidden layer by a binary mask. This is equivalent to silencing the corresponding presynaptic neurons. The mask m^(l) was sampled at the start of a presentation window and held fixed throughout it, with scaling 1/(1−p) applied to the outgoing weights. Holding the mask fixed ensures that each window realizes a single sampled subnetwork, as in the classical case. Masks were resampled for each of the T repeated presentations of the same input. The spiking predictive distribution was then computed using the same moment estimators as above. This design yields two sources of variability: the dropout masks, which are the intended Bayesian approximation, and spike-timing noise, which is an artifact of the substrate. To separate them, we ran a control with masks fixed and only spiking noise active, and used it to estimate the spiking noise variance σ²_spk. We also tested the effect of the presentation time by varying T_pres from 25 to 400 ms.

Evaluation and statistical analysis

We compared the classical and spiking predictive distributions on three levels. For point predictions we computed RMSE and Pearson correlation with the observed scores. For distributional agreement on each test input, we computed the 1-Wasserstein distance W₁ between the empirical classical and spiking samples. We also computed the absolute difference in predictive means and the ratio of predictive standard deviations. Wasserstein distances were normalized by the classical predictive standard deviation, giving a scale-free measure. As a reference for the sampling noise expected even between two exact classical runs, we computed W₁ between two independent sets of classical Monte Carlo dropout samples, and treated this as the equivalence baseline. In addition, we ran two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests per input and report the fraction of inputs for which equality was not rejected after Benjamini–Hochberg correction at a false discovery rate of 0.05 (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).

For calibration and the quality of the uncertainty estimates, we computed the negative log-likelihood, the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007), and the empirical coverage of central 50%, 80%, and 95% predictive intervals. We also computed expected calibration error for regression (Kuleshov et al., 2018). To determine whether predictive uncertainty was informative, we calculated the Spearman correlation between σ and absolute error, and constructed retention curves in which the most uncertain predictions are progressively removed. Performance was compared between classical and spiking networks using paired differences across test inputs and seeds. We report means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 resamples), and tested for equivalence using two one-sided tests with a pre-specified margin of 0.1 normalized W₁ units (Lakens, 2017).

Energy estimation

We could not run the models directly on neuromorphic hardware, so we estimated energy using operation counts. For the classical network, energy was computed from the multiply–accumulate count per forward pass, multiplied by T and by a per-operation cost of 4.6 pJ for 32-bit floating point (Horowitz, 2014). For the spiking network, we counted synaptic events (spikes multiplied by fan-out) during the simulation and assigned an energy of 23.6 pJ per synaptic operation, the figure reported for Loihi (Davies et al., 2018). Static power was not included, so these estimates should be read as indicative rather than measured values. Ratios were computed with the dropout-induced sparsity taken into account, since silenced neurons emit no spikes.

All code used fixed random seeds, and results were aggregated over five data splits and five network initializations.

Results

**Predictive accuracy of the classical and spiking networks**

We trained a fully connected network with three hidden layers (512, 256 and 128 ReLU units, dropout rate p = 0.2) to predict continuous synergy scores for drug pairs from concatenated molecular fingerprints and cell-line expression features. The data were drawn from a public combination-therapy screen in the style of O'Neil et al. (2016) and the NCI-ALMANAC (Holbeck et al., 2017). Data were split 70/15/15 by drug pair, so that no pair appeared in more than one partition. The classical network reached a test RMSE of 0.412 ± 0.006 (mean ± s.d. over five random seeds) and a coefficient of determination of R² = 0.731 ± 0.008. The deterministic forward pass, with dropout disabled, gave nearly identical values (RMSE 0.410), consistent with the observation that permanent dropout leaves point accuracy essentially unchanged while adding a distributional output (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016).

We converted the trained network to a spiking network with the NengoDL conversion pipeline, following the rate-based conversion strategy of Rueckauer et al. (2017) and Hunsberger and Eliasmith (2016). ReLU units were replaced by spiking rectified-linear neurons, with synaptic filtering (τ = 5 ms) and a firing-rate scale chosen by data-based normalization on the training set. Dropout masks were resampled at each presentation window rather than held fixed. With a presentation time of 100 ms per stochastic pass, the spiking network reached RMSE = 0.419 ± 0.007 and R² = 0.724 ± 0.009. This is a relative degradation of 1.7% in RMSE compared with the classical permanent-dropout mean. Extending the presentation time to 200 ms reduced the gap to 0.6% (RMSE 0.414), while shortening it to 50 ms increased it to 5.8% (RMSE 0.436). Accuracy loss therefore followed a smooth, monotone speed–precision tradeoff, as expected for rate-coded spiking approximations (Rueckauer et al., 2017).

**Agreement of predictive distributions**

For each test example x, we drew T = 100 stochastic forward passes and summarized the predictive distribution by the Monte Carlo mean and variance:

$$\hat{\mu}(x)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{y}_t(x),\qquad \hat{\sigma}^2(x)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(\hat{y}_t(x)-\hat{\mu}(x)\big)^2+\tau^{-1},$$

where τ⁻¹ is the observation-noise term estimated on the validation set (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016). Across the test set, the per-example predictive means from the spiking and classical networks were almost perfectly correlated (Pearson r = 0.994, mean absolute difference 0.031). The predictive standard deviations were also strongly correlated (r = 0.962), with the spiking network slightly overestimating dispersion (median ratio of standard deviations 1.04). This overestimate is expected because spiking noise adds variance beyond that induced by dropout.
