To compare full distributions, we computed the one-dimensional Wasserstein-1 distance between the 100 classical and 100 spiking samples for every test point. The median distance was 0.036 (interquartile range 0.021–0.062), equal to about 0.09 of the test-set RMSE. For comparison, the distance between two independent sets of 100 classical samples at the same input had a median of 0.027 (IQR 0.015–0.048). The spiking–classical discrepancy was therefore only 1.3 times the Monte Carlo sampling noise floor. A two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test at α = 0.05 rejected equality for 7.9% of test points for the spiking-versus-classical comparison, against 5.3% for the classical-versus-classical comparison. This is close to the nominal false-positive rate and indicates that the two predictive distributions are practically indistinguishable for the large majority of inputs. Gaussian-fit KL divergence gave the same picture, with a median of 0.011 nats.

**Calibration and uncertainty quality**

We evaluated whether the spiking approximation preserves the usefulness of the uncertainty estimates. The mean negative log-likelihood (NLL) under a Gaussian predictive density was 0.587 for the classical network and 0.601 for the spiking network. The deterministic network, with a single global noise estimate, gave 0.742, confirming that the stochastic ensemble is the source of the improvement. The empirical coverage of nominal 95% central predictive intervals was 93.1% (classical) and 93.8% (spiking), and nominal 80% intervals covered 78.4% and 79.2% of test targets, respectively. Both networks were slightly overconfident, a known property of dropout-based uncertainty (Ovadia et al., 2019). The calibration error, computed as the mean absolute deviation between nominal and empirical coverage over deciles of the quantile levels (Kuleshov et al., 2018), was 0.021 for the classical network and 0.018 for the spiking network. The slight improvement in the spiking case is consistent with the small amount of added variance compensating for classical underdispersion.

The practical value of uncertainty was assessed with a selective prediction experiment. Test examples were ranked by predictive standard deviation and the most uncertain fraction was removed. For the classical network, retaining the 80% most confident predictions lowered RMSE from 0.412 to 0.331, and retaining 50% lowered it to 0.254. For the spiking network, the corresponding values were 0.338 and 0.261. The Spearman correlation between predictive standard deviation and absolute error was ρ = 0.47 (classical) and ρ = 0.45 (spiking). Moreover, the 20% of pairs flagged as most uncertain by each model overlapped by 87%, so the two models would route nearly the same cases to expert review. Among synergistic combinations (score above the 90th percentile), the spiking network recovered the classical network's ranking with Spearman ρ = 0.97 on the mean prediction and a top-50 overlap of 46 of 50 compounds.

**Dependence on number of samples and simulation time**

The agreement between the spiking and classical distributions depended mainly on the number of stochastic passes, T, and the presentation time. With T = 10, median Wasserstein distance between the two methods was 0.071, falling to 0.044 at T = 30, 0.036 at T = 100 and 0.034 at T = 300. This indicates that beyond roughly T = 100 the remaining discrepancy is dominated by systematic spiking approximation error rather than sampling noise. Because the passes are independent given the dropout masks, they can be pipelined or executed in parallel on neuromorphic hardware. In our simulations, shortening the window to 50 ms while increasing T from 100 to 200 gave a lower NLL (0.598) than the 100 ms, T = 100 setting at the same total simulated time, which suggests that for UQ, more samples with shorter windows can be preferable to fewer, more precise samples.

**Estimated computational and energy cost**

Finally, we estimated the energy cost of T = 100 stochastic passes using spike counts recorded in Nengo and per-operation energy figures reported for Intel's Loihi (Davies et al., 2018) and for a conventional GPU baseline. These figures should be treated as projections, since the experiments themselves were run in simulation. The mean spike count was 1.9 × 10³ spikes per neuron population per 100 ms pass, with 18% of hidden units silent on a typical input. Under the synaptic-operation energy model, this yielded an estimated 0.9 mJ per test example for 100 passes on neuromorphic hardware, compared with an estimated 31 mJ for 100 dense forward passes on a GPU at batch size 1, a reduction of about 34-fold. The estimate decreased roughly linearly with presentation time and was relatively insensitive to the dropout rate over the range p = 0.1–0.3, because dropout reduced the spike count of the active network further.

Discussion and Conclusion

The central finding of this study is that permanent (Monte Carlo) dropout, a widely used approximation to Bayesian inference in deep networks (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016), can be carried out on a spiking neural network obtained by conversion from a conventional network, with little change to the resulting predictive distribution. Because the cost of dropout-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) scales linearly with the number of stochastic forward passes, the method moves the computational burden from training to deployment. Neuromorphic hardware is designed to reduce exactly this cost, and our results suggest the two can be combined without sacrificing the quality of the uncertainty estimates. In the combination-therapy regression task, the spiking and classical predictive means and variances agreed closely, and the differences were small relative to the spread of the predictive distribution itself. For a practitioner, this is the relevant criterion: a clinician or screening pipeline consumes the predictive interval, not the individual forward pass.

Several features of the approach likely explain this agreement. Rate-based conversion pipelines of the kind implemented in Nengo and NengoDL (Bekolay et al., 2014; Rueckauer et al., 2017) approximate each rectified-linear unit with a population of spiking neurons whose firing rate follows the original activation function. Dropout masks are applied to the activations in the same way in both networks, so the Bernoulli noise that underlies the approximate posterior is injected identically, and the spiking approximation contributes only an additional, comparatively small, perturbation. In effect, spiking noise adds to the variability of the predictive distribution, but its magnitude is controlled by synaptic filtering and the length of the presentation window, and it can be driven below the dropout noise. An important observation is that the two sources of variability are not equivalent in kind. Dropout noise reflects, under the variational interpretation, epistemic uncertainty about the weights, whereas spiking noise is a nuisance discretization error that carries no information about the data. Our results indicate that, in the regime tested, the second does not contaminate the first, but this should be verified rather than assumed for each new architecture and time window.

The implications for deployment are potentially significant. Neuromorphic platforms such as Loihi (Davies et al., 2018) and SpiNNaker (Furber et al., 2014) report large energy savings for event-driven inference relative to conventional processors, particularly when activity is sparse. Since permanent dropout multiplies inference cost by tens or hundreds of passes, even moderate per-pass savings accumulate substantially. This matters most at the edge, where power budgets rule out ensembles or repeated sampling, for example in portable diagnostic devices, implantable systems, or autonomous vehicles. A further possibility is that hardware stochasticity could be exploited directly: neuromorphic devices are often noisy, and with appropriate calibration, intrinsic noise or stochastic synapses might supply the Bernoulli masks at almost no additional cost. We did not test this, and doing so would require careful characterization of whether hardware noise has the correct statistical structure to serve as an approximate posterior (Neftci et al., 2016).

Several limitations should be stated plainly. First, our experiments were conducted in the Nengo simulator, not on physical neuromorphic hardware. Simulation captures the neuron and synapse dynamics but not the quantization of weights, limited fan-in, restricted precision, and communication constraints of real chips, each of which can degrade accuracy after conversion. Energy and latency claims are therefore projections based on published hardware characteristics, not measurements from our own experiments. Second, spiking inference requires simulating each input over a window of simulated time, so the latency of each pass is not negligible. If many stochastic passes must be run sequentially, wall-clock latency may offset energy gains in time-critical applications. Parallel replication of the network across cores can address this, but at a cost in chip area. Third, we evaluated a single dataset and a relatively shallow, fully connected architecture. Conversion losses are known to increase with depth, with architectures that include batch normalization, max pooling, or residual connections, and with activation functions that are not well approximated by rates (Diehl et al., 2015; Rueckauer et al., 2017). Whether the near-equivalence of predictive distributions persists in deeper convolutional or attention-based models remains open.

Fourth, the quality of the uncertainty itself is limited by the underlying method. Permanent dropout is an approximation whose posterior is known to be overly restrictive and sensitive to the dropout rate, which is typically fixed rather than learned (Osband, 2016; Ovadia et al., 2019). Our claim is therefore one of fidelity, that the spiking network reproduces what the classical dropout network would produce, and not that either yields well-calibrated uncertainty in an absolute sense. Where dropout-based UQ is miscalibrated, the spiking version will inherit that miscalibration. Likewise, we compared distributions through summary statistics and distributional distances on held-out data; this does not exclude differences in the extreme tails, which are relevant in safety-critical settings. Finally, the dataset used here, although representative of a domain where UQ matters, is of modest size, and we have not evaluated behavior under distribution shift, where the value of UQ is greatest and where small approximation errors might interact with out-of-distribution inputs in unexpected ways.

These limitations suggest a clear agenda. The most immediate step is deployment on physical hardware, with end-to-end measurement of energy per prediction, latency, and distributional agreement under realistic quantization. Next, the approach should be tested on deeper architectures and on additional UQ methods that share the same sampling structure, such as deep ensembles or stochastic-weight approaches, which may map differently onto spiking substrates. Calibration should be assessed explicitly, using proper scoring rules and coverage of predictive intervals, and under covariate shift. The possibility of using native hardware stochasticity as a source of dropout noise deserves systematic study, as does training networks that are spike-aware so that conversion error and dropout variability are jointly accounted for.

In conclusion, we have shown that approximate Bayesian inference through permanent dropout can be transferred to spiking neural networks with predictive distributions that are practically indistinguishable from those of the classical network in our drug combination application. By aligning a UQ technique whose cost lies in repeated inference with hardware designed to make inference inexpensive, this approach offers a plausible route to making uncertainty-aware deep learning practical at scale and on resource-constrained platforms. Confirming this on hardware and across broader model classes is the necessary next step before the energy benefits can be claimed with confidence.

Introduction

Diabetes mellitus has become one of the most pressing public health problems worldwide. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that more than 530 million adults are currently living with diabetes, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) accounts for roughly 90% of cases (Sun et al., 2022). Among its microvascular complications, diabetic nephropathy (DN) is of particular concern because it develops in approximately 30–40% of patients with diabetes and is now the leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in most developed and many developing countries (Alicic et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2015). In China, DN has overtaken primary glomerulonephritis as the most common cause of chronic kidney disease among hospitalized patients in several large centers (Zhang et al., 2020). Once overt proteinuria develops and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) begins to decline, patients face substantially increased risks of cardiovascular events, infection, and premature death, and the economic burden of renal replacement therapy is considerable (Afkarian et al., 2013). Identifying patients at highest risk of rapid progression, ideally using inexpensive and widely available markers, is therefore a clinical priority.

Current risk stratification in DN relies principally on eGFR and albuminuria or proteinuria (KDIGO CKD Work Group, 2013). These markers are indispensable but imperfect. A considerable proportion of patients with T2DM develop reduced eGFR without significant albuminuria, and others with heavy proteinuria show relatively stable kidney function for many years (Krolewski et al., 2014). Renal biopsy offers more granular information, and the pathologic classification proposed by the Renal Pathology Society (Tervaert et al., 2010) has been shown to correlate with renal outcomes in several cohorts (An et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2012). However, biopsy is invasive and cannot be repeated routinely. Consequently, there is continued interest in readily measurable biomarkers that reflect the underlying pathophysiological processes of DN, including chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and impaired erythropoiesis, and that might complement established predictors.

The red cell distribution width (RDW) is a component of the routine complete blood count that quantifies the variability in size of circulating erythrocytes (anisocytosis). Traditionally, it has been used in the differential diagnosis of anemia, where an elevated RDW suggests nutritional deficiency or mixed etiologies (Evans and Jehle, 1991). Over the last two decades, however, RDW has emerged as a prognostic marker in a variety of non-hematologic conditions. In a landmark analysis of patients with recent myocardial infarction, Felker et al. (2007) and subsequently Tonelli et al. (2008) reported that higher RDW was independently associated with death and cardiovascular events. Similar associations have been observed in heart failure, stroke, pulmonary hypertension, and in the general population (Salvagno et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2009). Elevated RDW has also been linked to components of the metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and the presence of diabetes itself (Engström et al., 2014; Lippi et al., 2009). Among patients with T2DM, higher RDW has been associated with poor glycemic control as reflected by glycated hemoglobin, and with microvascular complications including retinopathy and neuropathy (Malandrino et al., 2012; Nada, 2015).

Several mechanisms may explain why RDW tracks adverse outcomes. Systemic inflammation and oxidative stress can suppress erythroid maturation and shorten erythrocyte survival, releasing cells of varying size into the circulation (Förhécz et al., 2009). Proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α blunt the response of erythroid progenitors to erythropoietin, while chronic hyperglycemia promotes glycation and oxidative damage to red cell membranes, thereby altering their deformability and lifespan (Lippi et al., 2009). Reduced erythropoietin production by damaged renal interstitium, iron dysregulation, and deficiency of vitamin B12 or folate, which are common in patients with diabetes and kidney disease, may further contribute to anisocytosis. In the context of DN, all these processes converge, suggesting that RDW might serve as an integrated, low-cost indicator of the inflammatory and metabolic burden that drives renal injury.

Evidence directly linking RDW to kidney disease has been accumulating. In community-based and hospital-based cohorts, higher RDW was associated with prevalent CKD, lower eGFR, and faster kidney function decline (Afonso et al., 2011; Yonemoto et al., 2013). In patients with established CKD, RDW predicted mortality and cardiovascular events (Zhang et al., 2015), and in IgA nephropathy and other primary glomerular diseases it has been related to disease severity and progression (Yang et al., 2019). Within diabetic populations, several cross-sectional studies have reported higher RDW in patients with albuminuria than in those with normoalbuminuria (Zhang et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2019), and a few longitudinal studies suggest that RDW is associated with incident DN or with a decline in eGFR (Li et al., 2018). Clinically, patients with DN are often observed to have an elevated RDW, yet the available literature has important limitations.

First, most studies of RDW in diabetic kidney disease have defined DN clinically, on the basis of albuminuria and/or reduced eGFR, without histological confirmation. Because a substantial proportion of patients with T2DM and kidney disease have non-diabetic renal disease or superimposed lesions (Fiorentino et al., 2017), clinically diagnosed cohorts are heterogeneous, and associations may be confounded by other glomerular or tubulointerstitial diseases. Second, to our knowledge, no previous study has examined how RDW relates to specific pathologic features of biopsy-proven DN, such as glomerular lesion class, interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, interstitial inflammation, and vascular lesions, even though these features are strongly linked to prognosis. Third, evidence on whether RDW predicts hard renal endpoints, namely progression to ESRD, in patients with biopsy-proven DN is scarce, and it remains uncertain whether any such relationship persists after adjustment for conventional predictors such as eGFR, proteinuria, hemoglobin, and serum albumin, with which RDW is inevitably correlated.

To address these gaps, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of 175 patients with T2DM and biopsy-proven DN. Our objectives were threefold: (1) to compare clinical and pathological characteristics between patients with lower and higher RDW, using the cohort median (13.6%) as the cut-off; (2) to examine the correlations of RDW with eGFR and proteinuria as indicators of disease severity; and (3) to evaluate, using Cox proportional hazards models, whether RDW is associated with the risk of progression to ESRD during follow-up and whether any association is independent of established prognostic factors. By pairing a routinely available hematologic index with histologically verified disease and longitudinal renal outcomes, this study aims to clarify the potential role of RDW as a simple adjunctive marker of severity and prognosis in DN.

Methods

Study population and design

We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and biopsy-proven diabetic nephropathy (DN) who were hospitalized at a tertiary care renal center between January 2010 and December 2017. T2DM was diagnosed according to the World Health Organization criteria (fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, 2-hour plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L, or prior diagnosis with current use of glucose-lowering therapy) (American Diabetes Association, 2018). Renal biopsy was performed in patients with T2DM who presented with atypical features, such as rapidly declining renal function, sudden-onset heavy proteinuria, hematuria with dysmorphic red cells, or absence of diabetic retinopathy, and in whom the clinical diagnosis was uncertain. Only patients whose biopsy specimens showed typical diabetic glomerulopathy, without superimposed non-diabetic renal disease, were included.

Exclusion criteria were: (1) type 1 diabetes or other specific types of diabetes; (2) biopsy evidence of any coexisting primary or secondary glomerular disease, including IgA nephropathy and membranous nephropathy; (3) fewer than 6 months of follow-up (unless ESRD or death occurred earlier); (4) missing RDW or baseline serum creatinine values; (5) conditions known to affect RDW independently of DN, namely recent blood transfusion (within 3 months), active bleeding, hematological malignancy, known hemoglobinopathy, myelodysplastic syndrome, or treatment with erythropoietin-stimulating agents, iron, vitamin B12 or folic acid supplementation at the time of the baseline blood draw; (6) acute infection, active malignancy, or decompensated liver disease; and (7) already receiving renal replacement therapy at the time of biopsy. After applying these criteria, 175 patients were included in the final analysis. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the institutional ethics committee. Because of the retrospective design and use of anonymized data, the requirement for informed consent was waived.

Data collection

Baseline clinical and laboratory data were extracted from electronic medical records at the time of renal biopsy. Variables included age, sex, body mass index, duration of diabetes, history of hypertension, presence of diabetic retinopathy (assessed by fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist), systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and use of renin–angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors. Laboratory measurements, obtained after an overnight fast within 3 days before biopsy, comprised hemoglobin, RDW, mean corpuscular volume, white blood cell and platelet counts, serum albumin, creatinine, uric acid, total cholesterol, triglycerides, low- and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, fasting plasma glucose, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), and 24-hour urinary protein excretion. Complete blood counts were analyzed on an automated hematology analyzer using EDTA-anticoagulated venous blood, and RDW was reported as the coefficient of variation of red cell volume distribution (RDW-CV, %), calculated as

RDW (%) = (SD of red cell volume / mean corpuscular volume) × 100.

The laboratory reference range for RDW was 11.5–14.5%. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) creatinine equation (Levey et al., 2009):

eGFR = 141 × min(Scr/κ, 1)^α × max(Scr/κ, 1)^−1.209 × 0.993^Age × 1.018 [if female],

where Scr is serum creatinine in mg/dL, κ is 0.7 for women and 0.9 for men, α is −0.329 for women and −0.411 for men, min indicates the minimum of Scr/κ or 1, and max indicates the maximum of Scr/κ or 1. Proteinuria was expressed as grams per 24 hours. Hypertension was defined as blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg or use of antihypertensive medication.

Renal pathology

Renal biopsy specimens were processed for light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy using standard techniques. Paraffin sections (2–3 μm) were stained with hematoxylin and eosin, periodic acid–Schiff, Masson's trichrome, and periodic acid–silver methenamine. Two experienced renal pathologists, blinded to clinical data, independently reviewed all slides, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. Glomerular lesions were classified according to the Renal Pathology Society classification of diabetic nephropathy (Tervaert et al., 2010): class I, isolated glomerular basement membrane thickening; class IIa/IIb, mild/severe mesangial expansion; class III, nodular sclerosis (Kimmelstiel–Wilson lesions) in at least one glomerulus; and class IV, advanced diabetic glomerulosclerosis with more than 50% global glomerular sclerosis. Interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) was scored semiquantitatively (0, absent; 1, <25%; 2, 25–50%; 3, >50% of cortex involved), interstitial inflammation was scored (0, absent; 1, infiltration only around globally sclerotic glomeruli; 2, infiltration in areas with IFTA; both in relation to the extent of the cortical area), and arteriolar hyalinosis (0, absent; 1, at least one area of arteriolar hyalinosis; 2, more than one area; 3, circumferential hyalinosis in >1 arteriole) and large-vessel arteriosclerosis were graded according to the same classification. The percentage of globally sclerotic glomeruli was also recorded.

Grouping by RDW

Patients were stratified according to the median baseline RDW of the cohort (13.6%) into group 1 (RDW <13.6%) and group 2 (RDW ≥13.6%). Median-based dichotomization was chosen because no validated RDW cutoff exists for patients with DN, and it ensured balanced group sizes and sufficient events in each stratum. RDW was additionally analyzed as a continuous variable in correlation and regression models to avoid loss of information.

Follow-up and outcomes

Patients were followed from the date of renal biopsy until the occurrence of the primary endpoint, death, loss to follow-up, or the end of the observation period (June 30, 2019). Follow-up data were obtained from outpatient and inpatient records and by telephone interview when necessary. The primary endpoint was progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), defined as eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m², initiation of maintenance dialysis, or kidney transplantation, whichever came first (KDIGO, 2013). Time to ESRD was calculated in months. Patients who died before reaching ESRD or who were lost to follow-up were censored at the date of the last available contact.

Statistical analysis

Continuous variables were tested for normality with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Normally distributed data are presented as mean ± standard deviation and were compared between groups using the independent-samples t test; skewed data are presented as median (interquartile range) and were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables are given as counts and percentages and were compared using the χ² test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Ordinal pathological scores were compared using the Mann–Whitney U or Cochran–Armitage trend tests. Relationships between RDW and continuous clinical variables, including eGFR, 24-hour proteinuria, hemoglobin, and albumin, were evaluated using Pearson's or Spearman's correlation coefficients according to data distribution; proteinuria was log-transformed where appropriate. Multivariable linear regression was used to examine whether RDW remained associated with eGFR after adjustment for age, sex, hemoglobin, and diabetes duration.

Renal survival curves for the two RDW groups were generated by the Kaplan–Meier method and compared with the log-rank test. The association between RDW and the risk of ESRD was quantified using Cox proportional hazards regression, in which the hazard for individual i at time t is modeled as

h(t | x_i) = h₀(t) · exp(β₁x_i1 + β₂x_i2 + … + β_px_ip),

and hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were obtained as exp(β). We fitted a sequence of nested models: model 1 was unadjusted; model 2 was adjusted for age, sex, and diabetes duration; and model 3 was additionally adjusted for variables with clinical relevance or with p<0.10 in univariable analysis, namely baseline eGFR, 24-hour proteinuria, hemoglobin, serum albumin, HbA1c, systolic blood pressure, RAS inhibitor use, and pathological class. To avoid overfitting, the number of covariates was limited in accordance with the rule of approximately 10 events per variable (Peduzzi et al., 1996). Collinearity was assessed through variance inflation factors, with values >5 considered problematic. The proportional hazards assumption was verified using scaled Schoenfeld residuals and log–log survival plots. Potential non-linearity of the continuous RDW effect was explored using restricted cubic splines.

As a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the Cox models with RDW analyzed as a continuous variable (per 1% increase) and by tertiles. Missing data for covariates were infrequent (<5%) and were handled by complete-case analysis. The predictive value of RDW for ESRD was further assessed by receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, with discrimination summarized as the area under the curve.

All tests were two-sided, and p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using SPSS version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) and R version 3.6 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

Results

Baseline characteristics of the study population

A total of 175 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and biopsy-proven diabetic nephropathy (DN) were included in the analysis. The median RDW was 13.6% (interquartile range [IQR] 12.9–14.5%), and this value was used to divide the cohort into group 1 (RDW <13.6%, n = 87) and group 2 (RDW ≥13.6%, n = 88). Baseline demographic, clinical and laboratory characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The mean age of the whole cohort was 50.8 ± 10.4 years, and 118 patients (67.4%) were men. Age, body mass index, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and the prevalence of hypertension and diabetic retinopathy did not differ significantly between the two groups (all p > 0.05).

Patients in group 2 were more frequently female than those in group 1 (41.0% vs. 24.1%, p = 0.017) and had a longer duration of diabetes (median 9.0 [5.0–13.0] vs. 6.0 [3.0–10.0] years, p = 0.004). Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was significantly lower in the higher-RDW group (52.4 ± 26.8 vs. 69.7 ± 28.5 mL/min/1.73 m², p < 0.001), as were serum albumin (32.1 ± 6.4 vs. 35.4 ± 6.9 g/L, p = 0.002) and hemoglobin (110.3 ± 21.5 vs. 124.6 ± 20.8 g/L, p < 0.001). Serum creatinine was correspondingly higher in group 2 (p < 0.001). Twenty-four-hour urinary protein excretion tended to be greater in group 2 (3.9 [1.8–6.2] vs. 2.6 [1.1–4.8] g/24 h), although this difference only approached significance (p = 0.058). Fasting plasma glucose, glycated hemoglobin, total cholesterol, triglycerides and LDL-cholesterol did not differ between groups. The use of renin–angiotensin system inhibitors at baseline was also similar (73.9% vs. 77.0%, p = 0.64).

Renal pathologic findings

Pathologic lesions were classified according to the Renal Pathology Society criteria (Tervaert et al., 2010). Patients with higher RDW showed more severe glomerular damage. The distribution of glomerular classes differed significantly between groups (p = 0.011): class IV lesions were present in 21.6% of group 2 compared with 8.0% of group 1, whereas class IIa/IIb lesions were more common in group 1 (52.9% vs. 36.4%). The proportion of patients with class III lesions was comparable (31.0% vs. 34.1%). The percentage of globally sclerotic glomeruli was higher in group 2 (24.5 ± 18.2% vs. 15.8 ± 14.1%, p = 0.001). By contrast, the severity of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) showed only a nonsignificant trend toward higher scores in group 2 (score ≥2 in 52.3% vs. 40.2%, p = 0.115), and the degree of interstitial inflammation and arteriolar hyalinosis did not differ significantly between groups (p = 0.21 and p = 0.18, respectively).

Correlations between RDW and clinical parameters

In Spearman correlation analysis, RDW was inversely correlated with eGFR (r = −0.283, p < 0.001) and positively correlated with 24-hour proteinuria (r = 0.227, p = 0.003). RDW was also negatively associated with hemoglobin (r = −0.341, p < 0.001) and serum albumin (r = −0.236, p = 0.002), and positively associated with diabetes duration (r = 0.205, p = 0.007) and the percentage of globally sclerotic glomeruli (r = 0.264, p < 0.001). No significant correlation was found between RDW and HbA1c (r = 0.071, p = 0.35) or blood pressure. In a multivariable linear regression model including age, sex, hemoglobin, eGFR and proteinuria, eGFR (standardized β = −0.218, p = 0.006) and hemoglobin (β = −0.262, p = 0.001) remained independently associated with log-transformed RDW, whereas proteinuria did not (β = 0.087, p = 0.26), suggesting that the relationship between RDW and proteinuria was largely mediated through reduced kidney function and anemia.

Association of RDW with progression to ESRD

The median follow-up was 28.0 months (IQR 13.0–46.0). During follow-up, 81 patients (46.3%) reached end-stage renal disease (ESRD), defined as eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or initiation of renal replacement therapy. The proportion of patients reaching ESRD was considerably higher in group 2 than in group 1 (58.0% [51/88] vs. 34.5% [30/87], p = 0.002). Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly poorer renal survival in the higher-RDW group (log-rank χ² = 10.4, p = 0.001); the estimated 1-year renal survival rates were 78.4% and 91.9% in groups 2 and 1, respectively, and the 3-year rates were 41.2% and 66.5%. The median renal survival time was 34.0 months in group 2 and was not reached in group 1.

Table 2 shows the results of the Cox proportional hazards analyses. In the unadjusted model, higher RDW (≥13.6%) was associated with an increased risk of ESRD (hazard ratio [HR] 1.92, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.22–3.02, p = 0.005). When RDW was analyzed as a continuous variable, each 1% increase was associated with a 24% higher hazard (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.08–1.43, p = 0.003). After adjustment for age and sex (model 1), the association remained significant (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.16–2.94, p = 0.010). Additional adjustment for diabetes duration, systolic blood pressure and HbA1c (model 2) yielded an HR of 1.66 (95% CI 1.03–2.69, p = 0.037). However, when baseline eGFR, 24-hour proteinuria, hemoglobin and serum albumin were further included (model 3), the association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.73–2.00, p = 0.46). In this fully adjusted model, baseline eGFR (HR 0.97 per mL/min/1.73 m² increase, 95% CI 0.95–0.98, p < 0.001), proteinuria (HR 1.12 per g/24 h, 95% CI 1.05–1.20, p = 0.001) and the percentage of globally sclerotic glomeruli (HR 1.02 per 1%, 95% CI 1.01–1.04, p = 0.008) were the independent predictors of ESRD, whereas RDW was not. The proportional hazards assumption was verified using Schoenfeld residuals (global p = 0.39). Inclusion of RDW in model 3 did not significantly improve model discrimination (Harrell’s C-index 0.781 vs. 0.776, p = 0.52).

Subgroup and sensitivity analyses

The direction of the association between high RDW and ESRD was consistent across subgroups stratified by sex, age (<50 vs. ≥50 years), diabetes duration (<8 vs. ≥8 years) and presence of anemia (hemoglobin <120 g/L for women and <130 g/L for men), with no significant interaction (all p for interaction >0.10). Nevertheless, in the subgroup with baseline eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m² (n = 64), the unadjusted HR for high RDW was 2.31 (95% CI 0.94–5.68, p = 0.068), but the limited number of events (n = 14) precluded firm conclusions. When RDW was categorized into tertiles (<13.1%, 13.1–14.1%, ≥14.2%), a graded increase in the unadjusted risk of ESRD was observed (HR 1.00, 1.58 and 2.41; p for trend = 0.002), which again lost significance after full adjustment (p for trend = 0.51). Excluding patients with hemoglobin <90 g/L (n = 21) did not materially change the findings (unadjusted HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.09–2.91; fully adjusted HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.69–1.98).

Discussion

In this cohort of 175 patients with type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven diabetic nephropathy (DN), higher red cell distribution width (RDW) was associated with a more severe clinical and pathological phenotype: lower eGFR, lower albumin and hemoglobin, longer diabetes duration, and more advanced glomerular lesions. RDW correlated inversely with eGFR and positively with proteinuria. Patients with RDW ≥13.6% had a significantly higher unadjusted risk of progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), but RDW did not remain an independent predictor after adjustment for established prognostic factors. RDW therefore appears to be a marker of disease severity that overlaps substantially with baseline renal function and proteinuria, rather than an independent determinant of renal outcome in this population.

The association between RDW and renal function agrees with earlier work. Higher RDW has been linked to prevalent and incident chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the general population and in hospital-based cohorts (Afonso et al., 2011; Yonemoto et al., 2018), and to faster eGFR decline and ESRD in CKD patients (Zhang et al., 2015). In diabetes, elevated RDW has been related to microvascular complications, including retinopathy and albuminuria (Zhang et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018), and to cardiovascular and all-cause mortality (Patel et al., 2010). Our biopsy-based data extend these observations by showing that RDW also tracks histological injury, which is less susceptible to the misclassification that may affect clinically diagnosed DN, where non-diabetic kidney disease is frequently present (Fiorentino et al., 2017).

Several mechanisms could explain these findings, and they are probably not mutually exclusive. First, chronic low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress are central to DN pathogenesis (Navarro-González et al., 2011) and also disturb erythropoiesis. Inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α blunt erythropoietin responsiveness and impair iron mobilization, and they promote the release of immature reticulocytes of variable size, increasing anisocytosis (Pierce and Larson, 2013). Oxidative damage also shortens red-cell survival and enlarges the dispersion of cell volumes (Friedman et al., 2012). Second, relative erythropoietin deficiency from tubulointerstitial injury is common in diabetic kidney disease, often early and out of proportion to the loss of GFR (Thomas et al., 2003; Bosman et al., 2001). This could explain the lower hemoglobin in the high-RDW group. Third, nutritional deficiency, particularly of iron, folate and vitamin B12, which is common in patients with diabetes on metformin or with poor appetite in advanced CKD, can raise RDW. Fourth, hypoalbuminemia, which was more pronounced in our high-RDW group, is itself an indicator of inflammation, malnutrition and heavy proteinuria, and it has been tied to RDW in other settings (Salvagno et al., 2015). Finally, chronic hyperglycemia can alter erythrocyte membrane properties and deformability through glycation, which may contribute to heterogeneity in red-cell size (Kung et al., 2009). RDW thus appears to integrate several processes that also drive DN progression, which is consistent with its association with glomerular damage.

The loss of independence in multivariable models deserves careful interpretation. The most likely explanation is shared variance: RDW was correlated with eGFR, proteinuria, hemoglobin and albumin, which are themselves strong predictors of ESRD in DN (Zoppini et al., 2012; Tervaert et al., 2010). Adjusting for these covariates may absorb most of the prognostic information carried by RDW, suggesting that RDW lies on, or near, the causal pathway between systemic inflammation, anemia and renal progression, rather than acting independently. Over-adjustment for mediators can also attenuate associations that are biologically real. A second consideration is statistical power. With 175 patients and 81 events, the model could support only a limited number of covariates, and the confidence interval around the adjusted estimate may be wide enough to include a modest independent effect. Dichotomizing RDW at the median discards information and may reduce power further, and the 13.6% threshold is data-driven, so it should not be considered a clinically validated cut-off. Analyses of RDW as a continuous variable, with assessment of non-linearity, would be a useful next step.

Even without independent prognostic value, RDW has potential practical relevance. It is inexpensive, standardized and reported automatically with every complete blood count, so it requires no additional testing. It might serve as a simple flag for patients who warrant closer attention, such as screening for iron or vitamin deficiency, evaluation of inflammatory burden and more frequent monitoring of renal function. Whether RDW adds incremental discrimination beyond eGFR and proteinuria could be assessed formally by changes in the C-statistic, net reclassification improvement or integrated discrimination improvement, which we did not evaluate. Whether lowering RDW, for example by correcting nutritional deficiencies or treating inflammation, would alter renal outcomes is unknown, and our observational data cannot address causality.

This study has several limitations. It was a retrospective, single-center analysis of patients who underwent renal biopsy, so selection bias is likely: biopsy is generally performed in patients with atypical features or significant proteinuria, which limits generalizability to the broader T2DM population with milder disease. The sample was modest, and the relatively high proportion reaching ESRD (46.3%) reflects a high-risk referral population. RDW was measured at a single time point at baseline; RDW fluctuates with transfusion, acute illness, iron or vitamin supplementation and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, and we could not account for changes over time. We lacked data on iron indices, vitamin B12 and folate, erythropoietin levels, and inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein, so we could not test the proposed mechanisms directly. Medications that can affect RDW or progression, including renin–angiotensin system inhibitors, which lower hemoglobin slightly, and more recent agents such as SGLT2 inhibitors, may have varied across the follow-up period. Follow-up duration and the timing of ESRD ascertainment may also have differed between patients. In addition, the median split and the possibility of residual confounding mean the adjusted estimates should be interpreted cautiously. Finally, the study had no external validation cohort.

Future work should include larger, multicenter, prospective cohorts with serial RDW measurements, comprehensive hematinic and inflammatory profiling, and standardized pathological scoring, so that the contribution of RDW can be separated from that of anemia and impaired kidney function. Mediation analyses and joint modeling of longitudinal RDW and eGFR trajectories would help clarify whether RDW is a mediator, a marker or a modifiable contributor to progression.

In conclusion, higher RDW was associated with more severe renal dysfunction, greater proteinuria, worse glomerular pathology and a higher unadjusted risk of progression to ESRD in patients with biopsy-proven DN, although it was not an independent predictor of renal outcome. RDW should be viewed as an accessible integrative marker of disease severity and of the inflammatory and anemic milieu of advanced DN, rather than as a stand-alone prognostic tool. Confirmation in larger prospective studies is required before it can be incorporated into risk stratification.

Introduction

Events are the basic units through which documents describe what happens in the world, and understanding a text largely means understanding how its events relate to one another. A news report on an earthquake, for example, mentions the quake itself, the collapse of buildings, rescue operations, and subsequent aid pledges. Some of these mentions refer to the same real-world occurrence, while others describe distinct occurrences linked by time, causation, or narrative structure. Recovering these relations is important for downstream applications such as summarization (Daumé and Marcu, 2006), question answering (Narayanan and Harabagiu, 2004), knowledge base population (Ji and Grishman, 2011), and storyline extraction (Vossen et al., 2015). In this paper, we study two such relations: Event Coreference, which groups event mentions that refer to the same event, and Event Sequencing, which orders the subevents of a larger event in the sequence in which they are narrated within a script-like structure.

Event coreference resolution has received considerable attention over the past decade. Early work adapted entity coreference techniques to events, using pairwise classifiers over lexical, syntactic, and argument-overlap features (Bejan and Harabagiu, 2010; Lee et al., 2012). More recent systems incorporate distributed representations and neural architectures (Krause et al., 2016; Choubey and Huang, 2017; Lu and Ng, 2017), and shared tasks such as the TAC-KBP Event Nugget track (Mitamura et al., 2015, 2016) have provided standardized evaluation. A common feature of nearly all of this work is its decoding strategy. Following the mention-pair and mention-ranking paradigms of entity coreference (Soon et al., 2001; Denis and Baldridge, 2008; Durrett and Klein, 2013), systems typically link each mention to at most one antecedent, so the resulting structure is a forest in which each tree corresponds to one coreference cluster. This is a natural fit for coreference: coreference is an equivalence relation, so a single link to any earlier member of the cluster is sufficient to determine membership, and transitivity supplies the rest. The tree-like structure also admits efficient inference and learning, for example through latent antecedent trees (Fernandes et al., 2012; Björkelund and Kuhn, 2014).

Event sequencing, by contrast, has been studied less often and under different guises. Work on narrative schemas and scripts (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008, 2009; Pichotta and Mooney, 2016) learns typical orderings of events from large corpora, while temporal relation research (Pustejovsky et al., 2003; UzZaman et al., 2013; Ning et al., 2018) classifies pairwise relations such as BEFORE and AFTER between events on a document timeline. Our notion of sequencing is related to both but differs from each. Rather than asking about absolute or pairwise temporal order alone, we ask how the subevents of a complex event follow one another in the discourse, for instance that an attack is followed by an injury, an arrest, and a trial. These sequences are not equivalence classes. A subevent may follow several preceding events, may be followed by several, and a given event may participate in more than one sequence when a narrative branches or converges. Moreover, the relation is non-transitive in the sense relevant for annotation: a direct link between consecutive subevents carries information that would be lost if links were inferred from distant order.

This difference exposes a gap. If sequencing is decoded with the same antecedent-tree structure that works for coreference, each event can have only a single predecessor, and the output cannot represent branching or merging within a script. Such a restriction forces the model to discard valid links and to commit to one parent even when the text supports several. Conversely, relaxing the structure entirely, as in independent pairwise classification, yields outputs that may be inconsistent and that ignore global properties of the relation, such as the fact that sequence links should respect the narrative order of mentions and should not form cycles. Existing temporal ordering work often resolves such inconsistencies with global inference such as integer linear programming (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Do et al., 2012; Ning et al., 2017), but these approaches are typically designed for a single relation type and do not provide a shared decoding framework that can also handle coreference. As a result, the two relations are generally modeled by separate pipelines with incompatible assumptions, even though they interact: coreferent mentions should occupy the same position in a sequence, and sequence links between mentions should be consistent with their cluster membership.

These observations lead to our central research question: can a single decoding framework, more general than the antecedent tree, represent and learn both event coreference and event sequencing, while remaining competitive with specialized systems on each? A related question concerns the structure itself. We ask specifically whether the tree-like decoding that is effective for coreference is in fact inadequate for sequencing, and if so, what minimal relaxation is needed to capture sequencing structure without sacrificing the advantages of structured inference for coreference.

We address these questions by proposing a graph-based decoding algorithm. Events are treated as nodes, and relations are predicted as edges in a directed acyclic graph whose permitted topology is determined by the task. For coreference, the decoder is constrained so that each mention selects at most one antecedent, recovering the tree structure and the cluster semantics that follow from it. For sequencing, the constraint is lifted so that a mention may attach to multiple predecessors, which allows branching and merging while the acyclicity requirement and mention ordering still enforce coherent output. Because the decoder operates over edge scores and does not depend on how those scores are produced, it supports flexible feature sets, including lexical, discourse, argument, and embedding-based features, and allows task-specific features to be added without changing the inference procedure. The model is trained with a structured, margin-based objective so that learning matches the decoding used at test time.

We evaluate the approach on both tasks. On the TAC-KBP 2015 event coreference task, our system achieves state-of-the-art performance under the standard metrics (MUC, B³, CEAF-e, and BLANC; Vilain et al., 1995; Bagga and Baldwin, 1998; Luo, 2005; Recasens and Hovy, 2011). For event sequencing, we compare against a strong baseline that relies on temporal ordering of events and is informed by oracle information, and our system outperforms it despite that advantage.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we show, through analysis of the annotated data and through experiments, that the tree-like decoding structure standard in event coreference is unsuitable for event sequencing. Second, we introduce a graph-based decoding algorithm that unifies the two tasks and accommodates flexible feature sets. Third, we report state-of-the-art coreference results on TAC-KBP 2015 and sequencing results that surpass a strong oracle-informed temporal baseline. Finally, we discuss the challenges that remain in studying these event relations, including annotation sparsity, ambiguity in event granularity, and error propagation from upstream event detection.

Methods

**Data**

We evaluated the coreference system on the TAC-KBP 2015 Event Nugget corpus (Mitamura et al., 2015), which contains newswire and discussion-forum documents annotated for event nuggets (trigger spans with type and realis attributes) and within-document event coreference. Following the shared-task protocol, we trained on the 2015 training release (158 documents) and tested on the official 2015 evaluation set (202 documents). Ten percent of the training documents, sampled at random, were held out as a development set for feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. The final model was retrained on the full training set with the selected settings. The input to the coreference system was gold event mentions for the main experiments. We also report results on system-predicted mentions from a sequence-labeling nugget detector, to show how mention errors propagate.

Event sequencing was studied on the same documents, so that the two tasks share mentions and coreference clusters. A sequencing link connects an event to the event that immediately follows it in the narrative script of the document (Chambers & Jurafsky, 2008). Annotators marked a link only when the later event could be inferred to happen after the earlier one. Links are defined between coreference clusters rather than individual mentions, because coreferent mentions denote one event. Because a story can branch, an event may have several successors and several predecessors. We split the data at the document level in the same way as for coreference. Inter-annotator agreement was computed as Cohen's κ on a doubly annotated subset.

**Decoding structure**

Let a document contain mentions m_1, …, m_n in textual order. The usual approach to coreference is the latent antecedent tree (Yu & Joachims, 2009; Fernandes et al., 2012; Durrett & Klein, 2013). Each mention m_j selects a single antecedent a(j) ∈ {ε, m_1, …, m_{j−1}}, where ε is a dummy root that starts a new cluster. The set of selected edges forms a tree, and the connected components are the clusters. The score of an edge is a linear function of a feature vector:

s(i, j) = w · φ(m_i, m_j),  â(j) = argmax_{i<j or i=ε} s(i, j).

This single-parent constraint suits coreference, because transitivity means one antecedent link suffices to place a mention in a cluster. It is unsuitable for sequencing, where an event can have more than one valid predecessor, so forcing a single parent discards valid links and makes the output depend on arbitrary tie-breaking.

We therefore decode over a general directed graph G = (V, E). For coreference, V is the set of mentions. For sequencing, V is the set of clusters produced by the coreference stage. We write E_c and E_s for the coreference and sequencing edge sets. For each candidate pair (i, j) the model scores the edge with the task-specific weight vector w_t, t ∈ {c, s}. An edge is included when its score exceeds a threshold:

E_t = {(i, j) : w_t · φ_t(i, j) > τ_t}.

The threshold τ_t is tuned on the development set. Coreference keeps the tree constraint of at most one incoming edge per mention, so it uses the highest-scoring antecedent when that score exceeds τ_c, and otherwise links to ε. This makes the tree decoder a special case of the graph decoder. Sequencing places no limit on in-degree or out-degree, but we require the graph to be acyclic. Candidate edges are considered in descending score order, and an edge is skipped if it would close a cycle. This greedy procedure is not guaranteed to find the optimal DAG, but exact search is NP-hard in general (Chickering, 1996), and in preliminary experiments greedy search produced the same graphs as beam search on over 97% of documents. To keep the sequencing graph compact we apply transitive reduction to the output. An edge (i, k) is removed when a path i → j → k exists with both component edges selected.

**Learning**

Both tasks are trained with a structured perceptron (Collins, 2002) using the averaged weights. Gold coreference annotation gives only clusters, not antecedent choices, so the correct structure is latent. For each mention m_j we define the latent gold antecedent as the highest-scoring gold-coreferent predecessor under the current weights:

i*(j) = argmax_{i ∈ Gold(j)} w_c · φ_c(m_i, m_j),

where Gold(j) is the set of preceding mentions in the same gold cluster, or {ε} if m_j starts a cluster. The update at mention j is

w_c ← w_c + η [φ_c(m_{i*(j)}, m_j) − φ_c(m_{â(j)}, m_j)]

whenever â(j) ≠ i*(j). We use a cost-augmented variant (Fernandes et al., 2012), in which erroneous links to ε and erroneous non-root links receive different margin penalties (λ_FN and λ_FA). These two penalties were tuned for the trade-off between precision and recall.

For sequencing, the gold structure is observed at the cluster level, so no latent selection is needed. For each pair of clusters the update is

w_s ← w_s + η y_{ij} φ_s(i, j) · 1[y_{ij} (w_s · φ_s(i, j)) ≤ 0],

where y_{ij} ∈ {+1, −1} indicates whether the link is gold. Negative pairs are restricted to cluster pairs within a window of 10 sentences, because most gold links fall within this range. We train for 20 epochs with early stopping on the development set.

**Features**

The coreference features follow Liu et al. (2014) and Lu & Ng (2017). They include lexical match and lemma overlap of triggers, WordNet (Miller, 1995) synonymy, cosine similarity of pretrained word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013), event type and realis agreement, sentence and token distance, and argument overlap derived from a semantic role labeler and an entity coreference system. All of these are computed on mention pairs.

Sequencing features are computed on cluster pairs. We aggregate pairwise mention features by taking the maximum and the mean over all mention pairs in the two clusters. The features include the event types of both clusters, the order of their first mentions, the minimum sentence distance, and discourse connectives and temporal expressions near each trigger. For clusters that share a participant we add the participant's role in each event. We also add the signed difference of the clusters' positions in the document. Because the decoder scores each edge independently, any pairwise or cluster-level feature set can be used without changing inference. We exploit this by testing feature groups separately and in combination in the ablations.

**Baselines**

For coreference we compared against the top-ranked TAC-KBP 2015 systems (Mitamura et al., 2015), the tree-based latent antecedent model with the same features, and a mention-pair model with closest-first clustering (Soon et al., 2001). For sequencing we used a strong oracle-informed temporal baseline. It takes gold coreference clusters and orders them by the textual position of their first mention, since narrative order often approximates temporal order (Mani & Schiffman, 2005). It then links each cluster to its immediate predecessor in this ordering. This baseline therefore uses gold cluster information that our system does not receive in the end-to-end setting. We also report a variant of our model constrained to a single parent, to isolate the effect of the tree structure.

**Evaluation and statistical analysis**

Coreference was scored with the official TAC-KBP scorer (Pradhan et al., 2014), which reports MUC (Vilain et al., 1995), B³ (Bagga & Baldwin, 1998), entity-based CEAF (CEAF-e; Luo, 2005), and BLANC (Recasens & Hovy, 2011), together with their unweighted average. Sequencing was scored by precision, recall, and F1 over cluster-level links. Because the graph is transitive in meaning, we also report a variant that computes the same measures over the transitive closure of both gold and system graphs, so that systems are not penalized for omitting redundant edges.

Because the test set is small and metrics are not independent across mentions, we assessed significance by paired bootstrap resampling over documents (Berg-Kirkpatrick et al., 2012), with 10,000 resamples and a significance level of 0.05. Reported scores for the learned models are means over five runs with different random shuffles of the training data. Hyperparameters (η, τ_c, τ_s, λ_FN, λ_FA, and the negative-sampling window) were selected by grid search on the development set only.

Results

**Experimental Setup**

We evaluated event coreference on the TAC-KBP 2015 Event Nugget evaluation data (Mitamura et al., 2015), following the official protocol. The classifier was trained on the 2015 training documents (158 documents) plus the 2014 annotation release, with 20% of the training documents held out for tuning. The test portion contains 202 documents with 3,670 gold coreference clusters. We report the official scorer's metrics: MUC (Vilain et al., 1995), B³ (Bagga & Baldwin, 1998), entity-based CEAF (CEAF-e; Luo, 2005), and BLANC (Recasens & Hovy, 2011). The AVG score is the mean of the four F1 values. All coreference results use system-predicted event mentions from our nugget detector, whose type-sensitive F1 on the test set is 58.9. Event sequencing was evaluated on the same collection, using the "after" links and script-like sequences described in the Methods. We report precision, recall, and F1 over directed links, and a stricter sequence-level F1 that counts a predicted chain as correct only if all of its links are correct. All differences reported as significant were tested with a paired bootstrap resampling test over documents (10,000 samples, p < 0.05).

**Event Coreference**

Table 1 compares our graph-based decoder with the top KBP 2015 participants and with later published systems. Our system reaches an AVG F1 of 53.9, with MUC 31.4, B³ 49.8, CEAF-e 50.6, and BLANC 43.3 (the latter scored as F1). This is 1.6 points above the strongest system we compare against, the joint model of Lu and Ng (2017), at 52.3. It is also 3.2 points above the best official 2015 submission, 50.7, and 4.6 points above the mention-ranking system of Choubey and Huang (2017), which reaches 49.3 in our re-scoring. The gain over Lu and Ng comes mainly from MUC (+2.1) and BLANC (+2.4), the two metrics most sensitive to link-level recall. B³ and CEAF-e differ by less than 1 point. The AVG improvement over the best prior system is statistically significant (p = 0.03). The improvements on individual metrics are significant only for MUC and BLANC.

We also compared the graph decoder with other decoding strategies under identical features and the same pairwise classifier. A simple closest-first clustering of pairwise decisions (Soon et al., 2001) gives an AVG of 48.2. Best-first (antecedent-tree) decoding trained with a latent-antecedent perceptron, as in Durrett and Klein (2013) and Fernandes et al. (2012), reaches 51.8. Our graph decoder reaches 53.9. The graph decoder differs from the tree decoder in allowing a mention to retain links to multiple antecedents within a cluster, and the tree-to-graph gain of 2.1 AVG points is significant (p = 0.02). Most of it appears as higher recall: pairwise link recall on gold within-cluster pairs rises from 41.7 to 48.9, while precision falls only from 56.3 to 54.8. Cluster-level analysis shows the gain concentrated in larger clusters. For clusters of four or more mentions (11% of gold clusters, 39% of mentions), B³ F1 rises from 44.2 to 49.5. For singletons and pairs, the two decoders are statistically indistinguishable.

The flexible feature set also helps. Starting from a baseline with only lexical and surface features (head-word match, lemma overlap, type match, sentence distance), the system scores 47.6 AVG. Adding argument and entity-compatibility features, such as shared agent or patient, yields 50.9 (+3.3). Adding discourse features, such as same-paragraph and nearby-mention indicators, gives 52.2 (+1.3). Adding features derived from the sequencing relation, namely whether the two events have compatible predecessors or successors in the current partial graph, gives the final 53.9 (+1.7). Removing the sequencing-derived features reproduces the 52.2 configuration, so this effect is not a by-product of other features. These features are available only because the decoder maintains an explicit graph over events rather than a tree of antecedent choices.

**Event Sequencing**

For sequencing, the key question is whether the tree-like structure used for coreference suits the task. Analysis of the gold annotation shows that it does not. Among events with at least one gold predecessor in their sequence, 37.4% have two or more predecessors, and 28.9% have two or more successors. A decoder that selects one antecedent per mention, as in tree-based coreference decoding, therefore has a maximum attainable link recall of 62.6%, even with a perfect scorer. In contrast, the graph decoder has no such structural ceiling.

Table 2 reports sequencing results. The baseline is a strong temporal-based, oracle-informed system. It uses gold event mentions and gold coreference clusters, and it orders events by the gold temporal relation from the annotation layer (when available) and by textual order otherwise, linking each event to its immediate temporal neighbor. Despite its oracle information, it reaches only 34.6 link F1 (precision 41.8, recall 29.5), which shows that temporal order alone does not determine which events form a script-like sequence. A tree-decoding variant of our model, using a single best predecessor per event, reaches 36.9 F1 (precision 46.2, recall 30.7), consistent with its recall ceiling. Our graph decoder, using only predicted mentions and predicted coreference clusters, achieves 42.3 F1 (precision 45.1, recall 39.8). This is 7.7 points above the oracle-informed baseline and 5.4 points above the tree variant, and both differences are significant (p < 0.01). Recall improves most, by 10.3 points over the baseline and 9.1 over the tree variant, while precision is about the same as the tree variant (−1.1).

Sequence-level scores are lower for every system, reflecting the difficulty of constructing entire chains. The baseline scores 12.1 F1, the tree variant 13.5, and the graph decoder 19.8. We also ran the graph decoder on gold mentions and gold coreference to estimate the effect of upstream errors. Link F1 rises to 48.7 and sequence-level F1 to 26.4, so roughly 6 link-F1 points are lost to mention detection and coreference errors. Chain-length analysis shows a monotonic drop in accuracy: link F1 is 51.0 for sequences of length two to three, 41.5 for lengths four to six, and 30.2 for longer sequences. This suggests errors accumulate as the number of required links grows.

**Interaction Between the Two Tasks**

Because both tasks use the same decoder, we examined how they inform each other. Using predicted coreference clusters in sequencing features, instead of none, improves sequencing F1 from 39.5 to 42.3 (+2.8). Replacing predicted clusters with gold clusters raises it to 44.1, indicating that coreference quality is a moderate bottleneck. In the reverse direction, the sequencing-derived features add 1.7 AVG points to coreference, as noted above. Joint optimization was not attempted; these are pipeline results with one-way feature sharing in each direction.

**Error Analysis**

We manually inspected 100 sampled errors from each task. In coreference, 41% of false merges involved events of the same type with similar arguments but distinct real-world occurrences (for example, two separate attacks by the same group), and 27% of missed links involved mentions that required inference beyond lexical overlap, such as "the shooting" and "the incident." In sequencing, 36% of false positives were links to events that were plausible successors but belonged to a different script instance in the same document, and 29% of missed links involved events separated by more than three sentences. Annotator agreement on sequencing links is also lower than for coreference (Cohen's κ of 0.61 vs. 0.74 on a double-annotated subset of 20 documents), so part of the remaining error reflects genuine ambiguity in the task rather than model failure.

Discussion and Conclusion

Why tree decoding fits coreference but not sequencing

The central finding of this study is that the decoding structure matters, and that the appropriate structure depends on the relational semantics of the task. Event coreference is an equivalence relation. Each mention either begins a new event or attaches to an earlier mention of the same event, so a latent antecedent tree or a set of disjoint trees is a natural and efficient approximation (Durrett and Klein, 2013; Bengtson and Roth, 2008; Chang et al., 2013). Event sequencing differs in two ways. A script-like sequence is not partitioned into disjoint clusters, and a given event may be linked to more than one predecessor or successor, as when two preparatory events both precede a main event, or when an event begins several parallel subevents. Forcing each mention to choose a single antecedent therefore discards valid links by construction, and this limits recall regardless of how good the local scorer is. Our error analysis supports this reading. The tree-restricted variant lost most of its recall on mentions with multiple gold predecessors, and these cases are more frequent in sequencing than in coreference. The graph-based decoder avoids this limitation by scoring candidate edges jointly and enforcing only the constraints that the relation requires (transitivity and symmetry for coreference, acyclicity and sparsity for sequencing). In this sense our results echo earlier work on global inference for temporal and discourse relations (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Do et al., 2012; Denis and Muller, 2011), but extend it by showing that one decoding framework can serve two relations with different structural properties.

Interpreting the empirical results

On TAC-KBP 2015, the coreference system reached state-of-the-art performance. We attribute the improvement mainly to the decoder's ability to use pairwise evidence from mentions that are not adjacent in an antecedent chain, rather than to the feature set, which is deliberately conventional (lexical overlap, argument compatibility, embedding similarity, and discourse distance; cf. Lu and Ng, 2017; Peng et al., 2016). Ablations are consistent with this view. Removing graph-level consistency terms hurt more than removing any single feature family. The sequencing system outperformed a strong temporal baseline that was given oracle information. This should be interpreted carefully. The baseline reflects a natural hypothesis, that narrative order follows temporal order, and the oracle gives it the best possible conditions. That it still lost indicates that event sequencing is not reducible to temporal ordering. Sequencing as annotated depends on script knowledge, causal and enabling relations, and discourse salience, as well as on when events occurred (Schank and Abelson, 1977; Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Mostafazadeh et al., 2016). Events may be sequenced in a narrative sense even where their times are unspecified, and temporally ordered events may not be sequenced when they do not participate in a common storyline. The result should not be read as showing that temporal information is unhelpful. The decoder's flexible feature interface lets temporal signals enter as features rather than as hard constraints, and we believe the best systems will combine them with narrative cues.

Challenges in studying event relations

Several difficulties limit what can be concluded. First, the two relations interact with mention detection and with each other. Errors in event trigger identification propagate into both tasks, and we evaluated mainly under conditions where errors in upstream components are present but not systematically separated. Coreference decisions also constrain sequencing. Coreferent mentions should share their predecessors and successors, and sequencing links can sometimes provide evidence against coreference, since two events that are ordered relative to each other are unlikely to be identical. Our decoder permits joint reasoning of this kind in principle, but our reported systems treat the tasks mostly separately, and we have not quantified how much a fully joint model would gain. Second, annotation is difficult. Agreement on event coreference is known to be moderate because of partial identity, granularity differences, and ambiguous event boundaries (Hovy et al., 2013; Mitamura et al., 2015), and agreement on sequencing is likely lower still because annotators must decide which of many plausible orderings count as the narrative structure of a document. The consequences are twofold. Reported scores carry a noise ceiling that is hard to estimate, and the evaluation metrics for sequencing are less established than the standard coreference measures (MUC, B³, CEAF, BLANC; Pradhan et al., 2014). Because gold graphs may be incomplete, a prediction counted as an error may be a legitimate unannotated link, so precision is probably underestimated. Third, sequencing datasets are small, which limits the learning of script-level regularities and favors feature-engineered or lightly supervised models. Larger resources or transfer from pretrained language models (Devlin et al., 2019) might change the relative importance of features, though we would still expect the structural argument about decoding to hold, because it concerns the output space rather than the scorer.

Limitations

Our conclusions are bounded by several factors. The experiments use English news-style text, and sequencing behavior in other genres such as narratives, procedures, or clinical records may differ. The graph decoder uses approximate inference, and although it performed well, we cannot guarantee optimality or characterize its failures on very long documents, where the number of candidate edges grows quadratically and sparsification heuristics could remove true links. The sequencing baseline, while strong, represents one family of alternatives; other baselines using script induction or neural narrative models might narrow the gap. Finally, our comparison with prior coreference systems relies on published numbers and the shared task scoring setup, so differences in preprocessing and mention detection may account for some of the observed gain.

Implications and future work

For practitioners, the main implication is that the output structure should be matched to the relation being modeled, and that tree-structured decoders should not be adopted for new event relations simply because they work for coreference. A graph-based formulation costs little when the relation is tree-like and gains substantially when it is not. For the broader study of discourse and event structure, our results suggest that sequencing should be treated as a task in its own right with its own annotation guidelines and metrics, rather than as a by-product of temporal processing. Promising directions include joint modeling of coreference, sequencing, and causal or subevent relations in a single graph with cross-relation constraints (Peng et al., 2016; Ning et al., 2018), integration of neural encoders for richer contextual features, and evaluation methods that accommodate multiple valid orderings.

In conclusion, we have shown that tree-like decoding, which suits event coreference, is inadequate for event sequencing, and we have proposed a graph-based decoder that handles both tasks under a common framework with flexible features. The coreference system achieves state-of-the-art results on TAC-KBP 2015, and the sequencing system outperforms an oracle-informed temporal baseline. Together with the difficulties we have outlined in annotation, evaluation, and interaction between relations, these results indicate that event relations are rich enough to deserve dedicated modeling and that structure-aware decoding is a productive route to better document-level event understanding.

Introduction

Scene understanding has long been a central goal of computer vision, and its definition has expanded considerably over the past decade. Early work concentrated on recognizing objects and labeling pixels, whereas more recent efforts ask systems to produce rich, structured accounts of what an image contains. Dense captioning (Johnson et al., 2016), scene graph generation (Xu et al., 2017), and visual question answering (VQA) (Antol et al., 2015) all require models to relate visual evidence to language, and they have substantially broadened what we expect a vision system to do. Datasets such as VQA, CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2017), and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019) probe increasingly sophisticated skills, including counting, attribute comparison, spatial reasoning, and multi-step compositional inference. In principle, question answering is an open-ended format: any aspect of a scene that can be phrased as a question can be posed to a model.

In practice, however, the prevailing formulations are overwhelmingly about the present. Given an image, the question asks what is there, how many, what color, or what is to the left of what. Even tasks that involve video or commonsense, such as video question answering (Tapaswi et al., 2016) or visual commonsense reasoning (Zellers et al., 2019), mostly ask about events that were observed or about plausible explanations of what is already visible. The future state of a scene, and especially its dependence on an action that has not yet occurred, remains largely unexplored. Yet this is precisely the kind of reasoning that intelligent agents need. A robot deciding whether to push a cup, a person judging whether stacking one more box will topple a tower, or an assistant asked to predict the outcome of a plan all must reason about counterfactual, action-conditioned futures. Humans do this routinely and with apparent ease, drawing on an intuitive understanding of physics (Battaglia et al., 2013) that lets them mentally simulate how objects will move and collide.

In this paper, we study this capability by introducing a task that we call visual what-if question answering. The system is given an observation of the current scene, in the form of an image, and a question that contains a hypothetical action, such as "What happens to the red cube if the green sphere is pushed to the left?" The answer must describe some aspect of the scene after the action has taken place, for instance which objects end up in contact, which object ends up in a particular position, or whether an object remains in place. The task thus extends VQA along a new axis: instead of describing the scene as it is, the model must predict the scene as it would become, conditioned on an intervention.

This problem is difficult for several reasons. First, the answer is not directly observable in the input; it has to be inferred through a model of how the world evolves. Second, the outcome depends on object-object interactions, in which an action on one object propagates through collisions to others, so that small differences in geometry, position, or motion can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. Third, the question is expressed in natural language, so the system must ground the described action in the visual scene, translate it into a physical intervention, and finally map the resulting future state back into a linguistic answer.

One natural approach would be to train a monolithic end-to-end network that maps the image and question directly to an answer. Such models have been successful on many VQA benchmarks, but they must acquire the dynamics of the physical world implicitly from question-answer pairs, which is a weak and indirect supervisory signal. Related work on learned intuitive physics, including interaction networks (Battaglia et al., 2016), visual predictive models (Lerer et al., 2016; Mottaghi et al., 2016), and neural physics simulators (Chang et al., 2017), shows that data-driven prediction is possible, but also that generalization to novel configurations, numbers of objects, and long horizons is limited. Conversely, physics engines already encode rigid-body dynamics accurately and generalize by construction, but they operate on explicit symbolic scene descriptions rather than on pixels and language.

Motivated by this complementarity, we propose a hybrid model that integrates a physics engine into a question answering architecture. The model first perceives the scene and recovers an object-level representation including object identities, attributes, and positions.
