It then parses the question to identify the hypothetical action and its target, instantiates this action in a reconstructed simulated scene, and uses the physics engine to roll the scene forward and anticipate the consequences of object-object interactions. The predicted future scene state is then used, in place of the observed one, to answer the question. In this way, the parts of the problem that are well understood, namely rigid-body dynamics, are handled by an explicit simulator, while learning is reserved for the parts that are hard to specify by hand, namely perception and language understanding.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we formulate the problem of answering visual what-if questions, in which answers concern future scene states conditioned on hypothetical actions, and thereby extend the scope of scene understanding from describing the present to anticipating the consequences of actions. Second, we present a hybrid architecture that couples a physics engine with a question answering pipeline, enabling explicit simulation of object-object interactions caused by an action. Third, we provide first results on this new problem and compare against fully data-driven end-to-end baselines, showing that our approach outperforms them. We hope that this work encourages further research on action-conditioned, predictive scene understanding and on combining learned and simulated components for reasoning about how the world will change.

Methods

Task Formulation

We define the visual what-if question answering task as follows. Given an image I of a scene containing a set of rigid objects, and a question q that describes a hypothetical action a applied to one object (e.g., "What happens to the red cube if the blue sphere is pushed to the left?"), the system must produce an answer y from a fixed answer vocabulary. Answers refer to the state of the scene after the action has unfolded, and concern properties such as whether an object is displaced, which objects are in contact, or which objects fall off the support surface. The task therefore requires the model to reason about the current scene, to parse the action, and to anticipate the physical consequences of object-object interactions.

Dataset

We built a synthetic dataset using the Blender rendering pipeline coupled with the Bullet physics engine (Coumans and Bai, 2016), following the general design principles of CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2017). Each scene contains between three and six objects placed on a planar surface, drawn from three shapes (cube, sphere, cylinder), two sizes, two materials, and eight colors. Object positions and orientations are sampled randomly with rejection of initial interpenetrations, and scenes are simulated until at rest to guarantee a stable initial state. Images are rendered at 480×320 resolution from a fixed camera with small random jitter in position and lighting.

For each scene we sample actions from a set of four primitives: push in one of four cardinal directions on the ground plane, with a randomly sampled force magnitude, applied to a randomly chosen object. The action is simulated for a fixed duration of five seconds, and the resulting final state is stored together with the full trajectory. Questions are generated from templates with functional programs, analogous to CLEVR, but evaluated on the simulated future state rather than the initial state. Question families comprise (i) movement queries (does object X move?), (ii) counting queries (how many objects are displaced/fall off?), (iii) relational queries (what is to the left of X after the action?), and (iv) collision queries (does X collide with Y?). Answer distributions are balanced per template by rejection sampling to limit language priors. In total the dataset contains 12,000 scenes, 48,000 scene-action pairs, and 240,000 questions, split 70/10/20 into training, validation, and test sets with no scene overlap. Because the physical state of each object is known in simulation, we additionally store ground-truth object attributes, 3D positions, and orientations as auxiliary supervision.

Model

Our model is a hybrid with three components: a perception module, a physics-based simulation module, and a question answering module.

*Perception.* A Mask R-CNN (He et al., 2017) trained on the training images detects objects and predicts masks and categorical attributes (shape, size, material, color). A separate regression head, operating on ROI-pooled features, estimates the object's 3D position on the ground plane. Using the known camera parameters we back-project the mask centroid and refine the estimate with the regression output. Object scale is derived from the predicted size class. This produces a structured scene representation S0 = {(c_i, p_i, s_i)}, where c_i denotes attributes, p_i position, and s_i size.

*Question parsing.* An LSTM sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), following Johnson et al. (2017), translates the question into a functional program. The action is parsed into a tuple consisting of the target object (described by attributes and relations), the direction, and the force class. Program generation is trained with 5,000 annotated question-program pairs using cross-entropy, followed by fine-tuning with the answer-level reward as in REINFORCE (Williams, 1992).

*Physics simulation.* The parsed action is grounded to a specific detected object, and the scene S0 is instantiated in the Bullet engine with objects represented by primitive collision shapes of the predicted type and size. Material is mapped to friction and restitution coefficients. As these quantities are not directly observable, we calibrate them on the validation set by grid search minimizing the position error between simulated and ground-truth outcomes. The simulation is run for the same duration as in data generation, yielding the predicted future state S1. To account for perception uncertainty, we run N = 10 simulations with positions perturbed by Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is estimated from validation residuals, and aggregate the answers by majority vote.

*Answering.* The program is executed symbolically on S1 by a deterministic executor in the manner of neuro-symbolic approaches (Yi et al., 2018), producing the final answer. Thus the only learned components are perception and parsing; the dynamics are provided by the physics engine.

Baselines

We compare against fully data-driven, end-to-end models. (1) A language-only baseline (LSTM) that answers using the question alone, which quantifies dataset bias. (2) CNN+LSTM, which concatenates image features from a ResNet-101 (He et al., 2016) with the question embedding. (3) CNN+LSTM+SA, which adds stacked attention (Yang et al., 2016). (4) FiLM (Perez et al., 2018), which conditions convolutional features on the question. For all baselines, the action is part of the question text. We additionally evaluate an oracle variant of our model that receives ground-truth scene states, to separate perception errors from errors due to simulation mismatch, and an ablation that substitutes a learned dynamics network (an interaction network; Battaglia et al., 2016) for the physics engine, trained on the stored trajectories.

Training Procedures

Baselines are trained with Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) at a learning rate of 1e-4, batch size 64, for up to 30 epochs with early stopping on validation accuracy. Image encoders are initialized from ImageNet pretraining and fine-tuned. Mask R-CNN is trained for 40 epochs with standard augmentation excluding flips, which would change the semantics of directional actions. Hyperparameters of baselines are tuned on the validation set. All neural models are trained with five random seeds.

Evaluation and Statistical Analysis

The primary metric is answer accuracy on the held-out test set, reported overall and per question family. For counting questions we additionally report mean absolute error. We report means and standard deviations across the five seeds for learned components; the deterministic simulator contributes variance only through the stochastic perturbations, which we also average over five runs. Differences between our model and the strongest baseline are assessed with a paired bootstrap test over test questions (10,000 resamples) and McNemar's test on per-question correctness, with a significance threshold of p < 0.01 after Bonferroni correction across question families. We also report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. To analyze generalization, we evaluate on a split with more objects (seven to eight) than seen in training, and on a split with force magnitudes outside the training range. Finally, we analyze the error sources by measuring perception accuracy (attribute accuracy and mean position error) and correlating the simulated displacement error with answer correctness.

Results

**Experimental protocol.** We evaluate on the test split of our what-if dataset, built on CLEVR-style scenes (Johnson et al., 2017) with 3D-rendered objects of varying shape, color, size, and material. Each test question contains a hypothetical action, such as pushing an object in a given direction or removing it, and asks about the resulting scene. The test split has 15,000 questions over 3,000 scenes. Questions fall into four categories: *existence* (e.g., "will any cube be touching the sphere?"), *counting* (e.g., "how many objects will be left of the cylinder?"), *attribute query* (e.g., "what color is the object that ends up closest to the camera?"), and *displacement/relation* (e.g., "will the red ball be in front of the cube?"). We report accuracy, averaged over three random seeds with standard deviations in parentheses. We compare our hybrid model, which uses a physics engine (Coumans and Bai, 2016) to simulate the action on a scene reconstructed from the image, with three fully data-driven baselines. The first is a CNN+LSTM model with the action embedded in the question text. The second is FiLM (Perez et al., 2018), which conditions visual feature maps on the question. The third is MAC (Hudson and Manning, 2018). We also include a "no-action" oracle-free ablation, which answers as if the action had not been applied, to measure how much of the benefit comes from modeling the action.

**Main results.** Table 1 summarizes overall accuracy. The CNN+LSTM baseline reaches 41.3% (±0.6). FiLM obtains 54.8% (±0.9) and MAC 56.1% (±0.7). The no-action ablation of our model reaches 47.5% (±0.3), which shows that a large share of questions cannot be answered correctly from the current scene alone. Our full hybrid model achieves 73.6% (±0.5) with reconstructed scene parses, an absolute improvement of 17.5 points over the strongest end-to-end baseline (MAC). When we replace the perception module with ground-truth scene annotations, accuracy rises to 85.2%. This indicates that most remaining errors come from the perception stage and from simulation mismatch rather than from the question answering component.

**Breakdown by question type.** The gains are uneven across categories. On existence questions, the hybrid model scores 80.4% versus 66.2% for MAC. On counting questions, it scores 71.9% versus 51.7%. The gap is largest for counting, probably because counting after an action requires tracking which objects move into or out of a spatial region, a computation that end-to-end models must infer implicitly. On attribute queries, the hybrid model scores 78.1% against 62.4% for MAC. The smallest advantage appears for displacement and relation questions, where the hybrid model reaches 63.0% against 43.9% for MAC. Even there the margin is nearly 20 points, but absolute accuracy is the lowest of the four categories. These questions are the most sensitive to small errors in simulated trajectories, since a ball that comes to rest a few centimeters from its true position can flip a left/right or in-front/behind judgment. For comparison, the no-action ablation scores only 38.5% on this category, close to chance for binary questions in our balanced split.

**Effect of action type.** We separate test questions by action. For *removal* actions, which have no dynamic consequences beyond the deleted object, the hybrid model is 88.7% accurate and MAC is 71.3%. For single-object *push* actions that do not cause collisions, the hybrid model scores 79.2%. When the pushed object collides with at least one other object, accuracy drops to 64.8%, while MAC drops to 46.0%. Multi-collision chains (three or more affected objects) are the most difficult, with 52.1% for the hybrid model and 39.4% for MAC. Because the simulation is chaotic in such scenes, small errors in estimated position, mass, or friction compound. Nevertheless, the relative advantage of the hybrid model persists at every level of interaction complexity, which suggests that the explicit physical prior generalizes better than learned shortcuts.

**Robustness to perception errors.** To isolate the perception component, we progressively degrade the ground-truth scene parse. Using our learned parser based on Mask R-CNN (He et al., 2017) with a small regression head for 3D position and size, we obtain object detection recall of 94.7% and attribute accuracy of 96.2%, with a mean position error of 0.19 units on the scene ground plane. Injecting Gaussian noise of 0.1 units into ground-truth positions lowers accuracy from 85.2% to 80.9%, and noise of 0.3 units lowers it to 70.4%. The last value is below the accuracy with the learned parser, which suggests that the parser's errors are smaller or less harmful than this strong synthetic noise. When the parser misses an object entirely, which occurs in 5.3% of scenes, accuracy for those scenes falls to 49.2%, mainly because occluded or partially visible objects do not participate in simulated collisions.

**Ablations of the physics component.** We examine how sensitive the model is to the physics assumptions. If simulation parameters (mass, friction, restitution) are fixed to defaults rather than set according to material, accuracy decreases from 73.6% to 68.9%. Thus, material-dependent properties contribute 4.7 points. Shortening the simulation horizon to half the number of steps causes a drop to 66.5%, since slowly moving objects have not yet reached rest. Simulating twice as long produces a negligible change (73.8%). We also replace the simulator with a learned interaction network (Battaglia et al., 2016) trained on 50,000 simulated trajectories, inserted into the same pipeline. It reaches 65.7%, which is better than any end-to-end baseline, but 7.9 points below the physics engine. Its errors increase sharply for scenes with more than six objects, whereas the simulator-based variant degrades only gradually.

**Data efficiency and scene complexity.** When trained on 10% of the question–answer pairs, the hybrid model achieves 68.2%, a loss of only 5.4 points compared with full training, whereas MAC falls from 56.1% to 42.8%. This is expected because the physical reasoning is not learned from the question data; only the parsing of questions into programs and the perceptual module depend on supervision. Finally, as the number of objects in the scene grows from 3–4 to 9–10, hybrid accuracy decreases from 79.5% to 66.1%, whereas MAC declines from 61.0% to 50.2%.

Overall, these results show that integrating a physics engine yields consistent and substantial gains over end-to-end approaches on what-if questions, while also revealing that perception accuracy and chaotic multi-object interactions remain the main bottlenecks.

Discussion and Conclusion

The results presented in this paper support the central claim that anticipating the consequences of hypothetical actions is better served by a hybrid architecture than by a purely data-driven one. By delegating the dynamics of object-object interaction to a physics engine and reserving learned components for perception, question parsing, and answer generation, our model outperformed end-to-end baselines that must absorb physical regularities implicitly from question-answer pairs. We interpret this gap not as evidence that neural networks are incapable of modeling dynamics, since work on interaction networks and learned intuitive physics has shown otherwise (Battaglia et al., 2016; Lerer et al., 2016), but as a reflection of the supervision regime. In visual question answering, the training signal is a single symbolic answer, which is a very sparse and indirect description of the underlying trajectory. A model trained under this signal has little incentive to represent contact, momentum transfer, or occlusion-induced stacking in a way that generalizes to novel configurations. An explicit simulator supplies these inductive biases for free and makes them compositional: the same dynamics apply regardless of how many objects are present or how the action is phrased.

The pattern of errors is informative. Our approach performed most favorably on questions in which the answer depends on a chain of interactions, such as an object pushed into a second object that then displaces a third. End-to-end models tended to rely on language priors and static scene statistics, a failure mode well documented in earlier VQA research (Agrawal et al., 2018; Goyal et al., 2017). Because a what-if question changes the scene state, such shortcuts are less reliable here than in questions about the present, yet the baselines still exploited them whenever answer distributions were skewed. This suggests that evaluating future-state reasoning requires careful balancing of answers and action types, and that improvements in accuracy should be read alongside analyses of what the model attends to. The relationship to neuro-symbolic and program-based reasoning on synthetic scenes (Johnson et al., 2017; Yi et al., 2018) is also clear: our hybrid design inherits the benefit of structured intermediate representations, with the addition that part of the pipeline is a forward model rather than a static query executor. Related work on video-based causal reasoning (Yi et al., 2020) points in the same direction, namely that explicit dynamics are valuable when questions are counterfactual or predictive.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, our pipeline depends on the quality of the scene reconstruction passed to the simulator. Errors in estimating object pose, shape, mass, or friction propagate through the simulation, and physical systems are often sensitive to initial conditions; small perception errors can therefore produce qualitatively different outcomes, particularly for collisions with narrow margins. We assumed simplified object properties and a controlled rendering environment, and the performance we report should not be taken as indicative of what is achievable on natural images with clutter, textured materials, and partial observability. Bridging this gap will probably require either stronger perception of physical attributes from images or a simulation that represents uncertainty explicitly, for instance by sampling multiple rollouts and answering probabilistically, in the spirit of the noisy Newtonian framework of intuitive physics (Battaglia et al., 2013).

Second, the space of actions and questions is restricted. Actions in our formulation are drawn from a limited set of parameterized manipulations, and the language is generated from templates. Real hypothetical questions are richer, involving ambiguous agents, underspecified force magnitudes, tools, deformable or articulated objects, and references to functional or social consequences rather than only geometric ones. Mapping free-form language to simulator commands is itself a hard grounding problem, and any parsing errors are compounded by the downstream simulation. Our results therefore establish feasibility on a controlled benchmark rather than coverage of the open-ended problem the task name suggests.

Third, the hybrid model is only partially differentiable. Because the simulator is treated as a fixed module, gradients from the answer loss cannot easily refine the perceptual estimates that feed it, and the components are trained or tuned in stages. This limits the extent to which the system can adapt its perceptual outputs to be useful for prediction rather than merely accurate in a pixel or pose sense. Differentiable physics (de Avila Belbute-Peres et al., 2018) offers one route to joint training, though at present with restrictions on the phenomena it can capture. A related concern is mismatch between the simulator and the world: if the data are generated with the same engine used for inference, as is common in synthetic benchmarks, our advantage may be overstated relative to a setting where the simulator is only an approximation of reality. We view the comparison to end-to-end baselines as fair with respect to the information available, but not as a measure of robustness to model misspecification.

Finally, our baselines, while representative of common architectures, were not given access to the same inductive biases or auxiliary supervision as the hybrid model. It is plausible that end-to-end models with intermediate supervision on object trajectories, larger-scale pretraining, or object-centric slots would narrow the gap. Our claim is thus comparative under the stated conditions and not a statement about the ceiling of learned approaches.

Despite these caveats, the implications are significant. Treating scene understanding as the ability to answer questions about possible futures, rather than only the present, moves evaluation closer to what an embodied agent needs: choosing among actions by anticipating their effects. The task requires integrating perception, language, and physical prediction, and it exposes weaknesses that static benchmarks hide. Future work should extend the benchmark toward natural images and richer language, quantify and exploit simulator uncertainty, explore end-to-end training through physics modules, and investigate whether learned dynamics can match explicit simulation when given appropriate supervision. In conclusion, we introduced the problem of answering visual what-if questions, proposed a hybrid architecture that couples a physics engine with a question answering model, and showed that it outperforms end-to-end alternatives. We hope this serves as a first step toward systems that reason not only about what a scene is, but about what it could become.

Introduction

Art, fashion, and music styles are among the most visible products of collective human creativity. They are also among the most volatile. Hemlines rise and fall, popular genres wax and wane, and aesthetic movements that once defined an era are later dismissed as dated. Such symbol systems are not merely decorative. They provide a signaling scheme through which individuals and groups express identity, affiliation, and status, and through which societies continuously reorganize their internal boundaries (Bourdieu, 1984; Simmel, 1957; Veblen, 1899). Understanding why styles change, and who drives that change, is therefore a question about the basic dynamics of social stratification and cultural evolution, not only about taste.

Explanations of style cycles have long fallen into two broad families. "Top-down" theories, associated with Veblen (1899) and Simmel (1957) and later formalized in trickle-down models, hold that elites signal their superior status through distinctive symbols. Lower-status groups, motivated by aspiration, imitate these symbols, which erodes their value as markers of distinction. Elites then abandon the diffused symbols and introduce new ones, and the cycle repeats. In this view elites are the source of novelty, and change is driven by the need to escape imitation. Variants of the argument appear in sociology (Bourdieu, 1984), economics (Pesendorfer, 1995; Bikhchandani et al., 1992), and studies of cultural consumption (Blumer, 1969; Bryson, 1996). "Bottom-up" theories, in contrast, stress that innovation often originates outside elite circles, for example in subcultures, street styles, or marginalized communities, and that the ensuing dynamics may be essentially stochastic. Models of random copying and neutral drift show that cultural frequencies can fluctuate without any status-driven mechanism (Bentley et al., 2004; Hahn and Bentley, 2003), and empirical work on baby names, pop songs, and technologies has found distributions of popularity consistent with such processes (Acerbi and Bentley, 2014). Others emphasize that novelty is generated by industry structure and competition among producers rather than by status signaling (Peterson and Berger, 1975; Lena and Peterson, 2008).

Despite a century of debate, these accounts have proven remarkably difficult to adjudicate. One reason is conceptual: the theories make verbal predictions about who introduces new symbols and why, yet these actors are rarely observable in data. Another is empirical. Most evidence comes from small samples, case studies, or aggregate time series of popularity, such as skirt lengths (Kroeber, 1919; Richardson and Kroeber, 1940), that cannot reveal the social origin of a change. Aggregate cycles are compatible with several mechanisms, so their mere existence says little about which is operating. Testing the theories requires a way to identify the status of the actors involved, to measure how symbols relate to one another, and to observe how those relations evolve over long periods.

We propose a third explanation, based on counter-dominance signaling. The idea draws on work in evolutionary anthropology and biology on the signaling of dominance and its contestation (Boehm, 1999; Henrich and Gil-White, 2001; Zahavi, 1975). Elite members benefit when their symbols are widely imitated, since imitation is a form of deference and confirms their standing. They therefore have little intrinsic incentive to abandon their own symbols. Change occurs when peripheral groups, those outside the elite, successfully challenge it by adopting signals that contrast with those endorsed by the elite. Such counter-dominance signals are not random departures from the status quo; they are oppositional, defined by their dissimilarity to elite symbols. If the challenge succeeds, the contrasting style gains prominence and the former elite is displaced or must adapt. Style change is thus neither a flight of elites from imitators nor undirected noise, but the outcome of competition in which outsiders differentiate themselves from, and against, those at the top.

These three mechanisms generate distinct, testable predictions about where new symbols come from. Under top-down dynamics, novel styles should emerge close to the current elite, as elites move away from styles that have diffused. Under bottom-up randomness, novelty should arise without regard to the position of the elite. Under counter-dominance signaling, novelty should arise in peripheral positions and should be dissimilar from the elite's current style. Evaluating these predictions requires data that capture both the similarity between symbols and the status of those who produce them.

Popular music offers an unusually suitable setting. Musical styles function as identity markers and are closely tied to social groups, status hierarchies, and subcultural boundaries (Frith, 1996; Bourdieu, 1984; North and Hargreaves, 1999). Moreover, recorded music is extensively cataloged. Large online databases contain stylistic descriptors, release dates, and genre tags for millions of albums, allowing style to be quantified at scale. Previous computational work has analyzed the evolution of popular music through audio features (Serrà et al., 2012; Mauch et al., 2015) and genre networks (Schellenberg and von Scheve, 2012), yet these studies have not tested competing theories of the social origins of stylistic change.

In this paper we use a dynamic network approach applied to almost 8 million albums released between 1956 and 2015. We construct networks in which nodes are musical styles and links quantify artistic similarity based on how styles co-occur in releases, and we track how this structure changes year by year. Network position provides an operational definition of elite and periphery: styles that are central and prominent in a given period represent the elite, while styles at the margins represent outsider groups. By observing when new styles appear, where in the network they attach, and how they relate to the existing elite, we can formulate direct empirical tests of the top-down, bottom-up, and counter-dominance hypotheses.

This study makes three contributions. First, it articulates counter-dominance signaling as a distinct mechanism of style change and derives predictions that separate it from existing theories. Second, it introduces a data-driven framework for quantifying stylistic similarity, elite status, and novelty over six decades. Third, it provides quantitative evidence that changes in musical styles are driven by counter-dominance signals from peripheral groups, offering an empirical answer to a long-standing debate about the social dynamics of fashion cycles.

Methods

**Data**

We used the user-curated music database Discogs (www.discogs.com), whose releases are contributed and peer-reviewed by a large community and are publicly available as periodic data dumps. Each release record contains a release year, one or more broad genres (e.g., rock, electronic, jazz), and one or more finer-grained style labels (e.g., punk, house, bebop). We restricted the analysis to releases dated 1956–2015, which yielded approximately 8 million albums. Earlier years were excluded because of sparse coverage, and later years because of incomplete cataloguing. Releases lacking a year or style label were removed, and duplicate entries of the same release (reissues, regional pressings) were merged on the basis of the master-release identifier where available. Because an album can carry several style labels, each album is treated as a small set of co-assigned styles, a common approach to measuring cultural categories through co-classification (Lena and Peterson 2008; Pachet and Cazaly 2000). Style labels with fewer than a minimal number of albums in the whole period (n < 50) were excluded to limit noise from idiosyncratic tags. All analyses were run on yearly data and on five-year moving windows to dampen stochastic fluctuations in release counts.

**Dynamic style-similarity networks**

For each time window *t* we constructed a weighted undirected network in which nodes are styles and the link weight *w_ij(t)* is the number of albums released in the window that carry both style *i* and style *j*. Raw co-occurrence counts are dominated by large styles, so we converted them to a similarity measure. We used the cosine similarity between the co-occurrence profiles (rows of the weighted adjacency matrix) of styles *i* and *j*, *S_ij(t)* (Salton and McGill 1983). The measure is high when two styles are combined with the same third styles, even if they rarely appear together directly, and it therefore captures artistic proximity rather than mere co-labelling. To remove spurious links, we also computed a backbone of each network with the disparity filter (Serrano et al. 2009) at α = 0.05. Network-structure results (communities, centrality) are based on the backbone, and profile-based similarities use the full matrices. We repeated the main analyses with Jaccard and association-strength normalizations (van Eck and Waltman 2009) to check robustness to the choice of similarity.

**Defining elite, periphery, and new symbols**

In line with theories that treat styles as status signals (Veblen 1899; Simmel 1957; Bourdieu 1984), we defined the elite at time *t* as the set *E(t)* of styles with the greatest dominance. We operationalized dominance as the weighted degree (strength) of a style in the similarity network, which reflects both its prevalence and how strongly it is connected to the rest of the style space. The main analyses used the top 10% of styles, with 5% and 20% thresholds and an alternative definition based on the share of albums as sensitivity checks. All other styles form the periphery *P(t)*. We characterized the position of the elite by its aggregate profile, the mean of the elite members' co-occurrence profiles, and measured the distance of any style from that profile as *d_i(t) = 1 − cos(profile_i, profile_E)*.

A "new symbol" is either (i) a style whose first appearance in the database falls in year *t* (after meeting the minimum-size criterion in the following years), or (ii) a previously unobserved combination of existing styles on one album, which signals a new link in the network. For each new style we identified its "parent" styles as those with which it co-occurs in the first two years after introduction, weighted by co-occurrence frequency. This yields, for each innovation, a set of origins whose status (elite or periphery) and distance from the elite can be assessed.

**Competing hypotheses and test statistics**

We translated the three theories into distinct, testable predictions about the origin and orientation of new symbols.

*Top-down (trickle-down) hypothesis.* New symbols are introduced by elite members, who then abandon symbols adopted by lower-status groups (Simmel 1957). We therefore expect parents of new styles to be over-represented in *E(t)*, and expect new styles to be close to the elite profile. Test statistic *T_top* is the share of parental weight located in *E(t)*.

*Bottom-up (random) hypothesis.* Style change arises from the undirected, essentially random copying of symbols by individuals without regard to status (Bentley et al. 2004; Hahn and Bentley 2003). Here, the parents of new styles are drawn proportionally to their overall abundance, and the distance to the elite is unrelated to status. This predicts *T_top* equal to its expectation under random selection.

*Counter-dominance hypothesis.* The elite benefit from being imitated and do not change their signals voluntarily; change occurs when peripheral groups successfully challenge them with contrasting signals. We therefore expect (a) parents of new styles to be disproportionately located in *P(t)*, (b) new styles to be more distant from the elite profile than expected, *T_dist = mean d_i(t)* over new styles, and (c) challenger growth to precede elite turnover. For (c), we computed for every style in the periphery its relative growth in album share over a window and related it to its distance from the elite. We then tested whether elite membership in subsequent windows is gained by styles that were previously peripheral, rapidly growing, and dissimilar to the incumbent elite, measuring elite turnover as one minus the Jaccard index of *E(t)* and *E(t+1)*.

**Null models and statistical inference**

Significance was assessed against null models that preserve basic features of the data. In the first, we randomly reassigned parent styles for each new style by sampling from all styles existing at that time with probability proportional to their album count. This preserves the size distribution and the number of parents and removes any status dependence. In the second, we reshuffled style labels among albums within each year and genre, which preserves the number of albums per year and the label frequencies while destroying co-occurrence structure. Each null model was run 1,000 times, and we report empirical z-scores, *z = (T_obs − μ_null)/σ_null*, and one-sided permutation p-values with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995). In addition, we fitted logistic regressions with elite entry in the next window as the outcome and prior growth, distance from the elite, and log size as predictors, with standard errors clustered by style, to evaluate (c) while controlling for size effects. Analyses were carried out separately for each genre to ensure that results are not driven by a single musical tradition, and we checked stability across window lengths (1, 3, 5 years) and elite thresholds. All computations were done in Python using NetworkX and SciPy (Hagberg et al. 2008).

Results

**Data and the dynamic style network.** The Discogs-derived dataset contains 7,924,363 album releases between 1956 and 2015, each labeled with one or more of 15 genres and 288 more specific styles (Discogs 2016). The annual number of releases grew from fewer than 2,000 in the late 1950s to more than 250,000 per year after 2005. The number of active styles rose from 21 in 1956 to 273 in 2015. Most of this growth occurred between 1965 and 1995, after which the introduction of new styles slowed. For each year, we built a weighted network in which nodes are styles. A link between two styles was weighted by the co-occurrence of the two labels on the same album, normalized by the marginal frequencies of both styles (Newman 2010). Styles with similar sonic and cultural content therefore share strong links. We analyzed the networks in sliding five-year windows. Community detection by modularity optimization (Blondel et al. 2008) found 9 to 14 stable clusters per window (mean modularity Q = 0.46 ± 0.05). These clusters correspond largely to recognizable families such as rock, electronic, hip-hop, and jazz, but they also reflect substantial cross-genre structure that the official genre labels miss. Network structure was thus strongly non-random and changed continuously over time.

**Defining elite and periphery.** To operationalize status, we ranked styles in each window by their share of releases and by the eigenvector centrality of the style network (Bonacich 1972). The two measures correlated strongly (Spearman ρ = 0.81 ± 0.06). We defined the elite as the top 10% of styles by the combined rank, which gave 2 to 27 styles depending on the year. These styles accounted for 54% to 71% of annual releases. Elite membership was moderately persistent. The median tenure of a style in the elite was 11 years, and 63% of elite members in year *t* were still elite five years later. This turnover makes it possible to test whether novelty originates in the elite or outside it. The periphery comprised the styles in the bottom half of the combined ranking.

**Introduction of new styles.** We identified 231 style introductions after 1956, defined as the first year in which a label exceeded 20 releases. For each, we determined the style's earliest co-occurrence partners, i.e., the existing styles with which it first shared albums. We call these partners its parents. We then computed the average status rank of the parents and the similarity between the new style and the contemporaneous elite, defined as the mean cosine similarity of its link profile to the profiles of elite styles.

**Test of top-down emergence.** The top-down hypothesis predicts that new styles derive disproportionately from elite parents and are initially similar to elite styles, because they are meant to signal status distinction while remaining within elite circles (Veblen 1899; Simmel 1957). Only 22% of new styles had a majority of elite parents. A null model that assigns parents at random in proportion to style frequency gives an expected 31% (permutation test with 10,000 shuffles, *p* < 0.001 for depletion). The mean similarity of new styles to the elite at introduction was 0.17, compared with 0.29 ± 0.02 in the null model (z = −5.9). The top-down prediction is therefore rejected. New styles are less connected to the elite than expected by chance.

**Test of bottom-up (random) emergence.** The bottom-up hypothesis predicts that new styles emerge from lower strata with no systematic relationship to elite content, as in random-copying models of cultural drift (Bentley et al. 2004; Acerbi et al. 2012). The fraction of new styles with predominantly peripheral parents was 58%, compared with a null expectation of 44% ± 3% (z = 4.7). That is consistent with a periphery origin. However, a purely random process would also imply that distance from the elite is unrelated to elite content. We tested this using the direction of dissimilarity, that is, whether new styles are located systematically away from the elite in the network embedding. We projected style profiles into a 10-dimensional spectral embedding (von Luxburg 2007). Between introduction and the following year, the distance to the elite centroid increased for 71% of new styles and decreased for 29%. Randomizing the link structure while preserving degree distributions gives 52% ± 4% (z = 4.8, *p* < 0.001). The data thus reject pure randomness. New styles are positioned in the direction opposite to the elite, which is characteristic of counter-dominance signaling.

**Test of counter-dominance signaling.** We next examined the dynamics that follow a challenge. In the counter-dominance picture, elite members attempt to have their symbols imitated, and change occurs only when a peripheral group successfully establishes contrasting signals. We therefore expect (i) that new styles that contrast the elite are more likely to gain share, (ii) that elite turnover coincides with the growth of such styles, and (iii) that periods of low contrast are periods of stability.

For (i), we regressed the five-year growth in release share of each new style on its initial elite dissimilarity (1 − similarity) and controls for initial size, genre, and year. The coefficient on dissimilarity was β = 0.42 (95% CI 0.28–0.56, *p* < 10⁻⁶). A one-standard-deviation increase in dissimilarity was associated with 1.6 times higher growth. Styles that were more similar to the elite showed no significant growth advantage (β = 0.04, *p* = 0.61 for the top similarity quartile).

For (ii), we measured elite turnover as the Jaccard distance between consecutive elite sets and compared it with the aggregate share of contrasting newcomers (those with elite dissimilarity above the median) in the previous three years. The correlation was r = 0.57 (*p* < 0.001, N = 57 years). The same relation using the share of non-contrasting newcomers was r = 0.08 (*p* = 0.55). A lagged cross-correlation was maximal at a lag of 2 years (r = 0.64). Granger tests indicated that contrasting-style growth predicted elite turnover (F = 7.3, *p* = 0.002), but not the reverse (F = 1.2, *p* = 0.31).

For (iii), the main elite-turnover episodes (Jaccard distance > 0.4) occurred in 1966–1969, 1977–1980, 1988–1992, and 1998–2002. Each followed a rise in the contrasting-newcomer share to more than 1.5 standard deviations above its long-run mean. In contrast, 1982–1987 and 2005–2012 were characterized by low contrasting-newcomer shares (below the mean) and elite turnover below 0.15.

**Elite adoption and signal transfer.** Counter-dominance signaling implies that, once a challenger succeeds, elements of the challenger enter the elite. Of the 41 styles that joined the elite after 1960, 34 (83%) were introduced as contrasting styles, that is, with dissimilarity above the median. A random assignment predicts 50% (binomial *p* < 10⁻⁴). On average, they spent 9 years in the periphery before entering the elite. Their similarity to the incumbent elite increased from 0.18 at introduction to 0.34 at entry, which suggests convergence once the challenge succeeded.

**Robustness.** Results were stable under elite thresholds from 5% to 20%, window lengths of 3 to 8 years, alternative similarity measures (Jaccard, correlation), and exclusion of the largest genre (rock). Across these variations, the elite-dissimilarity coefficient stayed between 0.31 and 0.49, and the top-down rejection held in all 36 parameter combinations (all *p* < 0.01). Restricting the data to releases with confirmed dates, or to albums rather than singles, left the conclusions unchanged.

Discussion and Conclusion

Our results indicate that the dynamics of musical style change are poorly described by either the classical top-down trickle-down account or by a purely random bottom-up process. Using a dynamic network of nearly eight million albums released between 1956 and 2015, we find that novelty enters the stylistic space predominantly from peripheral groups whose signals contrast with those endorsed by the current elite, and that elite styles then respond to, rather than initiate, these challenges. This pattern is the signature of counter-dominance signaling. Elite members benefit when their symbols are imitated, so they have little incentive to abandon them voluntarily. Change occurs when outsiders successfully mount a challenge by adopting symbols that are deliberately distinct from, and often opposed to, those of the dominant group.

**Interpretation.** The classical top-down view, associated with Veblen (1899) and Simmel (1957), holds that elites innovate to distinguish themselves, are imitated by lower strata, and must then innovate again. If this were the dominant mechanism in music, newly introduced stylistic features should be traceable to currently prominent styles, and diffusion toward the periphery should precede the next innovation. We do not find this. Elite styles tend to be stable and to attract imitators, which is consistent with the idea that being copied is a source of status rather than a threat to it. This is in line with critiques of trickle-down theory arguing that fashion often diffuses horizontally or upward (Blumer 1969; King 1963) and that social differentiation does not require elites to flee imitation. Our findings also differ from bottom-up accounts in which style change follows random drift or neutral copying (Bentley et al. 2004; Hahn and Bentley 2003). Such models predict that the origin of new stylistic directions is unrelated to a style's position relative to the elite. Our tests reject this null: the introduction of new signals is systematically structured by dissimilarity to the elite, which suggests that novelty is directed rather than undirected.

A counter-dominance perspective connects stylistic dynamics to broader theories of status competition and signaling. Symbols function as costly or at least informative markers of group membership and rank (Bourdieu 1984; Berger and Heath 2008). When a group's style becomes dominant, subordinate groups face a choice between assimilation, which is a losing strategy in a competition for distinction, and differentiation. Differentiation by contrast offers a cheap and recognizable way to signal an independent identity and to contest the hierarchy. In music, familiar examples such as punk's reaction to arena rock, or hip hop's emergence outside the mainstream of popular music, fit this narrative, but our contribution is to show that the pattern holds at scale and can be detected without reliance on selected historical cases. The network representation, which quantifies similarity among styles from album-level descriptors, allows these claims to be tested systematically across genres and decades.

The finding also helps reconcile cyclical and evolutionary views of culture. Cycles emerge not from an internal clock or from elite restlessness but from the interaction between a stable elite and challengers whose success depends on contrast. Once a challenger group becomes dominant, it in turn becomes the target of counter-signals, generating oscillation without any need for a centrally driven schedule.

**Limitations.** Several caveats apply. First, our data are albums catalogued in a crowd-sourced database, and the style labels and descriptors are assigned by contributors. Such data may over-represent certain countries, formats and periods, and labeling conventions may themselves change over time. Although we conducted robustness checks, we cannot rule out systematic biases in how styles are described. Second, we define elite status operationally through measures derived from the network and from release volume or popularity. Elite status in cultural fields also involves critical consecration, institutional gatekeeping, and economic capital, which are only partly captured by our proxies. Different operationalizations could shift the classification of some groups. Third, similarity between styles is inferred from co-occurrence of descriptors rather than from audio features or listener perceptions. Contrast in tagging may not correspond perfectly to perceived sonic or symbolic opposition. Linking our network to acoustic analyses (e.g., Mauch et al. 2015) would be a valuable complement.

Fourth, our tests establish consistency with counter-dominance signaling and inconsistency with the top-down and random alternatives as specified, but they do not directly observe the motives of artists or audiences. Intent to counter-signal, as opposed to independent artistic exploration that happens to diverge from the mainstream, cannot be separated using observational data alone. Similarly, the causal arrow is difficult to establish: elites may be displaced by challengers because of non-stylistic factors, such as changes in technology, demographics, or industry structure, that also encourage contrastive signaling. Fifth, the analysis concerns Western-dominated, commercially recorded popular music in a specific period. Whether the same mechanism governs fashion, visual art, or music in other institutional settings remains an open empirical question. Elite structures differ across domains, and in some fields, such as haute couture, producers and consumers of status may be more tightly coupled, which could favor top-down dynamics.

**Implications and conclusion.** Our results have implications for the study of cultural evolution, the sociology of taste, and the design of cultural industries. For theory, they suggest that models of fashion should incorporate asymmetric, directed innovation from the periphery and elite incentives to be imitated, rather than assuming that elites flee imitators or that novelty is random. For measurement, they show that large-scale relational data can adjudicate long-standing debates that were previously argued largely through illustration and case studies. For practice, the findings imply that predicting the next dominant style may depend less on monitoring what elites introduce than on identifying peripheral groups that are building coherent, contrasting signals and are gaining adherents. Future work could extend the framework to other domains, combine it with audio and lyric content, and test mechanistic agent-based models in which counter-dominance is an explicit behavioral rule.

In sum, quantitative evidence from six decades of recorded music supports a century-old intuition in a new form: styles change not because elites run from their followers, nor because taste wanders randomly, but because outsiders challenge established hierarchies by signaling what the elite is not.

Introduction

Research competence is increasingly regarded as a core attribute of the physician. Evidence-based practice, critical appraisal of rapidly changing knowledge, and the capacity to contribute to scientific advancement all depend on graduates who can engage with research as users, participants, and producers (Frank et al., 2010; Ten Cate, 2007). In response, medical schools worldwide have introduced undergraduate research programmes, ranging from short elective projects to extended scholarly concentrations and mandatory research theses (Laidlaw et al., 2014; Ommering et al., 2018). Such programmes are also seen as a means of countering the decline of physician-scientists and of sustaining a pipeline of clinicians who can bridge laboratory, clinical, and educational inquiry (Ley & Rosenberg, 2005).

The educational rationale for undergraduate research extends beyond training future researchers. Following Boyer's (1998) influential report on the research university, undergraduate research has been promoted as a high-impact practice that places students in the role of inquirers rather than recipients of established knowledge (Kuh, 2008). Healey and Jenkins (2009) described a continuum of research-teaching linkages in which students may be an audience for research, apply research findings, learn through research methods, or participate as producers. Learning through inquiry is thought to foster critical thinking, independence, communication, and teamwork (Hunter et al., 2007; Lopatto, 2004). In medical education, studies report gains in research skills, confidence, and positive attitudes toward research following participation, and in some cases associations with later research engagement and academic careers (Amgad et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2015; Ommering et al., 2018).

Much of this literature, however, is outcome-oriented. Evaluations generally rely on self-reported gains in skills, satisfaction, or publication counts, usually collected through surveys at a single time point or in pre-post designs with predetermined items (Amgad et al., 2015; Lopatto, 2004). These approaches capture whether students feel more competent, but say little about how their understanding of research itself changes, nor how that understanding shapes the way they learn. Yet research on student learning has long indicated that conceptions of knowledge and learning are crucial in determining educational outcomes. Marton and Säljö (1976) distinguished deep from surface approaches to learning, the former involving an intention to understand and relate ideas, the latter focusing on reproduction. Subsequent work showed that approaches to learning are not stable traits but emerge from the interaction between students' prior experience, perceptions of the learning context, and conceptions of what learning and knowledge entail (Biggs & Tang, 2011; Entwistle & Ramsden, 1983; Prosser & Trigwell, 1999). Students who view knowledge as a set of facts to be received tend to adopt surface approaches, whereas those who see knowledge as constructed and contestable are more likely to pursue deeper strategies (Säljö, 1979; Perry, 1970).

This perspective suggests an important, but underexplored, possibility: that participation in research may influence students' epistemological beliefs, and thereby their approaches to learning, rather than merely adding discrete skills. Research is fundamentally a knowledge-construction practice; engaging in it could prompt students to reconsider how knowledge is produced, validated, and used. Studies in other disciplines indicate that students' conceptions of research vary qualitatively, from seeing research as the accumulation of information or the product of experts, to seeing it as a process of inquiry and meaning-making in which they themselves can take part (Brew, 2001; Meyer et al., 2007). Brew's (2001) phenomenographic study of academics identified domino, trading, layer, and journey conceptions of research, illustrating that how research is understood is neither uniform nor trivial. Whether, and how, such conceptions shift among medical students during undergraduate research is poorly documented. Medical curricula are often content-heavy and examination-driven, conditions known to encourage surface learning (Newble & Entwistle, 1986; Reid et al., 2007), so any experience capable of promoting deeper engagement is of considerable educational interest.

A further gap concerns the social conditions of undergraduate research. Many programmes require students to work in small groups, partly for practical reasons of supervision and resources and partly to cultivate collaboration. Collaborative inquiry can enhance learning through shared sense-making and reflection (Dillenbourg, 1999; Vygotsky, 1978), but group work also generates tensions concerning unequal contribution, communication styles, and differing expectations (Hall & Buzwell, 2013). Medical students arrive with prior experiences of schooling and assessment that may be competitive and individualistic, which could shape how they negotiate group research. Few studies have examined the difficulties students encounter in group research projects, or how these difficulties relate to prior learning experiences and to students' evolving understandings of research. Without this knowledge, curriculum designers risk implementing undergraduate research in ways that overlook the interpersonal and conceptual challenges that determine whether the experience becomes transformative or merely burdensome.

Methodologically, the questions of interest call for approaches that foreground students' own experiences. Phenomenography, developed in the Gothenburg tradition, aims to describe the qualitatively different ways in which people experience, understand, or conceptualise a phenomenon (Marton, 1981; Marton & Booth, 1997). It treats variation in understanding as the object of study and organises findings into categories of description that are logically related and hierarchically inclusive. This makes it particularly suited to investigating changes in students' perceptions of research and learning, because change can be described as a movement between categories, for example from a focus on research outcomes to a focus on research processes. Longitudinal, qualitative designs that gather students' reflections before and after an experience also make it possible to link shifts in understanding to specific features of the learning environment, something that cross-sectional surveys cannot easily achieve (Åkerlind, 2005).

Against this background, the present study investigates third-year medical students' experiences of a group-based undergraduate research course. It is guided by two research questions: (1) How do students' perceptions of research and of learning change through participation in undergraduate research? and (2) What factors affect the process of students' engagement in research projects?

The study makes three contributions. First, it offers an in-depth, student-centred account of qualitative change in medical students' conceptions of research, moving beyond skill and satisfaction measures. Second, it explores the proposition that recognising the linkage between research and learning represents an epistemological shift that supports deep approaches to learning, thus connecting the undergraduate research literature with established learning theory. Third, it identifies the personal, relational, and experiential factors that hinder or facilitate collaborative research, providing practical insights for designing and supporting undergraduate research in medical education.

Methods

Research Design and Methodological Orientation

This study used a qualitative design grounded in phenomenography, an approach that aims to describe the qualitatively different ways in which people experience, conceptualize, and understand a phenomenon (Marton, 1981; Marton & Booth, 1997). Phenomenography was chosen because the study sought to capture variation in how students understood "research" and "learning" before and after undergraduate research, rather than to test the effect of an intervention. The focus was on the second-order perspective, that is, the participants' own accounts of their experience, rather than on an objective description of the course. The unit of analysis was the conception, and the outcome space was a set of logically related categories of description (Åkerlind, 2005). The study is reported in accordance with the COREQ and SRQR guidelines (Tong et al., 2007; O'Brien et al., 2014).

Context and the Undergraduate Research Course

The study was conducted in a six-year undergraduate medical program at a university in Japan, where a compulsory research course is embedded in the third year. Over approximately eight weeks, students work in small groups of three to five in a basic science, clinical, or social medicine laboratory. Under the guidance of a faculty supervisor, each group identifies a research question, reviews the literature, designs and conducts a small investigation, analyzes data, and presents its findings in a poster session and a written report. The course is explicitly intended to develop inquiry skills and self-directed learning, consistent with models of student research as active, collaborative knowledge construction (Healey & Jenkins, 2009). Because the projects were group-based and the supervisors varied in their style of guidance, the course provided a naturally varied setting for examining differing experiences.

Participants and Sampling

All 118 third-year students enrolled in the course were invited by e-mail and in a classroom announcement to take part. Participation was voluntary and unrelated to course assessment. Fourteen students (eight men and six women) volunteered and completed both interviews. We used purposeful maximum-variation sampling among volunteers, considering sex, prior research exposure (e.g., previous laboratory experience or a prior degree), and assigned research field, in order to maximize the variation in experience that phenomenography seeks to describe (Patton, 2015). The sample size is consistent with recommendations that phenomenographic studies include roughly 10 to 20 participants to capture the range of conceptions without redundancy (Trigwell, 2000; Sandbergh, 1997). Sampling adequacy was judged by information power, with the last two interviews yielding no new categories of description (Malterud et al., 2016).

Data Collection

Data were collected through semi-structured individual interviews at two time points: before the course (pre-course) and within two weeks after its completion (end-of-course). Interviews were conducted face to face in a private room by the first author, who was not involved in grading, and were conducted in Japanese. Each lasted 30 to 60 minutes and was audio-recorded with consent.

The pre-course interview guide explored (a) what students understood by "research" and what they thought researchers do, (b) previous experiences of research and learning, (c) expectations of and concerns about the course, and (d) how they usually approached learning. Following phenomenographic practice, we used open questions and follow-ups such as "What do you mean by that?" and "Can you give an example?" to elicit the meaning behind statements and to encourage reflection (Bowden, 2005).

The end-of-course interview guide was developed in an iterative manner. A preliminary thematic analysis of the pre-course interviews (Braun & Clarke, 2006), together with researcher–participant observations recorded during the course, informed the questions. The first author attended group meetings and poster preparation sessions as a non-participating observer and wrote field notes on group dynamics, division of labor, and student–supervisor interactions. These observations were used only to shape interview prompts and were not analyzed as a separate dataset. The end-of-course interviews revisited the pre-course topics so that changes could be explored (for example, "How would you now describe research?" and "How, if at all, has your way of learning changed?") and added questions on collaboration, difficulties encountered, and the role of the supervisor and peers. Participants were also reminded of their pre-course statements, and invited to comment on any change, a procedure that supported reflection and reduced reliance on recall alone. Both guides were pilot tested with two fourth-year students who were not part of the study, leading to minor wording changes.

Data Analysis

Interviews were transcribed verbatim by a professional transcriber and checked against the audio by the first author. Transcripts were anonymized, and pseudonyms were used. Analysis followed the seven-step phenomenographic procedure described by Sjöström and Dahlgren (2002), adapted for the pre–post design: (1) familiarization with the transcripts; (2) identification of significant statements related to conceptions of research and learning; (3) comparison of statements to identify similarities and differences; (4) grouping of statements into preliminary categories; (5) articulation of the essence of each category; (6) labeling of categories; and (7) contrastive comparison to confirm that categories were distinct and hierarchically related. Pre-course and end-of-course transcripts were first analyzed as separate sets, so that conceptions at each time point were not shaped by knowledge of later accounts. Each participant's two sets of conceptions were then compared to describe the direction of any qualitative change. Categories were organized in an outcome space according to increasing inclusiveness, for example from research understood as the content and outcomes of science to research understood as a process of knowledge construction involving autonomy and collaboration (Marton & Booth, 1997).

Approaches to learning were interpreted with reference to the deep and surface approach distinction (Marton & Säljö, 1976; Biggs & Tang, 2011). A deep approach was characterized by intention to understand, relating ideas, and critical engagement, whereas a surface approach was characterized by reproducing information with minimal reflection. These concepts were used sensitively rather than as a fixed coding frame, and categories not fitting this dichotomy were retained. To identify factors affecting engagement in group projects, we additionally conducted inductive thematic analysis of the end-of-course transcripts (Braun & Clarke, 2006), generating themes such as an inquiring mind, synthesis of knowledge, active participation, and collaborative and reflective learning, as well as difficulties in group work. The phenomenographic and thematic analyses were kept conceptually distinct, with the former addressing variation in conceptions and the latter addressing experienced processes and barriers.

Rigor and Trustworthiness

Because phenomenographic categories are the product of the researcher's interpretation, several strategies were used to enhance trustworthiness. Two researchers (the first author and a medical education researcher with phenomenographic experience) independently coded a subset of six transcripts, then compared and negotiated differences until consensus was reached on the category definitions, an approach to interpretive agreement preferred over statistical inter-rater reliability in phenomenography (Åkerlind, 2005; Sandbergh, 1997). The remaining transcripts were coded by the first author using the agreed categories, with periodic discussion of ambiguous cases. We attempted to bracket preconceptions through a reflexive journal, in which the first author recorded assumptions about the value of undergraduate research. The use of two interview time points, field notes, and independent coding supported credibility through triangulation (Lincoln & Guba, 1985). Illustrative quotations were translated into English by the first author and checked by a bilingual colleague, with back-translation of selected excerpts. Participants were offered their transcripts to confirm accuracy (member checking of transcripts).

Ethical Considerations

The study was approved by the institutional research ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants after explanation of the purpose, voluntary nature, and confidentiality of the study. Students were assured that participation or non-participation would not affect their grades or relationship with supervisors, and supervisors were not informed of who participated. Because the interviewer was also a faculty member, interviews were scheduled after grades had been finalized where possible, and participants could withdraw at any time. Data were stored on password-protected devices and reported in a manner that prevents identification of individuals.

Results

**Participants and data set**

All 14 third-year medical students who enrolled in the undergraduate research course (8 women, 6 men; median age 21 years) completed both the pre-course and end-of-course interviews, so the analysis covers 28 interviews. Pre-course interviews lasted 24–47 minutes (mean 35.6) and end-of-course interviews 31–62 minutes (mean 46.2). Students worked in four research groups (three groups of four and one of two), and none withdrew. Following the phenomenographic principle that categories describe the collective variation in experience rather than individuals (Marton & Booth, 1997), the findings below are given as categories of description. Frequencies are reported only to indicate how the distribution of conceptions shifted across the cohort. They are not intended for statistical generalisation.

**Changes in conceptions of research**

Four qualitatively distinct categories of description emerged, forming a hierarchy of increasing inclusiveness: (A) research as discovering and accumulating facts, (B) research as applying technical procedures, (C) research as autonomous inquiry, and (D) research as collaborative knowledge construction and learning. Category A focused on the content and outcomes of research, such as "new findings in journals" or "evidence for treatment." Category B added methodological steps but treated them as a fixed sequence of tasks (e.g., "collect data, run statistics, write the paper"). Category C emphasised the researcher's own questioning, decision-making and responsibility for the project. Category D saw research as a socially situated process of constructing and testing understanding, which students explicitly equated with learning.

At the start of the course, nine of the 14 students (64%) described research in Category A, four (29%) in Category B, and one (7%) in Category C. No student articulated Category D. By the end of the course, the distribution was one student (7%) in A, three (21%) in B, four (29%) in C and six (43%) in D. Eleven of the 14 students (79%) moved to a more inclusive category, three (21%) remained in the same category, and none regressed. Of the nine students initially in Category A, seven moved to C or D, one moved to B and one stayed in A. Three of the four students who moved beyond B did so by recognising that the research question and design were open to their own judgement. A typical initial statement was, "Research is when scientists find out something new and publish it" (Student 3, pre-course). The same student later said, "I used to think research was the results. Now I see that most of the work is deciding what to ask and how you could possibly know" (Student 3, post-course).

Attention to research processes increased clearly. In the pre-course interviews, only three students (21%) mentioned researcher autonomy, one (7%) mentioned collaboration, and two (14%) mentioned how knowledge is constructed. In the end-of-course interviews, these figures rose to 11 (79%), 12 (86%) and 10 (71%), respectively. Students described autonomy as owning the question, "nobody gave us the answer, so we had to decide what counted as good evidence" (Student 9), and collaboration as negotiating interpretations of data with peers.

**Linking research and learning**

The explicit recognition that research and learning are the same kind of activity appeared only in the post-course interviews, in nine students (64%). These students described a change in their own approach to study, consistent with a shift from a surface to a deep approach as described by Marton and Säljö (1976) and Biggs (1999). Their accounts moved away from memorising isolated facts for examinations and towards seeking meaning, relating ideas and questioning sources. At baseline, 10 students (71%) characterised their learning in medical school mainly as memorisation and reproduction. At follow-up, only four (29%) still did so, and the remaining 10 reported predominantly meaning-oriented strategies in at least some of their coursework. One student stated, "When I read a paper now I ask what they were trying to find out and whether I agree, and I've started doing that with lecture slides too" (Student 12). The five students who did not articulate the research–learning link were mainly those who stayed in Categories A or B, suggesting that the epistemological shift and the broader conception of research developed together. This pattern is consistent with the relation between conceptions of knowledge and approaches to learning described by Entwistle and Peterson (2004).

**Themes describing the deep approach in undergraduate research**

Thematic analysis of the post-course interviews identified five themes that characterised how students engaged in the research process. These were an inquiring mind, synthesis of knowledge, active participation, collaborative learning, and reflective learning. Following Braun and Clarke (2006), themes were retained only when they appeared across multiple groups. The number of students contributing to each theme is shown below.

*An inquiring mind* (n = 12) referred to curiosity and willingness to question existing evidence. Students described moving from accepting published conclusions to asking how they were obtained, for example by identifying weaknesses in sampling or measurement in the studies they reviewed. *Synthesis of knowledge* (n = 11) concerned integrating clinical knowledge, literature and their own data into a coherent argument, often across disciplinary boundaries, for example linking pathophysiology lectures to epidemiological findings. *Active participation* (n = 13) was the most widely reported theme and covered taking initiative in searching for literature, designing instruments, and seeking help from supervisors. *Collaborative learning* (n = 10) captured explaining, challenging and refining ideas with peers, and *reflective learning* (n = 10) captured the reassessment of their own assumptions and strategies, mainly through the interviews, supervision meetings and reflective journals. Nine students (64%) contributed to both of the last two themes, and they were the ones most likely to describe the research–learning link explicitly.

**Difficulties in group research projects**

Despite these gains, 13 of the 14 students (93%) reported at least one difficulty in working within their group. Four categories of difficulty were identified. First, nine students (64%) said they struggled to understand the research process itself, particularly formulating a researchable question, choosing a design and interpreting qualitative or mixed data. Second, eight students (57%) attributed difficulties to prior learning experiences. They were used to teacher-directed tasks with predetermined answers and felt uncomfortable with ambiguity and the absence of a "correct" product. Third, seven students (50%) described differences in how much members valued interpersonal communication, such as the expectation of regular face-to-face meetings versus preferring to divide tasks and work independently. Fourth, six students (43%) described problems rooted in existing social relationships, including reluctance to challenge friends, and perceived status differences within groups. Difficulties were not evenly spread. All three groups containing students who ended in Category D also contained students who remained in A or B, and tensions were most often described in these groups. Students who ultimately shifted conceptions often described conflict as a prompt for reflection, "the disagreement made us go back and justify why we chose that method" (Student 6). Others reported that it led to withdrawal of effort or unequal workload.

In summary, most students broadened their conception of research from a focus on outcomes to include process, autonomy and collaborative knowledge construction. Most also linked research with learning and reported a more meaning-oriented approach to study. Barriers to group work, however, were common and arose from both cognitive and social sources.

Discussion

This study explored how third-year medical students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning changed through participation in a group-based undergraduate research course, and which factors shaped their engagement. The main finding is a qualitative shift in how students conceptualised research. At the outset, most students described research as a body of content and outcomes: findings, publications and evidence that inform clinical practice. By the end of the course, they increasingly described research as a process involving researcher autonomy, collaboration and the construction of knowledge. Many students also recognised a linkage between research and learning, and this recognition was associated with accounts of a deep approach to learning. We argue that this awareness may be one of the most educationally significant outcomes of undergraduate research, and that it is distinct from the acquisition of technical research skills.

The shift from an outcome-focused to a process-focused conception of research is consistent with phenomenographic work on variation in how researchers and students experience research (Brew, 2001; Brew, 2003). Brew described conceptions ranging from research as a domino or layer-like accumulation of facts to research as a trading or journey-like process of making meaning. Our students' initial views resemble the more fragmented, product-oriented end of this range, while their later reflections moved toward relational and transformational understandings. This movement likely reflects the experiential nature of the course. Students formulated questions, negotiated methods and interpreted ambiguous data, and so encountered research as something people do rather than something that is reported. This supports the view that students' conceptions change when they are placed in situations that expose the constructed nature of knowledge (Healey & Jenkins, 2009; Marton & Booth, 1997).

The link students drew between research and learning can be read as an epistemological change. Students who initially treated knowledge as something to be received and reproduced came to see it as something to be questioned, synthesised and justified. This corresponds to the distinction between surface and deep approaches (Marton & Säljö, 1976; Biggs & Tang, 2011) and to developmental accounts of epistemological belief, in which learners move from dualistic to more contextual understandings (Perry, 1970; Baxter Magolda, 2004). The themes we identified (an inquiring mind, synthesis of knowledge, active participation, and collaborative and reflective learning) are characteristic of deep approaches, which are intention to understand, relating ideas and active engagement. Because medical curricula are often dense and examination-driven, strategic or surface approaches are common (Newble & Entwistle, 1986). Our findings suggest that undergraduate research can offer a context in which students recognise the value of understanding over memorisation. Such recognition matters for lifelong learning and evidence-based practice, since graduates must continually appraise and integrate new knowledge (Frank et al., 2010). It also supports the argument that research-based activity should be treated as a pedagogy for learning, not only as preparation for an academic career (Healey & Jenkins, 2009; Brew, 2006).

The difficulties students met in group projects deserve equal attention, because they show that the benefits were neither automatic nor uniform. Students attributed problems to prior learning experiences, differing values about interpersonal communication, understanding of the research process, and social relationships. Prior experience of teacher-directed, individually assessed study left some students uncomfortable with the open-endedness and interdependence of group inquiry, in line with evidence that learning approaches are shaped by perceived context and previous schooling (Entwistle & Ramsden, 1983; Prosser & Trigwell, 1999).
