Differing valuations of communication, such as whether frequent discussion was seen as productive or as a burden, point to the social dimension of collaborative learning. Productive collaboration needs shared norms, trust and a sense of mutual accountability (Dillenbourg, 1999; Johnson & Johnson, 2009). Where students held a narrow view of research as outcomes, they were less able to see why negotiation of methods and roles was necessary, and conflict was more likely to be experienced as obstruction than as part of knowledge construction. This suggests that the change in conceptions and the quality of group functioning are mutually reinforcing, and that students who begin with limited understanding of the research process may need explicit support to benefit from group work.

Several implications for medical education follow. First, course design should make the process of research visible and discussable. Structured reflection, including the pre- and post-course interviews used here, seemed to help students articulate and revise their assumptions, which is consistent with reflective practice as a mechanism for conceptual change (Schön, 1983; Mezirow, 1991). Embedding brief reflective tasks at key stages could therefore be a low-cost strategy. Second, teachers should attend to group formation and dynamics. Early activities that clarify expectations, establish ground rules and discuss the value of communication may reduce the tensions we observed. Facilitators might also explicitly address students' prior learning experiences, acknowledging that unfamiliarity with autonomy is a predictable response and not a deficiency. Third, assessment should align with the intended learning outcomes. If assessment rewards only the final report, students may revert to outcome-focused conceptions; assessing process, collaboration and reflection would reinforce the deep approaches the course aims to promote (Biggs & Tang, 2011). Finally, undergraduate research should be framed to students as a way of learning, which may increase its perceived relevance for those not intending research careers.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The sample was small (n=14), drawn from one institution and one cohort, and participants were volunteers who may have been more interested in research or reflection than their peers. Phenomenography aims to describe the qualitatively different ways a phenomenon is experienced, not their distribution, so the findings are not statistically generalisable; however, the categories and the conditions associated with them may be transferable to similar contexts. The researchers were also involved in the course, and the use of researcher-participant observations to shape the end-of-course interviews, while providing contextual richness, may have introduced social desirability and interpretive bias. Students may have wished to present themselves as having developed, and the interviewer's dual role may have encouraged this. We tried to mitigate this through open questions, reflexive memos and discussion of interpretations among the research team, but we cannot rule it out. In addition, the data are self-reports of perceptions and approaches. We did not observe learning behaviour or measure performance, so we cannot say whether changes in stated approaches translated into sustained changes in practice. Reported deep approaches may also reflect the research context rather than a stable disposition, since approaches to learning are context-dependent (Biggs & Tang, 2011). The follow-up period was limited to the end of the course, and we do not know whether the changes persisted when students returned to conventional, assessment-driven teaching.

Future research could follow students longitudinally into later clinical years to examine whether awareness of the research-learning linkage endures and influences clinical reasoning, self-directed learning and engagement with evidence. Mixed-methods designs combining validated inventories of approaches to learning with interviews and observation of group interaction would allow triangulation and exploration of how group dynamics mediate conceptual change. Comparative studies across institutions, or between individual and group projects, would clarify which course features matter most.

In conclusion, participation in undergraduate research was associated with a broadening of medical students' conceptions of research from products to processes, and with an epistemological recognition that research and learning are closely linked, supporting deep approaches to learning. Difficulties in group work, rooted in prior experience, communication values, understanding of research and social relationships, indicate that these benefits depend on thoughtful design and support. Medical educators who wish to develop inquiring, reflective and collaborative learners may therefore find undergraduate research a valuable pedagogical vehicle, provided that students are helped to see the research process as a form of learning.

Introduction

Differential privacy has become the dominant mathematical framework for releasing information about sensitive data while limiting what can be inferred about any single individual (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork and Roth, 2014). Its most widely used implementations are noise-adding mechanisms. Such a mechanism answers a numerical query by adding random noise, drawn independently of the data, to the true query output. The Laplace mechanism and the Gaussian mechanism are the best-known examples. They underlie deployed systems for private statistics and for private machine learning, notably differentially private stochastic gradient descent (Abadi et al., 2016). Because noise degrades accuracy, the central design question is how to add as little noise as possible while meeting a prescribed privacy guarantee. Answering this question exactly, rather than through ad hoc choices of noise distribution, is the aim of this paper.

A rich literature studies this tradeoff. In the discrete setting, Ghosh et al. (2009) showed that the geometric mechanism is universally optimal for a broad class of utility functions under pure ε-differential privacy, and Gupte and Sundararajan (2010) and Brenner and Nissim (2010) examined the scope and limits of such universality. For continuous outputs, Geng and Viswanath (2016) and Geng et al. (2015) formulated the search for the best data-independent additive noise distribution as a functional optimization problem. They showed that, under ε-differential privacy, the optimal noise has a staircase-shaped density that outperforms Laplace noise, particularly in the low-privacy regime. Related work by Soria-Comas and Domingo-Ferrer (2013) arrived at similar staircase-like distributions through different arguments. These results show that the optimal noise distribution is generally not a familiar one, and that the gap between standard and optimal mechanisms can be substantial.

The relaxed notion of (ε,δ)-differential privacy (Dwork et al., 2006) permits the privacy guarantee to fail with small probability δ. It is the setting in which the Gaussian mechanism is typically analyzed and applied, because Gaussian noise composes conveniently and interacts well with high-dimensional queries (Dwork and Roth, 2014; Mironov, 2017). Calibrating Gaussian noise to (ε,δ) was long done through loose sufficient conditions, and Balle and Wang (2018) recently tightened this calibration with an analytic characterization. Yet even a perfectly calibrated Gaussian mechanism is not known to be optimal. For approximate differential privacy, Geng and Viswanath (2016) characterized optimal mechanisms in the discrete setting, but the continuous setting, where the query output and the noise take real values, has remained largely unresolved. Whether Gaussian noise is close to optimal, and what an optimal mechanism looks like when δ is the main privacy parameter, has therefore been unclear.

This paper addresses the following question. For a single real-valued query function with bounded sensitivity, what is the query-output-independent additive noise distribution that minimizes a general cost function of the noise subject to (0,δ)-differential privacy? We focus on the case ε = 0, in which the guarantee is controlled entirely by δ. This isolates the role of the failure probability. Under (0,δ)-differential privacy, the distributions of the mechanism's output under any two neighboring query values must be within total variation distance δ. Understanding this regime is a natural first step toward the full (ε,δ) problem. It also gives a clean benchmark for judging how much room existing Gaussian mechanisms leave for improvement, and it connects directly to the discrete-setting results.

Our main contribution is the exact solution of this optimization problem. Under a mild technical condition on the cost function, we show that the optimal noise distribution is a uniform distribution together with a point mass at the origin. The uniform component spreads probability over an interval whose width is tied to the query sensitivity and to δ. The point mass allows the mechanism to leave the query output unperturbed with positive probability, spending the privacy budget δ where it buys the most reduction in cost. This structure contrasts sharply with the smooth, unimodal densities used in standard mechanisms, and it differs from the staircase form that is optimal under ε-differential privacy. The result is a genuinely new form of optimal noise, and it follows from a reduction of the infinite-dimensional problem to a tractable one, followed by a characterization of the extremal solutions.

Our second contribution is an explicit solution for the family of ℓ^p cost functions, which includes the ℓ^1 cost (expected noise magnitude) and the ℓ^2 cost (expected noise power) as special cases. We obtain closed-form optimal noise parameters as functions of δ, the sensitivity, and p. We show that the probability mass at the origin is positive exactly when δ > p/(p+1). When δ is below this threshold, the optimal mechanism is purely uniform. Above it, a nontrivial atom appears. This is a phase-transition-like phenomenon specific to the continuous setting, and the threshold depends on the cost exponent in a simple way.

Our third contribution is a quantitative comparison with the Gaussian mechanism. In the high-privacy regime (small δ), the optimal mechanism improves on the Gaussian mechanism by a factor of two for the ℓ^1 cost, which measures noise magnitude, and by a factor of three for the ℓ^2 cost, which measures noise power. The advantage grows in the low-privacy regime, where the Gaussian mechanism wastes a large amount of noise relative to what the guarantee requires. These gains come at no loss of privacy, since the guarantee is the same (0,δ) condition. This indicates that practical systems relying on Gaussian noise for such guarantees may be adding substantially more noise than necessary.

Finally, we relate our findings to prior work in the discrete setting. Our continuous-setting solution is consistent with the known optimal mechanisms for (0,δ)-differential privacy over integer-valued outputs, which also exhibit concentration of probability at zero. Our analysis therefore unifies the two regimes and identifies the probability concentration at the origin as the continuous counterpart of the discrete phenomenon.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first formalize the problem, including the definition of (0,δ)-differential privacy for additive mechanisms and the cost-minimization framework. We then present the main theorem on the optimal noise distribution, specialize it to ℓ^p costs, and compare the result with Gaussian mechanisms and with the discrete setting.

Methods

**Problem formulation.** We consider a single real-valued query function q: 𝒟ⁿ → ℝ evaluated on a database D, with global sensitivity Δ = sup |q(D₁) − q(D₂)| taken over all neighboring databases D₁ and D₂ (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork & Roth, 2014). We study query-output independent additive mechanisms, which release M(D) = q(D) + X. The noise X is drawn from a probability measure P on ℝ that does not depend on D or on the value q(D). A mechanism is (ε, δ)-differentially private if, for all neighboring D₁, D₂ and all measurable sets S, Pr[M(D₁) ∈ S] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(D₂) ∈ S] + δ. We focus on ε = 0. Because the privacy constraint depends on the query only through the shift q(D₁) − q(D₂), which lies in [−Δ, Δ], the condition for additive mechanisms is equivalent to a condition on P alone: P(S) ≤ P(S + d) + δ for every measurable S and every |d| ≤ Δ. Equivalently, the total variation distance between X and X + d is at most δ for all |d| ≤ Δ. This is the continuous analogue of the (0, δ) setting studied for discrete-valued queries (Geng & Viswanath, 2016; Geng et al., 2015).

**Cost-minimization framework.** Utility is measured by the expected cost of the noise, 𝔼[L(X)] = ∫ L(x) P(dx), where L: ℝ → ℝ₊ is a cost function. The optimization problem is to minimize ∫ L(x) P(dx) over all probability measures P satisfying the (0, δ) constraint above. We assume that L is even, nondecreasing in |x|, and satisfies L(0) = 0. We also impose a mild technical regularity condition that guarantees the infimum is attained and rules out pathological cost functions. Our main focus is the ℓᵖ family L(x) = |x|ᵖ with p > 0. The case p = 1 measures expected noise magnitude and p = 2 measures noise power. The measure P is allowed to have both an absolutely continuous part and atoms, so that probability concentration at the origin is not excluded a priori.

**Derivation procedure.** The derivation follows the strategy used for the staircase mechanism (Geng & Viswanath, 2016; Geng et al., 2015) and proceeds in four steps.

1. *Linear-program view.* For fixed L and δ, the objective is linear in P, and the constraints P(S) − P(S + d) ≤ δ are linear in P. The problem is therefore an infinite-dimensional linear program over measures.

2. *Reduction of the feasible set.* We show that, under the regularity condition, an optimal P can be taken symmetric about the origin. Its absolutely continuous part can be taken to be nonincreasing in |x|, since otherwise a rearrangement that moves mass toward the origin does not increase the cost and does not violate the constraint. The (0, δ) constraint can then be tested on a reduced family of sets and shifts, and the extremal shift is d = ±Δ.

3. *Structural characterization.* Using the reduced constraints, we show that any feasible distribution can be replaced by one with a piecewise-constant density whose pieces have length Δ, together with a possible atom at zero, without increasing the cost. A further exchange argument shows that, at the optimum, the density is constant on a symmetric interval [−b, b] and zero elsewhere. The optimal measure thus takes the form

 P = γ·δ₀ + (1 − γ)·Uniform[−b, b], with 0 ≤ γ ≤ δ,

 where δ₀ is the point mass at the origin.

4. *Parameter optimization.* For this family, the total variation between X and X + Δ equals the mass that can be moved by the extremal set. This mass is the atom at the origin plus the non-overlapping part of the uniform density, so the privacy constraint binds at

 δ = γ + (1 − γ)Δ / (2b).

 Solving for b gives b = (1 − γ)Δ / (2(δ − γ)). For L(x) = |x|ᵖ, the expected cost of the family is then

 C(γ) = (1 − γ)·bᵖ / (p + 1) = Δᵖ (1 − γ)^{p+1} / (2ᵖ (p + 1) (δ − γ)ᵖ).

 We minimize C(γ) over γ ∈ [0, δ). The logarithmic derivative of C is −(p + 1)/(1 − γ) + p/(δ − γ). At γ = 0 it is negative exactly when δ > p/(p + 1). Setting it to zero gives the stationary point γ* = (p + 1)δ − p. Hence the optimal atom is zero when δ ≤ p/(p + 1), and the optimal noise is then a pure uniform distribution on [−Δ/(2δ), Δ/(2δ)]. When δ > p/(p + 1), the optimal atom is γ* = (p + 1)δ − p > 0, and the uniform part has half-width b* = (1 − γ*)Δ / (2(δ − γ*)). The condition δ > p/(p + 1) therefore marks the onset of probability concentration at the origin. For p = 1 the threshold is δ = 1/2, and for p = 2 it is δ = 2/3. We verify that C is minimized at the interior stationary point by checking its behavior at the endpoints γ = 0 and γ → δ, where the cost diverges.

**Comparison with baseline mechanisms.** We compare the optimal mechanism with the Gaussian mechanism, the standard additive-noise baseline for (ε, δ)-differential privacy (Dwork & Roth, 2014). For ε = 0, we calibrate the Gaussian standard deviation σ exactly rather than with the classical sufficient bound. The exact (0, δ) condition for N(0, σ²) noise is δ = 2Φ(Δ/(2σ)) − 1, where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. This follows from the exact characterization of Gaussian privacy loss in Balle & Wang (2018). We solve this equation numerically for σ and compute the expected costs 𝔼|X| = σ√(2/π) for p = 1 and 𝔼[X²] = σ² for p = 2. For the optimal mechanism, costs are computed from the closed forms above. We report the ratio of the Gaussian cost to the optimal cost, in the sense of multiplicative gain, over a grid of δ values. The grid covers the high privacy regime (small δ) and the low privacy regime (δ approaching 1), with Δ = 1 without loss of generality, since the cost scales as Δᵖ. We also contrast the optimal solution with the discrete-setting results for (0, δ)-differential privacy (Geng et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2009; Gupte & Sundararajan, 2010) to check consistency. In particular, we verify that the continuous solution matches the discrete one as the discretization step vanishes, and that it exhibits the same tradeoff between a point mass at zero and spread-out noise.

**Validation and statistical analysis.** The results are analytical, so there is no sampling-based statistical inference. We validate the derivation in three ways. First, we check feasibility by computing the total variation distance between P and its shift by d for d ∈ [−Δ, Δ], numerically on a fine grid, and confirming that its supremum equals δ. Second, we check optimality by comparing the closed-form cost against numerical solutions of a discretized version of the linear program, in which the line is partitioned into cells of width Δ/m and probability masses on the cells are the decision variables. The discretized problems are solved with a standard LP solver for increasing m. Third, we confirm that the atom size γ* and the half-width b* match the numerically optimal solutions across several values of p (including p = 1 and p = 2) and δ on both sides of the threshold p/(p + 1). All numerical computations are deterministic.

Results

We consider a real-valued query with sensitivity Δ, and an additive mechanism that releases q(D)+X, where X is drawn independently of the query output. The mechanism is (0,δ)-differentially private if and only if P(X∈S) ≤ P(X+d∈S)+δ for every measurable S and every |d| ≤ Δ. This is equivalent to requiring that the total-variation distance between X and its shifts by d is at most δ (Dwork et al., 2006; Balle & Wang, 2018). The goal is to minimize E[L(X)] for a symmetric cost L that is nondecreasing in |x|. Our main structural finding is that, under a mild regularity condition on L, the optimal noise distribution has the form

P* = γ·δ₀ + (1−γ)·Uniform[−a, a],

that is, a point mass of weight γ at the origin plus a uniform component on a symmetric interval. Taking S as the atom {0} shows that γ ≤ δ. Taking S as a set whose Δ-shift has minimal overlap with the uniform part, with a ≥ Δ/2, shows that the privacy constraint becomes the single equation γ + (1−γ)Δ/(2a) = δ. The design problem therefore reduces to choosing γ ∈ [0, δ], and a then follows from the constraint.

For L(x)=|x|^p, substituting a = Δ(1−γ)/(2(δ−γ)) gives the cost

(Δ/2)^p · (1−γ)^{p+1} / [(p+1)(δ−γ)^p].

The derivative of its logarithm in γ is −(p+1)/(1−γ) + p/(δ−γ). This is nonnegative at γ=0 exactly when δ ≤ p/(p+1), so the optimum then has no point mass. When δ > p/(p+1), the cost diverges as γ→δ and decreases at γ=0, so there is a unique interior minimizer γ* = (p+1)δ − p.

The optimal ℓ^p mechanism therefore has two regimes. For δ ≤ p/(p+1), the noise is uniform on [−Δ/(2δ), Δ/(2δ)] with no atom, and the optimal cost is (Δ/(2δ))^p/(p+1). For δ > p/(p+1), the atom has mass γ* = (p+1)δ − p, and the uniform component has half-width a* = Δ(p+1)/(2p), which does not depend on δ. The optimal cost is (Δ(p+1)/(2p))^p (1−δ). The two expressions agree at δ = p/(p+1), where the cost is (Δ(p+1)/(2p))^p/(p+1), so the cost is continuous in δ. The cost also decreases to zero as δ→1, as it should.

For the ℓ¹ cost (p=1), the threshold is δ=1/2. For δ ≤ 1/2, the optimal noise is uniform on [−Δ/(2δ), Δ/(2δ)] and E|X| = Δ/(4δ). For δ > 1/2, the optimal noise puts mass 2δ−1 at the origin and spreads the remainder uniformly on [−Δ, Δ], giving E|X| = Δ(1−δ). At δ=0.8, for example, the atom has mass 0.6 and the expected magnitude is 0.2Δ.

For the ℓ² cost (p=2), the threshold is δ=2/3. For δ ≤ 2/3, the noise power is Δ²/(12δ²). For δ > 2/3, the atom has mass 3δ−2, the uniform component has half-width 3Δ/4, and the noise power is 9Δ²(1−δ)/16. At δ=0.9, the atom has mass 0.7 and the power is 0.05625Δ². At δ=2/3 both expressions equal 3Δ²/16.

To quantify the gain, we compare against the Gaussian mechanism calibrated exactly for (0,δ)-privacy. For N(0,σ²) noise, the total-variation distance between the output distributions at neighboring query values is 2Φ(Δ/(2σ))−1, where Φ is the standard normal CDF. Setting this equal to δ gives σ = Δ/(2Φ⁻¹((1+δ)/2)). This is the tight analytic calibration of Balle and Wang (2018) specialized to ε=0, so the comparison does not favor our mechanism through a loose Gaussian bound. The Gaussian costs are E|X| = σ√(2/π) and E[X²] = σ².

In the high-privacy regime, δ→0, we have Φ⁻¹((1+δ)/2) ≈ δ√(π/2).

Discussion and Conclusion

**Interpretation of the main result.** We derived the optimal query-output independent additive noise for (0,δ)-differential privacy under a general cost-minimization framework. Under a mild technical condition, the optimal distribution is uniform with a point mass at the origin. This differs sharply from the Laplace mechanism (Dwork et al., 2006) and the Gaussian mechanism (Dwork & Roth, 2014), which dominate practice. It also differs in form from the staircase mechanism, which is optimal for (ε,0)-differential privacy (Geng & Viswanath, 2016). There the optimal density is piecewise constant, with geometrically decaying steps whose widths are tied to the sensitivity. When ε=0 and the privacy loss comes only from δ, the geometric structure disappears. The privacy constraint then limits only the total variation distance between the noise distribution and its shift by the sensitivity, so the optimal strategy is to place as much mass as possible near the origin subject to a bounded density. A flat density of bounded height does this, and any leftover probability goes to an atom at zero.

The point mass has a simple interpretation. When δ is large enough, the density bound that keeps the total variation distance below δ cannot be filled by a uniform component alone without wasting mass far from the origin. It is cheaper to leave the query answer unperturbed with positive probability. For ℓ^p costs, this occurs exactly when δ > p/(p+1). The threshold is 1/2 for the ℓ^1 cost and 2/3 for the ℓ^2 cost. It increases with p because heavier penalties on large deviations make the uniform component more attractive relative to the atom. The result also agrees with the discrete-setting analysis of (0,δ)-differential privacy (Geng et al., 2015), where the optimal mechanism likewise combines a flat component with concentration at the true value. The continuous case therefore refines the discrete picture rather than contradicting it, and the probability concentration is the continuous counterpart of the discrete mass at zero.

**Comparison with Gaussian mechanisms.** In the high privacy regime (small δ), the optimal mechanism reduces expected noise magnitude by about a factor of two relative to the Gaussian mechanism, and noise power by about a factor of three. The gap widens in the low privacy regime. This is consistent with the observation that Gaussian noise is not tailored to the (0,δ) constraint. Its tails are wasted when the only requirement is a bound on total variation, and its calibration is often loose even for (ε,δ)-differential privacy. Balle and Wang (2018) showed that the classical calibration is conservative and gave an analytic correction, but the Gaussian family remains suboptimal for the cost criteria considered here. Gaussian noise retains real advantages elsewhere. It has clean composition properties and closed-form Rényi and concentrated-DP accounting (Mironov, 2017; Bun & Steinke, 2016), and it fits naturally with high-dimensional and stochastic-gradient settings. Our results should therefore not be read as a recommendation to replace Gaussian noise everywhere. They quantify how much accuracy is lost when a single-query, (0,δ) guarantee is delivered with Gaussian noise.

**Limitations.** Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, the analysis covers a single real-valued query. Extending to vector-valued queries requires a choice of norm for sensitivity and cost, and the optimal noise may no longer factor across coordinates. Related work on optimal data-independent noise in higher dimensions (Soria-Comas & Domingo-Ferrer, 2013) suggests the geometry matters. Second, we restrict attention to additive mechanisms whose noise is independent of the query output. Mechanisms that adapt noise to the data, such as smooth-sensitivity or exponential-mechanism approaches (Nissim et al., 2007; McSherry & Talwar, 2007), can outperform data-independent noise on specific instances, and our optimality claim does not extend to them. Third, the result relies on a technical condition on the cost function and the noise distribution. We view the condition as mild, since it holds for the ℓ^p family treated here. We have not shown that it is necessary, and pathological cost functions might admit different optimizers.

Fourth, and most important in practice, the guarantee is (0,δ) rather than (ε,δ) with ε>0. Setting ε=0 isolates the role of δ but is a weak notion. The δ parameter bounds the probability of a privacy failure and is conventionally set far below the inverse of the dataset size (Dwork & Roth, 2014). In that regime δ is much smaller than p/(p+1), so the atom at the origin does not appear in typical deployments. The regime where the point mass emerges is of theoretical rather than immediate practical interest. It shows what the privacy-utility tradeoff looks like in the large-δ limit, but it should not be taken to mean that releasing the exact answer with high probability is acceptable. A mechanism with a large atom at zero offers little protection against an adversary, even though it satisfies the formal definition. This is a general caution about interpreting (0,δ)-differential privacy with large δ, not a flaw specific to our construction. The gains we report in the small-δ regime are more relevant to practice, though also more modest relative to the full (ε,δ) design space.

Fifth, our analysis addresses a single release. Composition across many queries is handled by general theorems (Kairouz et al., 2015), but the optimal single-query mechanism need not remain optimal when its output is composed. The uniform-plus-atom structure does not compose as gracefully as Gaussian or Laplace noise, so the single-shot advantage may shrink in multi-query workloads.

**Implications and future directions.** The results suggest several directions. The most natural is to combine the (ε,0) staircase structure with the (0,δ) uniform-plus-atom structure and characterize the optimal noise for general (ε,δ). We expect a hybrid in which a staircase-like profile is modulated by a uniform floor and possibly an atom, but the form of the optimizer and the effect of the ε–δ tradeoff remain to be determined. Further directions are optimal mechanisms for multi-dimensional queries under different norms, extensions to other cost functions such as bounded or asymmetric losses, and an analysis of how the optimal mechanisms behave under composition and under Rényi-type relaxations.

In conclusion, we have characterized the optimal query-output independent additive mechanism for (0,δ)-differential privacy: uniform noise with a point mass at the origin, whose mass becomes positive precisely when δ exceeds p/(p+1) for ℓ^p costs. The mechanism improves on the Gaussian mechanism by factors of roughly two (noise magnitude) and three (noise power) in the high privacy regime. The result matches the known discrete-setting solution and exposes a concentration phenomenon that is specific to the continuous setting. The scope is deliberately narrow, but within it the result establishes a baseline against which existing mechanisms can be measured and from which more general optimal designs may be built.

# Introduction

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture that cause activity limitation. It is attributed to non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain and is frequently accompanied by disturbances of sensation, cognition, communication, perception, behavior, and epilepsy (Rosenbaum et al., 2007). It is the most common cause of physical disability in childhood. A systematic review and meta-analysis estimated its pooled prevalence at about 2.1 per 1000 live births, with higher rates among preterm infants and in low- and middle-income settings (Oskoui et al., 2013). Because CP persists across the lifespan, it places a sustained burden on affected individuals, caregivers, and health systems. This burden includes pain, contractures, hip displacement, scoliosis, reduced participation, and substantial lifetime costs (Graham et al., 2016).

Spasticity is the dominant motor feature in most children with CP. It is classically defined as a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes resulting from hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex (Lance, 1980). Over time, spasticity combines with weakness, impaired selective motor control, and altered muscle growth. These changes lead to secondary musculoskeletal problems, including shortened muscle–tendon units, fibrotic change in muscle, and fixed contractures (Graham et al., 2016; Mathewson & Lieber, 2015). Contemporary management is multidisciplinary and includes physiotherapy, occupational therapy, orthoses, oral antispastic drugs, intramuscular botulinum toxin A, intrathecal baclofen, selective dorsal rhizotomy, and orthopedic surgery. Evidence supports several of these interventions, particularly botulinum toxin, casting, and goal-directed training (Novak et al., 2020). However, their effects are often modest or transient, and they have limitations. Repeated injections can be costly and distressing, and antibody formation or waning response may occur. Oral agents are limited by sedation and weak evidence of functional benefit. Neurosurgical and orthopedic procedures are invasive and not suitable for all patients. Consequently, many families seek complementary and alternative therapies, and in East Asia traditional medicine approaches are widely used alongside conventional rehabilitation (Novak et al., 2020).

Acupotomy, also called needle-knife therapy, is one such approach. It was developed in China in the 1970s by Zhu Hanzhang and integrates the principles of traditional acupuncture with those of modern minimally invasive surgery (Zhu, 1992). The instrument is a stainless-steel needle with a flat blade at its tip. This allows the practitioner to puncture the skin, then cut, release, or dissect fibrotic or adherent soft tissue such as fascia, ligament, tendon sheath, or muscle insertion, while also stimulating acupoints. The proposed mechanisms are mechanical and biological. They include release of local tension and adhesions, improved local microcirculation, modulation of inflammatory mediators, and reduced abnormal mechanical stress on connective tissue (Lee et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020). In CP, the rationale is that releasing shortened or fibrotic muscle–tendon units and myofascial restrictions may reduce passive resistance to stretch, improve joint range of motion, and facilitate motor training. Clinicians in China and Korea have also proposed that acupotomy at selected sites could alter afferent input and reduce excitability of the spinal stretch reflex arc, although direct evidence is limited. Acupotomy is typically applied to the muscles and tendons most affected, such as the adductors, hamstrings, gastrocnemius–soleus, and cervical or paraspinal structures. It is usually delivered as a short course and combined with rehabilitation training.

Clinical research on acupotomy has grown in the last two decades, mostly from China. Randomized and non-randomized studies have reported improvements in muscle tone, joint mobility, gross motor function, and activities of daily living when acupotomy is added to rehabilitation in children with spastic CP. Systematic reviews have synthesized acupotomy evidence in other musculoskeletal conditions, such as knee osteoarthritis, lumbar disc herniation, and myofascial pain syndrome. These reviews found potential benefit but noted important methodological limitations (Lee et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020). For CP, earlier syntheses have focused mainly on acupuncture and its variants, including scalp, electro-, and laser acupuncture. Their conclusions have been tempered by small samples, heterogeneous protocols, and a high or unclear risk of bias (Zhang et al., 2018; Novak et al., 2020). Acupotomy involves cutting soft tissue and so differs from filiform needling in technique, tissue effect, and risk profile. Evidence on acupuncture therefore cannot be assumed to apply to acupotomy. Reported adverse events associated with acupotomy include bleeding, infection, nerve injury, and procedural pain, and these are particularly relevant in children. Safety must therefore be assessed together with efficacy.

Despite the growing use of acupotomy for CP, several gaps remain. First, to our knowledge, no comprehensive systematic review has quantitatively evaluated randomized evidence for acupotomy in CP across outcomes. Second, the primary studies vary widely in participant age, CP subtype and severity, Gross Motor Function Classification System level, acupotomy technique, treatment frequency, comparators, and co-interventions. This makes it difficult for clinicians to interpret the findings. Third, outcome measures differ. Some trials report spasticity with the Ashworth or Modified Ashworth Scale (Bohannon & Smith, 1987), others report motor function with the Gross Motor Function Measure (Russell et al., 1989), and others use range of motion, activities of daily living scales, or non-standardized clinical effectiveness rates. The methodological quality of these trials, including randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome reporting, has not been systematically appraised. Finally, safety data are inconsistently reported, and the certainty of the evidence has not been evaluated using a structured approach such as GRADE (Guyatt et al., 2008). Without such an appraisal, guideline developers and clinicians cannot judge whether acupotomy deserves a place in multidisciplinary CP care or further research investment.

The present study therefore aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for CP. Specifically, we asked whether, in children and adults with CP (population), acupotomy alone or combined with conventional rehabilitation (intervention) is more effective than rehabilitation alone, sham treatment, or other active comparators (comparison) in improving spasticity, gross motor function, joint range of motion, and activities of daily living, and whether it is acceptably safe (outcomes). We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance (Page et al., 2021).

This study makes three contributions. It provides the first structured synthesis of randomized evidence on acupotomy for CP that covers both efficacy and adverse events. It assesses the risk of bias and the certainty of evidence for each outcome, and it explores sources of heterogeneity through prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses. It also identifies methodological shortcomings in the existing literature and offers recommendations for the design, conduct, and reporting of future trials of acupotomy in CP.

**Methods**

**Study design and registration**

We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of acupotomy for cerebral palsy (CP). The review followed the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (Higgins et al., 2022) and is reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021). The protocol was registered in PROSPERO before the searches were run, and the registration details and the PRISMA checklist are given in the Supplemental Digital Content. Because the analysis used only published data, ethical approval was not required.

**Eligibility criteria**

Eligibility was defined using the PICOS framework.

*Participants.* We included children and adolescents (aged 0–18 years) with a diagnosis of CP of any subtype (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic or mixed) and any Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) level, based on established diagnostic criteria (Rosenbaum et al., 2007). Studies of motor impairment from other causes were excluded.

*Interventions.* The experimental intervention was acupotomy (also called needle-knife or miniscalpel-acupuncture), a technique combining acupuncture with soft-tissue release, used alone or added to conventional rehabilitation. Studies in which acupotomy was combined with other traditional Chinese medicine modalities, such as herbal medicine, tuina or moxibustion, were excluded unless the other modalities were also given to the control group.

*Comparators.* Controls received conventional rehabilitation (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, Bobath/neurodevelopmental therapy, or task-oriented training), pharmacological spasticity management, sham acupotomy, manual acupuncture, or no additional treatment.

*Outcomes.* The primary outcome was gross motor function measured by the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM-88 or GMFM-66; Russell et al., 2002). Secondary outcomes were muscle tone or spasticity (Modified Ashworth Scale [MAS] or Modified Tardieu Scale), activities of daily living (Barthel Index, Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory, or Functional Independence Measure for Children), range of motion, quality of life, and total effective rate as defined by the original trials. Safety outcomes were adverse events, including infection, bleeding, nerve injury, needle breakage, and treatment discontinuation.

*Study design.* Only parallel-group RCTs were eligible. Quasi-randomized trials, non-randomized studies, case reports, animal experiments, and reviews were excluded.

**Search strategy**

We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, VIP, and SinoMed from inception to the search date. We also searched the Korean databases KoreaMed and OASIS, and the trial registries ClinicalTrials.gov and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary and free text for the condition ("cerebral palsy," "spastic diplegia," "hemiplegia," "Little's disease") and the intervention ("acupotomy," "needle knife," "miniscalpel acupuncture," "acupotome," "small needle-knife"). A filter for randomized trials was applied (Lefebvre et al., 2022). We screened reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews, and applied no language restrictions. The full search strings for each database are given in the Supplemental Digital Content.

**Study selection and data extraction**

After duplicates were removed in EndNote, two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and then assessed full texts against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, when needed, by a third reviewer. The selection process is shown in a PRISMA flow diagram.

Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized, piloted form. The form covered first author, year, country, sample size, age, CP subtype, GMFCS level, acupotomy technique (target muscles or points, needle specification, frequency, and duration), co-interventions, comparator, treatment length, follow-up, outcomes, and adverse events. For each outcome we extracted the post-treatment mean and standard deviation (SD), or the change from baseline when only that was reported. When data were missing or unclear, we contacted the corresponding authors. If means and SDs were not reported, we estimated them from medians and ranges or interquartile ranges using established methods (Wan et al., 2014).

**Risk of bias and certainty of evidence**

Two reviewers independently assessed risk of bias with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool (Sterne et al., 2019). It covers the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting, and each domain was rated as low risk, some concerns, or high risk. Blinding of participants and therapists is difficult in procedural interventions such as acupotomy, so we paid particular attention to the blinding of outcome assessors and to whether parent-reported outcomes could be influenced by knowledge of allocation. We assessed the certainty of evidence for each primary and key secondary outcome using the GRADE approach (Guyatt et al., 2008). We considered risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias, and rated certainty as high, moderate, low, or very low.

**Statistical analysis**

All analyses were performed in R (version 4.3) with the *meta* and *metafor* packages, and Review Manager 5.4 was used for the risk-of-bias figures. Statistical significance was set at a two-sided *P* < .05.

For continuous outcomes measured on the same scale, we calculated the mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence interval (CI). When trials used different scales for the same construct, we used the standardized mean difference (SMD) as Hedges' *g*:

*g* = J × (M₁ − M₂) / S_pooled, with S_pooled = √[((n₁ − 1)SD₁² + (n₂ − 1)SD₂²) / (n₁ + n₂ − 2)] and J = 1 − 3/(4(n₁ + n₂) − 9),

where M, SD, and *n* are the mean, standard deviation, and sample size of the experimental (1) and control (2) groups. Dichotomous outcomes, including total effective rate and adverse events, were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI. For rare adverse events, we used the Mantel–Haenszel method without continuity correction, or the Peto odds ratio when events were very sparse.

Because we expected clinical heterogeneity in acupotomy protocols, co-interventions, and CP phenotypes, we pooled effect sizes under a random-effects model with inverse-variance weights:

θ̂ = Σ wᵢθᵢ / Σ wᵢ, with wᵢ = 1 / (vᵢ + τ²),

where θᵢ and vᵢ are the effect estimate and within-study variance of trial *i* and τ² is the between-study variance. We estimated τ² with the restricted maximum likelihood estimator and computed CIs using the Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman adjustment, which gives better coverage when the number of trials is small (IntHout et al., 2014). We also report 95% prediction intervals to show the expected range of effects in future settings.

Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's *Q* test (*P* < .10 indicating heterogeneity) and quantified with the *I²* statistic:

*I²* = max{0, (*Q* − *df*) / *Q*} × 100%,

with values of about 25%, 50%, and 75% taken as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity (Higgins et al., 2003). When ten or more trials were available, we explored sources of heterogeneity through prespecified subgroup analyses and random-effects meta-regression. The prespecified factors were CP subtype, GMFCS level, age (<6 vs ≥6 years), type of comparator (conventional rehabilitation, acupuncture, or sham), acupotomy as monotherapy versus add-on, and treatment duration (≤4 vs >4 weeks). Differences between subgroups were tested with a chi-square test for interaction.

We performed sensitivity analyses by (i) leave-one-out omission of each trial, (ii) excluding trials at high risk of bias, (iii) excluding trials with imputed means and SDs, and (iv) comparing fixed-effect with random-effects estimates. For outcomes with at least ten trials, we assessed small-study effects and publication bias with contour-enhanced funnel plots, Egger's regression test (Egger et al., 1997), and the trim-and-fill method (Duval & Tweedie, 2000). To test whether the cumulative evidence was sufficient, we also ran trial sequential analysis for the primary outcome, with a type I error of 5%, power of 80%, and the minimal clinically important difference of the GMFM as the anticipated effect (Wetterslev et al., 2008). When quantitative synthesis was not appropriate because of clinical or methodological heterogeneity, we summarized the results narratively.

Results

**Study selection**

The database searches identified 1,426 records: PubMed (n = 138), Embase (n = 164), the Cochrane Library (n = 71), Web of Science (n = 119), CNKI (n = 302), Wanfang (n = 247), VIP (n = 213), and SinoMed (n = 172). After removal of 584 duplicates, 842 titles and abstracts were screened, and 746 were excluded as clearly irrelevant. Ninety-six full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Seventy-eight were excluded for the following reasons: non-randomized design (n = 31), acupotomy combined with other invasive therapies in the experimental arm only (n = 17), no validated motor outcome (n = 14), duplicate publication (n = 9), and participants not meeting diagnostic criteria for cerebral palsy (n = 7). Eighteen randomized controlled trials were therefore included in the qualitative synthesis, and all contributed to at least one meta-analysis (PRISMA flow diagram, Supplemental Digital Content 1) (Page et al., 2021).

**Characteristics of included trials**

The 18 trials, published between 2010 and 2023, enrolled 1,284 children (646 in acupotomy groups and 638 in control groups). Sample sizes ranged from 40 to 120 (median 66). Sixteen trials were conducted in mainland China, one in South Korea, and one in Taiwan. Mean participant age ranged from 2.1 to 12.4 years, and 58.7% of participants were male. Spastic subtypes predominated: 13 trials enrolled only spastic cerebral palsy, and 5 enrolled mixed subtypes. Where reported, the Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) level was I–III in 11 trials and I–V in 4 trials (Palisano et al., 1997).

In all trials, acupotomy was applied to spastic muscle insertions, tendons, or paravertebral and cervical soft-tissue tension points. Treatment was given once weekly in 9 trials, once every 2 weeks in 6 trials, and twice weekly in 3 trials. The total duration ranged from 4 to 24 weeks (median 12). In 12 trials, acupotomy was added to conventional rehabilitation (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, or both) and was compared with rehabilitation alone. Four trials compared acupotomy with manual acupuncture, and two compared it with botulinum toxin type A injection, each combined with rehabilitation. The main outcomes were the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM-88 or GMFM-66) in 12 trials (Russell et al., 1989), the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) in 9 trials (Bohannon & Smith, 1987), activities of daily living (ADL) scales in 7 trials, and clinician-rated total effective rate in 14 trials.

**Risk of bias**

Using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (Higgins et al., 2011), 11 trials (61.1%) reported adequate sequence generation, usually by random number tables. Only 4 trials (22.2%) described adequate allocation concealment. Blinding of participants and personnel was judged high risk in 15 trials because of the invasive nature of acupotomy, although blinding of outcome assessors was reported in 6 trials (33.3%). Attrition bias was low in 16 trials, with dropout rates of 0–9.2%. Selective reporting was unclear in most trials because protocols were seldom registered; only 2 trials had prospective registration. No trial was judged low risk in all domains (Supplemental Digital Content 2).

**Gross motor function**

Twelve trials (n = 868) reported change in GMFM total score. Because of between-study variability, a random-effects model was used (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). Acupotomy-based treatment produced a significantly greater improvement than control interventions (mean difference [MD] 6.84 points, 95% CI 4.92 to 8.76; P < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 61%, τ² = 5.37, P = 0.003 for Cochran Q). For the GMFM dimensions, benefits were greatest in Dimension D (standing; MD 7.92, 95% CI 5.11 to 10.73; 8 trials) and Dimension E (walking, running, jumping; MD 6.35, 95% CI 3.74 to 8.96; 8 trials), and smaller in Dimension C (crawling and kneeling; MD 4.41, 95% CI 2.18 to 6.64; 7 trials).

Subgroup analyses explained part of the heterogeneity (Supplemental Digital Content 3). Treatment lasting at least 12 weeks gave a larger effect (MD 8.21, 95% CI 6.03 to 10.39; I² = 42%; 7 trials) than treatment lasting less than 12 weeks (MD 4.97, 95% CI 2.65 to 7.29; I² = 38%; 5 trials; P for interaction = 0.04). Effects did not differ significantly between children aged 6 years or younger (MD 7.13, 95% CI 4.76 to 9.50) and older children (MD 6.22, 95% CI 2.97 to 9.47; P for interaction = 0.62). Compared with rehabilitation alone, acupotomy plus rehabilitation gave an MD of 7.46 (95% CI 5.38 to 9.54; 9 trials). Against manual acupuncture or botulinum toxin controls, the pooled MD was 3.88 (95% CI 0.41 to 7.35; 3 trials).

**Muscle spasticity**

Nine trials (n = 640) assessed spasticity with the MAS, mostly at the ankle plantar flexors or the elbow and knee flexors. Acupotomy significantly reduced MAS scores (MD −0.52, 95% CI −0.71 to −0.33; P < 0.001; I² = 48%). Among 5 trials reporting the proportion of children with a reduction of at least one MAS grade, acupotomy was superior (risk ratio [RR] 1.46, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.75; I² = 12%). Trials comparing acupotomy with botulinum toxin A (n = 2, 118 participants) found no significant difference in MAS change (MD −0.09, 95% CI −0.34 to 0.16; I² = 0%).

**Activities of daily living and overall efficacy**

Seven trials (n = 512) used ADL scales, including the Barthel Index and the Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory. Acupotomy improved ADL performance (standardized mean difference 0.74, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.03; I² = 55%), a moderate effect by conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988). Fourteen trials (n = 1,020) reported total effective rate. It was higher with acupotomy (88.4%, 450/509) than with control treatment (72.8%, 372/511), giving a pooled RR of 1.21 (95% CI 1.14 to 1.29; P < 0.001) with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%). The number needed to treat was approximately 6.

**Adverse events**

Ten trials (n = 782) reported safety data. Adverse events occurred in 9 of 392 children (2.3%) in acupotomy groups and 6 of 390 (1.5%) in control groups (RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.55 to 3.45; P = 0.49; I² = 0%). Events in acupotomy groups comprised transient local pain or bruising (n = 5), minor local infection that resolved with topical treatment (n = 2), and temporary post-procedural fatigue (n = 2). No serious adverse events, nerve injuries, or treatment-related withdrawals were reported. Eight trials did not report adverse events systematically.

**Sensitivity analyses and publication bias**

Leave-one-out analysis showed that no single study materially changed the pooled GMFM estimate (MD range 6.21–7.35, all P < 0.001). Excluding the four trials at highest risk of bias (inadequate randomization and attrition >5%) gave a similar but slightly smaller effect (MD 5.97, 95% CI 3.85 to 8.09; I² = 53%). Switching to a fixed-effect model yielded an MD of 6.12 (95% CI 5.30 to 6.94). Funnel plot asymmetry was apparent for the GMFM outcome, and Egger's test was significant (P = 0.03; Egger et al., 1997). The trim-and-fill method imputed three missing studies and gave an adjusted MD of 5.64 (95% CI 3.58 to 7.70). Egger's tests were not significant for MAS (P = 0.21) or total effective rate (P = 0.18).

**Certainty of evidence**

According to GRADE (Guyatt et al., 2008), the certainty of evidence was low for GMFM and ADL scores, downgraded for risk of bias and inconsistency (and for suspected publication bias in GMFM). It was moderate for MAS, downgraded for risk of bias, and low for total effective rate because of unblinded subjective assessment and imprecision in some trials. The certainty for adverse events was very low owing to inconsistent reporting and few events (Supplemental Digital Content 4).

Discussion and Conclusion

This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of acupotomy, a technique that combines acupuncture with a miniature surgical blade, in children with cerebral palsy (CP). Across the included randomized trials, acupotomy, mostly combined with conventional rehabilitation, was associated with greater improvements in gross motor function (GMFM-88) and lower muscle tone (Modified Ashworth Scale) than rehabilitation alone. Secondary outcomes, including activities of daily living and joint range of motion, tended to favor acupotomy. Adverse events were infrequent and mild, mainly local bleeding, transient soreness, and needle-site infection in a small number of cases. Because the methodological quality of the trials was generally low, these findings should be interpreted as encouraging but preliminary.

The direction of effect is biologically plausible. Spasticity and contracture in CP arise from upper motor neuron lesions and from secondary changes in muscle and connective tissue, including sarcomere elongation, extracellular matrix stiffening, and reduced muscle fiber length (Mathewson & Lieber, 2015; Graham et al., 2016). Acupotomy is intended to release adhesions and tension in fascia, tendons, and muscle insertions through minimally invasive cutting and stretching at selected sites, in the tradition of Zhu Hanzhang's work. Several mechanisms may explain a benefit. Mechanical release may reduce passive stiffness and improve muscle length and joint mobility, enabling more effective motor training. Needling of connective tissue can modulate local fibroblast behavior and nociceptive and proprioceptive afferent input (Langevin et al., 2011). Spinal and supraspinal modulation of stretch-reflex excitability has also been proposed for acupuncture-related techniques. Our data cannot test these mechanisms, but the concurrent changes in tone and motor function are consistent with a pathway in which reduced peripheral resistance facilitates functional gains.

The findings fit within the broader CP literature. Current guidelines favor goal-directed, task-specific training, botulinum toxin for focal spasticity, and selected surgical or neurosurgical interventions (Novak et al., 2020). Botulinum toxin type A reduces tone and improves function in the short term, but effects wane after about three months and repeated injections are costly (Multani et al., 2019). Acupotomy offers a potentially lower-cost alternative or adjunct, particularly in settings with limited access to toxin or orthopedic services. Previous reviews of acupuncture and related Chinese medicine modalities for CP have likewise reported favorable but low-certainty effects, with much of the evidence published in Chinese-language journals and conducted in a single national health care context. Our results are consistent with this pattern and add evidence specific to blade-based needling.

The size of the pooled effects must be viewed against clinically meaningful thresholds. Minimal clinically important differences for the GMFM are modest, roughly 1 to 3 points for the GMFM-66 depending on the child's Gross Motor Function Classification System level (Oeffinger et al., 2008). Whether the statistical differences we observed exceed these thresholds is uncertain, in part because trials seldom reported GMFM-66 or stratified by GMFCS level. Moreover, the typical follow-up was short, so we cannot determine whether benefits persist after treatment ends or whether they translate into participation, quality of life, or caregiver burden, the outcomes most valued by families (Rosenbaum et al., 2007).

Several limitations affect confidence in these conclusions. First, risk of bias was high or unclear in most trials. Randomization methods were often inadequately described, allocation concealment was rarely reported, and blinding of participants, therapists, and outcome assessors was usually impossible or not attempted. Because outcomes such as the MAS and GMFM involve subjective judgment, performance and detection bias likely inflated effects (Sterne et al., 2019). Second, heterogeneity was substantial for some outcomes. Trials differed in age, CP subtype, severity, acupotomy technique (site selection, blade type, frequency, number of sessions), and co-interventions. We used random-effects models and subgroup or sensitivity analyses where data allowed, but residual clinical heterogeneity limits the interpretability of any single pooled estimate. Third, small sample sizes and the possibility of publication bias are concerns. Funnel plot asymmetry and the predominance of positive results from a limited number of regions suggest that small negative studies may be missing (Egger et al., 1997). Fourth, safety reporting was inconsistent. Many trials did not state whether adverse events were monitored, so the apparent safety may reflect under-reporting. Given that acupotomy is invasive and is performed in children who may be unable to report discomfort, as well as the theoretical risks of nerve or vascular injury, infection, and procedural distress, rigorous harm surveillance is essential. Fifth, we restricted inclusion to published trials in specified languages and databases, which may have missed unpublished data. Applying the GRADE framework, we rated the certainty of evidence as low to very low for most outcomes, mainly because of risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision (Guyatt et al., 2008).

These limitations point to clear priorities for future research. Well-designed, adequately powered, multicenter randomized trials are needed, with preregistered protocols, centrally concealed allocation, and blinded outcome assessment. Sham-controlled designs, though challenging for an invasive technique, may be feasible using non-penetrating or superficial needling comparators, and active comparators such as botulinum toxin or standard acupuncture would clarify relative value. Standardized reporting of acupotomy procedures, for example through an extension of STRICTA, would improve reproducibility. Trials should use core outcome sets for CP, stratify by GMFCS level and CP subtype, include participation and quality-of-life measures, and follow children for at least six to twelve months. Objective measures of tone and muscle architecture, such as instrumented spasticity assessment, ultrasound, or shear-wave elastography, could also help test the proposed mechanisms. Economic evaluation and systematic collection of adverse events would further inform decision-making.

For clinical practice, the current evidence does not support replacing established, guideline-recommended interventions with acupotomy. However, it suggests that acupotomy may be considered as an adjunct to conventional rehabilitation for selected children with spasticity-dominant CP, provided it is performed by adequately trained practitioners under sterile conditions with informed parental consent and careful monitoring.

In conclusion, available randomized evidence indicates that acupotomy, mostly combined with rehabilitation, may improve motor function and reduce spasticity in children with CP, with few reported adverse events. The low certainty of evidence, driven by methodological weaknesses and heterogeneity, prevents firm recommendations. Rigorous, transparent trials with standardized interventions and patient-centered outcomes are required before acupotomy can be considered an evidence-based component of CP management.

Introduction

Obesity has become one of the defining public health challenges of the twenty-first century, and its burden is shifting toward low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Sub-Saharan Africa, long associated with undernutrition, is now experiencing a nutrition transition characterized by rising consumption of energy-dense processed foods, declining physical activity, and rapid urbanization (Popkin et al., 2012; Ford et al., 2017). Overweight and obesity among adults in the region have increased steadily over the past three decades, with the greatest burden among women and in urban populations (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, 2017). Kenya mirrors this pattern. National surveys indicate that a substantial proportion of urban adults, particularly women, are overweight or obese, and that obesity-related conditions such as hypertension and type 2 diabetes are increasingly common (Ministry of Health Kenya, 2015; Haregu et al., 2018). Because health systems in these settings are still contending with infectious diseases, the added burden of cardiometabolic disease poses a considerable strain on scarce resources.

Body mass index (BMI) remains the most widely used indicator for classifying obesity in clinical and population settings because it is inexpensive and simple to calculate. However, BMI cannot distinguish between lean mass and fat mass, nor does it capture where fat is stored in the body (Gallagher et al., 1996; Okorodudu et al., 2010). This limitation matters because the health risks of excess adiposity depend heavily on its distribution. Central, or abdominal, fat accumulation, particularly visceral adipose tissue surrounding internal organs, is metabolically active and is closely linked to insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, systemic inflammation, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease (Despres and Lemieux, 2006; Neeland et al., 2019). Measures of central adiposity such as waist circumference (WC) and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) have in many studies predicted cardiometabolic outcomes better than BMI (Yusuf et al., 2005; Coutinho et al., 2013).

The recognition that individuals with a BMI in the normal range may nonetheless carry excess abdominal fat has led to the concept of normal-weight central obesity (NWCO). Sometimes described as "metabolically obese normal weight" or "normal-weight obesity," this phenotype combines a normal BMI with a high waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio (De Lorenzo et al., 2006; Oliveros et al., 2014). Evidence from high-income countries suggests that people with NWCO face cardiometabolic risks comparable to, or even exceeding, those of people with general obesity. In an analysis of the Third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, Sahakyan and colleagues (2015) found that normal-weight individuals with central obesity had the highest long-term mortality, including cardiovascular mortality, of all BMI–fat distribution groups. Similar findings have been reported in European and Asian cohorts (Coutinho et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2019). The apparent paradox is thought to arise from the combination of relatively low lean mass and high visceral fat, which together promote adverse metabolic profiles while escaping detection by BMI-based screening (Oliveros et al., 2014). People with NWCO are thus unlikely to be identified as at risk or offered preventive advice.

Despite its potential importance, NWCO has received little attention in sub-Saharan Africa. Most African studies on obesity have relied on BMI alone, and those that have measured central adiposity have generally reported it separately from general obesity rather than examining their overlap (Tchernof and Despres, 2013; Kamadjeu et al., 2006). Where abdominal obesity has been assessed, prevalence has often been markedly higher than that of BMI-defined obesity, especially among women, suggesting that a considerable number of people with a normal BMI may carry excess central fat (Amoah, 2003; Ziraba et al., 2009). Yet the magnitude of NWCO has seldom been quantified, and it is unclear to what extent it varies by the measure used. WC and WHR are simple anthropometric proxies, while ultrasound-measured visceral and subcutaneous fat thickness provide more direct estimates of fat depots. Because these indicators capture different aspects of body composition, the estimated burden of NWCO is likely to depend on how it is defined, and comparisons across measures are rarely available in African populations.

Urban informal settlements are of particular concern. These settlements house over half of Nairobi's residents and are characterized by poverty, overcrowding, limited access to healthy food and safe spaces for physical activity, and weak health services (Ezeh et al., 2017). Residents are exposed simultaneously to food insecurity in early life and to obesogenic environments in adulthood, a combination that may favor central fat deposition and low lean mass (Wells, 2012; Haregu et al., 2018). Studies in Nairobi's informal settlements have documented a high prevalence of overweight and hypertension (Ziraba et al., 2009; Haregu et al., 2018), but information on fat distribution is limited. Moreover, the sociodemographic factors that predispose individuals to NWCO, such as sex, age, education, occupation, and wealth, are poorly understood in this setting. Identifying them is a prerequisite to targeting prevention efforts toward those at greatest risk.

This study addresses these gaps using data from the Africa Wits-INDEPTH partnership for Genomic Studies (AWI-Gen), a cross-sectional survey of adults aged 40–60 years in two urban informal settlements in Nairobi. The study had two objectives: first, to estimate the prevalence of general obesity and of central obesity assessed by four indicators (waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, visceral fat thickness, and subcutaneous fat thickness); and second, to determine the magnitude of NWCO and its sociodemographic predictors according to each indicator.

This work makes several contributions. It provides, to our knowledge, one of the first estimates of NWCO in an urban poor African population. It also compares four measures of central adiposity, including ultrasound-based fat thickness measurements that are rarely available in population surveys in LMICs, thereby clarifying how definition influences prevalence estimates. Finally, by identifying groups at higher risk, particularly women and older adults, the study provides evidence to inform screening strategies that go beyond BMI and to guide interventions and future longitudinal research on the health consequences of NWCO in sub-Saharan Africa.

Methods

Study design and setting

This analysis used data from the Africa Wits-INDEPTH partnership for Genomic studies (AWI-Gen), a population-based cross-sectional study of the genomic and environmental determinants of cardiometabolic disease in sub-Saharan Africa (Ramsay et al., 2016). The Nairobi arm was conducted between 2014 and 2016 by the African Population and Health Research Center in two informal settlements, Korogocho and Viwandani, which are covered by the Nairobi Urban Health and Demographic Surveillance System (NUHDSS) (Beguy et al., 2015). The two settlements are densely populated and characterised by poor housing, limited sanitation, and high unemployment. They differ somewhat in character: Viwandani is close to an industrial area and has a more mobile, employment-seeking population, whereas Korogocho is older and more residentially stable (Emina et al., 2011).

Study population and sampling

The target population was adults aged 40–60 years who were resident in the two settlements and registered in the NUHDSS. Participants were randomly selected from the surveillance database, stratified by sex and by age group, to give balanced representation across strata, in line with the AWI-Gen core protocol (Ramsay et al., 2016). Eligible individuals were those who had lived in the study area for a defined minimum period and who gave written informed consent. Pregnant women were excluded from anthropometric analysis because pregnancy affects body size and fat distribution. For the present analysis we also excluded participants with missing anthropometric or ultrasound data and, when examining normal-weight central obesity, those who were underweight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m²).

Data collection

Trained field staff collected data in a standardised, interviewer-administered questionnaire followed by a physical examination. The questionnaire covered sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, education, marital status, occupation or employment status, and settlement), lifestyle behaviours (tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and physical activity), and medical history. Educational attainment was grouped as none or primary, secondary, and tertiary. Employment status was grouped as full-time employment, part-time or casual work, self-employed, and unemployed. Physical activity was assessed with the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire (Armstrong & Bull, 2006). Household socioeconomic position was captured using an asset-based wealth index.

Anthropometric measurements

Measurements followed WHO STEPwise procedures (World Health Organization, 2008). Participants wore light clothing and no shoes. Height was measured to the nearest 0.1 cm with a portable stadiometer, and weight to the nearest 0.1 kg with a calibrated digital scale. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. Waist circumference was measured at the midpoint between the lower margin of the last palpable rib and the top of the iliac crest, and hip circumference at the widest part of the buttocks. Both were recorded to the nearest 0.1 cm with a non-stretchable tape. Waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) was computed as waist divided by hip circumference. Measurements were taken twice, and a third was taken if the first two differed by more than a pre-specified tolerance. The mean of the closest readings was used in analysis.

Ultrasound assessment of abdominal fat

Visceral and subcutaneous fat thickness were measured by trained sonographers using a portable B-mode ultrasound device with a convex transducer, following established protocols (Ribeiro-Filho et al., 2001; Stolk et al., 2001). With the participant supine and breathing normally, measurements were taken at the end of a gentle expiration to limit compression of abdominal tissue. Visceral fat thickness was defined as the distance between the internal surface of the rectus abdominis muscle and the anterior wall of the aorta, measured at the umbilical level. Subcutaneous fat thickness was defined as the distance between the skin–fat interface and the linea alba. The average of repeated measurements was used.

Outcome definitions

General obesity was defined as BMI ≥ 30 kg/m², and normal weight as BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m² (World Health Organization, 2000). Central obesity was defined using four indicators. By waist circumference, it was defined using sex-specific cut-offs recommended by the World Health Organization and International Diabetes Federation (Alberti et al., 2009; World Health Organization, 2011). By WHR, it was defined as ≥ 0.90 in men and ≥ 0.85 in women (World Health Organization, 2011). Visceral and subcutaneous fat thickness were dichotomised using sex-specific thresholds adopted from published ultrasound studies (Ribeiro-Filho et al., 2001; Stolk et al., 2001). Normal-weight central obesity was defined as the presence of central obesity by a given indicator in a participant with normal BMI (De Lorenzo et al., 2006; Sahakyan et al., 2015). Because four indicators were used, four separate normal-weight central obesity outcomes were created, and each was analysed independently.

Statistical analysis

Analyses were conducted in Stata (StataCorp, College Station, TX). Continuous variables were summarised as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges, depending on their distribution, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Prevalence of general obesity, central obesity by each indicator, and normal-weight central obesity by each indicator was estimated with 95% confidence intervals and compared by sex and age group using Pearson’s chi-square test (or Fisher’s exact test when expected cell counts were small). Differences in continuous measures between groups were assessed using t-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.

To identify predictors of normal-weight central obesity, we fitted separate multivariable logistic regression models for each indicator (Hosmer et al., 2013). In each model, the outcome was normal-weight central obesity versus normal weight without central obesity, so that the comparison group consisted of participants with normal BMI. Candidate predictors were chosen a priori from the literature and included sex, age group, education, marital status, employment status, settlement, wealth quintile, smoking, alcohol use, and physical activity (Sahakyan et al., 2015; Coutinho et al., 2013). Variables with p < 0.20 in bivariate analysis, together with those considered important on theoretical grounds, were included in the multivariable models. Results are presented as crude and adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors, and model fit using the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test. Statistical significance was set at a two-sided p-value < 0.05. Missing data were minimal, and complete-case analysis was used.

Ethical considerations

The AWI-Gen study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee (Medical) of the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, and by the ethics review committee of the African Medical and Research Foundation (AMREF) in Kenya, with research permission from the relevant national authorities. All participants gave written informed consent after the study procedures, risks, and benefits had been explained in a language they understood. Data were de-identified before analysis, and participants found to have abnormal clinical findings were referred to local health facilities for care.

Results

**Characteristics of the study participants**

The analysis included 1,001 adults aged 40–60 years from the two Nairobi informal settlements (Korogocho and Viwandani). The mean age was 49.7 years (SD 5.6). Women made up 50.4% of participants. Most participants had completed primary education or less (68.3%), and 41.2% were in full-time employment. Another 33.5% were self-employed or in casual work, and the remainder were unemployed or not working. Mean BMI was 25.6 kg/m² (SD 5.7) and was higher in women (27.0) than in men (24.2; p<0.001). Using WHO categories (WHO, 2000), 5.1% of participants were underweight, 47.3% were normal weight, 27.6% were overweight, and 20.0% had general obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²). General obesity was about four times as common in women as in men (32.1% vs 7.8%; p<0.001).

**Prevalence of central obesity by anthropometric and ultrasound measures**

Central obesity was common whichever indicator was used (Table 2). Using waist circumference (>88 cm in women, >102 cm in men), the prevalence was 52.0%. Using waist-to-hip ratio (≥0.85 in women, ≥0.90 in men; WHO, 2008), it was 53.5%. Ultrasound-measured visceral fat thickness classified 32.4% of participants as centrally obese, and subcutaneous fat thickness classified 49.2%. Prevalence was consistently higher in women than in men on every indicator:

- Waist circumference: 71.9% vs 31.8%.
- Waist-to-hip ratio: 69.6% vs 37.3%.
- Visceral fat thickness: 37.8% vs 27.0%.
- Subcutaneous fat thickness: 63.4% vs 34.9%.

All sex differences were statistically significant (p<0.001, except visceral fat thickness, p=0.002). Central obesity prevalence rose with age on most indicators. For waist-to-hip ratio it increased from 47.9% in participants aged 40–44 years to 60.2% in those aged 55–60 years (p for trend=0.004).

**Prevalence of normal-weight central obesity**

Normal-weight central obesity (NWCO) was defined as central obesity in a participant with a BMI of 18.5–24.9 kg/m². Its prevalence differed markedly with the indicator used. It was highest with waist-to-hip ratio (38.1%) and lowest with visceral fat thickness (18.1%). Intermediate values were 28.4% for waist circumference and 25.7% for subcutaneous fat thickness.

Because NWCO is expressed here as a proportion of all participants, these figures should be read alongside the proportion of participants with general obesity (20.0%). Among participants with normal BMI, the share with central obesity was substantial on every indicator. By waist-to-hip ratio, 44.6% of normal-weight participants had central obesity, compared with 21.3% by visceral fat thickness. By waist circumference the figure was 31.7%, and by subcutaneous fat thickness it was 29.4%. Nearly all participants with general obesity were also centrally obese by waist circumference (97.5%) and waist-to-hip ratio (91.0%). Concordance was lower for visceral fat thickness (78.4%), so some participants with a high BMI did not have visceral adiposity.

NWCO was more common in women than in men on all four indicators. By waist-to-hip ratio, 45.2% of women and 31.0% of men had NWCO. By waist circumference the figures were 36.1% and 20.6%. For visceral and subcutaneous fat thickness, the proportions were 20.9% vs 15.3% and 30.2% vs 21.1%, respectively.

**Agreement between indicators**

Agreement between the indicators of NWCO was moderate to low. Cohen's kappa between waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio was 0.46 (95% CI 0.40–0.52). Agreement between waist circumference and visceral fat thickness was 0.31 (0.24–0.38), and between waist-to-hip ratio and visceral fat thickness it was 0.27 (0.20–0.34). Only 9.6% of participants met the NWCO definition on all four indicators simultaneously, and 56.8% met it on at least one.

**Factors associated with normal-weight central obesity**

Table 3 shows the multivariable logistic regression results, which compared participants with NWCO against normal-weight participants without central obesity. Participants with general obesity or abnormal BMI were excluded from these models.

*Waist circumference.* Sex, age, and employment status were independently associated with NWCO. Women had much higher odds than men (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.42; 95% CI 2.28–5.13; p<0.001). Each five-year increase in age was associated with 1.28 times higher odds (95% CI 1.09–1.51; p=0.003). Compared with participants who were not working, those in full-time employment had higher odds of NWCO (aOR 1.86; 95% CI 1.12–3.09; p=0.016). Self-employed or casual workers did not differ significantly from the reference group (aOR 1.31; 95% CI 0.80–2.16). Education level, marital status, smoking, alcohol use, physical activity, and site were not significantly associated with NWCO after adjustment.

*Waist-to-hip ratio.* Older age was the only factor independently associated with NWCO. The odds increased by 1.35 for each five-year increase in age (aOR 1.35; 95% CI 1.14–1.60; p<0.001). Participants aged 55–60 years had 2.07 times higher odds than those aged 40–44 years (95% CI 1.31–3.27).
