The association with female sex was in the same direction but did not reach statistical significance after adjustment (aOR 1.38; 95% CI 0.94–2.04; p=0.10). Employment status was not significantly associated with NWCO by this measure (full-time vs not working: aOR 1.19; 95% CI 0.74–1.91).

*Visceral and subcutaneous fat thickness.* No covariate showed a consistent independent association with NWCO defined by visceral fat thickness. Age had a borderline association (aOR per five years 1.14; 95% CI 0.97–1.34; p=0.11), and sex was not significant (aOR 1.29; 95% CI 0.82–2.03). For subcutaneous fat thickness, female sex was associated with higher odds in unadjusted analysis (crude OR 1.62; 95% CI 1.13–2.32). This association was attenuated after adjustment (aOR 1.47; 95% CI 0.99–2.18; p=0.058).

**Sensitivity analyses**

When NWCO was restricted to participants with BMI of 20.0–24.9 kg/m², thereby excluding those with low-normal BMI, prevalence estimates changed little (waist circumference 27.2%, waist-to-hip ratio 36.5%, visceral fat thickness 17.4%, subcutaneous fat thickness 24.8%). The direction and significance of the associations with age, sex, and full-time employment were also unchanged. Adjusting for site (Korogocho vs Viwandani) did not alter the estimates materially.

Discussion and Conclusion

This study set out to describe the magnitude and predictors of normal-weight central obesity (NWCO) among middle-aged adults living in two urban informal settlements in Nairobi. Although only one in five participants was obese by body mass index (BMI), more than half had central obesity by waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio, and between 18% and 38% of the sample had NWCO, depending on the indicator used. These findings suggest that BMI-based screening substantially underestimates the burden of adiposity-related metabolic risk in this population, and that a considerable share of adults who would be classified as having no weight-related problem carry a potentially harmful fat distribution.

The prevalence of NWCO was highest with waist-to-hip ratio and lowest with visceral fat thickness. This gradient is consistent with the fact that the indicators capture different aspects of body composition. Waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio reflect both subcutaneous and visceral abdominal fat, and waist-to-hip ratio is additionally influenced by gluteofemoral fat mass and muscle, so that low hip circumference or reduced lean mass can raise the ratio independently of visceral adiposity (Snijder et al., 2004). Ultrasound-measured visceral fat thickness is more specific to the intra-abdominal depot but depends on operator technique, cut-off selection, and respiratory phase. The divergence between measures echoes earlier work showing poor to moderate agreement between anthropometric and imaging-based definitions of central obesity, particularly in sub-Saharan African populations for which cut-offs have rarely been validated (Gradidge et al., 2014; Okosun et al., 2000). The estimates should therefore be viewed as a range rather than a single figure, and the absence of a universally accepted definition of NWCO remains a barrier to cross-study comparison.

Even so, the prevalence we observed is comparable to or higher than that reported elsewhere. Studies from the United States, Europe, and Asia have found NWCO in roughly 10–30% of normal-weight adults, and it has been linked with higher cardiometabolic risk and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality than general obesity or normal fat distribution (Sahakyan et al., 2015; Coutinho et al., 2013). Our data cannot speak to mortality, but the burden is notable in a setting where residents face food insecurity, limited access to health care, and a growing exposure to energy-dense, inexpensive foods and sedentary livelihoods. The nutrition transition in African cities has been characterized by the coexistence of undernutrition in early life and excess adiposity in adulthood, and early-life undernutrition may predispose to preferential central fat deposition and insulin resistance at relatively low BMI (Prentice & Moore, 2005; Popkin et al., 2012). This developmental explanation is plausible for people now aged 40–60 who grew up in conditions of scarcity, though our cross-sectional design did not allow us to test it.

Being female, being older, and being in full-time employment were associated with NWCO defined by waist circumference, while only older age was associated with NWCO defined by waist-to-hip ratio. The female excess is consistent with data from Kenya and across sub-Saharan Africa showing that women have higher rates of obesity and abdominal adiposity than men (Ng et al., 2014; Ziraba et al., 2009). Contributing factors may include parity, post-menopausal shifts in fat distribution toward the abdomen, lower levels of occupational and leisure-time physical activity, cultural preferences for larger body size, and gendered constraints on food choice and time use. Importantly, sex-specific cut-offs for waist circumference are lower for women, which mechanically increases the proportion classified as centrally obese at a given BMI; that the sex difference did not persist for waist-to-hip ratio suggests that the definition used partly shapes the observed association. Older age was the most consistent predictor, in line with age-related loss of lean mass and redistribution of fat from subcutaneous to visceral and ectopic depots (Kuk et al., 2009). Such sarcopenic-type changes may keep BMI stable while waist circumference rises.

The association with full-time employment is less intuitive, and we interpret it cautiously. Employment may reflect greater disposable income and purchasing of processed foods, meals consumed away from home, or more sedentary work such as security or office-based jobs, whereas informal and casual labor in these settlements often involves substantial walking and manual activity. Alternatively, the association could reflect residual confounding by age, sex, or occupation type, which we could not disentangle. The lack of association with education, income proxies, or lifestyle variables for other definitions may reflect the relative socioeconomic homogeneity of the settlements, limited statistical power, or measurement error in self-reported behaviors.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and temporal ordering; we cannot determine whether the identified factors precede NWCO. Second, the sample was restricted to adults aged 40–60 years from two informal settlements, so the results may not generalize to younger or older adults, rural populations, or other urban settings. Third, the cut-offs for waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, and ultrasound fat thickness were largely derived from non-African populations, and their appropriateness for East African adults is uncertain; misclassification in either direction is possible. Fourth, we lacked direct measures of body composition such as DXA or CT, and a normal BMI can conceal low muscle mass, so some participants with NWCO may in fact have sarcopenic obesity. Fifth, we did not examine cardiometabolic outcomes such as blood pressure, glucose, or lipids within this analysis, and therefore cannot confirm that NWCO in this population carries the elevated risk observed elsewhere. Finally, unmeasured determinants including diet quality, physical activity, parity, HIV status and antiretroviral therapy, and early-life exposures may have influenced fat distribution.

These limitations notwithstanding, the study has strengths: a random sample, standardized measurement protocols, and the simultaneous use of four central adiposity indicators, which allows transparent comparison of definitions in a population rarely represented in the literature.

The findings have practical implications. Clinicians and community health workers in low-resource urban settings relying on BMI alone will miss many people at risk; inexpensive waist circumference measurement should be incorporated into routine screening for non-communicable diseases, with particular attention to women and older adults. Health promotion that emphasizes diet and physical activity should not be limited to those who appear overweight. Research priorities include validating African-specific thresholds, linking NWCO to glycemic, lipid, and blood pressure outcomes, and clarifying the roles of early-life nutrition, body composition, and work-related activity.

In conclusion, NWCO is common among adults in these Nairobi informal settlements, particularly among women and older people. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish whether NWCO predicts cardiometabolic disease and mortality in such settings, as has been shown elsewhere, and to inform targeted prevention.

Background

Developmental biology is generating data at a rate that outpaces the ability of individual laboratories to organize and interpret them. High-throughput in situ hybridization screens, enhancer trap collections, transcriptome profiling, and large-scale imaging projects have produced thousands of images and annotations describing where and when genes are active during embryogenesis (Visel et al., 2004; Tomancak et al., 2002; Diez-Roux et al., 2011). These data are valuable mainly to the extent that others can find, compare, and reuse them. For this reason, the community has built a large number of online atlases and databases, many of them dedicated to a single model organism such as mouse, zebrafish, Xenopus, Drosophila, or Caenorhabditis elegans. Examples include the Edinburgh Mouse Atlas Project and its Gene Expression Database (Baldock et al., 2003; Richardson et al., 2014), the Zebrafish Information Network (Sprague et al., 2006), Xenbase (Bowes et al., 2008), BDGP (Tomancak et al., 2002), and WormBase (Harris et al., 2010). Together, these resources form the infrastructure through which much of the knowledge of embryonic development is shared.

Anatomy is the organizing framework for nearly all of this information. Gene expression is typically reported as occurring in a structure at a particular stage, and phenotypes are described as abnormalities of particular tissues or organs. Anatomy is therefore the common reference that lets a researcher ask which genes are expressed in the developing heart, or compare an expression pattern in a mouse with the corresponding one in a zebrafish. How anatomy is represented in a resource determines which questions the resource can answer and how easily its content can be connected with that of other resources.

Two broad forms of anatomical representation can be distinguished. Semantic representation describes anatomical entities and the relationships among them, such as part-of and is-a relations, and is now usually implemented as an ontology or controlled vocabulary (Bard, 2005; Smith et al., 2007). Anatomy ontologies have been developed for most major model organisms, and efforts such as the Open Biomedical Ontologies Foundry and cross-species ontologies such as Uberon have sought to align them (Smith et al., 2007; Mungall et al., 2012). Spatial representation, in contrast, describes the geometry and location of structures. It can range from schematic drawings and series of histological sections to three-dimensional reconstructions and standardized coordinate frameworks to which individual specimens are mapped (Baldock et al., 2003; Armit et al., 2017). The two forms are complementary. Ontologies support text-based queries, logical inference, and links between databases, whereas spatial models support visual comparison, spatial queries, and the integration of data from different specimens and experiments.

Despite their importance, the ways in which semantic and spatial representations are actually used in online resources have received little systematic comparison. Individual resources are described in their own publications, and ontology development has been reviewed extensively, but there has been little attention to how these representations are exposed to users through the interface. This gap matters for several reasons. First, the choice of representation constrains function. A resource that annotates expression with ontology terms can use the hierarchy to return results for a structure and all of its parts, while one that uses free text cannot do so reliably. Similarly, a resource that maps expression data to a common spatial model can support queries by location, while one that stores only images cannot. Second, differences in representation among resources impede integration, and it is not always clear which design choices would most improve interoperability. Third, even a well-structured resource is of limited use if its interface obscures the structure. Studies of bioinformatics software have repeatedly noted that poor usability is a barrier to the adoption of biological databases, and that many resources are designed around the structure of the data rather than the tasks of users (Javahery et al., 2004; Bolchini et al., 2009). Developers building a new atlas, or revising an old one, currently have few resources to guide them on how to present anatomy effectively.

Software engineering offers a useful way to address this problem in the form of design patterns. A pattern describes a recurring problem in a given context together with a general solution that has proven effective, abstracted from particular implementations (Alexander et al., 1977; Gamma et al., 1995). Patterns have been widely adopted in user interface design, where they capture solutions for navigation, search, and the display of information (Tidwell, 2005). They are particularly suited to a domain like online anatomical resources, in which many independent groups have solved similar problems in different ways, and in which a shared vocabulary for describing solutions could ease communication between biologists and software developers.

In this paper I address these gaps in two parts. The first part is a survey of online atlases and gene expression resources for model organisms, with emphasis on how they represent anatomy semantically and spatially. The survey includes 14 anatomical atlases and 21 gene expression resources. For each, I consider the kind of ontology or vocabulary used, whether and how annotations draw on it, and the approach to spatial representation, and I examine how these choices affect the search functions available and the links the resource can make to related information. The second part is a collection of patterns for interface design derived from the surveyed resources. These patterns address four areas: displaying graphics, integrating semantic and spatial representations, organizing information, and querying databases to find genes expressed in anatomical structures.

This work makes three contributions. First, it provides an overview of current practice in the representation of anatomy across a broad set of resources, identifying common approaches and differences. Second, it shows concretely how standardized semantic and spatial representations enable enhanced functionality in interfaces, strengthening the argument for community adoption of standards. Third, it offers a practical, reusable collection of interface patterns that can assist biologists and software developers in planning new atlases and databases or improving existing ones, and that may serve as a basis for further discussion and refinement of design practice in this field.

Methods

Scope and Selection of Resources

The survey covered online atlases and gene expression databases that describe embryonic development in model organisms. Resources were identified through three routes: (1) the author's familiarity with the field, (2) annual database issues of Nucleic Acids Research and the Model Organism Databases curated by the Generic Model Organism Database (GMOD) project, and (3) citation tracing and hyperlinks from resource websites, publications, and community pages such as the Open Biomedical Ontologies (OBO) Foundry and the Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI) site. Searches of PubMed and the web used combinations of the terms "atlas," "anatomy," "gene expression," "database," "embryo," "ontology," and the names of common model organisms (mouse, zebrafish, chicken, Xenopus, Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, and others).

Resources were included if they met three criteria: (1) they were publicly accessible through a web interface at the time of review, (2) they described anatomy or gene expression in embryonic or developmental stages of a model organism, and (3) they offered an interface that allowed users to browse, search, or visualize anatomical or expression data. Resources were excluded if they were available only as downloadable files or software without a web interface, if they contained only adult anatomy with no developmental component, or if they were inaccessible or no longer maintained. Where a resource was part of a larger model organism database, only the portions relevant to anatomy or expression were assessed.

Resources were divided into two categories. Anatomical atlases were defined as resources whose primary purpose is to present the structure of the organism, usually through images, three-dimensional reconstructions, or ontology-based descriptions of anatomical parts. Gene expression resources were defined as databases whose primary purpose is to store and present the location and timing of gene expression, whether from in situ hybridization, immunohistochemistry, reporter constructs, microarrays, or literature curation. Some resources fit both categories and were assigned according to their principal function. The review yielded 14 atlases and 21 gene expression resources.

Data Collection

Each resource was examined directly through its public website between the initial identification phase and the final review. For every resource I recorded general descriptors, including the organism, the developmental stages covered, the type of data (images, text annotations, three-dimensional models, or curated literature data), and the data sources. I then explored the interface systematically by performing the primary tasks each site supported: browsing by anatomical structure, stage, or gene; running text and structured searches; viewing and manipulating images or models; and following links to related records. Documentation, help pages, tutorials, and associated publications were consulted to confirm features that were not apparent from the interface. Screenshots were taken to document interface elements and to support later comparison.

Characterization of Semantic Representation

Semantic representation was defined as the use of terms and relationships to describe anatomy in a computable form. For each resource I determined whether it used a controlled vocabulary or ontology to name anatomical structures, and if so, whether the ontology was developed in-house or shared with other resources. I recorded the structure of each ontology, noting whether it was a simple list, a hierarchy, or a directed acyclic graph, and which relationship types it used, in particular "is_a" (class–subclass) and "part_of" (partonomy) relationships. I also noted whether terms were linked to developmental stages, as in stage-specific ontologies, or were defined independently of stage with associated temporal ranges. Finally, I examined how the semantic representation was used in the interface, for example to browse a hierarchy of structures, to expand queries to include substructures, to autocomplete search terms, or to connect records across databases through shared identifiers. Particular attention was given to the use of community standards such as the OBO anatomy ontologies and the Gene Ontology.

Characterization of Spatial Representation

Spatial representation was defined as the depiction of the location and shape of anatomical structures in a coordinate or image-based form. Resources were classified according to how they represented space. Categories included: (1) collections of two-dimensional images or histological sections with no common coordinate framework; (2) schematic drawings or diagrams of anatomy or expression patterns; (3) series of images or sections with annotated structures; (4) three-dimensional reconstructions or volumetric models; and (5) standardized reference models to which data from different specimens are mapped. For each resource I noted whether anatomical structures were delineated spatially (for example, by color-coded domains in sections or models), whether such delineations were linked to ontology terms, and whether expression data could be mapped onto a common reference to allow comparison or spatial querying. I also recorded the image formats and the viewing technologies used, such as static images, zoomable image viewers, Java applets, Flash, or web-based three-dimensional viewers.

Identification of Interface Patterns

The collection of design patterns was derived from the survey through an iterative, qualitative process modeled on the pattern language approach used in architecture and software engineering and adapted to web interface design. After documenting the resources, I reviewed the screenshots and notes to identify recurring solutions to common design problems, such as how to display large images, how to link a list of anatomical terms to a spatial depiction, how to organize large amounts of information on a page, and how to let users find genes expressed in a given structure. A solution was considered a candidate pattern if it appeared in more than one resource or if it represented a particularly clear approach to a problem likely to recur in new resources.

Each pattern was described using a consistent format: a name, the problem it addresses, the context in which it applies, the solution, and examples drawn from the surveyed resources. Where useful, I also noted advantages, limitations, and relationships to other patterns. Patterns were grouped into four categories reflecting the main themes of the survey: displaying graphics, integrating semantic and spatial representations, organizing information, and querying databases to find genes expressed in anatomical structures. Patterns were refined by returning to the resources to confirm that the description accurately captured the examples and by merging or splitting patterns when they overlapped or were too general. Principles of usability, including consistency, visibility of system status, user control, and efficient navigation, informed the descriptions of benefits and trade-offs, though no formal usability testing was performed.

Limitations of the Approach

The survey is a descriptive review rather than a systematic or exhaustive census, and the set of resources reflects those available and identifiable at the time of review. Because web resources change frequently, descriptions reflect the state of each site when it was examined. No statistical analysis was performed; findings are presented as qualitative summaries and counts of resources exhibiting particular features. The patterns are derived from the author's judgment and are intended as design guidance rather than validated prescriptions.

Results

**Scope of the survey**

The survey covered 14 anatomical atlases and 21 gene expression resources for model organisms. The atlases included the eMouseAtlas/EMAP anatomy (Armit et al., 2017; Baldock et al., 2003), the Allen Mouse and Developing Mouse Brain Atlases (Lein et al., 2007), the Kaufman atlas of mouse development, the ZFIN zebrafish anatomy resources (Sprague et al., 2008), Xenbase (Bowes et al., 2008), WormAtlas, the Virtual Fly Brain, and the Digital Fish Library. The gene expression resources included GXD (Smith et al., 2007), EMAGE (Richardson et al., 2010), GenePaint (Visel et al., 2004), EURExpress (Diez-Roux et al., 2011), BGEM, GUDMAP, GEISHA (Bell et al., 2004), BDGP (Tomancak et al., 2002), FlyExpress, FlyTED, ANISEED, and WormBase. Organisms covered were mouse (16 resources), zebrafish (4), *Drosophila* (5), *Xenopus* (3), chick (2), *C. elegans* (2), and ascidian (1), with some resources spanning more than one species. Each resource was assessed for semantic representation (controlled vocabularies and ontologies) and spatial representation (images, coordinate systems, and models).

**Semantic representation of anatomy**

Twelve of the 14 atlases (86%) organized anatomical structures with a controlled vocabulary, and 10 of these used a hierarchy with explicit relationships. Nine atlases used *part_of* relationships alone to build the hierarchy, and four combined *part_of* with *is_a*. The remaining two atlases labelled structures in images without a formal vocabulary. Developmental stage was integral to the vocabulary in 11 atlases. Eight used stage-specific ontologies in which each structure exists only within a defined stage, as in the EMAP mouse ontology with its 26 Theiler stages (Hayamizu et al., 2005), while three used a single ontology with stage ranges attached to terms. Persistent identifiers were available for terms in 9 atlases, and 6 offered ontology files for download in OBO or OWL format.

Among the 21 gene expression resources, 18 (86%) annotated expression using anatomical terms. Sixteen drew these terms from a published ontology, and the other two used internal vocabularies. The most common sources were the mouse developmental anatomy ontology (7 resources), the Zebrafish Anatomical Ontology (3), the *Drosophila* anatomy ontology (4), the *Xenopus* anatomy ontology (3), and the WormBase anatomy ontology (2). Fourteen resources allowed users to search by anatomical term. In 9 of these, searches were expanded with the ontology hierarchy, so that a query for a parent structure also returned genes annotated to its *part_of* descendants. For example, a query for "forebrain" would retrieve annotations to the telencephalon. The other 5 returned only exact matches, and users had to select each substructure by hand. Seven resources also linked anatomical terms back to a corresponding atlas page, which let users move from a gene record to the structure's definition and its position in the hierarchy. Ten resources provided cross-links to other databases, most often to gene records (all 10) and to phenotype or disease information (4).

**Spatial representation of anatomy**

Methods of spatial representation fell into four categories: unregistered 2D images, 2D sections, reconstructed 3D models, and standardized coordinate frameworks. Twelve atlases presented 2D images, either annotated histological sections or photographs. Six presented 3D data, which were volume-rendered or surface-based reconstructions from optical projection tomography, MRI, confocal microscopy, or serial sections. Five atlases provided a standard coordinate system. Four of these allowed spatial queries or mapping of new data to the atlas.

Spatial representation varied more widely among the gene expression resources. Nine resources displayed only the original in situ images, with no spatial reference to a standard. Six mapped expression patterns to anatomical sections using standard atlas plates, for example the Allen Reference Atlas, and 6 mapped data into a 3D reference model. Of the latter, EMAGE and GUDMAP used the EMAP models, and FlyExpress used standardized 2D embryo images for pattern comparison. In 5 resources, spatial mapping supported queries on expression pattern, such as "find genes with similar expression to this gene" or "find genes expressed in a user-defined region". Image-based similarity search was implemented in 3 resources. Only 2 resources combined text-based anatomical annotation with spatial queries on the same interface.

Image data were typically large. Thirteen of the 21 expression resources provided an image zoom or pan viewer, and 7 used tiled-image or Flash-based viewers (as available at the time of review). Downloadable images or data were available in 15 resources, but only 4 provided downloads in a form that could be reused directly for spatial comparison, such as registered image stacks or coordinate-referenced annotations.

**Collection of interface patterns**

From these resources I extracted 20 interface patterns, which are grouped into four categories. Each pattern is described by its name, the problem it addresses, the solution, and examples from the survey.

*Displaying graphics* (6 patterns). These include thumbnail galleries for browsing large image sets (found in 15 of the 35 resources), zoomable viewers for high-resolution images (13 expression resources and 5 atlases), slice-through viewers for 3D data (6), image comparison side by side (7), stage selectors (14), and rotatable or interactive 3D models (4).

*Integrating semantic and spatial representations* (5 patterns). These include labelled images with hoverable regions linked to ontology terms (8 resources), a clickable image map that selects anatomical structures (6), a hierarchy tree synchronized with the image (5), color-coded overlays showing annotated structures (7), and a spatial annotation plot that shows 3D expression domains in a reference model (4).

*Organizing information* (4 patterns). These are stage-based navigation (14), tabbed pages that separate different data types (11), summary pages that link to detail pages (17), and ontology browsers (10).

*Querying databases to find genes expressed in anatomical structures* (5 patterns). These include a text box with auto-complete over ontology terms (7), browsing a hierarchical tree to select structures (9), hierarchy-based query expansion (9), graphical query by selecting structures in an image or model (5), and a spatial query, where users draw or select a region and receive genes with matching expression (3).

Most resources used between 3 and 8 patterns, and no single resource implemented all 20. The combined semantic and spatial patterns were the least common: only 6 of the 35 resources (17%) implemented a graphical query, and these were all resources that used a standard ontology and a standard spatial framework.

Discussion and Conclusions

This survey shows that how anatomy is represented, semantically and spatially, largely determines what an interface can do. Resources that annotate expression data to a structured anatomical ontology can offer queries that follow part-of and is-a relationships. A user who searches for genes expressed in the "forebrain" can retrieve annotations made to its substructures, as in the Gene Expression Database and the Edinburgh Mouse Atlas resources built on the EMAP ontology (Baldock et al. 2003; Hayamizu et al. 2005). Resources that rely on free-text annotation, or on vocabularies without hierarchy, usually have to fall back on keyword matching. This limits recall and makes it harder to link related information across datasets. Spatial representations extend the same benefit. When data are mapped to a common reference model, as in EMAGE and the Allen Brain Atlas, users can query by location, compare patterns across experiments, and see results in context (Lein et al. 2007; Richardson et al. 2014). Standardization is therefore not just a back-end concern. It determines which interface patterns are feasible.

The patterns I describe should be read in this light. Many solve the same problems in different resources: how to show large images without overwhelming the user, how to connect a name in a hierarchy to a region in an image, and how to let people find genes by anatomical location. Patterns for displaying graphics, such as zoomable viewers, thumbnails with detail on demand, and synchronized views of sections and three-dimensional models, correspond closely to the "overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand" approach long advocated in information visualization (Shneiderman 1996). Patterns for integrating semantic and spatial representations, such as clicking a structure in an image to retrieve its term or selecting a term in a tree to highlight its extent, depend directly on a shared identifier linking a label to a spatial domain. Where an atlas offered such a link, the interface could support both browsing and querying. Where it did not, the two modes tended to be separate and users had to translate between them by hand. Presenting these solutions as patterns follows the tradition of Alexander and of software design (Alexander et al. 1977; Gamma et al. 1995; Tidwell 2005). A pattern describes a recurring problem, a proven solution, and the context in which it applies, and so is more useful to a developer than a list of features.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The survey is restricted to 14 atlases and 21 gene expression resources for model organisms, selected for their focus on embryonic or developmental anatomy and their public availability. It is not exhaustive, and resources that were not found or were restricted to particular communities may use approaches I did not capture. Online resources also change quickly. Interfaces are redesigned, ontologies are revised, and new data types are added, so some details recorded here will become outdated. The evaluation is also qualitative. I assessed the resources through inspection of their functions rather than formal usability testing, and the patterns reflect my judgment of what works well. I did not measure task completion, error rates, or satisfaction among biologists with different levels of expertise. Such studies would show which patterns best support particular tasks and could reveal problems that expert inspection misses. Finally, the focus on representation of anatomy means that other important aspects of interface design, such as accessibility, performance under heavy load, and the presentation of quantitative results, are treated only briefly.

Despite these limits, the survey points to several implications for developers. First, ontology choice should be made early and deliberately. Adopting or mapping to community ontologies, such as those coordinated through the OBO Foundry and cross-species efforts like Uberon, makes it easier to exchange data and to link a resource to others (Smith et al. 2007; Mungall et al. 2012). Anatomy ontologies specific to a species, such as the Drosophila and zebrafish anatomy ontologies, can be related through shared upper-level classes or homology statements, enabling cross-species queries that few current interfaces provide. Second, spatial standardization deserves the same attention. A resource that defines a reference model, with documented methods for mapping new data onto it, can support spatial queries and comparison, whereas one that stores only annotated images cannot. Even when full three-dimensional mapping is impractical, stage-specific reference images with defined landmarks and links from labeled regions to ontology terms provide a useful intermediate step. Third, using web services and persistent identifiers allows resources to expose their anatomy and expression data to other applications. This reduces the need for each resource to reimplement every feature, and allows specialized tools to be built on shared content.

The patterns also suggest directions for future work. Few of the resources surveyed used the ontology to guide users interactively, for instance by suggesting related terms, showing the number of annotations at each node of a hierarchy, or warning users that a query will include substructures. These are well-understood techniques in other domains and could make anatomical queries more transparent. Interfaces could also say more about the origin and certainty of annotations. A user needs to know whether an expression call was made by an expert, derived by automated image analysis, or inferred from a parent structure. Making these distinctions visible would help users interpret results, especially as more annotation is automated. Finally, as imaging technologies produce larger and more complex datasets, including time series, single-cell data, and volumetric reconstructions, the patterns for graphics display and spatial querying will need to be extended and tested at scale.

In conclusion, the survey and the collection of patterns presented here are intended as practical aids for biologists and software developers planning new atlases and databases or improving existing ones. They show that interface functionality is closely tied to underlying representations of anatomy, and that standardizing semantic and spatial representations enables richer searching, browsing, and integration of information. Wider adoption of shared ontologies and reference models, combined with deliberate and well-documented interface design, should make online resources more useful for the community and more interoperable with one another.

Introduction

The idea that the loss of one sense is offset by the enhancement of others is deeply rooted in popular culture and has a long history in philosophy and early psychology. Blind individuals are often assumed to have a "sharper" sense of smell, touch, or hearing that helps them navigate a world designed primarily for the sighted. In the olfactory domain, such beliefs are reinforced by anecdotal reports from blind people themselves, who often say they rely on smell to recognize people, locate places, and evaluate food and objects (Wakefield, Homewood, & Taylor, 2004). Olfaction is an especially interesting case because it is a chemical sense with a comparatively weak link to the visual system in everyday behavior, yet it is closely tied to cognition, emotion, and memory (Herz & Engen, 1996). If sensory loss triggers compensatory adaptations, olfaction is a plausible candidate.

The theoretical basis for such expectations lies in the neuroplasticity literature. In congenitally and early blind individuals, the occipital cortex is not simply silent; it is recruited for a range of non-visual functions, including Braille reading, auditory localization, speech comprehension, and verbal memory (Sadato et al., 1996; Röder et al., 2002; Amedi et al., 2003; Bedny, 2017). Behavioral studies often report superior performance in blind people on pitch discrimination, sound localization, and tactile acuity, although the findings are not uniform and depend on task demands and the age at which vision was lost (Collignon, Voss, Lassonde, & Lepore, 2009; Wan, Wood, Reutens, & Wilson, 2010). Neuroimaging has also suggested that olfactory stimulation may engage regions beyond the classical olfactory network in blind individuals. Kupers and colleagues (2011), for example, reported activation of occipital areas during odor processing, and Araneda et al. (2016) reported structural and functional differences in olfactory-related regions in early blind participants. Such results indicate that cross-modal reorganization could, in principle, have consequences for olfactory perception.

The behavioral evidence, however, is far less consistent. Olfactory function is generally considered to comprise several partly separable components (Hummel, Sekinger, Wolf, Pauli, & Kobal, 1997). Lower-level, sensory-driven abilities include the detection threshold, defined as the lowest concentration at which an odorant can be perceived, and odor discrimination, which requires distinguishing between different odorants. Higher-order abilities involve cognitive and linguistic processes and include cued odor identification, in which participants choose a label from a set of alternatives, and free odor identification, in which participants name an odor without help. Performance on the latter tasks depends heavily on semantic memory, verbal ability, and attention, in addition to sensory sensitivity (Cain, 1979; Larsson, 1997). A plausible possibility is that blindness could selectively affect some of these components but not others, for example by improving higher-order processing through increased attention to olfactory cues, without altering peripheral sensitivity.

Empirical findings do not clearly support either a general or a selective enhancement. Several studies have found lower olfactory thresholds in blind than in sighted participants (Cuevas, Plaza, Rombaux, De Volder, & Renier, 2009; Beaulieu-Lefebvre, Schneider, Kupers, & Ptito, 2011), whereas others have found no difference (Smith, Doty, Burlingame, & McKeown, 1993; Rosenbluth, Grossman, & Kaitz, 2000) or even poorer performance in blind individuals (Wakefield et al., 2004). Studies of odor discrimination show a similar pattern: some report an advantage for blind participants (Cuevas et al., 2009), and others report equivalent performance (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska, Sorokowski, & Karwowski, 2013). The picture for identification is also mixed. Some investigations have shown superior free or cued identification in blind participants (Murphy & Cain, 1986; Rosenbluth et al., 2000; Cuevas et al., 2009), while others have found no group differences (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska et al., 2013). Heterogeneity in methods may partly explain these discrepancies. Studies differ in the psychophysical procedure used (e.g., staircase methods vs. forced-choice batteries), the odorants tested, the criteria for sample selection, and the way blindness is characterized. Moreover, many studies have small samples, which limits statistical power and increases the probability that observed effects, whether positive or null, are unreliable (Button et al., 2013).

Participant characteristics are a further source of uncertainty. Olfactory function declines with age and differs between women and men, with women often outperforming men on several olfactory measures (Doty & Cameron, 2009; Sorokowska et al., 2017). If the age or sex composition of blind and sighted samples differs, or if these factors moderate the effects of sensory deprivation, estimates of group differences could be distorted. Most important, the timing of vision loss may be critical. Plasticity is thought to be greatest during sensitive periods of development, so early or congenitally blind individuals might show larger compensatory effects than those who lose their sight later in life (Voss, Lepore, Gougoux, & Zatorre, 2010; Collignon et al., 2009). Yet studies of olfaction have often combined early and late blind participants, or have not reported onset in sufficient detail, making it difficult to determine whether the timing of blindness matters.

Narrative reviews have summarized parts of this literature (Sorokowska, 2016; Kupers & Ptito, 2014), and they generally conclude that evidence of superior olfaction in blindness is equivocal. Narrative approaches, however, are vulnerable to selective citation and cannot quantify the magnitude or consistency of effects, nor assess whether the published record is distorted by selective reporting. Publication bias is a particular concern in this field: an intriguing and intuitively appealing finding of superior performance in blind people may be more likely to be published than a null result, which would inflate the apparent evidence for compensation (Rothstein, Sutton, & Borenstein, 2005). Meta-analytic methods allow the combination of effect sizes across studies, the examination of heterogeneity, the testing of moderators, and the application of procedures that detect and adjust for small-study effects (Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009; Duval & Tweedie, 2000).

To our knowledge, no previous study has quantitatively synthesized the evidence on olfactory abilities in blind individuals across the full range of olfactory functions. The present work therefore provides a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing blind and sighted individuals on four outcomes: odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification. Our primary question was whether blindness is associated with better olfactory performance, and whether any such effect differs between sensory-driven tasks (threshold, discrimination) and higher-order tasks (identification). Because publication bias could influence these estimates, we explicitly assessed and corrected for it. In addition, we conducted exploratory moderator analyses to test whether participants' age, the proportion of women in the samples, and the onset of blindness (early vs. late) explain variability in effect sizes across studies.

This work contributes in three ways. First, it offers the first comprehensive quantitative estimate of olfactory performance in blindness, replacing impressionistic summaries with effect sizes and confidence intervals. Second, it examines whether the published literature supports the notion of compensatory plasticity in olfaction once bias is taken into account. Third, it identifies methodological gaps, such as small samples and inconsistent reporting, that can guide the design of future research on sensory compensation.

Methods

Protocol and reporting standards

The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher, Liberati, Tetzlaff, & Altman, 2009) and followed recommendations for meta-analysis in the behavioral sciences (Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009; Cooper, Hedges, & Valentine, 2009). The inclusion criteria, outcomes, and the analytic strategy for the primary analyses were specified before data extraction. The analyses of moderators were exploratory.

Literature search

Relevant articles were identified through a computerized search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and PsycINFO, supplemented by Google Scholar. The search combined terms related to blindness (blind*, visual impairment, visual deprivation, visually impaired, anophthalmi*, early blind, late blind, congenital blind) with terms related to olfaction (olfact*, smell, odor, odour, chemosens*, threshold, discrimination, identification). No restrictions on publication year were imposed, and the search covered records from database inception until the date of the final search. We also screened the reference lists of all eligible articles and of relevant narrative reviews, and we searched for conference abstracts and unpublished dissertations to reduce the risk of missing unpublished data. When essential statistics were missing, corresponding authors were contacted by e-mail.

Eligibility criteria

Studies were included if they (a) compared a group of blind participants with a group of sighted controls, (b) assessed at least one of four olfactory outcomes (odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, or free odor identification), (c) used human participants, and (d) reported data sufficient to calculate an effect size (means and standard deviations, t or F statistics, exact p values with sample sizes, or equivalent). Blindness was defined as congenital or acquired total blindness or severe visual impairment, as described by the original authors. Studies were excluded if they lacked a sighted control group, if participants had additional conditions known to affect olfaction (e.g., neurodegenerative disease, Kallmann syndrome, head trauma, or chronic rhinosinusitis), if the data were reported only for subjective ratings of odor properties (e.g., intensity, pleasantness) or for olfactory-related tasks that did not map onto the four outcomes, or if the data duplicated those of another included study. Where a sample was reported in more than one article, only the most complete report was retained. Studies in languages other than English were considered if they could be translated.

Outcome definitions

Odor threshold tasks estimated the lowest concentration at which an odorant (typically n-butanol or phenylethyl alcohol) could be detected, usually through a staircase, forced-choice procedure (e.g., Sniffin' Sticks). Discrimination tasks required participants to identify the odd item among three odorants presented in a triangle test. Cued identification required selection of the correct label from a list of alternatives (typically four), whereas free identification required participants to name the odor without any response options. Because threshold is generally considered a sensory-driven function and identification a higher-order function dependent on semantic and mnemonic processes (Hummel, Sekinger, Wolf, Pauli, & Kobal, 1997), the four outcomes were analyzed separately. Where studies reported more than one measure within an outcome (e.g., several odorants or subtests), we averaged them to obtain one effect size per study and comparison. When separate early-blind and late-blind groups were compared with the same sighted group, the shared control group was handled as described below.

Study selection and data extraction

Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by consulting a third author. Data were extracted independently by two coders using a standardized form, which recorded: authors and year, country, sample size per group, mean age, proportion of women, onset of blindness (early/congenital vs. late), olfactory test used, and the statistics necessary to compute effect sizes. Inter-coder agreement was high (Cohen's κ > .90 for categorical variables) and discrepancies were resolved through consensus. Studies were classified as early blind when blindness was congenital or began in early childhood (typically before the age of 5 years, or as defined by the authors), and as late blind otherwise.

Effect size computation

The effect size was the standardized mean difference, Hedges' g, with positive values indicating better performance in blind than in sighted participants. For threshold tasks, in which lower scores reflect higher sensitivity (in studies reporting concentration), the sign was reversed accordingly. For each study,

d = (M_blind − M_sighted) / SD_pooled, with SD_pooled = √[((n₁ − 1)SD₁² + (n₂ − 1)SD₂²) / (n₁ + n₂ − 2)],

and the small-sample correction

g = d × [1 − 3 / (4(n₁ + n₂) − 9)].

The sampling variance was

v_g = (n₁ + n₂)/(n₁n₂) + g² / (2(n₁ + n₂)) multiplied by the squared correction factor.

When only t or F values were reported, they were converted to d using standard formulas (Borenstein et al., 2009). For nonparametric tests, we converted exact p values or z statistics to equivalent effect sizes. When a study contained two blind subgroups compared with one control group, we combined the subgroups into one group (computing pooled means and standard deviations) for the main analyses and treated them separately only in the onset moderator analysis, where the shared control group's sample size was divided between the comparisons to avoid double-counting (Higgins & Green, 2011).

Meta-analytic model

Because we expected true effects to vary across studies due to differences in samples and procedures, we used random-effects models fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. The weighted mean effect was

ĝ = Σ wᵢgᵢ / Σ wᵢ, with wᵢ = 1 / (vᵢ + τ²),

where τ² is the between-study variance. Confidence intervals were computed with the Knapp–Hartung adjustment, which improves coverage when the number of studies is modest (Knapp & Hartung, 2003). Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran's Q, τ², and I² = max(0, (Q − df)/Q) × 100, and 95% prediction intervals were calculated (Higgins, Thompson, & Deeks, 2003; IntHout, Ioannidis, Rovers, & Goeman, 2016). Outlying and influential studies were examined through studentized residuals, Cook's distance, and leave-one-out analyses (Viechtbauer & Cheung, 2010).

Publication bias

Small-study effects and publication bias were evaluated with several complementary methods because no single method performs best under all conditions. We inspected contour-enhanced funnel plots and tested funnel asymmetry through Egger's regression test (Egger, Davey Smith, Schneider, & Minder, 1997) and Begg's rank correlation test. We applied the trim-and-fill procedure (Duval & Tweedie, 2000) to estimate the number of potentially missing studies and the adjusted effect. We additionally used PET-PEESE meta-regression (Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2014), in which g is regressed on its standard error (PET) or its variance (PEESE), the intercept representing the bias-corrected estimate, and p-curve analysis (Simonsohn, Nelson, & Simmons, 2014) to evaluate the evidential value of significant results. Fail-safe N was not used as the primary indicator because of its known limitations (Becker, 2005).

Moderator analyses

Three moderators were examined exploratorily: mean participant age (continuous), proportion of women in the total sample (continuous), and onset of blindness (early vs. late, categorical). Continuous moderators were tested through mixed-effects meta-regression, gᵢ = β₀ + β₁xᵢ + uᵢ + eᵢ, and categorical moderators through subgroup analyses with a pooled estimate of τ² across subgroups. Moderator tests were Wald-type tests with the Knapp–Hartung adjustment. Moderators were analyzed only when data were available for at least ten studies (continuous) or at least three studies per subgroup (categorical), and no correction for multiple testing was applied given the exploratory aim, which is acknowledged in the interpretation of the results.

Risk of bias

Study quality was appraised using an adapted checklist covering the clarity of blindness definition, matching of groups on age and sex, control for smoking and nasal health, use of validated olfactory tests, and blinding of the experimenter. Quality scores were used descriptively and in sensitivity analyses.

Software

All analyses were performed in R (R Core Team) using the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010), complemented by the dmetar and weightr packages for ancillary analyses. Statistical significance was set at α = .05, two-tailed.

Results

**Study selection and characteristics**

The search identified studies that compared olfactory performance in blind and sighted adults, and the final sample covered four olfactory domains. Eighteen studies assessed odor threshold (N = 1227; 590 blind, 637 sighted), 14 assessed odor discrimination (N = 940; 455 blind, 485 sighted), 14 assessed cued odor identification (N = 968; 468 blind, 500 sighted), and 7 assessed free odor identification (N = 443; 224 blind, 219 sighted). Many publications reported more than one olfactory measure, so the same participants contribute to more than one domain-specific analysis. Each domain was therefore analyzed separately, and no study entered the same analysis twice. Effects were expressed as Hedges' g (Hedges & Olkin, 1985), with positive values indicating better performance in the blind group. Threshold scores were reversed where lower values indicated greater sensitivity.

For each study, the standardized mean difference was

g = J · (M_blind − M_sighted) / SD_pooled, with J = 1 − 3/(4(n₁ + n₂ − 2) − 1).

Effects were pooled with random-effects models using restricted maximum likelihood estimation, as implemented in the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010). Heterogeneity was quantified with Cochran's Q and I² = max(0, (Q − df)/Q) × 100% (Higgins et al., 2003).

**Odor threshold**

The uncorrected random-effects model showed a small advantage for blind participants (g = 0.28, 95% CI [0.05, 0.51], z = 2.39, p = .017). Heterogeneity was substantial (Q(17) = 52.4, p < .001; I² = 68%; τ² = 0.14). Individual effect sizes ranged from g = −0.41 (Smith et al., 1993) to g = 1.02 (Cuevas et al., 2009), and fewer than half of the 18 comparisons were individually significant. Visual inspection of the funnel plot suggested asymmetry, with small studies showing larger positive effects. Egger's regression test confirmed this (intercept = 2.14, p = .018; Egger et al., 1997). Duval and Tweedie's (2000) trim-and-fill procedure imputed five missing studies on the left side of the funnel. The adjusted estimate was g = 0.09, 95% CI [−0.15, 0.33], which does not differ from zero. Leave-one-out analyses showed that the uncorrected estimate was unstable, with g ranging from 0.21 to 0.33 and the lower confidence bound crossing zero in seven of 18 iterations.

**Odor discrimination**

Across 14 studies, the pooled effect for discrimination was g = 0.21, 95% CI [−0.04, 0.46], z = 1.64, p = .101. Heterogeneity was moderate to high (Q(13) = 33.1, p = .002; I² = 61%; τ² = 0.10). Egger's test indicated funnel plot asymmetry (intercept = 1.87, p = .041). Trim-and-fill imputed three studies and reduced the estimate to g = 0.07, 95% CI [−0.19, 0.33]. Both the uncorrected and corrected results therefore indicated no reliable difference between blind and sighted participants. The leave-one-out analysis gave estimates between 0.15 and 0.27, none of which was significant.

**Cued odor identification**

For cued identification (14 studies), the uncorrected pooled effect was small and significant (g = 0.30, 95% CI [0.07, 0.53], z = 2.56, p = .010), with considerable heterogeneity (Q(13) = 35.8, p < .001; I² = 64%; τ² = 0.12). The largest positive effects came from small samples (n < 30 per group). Egger's test again suggested small-study effects (intercept = 2.31, p = .016). Trim-and-fill imputed four studies and yielded a corrected estimate of g = 0.12, 95% CI [−0.11, 0.35], p = .304. After correction, the cued identification advantage disappeared. Excluding any single study did not alter this conclusion, although the uncorrected effect lost significance when the two most extreme positive studies were removed (g = 0.19, 95% CI [−0.03, 0.41]).

**Free odor identification**

Seven studies compared free identification. The uncorrected pooled effect was g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.02, 0.74], z = 2.07, p = .039, with high heterogeneity (Q(6) = 19.7, p = .003; I² = 70%; τ² = 0.17). Because of the small number of studies, the test for funnel asymmetry had limited power. Egger's test was nevertheless marginal (intercept = 2.62, p = .058). Trim-and-fill imputed two studies and reduced the estimate to g = 0.15, 95% CI [−0.21, 0.51], p = .417. Removing any one study left the corrected estimate nonsignificant, and the corrected confidence interval was wide, so the free identification result should be treated with caution.

**Moderator analyses**

We examined three moderators: mean participant age, proportion of women in the combined sample, and onset of blindness (early vs. late). Age and sex composition were tested with mixed-effects meta-regression, and onset with subgroup comparisons. These analyses were exploratory, and several cells contained few studies.

*Age.* Mean age was unrelated to effect size in all domains (threshold: b = −0.004, SE = 0.008, p = .62; discrimination: b = 0.002, SE = 0.009, p = .81; cued identification: b = −0.006, SE = 0.008, p = .45; free identification: b = −0.011, SE = 0.013, p = .43). Age explained 0% of the between-study variance in every model.

*Proportion of women.* The proportion of women did not predict effect sizes for threshold (b = 0.41, SE = 0.52, p = .43), discrimination (b = 0.29, SE = 0.61, p = .64), cued identification (b = −0.35, SE = 0.58, p = .55), or free identification (b = 0.72, SE = 0.95, p = .47). The reported R² values were negligible (all < 4%).

*Onset of blindness.* Studies that reported results separately for early-blind and late-blind participants were included in the subgroup analyses (threshold: k = 9 and 6; discrimination: k = 7 and 5; cued identification: k = 8 and 5; free identification: k = 4 and 3). Early-blind participants did not differ significantly from late-blind participants in any domain. For thresholds, the early-blind effect was g = 0.24 [−0.06, 0.54] and the late-blind effect was g = 0.17 [−0.20, 0.54] (Q_between(1) = 0.12, p = .73). The corresponding subgroup contrasts were Q_between(1) = 0.31, p = .58 for discrimination, Q_between(1) = 0.46, p = .50 for cued identification, and Q_between(1) = 0.58, p = .45 for free identification. Residual heterogeneity remained high within subgroups (I² = 52–71%), so onset of blindness did not account for the variability across studies.

**Summary**

In all four domains, the uncorrected pooled effects were small and positive (g = 0.21–0.38) but heterogeneous, and three of the four reached nominal significance. Evidence of small-study effects was present in each domain. After correction for publication bias, all estimates shrank by more than half (g = 0.07–0.15) and their confidence intervals included zero. None of the tested moderators explained between-study variability. These results provide no robust evidence that blindness is associated with better olfactory threshold, discrimination, or identification performance.

Discussion and Conclusion

The present systematic review and meta-analysis set out to determine whether blindness is associated with superior performance in olfactory tasks. Across four domains (odor threshold, odor discrimination, cued identification, and free identification), we found no reliable evidence that blind individuals outperform sighted controls once the results were corrected for publication bias. Uncorrected estimates suggested small advantages for the blind in some domains, especially threshold and identification, but these shrank toward zero after trim-and-fill and related adjustments, and the funnel plots showed the asymmetry expected when small studies with positive findings are over-represented. Exploratory moderator analyses showed that participants' age, the proportion of women in the samples, and the onset of blindness (early vs. late) did not significantly account for the heterogeneity in effect sizes. Taken together, the data do not support the popular notion that blindness confers supra-normal olfactory abilities, whether at a sensory level (threshold) or at higher-order levels (discrimination and identification).

These findings fit with a broader picture in which compensatory plasticity in blindness is clearer for audition and touch than for chemosensation. Enhanced pitch discrimination, sound localization, and Braille-related tactile acuity have been documented repeatedly (Lessard et al., 1998; Röder et al., 1999; Wong et al., 2011), and are accompanied by cross-modal recruitment of occipital cortex (Sadato et al., 1996; Collignon et al., 2011). The olfactory system, however, differs in important ways. Olfactory input reaches the piriform cortex and orbitofrontal regions without an obligatory thalamic relay, and the system is less dependent on vision for spatial calibration than hearing or touch. Moreover, sighted individuals rarely depend on vision to resolve the identity of odors in everyday life, so the loss of vision may not generate the same functional pressure for compensatory reorganization. Neuroimaging studies have reported structural and functional differences in olfactory-related regions in blind people, such as altered orbitofrontal volume and enhanced responses to odors (Rombaux et al., 2010; Kupers et al., 2011; Araneda et al., 2016). Our results suggest that such neural differences do not necessarily translate into reliably measurable behavioral advantages, or that any behavioral effect is too small or too context-dependent to emerge consistently with standard psychophysical tests.

Why, then, have individual studies reported superior performance? Several explanations are plausible. First, small sample sizes are common in this literature, and blind populations are hard to recruit. Underpowered studies yield unstable estimates, and when positive findings are preferentially published, the literature overstates the effect. The attenuation of effects following bias correction is consistent with this account. Second, differences in task demands may matter. Cued and free identification depend on semantic knowledge, verbal abilities, and attention to odors, and blind individuals may differ from sighted ones in how much they attend to or label odors (Murphy & Cain, 1986; Cuevas et al., 2009) rather than in perceptual sensitivity. Where blind participants outperform controls on identification, the advantage might therefore reflect cognitive strategies, greater reliance on olfaction for object and person recognition, or enhanced memory, rather than altered sensory processing. Third, the sighted control groups often differ in uncontrolled ways, including education, smoking, and testing conditions, and some earlier studies did not screen carefully for olfactory dysfunction or for conditions that can accompany blindness, such as congenital anomalies that also affect olfactory structures.

The null moderator results should be interpreted cautiously. The lack of an effect of onset of blindness is notable, given the hypothesis that early visual deprivation during a sensitive period should produce the strongest reorganization (Voss, 2013). However, the number of studies that reported separate data for early- and late-blind groups was limited, and the definitions of "early" and "late" varied considerably, from birth to several years of age. Likewise, meta-regressions on mean age and sex composition are based on study-level aggregates and are therefore vulnerable to ecological bias and low power; they cannot rule out subgroup-specific effects, for instance among older blind adults, who might benefit from experience-dependent maintenance of olfactory function, or between women and men, who typically differ in olfactory performance (Sorokowski et al., 2019). Other potentially relevant moderators, such as duration of blindness, etiology, braille proficiency, or the use of olfaction in daily navigation, were rarely reported and could not be examined.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The between-study heterogeneity was moderate to substantial in some domains, reflecting differences in testing procedures (e.g., Sniffin' Sticks versus other threshold methods; different odor sets and numbers of response alternatives), which complicates the pooling of standardized mean differences. Publication bias corrections rely on assumptions that may not be met, particularly when heterogeneity is high, and different methods can produce different adjusted estimates; we therefore regard the corrected estimates as indicative rather than definitive. Our search, although systematic, may have missed unpublished work, which is directly relevant to the issue of selective reporting. In addition, the number of studies in the free identification domain was relatively small, reducing the precision of that estimate. Finally, a non-significant difference is not proof of equivalence. The confidence intervals around the pooled estimates are compatible with small effects in either direction, and we cannot exclude modest advantages that would be detectable only with much larger samples or more sensitive tasks.

These limitations point to clear directions for future research. Adequately powered, preregistered studies with well-characterized blind participants and carefully matched sighted controls are needed, ideally including registered reports to reduce selective publication. Standardized test batteries would improve comparability across laboratories, and reporting of individual-level data would permit individual participant meta-analysis and more precise moderator tests. Researchers should also distinguish perceptual from cognitive components of olfactory performance, for example by combining psychophysics with measures of odor imagery, odor memory, verbal labeling, and attention. Longitudinal and ecological approaches may reveal whether blind individuals use olfactory cues differently in daily life, even in the absence of superior thresholds. Neuroimaging studies could also clarify whether the observed cortical differences reflect functional compensation or simply altered use of the system.

In conclusion, the available evidence does not support the claim that blindness enhances olfactory threshold, discrimination, or identification once publication bias is taken into account. Anecdotal impressions of "heightened smell" in blind people may reflect greater attention to, and reliance on, olfactory information in everyday contexts rather than superior sensory capacity. Practically, this implies that rehabilitation and educational programs should not presume that olfactory skills will spontaneously compensate for visual loss; instead, any use of smell as an information channel may require explicit training and support. More rigorous and transparent research is necessary to determine whether subtle or context-specific advantages exist.
